COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY—ENTIRE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL—OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIMES OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, VERY CAREFULLY CORRECTED BY COMPARISON WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; AUGMENTED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED after the most extensive editions completed during the last three centuries; PROVIDED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY DISTRIBUTED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING ITS SUBJECT MATTER; ENLARGED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL, PROVIDED THEY POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDEXES: one of subjects, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any given topic; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon each text of each book of Scripture, and in what passages of their works. A most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others, if the following are weighed: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of reprinted works, the highly convenient and throughout consistently uniform format of the volumes, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but for the first time gathered together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

SECOND SERIES, IN WHICH APPEAR THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM GREGORY THE GREAT TO INNOCENT III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Library of the Universal Clergy, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical science. Patrology has been published in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition, consisting of two hundred and sixty volumes, is sold for 1,300 francs; the Greek-Latin edition, consisting of three hundred volumes, for 1,800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied there only in a Latin translation.

THOMAS THE CISTERCIAN AND JOHN ALGRIN, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 0009]

NOTICES

(Oudin, *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers and Writings*, vol. II, col. 1574; vol. III, col. 43)

I.

[Col. 0009A] THOMAS, a monk of the Cistercian abbey, was distinguished about the year 1180 not only in this chief monastery but also throughout the whole Cistercian order. As a learned man, diligently occupied with the Scriptures, which he continually held in his hands and constantly meditated upon in his mind, he wrote, with much labour, for Pons, bishop of Clermont, a notable and extensive Commentary in twelve books on the Song of Songs. Its dedicatory letter begins: “I am greatly astonished, and do not cease to marvel beyond what can be expressed,” etc. The prologue begins: “There are three epithalamia: the first historical,” etc. The first book begins: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. This is the voice of the Synagogue,” etc. I have seen it in manuscript in many libraries of abbeys of the Cistercian order, and indeed also printed at Paris in 1521 by Josse Badius Ascensius, and again at Lyons in 1571, and elsewhere.

The time when Thomas the Cistercian wrote this Commentary may be inferred from the preface addressed to Pons, bishop of Clermont. [Col. 0009B] But it is entirely certain from *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, p. 528, under the bishops of Clermont, that this Pons, formerly abbot of Grand-Selve and Clairvaux, was made bishop of Clermont in 1170. He held that see until 1189, when he died on 2 April. Thus he is called bishop of Clermont in a document of the abbey of Souvigny in 1173; in a charter of Saint Martin of Tours in 1174; and in 1175, together with Ainard, abbot of Saint-Illidius; for Ainard’s successor Pons confirms the gift of the church of Valbellez. There survives a letter of his to Maurice, bishop of Paris, and Stephen, abbot of Saint-Evroult; it is the third among the letters of Stephen of Tournai, whom editions wrongly call Peter instead of Pons. Thomas therefore wrote this work between 1173, when Pons was elected bishop of Clermont, and 1189, when he is recorded as having died on 2 April. William Cave seems to have placed him later than he ought, under the year [Col. 0009C] 1201 in the *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 701; by that time he appears already to have been dead, since he had flourished from as early as 1160. He is said to have lived until 1190, indeed even until 1200.

Many have written about the author of the aforesaid Commentary, and nearly all have been deceived. First of all, Charles de Visch, in his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, printed at Cologne in 1654, quarto, by Johann Busaeus, and at Douai in 1649, quarto, by Johann Serruvier, makes three Thomases, in different places—namely on pp. 310 and 312 of his *Library*—authors of this Commentary: one a monk of Cîteaux, another of Perseigne, and a third of Vaucelles in the diocese of Cambrai. Visch was misled by the inscriptions of manuscript codices of this Commentary on the Song of Songs, which very often occur under the name Thomas of Vaucelles, as in the Colbert Library, codex 2783, and in the Parisian Victorine Library, shelfmark F. 18.

Second was John Lepaige, author of the *Premonstratensian Library*, book I, chapter 17, p. 307, published at Paris in folio in 1633 by Aebrianus Taupinard. Out of affectation or reliance upon another’s authority, he attributed this Commentary of Thomas to a certain canon of the Church of Vicogne, doubtless in order to enrich his own order with an external writer. Therefore, when in 1680 I spent a considerable time at Vicogne and examined all the manuscript codices of that once distinguished library, I held, turned over, and read this Commentary. I found it anonymous, except that Thomas’s name alone was written upon it; nor did I find even the slightest letter there by which it might be attributed to some canon of Vicogne. But when I had found the same Commentary in many libraries of other orders, often anonymous and sometimes bearing the express name of this Cistercian Thomas, together with the prefatory letter to Pons, bishop of Clermont—and indeed when I had committed to memory the opening phrases of the letter, preface, and first book—I immediately understood it to be the very work of Thomas, Cistercian monk, so frequently seen by me in other libraries. Thus either good John Lepaige supposed that whatever was found anonymous in the manuscripts of Vicogne belonged to the brethren of Vicogne, or perhaps some other canon of Vicogne, sufficiently credulous in his own favour, deceived him—something which may, without concealment or envy, be affirmed of all Belgians under French or Spanish rule.

Third, with open warfare and banners joined, sought, by every kind of quibbling, to claim—indeed, to steal—this Commentary for an author of the Franciscan order. This was Paul of Rieti, an Observant Friar Minor. In misplaced zeal for his own John Scotus, so that he might render this Franciscan, whom they call the Subtle Doctor, more famous than others and dearer to the Friars Minor by writings still purloined, he rashly undertook—though his attempt was ultimately fruitless—to publish this Commentary at Rome in 1653, in folio, from the press of Stefano Caballi, under the false and fabricated name of John Duns Scotus, the Subtle Doctor, *On Solomon’s Song of Songs*. When John Malgorius, monk of Bonnevaux and general procurator of the Cistercian order at the Roman Curia, learned this, he opposed Paul of Rieti’s criminal attempts on behalf of his order and prevented the distribution of the impression already produced under the name of John Scotus. Yet Paul of Rieti did not abandon what he had begun. Counting his audacity as a legal title, he brought Malgorius the Cistercian—both defendant and innocent party—into court. When litigation had been undertaken, arguments adduced on both sides, and documents and proofs from manuscript codices and old editions produced, John Duns Scotus went away deprived of this Commentary on the Song of Songs, and Paul of Rieti, Observant Friar Minor, stood confounded, convicted of intolerable rashness and audacity. The definitive judgment, publicly issued by the Most Reverend Father, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, in 1655, in the eighth indiction, on the fifteenth day of March, definitively declared that the Book on the Song of Songs had been and was composed, produced, and published by the Reverend Father Thomas the Cistercian [Note: [Col. 0011D] See the complete judgment below.], etc.

I saw one copy of this Roman folio impression in the library of the Benedictines of Saint-Germain at Paris. From the first page through page 403, the last, it is headed *JOHN DUNS SCOTUS ON THE SONG OF SONGS*, etc., following the cited edition of the Friar Minor Paul of Rieti. But the title-page and the heading attached to the first page read: *THOMAS THE CISTERCIAN ON THE SONG OF SONGS, a work most useful to preachers; dedicated to the most eminent and most reverend prince James Nini, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, prefect of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, and most gracious protector of the sacred Cistercian order.* Paul of Rieti undoubtedly regretted that, by the furtive substitution of this Commentary on the Song of Songs, he had been unable to make John Scotus equal to Saint Thomas Aquinas. Would that similar attempts were restrained by similar censure, and that so many parents of anonymous writings were not discovered at will through partisan zeal. This is indeed a lengthy account, yet I could not depict the lawsuit more briefly. [Col. 0012B] We shall discuss it again briefly later, under the year 1220, when we treat the writings of John of Abbeville. In order to make his attribution without punishment and shamelessly, Paul of Rieti had removed the work’s preface addressed to Pons, bishop of Clermont, and had, on his own authority, inserted the name of John Scotus, who had not yet been born in the lifetime of this bishop and was about one hundred and forty years later. Thomas the Cistercian is treated by Charles de Visch in the *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, p. 310; by Antonio Possevino in the *Sacred Apparatus*; and incorrectly, as stated above, by William Cave in the *History of Ecclesiastical Writers* under the year 1201.

II.

[Col. 0011]

[Col. 0011C] JOHN ALGRIN, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Sabina, was surnamed “of Abbeville” from his birthplace, for he originated from this principal town of Ponthieu. A Parisian doctor of theology, he acquired a celebrated reputation in France for learning in 1220. Hence, as upright character was joined to the education of this exceptional mind, he later became dean of the very celebrated church of Amiens. As Alberic also writes in his manuscript chronicle, he was consecrated archbishop of Besançon in 1225, on the day after the feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist. At Anagni, Gregory IX—who had known him as master of the Parisian schools—made him cardinal bishop of the title of Saint Sabina in September 1227. He was immediately sent as legate to Portugal and Spain to preach the crusade, as it is called, against the Saracens. From there he was deputed by the same pope to Emperor Frederick II, whom he brought to amicable peace agreements.

He added brief [Col. 0011D] notes to Thomas the Cistercian’s extensive Commentary on the Song of Songs. Their prologue begins: “About to expound the Song of Songs in honour of Mother and Son,” etc. Josse Badius Ascensius published these, together with the aforesaid Commentary of Thomas the Cistercian, divided into twelve books, in folio at Paris in 1521. John Algrin added these brief notes to the Commentary of the said Thomas the Cistercian in 1233, during the time of Pope Gregory IX, as the cited Paris edition of Ascensius indicates—unless it is more plausible and probable that Ascensius merely chose at pleasure to combine both commentaries in the cited edition. For in the Cholet Library at Paris, codex 37, there is a manuscript, *Exposition on the Song of Songs by John of Abbeville, approved by the Roman Church in 1233*, as the manuscript title reads. The same work is found under the name John, cardinal and bishop of Sabina, in manuscript in the Utrecht Library, no. 252, K. K.; likewise together with Bede and others on the Song of Songs, no. 243, folio, as the catalogue has it, part I, p. 99, of the printed and manuscript books of this library, published in folio at Utrecht in 1670.

The same John wrote a Commentary, or Sermons, on the Psalter, surviving in manuscript in the libraries of Clairvaux and Longpont, shelfmark A. 4, folio. In both libraries there are manuscripts of the same John of Abbeville’s Sermons on the epistles and gospels of the entire year, as also in the abbeys of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme and Blessed Mary of Lyre, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and frequently elsewhere. He therefore wrote Sermons for the seasons and for the saints throughout the year. Henry of Ghent speaks of them thus in book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 38:

> John, called of Abbeville, formerly master of theology at Paris, archbishop of Besançon, and thereafter at Rome cardinal bishop, wrote sermons both for Sundays and for feast days. He briefly expounded the Gospel and apostolic readings; after this, sermons very extensive, with so many testimonies of Holy Scripture introduced that they could scarcely be committed to memory.

The more extensive Sermons survive in manuscript at Cambridge in the public library, codex 40, and in the archives of Caius College, codex 41; the shorter version, containing only brief expositions of the readings and apostolic passages, survives at Oxford in the library of Lincoln College, codex 271; and at Cambridge in the library of Pembroke College, codex 169. Likewise privately in the library of Baron Lumley, codex 155. They are similarly found in the more notable libraries of France: namely in the Royal Library at Paris, codex 4086, folio, which is nearly four hundred years old and includes a table of subjects. They begin: [Col. 0013A] “Together with the most holy mother Church,” etc. The first sermon on the Gospels begins: “When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem,” etc. “This Gospel serves for two Sundays,” etc. Also codex 4387, from folio 19 to the end, and 4512, quarto, three hundred years old. The same work is in the library of Saint Victor at Paris, shelfmark Q. Q. 18: Sermons on the Gospels, folio 1; Sermons on the Epistles, folio 109; Sermons for Saints’ Feasts, folio 154, etc. Others likewise at shelfmarks O O O 7 and R. R. 4. In the library of Saint-Germain at Paris, codices 403 and 654, though incorrectly in the latter under the name John of La Rochelle instead of John of Abbeville; for they begin with the same words as all the other manuscript codices mentioned above. Finally, they occur in the renowned Colbert Library, codices 1075 and 1744, and in the celebrated library of Lucelle Abbey, of the Cistercian order, desk 24, shelfmarks M and L.

Having returned to Rome in 1236, or rather 1237, he died on the fourth day before the Kalends of October [28 September]. See Francis Chifflet in the Sammarthani brothers’ *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, under “Archbishops of Besançon”; [Col. 0013B] and Jacques Chifflet in the work entitled *Besançon, Metropolis of the Sequani*. In Matthew of Westminster, under the year 1237, there are letters from Master John of Colonna, cardinal deacon, to Otto, papal legate in England that year and cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, concerning the state of the Roman Church, from which the Greeks had recently separated themselves. These letters testify that John of Abbeville, cardinal, died in that year; they make honourable mention of Master John of Abbeville, Parisian doctor, [Col. 0014A] formerly archbishop of Besançon and afterwards cardinal bishop of Sabina:

> “To the accumulation of sorrow is added that noble pillar which so magnificently sustained the fabric of the Church: the lord bishop of Sabina, of revered memory, has suddenly been taken from our midst. First struck by the pain of affliction, and finally harassed by a lingering illness, he departed to enter into the powers of the Lord, leaving his mother exposed incidentally to the fall of ruin, amid groaning and mourning.”

The principal cause of mourning was the schism of the Greeks. Having expelled their Latin emperor Baldwin, son of Peter, count of Auxerre, they had made Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, an antipope and had added new errors to their old ones:

> “When such wickedness and oppression had been seen, the Greek Church rose up against the Roman Church by expelling its emperor and obeying only its archbishop of Constantinople, named Germanus; he insolently spreads not only the ancient errors of the Greeks but also new and invented ones, and raves monstrously away from the Catholic religion.”

John of Abbeville is discussed by Henry of Ghent in book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 38; Aubertus Miraeus in his scholia on that chapter; Antonio Possevino, vol. I of the *Sacred Apparatus*, folio 810; the fifth century of the *History of the University of Paris*, under the year 1237, folio 163, and in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Academics*, folio 692; and William Cave in the *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1227, p. 713, where he wrongly writes that John died in 1236.

[Col. 0013]

DEFINITIVE JUDGMENT, IN PUBLIC FORM, OF THE MOST REVEREND FATHER, MASTER OF THE SACRED PALACE, by which he definitively declared that the book on the Song of Songs had been and was composed, produced, and published by the Reverend Father Thomas the Cistercian; and that it had been and was wrongly and improperly procured by the Reverend Father Paul of Rieti, Friar Minor, and the other parties to the suit to be printed and published under Scotus’s name; with an injunction that it must not be printed, sold, or accepted for use under Scotus’s name, but only under the name Thomas the Cistercian.

In the name of the Lord. Amen.

Let it be clearly apparent and known to all everywhere by this present public instrument that, in the year from the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1655, in the eighth indiction, on the fifteenth day of March, during the vacancy of the Apostolic See following the death of Pope Innocent X of happy memory, on behalf of the Reverend Father John Malgoirez, general procurator of the Cistercian Order, principal party, etc., against the Reverend Father Paul of Rieti, of the Observant Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, and others in their named capacities, etc., Charles, most eminent Lord Cardinal, mandatory of the Vicar, on the eleventh day of the same month caused him to be cited before the Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, in order that, after the setting aside of any prejudicial decree, all and each of the substantial time-limits nullly and negligently observed by virtue of whatsoever faculties might be renewed; that the present party might be absolved from censures for the purpose of concluding and hearing definitive judgment at the suit of the aforesaid principal party, etc. The same requested and obtained as above, and also that the matter might be concluded, pronounced, and decided as in the schedule which the said Most Reverend Father Master, having before him, saw, read, and subscribed, and then delivered to me; its tenor is registered below. Concerning all this, etc. Done on Monte Quirinale, in the rooms of the dwelling of the said Most Reverend Father Master, in the presence of Brother Antonio Posterla, a Roman of the Order of Preachers, and Lord Sebastiano Trifoglio of Nepi, witnesses specially called, present, and requested for all and each of the aforesaid matters. The tenor of the aforesaid schedule, mentioned above, is as follows:

The name of Christ having been invoked, sitting as a tribunal and having God alone before our eyes, by this our definitive judgment, which we issue in writing upon the advice of jurists, in the action and actions which have been and are pending before us in first instance between the Reverend Father Paul of Rieti, of the Observant Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, and the other parties to the suit as plaintiffs on the one side, and the Reverend Father John Malgoirez, general procurator of the Cistercian Order, defendant, concerning the printing and publication of the book entitled *On the Song of Songs* under the name of Scotus, and the declaration that it was not composed and produced by the Reverend Father Thomas the Cistercian, and other matters, etc.; the case having most recently been remitted to us by the most eminent Cardinal Giulio Sacchetti, Prefect of the Signatura of Justice, at the request of either party: [Col. 0015] We say, pronounce, decree, and definitively adjudge that the aforesaid book on the Song of Songs was and is composed, produced, and published by the aforesaid Reverend Father Thomas the Cistercian; and that it was and is erroneously and improperly procured by the said Reverend Father Paul and the other parties to the suit to be printed and published under the name of Scotus. Therefore, the said book ought not, could not, ought not now, and cannot now be published, sold, or received for use under the said name of Scotus; and, to this end, publication and sale of the same book under the said name of Scotus were and are forbidden to them. In its place the name of the said Father Thomas the Cistercian was and is to be inserted and printed, as we enjoin and prohibit. Moreover, the molestations, vexations, disturbances, and claims brought, made, and maintained by the said Father Paul and the others were and are erroneous and de facto brought, made, and maintained. Concerning the aforesaid matters, perpetual silence was and is to be imposed upon the same Father Paul and his fellow litigants; as such, we declare the said molestations, etc., and impose perpetual silence upon them. We absolve the said Reverend Father Paul and the other parties to the suit from costs, for just causes moving our mind, provided, however, that they acquiesce in this our judgment; otherwise we condemn them. And thus we say, etc., not only, etc., but in every respect, etc.

Thus have I pronounced, I, Raymond Capisuccus, of the Order of Preachers, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace.

In place of the + sign.

And because Lord John Garzias of Valencia, notary of the Curia of the Most Eminent and Most Reverend Lord Cardinal Vicar, was requested concerning the aforesaid matters: therefore I, Antonio Francesco Maria Simius of Pistoia, citizen of Rome, public notary, registered in the Archive of the Roman Curia, and administrator of the office of the aforesaid Lord John Garzia, subscribed and published this instrument of judgment, and, being requested and required, marked it with my customary sign, etc.

ROME, from the Press of the Reverend Apostolic Chamber.

1655.

With permission of superiors.

[Col. 0015]

THE SONG OF SONGS, with two plainly outstanding Commentaries: one by the venerable Father Brother THOMAS, Cistercian monk; the other by the most reverend Cardinal Master JOHN HALGRIN of Abbeville.

(At the expense and under the care of Josse Badius Ascensius, sworn bookseller of the illustrious University of Paris, on the Nones of February before Easter, 1521, folio.)

DEDICATORY LETTER

Josse Badius ASCENSIUS sends greetings to the Father Lord EDMUND, foremost among those to be revered, most prudent superior of the renowned house of Clairvaux of the Cistercian order.

Behold, venerable abbot, the Commentaries on the Song of Songs by the most learned and exceptionally devout Father Thomas, monk of Cîteaux. Long desired through the requests of many, they seemed to us most worthy of being committed first to your reverend fatherhood and then to our press, so that they might be printed—for we gave you the opportunity to inspect them last year, when you were staying in Paris. Now at last printed, they are also inscribed and dedicated to you for many reasons.

The first that occurs is that their author seems to me to have belonged not only to that order and profession but also to your house and community. For he displays a diligent training in the divine Scriptures after the manner of the mellifluous doctor Saint Bernard, a milky eloquence, and a Daedalian diligence, more than bee-like, in gathering honeycombs from the flowers of sacred Scripture. The second is that, in so great an order, I know of no house from which—without prejudice to less well-known houses, as we should say—there have emerged more interpreters of divine wisdom and cultivators of distinguished books. The third is that I have hitherto had no such close acquaintance with fathers of another monastery as with these venerable fathers from Vauprès and Cangé. Through them we have issued not a few books, neither to be regretted nor previously printed in France; and, while they studied here, I knew them to be of the purest spirit along with the most distinguished professors of theology, Master John de Burrey, Master Nicholas Boucherat, and now Master Francis Mauroy, soon to be called to the degree.

The fourth and last reason, not to be long-winded, is that your venerable humanity, courtesy, and prudence were made known to me by your most honourable services before you entered upon this profession, as you remember. Thus I am accustomed to extol in the highest terms the modesty and prudence of the fathers of that monastery. Their modesty, indeed, because in selecting a superior they took account neither of age nor birth; their prudence because even in its flowering they recognised the powers and fruits of your character. Receive favourably, therefore, our most welcome patron, and consider these Commentaries—worthy of much praise—still more praiseworthy on this account: that we have inscribed them to your most honourable name, which expected nothing of the kind. Farewell.

From our printing-house in the illustrious University of Paris, on the Ides of February, in the year 1521 according to Roman reckoning.

PREFACE OF THOMAS THE CISTERCIAN TO PONS, BISHOP OF CLERMONT

[Col. 0017]

[Col. 0017A] To the reverend father, Lord PONS, by the grace of God bishop of Clermont: Brother THOMAS, however insignificant a Cistercian monk, offers his whole self in carrying out his commands.

I am greatly astonished, and I do not cease to marvel beyond what can be expressed, that one so exalted has invited one so small, one so eloquent one so unlearned, one so spiritual one so irreligious, to express the spiritual sweetness of the Song of Songs—not so much by enticements as by compelling him with a scourge made from the cords of charity. For who would believe that, after Origen’s honey, Gregory’s spices, Bede’s fragrances, and blessed Bernard’s balsams—whose manifold riches cannot be counted—there remains even a drop of spiritual understanding for posterity to squeeze out from the dregs of the letter? [Col. 0017B] Therefore, “I am hemmed in on every side. For I am constrained, and I do not know which of the two I should choose” [Note: [Col. 0017] Phil. 1; Dan. 13:8.]. If I do it, I fear the shame of insufficiency. “But if I do not do it, I shall not escape” the pit of disobedience.

Therefore, out of reverence for so excellent a person, exposing myself to men’s mockery and considering Daniel’s saying, “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” [Note: [Col. 0017] Dan. 12.], I labour, with Ruth the Moabite—whose name means “inspired”—in the field of Boaz, whose name means “in strength,” that is, in the Scripture of Christ, who is the mighty God, to gather after Origen and the other aforementioned reapers ears of grain, that is, meanings wrapped in the chaff of the letter. In truth, I free each verse from its covering of chaff by a short or concise exposition. Then, arranging the elucidated [Col. 0017C] meaning in a manifold division, I afterwards, like an ingenious bee, range through the little flowers of Scripture, confirming by the strength of their testimony what has been expounded and distinguished. When this shall have been presented to our Naomi, whose name means “beautiful”—that is, to the desire of so great a father—even if it does not suffice to satisfy his soul, it may nevertheless excuse the deficiency of its writer: that beautiful soul, I mean, which is so lovely in form and so sweet amid the bridegroom’s delights that it confidently cries: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0017] Song 1.].

On the three epithalamia

There are three epithalamia: the first historical, the second philosophical, the third theological. The first treats of the lawful union of male and female; the second expresses the union of the eloquence of the trivium and the wisdom of the quadrivium; the third, the union [Col. 0018A] of bride and bridegroom, God and soul, Christ and Church. God established the first in Adam and Eve, saying: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife” [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 2.]; Martianus sets forth the second in treating the marriage of Philology and Mercury; Solomon sets forth the third in this work, treating the spiritual marriage of bridegroom and bride. In the first, children are begotten to serve their Creator; in the second, they are instructed that they may know something of God; in the third, they are invited to enjoy God himself. But those who belong to the first “served the creature rather than the Creator” [Note: [Col. 0017] Rom. 1.]; and those who belong to the second, “although they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give him thanks” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ibid.]. Therefore, in place of the third, “they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God” [Note: [Col. 0017] Rom. 2.].

For this reason, “the Father [Col. 0018B] of mercies and God of all consolation” [Note: [Col. 0017] 2 Cor. 1.], wishing to recall lost humanity to the heavenly kingdoms, took counsel with the citizens above and resolved that his Son should undertake this embassy. To him the Father said:

> “Faithful minister of my commands, my son,” he said [Note: [Col. 0017] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book II.]

You see that “the earth has been given into the hand of the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0017] Job 9.]. “The holy man has perished from the earth; there is no righteous man among humankind. All lie in wait for blood; each hunts his brother unto death” [Note: [Col. 0017] Mic. 7.]. “And now, what have I here?” says the Lord, “since my people has been taken away for nothing?” [Note: [Col. 0017] Isa. 52.]. You know that your brothers are tending the sheep, namely in Shechem. Come, I will send you to them, that you may see whether all goes well with them. When he answered, [Col. 0018C] “Here I am” [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 37.], the Father added: There is there a maiden of surpassing beauty, of David’s royal lineage, who has always been pleasing to me through the merit of her chastity and the confession of our virtue. Let her become your bride, “to beget new children, whom a mother may nourish for me unto the new infancy of grace” [Note: [Col. 0017] Office for Holy Saturday.]. For I shall

> “Join her to you in firm marriage and dedicate her as your own.” [Note: [Col. 0017] Vergil, *Aeneid*, book I, v. 63.]

Nevertheless, “mercy and truth shall go before your face” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 88.]; charity shall accompany your steps. For mercy shall make her without spot, truth without wrinkle, charity without hardness: without the spot of impurity, without the wrinkle of duplicity, without the hardness of obstinacy. Truth instructs her in faith; mercy raises her to hope; charity to love. Then the king commanded them to hasten. But they, no less than commanded, run faster than the breeze.

[Col. 0019A] They had come to the gates. Then Truth, ever rejoicing in the nakedness of speech, cried out: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” [Note: [Col. 0019] Rev. 3]. But Mercy, sympathetic to virginal modesty, added more gently: “If anyone opens to me, I shall enter in to him, and I shall dine with him, and he with me” [Note: [Col. 0019] Ibid.]. Then the Virgin came, advancing bashfully from her secret shade; the doors opened easily upon their hinges. At the first sight the most beautiful Virgin was astonished. But they greeted her with peaceful words of good omen. Then Truth, flattering no one, said: “The Lord shall come manifestly; our God shall not be silent. Fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 49].

But she, frightened by the harshness of these words, replied:

> . . . . Do you bring peace, or arms?

[Col. 0019B]

> And who at last are you, from what shores have you come? [Note: [Col. 0019] Virgil, *Aeneid*].

Then Mercy, tempering her modest words with a certain serenity, spoke thus with a gentle countenance: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your father and the house of your father, and the king shall desire your beauty” [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 44]. “You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall not be called Desolate, because the Lord has taken pleasure in you. For as a young man dwells with a virgin, so shall your bridegroom dwell with you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” [Note: [Col. 0019] Isa. 62]. We are not inhabitants of this world, but strangers; nor have we entered the world in order to delight in remaining in it, but to pass through it. “For we all hasten toward one goal; our citizenship is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0019] Phil. 3]. You await one Savior.

This is the place which, if boldness be granted to my words, I should not indeed fear to call the great king’s palace. There the royal hall gleams with golden robes. There,

> . . . . . . Preceded by a white fleece,  
> The virginal Lamb—a sheep—enters wholly white; likewise the whole flock [uncertain: *grexque*].

The gate stands open for his soldiers; he who serves as a soldier enters.

Then:

> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.  
> If under her guidance any traces of our crime remain,  
> They shall be rendered void, freeing us from perpetual fear of punishment [Note: [Col. 0019] Virgil, *Eclogue* IV, 7, 13–14].

And she said:

> I do not indeed deem myself worthy of so great an honor [Note: [Col. 0019] Ibid.];

yet I desire to hear these things from the mouth of Truth.

Then Truth said: “What do you seek to hear? Do you not know that ‘God is great and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain’ [Col. 0020A; Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 47]? Hear of his riches: ‘The Father appointed him heir of all things’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Heb. 1]. Hear of his Wisdom: ‘Through whom also he made the worlds’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Ibid.]. He is beautiful, ‘being the radiance of glory and the image of his substance’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Ibid.]. He is mighty: ‘upholding all things by the word of his power’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Ibid.]. Hear what he accomplishes: ‘making purification for sins’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Ibid.]. Hear of his exaltation: ‘he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Ibid.].

“Hear these matters more fully. He is rich, for ‘the Father subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and besides them the beasts of the field’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 8]. He is wise, because in him ‘are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Col. 2]. He is beautiful, because the bridegroom is ‘beautiful in form beyond the sons of men’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 44], and sun and moon marvel at his beauty. [Col. 0020B] ‘Into whom angels desire to look’ [Note: [Col. 0019] 1 Pet. 1]. ‘For he is the brightness of eternal light’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Wis. 7]. He is mighty because ‘his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Dan. 7]. He performs good things because through him ‘the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise again, and the poor receive the Gospel’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Matt. 11]. He is exalted, ‘whom dominions adore and powers tremble before’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Preface of the Mass].

“Such is our king: ‘I am Truth’ [Note: [Col. 0019] John 14]. This is Mercy. We have come peaceably. For our king is our peace, ‘who made both one’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Eph. 2]. Here is deceit; in heaven is peace. For the highest realms possess peace; discord disturbs the least things. But there shall be peace in our land when he comes. For ‘Glory to God in [Col. 0020C] the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Luke 2]. With him Charity shall come, through whom, by our intercession, you shall receive grace. But the king himself shall give glory. For ‘God loves mercy and truth; the Lord shall give grace and glory’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 83].”

Then, as she had been suffused with virginal shame,

> A bashful blush had tinged her golden cheeks,

and she added: “‘This has been done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 117].”—“‘Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Luke 1]. Let therefore our king come and ‘kiss me with the kiss of his mouth’ [Note: [Col. 0019] Song 1].”

## Prologue to John of Halgrin of Abbeville, Dean of Amiens and Cantor of Abbeville, Cardinal of Sabina, His Commentaries on the Song of Songs in Praise of the Virgin Mary

[Col. 0019]

[Col. 0019D] Intending to expound the Song of Songs in honor of Mother and Son, I, poor and limited in understanding, implore the Mother’s aid and humbly seek the Son’s favor: that she who bore the eternal Word in time may obtain for me a word in praise of the [Col. 0020D] Word; and that the Word of the Father made human in the Virgin may suggest to me words in praise of his Mother.

Therefore, since a song is called an exultation of the mind, this song is deservedly named the *Song of Songs* because of the excellence of the persons exulting in one another therein. For it contains the pleasant and mutual rejoicing of Mother and Son—namely, the blessed Virgin and the Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 0022A] Here the Mother rejoices in the Son; here the Son delights in the Mother. Here the Son describes the Mother’s privileges; here the Mother describes the Son’s excellence. Four persons speak in this song: the Mother, the Son, the angels who attend the Son as Lord, and the young women who attend the Virgin as their lady, as the following sequence of Scripture will make clear.

## The Most Learned Commentary on the Song of Songs by the Reverend Father Thomas, Cistercian Monk

[Col. 0021]

# Book I

[Col. 0021]

## Chapter 1

[Col. 0021B]

### “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

[THOMAS.] This is the voice of the Synagogue, which had learned from angels and heard from prophets that Christ would come into the world. Thus, inflamed with desire for him, she cries: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”—that is, let him come to instruct and save me. Let him no longer send angels, patriarchs, or prophets; but let the one who is to come come in his own person. His kiss is the instruction of his own mouth. Let him therefore come and instruct me with his own mouth. Yet let him also patiently receive the touch of my mouth—that is, let him not disdain to hear me asking about the way of salvation.

We believe that this desire was fulfilled when, [Col. 0021C] seated upon the mountain, he taught his disciples, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0021] Matt. 5], and so forth. There he gave a kiss, because, opening his mouth, he promised to his apostles the joy of the heavenly kingdom.

There is a fourfold kiss: the kiss of the flesh, the kiss of the devil, the kiss of a human being, and the kiss of the Beloved. From the first comes a lustful kiss; from the second, a poisonous one; from the third, a domestic one; from the fourth, a holy one. Of the first, Proverbs says concerning the foolish woman: “She seized the young man and kissed him” [Note: [Col. 0021] Prov. 7]. Joab gave the second to Amasa when, taking hold of his chin, he kissed him, saying, “Hail, brother,” and killed him [Note: [Col. 0021] 2 Sam. 20]; Judas also gave it to Christ, saying, “Hail, [Col. 0021D] Rabbi,” and betrayed him [Note: [Col. 0021] Matt. 26]. Isaac gave the third to his son Jacob, saying, “Give me a kiss, my son” [Note: [Col. 0021] Gen. 27]. Of the fourth the Apostle says: “Greet one another with a holy kiss” [Note: [Col. 0021] Rom. 16].

The first is evil, the second worse, [Col. 0022B] the third good, and the fourth better. Since the first is shameless, the second wicked, the third familial, and the fourth religious, the holy soul chooses this fourth above the rest. For it despises the first, flees the second, passes over the third, and desires the fourth. Hence it cries: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Three things are observed in a kiss: the lips of those kissing join together, their inward breaths mingle, and their bodies draw near to one another. In the first occurs the joining of natures; in the second, the union of spirits; in the third, the sharing of sufferings. These are, respectively, the natures of man and the Word; the divine and human spirits; and the sufferings of Christ and the Christian. Of the first: “The Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0021] John 1]; of the second: “He who is joined to God is one spirit with him” [Note: [Col. 0021] 1 Cor. 6]; of the third: “If we have been [Col. 0022C] planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be in that of his resurrection” [Note: [Col. 0021] Rom. 6].—“For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” [Note: [Col. 0021] 2 Tim. 2].

Again, in the moral sense, lips are instruments of speech; therefore, their union signifies the mutual exchange of fraternal prayers. In the mingling of breaths is harmony of wills; in the union of bodies, the bearing of burdens. Of the first, the Apostle James says: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved” [Note: [Col. 0021] Jas. 5]. Of the second, Acts of the Apostles says: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” [Note: [Col. 0021] Acts 4]. Again, there was in them one spirit and “one faith” [Note: [Col. 0021] Eph. 4]. Of the third: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you shall fulfill the law of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0021] Gal. 6].

Of these three things the Apostle says: “May God the Father grant you to think the same thing toward one another, so that being of one mind [Col. 0022D] you may with one mouth glorify God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0021] 1 Cor. 15]. Those think the same thing toward one another who, compassionately sharing others’ sufferings in their heart [Col. 0023A] and bearing them in their body, make others’ pains their own by grieving with them.

In this desired kiss, the Word is the one who kisses, the flesh that which is kissed, and the God-man the kiss. Again, there is a kiss at the feet, for the remission of sins; a kiss at the hands, for thanksgiving; and a kiss at the mouth, for love. In the first, the beginnings of our way of life are dedicated; the second is granted to those making progress; the third is experienced only by the perfection of reason. Again, the first is in confession, the second in devotion, the third in contemplation. Again, the Father is the one kissing, the Son the one kissed, and the Holy Spirit the kiss. This third kiss tastes sweeter, is tasted more rarely, and is understood with greater difficulty.

The soul does not seek the *suavium*, the kiss of shameless women; nor the *basium*, the kiss of married persons; but the *osculum*, the kiss of friends: that the bridegroom may kiss the bride, Christ the Church, God the soul. The bridegroom’s lips are mercy and truth. The bridegroom’s lips are fear and love.

She who seeks the kiss must possess three things: repentance, purity, and spiritual fervor. The first seeks pardon, the second illumination, and the third an increase of virtues. There must be repentance, by which she blushes for past evils; purity, by which, through a good conscience, she presents herself clean with confidence before the Creator’s gaze; and spiritual fervor, by which she always kindles herself toward the higher pursuits of virtue. In this fervor love and desire must be considered: love, by which she ardently loves the good things God has granted her; desire, [Col. 0023C] by which she eagerly hastens toward what she has not yet attained.

Here we may consider three kisses: reconciliatory, remunerative, and contemplative. The first is received at the feet, the second at the hands, and the third at the mouth. In the first, remission of sins is received; in the second, the gift of virtues; in the third, knowledge of mysteries.

Again, there is a kiss of teaching, of nature, and of grace. In the first, through preachers God makes his love known to us; in the second, he illumines us by the brightness of natural good; in the third, he exalts us by the charisms of special grace. Thus, from the first we have charity; from the second, brightness; from the third, manifold grace.

Again, in this age the bride sought a wondrous [Col. 0023D] exchange: namely, that divinity should come, to which our humanity might be joined. Hence the Church sings: “O wondrous exchange! The Creator of the human race, taking an animate body, deigned to be born of a Virgin; and, coming forth as man without seed, bestowed his Godhead upon us.” *Commercium* (“exchange”) is derived from *com* and *mercor* (“to trade”). There is a threefold exchange. The first was execrable; the second miserable; the third wondrous. The first was made by the plotter against the human race; the second by the propagator of the human race; the third by the Creator of the human race. The first assumed the form of a serpent; the second put on [Col. 0024A] garments of skin; the third took an animate body. The first scorned divine exaltation; the second disdained obedience; the third deigned to be born of a Virgin. The first gave wickedness in exchange for righteousness; the second received misery in exchange for glory; the third, coming forth as man without seed, bestowed his Godhead upon us.

The first is therefore rightly called execrable, because it was made by the plotter against the human race, who took the form of a serpent and, scorning divine exaltation, gave wickedness in exchange for righteousness. Of this Paul says: “But I am carnal, sold under sin” [Note: [Col. 0023] Rom. 14]. And Isaiah: “You were sold for nothing, and without silver you shall be redeemed” [Note: [Col. 0023] Isa. 42]. In it the devil, Eve, and Adam came together. Every buyer says: “It is bad, it is bad” [Note: [Col. 0023] Prov. 20]. But [Col. 0024B] Adam and Eve said: “It is good, it is good” [Note: [Col. 0023] Gen. 3]. The devil said: “Let there be one purse for us all” [Note: [Col. 0023] Prov. 1].

In it the devil placed, first, the blandishments of flattery; second, the sharpness of subtle temptation; third, the deception of a false promise; fourth, the heavy weight of enduring wickedness. Hence Ezekiel, chapter 27: “The Carthaginians, your merchants, filled your markets with silver, iron, tin, and lead.” The first is understood in the brightness and sound of silver; the second in the sharpness of iron; the third in the gleam of tin; the fourth in the heaviness of lead. Thus the devil puts into this purse suggestion, Eve delight, Adam consent, and all alike sin.

Therefore in the first exchange they buy [Col. 0024C] serpentine teeth; in the second, thorns and thistles; in the third, God and the angels. Hear of the serpentine teeth: “The woman shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” [Note: [Col. 0023] Gen. 3]. Hear of the second: “When you work the earth, it shall not yield its fruits; but it shall germinate thorns and thistles for you” [Note: [Col. 0023] Ibid.]. Of the third: “Come, buy wine and milk without silver and without any exchange” [Note: [Col. 0023] Isa. 55]. The wine is Christ’s divinity, while the milk is his humanity, for milk is born from flesh.

The second exchange was miserable, in which the propagator of the human race put on garments of skin because he disdained obedience and received misery in exchange for glory. For “man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts [Col. 0024D] and became like them” [Note: [Col. 0023] Ps. 48]. In this exchange, indeed, “they exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf eating hay” [Note: [Col. 0023] Ps. 109].—“They gave all their precious things for food, to restore the soul” [Note: [Col. 0023] Lam. 1]. By their hands and feet they summoned death to themselves.

For in this exchange they bought for themselves thorns and thistles: thistles, that is, temptations that afflict the body outwardly; thorns, which penetrate more deeply, that is, spiritual suggestions that prick inwardly. Thus, in the first exchange, the man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho is stripped; in the second, he is wounded; in the third, his wound [Col. 0025A] is poured over with wine and oil [Note: [Col. 0025] Luke 10]. He is stripped of gratuitous gifts, wounded in natural gifts, and drenched with the oil of the Spirit and the wine of the Lord’s blood.

The third exchange was wondrous, because “the Creator of the human race, taking an animate body, deigned to be born of a Virgin; and, coming forth as man without seed, bestowed his Godhead upon us” [Note: [Col. 0025] Office of the Church]. For divine Wisdom incarnate was that strong woman who “considered a field and bought it; from the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard” [Note: [Col. 0025] Prov. 31]. The field is the world; the vineyard is the Church. Therefore, “You were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body” [Note: [Col. 0025] 1 Cor. 6]. Behold, he says: “I come quickly, and my reward is with me” [Note: [Col. 0025] Rev. 22]; “her price is from afar and from the uttermost bounds” [Note: [Col. 0025] Prov. 31]. Therefore, that you may be satisfied, hasten to this [Col. 0025B] exchange: buy and eat.

But many say: “I am rich and need nothing” [Note: [Col. 0025] Rev. 3]. But look, man, for “you are wretched and pitiable”: wretched in yourself, pitiable to those who look upon you. For you are “poor, naked, and blind” [Note: [Col. 0025] Ibid.]: poor, because you do not possess treasure in heaven; naked, lacking the garment of virtue; blind, because you do not understand the mystery of the Incarnation. Therefore, in this exchange buy the gold of divinity, the garment of virtue, and eye-salve—that is, faith in the Incarnation.

This gold is fiery, tested, and pure: fiery in divinity, tested in charity, pure in passion, without the defilement of sin. Of the first: “His head is the finest gold” [Note: [Col. 0025] Song 5]; of the second: “Our God is a consuming fire” [Note: [Col. 0025] Heb. 12]; of the third: “I gave my body to those who struck me and my cheeks to those [Col. 0025C] who plucked them; I did not turn my face from those who rebuked and spat upon me” [Note: [Col. 0025] Isa. 50]; of the fourth: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0025] 1 Pet. 2]. Of the garment: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” [Note: [Col. 0025] Song 4]. Of the eye-salve: “Your name is oil poured out” [Note: [Col. 0025] Song 1].

Therefore, let us buy gold for redemption, a garment for adornment, and eye-salve for illumination. This gold “redeemed Israel from all his iniquities” [Note: [Col. 0025] Ps. 129]. The garment adorns, so that “all the glory of the king’s daughter may be within, in golden fringes” [Note: [Col. 0025] Ps. 44]. The eye-salve illumines, because through it “the people of the Gentiles who walked in darkness saw a great light” [Note: [Col. 0025] Isa. 9].

Behold the wondrous exchange. Hear the three things that [Col. 0025D] follow: “taking an animate body,” and so forth. In the first, the Savior’s kindness appeared; in the second, his humility was shown; in the third, his generosity. First, he freed us from the devil; second, he conformed us to himself; third, he enriched us with his kingdom. Hear the first: by taking an animate body he consumed the serpent’s form, unstitched the loincloths, and stripped from us the garment of skin. First, he put on our misery; second, he weakened the devil’s deceit; third, he restored man unto glory.

The first was in order that he might free us from sins [Note: [Col. 0025] [ [Col. 0025] This note appears at the foot of columns 25 and 26, but the callout number (89*) has not been printed in the text.] Ps. 73]; [Col. 0026A] the second, that he might thwart the devil’s wiles; the third, that he might distinguish man with the robe of joy. Of the first: “He himself bore our sins,” namely “in his body upon the wood” [Note: [Col. 0025] 1 Pet. 2]; of the second: “You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters.”—“You broke the heads of the dragon” [Note: [Col. 0025] Ibid.]; of the third: “Quickly bring forth the first robe” [Note: [Col. 0025] Luke 15]. Again: “Putting off the old man with his deeds, put on the new, that you may walk in newness of life” [Note: [Col. 0025] Rom. 6].

Behold kindness. Humility follows, because he deigned to be born of a Virgin: he descended from heaven to Nazareth, willed to be born in Bethlehem, and endured death in Jerusalem. This descent took place through the Virgin. For she “became like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar” [Note: [Col. 0025] Prov. 31], because by the virginal vessel he came from Nazareth to [Col. 0026B] Bethlehem, which is called the house of bread. For he is “the living bread who came down from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0025] John 6].

There are three breads. The first is barley bread, the second ash-cake bread, the third fine-flour bread. The first is for those converting; the second for those fighting bravely; the third for those delighting in heavenly things. The first has some harshness, the second much humility, the third very great sweetness. The first pricks with the goads of repentance; the second has the ashes of self-abasement; the third the whiteness of innocent purity. With the first Christ fed five thousand people [Note: [Col. 0025] Ibid.]; Elijah had the second as consolation [Note: [Col. 0025] 3 Kings 19]; the third, from the table of offering, was allotted for the use of priests [Note: [Col. 0025] Exod. 25]. Christ himself was manna in the desert [Note: [Col. 0025] John 6], bread from heaven in the flowering garden, bread of angels in the kingdom. Of these three David says: [Col. 0026C] “He rained manna upon them to eat, and gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” [Note: [Col. 0025] Ps. 77].

Again, there are three breads. The first is ash-cake bread, the second is turned-over bread, the third neither ash-cake nor turned-over. The first is God-man; the second is man-God; the third, “God, my God.” The first is before the resurrection; the second is in the resurrection; the third “shall refashion our lowly body, conformed to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0025] Phil. 5]. The first is food for body and soul in pilgrimage; the second is food for the soul in expectation; the third is food for the delicately nourished, in the contemplation of divinity. Of the first: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh” [Note: [Col. 0025] John 6]; of the second: [Col. 0026D] “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0025] Ibid.]; of the third: “Man ate the bread of angels” [Note: [Col. 0025] Ps. 77].

That we may find this bread, let us pass over to Bethlehem, which is called the house of bread. Let us go, pass over, pass through. First, that we may seek; second, that we may see; third, that we may find. Of the first: “Go and inquire diligently concerning the child” [Note: [Col. 0025] Matt. 2]; of the second: “Let us pass over to Bethlehem and see this Word that has come to pass” [Note: [Col. 0025] Luke 2]; of the third: “When I had passed by, I found him whom [Col. 0027A] my soul loves” [Note: [Col. 0027] Song 3].

Let us therefore hear the Word that was uttered: “Let us see the Word that has come to pass” [Note: [Col. 0027] Luke 2]. Let us love the Word that was made flesh [Note: [Col. 0027] John 1]. The first was from the angel, the second in the manger, the third in the Virgin’s womb. Of the first: “Receive my words in your ears, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 6]; of the second: “Let us see this word that has come to pass” [Note: [Col. 0027] Luke 2]; of the third: “The Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0027] John 1]. The first is the joyfulness of the angelic voice; the second, Christ’s nativity; the third, incarnate Divinity.

Let us hear the oracle, see the miracle, and run to the spectacle: the oracle of the prophets, the miracle of the angels, the spectacle of the shepherds. The first made us certain, the second made us joyful, the third shall make us blessed. Why then, human being, are you [Col. 0027B] anxious about a royal dwelling when your God lies in a manger and there is no room for him in the inn [Note: [Col. 0027] Luke 2]? Why do you think about clothing? Behold, Christ is wrapped in a cheap little cloth [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid.]. Why do you labor over a company of retainers? Your Savior lies with ox and ass. Why are you anxious about dominion? The King of Glory obeys the command of Joseph and Mary.

Behold, you have heard of humility; hear of generosity: “Coming forth as man without seed, he bestowed his Godhead upon us” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ecclesiastical Chant at Vespers of the Annunciation]. For from this birth there shall be given to us lilies in place of dung, purple in place of sackcloth, glory in place of shame: lilies of purity delightful forever instead of the dung of carnal foulness; purple of immortality instead of the sackcloth of the corruptible body; the glory of divine contemplation instead of the shame of worldly calamity. May we see him reigning [Col. 0027C] with the Father and the Holy Spirit without end. Amen.

### “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

[CARDINAL [Note: [Col. 0027D] That is, John Algrin.].] At the beginning of this song, therefore, the Mother is introduced speaking and asking for the grace of the Holy Spirit and the union of the divine nature with the human, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” She leaves unstated the subject of the verb, or nominative, as certain and impressed upon her mind; God the Father is understood.

The Son is called the Father’s mouth because, just as he is called the Father’s arm, because through him the Father accomplishes all things, so he is called his mouth because through him the Father speaks to us and through him breathes forth that sound of which it is written: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound” [Note: [Col. 0027] Acts 2]. As Gregory says on that passage in Job: “My heart shall hear the hearing in the terror of his voice, and the sound proceeding from his mouth” [Col. 0027D; Note: [Col. 0027] Job 37].

Yet many things are indicated in a kiss. For the person kissing another breathes his own spirit toward that person, and it is in this sense that the word “Let him kiss” is understood. A kiss also contains the sweet and delightful union of two persons. It is likewise the sign of love, reconciliation, and peace; and all these are connoted by a kiss.

The blessed Virgin therefore says: “Let God the Father kiss me, by breathing his Spirit upon me.” The angel promised that this petition would be fulfilled when he said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you” [Col. 0028A; Note: [Col. 0027] Luke 1], as if to say: From above, from the Father of lights, the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, so that, as happens in a kiss, the Father shall breathe his Spirit toward you.

The blessed Virgin therefore says: “Let God the Father kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” that is, in the kiss of his Son, who kisses human nature. In this kiss there is the sweet union and delightful conjunction of the two natures in Christ; it is the sign of God’s love toward humankind, and likewise of the peace and reconciliation of God and humanity.

And just as, in this petition, the blessed Virgin joined the Father’s kiss to herself with the Son’s kiss of human nature, so the angel, having said to the Virgin, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid.]—in which statement he signified the Father’s kiss to the Virgin—then, joining to this kiss the Son’s kiss of human nature, immediately added: “And the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Col. 0028B; Note: [Col. 0027] Ibid.], as if to say: “You”—that is, for your honor, that he may honor you with the title Mother of God. The power of God the Most High, the Father—namely, the Son, who is called both the power and the arm of God the Father—shall overshadow: that is, shall make a covering. For, by taking flesh from the Virgin’s flesh, he made it a covering for the divine nature and veiled the splendor of Divinity beneath the shadow of flesh.

### “Because your breasts are better than wine.”

[THOMAS.] As though she said: Therefore, in your coming I desire to be refreshed by your eyes, because the gifts that you sent through your heralds surpass all things beyond comparison. Wine here signifies the fervor of legal knowledge; the breasts, [Col. 0028C] however, the elementary teachings of evangelical faith. Hence Paul: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0027] 1 Cor. 3]. Therefore your breasts are better than wine, because the rudiments of the New Testament immediately make fit for entrance into heavenly life all whom they regenerate from water and the Spirit—something the Law could not do: “For the Law brought nothing to perfection” [Note: [Col. 0027] Heb. 7].

The Beloved also has wine—that is, the perfection of teaching—far better than the wine of the Law. Of this, much later, it follows: “I drank my wine with my milk” [Note: [Col. 0027] Song 5]. The bridegroom has two breasts, and the bride has two. The bridegroom’s first is long-suffering, which has milk—that is, waiting for the sinner—as in Paul: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering?” [Note: [Col. 0027] Rom. 2]. The second is clemency, [Col. 0028D] and it has milk—that is, the receiving of the penitent, or readiness to forgive—as in the prophet: “Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0027] Isa. 55].

The bride also has two breasts. The first is that of rejoicing-with, and it pours out the milk of exhortation; the second is that of compassion, and it has the milk of consolation. For she knows how “to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep” [Note: [Col. 0027] Rom. 12].

The bridegroom also has two breasts: mercy and truth—mercy for pardoning, [Col. 0029A] truth for instructing. There is a threefold mercy of God. The first is beautiful, the second spacious, the third precious. The beautiful mercy cleanses the vices of souls and bodies; the spacious mercy enriches with the wealth of spiritual charisms; the precious mercy fills to abundance with the delights of heavenly beatitudes.

The first is beautiful because it makes the soul beautiful, so that “all her glory,” namely that of the king’s daughter, “is within” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 44]. The second is spacious because “his going forth is from the summit of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 18]. The third is precious because “her price is from afar and from the uttermost bounds” [Note: [Col. 0029] Prov. 31]. The first is beautiful because it makes the soul whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire [Note: [Col. 0029] Lam. 4]; the second spacious because “she reaches mightily from end to end” [Note: [Col. 0029] Wis. 8]; the third precious because it shall bring us “into an inheritance [Col. 0029B] incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading” [Note: [Col. 0029] 1 Pet. 1].

Of the first, the prophet says: “Mercy is beautiful in a time of affliction, and like a rain-cloud in a time of drought” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ecclus. 35]. Of the second: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 32]; and, “O Lord, your mercy is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 35]. Of the third: “For God loves mercy and truth; the Lord shall give grace and glory” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 83].

The first, called beautiful, bestows four beauties on the soul. Seek these below in the second book. First, it afflicts the heart with contrition; second, it softens the heart toward love of God; third, it bathes it, as with heavenly dew, in the goods above. This is according to the threefold interpretation of the name. By the first, *misericordia* is called, as it were, *miserum cor dans*, “giving a wretched heart”; by the second, it is called, as it were, *mittens seorsum rigorem cordis*, “sending away the hardness of the heart”; by the third, mercy is called that which waters hearts with wondrous sweetness.

This concerns the first breast; the second is truth. This truth is threefold. The first is in the assumption of flesh; the second in promise; the third in recompense. Of the first: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” [Col. 0029C; Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 84]. Of the second: “Your word is truth” [Note: [Col. 0029] John 17]. Of the third: “His mercy has been confirmed upon us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 116].

Likewise the bride has two breasts, namely mercy and truth. The first has milk—that is, compassion; the second, knowledge and assurance. Again, this mercy is threefold. The first is to forgive an enemy and pray for him; the second is to tear a sinner away from his sin; [Col. 0029D] the third is to relieve the need of the poor from one’s own resources. Again, there are three truths of the human being. The first is the truth of confession, the second the truth of faith, and the third the truth of every action.

Since, therefore, the bride asks for a kiss, she sees these breasts meeting one another in the drawing-near of their bodies, so that the bridegroom’s left is opposite her right, and his right opposite her left. In each case, the right is truth and the left mercy. Thus the three human truths meet the three mercies of God. The bride’s right breast [Col. 0030A] meets the bridegroom’s left breast. Therefore the truth of confession meets the first mercy of God, namely the beautiful mercy. For in the truth of confession forgiveness of sins is obtained, which belongs to the first mercy. Therefore the truth of God, which is the second truth, meets the spacious mercy; because spiritual charisms, which belong to the second mercy, are built upon true faith. The third truth, which is to do all things truly for God’s sake, meets the third mercy, namely the precious mercy. For whoever performs works for God’s sake receives a precious reward. Likewise, the three truths of God meet the three human mercies. For the first truth of God is in the assumption of flesh. This meets the first human mercy, which is to forgive an enemy and pray for him. For this purpose Christ assumed true [Col. 0030B] flesh: that he might mercifully forgive sins and pray for his enemies. The second truth of God, which is in the promise, meets the second human mercy, which is to tear a sinner away from sin. For God promises the kingdom of heaven to such persons. The third truth of God, which is that of recompense, meets the third human mercy, which is to relieve the need of the poor from one’s temporal goods; because for temporal and perishable goods God will repay eternal and unchangeable goods.

In the first meeting Stephen says: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” [Note: [Col. 0029] Acts 7.]; and Truth, who is God, meets him, because “he saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ibid.]. And the good Father was moved with compassion for the prodigal son [Col. 0030C] [Note: [Col. 0029] Luke 15.]. For the second Daniel says: “Those who have been learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who have instructed many unto righteousness, like bright stars for eternity” [Note: [Col. 0029] Dan. 17]. Jesus Christ had compassion upon the mother of the young man who, already dead, was being carried out beyond the gate [Note: [Col. 0029] Luke 7.]. Of the third it is written: “I was hungry and you gave me food” [Note: [Col. 0029] Matt. 25], etc.

The truth of promise follows: “Come, blessed of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ibid.]. Thus the Samaritan, moved by mercy for the man wounded by robbers, poured in wine and oil; and gave two denarii on his behalf [Note: [Col. 0029] Luke 10.]. In the denarii temporal assistance is signified; in the wine, the giver’s joy; in the oil, the sweetness of gentleness; because “God loves a cheerful giver” [Note: [Col. 0029] II Cor. 9], and one who is gentle toward the poor. These meetings occur in God’s threefold mercy: beautiful, spacious, precious. “For she reaches mightily from end to end” [Note: [Col. 0029] Wisd. 8]; that is, she does not abandon you from the beginning of your conversion, provided, however, that truth accompanies her. For these accompany you, go before you, and follow you. The first meeting goes before; the second accompanies; the third follows. They go before; hence David: “Mercy and truth shall go before thy face” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 58]. They accompany; hence the same writer: “For mercy shall be built up in the heavens; thy truth shall be prepared in them” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 58].

But there are some who [Col. 0031A] reject these mercies; some who neglect them; some whose mercy is momentary; and some whose mercy is enduring. The first are criminals, the second lukewarm, the third changeable, the fourth steadfast. Of the first the prophet says: “There is no mercy, no truth, no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, theft, murder, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” [Note: [Col. 0031] Hos. 4]. Of the second: “Judgment without mercy shall be given to one who has not shown mercy” [Note: [Col. 0031] Jas. 2]. Of the third: “Your mercy is like a morning cloud, and like dew passing away in the morning” [Note: [Col. 0031] Hos. 6]. Of the fourth, Job says: “Compassion grew with me, and came forth with me from my mother’s womb” [Note: [Col. 0031] Job 31]. But it should be noted that God is called mercy, as in: “My God is my mercy” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 58]. [Col. 0031B] God’s mercy is also spoken of; hence: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 32]. And man’s mercy is also spoken of; hence we read: “The faithful mercies of David” [Note: [Col. 0031] Isa. 55].

The ancient fathers received Mercy, who is God, at the doorway of the temple, through faith and prophetic revelation. We Christians received him in the middle of the temple, through his incarnation. The blessed shall receive him in the sanctuary of the temple through glorification. Likewise, the blessed Virgin received him at the doorway of her temple in the angelic annunciation; in the middle of the temple in conception; in the sanctuary of the temple in her assumption. We too have received these three mercies of God: the first at the doorway of the temple, when, purified, we pass from darkness to light; the second in the middle of the temple, [Col. 0031C] when, in the fragrance of virtues, we meet Christ; the third we shall receive in the sanctuary of the temple, when, seeing God in his brightness, we shall praise him forever with the angels. These are Job’s three daughters: the first is she who is called Day, the second Cassia, the third Horn-of-antimony [*Cornustibii*] [Note: [Col. 0031] Job 42], because we shall praise God without end.

## Fragrant with the finest ointments

[THO.] The finest ointments are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which Christ’s words are fragrant; for apostolic men, ministers of the milk of the Gospel, progress in the love of virtues through the anointing of the Spirit. John speaks of this: “May the anointing which you received from him remain in you” [Note: [Col. 0031] I John 2]. Likewise, men of good repute are fragrant with the finest ointments, whose scent preachers spread far and wide, as they themselves say: “But thanks be to God, who always [Col. 0031D] leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and through us makes manifest in every place the fragrance of his knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0031] II Cor. 2].

There is an ointment of contrition, an ointment of devotion, and an ointment of piety. The first is piercing, producing pain; the second tempering, relieving pain; the third healing, even driving out sickness. The first is poured upon Christ’s feet, the second upon his head, the third upon his whole body. The first is good, the second better, the third best. From the first we have the benefit of forgiveness; from the second, the consolation of exultation; in the third we give thanks to Christ for [Col. 0032A] the work of our redemption, in which its manner and fruit are contained.

Hear the fruit: “They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing” [Note: [Col. 0031] Luke 6]. The measure will be good in the general resurrection; pressed down in the solidity of bodies; shaken together in agility; overflowing in brightness and the vision of God. But there is flowing, outflowing, through-flowing, and overflowing. Flowing is in the first cleansing from sins; outflowing is in the grace of virtues, when an example is given to one’s neighbor; through-flowing is the perfect devoutness that endures to death; overflowing is the abundance of blessedness, when we shall see God face to face. But its fruit will be in the soul. Now in the soul we see reason, will, and memory. By these, reason is often deceived in judgments, [Col. 0032B] will is tossed by disturbance, and memory is confounded by forgetfulness. But God will be fullness of light for reason, abundance of peace for the will, and continuation of eternity for memory. God as Truth will accomplish the first; God as Love the second; God as Eternity the third. My trinity has become entangled in errors, pains, and fears. Hence: “My heart has been troubled” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 54], and thence pain. “My strength has forsaken me” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 37], and thence dread. “And the light of my eyes, even that is not with me” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ibid.], and thence terror. But then error will depart from reason, pain from will, and fear from memory.

The manner of our redemption was Christ’s self-emptying: he emptied himself even unto flesh, unto the cross, unto death [Note: [Col. 0031] Phil. 2]. The first was an act of humility, the second [Col. 0032C] of condescension, the third of gentleness: namely, to be clothed in flesh, tortured on the cross, and punished by death. These ointments are called, or understood as, gifts of spiritual grace, which console, cherish, restore, and strengthen mortal hearts: they console by removing sorrow; refresh by relieving the burdens of frail condition; restore by healing with inward sweetness; strengthen by fortifying with the shield of patience. Of the first Paul says: “Confirm love toward him” [Note: [Col. 0031] II Cor. 2], etc. For the second, David restored the Amalekite youth, so that he became his guide. Of the third the Bride says: “Eat, friends, and be drunk, beloved ones” [Note: [Col. 0031] Song 5]. Of the fourth Paul says: “In all things take up the shield of faith, by which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one” [Note: [Col. 0031] Eph. 6].

Likewise, there are good ointments, better ones, and the finest. Good are those of [Col. 0032D] consolation in the reconciliation of sins; better, those of love in the imparting of virtues; finest, those of contemplation in the revelation of heavenly things. But let us consider the cause of these nuptials.

When the supreme Craftsman was establishing the laws of the heavenly kingdom, he entrusted the entire governance of his kingdom to three virtues: to power he entrusted the crown, to wisdom the scepter, to kindness the seal. In the crown is understood the singular preeminence of divine dignity; in the scepter, the rule of just severity; in the seal, the consolation of inexhaustible piety. Power says: [Col. 0033A] “I will not give my honor to another” [Note: [Col. 0033] Isa. 42]. Of wisdom it is said: “Wisdom conquers malice” [Note: [Col. 0033] Wisd. 7]. Of piety: “His compassions are over all his works” [Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 144]. Therefore it belongs to power to defend inviolably the glory of heavenly honor; to wisdom, to cast down its despisers with just severity; to kindness, after their fall, to forgive those seeking mercy.

That Lucifer wished to seize such power; but he could neither constrain by force the possessor of so great a glory, because he was supremely powerful; nor ensnare him by fraud, because he was supremely wise; nor expel him through hatred on the part of his own, because he was supremely kind; nor succeed him by succession, because he is immortal. Thus he brought forth the injustice of pride, conceived the pain of envy, and gave birth to the iniquity of defiant audacity [Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 7]. The first arose because, since he could not be preferred, he sought to make himself equal [Col. 0033B] to the Creator; the second, because he could not be made equal to his glory, wasted away from envy of it; the third despised him by whose majesty he was overwhelmed.

Likewise, there is a good ointment, a better one, and a best. The first heals inwardly and darkens outwardly; the second strengthens inwardly and smooths outward pustules; the third gladdens. The first is of humility, the second of purity, the third of religious honorableness. Of this Exodus says: “The flesh of man shall not be anointed with it” [Note: [Col. 0033] Exod. 30]. A man is called the human spirit, and it is anointed with this threefold ointment. The woman is called the human flesh, and those who lead a womanish life are said to be anointed with this second ointment. Hence in the Old Testament we read not of women being anointed, but of men.

Three men are anointed with these three ointments. The first is, before men, a man whose life is contemptible; the second, a man whose life is irreproachable; the third, a man whose life is venerable. Through the first vainglory is checked in the weak; through the second, “The mouth of those who speak iniquity is stopped” [Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 62]; through the third, life and teaching are brought to perfection. Hence the first is called a man avoiding ruin, the second a man vigorous in rigor, the third a man governing the way of righteousness.
