Through the first a new religious order is defended from vainglory; through the second, an abundance of virtues is strengthened; through the third, an abundance of graces flourishes and bears fruit. Therefore the poet says of the first:

> While a new branch is growing together in its green bark,  
> Let any breeze shake it, and it will fall tenderly.  
> [Note: [Col. 0033] Ovid.]

Of the second:

> Afterwards, hardened by time, it also withstands the winds.  
> [Note: [Col. 0033] Ibid.]

[Col. 0033D] Of the third:

> And the firm tree will possess its adopted riches.  
> [Note: [Col. 0033] Ibid.]

The first ointment possessed by the man whose life is contemptible is made from three things. First, he presents himself as a sinner; second, as abject and worthless; third, as an unprofitable servant. For in this way the humble person assumes the appearance of a sinner. He conceals temporal graces. He makes little of the good that he does. Of the first that publican said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” [Note: [Col. 0033] Luke 18]. In opposition to the second Elihu spoke when he said: “I am full of words, and the spirit of my belly constrains me. [Col. 0034A] I too will show my knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0033] Job 32]. In opposition to the third that Pharisee said: “God, I give thee thanks that I am not like other men—robbers, adulterers; I fast twice in the Sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0033] Luke 18], etc.

The second ointment, possessed by the man whose life is irreproachable, is made from four things. He must be irreproachable in the sight of God, in the sight of his teacher, in the sight of his brother, and in the sight of his enemy. The first must be achieved by a pure conscience, the second by obedience, the third by discipline, the fourth by abstinence. Of the first Job says: “For my heart has not reproached me throughout my life” [Note: [Col. 0033] Job 27]. Of the second the Lord reproves Adam, saying: “Because thou hast obeyed the voice of thy wife more than mine, thou shalt be cursed upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0033] Gen. 3]. And Samuel says to Saul: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” [Note: [Col. 0033] I Sam. 15]. [Col. 0034B] Of the third Paul reproves Peter: “I resisted him,” he says, “to his face, because he was blameworthy” [Note: [Col. 0033] Gal. 2]. For he ate with the uncircumcised. Of the fourth the Apostle says: “Be without blame in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world” [Note: [Col. 0033] Phil. 2]. And Peter: “I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul, maintaining good conduct among the Gentiles, so that, in that wherein they speak against you as evildoers, from good works” [Note: [Col. 0033] I Pet. 2], etc.

The third ointment, used by the man whose life is venerable, is made from four things. The first is truth in teaching; the second, cheerfulness in affability and expression; the third, gravity of discipline; the fourth, dignity of person. The first instructs toward truth; the second [Col. 0034C] displays kindness of heart; the third excludes frivolity; the fourth gives authority to the rest. Job showed himself to be such a man. Hence he says: “They waited for me as for rain, and opened their mouth as for the latter rain” [Note: [Col. 0033] Job 29]; behold the first. “If I laughed at them, they did not believe it” [Note: [Col. 0033] Ibid.]; behold the second. “And the light of my face did not fall to the ground” [Note: [Col. 0033] Ibid.]; behold the third. “When I wished to come to them, I sat first” [Note: [Col. 0033] Ibid.]. But lest this should seem to smell of pride, he says: “When I sat like a king with an army around me, I was nevertheless a comforter of mourners” [Note: [Col. 0033] Ibid.].

Thus Job was anointed in the first way, sitting on the dunghill and scraping his sores [Note: [Col. 0033] Job 2]. Daniel in the second: when an attempt was made to remove him from the king’s side, no wrongdoing was found [Note: [Col. 0033] Dan. 6]. Moses in the third: when he [Col. 0034D] entered the tabernacle, the children of Israel, standing at the entrances of their tents, looked upon his back [Note: [Col. 0033] Exod. 32].

As a figure of the first, blue skins and red-dyed ram skins over the tabernacle were covered with a sackcloth of hair. Yet, according to the sequence of the text, it appears that the blue skins were placed underneath [Note: [Col. 0033] Exod. 26]. But because Bede says that the haircloth coverings protected the inward beauty from stormy weather, it could be that in a storm the coverings were laid underneath for protection, while in clear weather the red-dyed and blue skins were laid underneath as ornament. This is also to be understood [Col. 0035A] wherever it may be found elsewhere in this work. As a figure of the second, the ark was coated inside and outside with pitch [Note: [Col. 0035] Gen. 6], lest any crack give the flood a place to enter. As a figure of the third, the ark of the covenant was overlaid within and without with the purest gold [Note: [Col. 0035] Exod. 25], so that it might appear splendid to men and to God. The venerable man of life was blessed Benedict.

Blessed in gift, through prevenient grace; blessed in name, pouring forth the good fragrance of reputation; blessed in divine power, accomplishing all things. In these three there is a threefold grace. The first consumes, the second sows together, the third completes: consuming sins, sowing good works together, completing merits. Of the first Paul says: “But when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace” [Note: [Col. 0035] Gal. 1]. Of the second, the same writer: “I have labored more [Col. 0035B] than all; yet not I, but the grace of God with me” [Note: [Col. 0035] I Cor. 15]. Of the third John says: “From his fullness we have all received grace for grace” [Note: [Col. 0035] John 1]. Of the first: “He recognized him in his blessings” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ecclus. 44], etc. And: “He magnified him in the sight of the Lord.” “Lord,” he says, “thou hast gone before with blessings of sweetness” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 20]. This consumes sins.

Hear the grace that sows together through the good fragrance of the name: “Behold,” he says, “the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field which the Lord has blessed” [Note: [Col. 0035] Gen. 27].—“A good name,” says the Wise Man, “is better than precious ointments” [Note: [Col. 0035] Prov. 22]. For he who sows together—that is, sows with others through a good fragrance—our Lord God will give him an inheritance in an everlasting name [Note: [Col. 0035] Ecclus. 15]. Hear the grace that sows together: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence. [Col. 0035C] He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which sends out its roots toward moisture; and he shall not fear when heat comes. His leaf shall be green, and in time of drought he shall not be anxious, nor shall he ever cease to bear fruit” [Note: [Col. 0035] Jer. 17].

Hear the completing grace in which Benedict is blessed in divine power: “The Lord,” he says, “gave him the blessing of all nations, and confirmed his covenant upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ecclus. 44]. For there are three nations whose blessing he possessed: the nation of pagans, the nation of Jews, and the nation of Christians. He possessed the blessing of pagans when, fleeing idolatry, he maintained the worship of the one true God. He merited the blessing of the Jews by following not the letter but the spirit, not ceremonies but the sacrament, not [Col. 0035D] the hardness of the law but the moderation of grace. He merited the blessing of Christians by fleeing from sin to holiness, ascending from virtue to virtue, and passing from the misery of the world to blessedness; for then God confirmed his covenant upon his head.

A covenant is first drawn up, second established, third confirmed. It is drawn up when it is written; established when witnesses are brought forward; confirmed when a seal is applied. It is drawn up over the feet, established over the hands, confirmed [Col. 0036A] over the head. It is drawn up over the feet of the affections, when by good will a person is added to the elect in the book of life; it is established over the hands, when testimony is rendered to him from good works. It is confirmed over the head, when a crown of glory is repaid for his merits. Christ showed the covenant drawn up: “At the head of the book it is written of me” [Note: [Col. 0035] Heb. 10]. Hence he says to his disciples: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0035] Luke 10]. Of the testimony of works he says: “The works which I do bear witness concerning me” [Note: [Col. 0035] John 5]. And the Apostle: “Having testimony from those who are within and from those who are without” [Note: [Col. 0035] I Cor. 5]. Hear it confirmed in Christ by the seal: “John saw in the Apocalypse an angel coming down from heaven, with a golden crown upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0035] Rev. 10]. And elsewhere in the same book: [Col. 0036B] “And a rainbow upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ibid.]; and in the same book, in a figure of Christ’s members, he saw others having the seal of the living God upon their foreheads, as a sign that the covenant was established upon their heads [Note: [Col. 0035] Rev. 9].

## Your name is oil poured out

[THO.] Christ is called oil because of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which he received not by measure but in fullness. Hence it is called poured out, not dripped. Thus Christ is also called anointed. Hence David: “God, thy God, has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy companions” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 44]. Therefore it is called poured-out oil because he is full of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out abundantly after his ascension, not only upon Jews but also upon others, as he foretold through the prophet: “I will pour out [Col. 0036C] of my Spirit upon all flesh” [Note: [Col. 0035] Isa. 44].

There is the oil of the Holy Spirit. Hence: “That he might suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone” [Note: [Col. 0035] Deut. 32]. And Job: “The rock poured out for me streams of oil” [Note: [Col. 0035] Job 29]. And the prophet: “The yoke shall rot away before the oil” [Note: [Col. 0035] Isa. 10]. There is also the oil of mercy. Hence David: “And my flesh has been changed because of oil” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 108]. There is also the oil of gladness. Hence David: “That he may make the face cheerful with oil” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 103]. There is also the oil of love. Hence Solomon: “Let thy garments be white at all times, and let oil not be lacking from thy head” [Note: [Col. 0035] Eccl. 9]. There is also the oil of a good conscience, which “the five prudent virgins took in their vessels with their lamps” [Note: [Col. 0035] Matt. 25]. There is also the oil of consolation, which the Samaritan poured into the man wounded by robbers [Note: [Col. 0035] Luke 10]. Flattering speech is also called oil. Hence [Col. 0036D] David: “Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 140]. There is also the oil of heretics: subtle and bland deception. Hence Solomon says of the wandering woman: “Her throat is smoother than oil” [Note: [Col. 0035] Prov. 5].

O sweet pouring-out of the oil—of which this discourse speaks—intoxicating angels, satisfying saints, giving life to the dead, justifying sinners, making mourners glad, scattering hell, redeeming the world, restoring heaven! This oil made the child in Fourth Kings yawn seven times [Note: [Col. 0035] IV Kings 4]. Four of these yawns belong to the feeling of compunction; [Col. 0037A] three belong to the sound of confession. It restores inward assent by fourfold compunction, namely a double shame and a double fear. First consider your Lord, your Maker, God your beneficent Father. Let your fear answer to the first and the last; shame to the two middle terms.

The conscience is cleansed by a threefold judgment: one’s own, another’s, and God’s. Hence Paul: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you, or by a human day” [Note: [Col. 0037] I Cor. 4]: this is another’s judgment. “But neither do I judge myself” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ibid.]: this is one’s own. “But the one who judges me is the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ibid.]: this is God’s. Things known to oneself are judged by one’s own judgment; doubtful things by another’s; things wholly unknown by God’s. One’s own judgment is made to wash away guilt; another’s to water a neighbor’s infamy; God’s, lest through hidden sin someone fall into Gehenna. [Col. 0037B] Therefore the first must be done diligently, the second endured bravely, the third eagerly desired. In the first a person performs judgment and justice; in the second the neighbor performs wickedness; in the third God performs mercy. Of the first: “Judge justly, sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 57]. Likewise: “I have performed judgment and justice” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 118]. Likewise: “Love justice, you who judge” [Note: [Col. 0037] Wisd. 1]. Of the second: “Who are you that you judge your brother?” [Note: [Col. 0037] Rom. 14]. “For in judging another you condemn yourself” [Note: [Col. 0037] Rom. 2]. Likewise: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged” [Note: [Col. 0037] Matt. 7]. Likewise: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” [Note: [Col. 0037] I Cor. 4]. Of the third: “But the one who judges me is the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ibid.]. [Col. 0037C] Likewise: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 42]. Likewise: “When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world” [Note: [Col. 0037] I Cor. 11]. Behold the four yawns and the three in the threefold judgment, or the three in confession, as was proposed.

There are three in confession, for it must be humble, pure, and faithful. Now humility is beginning, progressing, and perfecting. The first is in the heart, the second in work, the third in endurance. Truth in the heart, arising from knowledge of oneself, produces the first; holiness in work, arising from good conduct, displays the second; love, armed with the shield of patience, perfects the third in endurance. This is humble confession.

Second, confession must be pure. Four things impair the purity [Col. 0037D] of confession. There are those who confess certain sins but not others: this is signified in Ananias and Sapphira, who kept back part of the price of the field [Note: [Col. 0037] Acts 5]. Others confess everything but conceal the manner—that is, the circumstances. David signified this when he said concerning Saul and Jonathan: “How the mighty have fallen in battle” [Note: [Col. 0037] II Sam. 1]. Others make excuses, like Adam: “The woman,” he says, “gave me, and I ate” [Note: [Col. 0037] Gen. 3]. Others conceal the multitude or gravity of their sins beneath ornate words: these are the girdles with which Adam and Eve covered their shameful parts [Note: [Col. 0037] Ibid.].

Faithful confession [Col. 0038A] consists in three things: namely, if it has hope of pardon, hope of grace, and hope of glory—hope of pardon, by which sin is forgiven; of grace, by which one performs good; of glory, by which the good one does is rewarded. Or, as a certain wise man says, there are four judgments: according to foreknowledge, according to cause, according to operation, and according to recompense. According to foreknowledge, we were judged from the beginning; according to cause, we are judged inwardly every day; according to operation, we are judged outwardly from works; according to recompense, we shall be judged at the general judgment. Of these, the first two are hidden and the last two manifest. Human judgment is not admitted in the two hidden judgments; in the judgment of operation, God grants power to men; in the judgment of recompense [Col. 0038B] each person shall be judged by God before men. The first is hidden and unchangeable; the second hidden and changeable; the third manifest and changeable; the fourth manifest and unchangeable.

Likewise, judgment is said to occur when a sentence is formulated, and judgment is said to occur when a sentence is pronounced. In formulating the sentence of every judgment, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit judge together. In pronouncing the sentence, the Son alone judges, because in his divinity he formulates the sentence with the Father and Holy Spirit; in his humanity, he alone is to pronounce the sentence. Hence, concerning the formulation of sentence according to his humanity, he said: “I judge no one” [Note: [Col. 0037] John 8]. Concerning the pronouncement of sentence, he says: “As I hear, so I judge” [Note: [Col. 0037] John 5]. Likewise it is said: “He gave all judgment to the Son” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ibid.]. For as he [Col. 0038C] hears in formulation, so he speaks in pronouncement.

The beloved’s name is understood in three ways. For the name is called divine wisdom; it is also called Christ’s good repute; and it is also called particular knowledge. Of the first: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar” [Note: [Col. 0037] Isa. 3]. Of the second: “A good name is better than precious ointments” [Note: [Col. 0037] Eccl. 7]. Of the third he said to Moses: “I have known thee by name” [Note: [Col. 0037] Exod. 33]. The first is oil poured out, the second spread abroad, the third lavishly poured forth. The first is from heaven, the second in Judaism, the third in the world. The first through self-emptying; the second through teaching, miracles, and conduct; the third through Gospel and apostolic preaching. This oil was poured out so that the pain of the wound of the man wounded by robbers might be softened; it was spread abroad so that the hardness of the Jews might be softened; it was poured over so that the hidden sacrament might shine forth. The first is for forgiveness, the second for devotion, the third for faith. As a figure of the first, there was the oil that the Samaritan poured into the wounded man [Note: [Col. 0037] Luke 10]. As a figure of the second, “Jacob set up a stone as a memorial, pouring oil upon it” [Note: [Col. 0037] Gen. 18]. As a figure of the third, the Lord said to Moses: “You shall make the purest oil from olives for preparing the lamps” [Note: [Col. 0037] Exod. 35].

That first oil, namely divine wisdom, is poured out, poured forth, and infused. It is poured out from the Father’s throne; poured forth from the Virgin’s womb; [Col. 0039A] infused into the human heart. The first, that it might call lost man back to the heavenly kingdoms; the second, that it might place him in Abraham’s bosom; the third, that the human heart might savor the things above. On account of the first it was said to Samuel: “Take a horn of oil, that you may anoint the son of Jesse” [Note: [Col. 0039] I Sam. 16]. For the Father, who is called power, is signified through the horn, in which lies all the defense of horned animals. On account of the second it is said to the same man: “Take a flask of oil and anoint Saul” [Note: [Col. 0039] I Sam. 10]. A flask (*lenticula*) is an earthen vessel, but square. This is the Virgin Mary: earthen, that is, frail, because mortal; but square, that is, solid, because inviolate. On account of the third, “the prudent virgins took oil in their lamps” [Note: [Col. 0039] Matt. 25].

O venerable outpouring, through which infusion was made, perfusion was given, renewal was procured, [Col. 0039B] and confusion shall be taken away! Infusion of divinity; perfusion of devotion; renewal unto incorruption; confusion at the eternal examination. The first in the Virgin, the second in the heart, the third in the body, the fourth in the examination of good and evil persons. Of the first: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 71]. Of the second: “But I shall delight in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 103]. Of the third: “We shall see him as he is, because we shall be like him” [Note: [Col. 0039] I John 5]. Of the fourth: “On that day thou shalt not be confounded because of all thy inventions by which thou hast transgressed against me” [Note: [Col. 0039] Zeph. 3].

The infusion was made when “the Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0039] John 1]. The perfusion of devotion occurred because “he dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid.]. The renewal of the body will occur when “we shall see his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid.]. The confusion of iniquity shall be removed when “we shall see [Col. 0039C] him full of grace and truth” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ibid.].

Likewise, knowledge of God is threefold. The first is that he exists; the second, what he is not; the third, what he is. Of the first: “One who approaches God must first believe that he is” [Note: [Col. 0039] Heb. 11]. Of the second: No small part of understanding consists in understanding, while we are not yet able to understand what God is, what he is not. Of the third: “Then I shall know him as I also am known” [Note: [Col. 0039] I Cor. 13]. The first cleanses from brutish ignorance; the second purifies from foolish idolatry; the third sanctifies and frees from the second death.

The Father now protects us through himself, now through the Son, now through the Holy Spirit. Of the first, to Leviathan in Job: “Nevertheless, preserve his life” [Note: [Col. 0039] Job 2]. Of the second: “His truth shall surround thee with a shield” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 90]. Of the third: “Thou hast crowned us with the shield of thy good will” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 5].

[Col. 0039D] Therefore the young maidens loved thee exceedingly.

[THO.] The maidens are souls reborn in Christ, having cast off the filth of the old man. They therefore love the Beloved because they have obtained from him remission of sins and received the gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which they may advance in the virtues. Hence they say: “The charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us [Note: [Col. 0039] Rom. 5.].” The faithful of old were also maidens, who likewise held the hope of eternal life in Christ who was to come. [Col. 0040A] Therefore, expressing their desire, the Church represents them every year by solemnly singing: “O Adonai and leader of the house of Israel [Note: [Col. 0039] Office of Advent], who appeared to Moses in the fire of the flame of the bush [Note: [Col. 0039] Exod. 3], and gave the law on Sinai [Note: [Col. 0039] Exod. 19], come to redeem us with an outstretched arm [Note: [Col. 0039] Exod. 6].” Because the people sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0039] Luke 1] had heard that Christ would come—he who would free them from the yoke of slavery, go before them in battle, kindle them to virtue, and order their life—they cry out: “O Adonai,” and so forth.

One must observe four things here: lord, leader, fire, and lawgiver. He is Lord, by whom we are protected; leader, whom we follow; fire, by which we are kindled; lawgiver, by whom we are instructed: Lord, by whom we are protected from the assembly of the wicked; leader, whom we follow [Col. 0040B] into battle; fire, by which we are kindled to love; lawgiver, by whom we are instructed to live religiously. He is Lord, by whom we are protected from the assembly of the wicked, so that we may be freed from the devil’s yoke, “rescued from the most harsh rule of Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0039] Hymn of the Church]”; leader, whom we follow into battle, so that we may be able to stand firm on the evil day [Note: [Col. 0039] Eph. 6]; fire, by which we are kindled to love, so that we may hear: “I love those who love me; and if anyone loves me, he shall be loved by my Father [Note: [Col. 0039] John 14]”; lawgiver, by whom we are instructed to live religiously, so that “we may live soberly, justly, and godly in this age [Note: [Col. 0039] Titus 2].”

Of the first: “You protected me from the assembly of the wicked, from the multitude of those working iniquity [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 63].” Of the second: “In your mercy you were leader to your people whom you redeemed [Note: [Col. 0039] Exod. 15].” Of the third: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire [Col. 0040C] but that it should burn [Note: [Col. 0039] Luke 12]?” David sought the fourth when he said: “Set a law before me, O Lord, in your way, and direct me upon a straight path because of my enemies [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 26].”

The Lord was sought by the ancient Fathers when they said: “O Adonai [Note: [Col. 0039] Judith 16],” which means “Lord.” And rightly they first seek the Lord, that he may aid them in the three things belonging to a lord. For he ought to be just, merciful, and beneficent: just, to punish rebels; merciful, to pardon suppliants; beneficent, to reward those who love him. Hence this name *Dominus*, “Lord,” is interpreted in three ways: according to the first, Lord means “one giving threats”; according to the second, “one alone mitigating pains”; according to the third, “one giving a gift.”

[Col. 0040D] Hear of the just one: “God is a just, strong, and patient judge. Is he angry every day? [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 7]” Hear David on mercy: “When I said, ‘My foot has slipped,’ your mercy, O Lord, helped me [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 93].” Hear of the beneficent one: “For the Lord will give kindness, and our land will yield its fruit [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 84].” Beneficence is indeed liberality in things. What could he have given more liberally than himself, for whom the Fathers, longing, cried: “O Adonai [Note: [Col. 0039] Judith 16]”?

For he himself is Lord, himself [Col. 0041A] ruler, himself reigning. He is Lord in eternity, ruler in time, reigning in operation. He has the first naturally as a disposition, the second in use, the third in effect. For sometimes we possess the use of a thing though not its exercise: thus a horse in a stable has the capacity for walking, though it does not walk. Of the first: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand [Note: [Col. 0041] Ps. 109].” Of the second: “Behold, the Lord, the ruler, comes [Note: [Col. 0041] Isa. 3].” Of the third: “Remember me, O God, almighty ruler [Note: [Col. 0041] Jer. 15].” Therefore he invokes Christ as Adonai, so that he who rules eternally as the Father’s equal may rule in use by coming into his mother’s womb, and may rule in act by redeeming from the prison of the devil.

This name *Adonai* is significantly placed; it has six letters, because six is the first perfect number, to show that he rules perfectly when he creates; [Col. 0041B] perfectly when he re-creates; and perfectly when he restores. He showed the first in the creation of the world, the second in the Passion, the third in the Nativity. Thus, as regards the first, he created all things in six days, and Adam was created on the sixth day [Note: [Col. 0041] Gen. 1]. As regards the second, he suffered on the sixth day [Note: [Col. 0041] Matt. 27]. As regards the third, as they say, he was born on the sixth day without the corruption of sin, so that through him humankind might rise incorruptible from this mortality.

But if through the Lord we are freed from the devil’s yoke, since “a great way still remains [Note: [Col. 0041] III Kings 19],” in which “the life of man upon earth is warfare [Note: [Col. 0041] Job 7],” it is necessary that he be leader of the house of Israel: leader in danger, leader in battle, leader in pilgrimage. In danger, where perplexity constrains us amid the ambiguity of evils; in battle, where the importunity of adversaries [Col. 0041C] oppresses us; in pilgrimage, lest faintheartedness weary us through tedium. Therefore in the first he is a counsellor; in the second, a helper; in the third, a comforter: counsellor, so that in flight from perplexity we may be more discerning; helper, so that in battle we may be stronger; comforter, so that we may make our pilgrimage more cheerfully.

He can do the first because he himself is “Wonderful, Counsellor [Note: [Col. 0041] Isa. 9].” Why then are you disturbed by sorrow? Is he not your counsellor, or has your comforter failed you? In the second case say: “The Lord God is my helper, and therefore I have not been confounded [Note: [Col. 0041] Isa. 50].” In the third he cries: “Comfort, comfort my people [Note: [Col. 0041] Isa. 40].”

He is truly leader of the house of Israel, because in the first case he brought them forth from darkness and the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0041] Ps. 106], namely, from perplexity; in the second, “he brought them out of [Col. 0041D] their necessities [Note: [Col. 0041] Ibid.],” namely, from battle; and in the third, “he led them by the right way,” namely, the way of pilgrimage, “that they might go to a city of habitation [Note: [Col. 0041] Ibid.].”

At the crossing of the Red Sea Moses was leader in danger [Note: [Col. 0041] Exod. 14]; Judas Maccabaeus in battle [Note: [Col. 0041] I Macc. 3, etc.]; and the angel Raphael in Tobias’s pilgrimage [Note: [Col. 0041] Tobit 5, etc.]. Under the first, the perplexed people escaped; under the second, they triumphed; under the third, Tobias brought medicine to his father. Let us consider Susanna under perplexity, Joshua under battle, and Elijah beneath the juniper tree under pilgrimage. Susanna received counsel under this leader through Daniel [Note: [Col. 0041] Dan. 13]; Joshua received help through [Col. 0042A] prayer and the uplifted hands of Moses [Note: [Col. 0041] Exod. 17]; Elijah received comfort when the angel brought water and bread baked under ashes [Note: [Col. 0041] III Kings 19].

Let us therefore see how this leader’s counsel delivers in danger. These things appear in Susanna. She first said: “I am hemmed in on every side, and I do not know what to choose [Note: [Col. 0041] I Macc. 4, 5, etc.; citation apparently corrupt].” But hear her choice: “It is better for me to fall into the hands of men than to forsake the law of my God.” Daniel thus scattered the counsel of the elders: “Separate them from one another, and I will judge them.” And he convicted them. Hear how she was freed from perplexity: “And innocent blood was saved on that day.” Behold, our leader gave counsel in danger.

Hear of help in battle, shown to us in the war of Judas Maccabaeus. When Judas Maccabaeus returns from battle, the hindmost follows [Col. 0042B] the hindmost; he gathers the scattered, because he calls contrary movements of the soul back to unity of mind. He raises the weary as he consoles those whom the strain of a prolonged journey presses and breaks. He rebukes the slow, accusing their sloth lest they be captured by enemies. He instructs the wounded not to despair, but directs, recalls, and kindles them toward hope of salvation. He supports the burdened and, lest they sink under their burden, urges them by words and examples.

By the wounded we mean those whom we see struck by the devil’s darts. The burdened are those who groan in sorrow under the burden of a long course of life. He exhorted the people along the way until they came into the land of Judah, that is, of confession—not only of sin, but also of faith and divine praise. Behold, help in battle.

[Col. 0042C] Consolation in pilgrimage follows.

This leader comforts pilgrims by three consolations: love, meditation, and reading. These are the three things which were in Solomon’s Temple [Note: [Col. 0041] III Kings 7]: a golden altar, a golden table, and a golden lampstand. Let the altar therefore be love, the table reading, and the lampstand meditation. The purity of the gold in the altar is a mind perfect in love; the purity of the gold in the table is sound understanding in reading; the purity of the gold in the lampstand is pure affection in meditation. Thus love should seek nothing carnal, reading should teach nothing heretical, and meditation should desire nothing earthly.

Incense is kindled upon the altar, loaves are placed on the table, and a lamp upon the lampstand: incense of prayer, loaves of refreshment, a lamp of knowledge. By prayer God is sought; by refreshment he is [Col. 0042D] tasted; in the light of knowledge he is seen. In seeking he is desired; when tasted he becomes sweet; when known he is loved. The incense has fragrance, the loaves flavour, knowledge love. Prayer indeed breathes forth God; the loaves have savour; knowledge loves. God imparts sweetness to fragrance, sweetness to savour, and delight to love. Therefore let the fragrance be sweet, the taste sweet, and the love delightful.

Thus you have from this leader counsel in danger, help in battle, and comfort in pilgrimage. You have the Lord; you have the leader. It follows that he appear in fire through the bush.

[Col. 0043A] The roughness of the bush is the mortal flesh, full of pains, which he assumed from the Virgin. The fire signifies the love which he had for us when he came into the world. The bush seemed to burn and was not consumed [Note: [Col. 0043] Exod. 3], because his flesh, which died for love of us, seemed given over to decay, although it rose more glorious. Therefore fire is the love of God, which has six properties. It is dry, hot, light, mobile, subtle, and sharp: dry, to dry out the moist; hot, to inflame the cold; light, to lift up the heavy; mobile, to arouse the sluggish; subtle, to thin the gross; sharp, to pierce the hard.

The moist are so through carnal pleasure; the cold through fear; the heavy through worldly care; the sluggish through faintheartedness; the gross through dullness of the senses; the hard through obstinacy. It dries the moist [Col. 0043B] through abstinence, inflames the cold to repentance, lifts the heavy toward heavenly desires, arouses the sluggish to works of charity, thins the gross by understanding, and pierces the hard by loving wisdom.

It dries the moist, of whom it was said: “Let him who is in filth become still more filthy [Note: [Col. 0043] Rev. 22].” They cried: “I am fixed in the mud of the deep, and there is no firm ground [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 68].” But once dried, they say: “He brought me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 39].” It inflames the cold, who said: “I have become like a wineskin in frost [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 118].” But now, “my heart has been inflamed, and my inward parts have been changed; I became like a beast before you [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 72],” bearing the burden of penitence.

It lifts the heavy, to whom it was said: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 4]” He spread his wings, took them up, and bore them on his shoulders, so that they may say: “My soul desires you in the night; and my spirit in my inmost parts will watch for you in the morning [Note: [Col. 0043] Isa. 26].” It arouses the sluggish who heard: “Because of the cold, the sluggard would not plough; therefore he shall beg in summer, and nothing shall be given him [Note: [Col. 0043] Prov. 20].” But now, once aroused, they say: “Our hands are rounded and golden, full of hyacinths [Note: [Col. 0043] Song 5].” Rounded, because free from the scruple of vanity; golden because of works of charity; full of hyacinths because heavenly recompense is expected from this.

It thins the gross, who were “like horse and mule, which have no understanding [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 31],” who “did not know and did not understand [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 81].” Now it is promised them: “I will give you understanding and instruct you in the way [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 31].” Loving wisdom pierces those hardened by obstinacy. To them it was said [Col. 0043D] through the prophet: “We know that you are hard, and your brow is bronze [Note: [Col. 0043] Isa. 48].” But now they seek the things above and savour the things above [Note: [Col. 0043] Col. 3]. “For you gave them bread from heaven, O Lord, having every delight of flavour [Note: [Col. 0043] Wis. 16].”

Behold, you have the Lord, the leader, and the fire. But unless one proceeds rightly in all these things, nothing has been accomplished. Therefore there follows: “And you gave him the law on Sinai.”

The law is threefold: human law, Mosaic law, and evangelical law. The first was given for civil [Col. 0044A] concord, the second because of hardness of heart, and the third for the abundance of charity. The first deals with acquiring, retaining, and recovering possessions. In the second are certain harsh commandments, certain ceremonial ones, and certain moral ones. In the third one is taught to pardon the sinner, pray for persecutors, and love enemies.

But there is a moral law which teaches us to order the virtues, triumph over the devil, and commit to effect the good that is in the heart. These are the three things which were upon the wall of the Temple: cherubim, palms, and projecting varied carvings [Note: [Col. 0043] III Kings 6]. *Cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge,” so that we may know how to order our morals, having zeal for God according to knowledge [Note: [Col. 0043] Rom. 10], and may know “how to be hungry and to be filled, to abound and to endure need [Note: [Col. 0043] Phil. 4].”

Let us also know how to fly with two wings, namely hope and love, and how with two wings to veil our face against vainglory. The first is reverent modesty, by which, like Rebecca with a veil [Note: [Col. 0043] Gen. 24], we cover our face, not wishing to be seen. The second is contempt for popular favour received through the ear, so that, after the ear is cut off from Malchus by Peter with the sword of God’s word, we may thereafter deserve to be healed by Christ [Note: [Col. 0043] Luke 22], and may stop up our ear lest we hear the blood of vain glory. Behold the cherubim.

There are also palms, that is, triumph over the devil. In this we ought first to consider the fitting occasion for engaging; second, to resist manfully; third, to give thanks to God for victory. Thus Judith waited until she found Holofernes drunk and asleep; second, she cut off his head; third, she offered the canopy together with the head in the Temple with thanksgiving [Note: [Col. 0043] Judith 10–14]. Behold victory over the devil.

We must also commit to effect the good which we have within us. These are the projecting carvings: things inwardly present but outwardly manifested in work. For example, let kindness appear in countenance, mercy in deed, humility in dress, gentleness in living with others, and patience in tribulation. Kindness appears in countenance when a person is mild in speech, sweet in appearance, and modest in gesture. Mercy appears in deed when one has compassion on the wretched, helps the needy, and weeps with those weeping for sins. Humility appears in dress if there is poverty in clothing, lowliness in works, and submission in lowly matters. Gentleness appears in living with others if one gladly bears the burdens of the brethren, reconciles those in discord, and gives consolation [Col. 0044D] to the wearied. Patience appears in tribulation if one does not curse again the person who curses him, does not strike back one who strikes him, and gives his own goods to one who takes them. These are the projecting carvings.

Therefore, since the ancient Fathers did not seek the first law, and likewise abhorred the second because it was severe and “brought no one to perfection [Note: [Col. 0043] Heb. 7],” they sought not that the old law should now be given to them through Moses, but that he himself should come, in order to lead us out of the dark prison, redeeming us with an outstretched arm [Col. 0045A] upon the cross. Thus they might live truly under the Gospel, held fast in his embrace, and might cry with the Bride: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me [Note: [Col. 0045] Song 2].”

He loved us in three ways: sweetly, wisely, and strongly. It was sweet that he clothed himself in flesh for us; wise that he avoided fault; strong that he endured death. Thus he sought us in flesh, loved us in wisdom, redeemed us in power; in assuming flesh he condescended to me, in avoiding fault he took counsel for himself, and in accepting death he satisfied the Father. He is a sweet friend, a prudent counsellor, a strong helper. In the first he wills to save me; in the second he knows how to save me; in the third he is able to save me. “Go, and do likewise [Note: [Col. 0045] Luke 10].”

Love sweetly, wisely, and strongly: sweetly, lest, enticed; wisely, lest deceived; strongly, lest [Col. 0045B] oppressed, we be turned away from love of the Lord—lest the glory of the world or pleasure of the flesh draw you away. Let Christ, Wisdom, become sweet to you above these things, lest you be seduced by the spirit of error. Let Christ, Truth, shine upon you. Let Christ, the Power of God, strengthen you, lest adversity break you. Let charity inflame your zeal, knowledge form it, and constancy strengthen it. Let love be fervent, circumspect, and unconquered; let it have neither lukewarmness, nor lack discernment, nor become timid. Hence in the Gospel: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength [Note: [Col. 0045] Mark 12].” Therefore love with the whole affection of your heart; love with your soul, that is, with entire circumspection; love with all your strength, so that you need not fear even to die for his love.

Likewise, love on account of temporal, spiritual, [Col. 0045C] and eternal goods. On account of temporal goods, since “nothing is lacking to those who fear God,” nor to those who love him in truth. On account of spiritual goods, of which there are two kinds: reward and mercy. Hence: “You who love the Lord, hate evil; the Lord preserves the souls of his saints [Note: [Col. 0045] Ps. 96].” The second is grace. Hence David says: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength [Note: [Col. 0045] Ps. 17],” and so forth. Likewise, on account of eternal goods, because God has prepared invisible goods for those who love him, so that, loving him in all things and above all things, we may obtain his promises, which surpass every desire.

These are the six wings, the six seraphim: “Six wings,” he says, “to one and six to the other [Note: [Col. 0045] Isa. 6].” The six wings are the six works of mercy [Note: [Col. 0045] Matt. 25]: feeding and giving drink to the hungry, as Job says: [Col. 0045D] “If I ate my morsel alone and the orphan did not eat from it [Note: [Col. 0045] Job 31].” Clothing the naked; likewise: “If his sides have not blessed me, and if he was not warmed from the fleece of my sheep [Note: [Col. 0045] Ibid.].” Receiving the stranger; likewise: “The stranger did not remain outside, and my door stood open to the traveller [Note: [Col. 0045] Ibid.].” Consoling the sorrowful; likewise: “When I sat as a king surrounded by an army, I was a comforter of those who mourned [Note: [Col. 0045] Job 29].” Visiting the sick and imprisoned; likewise: “The blessing of the poor came upon me [Note: [Col. 0045] Ibid.].” Burying the dead: this was the virtue of Tobias [Note: [Col. 0045] Tobit 1, 2, etc.]. Behold the six wings.

[Col. 0046A] For all these reasons the Beloved is to be loved, because they are from him, as James says: “Every good giving,” he says, “and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow of variation [Note: [Col. 0045] Jas. 1].” For there is a good gift, a better gift, a best gift, and a perfect gift. The good gift is temporal goods by which we are sustained. The better gift is mercy, through which sins are forgiven. The best gift is grace, through which we ascend from virtue to virtue. The perfect gift is glory, which we shall enjoy forever.

Of the first, in the Gospel: “If you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children [Note: [Col. 0045] Matt. 7],” and so forth. Of the second: “For your mercy is better than lives [Note: [Col. 0045] Ps. 62].” Of the third: “It is best to strengthen the heart by grace [Note: [Col. 0045] Heb. 13].” Of the [Col. 0046B] fourth: “We shall all come to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ [Note: [Col. 0045] Eph. 4].”

The first is from below, because temporal things grow from the earth; and so too is the second, because mercy concerns sins which are from the world. The third and fourth are from above—that is, grace and glory—because the best gift and the perfect gift descend from the Father of lights [Note: [Col. 0045] Jas. 1]. Job had received these goods from the hand of the Lord. Hear of temporal goods: “He had five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred she-asses [Note: [Col. 0045] Job 1],” and so forth. Hear of the better good, that is, mercy: “You granted me life and mercy, and your visitation guarded my spirit [Note: [Col. 0045] Job 10].” Hear of the third, the best good, namely grace, by which he ascended from virtue to virtue in order to contemplate God: “By hearing of the ear,” he says, [Col. 0046C] “I heard you; but now my eye sees you. Therefore I reproach myself and do penance in ashes and dust [Note: [Col. 0045] Job 42].” Hear of the fourth, the perfect good which he awaited, namely the vision of God: “For I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and in my flesh I shall see God my Saviour [Note: [Col. 0045] Job 19].”

Opposed to these four goods are four evils, that is, four kinds of afflictions, which we ought to endure patiently: loss of possessions, affliction of the body, insults in speech, and forced labour. The Lord recalls these in the Gospel as follows. Of the first: “If anyone takes your tunic, give him your cloak as well [Note: [Col. 0045] Matt. 5].” Job endured this when he lost all [Col. 0046D] his substance [Note: [Col. 0045] Job 1]. “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also [Note: [Col. 0045] Luke 6].” This is said of the second. Job endured it when he was struck with a grievous ulcer [Note: [Col. 0045] Job 2]. Of the third: “Pray for those persecuting and slandering you [Note: [Col. 0045] Luke 6].” Likewise: “Bless, and do not curse [Note: [Col. 0045] Rom. 12].” Job endured this also. Hence he says: “You prepare words to reproach me; nevertheless carry out what you intend [Note: [Col. 0045] Job 6].” Of the fourth: “If anyone compels you to go one mile, go with him two miles [Note: [Col. 0045] Matt. 5].” David also endured this. For when Saul compelled him [Col. 0047A] to seek one hundred foreskins, he paid two hundred [Note: [Col. 0047] I Kings 18 and elsewhere].

God is called the Father of lights [Note: [Col. 0047] Jas. 1] because he made four lights. First he made the firmament; second, the lights, namely the sun and moon; afterwards it is said, “and the stars” [Note: [Col. 0047] Gen. 1]. These are assigned to the four gifts. The light of the stars is distinguished by varied rays. This is particular prudence, by which we know how to distinguish the use of one thing from that of another and do not sin through error. This is the light by which God enlightens every person coming into this world [Note: [Col. 0047] John 1], namely, the reason of discernment.

The moon, which shines at night, is divine inspiration, by which we recognize our sins. Hence David: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 12].” Likewise: “My God, enlighten my darkness [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 17].” The sun, which [Col. 0047B] shines by day, is spiritual understanding, by which we savour and contemplate heavenly things. Hence David: “Send forth your light and your truth; they themselves have led me [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 42].” The firmament, which shines more fully, is eternal brightness. Hence: “That city has no need of sun or moon to shine in it, because the brightness of God will illuminate it, and the Lamb will be its lamp [Note: [Col. 0047] Rev. 21].”

These things have been said according to four interpretations of this name, *lumen*, “light.” First, *lumen* is said to be *luens mene* [μὴν], “dispelling deficiency,” which is ignorance of things. Second, it is said to be “dispelling the night of the mind,” that is, the darkness of sins. Third, it is said to be the “light of the mind,” by which the mind is illuminated to know God. Thus when the blind man was asked, “What do you wish me to do for you?” he said: [Col. 0047C] “Lord, that I may see the light [Note: [Col. 0047] John 10].” And David says: “Send forth your light and your truth [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 42].” Fourth, *lumen* is said to be the “light of the world”: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God forever [Note: [Col. 0047] Matt. 5].”

For with him “there is no change nor shadow of variation [Note: [Col. 0047] Jas. 1].” This notes two things by which the knowledge of things is obscured among us: the change of substances and the succession of accidents. Change of substances is the reciprocal transformation of the elements: earth is made subtle into water, water into air, air into fire; and conversely, fire is condensed into air, air into water, water into earth. This change makes a thing less knowable. Likewise, there is succession of accidents, because a thing is now white, now black; now sitting, [Col. 0047D] now standing; and so forth. This succession obscures the knowledge of things. But there is none of this there; and therefore there will be full knowledge of Creator and creature. Likewise, I still have grounds for loving God.

There are four reasons why men are loved: power, wisdom, riches, and beauty. Hence Virgil, addressing one from whom he wished to be loved, speaks of riches:

> May new milk not fail me in summer nor in cold;

of power:

[Col. 0048A]

> A thousand of my waters wander on Sicilian mountains;

of wisdom:

> I sing the song which Dircaean Amphion was wont to sing  
> whenever he called his herds upon Attic Aracynthus;

of beauty:

> Nor am I so ugly: lately I saw myself upon the shore,  
> when the sea stood calm before the winds. . . . . .

For these four reasons God is to be loved. For he is wise in creation: “The Lord founded the earth by wisdom [Note: [Col. 0047] Prov. 3].” He is powerful in governance, because “God is able to raise up children of Abraham from stones [Note: [Col. 0047] Matt. 3].” And: “His power is an everlasting power which shall not be taken away [Note: [Col. 0047] Dan. 7].” He is rich, because “the Father has subjected all things beneath his feet: sheep and oxen, birds [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 8; Heb. 2].” According to his humanity: “Beautiful in form above [Col. 0048B] the sons of men [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 44].” According to his divinity: “He is the brightness of eternal light and a spotless mirror [Note: [Col. 0047] Wis. 7],” “into which angels desire to look [Note: [Col. 0047] I Pet. 1].”

Paul says of these: “Whom he appointed heir of all things [Note: [Col. 0047] Heb. 1]”—behold, riches; “through whom he also made the ages [Note: [Col. 0047] Ibid.]”—behold, wisdom; “who, being the brightness of glory and the figure of substance [Note: [Col. 0047] Ibid.]”—behold, beauty; “and bearing all things by the word of his power [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 118]”—behold, power. For these reasons he is to be loved.

Likewise, the love of maidens is one thing, that of young men another, and that of old men another. The maidens’ love is sweeter, young men’s stronger, old men’s more mature. In the first there is remission of sins; in the second, exercise of virtues; in the third, their perfection. The first is humble in the sinful Mary, fervent in Peter, [Col. 0048C] pious and sweet in John. The second sleeps as regards worldly things, keeps watch in spiritual things, and languishes because his soul has failed for the salvation of God [Note: [Col. 0047] Phil. 4]. The third hears ineffable words: silence, namely that peace “which surpasses all understanding [Note: [Col. 0047] Exod. 3].”

The first drives his sheep, that is, the affections of sensuality, into the inner part of the desert, seeing the bush which was not consumed [Note: [Col. 0047] Deut. 5], that is, the mystery of the Incarnation. The second ascends the mountain and hears from the Lord—that is, he is hidden in the secret place of his face: “But you, stand here with me, and I shall teach you the laws and commandments which you shall set before the children of Israel [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 30].” The third is buried by the Lord on the mountain—that is, hidden in the secret place of his face [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 41].

The first hears from men: “Where is your God?” The second remembers [Col. 0048D] and pours out his soul within himself [Note: [Col. 0047] Ibid.]. The third passes to the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God [Note: [Col. 0047] Ibid.]. The first serves faith, the second hope, the third charity. And as faith begets us for God, hope nourishes us, and charity brings us to perfection, so the first state dedicates to God in us the human affection; the second strips off the old man with his deeds; the third perfects and conforms us to God.

Because your breasts are better than wine.

[CARD.] In this sequence of words three clauses are gathered under this expression, by which three reasons are given [Col. 0049A] why the Blessed Virgin is greatly loved by the maidens. And these two expressions, “because” and “therefore,” correspond to one another. They may be words of the Son to his Mother. They may be words of angels to the Virgin, who, seeing the maidens standing beside the Virgin, say to her: “Therefore these maidens loved you exceedingly”—that is, very greatly—“because your breasts are better than wine, because your breasts are more fragrant than the finest ointments, because your name is oil poured out.”

The maidens are faithful souls, made new through grace rather than old through sin; not barren in old age, but fruitful in spiritual gifts; strong, not weak like old women; neither bent over nor “fixing their eyes downward upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 16],” but upright through heavenly desire and raised toward heaven. By reason of the service of their devotion, these souls always stand beside the Blessed Virgin, loving her and loving in her these supreme causes of love: namely, because her breasts are better than wine.

For the breasts of the Blessed Virgin have an effect more powerful and more abundant than wine. Wine can intoxicate a man, so that he forgets past offences and becomes ready to pardon and liberal in giving. But the Virgin’s breasts could, as it were, intoxicate God. For after he drank milk from his Mother’s breasts, as though, with the sweetness of milk, he had also drunk the sweetness of mercy, he cast our sins behind his back, out of his sight [Note: [Col. 0049] Isa. 38], and became liberal in granting forgiveness of sins, liberal in granting grace and [Col. 0049C] the righteousness of works.

Likewise the young maidens love the Blessed Virgin because her breasts are more fragrant than the finest ointments. For in her breasts breathes the fragrance of him who suckled at them. Anointed with the finest ointments, in the fullness of charisms and healing graces, he comes to the Bride—or to the sinful soul—that he may heal it of every leprosy and join it to himself in sacred marriage.

Likewise the Blessed Virgin is deservedly loved by the maidens because her name is oil poured out. For just as oil floats above liquid substances, so her name and the invocation of her name surpass all names of saints and invocations of names, exceeding them in the efficacy of help, in the obtaining of divine grace, and in the flight of demons.

[Col. 0049D] Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.

[THO.] Thus far the Synagogue, which in devoted faith awaited Christ’s coming. From that point, at the beginning of this song, she answered the prophets: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” that is, let him appear to me in person and bestow upon me examples for living and gifts. Then, in the following verses, she shows what kind of gifts his are, to be desired by the faithful. Here the voice of the Church is added: namely, of those who would come to faith after the time of the Incarnation. The former prayed that he might come; the latter, that he might draw her after himself, whom she already knows to have ascended, and draw her who would not ascend by herself.

[Col. 0050A] As if she said: “By myself I cannot do it; but may your good works, examples, manner of life, and all the other things which you wrought religiously and miraculously in the world draw me.” He who wishes to be drawn is compared to “a man seeking good pearls; having found one precious pearl, he went away, sold all that he had, and bought it” [Note: [Col. 0049] Matt. 13.]. This pearl is the kingdom of heaven which we await. Hence Solomon says: “Expectation is a most welcome jewel to one who waits; wherever he turns, he will understand prudently” [Note: [Col. 0049] Prov. 17.].

Now there is a welcome jewel, a more welcome jewel, and a most welcome jewel. The welcome jewel is the soul still laboring in this pilgrimage. More welcome is that which, now stripped of its body, is still in expectation. Most welcome it will be when, having received its body again, it fully enjoys the vision of God.

Concerning the welcome jewel:

[Col. 0050B] 7 A welcome jewel ought to possess purity, gentleness, and brightness. Purity lies in the correction of vices; gentleness in the ordering of conduct; brightness in the contemplation of God. There must be purity free from the contagion of carnal desire; gentleness without the scruple of murmuring, hatred, and envy; brightness without the scruple and cloud of worldly care.

Hear of purity: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0049] II Cor. 7.]. Hear of gentleness; the same says: “We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure; we are reviled, and we entreat” [Note: [Col. 0049] I Cor. 4.]. Hear of brightness; again: “With unveiled face we behold the glory of God, that we may be transformed into the same image from brightness to brightness” [Col. 0050C] [Note: [Col. 0049] II Cor. 3.].

The more welcome jewel has its purity: namely, the inability to sin, because “they are without blemish before the throne of God” [Note: [Col. 0049] Apoc. 14.]. Its gentleness is complete freedom from pain, because already “God has wiped every tear from the eyes of his saints; and there shall no longer be mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, since the former things have passed away” [Note: [Col. 0049] Apoc. 21.]. Its brightness is that light by which they rejoice to see the brightness of their homeland, because “light has arisen for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart” [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 96].

When the resurrection of the most welcome jewel has been celebrated, there will be purity in the body—incorruption in the body—when “this corruptible thing puts on incorruption” [Note: [Col. 0049] I Cor. 15]. In the soul there will be perfect concentration upon God, upon the Lord; for souls still have some regard for their bodies, so that they cannot attend perfectly to God until they receive them again.

[Col. 0050D] Hence the souls beneath God’s altar seem to murmur, saying: “How long will you not avenge, Lord, our blood upon those who are on the earth?” [Note: [Col. 0049] Apoc. 6.] There will then be gentleness, a tranquillity between body and soul, so that the flesh neither “desires against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0049] Gal. 5]. For the flesh will obey the spirit, nor will the spirit demand anything undue from the flesh. For “the bridegroom will rejoice over the bride” [Note: [Col. 0049] Isa. 62]. There will be brightness in the body, of which it is said: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” [Note: [Col. 0049] Matt. 13]. In the soul there will be the vision of God. Hence: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0049] Matt. 5].

Seeing and desiring these things, the bride says:

[Col. 0051A] “Draw me after you” [Note: [Col. 0051] Song 1.]: first, by mercifully drawing me out of the depth of sins; second, by steadfastly directing me in the way of uprightness; third, by pouring into the depths of my heart the affection of a most ardent and sweet love. These are the ointments in whose fragrance the bride promises that she will run, when she adds: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.”

The first ointment is mercy, the second grace, the third glory. The fragrance of the first is pardon; of the second, God’s generosity; of the third, God’s magnificence. Of the first: “Like chosen myrrh I gave forth sweetness of fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ecclus. 24]. Of the second: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” [Note: [Col. 0051] Gen. 27]. Of the third: “While the king was reclining, my nard gave forth its fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0051] Song 1].

The first draws back; the second draws; the third attracts.

[Col. 0051B] The first draws back from the depth of vices; the second by the cord of virtues; the third by the sweetness of rewards. In the fragrance of the first we walk; in the fragrance of the second we run; in the fragrance of the third we fly. This is the ineffable fragrance, the sweetness of divine delight. Hence Jacob: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” [Note: [Col. 0051] Gen. 27]. And John: “Your fragrance has stirred eternal longings within me.”

Concerning this Jacob said to his sons: “Take with you some of the best fruits of the land: a little resin, honey, storax, stacte, terebinth, and almonds” [Note: [Col. 0051] Gen. 43]. There are good fruits of the earth, better ones, and the best. Good are the fruits of repentance, in uprooting vices. Better are those of devout devotion, in exercising virtues. Best are those of divine contemplation, in the knowledge of

[Col. 0051C] heavenly things.

By resin, which is bitter, repentance is signified; by honey, divine consolation given to the penitent. Storax is a tree in Arabia, from whose twigs a tear flows; but if it falls to the ground, it is unclean, whereas that gathered from the branches is clean. The drops that fall to the ground signify those who shed tears in order to appear holy; but those which cling to the stalks signify tears shed by us solely from love of God. Hence David: “You have set my tears in your sight” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ps. 55].

Stacte is a twig with stout bark and purple leaves; it has the colour of pepper. The twig is the restraint of discipline, by which we chastise unlawful impulses. The strength of its bark is patience, by which we endure courageously. Purple is the dignity

[Col. 0051D] of the kingdom toward which we strive. The heat of pepper is the fervor by which we are always kindled, lest we grow lukewarm. For there are three things that make a holy person perfect: discipline, dignity, and charity. Discipline is for the suppression of vices; dignity for the freedom of virtues; charity for the affection of inward advancement.

The terebinth produces resin surpassing all others. This signifies tears of higher compunction. Hence David: “I poured out my soul within me, because I shall pass to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ps. 41].

Almonds blossom earlier than the rest,

[Col. 0052A] and milk is pressed from them. This is the figure of charity, from which we ought to begin and by which we ought to nourish even little strangers. Or otherwise: almonds are a healing fruit; the pressed milk is nourishing food. In their blossom is the security of expectation; in the pleasantness of the blossom, eternal delight. Therefore charity is health for the sick, nourishment for little ones, expectation for the righteous, and joy for the blessed.

Of the first: “He has seized us, and he will heal us” [Note: [Col. 0051] Hos. 6]. “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” [Note: [Col. 0051] Jer. 17]. Of the second: “Like newborn infants, desire rational milk without deceit” [Note: [Col. 0051] I Pet. 2]. Again: “A man will feed a young cow and two sheep, and from the abundance of milk he will press butter” [Note: [Col. 0051] Isa. 7]. Of the third: “I waited expectantly for the Lord, and he inclined to me” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ps. 39]. Again: “Wait for me on

[Col. 0052B] the day of my resurrection to come” [Note: [Col. 0051] Zeph. 3]. Of the fourth: “With unveiled face we behold the glory of God, that we may be transformed into the same image from brightness to brightness” [Note: [Col. 0051] II Cor. 3].

This is called working charity, because “God works this in us because of the exceeding charity by which he loved us” [Note: [Col. 0051] Eph. 2]. These are God’s gifts, and therefore we say: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” Or thus: in the renown of your name, which is compared to ointment; or in faith in eternal goods; or in consideration of your miracles.

“We shall run,” she says, “in the fragrance of your ointments.” Some walk after this fragrance, some run, and some fly. Those walk who are still hindered by many temptations; those run who are delayed by the care of dependents and temporal matters; those fly who have cast off every worldly care.

Thus Ezekiel’s living creatures are read to have walked: “Each of them walked before its face,” or “before its own face.” They ran: “Where,” he says, “the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ezek. 1]. For to go in the impulse of the spirit is to run; and they flew: “Their faces,” he says, “and their wings were stretched upward” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ibid.], and they flew with two wings.

[Col. 0052C] Isaiah says: You who are burdened with temptations [Note: [Col. 0051] Isa. 24], “walk while you have the light” [Note: [Col. 0051] John 12]. “But see how cautiously you walk” [Note: [Col. 0051] Eph. 5], like the living creatures. For each walked before its own face, advancing from virtue to virtue, not returning behind it to sins. “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ps. 118]. “For one who walks with God walks confidently” [Note: [Col. 0051] Prov. 10].

Of running it is said: “Those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives the prize. Run in such a way that you may obtain it. I,” says the Apostle, “so run, not as though toward an uncertainty” [Note: [Col. 0051] I Cor. 9]. “Let us therefore run toward the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” [Note: [Col. 0051] Heb. 12], so that at the end we may say: “I have fought the good fight; I have completed the course” [Note: [Col. 0051] II Tim. 4].

Again: Fly, you who have cast off worldly care, namely with the wings of love and desire. Of these the philosopher says: “For there are wings

[Col. 0053A] swift to me, which may climb the heights of heaven”; so that it may be said: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” [Note: [Col. 0053] Isa. 60]. Again: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and be at rest?” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 54], away from temporal misery.

As John says in the Apocalypse: “I heard,” he says, “the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven and saying: Woe, woe, woe to those dwelling on the earth” [Note: [Col. 0053] Apoc. 8]. The first woe is for guilt, the second for worldly tribulation, the third for eternal punishment.

Jesus, walking beside the Sea of Galilee: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 18]; “he mounted the cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 17]. Let us therefore walk, because Christ walks with us, that “we may walk in newness of life” [Note: [Col. 0053] Rom. 6]. Let us run, because he

[Col. 0053B] runs with us, that we may run without stumbling toward his promises. Let us fly, because he flies with us toward the joys above, so that amid worldly changes our hearts may be fixed where true joys are.

The bride also has ointments of her own. The first is modest love, the second strong love, the third sweet love. The first arises from contrition of heart, confession by the mouth, and the pouring forth of tears. Of the first: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 50]. Of the second: “Confess your sins to one another” [Note: [Col. 0053] Jas. 5]. Of the third: “May your eyes bring down waters, and your eyelids a fountain of tears” [Note: [Col. 0053] Jer. 9].

Strong love likewise consists of three things: it scorns fear, seeks pain, and does not flee shame. It scorns fear,

[Col. 0053C] because “the Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 26]. And: “Deliver me, Lord, and set me beside you, and let the hand of anyone whatsoever fight against me” [Note: [Col. 0053] Job 17]. It seeks pain: “Let rottenness enter into my bones and bubble beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0053] Hab. 3]. And Job: “Who will grant that my petition may come, and that God may give me even what I ask? May he who began himself crush me, release his hand, and cut me off” [Note: [Col. 0053] Job 6]. It does not flee shame: “All day my shame is ever before me, and confusion of face has covered me” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 43].

Sweet love has three forms: contempt for temporal things, as Paul says: “The things that were gain to me became losses for Christ, for whose sake I have counted all things as loss and have considered them as dung, that

[Col. 0053D] I may gain Christ” [Note: [Col. 0053] Phil. 3]. It also has particular and spiritual desire: “Before you is all my desire and my groaning” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 37]. And: “My soul shall desire you in the night; and with my spirit in my inward parts I shall watch for you in the morning” [Note: [Col. 0053] Isa. 26]. It also has heavenly joy: “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0053] Isa. 61]; and: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep festival, all you who love her; rejoice with great joy” [Note: [Col. 0053] Office of the Church, Fourth Sunday in Lent, Introit].

The first is produced in the water-cellar, the second in the wine-cellar, the third in the spice-cellar. For in the first

[Col. 0054A] sins are washed away; in the second the lukewarm are kindled; in the third those made sweet are fragranced with heavenly spices. In the first it is said: “Wash yourselves; be clean” [Note: [Col. 0053] Isa. 1]. Hence Peter: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and head” [Note: [Col. 0053] John 13], that is, not only my affections, but also my works and senses, which are active in the head.

Of the second: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” [Note: [Col. 0053] Luke 12]. Of the third John the Evangelist says: “Your fragrance has stirred eternal longings within me.”

The first was prepared by Mary of James, whose name means “supplanting,” because sins are washed away by it; the second by Mary Magdalene, whose name means “tower of strength,” because the weak are strengthened by it; the third by Mary Salome, whose name means “peaceful,” because by it heavenly sweetness is conferred upon the peaceful. Perhaps Mary Magdalene took part in preparing these three.

[Col. 0054B] She took part in the first when she lay modestly at the Lord’s feet [Note: [Col. 0053] John 19]; in the second, when with such persistence she sought the buried Lord [Note: [Col. 0053] John 20]; in the third, when, finding him in the form of a gardener, she said: “Rabboni”—which means “Teacher” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ibid.].

Behold the joy which she announced to the world, announced to the Church, and announced to the company of the apostles. To the world, while, as herald of the risen one, she filled the world with joy. To the Church:

> That empress of the world,  
> that blessed sinner,  
> poured forth the beginnings  
> of joy into the Church.

To the company of the apostles:

> Christ bore to the brethren,  
> made sorrowful by his death,  
> the joys they had awaited.

[Col. 0054C] The first cellar is called the water-cellar because it has tears of contrition; the second, tears of compassion; the third, tears of devotion. The first wash the sinner, the second give drink to the wretched, the third water the devout. In their figure Christ wept three times, as is read: first at the tomb of Lazarus [Note: [Col. 0053] John 11]—behold, tears of contrition; second, “Seeing the city, he wept over it” [Note: [Col. 0053] Luke 19]—behold, tears of compassion; third, when, with the Passion approaching, he went alone up the mountain to pray [Note: [Col. 0053] Mark 6]. “And his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the earth” [Note: [Col. 0053] Luke 22]. There he wept out of devotion for the future resurrection, as Paschasius says on that passage of Jeremiah’s lamentation: “Streams of waters ran down from my eyes in contrition for my people”

[Col. 0054D] [Note: [Col. 0053] Lam. 3].

“Draw me after you,” etc.

[CARD.] This saying pertains to the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin. The Blessed Virgin directs her speech to the Son, saying: “Draw me after you,” as if she said: “You, assumed to the Father’s right hand, assume your mother into glory.” And she rightly says, “Draw me after you,” so that in the word “draw” she signifies that grace, as if by force, sets free will aright. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things”

[Col. 0055A] [Note: [Col. 0055] Wis. 9].

But the young women, hearing of their lady’s Assumption, reply: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” [Note: [Col. 0055] Song 1]. “We shall run,” swift 8 with longing to follow; “we shall run,” strong in faith; we shall run as light and agile persons, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Casting aside every weight and the sin which surrounds us, let us run with patience toward the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame” [Note: [Col. 0055] Heb. 12].

“We shall run,” I say, “in the fragrance of your ointments.” The ointments of the Blessed Virgin are preparations of spiritual charisms, placed among the very richnesses of virtues, which enrich her as though by their own

[Col. 0055B] substance; by their fragrant sweetness and delight of scent they delight us and invite us to run in good works.

When, however, the Blessed Virgin had been assumed into the ethereal bridal chamber and had attained what she requested, she adds:

“**The king has brought me into his cellars.**”

[THO.] The cellars of the eternal king are the inward joys of the heavenly homeland. Into them the holy Church has now been introduced by faith, and into them it will in the future be introduced more fully in reality. The bride speaks to the young women, that is, the Church of Christ to faithful souls, namely her members newly reborn in Christ: “Therefore I pray Christ the bridegroom that he himself may help us, who run after him, giving us his hand lest we fail, because I have already tasted beforehand the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom; I have already tasted that the Lord is sweet” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 99]. “I have already learned, through his revelation, the good things

[Col. 0055C] prepared for me in heaven.”

She had said that one must run, and in what one must run. Behold where one must run: namely, into the wine-cellar, into which she has already been introduced. There human beings are refreshed by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 4]. They are refreshed by the grain of instructive doctrine; they are made drunk by the wine of particular and spiritual fervor; they are anointed with the oil of sweet devotion. The first is for oneself, the second for God, the third for one’s neighbor. The first is for oneself, “that bread may strengthen the human heart” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 103]; the second for God, “that wine may gladden the human heart” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ibid.], that is, that fervor may make one glad in God; the third for one’s neighbor, that one may outwardly “make the face cheerful with oil” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ibid.].

Of the first it is said: “Strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 67]. Of the second: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again

[Col. 0055D] I say, rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0055] Phil. 4]. Of the third Paul says: “God loves a cheerful giver” [Note: [Col. 0055] II Cor. 9].

In this work we see that the bride wishes to be with the bridegroom: namely, in the garden, in the cellar, and in the chamber. Therefore let the simple history be the garden, the moral sense the cellar, and the secret of contemplation the chamber. In the history are three things: the creation of heaven and earth, reconciliation, and restoration. Creation is like gardening or planting; reconciliation, like the sprouting of things sown or planted. For in its season, when the heavens dropped dew from above and the clouds rained

[Col. 0056A] the Righteous One, the earth opened and brought forth the Savior [Note: [Col. 0055] Isa. 45], through whom the reconciliation of heaven and earth was accomplished. Restoration will come at the end of the age.

In the cellar are three rooms: the first, of discipline; the second, of nature; the third, of grace. In the first you learn to be lower; in the second, equal; in the third, higher—that is, under another, with another, above another; or thus: to be subject, to exist together, to preside. First you learn to be a disciple, second a companion, third a master.

The king’s chamber is the hidden place of contemplation. But there is not only one chamber, because there are many queens and concubines. One woman obtained a place at the Lord’s feet [Note: [Col. 0055] Luke 7]. Another found devotion at his head [Note: [Col. 0055] Matt. 26]. Thomas at his side [Note: [Col. 0055] John 20], John on his breast [Note: [Col. 0055] John 21], Peter in the Father’s bosom [Note: [Col. 0055] Matt. 16], and Paul in the third heaven [Note: [Col. 0055] II Cor. 12] attained the grace of this secret. The first

[Col. 0056B] woman attained it in the depth of humility; the second in the firmness of hope; Thomas in the firmness of faith; John in the breadth of charity; Peter in the light of truth; Paul in the depth of Wisdom.

There is a place with the bridegroom from which he determines his laws and orders his counsels “in weight and number and measure” [Note: [Col. 0055] Wis. 11]. And there is a place in which the judge’s punitive attention is directed against the reprobate soul: “Terrible in counsels above the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 65]. Yet in neither the first nor the second is there perfect repose for the contemplative. In the first God appears as though concerned; in the second, as though troubled. The one is the aid of the teacher; the other, the tribunal of the judge. But there is a third place where the bridegroom is seen at rest—not as teacher, not as judge, but as bridegroom. O place of true repose, in which God is seen neither as troubled by anger nor as preoccupied

[Col. 0056C] by care, but his will is seen in it to be “good, pleasing, and perfect” [Note: [Col. 0055] Rom. 12].

Behold three times, three merits, and three rewards: times in the garden, merits in the cellar, and rewards in the threefold contemplation of the chamber.
