These cellars have three rooms: the first is that of Scripture, the second of the soul, the third of the heavenly homeland. In the first is received water of refreshment; in the second, wine of joy; in the third, oil of sweetness.

The water of the first is threefold. The first is secular prudence, the second literal knowledge, the third heavenly wisdom. The first comes from a muddy pool; the second from a flowing stream; the third from a most pure spring. The first comes from a muddy pool because it concerns temporal matters, which disturb the soul; the second from a flowing stream,

[Col. 0056D] because it concerns philosophical eloquence and opinion, which ought swiftly, like a stream, to pass from our memory; the third comes from a most pure spring because it concerns heavenly things, which ought to water our soul.

These are the three wells which Isaac’s servants dug [Note: [Col. 0055] Gen. 26]. They called the first “Accusations,” the second “Enmities,” and the third “Abundance,” or “Sevenfold,” because the Philistines—that is, demons loving what belongs to another—accuse us over temporal things. But in literal knowledge they are hostile to us unless we turn it back toward theological understanding. For in the sevenfold Spirit we possess an abundance of grace.

[Col. 0057A] The first is the corrupted water in Jericho [Note: [Col. 0057] IV Kings 2]; the second is the bitter water of Marah in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0057] Exod. 15]; the third is the water which Moses brought out from the rock [Note: [Col. 0057] Exod. 17]. The first is Jericho’s water—Jericho being understood as the world—that is, secular prudence, which is corrupt if anything other than the glory of God is sought from it. But Elisha, that is, “God my Lord,” places salt, that is, the savor of God, in a new vessel, that is, a newly converted heart; he blesses it, puts it into the water, and thus Elisha says: “Behold, I have healed these waters, and there shall no longer be death or corruption in them” [Note: [Col. 0057] IV Kings 2]. Thus secular prudence serves God and so ceases to be corrupt.

Marah, that is, literal knowledge, is bitter to the religious soul unless wood is put into it—that is, unless Christ’s cross is preached in it—as Paul says: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified”

[Col. 0057B] [Note: [Col. 0057] I Cor. 2].

The third is water from the rock, which Moses struck with a rod [Note: [Col. 0057] Exod. 15]: “And the rock was Christ” [Note: [Col. 0057] I Cor. 10], who, struck on the cross, brought water from his side [Note: [Col. 0057] John 19] and sent the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0057] Acts 2]. This is “the rushing of the river which makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0057] Ps. 45], the fountain of gardens.

In the cellar there is a threefold wine. The first is thanksgiving to God for one’s first conversion. Hence: “You have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine into which you were delivered” [Note: [Col. 0057] Rom. 6]. The second is the glory of conscience. Hence the same Apostle: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0057] II Cor. 1]. The third is joy from the infusion of grace. Hence again: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0057] Rom. 5].

In the cellar of the heavenly homeland

[Col. 0057C] there are four sweetnesses of oil: the glorification of bodies, association with angels, sitting at the Father’s right hand, and the vision of God. This is the Apostle’s surpassing greatness: “May God,” he says, “give you the enlightened eyes of your heart, that you may know what is the surpassing greatness of his power” [Note: [Col. 0057] Eph. 1]. The abiding greatness is the glorification of bodies; the eminent greatness is association with angels; the pre-eminent greatness is sitting at the Father’s right hand; the surpassing greatness is seeing God face to face.

Whoever wishes to see God face to face must be near him, turn toward him, and allow no obstacle to intervene. Therefore, that we may contemplate him, let us be near through the pursuit of righteousness; let us remove every obstacle of sin from ourselves through the guarding of innocence.

[Col. 0057D] We turn toward him by the devout affection of tireless diligence. Thus Jacob saw the angels [Note: [Col. 0057] Gen. 28], but first he supplanted vices. And how? Let us see. First he killed the kids; second, he skinned them; third, he cooked them [Note: [Col. 0057] Gen. 27]. These two kids are our body and soul. They must be killed, because the soul must be killed to the life of perverse will, and the flesh must be mortified by the exercise of perverse or wicked action. They must also be skinned, because the soul must be separated from the inclination of a left-handed intention, and the flesh stripped of delight in unlawful pleasure. They must also be cooked, so that,

[Col. 0058A] tested by the fervor of charity, they may offer a refreshment pleasing to God. Spiritual wine of joy must also be offered, because “God loves a cheerful giver” [Note: [Col. 0057] II Cor. 9].

Therefore through these things the soul merits the Father’s blessing: “May God give you of the fatness of the earth,” that is, lower compunction, “and abundance of the dew of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0057] Gen. 27], that is, higher compunction. Accordingly, the faithful soul, observing such consolations from God, adds:

“**The king has brought me into his cellars.**”

[CARD.] Into the heavenly cellars, that he may refresh me with his choicest goods. But the angels, who stand before the Son, seeing her exalted above the angelic choirs into the heavenly realms and rejoicing at her exaltation, add:

[Col. 0058B] “We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts above wine.”

[THO.] As if it said: “We ourselves do not at all exalt ourselves over the gifts received; rather, in everything wherein we live well, we shall always exult and rejoice in your mercy, remembering in every respect with how great a loving-kindness you have deigned to refresh us, and how you have mitigated the severity of the Law by the grace of evangelical faith: true consolations.”

Hear what Jacob did when his brother came to meet him with four hundred men, that is, with the principal vices: fear, greed, joy, and sorrow. Hence the poet:

> They fear, desire, rejoice, and suffer pain;  
> nor do they look upon the air,  
> shut up in darkness and a blind prison.  
> [Note: [Col. 0057] Virgil.]

[Col. 0058C] First the maidservants with their sons, second Leah with her children, third Rachel and Joseph, are set before him [Note: [Col. 0057] Gen. 33]. By Leah’s maidservant is signified fear of wicked action; by Rachel’s maidservant, fear of error; by their sons, the good things that proceed from them; by Leah, the active life; by her sons, the virtues proceeding from it; by Rachel, the contemplative life; by Joseph, whose name means “increase,” the progress of desire.

Therefore it says: “We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts above wine.” A person is drawn in two ways: by fear and by consolation. Fear is signified in wine; the soothing comfort of consolation in breasts. Therefore we shall rejoice more on account of consolation than fear. Hence the prophet:

[Col. 0058D] “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep festival, all you who love her; rejoice with great joy” [Note: [Col. 0057] Introit of the Mass, Fourth Sunday in Lent].

First, we should rejoice over the removal of calamity. Second, we keep festival in the acquisition of some solemnity or dignity. Third, we rejoice with great joy on account of possessing blessedness. The people of Israel rejoiced when it crossed the sea; it kept festival when it received the Law and erected the tabernacle for God; it rejoiced with great joy when it received the promised land as an inheritance.

First it is given milk to drink; second, it is satisfied from the breasts of her consolation [Note: [Col. 0057] Isa. 66];

[Col. 0059A] third, it feasts from entry into her glory.

There are many kinds of consolation. There is consolation in deliverance from danger. Hence David: “Perform for me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see it and be ashamed, because you, Lord, have helped me and consoled me” [Note: [Col. 0059] Ps. 85]. There is also consolation in attaining what one desires. Hence the Lord: “As a mother comforts her children, so I also shall comfort you, and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted” [Note: [Col. 0059] Isa. 66]. There is also consolation in meditation on the divine word. Hence Paul: “Whatever things have been written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope” [Note: [Col. 0059] Rom. 15]. There is a comforter in receiving the Holy Spirit. Hence the Lord: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come. But if I am assumed, I shall send

[Col. 0059B] him.” For *Paraclete* means “comforter” [Note: [Col. 0059] John 16].

There are those who mock God, those who leap for themselves, those who leap back to God, and those who exult in God. The first are the ungodly; the second, the tempted; the third, the consoled; the fourth, the devout. The first do so by commanding Christ’s humiliation and passion; the second by leaping over the difficulties of temptations; the third by returning thanks to God for their consolation; the fourth by expressing outwardly, not only in voice but also in bodily gesture, the eternal joy of divine love.

Those who mock are so called in contrast to those who leap. Those who leap, simply speaking, are those who frequently spring. Those who leap back (*resultantes*) are those who spring back with respect to their voice: that is, who return to God, by thanksgiving, benefits received from him. Those who exult (*exsultantes*) are those who leap outwardly:

[Col. 0059C] namely, from the joy of the heart into bodily gesture.

They mocked God, crying: “Hail, King of the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0059] Matt. 27]. The prophet taught them to leap for themselves, saying: “Go out from Babylon and flee from the Chaldeans” [Note: [Col. 0059] Isa. 48]. Christ himself leapt back when he said: “I give thanks 9 to you, Father, because you always hear me” [Note: [Col. 0059] John 11]. David taught exultation when he said: “All nations, clap your hands” [Note: [Col. 0059] Ps. 46].

Paul showed all these in himself. First he says: “I was a blasphemer and persecutor, because I persecuted the Church of God” [Note: [Col. 0059] I Tim. 1]—behold, mockery. “Immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood” [Note: [Col. 0059] Gal. 1]—behold, leaping. “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0059] I Cor. 15]—behold, leaping back. “I desire men in every place to pray, lifting up pure hands” [Note: [Col. 0059] I Tim. 2]—behold, by the hands, mockery.

They mock God through blindness, through the weakness of life,

[Col. 0059D] and by diminishing his power: through blindness, when they think that God does not know their sins; through weakness of life, when they believe that he endured death because of his own offense; by diminishing his power, because they do not believe that he will come to judge sins.

Of the first they said: “The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand” [Note: [Col. 0059] Ps. 93]. Of the second: “The fool said in his heart: There is no God” [Note: [Col. 0059] Ps. 13]. Again, the Jews said to Pilate: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you” [Note: [Col. 0059] John 18]. Of the third, through the prophet:

[Col. 0060A] “He will do nothing, either good or evil.”

This mockery was prefigured by the mockery inflicted upon Samson by the Philistines. First they blinded him; second, they assigned him to the mill; third, they made him perform before them [Note: [Col. 0059] Judg. 16]. That blinding signifies the blindness by which they think that God is ignorant of their sins. Assignment to the mill, however, signifies the Passion imposed upon Christ by them because of sin and punishment, although he was free from guilt.

We, however, like a grain of wheat, are ground between two millstones, namely guilt and punishment. They make Samson play when they mock his future judgment; but these things also apply morally to the spirit. Samson is the human spirit; the Philistines are demons. They first blind it by taking away the spirit of understanding. [Col. 0060B] They make it grind when they make it labor by committing sin. They make it play before them when they make it wander freely through every unlawful thing. Of the first: “How the Lord in His wrath has covered the virgin daughter of Zion with darkness [Note: [Col. 0059] Lam. 2.]!” Of the second: “All her persecutors seized her amid straits [Note: [Col. 0059] Lam. 1.].” Of the third: “Jerusalem has grievously sinned; therefore she has become unstable [Note: [Col. 0059] Ibid.].” Those who leap over the pit of diabolical deception dance for them: the pit of despair, the pit of error. Of the first: “Foxes have dens, and birds of heaven nests [Note: [Col. 0059] Matt. 8.].” Of the second: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the hole which he made [Note: [Col. 0059] Ps. 7.].” The pit is the world. He opens it by digging who follows its pleasures, until, reaching the depth of evils, he despises [Note: [Col. 0059] Prov. 18.]. He falls into the [Col. 0060C] hole when, because of the greatness of his sins, he falls into despair. He made this hole when he sinned. Of the third it is said: “If a blind man leads a blind man, will not both fall into a pit [Note: [Col. 0059] Matt. 15.]?” Of those leaping over these pits Samuel says to Saul: “You will find two men near Rachel’s tomb, at the border of Benjamin, at midday, leaping over great pits [Note: [Col. 0059] 1 Sam. 10.].” These two men are spirit and body. The spirit is a man because it flourishes in virtues. The body is a man when it obeys the spirit in works of virtue. They leap over these three pits. They leap over the pit of diabolical deception near Rachel’s tomb. Rachel means “sheep” or “seeing the beginning.” Her tomb is in the heart, in which are sheep-like simplicity and the truth of sight for discerning motions. Against such deceptions the pit does not obstruct them. They leap over the pit [Col. 0060D] of despair who are at the borders of Benjamin. Benjamin means “son of the right hand,” that is, Christ, who sits at the Father’s right hand. His borders, according to His humanity, are beginning and end: the humility of His birth and the ending of His death.

Therefore, following humility and trusting that they are saved through His Passion, those who are at Benjamin’s borders leap over the pit of despair. Benjamin means “son of the right hand,” that is, Christ. They leap over the pit of error when they are at midday—that is, in clear day—[Col. 0061A] namely, when they possess the spirit of understanding that does not permit them to err. They resound to God, giving thanks. They give thanks to God for three things: for evils which, through God’s grace, they have been able to avoid; for goods which, with God as author, they are able to do; and for the heavenly goods which they await from His promise. For these things the children of Israel gave thanks to God after crossing the Red Sea, when they said: “Let us sing to the Lord, for He has been gloriously honored, when He cast horse and rider into the sea [Note: [Col. 0061] Exod. 15.].” Behold the first: “The Lord is my strength and my praise [Note: [Col. 0061] Ibid.].” Of the second: “You have been a leader in Your mercy to the people whom You redeemed, and You carried them in Your strength to Your holy dwelling [Note: [Col. 0061] Ibid.],” behold the third. Of the first David says: “You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet [Col. 0061B] from falling [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 55.],” behold the first. Of the second: “I will sing to the Lord, who grants good things to me [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 12.].” Of the third: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 114].” Again, of the first: “Bless the Lord, O my soul [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 102.].” Why? Because “He forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities, who redeems [Note: [Col. 0061] Ibid.],” etc.; this is of the first. Of the second: “Who crowns you with mercy and compassion, who satisfies your desire with good things [Note: [Col. 0061] Ibid.].” Of the third: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s [Note: [Col. 0061] Ibid.].” As a figure of these three, in Leviticus we find three kinds of animals sacrificed to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0061] Lev. 11.]: unclean animals, such as the goat, which is a lustful animal—and this for the first; clean animals, such as ox and sheep, in the figure of the second; turtle-dove and dove, which fly upward, [Col. 0061C] in the figure of the third. They exult in God, conceiving in their hearts joy from heavenly things. This exultation has three elements. For one who exults ought to have jubilation in the mouth, a psaltery in the heart, and a timbrel in the body: jubilation, namely, the voice by which he praises God; the psaltery, namely, spiritual joy in the heavenly things he desires; the timbrel, namely, a bodily gesture in which he expresses both. Thus David: “Raise a joyful shout to the God of Jacob; take up the psaltery and strike the timbrel [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 80.].”—“I shall sing psalms with the spirit; I shall sing psalms also with the mind [Note: [Col. 0061] 1 Cor. 14.],” says the Apostle of the first two. “Of the third: ‘Glorify and bear God in your body [Note: [Col. 0061] 1 Cor. 6.].’” David performed these three when he brought the ark of the Lord into Jerusalem. “He brought,” it says, “the ark amid jubilation [Note: [Col. 0061] 2 Sam. 6.],” which is of the first. [Col. 0061D] Of the second: “Lord,” he says, “I have joyfully offered all these things to You [Note: [Col. 0061] 1 Chron. 29.].” Of the third it is said that Michal, Saul’s daughter, saw David dancing before the ark of the Lord and despised him in her heart [Note: [Col. 0061] 2 Sam. 6.].

It should be noted that among those who exult, some exult to the Lord, some in the Lord, and some with the Lord: to the Lord, because they have been delivered from sins and tribulations; in the Lord, as the righteous; with the Lord, as the blessed. The first give thanks for their deliverance; the second praise God for His benefits; the third see God face to face. [Col. 0062A] The first say: “Exult in God, our helper [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 80.].” To the second it is said: “Exult, righteous ones, in the Lord; praise befits the upright [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 32.].” Of the third: “O how glorious is that kingdom in which all the saints rejoice with Christ [Note: [Col. 0061] Office of the Church]!” In the first there is some bitterness; in the second, much sweetness; in the third, complete happiness. Of the first: “The apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Christ’s name [Note: [Col. 0061] Acts 5.].” Of the second: “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God, because He has clothed me with garments of salvation [Note: [Col. 0061] Isa. 61.].” Of the third: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice upon their beds [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 149.].” These are mindful of the Bridegroom’s breasts, which are consolations; but they use them differently. Those who press upon them violently [Col. 0062B] draw out blood; those who dance suck milk; those who resound press out wine; those who rejoice receive fragrances: blood of wickedness, milk of teaching, wine of spiritual fervor, fragrances of heavenly sweetness—blood that kills the righteous man, milk that nourishes little ones, wine that warms the lukewarm, fragrances by which the soul may sleep and rest in peace, all together [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 4.]. Of the first it is said: “He who presses the breasts violently draws out blood.” Of the second: “That you may drink milk and suck at the breasts of her consolation [Note: [Col. 0061] Isa. 66.].” Of the third, this work continues: “And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine [Note: [Col. 0061] Song 7.].” Of the fourth it has already been said in this work: “Your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments.” The first are mindful of these breasts against wine, [Col. 0062C] the second beneath wine, the third on account of wine, the fourth above wine.

We shall exult and rejoice.

[CARD.] We shall exult, as though expressing our joy by a certain gesture, and we shall rejoice in You in mind. But because the angels had previously said to the Blessed Virgin, “Therefore the young maidens loved You exceedingly, because Your breasts are better than wine,” lest the feminine gender of the name “young maidens,” applied to holy souls, suggest some weakness, they repeat the same thought and call the same souls whom they had called young maidens “the upright”: as it were manly, not effeminate; upright, not bent crooked by corrupt old age. And they say:

[Col. 0062D] The upright love You.

[THO.] Therefore we shall exult not in ourselves but in You, mindful of Your gifts, because all whose hearts are not crooked but upright love You before all things and above all things; nor can those be upright who set anything before Your love. When he said above, “The young maidens loved You,” he meant by youth the uprightness of heart. Likewise, “The upright love You,” because no one but the upright can truly love God. Whoever has violated the uprightness of justice in deed, word, [Col. 0063A] or thought vainly believes that he loves God. This is uprightness of mind, not of body, although perhaps for this purpose man has eyes raised toward heaven. Those who seek earthly things are crooked; those who seek heavenly things are upright. “Seek the things above, not those which are upon earth [Note: [Col. 0063] Col. 3.].” Hence the poet [Note: [Col. 0063] Ovid]:

> While all other animals look downward toward the earth,  
> He gave man an uplifted countenance, and commanded him  
> To gaze upon heaven and raise his erect face toward the stars.

You are crooked if you seek your own glory, envy one who prospers, slander one who is absent, or repay one who harms you. This uprightness must be preserved in many ways. Let each person be upright in thought, will, action, and office. Let him be upright in thought, so that he rejects deceptive phantasms and delights himself only in the understanding of truth. Thus David: [Col. 0063B] “You have prepared directions; You have executed judgment and justice in Jacob [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 98.].” Direction, therefore, refers to reason; judgment, to understanding; justice, to choice. For reason loves, understanding judges, and will chooses. Therefore, the uprightness of thoughts consists in directing every motion of the heart according to the rule of reason and, by the judgment of truth, adhering to devout meditations. Secondly, it consists in inflexibly joining to the understanding the affections of a will pleasing to God. For, as blessed Augustine says, the spiritual man strives to preserve health in the body, truth alone in thought, and peace alone in action. There is also uprightness of office, when a person strives, in the office entrusted to him, to carry out what is useful and honorable. There is also uprightness when one extends uprightness of heart to uprightness of speech. [Col. 0063C] Hence Paul says: “That you may be sincere and children of God [Note: [Col. 0063] Phil. 2.],” that is, sincere with a pure heart and straightforward in speech. There is also uprightness when minds placed in prosperity praise divine clemency, and in adversity accuse their own sins. Thus David: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 72.]!” And above all this uprightness must be preserved: that every work undertaken be directed to heavenly things through a right intention.

Therefore the upright love God: those who seek divine things alone, love heavenly things alone, and desire to enjoy eternal goods alone. There must be uprightness in heart, work, and speech: in heart, by thinking good things, because “the Lord is near to those who are upright in heart [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 33.]”; [Col. 0063D] in work, by doing good things, because “their feet were straight feet [Note: [Col. 0063] Ezek. 1.],” etc.; in speech, by speaking good things. Hence: “Put a right and well-sounding word in my mouth [Note: [Col. 0063] Job 8.].” Of the first it is said of Job: “That man was simple and upright [Note: [Col. 0063] Job 1.].” Of the second, to the same man: “If you walk pure and upright, the Lord will immediately awaken for you [Note: [Col. 0063] Job 8.].” Of the third it is said to Job’s friends: “You have not spoken rightly before Me as My servant Job has [Note: [Col. 0063] Job 42.].” Again, there must be uprightness in weight, number, and measure [Note: [Col. 0063] Wis. 11.]: in the measure of works and words, lest they exceed due bounds or fall short; [Col. 0064A] in the number of affection—that is, in form—lest it remain formless and disordered; in the weight of love, that we may know how much each person ought to be valued. In the measure of works: that you give the greater person submission, the equal fellowship, the inferior protection; in the measure of words: confession to yourself, preaching to your neighbor, prayer for yourself and your neighbor, praise to God. In number, fear of God should restrain the motions of sensuality; intention should aspire to its due end; reason should arrange the manner of walking; and affection should proceed as reason has ordained. In the weight of love, we must see what is to be sought, what avoided, what preferred, and what postponed. Augustine says literally: in measure, namely, of greatness and smallness; in number, of multitude [Col. 0064B] and fewness; in weight, of lightness and heaviness. Again, God is measure without measure, number without number, weight without weight. Again, uprightness is nothing other than justice which produces peace. Hence it is said: “Justice and peace have kissed [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 84.],” that is, the justice of man and the peace of God; likewise, the justice of God and the peace of man. There is a threefold justice of man. The first is natural equity; the second, the fellowship of virtues under charity; the third, freedom from sin. The first excludes the unjust; the second makes one religious; the third makes one glorious. Christ taught the first when He said: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another [Note: [Col. 0063] Job 4; Matt. 7.].” He taught the second thus: “Unless your justice exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0063] Matt. 5.].” The third thus: “The righteous shall shine [Col. 0064C] like the sun in the kingdom of their Father [Note: [Col. 0063] Matt. 13.].” The first turns away from evil; the second does good; the third shall reap in joy. The first avoids guilt; the second runs by the straight way toward the homeland; the third shall receive the glory of blessing. Of the first David says: “I have done judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who slander me [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 118.].” Of the second: “The Lord led the righteous man by straight paths and showed him the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0063] Office of the Church].” Of the third: “All who love Your name shall glory in You, because You will bless the righteous [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 5.].”

Again, there are three peaces of God: the first from human perversity, the second from temptation, the third from the pain of corruption. David recalls them. Of the first: “For the sake of my brethren and companions, I spoke peace concerning you [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 121.].” [Col. 0064D] Of the second: “Let peace be in your strength and abundance in your towers [Note: [Col. 0063] Ibid.].” Of the third: “Pray for the things that make for Jerusalem’s peace, and for abundance for those who love you [Note: [Col. 0063] Ibid.].” Of the first Job says: “The beasts of the earth shall be at peace with you [Note: [Col. 0063] Job 5.].” Of the second, the same man says: “If you rise early to God and entreat the Almighty; if you walk pure and upright, He will immediately awaken for you and restore the dwelling of your justice in peace [Note: [Col. 0063] Job 8.].” Of the third David says: “In peace I shall sleep and rest together [Note: [Col. 0063] Ps. 4.].” The first peace and the first justice kiss one another. Hence: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and [Col. 0065A] the hills justice [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 71.].” The second peace and the second justice kiss one another. Hence: “In his days justice shall arise, and peace shall abound [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid.].” The third peace and the third justice kiss one another. Hence: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace, upon David’s throne and over his kingdom: namely, that He may establish and strengthen it in judgment and justice [Note: [Col. 0065] Isa. 9.].” Again, conversely, there is a threefold justice of God and a threefold peace of man, which kiss one another.

The first justice, therefore, is in the ordering of things; the second in the equity of judgments; the third in freedom from sin. The first: all things are ordered in weight, number, and measure [Note: [Col. 0065] Wis. 11.]; the second: “He will render to each according to his works [Note: [Col. 0065] Rom. 2.]”; the third is in the divine essence. Of the first it is said: “God, Creator of all [Col. 0065B] things, terrible and strong, just and merciful [Note: [Col. 0065] 2 Macc. 1.].” Of the second: “You are righteous, O Lord, and Your judgment is right [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 118.].” Of the third: “Your justice is justice forever [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid.].” The first has wisdom as its guide; the second has mercy as its companion; the third belongs to power. Wisdom is the Son; mercy is given by the Holy Spirit; power is the eternal Father. The first is governed through wisdom; the second is moderated through mercy; the third is possessed without defect through power. Of the first: “The Lord founded the earth by wisdom; He established the heavens by prudence [Note: [Col. 0065] Prov. 3.].” Of the second: “Light has arisen in darkness for the upright: merciful, compassionate, and just [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 111.].” Of the third: “His power is an eternal power which shall not be taken away, and His kingdom [Col. 0065C] shall not be destroyed [Note: [Col. 0065] Dan. 4.].”

From these depend three peaces, which kiss them: the peace of the world, the peace of the human race, and the peace of God. The first is in nature; the second comes from grace; the third will be in glory. The first prevents the collision of the elements; the second causes one to hate evil and love God and neighbor; in the third, God is undisturbed, so that evil and the scourge do not come near Him [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 90.]. The first peace and first justice kiss one another; the second peace and second justice; the third peace and third justice. The first peace arises from the proportioned creation of the world; the second from fear of judgment; the third because there can be no disturbance in God, where there is no stain of sin. To this end the upright rightly labor: that by the first they may have temporal tranquility here, by the second purity of heart, [Col. 0065D] and by the third that supreme blessedness. But the upright ascend to uprightness by a threefold step. First they correct, second they govern, third they direct. They correct iniquity, govern their own simplicity, and direct their steps toward that city of peace. They correct through satisfaction, govern through regular discipline, and direct through the clarity of inward contemplation. They correct through contrition, confession, and satisfaction. This is the perfection of uprightness. Of the first David says: “By what means does a young man correct his way? By keeping [Col. 0066A] Your words [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 118.],” by which You teach us the ways of satisfaction. Of the second the satirist says [Note: [Col. 0065] Horace]:

> Rule your mind; unless it obeys,  
> it commands. Restrain it with reins; subdue it with lashes.

Of the third: “The dawn from on high has visited us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace [Note: [Col. 0065] Luke 1.].” The first begin to love; the second grow in love; the third attain the highest degree of love.

The upright love You, mindful of Your breasts above wine.

[CARD.] As though he said: Therefore they love You, because they hold firmly fixed in their memory that Your breasts are better than wine, as has been explained above.

I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0066B] [THO.] After the holy Church has been brought into Christ’s wine-cellars—that is, through knowledge and hope of heavenly goods—after she has learned to love with an upright heart and to rejoice and exult in His grace alone, it remains to show what conflict she undergoes for that same love and for the acquisition of the goods which she has borne, and what affliction she endures: namely, what she says, “I am black, but beautiful.” Black under the adversity of oppressions, but beautiful through the beauty of virtues—indeed, so much more beautiful in God’s sight as she is harassed by the greater pressures of the foolish. By the daughters of Jerusalem, to whom she speaks these words, he means souls instructed in heavenly mysteries and longing for the heavenly habitation of their homeland. Because she had said, “The upright love You,” lest she seem perhaps not upright to the weaker persons—whom here he calls [Col. 0066C] daughters of Jerusalem—because of the tribulations she endures, she says: although I am black through tribulations, I am nevertheless inwardly beautiful through charity. I am black through pressures, beautiful through virtues; black through the pursuit of humility, but beautiful through heavenly desires; black in the eyes of the foolish, but beautiful to the understanding of the wise; black because of the memory of sins, but beautiful because of contemplation of heavenly things; black to those living perversely, by threatening eternal punishments; beautiful to those living holy lives, by promising eternal joys; black through the body’s lowliness and humility, beautiful through the soul’s holiness. I am black on earth, beautiful in heaven; black in suffering temporal evils, beautiful in hoping for everlasting goods. Hear the beautiful one: “Rejoicing in hope [Note: [Col. 0065] Rom. 12.].” Hear the black one: “Patient in tribulation [Col. 0066D] [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid.].” Paul was black when stoned [Note: [Col. 0065] 2 Cor. 11.], beautiful when caught up to the third heaven [Note: [Col. 0065] Ibid.]. Black, he said: “We have become like the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all things to this day [Note: [Col. 0065] 1 Cor. 4.].” Beautiful, he said: “With unveiled face we behold the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0065] 2 Cor. 3.].” Tribulation is the chief road to God or to the kingdom, because “all who wish to live godly lives in Christ Jesus suffer persecution [Note: [Col. 0065] 2 Tim. 3.].” Therefore, being set in this pilgrimage, she cries: “I am black, but beautiful.”

Three things afflict travelers: the difficulty [Col. 0067A] of roads, the ambushes of robbers, and the heaviness of burdens. There are four difficulties of roads: for they are muddy, stony, steep, and precipitous. They are muddy with the marshes of pleasures, stony with the rocks of scandals, steep with the prosperities of successes, precipitous with the failures of adversities. Of muddy roads it is said: “I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm footing [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 68.].” Of stony roads: “Lest at any time you strike your foot against a stone [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 90.].” Of precipitous and steep roads together: “They rise up to the heavens and go down to the depths [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 106.].” Therefore the way ought to be clean, straight, level, neither dark nor slippery. Let it be clean from carnal contamination, as in that saying: “My God, His way is undefiled [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 17.].” Let it be straight in intention; level, free from scandal, hatred, anger, envy, and detraction, so that “crooked things may become straight and rough places [Col. 0067B] level ways [Note: [Col. 0067] Luke 3.],” so that they may not be dark through error or slippery through levity and dissoluteness, so that there may not be “darkness and slipperiness in their way [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 34.].” Again, the ambushes of robbers on the road afflict travelers. For they set snares sometimes at the beginning of the way, sometimes in the middle, sometimes at the end. At the beginning: “The snares of death have anticipated me [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 17.].” In the middle: “In this way in which I was walking, they hid a snare for me [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 141.].” Of the snare at the end the saints say: “The snare is broken, and we have been delivered [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 123.].” Adam encountered the first [Note: [Col. 0067] Gen. 1]; the second, the ten men who were coming to worship in Jerusalem, whom Ishmael of royal blood killed in the middle of the way [Note: [Col. 0067] Jer. 41]; the last, Jonathan son of Saul, when at the end of his victory he ate a honeycomb [Note: [Col. 0067] 1 Sam. 14]. Of the first it is said: “They became [Col. 0067C] her enemies at the head [Note: [Col. 0067] Lam. 1.].” Of the second: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path [Note: [Col. 0067] Gen. 49].” Of the last: “The woman shall crush his head, and you shall lie in ambush for her heel [Note: [Col. 0067] Gen. 3.].” Again, the heaviness of burdens afflicts travelers. Some say there are five burdens; others eleven, as Isaiah does [Note: [Col. 0067] Isa. 13, 14, etc.]; others only three, which are called burdens of burdens. Of the five: the first is called the law. Hence: “This is a burden which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear [Note: [Col. 0067] Acts 15.].” The second is called the labor of works. Hence: “Come to Me, all you who labor and are burdened [Note: [Col. 0067] Matt. 11.].” The third is called temporal misery. Hence: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all [Note: [Col. 0067] Sir. 40.].” [Col. 0067D] The fourth is called sin. Thus Isaiah: “Release those who are broken free, and break every burden [Note: [Col. 0067] Isa. 58.].” The fifth is called God’s judgment, or that eternal misery. Hence: “Each shall bear his own burden [Note: [Col. 0067] Gal. 6.].” In Isaiah we read of eleven burdens [Note: [Col. 0067] Isa. 13, 14, etc.], namely: the burden of Babylon, the burden of the Philistines, the burden of Moab, the burden of Damascus, the burden of Egypt, the burden of the wilderness of the sea, the burden of Dumah, the burden in Arabia, the burden of the valley of vision, the burden of Tyre, and the burden of the beasts of the south. By their very number these signify the transgression of sin.

[Col. 0068A] Therefore, just as in divine speech one speaks simply of “Songs” and of “the Song of Songs,” so too there are burdens simply so called and burdens of burdens. Burdens simply so called are individual crimes or individual kinds of tribulation. Burdens of burdens, however, are the excessive immensity of sins or tribulations. There are, then, three burdens of burdens: vanity, iniquity, and calamity. Vanity of the world, iniquity of the soul, calamity of hell. Vanity blinds; iniquity casts down headlong; calamity torments. Vanity of the world takes away contemplation of heavenly things; iniquity of the soul takes away love of God and neighbor; the calamity of Tartarus takes away the inclination toward good and the soul’s devotion. Vanity of the world makes one vicious; iniquity of the soul makes one hateful; the calamity of hell makes one liable to punishment. Vanity makes one incestuous; iniquity makes one hostile; calamity makes one perpetually [Col. 0068B] sorrowful. Vanity presses down; iniquity bends and weighs down; calamity breaks. Of these burdens, one is carried on the head, another in the arms, another on the shoulders. The burden on the head is vanity in the mind; the burden in the arms, iniquity in action; the burden on the shoulders, the calamity of Gehenna. The first defiles affection; the second dishonors action; the third kills the subject. Of these three Hosea says: “You have plowed impiety, reaped iniquity, and eaten the fruit of lies [Note: [Col. 0067] Hos. 10.].” Impiety is plowed when someone, from devotion to the world, meditates upon vanity; he reaps iniquity when from thought he gathers a wicked deed; he eats the fruit of lies when, according to what he has done in the body, he receives his due in hell. Of vanity, some are subjects, others associates, others superiors. The first are carnal, the second [Col. 0068C] spiritual, the third intellectual. The first give their sense to curiosity; the second to human necessity; the third devote themselves to contemplated truth. In the first order, sense and thought are defiled; in the second, affection is adorned and action made honorable; in the third, understanding is elevated and reason is quickened. The first voluntarily subject themselves to the world; the second serve the world unwillingly; the third utterly despise the world. The first, therefore, are brutish; the second active; the third contemplative. We can say similar things about iniquity. For some love iniquity but do not preach it; some both love and preach it; others love it, preach it, and defend it. Iniquity, therefore, has three principal kinds: impiety, crime, and malice. Impiety concerns [Col. 0068D] God; crime, oneself; malice, one’s neighbor. The impious are so by despising commandments; the criminal by plunging themselves into vices; the malicious by corrupting their neighbors. The first order is those “whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame [Note: [Col. 0067] Phil. 3.].” The second order is those who “have proclaimed their sins like Sodom [Note: [Col. 0067] Isa. 3.].” The third is those who have become “like molten shields [Note: [Col. 0067] Job 41.].” The first are those who “cast their innermost parts upon the ground [Note: [Col. 0067] Ezek. 29].” The second are those who say: “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither, for this is our portion and this is our lot [Col. 0069A] [Note: [Col. 0069] Wis. 2.].” The third are those who say: “The way of the Lord is not just [Note: [Col. 0069] Ezek. 18.].” Thus they sin first against the Father, second against the Son, third against the Holy Spirit: against the Father by acting against His will; against the Son, against His humility; against the Holy Spirit, against His charity. The calamity of hell likewise has three kinds. The first is bitterness of conscience; the second hatred of justice; the third despair of pardon. The first are miserable because conscience gnaws at them; the second more miserable because justice displeases them; the third most miserable because no mercy of pardon looks upon them.

Although these are burdens of burdens, there are others which are only burdens. Above, we set out Isaiah’s eleven burdens, which express eleven kinds of vices and eleven kinds of worldly concerns; and let us discuss first the vices, [Col. 0069B] then the concerns. In the burden of Babylon pride is noted; in Moab indignation, and especially arrogance; in the Philistines the perverse curiosity of the senses individually; in Damascus, avarice expressly; in Egypt, altogether gluttony and drunkenness; in the wilderness of the sea, the presumption of singularity; in Idumea, superstition; in Arabia, feigned love; in the valley of vision, blindness of soul; in Tyre, boasting of riches and arrogance; in the beasts of the south, the dissolution of religious life is expressed. These are the kinds of vices. Now let the burdens of worldly concerns be set forth. The first of these is worldly power; the second, pagan learning; the third, dog-like eloquence; the fourth, nobility of blood; the fifth, beauty of body; the sixth, the virtue of a spouse; the seventh, the example of children; the eighth, the loyalty of friends; [Col. 0069C] the ninth, the humble obedience of subjects; the tenth, abundance of temporal goods; the eleventh, peaceful possession of all the aforesaid things. Vanity, therefore, is attached to worldly concerns; iniquity to vices; and the calamity of Gehenna to punishments. That vanity presses many down with its burden is attested by the Apostle: “Creation was made subject to vanity, not willingly [Note: [Col. 0069] Rom. 8.].” In the Psalm, concerning the burden of iniquity: “My iniquities have passed over my head and, like a heavy burden, have weighed me down [Note: [Col. 0069] Ps. 37.].” Of the burden of calamity the Savior says: “I have trodden the winepress alone [Note: [Col. 0069] Isa. 63.].” Of the first in Ecclesiastes [Note: [Col. 0069] ch. 1.]: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” Of the second in Zechariah: “Iniquity sits upon a talent of lead [Note: [Col. 0069] Zech. 5.].” Of the third in the Psalm: “Destruction and [Col. 0069D] unhappiness are in their ways [Note: [Col. 0069] Ps. 13.].”

There are also other burdens very unlike these. The first is that of administration, the second that of religious life, the third that of love. The first is borne by prelates; the second by those mortified to this world; the third by those perfected “in the cubit” (in cubito; the reading is uncertain). The first strengthen the Church’s estate; the second adorn her face; the third commend her very power. To the first it is said: “My daily pressing concern is the care of all the churches [Note: [Col. 0069] 2 Cor. 11.].” Of the second: “My soul has chosen hanging, and my bones death [Note: [Col. 0069] Job 7.].” Of the third: “Whether Paul, Cephas, or Apollos, all are yours [Note: [Col. 0069] 1 Cor. 3.].” The first order is those who bend beneath [Col. 0070A] God and bear the world; the second, those who mortify their flesh; the third, those who are wounded by love for their neighbor through each and every hardship.

Stewardship comprises within itself three burdens: first, the occupation with external matters; second, anxious concern for conduct; third, the endurance of hardships. By the first it serves the needs of subjects; by the second it provides for the purity of their morals; by the third it makes supplication, as expedient, amid adversity. The first is the business of the world; the second, watchfulness over oneself; the third, concern for one’s neighbour. It must be necessary in the first, honourable in the second, useful in the third: necessary, lest it seek superfluities without restraint; honourable, lest by living effeminately it corrupt the morals or minds of others; useful, insofar as it goes before its subjects toward pardon, grace, and glory. Thus it is necessary in life, honourable in reputation, useful in teaching.

Religion likewise consists in three things: namely, mortification of the flesh, devotion of the spirit, and compassion for one’s neighbour. Hence the Saviour, when giving instruction concerning prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, referred fasting to the mortification of the flesh, almsgiving to compassion for one’s neighbour, and prayer to the devotion of the spirit. The first is abstinence from evil; the second, the fragrance of good; the third, the joy of a purified mind.

The burdens of love, however, are three. For one thing is required of us by our neighbour, another by the angel, another by God. Our neighbour requires kindness from us; the angel, purity; God, perfect charity. Our neighbour requires the services of humanity; the angel, desires of sincerity; God, pursuits flowing with sweetness. [Col. 0070C] Our neighbour demands a devout act; God requires an utterly pure understanding.

Behold, concerning all the foregoing the bride had said, “I am black”; concerning these she says, “but beautiful.” For, as the bridegroom says in the same Song: “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely, terrible as an ordered army in battle-array” [Note: [Col. 0069] Song 6.]. Beautiful to the world, sweet in affection, lovely in understanding. Beautiful in the honour of her reputation, sweet in the usefulness of her teaching, lovely in the necessity of her lofty life. Beautiful in example, sweet in speech, lovely in counsel. Beautiful in works, sweet in character, lovely in the elevations of the mind. Beautiful to her neighbour, sweet to the angel, lovely to the bridegroom.

Again, it is said of her: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish in you” [Note: [Col. 0069] Song 4.]. And truly: because she is neither conquered by the enemy, nor corrupted by the world, [Col. 0070D] nor seduced by her neighbour, nor crushed by the flesh, nor puffed up in mind. Truly beautiful, whom neither action corrupts, nor affection infects, nor understanding obstructs: action by wickedness, affection by vanity, understanding by being cut off from the brightness of heavenly things.

Therefore there is no blemish in her, in whom the suggestion of the evil one does not prevail. The threats and promises of the world are foul to her; the flesh’s enticement lies powerless; the mind’s pride is choked. The burdens, then, are evidently fourfold. Some are of God, some of the soul, some of the world, some of hell. We subdivided these above; now let us consider others.

Some goods are for the soul’s health, some for its firmness, some for its beauty, others for its enlargement: justice for health, fortitude for firmness, prudence for beauty, temperance for enlargement. For there are four things that instruct, adorn, establish, and strengthen the soul: counsels, services, aids, and remedies. Counsels pertain to prudence; services to justice; aids to fortitude; remedies to temperance. Counsels enlighten the blind; services make people devout; aids strengthen the weak; remedies heal the sick. Counsels drive out ignorance; services, envy; aids, weakness; remedies, covetousness. They make teachers of wisdom, lovers of justice through services, defenders of truth through aids, lovers of blessedness through remedies.

Christ himself bestowed this upon [Col. 0071B] his Church: for he gave counsels of life, services of justice, aids of steadfastness, remedies of repentance—counsels by teaching men [Note: [Col. 0071] Mark 1.], services by feeding the crowds [Note: [Col. 0071] John 6.], aids by judging the causes of the widow and orphan [Note: [Col. 0071] Jer. 32.], remedies by going about “and healing all who were oppressed by the devil” [Note: [Col. 0071] Acts 10.].

Therefore he gave counsels on the mountain, services beside the sea, aids in the upper room, remedies on the cross. Through counsels the soul comes from natural ignorance, as from the eastern quarter. Through services it returns from the heat of concupiscence, as from the southern region. Through aids it is drawn back from the coldness of malice, as from the northern brightness. Through remedies it is led away from the setting of vices, as from the western quarter.

In her are commandments for health, [Col. 0071C] counsels for weakness, charisms for beauty, precepts for enlargement; obedience for health, steadfastness for firmness, patience for beauty, remedies of repentance for enlargement; apostles for health, martyrs for firmness, virgins for beauty, confessors for the fragrance of enlargement; charity for health, humility for firmness, continence for beauty, mercy for enlargement. Adorned with such things, she says, “I am black and beautiful,” in accordance with what is found in the Proverbs of Solomon.

There are three women: two pursue the foul pursuits of the flesh; the third reproves the wickedness of morals, explains the laws of honourableness, and promises peace and glory to those who obey them. The first is sweetness of the flesh; the second, worldly pomp; the third, spiritual wisdom. The sweetness of the flesh tempts by softness and conquers by the will. Worldly pomp tempts by glory and conquers by excellence; spiritual wisdom begins with austerity and draws by pleasantness. Each one “speaks out of the abundance of the heart” [Note: [Col. 0071] Matt. 12.]. The first speaks shameful things, the second harmful things, the third healing things.

The first, whom Solomon calls “talkative and wandering, unable to endure quiet, nor able to keep her feet at home; now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait by the corners” [Note: [Col. 0071] Prov. 7.], says: “I have woven my bed with cords; I have spread it with embroidered coverings from Egypt; I have sprinkled my couch with myrrh, [Col. 0072A] aloes, and cinnamon. The ways of hell are her house, penetrating to the lower regions of death” [Note: [Col. 0071] Ibid.].

The second, called the excellence of the world, is she who is said to be “foolish and clamorous, sitting at the door of her house upon a seat in the high place of the city” [Note: [Col. 0071] Prov. 9.]. She also says: “Whoever is simple, let him turn aside to me”; and she says to the foolish: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is pleasant” [Note: [Col. 0071] Ibid.]. But hear the end: “And he did not know that giants are there, and that her guests are in the depths of hell” [Note: [Col. 0071] Ibid.].

The third woman speaks against both and calls her hearers back from fellowship with either. Thus she says: “O men, I cry out to you; my voice is to the children of men. Blessed is the man who hears me, who watches daily at my doors and keeps watch at the posts of my entrance. Whoever finds me finds life and draws salvation from the Lord; but whoever sins against me injures his own soul” [Note: [Col. 0071] Prov. 8.].

Thus three persons are introduced, namely women; three persons are addressed; and three subjects are discussed. The first woman speaks soft things to the young man; the other, lofty things to the little one; the third, saving things to men and children of men. But if we are men—for man is the image and glory of God—let us hear her who speaks manly things. Let us hear her, but first let us approach her. For she is the strong woman whose praise is sung at the end of Proverbs; whose face is the image of the Father; whose eyes are the brightness of understanding; whose beauty is the radiance of light; whose nature, splendour, and figure are the substance of God. Therefore let us hear her, but first let us approach her. Let us approach her, but first [Col. 0072C] let us seek her.

The first woman makes the way unclean; the second makes it crooked; the third makes it straight. With the first the unclean walk; with the second, the proud; with the third, the blessed. For this one leads out from vices, leads onward through virtues, and leads into the homeland.

One woman is not black but beautiful; another is black and beautiful; another is neither black but beautiful [an evidently corrupt formulation]; another is not beautiful but black. The first is the Queen of Heaven; the second, the Bride of the Lamb on earth; the third, the wife of the world; the fourth, the spouse of the devil. The first consists of those who rejoice with Christ in heaven; the second, of faithful people journeying on earth; the third, of those whom the vanity of the world has swallowed up; the fourth, of those whom wickedness afflicts with punishments and calamity torments in hell.

There are four kinds of espousal by which the aforesaid kinds of women are espoused: namely, the joy of divine contemplation, the grace of pardon, the concupiscence of the world, and the misery of hell. By the first is espoused the company of blessed angels; by the second, the glorious unanimity of righteous people; by the third, the destructive vanity of the reprobate; by the fourth, the dreadful wretchedness of the utterly wicked in hell. The first are at rest; the second stand in battle-line; the third lie shamefully prostrate; the fourth are mercilessly consigned to prison.

The first is the Jerusalem above, our mother; the second and third are, in the Lord’s threshing-floor, wheat and chaff together; the fourth is tortured by misery in hell. In the first [Col. 0073A] are all things of glory and nothing of misery; in the second, much glory but some misery; in the third, much misery but scarcely any grace; in the fourth, no glory at all but every kind of misery. Therefore let the first rejoice above with Christ; let the second prepare herself for the bridegroom; let the third commit fornication with the world; let the fourth be tortured with the devil.

The second, then, should prepare herself for the bridegroom in such a way that she is black through repentance but beautiful through obedience; black through humility, beautiful through charity; black through the battle of temptations, but beautiful through steadfastness in virtues; black through service, but beautiful through desire; black through the practice of religion, beautiful through the sincerity of contemplation; black in carnal things, beautiful in spiritual things; black in active matters, beautiful in contemplative matters.

Christ himself was black, yet beautiful in his blackness. See him black: soiled with filthy garments, smeared with spittle, bruised with wounds, pale in death; and yet “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0073] Ps. 44]. Behold, beautiful in his blackness, beautiful in the Transfiguration, beautiful in the Resurrection, beautiful in divinity.

Likewise, the soul is beautiful in its blackness. Hence Paul: “Not only so, but we glory also in tribulations” [Note: [Col. 0073] Rom. 5]. Again: “I will gladly,” he says, “glory in my weaknesses” [Note: [Col. 0073] 2 Cor. 12]. Again: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0073] Gal. 6]. A conscience is beautiful, as in the saying: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0073] 2 Cor. 1]. Beautiful in an abundance of virtues: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed round with variety in golden fringes” [Col. 0073C] [Note: [Col. 0073] Ps. 44]. Beautiful in contemplation: “With unveiled face we behold the glory of God, that we may be transformed into the same image from glory to glory” [Note: [Col. 0073] 2 Cor. 3]. This concerning the blackness and beauty of the bridegroom.

“Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.”

[THO.] Kedar was a son of Ishmael, of whom it was said: “His hand shall be against all, and the hand of all against him” [Note: [Col. 0073] Gen. 16]. Of him it was said: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” [Note: [Col. 0073] Ps. 119]. Kedar is interpreted “darkness.” The peoples descended from him did not at times know how to have peace.

What then means: “I am black but beautiful, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon”? Make the distinction thus: black like the tents [Col. 0073D] of Kedar, beautiful like the skins of Solomon. For the holy Church is so often darkened by the afflictions inflicted by unbelievers, as though she were the general servant of the entire world. Hence the Lord says: “You shall be hated by all men for my name’s sake” [Note: [Col. 0073] Matt. 10].

Solomon made tents from the skins of dead animals. So the Lord constituted his Church from those who mortify themselves for his sake. Therefore he himself says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” [Note: [Col. 0073] Matt. 16].—“Mortify,” he says, “your members which are upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0073] Col. 3].

Or thus: “I am black like the tents of Kedar among carnal people and false brethren; beautiful like the skins of Solomon among spiritual people.” Or: she is called black like the tents of Kedar on account of Christ’s Passion, beautiful like the skins of Solomon on account of his glorious Resurrection.

We read of four kinds of tents: the tent of the Idumeans, from Edom, which is called *eduliumi* [uncertain reading]; the tent of Kedar; the tent of Jacob; and the tent of the Lord of hosts. Of the first: “The tents of the Idumeans and the Ishmaelites have made a covenant against you” [Note: [Col. 0073] Ps. 82]. Of the second, in this place; of the third: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0073] Ps. 86]; of the fourth: “How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts” [Note: [Col. 0073] Ps. 83].

The first is the shadow of worldly pleasure. [Col. 0074B] The second is penitential affliction. The third is delight in things above. The fourth is the happy dwelling of the heavenly city. In the first are those “who make provision for the flesh in its desires” [Note: [Col. 0073] Rom. 13]; in the second, those “who have crucified their flesh with its vices and concupiscences”; in the third, those “whose citizenship is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0073] Gal. 5]; in the fourth, those who have already learned by experience that “there are many dwelling-places in the house of God the Father” [Note: [Col. 0073] John 14].

In the first is the tent of sinners; in the second is a shelter from the heat of vices; in the third we are secure from the storm of worldly intercourse; in the fourth we shall be hidden from the rain of transient mortality. God gave the first “over to dishonourable passions and to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are unfitting” [Note: [Col. 0073] Rom. 1]. Those in the second cry: “For your sake we are put to death all day long” [Col. 0074C] [Note: [Col. 0073] Rom. 8]. Those in the third say: “As the eyes of a handmaid are upon the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he have mercy on us” [Note: [Col. 0073] Ps. 122]. Of those in the fourth it is said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” [Note: [Col. 0073] Ps. 83].

Those in the first remain outside even the court of Moses’ tent, wandering lawfully through unlawful things. But those in the second remain in the court, offering to God sacrifices of body and soul. Those in the third remain in the first tent, called the Holy Place, where are the seven lamps of the lampstand: the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit given by Christ. Those in the fourth remain in the second tent, called the Holy [Col. 0074D] of Holies, where they see the cherubim, the gilded ark, and the mercy-seat. There indeed they find full knowledge. There they see Christ’s flesh glorified. There they see Christ as advocate for us with the Father, to obtain for us grace here and glory there.

Elijah passed through these four tents. He avoided the first when fleeing from the face of Jezebel [Note: [Col. 0073] 3 Kings 19]; he dwelt in the second when he fell asleep beneath a juniper tree, asking that his soul might die [Note: [Col. 0073] Ibid.]; he hastened to the third, journeying toward Horeb, the mountain of God [Note: [Col. 0073] Ibid.]; he passed into the fourth when he was carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses [Col. 0075A] [Note: [Col. 0075] 4 Kings 2].

We have called the first that of the Idumeans, who are impatient of abstinence. Those who are in it break patience, corrupt chastity, and empty mercy: the first because they are grumblers, the second because they are lustful, the third because they are avaricious. Grumblers do not heed the voice by which God corrects them; in the lustful the Son of the Virgin does not dwell; for those who burn with avarice above all others eternal fire is prepared.

Of the first it is said: “And they murmured in their tents; God will not hear them” [Vulgate: “they did not hear the voice of the Lord”] [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 105]. Of the second the Apostle says: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no authority to eat” [Note: [Col. 0075] Heb. 13], that is, those who serve carnal pleasure. Of the third Job says: “Fire shall devour the tents of those who gladly receive gifts” [Note: [Col. 0075] Job 15].

But because you do not dwell in this tent: “Lord, if you wish, let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” [Note: [Col. 0075] Matt. 17]. These are the three tents proposed by us, the first having been rejected. Of these three, then, the first is Moses’, whose name means “saved from the waters,” because in it we escape from the waters of sins. The second is Elijah’s, whose name means “My God is the Lord,” because in it we see God through a mirror and in an enigma [Note: [Col. 0075] 1 Cor. 13]. The third is Jesus’, whose name means “Saviour,” because through Jesus we shall there receive salvation of body and soul.

In these three must be performed those dedications which we read of in the Old Testament. Solomon performed the first by dedicating the Temple in autumn [Note: [Col. 0075] 2 Kings 7]; the children of Israel performed the second, on their return from the Babylonian captivity under King Cyrus, in spring [Note: [Col. 0075] 1 Esdras 6]; Judas Maccabaeus performed the third [Col. 0075C] in winter [Note: [Col. 0075] 1 Macc. 4]. The first dedication was called *dedicatio*, the second *scenopegia* (“feast of tabernacles”), the third *encaenia* (“renewal”). Therefore the last belongs to the first tent, the second to the second, the third to the third.

To dedicate is to raise something from common use to solemn and divine use, or newly to begin its use again. In the first of these three we find three things: first, that our conscience, relieved as though of a certain burden of sins, is raised from the earth to do good works; second, that in it one is hidden and protected against temptations, whether violent or deceitful; third, that because of the burden which we feel in it we groan, that we may be clothed upon in incorruption.

Of the first Job says: “If you remove the iniquity which is in your hand, and injustice is not in your tent, then you shall be able to lift up [Col. 0075D] your face without blemish” [Note: [Col. 0075] Job 11]. Of the second David says: “For he has hidden me in his tent; in the day of evils he has protected me in the secret place of his tent” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 26]. Of the third the Apostle says: “We who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed upon” [Note: [Col. 0075] 2 Cor. 6].

Those dwell in these who flee the dwelling-place of the first. Hence: “I chose to be cast down in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 83]. “The putting off of this tent is swift,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0075] 2 Pet. 1]. These [Col. 0076A] are the tents of Kedar [Note: [Col. 0075] Song 1], because penitents are thus considered dark by men. This also is the tent made by Moses [Note: [Col. 0075] Exod. 26].

The second of these three tents is that made by Elijah [Note: [Col. 0075] 3 Kings 19]. This, we said, is the tent of Jacob [Note: [Col. 0075] Gen. 35]. In it are found the secret consolation of the Holy Spirit, beauty from contemplation of things above, and rejoicing which breaks forth into praise because of one’s righteousness and hope of heavenly goods. Of the first Job says: “When God was secretly in my tent, and my servants round about me” [Note: [Col. 0075] Job 29]; of the second Balaam says in the book of Numbers: “How beautiful are your tents, O Jacob, and your tents, O Israel” [Note: [Col. 0075] Num. 24]; of the third: “The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 117].

The third tent is called Jesus’, because our salvation is in it; it is “not made with hands, that is, not of this creation” [Note: [Col. 0075] Heb. 9]. One ascends to it by a threefold step: avoidance of evil, performance of good, secondly prayer, thirdly the shedding of blood. Of the first: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tent?” The answer is: “He who walks without blemish and works righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 14]. Of the second: “We shall enter into his tent; we shall worship in the place where his feet stood” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 139]. Of the third: “Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tent not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, nor through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” [Note: [Col. 0075] Heb. 9].

Likewise, Christ had these three tents. He had the first, the tent of Kedar, in his Passion [Col. 0076C] and also throughout his whole life in the world, yet with holiness; the second, in the Resurrection and Ascension; the third, in the bosom of the Father’s glory. The first is venerable through holiness, the second visible through brightness, the third admirable through the greatness of glory. Of the first: “The Most High sanctified his tent” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 45]; of the second: “He placed his tent in the sun” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 18]; of the third: “I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tent, even unto the house of God” [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 41].

Behold how the bride is black like the tents of Kedar. It follows:

How is she beautiful like the skins of Solomon? There are four kinds of skins. There are the skins of the land of Midian; skins from sacrifices; Adam’s skins; and Solomon’s skins. The first are the appearance of a perverse way of life; [Col. 0076D] the second are vain glory sought from good works; the third are patience under afflictions; the fourth are uprightness and grace in good works.

The first are called the skins of the land of Midian. For Midian is interpreted “from judgment.” Such persons are troubled because of their sins and fear the judgment to come. Hence it is said: “The skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled” [Note: [Col. 0075] Hab. 3]. The second are called skins from sacrifices. Hence in Leviticus: “When you offer a sacrifice of oxen or sheep, once the skin has been removed, you shall cut the limbs into pieces” [Note: [Col. 0075] Lev. 1]; that is, [Col. 0077A] you shall remove vain glory from the good deeds you perform. The third are called Adam’s skins. For after his sin the Lord made him garments of skins [Note: [Col. 0077] Gen. 3]; that is, he clothed him in this temporal misery, that he might suffer afflictions in the world. In this passage, however, the fourth kind is meant, called the skins of Solomon.

The first are hairy, the second spotted, the third reddened, the fourth hyacinth-coloured. The first, the hairy skins, are those of the kids which Jacob prepared for his father and with which he covered himself that he might be thought hairy [Note: [Col. 0077] Gen. 27]. This was Christ, who appeared to the Father in the likeness of flesh [Note: [Col. 0077] Rom. 8]. The second are called spotted. Hence, under the Law, an animal that has a blemish is forbidden in sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0077] Lev. 1, etc.]. For one has a blemish who, in doing good, seeks human praise from it [Note: [Col. 0077] Matt. 6]. The third are called reddened because of the shedding of blood by martyrs, [Col. 0077B] and also by others who are ready to shed their blood for Christ, and who “went about in sheepskins and goatskins” [Note: [Col. 0077] Heb. 11]. The fourth are called hyacinth-coloured because of the beauty of heavenly life. Hence the bride is here called beautiful, like the skins of Solomon. Of these two it is said: “Over the tent of the covenant were hyacinth skins and reddened ram skins” [Note: [Col. 0077] Exod. 25].

Passing over the others, let us treat of the skins of Solomon.

They are commendable for three things: strength, softness, and beauty. The first is produced by patience in adversities; the second by obedience rendered to masters; the third by the varied adornment of virtue. Therefore these skins are first prepared, second anointed, third painted. They are prepared by the preparation of regular discipline; [Col. 0077C] anointed by the anointing of spiritual grace; painted by diverse virtues.

For the first, the Apostle directs us, saying: “Putting off the old man with his deeds, put on the new man” [Note: [Col. 0077] Eph. 4]. And Solomon: “My son, hear the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother” [Note: [Col. 0077] Prov. 1]. Of the second: “You have an anointing from the Holy Spirit, and it teaches you concerning all things” [Vulgate: “and you know all things”] [Note: [Col. 0077] John 2]. Of the third: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed round with variety in golden fringes” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 44]. Of the first: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul” [Note: [Col. 0077] Job 2]. Of the second: “Stretching out heaven like a skin.” Here the third is commended when it is said [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 103]: The bride is beautiful like the skins of Solomon.

[Col. 0077D] “Do not consider that I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me.”

[THO.] As though she said: O souls devoted to God, do not marvel that I am despised by men, because the heat of temptations, which I do not cease to endure for the sake of my inner beauty, renders me dark outwardly—though heavenly grace has granted that I should be lovely inwardly. For the true Sun of righteousness, for whose love I endure these things, is the cause.

For just as those who remain at home generally have white limbs, whereas those who labour in the field generally have dark ones, so the Church appears white in peace; but the more ardently one girds oneself for spiritual pursuits, the more fiercely does the devil’s temptation rage against one. Therefore, because the bride is beautiful inwardly by faith and virtues, but scorched outwardly by tribulations, she says that Christ is the cause.

The holy soul has a threefold colour: first, loftiness; second, delight; third, charity. Loftiness, because it is esteemed great before God and men; delight, by which it takes spiritual pleasure in God; charity, by which it contemplates heavenly things. Of the first the Apostle says: “Thus let a man regard us” [Note: [Col. 0077] 1 Cor. 4], etc. Again: “Providing good things not only before God, but [Note: [Col. 0077] Rom. 23],” etc. Of the second David says: “They shall utter the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they shall exult in your righteousness” [Col. 0078B] [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 144]. Of delight it is written: “The Lord had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning” [Note: [Col. 0077] Gen. 2]; and: “Those who feasted luxuriously perished in the ways” [Note: [Col. 0077] Lam. 4]; and: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 35]. Of the third: “With unveiled face we behold the glory of God” [Note: [Col. 0077] 2 Cor. 3].

Concerning these it was said of Abraham: “Abraham went on increasing” [Note: [Col. 0077] Gen. 26]. This is the first; “and prospering” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid.]. This is the second; “toward the south” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid.]. Behold the third: “until he became great” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ibid.].

And in Christ we find these three colours: loftiness in the display of miracles, delight in prayer, brightness in the Transfiguration. Of the first it is said that “they regarded him as a prophet” [Note: [Col. 0077] Matt. 15]. Of the second, at Lazarus’ tomb: [Col. 0078C] “I thank you, Father, because you always hear me” [Note: [Col. 0077] John 11]. Of the third: “His face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow, such as no fuller on earth can make” [Note: [Col. 0077] Mark 9].

The sun is understood in many ways. Here we find three suns, which discolor the bride here in a threefold colour. The first sun is Christ; the second, tyrannical persecution; the third, temptation. Of the first: “The sun and moon stood in their habitation” [Note: [Col. 0077] Hab. 3]. Of the second, in the Gospel: “Seeds which had no root withered when the sun rose” [Note: [Col. 0077] Matt. 13]. Of the third, in the Law: “If anyone is defiled by a nocturnal dream, let him remain outside the camp; and after washing with water, let him return to the camp after sunset” [Note: [Col. 0077] Deut. 23].

The first sun discolours through love, the second through pain, the third [Col. 0078D] through sorrow. The first sun discolours the soul when, through its love, it descends from loftiness to humility; the second, when the delight by which it rejoices in the Lord is diminished through tribulation; the third, when the brightness by which it contemplates heavenly things is darkened by an unclean suggestion.

David gives an example of the first: from royal loftiness, through love of the first sun—that is, of Christ—he descended, stripped like a buffoon, to dance before the ark of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0077] 2 Kings 7]. Job gives an example of the second. For, burned by the second sun—that is, by Satan’s persecution—his delight in God was diminished, and he spoke thus: “My harp has been turned into mourning, and my joy into the voices of those who weep” [Note: [Col. 0079] Job 30]. The Psalmist complains that he was discoloured by the third sun, when he shows that through temptation he had fallen away from heavenly contemplation, saying: “My heart is troubled; my strength has forsaken me, and even the light of my eyes is not with me” [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 37]. Also by the second sun, that is, tribulation.

The soul is discoloured by those three colours. Hence in Job, concerning the first: “When I sat as a king with an army around me, I was nevertheless a comforter of mourners” [Note: [Col. 0079] Job 29]: behold, loftiness. “Now those younger than I in days mock me” [Note: [Col. 0079] Job 30]: behold humility, which discolours. Of the second: “I washed my feet with butter, and the rock poured out streams of oil for me” [Note: [Col. 0079] Job 29]: this is exultation in [Col. 0079B] God. “My soul is weary of my life” [Note: [Col. 0079] Job 10]: behold discoloration. Of the third: “Who will grant that I might be as in former months, in which God guarded me, when his lamp shone over my head and by his light I walked in darkness?” [Note: [Col. 0079] Job 29]. Behold the brightness of contemplation. “Why do you hide your face, and reckon me your enemy?” [Note: [Col. 0079] Job 13]. Behold discoloration also by the third sun, that is, temptation.

The soul is discoloured by these three colours. Therefore Jeremiah says in Lamentations, concerning the first: “The princess of provinces has become tributary” [Note: [Col. 0079] Lam. 1]; concerning the second: “Those who feasted luxuriously have perished in the ways; those who were nourished in saffron have embraced dung” [Note: [Col. 0079] Lam. 4]; concerning the third: “How the Lord in his anger has covered the virgin daughter of Zion with darkness” [Col. 0079C] [Note: [Col. 0079] Lam. 2].

Again, the first sun, that is, Christ, coloured, discoloured, and recoloured the Church. He coloured her in the Nativity, discoloured her in the Passion, recoloured her in the Resurrection.
