In the Nativity, with a new brightness: “Light has risen in darkness for the upright” [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 111]; and: “For those dwelling in a land of the shadow of death, a light has risen” [Note: [Col. 0079] Isa. 9]. In the Passion, with the darkening of darkness: “Darkness came over the whole earth” [Note: [Col. 0079] Matt. 27], while he hung on the cross. Also through the despair of certain persons, and the fear and flight which befell his disciples in the Passion. In the Resurrection he recoloured her through the glorification of the flesh; and when he was raised in the clouds and gave hope that he would refashion the body of our humility, conformed to the body of his glory [Col. 0079D] [Note: [Col. 0079] Phil. 3].

This same sun also coloured the blessed Virgin at the Conception, discoloured her in the Passion, and recoloured her in the Assumption. Her colouring was the grace that came to her aid; her discoloration, the pain of the Passion; her recolouring, the glory of immortality. Hear the colour: “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you” [Note: [Col. 0079] Luke 1]. Hear the discoloration: “Woman, behold your son” [Note: [Col. 0079] John 1]. Hear the recolouring: “I saw the beautiful one ascending like a dove above the streams of waters” [Note: [Col. 0079] Gal. 1].

This sun also colours the soul by the infusion of grace, discolours it by the withdrawal of that same grace, and recolours it by the restoration of what was withdrawn. The Apostle was coloured [Col. 0080A] when he said: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, immediately I did not confer with flesh and blood” [Note: [Col. 0079] Isa. 38]. Hezekiah was discoloured when he said: “My life has been cut off as by a weaver; while I was still beginning, he cut me off” [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 50], namely, by withdrawing grace. David wished to be recoloured after sin when he said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” [Note: [Col. 0079] Jer. 17].

Therefore the first sun makes the soul pale with love, the second dark with labour, the third moist with sorrow. For it weeps for a threefold reason: it fears, through temptation, that it may incur ugliness, weakness, and death. For the soul, yielding to temptation, first becomes ugly, secondly weak, thirdly dead. It is ugly at the first thought. [Col. 0080B] Hence it cannot be said: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend.” It becomes weak in the pleasure of the thought. Hence it cries: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0079] Ezek. 18]. It is dead in the commission of sin. Hence: “The soul that sins, it shall die.”

A devout soul, moreover, pours forth four kinds of tears. For it weeps: first, because of its sojourn in this misery; second, because of the sorrow of sin; third, because of the horror of Gehenna; fourth, because of desire for the homeland. The first give drink to the thirsty soul; the second wash the unclean one; the third moisten the dry soul; the fourth water the soul already made fruitful. Of the first it is said: “You will give us drink in tears by measure [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 79].” Of the [Col. 0080C] second: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 6].” Of the third: “The Lord has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 104].” Of the fourth: “With my tears I shall water my couch [Note: [Col. 0079] Ps. 6].”

These are the four rivers which go forth from Paradise. The first are the first river, called Phison, which is interpreted “change of countenance,” “which encircles the land of Havilah [Note: [Col. 0079] Gen. 2],” interpreted “bringing forth”; because there, with these tears, are pains like those of a woman in labour. On account of the burden of misery there will be a change of countenance—that is, corruption shall encompass corruption—where also the finest gold is produced; for from this corruptible earth gold shall be made, that is, an incorruptible body, when all the streets of Jerusalem are paved with [Col. 0080D] pure gold [Note: [Col. 0079] Tob. 13].

The second tears are the second river, called Gehon, that is, “a gaping of the earth,” and it “encircles the land of Ethiopia [Note: [Col. 0079] Gen. 2].” Ethiopians are compared with sinners because of their blackness; for tears over sins so surround sinners as to bring about a gaping of the earth—that is, of the heart—through confession.

The third tears are the third river, called Tigris because of its swiftness, and it “goes against the Assyrians [Note: [Col. 0079] Ibid.].” In many places we find Assyrians used for adversaries, as here, because they greatly opposed the children of Israel. For sinners, seeing the punishments which these adversaries [Col. 0081A] prepare for the wicked, swiftly break forth into tears, that they may deserve to be delivered from them; and thus this river goes against the Assyrians.

The fourth tears are the fourth river, called Euphrates, and it is interpreted “fruit-bearing,” because tears of devotion have abundant fruit. This river is not said to encircle any land, because tears of devotion pour themselves out more around one’s own heart than toward another matter. These water, because they affect the human heart with a certain richness. David rejoices to be washed with these tears, saying: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow [Note: [Col. 0081] Ps. 50].”

The first sun, namely Christ, was discoloured in the Passion; but in the Resurrection he is recoloured by the brightness of glory. Hence: “When the sun, which had previously been clouded, shone forth, a great fire was kindled, so [Col. 0081B] that all marvelled [Note: [Col. 0081] 1 Macc.].” This sun is Christ, who first wrapped himself in a cloud; second, possessed splendour; third, sent forth the heat of fire; fourth, produced wonder: the cloud of assumed weakness, the splendour of glorified humanity, the fire of charity, the wonder of majesty.

The first is so that by his example we may endure the sufferings of this present time [Note: [Col. 0081] Rom. 8]; the second, so that we may sigh for the glory “which shall be revealed in us [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid.]”; the third, so that “the charity of God may be poured into our hearts [Note: [Col. 0081] Rom. 5]”; the fourth, so that we may see how wonderful God is in his saints [Note: [Col. 0081] Ps. 67].

In the first respect the sun of righteousness had a rising, a darkening, and a setting: its rising in a stable, its darkening in a cloud, its setting on the gibbet. The first was by being born of the Virgin; [Col. 0081C] the second by the veil of the flesh; the third by the burden of the Passion. Of the first: “The sun rose and they were gathered together [Note: [Col. 0081] Nah. 3].” Habakkuk says of the stable: “I considered your works and was afraid [Note: [Col. 0081] Hab. 1], in the midst of two animals.” Of the second: “When [Note: [Col. 0081] Exod. 40] the tabernacle had been completed, a cloud covered it”; and: “I shall cover the sun with a cloud [Note: [Col. 0081] Ezek. 32]”; and: “The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt [Note: [Col. 0081] Isa. 19].” Of the third: “The sun knew its setting [Note: [Col. 0081] Ps. 103]”; and: “The sun shall set at noon [Note: [Col. 0081] Amos 8].”

In the first a new grace appeared; in the second, God’s wisdom lay hidden; in the third, prudence was displayed. The first was for the strengthening of morals; the second, for the proving of faith; the third, for resurrection. The first, that we may live honourably; the second, that we may believe; the third, that we may live with Christ. Of the first: “The [Col. 0081D] grace of God our Saviour has appeared to all people, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this age [Note: [Col. 0081] Tit. 2].” Of the second Martha says: “I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who came into this world [Note: [Col. 0081] John 11].” And Peter: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God [Note: [Col. 0081] Matt. 16].” Hence: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen [Note: [Col. 0081] Heb. 11].” Wisdom was veiled when “the Word was made flesh [Note: [Col. 0081] John 1].” Of the third: “For if we died with [Col. 0082A] Christ, we believe that we shall live with him. For if we have been made planted-together in the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be of his resurrection [Note: [Col. 0081] Rom. 6].”

In the first we are watered; in the second, planted; in the third, planted together: watered by the dew of grace, planted by the rooting of faith, planted together by participation in death. In the first, the earth of our heart is softened; in the second, the root of faith grows warm; in the third, human nature grows together. Of the first: “I shall be like dew; Israel shall bud like the lily [Note: [Col. 0081] Hos. 14]”; and Isaiah: “As rain and snow descend from heaven and make the earth drunk and soak it and cause it to germinate, so shall the word be which proceeds from my mouth [Note: [Col. 0081] Isa. 55].” Of the second: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it [Note: [Col. 0081] Ps. 79].” Likewise: “You planted its roots, and it filled the earth [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid.].” Of the third: [Col. 0082B] “If we have been made planted together [Note: [Col. 0081] Rom. 6],” etc.; and Christ to the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink [Note: [Col. 0081] Matt. 20]?”

Behold, this sun was in a filthy garment, in flowering flesh, in a radiant face: in the filthy garment of our corruption; in the flowering flesh of resurrection; in the radiant face of paternal glorification. In the first, “we saw him as though a leper, struck by God and humbled [Note: [Col. 0081] Isa. 53]”; in the second the Father “stored up joy and exultation over him [Note: [Col. 0081] Ecclus. 15].” The third is “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world [Note: [Col. 0081] John 1].”

Hear of the filthy garment: “Why is your clothing red, and your garment like that of those treading in the winepress [Note: [Col. 0081] Isa. 63]?” Likewise: “Their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I defiled all [Col. 0082C] my clothing [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid.].” For this is Jesus the high priest, who in Zechariah was seen in filthy garments [Note: [Col. 0081] Zech. 3]. This garment is Joseph’s tunic, which his brothers dyed with the blood of a goat [Note: [Col. 0081] Gen. 37]. He was clothed with this filthy garment before the Resurrection; but in the Resurrection, with flowering flesh. Hence: “And my flesh flowered again [Note: [Col. 0081] Ps. 27]. Behold, winter has passed; flowers have appeared in our land [Note: [Col. 0081] Song 2].”

Truly, flowers. For Christ’s flesh flowered with the privilege of three flowers. The first was the rose, that is, the flower of the field; the second, the lily of the valleys; the third, the almond blossom. The first was freedom from sin; the second, virginity from a virgin; the third, the joy of resurrection. The first grows from thorny ground without a thorn; the second from uncultivated ground without stain; the third from rock without hardness. [Col. 0082D] The first, indeed, was from the Jewish people; the second, from the Virgin’s womb; the third, from the tomb. The first is from Aaron’s rod, which blossomed [Note: [Col. 0081] Num. 17]; the second proceeded from the root of Jesse [Note: [Col. 0081] Isa. 11]; the third from the almond tree that blossomed [Note: [Col. 0081] Eccl. 12], through which man shall return to the house of eternity.

The first is the flower of the field, that is, the rose which is born from a thorn yet knows no sting, because Christ was born from sinners, “who committed no sin [Note: [Col. 0081] 1 Pet. 2].” The second is the lily, proceeding and born from a green stalk, because the Virgin bore the virgin Christ and suffered no loss of [Col. 0083A] virginity. The third is the almond blossom, which produces its flower before other trees, because Christ rose as the first fruits of those who sleep [Note: [Col. 0083] 1 Cor. 15], or of those who die, or as the firstborn of the dead [Note: [Col. 0083] Col. 1].

Therefore, you who seek to be cleansed from sins, bear fruit like a rose planted beside streams of water. You who strive after virginity, possess, like the lily, the fragrance of sweetness. You who aspire to the resurrection, look upon the almond tree, through which man shall return to the house of his eternity [Note: [Col. 0083] Eccl. 12].

This almond tree had a leaf, a flower, and fruit: the leaf, namely, the word of instruction; the flower, the joy of resurrection; the fruit, confession of the Father. The first in preaching, the second in resurrection, the third in ascension. Through the first we have received knowledge of truth; [Col. 0083B] through the second we shall receive the robe of joy; through the third, the brightness of divinity. Of the first: “And its leaf shall not fall [Note: [Col. 0083] Ps. 1].” Likewise: “And its leaf shall be green [Note: [Col. 0083] Jer. 17].” Of the second: “The Lord clothed him in a robe of joy [Note: [Col. 0083] Ecclus. 45].” Of the third: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had before the world was made [Note: [Col. 0083] John 17].”

Behold the filthy garment; behold the flowering flesh. There follows the radiant face. Of this it is said: The face of Moses became radiant when the Lord looked upon him [Note: [Col. 0083] Exod. 34]. That Moses is Christ, upon whom the Lord looked when he raised him from the dead. Hence: “But God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day [Note: [Col. 0083] Acts 13].”

Thus the sun, which had previously been clouded, shone forth. For this sun shone, shone into, and shone back: it shone in [Col. 0083C] glorified flesh, shone into the faithful mind, and shone back in our body. First, by the glory of resurrected flesh; second, by devotion and understanding; third, by work and patience. Of the first John in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0083] ch. 1] saw a man, and “his face was like the sun shining in its strength.”

Of the second, Ambrose:

> And, true Sun, come down,  
> Shining with perpetual brightness;  
> Pour the radiance  
> Of the Holy Spirit into our senses.

Hence: “The new light of your splendour has shone into the eyes of our mind [Note: [Col. 0083] Preface of the Mass].” Of the third: “The sun shone upon the golden shields [Note: [Col. 0083] 1 Macc. 6].”

In opposition to the first, this sun lay hidden in the cloud of misery; in opposition to the second, in the cloud of ignorance; in opposition to the third, in the cloud of our deformity. Of [Col. 0083D] the first, in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0083] Rev. 6]: “The sun became as sackcloth of hair.” Of the second: “Like wax which melts they shall be taken away; fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun [Note: [Col. 0083] Ps. 57].” Of the third, in the Apocalypse: “One of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the wrath of God poured out his bowl upon the sun [Note: [Col. 0083] Rev. 1],” that is, upon Christ. The bowl of God’s wrath is poured out when, because our sins demand it, Christ’s patience and pattern of action are either not granted to us, or, once granted, are not preserved.

Likewise, this sun shone forth in his Nativity, shone forth in his works, and shone forth in his Transfiguration: in the Nativity, through the revelation of [Col. 0084A] stars and angels; in his works, through the performance of miracles; in the Transfiguration, through the manifestation of future glory. In the first it is shown that he came; in the second, who came; in the third, for what purpose he came: that he came whom prophecy had foretold; who came, namely the power of God and the wisdom of God [Note: [Col. 0083] 1 Cor. 1]; for what purpose he came, namely that he might transfer us from this misery to glory.

Hear the first: “For you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness shall rise [Note: [Col. 0083] Mal. 4].” Hence at the Lord’s birth the Church sings [Note: [Col. 0083] Mass at cockcrow]: “Light shall shine upon us today, because the Lord has been born for us.” Of the second: “The sun and moon stood in their habitation, in the light of your arrows [Note: [Col. 0083] Hab. 3],” that is, in the splendour of the brightness of your dwelling. Of the third: “His face shone like the sun, and his garments were white as snow [Note: [Col. 0083] Matt. 17].”

From this sun, thus shining forth, a great fire was kindled. This fire is threefold: fire at the tomb, fire in the assembly of the apostles, and fire in the human heart. The first shines yearly; the second, once and uniquely; the third, frequently and spiritually. The first was great and a testimony to Christ’s resurrection; the second was great and a sign of the Holy Spirit’s coming; the third is great—the fire which our Lord Jesus Christ sent into the earth and wished vehemently to be kindled [Note: [Col. 0083] Luke 12]. In the first all marvel at the truth of the Son’s resurrection; in the second, at the Father’s power and majesty; in the third, at the kindness of the Holy Spirit.

The first fire was prefigured by the fire which Moses saw in the bush [Note: [Col. 0083] Exod. 3]. Just as that fire showed the bush, which seemed liable to decay, to be incorruptible, so [Col. 0084C] that Paschal fire, which is divinely kindled yearly at the tomb, bears witness to the Lord’s true resurrection. Of the second: “There appeared to the apostles divided tongues, as of fire, and it sat upon each of them [Note: [Col. 0083] Acts 2].” Of the third, the Sun himself, namely Christ, said: “I came to send fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it burn [Note: [Col. 0083] Luke 12]?” This fire is charity.

*I am black, but beautiful,* etc.

[CARD.] This song proceeds in the manner of a prophet: for it suddenly changes persons and suddenly changes times. A little earlier the Blessed Virgin had spoken of the joy of her Assumption, and the angels had spoken of the same; now the Blessed Virgin speaks of the sorrow which she had at the time of her Son’s Passion, and she turns [Col. 0084D] her speech toward the young women, saying: “I am black, overcome by sorrow of heart.” Or thus: “I am black, despised, darkened, obscured, discoloured, because the dying sun discoloured me; the darkened and obscured sun made me colourless.” Of this obscuring and darkening of the sun Isaiah speaks when he speaks of Christ’s Passion: “There is neither form nor beauty; and we saw him, and there was no appearance: despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and knowing weakness; and his face was as though hidden, and despised; therefore we did not esteem him [Note: [Col. 0083] Isa. 53].”

For in the Passion there did not [Col. 0085A] appear in Christ the form or beauty of majesty; but, because of the likeness of sinful flesh, he was regarded as though a leper. Hence Isaiah: “And we considered him as though a leper [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid.].” For the countenance of divine power was hidden in him, while, amid sufferings, the weakness of human nature appeared; and thus he was considered despised [Note: [Col. 0085] Isa. 53], nor was he regarded as the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0085] Mark 15].

Therefore, since he was so despised, his mother too was despised; since he was so darkened, his mother too was darkened, nor was she considered the Mother of God. She therefore says: “I am black in the appearance and opinion of unbelieving people, but in truth I am beautiful. I am black in appearance, and despised as the mother of a leper, but beautiful in the reality of truth and glorious as the Mother of the true God. I am black like the tents of Kedar, because I am not considered the tent of the King of righteousness, [Col. 0085B] but like other mothers, whose wombs are tents of children of sorrow and darkness.” Thus she was reckoned among the tents of Kedar, which is interpreted “darkness” or “sorrow.”

Nevertheless, I am beautiful like the skins of Solomon—like the skins dedicated [Col. 0086A] to the true Solomon, the true peaceful one, Christ. For just as those skins contained the typical ark, so I contained within my womb the true ark, namely Christ: his flesh is signified by the ark, his soul by the golden urn which was in the ark, and his divinity by the manna. And just as the skins protected the whole tabernacle, so under the shadow of my protection I protect the whole Church.

I am indeed like a scarlet skin, because through compassion in suffering I was dyed in the Passion of my Son; likewise like a hyacinth-coloured skin through contemplation and love of heavenly things. Therefore do not consider, O daughters of Jerusalem, that I am dark; rather consider that I am beautiful. For I am dark because the sun discoloured me, he in whose Passion “there was neither form nor beauty [Note: [Col. 0085] Isa. 53].” Yet he shall receive form and beauty, and I likewise shall receive them with him. For through the glory of the Resurrection he shall be believed to be God, and I shall be believed to be the Mother of God.

Concerning this darkening of the Blessed Virgin in the opinion of unbelieving Jews, she herself adds:

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0085]

[Col. 0085B] *The sons of my mother fought against me.*

[THO.] This is the voice of the primitive Church, which endured the wars of tribulation from the Synagogue itself, from which it drew its carnal origin, as the Acts of the Apostles teach most fully. But the Church at Jerusalem was one and was scattered throughout the world [Col. 0085C] by this conflict, so that more might be born from it.

Our mother is Eve. She bore three sons. For she is the mother of all living. The three sons whom she bore are culpable impulses, penal afflictions, and perverse brothers. For from her sin took its beginning, misery came into the world, and the human race was born from her. These are the sons of our mother: the first fight against us, the second around us, the third against us. Of the first the Apostle says: “I find another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin [Note: [Col. 0085] Rom. 6].” Of the second David says: “The sorrows of death surrounded me, and the perils of hell found me [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 17].” Of the third, in the book of Maccabees: [Col. 0085D] “The nations gathered in a great multitude to fight against us [Note: [Col. 0085] 1 Macc. 1].”

The first fight by staining, the second by bringing death, the third by murmuring. Of the first the Psalmist complains: “God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 78].” Those nations are shameful impulses; our heart ought to be the inheritance. Of the second: “The sorrows of death surrounded me [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 17].” Of the third the same author says: “Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 13].”

The Psalmist glories that he has been delivered from the first, saying: “My protector, and in him I have hoped, who subdues my people [Col. 0086B] beneath me [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 143].” The Apostle complains of the second, saying: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0085] Rom. 7].” Of the third David prayed, saying: “Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and [Col. 0086C] free me from those rising against me [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 58].” Likewise of them: “Sinners have built upon my back [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 128].” Likewise: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has exalted treachery against me [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 40].”

He prayed concerning these three when he said: “Deliver me from the mud, that I may not sink [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 68]”—behold the first; “free me from those who hate me [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid.]”—behold the third; “and from the depths of the waters [Note: [Col. 0085] Ibid.]”—behold the second.

But hear how you may triumph over them. Against the first, keep before your eyes the remembrance of death; against the second, make virtue out of necessity; against the third, show yourself blameless in all things. For remembrance of death will prevent the first enemies—that is, unlawful impulses—from [Col. 0086D] taking effect. Necessity converted into virtue will bring you merit. If you show yourself blameless in all things, you will confound the adversary.

Hear of the first: “Son,” says Solomon, “remember your last things, and you shall never sin [Note: [Col. 0085] Ecclus. 7].” For it is written: “O death, how bitter is the memory of you to a righteous man [Note: [Col. 0085] Ecclus. 41].” This bitterness will restrain the pleasures of thoughts.

Hear of the second: “Father,” says the Saviour, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. But if it cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done [Note: [Col. 0085] Matt. 26].” “If it must be so,” Jacob says to his sons, “do what you will [Note: [Col. 0085] Gen. 43].” Therefore you too, [Col. 0087A] moved by such great examples, in every distress say to the Lord: “Your will be done [Note: [Col. 0087] Matt. 26].”

Hear also what the Apostle says of the third: “In all things show yourself an example of good works: in doctrine, in seriousness, in integrity, in sound speech beyond reproach, so that one who is opposed may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say of us [Note: [Col. 0087] Tit. 2].”

In a figure of these three, as they made for the promised land, the children of Israel fought with beasts and serpents, with the thorns and briars of the desert, and with hostile human beings. These serpents and beasts are the poisonous and beastlike impulses of the soul. The principal impulses of the soul are four, to which all the others are referred: love of pleasure; envy, which is hatred of another’s happiness; love of exaltation; and ungovernable anger. The Psalmist expressed these four when he said: “You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 90].”

The asp, then, is love of pleasure. For as the asp flatters with its face and has a sting in its tail with which it strikes, so pleasure is attractive in the experience of it, but it stings at the end, when penance is done or punishment is suffered in hell. For it is written: “Pleasure has punishment [Note: [Col. 0087] 1 John 4].” Hence the poet says [Note: [Col. 0087] Horace, *Satires* I.1.55]:

> Despise pleasures: pleasure bought with pain does harm.

And another:

> Few things are owed to pleasure; more are owed to health.

Whoever acts thus walks upon the asp.

The basilisk [Col. 0087C] signifies envy. For just as the basilisk kills by its glance the one whom it sees, so the envious person wears away another’s advantages and kills himself by punishments before he kills another. Hence Solomon: “Envy kills the foolish man, and anger slays the little one [Note: [Col. 0087] Job 5].” And the poet:

> Nothing is more just than envy: it immediately gnaws at  
> Its own author, tormenting his mind.

For, as the same poet says [Note: [Col. 0087] Horace, *Satires* I.2.57]:

> The envious man wastes away at another’s abundant wealth.

Hence that saying of the poet [Note: [Col. 0087] Ibid.]:

> The Sicilian tyrants devised  
> No greater torment than envy.

And another [Note: [Col. 0087] Ovid, *Epistles from Pontus* III.3.102]:

> Envy is an idle vice; it does not rise to noble character,  
> But creeps like a hidden viper upon the lowest ground.

The lion, which is called king of the animals, signifies love of [Col. 0087D] exaltation. To those who seek this it is said: “Do not think lofty thoughts, but fear [Note: [Col. 0087] Rom. 11].” “For the Lord is exalted: he looks upon humble things, and knows lofty things from afar [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 137].” “The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars, and the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 28],” that is, the exalted. Hence the Lord himself, who is the wisdom of the Father, says: “I alone have gone round the circuit of heaven [Note: [Col. 0087] Ecclus. 24].” And it follows: “By my own power I have trodden down the necks of all the proud and exalted [Note: [Col. 0087] Ibid.].” And in the Psalm: “You cast them down when they were lifted up [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 72].” Therefore:

> [Col. 0088A] He who seeks the heights must avoid a fall.  
> He who lies upon the ground has nowhere from which to fall.

The dragon, of fiery nature, signifies immoderate anger. Of this the Saviour says: “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to the council [Note: [Col. 0087] Matt. 5].” Hear the poet:

> Whoever will not govern anger  
> Will wish undone what pain and the mind have advised him to do.

The same author:

> Anger is a brief madness; rule your mind. Unless it obeys, it rules:  
> Curb it with reins; crush it with lashes.

“Be angry, and do not sin [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 4].” To be angry is human; but it is a fault to remain long in anger. Hence Horace says of himself:

> Quick to anger, yet I wished to be easy to appease.

Behold the first enemy with whom we fight, namely [Col. 0088B] unlawful impulses, which are the sons of our mother Eve, because she bore them.

These are the beasts and serpents with whom the children of Israel fought. They also fought “with thorns and briars in the desert [Note: [Col. 0087] Judg. 8],” by which our misery is signified. Against the first we fought by remembering death; against these, however, by making virtue out of necessity. Thus we shall make gain for ourselves when we acknowledge our weakness. Hence David: “I was turned in my affliction while the thorn was fixed in me [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 31].”

This is Adam’s curse: “When you have cultivated the earth,” God says, “it shall not yield its fruit [Note: [Col. 0087] Gen. 4], but it shall bring forth thorns and briars for you [Note: [Col. 0087] Gen. 3].” This enemy will never fail until that saying of the prophet Hosea is fulfilled: “The Lord shall bring a burning wind [Col. 0088C] from the desert, and it shall water the torrent of thorns and dry up the veins of death [Note: [Col. 0087] Hos. 13].” Meanwhile Christ, coming, watered the thorns by his grace, so that they might be borne more lightly.

The last enemy, namely the slandering brother, is conquered, as stated, by blamelessness. Hence in the Catholic Epistle: “Who among you is wise and disciplined? Let him show by good conduct his works, so that he may make the imprudence and ignorance of men silent [Note: [Col. 0087] Jas. 3].”

Likewise, the sons of the handmaid fight against us; the sons of the stepmother; the sons of the sister; and the sons of the mother. Our stepmother is the synagogue of Jews or pagans, whose warfare is sufficiently frequent and open. That is not under discussion here. But the sons of the handmaid fight against us, that is, impulses of the flesh; and the sons of the sister, that is, of the Church militant—that is, prelates, tyrants, heretics. Of her it is said: “Our little sister has no breasts [Note: [Col. 0087] Song 8].” The sons of the mother also fight: that is, of Jerusalem, which is free and above, which is our mother—namely, the evil angels, who departed from her through pride.

Thus the first conflict is with our body; the second with the prelate, tyrant, and heretic; the third with the devil. In the first one must flee. Hence the Apostle: “Flee fornication [Note: [Col. 0087] 1 Cor. 6].” In the second one must endure patiently. Hence: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation [Note: [Col. 0087] Jas. 1].” In the [Col. 0089A] third one must resist manfully. Hence: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you [Note: [Col. 0089] Jas. 4].” But these matters will be discussed more fully in what follows.

*The sons of my mother fought,* etc.

[CARD.] The sons of my mother, the Synagogue, fought against me, denying that I was the Mother of God and denying that my Son was God. Since they rejected my help and service, I left their faithlessness and passed over to the care of the faithful nations. This is what follows:

*They made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.*

[THO.] As if she said: “This I gained from persecution: that I became keeper of many vineyards, that is, Churches, after that primitive one founded at Jerusalem, which their storm dispersed.” But the statement that she did not keep the vineyard must be referred not to intention but to place. For although its material fabric was destroyed, the integrity of faith remained.

The bride sometimes speaks in the person of subjects and sometimes in the person of prelates, as here. This vineyard is the Church or a soul planted in faith, rooted in charity, dug over with the hoe of discipline, manured with the tears of penitents, watered with the words of preachers; and thus it abounds in wine, in which is gladness—that is, holy devotion.

Likewise, let us call the faith of this vineyard the vine; its virtues, the branches; its work, the cluster; its devotion, the wine. Religion is a vineyard whose Father is the husbandman, whose Son is the vine, and whose branches are the righteous. The Father is the husbandman because he digs through confession and contrition, prunes through the satisfaction of penance, and manures through the shedding of tears. The vine, whose roots cling to [Col. 0089C] the earth, is the Son, who is the foundation in religion: “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus [Note: [Col. 0089] 1 Cor. 3], in whom every structure, built together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0089] Eph. 2].”

The branches are the righteous, who are born from Christ the vine and abound in his verdure and moisture. Thus the Father purges; the Son founds. The branch abounds in verdure and moisture. The Father purges, so that there may be “religion pure and undefiled [Note: [Col. 0089] Jas. 1].” The Son founds, so that it may be rooted and founded in charity [Note: [Col. 0089] Eph. 3]. The branch abounds in the moisture—that is, the grace—of the vine, so that amid temptations it “may not be scorched by the pressure of flame which surrounded it in the midst of fire [Note: [Col. 0089] Ecclus. 51].”

There are four vineyards. The first is in the perishing joys of the reprobate. Hence it is said: “Their vineyard is of the vineyard of Sodom [Note: [Col. 0089] Deut. 32].” The second is that of religious life, which Ahab desired in order to take it from Naboth [Note: [Col. 0089] 3 Kings 21]. The third is the vineyard of the Church, of which it is said: “You transferred a vine from Egypt, cast out the nations, and planted it [Note: [Col. 0089] Ps. 79].” The fourth is in good consciences. This is the vineyard of Sorec [Note: [Col. 0089] Judg. 16], that is, “chosen.”

In the first, Lot—that is, “turning aside”—is made drunk in the mountains by his two daughters, namely glory and greed, serving drink; and he commits incest [Note: [Col. 0089] Gen. 10]. For the second Naboth dies [Note: [Col. 0089] 3 Kings 21], lest it be surrendered while [Col. 0090A] he lives. In the third the Saviour becomes drunk when “he became like a mighty man overcome with wine [Note: [Col. 0089] Ps. 77],” so that he might die for it. Noah planted the fourth, became drunk, and was uncovered in his tent and mocked by his son [Note: [Col. 0089] Gen. 9]. We have called the fourth conscience; how it ought to be cultivated is discerned from the cultivation of a material vineyard.

Among the other implements, there are four that contribute to cultivating the vineyard: trenching around it, pruning, layering, and digging. To trench around it is to open the soil around the root and make, as it were, channels through which water may flow away, lest it do harm by its excess; to prune is to cut off useless branches; to layer is to extend a shoot lengthwise beneath the earth, as though planting it further on; to dig is to open the soil around the root in order to seek out faults [Col. 0090B]. In trenching we receive the remedies of confession. Thus Joel says: “Rend your hearts, and not your garments” [Note: [Col. 0089] Joel 2.]. Pruning is the cutting off of sins through repentance and amendment of life. Hence, later on: “The time for pruning has come” [Note: [Col. 0089] Song 2.]; and: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0089] 2 Cor. 6.]. There will also be another time of pruning, when this corruptible body shall put on incorruption [Note: [Col. 0089] 1 Cor. 15.]. Layering is constancy in the exercise of virtues, covered by humility as by a turf of lowly earth. Hence the Apostle: “Let us not grow weary in doing good; for in its due season we shall reap, if we do not grow weary” [Note: [Col. 0089] Gal. 6.]. By digging we understand the daily examination of our heart, in which we must have, first, watchfulness; secondly, [Col. 0090B] discernment; thirdly, deliberation. In watchfulness present, past, and future sin is detected; in discernment what has been detected is judged; in deliberation it is ordered what ought, or ought not, to be done. Concerning the first: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” [Note: [Col. 0089] Prov. 4.]; likewise: “My son, when you come to serve God, prepare your soul for temptation; humble your heart, and endure” [Note: [Col. 0089] Ecclus. 2.]: humble it, lest it exalt itself in prosperity; endure, lest it collapse in adversity. Concerning the second, let it be said: “I have done judgment and justice” [Note: [Col. 0089] Ps. 121]; concerning the third: “Lord, teach me to do your will, for you are my God” [Note: [Col. 0089] Ps. 142].

The Lord taught Jeremiah how this vineyard ought to be cultivated, saying [Note: [Col. 0089] ch. 1]: “Behold, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, that you may uproot and destroy, scatter and overthrow, build and plant” [Col. 0090C]. The nations and kingdoms are vices and demons. Thus there are those who are set over nations and kingdoms; those who are appointed over nations and kingdoms; and those who are established over nations and kingdoms. The first are drawn away and enticed by their own desires [Note: [Col. 0089] Jas. 1.]; the second guard Solomon’s bed, holding swords and being highly trained for war [Note: [Col. 0089] Song 3.]; the third are conquerors and friends of God [Note: [Col. 0089] Jas. 2.]. The Lord recalls the first from the slavery of sin to the liberty of grace; he invites the second to long-suffering; he instructs the third [Col. 0091A] for the benefit of their brethren. The first, serving in mud and brick [Note: [Col. 0091] Exod. 1.], depart Egypt with Moses [Note: [Col. 0091] Exod. 12]; the second fight the Amalekites under Joshua [Note: [Col. 0091] Josh. 9, 10, etc.]; the third, preaching, prepare Christ’s way with John [Note: [Col. 0091] Matt. 3.].

The Church laments the first, because “their little children were led captive before the face of the pursuer. For all her persecutors overtook her amid straits” [Note: [Col. 0091] Lam. 1.]. Hence Paul: “Awake, you who sleep; arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” [Note: [Col. 0091] Eph. 5.]. And the Lord says through the prophet: “What is it, Israel, that you are in the land of enemies? You have grown old in a foreign land; you are defiled with the dead; you are counted among those who go down into hell” [Note: [Col. 0091] Baruch 3.]. Hence the prophet: “Shake yourself from the dust; arise, sit down, Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0091] Isa. 52.] [Col. 0091B]. Likewise: “Go out from Babylon, and flee from the Chaldeans” [Note: [Col. 0091] Isa. 48.].

To the second it is said: “Be strong in battle and fight against the ancient serpent; for no one shall be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” [Note: [Col. 0091] 2 Tim. 2.]. Likewise: There is no crown where there is no contest; but be long-suffering, because the end, not the contest, crowns.

Therefore, one who fights must abstain from harmful things, look to eternal rewards, and assail the enemy cautiously. Of these three things the apostle Paul says [Note: [Col. 0091] 1 Cor. 9]: “Everyone who contends in the contest abstains from all things”—this is the first; “Therefore I run thus, not as toward an uncertainty”—this is the second; “Thus I fight, not as one beating the air”—this is the third. Concerning the third group: “Feed the Lord’s flock which is among you, not for the sake of shameful gain, nor as lording it over the clergy” [Note: [Col. 0091] 1 Pet. 5.] [Col. 0091C]. They ought therefore to distribute God’s precepts simply, to exercise care over God’s flock, and mercifully to pardon sinners. Hence Paul: “He who gives, with simplicity; he who presides, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness” [Note: [Col. 0091] Rom. 12.].

Therefore he must rebuke the unwilling, entreat the well-disposed, and reprove the obstinate. Hence the Apostle: “Rebuke, entreat, reprove” [Note: [Col. 0091] 2 Tim. 4.]. These three were found in John. Concerning the first: “John rebuked Herod because of Herodias” [Note: [Col. 0091] Luke 3.]; concerning the second: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” [Note: [Col. 0091] Matt. 3.]; concerning the third: “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the wrath to come?” [Note: [Col. 0091] ibid.]. Therefore, because John perfected the first, “the Lord appointed him ruler over all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0091] Ecclesiastical Office]; because he fought well with the second, “the Lord established for him a covenant of peace” [Note: [Col. 0091] ibid.] [Col. 0091D]; because he instructed others, he was “the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord appointed over his household” [Note: [Col. 0091] ibid.], for “those who have been learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto righteousness as stars for everlasting ages” [Note: [Col. 0091] Dan. 13.].

For this reason the Lord appointed him to uproot [Note: [Col. 0091] Jer. 1.], that is, so that every plant which my Father has not planted may be uprooted [Note: [Col. 0091] Matt. 15.]; and to destroy, namely, so that everything which builds toward Gehenna may be destroyed [Col. 0092A]; to scatter [Note: [Col. 0091] ibid.], namely, so that oppressive bundles and every bond of impiety may be loosed [Note: [Col. 0091] Isa. 58.]; to overthrow the walls of Jericho with a shout [Note: [Col. 0091] Josh. 6.]; to build gold, silver, and precious stones in love [Note: [Col. 0091] 1 Cor. 3.]; and to plant a tree “beautiful to look upon and sweet for eating” [Note: [Col. 0091] Gen. 3.]. Likewise, he is to uproot the beginning of evil will; destroy the lead, bronze, and iron of weighty impiety; scatter the multitude of amassed iniquity; overthrow the hardness of obstinacy; build a dwelling-place of love; and plant the verdure of heavenly delight [Note: [Col. 0091] Jer. 1.].

We must therefore uproot the evil root from the field of which Solomon says: “I passed by the field of a slothful man and by the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled everything, and thorns had covered its surface” [Col. 0092B] [Note: [Col. 0091] Prov. 24.]. Unless you uproot the root of these plants, “God will uproot you from your dwelling and your root from the land of the living” [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 51.]. For already the axe has been laid to the root of your tree [Note: [Col. 0091] Matt. 3.]. Therefore:

> Meet the disease as it comes,
>
> For an evil tree drives its roots deeper.

Therefore, if you wish to eradicate the root of evil will:

> Resist beginnings; medicine is prepared too late  
> When evils have gained strength through long delay.

[Note: [Col. 0091] Ovid.]

Whoever wishes to uproot this root must first open the soil with the hoe; secondly, seize the exposed root with the hand and draw it out; thirdly, scatter it once drawn out with a fork: with the hoe of confession, the hand of satisfaction, and the fork of rejection. Concerning the first: “Open to me, my sister, my bride” [Note: [Col. 0091] Song 5.]. Likewise: “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved, but he had turned aside and passed on” [Col. 0092C] [Note: [Col. 0091] ibid.]. Hence, to Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall” [Note: [Col. 0091] Ezek. 8.]. Apply your hand in order to uproot it, because where there is pain there is the hand, lest some root of bitterness springing up above should hinder, so that through it many may be defiled. If “the sluggard hides his hand under his armpit and does not bring it even to his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0091] Prov. 19.]. Thirdly, let the fork of scattering also be applied, so that it may be said: “I have hated and abominated iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 118.]. “For he who is baptized by a dead person, if he touches the dead again, what profit is there in that washing?” [Note: [Col. 0091] Ecclus. 34.]

But now let us praise the glorious man who has been set before us to uproot: wonderful in birth, wonderful in usefulness, wonderful in holiness—miraculous in birth, fruitful in usefulness, glorious in holiness. Truly miraculous in birth, by which barrenness is made fruitful [Col. 0092D]; fruitful in usefulness, by which the sinner is justified; glorious in holiness, by which he is commended by the Lord. Hear the first: “This is the sixth month for her who is called barren” [Note: [Col. 0091] Luke 1.]; concerning the second: “He prepared the way of the Lord in the wilderness” [Note: [Col. 0091] Matt. 3.]; concerning the third: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” [Note: [Col. 0091] Luke 7.]. This man was wonderful, lovable, ineffable: wonderful in birth, praiseworthy in preaching, ineffable in manner of life [Col. 0093A]. Wonderful, because he made barren nature blossom again; lovable, because by preaching he repaired the loss of fallen man; ineffable, because in praise he surpassed the measure of the human race. No knowledge comprehends the first; in the second, human continence was restored; no eloquence can unfold the third. For he was the marvel of philosophers, counsel for the desolate, the privilege of divine praise. Truly, he was the marvel of philosophers, “who, though they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks. Therefore the Lord gave them over to a reprobate mind” [Note: [Col. 0093] Rom. 1.]. He was counsel for the desolate. Hence: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” [Note: [Col. 0093] Matt. 3.]. He possessed the privilege of divine praise. Hence: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” [Col. 0093B] [Note: [Col. 0093] Luke 7.].

He was also set to destroy the construction of sin. This construction is threefold: one construction leads to Gehenna, another to purgatory, another to glory. The first consists in mortal sins, the second in venial sins, the third in works of charity. In the first are built lead, bronze, and iron; in the second, wood, hay, and straw; in the third, gold, silver, and precious stones. But now let us speak of the first, which John destroyed. In it there is lead, which oppresses; bronze, which deceives; iron, which crushes works: lead because it is heavy; bronze because it deceives by its golden colour; iron because it crushes, being hard. The first is mortal sin; the second, worldly sin; the third, the hardness of obstinacy in fraternal hatred and the sin of apostasy [Col. 0093C]. Concerning the first: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” [Note: [Col. 0093] Wis. 9.]. This is the talent of lead on the mouth of the vessel in which impiety was. Concerning the second—that is, worldly sin, which is deceptive and vain glory—Solomon says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” [Note: [Col. 0093] Eccles. 1.]; and Isaiah: “Your gold has become rusty” [Note: [Col. 0093] Isa. 60.]. Concerning this and the third, namely iron, the prophet Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0093] ch. 48]: “We know that you are hard, that your brow is bronze, and your neck an iron sinew.” Concerning the third Stephen says: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0093] Acts 7.]. For just as iron masters the other metals by its hardness, so the hardness of obstinacy [Col. 0093D], which is contrary to charity, destroys the other virtues. For where charity is destroyed, it follows that no other virtue remains.

John destroyed the first in himself by subduing the flesh, when he ate honey and locusts and bound his loins with a leather belt [Note: [Col. 0093] Matt. 3.]. He destroyed the second when, though he could have been called Christ, he refused and said: “I am not the Christ” [Note: [Col. 0093] John 1.]. He taught the destruction of the third when he said: “Repent” [Note: [Col. 0093] Matt. 3.].

There follows the scattering of the bonds of impiety, which are threefold. The first is an accumulation of vices; the second, a faction of conspirators; the third, a gathering of heretics. The first attacks, as though it fights within; the second attacks, as though it fights against obedience; the third resists, as though it fights by resisting the Church. The first harms conscience; the second flees obedience; the third dissolves the Church’s harmony. Concerning the first, in the Song: “Each man’s sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night” [Note: [Col. 0093] Song 3.] [Col. 0094A]; concerning the second: “My mother’s sons fought against me”; concerning the third: “Catch for us the little foxes that lay waste the vineyards” [Note: [Col. 0093] Song 2.]. Likewise, concerning the first: “My iniquities have passed over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed me down” [Note: [Col. 0093] Ps. 37.]; concerning the second: “Let us put wood into his bread” [Note: [Col. 0093] Jer. 11.]; concerning the third: “A gathering of bulls among the cows of the peoples, that they may exclude those tested by silver” [Note: [Col. 0093] Num. 15.].

The first is figured by the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath and was stoned; the second by Korah, who was swallowed by the earth because of his conspiracy [Note: [Col. 0093] Num. 16.]; the third by Achan son of Carmi, who was covered with stones because of theft [Note: [Col. 0093] Josh. 7.].

There follows:

> And overthrow, namely, the walls of Jericho—that is, the hardness of obstinacy—which is threefold.

For there is a hardness which follows one’s own counsel and not another’s; one which retains sin for a long time; and one which makes a person sluggish in doing good. In the first, discernment is idle; in the second, confession is despised; in the third, love is held of little account. Reason illuminates the mind; confession examines the heart; discernment removes envy. Concerning the first, Abigail says to David about her husband Nabal [Col. 0094C]: “My lord, this man is harsh and foolish, according to his name” [Note: [Col. 0093] 1 Sam. 25.]. Concerning the second: “According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day...” [Note: [Col. 0093] Rom. 2.]. By this Pharaoh’s heart was hardened [Note: [Col. 0093] Exod. 7.]. Concerning the third: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0093] Acts 7.]. Likewise: “He who shuts his ear to the cry of the poor shall cry out and shall not be heard” [Note: [Col. 0093] Prov. 21.].

Do you wish to overthrow these three hardnesses? Hear how the walls of Jericho fell. First, the Israelites went around the walls; second, they shouted; third, they sounded the trumpets. Therefore, against the first, that you may distinguish what advantage and disadvantage follow from one’s own or another’s counsel, you must go around it frequently [Col. 0094D]; against the second, shout through confession and prayer; against the third, sound the trumpets of preaching. Concerning the first: “Do all things with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” [Note: [Col. 0093] Ecclus. 32.]; concerning the second: “I said: I shall confess my injustice against myself to the Lord. For this every saint shall pray to you” [Note: [Col. 0093] Ps. 31.]; concerning the third: “Love righteousness, you who judge the earth” [Note: [Col. 0093] Wis. 1.].

There follows: Build, namely, gold, silver, and precious stones: red gold, white silver, shining stones [Note: [Col. 0093] 1 Cor. 3.]. Red gold [Col. 0095A] is the burning of charity; white silver, the preaching of the innocent teacher; shining stones, the brother’s illumination through good works. And plant the shoots. This tree is Christ, who must be planted in our hearts. For he is gentle to the touch, beautiful to look upon, sweet for eating: the first in the earthly city, the second when mortality has been laid aside, the third in eternal blessedness. The first is in patience; the second in the glory of resurrection; of the third it is said: “Man ate the bread of angels” [Note: [Col. 0095] Ps. 77.] in glory.

> They made me keeper in the vineyards of the nations.

[CARD.] “My vineyard, from which I was born”—namely, the Synagogue—“I did not keep, because of its unbelief.” 16 Because the blessed Virgin had called herself keeper of the vineyards [Col. 0095B], in order to know which branch is in the vine and which is outside the vine, she asks to be shown by her Son which sheep is in the Lord’s flock and which is outside the flock, lest she wander uncertain and doubtful as to upon whom she should expend her labours. Therefore she says:

> Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.

[THO.] As though she said: “For this reason I love you with my whole mind: because I see that without your grace I can possess no virtue.” She also identifies him as shepherd when she says, “where you pasture,” according to that saying of the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd” [Note: [Col. 0095] John 10.], who pasture my sheep and lie down among them at midday. For he refreshes the hearts of his own with the remembrance of heavenly sweetness, lest they wither inwardly; and, as with the heat of midday, inflames them with the fire of charity.

Because she had said, “They made me keeper in the vineyards” [Note: [Col. 0095] Song 1.]—that is, to guard churches, souls, and consciences—and has no means of guarding if she does not know him whose they are, she cries: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves.” In the kingdom he will appear to all as he is [Note: [Col. 0095] 1 John 3.]; in exile he appears in four ways. First, in created things: “For the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are perceived through the things that have been made” [Note: [Col. 0095] Rom. 20], because in them God’s power and wisdom appear. Secondly, as he appeared to the ancients in visible forms: in fire [Note: [Col. 0095] Exod. 3.], a cloud [Note: [Col. 0095] Exod. 13.], a dove [Note: [Col. 0095] Matt. 3.], and an angelic appearance, as to Abraham [Note: [Col. 0095] Gen. 22.]. Thirdly, in the flesh, in which “he was seen upon earth and conversed with men” [Note: [Col. 0095] Baruch 3.]. Fourthly, spiritually in contemplation [Col. 0095D]. The bride desires to see him in this manner when she says, “Tell me, you whom my soul loves,” so that afterwards she may see him in the homeland as he is [Note: [Col. 0095] 1 John 3.], where desire will not be sated, sweetness will not withdraw itself, truth will not defraud, and eternity will not fail. Hence, from longing she cries: “My soul shall desire you in the night, and also with my spirit within my inmost parts” [Note: [Col. 0095] Isa. 26.].

Meanwhile, however, the Word of God manifests himself inwardly in a spiritual manner, because he is a word not sounding but penetrating; not talkative but effectual; not clamouring in the ears but gently winning the affections. He is a face not formed but forming; not striking the bodily eyes, but gladdening the countenance of the heart; pleasing by the gift of love, not by colour [Col. 0096A]. This beloved is sought sometimes by the good, sometimes by the evil; but they seek with differing ends. The good find the beloved; the evil do not find him, though they seek, because they do not seek fittingly. “For the abyss says, ‘He is not in me,’ and the sea says, ‘He is not with me.’ Nor is he found in the land of those who live pleasantly” [Note: [Col. 0095] Job 28.]. The abyss is deep curiosity; the sea, the swelling of the world; the land of those living pleasantly, carnal pleasure. He is not here, but “his price is from afar and from the uttermost bounds” [Note: [Col. 0095] Prov. 31.].

There are four things without which no one reaches and enters into the powers of the Lord: knowledge of the way, provisions, caution on the way against enemies, and a guide for the way. The way prevents you from wandering; provisions prevent you from failing; caution enables you to look to yourself; the guide leads you and provides help [Col. 0096B]. Thus you seek rightly, proceed safely, approach joyfully, and are told: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” [Note: [Col. 0095] Matt. 25.]. Thus a place pertains to joy, a way to expedition, provisions to sustenance, caution to instruction, and a guide to service. The Saviour says of the way: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0095] John 14.]. Of provisions: “Who, desiring to build a tower, does not first calculate the necessary costs?” [Note: [Col. 0095] Luke 14.] Of caution: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” [Note: [Col. 0095] Matt. 10.]. Of guides: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0095] Matt. 18.].

Knowledge of the way is therefore useful, because there are ways which seem right to men and are not; likewise caution—not, indeed, worldly caution, because “the prudence of the flesh is hostile to God” [Note: [Col. 0095] Rom. 8.]. Nor should provisions consist of “the leaven of malice and wickedness, but of the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” [Note: [Col. 0095] 1 Cor. 5.] [Col. 0096C]. One must have a guide, not one who transforms himself into an angel of light [Note: [Col. 0095] 2 Cor. 11.], by whose leading death entered into the world [Note: [Col. 0095] Rom. 5.], but one who is benevolent, provident, invincible: benevolent, that he may rejoice with us; provident, that he may give counsel; invincible, that he may defend. Therefore we must consider first the way, secondly provisions, thirdly caution, fourthly the guide.

Three things contribute to knowledge of the way: the way, a sign, and a number. In the way expedition is bestowed; by the sign certainty; by the number the depth of the mystery is opened. In the way I adore the person of the Redeemer; in the sign I recognize the instrument of salvation [Col. 0096D]; in the number I understand the causes of the mysteries. The number six signifies the person of man, who was created on the sixth day [Note: [Col. 0095] Gen. 1.] and was restored at the sixth hour of that same day. Thus the way, number, and sign are the Redeemer, the redeemed person, and the manner of redemption. Therefore the way is Christ; the cross is the sign of the way, yet “a sign that shall be contradicted” [Note: [Col. 0095] Luke 2.]. Christ came to us by such a way: undergoing harsh things in order to draw us to himself; teaching saving things in order to instruct us; enduring unworthy things in order to gain us; dying for us in order to redeem us.

He left this way [Col. 0097A] to us, that we might walk in it, if not by equality of life, then by likeness of character, the practice of piety, and imitation of virtues. Since we could not see him in his own nature, man appeared among men, a ray in a cloud, light in concealment, affection in effect, the Word in flesh, divinity in humanity. Follow, then, him who for you grew pale in death, was troubled on the cross, had his face smeared with spittle, was struck with lashes, was beaten on the head with a reed, and had his entrails stretched upon the cross. If you ponder these things, speak them, correct, exhort, and warn against them, you keep the way to heaven. On this way the sign is a standard, and “a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night” [Note: [Col. 0097] Exod. 13.]. An example is a sign for one journeying; a standard for one fighting; a cloud for one making progress; fire for one labouring; an example for one working. A sign drives away deception [Col. 0097B]; a standard arms for battle; a cloud provides shade; fire supplies the service of light. An example is the pattern of virtues and the spectacle of action.

On this way there are three dwelling-places, that we may make a journey of three days in the wilderness. Hear: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0097] John 14.]; and fittingly: “In him we live and move and are” [Note: [Col. 0097] Acts 17.]. These three correspond to the three preceding words: by life we live, on the way we move, in truth we stand. There are three dwelling-places: the first is the way, the second truth, the third life.

Concerning the first dwelling-place. The first dwelling-place is repentance. It has three upper rooms. The first is in renunciation, the second in frugality, the third in discipline. Renunciation concerns what is commanded; frugality, superfluities; discipline, necessities. Renunciation is a matter of necessity [Col. 0097C]; frugality a matter of choice; discipline a matter of freedom. Therefore discipline cuts away lawful and necessary things; frugality removes unlawful and superfluous things; renunciation removes forbidden and ruinous things. In the first, wrongdoing is condemned; in the second, desire is corrected; in the third, the merit of greater grace is accumulated. But not all can ascend higher, because there are differences among those who travel, distinctions among those who arrive, and degrees among those who ascend. Let one to whom the ability to enter the second or third upper room has not been given humbly take a place in the first. Let him remain on the first step until he hears: “Friend, go up higher” [Note: [Col. 0097] Luke 14.]. Therefore, if you have put to death ruinous things, you have entered the first upper room of the first dwelling-place; if you have cut away superfluities, you have ascended to the second; if you strive also to restrain necessary things [Col. 0097D], you have been received into the third.

There follows the second dwelling-place and its three upper rooms. Its first level is rectitude of action; its second is called purity of meditation. For it is not enough that what is outside be cleansed, unless the inward things are purified. This is done by guarding the heart, as Solomon says: “With all vigilance guard, or keep, your heart, because from it life proceeds” [Note: [Col. 0097] Prov. 4.]. This guarding is divided in three, because the mind is attacked in its thoughts by a threefold battle-line of vices. It is attacked by pleasant things, deceptive things, and harsh things. Every [Col. 0098A] holy thought, when assailed, succumbs either by bending under harmful sweetness, being confounded by error, or being cast down by the harshness of temptation. Against these three are opposed sweetness, truth, and strength. Spiritual sweetness attracts; truth instructs; strength defends. Sweetness produces joy; truth enlightens the understanding; strength supplies aid: joy, that you may burn fervently; understanding, that you may examine; aid, that you may not succumb.

Many receive this sweetness from the Holy Spirit, “but do not know whence it comes or whither it goes” [Note: [Col. 0097] John 3.]. For they do not know whether they have received it to their benefit or detriment. Therefore, if, after sweetness has been received, the discipline of truth is not observed, an entrance is opened to errors; and thus, when the Spirit departs, sweetness is withdrawn at the same time. Thus “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the feigned and withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding” [Col. 0098B] [Note: [Col. 0097] Wis. 1.]. Therefore sweetness must be kindled by the light of truth, so that you may rejoice alike in the gift received and recognize the power of the giver. Yet some have both, but are not strong in temptation. “Woe to those who have lost endurance” [Note: [Col. 0097] Ecclus. 2.]. These are “the sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, who turned back in the day of battle” [Note: [Col. 0097] Ps. 77.]. For they are “like a leaf carried away by the wind” [Note: [Col. 0097] Job 13.], and “like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0097] Ps. 1.]. It is therefore better to have true thoughts than pleasant ones, and better to have thoughts true and strong than pleasant and true. Where these three are, there is the anointing of the Holy Spirit; where they are not, there intervene enticement, seduction, and fickleness. Therefore let thought be sweet, that it may please; true, that it may not deceive [Col. 0098C]; strong, that it may endure. Let it be sweet, lest it embitter or defile; true, that it may earn reward; strong, because a thought cannot be lovable unless it delights, praiseworthy unless it purifies, or reward-worthy unless it perseveres.

For these three reasons it is said that the Holy Spirit has knowledge of speech, because he makes those whom he fills possess it. The Holy Spirit speaks to thoughts with three voices, and whoever searches him out becomes a hearer of his tongue. The first is: “Receive what is offered; for it is sweet.” The second: “Understand the gift and the cause of the gift which is offered; for it is deep.” The third: “Guard the gift and the understanding of the gift which is offered; for it is most powerful.” The first is the infusion of sweetness; the second, the inquiry of truth [Col. 0098D]; the third, the perseverance of both in the recompense of strength. The soul then has knowledge of the voice when, in the fullness of anointing, it rejoices, is enlarged, and strengthened—sweetly, faithfully, happily, firmly. Thus the instructed mind hears the Spirit’s speech, receives his presence by feeling, examining, and guarding, lest it be deceived by some seduction. In the first upper room we are refreshed by what is set before us; in the second we examine it; in the third we labour, that delight may be continual and comprehension of what is set before us certain.

Concerning the third dwelling-place. Having attained the first dwelling-place [Col. 0099A], namely rectitude of work, and the second, namely purity of meditation, let us approach the third, namely the sublimity of contemplation. The body ministers to outward things; the soul orders inward things; the spirit contemplates higher things. Thus spirit, soul, and body shall be saved for the day of the Lord, if the spirit tastes heavenly things, the soul meditates on rational things, and the body orders lower things in its senses. There are bodily visions, imaginative visions, and intellectual visions. Bodily visions are those through which bodies are seen; imaginative visions, those through which likenesses of bodies are viewed; intellect concerns things which lack dimensions.

Among intellectual things, some in their own nature have neither increase nor decrease, such as number, measure, and weight. Others occur temporally and are variable, such as faith, hope, and charity; others naturally decline and are variable, such as reason, intelligence, and memory; others, if it may be said, are everlasting: God’s power and divinity. The following is the rationale of the first three [Col. 0099B]. In the first, arrangement is instituted; in the second, the inspiration of visitation; in the third, rational knowledge. Arrangement concerns things made; inspiration, those redeemed; knowledge, natural things. In the last, nature is adorned; in the middle, grace is received; in the first, the natural life of all things is considered. In the last, the soul understands the honour by which it was made in the image of God, who made it [Note: [Col. 0099] Gen. 1.]; in the middle, it reveres the grace by which it is formed after the likeness of him who chose it; in the first, it contemplates the pattern according to which, and through which, God ordered all things [Note: [Col. 0099] Wis. 11.] and re-formed it.

The fourth reality is God the Trinity: three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Contemplation of this alone is as precious as it is rare. This division is threefold. For God is one way in himself, another way in the image which he himself made, and another way in the creatures which he himself made. In this dwelling-place the first upper room is the vision of the divine substance in natures; the second, the vision in the image; the third, the vision in himself. Therefore, if spiritual eyes are raised there, the beloved is found, insofar as our weakness is granted in this exile. Afterwards, however, he shall be found more fully by the blessed and seen in the kingdom. “For now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears [Col. 0099D], we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” [Note: [Col. 0099] 1 John 3.] in his glory. Thus according to the first dwelling-place the Creator will be seen and found. 17 According to the second, the lover will be found; according to the third, the Saviour will be found. This will take place when death has been swallowed up in victory [Note: [Col. 0099] 1 Cor. 15.]. When this is seen, perfect glory will be ours. But meanwhile, to see him in this exile, at least “through a mirror and in an enigma” [Note: [Col. 0099] 1 Cor. 13.], is for us a great consolation and a relief upon the way.

Accordingly, we must note the ways in which he presents himself to us in this song. [Col. 0100A] We observe him presenting himself under four aspects. At times, like a bashful bridegroom, he seeks the secret embraces of the holy soul and delights in kisses. Hence she cries: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” But now he displays himself in oil and ointments as a physician, for delicate and infirm souls. Hence they cry: “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments.” Now, like a traveler, he keeps company alike with the bride and the young woman, relieving the weariness of the road by sweet conversation, so that they may eagerly say: “Draw me after you.” Likewise: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?” [Note: [Col. 0099] Luke 24.] At times he comes forward like a very wealthy householder, intending to show his riches. Hence: “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices” [Col. 0100B] [Note: [Col. 0099] Song 5.]. And thus he brought the bride into his secrets. No wonder: “The heart of her husband trusts in her.” [Note: [Col. 0099] Prov. 31.] He redeemed her when poor, proved her faithful, and embraces her as lovable. In kisses he is affectionate and gentle; in oil and ointments merciful and abounding in the tender bowels of pity and compassion; on the road cheerful and gracious, full of grace and consolation; in the display of riches he shows himself a lavish rewarder: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.”

The Bride says: “Show me your ways, O Lord,” [Note: [Col. 0099] Ps. 24.] that is, righteousness. Hence elsewhere: “He led me along the paths of righteousness.” [Note: [Col. 0099] Ps. 22.] Likewise another says: “Tell me why you judge me thus.” [Note: [Col. 0099] Job 10.] The inquiring soul never ceases to seek these three things of God: righteousness, judgment, and the place of the bridegroom’s glorious dwelling [Col. 0100C]—as the road on which it walks, the caution by which it walks, and the abode to which it walks. Of this the Prophet says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” [Note: [Col. 0099] Ps. 26.]

Rightly does the bride seek these three things: that, through the beauty of righteousness, she may be beautiful; through knowledge of judgments, cautious; through desire for the bridegroom’s glory, chaste. For it befits the bride of the Lord to be beautiful, learned, and chaste. And this is the bride’s final petition. At noon the sun is higher, hotter, and brighter. The Lord lies down in the hearts of those who remain steadfast in an exalted purpose of holiness. He is fed in those who burn with the ardor of heavenly longing. He is loved by those who shine with the brightness of heavenly wisdom. Likewise, he lies down upon the bed [Col. 0100D] that is a pure conscience; he pastures in the inner chamber of the heart, where virtues abound; he is loved in the garden of spiritual affection, where grace delights in devotions as though in blooming flowers of spring.

Likewise, noon is threefold, according to the threefold interpretation of this name. The first is the brightness of contemplatives still laboring in this pilgrimage; the second, the brightness of saints who, stripped of their bodies, still remain in expectation; the third, that of angels and saints who, once the resurrection has been accomplished, will see God more clearly than those of the second noon, because they will see face to face.

The first is called *meridies* (“noon”), as though *moerens dies*, “a mourning day,” [Col. 0101A] because in it we both mourn our sins and earn growth in the virtues. The second is called *meridies* as though *medidies*, that is, “midday,” because its brightness is clearer than the first but dimmer than the third. The third is called *meridies* as though *mera dies*, “a pure day,” because it is brighter than the rest.

It should be noted that the Beloved is fed in us by taking delight, and lies down in us by resting. He is fed in good will; he is fed in works of mercy; he is fed in chastity. Of the first: “My food is to do the will of him, the Father, who sent me.” [Note: [Col. 0101] John 4.] Of the second: “I was hungry and you gave me food.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Matt. 25.] Of the third: “He who pastures among the lilies, enclosed,” [Note: [Col. 0101] Song 6.] etc.; likewise: “He who pastures among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Song 2.]

Likewise, he lies down among those characterized by charity; he lies down among the humble and quiet; he lies down [Col. 0101B] in the sanctification of unity. Of the first: “If anyone loves me, he keeps my word, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.” [Note: [Col. 0101] John 14.] Of the second: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, unless upon the humble and quiet man who trembles at my words?” [Note: [Col. 0101] Isa. 66.] Of the third: “Likewise I rested in the sanctified city.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Sir. 24.]

But in the second and third noons we shall be pastured by him and rest in him. Hence they shall pasture and recline, and there will be none to terrify them. In the first, when Abraham was at the entrance of his tent in the very heat of noon, he saw three angels and fed them beneath the oak of Mamre: namely, with unleavened bread, that is, chastity of soul and body; and sobriety; and milk, that is, simplicity of intention; and butter, that is, the richness of devotion; and a fatted calf, [Col. 0101C] that is, the cheerful sacrifice of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0101] Gen. 18.]

In the second, Jacob, in the very heat of the day—that is, at noon—watered his sheep in channels, where before the eyes of the mating sheep he placed rods of poplar, almond, and plane trees, partly stripped of bark, so that they might conceive offspring like them. [Note: [Col. 0101] Gen. 30.] Jacob is that good shepherd who laid down his soul for his sheep [Note: [Col. 0101] John 10.] and deigned to die for his flock, in order to supplant our vices. But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture. [Note: [Col. 0101] Ps. 78.] The waters are the heavenly joys of the saints. Hence: “The rush of the river gladdens the city of God.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Ps. 45.] He leads us to them whenever he raises us to contemplate those joys.

There he places three sorts of rods, that we may produce similar offspring: namely, the patience [Col. 0101D] and humility of the saints, the charity of Christ, and the purity of angels. The first is designated by poplar rods, because through crushing the poplar yields an ointment by which swellings of wounds are reduced. This is the humility and patience of the saints. Christ’s charity is signified by almond rods, because milk is pressed from them for nourishment, and it is healing food. For charity heals sins and nourishes little ones. By plane-tree rods is signified the purity of angels, because plane trees bear no fruit. They are partly stripped of bark because “we know in part, and we prophesy in part.” [Col. 0102A] [Note: [Col. 0101] 1 Cor. 13.]

David answered Achish concerning this threefold noon: “Where have you raided today?” And he replied: “Against the south of Judah, against the south of Jerahmeel, and against the south of the Kenites.” [Note: [Col. 0101] 1 Sam. 27.] The first is the noon of Judah, whose name means “confession,” in which he plunders who, seeing his own sin, rescues himself from the devil through confession. The second is the noon of Jerahmeel, in which he plunders who, through God’s mercy and through his works, is transferred from this misery to rest; for Jerahmeel means “mercy of God.” There is a mercy of God by which we are here freed from sin. But there is a greater mercy of God in heaven, by which souls are freed from this exile. Hence: “O Lord, your mercy is in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Ps. 35.]

He plunders toward the noon of the Kenites who here [Col. 0102B] plunders in such a way that, in a glorified body, he may rejoice before God in the kingdom. For *Ceni* means “my nest,” or “my treasury,” or “my possession.” Of the first: “The sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest where she may lay her young.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Ps. 83.] Of the second: “Lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Matt. 6.] Of the third: “They shall possess double in their land.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Isa. 61.]

The third noon is called *mera dies*, “pure day,” because then God will be seen purely—that God whom religious people now see through a mirror and in an enigma [Note: [Col. 0101] 1 Cor. 13.]—and in four ways. We see his nature and lament our own misery. Abraham saw thus when he said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Gen. 18.] Second, we see his purity, consider the uncleanness of our sins, and blush, like Isaiah: “Woe [Col. 0102C] is me,” he says, “for I am a man of unclean lips,” and this after I saw the Lord seated upon a lofty throne. [Note: [Col. 0101] Isa. 6.] And Job: “I had heard of you by hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Job 42.] Therefore I reprove myself and do penance in dust and ashes.

Third, we see his riches and groan over our own poverty.
