Hence, when Daniel had seen the angel, he said: “I fell to the ground, and no spirit remained in me, nor had I any strength left.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Dan. 10.] And Ezekiel’s living creatures: “When there was a voice above the firmament which was over their heads, they stood and lowered their wings,” [Note: [Col. 0101] Ezek. 1.] —[uncertain printed reading: “le le. l. humiliantia” (sic)]—humbling themselves after hearing of riches and recognizing their own poverty. Fourth, we see him as though face to face, when we see him merciful and [Col. 0102D] concerned for our salvation, as Jacob saw him: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Gen. 32.]

Behold the noon at which Joseph is to eat bread with his brothers, that is, Christ, as he promised: “You are those who have remained with me in my trials, and I appoint for you a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.” [Note: [Col. 0101] Luke 22.] Joseph is interpreted “increase.” For Christ was increased in our corruption, in age and wisdom; in the resurrection, in the glory of immortality; in [Col. 0103A] the ascension, in exaltation at the Father’s right hand; in the general resurrection, when the Church militant will be gathered to him. The bride desires to see him such in this pilgrimage when she says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves.” For without the vision of him she can easily go astray.

“Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

[THO.] The companions may be called heretics, because they bear about either the confession of his name or his mysteries. His companions are also called any believers whatsoever, even if evil: schismatics, thieves, hirelings, Simoniacs, and all such persons. Whoever conforms himself to their corrupt doctrines or deeds imitates their flocks by wandering, ignorant of what in them pleases or displeases God. Therefore the bride asks to be illuminated [Col. 0103B] by that noonday light in which the Beloved dwells above, because every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights. [Note: [Col. 0103] Jas. 1.] There is the unchangeable noon.

Three kinds of Christ’s companions are named: by name, not by divine power; in number, not in merit; in body, not in mind. The first are heretics, the second schismatics, the third Catholics who live wickedly. Or Christ is said to have companions, namely the virtues. But because vices disguise themselves in the respectable appearance of virtues, she fears this wandering. For guile imitates prudence, rashness fortitude, obstinacy liberty, restlessness diligence, and sloth the gravity of good character.

Wandering has several outlets: of thought, speech, and action. David says of the wandering of the heart: “My heart has forsaken me.” [Note: [Col. 0103] Ps. 39.] Solomon says of the wandering of speech: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue.” [Note: [Col. 0103] Prov. 18.] And James: “No human being can tame the tongue.” [Note: [Col. 0103] Jas. 3.] Isaiah says of the wandering of deeds: “Strengthen the weak hands and the feeble knees.” [Note: [Col. 0103] Isa. 35.]

These, like Cain [Note: [Col. 0103] Gen. 4.], are wanderers through disordered desire and fugitives through a guilty conscience. Thus the saying of Cain aptly applies to them: “Whoever finds me will kill me.” [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid.] For whatever temptation attacks a mind deserted by divine counsel overthrows it. Likewise, heretics make their flocks wander through doctrine, schismatics through conspiracy, and wickedly living Catholics through the example of evil conduct. The flocks of the first follow into error of faith, those of the second into disturbance of peace, [Col. 0103D] and those of the third into moral dissolution.

Ishmael, separated from his brother Isaac, with whom he was playing, they say, otherwise than was proper [Note: [Col. 0103] Gen. 21.], represents the first, that is, the heretics. For it is said that he compelled Isaac to worship his idols. Cain, who first disturbed peace by killing his brother [Note: [Col. 0103] Gen. 4.], represents the second, that is, schismatics. Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, who left the camp of Israel to see the women of the region, and whom Shechem son of Hamor seized and violated [Note: [Col. 0103] Gen. 34.], represents the third, that is, those who live wickedly.

Three others are called wanderers according to a threefold interpretation of this name. [Col. 0104A] The first is called *vagus*, “wandering,” as though *varia agens*, “doing diverse things,” namely by corrupting the unity of faith. The second, the schismatic, is called *vagus*, that is, *vas agonis*, “a vessel of struggle,” while he disturbs peace by his conflicts. The third, the wickedly living Catholic, is called *vagus*, that is, *vana gustans*, “tasting vain things,” while in thought, speech, and action he tastes the vanity of the world.

Likewise, I know that someone has said that demons are rightly called companions, because they transform themselves into an angel of light [Note: [Col. 0103] 2 Cor. 11.]. We know that by their cunning devices they deceive human beings, often transfer Christ’s flocks into their own flocks, and make them their own. Therefore the ancient Fathers cried out with great longing that the Sun of righteousness might rise for them, thus: “O rising Splendor of eternal light and Sun of righteousness, come; and illumine him who sits in darkness and the shadow of death.”

[Col. 0104B] Three persons, very unlike one another, meet us: the devil, Adam, and Christ. The first was the beginning of sin, the second of human misery, the third of redemption and grace. The first was falling; the second an inhabitant of eternal light; the third one who raises up. The first kindled the sun of malice; the second experienced the sun of tribulation and distress; the third is the Sun of righteousness. The first lost the brightness of the angelic host; the second descended into the darkness of a miserable lot; the third came to enlighten those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. [Note: [Col. 0103] Luke 1.]

Thus the devil first fell in three ways: he fell from heaven, fell in the world, and falls into hell. First, because of pride; second, because of Christ’s victory; third, he falls into Gehenna. Isaiah recalls this threefold fall as follows: “How you have fallen, Lucifer, [Col. 0104C] from heaven, you who rose in the morning!” [Note: [Col. 0103] Isa. 14.] Behold the first. “You have fallen to the earth, you who wounded the nations!” [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid.] Behold the second. And shortly afterward he says: “You shall be dragged down to hell.” [Note: [Col. 0103] Ibid.] Behold the third.

Accordingly, the first teaches us not to be proud, lest we sin against God; the second, not to envy, lest we sin against our neighbor; and the third, not to be obstinate in ourselves, lest we descend into hell. He was the robber of inward light. This inward light is human reason, illuminated by God in a threefold way: knowledge, understanding, and wisdom. Knowledge distinguishes the uses of temporal things; understanding philosophizes concerning invisible things; wisdom knows and loves God. These are the three lights. [Col. 0104D] Of them it was said: “God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars.” [Note: [Col. 0103] Gen. 1.]

But the devil stole knowledge when he caused Adam to turn use into misuse, understanding into ignorance, and wisdom into forgetfulness of God. Tobias instructed his son concerning knowledge as follows: “If you have much, give abundantly; if little, strive gladly to share even that.” [Note: [Col. 0103] Tob. 4.] And: “He who ministers well will acquire for himself a good rank.” [Note: [Col. 0103] 1 Tim. 3.] David, concerning understanding: “And now, O kings, understand; receive instruction, you who judge the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0103] Ps. 2.] And the Lord to his disciples: [Col. 0105A] “Are you also still without understanding?” [Note: [Col. 0105] Matt. 15.] The Apostle, concerning wisdom: “Set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Col. 3.]

See how the devil is a robber of inward light. It follows how he kindles the sun of malice. This sun of malice inflames excessively, dries grievously, and shines inopportunely: it inflames by temptation, dries up devotion, and shines by ostentation. Against the first David promises us: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Ps. 120.] To the second belongs that Gospel seed of which the Lord says: “When the sun rose, it was dried up, because it had no moisture.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Matt. 13.] Of the third Job says: “If I have looked upon the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Job 31.]

Through this sun the devil himself lost the brightness of the angelic host. In opposition to the fact [Col. 0105B] that he sinned by pride against God, “Christ emptied himself,” [Note: [Col. 0105] Phil. 2.] and by his example teaches us not to sin against our neighbor. Otherwise, “it would be better for us that a millstone be hung around our neck and we be drowned in the deep.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Matt. 18.] Nor should we be obstinate like him, because the Lord “has brandished his sword, stretched his bow, and made it ready,” [Note: [Col. 0105] Ps. 7.] in order to “send such persons into outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Matt. 22.] Thus the first, the devil, was falling.

It follows that the first man was dying through him. Hence in the Apocalypse: “His name was Death.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Rev. 6.] Therefore a human being dies temporally; dies spiritually and beneficially; and dies spiritually and damnably. First, he dies by the general law of dying; second, he dies to sin; third, he dies to righteousness. Christ assumed the first, taught the second, and condemned the third. Of the first, one frequently hears in Genesis: “He lived so many years and died.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Gen. 5.] Of the second: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Col. 3.] Of the third: “The soul that sins shall itself die.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Ezek. 18.]

The devil, therefore, was falling irreparably; but man was dying reparably. Christ, the Rising One, came so that the latter—not the former—might mercifully be restored to life. The former was the robber of inward light; the latter an inhabitant of eternal light. Therefore the Splendor of eternal light came. The eternal light inhabited by humankind is full of miseries. [Note: [Col. 0105] Job 14.] For it has interruption, temptation, and deception: interruption [Col. 0105D] by the recurrence of nights; temptation because a crowd of objects of desire comes upon it; deception because human judgment is often mistaken. By the first it fails; by the second it kills; by the third it is not sufficient for investigating adversity.

Against the first, one prayed, saying:

> And may the night breathe forth a new light,  
> which no night may interrupt,  
> and may it shine with unceasing faith.

Against the second, David says: “You light my lamp, O Lord my God; enlighten my darkness, for in you I shall be delivered from temptation.” [Col. 0106A] [Note: [Col. 0105] Ps. 17.] Against the third he says: “Send forth your light and your truth,” [Note: [Col. 0105] Ps. 42.] that is, your true light, because ours is vain.

Seeing these three things, Job said: “Why is light given to the wretched, and life to those in bitterness of soul, who await death and it does not come, as though digging for treasure?” [Note: [Col. 0105] Job 3.] The first kindles the sun of malice. But this man experiences the sun of tribulation and distress. This sun kindles the heat of carnal temptations, the vexations of persecutions, and weariness of life. The first draws to defilement, the second to impatience, the third to acedia.

Of the first it is said in the Law: “Whoever has been defiled by a nocturnal emission shall not return to the camp until sunset,” [Note: [Col. 0105] Deut. 23.] [Col. 0106B] that is, until temptations cease. As a figure of the second: “The sun burned fiercely upon the head of Jonah the prophet.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Jonah 4.] Hence he became impatient. As a figure of the third, the sun heated the head of the boy, son of the Shunammite woman, who cried: “My head hurts.” [Note: [Col. 0105] 2 Kings 4.]

Elijah experienced these three when he was under the juniper tree: [Note: [Col. 0105] 1 Kings 19.] he fled carnal temptation when he fled from Jezebel; persecution by the pricks of the juniper; and the third when he asked that his soul might die. At the rising of the Sun of righteousness the world is made young again; in its splendor it flowers anew; when the sun appears it grows warm again. It is made young again by the emergence of the newness of things; flowers anew by the expulsion of the multiplicity of things; grows warm again when the night’s chill is driven out. For the Church is renewed in Christ’s Incarnation, flowers anew in the resurrection, and grows warm again in the ascension: in the Incarnation, [Col. 0106C] forgiveness of sins; in the resurrection, joy; in the ascension, the grace of the sevenfold Spirit sent down.

Of the first: “Behold, a great prophet will come, and he himself will renew Jerusalem.” And: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Rev. 21.] And the angel: “Behold, I make all things new.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Ibid.] Of the second: “The almond tree will flower, the locust will grow fat, and the caper berry will be scattered.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Eccl. 12.] “And I saw a mighty angel descending from heaven, and the whole earth was illumined by his glory.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Rev. 18.] Of the third: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it burn?” [Note: [Col. 0105] Luke 12.] Hence: “An angel stood beside the altar of the temple, holding a golden censer in his hand; and he filled it from the fire of the altar and cast it upon the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Rev. 8.]

[Col. 0106D] It should be noted that this sun rises from us, rises in us, and rises for us: from us corporeally, in us spiritually, and for us causally. Corporeally and temporally, whence he endured the defect of death; spiritually, by inspiring the affection of his love; causally, because his rising was the cause by which we obtained the effect of salvation. Of the first: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Eccl. 1.] Of the second: “The sun rose, and they were gathered together and were placed in their dens.” [Note: [Col. 0105] Ps. 103.] They will be gathered [Col. 0107A] into the unity of faith [Note: [Col. 0107] Eph. 4.] and placed in the dens of their hearts, resting in a good conscience. Of the third: “For you who fear my name the Sun of righteousness shall rise.” [Note: [Col. 0107] Mal. 4.]

He is likewise the creator of external light, the inspirer of inward light, and the splendor of eternal light: of external light for seeing and using creatures; of inward light for the salvation of souls; of eternal light for the glory of the blessed. Of the first he said: “Let there be light, and there was light.” [Note: [Col. 0107] Gen. 1.] Of the second: “They will go in the light of your arrows, in the brightness of your flashing spear.” [Note: [Col. 0107] Hab. 3.] These arrows are various movements of charity in the heart. Their light is the spirit of understanding. Of the third: “Perpetual light shall shine upon your saints, O Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0107] Ps. 129.] Likewise it is said of God that “he alone possesses immortality and inhabits inaccessible light.” [Note: [Col. 0107] 1 Tim. 6.]

We see the first in birth; the second through a mirror and in an enigma; the third we shall see in truth. The first is beneath the sun; the second in the sun; the third above the sun. Of the first Solomon says: [Col. 0107B] “I saw all things that are under the sun, and behold, all is vanity.” [Note: [Col. 0107] Eccl. 1.] Of the second: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.” [Note: [Col. 0107] 1 Cor. 13.] Of the third: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” [Note: [Col. 0107] John 1.] Christ is the splendor of this light, since by the brightness of his miracles he shows that this is above. Christ is also called the Sun of righteousness. [Note: [Col. 0107] Mal. 4.]

This righteousness grants, distributes, and repays. It grants gratuitous gifts, distributes gifts already granted, and repays rewards for merits. Of the first: “You granted him the desire of his heart.” [Col. 0107C] [Note: [Col. 0107] Ps. 20.] Of the second: “Distribute his houses, that you may recount them to another generation.” [Note: [Col. 0107] Ps. 47.] And the Apostle: “If I distribute all my possessions into the bosom of the poor but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.” [Note: [Col. 0107] 1 Cor. 13.] Of the third: “Repay your servant; give me life, and I shall keep your words.” [Note: [Col. 0107] Ps. 118.]

By the first, God “justifies the ungodly”; [Note: [Col. 0107] Rom. 4.] by the second, “he distributes to each as he wills,” such as kinds of tongues and interpretations of utterances; [Note: [Col. 0107] 1 Cor. 12.] by the third, God will render a reward for the labors of his saints. [Note: [Col. 0107] Wis. 10.] The first is the Sun of righteousness because it shines in the devout heart; the second shines upon the world; the third will shine in judgment. The first leads a person out of the darkness of sin; the second, out of the darkness of ignorance; the third, out of the shadow of death, that is, worldly misery.

[Col. 0107D] “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

[CARD.] As though she said: “O my son, whom my soul loves with special affection, tell me at noon—that is, in full light and manifest knowledge—where you pasture, that is, where you fulfill the office of shepherd, and where you lie down, that is, where you make the sheep lie down, just as you say through Ezekiel: ‘I will pasture my sheep, and I will make them lie down.’” [Note: [Col. 0107] Ezek. 34.] And concerning the office of shepherd which he performs, he adds: “I will seek what was lost; I will bring back what had been cast away; I will bind up what was broken; I will strengthen what was weak; and I will preserve what is strong and fat.” [Col. 0108A] [Note: [Col. 0107] Ibid.]

Or thus: “Tell me where you pasture,” namely where you feed your people “with the bread of life and understanding and give them to drink the water of saving wisdom,” [Note: [Col. 0107] Sir. 15.] all of which takes place in the Church of the faithful. “Tell me where you lie down,” that is, in whose minds you rest, because “foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man scarcely has where to lay his head.” [Note: [Col. 0107] Matt. 8.] I seek all these things so diligently lest, without possessing knowledge and discernment concerning them, I, uncertain and wavering as to those upon whom I ought to expend the care of maternal guardianship, begin to wander and spend my labors after wandering flocks—not yours, but those of your companions. By Christ’s companions he means heretics, who steal sheep from [Col. 0108B] Christ’s flock and lead them astray and wandering through errors and byways.

“If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and go after the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds.”

[THO.] As though the Beloved said: “Why do you complain, as though in temptation you could be abandoned by me, and as though you had been blackened by persecutions while keeping our vineyard—although I have already made you beautiful by baptism and have decreed that you should be made more beautiful by the testing of tribulations? But if you do not know these things, nor remember that no one ‘will be crowned unless he has contended lawfully,’ [Note: [Col. 0107] 2 Tim. 2.] depart from my fellowship and go after the tracks of the flocks—that is, imitate the various actions of those who wander—and pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds; that is, nourish lost [Col. 0108C] hearers, following the teachings of foolish masters. For I commanded you to pasture my lambs with the word of doctrine, and to suffer adversity for them and even to die. Therefore, if you do not know that you are betrothed to me on this condition, pasture your kids with the wandering teachings of other masters.”

Because she had said, “Tell me, you whom my soul loves,” the bride wished to advance to contemplation of God, which she could not attain unless she first had knowledge of herself. She is here invited to seek it when it is said: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful,” etc. We return to self-knowledge in three ways. First, when we recall our sins to memory and reflect how deformed we were in them. Hence David says: “My iniquities [Col. 0108D] have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me. My wounds have rotted and festered because of my foolishness.” [Note: [Col. 0107] Ps. 37.] And hence Paul says: “I am the least of the apostles, not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.” [Note: [Col. 0107] 1 Cor. 15.]

The second way is when we recognize our misery, saying with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” [Note: [Col. 0107] Rom. 7.] The first humbles us through the memory of sin; this one makes us sad because of the condition of present wretchedness. The former makes us submissive; [Col. 0109A] the latter vigilant. Nor is it surprising, when a person sees himself surrounded by dangers, subject to the mockery of demons, exposed to the insults of wicked persons, open to the snares of the deceitful, worn down by temptations, driven by prosperity, and driven or urged by adversities toward deadly sorrow.

The third way is when we contemplate that dignity by which we were created in the likeness and image of God. [Note: [Col. 0109] Gen. 1.] The Prophet rebukes the negligent soul, wandering far from this contemplation, as follows: “What has happened, Israel, that you are in the land of enemies? You have grown old in a foreign land; you have dwelt—or have been numbered—with the dead; you have been reckoned with those who are in hell.” [Note: [Col. 0109] Baruch 3.]

For our land is the remembrance of our Creator, in which we sow the seeds of faith and conduct [Col. 0109B] and from which we reap the fruit of divine contemplation and eternal blessedness. The foreign land that belongs to enemies is called forgetfulness of God. Therefore one is in the land of enemies who, by sinning, forgets God. One grows old in the foreign land when sin is drawn into habit. One dwells with the dead when one delights in the act. One is reckoned with those in hell when the magnitude of sin leads one into despair.

For the soul to have knowledge of its own beauty, it must consider these three things: dignity, knowledge, and virtue. Dignity, by which it may rejoice that it surpasses the other animals; knowledge, by which it knows and recognizes that it possesses this same dignity, yet does not possess it from itself; virtue, by which it strives to seek God, in whose image it was made [Note: [Col. 0109] Gen. 1.], [Col. 0109C] and, having found him, to cling to him. If the soul is ignorant of these things, it does not know itself, but goes after the tracks of the flocks—that is, of worldly thoughts—or of flocks, that is, of deceived souls. Concerning these, it was said above in section 19: “Beside the tents of the shepherds.” Tents belong to those who are passing through; houses, to those who remain. Therefore, tents are the pleasures of the world, which pass away; or our bodies devoted to pleasures. Their shepherds are those who feed them well, or invite others to this by their example. Beside them kids are fed—that is, wanton impulses. Or the shepherds are heresiarchs, beside whose tents, that is, conventicles, kids are fed—that is, sinners.

“Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared [Col. 0109D] to the senseless beasts” [Note: [Col. 0109] Ps. 48]. He failed to know two things: namely, that he is clay, and in this he was compared to beasts; and he failed to know God’s judgment, by which a human being, not a beast, will be punished. Therefore he goes after the tracks of the flocks. The first stage of a soul’s departure from God is not to know itself and not to know God’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0109] Isa. 28]; the second is to go forth from the spirit into the vices of the flesh, from the goods of the soul to worldly desires, from the inward repose of the mind to the noise and burdens of the world; the third is to follow the tracks of the flocks, because one who is now likened to a beast in wantonness will be worse than a beast in punishment.

Relevant to this self-knowledge [Col. 0110A] is the fact that “Moses made a bronze basin from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle” [Note: [Col. 0109] Exod. 38]. Holy women are holy souls, which keep watch at the entrance of the tabernacle—that is, toward contemplation of the heavenly homeland, which is the tabernacle of the blessed. Hence: “We shall enter into his tabernacle” [Note: [Col. 0109] Ps. 131]. From their mirrors—that is, from their contemplations—he made a bronze basin, in which the priests washed; that is, he gathered an abundance of tears from their contemplations. More will be said below about these mirrors. Solomon says of these contemplatives: “The path of the righteous, like a shining light, goes forth and increases unto the perfect day” [Note: [Col. 0109] Prov. 4].

There is a path of deceivers, a path of the wicked, and a path of the righteous. The first overreaches like a deceptive light [Col. 0110B]; the second falls upon one like a flattering light; the third goes forth like a shining light. The first promises false rest; the second entices by the appearance of the world; the third increases unto the perfect day. Of the first: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path” [Note: [Col. 0109] Gen. 40]. And Job says: “Consider the paths of Theman” [Note: [Col. 0109] Job 6]. Theman means “the south,” namely dissolution of life. Saba means “a net,” that is, deception. This path overreaches. Hence: “Do not be less righteous” [Note: [Col. 0109] Eccl. 7]. Like a deceptive light, it promises false rest when “an angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light” [Note: [Col. 0109] II Cor. 11].

Of the second: “The path of the wicked is dark” [Note: [Col. 0109] Prov. 4]. The Lord meets them thus: “I will hedge up your way with thorns; I will fence it with a wall, and you shall not find your paths” [Note: [Col. 0109] Hos. 2]. This path advances like a flattering light. “Woe to those who call darkness [Col. 0110C] light, and light darkness” [Note: [Col. 0109] Isa. 5]. This light does not endure. Hence in Job: “Their light shall be taken away from the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0109] Job 38]. This is the light of this world which entices, “because the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light” [Note: [Col. 0109] Luke 16]. These have gone lame from their paths. Let us now return, therefore, to the path of the righteous.

But there is a righteous person who lives by faith [Note: [Col. 0109] Hab. 2], and there is a righteous person who is confident like a lion [Note: [Col. 0109] Prov. 8]. The first raises himself from earthly things; the second corrects one subject to him; the third loves intensely. The first enters a straight path; the second despises sudden death; the third longs for true life. The Lord leads the first by the path of the commandments, shows him the chief good, and gives him knowledge for discerning good and evil. Hence it is said:

[Col. 0110D] “The Lord led the righteous man by straight ways” [Note: [Col. 0109] Office of the Church]: behold the first; “and showed him the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid.]: behold the second; “and gave him the knowledge of holy things” [Note: [Col. 0109] Ibid.]: behold the third.

Of the first: “The path of the righteous is straight; the way of the righteous is straight for walking” [Note: [Col. 0109] Isa. 26]. Likewise: “Lead me in the path of your commandments, because I have desired it” [Note: [Col. 0109] Ps. 118]. The second sought what she asked for, saying: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves: where do you feed, where do you lie down at noon?” [Note: [Col. 0109] Song 1]. And Moses: “Show me yourself” [Note: [Col. 0109] Exod. 33]. Of knowledge: “I desired the knowledge of God more than a holocaust” [Note: [Col. 0109] Hos. 6]. As though he said: “If [Col. 0111A] the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come in the night, he would not permit his house to be broken into” [Note: [Col. 0111] Luke 12].

The second righteous person does not fear sudden death, for he sees a refuge prepared. God gives maturity for counsel and an undefiled life as a helpful example. Of the first: “If the righteous man is overtaken by death, he shall be at rest” [Note: [Col. 0111] Wis. 4]. Of the second: “Venerable old age is not that which is long-lasting, nor measured by the number of years” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid.]. Of the third: “An undefiled life is the age of old age” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid.].

The third already rejoices that he is under God’s protection, secure from the affliction of hell, and destined for the delight of peace. Of the first: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” [Note: [Col. 0111] Wis. 3]; of the second: “And the torment of malice shall not touch them” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid.]; of the third: “They seemed, in the eyes of the foolish, to die; but they are in peace” [Col. 0111B] [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid.].

These are the three Magi. The first offers myrrh, the second incense, the third gold [Note: [Col. 0111] Matt. 2]: myrrh, namely the bitterness of satisfaction; incense, the fragrance of a good reputation; gold, the brilliance of heavenly illumination. The first says: “My hands have dripped myrrh, and my fingers are full of the finest myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0111] Song 2]. No wonder, because “my beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me” [Note: [Col. 0111] Song 1]. To the second it is said: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” [Note: [Col. 0111] Song 4]. No wonder, because my beloved was “like sweet-smelling incense in the days of summer” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ecclus. 50]. On behalf of the third it is said: “The sun shone upon the golden and bronze shields, and the mountains gleamed from them” [Note: [Col. 0111] I Macc. 6]. For it is said of the beloved: “His head is finest gold” [Note: [Col. 0111] Song 5].

Therefore the first prays to God; the second worships God; the third honours the king. The first is in [Col. 0111C] hope, the second in faith, the third in charity. To the first it is said: “Be subject to the Lord and pray to him” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ps. 36]; for the second, the angel says to John in the Apocalypse: “Worship the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0111] Rev. 22]; for the third: “The king’s honour loves judgment” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ps. 38]. In the first, he is Redeemer; in the second, Justifier; in the third, Restorer.

The first therefore travels a hard path; the second, a straight path; the third, a peaceful path. The first walks in deficiency; the second in progress; the third in affection. Of the first: “For the words of your lips I have kept hard ways” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ps. 16]; of the second: “The path of the righteous is straight; the way of the righteous is straight for walking” [Note: [Col. 0111] Isa. 26]; of the third: “Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful” [Note: [Col. 0111] Prov. 3].

The first mourns his own negligence; [Col. 0111D] the second is very watchful in virtues; the third applies great diligence in preserving love. The first confesses his own ugliness; the second has solicitude as his companion; the third offers God the richness of devotion. Of the first: “The righteous man is the accuser of himself at the beginning” [Note: [Col. 0111] Prov. 18]; of the second: “The righteous gives his heart to rise early in the morning, to watch for the Lord who made him” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ecclus. 39]; of the third: “The offering of the righteous makes the altar rich” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ecclus. 35].

The first brings his gift to Christ’s feet; the second to his hands; [Col. 0112A] the third to his breast. The first is at the mercy-seat; the second in the refectory of the tabernacle; the third on Solomon’s golden couch. The first will find forgiveness; the second, the refreshment of the Comforter; the third, peace and devotion. The first says: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” [Note: [Col. 0111] Luke 13]. To the second Elijah is told: “Arise, eat, for the journey remaining for you is great” [Note: [Col. 0111] II Kings 29]; and the bride says: “Eat, friends, and be intoxicated, beloved ones” [Note: [Col. 0111] Song 5]. Of the third: “I sleep, but my heart watches” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid.]. Mary Magdalene received the first at the Lord’s feet [Note: [Col. 0111] Luke 10]; the apostles received the second at supper [Note: [Col. 0111] Matt. 26]; John the Evangelist, reclining on the Lord’s breast, received the third [Note: [Col. 0111] John 2].

Each of these is like the path of the righteous, which shines like light. This light is threefold: there is a light which announces Christ; there is one which leads to Christ; and there is one which glorifies Christ. It announces him as coming, leads to him as helper, and glorifies the one who has attained fulfilment in Christ. Of the first it is sung: “Light shall shine upon us today” [Note: [Col. 0111] Office of the Church]; of the second: “They shall go in the light of your arrows, in the brightness of your flashing spear” [Note: [Col. 0111] Hab. 3]. Of the third: “Everlasting light shall shine upon your saints, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0111] Office of the Church].

Hence we read that three lights appeared in connection with Christ. The first appeared to the shepherds at his birth, because “the glory of God shone around them” [Note: [Col. 0111] Luke 2]; the second at the appearance of the star. Hence: “The star flashes like a flame” [Note: [Col. 0111] Office of the Church]; the third at the Transfiguration. Hence: “His face shone like the sun” [Note: [Col. 0111] Matt. 17]. Through the first appeared Christ’s humanity; through the second, his goodness; through the third, his truth. His humanity diminished the devil’s power; his goodness [Col. 0112C] relieved our weakness; his truth showed his own blessedness. In the first he assumed our misery; in the second he showed us his mercy; in the third he will raise us to the excellence of angels.

Of the first light it is said: “The light shines in the darkness” [Note: [Col. 0111] John 1]; of the second: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid.]; of the third: “And the life was the light of men” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ibid.]. By the first, therefore, we were liberated from the devil and made joyful; by the second, redeemed by Christ; by the third, we shall be exalted. Of the first: “Light has risen for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ps. 96].

Hence we read: “There was a small city, and few men in it; and a mighty king besieged it. And one poor man was found in it [Col. 0112D] who delivered it by his wisdom; and afterwards no one remembered him” [Note: [Col. 0111] Eccl. 9]. This city is the world, in which Christ was born. Hence: “And a man was born in her” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ps. 86]; and: “He delivered the poor man from the powerful, and the poor man who had no helper” [Note: [Col. 0111] Ps. 71]. Concerning this it is said: “You appeared, O Christ, light from light.” Christ is called “anointed,” for he anoints us. Hence: “Your name is oil poured out.” In this light goodness appeared. “Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” [Note: [Col. 0111] Rom. 2].

Of the third: “Behold, the Lord will come, and all [Col. 0113A] his saints with him; and on that day there shall be great light” [Note: [Col. 0113] Office of the Church]. This light makes the perfect day toward which the path of the righteous increases. But it should be noted that there is a day made, a day unmade, a day remade, and a perfect day. The first was the infusion of grace; the second, the confusion arising from sin; the third, Christ’s incarnation; the fourth, the manifestation of glory. God inspired the first; sin darkened the second; Christ restored the third; from eternity God prepared the fourth for the righteous.

Of the first: “The light of one day shall be as the light of seven days” [Note: [Col. 0113] Isa. 30], namely, of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit which were in Adam. Of the second: “May the day perish on which I was born” [Note: [Col. 0113] Job 3]; and: “I did not desire the day of man; you know it” [Note: [Col. 0113] Jer. 17]; and: “My days declined like a shadow” [Note: [Col. 0113] Ps. 101]. Of the third: “Abraham rejoiced to see [Col. 0113B] my day; he saw it and was glad” [Note: [Col. 0113] John 8]. Of the fourth, in this place. Likewise: “And his throne is as the days of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0113] Ps. 88], in which “the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” [Note: [Col. 0113] Ps. 83]. May Christ Jesus himself bring us to it, “to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages” [Note: [Col. 0113] Rom. 16]. Amen.

*If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women.*

[CARD.] These are the words of the Son, who does not answer his mother’s question, but rather shows that the question has no place, because his mother can and ought to benefit not only those who are in the flock, but also those who are not of the flock; not only branches that are in the vine, but also those cut off from the vine; and can not only preserve grace for the righteous, but also obtain pardon for the guilty [Col. 0113C].

Therefore he says: *If you do not know yourself*—that is, “Do you not know yourself?” The word *yourself* should be pronounced emphatically, as though he were saying: “Do you not know that you are the star of the sea, who directs not only those who deserve well, but brings wandering and straying people back to the harbour of salvation? Do you not know that you are mediator between God and human beings, so that you may return sinners, who are at variance with your Son, to concord? Do you not know that you are the most beautiful among women, and therefore most powerful in interceding for sinners? Do you not know that, because of your beauty, your voice is sweet [Note: [Col. 0113] Song 2], desirable to me, and your prayers powerful?”

Hence below: “Let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet” [Note: [Col. 0113] Ibid.]; indeed it is sweet because “your face is beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0113] Ibid.]. Having heard and understood these things more fully, the mother, drawing and understanding much from the Son’s few words [Col. 0113D]—that she ought to direct her efforts not only to the righteous but also to sinners, not only to sheep in the fold but also to those who wander—immediately takes up prayer to the Son on their behalf, saying: “Go forth, and go after the tracks of the flocks, and feed your kids beside the tents of the shepherds.”

As if she said: “You have taught me, Son: I no longer fail to know myself as the star of the sea and the reconciler of wandering sheep. And because I have been taught this by you, I beg you, dearest Son, go forth from the confines of severity into the breadth of mercy, and follow the tracks of the flocks, so that you may carry fugitive and wandering sheep on your shoulders back to the fold” [Note: [Col. 0113] Luke 15], [Col. 0114A] “and feed with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” [Note: [Col. 0113] I Cor. 5] the sinners who are kids and children of uncleanness by fault, yet yours by nature; who are kids beside the tents of holy shepherds. For heretics, signified by these kids, are said to be beside the tents of holy shepherds because, although the admixture of falsehood prevents them from being in the tents of the Church, they are not altogether far from those tents, since they retain something of the doctrine of truth.

*I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.*

[THO.] That is: while you were still acting wickedly in Pharaoh’s chariots, I compared you to my cavalry, considering that I had predestined you, and compared you to my horses [Col. 0114B]. For all who live wickedly are horses in Pharaoh’s chariots—that is, under the rule of him who drives those chariots, namely the devil. All who live well, however, are in God’s chariots—that is, under his rule—and he is their rider.

Because the bride’s presumption was sharply and unreservedly rebuked, lest she remain too sorrowful, certain good things which she had already received are recalled to her mind, and certain things not yet received are promised to her. She is also declared beautiful and called beloved, and it is said: “I made you strong to fight against Pharaoh’s chariots.” This warfare in us is an actual spiritual warfare. There the people are brought out from Egypt; here, the human being from the world. There Pharaoh is overthrown; here, the devil. There Pharaoh’s chariots are overturned [Note: [Col. 0113] Exod. 13, 14]; here carnal desires [Col. 0114C] which wage war against the soul are cast down [Note: [Col. 0113] I Pet. 2]. Those were by waves; these, by weeping: those watery, these bitter.

There are three chariots of Pharaoh: the first, of malice; the second, of luxury; the third, of avarice. The chariot of malice has four wheels: cruelty, impatience, boldness, and shamelessness. This chariot is swift to shed blood [Note: [Col. 0113] Ps. 13]; it is checked neither by innocence, delayed by patience, restrained by fear, nor inhibited by shame. It is drawn by two swift horses: earthly power and worldly pomp. Two charioteers preside over them: pride and envy. Pride drives the pomp; envy, the power. Whoever stands firmly in himself is oppressed by pride, modest through gravity, firm through humility, sound through purity [Col. 0114D]. He will not be lightly swept away by the breeze of this vanity.

The chariot of luxury has four wheels: gluttony of the belly, lust for intercourse, softness of clothing, and dissolution into idleness and pleasure. It is drawn by two horses: prosperity in life and abundance of possessions. Two charioteers preside over them: the torpor of sloth and faithless security. They have neither spurs nor whips; rather, they use a canopy to make shade and a fan to stir up wind. The canopy is dissimulation, making shade and protecting from the heat of cares; the fan is prodigality, bringing the wind of flattery.

[Col. 0115A] The chariot of avarice turns upon four wheels of vices: cowardice, inhumanity, contempt for God, and forgetfulness of death; the beasts drawing it are tenacity and rapacity. It has one charioteer: the love of possessing. These are Pharaoh’s chariots.

There are also three chariots of God. There is Elijah’s chariot, the chariot that is Elijah, and the chariot of the eunuch of Queen Candace. The chariot that is Elijah is the one concerning which Elisha cries: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” [Note: [Col. 0115] IV Kings 13]. For he who patiently bears those subject to him, as Elijah bore Israel, is this chariot, called that of patience or fatherhood. It has four wheels: first, the administration of temporal affairs; second, active compassion for infirmities; third, consolation in temptation; fourth, glorying in injury inflicted by subjects.

Of the first the Apostle says: “He who gives, with simplicity” [Col. 0115B] [Note: [Col. 0115] Rom. 12]; and: “He who has ministered well shall acquire a good rank” [Note: [Col. 0115] I Tim. 3]. Of the second: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0115] Gal. 6]. Of the third: “If a person is caught in some offence, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid.]. Of the fourth: “We are cursed, and we bless; enduring persecution, we bear it” [Note: [Col. 0115] I Cor. 4].

Two horses draw this chariot: mercy with cheerfulness, and concern for a brother’s salvation and for rendering an account. Of these two the Apostle says: “He who presides, with diligence; he who ministers, with cheerfulness” [Note: [Col. 0115] Rom. 12]. The charioteer is the teacher himself who instructs. For the chariot of Israel and its charioteer are the same.

But Elijah’s chariot is fiery, of which it is said: “A fiery chariot and fiery horses separated the two of them” [Col. 0115C] [Note: [Col. 0115] IV Kings 2]. This is the chariot of charity. Its four wheels are four fervours. The first is zeal for God, that he may be honoured. Hence: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” [Note: [Col. 0115] Ps. 68; John 2]. The second is zeal for one’s neighbour, that he may be saved. Hence: “For I am jealous of you with God’s jealousy” [Note: [Col. 0115] II Cor. 11]. Of this: “My heart grew hot within me” [Note: [Col. 0115] Ps. 38]. Of the first: “In my meditation fire blazed forth” [Note: [Col. 0115] Ibid.]. The third is fervour in mortifying the flesh: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” [Note: [Col. 0115] Gal. 5]. Hence: “For in the fire of my zeal all the earth shall be devoured” [Note: [Col. 0115] Zeph. 1], that is, everything earthly. The fourth is fervour of devotion. By this, “My heart was inflamed, and thus my inward parts were changed” [Note: [Col. 0115] Ps. 72]. Hence Elijah was told: “What are you doing here, Elijah?”—“I have been zealous with zeal for the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0115] I Kings 10]. Of these two it is said: “Burn my inward parts and my heart” [Col. 0115D] [Note: [Col. 0115] Ps. 25].

Two horses draw this chariot: love and desire. Of the first: “Your love is strong as death,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0115] Song 2]. Of the second: “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus while he spoke to us on the way?” [Note: [Col. 0115] Luke 24]. Its charioteer is contemplation, which guides these horses. Hence David: “Send forth your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain” [Note: [Col. 0115] Ps. 42].

There is also the chariot of the eunuch of Queen Candace [Note: [Col. 0115] Acts 8], namely the chariot of chastity. For eunuchs [Col. 0116A] are those who exercise continence for the love of God. Likewise, it has four wheels. The first is contempt for intercourse, because of the contamination of the fleshly stain. Hence the Apostle: “Every sin which a person commits is outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body” [Note: [Col. 0115] I Cor. 6], namely by staining it. The second is hatred of it, because it can scarcely exist without an admixture of sin. Hence, according to the Pseudo-Pythagorean, a fornicator is properly called a person excessively enamoured of his wife. The third is abstinence from intercourse, because devotion to God is hindered by the consent of husband and wife and the rearing of children. Hence the Apostle: “Such people shall have tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0115] I Cor. 7]. The fourth is abstinence because of the dignity of the virtue of chastity. Hence Augustine: “No fruitfulness of marriage can [Col. 0116B] be compared to holy virginity.”

The two horses are two privileged and singular miracles, namely those in Christ and Mary. In Mary, because virginity gave birth; in Christ, because divinity united to itself a virgin through humanity. The charioteer is the reward in the homeland: namely, that virgins will cling to Christ more intimately than others, as Augustine says: “Others will follow Christ in the kingdom in all things, except when he proceeds in the beauty of virginity.”

In such a chariot sits the eunuch, namely every person continent in Christ. And it is read in Isaiah: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter” [Note: [Col. 0115] Isa. 53], because such persons are worthy to preach Christ’s passion. But because virginity alone does not suffice for understanding, Philip—whose name is interpreted “mouth of a lamp”—sits in the same chariot [Note: [Col. 0115] Acts 8], so that instruction from teachers may supply what the virgin cannot understand by himself [Col. 0116C].

The chariot of luxury pursues Israel, lest it crucify its flesh with vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0115] Gal. 5]; the chariot of avarice, lest it redeem its sins with alms and its iniquities with mercies to the poor [Note: [Col. 0115] Dan. 4]; the chariot of malice, so that it may not act simply but may defraud its brother in every transaction [Note: [Col. 0115] I Thess. 4]. Three other chariots oppose these: the chariot of chastity carries them beyond the waters of pleasures; the chariot of patience leads them through the desert; and the chariot of charity transports them from the Jordan into the land of their fathers [Note: [Col. 0115] Exod. 12].

Therefore, those who wish to flee Egypt sometimes have the sea before them, sometimes around them, and sometimes behind them. The sea is the world, which a person has before him as an obstacle, around him as an aid, and behind [Col. 0116D] him as a support: as an obstacle, lest he be converted; as an aid, so that, exercised by temptations, he may not be found idle; as a support, so that, when the world’s pleasure is wholly cast off, no way of tempting may remain to the devil. In the first is fear; in the second, labour; in the third, sorrow: fear of future dangers, labour in present conflicts, sorrow over past evils. Fear arises from faintheartedness; labour belongs to the virtue of patience; sorrow comes from compunction.

In the chariot of luxury sat the two elders seeking to defile [Col. 0117A] Susanna [Note: [Col. 0117] Dan. 13]. In the chariot of avarice I know that Ananias and Sapphira sit [Note: [Col. 0117] Acts 5]; in the chariot of malice, Jezebel pursuing Elijah [Note: [Col. 0117] III Kings 19]. Likewise, Susanna sat in the chariot of chastity, Job in the chariot of patience, and Mary Magdalene in the chariot of charity: Susanna when she refused violation; Job when, in adversity, he praised God; Mary when “many sins were forgiven her, because she loved much” [Note: [Col. 0117] Luke 7].

Susanna sings: “I will not abandon the law of my God. It is better for me to fall into the hands of men” [Note: [Col. 0117] Dan. 13]. Job sings: “As it pleased the Lord, so it was done; blessed be the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0117] Job 1]. Mary Magdalene sings: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” [Note: [Col. 0117] John 20].

Sitting in the first, Jesus Christ was raised into heaven [Note: [Col. 0117] Acts 1], because “the chariot of God is multiplied ten thousand times; the Lord is among them in holy Sinai” [Col. 0117B] [Note: [Col. 0117] Ps. 67]. Sitting in the second, Elijah was taken up, because a fiery chariot and fiery horses separated him from Elisha [Note: [Col. 0117] IV Kings 2]. Sitting in the third, the eunuch was baptized by Philip [Note: [Col. 0117] Acts 8].

*I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.*

[CARD.] These are the words of the Son to the Mother; and this little verse, together with those following, looks back to the earlier verse: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women!” For, that she may not be ignorant of herself, he here teaches her how great is her power against spiritual wickedness. And because he called her the most beautiful among women, he next adds concerning her beauty.

He says, therefore: “O my beloved, more beloved to me [Col. 0117C] than all others, in frightening and crushing Pharaoh’s chariots I have compared you to my cavalry.” Pharaoh’s chariots are Satan’s malice, which fights against faithful souls as though on four wheels: in four vices opposed to the four cardinal virtues. Christ’s cavalry, however, may be understood as the army of saints. In its battle line, spirits preside over bodies as horsemen, hold the flesh back with the bridle of temperance lest it rush headlong after desires, and urge it, lest it be sluggish and disobedient, with the goads of divine fear and love, like spurs, toward the course of good works. These are the horses which Joshua is recorded to have hamstrung, not killed, lest they run too fast, yet so that they might still be fit for ploughing and bearing burdens [Note: [Col. 0117] Josh. 11].

For the flesh is not to be killed but chastised, lest it be proud and wanton; and, in order that it may be obedient to good works, it must be reduced to servitude. Thus this cavalry or army, to which the blessed Virgin is compared in frightening, troubling, and putting spiritual wickedness to flight, is that ordered battle line of the camps of the saints; and the one blessed Virgin is compared to them all in striking terror into malicious spirits. As it is said below: “Terrible as an ordered battle line of camps” [Note: [Col. 0117] Song 6].

Christ’s cavalry can also be understood as that triumphant warfare by which [Col. 0118A] he fought against the devil, seated upon the horse of the flesh. Of this cavalry Habakkuk says to the Lord: “And your cavalry is salvation” [Note: [Col. 0117] Hab. 3]. For his cavalry against the devil’s assaults was humanity’s salvation. In this passage another translation also says: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my horse among Pharaoh’s chariots.”

This is the horse of which Zechariah says: “I saw in the night, and behold, a man riding upon a red horse” [Note: [Col. 0117] Zech. 1]. This is the horse of assumed humanity, reddened by its own blood; God, seated upon it as upon a horse, triumphed over the devil. Therefore the Son says: “In frightening and crushing Pharaoh’s chariots, though I have not made you equal to my cavalry—or to my horse—I have nonetheless compared you to it, O most beloved Mother; because, although maternal virginity in its humanity is not equal to divinity in frightening and crushing the devil’s camps, it is nevertheless more like it in these matters than all others.”

After this he praises the Mother’s beauty and says:

*Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.*
[THO.] It is the custom of the turtledove, once it has lost its mate, never thereafter to attach itself to another, but always, in solitude, to mourn the absent one. Such is the holy soul, which groans in longing for the Bridegroom—that is, Christ—from whom it seems to be separated while it lives in this exile. Since it does not find him whom it loves, it withdraws itself from every alien love; and thus, with a certain modesty, suffusing its outward cheek—that is, both the left and the right, namely the inward—with a kind of blush, it makes them shine with the beauty of chastity: preserving outward discipline and inward purity.

He reveals the Bride’s modesty, praising her for shamefastness and chastity. The Bride’s face is her intention. The two cheeks are the thing and the cause: that is, what she aims at and why. For from these two either the beauty or the ugliness of the soul is judged. To aim, as it were, at God, though not for God but for the world, belongs to the worldly soul; it has no beautiful cheek at all. To aim, as it were, at God, but not for God’s sake, is hypocrisy. Though one cheek may seem beautiful, dissimulation disfigures it. But if she directs herself toward God because of a present necessity of life, we call her face somewhat darkened by the vice of faint-heartedness. If, however, she tends toward something other than God, yet performs Martha’s service for God’s sake, we do not call her ugly; but she has not attained the perfection of beauty.

Among the lofty exercises of the saints these virtues are principal, because they render persons dear to God and worthy of reverence among human beings: faith, modesty, chastity, frugality, humility, innocence, simplicity, and the mind’s lofty intention toward God. Understand these in the turtledove. It preserves faithfulness to its mate, since after his death it refuses to be joined to another; it is adorned with modesty, since it permits union with no one without lawful right; it shines with chastity, since it displays nothing unseemly or turbulent in its habits; it is adorned with frugality, since it feeds not on flesh but on pure grain; it preserves humility, since it gives utterance to groaning instead of song; it follows innocence, since it is known not to inflict injury even upon the smallest animals; it delights in simplicity, since it is not known to practise deceit even with deceitful birds. It loves mountain heights and trees, and rejoices in its solitary wandering.

There are three kinds of modesty, by which a person is ashamed to speak of his sins. A twofold modesty is praiseworthy: that by which a devout soul, “providing good things before God and men” [Note: [Col. 0119] 2 Cor. 8.], is ashamed in every way of whatever is unseemly before God and unbecoming before human beings—whether to think it in the mind, utter it with the tongue, or perform it in deed. The virtue of chastity renders us venerable among human beings, desirable to angels, approved and beloved by God himself. This virtue cleanses the conscience, preserves affection, enlightens the understanding, strengthens the devout purpose of the mind, draws friends, restrains adversaries, confounds demons, invites angels, shuts hell, opens heaven, and stands before God himself with confidence.

Innocence too is commended in the turtledove. It is steadfastness of life, sweetness of self-restraint, tranquillity of mind, security of heart, the seat of virtue, the hall of wisdom. Our conscience is the face of the inward person. Hence, later: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” [Note: [Col. 0119] Cant. 2.]. For by it we are known to God. It has two cheeks. The first is shame, by which the purified conscience blushes when struck by temptations; the second is that by which it is ashamed of being puffed up by empty favour on account of the good things it does.

There are seven kinds of temptations of which it blushes: the first is importunate; the second doubtful; the third sudden; the fourth hidden; the fifth violent; the sixth deceitful; the seventh entangled. The importunate temptation is that which we can scarcely remove from the eyes of our memory: though often driven away, it often returns and never ceases to trouble the mind. The doubtful temptation is that which so wraps the mind in a cloud of uncertainty that it does not know what certain thing it ought to hold. The sudden temptation is that which forestalls the judgment of reason, so that the mind, overtaken by its onset, cannot anticipate its snares and is carried through delight more quickly than it can be fortified by circumspection. The hidden temptation is that through which we often neglect the very point at which we ought to be watchful; for it causes a harmful matter not to be brought under consideration. The violent temptation is that which can scarcely, or never, be overcome by human effort. The deceitful temptation seduces the mind, so that it calls good evil, and conversely. The entangled temptation is that by which the mind is assailed by various vices at one and the same time, so that it may stumble in at least one.

The importunate temptation is that which presses insolently; the doubtful, that which envelops the mind in a cloud of uncertainty; the sudden, that which forestalls the judgment of reason; the hidden, that which evades the judgment of deliberation; the violent, that which exceeds the strength of the mind; the deceitful, that which seduces the mind; the entangled, that which attacks it with various vices.

Of the first, called importunate, Job says: “Waters hollow out the stone, and the earth is gradually consumed by washing” [Note: [Col. 0119] Job 14.]. Again, of the second, namely the doubtful, Job says: “Therefore my thoughts succeed one another in variety, and my mind is carried away in different directions” [Note: [Col. 0119] Job 20.]. Of the third, namely the sudden, Jeremiah says: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0119] Job 20.]: that is, than the mind’s watchful perceptions. For the fourth, namely the hidden, Job prayed to the Lord, saying: “How many iniquities and sins have I? Show me my crimes and offences” [Note: [Col. 0119] Job 13.]. Job also says of the violent temptation, which is the fifth: “As through a breached wall and an open gate, they rushed in upon me and rolled onward amid my miseries” [Note: [Col. 0119] Job 30.]. Of the sixth, namely the deceitful, Solomon says: “There are ways which seem right to men, but their end leads to death” [Note: [Col. 0119] Prov. 16.]. Of the seventh, that is, the entangled, it is said of Behemoth: “The sinews of his testicles are interwoven” [Note: [Col. 0119] Job 40.].

Against these seven David said: “Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 118]. And it should be noted that the first is more dangerous than the second and third, and so in order than the rest. David briefly sets forth these seven kinds of temptation when he says: “His truth shall surround you with a shield” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 90]. Against the first, which is importunate, we set the shield, when it is said: “His truth shall surround you with a shield.” Against the doubtful it is said: “From the terror of the night.” For what occurs at night is uncertain. Concerning the sudden it is said: “From the arrow that flies” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid.], because it wounds suddenly.

This arrow sometimes flies by night and sometimes by day. By night: “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at those upright in heart” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 10]. It flies by night when it suddenly strikes the mind and disguises as good the evil it urges. It flies by day when it precipitately suggests an evil which it does not fail to know is evil. Hence: “From the arrow that flies by day” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 90]. Of the hidden temptation: “From the business that walks in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid.], because “he who does evil hates the light” [Note: [Col. 0119] John 3]. Of the violent: “From the assault” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 90], because one must run strongly against a violent enemy. Against the deceitful it is said: “From the noonday demon” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid.]. At noon the sun is both brighter and hotter. For then the devil comes to us with brightness and heat: namely, when he transforms himself into an angel of light. Of the manifold temptation it is said: “A thousand shall fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ibid.].

A soldier bears a shield in his left hand and a sword in his right. There are likewise two kinds of vices, carnal and spiritual; some therefore are exercised carnally, others spiritually. Carnal vices are on the left, spiritual vices on the right. Those on the left are repelled by the thrust of the shield; those on the right by the stroke of the sword. Discipline of the body is placed on the left, discipline of the spirit on the right.

Of the importunate temptation it is said: “All day long they prepared battles” [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 130]; of the doubtful: “He poured contempt upon princes and made them wander in a trackless waste, not on a road” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 106]; of the sudden: “The snares of death overtook me” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 17]; of the hidden: “For you light my lamp, O Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.]; of the violent: “Behold, they have seized upon my life; the mighty have rushed upon me” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 58]; of the deceitful: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 119]; of the manifold: “Those who hate me without cause have multiplied against me” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 68].

Again, of the importunate: “All day long, attacking, he afflicted me” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 55]; of the doubtful: “They wandered in a wilderness, in a waterless place” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 106]; of the sudden: “They came before me in the day of my affliction” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 17]; of the hidden: “Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 18]; of the deceitful: “Who planned to trip up my steps” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 139]; of the manifold: “I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 3].

The importunate temptation troubles the mind; the doubtful perpetually agitates it; the sudden wounds it; the hidden blinds it; the violent continually oppresses it; the deceitful makes it foolish; the manifold tears it apart. Thus the first disturbs, the second agitates, the third wounds, the fourth blinds, the fifth weakens, the sixth makes foolish, and the seventh tears apart. Behold, one cheek is beautiful when it always blushes at these things. The other will be beautiful if it is not exalted by empty favour because of its good deeds.

The vain are accustomed, first, gladly to look upon their own good works and to show them to others; second, when praised by others, gladly to listen; third, to magnify themselves in their hearts; fourth, to proclaim their works with their own mouths. Job removed these four things from himself when he said: “If I saw the sun when it shone” [Note: [Col. 0121] Job 31]—behold the first—“and the moon moving brightly” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.]—behold the second—“if my heart rejoiced secretly” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.]—behold the third—“and if I kissed my hand with my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.]—behold the fourth.

To see the sun is gladly to regard one’s good deeds and display them to others. Hence the Lord: “Take care not to do your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them” [Note: [Col. 0121] Matt. 6]. The moon shines when one’s reputation is on the lips of the people [Note: [Col. 0121] Something appears to be missing here.], who are sellers of oil; but let him say: “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ps. 140]. And Isaiah: “My people, those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ch. 3]. They rejoice secretly in their hearts when, after seeing and hearing these things, they esteem themselves great. But the Apostle intervenes: “He who thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” [Note: [Col. 0121] Gal. 6]. They kiss their own hand with their own mouth when they proclaim their works with their own mouth, like that Pharisee: “God, I thank you that I am not like other men” [Note: [Col. 0121] Luke 18]. And then: “I fast twice on the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess” [Note: [Col. 0121] Ibid.]. When the Bride is ashamed of these things, the other cheek is beautiful, and it is said to her: “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.”

## Your neck is like necklaces

[Col. 0122A] The Bride’s neck is the preachers of the Church. In necklaces, gems are set in gold. Gold signifies wisdom and stones signify works. Thus the Bride’s neck is like necklaces, because the preacher clothes himself inwardly with wisdom and outwardly performs the works which he sees in wisdom. The spiritual head is Christ; the neck, understanding; the body, dispositions and affections. Therefore, through this neck spiritual grace, like food, is conveyed from Christ the head into the body of dispositions and affections.

This neck is not so much adorned with a necklace as compared to one, because of the purity, truth, and gentleness of understanding: purity from sin, truth in the knowledge of heavenly things, and gentleness in the ordering of conduct. Again, preachers are signified by the neck, through which the word of preaching is uttered and the secret of the heart is disclosed. Thus the body of the Church is joined to Christ its head.

A necklace is a woman’s ornament: it veils what ought to be covered, adorns outward things, and drives away corrupters. In this is signified the threefold providence of teachers. Some disclose by words the things that ought to be said from the Scriptures; some veil the things that ought to be said and preserve the flock entrusted to them from heretical corrupters. Moses displays a precious necklace when, concerning sacrifices, he taught that some things were to be offered through fire to God alone; some were for priests only; some for priests and their sons; and some were also to be taken as food by laypeople.

The first things are so hidden that they must be left to God alone. Hence, of the typical lamb: “If anything remains, it shall be burned with fire” [Note: [Col. 0121] Exod. 12]. Things to be eaten by the priest alone are those which spiritual persons grasp, so that they may love them but not teach them. Hence: “I heard unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter” [Note: [Col. 0121] 2 Cor. 12]. Those to be handled with the priests and the priests’ sons signify the precepts of perfection and those sublime mysteries of faith; those to be shared with laypeople are the common ordinances of wholesome life, which defend from corrupters when they stand as a wall for the house of God against heretics, schismatics, and violent persons [Note: [Col. 0121] Ezek. 13].

Again, our head is divinity and our body humanity. The Blessed Virgin is the neck, in whom divinity was joined to humanity; she is called like a necklace because of her ineffable chastity, signified by the necklace. Through the neck inward air is emitted and outward air drawn within, because through her mediation our inward devotion is presented to God and God’s mercy is returned to us. Again, saliva is drawn through the neck from the head into the body, because through her grace is obtained from God for the human race. Hence Job: “How long will you not spare me, nor leave me until I swallow my saliva?” [Note: [Col. 0121] Job 1.]

Again, speech is emitted through the neck, because from her the incarnate Word of the Father was born. Word, I say, of the active gender, because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” [Note: [Col. 0121] John 1]. Word of the passive gender, because “he suffered for us, leaving you an example that you should follow in his footsteps” [Col. 0123A] [Note: [Col. 0123] 1 Pet. 2]. Word of the deponent gender: for in death he laid aside his own single oldness and our double oldness, namely his own punishment and our guilt and punishment. Hence: “He himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” [Note: [Col. 0123] Isa. 53]. He laid aside guilt when “he bore our sins in his body upon the tree” [Note: [Col. 0123] 2 Pet. 2]. He will lay aside punishment when “he will transform the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0123] Phil. 3]. Word of the neuter gender, because he is neither merely man nor merely God. Word of the common gender, because he is both man and God.

Necklaces are made of gold and precious stones; and teachers ought to be golden vessels in the house of God, furnished with wisdom and precious stones—that is, good works—by which streams of grace are offered to the people. Hence it is written: “Simon son of Onias, like a solid vessel of gold, adorned with every precious stone, offered streams of grace to the people, and received a robe of glory at the consummation of virtue” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ecclus. 50].

But it should be noted that there are five kinds of vessels: earthen, wooden, bronze, silver, and gold. The first are carnal persons; the second, the proud; the third, penitents; the fourth, continent persons; the fifth, wise prelates. The first contain mud; the second, wind; the third contain myrrh; the fourth, lilies; the fifth, spices. Mud is luxury; wind, pride; myrrh, the bitterness of penitence; lilies, the whiteness of virginal purity; spices, the fragrances of inward virtue.

Of four of these the Apostle says: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay” [Note: [Col. 0123] 2 Tim. 2]. Of the bronze vessel the Law says: “If the vessel in which the sacrifice is offered is bronze, it shall be scoured and washed with water, and it shall be clean” [Note: [Col. 0123] Lev. 6]. The first are vessels of dishonour; the second, of wrath; the third, of mercy; the fourth, of exile; the fifth, of election. Of the first: “Does the potter have power over the clay to make one vessel for honour, another for dishonour?” [Note: [Col. 0123] Rom. 9]. Of the second and third: “God endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ibid.]. The first two are vessels of the foolish shepherd. Of the fourth the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Make for yourself vessels of exile” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ezek. 12]. Of the fifth the Lord says of Paul: “This man is a vessel of election to me, to bear my name among the nations” [Note: [Col. 0123] Acts 9].

Hear of mud: “I shall grind them like dust before the face of the wind; I shall wipe them out like the mud of the streets” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 17]. And of wind: “A whirlwind wind comes from the north” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ezek. 1]. And of myrrh: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts” [Note: [Col. 0123] Cant. 1]. And of lilies: “My beloved is like a gazelle and a young stag; he feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline” [Note: [Col. 0123] Cant. 2]. And of spices: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; breathe upon my garden, and its spices shall flow forth” [Col. 0124A] [Note: [Col. 0123] Cant. 4].

Hear of the mud of the earthen vessel: “Come, let us fill ourselves with wine and precious ointments” [Note: [Col. 0123] Wis. 2], etc. Of the same David says: “I am stuck fast in deep mire, and there is no firm ground” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 68]. Thus he rejoices that he has been delivered: “He brought me out of the pit of misery and from the mire of filth” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 39]. These are those “whose god is their belly” [Note: [Col. 0123] Phil. 3]; but the Lord “will break them like a potter’s vessel” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 2]. Hear how: “They hold tambourine and lyre; they rejoice at the sound of the instrument; they spend their days in prosperity, and in an instant descend to hell” [Note: [Col. 0123] Job 21].

Wood, which grows upward, signifies pride. Hear this wind: “I will ascend, says Satan, above the heights of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0123] Isa. 14]. Hence Job: “A vain man is lifted up in pride, and thinks himself born free like a wild ass’s colt” [Note: [Col. 0123] Job 11]. Hence it is said to him: [Col. 0124B] “Why does your heart lift you up, and why do you hold your eyes astonished, as though thinking great things?” [Note: [Col. 0123] Job 15.] But the Lord will break such persons. For “he will humble the eyes of the proud, and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 28].

Bronze vessels are penitents. Of these the Law says: “The bronze vessel shall be washed with water, scoured, and made clean” [Note: [Col. 0123] Lev. 6]. It shall be washed with water in confession, scoured in satisfaction, and made clean in one’s manner of life. Behold myrrh. Of the first: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 6]. And the Apostle: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit” [Note: [Col. 0123] 2 Cor. 7]. Of the second, he says: “I beseech you to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” [Note: [Col. 0123] Rom. 12]. Of the third, he says: “Do all things without murmurings and disputings, that [Col. 0124C] you may be blameless and simple children of God, without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation” [Note: [Col. 0123] Phil. 2]. Isaiah: “Wash yourselves; be clean” [Note: [Col. 0123] Isa. 1].

Silver vessels are virgins, namely “silver tested by fire” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 11], that is, by the temptations of the flesh. These are the “silvered wings of the dove” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 67], namely of the Church, which is a virgin. “Her head is Christ” [Note: [Col. 0123] Eph. 5]. The wings are virgins who fly higher than others. For “they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” [Note: [Col. 0123] Rev. 14]. In them are lilies, among which Christ rests; he who feeds among the lilies, surrounded by choirs of virgins, “who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline” [Note: [Col. 0123] Cant. 2]. To them Paul says: “I have espoused you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” [Note: [Col. 0123] 2 Cor. 11]. There are also golden vessels, namely the wise, in whom are the fragrances of virtues.

[Col. 0124D] But it should be noted that there are vessels for washing, vessels for refreshment, and vessels for the veneration of God. The first reconcile us to God; the second instruct our neighbour; the third invite God to love us. In figure of the first, the angel placed at Elijah’s head a cake baked under ashes and a vessel of water [Note: [Col. 0123] 3 Kgs. 19]. And Jacob said to his sons: “Take with you in your vessels the best fruits of the land, and bring presents to the man” [Note: [Col. 0123] Gen. 43]. Of the second it is said that, at King Ahasuerus’s banquets, “those who were invited drank from golden cups, and food was brought in various vessels” [Col. 0125A] [Note: [Col. 0125] Esth. 1]. “And the son brought vessels to his mother, and she poured [oil] into them” [Note: [Col. 0125] 4 Kgs. 4]. For the third: “The wise virgins took oil in their vessels with their lamps, and went out to meet the bridegroom and bride” [Note: [Col. 0125] Matt. 25].

There are golden vessels which never possess spices; some possess them but do not retain them; others possess them and always preserve them undefiled. The first are wise persons shining in knowledge without virtue; the second are wise persons shining in knowledge with virtue, but losing it in temptation; the third are wise persons with knowledge and virtue, which they preserve steadfastly. Of the first: “Babylon was a golden cup in the Lord’s hand; all nations drank of her wine” [Note: [Col. 0125] Jer. 51]. The second are the vessels of the Temple of Jerusalem, which Nebuzaradan, captain of the cooks, carried to Babylon [Note: [Col. 0125] Jer. 52]. Hence Jeremiah: “How the gold has grown dim; the finest colour has changed!” [Note: [Col. 0125] Lam. 4]. Of the third it is said in the Apocalypse of the elders: “Each had golden harps and bowls full of perfumes” [Note: [Col. 0125] Rev. 5].

Hence it is said: “Simon son of Onias, like a solid vessel of gold, adorned with every precious stone, offered streams of grace to the people, and received a robe of glory at the consummation of virtue” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ecclus. 50]. Of the second it is said: “How the gold has grown dim; the finest colour has changed!” [Note: [Col. 0125] Lam. 4]. Of this one it is said: “Like a solid vessel of gold” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ecclus. 50].
