Of the third it is said: “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” [Note: [Col. 0125] Lam. 4]. Of this one: “Adorned with every precious stone” [Note: [Col. 0125] Rev. 21]. [Col. 0125C] Of the failure of that one: “Those who fed delicately perished in the streets” [Note: [Col. 0125] Lam. 4]. Of this one: “He offered streams of grace to the people.” Of that one: “Those nurtured in scarlet embraced dung” [Note: [Col. 0125] Lam. 4]. Of this one: “He received a robe of glory at the consummation of virtues” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ecclus. 50].

That, then, is “adorned with every precious stone.” Precious stones are virtues in habit; precious stones are works in act; precious stones are religious persons in assembly. The first are an ornament of spirits, the second of bodies, the third of congregations. Therefore, the interconnection of virtues adorns the righteous person inwardly; the differentiation of works adorns outwardly; the consolation of religious persons adorns at the side. Of the first, to Lucifer: “Every precious stone was your covering” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ezek. 28]. Of the second Paul says: “Others build with gold, silver, precious stones” [Col. 0125D] [Note: [Col. 0125] 1 Cor. 3]. Of the third: “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” [Note: [Col. 0125] Lam. 4].

Isaiah also says of these: “I shall lay your stones in order, found you upon sapphires, make your battlements jasper, and your gates sculptured stones” [Note: [Col. 0125] Isa. 54]. Sapphire is of a heavenly colour: namely, the virtues which are the foundation of the whole spiritual building. Jasper is of a green colour: it signifies good works which do not wither through failure, and these are the battlements, for with them we fight. The sculptured stones are religious persons, who carve themselves with continual scourging while they chastise the body and watch their hearts. They are also gates, because by their example they lead others to the kingdom. Such a golden vessel offered streams of grace to the people.

There are three streams of grace: tearful penitence, literal knowledge, and heavenly wisdom. The first cleanses; the second makes fruitful; the third floods. The first washes away foulness; the second instructs toward love; the third imparts savour. Of the first: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ps. 6]. Of the second: “Behold, I turn toward them as a river of peace” [Note: [Col. 0125] Isa. 66], which is brotherly charity. Of the third: “And as a flooding torrent, the glory of the nations” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ibid.], which is heavenly savour.

Of the first: he offered streams of grace to the people, that they might be invited to [Col. 0126B] penitence. Of the second: he offered streams of grace to the clergy, that they might be instructed in the Catholic faith. Of the third: he offered streams of grace in the cloister, that they might savour “the things above, not those upon earth” [Note: [Col. 0125] Col. 3], and therefore “received a robe of glory at the consummation of virtue” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ecclus. 50].

But it should be noted that first we receive righteousness, or the robe of righteousness; second, the robe of saving joy and wisdom; third, the robe of glory: the first at the beginning of virtue, the second at the perfection of virtue, the third at the consummation of virtue. With the first we receive righteousness; with the second, the joy of rest; with the third, the glory of the incorruptible body. Of the first, the father commanded that the first robe be brought forth for his returning prodigal [Col. 0126C] [Note: [Col. 0125] Luke 15]. Of the second it is said in the Apocalypse: “A white robe was given to each of them” [Note: [Col. 0125] Rev. 6]. Of the third: The Lord loved him and adorned him; “he clothed him with a robe of glory” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ecclus. 45]. Of the third: “He clothed me with the garment of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0125] Isa. 61]. Of the first: “And he surrounded me with the garment of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0125] Ibid.].

“Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove; your neck is like necklaces.”

[CARD.] In the cheeks a woman’s beauty shines forth, and a distinguishing mark is observed. In the turtledove, chastity is signified. The Son therefore commends his Mother’s cheeks, not for the brightness of their skin but for the beauty of modesty and virginal chastity. Necklaces are ornaments of the neck and encircle it. Through the neck, moreover, the voice goes out and food enters. Her necklaces, therefore, were moderation in speech and temperance in food. For she did not speak much like a chatterer, but, as the Gospel has it, “silently kept all these words in her heart” [Note: [Col. 0125] Luke 2]; and, as though dried up by abstinence, she compared herself shortly before to Solomon’s skins. The Son adds concerning her ornaments:

## We shall make for you golden chains, patterned with silver

[THO.] *Murenulae* are little chains by which necklaces are fastened to the neck, because wisdom and religion are joined to preachers through the Scriptures; for sacred Scripture is understood through the *murenulae*. They are rightly called golden and patterned with silver, because holy Scripture shines with wisdom and is taught throughout the world by resonant preaching. As gold signifies wisdom, so silver signifies preaching.

Because “we shall make” is said in the plural, we believe this to be the voice of the companions rather than of the Bridegroom. The Bride had said: “Show me him whom my soul loves.” But he cannot be seen except with the pure eyes of hearts: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0127] Matt. 5]. But they cannot be pure except through faith, as it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” [Note: [Col. 0127] Acts 15], and “faith comes by hearing” [Note: [Col. 0127] Rom. 10]. Therefore the adornment of the ears is placed first, as though they said: “Hear, daughter, and see” [Note: [Col. 0127] Ps. 44]. Hear first, that you may see afterwards. For the Bridegroom will give joy and gladness to your hearing [Note: [Col. 0127] Ps. 50] when you see him.

They offer her golden chains patterned with silver, that by faith she may know what she ought to believe concerning gold, that is, the splendour of divinity, and silver, namely Christ’s humanity. This is that appearance of electrum of which Ezekiel says: “From its midst, as it were, the appearance of electrum” [Note: [Col. 0127] Ezek. 1], that is, from the midst of the fire. Electrum is made of silver and gold. Or gold signifies wisdom and silver eloquence, with which she may preach to her subjects, so that the desired vision of the Bridegroom may precede and then follow, as Jacob is shown in Leah and Rachel [Note: [Col. 0127] Gen. 29].

Again, lovers are accustomed to furnish their brides with precious ornaments in order to kindle their love for them more ardently. Thus Christ does for the Church. He cleanses her in the washing of baptism, confirms and strengthens her by the sacrament of his body and blood, and enlightens her through the mysteries of the Scriptures, so that she may love her cleanser, defender, and illuminator. These golden chains are divine writings, by reason of their wisdom and silver eloquence. They are ornaments of the ears: chains of gold, subtly patterned with silver in the form of a worm, called a *teredo* or *terebella*, because it bores through hard wood. Thus these chains shine with the gold of heavenly wisdom and the silver of life-giving eloquence; and now through rebukes, now through consolations, now through the allurements of heavenly promises, and now through threats of infernal punishments, they soften hard hearts.

Brides are commonly adorned especially with three ornaments found in this Song: rings—“his hands are rounded and golden, full of hyacinths” [Note: [Col. 0127] Cant. 5]. This is said of the Bridegroom; but we believe that he possesses rings in order to adorn the Bride with them. Then chains, as above: “We shall make for you golden chains.” And necklaces: “Your neck is like necklaces.” In rings, a girdle; in chains, a sign; in necklaces, a seal. The girdle is temperance; the sign, obedience; the seal, chastity. The girdle of temperance prevents the hand from being loosened for unlawful works; the sign of obedience enables her, instructed by the divine utterance signified by silver and divine wisdom signified by gold, to obey wisely; the seal of chastity prevents a shameful movement from staining chastity.

The seal of necklaces does three things. It conceals inward things, lest some shameful thought arising against the resolve of chastity burst out; it adorns outward things, so that she appears modest and of sober gravity; and it restrains shameless hands from unlawful touch, lest through the touch of another’s flesh the fire of lust burn hot. The Bride is also adorned with garments.

A threefold garment belongs to the bride. The first is the brightness of a religious way of life; the second, bodily chastity; the third, innocence and charity. The first is worn in days of labour; the second in days of festivity; the third at the reception of the king. The first is worn for one’s neighbour; [Col. 0128B] the second for an angel; the third for God. For by the first one’s neighbour is edified; by the second the angel rejoices in purity; by the third God delights in innocence and charity. Of the first: “That strong woman made herself a quilted garment [Note: [Col. 0127] Prov. 31.],” as though triangular, because religious life consists in three things; or, according to others, *stragulata* derives from *stratus*, “a covering,” because it is a garment by which a bed is covered and by which a person is nonetheless clothed. Hence it is thought to be triangular in the manner of a cloak: in restraint of the members, obedience to commandments, and patience under persecutions [Note: [Col. 0127] Isai. 33.]. Of the first it is said: “Who stops his ears lest he hear of bloodshed, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil” [Note: [Col. 0127] Eccle. 4.]. Of the second: “Obedience is better than sacrifices.” Of the third: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” [Note: [Col. 0127] Luc. 21.].

Of the second [Col. 0128C] garment: “The same woman made fine linen, and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite” [Note: [Col. 0127] Prov. 31.]. That is, she made fine linen, the whiteness of chastity; she delivered a girdle to the Canaanite, that is, restraint of agitation. For “Canaanite” means “agitation,” and Christ’s body was wrapped in fine linen [Note: [Col. 0127] Luc. 23]. Of the third garment: “Purple and fine linen are her clothing” [Note: [Col. 0127] Prov. 31.]. Purple signifies charity; fine linen, innocence. Christ was clothed in the first at the Transfiguration: for “his garments became white as snow” [Note: [Col. 0127] Matth. 17.]. In the second: the two men at the Ascension [Note: [Col. 0127] Act. 1.]. In the third: the angel at the Resurrection [Note: [Col. 0127] Matth. 28.]. For his face was red because of charity, his garment white because of an innocent life.

In the first there is the fragrance of incense; in the second, an inestimable fragrance; in the [Col. 0128D] third, the fragrance of fullness. Of the first: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” [Note: [Col. 0127] Cant. 4]; of the second: “whose fragrance in his garments was altogether beyond estimation”; of the third, when Isaac perceived the fragrance of his garments, he said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” [Note: [Col. 0127] Gen. 27.].

Behold the adornment of the bride’s garments. Yet, for her greater beauty, another adornment is added from what follows: she is adorned with brightness, “adorned with a variety of flowers.” Hence it follows: “And as days of spring, flowers of roses surrounded her, and [Col. 0129A] lilies of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0129] Eccli. 50.].

Here it must be known that there are winter days, inward days, and spring days. The first are temporal, the second spiritual, the third heavenly. Of the first: “I have not desired the day of man; you know it” [Note: [Col. 0129] Jer. 17.]; of the second: “They turned night into day, and again after darkness I hope for light” [Note: [Col. 0129] Job 17.]; of the third: “And his throne is as the days of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 88.]. In the first the soul is surrounded by the calamity of tribulations; in the second, by the ardours of desires; in the third, by flowers of roses and lilies. Of the first, Job says: “Let the day perish on which I was born” [Note: [Col. 0129] Job 3.]; of the second: “Day utters speech to day, and night makes knowledge known to night” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 18.]; of the third: “And, as days of spring, flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys surround her.”

Thus illuminated, this soul ascends: first through [Col. 0129B] the steps of virtues; second, to a lofty heart; third, to the ethereal bridal chamber. Of the first: “He has set ascents in his heart. They shall go from strength to strength” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 83.]. Of the second: “Let man ascend to a lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 63.]. Of the third: “The Virgin Mary was assumed into the ethereal bridal chamber” [Note: [Col. 0129] Offic. Eccles.]. In the first she ascends painfully; in the second preciously; in the third gloriously. Nor is this surprising: for she ascends above streams of water. First she ascends from the valley of tears; second, from the flow of graces; third, from the torrent of delights. In the first, cleansed; in the second, made fruitful; in the third, satisfied. Of the first: “He has set ascents in his heart in the valley of overflowing tears” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 83.]; of the second: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 45.]; of the third: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 35.].

Likewise, there is a threefold bridal chamber: one is virginal; one special and spiritual; and one ethereal. [Col. 0129C] Of the first: “And he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 18.]. Of the second: “Adorn your bridal chamber, O Zion, and receive Christ the King” [Note: [Col. 0129] Offic. Eccles.]. Of the third: “The Virgin Mary was assumed into the ethereal bridal chamber” [Note: [Col. 0129] Ibid.]. In the first he took our weakness; in the second he experiences the sweetness of our devotion; in the third he displays his majesty. In the first, indeed, he was “made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” [Note: [Col. 0129] Philipp. 2.]. In the second he “rests like a solitary sparrow on the roof” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 101.]. In the third: “The King of kings sits upon a starry throne” [Note: [Col. 0129] Offic. Eccles.].

Thus adorned, the bride ascends to her bridegroom. Christ’s first birth was in a virgin’s womb; but there was, as it were, a second in baptism and, as it were, a third in the Resurrection. These are the matters discussed here. On the fortieth day after his birth, the Lord was presented in the Temple. After his baptism, fasting forty days, he was tempted by the devil and set upon the pinnacle of the Temple. Forty days after the Resurrection, he was assumed into heaven by the Father. Behold three, as it were, births: the first fleshly, but without sin; the second sacramental, but without effect in him, because he had no sin for baptism to remove; the third [Col. 0130A] heavenly and in glory. These three births are followed by three forties. In the first he was hidden; in the second he laboured; in the third he rejoiced. After the first he was brought to the Temple by his parent; after the second he was placed upon the Temple by the enemy; after the third he was assumed into heaven by the Father.

Therefore the first period of forty is wholly one of purification; the second, of testing; the third, of contemplation. In the first, the flesh acquires chastity, the soul security, and the spirit usefulness and subtlety. Thus the flesh becomes purer, the soul stronger, the spirit clearer. Hence, in the purification which follows the first forty days, three animals were offered by command of the Law. The turtledove signifies chastity of the flesh, because it does not enter a marriage again. The lamb signifies the patience and [Col. 0130B] gentleness of the soul, because when struck it does not resist. The dove signifies the spirit, namely humility and subtlety, because it flies higher.

Elijah fasted the first forty while fleeing Jezebel [Note: [Col. 0129] III Reg. 19.], whose name means “vain flux,” that is, the enticement of the flesh; Christ fasted the second in the desert [Note: [Col. 0129] Matth. 4.], tested among thistles and thorns; Moses fasted the third upon the mountain, beholding the riches of divine utterance [Note: [Col. 0129] Exod. 20.]. These fasts are set in this number because forty has precisely three divisions: first, into two twenties; second, into four tens; third, into eight fives. In the first forty, that of purification, we fast by restraining the five senses, so that our flesh may receive the eighth, resurrection; in the second, that is, of testing, we fast while acquiring for ourselves the four virtues, so that [Col. 0130C] the soul may receive the tenarius, which the householder gave to the labouring workers [Note: [Col. 0129] Matth. 20.]; in the third, that is, of contemplation, we fast so that, as it were, receiving two twenties, we may receive the twofold robe of glorification.

Therefore, in the first, that is, purification, let the flesh be cleansed from deed, the soul from thought, and the tongue from evil speech. This is the first forty, of purification. The second, of testing, follows. For we fast that we may be tested and may be able to endure testing. It should be noted, moreover, that testing is threefold: the first is made by the guidance of reason, the second by experience, the third by miracles. The first is philosophical, the second active, the third anagogical. Through the first, a person becomes more discerning; through the second, stronger; through the third, more devout: more discerning because by reason he distinguishes truth from falsehood; [Col. 0130D] stronger through continual endurance; more devout because of the new and wondrous things he has seen.

Of the first the Apostle says: “Test all things; hold fast what is good; abstain from every evil hope” [Note: [Col. 0129] I Thess. 5.]. For he wished this testing to be made by the guidance of reason. Of the second he said: “But let a person test himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup” [Note: [Col. 0129] I Cor. 11.]. For he wished this to be made through the experience of tribulations. Of the third: “Your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my works” [Note: [Col. 0129] Psal. 94.], [Col. 0131A] namely, the miracles which I performed for them in the desert—when he dried up the sea, rained manna, and so forth.

Paul instructed us concerning the first when he said: “The invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made from the creation of the world, are clearly perceived” [Note: [Col. 0131] Rom. 1.]. Concerning the second: “In all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience” [Note: [Col. 0131] II Cor. 6.]. Paul received the third while going to Damascus, because he heard a voice and saw no one, when “the brightness of God shone around him, and afterwards he was blinded” [Note: [Col. 0131] Act. 9.]. For through these miracles he proved Christ to be God. Hence “he preached in the synagogue, affirming that this is Christ, the Son of God” [Note: [Col. 0131] Ibid.].

We fast the third forty days in order that we may become more subtle for contemplation. For the more the flesh is attenuated, the more the spirit [Col. 0131B] is made subtle. We contemplate three things above: the abundance of the heavenly city, the joy of its citizens, and the glory of its king. There is abundance because it will be filled with every good thing; joy because God will be seen face to face; glory because every creature will be subject to God. There is abundance because “the righteous shall neither hunger nor thirst any more” [Note: [Col. 0131] Apoc. 7.], where “they shall be made drunk with the abundance of God’s house” [Note: [Col. 0131] Psal. 35.]. Hence: “Let the righteous feast and rejoice in the presence of God” [Note: [Col. 0131] Psal. 67.]. The citizens will have joy: hence, “In their land they shall possess double things; everlasting joy shall be theirs” [Note: [Col. 0131] Isai. 61.], because “they rejoiced before you as those rejoice at harvest” [Note: [Col. 0131] Isai. 9.]. “I rejoiced at the things said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0131] Psal. 121.]. The king will have glory, because “God shall be wonderful in his saints, glorious in his majesty” [Note: [Col. 0131] Psal. 67.]. [Col. 0131C] For the whole earth shall be full of his majesty.

Therefore behold the city’s beauty, the citizens’ love, and the king’s honour: beauty from brightness, love from charity, honour from majesty. Hear of beauty from brightness: “She shall shine with splendid light” [Note: [Col. 0131] Tob. 13.]. For she “has no need of sun or moon, because the Lamb shall be her lamp” [Note: [Col. 0131] Apoc. 21.]. Hear of charity: “Charity never fails” [Note: [Col. 0131] I Cor. 13], for “many waters cannot quench charity, nor can rivers overwhelm it” [Note: [Col. 0131] Cant. 8.]. Hear of the king’s honour: in the Apocalypse it is written, “The twenty-four elders fell upon their faces, worshipping him who sits upon the throne, and laid down their crowns before the feet of him who sits upon the throne” [Note: [Col. 0131] Apoc. 4.]. Behold the honour. This is the king’s resting-place, in which the bride’s nard gives its fragrance. [Col. 0131D] Of this the following speaks.

> “We shall make for you golden chains, variegated with silver.”

[CARD.] *Murenulae* are ornaments for women, namely certain little chains interwoven with golden and silver rods; and therefore they are called variegated or distinguished with gold and silver. In gold, because it is more malleable than other metals, obedience is signified. Because of its price, wisdom—more precious than all riches—is signified. The ardour of charity too, because of its fiery colour, is denoted by gold. Christ therefore says: “We—namely Father, Son, and [Col. 0132A] Holy Spirit—shall make for you golden chains.” For towards these ornaments of the Virgin, the Father contributes the virtue of obedience, the Son the splendour of wisdom, and the Holy Spirit the ardour of love; these three, like little rods, are joined in the chains by a fitting craftsmanship. For charity, which burns, is joined to obedience, lest it be sluggish; obedience, which is humble, is joined to knowledge, lest it be puffed up [Note: [Col. 0131] I Cor. 8.]; and knowledge, which guides, is joined to love, lest zeal be erroneous. These little chains are variegated or distinguished with silver, for the brightness of bodily purity, signified by silver, contributes to the grace and beauty of the graces already mentioned.

But since a little earlier the Son called his mother [Note: [Col. 0131] Cant. 1.] his friend—and a true friend is one who both is loved and [Col. 0132B] loves—he immediately shows what God loved in her and how greatly she herself loved him who loved her. Therefore he says:

> “While the king was at his resting-place, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

[THO.] Christ entered his resting-place when he ascended into heaven. There the bride’s nard gave forth its fragrance when the Church’s virtue spread far and wide a sweet report of goodness. For from there he sent the Holy Spirit, filling the apostles with grace [Note: [Col. 0131] Act. 2.], so that in speech and action they might give the sweet fragrance of reputation, namely Christ’s humility and charity; for nard is a small and warm herb.

Rebuked by the bridegroom, the bride, her cheeks somewhat flushed with shame, answers his companions concerning what they had thought of him in that rebuke; [Col. 0132C] this she does through the following three chapters.

In the first, she declares humility—“while the king was”; in the second, charity—“a bundle of myrrh”; in the third, delight—“a cluster of cypress.” Nard is a warm and small herb, by which humility, arising from fervent love, is signified. I say this because there is a humility produced by truth: it has no warmth. And there is humility shaped and inflamed by charity. The latter consists in affection, the former in knowledge. The first teaches one, reproved by the light of truth, “not to think high things” [Note: [Col. 0131] I Tim. 6.]; the second, aided by the gift of charity, voluntarily to associate with the humble [Note: [Col. 0131] Rom. 12.]. The first is a matter of necessity, the second of will.

This humility of the bride spreads [Col. 0132D] its good fragrance like nard: warm with love, vigorous in devotion, fragrant in reputation. This humility is voluntary, perpetual, and fruitful. The king’s resting-place is the Father’s bosom, because the Son is always in the Father. Or the resting-place means repose in glory after the Ascension. The king’s resting-place is tranquility of heart, through which the Word of God rests piously in the heart and there kindles us to love and humility, which are signified in the warmth and smallness of nard. Thus he says: “While the king was at his resting-place, my nard gave forth its fragrance,” that is, it poured out humility and charity.

A fragrance sometimes comes from burning; sometimes from the breathing of a wafting breeze; sometimes from the crushing of spices. Therefore, when anyone, set aflame by the fire of divine love, gives himself to almsgiving and the other works of mercy and charity, he scatters, before the eyes of those who see it, a fragrance from burning. But when you learn that someone rich in the grace of spiritual virtues, or praiseworthy through the splendour of teaching or the glory of miracles, spreads a renowned reputation far and wide, recognize that the air is being filled with fragrance from divine flowers. But if you see someone worn down by the afflictions of illness, troubled by the harassments of persecution, or crushed by torments for God, and in all things giving thanks and enduring everything with a joyful soul and cheerful face, marvel that from the crushing of precious spices [Col. 0133B] a glorious fragrance rises even to heaven.

The bridegroom’s resting-place is threefold: the first is in a virgin’s womb, the second in the tomb, the third on the Father’s throne. Of the first it is said: “Issachar is a strong donkey lying down between the boundaries” [Note: [Col. 0133] Gen. 49.]. “Issachar” means “reward.” For the Beloved gave himself as our price. He lay down between the boundaries because he stood midway between divinity and humanity. Divinity, therefore, is the greater extreme, humanity the lesser; Christ, who is from these two, is the middle term. Therefore let us form a syllogism: let the major term be predicated of the middle, the middle of the minor, and thus, through the middle, the major of the minor. We argue thus: Christ is God; but Christ is also man; [Col. 0133C] therefore man is God.

Of the second resting-place it is said: “Resting, you lay down like a lion and lioness” [Note: [Col. 0133] Ibid.]. In the first he was a donkey by reason of humanity, but strong by reason of divinity. In the second he lay down by reason of humanity, but rose strong as a lion by reason of divinity. Of the third: “All shall feed and lie down, and there shall be none to terrify them” [Note: [Col. 0133] Soph. 3.]. They shall feed upon the vision of God; they shall lie down free from labours in eternal rest; there shall be none to terrify them, because they shall be secure in God’s protection.

In the first, our nard gave the fragrance of humility; in the second, myrrh removed the corruption of our old age; in the third, the cluster sent forth the wine of spiritual delight and delightful spirituality. The fragrance of humility has three degrees. There is humility produced by truth; a second, displayed by holiness; [Col. 0133D] and a third, perfected by charity. The first is in the heart, the second in the practice of works, the third in suffering. Of the first: “He shall save the humble in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0133] Psal. 33.]. Of the second: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things” [Note: [Col. 0133] Eccli. 3.]. Of the third: “I have been afflicted and humbled exceedingly; I roared from the groaning of my heart” [Note: [Col. 0133] Psal. 37.]. David displayed the first when he said: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” [Note: [Col. 0133] Psal. 21.]; the second, when he danced before the Ark of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0133] II Reg. 6.]; the third, when Shimei stoned him and cursed the king [Note: [Col. 0133] III Reg. 2.].

In the second resting-place myrrh removed the corruption [Col. 0134A] of our old age. Human oldness is twofold: that of guilt and that of punishment. Christ assumed one of these, namely punishment. Therefore he lay in the tomb for two nights because of our twofold oldness, and one day because of his own single oldness. He removed the oldness of guilt by forgiving past sins; by turning people away from and forgiving present sins; and, as to future sins, not by forgiving them, but by bestowing the grace through which they may be avoided. He removed the oldness of punishment: eternal punishment, by wholly destroying it so that the repentant do not experience it; purgatorial punishment, by setting a limit to it; temporal misery, not by wholly destroying it, but by weakening it and by making it no longer feared. Hence Peter, who denied at the voice of a maidservant [Note: [Col. 0133] Matth. 26.], after the myrrh of the Passion voluntarily offered himself to death.

In the third [Col. 0134B] resting-place, the cluster—that is, Christ—sent forth the wine of delight, that is, the grace of his love. Wine naturally intoxicates, warms, and makes glad; likewise the love of Christ intoxicated the apostles after the Resurrection so that they despised the world; it kindled them with desire for God; it gladdened them in hope of future goods. Of the first: “Do not be surprised if the world hates you” [Note: [Col. 0133] I Joan. 3.]. They say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” [Note: [Col. 0133] Galat. 6.]. Of the second: “Lord, your name and your memorial are in the desire of the soul. My soul shall desire you in the night, and my spirit also within my inmost parts” [Note: [Col. 0133] Psal. 134.]. Of the third: “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God, because he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and surrounded me with a robe of joy” [Note: [Col. 0133] Isai. 61.].

He will clothe me with a garment of salvation when [Col. 0134C] he clothes me with the glory of incorruption in likeness of the Lord’s Resurrection; he will surround me with a garment of righteousness when he glorifies the soul, making it immune from sin and suffering. And so all shall possess double things in their land, that is, the glory of body and soul.

The soul too has a threefold resting-place, in which it is refreshed with the bridegroom by spiritual feasts. Thus there are three banquets at which it is refreshed: the first, of bodies; the second, of souls; the third, of angels. At the first we eat to acquire strength; at the second, to console the soul’s hunger; at the third, for delightful satiation. Servants partake of the first; friends eat at the second; the dearest are intoxicated at the third. [Col. 0134D] In figure of these, we read that Christ celebrated three banquets. The first was at the approach of the Passion, when he ate the Passover with his disciples [Note: [Col. 0133] Matth. 26.]. The second was at the Ascension, when, while eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0133] Act. 1.]. The third he promised to his soldiers: “I,” he said, “appoint for you a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0133] Luc. 22.].

Of the first: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” [Note: [Col. 0133] I Cor. 15.]. Of the second: “Eat rich foods and drink mead” [Note: [Col. 0133] Prov. 9.]. Of the third, the angel says to Tobias: “I use immortal food and drink that cannot be seen” [Note: [Col. 0135] Tob. 12.]. [Col. 0135A] At the first, we must sustain the servant with food, adorn him with discipline, and burden him with works. Hence: “Food, a rod, and a burden for a donkey; bread, discipline, and work for a servant.” At the first, before he eats, the righteous person sighs; at the second, before he eats, he breathes freely; at the third, before he eats, he breathes upward. He sighs, fearing God’s judgments; he breathes freely in a pure conscience; he breathes upward toward heavenly joys.

At the first, therefore, we must observe what, how much, and when we eat. First, lest luxuries be sought; second, lest we pass the bounds of need; third, lest we neglect the time of abstinence. First, lest the grace of prayer be excluded; second, that almsgiving may be made from what remains; third, that penance may be performed. Therefore, before we eat, we must have three sighs. First we sigh in order to flee [Col. 0135B] hell; second, that sin may be removed; third, that we may return to the kingdom. Of these: “Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is better than storing up treasures of gold. It is what delivers from death, cleanses sin, and causes one to find eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0135] Ibid.].

For the first Job sighed, saying: “Leave me a little while, that I may bewail my pain before I go, never to return, to a land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death” [Note: [Col. 0135] Job. 10.]. For the second he sighs thus: “I have sinned. What shall I do to you, O guardian of men? Why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity?” [Note: [Col. 0135] Job 7.] For the third he sighs thus: “As a deer desires shade, and as a hired labourer awaits the end [Col. 0135C] of his work, so I have had empty months, and have counted laborious nights for myself” [Note: [Col. 0135] Ibid.].

But when there is sighing in the heart, there comes a roar of prayer in the mouth and overflowing waters in the eyes, that is, tears. Thus the three sighs have three roars: there is the roar of one threatening, the roar of one weeping, and the roar of one desiring—the first threatening hell, the second mourning affliction, the third desiring the kingdom. Of the first: “The lion shall roar; and who shall not fear?” [Note: [Col. 0135] Amos 3.] And: “The Lord shall roar from Zion, and from on high shall utter his voice” [Note: [Col. 0135] Amos 1.]. Of the second: “Esau roared with a great and very bitter cry” [Note: [Col. 0135] Gen. 27.]. Of the third, in this place.

The first has waters that make fruitful, the second overflowing waters, the third cleansing waters. For the first waters, that is, tears, lead to peace; the second wash away foulness; the third impart savour. Of the first: “Behold, I turn aside to them like a river of peace” [Note: [Col. 0135] Isai. 66.]. Of the third: “And like an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations” [Note: [Col. 0135] Ibid.]. Of the second: “Every night I shall wash my bed; I shall drench my couch with my tears” [Note: [Col. 0135] Psal. 6.]. In figure of these tears, Jesus wept three times: at the tomb of Lazarus [Note: [Col. 0135] Joan. 11.]; again, “seeing the city, he wept over it” [Note: [Col. 0135] Luc. 19.]; third, when the Passion was imminent, when he prayed alone on the mountain [Note: [Col. 0135] Matth. 14.], there he wept.

Paschasius says on Jeremiah: “Streams [Col. 0136A] of waters flowed down from my eyes” [Note: [Col. 0135] Thren. 3.]. These are the overflowing waters, namely: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0135] Psal. 45.]. Behold the first banquet. But at the second banquet, before I eat, I breathe freely with an unstained conscience. For one who feels the worm of a wicked conscience does not rest; no guilty person is absolved from it. For a disturbed conscience always forebodes cruel things. A good conscience has three things here: it has glory, does not fear disgrace, and awaits a crown. Of the first Paul says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0135] II Cor. 1.]. Of the second, the poet:

> A mind conscious of rectitude laughs at the falsehoods of reputation.

Of the third:

> The mind conscious to itself of rectitude shall receive worthy rewards.

[Col. 0136B] In this spiritual banquet there are four dishes. The first is innocence and simplicity in action; the second, a conscience free from the corruption of sin; the third, sweetness in devotion; the fourth, Abraham’s feeding of the angels beneath the oak of Mamre. For the first he gave milk; hence the Apostle: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0135] I Cor. 3.]. For the second, unleavened loaves. The same Apostle: “Let us feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” [Note: [Col. 0135] I Cor. 5.]. For the third, butter. The same Apostle: “Set your minds on things above” [Note: [Col. 0135] Coloss. 3.]. For the fourth, he cooked a calf from the herd; hence the bride in the Song: “Eat, friends, and be intoxicated, dearest ones” [Note: [Col. 0135] Cant. 5.]. For because of the sweetness of the Passion Christ ate “a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 0135] Luc. 24.]. This same thing was “John’s wild honey” [Note: [Col. 0135] Matth. 3.].

At the third banquet, before [Col. 0136C] they eat, they breathe upward. Hence David: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” [Note: [Col. 0135] Psal. 41.], where it says: “With the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting” [Note: [Col. 0135] Ibid.]. And the bride in the Song: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.” At that third banquet: “Man ate the bread of angels” [Note: [Col. 0135] Psal. 77.], where all “shall feed and lie down, and there shall be none to terrify them” [Note: [Col. 0135] Sophon. 3.]. Then “they shall rejoice in the Lord’s good things: in grain, wine, and oil” [Note: [Col. 0135] Jer. 31.]: in grain, because they shall see Christ’s humanity glorified; in wine, because they shall know by experience the charity of God the Father; in oil, because they shall taste the sweetness of the Holy Spirit. “And their soul shall be like a watered garden, and they shall hunger no more” [Note: [Col. 0135] Ibid.], because “we shall be satisfied when your glory appears, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0135] Psal. 16.]. [Col. 0136D] In which glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, you live and reign as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

Those who are at the first banquet recline in the lowest place; those at the second recline in the middle; those at the third recline in the first place. The first do so through humility, the second through truth, the third through dignity: through humility, because they consider themselves unworthy of heaven; through truth, because, considering all temporal things, they despise them and pant after heavenly things; through dignity, because they reign with [Col. 0137A] Christ. Of the first: “I have sinned beyond the number of the sand of the sea.” Of the second Paul says: “Forgetting the things behind, and stretching myself toward the things before, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling” [Note: [Col. 0137] Philipp. 3.]. Of the third: “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven, who have followed Christ’s footsteps.”

> “While the king was at his resting-place, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

[CARD.] Nard is a low-growing herb and signifies humility. Therefore the sense is: “While the king was at his resting-place”—while the Son was still in the Father’s bosom, not yet made visible—“my nard,” that is, my humility, “gave forth its fragrance” in his sight; and thus it pleased him. “For he has regarded the humility [Col. 0137B] of his handmaid; behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed” [Note: [Col. 0137] Luc. 1.]. But concerning her love for the Son:

> “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts.”

[THO.] Myrrh preserves bodies from decay by its bitterness. We apply it to bodies so that they may not rot, when, following Christ’s example, we restrain our bodies from the corruption of lust through mortification of the flesh, lest, if we leave them unseasoned, they become food for everlasting worms. It is called a little bundle because virtues bound together within us have little weight for those who love them. It dwells between the breasts because, in love of God and neighbour, a dwelling is prepared for Christ. Formerly he was “king,” now “beloved”; formerly he was at the royal table, now he is between the bride’s breasts. Great is the power of humility, to which the majesty of divinity so readily bows itself.

Myrrh is bitter, a hard and harsh thing, and signifies tribulation. Foreseeing that this was impending for the sake of her beloved, she speaks it joyfully, confident that she will undergo all things courageously. Therefore she says not a great bundle but a little bundle, and regards as small whatever she may suffer for his love. Aptly, a little bundle, because “a little one is born to us” [Note: [Col. 0137] Isa. 9]; aptly, a little bundle, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0137] Rom. 8]. Likewise: “For that which is at present momentary and light worketh in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory on high” [Note: [Col. 0137] 2 Cor. 4]. One day there will be for us an immense accumulation of glory which is now [Col. 0137D] a little bundle of myrrh [Note: [Col. 0137] Song 1]. And, lest she seem to presume concerning herself, but rather concerning God’s help which she has in her heart, she says: “It shall dwell between my breasts.” Hence she can confidently say: “Though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, for thou art with me” [Note: [Col. 0137] Ps. 22].

That bitter myrrh I would rightly call the insults, spittle, blows, nails, cross, and the other bitterness which he suffered for us. Nor shall I pass over the myrrh with which he was given drink on the cross [Note: [Col. 0137] Mark 15], nor that with which he was anointed in the tomb [Note: [Col. 0137] John 19]. In the first [Col. 0138A] he took upon himself the bitterness of my sins; in the second he consecrated the future incorruption of my body. Remember what the bride bore in the midst of her breasts: Mary in her womb, Simeon in his arms, Joseph on his shoulder. We bear him between our breasts by thinking of him; in the womb, by nurturing him with holy devotion; in the arms, by imitating his works; on the shoulders, by gladly enduring his sufferings.

Myrrh is bitter and pleasant in fragrance: bodies anointed with it do not know decay, because of its bitterness; yet it gives forth a pleasing odour. Hence John hears not only men but angels rejoicing and saying: “Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing for ever and ever. [Col. 0138B] Amen” [Note: [Col. 0137] Rev. 5]. He receives power in his birth, by which he was born without sin of the Virgin; divinity in baptism, when by the Father’s voice he was declared from heaven to be the beloved Son of God [Note: [Col. 0137] Matt. 3]; wisdom in preaching; strength in suffering; honour in resurrection; glory in ascension; blessing in the gathering of the elect into heaven.

See to what great glory Christ came through the myrrh and ignominy of the Passion, so that, encouraged by his example, we may hope through suffering to attain his glorious resurrection—yet with his grace going before: “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0137] Rom. 8].

There are three kinds of sufferings: sufferings of past time, sufferings of this time, and [Col. 0138C] sufferings belonging to no time. The first are imposed by necessity; the second arise from free will; the third arise from bondage to perpetual corruption. Of the first the Apostle says: “Every creature is subject to vanity, not willingly” [Note: [Col. 0137] ibid.]; of the second: “We, having the first fruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of the sons of God, the redemption of our flesh” [Note: [Col. 0137] ibid.]; of the third: “Every creature shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God” [Note: [Col. 0137] ibid.].

The first excluded former glory; the second work toward present glory, but are not comparable to future glory; the third do not belong to it. Former glory was in paradise; present glory is in the human heart; future glory will be in the kingdom. The first was in the temperance of the original state; the second in a pure conscience; [Col. 0138D] the third, when the affliction of this misery shall cease. The first passed away, because the first parents changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay [Note: [Col. 0137] Ps. 105], and all its glory is as the flower of hay [Note: [Col. 0137] Isa. 40]. Of the second, which is in the heart, it is said: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0137] 2 Cor. 1]. Of the third: “I shall be satisfied when thy glory appears” [Note: [Col. 0137] Ps. 16].

But in order that it may possess perfect testimony, it must first have beauty, second ardour, third splendour: the beauty of purity, the ardour of charity, the splendour [Col. 0139A] of truth. Purity, so that it may have no sin; charity, by which it loves God, has zeal for its neighbour, and a desire for sufferings; truth, by which it knows the blessedness of angels. Of these three it is said: “The glory of Lebanon is given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon” [Note: [Col. 0139] Isa. 35]. Carmel is called the knowledge of circumcision, which belongs to the first; Sharon, succession, which belongs to the second; Lebanon, whitening, which pertains to the third.

Therefore one must be circumcised in heart from unlawful thought; in mouth, from superfluous speech; in body, from evil action. Of the first: “Perverse thoughts separate from God” [Note: [Col. 0139] Wis. 1]; of the second: “Abstain from useless murmuring, and spare your tongue from detraction” [Note: [Col. 0139] ibid.]; of the third: “You shall do no servile [Col. 0139B] work” [Note: [Col. 0139] Num. 28]. Hence the Apostle says: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of our flesh: as you yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so yield your members to serve cleanness unto sanctification” [Note: [Col. 0139] Rom. 6]. Again: “Thanks be to God that, though you were once servants of sin, you have obeyed that form of teaching into which you were delivered” [Note: [Col. 0139] ibid.]. Behold the beauty of Carmel; behold the fine flour offered to God in sacrifice.

Sharon—that is, kindling—is a threefold ardour. The first is in the love of God; the second, in the mortification of the flesh; the third, in rebuking a brother. Behold, the fine flour is cooked: this is the threefold sacrifice—first, that from the oven, namely the love of God; second, that from the griddle, namely the affliction [Col. 0139C] of the flesh; third, that from the frying-pan, namely the correction of a brother. Of the first: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames” [Note: [Col. 0139] Song 8]; and: “The likeness of the living creatures was like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps” [Note: [Col. 0139] Ezek.]. The oil of devotion is poured over it. Hence: “Thou hast made my head fat with oil” [Note: [Col. 0139] Ps. 22].

Of the second: “Let rottenness enter into my bones” [Note: [Col. 0139] Hab. 3], etc. And Job: “Who will grant that my request may come, and that the Lord may grant me what I await? May he who began crush me; may he loose his hand and cut me down” [Note: [Col. 0139] Job 6]. Here too the oil of gladness is poured over it, “that it may gladden the face with oil” [Note: [Col. 0139] Ps. 103]. For God loves a cheerful giver [Note: [Col. 0139] 2 Cor. 9].

Of the third, Mattathias says: “Why was I born to see the evils of my nation?” [Note: [Col. 0139] 1 Macc. 2]. And Elijah, standing on the rock: “I have been zealous with zeal [Col. 0139D] for the Lord, because the children of Israel have forsaken his covenant” [Note: [Col. 0139] 3 Kings 19]. Here the oil of consolation is poured over it, which the Samaritan pours upon the man wounded by robbers [Note: [Col. 0139] Luke 17]. Behold Sharon.

Lebanon follows—that is, whitening. In the first it had beauty, so that it might be said: “Thou art wholly beautiful, my friend; thou art wholly beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0139] Song 4]. In the second, ardour, so that it may be said: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall blaze forth” [Note: [Col. 0139] Ps. 38], and: “My heart was inflamed and my reins were changed” [Note: [Col. 0139] Ps. 72]. “Was not our heart burning [Col. 0140A] within us” concerning Jesus [Note: [Col. 0139] Luke 24]? The third has splendour. Hence it is said: “With unveiled face we behold the glory, that we may be transformed into the same image” [Note: [Col. 0139] 2 Cor. 3].

Therefore, when these three degrees of ardour have been attained, let it be said: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0139] 2 Cor. 1]. Of the first: “Who can glory that he has a clean heart?” [Note: [Col. 0139] Prov. 20]. Of the second: “We glory in the hope of the glory of the sons of God.” Of the third: “And not only so, but we also glory in tribulations” [Note: [Col. 0139] Rom. 5]. In this splendour, then, we see that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us [Note: [Col. 0139] Rom. 8].

Now indeed it is not yet revealed, because we see only “through a glass in an enigma” [Note: [Col. 0139] 1 Cor. 13]. “For now we are the sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that, when he appears, we shall be like [Col. 0140B] him, because we shall see him as he is” [Note: [Col. 0139] 1 John 2]. For then “the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see the salvation of our God” [Note: [Col. 0139] Isa. 48; Luke 3]. For the Lord shall build Zion, “and he shall appear in his glory” [Note: [Col. 0139] Ps. 101], when “the wicked man shall be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” [Note: [Col. 0139] Isa. 26]. Then, therefore, it will be manifest that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0139] Rom. 8], then through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever.

“A little bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he shall dwell between my breasts.”

[CARD.] As though she said: The beloved who is mine, mine singularly and specially, is himself a little bundle of myrrh—that is, a bound collection of many bitternesses. And this little bundle shall dwell between my breasts, enclosed in my heart; for I cannot but suffer with him, I cannot but die with him, whom I bore, whom I suckled. Nor can I in any way fail to love him who endured so many bitternesses for me. But because she had said how deeply embittered she had been in the Passion of her Son, she next adds, concerning the joy of his resurrection and the consolation of her sorrow in the fruit of the Passion:

“A cluster of cypress-blossom is my beloved to me in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

[THO.] In Cyprus the vineyards are larger than elsewhere. Cyprus is the universal Church, which nourishes many vineyards insofar as it produces the wine of charity, which gladdens [Col. 0140D] the heart of man [Note: [Col. 0139] Ps. 103], for particular churches. Engaddi means “fountain of the kid.” Formerly a kid was sacrificed for sins [Note: [Col. 0139] Lev. 16]. The fountain of the kid is Christ’s baptism: when the body is immersed in it, it is washed from sins through faith in Christ, who died for sins. He who was myrrh in death is a cluster in resurrection. “For he died for our sins and rose again for our justification” [Note: [Col. 0139] Rom. 4], “that, dead to sins, we may live unto righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0139] 1 Pet. 2]. Thus, by mourning sins, you drank the bitterness of myrrh. But if [Col. 0141A] you have taken breath in the hope of life, you have drunk the wine which gladdens the heart of man.

Engaddi means “fountain of the kid,” or “eye of temptation.” It has vineyards, namely peoples who are in the fountain of the kid—that is, in baptism or in the tears of penitents—and who have an eye that sees temptations approaching. To these the beloved is a cluster pouring out wine, that is, the joy of his resurrection; and they themselves long for it, lest they be swallowed up by an excessive sorrow [Note: [Col. 0141] 2 Cor. 2]. Morally, Cyprus is called sadness or mourning, in which is this gladdening cluster. For in the practice of compunction the joy of consolation is found. Hence: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Note: [Col. 0141] Matt. 5].

This order is also found historically. First Mary Magdalene poured the precious fragrance of nard upon the head and feet of the reclining Lord [Note: [Col. 0141] Matt. 26]. Then the disciples anointed the crucified one with myrrh [Note: [Col. 0141] John 19]. Then he became a cluster of cypress-blossom when he gladdened them with the joy of resurrection. Hear the joy:

“The Lord rose, and, meeting the women, said: ‘Hail.’ Then they came up and held his feet” [Note: [Col. 0141] Matt. 28].

Three things are set before us, fragrant with the sweetness of divine mercy: that he rose, that he met the women, and that he greeted them. In the first he set before us glory; in the second he gave confidence; in the third he bestowed joy: glory, for which we may sigh; confidence, by which we may aspire; joy, beneath which we may take breath. We sigh through desires; we aspire from a pure conscience; we take breath from the constriction [Col. 0141C] of sorrow.

The bride sighed when she said in the Song: “Tell my beloved that I languish for love” [Note: [Col. 0141] Song 5]. She aspired when she said: “I shall rise and go around the city; through the lanes and streets I shall seek him whom my soul loves” [Note: [Col. 0141] Song 3]. She took breath when she said: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” [Note: [Col. 0141] Song 2]. O with what mighty embrace he embraced me on the cross, on which water flowed from his side, blood streamed from his heart, and his soul departed from his body. This rich merchant brought his wares, wrapped up, at his coming. Hence: “Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me” [Note: [Col. 0141] Rev. 22]. For “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” [Note: [Col. 0141] Jas. 1].

In the Passion the sackcloth was torn. Hence: “Thou hast torn my sackcloth [Col. 0141D] and hast clothed me with gladness” [Note: [Col. 0141] Ps. 29]. In it we saw him as a leper, struck by God and humbled [Note: [Col. 0141] Isa. 53]. In the resurrection he cast off the purple. “For with unveiled face we behold the glory of the Lord,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0141] 2 Cor. 13]. Or thus: “The locks of his head are like royal purple bound in channels” [Note: [Col. 0141] Song 7]. This purple is Christ’s glorified flesh; the bride’s head is Christ, and his hair his imitators, who are like royal purple because the glory of resurrection is owed to them. This purple is bound in channels because it is now worshipped in heaven by angels [Col. 0142A]. The fountain of graces is in heaven; but when it is ministered to us through angels, it is poured out as though through channels.

This glory is threefold, because resurrection is threefold. The first is miraculous, the second virtuous, the third glorious. The first is from temporal death to temporal life; the second, from spiritual death to spiritual life; the third, from temporal death to incorruptible life. In the first the Church grows together; in the second the spirit revives; in the third human nature blooms again. Of the first: “Women received their dead raised to life” [Note: [Col. 0141] Heb. 11]. Again: “The deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor have the gospel preached to them” [Note: [Col. 0141] Matt. 11]. Of the second: “They told Jacob: ‘Joseph your son is alive.’ When he heard it, his spirit revived” [Note: [Col. 0141] Gen. 45]; [Col. 0142B] and: “My son was dead and has come alive again; he was lost and is found” [Note: [Col. 0141] Luke 15]. Of the third: “Christ rose, the first fruits of those asleep” [Note: [Col. 0141] 1 Cor. 15]; and: “My flesh has blossomed again” [Note: [Col. 0141] Ps. 27]; and: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” [Note: [Col. 0141] Ps. 91]; and: “The righteous shall bud like a lily and shall flower for ever with the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0141] Office of the Church].

The first occurred in Lazarus; the second in the prodigal son; the third in Christ. By Christ, because he raised three dead persons [Note: [Col. 0141] Luke 7 and 8; John 11]. With Christ: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above” [Note: [Col. 0141] Col. 3]. In Christ, because “as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0141] 1 Cor. 15]. The first is glorious. Hence the Lord says to Martha: “Did I not tell thee: If thou believest, thou shalt see the glory of God?” [Note: [Col. 0141] John 11]. [Col. 0142C] The second is more glorious, because “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” [Note: [Col. 0141] Ps. 44]. The third is most glorious: “The body is sown dishonourable; it shall rise in glory” [Note: [Col. 0141] 1 Cor. 15], “when with unveiled face we shall behold the glory of God” [Note: [Col. 0141] 2 Cor. 3].

By this resurrection the Lord rose and showed his glory, that we might sigh for it. This resurrection brought our imperfection to perfection, restored our exile to paradise, and restored our dead person to life. He himself, rising, taught the first thus: “If thou wilt be perfect, sell all that thou hast and give to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0141] Matt. 19]. Of the second it is said [Note: [Col. 0141] Office of the Church]:

> He was raised above the clouds,  
> And gave hope to believers,  
> Opening paradise,  
> Which the first-created man had closed.

[Col. 0142D] Of the third: “As all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0141] 1 Cor. 15], because sinful man was dead and came alive again; he had been lost through Adam’s fault and was found through Christ rising from the dead [Note: [Col. 0141] Luke 15].

Second, he met the women [Note: [Col. 0141] Matt. 28], in order to give the confidence by which we may aspire. The Lord meets the weak, the desolate, and the saints: the weak, that he may strengthen them through patience; the desolate, that he may restore them in joy; the saints, that he may satisfy their desire with the presence of his glorified flesh. In the first sense Peter saw Christ meet him; in the second he met [Col. 0143A] the women; in the third he met the angels in the Ascension. “For his going forth is from the height of heaven, and his meeting is unto its height” [Note: [Col. 0143] Ps. 18].

As a figure of the first, Isaac came to meet Rebekah, and she herself descended from the camel [Note: [Col. 0143] Gen. 27]. Rebekah means patience. As a figure of the second, the father met the prodigal son [Note: [Col. 0143] Luke 15]. As a figure of the third, Melchizedek, with bread and wine, met Abraham returning from battle [Note: [Col. 0143] Gen. 14]. Behold, he will give us confidence, that we may aspire.

Third, he added, “Hail” [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 28], that in joy we might take breath. We find three salutations of God full of devotion. Raphael brought the first to Tobias [Note: [Col. 0143] Tob. 5], Gabriel the second to Mary [Note: [Col. 0143] Luke 1], and today the Lord the third to the women. The first he sent and delayed; the second he commanded and brought; the third he offered and brought. [Col. 0143B] Of the first: “Thou who sendest salvations to Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0143] Ps. 43]; of the second: “My spirit hath rejoiced in God my saviour” [Note: [Col. 0143] Luke 1]; of the third: “Our salvation is in thy hand” [Note: [Col. 0143] Gen. 47].

In the first there was a slower feeling, in the second a more discerning one, in the third a more ardent one. For in the first, when the angel says, “May joy be always with thee,” Tobias says: “What joy shall there be for me?” [Note: [Col. 0143] Tob. 5], etc. In the second Mary says: “How shall this be, since I know not a man?” [Note: [Col. 0143] Luke]. In the third: “They came up and held his feet” [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 28]. He who is greeted is held more eagerly in love, more firmly in memory, and more healthfully in hope.

Accordingly, beside the three words of greeting, we read in Scripture three defective words, because on this way [Col. 0143C] there is no perfect salvation: *avete*, *valete*, *salvete*. In the first, *avete* is said, as though *avide tenete*, “hold eagerly.” This *ave* is written four times. The first was admonitory, the second deceptive, the third mocking, the fourth consolatory. The angel brought the first to Mary [Note: [Col. 0143] Luke 1], a disciple brought the second to Christ [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 26], a pagan brought the third to the crucified one [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 27], and Christ brought the fourth to the women [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 28]. The first was followed by the fruit of virginal fertility; the second incurred the crime of violated majesty; the third, the sin of ingratitude; the fourth conceived assurance both of the Lord’s resurrection and of ours. In the first we praise new grace; against the second let us seek caution; against the third let us seek patience; in the fourth we conceive joy. Beside the second, *valete* means, as it were, *valide tenete*, “hold firmly”; beside the third, *salvete* means “hold fast to your salvation.” Behold the joy beneath which we take breath.

Of this greeting, namely: “Then they came up,” through confidence in the greeting, “in order to seize him” [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 26]. First we ought to withdraw, second to approach, third to go beyond: to withdraw by fleeing sin; to approach by imitating Christ; to go beyond by contemplating heavenly joys. In the first we are freer; in the second more secure; in the third more joyful. The prophet admonished us concerning the first [Col. 0144A] thus: “Go out from Babylon and flee from the Chaldeans” [Note: [Col. 0143] Isa. 48]; concerning the second: “Come to him, and you shall be enlightened” [Note: [Col. 0143] Ps. 33]; concerning the third: “I said in the excess of my mind: ‘I am cast away from before thine eyes’” [Note: [Col. 0143] Ps. 30].

It should be noted that some hold his feet, some his breast, some his head. Those hold the feet who have affection toward his humanity; his breast, those who marvel at the union of divinity and humanity; his head, those who contemplate majesty. The first trust in mercy and truth; the second burn with charity; the third shine with brightness. Thus the first held his feet and say: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps” [Note: [Col. 0143] 1 Pet. 2]. The second, marvelling, say: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0143] John 1]. [Col. 0144B] The third say: “With unveiled face we behold the glory of God” [Note: [Col. 0143] 2 Cor. 3].

Mary Magdalene held his feet when she bathed them with tears [Note: [Col. 0143] Luke 7]; John the Evangelist held his breast when he reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper [Note: [Col. 0143] John 21]; that woman held his head when she poured nard upon the head of him reclining [Note: [Col. 0143] Mark 14]. Those who hold his breast with Joseph, the noble councillor [Note: [Col. 0143] Mark 15], bury him in their heart. Thus, with Joseph, they season him with spices, wrap him in a clean linen cloth, and seal the stone [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 27]: with spices of desire and love, with the linen of purity, and with the stone of strength. Yet by the stone is signified now hardness, now strength. Therefore, because of the strength of love, he must be enclosed in the stone. But lest we be hard in dispensing the good which lies hidden within us, the stone must be rolled away by the angel of great counsel [Note: [Col. 0143] Isa. 9, according to the LXX]—that is, [Col. 0144C] hardness must be removed.

This hardness is threefold: first, that of the obstinate sinner; second, that of the miserly wise man; third, that of stern strength. The first is the stone beneath which Lazarus was decaying [Note: [Col. 0143] John 11]; the second, that beneath which the well was covered [Note: [Col. 0143] Gen. 28]; the third, the stone in which the Lord was buried [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 27]. The first was rolled away by a Jew; the second by Jacob together with the shepherds; the third by the angel of great counsel.

Of the first the Lord says to the Jews: “Take away the stone” [Note: [Col. 0143] John 11]. “Jew” is interpreted “confessing,” because confession takes away the hardness of obstinacy. Of the second it is said: “When Jacob, who is called supplanter, went into Mesopotamia of Syria, he rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well together with the shepherds” [Note: [Col. 0143] Gen. 28]; that is, Christ, who supplants sins together with the teachers [Col. 0144D] of the Church, brings it about that they distribute to others the knowledge which they hide in themselves. Of the third it is said: “The angel of the Lord came and rolled away the stone” [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 28]; that is, Christ by his visitation causes those who are strong in love, putting aside the austerity of severity, to begin to be gentle toward their neighbours.

“A cluster of cypress-blossom is my beloved to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

[CARD.] The island of Cyprus produces clusters large and sweet. But Cyprus is interpreted “flowering.” Therefore the mother, showing [Col. 0145A] her joy at the resurrection of her Son, says: My beloved is to me a cluster of cypress-blossom, that is, the sweet joy of flowering. For his flesh has flowered again; my bitterness has been changed into sweetness, my sorrow has been changed into joy; and I, who had withered with him in his death, bloom again with him as he flowers. He too has become to me a cluster of cypress-blossom—that is, sweet and great joy—in the vineyards of Engaddi, when I consider the fruit of his Passion, which appears in the vineyards of Engaddi.

Engaddi is a place where there are balsam trees, which he calls vineyards because they are cultivated in the manner of vineyards. Engaddi is interpreted “fountain of the kid.” Therefore, through the balsam trees which arise and grow in Engaddi are signified Christ’s faithful, who are spiritually born in Engaddi—that is, [Col. 0145B] in the fountain of the kid, namely the font of baptism, where the kid is washed and becomes a lamb—and, rooted in faith, grow and advance so that, like balsam trees, they may flow with spiritual richness. When the mother has said these things, the Son returns to continue his praise of the mother’s beauty, saying:

“Behold, thou art beautiful, my friend; behold, thou art beautiful: thy eyes are doves’ eyes.”

[THO.] Twice he calls her beautiful. Indeed, to one to whom he gives love of God and neighbour, he imparts a double beauty, in which he delights and which he praises. Her eyes are called those of doves because, while she groans among temporal things, she is borne by desire toward eternal things, and in simplicity guards her senses. A dove moans instead of singing. Such is the holy soul which, when it sees the reprobate chattering in love of the world, itself attends to heavenly desire, fearing, while it is delayed, lest it lose what it loves.

Or the dove’s eyes are preachers, who keep the simplicity they preach and, despising visible things, pant for eternal things with many groans. From love of the bride comes presumption; from love of the bridegroom, indignation, as the outcome proves. For correction followed presumption; cleansing, correction; reward, cleansing. Pride now yields where the affection of love grows strong. Therefore the beloved calls her, once cleansed, “friend,” repeats “beautiful,” and immediately hears the same exchange from her. Here he calls her beautiful because the soul’s beauty is twofold: humility and innocence. Hence David: “Thou shalt sprinkle [Col. 0145D] me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed”—that is, with humility, signified by a small herb. And it follows: “Thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” [Note: [Col. 0145] Ps. 50], because, washed by thee, I shall be innocent.

And because, rebuked by him for what she had asked—namely, to see the beloved as a little bundle of myrrh—she had humbled herself when she saw him, she deserved to hear: “Thy eyes are doves’ eyes,” that is, simple, because now “thou dost not walk in great matters nor in things too wonderful for me” [Note: [Col. 0145] Ps. 130]. Or, because the Holy Spirit appeared in this bird, spiritual vision is understood, to which she is now conveyed through her humility.

The bride had praised the bridegroom’s reclining, which had kindled her to display holy sweetness; she praises his Passion, by which he had trained her to suffer—that which nourishes virtues; she magnifies the glory of his resurrection, by which he had raised her to the hope of blessed immortality; she exalts the grace of the Spirit, by which he had led her into virtue. Behold, the bridegroom’s mercy gratefully beholds and gently receives her most diligent devotion; and thus, by proclaiming it, reveals her beauty, saying:

“Behold, thou art beautiful, my friend.” Beautiful in pure works, living soberly, righteously, and piously [Note: [Col. 0145] Titus 2]; beautiful in simplicity of heart, persevering in good deeds with the sole aim of eternity; beautiful in life, beautiful in teaching, beautiful in observance of the law—dispensing temporal things justly; beautiful in evangelical perfection, [Col. 0146B] leaving all things for God’s sake; beautiful in body, bravely overcoming the pleasures of the flesh; beautiful in soul, utterly uprooting from the mind the desires of the world; beautiful in flesh, preserving chastity; beautiful in mind, keeping inviolate charity toward God and neighbour; beautiful in prosperity, not becoming proud; beautiful in adversity, remaining untroubled; beautiful in subjection, by obeying; beautiful in prelation, by furnishing those subject to her with guidance toward life through words and examples; beautiful in private, beautiful in public, beautiful in silence, beautiful in speech, beautiful in gentleness, beautiful under the persecution of the proud. Now let us see by an example how this beauty is formed in us.

[Col. 0146C] One who intends to make a beautiful image first cuts wood from its natural root; then, when the branches have been cut away, he places it in a suitable place for the work; afterward he shapes and whitens the image; then he beautifully paints it with varied colours. Let us therefore consider a person clinging at some time to vices as a tree of the earth. For a tree signifies a human being, as in the Gospel: “A good tree brings forth good fruit” [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 7]. First, therefore, let us separate the person from worldly things, as the root from the earth. Next, the branch of vices is put in a suitable place when the person is placed in religious life. A form is impressed upon him when he is fashioned after God’s image. He is whitened by innocence; the variety of colours is the beauty of virtues; the field for these colours is the human and pure heart.

[Col. 0146D] For an impure heart is scattered by some thoughts, inflamed by others, stretched out by others, contracted by others, defiled by others, disturbed by others. Angry thoughts scatter it; proud thoughts inflame it; ambitious thoughts stretch it out; fearful thoughts contract it; lustful thoughts defile it; vain thoughts disturb it. Thus Isaiah says of these [Note: [Col. 0145] ch. 13]: “There wild beasts shall lie down, and dragons shall rest there; ostriches shall dwell there, and shaggy creatures shall dance there; owls shall answer one another, and sirens in temples of pleasure.” Wild beasts scatter; dragons inflame; ostriches stretch out; shaggy creatures disturb; owls contract; sirens defile.

[Col. 0147A] “Thy eyes,” he says, “are doves’ eyes.” Where the eye is truly single, it must have charity in its intention and truth in its choice. Hence the Lord says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” [Note: [Col. 0147] Matt. 10]. Therefore let it possess this purity, that it may not wish to deceive, and this caution, that it cannot be deceived.

Again, one eye is good, another better, another evil, another worse. There is one who loves good and does evil unknowingly: he is good, yet not simple but manifold. There is one who does good and understands wisely: he is simple. There is one who understands good, does evil, and does not love it: he is wicked. Of the first: “Ephraim is a deceived dove, without heart” [Note: [Col. 0147] Hos. 7]. Of the second: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” [Note: [Col. 0147] Matt. 10]. Of the third it is said that “the children of this world are more prudent in their generation than the children of light” [Note: [Col. 0147] Luke 16]. Of the fourth: “Their foolish heart was darkened, and they were given over to a reprobate mind” [Note: [Col. 0147] Rom. 1].

The dove sometimes signifies the Holy Spirit, as: “I saw the bride ascending like a dove from the branches of the trees” [Note: [Col. 0147] Office of the Church]; sometimes the foolishness of fools, as: “Ephraim, a deceived dove, without heart” [Note: [Col. 0147] Hos. 7]; sometimes the simplicity of the saints’ intention. Hence: “Who are these that fly as clouds, and as doves to their windows?” [Note: [Col. 0147] Isa. 60].

A dove feeds on pure grain; utters a moan instead of song; recognizes from its shadow in waters the flight of a hawk; nests in a rock; has no gall; flies in flocks; and looks upon all things simply. All these things suit the bride spiritually. For by purity of life she delights, as it were, [Col. 0147C] in pure grain; she rejoices in the devout compunction of her heart; in the sacred Scriptures she perceives and avoids the snares of demons; in the wounds of Christ’s Passion she builds for herself a sweet resting-place for the mind; without the bitterness of malice, she is severe against sinners’ offences; she loves the concord of the brethren; whatever she sees, she beholds without covetousness and considers without ambition. Therefore let it be said:

“Behold, you are fair, my beloved, behold, you are fair.” There are four beauties of the bride: in chastity, in purity of conscience, in outward conduct, and in contemplation. Of chastity it is said: “Behold how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity” [Note: [Col. 0147] Wisd. 4]; of conscience: “Forget your people [Col. 0147D] and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty” [Note: [Col. 0147] Ps. 44]; of conduct: “Strength and beauty are her garment” [Note: [Col. 0147] Prov. 31]; of contemplation: “Coming from Lebanon, how fair you have become, my beloved” [Note: [Col. 0147] Song 4]. Likewise, of these four it was said: “Whiter than snow, brighter than milk, more ruddy than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire” [Note: [Col. 0147] Lam. 4]. The whiteness of snow signifies bodily purity; its coldness, the cooling of the heart: and this belongs to chastity. The whiteness of milk signifies innocence—for it is the food of little children—and simplicity. [Col. 0148A] And this concerns conscience. Ivory is a strong animal, whose white bones acquire redness in the course of time. For those who live well must be strong in the exercise of virtues; white, because of the brightness of their example toward their neighbour; and red because of the fervour of the righteous. This concerns conduct. Sapphire has the colour of heaven, on account of contemplatives, who consider heavenly things.

Judith signifies chastity: Holofernes was captivated by her beauty, and she cut off his head, lest he corrupt her [Note: [Col. 0147] Judith 13]. Abishag the Shunammite signifies beauty of conscience: the beautiful young woman warmed the feet of aged David [Note: [Col. 0147] III Kings 1], that is, our affections. In the figure of Sarah is the beauty of conduct: Pharaoh, who seized her because of her beauty, could not corrupt her while God protected her, and [Col. 0148B] she returned to her husband with gifts [Note: [Col. 0147] Gen. 20; printed “Ged. 20”]. The beauty of Rachel [Note: [Col. 0147] Gen. 29] is the beauty of contemplation.

The first beauty is against the spirit of fornication; the second against the spirit of faithless security; the third against the spirit of faint-heartedness and dissipation; the fourth against the spirit of blindness. Of the first, Paul says: “Flee fornication; God will judge fornicators and adulterers” [Note: [Col. 0147] I Cor. 6]. Of the second: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” [Note: [Col. 0147] Prov. 28], “and he who is hard of heart shall fall into evil.”

[Note: [Col. 0147] Ovid.] “Love is a thing full of anxious fear.” Of the third, Paul says: “Correct the disorderly, comfort the faint-hearted” [Note: [Col. 0147] I Thess. 5]. Again: “I hear that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work but meddling in everything” [Note: [Col. 0147] II Thess. 3]. Of the fourth, David says: “The enemy [Col. 0148C] has persecuted my soul; he has humbled my life to the ground; he has placed me in darkness like those dead of old” [Note: [Col. 0147] Ps. 142].

These are the four evil angels whom John saw in the Apocalypse. “I saw,” he says, “four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth, and they held the four winds, lest they should blow upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0147] Rev. 7]: namely, the four breathings of the Holy Spirit which produce these beauties. The first wind cools the heat of lust; the second cleanses the threshing-floor of conscience from the chaff of perverse thoughts; the third, by its serenity, removes the unseasonable rigour of winter, that is, dissipation and faint-heartedness; the fourth drives away the cloud of worldly anxiety, so that heaven may appear more freely in contemplation. These [Col. 0148D] four spirits restrain them, lest they make the bride beautiful.

“Your eyes are those of doves.” There are the eyes of kites; there are the eyes of doves.
