Of the former: “The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0147] Prov. 17]; of the latter: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” [Note: [Col. 0147] Eccl. 2]. Earthly persons are called “earth,” namely those who love earthly things. There are three ends of this earth: pleasure, vanity, and malice. Likewise, there are three eyes of fools: the lustful, the proud, and the wicked. Of the lustful eye it is said: “An immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest mind [Col. 0149A].” Of the proud eye: “A generation whose eyes are lofty, and whose eyelids are raised on high” [Note: [Col. 0149] Prov. 30]. Of the wicked eye: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” [Note: [Col. 0149] Matt. 6]. The lustful eye is directed toward the end of pleasure; the proud toward the end of vanity; the wicked toward the end of malice.

Adam had the lustful eye when he saw that the tree was beautiful to the sight and sweet for eating, and the eyes of both of them were opened [Note: [Col. 0149] Gen. 3]. Jonathan had the proud eye when, after his victory had been achieved, he ate a little honey and his eyes were enlightened [Note: [Col. 0149] I Kings 14]. Balaam had the wicked eye when he gave Balak counsel by which the children of Israel might be deceived [Note: [Col. 0149] Num. 24]. Hence it is said: “A man whose eye is closed” [Note: [Col. 0149] ibid.], “who, falling, has open eyes”; “the eyes of the wise are in his head” [Note: [Col. 0149] Eccl. 2].

There are three heads: our spirit, [Col. 0149B] Christ, and God. Hence the Apostle: “The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ; the head of Christ is God” [Note: [Col. 0149] I Cor. 11]. The man is the spirit; the woman, the flesh. Likewise, there are three eyes of the dove. The first is circumspection; the second, devout inquiry; the third, contemplation. Of the first David complains: “The light of my eyes—even that is not with me” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 37]. Of the second, Simeon says: “Do you think that these eyes will see him through whom the eyes of the heart will be unveiled?” Of the third: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 122].

The first is directed toward the head which is the spirit. Hence: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 12]. The second toward the head which is Christ. Hence: “After I see the places of the nails with Thomas, I shall say: My Lord and my God” [Note: [Col. 0149] John 20]. The third toward the head which is God. [Col. 0149C] Hence: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you rest at noon” [Note: [Col. 0149] Song 1]. The first is circumspection for the exclusion of vices and preservation of virtues; the second, devout inquiry for remembrance of Christ’s benefits; the third, contemplation for knowledge of heavenly things.

“Behold, you are fair, my beloved, behold, you are fair; your eyes are those of doves.”

[CARD.] Because the fragrance of nard had passed from mother to son. Nard is a low-growing and warm herb. Behold, he commends the mother on both accounts and says: “Behold, you are fair, my beloved,” because of the beauty of humility; “behold, you are fair,” because of the warmth of love. Because of beauty you are beloved; and because of your simplicity you are mine, singularly and properly. This simplicity, indeed, [Col. 0149D] he expresses when he says: “Your eyes are those of doves.” For simplicity and innocence are signified in doves. The eyes, however, are two: understanding and affection. These dove-like eyes are innocent and simple when the understanding is without error and understands nothing in the truth of Scripture except truth; and when the affection is toward God without worldly desire, and in God’s work desires nothing worldly, seeks nothing but God.

“Behold, you are fair, my beloved, and comely.”

[THO.] She stands on high, and has raised herself to the lofty summit of the mind [Col. 0150A]: she who, with dove’s eyes, sees the king in his beauty. That he calls him fair and adds comely means according to both natures. The beloved is called fair and comely because he is seen by the lover, both in humanity and in divinity, without the blemish of reproach. As the soul follows him in desire, it forgets earthly things and becomes more beautiful. He is fair in creating all things; comely in redeeming what was lost. Fair in equality with the Father, the Word, God with God; comely in the virginity of his mother, the Word made flesh [Note: [Col. 0149] John 1]. Fair in bestowing blessed glory upon the righteous; comely in granting pardon to penitents.

He is also fair not only in himself but also in the Church, which is his body [Note: [Col. 0149] Col. 1], which he made fair in creation, and comely in redemption, so that she may be [Col. 0150B] lovable to the bridegroom, desirable to angels, and venerable to all good persons.

There are four beauties of the bridegroom. The first is in his mortal body, because he was “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 44]. The second is in the Transfiguration. Hence: “His face was like the sun, and his garments white as snow” [Note: [Col. 0149] Matt. 17]. The third is in glorified humanity. Hence: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe, walking on” [Note: [Col. 0149] Isa. 63]. The fourth is in divinity. Hence: “His eyes shall see the king in his beauty” [Note: [Col. 0149] Isa. 63]. In the first he honoured our weakness; in the second he showed the character of future blessedness; in the third, the reality of future incorruption; in the fourth he will restore the image and likeness lost in Adam, when his members shall share in that form. Even now they are [Col. 0150C] made comely, not by bodily fitness but by the commendation of virtues.

But, to draw one example from among many: such is that friend of the bridegroom—I mean John the Baptist—who is commended in the Gospel for such beauty as follows: “This child will be great before the Lord; he will drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he will eat nothing unclean; and many will rejoice at his birth” [Note: [Col. 0149] Luke 1]. Behold, here he is found commendable in three respects: commendable before God, strict with himself, gracious toward his neighbour. In the first is pre-eminence in holiness; in the second, restraint of pleasure; in the third, joy at his birth. By the first we strive to please God; by the second to guard ourselves; by the third to draw our neighbour.

[Col. 0150D] “‘He will,’” he says, “‘be great before the Lord.’” A person may be great in his own eyes; great before the world; great before a religious person; or great before the Lord. The first comes from consciousness of some grace; the second from power, riches, nobility, or rank; the third from good conduct; the fourth from the perfection of charity. The first is deformed with the devil; the second conformed to this world; the third re-formed by Christ; the fourth formed by the Holy Spirit.

The devil was great in his own eyes when he said: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” [Col. 0151A] [Note: [Col. 0151] Isa. 14]. Thus Simon Magus too thought himself to be someone great [Note: [Col. 0151] Acts 8]. Of the second: “Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians” [Note: [Col. 0151] Isa. 36]. Of the third, it is said of Job: “That man was great in all his work” [Note: [Col. 0151] Job 1]. Of the fourth: “Isaac went on growing and advancing until he became exceedingly great” [Note: [Col. 0151] Gen. 26].

The devil was great in his own eyes. Of him Ezekiel speaks [Note: [Col. 0151] chap. 17]: “A very great eagle, with great wings, long in the stretching out of its limbs, having feathers and many colours, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and carried it away into the land of Sennaar [Chanaan].” Of such persons the Apostle says: “He who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself” [Note: [Col. 0151] Gal. 6]. Again: “What do you have that you have not received? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” [Note: [Col. 0151] I Cor. 4]. Therefore: “The greater you are, humble [Col. 0151B] yourself in all things” [Note: [Col. 0151] Ecclus. 3].

The Pharisee was great in his own eyes when he said: “I am not as other men are, nor even as this Publican” [Note: [Col. 0151] Luke 18]. John was not great in his own eyes when he said: “He who comes after me has been made before me; I am not worthy to loose the strap of his sandal” [Note: [Col. 0151] Mark 1]. Such a person deforms himself with the devil, because he who was first made in the image and likeness of God “was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” [Note: [Col. 0151] Ps. 48].

There is another who is great before the people: first, in power, by which he is proud, not considering how Nebuchadnezzar fell when he said: “Is this not Babylon, which I have built, for the glory and beauty of my kingdom?” [Note: [Col. 0151] Dan. 4]. Behold power. But no power endures long. For a voice was [Col. 0151C] made to him: “To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom is taken away from you” [Note: [Col. 0151] ibid.], and he was changed into an ox.

Likewise, prelates are great by rank, of whom it is said: “Iniquity went forth from the elders who ought to govern the people” [Note: [Col. 0151] Dan. 13]. These are Nadab and Abihu, who, offering strange fire, died before the Lord [Note: [Col. 0151] Num. 3]. Of these it is said in the law: “When you choose one from among our least, he shall not multiply horses, nor lead the people back into Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0151] Deut. 17]. They labour to appear great before the people. And why should they not, when it is said:

[Note: [Col. 0151] Juvenal, Satire 3.]

How often Fortune, eager for jesting,  
raises men from low estate  
to the highest peaks of affairs.

To the powerful it is said: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments. For those who preside, a most severe judgment [Col. 0151D] shall be made” [Note: [Col. 0151] Wisd. 6], that is, for prelates.

Those who are great by nobility say: “We are Abraham’s seed and have never been slaves to anyone” [Note: [Col. 0151] John 8]. Hear the philosopher:

[Note: [Col. 0151] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy.*]

Why do you boast of lineage and ancestors?  
If you look to your beginnings  
and to God your author,  
none proves base-born,  
unless, cherishing worse things in vices,  
he abandons his own origin. If you are wicked—

[Col. 0152A] [Note: [Col. 0151] Juvenal, Satire 8.]

The nobility of your very parents begins to stand against you  
and to hold a bright torch before your shameful deeds.

Because:

[Note: [Col. 0151] ibid.]

Every vice of the mind bears a crime in itself  
so much the more conspicuous as he who sins is thought greater.

And:

[Note: [Col. 0151] ibid.]

It is wretched to depend on another’s fame.  
I would rather that Thersites were your father, provided that you  
were like Aeacides and took up the arms of Vulcan,  
than that Achilles should beget you, yet make you like Thersites.

Likewise:

[Note: [Col. 0151] Ovid.]

Majesty and love do not agree well,  
nor do they remain in one dwelling-place.

And:

[Note: [Col. 0151] ibid.] “Nobility lies beneath love.”

David kept these things far from himself, saying thus in Psalm 130: [Col. 0152B] “I have not walked in great things, nor in wonders above me” [Note: [Col. 0151] Ps. 130]. And John: “Are you Elijah? I am not. Are you the prophet? No” [Note: [Col. 0151] John 1].

He was great in wealth, “that rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day” [Note: [Col. 0151] Luke 16]. And so was he to whom the Lord said: “Fool, this night they shall require your soul of you; and the things you have prepared, whose shall they be?” [Note: [Col. 0151] Luke 12].

Those are great in wisdom who “are wise to do evil, but are unwilling to do good” [Note: [Col. 0151] Jer. 4]. “This wisdom does not descend from above, but is earthly, animal, devilish” [Note: [Col. 0151] Jas. 3]. These, “when they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts; claiming to be wise, they became fools” [Col. 0152C] [Note: [Col. 0151] Rom. 1]. “I shall destroy,” he says, “the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” [Note: [Col. 0151] I Cor. 1]. “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; he also chose the weak things to confound the strong” [Note: [Col. 0151] ibid.].

All these did not give thanks to God for their greatness, as did the elders of the Apocalypse, who fell upon their faces to worship him who sat upon the throne and cast their crowns before the throne [Note: [Col. 0151] Rev. 5]. These are conformed to this world. Hence the Apostle: “Do not be conformed to this world” [Note: [Col. 0151] Rom. 12].

Of the third sort, because they are re-formed by Christ, it is said: “But be re-formed in the newness of your mind” [Note: [Col. 0151] ibid.]. These are great before a religious person, just as “Job was great among all the easterners” [Note: [Col. 0151] Job 1]. For easterners are those who begin to know God. Job is great among them, while, admiring [Col. 0152D] his conduct, they follow him. Hence, “those who instruct many in righteousness shall shine as stars for everlasting eternities” [Note: [Col. 0151] Dan. 12]. Hence: “When the living creatures went, the wheels beside them went also” [Note: [Col. 0151] Ezek. 1]. Such people provide both for themselves and for their neighbour. Hence the poet:

He both moves his own wings and looks back at those of his young.

For they have two wings by which they are raised, and two by which their subjects are protected. Hence: “The two wings of each were joined” [Note: [Col. 0151] ibid.], that is, hope and love; [Col. 0153A] “and two covered their bodies” [Note: [Col. 0153] ibid.], namely fear and repentance, which the teacher proclaims to his own body, that is, to his subjects, of whom he himself is the head.

John the Baptist was great in this manner in preaching and conduct. Thus Elizabeth, the wife of Zacharias, bore a great man, John the Baptist, the forerunner of the Lord: “He who does and teaches men thus shall be called great in the kingdom of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0153] Matt. 5].

Those of the fourth sort are formed by the Holy Spirit, when all virtues are referred through charity—the form of virtues—to heavenly joys. Of these it was said: “Isaac went on growing and advancing until he became great” [Note: [Col. 0153] Gen. 26]. Isaac—that is, the joyful one—first grows by departing from sin; he advances by ascending from virtue to virtue. He becomes great by helping others to advance; [Col. 0153B] exceedingly great by having his whole manner of life in heaven.

Hence it is said: “Joseph, a growing son; a growing son and beautiful in appearance” [Note: [Col. 0153] Gen. 49]. In the first is “a growing son”; in the second, Joseph; in the third, “a growing son”; in the fourth, “beautiful in appearance.” Therefore his father blessed him thus: “The Almighty shall bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that lies beneath, blessings of breasts and womb” [Note: [Col. 0153] ibid.]. John possessed the blessing of the deep that lies beneath when Christ visited him in hell; that of heaven above when he ascended to heaven with him; that of breasts was bestowed on him through the grace by which he offered his neighbour the milk of teaching; that of the womb through the miracles wrought concerning him in the womb. For he was conceived in the womb, announced by an angel in the womb, sanctified in the womb, [Col. 0153C] and made a new prophet in the womb, when Christ was recognized by him. [Note: [Col. 0153] Luke 1.]

Behold, he was great before the Lord, as Christ says: “Among those born of women, none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” [Note: [Col. 0153] Luke 7]. Therefore beyond the others he was called “a burning and shining lamp” [Note: [Col. 0153] John 5]: burning through exceedingly great love, shining by pointing out Christ with his finger. Behold how he was commendable before God.

It follows how he was strict with himself: “He shall drink neither wine nor strong drink” [Note: [Col. 0153] Luke 1], “and shall eat nothing unclean” [Note: [Col. 0153] Deut. 14]. In wine is understood unsuitable merriment; in strong drink, excessive sadness; in what is unclean, the unruliness of the flesh. Against the first he devoured locusts; against the second he ate honey; against the third he clothed himself in camel’s hair.

Wine is from the vineyard [Col. 0153D] of Sodom. Strong drink, although every beverage able to intoxicate is called by the general name, is here particularly that which is made from fruit juice and is harsh. “Unclean” means whatever is unlawful to eat. “All things,” says the Apostle, “are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, but their mind and conscience are defiled” [Note: [Col. 0153] Titus 1]. The clean person uses things with equanimity, to endure want; with temperance, lest abundance corrupt him; and with charity, lest by taking them himself he scandalize another’s conscience, or [Col. 0154A] be scandalized against another on account of difference in foods. Of the first two the Apostle says: “I know both how to be hungry and how to be satisfied, how to abound and how to suffer want” [Note: [Col. 0153] Phil. 4]. Of the third: “Asking no questions on account of conscience” [Note: [Col. 0153] I Cor. 10]. I mean not your conscience, but that of the other.

Hear how he was gracious toward his neighbour: “And many will rejoice at his birth” [Note: [Col. 0153] Luke 1]. We celebrate three births: those of John, of the Blessed Virgin, and of the Saviour. The first stood between grace and law; the second, between the Virgin’s son and the sinner; the third, between God and man. The first was the dawn-star before the light; the second, like a bright dawn; the third, like the sun rising from the eastern region. Of the first the poet says [Note: [Col. 0153] Virgil, *Eclogue* 8.17]:

Be born, and, coming before the day, bring on the lofty Lucifer.

Of the second: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn?” [Col. 0154B] [Note: [Col. 0153] Song 6]. Of the third: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall arise” [Note: [Col. 0153] Mal. 4]. John announced the light, that is, Christ; Mary brought forth the one announced; Christ, brought forth from the womb, enlightened the world.

Our birth too is threefold: the first temporal; the second spiritual; the third immortal. In the first we are born into the world; in the second, from God; in the third, we shall be with God. Of the first: “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow; but when she has borne, she no longer remembers the anguish for joy that a human being has been born into the world” [Note: [Col. 0153] John 16]. Of the second: “Everything born of God conquers the world” [Note: [Col. 0153] I John 6]. And: “Unless a person is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0153] John 3]. Of the third: the birthdays of saints are proclaimed in the Church. And Job says: “When you think yourself consumed, [Col. 0154C] you shall rise like the morning star” [Note: [Col. 0153] Job 11]. A man thinks himself consumed in death, but he shall rise like the morning star in the general resurrection.

The first birth is Herod’s; the second, Mary’s and John’s; the third, the Saviour’s. At the first earthly persons rejoice; at the second, the righteous; at the third, the saints. The first tends toward failure; the second has perfection; the third brings the effect to completion. At the first the woman rejoices, “because a human being has been born into the world” [Note: [Col. 0153] John 16]. Of the second and third: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0153] Phil. 4]. Of the first: “The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful” [Note: [Col. 0153] John 16]. Of the second: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” [Note: [Col. 0153] ibid.]. Of the third: “No one shall take your joy from you” [Note: [Col. 0153] ibid.].

Those of the first sort “take up tambourine and harp and rejoice at the sound of the pleasing instrument” [Col. 0154D] [Note: [Col. 0153] Job 1]. Those of the second “draw water with joy from the springs of the Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0153] Isa. 12]. Those of the third experience that evangelical saying: “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0153] Matt. 3].

Of the first: “Laughter shall be mixed with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy” [Note: [Col. 0153] Prov. 14]. Again: “I judged laughter to be error, and said to joy: Why are you vainly deceived?” [Note: [Col. 0153] Eccles. 2]. Therefore James says: “Let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into voices of weeping” [Note: [Col. 0153] Jas. 4]. “May joy always be yours,” the angel says to Tobias [Note: [Col. 0153] Tobit 5]. And he replies: “What joy shall there be for me, [Col. 0155A] who sit in darkness and cannot see the light of heaven?” [Note: [Col. 0155] ibid.].

Despising this temporal joy, on account of the third joy it is said: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep festival, all you who love her” [Note: [Col. 0155] Office of the Church, fourth Sunday in Lent]. “Rejoice with great joy, all you who mourned over her” [Note: [Col. 0155] Isa. 66]. Of the second he says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0155] Rom. 14]. Again: “If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice because I go to the Father” [Note: [Col. 0155] John 14]. Again: “I shall come to you, and your heart shall rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0155] John 16]. These “draw water with joy from the springs of the Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0155] Isa. 12].

There are three springs which pour out for us water from heaven: the spring of mercy, the spring of grace, and the spring of glory. The first is the spring of kids; the second, the spring of gardens; [Col. 0155B] the third, the spring of good things. The first washes the unclean; the second waters the dry; the third gives drink to the thirsty. Of the first: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman” [Note: [Col. 0155] Zech. 1]. Of the second: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters” [Note: [Col. 0155] Song 4]. Of the third, Boethius says:

Grant, Father, that the mind may ascend  
to your exalted seat;  
grant that it may behold the fountain of good.

Of the first, “we draw water with joy from the springs of the Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0155] Isa. 12] when we rejoice that sin has been forgiven. The angels too have “joy over one sinner who repents” [Note: [Col. 0155] Luke 15]. And the father says: “Son, it was fitting to rejoice and feast, because my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” [Note: [Col. 0155] ibid.].

We draw from the second when he is born in us. [Col. 0155C] Therefore we rejoice: “For the woman who has given birth” [Note: [Col. 0155] John 16], that is, the soul which does penance, “no longer remembers her affliction, because a human being has been born into the world” [Note: [Col. 0155] ibid.]. This is the birth of John, whose name means “the grace of the Lord,” at which many rejoice when they receive it.

Those draw from the third who conceive heavenly joys and, because of joy, endure tribulations. Hence: “The apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been counted worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0155] Acts 5]. Hence, of Stephen:

He, with his head prepared,  
joyfully received the stones.

And Lawrence:

I plainly rejoice,  
because I have deserved  
to become [Col. 0155D]  
a sacrifice of Christ.

From the first, the Son gives a draught by forgiving sins; from the second, by pouring in the grace of the Holy Spirit; from the third, the Father gives a draught by setting joys before us. Of these it is said: “Count it all joy, brothers, when you fall into various temptations” [Note: [Col. 0155] Jas. 1]. For temporal joy is no joy; spiritual joy is some joy. [Col. 0156A] But eternal joy is all joy, and “no one shall take that joy from you” [Note: [Col. 0155] John 16]. Hence the prophet: “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God” [Note: [Col. 0155] Isa. 61].

Thus it was said figuratively in the history: “Mordecai, going out from the palace and from the presence of the king” [Note: [Col. 0155] Esther 8], that is, Christ coming from the Father’s hidden place to transfer the elect, “shone in royal garments, hyacinth-blue and air-coloured” [Note: [Col. 0155] ibid.], that is, with the holy angels coming down with him for judgment: they are hyacinth-blue; the saints of this world are air-coloured—not of heaven, yet as it were suspended in the air above earthly things. “Bearing a golden crown upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0155] ibid.], namely, the sign of royal dignity; “clothed in a silk and purple mantle” [Note: [Col. 0155] ibid.], that is, in glorified flesh, which is called silken because silk is born from worms, [Col. 0156B] and Christ from mortals. Hence he too is called a worm; purple because of the Passion. “And the whole city exulted and rejoiced” [Note: [Col. 0155] ibid.], that is, the triumphant Church received by him. “To the Jews also a new light seemed to arise,” that is, to those who truly confess, together with “joy and honour and dancing” [Note: [Col. 0155] ibid.]. Then all “shall come and rejoice in the good things of the Lord, over grain, wine, and oil” [Note: [Col. 0155] Jer. 31]: in seeing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

That king is called Ahasuerus, which means “his blessedness” or “his court.” His wife is Esther, that is, “hidden.” This is the Church, which still lies hidden in the darkness of this misery. In accordance with the saying: “Now we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” [Note: [Col. 0155] I John 3]. Mordecai means “pure myrrh,” namely Christ, called myrrh because of the bitterness [Col. 0156C] of the Passion; “pure,” because he will meet us without sins, to transfer us into the kingdom of God the Father. Then there will be joy for you, when corruption has been laid aside; honour from God’s calling; and dancing from the agility of bodies.

“Behold, you are fair, my beloved, and comely.”

[CARD.] “Our little bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress.” Thus the mother returns praises for praises to the son, saying: “Behold, my beloved, you are fair according to divinity and comely according to humanity.” And because he had now several times called her his beloved, while beloved man and beloved woman dwell together in the same bed and the same house, she immediately speaks of the bed and the house. [Col. 0156D] “For Christ remains in the one who loves him” [Note: [Col. 0155] John 6]; but whoever loves the Son loves the Mother also, and thus each remains in the one who loves the other. Yet in different ways. For the Son remains in the heart of one who loves him through indwelling grace; the Mother, through that person’s devotion and the inseparable fellowship of Mother and Son, in the affection of devout love. Therefore she says:

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0157]

[Col. 0157A] **29. Our little bed is flowering.**

[THO.] The bed of the soul is rest. For, while it loves the bridegroom singly, it withdraws itself, as far as it can, from the disturbance of the world, gathers virtues by which it may please him, and, while it scorns temporal things, spreads for him a little bed of tranquillity in which he delights in the flowers of virtues. Having found the opportunity, the bride announces the adorned chamber, pointing out the little bed with her finger. The beloved invites her to rest and, with those going to Emmaus, unable to bear the burning of his heart, draws them to the lodging-place of the mind. He compels them to stay with him overnight, and speaks with Peter: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” [Note: [Col. 0157] Matt. 17].

In this chapter and the two following, the condition of the Church is fittingly set forth: Christ, the authority of prelates; the beauty of the clergy; the repose of monks; [Col. 0157B] and the discipline of the people. In the Church, I think the little bed on which one rests means cloisters and monasteries, in which we are free from secular cares. This little bed is flowering with the institutions and examples of the Fathers, with which the conduct of the brethren is sprinkled as though with flowers. The house is the popular assembly of Christians, whom beams placed on high—that is, the rulers of the churches—protect. The ceilings which adorn it are the well-ordered morals of the clergy. That the beams are called cedar and the ceilings cypress means that prelates and clergy ought to give a good fragrance to others and remain incorruptible, lest they be corrupted by vices.

Is this little bed righteousness? You know what righteousness: “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my spirit rest, except upon one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?” [Note: [Col. 0157] Isa. 66]. [Col. 0157C] Therefore, if anyone is such, he becomes God’s little bed.

It should be noted that a flower offers beauty to the sight, softness to the touch, and sweetness to the smell. Therefore understand in beauty contemplation, which invitingly calls, sweetly draws, and ardently kindles; in softness, patience, which meets threats and curses, confronts persecutors with prayers, repays kindness to those who injure, and charity to those who hate; and in fragrance, receive the sweet reputation of the saints before God. These say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” [Note: [Col. 0157] II Cor. 2]. This flower signifies hope and sometimes the patience of the saints, because it refreshes by its softness, delights by its appearance, and soothes by its fragrance. Thus patient persons endeavour to overcome the angry by gentleness, the envious by humility, and the contentious by devout silence. Therefore the little bed of spiritual union is rightly called flowering, because Christ rests sweetly in those hearts in which the beauty of wisdom, the tranquillity of prudence, and the sweet fragrance of heavenly hope reign.

There are four beds. The first is foul; the second firm; the third white; the fourth flowering. [Col. 0158A] The first is foul with the stench of lust; the second firm through preservation of marital faith; the third flowering through the change of one’s former life, as it were from blackness into whiteness; the fourth white through the pleasant charm of virginal delight. The first belongs to fornicators; the second to married persons; the third to the continent; the fourth to virgins.

Of the first the Apostle says: “Not in revelling and drunkenness, not in chambers and shamelessness” [Note: [Col. 0157] Rom. 13]. Those belong to this bed who “burned in their desires toward one another, males committing shamefulness with males.” But “those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0157] Rom. 1]. For if anyone violates the temple of God, God shall destroy him [Note: [Col. 0157] Gal. 5]. “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” [Note: [Col. 0157] I Cor. 3]. And: “Taking the members of Christ and making them members [Col. 0158B] of a prostitute” [Note: [Col. 0157] I Cor. 6]. Again: “He who fornicates sins against his own body” [Note: [Col. 0157] ibid.].

Sometimes these defilements arise from bad habit. Hence the poet says [Note: [Col. 0157] Horace, *Epistles* I]:

We are a number, born to consume the fruits—  
suitors of Penelope, idlers, and the companions of Alcinous . . .  
for whom it was pleasant to sleep until midday  
and to prolong carelessness to the sound of the lyre.

Sometimes they arise from riches. Hence another poet says [Note: [Col. 0157] Juvenal, *Satire* 6]:

Riches have broken the ages with shameful luxury.

Wealth nourishes wanton love. [Note: [Col. 0157] Ovid.] Hence Horace, in the first book of the *Satires*: [Note: [Col. 0157] Epistle 18.]

> … Eutrapelus, whenever he wished to harm someone,  
> gave him costly clothes: for the man, now happy,  
> will sleep until daylight and prefer a prostitute  
> to honourable duty.

[Col. 0158C] Let those who lie in this bed know that God will judge fornicators and adulterers. [Note: [Col. 0157] Heb. 13.]

The second bed is firm. For God said: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate.” [Note: [Col. 0157] Matt. 19.] Here faith excuses from sin, by which spouses do not unite with another; hope of offspring, to be dedicated to divine worship; and sacrament, because Christ and the Church are represented in them. [Note: [Col. 0157] Eph. 5.] Married persons ought to possess purity in three respects in this bed. For they ought mutually to render obedience to one another in bodily intercourse. This is the bed of Abraham, whose name means “exalted father,” as one who rules, and of Sarah, whose name means “princess,” because she ought to obey her husband in rendering what is due; this was said with reference to the first point.

The second is represented by the bed of Isaac, whose name means [Col. 0158D] “joy,” and of Rebecca, whose name means “patience,” because they should rejoice and endure together; that is, by common consent they ought patiently to devote themselves to seeking the joys above. The third is represented by the bed of Jacob, whose name means “supplanter,” and of Rachel, whose name means “seeing the beginning,” because together they must overthrow vices and seek eternal joys. They ought [Col. 0159A] to be intent upon God, devoting themselves to prayer, overthrowing vices, and, because of incontinence, returning together again. [Note: [Col. 0159] I Cor. 7.]

At times they are commanded to render one another what is due, for the firmness of faith; at times they are urged to abstain from embraces for the sake of prayer; at times they are permitted to return to embrace because of weakness. [Note: [Col. 0159] Ibid.] On the first, Paul says: “The husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does; likewise the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ibid.] On the second, he says: “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ibid.] And he adds concerning the third: “Then return to one another, lest Satan tempt us because of our incontinence.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ibid.] Of the time given to prayer it is said: “Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber, and [Col. 0159B] the bride from her bridal room.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Joel 2.]

Those who lie in this third bed cannot devote themselves to contemplation because of the concerns belonging to marriage; they are, as it were, in darkness. Hence Job: “In darkness I have made my bed.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Job 17.] Therefore the bride herself, placed in this condition, says: “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him. A little while after I had passed on, I found him whom my soul loves; I held him and will not let him go until I bring him into my house and into the chamber of my mother.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Song 3.]

Observe the order of the words: she passes on, finds, holds, and brings him into her mother’s chamber—that is, into the chamber of the continent, who is fit for contemplation. She passes on by abandoning the first embraces; she finds by knowing with a purer understanding; [Col. 0159C] she holds by cleaving to him courageously and with steadfast purpose; she brings him into my chamber by drawing him with sweet devotion into a chaste heart and body. To such a person it is said: “When you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Matt. 6.] Such a person answers those who trouble him: “Do not trouble me. For my door is now shut, and my children are with me in my bed,” [Note: [Col. 0159] Luke 11.] that is, good works in a chaste heart. He is white because he has been washed by the tears of repentance. Hence David: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ps. 6.] The paralytic now carries his bed, by which he was previously carried. [Note: [Col. 0159] Mark 2.] And Judith, the chaste widow, slays Holofernes in this bed—that is, the movement of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0159] Judith 13.] How much [Col. 0159D] better this bed is than the marital one the Apostle shows thus: “Are you released from the law of a husband? Do not seek marriage.” [Note: [Col. 0159] I Cor. 7.]

There follows the fourth, namely virginal rest. There are three privileged flowers by which it is called flowery. The first is Christ, the second the Virgin Mary, the third John the Evangelist. For Christ says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Song 2.] In the figure of the Blessed Virgin, Aaron’s rod flowered. [Note: [Col. 0159] Num. 17.] Through the merit of virginity, manna was found in John’s tomb in place of his body. But morally there are also these three flowers: the lily of virginity, [Col. 0160A] the violet of humility, and the rose of charity; for without these three virginity is less perfect. Upon a bed fragrant with such flowers the bridegroom lies, so that the bride may say to him: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Song 1.] “These follow the Lamb wherever he goes.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Rev. 14.]

> Where the Lamb, the virgin sheep, goes before, white in fleece,  
> and every shining-white flock enters—namely, through pleasant green meadows.

The disadvantage of the first bed is estrangement from God; the usefulness of the second, the propagation of humankind; the usefulness of the third, leisure for God; the usefulness of the fourth, knowledge of the angels. Our little bed is flowery, because in such a bed we contemplate; what we contemplate we sweetly savour; and at the tasted savour we are astonished. God willed this to be [Col. 0160B] shown in Adam, when Scripture said: “The Lord cast a sleep upon Adam.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Gen. 2.]

It should be observed that the Lord cast sleep, savour, and astonishment: sleep, by which he might contemplate God; savour, by which he might delight in the things contemplated; astonishment, by which he might abhor sin. In the first, he formed Eve; [Note: [Col. 0159] Ibid.] in the second, Adam tasted the fruit; [Note: [Col. 0159] Gen. 3.] in the third, he hid himself from the face of God. [Note: [Col. 0159] Ibid.] For these three things which God gave for use, man turned to misuse. Of the first: “I sleep, but my heart watches.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Song 5.] Of the second: “Set your taste upon the things above.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Col. 3.] Of the third: “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are made numb.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Jer. 31.]

Therefore it must be known that there is a threefold sleep. The first is for cherishing wickedness; the second for restoring weakness; [Col. 0160C] the third for contemplating majesty. Of the first: “They slept their sleep, and all the wealthy men found nothing in their hands.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ps. 75.] Of the second: “If he sleeps, he will be safe.” [Note: [Col. 0159] John 11.] Of the third: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ps. 67.]

Of the first: “How long will you sleep, sluggard?” [Note: [Col. 0159] Prov. 6.] And: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Eph. 5.] And: “Those who sleep by night say: ‘It is now time for us to rise from sleep.’” [Note: [Col. 0159] Rom. 13.] Some of these sleep under the pursuit of sin; others because they conceal sin under silence; a third group because they are weighed down by weariness of making satisfaction. The first are blinded by God’s judgment; the second are raised up by a neighbour’s admonition; the third are roused by God’s consolation. The first was Samson in Delilah’s lap; [Note: [Col. 0159] Judg. 16.] the second Jonah in the depths of the bilge; [Note: [Col. 0159] Jonah 2.] the third Jonah beneath the shade of the prickly juniper. [Note: [Col. 0159] Jonah 4.]

[Col. 0160D] Of this it is said: “While people slept, the enemy sowed tares over the seed.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Matt. 13.] For there are three seeds over which the devil sows tares while people here sleep in sleep. There is the seed which is the divine word; there is the seed which is virtue; there is the seed which is Christ. Of the first: “The seed is the word of God.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ibid.] Of the second: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation.” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ps. 125.] Of the third: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone.” [Note: [Col. 0159] John 12.] Again: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Gen. 28.] [Col. 0161A] Again: “And to your seed, which is Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Gal. 3.] Again: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Isa. 1.] Behold the harms of the first kind of sleeping.

Of the second, which restores weakness: “If I give sleep to my eyes, and slumber to my eyelids.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 131.] Again: “Arise, hasten, my beloved.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Song 2.] Arise, lest you forget God. Hasten, lest the day of death overtake you. Come to the joys of the heavenly festival. “Winter has passed,” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] namely, the fear of hardship. “The rain has gone away,” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] namely, love of worldly pleasure. “Flowers have appeared,” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] that is, hope of heavenly joy. For such a winter brings forgetfulness of God. Such rain impedes the swiftness with which punishments are fled. Such hope kindles one toward the heavenly festival.

We find that Jacob [Col. 0161B] put sleep under command in these three respects. Of the first: when fleeing his brother, he slept upon a stone and, awakening from sleep, said: “Truly the Lord was in this place, and I did not know it.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Gen. 28.] As though he said: “Since I slept long, I forgot God; but waking, I find him.” Against the second—that is, against self-will—he said: “By night and day, in frost and heat, I was scorched; sleep fled from my eyes.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Gen. 31.] Concerning the third it is said: “They told Jacob, ‘Joseph your son lives.’ On hearing this his spirit revived, and, awakening as from a heavy sleep, he said: ‘I shall go and see him.’” [Note: [Col. 0161] Gen. 45.]

Of the first it is said: “Arise in the night, at the beginning of your watches.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Lam. 2.] The foolish virgins slept with the second kind of sleep; the prudent ones with the third. For thus it is written: [Col. 0161C] “While the bridegroom delayed, they all became drowsy and slept.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Matt. 25.] But differently: the foolish in the first manner; the prudent in the second.

Of the third, which is for contemplating majesty, it is said: “I sleep, but my heart watches”; [Note: [Col. 0161] Song 5.] and: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of the dove are silvered.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 67.] “Among the midst of the lots,” that is, between the New and Old Testaments, or between temporal and heavenly things; between these, as it meditates upon both, the soul is suspended. Hence Job: “My soul chose hanging, and my bones death.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Job 7.] Hence it is said: “Issachar, a strong ass lying down between the boundaries, saw that rest was good and that the land was very good.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Gen. 29.]

One sleeping thus contemplates hellish things, worldly things, and heavenly things: hellish things, in which he finds [Col. 0161D] calamity; worldly things, in which he finds changeability; heavenly things, in which he finds happiness. Abraham saw these three when sleep overtook him: “For a dark gloom came to pass.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Gen. 15.] Behold worldly things. “And he saw a smoking furnace,” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] namely hellish things; “and a blazing lamp,” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] namely heavenly things.

For the first, Pharaoh’s baker in prison dreamed his own trial. [Note: [Col. 0161] Gen. 10.] For the third, the cupbearer dreamed his own [30] salvation. [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] For the middle, Pharaoh dreamed, in cows now fat and now lean, of worldly [Col. 0162A] changeability. [Note: [Col. 0161] Gen. 41.] Behold the three sleeps: the first the Lord sends forth, the second he permits, the third he sends in.

The Lord also sent in savour; but there are some who savour carnal things, and some who savour heavenly things. [Note: [Col. 0161] Rom. 5.] The first delight in feasting and drunkenness, the second in vanity, the third in truth. The first savour infects the spirit, the second deceives, the third leads to the kingdom. Of the first: “Those who are in the flesh savour the things of the flesh.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] Of the second: “Do not be high-minded”; [Note: [Col. 0161] Rom. 12.] and: “Do not think proudly, but fear.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Rom. 11.] Of the third: “Set your taste upon the things above.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Col. 3.]

Of the first, Job says: “Can anyone taste what, when tasted, brings death?” [Note: [Col. 0161] Job 6.] Of the second: “When Christ had tasted vinegar mixed with gall, he would not drink it,” [Note: [Col. 0161] Matt. 27.] namely, the deceits and bitternesses of the world. [Col. 0162B] Of the third: “The strong woman tasted and saw that her trade was good.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Prov. 18.] Therefore, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 33.]

The children of Israel tasted these three savours in the desert. The first, when they turned back to the pots of meat, saying: “Who will give us flesh to eat?” [Note: [Col. 0161] Num. 11.] The second, when they said: “We remember the melons, leeks, onions, and other things.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] The third, when they ate manna. [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] Adam had the first when he ate the fruit; [Note: [Col. 0161] Gen. 3.] the second, when the serpent said: “You shall be as gods”; [Note: [Col. 0161] Ibid.] the third before the Fall, when he enjoyed converse with God. But after the Fall God sent in astonishment at the sin committed, so that he [Col. 0162C] could say: “The groans of death surrounded me; the pains of hell surrounded me.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 17.]

But there is a groaning of death, a medicinal groaning, and a life-giving groaning. The first surrounds, the second cleanses, the third makes fruitful: it surrounds, so that we may behold the world and flee its beauty; it cleanses the stench of sin; it makes fruitful, so that affection may grow into a higher love. Of the first, in this place: “Before I eat, I sigh.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Job 3.] Of the second: “I have laboured in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 6.] Hence Jeremiah: “Woe to us, for we have sinned, because the crown of our head has fallen.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Lam. 5.] Again: “It is through the mercy of God that we are not consumed, because his mercies have not failed.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Lam. 3.] Of the third: “Lord, [Col. 0162D] before you is all my desire, and my groaning is not hidden from you.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps.] Hence: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps.] Again: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Song 1.]

There follows: “The pains of hell surrounded me.” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 17.] There are pains of hell; there are pains of the world, which a person should endure patiently; and there are pains of the human heart, by which a person is reconciled to God. A person suffers the first because of wickedness; the second from necessity; the third willingly. Of the [Col. 0163A] first, in this place: “Leave me a little while, that I may lament my pain, before I go to the land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Job 10.] Of the second, David says: “My life fails in pain and my years in groanings.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ps. 30.] Hence it was said to Eve: “In pain you shall bear your children.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Gen. 3.] And to Adam: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ibid.] And Job: “Man is born for labour, and the bird for flight.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Job 5.] Of the third: “How long shall I lay up counsels in my soul, pain in my heart by day?” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ps. 12.] because God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart. [Note: [Col. 0163] Ps. 50.]

Christ is said to have suffered these three pains for the human race. He suffered the first when he endured punishment in order that it might be excluded from us. Hence Jeremiah: “Truly he bore our infirmities and [Col. 0163B] carried our pains.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Isa. 53.] And the second, again: “We saw him as the last of men, a man of pains.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ibid.] And the third; hence the same author: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any pain like my pain.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Lam. 1.]

Our little bed is flowery.

[CARD.] As if he said: If the little bed is ours, it is flowery; that is, if anyone’s conscience is to us a bed of rest, it is itself flowery, possessing both beauty and fragrance: beautiful through the adornments of virtues, and fragrant in works through example. Then he adds concerning the houses:

The beams of our houses are of cedar.

[THO.] By cedar beams we understand preachers. [Col. 0163C] For as cedar is incorruptible and tall wood, so preachers ought neither to be corrupted by a price, so as to be bent away from justice, nor fail to seek and savour the things above. [Note: [Col. 0163] Col. 3.] The roof is hope of heavenly things; while it draws us back from the desire for temporal things, it preserves us through patience from the storm of temporal things. For patience itself serves in place of timbers: it supports, as though they were the boards of a roof, whatever heavenly hope accomplishes. The beams are cedar because patience gives a good fragrance to neighbours who see it and, because it guards it, does not allow what is beneath it to rot through vices.

Of the guarding of this house it is written in the book of Numbers, under the name of the tabernacle: “Judah shall pitch tents to the east.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Num. 2.] This tabernacle is our heart. Around it Judah is commanded to [Col. 0163D] pitch his tent to the east, Reuben to the south, [Note: [Col. 0163] Ibid.] Ephraim to the west, [Note: [Col. 0163] Ibid.] and Dan to the north. [Note: [Col. 0163] Ibid.] East is the illumination of grace; south, the kindling of charity; west, the administration of temporal things; north, the disturbance of temptation. At the east a person keeps watch diligently, that he may see and correct his transgressions; at the south, that he may love heavenly things and raise his heart to them; at the west, that while administering temporal matters, he may subdue the world to himself; at the north, that he may foresee and drive away temptations.

Of the first, the prophet says: “Who raised up the righteous one from the [Col. 0164A] east?” [Note: [Col. 0163] Isa. 41.] The righteous one is raised from the east when, through the illumination of grace, a sinner is made righteous. Of the second: “Abraham went up from the south into Bethel.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Gen. 13.] Bethel means “house of God.” Therefore one goes up from the south into Bethel when, through the fervour of love, one dwells in heaven. Of the third: “The sun knew its setting.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ps. 103.] The sun knows its setting when contemplatives return to ministry without harm to themselves. Of the fourth: “A storm-wind came from the north.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ezek. 1.] The storm-wind comes from the north when temptation is breathed forth by the devil. But “in the midst was the appearance of electrum,” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ibid.] when in it we feel Christ’s help.

The bride lies toward the east when he said to her: “Who is this who comes forth like the dawn rising?” [Note: [Col. 0163] Song 6.] She wished to lie toward the south [Col. 0164B] when she said: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Song 1.] She feared to descend toward the west when she said: “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” [Note: [Col. 0163] Song 5.] Hence the beloved says: “Arise, hasten, my beloved.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Song 1.] She lay toward the north when she said: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Song 4.]

Therefore Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun pitch their tents to the east. Judah means “confession”; Issachar, “reward”; Zebulun, “dwelling of fear.” First, a person must confess; second, reward must be recognized; third, strength must be possessed: by the first, that one may reveal one’s conscience; by the second, that one may know for what purpose one exercises one’s evil; by the third, that one may suffice for doing penance. Judah therefore keeps watch, lest [Col. 0164C] shame impede confession; Issachar, lest ignorance of the reward make one languish; Zebulun, lest experience of labour cease through faintheartedness. Of the first: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Jas. 5.] Of the second: “To the one who conquers I shall give a white stone.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Rev. 2.] Of the third: “Be strengthened, you fainthearted.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Isa. 35.] “Lift up the slack hands and strengthen the weak knees.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Heb. 12.]

Consider these three in Issachar: “A strong ass lying down between the boundaries, he saw that rest was good and that the land was very good, and he put his shoulder beneath the burden to bear it.” [Note: [Col. 0163] Gen. 49.] Good rest is cessation from sin; the very good land is the kingdom to be given as reward; he puts his shoulder beneath the burden by labouring courageously.

Paul possessed these three. Of the first: “I was a blasphemer and persecutor, because I persecuted the Church of God”; [Note: [Col. 0163] I Tim. 1.] behold Judah. Of the second: “For the rest, the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord will render to me on that day.” [Note: [Col. 0163] II Tim. 4.] Of the third: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck.” [Note: [Col. 0163] II Cor. 11.]

These three were represented in David. First he confessed his weakness, saying: “I cannot walk thus armed”; [Note: [Col. 0163] I Sam. 17.] second, he awaited Saul’s daughter as a reward; [Note: [Col. 0163] Ibid.] third, he was strong in overthrowing his opponent. Behold Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun to the east.

[Col. 0165A] There follows, to the south, Reuben, Simeon, and Gad. Reuben means “vision”; Simeon, “obedient”; Gad, “girded.” Whoever wishes to preserve the kindling of love must first see, second obey, third gird himself. First, that they may be skilled; second, subject; third, ready: skilled for contemplation of glory, subject to God’s justice, ready for the road to the homeland. Of the first, David says: “My heart was inflamed and my inward parts were changed”; [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 72.] of the second: “I became as a beast of burden with you, yet I am always with you”; [Note: [Col. 0165] Ibid.] of the third: “You held my right hand and led me according to your will.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ibid.]

Through the first God is more desirable; through the second, more merciful; through the third, nearer. The bride had felt him more desirable when she said: “His throat is [Col. 0165B] most sweet, and he is wholly desirable.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Song 5.] Hezekiah found him more merciful: God prolonged his life because he obeyed the Lord, for he said: “Remember, Lord, how I have walked before you,” [Note: [Col. 0165] IV Kings 20.] namely, in obedience. Again, he became nearer to the bride because she had girded herself to seek him, saying: “Through the streets and squares I shall seek him whom my soul loves.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Song 3.] And then follows: “A little while after I had passed on, I found him whom my soul loves.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ibid.] Behold, he is nearer.

Thus, “Reuben shall pitch his tent to the south,” [Note: [Col. 0165] Num. 2.] so that the eye may be open; Simeon, so that the mind may be ready; Gad, so that the step may be straight: the eye, lest it be disturbed by worldly care; the mind, lest it be bent down by self-will; the step, lest [Col. 0165C] the weights of sins impede it. The first, lest Reuben become Tobit, blinded by a swallow’s dung; [Note: [Col. 0165] Tobit 2.] the second, lest Simeon be like Korah, devoured by fire for disobedience; [Note: [Col. 0165] Num. 26.] the third, lest Gad be burdened like the children of Israel with mud and brick. [Note: [Col. 0165] Exod. 1.] For Reuben would say: “The light of my eyes—even it is not with me”; [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 37.] Simeon: “My heart is troubled; my strength has forsaken me”; [Note: [Col. 0165] Ibid.] Gad: “I am stuck in deep mud, and there is no firm ground.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 68.]

Concerning the two first corners: in the Law the children of Israel had four fringes at the four corners of their garments, lest they follow their own thoughts and their eyes, which commit fornication upon diverse things. [Note: [Col. 0165] Deut. 22.] The garment is our manner of life. It has four corners: our manner of life ought to regard God, ourselves, our neighbour, and our enemy, so that it may give [Col. 0165D] God honour, ourselves beauty, our neighbour love, and our enemy fear. The fringes are the four special commandments of God: love of God, oneself, neighbour, and enemy. The hyacinth-coloured cord, which has the colour of heaven, is remembrance of the heavenly homeland, which we ought constantly to have.

Therefore let Reuben pitch his tent to the south and say: “To you I have lifted up my soul, my God; in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 24.] And Gad: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Isa. 2.]

To pitch a tent toward the west is, for one descending from contemplation to action, to employ vigilance. [Col. 0166A] Such persons deal with the vices of subjects, the use of temporal things, and the ordering of offices. In the first, the fruit of virtues is often diminished, love of God weakened, and love of the world fixed in the memory. For one can scarcely deal with vices without incurring a stain. “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ecclus. 13.] Of these the Lord says through the prophet: “I expected my vineyard to yield grapes, and it yielded wild grapes.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Isa. 5.]

Again, in the second: one can scarcely handle temporal matters without loving heavenly things less. Thus Gregory says: “The more each person gives himself to love of the world, the more he is separated from love of heavenly things.” Hence: “When you cultivate the earth, it shall not give its fruit.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Gen. 4.] In the third: one can scarcely be appointed over offices without being bitten by [Col. 0166B] ambition for them. Again, concerning these, the Lord says through the prophet: “They reigned without me; princes arose, and I did not know it.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Hos. 8.]

Therefore Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh pitch tents toward the west. Ephraim comes to the aid of those who extirpate sin; Benjamin, of those who deal with temporal matters; Manasseh, of those who order offices. The first, therefore, is to be summoned to the usefulness of fruits; the second, to the sweetness of love; the third, to flee the vanity of ambition. Of the first let it be said: “Bear fruit like a rose planted by streams of water”; [Note: [Col. 0165] Ecclus. 39.] to the second: “Be imitators of God as most dear children, and walk in love”; [Note: [Col. 0165] Eph. 5.] to the third: “Forget your people and your father’s house.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 44.]

To the first [Col. 0166C] Christ says: “Go and bear fruit”; [Note: [Col. 0165] John 15.] to the second: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him”; [Note: [Col. 0165] John 14.] to the third: “Freely you received; freely give.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Matt. 10.] Let us pass to the north.

There are persons tempted because they do not distinguish truth from falsehood; there are those who place their salvation in the world; and there are those who despair. The first are heedless, the second enticed, the third deceived. [31] The heedless are so because they do not possess the spirit of devotion and discernment; the enticed, through love of worldly affection; the deceived, through ignorance of divine mercy. To the first it is said: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Isa. 5.] To the second: “Let there be no meadow through which our luxury does not pass, for this is our portion and this is our lot.” [Col. 0166D] [Note: [Col. 0165] Wis. 2.] To the third: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness.” [Note: [Col. 0165] Gen. 4.]

Therefore, that they may be guarded, these pitch their tents toward the north: Dan, whose name means “judgment”; Asher, whose name means “happiness”; Naphtali, whose name means “expansion.” Let Dan summon them to the judgment of truth; Asher, to love of heavenly happiness; Naphtali, to hope in divine mercy. Let Dan say: “Judge justly, sons of men”; [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 57.] Asher: “O how glorious is the kingdom in which all the saints rejoice with Christ”; [Note: [Col. 0165] Church Office.] and Naphtali say: “Hope in him, all congregation of the people; pour out your [Col. 0167A] hearts before him: God is our helper for ever.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ps. 61.]

In these beams I find three things: in teachers, instruction; in the afflicted, mercy; in disciples, obedience. For they carry the tiles, as though supporting subjects; and the tiles rest upon them, as receiving their form from the teacher. Thus in the teacher we find instruction in words, conduct, and works; in the afflicted, the mercy of consolations; in disciples, obedience in carrying out commands. “Christ fulfilled these things when the only son of his mother was being carried out dead.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Luke 7.] He instructed by word, saying: “Young man, I say to you: Arise.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ibid.] He came near in conduct; he touched the bier in works. Mercy was shown toward the afflicted when the Lord saw those weeping and “was moved with mercy.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ibid.] Obedience was shown when, at [Col. 0167B] his command, “the one who had been dead sat up.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ibid.]

A teacher ought to possess words of doctrine, because “the lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Mal. 2.] Otherwise they are blind guides of the blind: “If a blind person leads a blind person, both fall into a pit.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Matt. 15.] And Isaiah says: “Their watchmen are all blind; they are all dumb dogs, unable to bark.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Isa. 56.] For they ought to draw people by words, attract them by conduct, and invite them by works. Thus the Apostle says: “In all things present yourself as an example of good works: in teaching, in dignity, in integrity.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Titus 2.] In teaching, as regards words; in dignity, as regards conduct; in integrity, as regards works. And not only with dignity of conduct, but also with sweetness. Hence Paul says: “Let the one who presides do so with diligence; the one who gives, [Col. 0167C] with simplicity; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Rom. 12.] And concerning disciples: “I beseech you to walk worthily, with humility and gentleness, with patience bearing one another in charity, diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Eph. 4.]

For teachers make disciples like themselves:

> Do you really expect a mother to produce honourable children,  
> or manners other than those she has herself? It is useful, indeed,  
> for an old depraved woman to produce a depraved little daughter.  
> [Note: [Col. 0167] Juvenal, *Satires* 6.]

“When the living creatures moved, the wheels beside them also moved; and when they were lifted up from the earth, the wheels likewise were lifted up, following them.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ezek. 1.] And concerning works: “Let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Matt. 5.] Again: “And let burning lamps be [Col. 0167D] in your hands.” [Note: [Col. 0167] Luke 12.]

Otherwise they will be like the messengers whom David sent to Hanun, who sent them back after shaving half their beards and half their hair, and cutting off their garments to the buttocks, so that their excrement appeared. [Note: [Col. 0167] II Sam. 10.] Teachers are David’s messengers when they announce the commandments to sinners by speech. They have hair hanging from and adorning the head—that is, good conduct in the heart, the ornament of the soul. They have a beard, the sign of manliness, that they may be strong and steadfast in adversity. They are adorned with garments—that is, [Col. 0168A] with honourable conduct.

Hanun means “their pain,” representing sinners. When teachers ought to heal their pains, the teachers themselves are often corrupted by the perversity of their hearers. These shave off half the hair when, by their example, they partly diminish teachers’ good conduct; they shave off half the beard when they make them weaker; they cut short their garments when they make them more negligent than usual in good conduct. Thus their excrement appears when, good conduct having been diminished, their sins become visible. Behold the instruction of teachers; there follows mercy toward the afflicted.

But it should be noted that there is mercy toward oneself, mercy toward one’s brother, and fatherly mercy. The first is directed toward oneself, the second toward one’s neighbor, the third [Col. 0168B] from a father toward his son. The first is exercised through contrition, the second through compassion, the third through correction. Of the first it is said: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ecclus. 30]. Of the second it is said: The Samaritan, moved by mercy, poured wine and oil upon the man wounded by robbers [Note: [Col. 0167] Luke 10]; and the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” [Note: [Col. 0167] Matt. 5]. Fatherly mercy does three things: it remits guilt, corrects error, and consoles bitterness. Of the first it is said: “That good father, seeing from afar his returning son—that is, the prodigal—was moved by mercy and ran to meet him” [Note: [Col. 0167] Luke 15]. Of the second it is said: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” [Note: [Col. 0167] Hab. 3]. For whom the Lord loves, he corrects; indeed, he scourges every son whom he receives [Note: [Col. 0167] Heb. 12]. “For he is patient and greatly merciful” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ps. 102]. [Col. 0168C] “Because he will not be angry for ever, nor threaten eternally” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ibid.]. And therefore he is angry and corrects now. Of the third we have an instance in the present example. For Jesus saw the weeping widow and a great crowd with her, and was moved by mercy [Note: [Col. 0167] Luke 7]. Thus much concerning mercy. Obedience follows.

The dead young man displayed this obedience, because at the Lord’s command, “he who had been dead sat up” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ibid.]. It should also be known that obedience is threefold. The first is rendered to a superior, the second to an equal, the third to an inferior. The first is obedience of necessity, the second of kindness, the third of humility. The first discharges a debt; the second renders service; the third is a marvel. Christ fulfilled the first, having become “obedient to the Father unto death” [Note: [Col. 0167] Phil. 12; apparently an erroneous citation]. Of this the Apostle says: “Children, obey your parents” [Col. 0168D] [Note: [Col. 0167] Col. 3]. And: “Servants, obey your masters” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ibid.]. And: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers” [Note: [Col. 0167] Rom. 13]. Of the second the same author says: “Outdoing one another in showing honour” [Note: [Col. 0167] Rom. 12]. The same speaks of the third: “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake” [Note: [Col. 0167] 1 Pet. 2]. This is relevant to the fact that Jesus set a little child in the midst of the disciples and said to them: “Unless you become like this little child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0167] Matt. 18]. And elsewhere he says: “Let the greater among you become as the lesser” [Note: [Col. 0167] Luke 22]. But he himself [Col. 0169A] was subject to Mary and Joseph [Note: [Col. 0169] Luke 2]. Likewise, he washed his disciples’ feet [Note: [Col. 0169] John 13], although he was greater than they.

It should be noted that some die inwardly in the soul; some outwardly in the body; and some are obstinate in both. The first simply die inwardly in the soul; the second in two ways; the third both die and are buried. Of the first it is said: “The soul that sins shall itself die” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ezek. 18]. Of the second the Law says: “Whoever does this or that, let him die the death” [Note: [Col. 0169] Exod. 21]. Of the third it is said: “The rich man died and was buried in hell” [Note: [Col. 0169] Luke 16]. In the figure of the first, the dead girl lay in her mother’s chamber [Note: [Col. 0169] Luke 8]. In the figure of the second, this young man, his mother’s only son, was already being carried outside the city gate [Note: [Col. 0169] Luke 7]. In the figure of the third, Lazarus had been dead four days and was horribly foul-smelling [Note: [Col. 0169] John 11].

But the soul, [Col. 0169B] as has been said elsewhere, first becomes ugly, secondly sick, and thirdly dead. In the first case it cannot be said: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved” [Note: [Col. 0169] Song 4]. Of the second it is said: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” [Note: [Col. 0169] Jer. 17]; and: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ps. 40]. Of the third: “The soul that sins shall itself die” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ezek. 18]. For a heart thus tempted is the jar which Zechariah saw, in the midst of which wickedness sits [Note: [Col. 0169] Zech. 5]. And two women carried her away into the land of Shinar; this is called “their stench.” But the angel cast a leaden mass into the mouth of the jar, so that wickedness might not come out: that is, Christ opposes difficulty to the iniquity conceived, lest it proceed to action.

The four bearers carrying the dead young man are these: gluttony, [Col. 0169C] idleness, lust, and softness of dress. Of this Ezekiel says: “A very great eagle, of great wings, with a long extension of limbs, having feathers and many colours, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar; it plucked off the tops of its branches” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ezek. 17]. It came to Lebanon, which is interpreted “whitening,” that is, to the Church; it took the marrow of the cedar, that is, devotion of a heart formerly fragrant and lofty; it plucked off the topmost branches, that is, the usefulness of words, according to the saying: “The end of prayer is better than its beginning” [Note: [Col. 0169] Eccl. 7]. It carried it away from the land of Canaan, which is interpreted “the movement,” namely, of the north wind, that is, from the good works of its former manner of life, by persuading it; “and it carried it into the land of Shinar” [Note: [Col. 0169] Dan. 1]. It is said to have great wings because of its swift tempting; a long extension of limbs [Col. 0169D] because of the power permitted it by God; feathers because of its gentleness; and colours because of its manifold deception.

Of that man dead four days the prophet says: “What is it, Israel, that you are in the land of enemies? You have grown old in a foreign land; you have dwelt with the dead; you have been reckoned among those who are in hell” [Note: [Col. 0169] Baruch 3]. The sinner is in the land of enemies through evil action; he grows old in a foreign land through habit; he dwells with the dead through falling away; he is reckoned among those in hell through despair.

[Col. 0170A] The beams of our houses are cedar; our panelled ceilings are cypress.

[CARD.] Beams, indeed, give strength to a house; ceilings give it beauty. Houses are holy souls. Therefore the beams are virtues and graces, without which there is no salvation; but the ceilings are the varieties of ministries and workings, and certain graces which adorn the soul, though they are not necessarily required for salvation, such as prophecies, kinds of tongues, miracles, discernment of spirits, and things like these [Note: [Col. 0169] 1 Cor. 12]. Like ceilings, these collapse if they do not adhere firmly to the beams. Thus the beams of houses ought to be cedar, so that the virtues neither become worm-eaten nor rot, but, rooted in the depths through humility, grow boundlessly [Col. 0170B] like the cedar.

Our panelled ceilings are cypress.

[THO.] Ceilings fill and adorn houses. Cedar and cypress, which do not decay, signify the elect, who, despising temporal things, become eternal; desiring eternal things, they are ceilings for adornment, as was said. The Church is adorned in three classes of persons. There is the adornment of rulers; the adornment of prelates; and the adornment of subjects. Rulers in the Church are adorned with justice; prelates with knowledge, wisdom, and endurance; subjects with discipline and obedience. In the first, the ruler is formidable; in the second, the prelate venerable; in the third, the subject lovable. On account of these three, lions, oxen, and cherubim were carved on the bases of the Temple [Note: [Col. 0169] 3 Kings 7]: namely, the cherubim signify fullness of knowledge; the lions, the prelates; and the oxen, subjects who bear the yoke. [Col. 0170C]

In the first case, Ahasuerus was formidable, because, sitting upon his throne, he held a golden sceptre. When Queen Esther saw him, she nearly fell to the ground from fear; one of her handmaids supported her head lest it fall to the ground, while another supported her cloak [Note: [Col. 0169] Esther 15]. The first handmaid is confidence in inward innocence, which supports the head—that is, reason—lest it be able to wander. The other handmaid is confidence in good works, which supports the cloak—that is, good conduct—lest it fall into the dust; that is, lest anyone be able to defile it before the Judge by some mark of shamefulness.

As a figure of the second, Aaron, as a sign of knowledge, wore the *logion*, that is, the breastpiece, [Col. 0170D] upon his breast [Note: [Col. 0169] Lev. 8]; as a sign of endurance, the ephod upon his shoulders; and the golden plate upon his forehead [Note: [Col. 0169] Ibid.], as a sign of wisdom. A prelate ought to possess knowledge by which to know how to order the Church, and endurance by which he must bear the burdens of the weak. Hence this breastpiece and ephod, in which burdens are denoted, were joined by golden chains—that is, by mutual works of charity. A prelate ought to have courage, knowledge, and chastity: the first in relation to a tyrant, the second in relation to a subject, and the third in relation to himself; so that he may rebuke the tyrant, instruct the subject, [Col. 0171A] and himself appear blameless.

These are the three things which walk well. The first is the lion, which fears no encounter with any animal, because the righteous is confident as a lion [Note: [Col. 0171] Prov. 28]. The second is the ram, leader of the sheep, who lays down his life for his sheep [Note: [Col. 0171] John 10], that he may be the ram sacrificed for Isaac [Note: [Col. 0171] Gen. 22]. The third is “a cock girded about the loins” [Note: [Col. 0171] Prov. 30]. This is the cock which rouses those lying down and reproves the sleepy; to it it is said: “Let your loins be girded” [Note: [Col. 0171] Luke 12]. In the figure of the third, the children of Israel, when approaching the altar, were clothed in tightly fitting linen [Note: [Col. 0171] Exod. 28]. Linen cloth is soft and receives whatever folds are made in it; this pertains to obedience, which is ready for all things.

That it is tightly fitting refers to discipline, which binds what is loose. The first adornment, namely justice, [Col. 0171B] has four elements. Thus a judge ought to be discerning: he should console the wretched, diligently investigate whatever doubtful matter arises, punish the guilty according to the measure of the offence, and mercifully free the oppressed. Of these Job says: “I put on justice, and I clothed myself with my judgment as with a diadem” [Note: [Col. 0171] Job 29]. Of the first: “When I sat as a king surrounded by an army, I was nevertheless the comforter of mourners” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ibid.]. Of the second: “The cause which I did not know, I investigated diligently” [Note: [Col. 0171] Job 29]. Of the third: “I broke the jaws of the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ibid.]. Of the fourth: “And from his teeth I snatched the prey” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ibid.].

Of prelates the Apostle says: “Let the priests who rule well be held worthy of double honour” [Note: [Col. 0171] 1 Tim. 5], namely because of knowledge and wisdom. Likewise: “I desire a bishop to be [Col. 0171C] blameless, hospitable, chaste, orderly” [Note: [Col. 0171] 1 Tim. 3], so that this may be fulfilled: “Let your light shine before men” [Note: [Col. 0171] Matt. 5]. Of subjects the same author says: “I beseech you to walk worthily of the calling by which you were called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing one another in the charity of faith, or of the Spirit, in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 0171] Eph. 4].

Subjects ought to advance in four things. First, they should seek spiritual gain, by which they may live; afterwards, they should join themselves to a community of religious, so that their path may be safe; third, they should flee with their troubles to God; fourth, they should labour with the body and have their conversation in heaven with the spirit. These are the four smallest things of the earth, and they are wiser than the wise. The first is: “The ant, which labours in summer in order to live in winter.” Hence Solomon says: “Go to the ant, [Col. 0171D] O sluggard, and consider her ways; and learn wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0171] Prov. 6]. Hence: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0171] 2 Cor. 6]. And the Lord: “Walk while you have the light” [Note: [Col. 0171] John 12]; and: “Trade while it is day” [Note: [Col. 0171] Luke 19].

The second is “the locust, which has no king and all flies in companies” [Note: [Col. 0171] Prov. 37].
