For subjects entering religious life have no king in this world; but they dwell together, because of the saying: “Woe to one alone, because, if he falls, he has no one to lift him up” [Note: [Col. 0171] Eccl. 4]; and: “If two sleep together, they keep [Col. 0172A] one another warm” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ibid.]. “Behold how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ps. 132]. And John: “The love of Christ has gathered us into one; let us fear and love Christ God.” And Peter: “Be compassionate, lovers of the brotherhood” [Note: [Col. 0171] 1 Pet. 3].

The third is “the coney, a weak people, which makes its dwelling in the rock” [Note: [Col. 0171] Prov. 30]; “and the rock was Christ” [Note: [Col. 0171] 1 Cor. 10], who says to Peter: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church” [Note: [Col. 0171] Matt. 16].

To this rock flee those entangled among rocks, those burdened by temptations, and those endowed with virtues: the first, that they may be converted; the second, that they may be delivered; the third, that grace may increase in them. Of the first: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ps. 103], in whom the spines signify sins. Of the second, namely, “the coney, a weak people, makes its [Col. 0172B] dwelling in the rock.” Of the third: “Come, my bride, my dove, my beautiful one, into the holes of the rock, into the cleft of the wall” [Note: [Col. 0171] Song 2].

The fourth is “the lizard, which walks with its hands and dwells in the house of the king” [Note: [Col. 0171] Prov. 30]. For we ought to labour with our hands and dwell in heaven with the spirit. Of labour it is said: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall go well with you” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ps. 127]; and: “My soul is in my hands” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ps. 118], namely, so that you may say: “My hands have dripped myrrh, and my fingers are full of most choice myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0171] Song 5]. Therefore, “whatever your hand finds that it can do, do it diligently; for there is neither work nor reasoning nor wisdom nor knowledge among the dead, whither you hasten” [Note: [Col. 0171] Eccl. 9]. Meanwhile the spirit ought to dwell in heaven: [Col. 0172C] this is to dwell in the king’s house. Hence Paul says: “Our conversation is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0171] Phil. 3]; and: “Set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0171] Col. 3]. Stephen laboured bodily upon earth when, rejoicing, he received the stones [Note: [Col. 0171] Acts 7]; meanwhile he dwelt in heaven when he said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and Jesus standing at the right hand of the power of God” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ibid.].

Of the first, when he is thus adorned, it is said: “You have loved justice and hated iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ps. 44]. The prelates will hear: “Many will praise his wisdom, and his name shall not be blotted out for ever” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ecclus. 39]. Subjects cry: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ps. 118], so that afterwards they may be able to say: “Your discipline corrected me unto the end, and your very discipline will teach me” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ps. 17]. These ceilings, if such persons are found, are cypress [Col. 0172D] ceilings, and it shall be said of them: “Blessed is the man who dwells in wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ecclus. 14]; concerning prelates: “And who meditates upon justice” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ibid.]; concerning rulers: “And who in understanding considers the circumspection of God” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ibid.].

But if vice is found beside them, the ceilings will not be cedar, for example: if reward or favour corrupts a ruler while he administers justice; if ambition or pride adheres to a prelate’s knowledge or wisdom; or if hypocrisy and vainglory attach to a subject’s discipline and obedience. Of rulers Isaiah says: “Your rulers are faithless, companions of thieves; all love gifts and pursue rewards” [Note: [Col. 0173] Isa. 1]. They are faithless in neglecting their office; companions of thieves in concealing the truth; they love gifts and pursue rewards; and therefore they do not shrink from judging falsely.

Of prelates the same writer says: “Your gold has rusted” [Note: [Col. 0173] Jas. 5]. “Your silver has become dross; your wine has been mixed with water” [Note: [Col. 0173] Isa. 1]. Your gold is wisdom. It becomes rusty when pride is mingled with it; silver becomes dross when a preacher’s eloquence is despised on account of the dishonour of his life; wine is mixed with water when charity grows cold. Hence in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0173] Rev. 2] a certain prelate, under the name of an angel, is told: “I have something against you, because you have abandoned your first charity. [Col. 0173B] Do your first works; otherwise I shall come and remove your candlestick from its place.” Likewise, concerning these men: “The illustrious sons of Zion, and those first clothed in gold, how have they been reckoned as earthen vessels, the work of the potter’s hands!” [Note: [Col. 0173] Lam. 4]. They were called gold when they were wise; now they are earthen vessels because they are muddy through sin.

Of subjects the same author says: “Those who fed luxuriously have perished in the ways; those who were reared in saffron have embraced dung” [Note: [Col. 0173] Ibid.], while they entangle themselves in sins, abandoning their neighbour. He feeds luxuriously who is nourished by his teacher’s sweet doctrine. But they have perished in the paths by which the kingdom of heaven is sought, when, neglecting doctrine, they stray from their purpose and so die in soul. Saffron gives a good scent and has a brilliant colour. Thus those are reared in saffron who conform themselves to the good fragrance of their neighbour’s reputation and the brightness of his visible works. But they embrace dung when they entangle themselves in sins, abandoning their neighbour and their works.

There is also moral adornment, namely in the body, in the soul, or in both. But what is exterior, namely in the body, is no adornment; what is in the soul is some adornment; but what is in both is complete adornment. Of the first David says: “Their daughters are fashioned and adorned after the likeness of a temple” [Note: [Col. 0173] Ps. 103]. For they are not truly God’s temple, yet they bear its likeness. Of these the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” [Note: [Col. 0173] Matt. 7]. Likewise, he calls the Pharisees whitewashed tombs, [Col. 0173D] because outwardly they are verdant, but within they are full of dead men’s bones and every uncleanness [Note: [Col. 0173] Matt. 23]. Therefore Paul said to one such man, namely the priest Ananias: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” [Note: [Col. 0173] Acts 23]. Hence the Lord said to his apostles: “See that you do not perform your justice before men, in order to be seen by them” [Note: [Col. 0173] Matt. 6].

Of inward adornment it is said in Job: “The Spirit of the Lord adorned the heavens, and by his hand acting as midwife the twisted serpent was brought forth” [Note: [Col. 0173] Job 26]. Hence: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” [Note: [Col. 0173] Ps. 44]. Of both it is said [Col. 0174A] in the book of Maccabees: “They adorned the face of the temple with golden crowns, and dedicated the altars to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0173] 1 Macc. 4]. “The temple of God is holy, which you are” [Note: [Col. 0173] 1 Cor. 3]. Its face is outward conduct, by which a person is known by other people, as though by the face, whether he is regarded as good or evil. Thus this face is adorned with golden crowns when wisdom is perceived through his outward conduct; the person who, living thus, deserves a crown shapes himself inwardly according to the way he conducts himself outwardly. Hence follows: “And they dedicated the altars to the Lord,” that is, their own heart, which is the altar, when with groaning they lament their sins in it and thereby dedicate it inwardly to God by treating it as his own.

Thus, “The heavens and the earth and all their adornment were perfected” [Note: [Col. 0173] Gen. 2]. For the soul is called heaven, and it is adorned [Col. 0174B] when the soul is decorated with virtues. But the body is called earth because it was made from earth; this earth is adorned when good outward conduct is practised. The first are Bel, god of Accaron, muddy within and bronze without; the second, Solomon’s Temple, stone without and gold within; the third, the ark of the Lord, gilded inside and out with purest gold. Therefore these ceilings are cypress if they have been strengthened in such a good purpose that they cannot be corrupted by any delusion of the devil, the world, or the flesh, as the Apostle says: “Who shall separate us from the charity of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” [Note: [Col. 0173] Rom. 8].

Perhaps she had heard: “Adorn your bridal chamber, [Col. 0174C] Zion, and receive Christ the King” [Note: [Col. 0173] Church Office for the Purification]; and, stirred by vehement longing of spirit, she says that she has adorned not only the bridal chamber but also the bed and the house. For we have the house of our flesh, the bridal chamber of the heart, and the little bed of conscience. In the house, public affairs are administered; in the bridal chamber, there is secret deliberation concerning what is to be administered; in the bed, judgment is made.

For with our members we sometimes do good and sometimes evil: evil, namely crime against ourselves, injustice against our neighbour, and impiety against God; good, namely works of penitence toward ourselves, mercy toward our neighbour, and piety toward God. In the bridal chamber we deliberate concerning deeds to be done and their circumstances, namely these:

Who, what, where, by what aids, why, how, when. [Col. 0174D] In conscience we judge whether matters deliberated or accomplished are true or false, good or evil, advantageous or disadvantageous. But since every adornment is vain unless the things to be adorned are first cleansed, conscience must be cleansed by contrition, the bridal chamber of the heart by confession, and the house of the body by the satisfaction of penance. Contrition is true if one grieves over sin. Hence David: “My sorrow is ever before me” [Note: [Col. 0173] Ps. 37]. If one hates it, if one abominates it. Hence the same writer: “I have hated and abominated iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0173] Ps. 108].

Four things hinder confession. [Col. 0175A] There are those who conceal part of their sin, as Ananias and Sapphira concealed part of the money [Note: [Col. 0175] Acts 5]. There are those who confess everything but keep silent about the manner of it. David sought the manner when he said: “How have the mighty fallen in battle?” [Note: [Col. 0175] 2 Sam. 1]. Under “manner” I include all the aforesaid circumstances: what, who, where, and so forth. There are those who say the whole thing and later confess it, but make excuses, like Adam: “The woman,” he says, “whom you gave me, gave to me, and I ate” [Note: [Col. 0175] Gen. 3]. There are those who speak in embellished words so that their sin may seem less serious. These are the loincloths made from the leaves of trees with which the first parents covered their nakedness [Note: [Col. 0175] Ibid.]. For leaves signify words. Hence Horace [Note: [Col. 0175] *On the Art of Poetry*]:

> As forests change their leaves with the declining years,  
> The first fall; so the old generation of words perishes.

[Col. 0175B] The house of the body is cleansed by penance. Penance is threefold, for it is performed either in this life, in purgatory, or in Gehenna. The first is voluntary and terminable; the second necessary and terminable; the third necessary and interminable. The Lord set these before David through Gad the seer when David sinned by numbering the people: namely, either pestilence in his land, which is the first; or famine in the land, which is the second; or capture by enemies, which is the third. And the lighter one was given him, namely because he left everything to divine ordering. The house of the body is adorned by good conduct.

Conduct is threefold. For we ought to conduct ourselves in the cloister, in the world, and [Col. 0175C] in heaven: in the cloister with religious brothers; in the world with the perverse; and in heaven with angels. With brothers, by conforming ourselves to them in discipline; with the perverse, by enduring their insults; with angels, by thinking upon heavenly things. Of the first: “You endured a great struggle of sufferings”; of the second: “with reproaches and tribulations”; of the third: “having become companions of those so conducting themselves,” says the Apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0175] Heb. 10]. Of the second: “I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul, keeping our conduct good among the Gentiles, so that, in that wherein they speak against us as evildoers, they may glorify God on the day of visitation” [Note: [Col. 0175] 1 Pet. 2]. Of the third: “But our [Col. 0175D] conversation is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0175] Phil. 3].

For this reason there were over the tabernacle of Moses coverings of goat-hair cloth, skins of rams dyed red, and blue skins [Note: [Col. 0175] Exod. 26]. The coverings, which are cheap, signify the conduct of cloistered persons, who regard themselves as cheap and abject. The red skins pertain to the patience of those enduring the perverse. The blue skins, because they have heaven’s colour, pertain to contemplation with the angels. The bridal chamber is adorned by love of God and neighbour. Love is modest, strong, sweet, and wise. Thus in Solomon’s Temple there was a wall of mortar [Col. 0176A] and stone [Note: [Col. 0175] 3 Kings 5]; secondly fragrant wood; thirdly gold. Mortar, which is mud and lies hidden among the stones, signifies modest love; the stones, strong love; the fragrant wood, sweet love; and the gold, wise love.

Modest love is found in three things: injury to faith, theft, and betrayal. It is ashamed because it has injured by sinning the faith which it vowed in baptism; it is also ashamed because it has committed theft by concealing sins; and it is ashamed, moreover, because it has committed betrayal by handing over to the devil its heart and members, which will be God’s dwelling-place. Of the first the Apostle says: “They have made void their first faith” [Note: [Col. 0175] 1 Tim. 5]. Of the second, Job: “If I have hidden my sin as a man does, and concealed my iniquity in my bosom” [Note: [Col. 0175] Job 31]. Of the third: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” [Note: [Col. 0175] 1 Cor. 3]. “Shall I then take the members [Col. 0176B] of God and make them the members of a harlot?” [Note: [Col. 0175] 1 Cor. 6]. And the Lord: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” [Note: [Col. 0175] Luke 9].

Strong love is found in three things: it despises fear, seeks suffering, and does not flee shame. Of the first: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” [Note: [Col. 0175] Ps. 26]. Of the second Job says: “Deliver me, Lord, and set me beside you, and let the hand of anyone fight against me” [Note: [Col. 0175] Job 17]. And Habakkuk: “Let rottenness enter into my bones, and beneath me let it bubble forth, that I may rest in the day of tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0175] Hab. 3]. Of the third David says: “For your sake I bore reproach; shame covered my face” [Note: [Col. 0175] Ps. 68].

These are the three mighty men who brought David water from the spring at the gate of Bethlehem: Eleazar, Shemaiah, and Jeshbaam. Eleazar [Col. 0176C] means “the help of my God”; he is assigned to the first. Shemaiah means “obedient to the Lord,” and fits the second. Jeshbaam means “becoming foolish,” and fits the third. That spring is the sweet remembrance of the heavenly homeland, because through this threefold strength one comes to that sweetness and pleasantness which is signified by the fragrance of cypress wood.

The love of God is sweet in three respects: in mercy, in grace, and in glory—through mercy, for the remission of sins. Hence David: “The Lord is sweet to all; his mercies are over all his works” [Note: [Col. 0175] Ps. 144]. In grace, for the infusion of spiritual gifts. Hence David: “They shall utter the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness, and shall exult in your justice” [Note: [Col. 0175] Ibid.]. In glory, for the expectation of heavenly joys. Hence the same David: “Taste and [Col. 0176D] see how sweet the Lord is” [Note: [Col. 0175] Ps. 33].

Love is wise in avoiding the wiles of the devil, in considering love’s beginning and end, and in ordering one’s affections in the ascent from one thing to another. Hence Wisdom conquers malice and therefore reaches from its own beginning-end to its furthest end [the Latin wording is uncertain]; and it has sweetly ordered all things—one’s affections in ascending [Note: [Col. 0175] Wis. 7]. Behold the house; behold the bridal chamber. The little bed of conscience follows.

But it should be known that there is one kind of conscience that is seared; hence Paul: “having a seared conscience” [Note: [Col. 0175] 1 Tim. 4]; another good; hence the same: “from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith” [Note: [Col. 0177A] 1 Tim. 1]; another flourishing; hence again: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0177] 2 Cor. 1]. The seared conscience is liable to guilt; the good one is without crime. The flourishing conscience is adorned with many virtues, and especially with violet, lily, and rose: that it may be conscious of Christ’s humility, chastity, and charity. For this reason the Bridegroom subsequently says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0177] Song 2].

Or thus: among consciences, one is good and another evil. The good conscience is threefold: it is good, secure, and glorious. The first is sound, the second serene, the third delightful: sound, because it is free from wickedness; serene, because it is relieved of worldly anxiety; delightful, because it already dwells amid the joy of the angels. Of the first: “The fulfillment of the law is charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith” [Note: [Col. 0177] 1 Tim. 1].

[Col. 0177B] Likewise, a good conscience is a possession that has no sin in the conscience. Concerning it, the Law says: “When you have taken a captive woman, if she pleases you, you shall shave all the hair of her flesh and take her as your wife” [Note: [Col. 0177] Num. 8]. Of the second, Job says: “Behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who knows me is on high” [Note: [Col. 0177] Job 16]. This is that strong woman who provides for her household and, weaving a garment for her husband, conducts trade. Of the third: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0177] 2 Cor. 1]. This is the bride who delights in the Bridegroom’s kiss.

The first says: “I have washed my feet: how shall I defile them? I have taken off my tunic: how shall I put it on?” [Note: [Col. 0177] Song 5]. The second says: “I sleep, but my heart watches” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ibid.]. The third says: “Our little bed is flowering” [Note: [Col. 0177] Song 1].

Likewise, one evil conscience is seared, another defiled, another troubled: seared, because it is inflamed by the burning heat of perverse desire; [Col. 0177C] defiled, because it rots in filth through continual desire; troubled, because, seeing sin on one side and the punishments of hell on the other, it lives always in horror while continually sinning. Of the first the Apostle says: “There are some who have their conscience seared” [Note: [Col. 0177] 1 Tim. 4]. Two daughters of the leech rule it, “who always say: Bring, bring” [Note: [Col. 0177] Prov. 30], that is, pleasure and avarice.

Of the second, the same says: “Their mind and conscience are defiled” [Note: [Col. 0177] Titus 1]. This conscience sits in the ephah [Note: [Col. 0177] Zech. 5] together with impiety, and two women carry it into the land of Shinar [Note: [Col. 0177] Dan. 1], a name meaning “their stench”: namely, worldly prosperity and an abundance of temporal things. For the third: “Two harlot women contended before King Solomon” [Note: [Col. 0177] 3 Kings 3], that is, fear and unfaithful security. For fear wishes its son—that is, a good work—to live, while unfaithful security wishes to kill it. Hence a cruel, troubled conscience is always presumptuous.

The house of God is the soul of the righteous. Its foundation is fear, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 110]. From this arise two walls, innocence and mercy. For the whole structure is made firm by these. Hence blessed James the Apostle says: “Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulations, and to keep oneself undefiled from this world” [Note: [Col. 0177] Jas. 1]. The first refers to mercy; [Col. 0178A] the second to innocence.

See how the wall of innocence rises from the foundation of fear. Fear of the Lord produces examination of oneself; self-examination, self-knowledge; self-knowledge, repentance; repentance, sorrow; sorrow, confession; confession, amendment; amendment, cleansing; cleansing, purity; and purity confers perfect innocence.

See, by another process, how the wall of mercy rises from fear: fear for the miserable produces consideration; consideration, compassion; compassion, the desire to help; and the desire to help, according to one’s capacity, exercises the full virtue of mercy. David invites us to these two things, saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 3].

The roof is hope of heavenly things. While it draws us back from the desire for temporal things, [Col. 0178B] it preserves us from the storm of temporal things through patience. For patience itself takes the place of rafters.

“No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0177] 1 Cor. 3]. Those who wish to build ought to consider the ground, the foundation, and the structure founded upon it. The ground is the place of the heart; the foundation is Christ; the founded structure is a good work, both inward and outward. Let the first have purity, the second stability, the third right order: the first, lest it have the mud of sins; the second, lest its purpose be unstable; the third, lest anything be done disorderly.

Of the first Paul says: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit” [Note: [Col. 0177] 2 Cor. 7]. Of the second: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? [Col. 0178C] Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword?” [Note: [Col. 0177] Rom. 8]. Of the third the bride says in the Song: “He has ordered charity within me” [Note: [Col. 0177] Song 2].

Hear of the first: “Prepare your hearts” [Note: [Col. 0177] 1 Kings 7]: behold the ground for the Lord. Behold the foundation: “And serve him alone” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ibid.]. Behold the founded structure: “Thus that house will be built.” Of it it is said:

> A whirlwind which no one  
> shakes, nor wandering  
> winds demolish,  
> nor storm-clouds penetrate.

For the storm-clouds of carnal pleasure do not penetrate the ground; the whirlwind of adversity does not shake the foundation; and the winds of vanity do not demolish the founded structure.

David was cleansing the place when he said: “If I give sleep to my eyes [Col. 0178D] and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 131]. For if the ground is muddy, Christ the foundation will not be laid there; rather, he will cry: “Deliver me from the mire, lest I be stuck fast” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 68]. But if he has perhaps entered it, he will cry: “I am stuck fast in deep mud, and there is no firm ground” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ibid.]. When he has emerged, he will give thanks thus: “The Father brought me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs” [Note: [Col. 0177] Ps. 39].

Upon this ground sinners build three edifices. They lay temporal goods as a foundation and build pride upon it. Likewise, they lay [Col. 0179A] the concupiscence of the flesh as a foundation and build wantonness upon it. Likewise, they lay garrulousness as a foundation and build blasphemy, murmuring, and insult upon it.

The first building is the tower of Babylon, made of bricks [Note: [Col. 0179] Gen. 11], that is, temporal goods. Unbaked bricks are temporal goods acquired wickedly and spent luxuriously. Hence it is said: “We shall build with unbaked bricks.” Baked bricks are temporal goods wickedly acquired. These are baked when a person becomes hardened in them by retaining them wickedly. Thus the children of Israel baked bricks for Pharaoh in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0179] Exod. 1]. And Isaiah says: “My belly shall sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick” [Note: [Col. 0179] Isa. 16].

The other two are Pithom and Rameses, which the children of Israel built in Egypt for King Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0179] Exod. 1]. The second [Col. 0179B] building, therefore, is Rameses, interpreted as “the agitation of the moth,” namely carnal desire. The third building is Pithom, called “the gaping mouth,” namely useless talkativeness. In such ground are “creeping things without number” [Note: [Col. 0179] Ps. 103].

Therefore one must first dig in such ground, as Ezekiel says: “Son of man, dig through the wall.” And he dug and found images of quadrupeds, creeping things, and birds [Note: [Col. 0179] Ezek. 8]. Quadrupeds are those who, touching the earth with their hands as though with feet, handle temporal things beyond measure. Creeping things are voluptuaries, who creep with mouth, breast, belly, and tail: with the mouth, by speaking wantonly; with the breast, by thinking so; with the belly, by devoting themselves to its fulfillment; with the tail, by persisting in these things. The birds, however, are the proud. Therefore these things are cleansed away, so that the house may be built.

For it is written: [Col. 0179C] “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” [Note: [Col. 0179] Ps. 126]. In it, “no one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0179] 1 Cor. 3]. Therefore he is placed like a stone in the foundation, of whom it is said: “Jacob set up a stone as a monument, pouring out prayer to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0179] Gen. 35].

This stone some leave at the bottom; some suspend in the middle; some set upright at the top. The first are carnal people; the second, those who live moderately; the third, those devoted to God. The first have faith but do not act; the second “use the world as though not using it” [Note: [Col. 0179] 1 Cor. 7]; the third live in heaven [Note: [Col. 0179] Phil. 3].

Of the first James the Apostle says: “Faith without works is dead” [Note: [Col. 0179] Jas. 2]. Of the second John [Col. 0179D] the Apostle says: “Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need and closes his bowels against him, how does the charity of God remain in him?” [Note: [Col. 0179] 1 John 3]. To these it is said: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” [Note: [Col. 0179] 1 John 2]. The third say with Paul: “The things which were gains to me have become losses for Christ, for whose sake I have counted all things loss; and I count them as dung, that I may gain Christ” [Note: [Col. 0179] Phil. 3]. Likewise the same Apostle says: “But one thing: forgetting those things which are behind, [Col. 0180A] and stretching myself toward those things which are before, I press toward the prize of the heavenly calling” [Note: [Col. 0179] Ibid.].

Thus the first leave it at the bottom in danger; the second balance it in the middle as a mirror; the third set it upright at the top as a monument: the first in the danger of damnation; the second in the mirror of self-knowledge; the third in the monument of divine praise. For of the first: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0179] Rom. 1]. Of the second: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go forth and follow the tracks of your flocks” [Note: [Col. 0179] Song 1]. The third say: “I shall praise my God in my life” [Note: [Col. 0179] Ps. 145].

The first pour out honey; the second, wine; the third pour oil from above: honey of carnal pleasure, wine of penitential austerity, oil of devotion. This honey [Col. 0180B] is forbidden in sacrifice. Wine and oil are poured by the Samaritan upon the man wounded by robbers [Note: [Col. 0179] Luke 10].

Behold, concerning the foundation: “Upon this foundation some build wood, hay, stubble” [Note: [Col. 0179] 1 Cor. 3], that is, certain movements of venial sins: vanity about deeds, which is wood; gracefulness of the body, which is hay, because “all flesh is hay” [Note: [Col. 0179] 1 Pet. 1]; and brilliance of speech, which is stubble, with which the ancients were accustomed to sing.

As a figure of the first, when Paul was gathering brushwood, a viper that lay hidden within sprang out from it and fastened upon his hand; he courageously shook it off [Note: [Col. 0179] Acts 25]. As a figure of the second, Absalom sat upon a mule—that is, foolish flesh—and the wind of self-exaltation lifted up his hair—that is, the thoughts of his heart—and they clung to an oak, that is, to the hardness of obstinacy. [Col. 0180C] Joab—that is, the devil—came upon him and pierced his heart with three spears [Note: [Col. 0179] 2 Kings 18], namely these: the proud person is cruel to an inferior, is indignant at an equal, and envies a superior. Against the first, according to the poet, he ought to:

> Spare the subjected and subdue the proud.

[Note: [Col. 0179] Vergil, *Aeneid* VI.353.]

Of the second another said:

> Caesar could no longer endure a superior,  
> nor Pompey an equal.

[Note: [Col. 0179] Lucan I.125.]

As a figure of the third, John saw in the Apocalypse “three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the mouth of the dragon” [Note: [Col. 0179] Rev. 16].

Others “build upon it gold, silver, precious stones” [Note: [Col. 0179] 1 Cor. 3]: gold of wisdom and charity; silver of innocence and chastity; precious stones of inward and outward work. In [Col. 0180D] the figure of the first, there were two golden cherubim in the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0179] Exod. 25]. In the figure of the second, Moses had two silver, hammered trumpets by which the people were summoned in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0179] Num. 10]. In the figure of the third, it is said of Ezekiel’s living creatures: “Under their wings were human hands in their four parts” [Note: [Col. 0179] Ezek. 1].

For the wings are inward works, and human hands outward works. Those which are beneath the wings are more excellent than outward things because they are inward. Outward works are in four parts: first, a person performs works of repentance for himself; second, works of mercy for his neighbor; third, works of perfection for his enemy; fourth, works of piety toward God are performed. And this concerning the construction of the spiritual house.

### 34. The ceiling panels ought to be of cypress.

[CARD.] For although those graces which are signified by the ceiling panels spread out below and are manifested for the benefit of neighbors, they nevertheless rise to a point, like the cypress, and are drawn together into one. For they tend toward him who is truly one, and direct themselves toward that one thing of which the Prophet says: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek” [Note: [Col. 0181] Ps. 26].

But because he had promised a flowering bed [Note: [Col. 0181] Song 1], the Son shows that the bed does not flower unless, through humility, it is a little bed; and that no one flowers unless he himself flowers in that person, since his Spirit does not rest except upon the humble [Col. 0181B] [Note: [Col. 0181] Isa. 66].

> I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.

[THO.] Christ aptly calls himself a flower because, while he extirpates the thorns of sins, he adorns the bride’s mind with the beauty of righteousness; and while he applies heavenly desire to the seas of the heart, he refreshes the inward parts of the soul as if by fragrance.

What is in the field lies open to all: namely, the violet of humility, by which he places himself beneath all, and the rose of charity, which spreads itself by doing good even to those who act wickedly. Gardens are usually enclosed in valleys because the ground is rich. There is the lily of chastity, which always rejoices to be kept enclosed.

That this adornment belongs not to the bride but to the Bridegroom is suggested by the Bridegroom when he says: “I am the flower [Col. 0181C] of the field and the lily of the valleys.” The flower is at one time in the bridal chamber, at another in the field, at another in the garden. The bridal chamber is the conscience filled with the flowers of good works. A flower is not born in the bridal chamber but is brought from elsewhere, because good works are done not by us but by God’s grace.

The field flowering without human cultivation is the blessed Virgin; its flower is her Son. Likewise, the garden is the human heart: there the flower of charity—that is, Christ—grows through human cultivation, though this is more divine than human. Likewise, the flower is virginity; the flower is marriage; the flower is good action. Virginity is in the garden, marriage in the field, and good work in the bridal chamber. Virginity is fittingly in the garden, since solitude is its friend. Mothers are fittingly in the field, since they are exposed to the mockery of all. Good action is deservedly also in the bridal chamber, [Col. 0181D] since it both makes the conscience peaceful and renders it secure.

Therefore the Lord is the flower of the garden; the Virgin is the rod; he is born from the Virgin. Likewise, he is the flower of the field, the martyr, the crown of martyrs, the pattern of martyrdom. Finally, he was led outside the city, suffered outside the camp [Note: [Col. 0181] Heb. 13], and was hung upon wood [Note: [Col. 0181] Matt. 27; Acts 10]; and thus Christ is compared to a flower in many ways.

By nature a flower is joyful. It is pleasant to behold, sweet to smell, delightful to touch. Therefore, in order to awaken our desire for the blessedness of his vision, through the beauty of a flower he sets his own beauty before us, so as to kindle our affections toward the taste of inward sweetness. Through the fragrance of a flower [Col. 0182A] he brings his sweetness to our remembrance, so as to invite our love to the joy of his blessed fellowship. Through the pleasantness of a flower he promises us the ineffable delight of his penitence.

Breadth is considered in a field; depth is seen in a valley. Therefore, in those who enlarge themselves by charity let there be the flower of the field; in those who humble themselves let there be the flower of the valleys. Likewise, three things are considered in the lily: greenness in its leaves, whiteness in its flowers, and golden color in its seeds. In the greenness, which benefits the eyes, faith is understood. In the white flower, from which fruit proceeds, hope is suggested to us. In the golden seed, both by its value and by its color, charity is set before us.

“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys,” as though he said:

[Col. 0182B] I am he who glorifies those enlarged by charity, exalts the humble, enlightens believers, strengthens those who hope, and kindles those who love.

It should be noted that “flower” sometimes signifies vanity, sometimes the grace and sweetness of virtues; sometimes it signifies the hope of fruit, sometimes the joy of heavenly things. This is according to four etymologies of the word. In the first sense, *flos* (“flower”) is so called as a separately passing honor of hay (*feni labens honor seorsum*); in the second sense, it is so called as spreading its fragrance widely; in the third, it is so called, namely as “fruit tasting the aid of what follows” (*fructus libans opem sequentis*); in the fourth sense, it is so called as producing the glad fragrance of sweetness.

For flower in the sense of birth, we find it said in [Col. 0182C] Isaiah: “All flesh is hay, and all its glory is like the flower of hay” [Note: [Col. 0181] ch. 40]. In the second sense, namely for the grace and sweetness of virtues, it is said: “Bloom, flowers, like a lily; give fragrance and put forth leaves in grace” [Note: [Col. 0181] Sir. 39]. In the third sense, for hope, it is said: “Let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers are bringing forth fruit” [Note: [Col. 0181] Song 7]. In the fourth sense, concerning the joy of heavenly things, we read: “The righteous shall sprout like a lily and shall flower forever before the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0181] Church Office].

In Solomon we find three kinds of vanity, as though folded together in this saying: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, says Ecclesiastes” [Note: [Col. 0181] Eccl. 1]. From these we learn that one vanity is of mutability, another of covetousness, another of punishment. The first is in perishable things, from their condition; [Col. 0182D] the second in the heart, from disordered love of things; the third in the body, from mortality. The first is natural and fitting; the second blameworthy because perverse; the third penal and wretched. The first is the cause of sin; the second is sin; the third is the punishment of sin. The first reproves the second; the third punishes it.

The first is vanity because it shows itself to possess what it does not possess, and cannot remain in what it possesses. In the second are “the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life” [Note: [Col. 0181] John 2]. In the third, however, are wearing-down and dissolution. Wearing-down is that by which a person is afflicted every day through temporal misery; dissolution is that by which the soul is separated from the body in death. Thus the whole human being is vanity so long as he is kept in this wretched exile.

We also find “flower” used of the adornment of virtues. There are three adornments: the first belongs to outward conduct alone; the second to outward conduct together with the inward ordering of character; the third belongs to future incorruption. The prophet Isaiah seeks the first when he says: “The Lord will take away from you ornaments, little crescents, and mirrors from your shoes” [Note: [Col. 0183A] Isa. 3]. Of the second we find in the Book of Maccabees: “They adorned the face of the temple with golden crowns and dedicated the altars to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0183] Macc. 4]: the face, namely, of outward conduct; the altar, namely, of the heart. Of the third: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, [Col. 0183B] coming down from heaven, prepared by God, like a bride adorned for her husband” [Note: [Col. 0183] Rev. 21].

The first is that of hypocrites; the second, that of religious persons; the third, that of the blessed. The first is a pretence of good; the second, the fragrance of good; the third, the consummation of good.

Hope also is threefold. The first is hope of pardon, the second hope of grace, the third hope of glory. Of the first: “Our fathers hoped in you; they hoped, and you delivered them” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 21], namely from sins. Of the second it is said: “They hoped in you and were not confounded” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ibid.], but were filled with grace. Of the third Job says: “I shall see God my Savior.” And he added: “This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom” [Note: [Col. 0183] Job 19].

Likewise, heavenly joy is threefold: the incorruption of bodies, fellowship with angels, and the vision of God. The prophet calls us to the first thus: “Rejoice, [Col. 0183C] daughter of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0183] Zech. 9]. Of the second: “It will be good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together as one” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 132]. Of the third: “He has stored up joy and exultation for him” [Note: [Col. 0183] Sir. 15].

Likewise, the Beloved is called “the flower of the field, the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0183] Song 2]. What is in the field lies open to all. The flower of the field is the rose, fiery in color, signifying the Holy Spirit, who appeared in fire [Note: [Col. 0183] Acts 2]. The lily, naturally white, is Christ: born from sinners as though from earth, yet having none of human sin. In valleys mists endure longer and shield lilies from the severity of heat.

Therefore, in the field is the manifest character of Christ’s way of life; in the fiery color of the rose is the charity of the Holy Spirit in him, as illumination—that is, understanding; in the cloud is protection in every temptation, where violence had no place in Christ [Col. 0183D]. For in these three things the fullness and abundance of the Holy Spirit in him is proved.

Against the first it is said: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from what is feigned” [Note: [Col. 0183] Wis. 1]; against the second: “and will withdraw from thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ibid.] “that are without understanding”; against the third: “and will be rebuked by iniquity coming upon it” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ibid.]. For these three drive the Holy Spirit from the human heart: the first is duplicity, the second obscurity, the third iniquity. Duplicity is that by which a hypocrite, inwardly evil, outwardly pretends religious devotion; obscurity is that by which he knows neither himself nor God; iniquity is that by which he offends his neighbor.

In the first: “The earth was empty” [Note: [Col. 0183] Gen. 1], because religion without foundation has no firmness. In the third: “The earth was void” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ibid.], because iniquity expels charity. In the second: “Darkness was upon the face of the abyss” [Note: [Col. 0183] Gen. 1], because he knows neither himself nor his Creator. But “the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ibid.], awaiting, as it were, the sinner’s uncertain return.

It should be noted that iniquity comes, reaches, and comes upon. It comes when it first attacks; it reaches when the tempted person consents; it comes upon when it intends to bring him to the act. In the first, the zeal of holy conduct and meditation melts away; in the second, good [Col. 0184B] will vanishes; in the third, charity grows cold.

Behold, the earth is void; but against the first it is recalled thus: “Come, Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0183] Invocation to the Holy Spirit]; against the second: “Fill the hearts of your faithful”; against the third: “And kindle in them the fire of your love.” This is the cloud of the Holy Spirit. Hence, when the tabernacle was completed, a cloud covered it and the glory of the Lord filled it [Note: [Col. 0183] 3 Kings 8]. Christ built it; glory filled it; cloud covered it: the first in the Passion, the second in the Resurrection and Ascension, the third in the sending of the Holy Spirit.

And in us, we build by imitating Christ’s Passion; glory fills us if we yearn for his Resurrection and Ascension; the cloud covers us through the mission of the Holy Spirit. In opposition to these three things, we read that the Holy Spirit appeared in three [Col. 0184C] forms: against duplicity, in the form of a dove—behold, the field; against obscurity, in fire—behold, the rose of fiery color; against iniquity, in a cloud—behold, the lily in the valley, knowing not the heat of the sun through the relief of the interposed morning mist.

The first is so that he may fill up duplicity; the second, so that he may illuminate obscurity; the third, so that he may cool the heat of tempting iniquity with dripping dew. Through the first returns the spirit of unity; through the second, the spirit of truth; through the third, the spirit of charity: unity in conduct, truth in speech, charity in affections.

Of the first: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 0183] Eph. 4]. Of the second: “I shall ask my Father, and he will send you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth” [Note: [Col. 0183] John 14]. Of the third: “Lord, pour into us the spirit of your charity” [Note: [Col. 0183] Church Office].

There are three kinds of duplicity: the first of malice, the second of vainglory, the third of self-will and inconstancy. The first is that by which someone pretends to love one against whom he plots evil. The second is that by which a hypocrite feigns himself in order to receive human praise. The third is that by which a fool is changed like the moon: an inconstant person, living under a rule, judges that things ought to be done otherwise, and appears wiser than all others in his own eyes.

Of the first: two are in the field. For this is the field in which Abel is slain by Cain [Col. 0185A] [Note: [Col. 0185] Gen. 4]. Of the second: two are in the bed in which the Beloved is sought at night and not found [Note: [Col. 0185] Song 3]. Of the third: two are at the mill, in which the captive woman is slain with the firstborn of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0185] Exod. 11].

The first are those who “speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ps. 27]. Of the second: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” [Note: [Col. 0185] Matt. 7]. Of the third: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent before yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0185] Isa. 5].

Of the first: “They spoke with mouth and heart” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ps. 11]. Of the second: “Woe to you who are double in heart” [Note: [Col. 0185] Sir. 2]. Of the third: “A double-minded man is inconstant in all his ways” [Note: [Col. 0185] Jas. 1].

Against these three duplicities there is found a threefold unity of the Holy Spirit. Against the first, unity of heart [Col. 0185B] toward one’s brother; against the second, unity of heart in outward action; against the third, unity of heart in regular observance. Hence it is said of the bride in the Song: “One is my dove, one is my beautiful one, one is she to her mother” [Note: [Col. 0185] Song 6]. Behold the threefold unity.

Of the first: “There was one spirit and one faith in them, and the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” [Note: [Col. 0185] Acts 4]; and: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ps. 132]. As a figure of the second: “The angel of the Lord descended into the pool” [Note: [Col. 0185] John 15], etc. As a figure of the third: “Ten lepers were cleansed, and no one returned except one to give glory to God” [Note: [Col. 0185] Luke 17].

Because of the first it is said: “Two are in the field; one shall be taken,” namely the soul that is in the first unity, “and [Col. 0185C] the other shall be left” [Note: [Col. 0185] Matt. 24], namely the soul that is in otherness. Because of the second: “Two are in the bed; one shall be taken and the other left” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ibid.]. Because of the third: “Two are at the mill; one shall be taken and the other left” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ibid.].

On account of these three unities, we read of a threefold dove signifying the Holy Spirit. The first was in the ark beneath the flood [Note: [Col. 0185] Gen. 8]; Moses commanded the second to be offered in sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0185] Lev. 1, 5, etc.]; the third appeared above the Lord at his baptism [Note: [Col. 0185] Matt. 3]. The first brought an olive branch to the ark, that is, peace. The second is offered “with its head twisted toward its little wings,” so that the hypocrite may be taught to turn back the head, which is the soul, toward the little wings, that is, toward the outward exercise of virtue. The third remained upon the Lord, so that it might recall the duplicity of inconstancy to stability—that is, against self-will. Hence [Col. 0185D] the Lord says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” [Note: [Col. 0185] John 6].

Thus further, “the Holy Spirit of discipline will not flee from what is feigned” [Note: [Col. 0185] Wis. 1], because duplicity has been filled up through the Holy Spirit. But it “is rebuked by iniquity coming upon it” [Note: [Col. 0185] Wis. 1], that is, by the heat of temptation which induces sin. Against this the Holy Spirit appeared in a cloud [Note: [Col. 0185] Matt. 17], with dew of refreshment dripping down.

“The Holy Spirit also appeared in [Col. 0186A] fire” [Note: [Col. 0185] Acts 2], in order to enlighten the dark heart. For there are three sins against the Holy Spirit which darken the heart. The first is the sin of despair; the second, presumption; the third, envy of brotherly charity. Of the first Cain says: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon” [Note: [Col. 0185] Gen. 4]. Of the second, in the Apocalypse: “I sit as a queen; I am not a widow; and I shall not see mourning” [Note: [Col. 0185] Rev. 18]. Of the third John says in his Catholic Epistle: “There is a sin unto death; concerning it I do not say that anyone should pray” [Note: [Col. 0185] 1 John 5].

Therefore, that he may enlighten, the Holy Spirit appears against this in fire: to consume, to kindle, and to illuminate—to consume sin, to kindle works of virtue, and to illuminate for the revelation of heavenly things.

[Col. 0186B] Hence philosophers say: Fire is sharp, mobile, subtle. Thus the fire of the Holy Spirit is sharp because it pierces when it penetrates the sinner’s heart through contrition; mobile because it rouses the sluggish person to action; subtle because it reveals heavenly things. In the first it pierces; in the second it joins; in the third it anoints. It pierces crimes, joins covenants, anoints the inward parts. It pierces crimes with the bitterness of contrition; joins covenants by the pledge of an infused spirit; anoints the inward parts with the sweetness of love.

In the first, “there was suddenly made a sound from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0185] Acts 2], which, by piercing as though in rebuke, consumes sin. In the second, a mighty Spirit came [Note: [Col. 0185] Ibid.] in order to kindle. In the third, he fills the whole house [Note: [Col. 0185] Ibid.] while enlightening it to see heavenly things.

In the first he is called *vehemens* (“mighty”), as though *vae adimens* (“taking away woe”); in the second *vehemens*, as though *vehens mentem* (“bearing the mind along”); in the third *vehemens*, as though *vehens a mente* (“bearing away from the mind”).

Hear of the sharp one, who pierces and consumes sins: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” [Note: [Col. 0185] John 20]. And Job [Note: [Col. 0185] Job 4]: “When the spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh stood on end,” that is, sins. Hence it is said in Ezekiel: “Come, spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ezek. 37].

For the Holy Spirit comes and brings the spirit of divine inspiration from the west, when he restores the fallen sinner; he comes from the north, from which “all evil is spread abroad” [Note: [Col. 0185] Jer. 1], when he overcomes in us the devil’s temptation; he comes from the south when he inflames our heart to love; he comes from the east when he enlightens it to know heavenly things.

But those to whom [Col. 0186D] it seems absurd that spirit should bring spirit should know that three are called spirits properly, and three improperly. Properly: the divine Spirit, the human spirit, and the angelic spirit, whether good or evil. Improperly: first, the spirit of diabolical suggestion; second, a human breath; third, divine inspiration. Therefore the three principal spirits bring forth the three improper ones.

Of the first: “We have not received the spirit of this world,” says the Apostle [Col. 0187A] [Note: [Col. 0187] 1 Cor. 2], that is, the world’s pride. Again: “Some are puffed up by the spirit of their flesh” [Note: [Col. 0187] 1 Cor. 4], that is, by carnal pleasure: here it is brought in by the diabolical spirit. Of the second, the same Apostle says: “If I pray with the tongue, my spirit prays” [Note: [Col. 0187] 1 Cor. 14], that is, breath. This breath is brought in by the human spirit also. Of the third, in the Apocalypse: “Grace to you and peace from him and from the seven spirits who are about his throne” [Note: [Col. 0187] Apoc. 1]. These seven spirits are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, as Hamno says in his commentary on the Apocalypse: namely, the spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0187] Isa. 11]. This spirit is brought in by the Holy Spirit. We have said these things lest those ignorant of the names of the virtues should deceive themselves or be deceived by others. The spirit of God’s wrath is also spoken of. Hence: “My Spirit shall not [Col. 0187B] remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” [Note: [Col. 0187] Gen. 6]; that is, I shall not condemn them forever, because they are made of frail material, but [I shall condemn] the angels, who are spirits. Of these it is read in the Apocalypse: “Four angels held the four winds, lest they should blow” [Note: [Col. 0187] Apoc. 7].

Hear of the spirit as mobile and proceeding to works: “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” [Note: [Col. 0187] Ezek. 1]. Again: “Wherever the spirit went, the spirits went likewise, as did the wheels following it” [Note: [Col. 0187] Ibid.]. And: “Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” [Note: [Col. 0187] Matt. 4].—“The spirit goes round about, traversing all things, and returns to its circuits,” says Solomon [Note: [Col. 0187] Eccl. 1]. It traverses when it searches the heart for sins of thought; then the members for sins of action; afterward the tongue for [Col. 0187C] sins of speech, “because,” he says, “God is the witness of his reins, the true searcher of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue” [Note: [Col. 0187] Wisd. 1]. It returns to its circuits when it comes again to the heart, to kindle it to love; to the members, to stir them to action; and to the tongue, to stir it to confess and praise God. “For the Spirit of the Lord fills the world” [Note: [Col. 0187] Ibid.], whom they call the soul of the world. Hence Virgil:

> In the beginning, a spirit within nourishes  
> heaven and earth, the liquid plains,  
> the shining globe of the moon, and Titanian stars;  
> and mind, infused through all the limbs,  
> moves the whole mass and mingles with the vast body.  
> [Note: [Col. 0187] Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VI.]

“Those who are led by the Spirit of God, they are the children of God” [Note: [Col. 0187] Rom. 8].

Hear of the subtle and illuminating spirit: “The Spirit,” says Paul, “searches all things, even the depths of God” [Note: [Col. 0187] 1 Cor. 2]. Again he says: [Col. 0187D] “God has revealed them to us through his Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0187] Ibid.]. “Those who are according to the spirit perceive the things of the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0187] Rom. 8]. “The spirit led me,” says Ezekiel, “to a great and broad mountain, and showed me the building of a city facing south” [Note: [Col. 0187] Ezek. 40]. This is the heavenly country for which we labor, that we may arrive there, the Holy Spirit guiding us and consoling our labors, as the poet says [Note: [Col. 0187] Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. I]:

> … perhaps one day it will help to remember even these things.  
> Endure, and preserve yourselves for more favorable circumstances.  
> O you who have suffered heavier things, God will grant an end to these also,  
> through varied chances and through so many hazards of affairs.  
> [Col. 0188A] We make for Latium, where the fates show us peaceful homes.

Let us therefore seek that the Holy Spirit may first be infused, secondly spread abroad, and thirdly poured forth. First, that the infusion of the Holy Spirit may cleanse our hearts and fertilize them by the inward sprinkling of his dew, so that the Holy Spirit, when he comes, may find in us a dwelling prepared for himself [Note: [Col. 0187] Church Office]. Secondly, that he may set us ablaze with that fire of the Holy Spirit which our Lord Jesus Christ sent upon the earth and strongly desired to be kindled [Note: [Col. 0187] Luke 12], so that we may say: “The charity of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0187] Rom. 5]. Thirdly, that he may be poured out upon us, and that the saying of the prophet Joel may be fulfilled: “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and [Col. 0188B] your sons and daughters shall prophesy” [Note: [Col. 0187] Joel 2], so that the Spirit who proceeds from the Father may illuminate our minds and lead us into all truth, as his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, promised [Note: [Col. 0187] Church Office], to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

[CAR.] He does not say, “I am the flower of the mountains,” but “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” A twofold humility is signified by the field and the valleys. For there are some who humble themselves before their superiors, and measure themselves humbly in relation to themselves and their equals; these are represented by the fields. The Apostle showed himself such when he said: “For we do not dare to insert or compare ourselves among certain persons who commend themselves; but they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, do not glory without measure” [Col. 0188C] [Note: [Col. 0187] 2 Cor. 10].

There are others who humble themselves beneath their equals and inferiors, like land which descends from its level and makes a valley. The Apostle showed himself such when he said: “I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle” [Note: [Col. 0187] 1 Cor. 15]. This also should be observed: the lily rises to bloom upon a stem higher and stronger than those of other plants; and because greater humility rises and advances further, while lesser humility does so less, the flower is assigned to the field and the lily to the valleys. But because, in proportion as each person grows in Christ through humility, Christ grows in him, Christ himself, to show this, says of himself: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” [Col. 0188D] Then, continuing the praise of his mother which he had begun, he says:

> As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among daughters.

[THO.] The bride is rightly called like a lily among thorns, because, although many confess Christ in word together with the Church, they do not do so in works, but follow the world’s anxieties. That soul alone is worthy of the dignity of the lily which, raising itself toward heavenly beauty, preserves for itself the whiteness of purity in heart and body, refreshes its neighbors with the fragrance of good works, and, spreading the fragrance of good repute among people, kindles them to good conduct.

There is a lily beneath thorns, a lily among thorns, and a lily above thorns. The lily is chastity. It is a lily beneath thorns when virginity is possessed together with sin; for both sin and temptation are thorns. Hence: “I was turned in my misery while the thorn was fixed in me” [Note: [Col. 0189] Ps. 31]. The lily is among thorns when virginity is assailed by many temptations. The lily is above thorns when the assault of temptations has been overcome. God threatens the first through the prophet: “The sword shall lay them waste without, and terror within: young man together with virgin, the suckling child with the old man” [Note: [Col. 0189] Deut. 32]. Of the second Jeremiah says: “Her priests groan, her virgins are squalid, and she herself is oppressed with bitterness” [Note: [Col. 0189] Lam. 1]. Of the third: “They are virgins and follow the Lamb wherever [Col. 0189B] he goes” [Note: [Col. 0189] Apoc. 14].

The foolish virgins represent the first: they had the shining lamps of virginity, but did not receive the oil of charity [Note: [Col. 0189] Matt. 25]. The wise virgins represent the second: they both had the lamps of virginity and received the oil of charity, but, wearied by temptations, “all dozed and slept” [Note: [Col. 0189] Ibid.]. They represented the third when, having laid aside every anxiety, they entered the wedding with the bridegroom [Note: [Col. 0189] Ibid.].

The first virginity was that of the dancing girl, that is, Herodias’s daughter [Note: [Col. 0189] Matt. 14], who was the daughter of sin. The second was that of blessed Agnes, who endured suffering lest she serve the marriage-bed. The third was that of the Blessed Virgin Mary, who experienced no sting of lust, overshadowed by the grace of the Holy Spirit. It should be noted that in Sacred Scripture virginity is sometimes compared to the lily [Col. 0189C] in the female sex and sometimes in the male; sometimes Christ, the virgin, is compared to the lily itself. Of the first it says here: “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among daughters”; of the second: “The righteous shall blossom like the lily” [Note: [Col. 0189] Hos. 14]; of the third it has been said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0189] Song 2].

Behold a threefold virginity. The first is more modest, the second stronger, the third more perfect: the first more modest because of the consciousness of sin that seduced humankind; the second stronger in vigor and discernment, because it governs itself and woman; the third more perfect, because the sting of the flesh did not bite Christ. Concerning the first it was said that a woman ought to veil her face [Note: [Col. 0189] 1 Cor. 11], and that woman shall be under the power of man [Note: [Col. 0189] Gen. 3]. Concerning the second it is said: “Man is the glory [Col. 0189D] of God, because he was created by him; but woman is the glory of man” [Note: [Col. 0189] 1 Cor. 11], by whom she is governed. Of the third it was said that Christ “did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0189] 1 Pet. 2].

Christ’s virginity, therefore, is the more perfect, and it is set before prelates as an example. But if a prelate is to possess a perfect life, these things must concur: in the heart, he must have the seasoning of wisdom and charity by which he may benefit his neighbor; in the outward person, a form of religious conduct as an example; inwardly and outwardly, the purity of chastity to restrain lust. Therefore in the tabernacle there was a lampstand [Col. 0190A] upon which were cups, little spheres, and lilies [Note: [Col. 0189] Exod. 25]: cups for offering wisdom and charity to subjects; the little spheres, smoothed by the process of turning, free from every roughness, signify perfection through holy conduct; the lilies, the delight of chastity.

It should also be noted that Scripture records lilies in three places: in a valley, in a thorn-brake, and in a field. Of the first it says here: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0189] Song 2]. Of the second: “As a lily among thorns.” Of the third the Lord says in the Gospel: “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. Amen I say to you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed as one of these” [Note: [Col. 0189] Matt. 6]. Thus the lily is in the valley: that is, virginity founded in humility; in the thorn-brake: patience proved in tribulation; in the field: [Col. 0190B] made fruitful with a hundredfold yield and gladdened by manifest splendor.

Virginity was fruitful in humility in her who said: “The Lord has looked upon the humility of his handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0189] Luke 1]. In blessed Anne, patience was proved: she chose rather to be killed than defiled. In those persons it is heaped up with a hundredfold fruit who, because of the merit of chastity, “follow the Lamb wherever he goes” [Note: [Col. 0189] Apoc. 14], and [it is] manifest. Hence: “How beautiful is the chaste generation with charity” [Note: [Col. 0189] Wisd. 4].

Again, because the bridegroom had praised her, lest perhaps she be deceived by excessive security, he says that the soul cannot live in this life without temptations, comparing her to a lily, and thorns to temptations or tempters, whom he here calls daughters because of their weakness. They are not good daughters, because they prick; therefore they must be feared. A thorn is guilt; a thorn is punishment; a thorn is a false brother; a thorn is an evil neighbor [Col. 0190C]. Thorns are in the earth, in the air, and in your flesh. To dwell among these and remain unharmed belongs to divine power, not human strength. It is a work of virtue to live well among the wicked, to retain innocence among evildoers; and it is greater still to be peaceable with those who hate peace [Note: [Col. 0189] Ps. 119], and more perfect to love them and do them good.

The lily is bitter to the taste and sweet in fragrance. It is Christ himself who, through the taste of his bitter Passion, poured out for us the fragrance of eternal salvation. Likewise, the mind must be healed and ordered through meditation and prayer, lest it be windy through vainglory, swollen through pride, rotten through envy, cast down through useless sorrow, dissipated through foolish joy, contracted through [Col. 0190D] empty swelling, torn through anger, blinded through avarice, chained through gluttony, defiled through lust, or vain through curiosity.

Hear of the swelling of pride: “Behold, the Lord passes by, overturning mountains and crushing rocks” [Note: [Col. 0189] 3 Kings 19], etc. Hear of the wind of vainglory: “A wind came from the wilderness and shook the four corners of the house” [Note: [Col. 0189] Job 1], etc. Hear Solomon on the mind rotted by envy: “Soundness of heart is the life of the flesh; envy is the rottenness of the bones” [Note: [Col. 0189] Prov. 14]. The Apostle tells how useless sorrow casts down and kills the mind: “The sorrow of the world works death” [Note: [Col. 0189] 2 Cor. 7]. Hear of [Col. 0191A] foolish joy and how it dissipates the mind: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” [Note: [Col. 0191] Exod. 32], and even worshipped idols. Hear Solomon on empty fear: “The sluggard would not plow because of the cold; therefore he shall beg in summer, and nothing shall be given him” [Note: [Col. 0191] Prov. 20].

Hear how anger tears the mind apart. The thoughts of the angry are a brood of vipers which devour their mother in the womb. Hear how avarice blinds the mind: “Gifts also blind the wise” [Note: [Col. 0191] Deut. 16]. Through gluttony the mind is chained, because a mind bound by it is led through everything. Lust defiles those who indulge in it. This is manifest, because “he who fornicates sins against his own body” [Note: [Col. 0191] 1 Cor. 6]. Dinah teaches by her own example how curiosity stretches the heart wide [Note: [Col. 0191] Gen. 34].

The lily signifies faith in its root, [Col. 0191B] which lies hidden in the earth because faith concerns hidden things; hope in its stalk rising upward; chastity in its flower; charity in the golden grains within; and fear in the club-shaped central pistil. The root is pale, signifying the repentance of believers. This is threefold: namely, in abstinence, whence the Lord says, “When you fast, do not become sad like the hypocrites” [Note: [Col. 0191] Matt. 6]; secondly, in the giving of alms: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet” [Note: [Col. 0191] Ibid.]; thirdly, in tearful prayer: “When you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” [Note: [Col. 0191] Ibid.]. The stalk has green leaves.

For hope flourishes with the four cardinal virtues. Hope is just if it gives to each person what is his [Col. 0191C] due. Hence: “Be strong in battle and fight against the ancient serpent.” Let it be prudent, so as to beware the suggestions of demons and false brethren. Hence: “Be prudent as serpents” [Note: [Col. 0191] Matt. 10]. Let a person be strong against violent temptation and adversity. Hence: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” [Note: [Col. 0191] Matt. 22]. Let a person be temperate in word, deed, and thought, and possess sobriety in bodily nourishment. Of thought it is said: “Do not let the sun set upon your anger” [Note: [Col. 0191] Eph. 4]. Of deed: “Let him who stole steal no more; rather let him labor with his hands at what is good, that he may have something to give to one who suffers need” [Note: [Col. 0191] Ibid.]. Of speech: “Let no evil word proceed from your mouth” [Note: [Col. 0191] Ibid.]. Of sobriety: “Not in feasting and drunkenness, [Col. 0191D] not in beds and indecencies” [Note: [Col. 0191] Rom. 13].

The flower, which signifies chastity, has six white petals, because there are six things that preserve uncorrupted chastity: sobriety, work, austerity of dress, restraint of the senses, graciousness of speech with propriety, and avoidance of opportunity, person, place, and time. Of the first, as has already been said: “Not in feasting and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies” [Note: [Col. 0191] Ibid.]. “Lot is an example of this: drunk, he committed incest” [Note: [Col. 0191] Gen. 19].

Gluttony occurs in five ways: through the natural ardor of appetite, as Esau desired lentils [Note: [Col. 0191] Gen. 25]; through more costly food, as the children of Israel turned in their hearts back to the pots of meat in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0191] Exod. 16]; through too elaborate preparation, as the sons of Eli demanded raw meat from the children of Israel in order to prepare it more elaborately for themselves; by taking more, as the Sodomites did, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0191] 2 Kings]: “The iniquity of Sodom was idleness and fullness of bread”; and by anticipating the hour of need, as Jonathan son of Saul did when he ate a honeycomb after the victory [Note: [Col. 0191] 1 Kings 2].

[Col. 0192A] Of the second: idleness is the enemy of the soul. Hence the poet:

> If you take away leisure, the arts of desire perish.

Again:

> Leisure nourishes the body, and the mind feeds upon it.

The Sodomites are an example of this, as has been said. [Col. 0192B] Of the third: “Not in costly clothing, nor in braided hair, or gold, or pearls” [Note: [Col. 0191] 2 Tim. 2]. The Moabite women are an example of this: they adorned themselves in order to cause the children of Israel to sin with them [Note: [Col. 0191] Num. 25]. Of the fourth the prophet says: “Death has entered through your windows and entered your house, to destroy your little children there” [Note: [Col. 0191] Jer. 9], as was said of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter [Note: [Col. 0191] Gen. 24]. Of the fifth it is written: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” [Note: [Col. 0191] Prov. 18]. Again: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” [Note: [Col. 0191] 2 Cor. 15], as Potiphar’s wife said to Joseph: “Sleep with me” [Note: [Col. 0191] Gen. 39]. Of the sixth Paul says to Timothy: “Avoid younger widows” [Note: [Col. 0191] 1 Tim. 5]. Hence Tamar, David’s daughter, was violated by her brother Amnon because she entered the chamber alone with him [Note: [Col. 0191] 2 Kings 3].

Within the flower are six golden grains, namely [Col. 0192C] charity. God is loved in three ways and for three reasons. He is loved sweetly, strongly, and wisely. Behold the three ways. He loved sweetly who said: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you” [Note: [Col. 0191] Ps. 30], namely with the fear of God, which accompanies love. He wished to love strongly who said: “I shall love you, O Lord, my strength” [Note: [Col. 0191] Ps. 17]. He taught us to love wisely who said: “The faithful shall rest in love” [Note: [Col. 0191] Wisd. 3].

God is loved for three reasons: for temporal goods; for spiritual goods on the way; and for eternal goods in the homeland. For temporal goods: because those who fear God lack nothing, nor do those who love him in truth [Note: [Col. 0191] Ecclus. 12]. For spiritual goods: whence Christ says, “If anyone loves me, [Col. 0192D] he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: [Col. 0191] John 14]. Again, for eternal goods: “For eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” [Note: [Col. 0191] 1 Cor. 2].

Concerning the first three it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” [Note: [Col. 0191] Mark 12]: first by desiring sweetly; second by discerning wisely; third by holding firmly in memory. Of the other three it is said: “In [Col. 0193A] him we live, move, and are” [Note: [Col. 0193] Acts 17]. First, because, that we may live temporally, he grants us the use of temporal things; we move by ascending through the degrees of spiritual things; we are, so that beyond these temporal things we may attain the eternal life of angels.

In the middle of the lily is the club, namely fear of God. But this club has three points, because there are three fears in addition to natural fear.

The first is servile, the second initial, the third filial. Servile fear is that by which punishment is feared and righteousness is not loved. This fear is not in charity. Of it the poet says [Note: [Col. 0193] Horace, *Epistles* IV, Epistle 16, v. 52]:

> The wicked hate to sin through fear of punishment;  
> you will admit nothing through love of virtue.

Initial fear is that by which punishment is partly feared and righteousness partly loved. Hence David: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 110]. Filial fear is that by which righteousness is so loved that punishment is not feared. Hence David: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for age upon age” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 16].

The pallor of repentance restrains sin, lest faith be void. The greenness of virtues orders morals, lest hope be vain. The sixfold number of petals preserves chastity, lest it be corrupted. Golden charity makes chastity fruitful, so that it may bear fruit. Fear pricks charity, lest it become lax. Although this lily is so ordered, it nevertheless feels the thorns of temptations. It has thorns beneath it, around it, beside it, within it, and above it. It has beneath it the thorns of riches; hence it is said: “The seed fell among thorns” [Note: [Col. 0193] Luke 8]. It has around it the thorns of false brethren. Hence [Col. 0193C] the prophet Nahum says: “Like thorns entwining one another, feasting and drinking together, they shall be confounded” [Note: [Col. 0193] Nah. 1]. For subjects entwine themselves against their masters by conspiracy. It has beside it the thorns of carnal pleasures. Hence, when the Lord cursed Adam: “When you have worked the ground, it shall not yield its fruit, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” [Note: [Col. 0193] Gen. 4]. Within it they have thorns of foolish thoughts. Hence Solomon says: “I passed by the field of the sluggard and the vineyard of the foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled everything, and thorns covered its surface” [Note: [Col. 0193] Prov. 24]. That field is the human heart. It has above it thorns, namely demons who are in the air. Hence David: “I was turned in my misery while [Col. 0193D] the thorn was fixed in me” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 31].

Three thorns are fixed in the human heart. “These are the three spears which Joab fixed in Absalom’s heart” [Note: [Col. 0193] 2 Kings 18]. First the devil hinders good from being done; second, he extinguishes what has been accomplished; third, he leads a person into obstinacy, so that the sinner does not seek from God the remedy of repentance for these sins. There is a worst thorn that pricks inwardly, namely anger. He who says, “Be angry and do not sin” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 4], taught that it must be avoided. The Apostle teaches the same thing, adding: “Do not let the sun set upon your anger; [Col. 0194A] do not give place to the devil” [Note: [Col. 0193] Eph. 4].

Anger is threefold. There is the anger of the sinner, the anger of the brother, and the anger of the teacher. The first contains sin; the second does not recognize sin; the third avoids sin. The first burns in patience; the second grieves over sin; the third removes sin. The first has a defect; the second an affection; the third an effect. Of the first it is written: “The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God” [Note: [Col. 0193] Jas. 1]. Of the second David and the Apostle say, as already stated: “Be angry and do not sin” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 4]. Of the third Habakkuk says: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” [Note: [Col. 0193] Hab. 3].

Of the first the poet says [Note: [Col. 0193] Horace, *Epistles*, bk. I, ep. 2, v. 63]:

> Anger is brief madness. Rule your mind: unless it obeys,  
> it commands; curb it with reins, restrain it with chains.

Again [Note: [Col. 0193] Ibid.]:

> [Col. 0194B] … Whoever will not govern anger  
> will wish undone what pain and mind have urged.

Again Boethius:

> Let him who wishes to be powerful  
> tame his fierce passions.  
> For though the farthest land  
> should tremble at your anger,  
> and farthest Thule serve you,  
> yet if you cannot conquer dark cares  
> and drive away wretched complaints,  
> that is no power.

Again [Note: [Col. 0193] Horace, *Odes*, II.2.9]:

> You will rule more widely by mastering your greedy  
> spirit than if you joined Libya to distant  
> Gades, and each Carthaginian  
> served one man.

Again: “Whoever is angry with his brother is liable to death” [Note: [Col. 0193] Matt. 5]. Blessed Benedict says, “Not to carry anger through to completion.” Of this, the prophet Jeremiah says: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is from the direction of the north” [Note: [Col. 0193] Jer. 4]. The boiling pot is the heart inflamed by anger; its face, that is, its intention, is turned toward the north, that is, the devil, who by blowing—by breathing upon it more strongly—kindles anger ever more and more.

In a figure of the second, Ezekiel saw a man from the navel upward like a flame of fire [Note: [Col. 0193] Lam. 2]. This signifies the ardor of anger in the heart: namely, the anger by which a brother is angry in his heart against his own sin. Hence David: “I saw the transgressors and wasted away, because they did not keep your words” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 18]. Again: “My zeal made me waste away, because my enemies forgot your words” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ibid.]. [Col. 0194D] And: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 68]. This is like flour fried with oil in a pan.

The third anger rebukes sin, now in word, now in deed. In word, thus: “And sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ezek. 4]. Hence Paul says: “Rebuke the unruly, comfort the faint-hearted, support the weak” [Note: [Col. 0193] 1 Thess. 5]. Again: “Argue, beseech, rebuke” [Note: [Col. 0193] 2 Tim. 4]. Again: “O senseless Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth?” [Note: [Col. 0193] Gal. 3]. In deed it is found: “In his hand is fiery brightness” [Note: [Col. 0193] Deut. 33], namely, he who was seen by Moses. Hence the Apostle says: [Col. 0195A] “What do you wish?
