Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” [Note: [Col. 0195] 1 Cor. 4].

Phinehas burned with this anger when, enraged, he seized a dagger and pierced in the genitals an Israelite having intercourse with a Midianite woman [Note: [Col. 0195] Num. 25]. Similarly Mattathias, when his reins trembled on seeing one of the Israelites sacrificing to idols, said: “Woe is me! Why was I born to see the evils of my nation?” and there he killed him [Note: [Col. 0195] 1 Macc. 2]. And James the Apostle: “If anyone has gone astray and someone converts him, you should know that whoever causes a sinner to be converted from the error of his way will save his soul from death” [Note: [Col. 0195] Jas. 5].

Behold the three angers. Upon the first the sun sets; to the second it draws near; the third it kindles: it sets by taking away brightness; it draws near by granting purity; it kindles by inflaming charity.

[Col. 0195B] It should be noted that the sun sometimes sets beneath anger, sometimes into anger, and sometimes over anger: beneath anger when anger darkens knowledge of temporal things; into anger when anger darkens understanding of spiritual things; over anger when anger darkens wisdom of heavenly things. For, as someone says:

> Anger prevents the soul from being able to see the truth.

In the first case, “the sun became as a sackcloth of hair” [Note: [Col. 0195] Apoc. 6]. Of the second it is said: “I shall cover the sun with a cloud” [Note: [Col. 0195] Ezek. 32]. Of the third: “The sun set at midday” [Note: [Col. 0195] Amos 8]. Therefore in the first anger the sun is at evening sunset; in the second it is at morning rising; in the third it is at midday’s center. Of the first: “The sun shall set at midday” [Note: [Col. 0195] Ibid.]; of the second: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise” [Col. 0195C] [Note: [Col. 0195] Mal. 4]; of the third: “Do not consider me dark, because the sun has discolored me” [Note: [Col. 0195] Song 1].

The sun draws near to the second. Hence it is said: “Jesus came near and touched the bier of the dead youth” [Note: [Col. 0195] Luke 7], namely the scrupulous conscience, that it may live by grieving charitably over a neighbor’s sin. It kindles the third; hence: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it burn?” [Note: [Col. 0195] Luke 12].

It follows: “Do not give place to the devil” [Note: [Col. 0195] Eph. 4]. First people give the devil sport; secondly, a hearth; thirdly, a place. A person gives him sport when he is invisibly seduced by the devil’s deceits; a hearth, when he is drawn or set aflame by violent temptation; a place, when he becomes obstinate in either. Of the first it is said: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God” [Col. 0195D] [Note: [Col. 0195] 1 John 4]; “For an angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light” [Note: [Col. 0195] 2 Cor. 11]. Of the second: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” [Note: [Col. 0195] 1 Pet. 5]. Of the third: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” [Note: [Col. 0195] Luke 9].

Again, concerning the lily.

A thorn sometimes pricks the lily in its root, sometimes in its stalk, sometimes in its flower, sometimes it pricks the grains, sometimes the club: in the root, when it mocks repentance; in the stalk, when it envies virtuous conduct; in the flower, when it plots against chastity; in the grains, when it opposes charity; in the club, when it abominates the fear of God. First it mocks repentance, calling it hypocrisy or indiscretion; secondly it envies virtuous conduct because it cannot rise to its esteem; [Col. 0196A] thirdly it plots against chastity in order to fulfill the defilement of its flesh; fourthly it opposes charity in order to sow dissension among brothers; fifthly it abominates fear, maintaining that it is the delusion of faint-heartedness.

Tobias’s wife pricked him in the root when she said: “Now your alms and prayers are apparent” [Note: [Col. 0195] Tob. 2]. And Job’s wife, saying to him: “Do you still remain in your simplicity? Bless God and die” [Note: [Col. 0195] Job 2]. But at judgment it will be said to these: “Are not these those whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach? Behold how they are counted among the sons of God” [Col. 0196B] [Note: [Col. 0195] Wisd. 5].

Cain pricked in the stalk by envying his brother [Note: [Col. 0195] Gen. 4]; Joseph’s brothers by envying Joseph [Note: [Col. 0195] Gen. 37]; and Saul by envying David [Note: [Col. 0195] 1 Kings 18]. For the envious person always grows thin at another’s prosperity. Hence the Apostle: “Do not be envious of one another, provoking one another” [Note: [Col. 0195] Gal. 5]. Envy of a brother’s grace is sin against the Holy Spirit. Hence Job: “Anger kills the fool, and envy slays the little one” [Note: [Col. 0195] Job 5]. This is one of the primal vices, as it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” [Note: [Col. 0195] Wisd. 2].

The woman pricked in the flower when she urged Joseph to fornication [Note: [Col. 0195] Gen. 39]; likewise the elders [did] Susanna [Note: [Col. 0195] Dan. 13], and Amnon [did] his sister Tamar [Col. 0196C] [Note: [Col. 0195] 2 Kings 13]. Hence Solomon: “The foolish woman gently takes hold of a young man, kisses him, and brings him into her house. But he follows her like an ox led to sacrifice, not knowing where he is going” [Note: [Col. 0195] Prov. 7].

Dathan, Abiram, and Korah pricked the golden grains of charity when they disturbed the people of Israel [Note: [Col. 0195] Num. 16]. Of such persons the Apostle says: “Would that those who trouble us might even cut themselves off.” And the Lord showed what he deserves: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble …” [Note: [Col. 0195] Gal. 5; Matt. 18]. “When you enter the land which the Lord is to give us,” he says, “build an altar to the Lord from stones which iron has not touched” [Note: [Col. 0195] Deut. 27]. The land is the religious life into which we enter; the altar is the unity of the brethren; the stones are our hearts, from which this unity is made. The iron of discord must not touch these stones.

The devil pricked the club of fear when he said to Eve: [Col. 0196D] “Why has God commanded you not to eat of the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil?” And she: “Lest perhaps we die,” that is, “We fear him, lest perhaps he kill us.” And he: “Do not fear. You shall by no means die” [Note: [Col. 0195] Gen. 3]. The thief said to the thief: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation?” [Note: [Col. 0195] Luke 23].

> As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among daughters.

[CAR.] As if he said: As the lily is incomparable with thorns, so among the daughters of humankind none is found comparable to my mother. For all the others have thorns; she shines like a lily without a thorn. It follows in the person of the mother:

> As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among sons.

[THO.] She who has been praised by him praises him. It is a small praise, because it is the praise of one who is small. But here he is not praised as great: “The Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy” [Note: [Col. 0197] Ps. 95]; rather, he is a little Lord and exceedingly lovable: namely, the little child who was born for us [Note: [Col. 0197] Isa. 9]. Here majesty is not exalted, but humility is commended. He is preferred to the strength and wisdom of men, who are unfruitful trees of the woods, while he himself produces fruit. Therefore, because what tastes sweeter to the bride is that which humbles itself, [Col. 0197B] she more gladly exalts grace, prefers mercy, and marvels at condescension. Although such persons are barren, nevertheless he calls them sons—those whom the Bridegroom, by his own blood, has made sons to his Father. This is the apple tree from whose shade and fruit the bride, in what follows, declares herself glad in this way: “Under his shade, whom I had desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0197] Song 2]. Rightly she desires his shade, from which she was to receive refuge, refreshment, and nourishment alike. Although the others have a shade of consolation, they do not furnish the fruit of life. But Christ refreshes from the heat of vices and feeds with the delight of virtues. His shade is his flesh. His shade is his faith. Christ’s flesh overshadowed Mary; Christ’s faith, however, has overshadowed me. Meanwhile, let us feed upon Christ’s flesh, venerate the mysteries, [Col. 0197C] follow the examples, preserve the faith; and thus we shall live in his shade. But the bride did not say, “We shall live,” but “I sat,” which is greater, because it belongs to one at rest; and this rest is in contemplation, by which she tastes the joys above. Hence she says: “And his fruit is sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0197] ibid.]. Yet this is in the shade, because it is through a mirror and in an enigma, but afterward face to face [Note: [Col. 0197] 1 Cor. 13]. The Beloved is aptly compared with an apple tree: his appearance surpasses the appearance both of men and of angels; his fragrance, all sweetness of scent; his taste, all sweetness. Of his appearance: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0197] Ps. 44]. But this concerns men. What of angels? “Into whom angels desire to look” [Note: [Col. 0197] 1 Pet. 1]. Of fragrance: “His fragrance is above all spices” [Note: [Col. 0197] Song 4]. This fragrance [Col. 0197D] blessed John perceived when he said: “Your fragrance has stirred eternal desires within me.” Of taste it is said: “The Lord is sweet and upright” [Note: [Col. 0197] Ps. 24]. And again: “You gave them bread from heaven, having every taste” [Note: [Col. 0197] Wis. 16].

Therefore wonderful is he whose appearance transcends all beauty, whose fragrance transcends all sweetness of scent, whose taste transcends all sweetness. And if we consider him insofar as he is the Wisdom of the Father, we see in him inestimable beauty, ineffable fragrance, incomparable taste. Hear concerning his appearance: “He is the brightness of eternal light” [Note: [Col. 0197] Wis. 7]. Wisdom herself [Col. 0198A] says concerning fragrance: “My fragrance is unmixed balsam” [Note: [Col. 0197] Sir. 24]. Balsam, from which chrism is prepared, here signifies the sacraments of the Church. Receiving them with the breathing-in of divine grace, Wisdom purifies, exalts, and enlightens them. She purifies by faith in the divine mysteries, exalts by hope of heavenly rewards, enlightens by the charity of contemplation and divine love. Of taste it is written: “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 0197] ibid.]. “My memory is in the generations of the saints” [Note: [Col. 0197] ibid.]. We also find these three, brothers, in the Lord’s words where he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0197] John 14]. His way is his commandments. Hence it is said: “Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful” [Note: [Col. 0197] Prov. 3]. Truth is compared to fragrance, because just as [Col. 0198B] fragrance is drawn from hidden things, so too taste is in the homeland: “In peace, in the selfsame place, I shall sleep and rest” [Note: [Col. 0197] Ps. 4]. And his appearance is in counsels, his fragrance in promises, his taste in rewards. Likewise, let us be beautiful by innocence, fragrant by obedience, savory by contemplation. Again, apple-tree blossoms are some white, some purple, some rosy. The Beloved was white, being born sinless from the Virgin; purple through the Passion, triumphing over the devil; rosy in beauty, manifesting the glory of the resurrection. In winter the apple tree is more lowly than the other trees; in summer it is more beautiful than all. Such are the righteous, who are now lowly but in the homeland will bloom beyond the rest. “For now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that, when he appears, [Col. 0198C] we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” [Note: [Col. 0197] 1 John 3].—“For when Christ, our life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory” [Note: [Col. 0197] Col. 3]. The shade of this tree is divine protection, to which we flee whenever we are weighed down by temptations. Its fruit is the spiritual understanding of the Law: they possess it in the mouth who do not wish to seem wise; in the throat, those who love God in their heart.

Perhaps this is Nebuchadnezzar’s tree, which he saw in a dream: it was great in the midst of the earth, and its height was immense [Note: [Col. 0197] Dan. 4]. Observe: this tree was great; it was high; it stood in the midst of the earth; it spread itself toward many and great things through virtue. It raised itself toward high things through subtlety; it also stood amid the innermost things through intention; [Col. 0198D] it extended itself to mighty things, raised itself to the highest things, and remained fixed amid the innermost things. It was among great things through practice; among the highest, through study; among the innermost, through desire. Therefore, because it did mighty things, it was great; because it desired inward goods, it was in the midst of the earth; because it thought subtly about sublime things, its height was great. “It was great,” he says, “and strong; moreover, its height touched heaven” [Note: [Col. 0197] ibid.]. Great for doing good, strong for enduring evil, lofty for contemplating sublime things; great in deeds, strong in contemplations, sublime in [Col. 0199A] investigations. It is further said of it: “Its leaves were most beautiful, its fruit abundant, and in it was food for all” [Note: [Col. 0199] Dan. 4]. In the leaves are words; in the fruit, knowledge; in the food, teaching. The most beautiful leaves are eloquent words; the abundant fruit is learned understanding, manifold insight. Food for all is complete instruction for everyone, discriminating admonition for each person. “Under it dwell the animals and beasts, and in its branches the birds of heaven made their abode” [Note: [Col. 0199] ibid.]. The animals are those who pursue temporal things; the beasts, the carnal; the birds, the spiritual. For both the carnal and those occupied with carnal things are under its power. The spiritual cling nearer to it, as though in its branches. Yet they sometimes descend from contemplation: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place.” [Col. 0199B] The sun of understanding rises toward contemplation; it sets through the reflected brilliance of the heavenly light; it returns to its place through examination or knowledge of itself. There, reborn through self-knowledge, it turns to contemplation through the south of heavenly brightness and bends toward the north through contemplation of infernal felicity.

There were three trees in paradise [Note: [Col. 0199] Gen. 2]. The first was that of the knowledge of good and evil, by which human obedience might be tested; the second, by which man might be nourished; the third, that of life, by which life might be preserved. At the first, man fell into guilt; separated from the second, he lost nourishment; deprived of the third, he lost the glory of incorruption. Therefore, that this threefold loss might be restored, Christ is compared with an apple tree. This apple tree [Col. 0199C] is wrinkled in winter, fruitful in autumn, beautiful in summer: wrinkled by the harshness of cold, fruitful by the abundance of apples, beautiful by the delightfulness of flowers. Christ possessed the first in the Passion; the second in preaching or in the mission of the Holy Spirit; the third in the resurrection. Hear the first: “He has neither appearance nor beauty; and we saw him as though leprous, struck by God, and humbled” [Note: [Col. 0199] Isa. 53]. Of the second: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” [Note: [Col. 0199] Matt. 11]; and: “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0199] John 30]. Of the third: “Who is this that comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah, this one beautiful in his robe?” [Note: [Col. 0199] Isa. 63]. In the first, he destroyed the sin of the first tree; in the second, he restored spiritually the nourishment of the second tree; in [Col. 0199D] the third, the life of the third tree, namely the glory of the body. Again, this apple tree made three shades: the shade of death, which came because of sins; the shade of refreshment for the righteous; and the shade of secure rest for the blessed.

There are four shades of death. The first is the world; hence: “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, for you are with me” [Note: [Col. 0199] Ps. 137]. The second is temporal affliction. Hence: “You have humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us” [Note: [Col. 0199] Ps. 43]. The third was endured by the righteous in hell [Col. 0200A] before Christ’s coming; hence it is said: “Come and bring forth the captive from the prison-house and from the shadow of death.” The fourth is the concealment of sin; hence Job says: “There are no darknesses and no shadow of death, where those who work iniquity may hide themselves” [Note: [Col. 0199] Job 34].

The shade of refreshment is threefold. The first is from guilt, the second from temptation, the third from tribulation. From guilt: Job says, “As the stag desires the shade, and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work, so have I had empty months” [Note: [Col. 0199] Job 7]. From temptation: the angel says to Mary, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Note: [Col. 0199] Luke 1]. From tribulation: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” [Note: [Col. 0199] Ps. 16]. The shade of secure rest shall be in the kingdom, namely the tabernacle—the glorified body of Christ—shall be a shelter [Col. 0200B] by day, that is, for the righteous from the heat of temptations, from the whirlwind of tribulations, and from the rain of sinners. Under the shade of this apple tree some sigh, some breathe again, and some aspire. Under the first they sigh beneath a heavy burden; under the second they breathe again as their weakness is eased; toward the third they aspire, that they may be without every pain. The fruit of this apple tree brings weakness to some, health to some, delight to some: weakness to unbelievers, health to penitents, delight to lovers. To unbelievers it brings weakness because it does not taste good to them; to penitents, health, for it is bitter but useful to them; to lovers, delight, who say with the bride: “His fruit is sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0199] Song 2]. Of the first: “Get behind me, Satan; you do not savor the things that are of God” [Col. 0200C] [Note: [Col. 0199] Matt. 16]. “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame: they savor earthly things” [Note: [Col. 0199] Phil. 3]. Of the second it is said: “Although that which is outside—our old man—is corrupted, yet that which is within is renewed day by day” [Note: [Col. 0199] 2 Cor. 4]. Of the third: “They shall be intoxicated by the abundance of your house” [Note: [Col. 0199] Ps. 35]. And again: “They shall feast from the entrance of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0199] Sir. 39].

Again, there are reprobate sons, upright sons, and proved sons. The first are evil, appointed for death; the second are good, predestined for life; the third are angels. The first are wicked; the second elevated by virtues; the third already blessed.

Of the first Isaiah says: “Woe to the sinful nation, the people weighed down with iniquity, the evil seed, the wicked sons” [Note: [Col. 0199] Isa. 1]. Of the second: “Brothers, now we are children of God” [Note: [Col. 0199] Rom. 8]; [Col. 0200D] and David: “I said: ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” [Note: [Col. 0199] Ps. 81]. Of the third Job says: “When the sons of God stood before the Lord, Satan also stood among them” [Note: [Col. 0199] Job 1]. The same author: “Who laid the cornerstone, when the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?” [Note: [Col. 0199] Job 38], that is, the angels. Among the first the Beloved is like an apple tree among the trees of the woods; among the second, like an almond tree among the trees of gardens [Note: [Col. 0199] Eccl. 12]; among the third, like the tree of life among the trees of paradise [Note: [Col. 0199] Gen. 2]: among the trees of the woods, which signify barrenness; of gardens, fruitfulness; of paradise, delight. Of the first: “A bad [Col. 0201A] tree cannot bear good fruit. For every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” [Note: [Col. 0201] Matt. 7]. Of the second: “A good tree cannot bear bad fruit” [Note: [Col. 0201] ibid.]. “Its leaf shall be green, and in the time of drought it shall not be anxious, nor shall it ever cease to bear fruit” [Note: [Col. 0201] Jer. 17]. Of the third: “The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning” [Note: [Col. 0201] Gen. 2]. But that heavenly paradise is more delightful, in which, as it is written, “the angels continually behold the face of the Father” [Note: [Col. 0201] Matt. 18]. For the first decline into worse things, the second advance into better things, and the third already receive glory. Of the first: “He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” [Note: [Col. 0201] John 1]. These are the trees of the woods which, as Scripture says, when they sought for themselves a king conformed to their own morals, were rejected by [Col. 0201B] the olive, the fig, and the vine, and chose for themselves the bramble as king [Note: [Col. 0201] Judg. 9], that is, the devil. Concerning the second, the Beloved himself says in the Song: “I went down into my garden, to see the fruits of the valleys and to observe whether the vines had flowered and the pomegranates budded” [Note: [Col. 0201] Song 6]. Ezekiel indicated the third, that is, the angels, in this manner: “When I turned, behold, on the bank of the torrent there were very many trees on either side” [Note: [Col. 0201] Ezek. 47]. That torrent is heavenly blessedness. Augustine speaks thus of it: “Some drops flow down to us through devotion.” Hence: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0201] Ps. 45]. The trees—that is, the angels—are on either side: some descend to us in order to minister to us; others always stand before God, praising him. But first [Col. 0201C] let us see how he was among the trees of the woods.

Among taller trees the apple tree is small; among smooth trees, rough; among level trees, as it were thorny. So Christ was most humble among the proud; full of sorrows among those living delicately; reckoned a sinner among those who justified themselves. See the proud Jews: “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me” [Note: [Col. 0201] Ps. 21]. See the humble one: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0201] Phil. 2]. Behold the little one in the manger [Note: [Col. 0201] Luke 1], the little one offered in the temple [Note: [Col. 0201] Luke 2], the little one fleeing into Egypt [Note: [Col. 0201] Matt. 2]. See those who are smooth by soft living. James says: “You have feasted upon the earth and nourished your hearts in luxuries” [Note: [Col. 0201] Jas. 5]. Conversely, see him full of sorrows, namely “a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness” [Note: [Col. 0201] Isa. 63]. Hear of the level ones, that is, [Col. 0201D] those who justify themselves: “‘Hypocrites,’ says the Lord, ‘you tithe rue, cumin, and every herb’” [Note: [Col. 0201] Luke 11; Matt. 23], “justifying yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0201] Luke 16]. Conversely, Christ is said to be, in the words of the man born blind: “We know that this man is a sinner” [Note: [Col. 0201] John 9]. For he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh [Note: [Col. 0201] Rom. 8].

Again, it seems marvelous that the trees of the woods grow from mother earth in themselves, without grafting from another tree. But the apple tree, producing a trunk from mother earth, receives by grafting a shoot taken from elsewhere. Thus Christ, taking flesh from the Virgin Mother as it were a trunk, [Col. 0202A] had divinity as it were a shoot—not from his mother, but coming from heaven—in unity of person. Therefore one delights to cry out, one delights to say with the Church: “See the miracle of the Lord’s Mother.” But that we may examine more carefully: behold the oracle, behold the seal, behold the miracle. The oracle is that of prophetic truth; the seal, of unimpaired virginity; the miracle, of virginal fruitfulness. At the first, the ancient fathers awoke as though from a heavy sleep. The second is the sign that we shall rise again with an incorrupt body. The newness of the miracle promises us newness of body and soul in the kingdom. Of the first: “Jacob, awaking as though from a heavy sleep, said: ‘Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it’” [Note: [Col. 0201] Gen. 28], namely, that his coming was so near. This awakening [Col. 0202B] was for the Nativity, and there was another for the Resurrection. Hence it is said: “They told Jacob, ‘Joseph your son lives.’ When he heard it, he awoke as though from a heavy sleep; yet he did not believe” [Note: [Col. 0201] Gen. 45]. Of the second: “This corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality” [Note: [Col. 0201] 1 Cor. 15]. For the third: “The Lord shall make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” [Note: [Col. 0201] Jer. 31]. And thus the prophet shall come, and he himself shall renew Jerusalem, when “your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” [Note: [Col. 0201] Ps. 102].

A threefold oracle was given concerning him: the oracle of prophecy, the oracle of the angelic announcement, and the oracle of the widow Anna. By the first it was announced that he would come; by the second, who he was and of whom he would be born; by the third, what he would do. Of the first: “God shall come from [Col. 0202C] the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran” [Note: [Col. 0201] Hab. 3]. Of the second: “That holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” [Note: [Col. 0201] Luke 1]. Of the third: “Behold, he is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted” [Note: [Col. 0201] Luke 2]. For the fall of idols, for the resurrection of the dead, and for the sign of miracles: for the fall of idols, by fleeing into Egypt; for the resurrection of the dead, when many bodies rose with Christ; for the sign of miracles, by raising the dead and healing the sick. Of the first: “The Lord shall enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be shaken before his face” [Note: [Col. 0201] Isa. 19]. Of the second: “Many bodies of the saints who had slept arose” [Note: [Col. 0201] Matt. 27]. Of the third: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign” [Note: [Col. 0201] Matt. 12]. Again, for the fall through descent into guilt; for resurrection through restoration by pardon; for a sign through the disgrace of the cross. In the first they were scandalized; in the second they were visited by God; in the third they were restored by his death. This, then, concerning the threefold oracle. Hear concerning the threefold seal.

For there is a seal of likeness, a seal both of the other virtues and of chastity, and a seal of concealment. The first is the expression of likeness, the second the observance of virtues, the third the veiling of a secret. The first was [Col. 0203A] broken in heaven through the pride of the devil, the second in paradise through human disobedience, the third through Christ’s coming into the world. Of the first: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of paradise” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ezek. 28]. Of the second: “He seals up the stars” [Note: [Col. 0203] Job 9], that is, the Lord preserves virtues. Of the third: “You are worthy, Lord, to receive the book and loose its seven seals” [Note: [Col. 0203] Rev. 5]. Hear also of the miracle of the Mother of God: a virgin conceived, a virgin gave birth, a virgin remained. By means of this miracle was born he who orders all miracles. He wrought miracles in three realms:

In the motions of the elements, in brute animals, and in human beings. In the first he was shown to be the Creator of the world; in the second, the ruler of nature; in the third, the restorer of humankind. [Col. 0203B] In the first, the sea made itself passable on foot [Note: [Col. 0203] Exod. 13], a new star appeared [Note: [Col. 0203] Matt. 2], and the sun was darkened at the Passion [Note: [Col. 0203] Matt. 27]. In the second, he sent evil spirits into swine [Note: [Col. 0203] Mark 5], and Balaam’s ass spoke [Note: [Col. 0203] Num. 22]. In the third, he healed the sick and raised the dead [Note: [Col. 0203] Mark 1; John 11]. Finally, he delivered from all corruption. Receive in this apple tree the oracle, the seal in its flowers, and the miracle in its fruits. For its leaves, whispering in the breeze, display the oracle; its fruits, born from flowers by a hidden principle, display the miracle. Of these three Job says: “Moreover, a hidden word was spoken to me, and my ear stealthily received the veins of its whisper” [Note: [Col. 0203] Job 4]. Behold the voices of the oracle, namely hidden prophecy. And it follows: “When a spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh stood on end” [Note: [Col. 0203] ibid.]. When the Holy Spirit overshadowed the Virgin, he made as it were a passing. But given to the apostles, he did not pass by, but remained with us. Therefore, looking upon the Virgin’s seal preserved by the Holy Spirit, rightly the hairs of my flesh stand on end—that is, we fear carnal sins. Behold concerning the seal. And it follows: “One stood whose face I did not recognize; an image was before my eyes” [Note: [Col. 0203] ibid.]. Behold the miracle: Christ appears through overshadowing.

Behold the apple tree among the trees of the woods. He is also among the trees of gardens as an almond tree. The almond tree blooms before the others, grows rich in oil, and, through its fruit, which is wholesome, weakness does not gain strength. Thus Christ excelled all other martyrs in the flower of blood, all other righteous persons in virtues, all other saints in miracles. Hence it is said: “I am the flower of the field and [Col. 0203D] the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0203] Song 1]. Beyond all others he abounded in the oil of charity; for through him “the love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0203] Rom. 5]. He himself is healing food. Hence Ezekiel says: “Its fruit shall be for healing, and its leaves for medicine” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ezek. 47]. Of these three Solomon says: “The almond tree shall bloom” [Note: [Col. 0203] Eccl. 12]—behold the first. “And the locust shall grow fat” [Note: [Col. 0203] ibid.]—behold the second. “And the caper plant shall be scattered” [Note: [Col. 0203] ibid.]—behold the third. For the caper plant is a corrupting herb, because our corruption [Col. 0204A] shall cease. It follows: “And man shall return to the house of his eternity” [Note: [Col. 0203] ibid.], where the Beloved shall be like the tree of life among the trees of paradise, namely the angels and saints.

“Like an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons.”

[CARD.] The apple tree indeed produces fruit with a red flower. Thus Christ produced the Church from the blood of his Passion. The Church is signified by the pomegranate, because in the unity of faith the Church gathers together diverse ranks and, within those ranks, diverse persons, just as the pomegranate contains diverse cells under one rind and many seeds within those cells. Therefore, as the apple tree is incomparable to all trees of the woods in its fruit, so among the sons of men no one is comparable to Christ. For we are [Col. 0204B] like trees of the woods, barren and unfruitful in comparison with him, and “all our justices are like the garment of a menstruous woman” [Note: [Col. 0203] Isa. 64]. It follows:

“Under his shade, whom I had desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat.”

[THO.] In this tree the bride says that she found three things: the desired shade, sitting in the shade, and sweetness of fruit. By the first we understand refreshment; by the second, repose; by the third, spiritual nourishment: refreshment from the heat of vices, repose from the discomfort of disturbances, nourishment from the taste of heavenly joys. By the first a person escapes the devil’s snare; by the second, renders service to God; by the third, kindles spiritual desire. In the first he will be [Col. 0204C] like a tree which “sends forth its roots toward moisture and shall not fear when the heat comes” [Note: [Col. 0203] Jer. 17]. Of the second Job says: “How long will you not spare me, nor leave me until I swallow my spittle?” [Note: [Col. 0203] Job 7]. Again: “Depart a little from him, that he may rest” [Note: [Col. 0203] Job 14]. Again: “He does not allow my spirit to rest” [Note: [Col. 0203] Job 9]. In the third: “The Lord shall feed him with the bread of life and understanding, and shall give him to drink the water of saving wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0203] Sir. 15].

The first person, who seeks to be in the shade, suffers a threefold heat: heat from the burning of the sun, from material fire, and from a diseased lung. The first is above him, the second beside him, the third within him. The heat coming from the sun is God’s wrath; that from fire, desire for worldly things; that from the lung, malice. God’s wrath, by which grace is withdrawn from the sinner; desire, by which carnal longing is kindled; malice, by which one devises evil against one’s neighbor. Of the first it is said: “Your wrath shall burn like fire” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ps. 88]. Of the second Paul says: “They burned one toward another in their desires, men committing shameful acts with men” [Note: [Col. 0203] Rom. 1]. Of the third Jeremiah says: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is from the face of the north” [Note: [Col. 0203] Jer. 1]. For this pot is the human heart, boiling with malice; and the north is the devil, kindling malice with the breath of evil inspiration.

[Col. 0205A] Against this threefold heat one must flee to a threefold shade. Against the first is the shade of divine mercy; against the second, the shade of the Lord’s Passion; against the third, the shade of wisdom: mercy, by which the hand of the Lord is moderated in anger; the Lord’s Passion, by whose imitation desire is restrained; wisdom, by which malice is conquered. Of the first Habakkuk says: “When you are angry, you shall remember mercy” [Note: [Col. 0205] Hab. 3]. Likewise David: “He abounded so as to turn away his wrath, and did not kindle all his anger” [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 77]. Such a person can say with Isaiah: “He protected me in the shadow of his hand” [Note: [Col. 0205] Isa. 49], so that the Son of God is called the hand of God, like the right hand by which he works all things. To him, therefore, it is said: “By day the sun shall not burn you” [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 120].

Of the second, that is, the shade of the [Col. 0205B] Lord’s Passion, Peter says: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought” [Note: [Col. 0205] 1 Pet. 4]. For he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins, so that during the time remaining in the flesh he may live no longer according to human desires, but according to the will of God. As though he said: The thoughts of the Lord’s Passion will be weapons for us against worldly desires. And if you suffer with Christ, your sins will cease. To such a one it is said: “He shall overshadow you with his shoulders” [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 90]. Thus, when you walk through fire, you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not blaze in you.

Of the third it is said that wisdom will conquer the malice which fights in you against innocence, so that you may say: “You have overshadowed my head in the day of battle” [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 139]. Jonah was overshadowed under an ivy plant as a figure of the first [Note: [Col. 0205] Jonah 4]; Elijah under a juniper tree as a figure of the second [Note: [Col. 0205] 3 Kings 19]; [Col. 0205C] Nathanael under a fig tree as a figure of the third [Note: [Col. 0205] John 1]. Christ was for him ivy, juniper, and fig tree: ivy in the Incarnation, juniper in the Passion, fig tree in the Resurrection. For just as ivy has a lowly trunk yet remains forever green in its leaves, so Christ appeared lowly and despised in the flesh, yet flourished with everlasting virtues, or with the incorruption of divinity. Hear of the lowly trunk: “He has neither appearance nor beauty” [Note: [Col. 0205] Isa. 63]. Hear of the greenery: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 44]. Therefore whoever is under his shade does not feel the heat of vices. For he came to take away the sins of the world [Note: [Col. 0205] John 1]: “For we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who became a propitiation for our sins” [Note: [Col. 0205] 1 John 2].

He was a juniper tree in [Col. 0205D] the Passion. Hear its thorns: vinegar, gall, reed, spittle, nails, lance [Note: [Col. 0205] Matt. 27]. But hear also other thorns which prick us: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” [Note: [Col. 0205] Matt. 16]. Hear the greenness of these thorns: “Although that which is outside—our old man—is corrupted, yet that which is within is renewed day by day” [Note: [Col. 0205] 2 Cor. 4]. But in all these things the Lord consoles him. For the angel of the Lord brought Elijah bread and water under this juniper tree [Note: [Col. 0205] 3 Kings 19]. Hear the consolation: “Although [Col. 0206A] sufferings abound in us for Christ, consolations also abound through Christ. Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0205] 2 Cor. 1].

Whoever is in the shade of the fig tree does not fear the heat of malice, but is told what was said to Nathanael: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” [Note: [Col. 0205] John 1], because the wise person, while meditating upon the joy of the Resurrection, tastes the sweetness of the fig: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Let us feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” [Note: [Col. 0205] 1 Cor. 5]. Behold, this person now has refreshment in the shade from the heat of vices. There follows repose from the discomfort of disturbances.

[Col. 0206B] In the third place, let us come to the refreshment of heavenly joys. As a figure of these three things, the Lord bestowed three things upon the Israelites in the wilderness: for the first, a cloud for coolness; for the second, festivals for repose; for the third, He gave most sweet manna. There follows sitting beneath the shadow. This repose of sitting is sought for five purposes. For we sit, first, in order to judge ourselves; second, in order to humble ourselves; third, in order to relieve our weakness; fourth, in order to instruct others; fifth, in order to reign. For the first, Jesus sat opposite the treasury, judging the woman who offered more than all the others [Note: [Col. 0205] Mark 12]; for the second, He sat upon an ass [Note: [Col. 0205] Matt. 21; John 12]; and among the teachers, hearing and asking questions [Col. 0206C] [Note: [Col. 0205] Luke 2]; for the third, weary from His journey, He sat beside the well [Note: [Col. 0205] John 4]; for the fourth, sitting on the mountain He taught the crowds [Note: [Col. 0205] Matt. 5]; for the fifth, “He sits at the right hand of God” [Note: [Col. 0205] Mark 16].

Of the first it was said in Daniel: “The court sat, and the books were opened” [Note: [Col. 0205] Dan. 7], that is, the books of consciences—not like those of whom David says: “Princes sat and spoke against me” [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 118]. Of the second: “Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 126]. Not like Absalom, sitting upon the mule of folly, whose hair—that is, his thoughts—the wind of pride carried away, and thus he perished [Note: [Col. 0205] II Kings 18]. Of the third it was said to the apostles, wearied by grief at the Lord’s Passion: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” [Note: [Col. 0205] Luke 24]. Not like the people [Col. 0206D] who “sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” [Note: [Col. 0205] Exod. 32]. Of the fourth, Job says: “When I came to them, I sat as the first; and when I sat as a king with his army standing round him, I was nevertheless the comforter of the mourning” [Note: [Col. 0205] Job 29]. Not like those of whom it is said: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat in Moses’ seat” [Note: [Col. 0205] Matt. 23]. Of the fifth: “You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0205] Matt. 19]. Thus it will no longer happen that he should fall as that one fell who said: “I shall sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north; above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne” [Col. 0207A] [Note: [Col. 0207] Isa. 14].

Behold, this man was first in the shadow, that he might be cooled from the heat of vices. Behold, now he sits in it, resting from disturbance and intent upon the study of holy meditations. It remains that, in this shadow, he should be refreshed by the taste of heavenly joys, so that he may say: “Its fruit is sweet to my throat.” This fruit is sweet in the mouth, sweeter on the palate, sweetest in the throat: in the mouth, that is, in the discourse by which it is preached and praised; on the palate, namely in the frequent meditation by which it is drawn in; in the throat, namely in the discerning love by which it is tasted.

Of the first: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0207] Ps. 118]. Of the second: “Your name and your memorial are in the desire of the soul” [Note: [Col. 0207] Isa. 26]. With regard to the third, the bride says: “I ate [Col. 0207B] my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk” [Note: [Col. 0207] Cant. 5].

This food has a manifold use: it makes the lax bitter; it makes what is bitter sweet; it strengthens the weak; it gladdens the devout. It makes bitter through compunction; makes sweet through consolation; strengthens through patience; gladdens because, having now obtained the first robe, one confidently awaits the second. Of the first food, Boaz says to Ruth: “Eat bread with our maidens, and dip your morsel in vinegar” [Note: [Col. 0207] Ruth 2]—behold bitterness. Of the second, the prophets cried to Elisha: “Man of God, there is death in the pot” [Note: [Col. 0207] IV Kings 4]. He put in meal, and the food was sweetened. For the third, we read that an angel offered food to Elijah as he lay beneath the juniper tree, “and he walked in the strength of that food as far as [Col. 0207C] Mount Horeb, the mountain of God” [Note: [Col. 0207] III Kings 19]—behold strength. Of the fourth, we read that the good Father killed the fatted calf for his returning prodigal son; prepared a feast; ordered the first robe to be brought; and said to the firstborn: “Son, it was fitting to rejoice and feast, because my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost [Col. 0208A] and has been found” [Note: [Col. 0207] Luke 15]. With this food “the poor shall eat and be filled” [Note: [Col. 0207] Ps. 21].

Servants desire to be in this shadow; friends desire it; those acquainted with heavenly secrets desire to feast. For servants hate to sin, lest they pay penalties; friends desire repose, that they may apply themselves to meditations; those who know the secrets desire to sit, that they may now live with the saints. Of the first, Job says: “As the stag longs for the shadow, and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work” [Note: [Col. 0207] Job 7]. Of the second, here: “Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat.” Of the third, Jeremiah says: “In his shadow we shall live among the nations” [Note: [Col. 0207] Lam. 4].

“Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat.”

[CARD.] In this verse and the following, the Blessed Virgin shows that the two things promised to her by the angel [Col. 0208B] have been fulfilled. She says therefore: “Under his shadow, whom I had desired, I sat.” For she desired the Most High, and in desiring prayed: “Let my beloved come into my garden” [Note: [Col. 0207] Cant. 5]. But it was said to her by the angel: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Note: [Col. 0207] Luke 1], that is, shall make a shadow which will be for your protection and refreshment. For He made a shadow when He assumed flesh, so that, beneath the shadow of flesh, the hidden divinity might lie concealed.

She says therefore: I desired the Most High, and He made a shadow for me; and so beneath His shadow, whom I had desired, I sat, having refreshment and protection from Him. And His fruit, whom I had desired—or the fruit of that shadow, that is, of the humanity assumed—was sweet to my throat. That fruit is the resurrection [Col. 0208C] and the ascension into heaven, in the sweetness of whose fruit the spiritual throat of the soul delights. Next she shows fulfilled the other promise of the angel: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you” [Note: [Col. 0207] Ibid.], when she says:

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0207]

[Col. 0207D] “The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered love within me.”

[THO.] After a very sweet and intimate conversation with that beloved one, the bride returns when he departs, intending to see the young women. Refreshed and inflamed by his love, she appears like one intoxicated; and, as though responding to their astonishment at the novelty and their inquiry into its cause, she says that she rightly burns with wine because she has entered the wine-cellar.

In this cellar are two ecstasies of contemplation: one in the understanding, the other in affection; one in light, the other in fervor; one in imagination, the other in devotion. Therefore, one who is inflamed by these is rightly said to have been in the wine-cellar. Where zeal is intense, discretion is necessary; and this is [Col. 0208D] the ordering of love. Therefore, the more fervent the zeal, the more vehement the spirit, the more lavish the love, the more necessary is an order that restrains zeal, tempers spirit, and orders love.

Love exists in affection and also in action. According to that which is in action, we work; according to that which is in affection, we love. Of the former: “If your enemy thirsts, give him drink” [Note: [Col. 0207] Rom. 12]. Of the latter: “If you love me, keep my words” [Note: [Col. 0207] John 14]. There is an affection which flesh produces; there is one which reason governs; there is one which wisdom establishes. The Apostle says that the first is not subject to the law of God [Note: [Col. 0207] Rom. 8]; the second consents to the law of God because it is good [Note: [Col. 0207] I Tim. 1]; the third tastes and knows that the Lord is sweet [Note: [Col. 0207] Ps. 33]. This last enlightens the first and [Col. 0209A] rewards the second. The first is sweet but base; the second dry but strong; the third rich and pleasant.

Both active and affectionate love have an order, but in a reversed order. For active love puts lower things first; affectionate love puts higher things first. In affection, love of God is preferred to human beings; and among human beings, the more perfect to the weaker; heaven to earth; eternity to time; soul to flesh. In active love, however, the order is reversed but necessary, since it begins with the lowest. Yet it should not be a respecter of persons, nor consider the worth of things, but the needs of human beings. Affectionate love, however, established by wisdom, observes distinctions: there are greater, less great, least, and very least things. The truth of love makes the former order; the truth of love claims the latter for itself. For love is true in this: that those who need more receive first. And truth is dear in this: if we maintain an order in affection rather than that order of practical reason. Then we shall be able to say: “He ordered love within me.”

We understand loftiness in the tree, sweetness in the fruit, security in the shadow: loftiness of virtue, sweetness of love, security of protection. Thus the bride is more freely at leisure to behold heavenly joys. Hence follows:

“The king brought me into the wine-cellar,” that is, into the knowledge of heavenly joys. We are brought into it sometimes through servants, sometimes through friends, sometimes through the king himself. For some turn to contemplate these things through fear; some through desire for reward; some through love of the Creator. [Col. 0209C] Penitence leads the first; obedience, the second; love, the third. Thus He first made one His servant through fear; afterward, His friend through obedience; then, His son through love.

Or He brings one into the cellar, that is, into sacred Scripture: first, giving it to drink according to the historical sense; second, the moral; third, the allegorical; fourth, the anagogical. Happy is the order in which love draws those hastening toward their homeland, aids those who run, and receives those who arrive.

Love is a fountain with two streams within it: one is love of the world, namely cupidity; the other is love of God, namely charity. This is the Jordan which divided itself in two for the passage of the children of Israel. The lower part flowed away, failed, and reached the Dead Sea. For in love of the world we flow away through unlawful things, fail from good things, and earn death in the world. The upper part stood still, [Col. 0209D] grew into a great mountain [Note: [Col. 0209] Dan. 2], and overflowed as far as Sarchan, which is interpreted “their tribulation,” because through love we stand still by ceasing from sins, grow into a mountain by accumulating virtues, and return as far as Salechan [Note: [Col. 0209] Josh. 13] by enduring sufferings for God’s love.

There are three things that may rightly be loved: God, neighbor, and world. God is above us, neighbor beside us, the world beneath us. Let God have three, the neighbor two, and the world one movement in the course of our desire. Thus love is ordered. Desire runs from God when it receives from Him that by which it loves Him. [Col. 0210A] It runs with God when it longs to rest in Him. There are two relations to a neighbor: desire can run from a neighbor and with a neighbor, but it cannot run into a neighbor. It runs from a neighbor, that we may rejoice in that neighbor’s salvation; with a neighbor, that we may have the neighbor as a companion on God’s way. But not into a neighbor, so as to place hope and trust in that neighbor. Desire does run from the world, however, when, on beholding God’s works in it, it turns more ardently to His praise—but neither with the world nor into the world.

Again, love has two orders: one, by growing in itself; the other, by discerning persons.

40. In itself it is first conceived, second born, third nourished, fourth strengthened, fifth perfected. It is conceived in good will, born in mercy, nourished in grace, strengthened in patience, perfected in wisdom: in good will that agrees with God’s will; in mercy with action; in grace with devotion; in patience with expectation of reward; in wisdom with contemplation. Of the first: “To do your will, O my God, I have desired” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 39]. Of the second, Job says: “I was an eye to the blind, a foot to the lame,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0209] Job 29]. Of the third: “I remembered God and was delighted, and I was exercised” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 76]. Of the fourth: “Who shall separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress?” etc. [Note: [Col. 0209] Rom. 8]. Of the fifth: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 33]. See by contemplation; taste by wisdom.

In the first is “the spirit of fear”; in the second, “the spirit of knowledge”; in the third, “the spirit of piety”; in the fourth, “the spirit of fortitude [Col. 0210C] and counsel”; in the fifth, “the spirit of wisdom and understanding” [Note: [Col. 0209] Isa. 11].

In discerning persons, the order is this: first, God; second, the person himself; third, one’s neighbor among neighbors—first parents, second members of one’s household, third enemies. And all these must be loved more than our own body. Behold what is due to each: “We ought to love God with all the heart, with all the soul, with all the mind” [Note: [Col. 0209] Mark 12], according to the three properties of the soul. For there is the animating principle, which gives life to the body and supplies powers to the senses; reason, which discerns; and affection, which desires. “We love with all the heart” if our whole affection is directed toward God; “with all the soul” if whatever the animating principle does advances to God’s praise; “with all the mind” if thought, memory, and reasoning serve in seeking and finding God [Col. 0210D].

To the soul, however, we ought to provide help, follow its counsel, and render service: the first in battle, the second on the way, the third in the bedchamber. Help, namely works of penitence, because “the flesh lusts against the spirit” [Note: [Col. 0209] Gal. 5]; counsel, that we may have discernment on the way of virtues: “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ezek. 1]; service, by guarding the entrances of the chamber, that is, the senses, lest concern for temporal things enter and disturb the chamber of contemplation: “Food, a rod, and a burden for the ass” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ecclus. 33]. Food, lest it fail; a rod, that [Col. 0211A] it may maintain discipline; a burden, lest it grow wanton in idleness.

To our neighbor we ought first to give, to convert, and to forgive: to give, so that the needy may be refreshed; to convert, so that sinners may not die; to forgive, so that we may forgive those who sin against us, lest we be without mercy and without brotherhood.

In this cellar we believe that the bride was not merely made drunk with the wine of gladness, but that she also received oil from it: not oil by which she might seduce her neighbor, but by which she might anoint her children with consolation, soothe them with the affection of love, and enlighten them with the splendor of charitable work. For there are children of the oil of seduction; children of the oil of consolation; children of the oil of love; and children of the oil of splendor. The first oil is taken for human uses; the second a woman pours into vessels supplied by her son; the third the wise virgins take at the bridegroom’s coming [Note: [Col. 0211] Matt. 25]; [Col. 0211B] the fourth comes from the Mount of Olives.

Those anointed with the first resist the ruler of the whole earth; those with the second stand firm under the ruler of the whole earth; those with the third press on under the ruler of the whole earth; those with the fourth stand before the ruler of the whole earth. The first resist the ruler of the whole earth: they are those who are wise according to the earth [Note: [Col. 0211] Phil. 3]. The second stand firm, “bearing one another’s burdens” [Note: [Col. 0211] Gal. 6]. The third press on, “running toward the contest set before them” [Note: [Col. 0211] Heb. 12], because love of God is never idle in them. The fourth stand before Him, because they contemplate the creature and the Creator.

The first deceive in three ways. Heretics deceive the simpler people by sweetness of speech; lovers of glory deceive flatterers; worshipers of their own bodies deceive themselves. Of the first Solomon says: “The lips of a harlot drip honeycomb, and her throat is more shining than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood” [Note: [Col. 0211] Prov. 5]. Of the second, David says: “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ps. 140]. The Lord says in the Law of these three: “You shall offer clear, pure oil, beaten with a pestle” [Note: [Col. 0211] Lev. 24]: “clear,” against the obscurity of heretical opinion; “pure,” against the deception of flatterers; “beaten with a pestle,” because of mortification of the flesh. Against the third: “The flesh of man shall not be anointed with it” [Note: [Col. 0211] Exod. 30]. This threefold oil is taken for human, not divine, uses; and thus they resist the ruler of the whole earth.

These are signified by Job’s three friends, who bring oil when they come, as it were, to comfort him [Note: [Col. 0211] Job 2]. The first is Eliphaz the Temanite, whose name is said to mean “contempt of my God.” The second is Bildad the Shuhite, which signifies “inveterate talkativeness.” For the tongue of a flatterer is wind. Thus: “Let old things depart from your mouth, [Col. 0211D] you who speak new and true things” [Note: [Col. 0211] I Kings 2]. Hence: “They shall speak in new tongues” [Note: [Col. 0211] Mark 16]. This oil the foolish virgins sought, saying: “Give us some of your oil” [Note: [Col. 0211] Matt. 25]. To them it is said: “Go rather to those who sell and buy for yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ibid.]. In Isaiah: “My people, those who call you blessed, they deceive you” [Note: [Col. 0211] Isa. 3]. And the Apostle: “We were never among you with words of flattery, God knows” [Note: [Col. 0211] I Thess. 2]. And the pagan poet:

[Col. 0212A]

> Remember to beware smooth and lisping words.

The same poet:

> The pipe sings sweetly while the fowler deceives the bird.

The powerful are often anointed with this oil. Hence the poet:

> … There is nothing that a man can believe about himself  
> he cannot do, when power equal to the gods is praised.

The third is Zophar the Naamathite, that is, “one who scatters the mirror of beauty.” For contemplation of heavenly things is the mirror of beauty; but the voluptuous care of the flesh scatters it. Hence it was said of the elders who sought to fulfill fleshly desire in Susanna: “They perverted their minds so that they might not see heaven” [Note: [Col. 0211] Dan. 13]. Hence Boethius:

> Cast off the mists and weight of earthly matter,  
> and shine with your own splendor.

[Col. 0212B] Of this oil it is said that “the Israelite people grew thick, fat, and broad” [Note: [Col. 0211] Deut. 32]: thick through outward care; fat through superfluous thought; broad when it rejoices in publicized guilt.

The second are children of the oil of consolation. They stand firm under the ruler of the whole earth when, for love of Him, they bear others’ burdens by consoling them. Wine was first poured upon the man wounded by robbers [Note: [Col. 0211] Luke 10], that is, the austerity of penitence. But pain still remains in the wound unless it is removed by the pouring in of oil.

This pain is threefold. First, sometimes while people grieve for their sins, they are swallowed up by excessive sorrow; second, they are wearied beneath the burden of satisfaction; third, they are frightened in temptation. “As Isaiah says, the wound is not yet bound up or healed by medicine, nor soothed with oil” [Col. 0212C] [Note: [Col. 0211] Isa. 1]. But these children pour in oil: against the first, by preaching that God’s mercy is abundant; against the second, that thereby they escape the misery of hell; against the third, that in this way they earn the crown of glory.

Of the first he says: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” [Note: [Col. 0211] Rom. 5]. And: “If the wicked turns from his wickedness which he has done, he shall give life to his own soul” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ezek. 18]. Of the second he says: “The Lord will not judge twice in the same matter”; for, if penitence is done here, the misery of hell will not be felt, and thus “a double tribulation shall not arise” [Note: [Col. 0211] Nahum 1]. Of the third he says: “No one shall be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” [Note: [Col. 0211] II Tim. 2]. And: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness” [Col. 0212D] [Note: [Col. 0211] II Tim. 4].

Through the first, “the face is made glad with oil” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ps. 103], that is, the conscience; through the second, “the yoke rots away because of the oil” [Note: [Col. 0211] Isa. 10]; through the third, “the swollen wound is soothed with oil” [Note: [Col. 0211] Isa. 1]. Against these three evils, a child is anointed in three places in baptism: with oil upon the breast against sorrow; with oil between the shoulders, that the child may be strong against the burden of satisfaction; with chrism upon the head, which is made from balsam and oil, that the child may have discernment and season the senses which abound in the head, and so have courage against temptation.

As a figure of these three things, “Jacob set up a stone as a pillar, [Col. 0213A] pouring oil over it” [Note: [Col. 0213] Gen. 28]. He sets up a stone as a pillar when he converts hard hearts to God and turns error toward penitence. He pours oil over it by offering this threefold consolation.

The oil of love has threefold sweetness. First, the lover delights, at the bridegroom’s coming, in embraces and kisses; second, in the rich nourishment of refreshment; third, if able to render a work of strenuous service. The first happens when the beloved’s presence comes through sweet meditation; the second, when one whose heart is set above savors heavenly things [Note: [Col. 0213] Col. 3]; the third, when one delights to endure hard and harsh things for Him.

Of the first: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0213] Cant. 1]. Of the second: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar.” Of the third: “Your love is strong as death, your zeal as hell” [Note: [Col. 0213] Cant. 8]. Of the first David says: “My soul refused consolation; I remembered God and [Col. 0213B] was delighted” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ps. 76]. Of the second, the same says: “Dwell in the land, and you shall be fed by its riches. Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ps. 36]. Of the third: “Rejoicing in tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0213] Rom. 12].

With this oil the tabernacle is anointed; its vessels are anointed; Aaron also is anointed for the priesthood: the tabernacle of the heart, in which God may be received; the vessels in which His soul may feast; Aaron, that the strong man may delight amid sufferings. “For God loves a cheerful giver, so that He may make his face glad with oil” [Note: [Col. 0213] II Cor. 9]. Of the first: “Cast your thought upon the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ps. 54]. Of the second: “And He Himself shall nourish you” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ibid.]. Of the third: “He will not allow the righteous to be shaken forever” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ibid.].

This threefold oil the beloved brought us: the first [Col. 0213C] at His birth, the second at His resurrection, the third in His Passion. The first was of outpouring, the second of exultation, the third of satisfaction. He is loved first because in becoming incarnate He emptied Himself; second because, by showing us the glory of resurrection, He made us glad; third because, by sanctifying us through His Passion, He strengthened us. Of the first: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women loved you greatly” [Note: [Col. 0213] Cant. 1]. Of the second: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ps. 44]. Of the third: “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ps. 88].—“For Christ, in order to sanctify the people by His blood, suffered outside the gate” [Note: [Col. 0213] Heb. 13].

Those anointed with this oil press on under the ruler of the whole earth. For its sweetness draws them meanwhile so that [Col. 0213D] they say: “I shall not let you go unless you bless me” [Note: [Col. 0213] Gen. 32].

The fourth oil is from the Mount of Olives, which is called the mountain of three lights. For in it are the light of the oil growing upon it, the light of the lamp shining from the Temple, and the light of the sun from the eastern side. The first is that by which a person is illumined by natural reason; the second, that by which a person is illumined by those things “which Jesus began to do and teach” [Note: [Col. 0213] Acts 1], namely teaching and action; the third illumines through miracles and spiritual revelation. By the first [Col. 0214A] comes knowledge from creatures; by the second, the way of salvation is known; by the third, the goal of blessedness. By the first we discern the natures of things; by the second, between virtue and vice; by the third, between rest and exile. God “enlightens every person coming into this world” by the first [Note: [Col. 0213] John 1]; of the second it is said: “I am the light of the world” [Note: [Col. 0213] John 8]; of the third: “The light shines in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0213] John 1].

Two children of the oil of splendor were anointed with this oil. First, Peter, when he knew how to distinguish fish from fish [Note: [Col. 0213] Matt. 13]; second, when after his denial he wept bitterly [Note: [Col. 0213] Matt. 26]; third, when the angel appeared to him in prison and he said: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel” [Note: [Col. 0213] Acts 12]. Likewise Paul: first, when he said: “The invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made from the creation of the world, are seen” [Note: [Col. 0213] Rom. 1]; second, when he said: “But when it pleased [Col. 0214B] Him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through His grace, etc., immediately I did not consult flesh and blood” [Note: [Col. 0213] Gal. 1]; third, when, “having been caught up, he saw secret things which it is not permitted for a man to speak” [Note: [Col. 0213] II Cor. 12].

These, moreover, are the spies of Jericho [Note: [Col. 0213] Josh. 6], which is called “moon” on account of changeability and signifies the world. Anointed first with oil, they lie hidden in the house of Rahab the harlot; second, they proceed through the plains; third, they climb to the mountains. We climb to these mountains when we investigate the need of our brothers, our own conscience, the devil’s cunning, and the glory of our homeland.

The need of our brothers is threefold: there is the need of the poor, the need of sinners, and the need of the dead. The first need temporal goods; [Col. 0214C] the second spiritual goods; the third suffrages and prayers. Of the first: “Redeem your sins with alms and your iniquities with mercies to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0213] Dan. 4]. Of the second: “If a person is caught in any fault, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness” [Note: [Col. 0213] Gal. 6]. Of the third: “The most valiant man Judas, after a collection had been made, sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem, to offer them there for the sins of the dead” [Note: [Col. 0213] II Macc. 12]. Likewise: “It is therefore a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ibid.].

These investigate their brothers’ need, and in three ways investigate their own conscience: lest it be weak, base, or sluggish—weak in resistance, base through sin, sluggish in doing good.

41. Lest of the first it be said: “My strength has been weakened in poverty, and my bones have been troubled” [Col. 0214D] [Note: [Col. 0213] Ps. 30]; of the second: “All her beauty has departed from the daughter of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0213] Lam. 1]; of the third: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep?” [Note: [Col. 0213] Prov. 6]. The first, therefore, must take care not to fall in battle; the second, not to displease the beloved; the third, not to lack a reward. Of the first it is said: “All her persecutors overtook her amid straits” [Note: [Col. 0213] Lam. 1]. Of the second: “All who glorified her despised her, because they saw [Col. 0215A] her shame” [Note: [Col. 0215] Ibid.]. Likewise: “Their faces have become blacker than coals, and they are not recognized in the streets” [Note: [Col. 0215] Lam. 4]. Of the third: “The sluggard would not plow because of the cold; therefore he shall beg in summer, and nothing shall be given to him” [Note: [Col. 0215] Prov. 29].

In three ways also one investigates the devil’s cunning. He deceives through poverty, through abundance, and through the appearance of good. Through poverty, in order to drive a person to blaspheme or steal; through abundance, in order to dissolve a person through unlawful pleasures; through an appearance of good, lest the sin he suggests should appear as such. Against the first and second, Solomon says: “Give me neither riches nor poverty” [Note: [Col. 0215] III Kings 3]. Against the third: “Give me, Lord, wisdom, the assistant who sits beside your throne, that she may be with me and labor with me” [Note: [Col. 0215] Wis. 9].

For this purpose the devil took Job’s temporal goods away, that he might blaspheme or steal [Note: [Col. 0215] Job 1]. And straw was taken away from the children of Israel by the Egyptians [Col. 0215B] [Note: [Col. 0215] Exod. 5]. People often steal more because of shame at poverty than because of the hardship of hunger. Hence that satirist [Note: [Col. 0215] Juvenal, *Satires* 3.152]:

> Unhappy poverty has nothing harsher in itself  
> than that it makes people ridiculous.

Through riches the devil drew the rich man of the Gospel into pleasure and thus into death [Note: [Col. 0215] Luke 16]. Through these also he tempted Christ, saying: “All these things I will give you if, falling down, you worship me” [Note: [Col. 0215] Matt. 4]. For these dissolve moral character; hence the poet [Note: [Col. 0215] Juvenal, *Satires* 6.268]:

> Riches have broken the ages with shameful luxury.  
> Luxurious love is nourished by riches.

Through the appearance of good he deceived the first parents, saying: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” [Note: [Col. 0215] Gen. 3]. Hence the prophet says: [Col. 0215C] “Ephraim is a deceived dove, without heart; strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it” [Note: [Col. 0215] Hos. 7]. Hence the poet [Note: [Col. 0215] Horace, *Art of Poetry* 437]:

> Let intentions hidden beneath a fox never deceive you.

They also investigate the glory of the homeland. These are the children of oil, namely of that oil concerning which Exodus says: “Tell the children of Israel to bring you pure oil from olive trees, crushed with a pestle” [Note: [Col. 0215] Exod. 27]. This oil is devotion. The olive, which is the sign of peace, signifies tranquility of heart; its purity, that it be without admixture of sin; its being beaten with a pestle, that it be tested by the distresses of adversity. Aaron, whose name means “mountain of strength,” that is, Christ, shall put fire upon it: Christ adds the fire of His grace to our devotion, by which we are kindled and illumined.

[Col. 0215D] This lamp stood outside the veil [Note: [Col. 0215] Ibid.], that is, in the Holy Place, so that through the midst of the veil—that is, heaven—we may see, through a mirror and in an enigma [Note: [Col. 0215] I Cor. 13], those things which are in the Holy of Holies, that is, in the kingdom of heaven. There is the ark overlaid with gold within and without [Note: [Col. 0215] Exod. 25], that is, the human being glorified in body and soul. Above are the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat [Note: [Col. 0215] Ibid.], that is, Christ. This is the angelic nature praising God. In their midst is the mercy-seat [Note: [Col. 0215] Ibid.], that is, Christ, joining lowest things to highest, human beings to angels, human things to divine things, [Col. 0216A] because He has made the homeland of sun and pole a single commonwealth. These two children of oil stand before Him: previously through a mirror, now through truth and the vision of God, whose honor and glory are unto ages of ages. Amen.

“The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered love within me.”

[CARD.] And this pronoun *me* denotes distinction and special significance; and the meaning is: the King brought me, uniquely and chiefly, into the wine-cellar of the Holy Spirit—that is, into the fullness of graces which gladden the soul—not giving me one measure of His wine, but the whole cellar. And He ordered love within me, that is, in my person, when He entrusted the bodily care of His mother to John, his fellow in the flesh, and the spiritual care of the Church especially to Peter, who loved Him [Col. 0216B]. Or thus: He ordered love within me, so that I who loved Him more ardently should consequently love my neighbor also. Hence, immediately, as though kindled by the fervor of love, she cried out to all souls:

> “Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love.”

[THO.] The Bride, cooled by the shade of Him whom she had desired, fed with fruit, and given drink from the cup, shows, when He departs, that she languishes from love of Him. Hence she seeks the remedies of flower and fruit. In the flower is shown the manner of life of the foolish; in the fruit, the strength of those making progress; in their use, their devotion. Again, the flower is faith in the soul, the fruit is work in the hand, and their use is reward in the homeland. There is a threefold languor of love in the soul. For it languishes from baseness, anxiety, and instability. From baseness, because it fears impurity; from anxiety, because it laments its own poverty; from instability, because it regards its own endurance with suspicion. It fears impurity lest the Bridegroom have departed because of sin; poverty lest He disdain to return because of a lack of virtues; endurance lest its fervour grow cold through weariness. Against these three it seeks a threefold remedy: against the first, the pleasantness of flowers; against the second, the abundance of fruits; against the third, the Bridegroom’s left hand beneath its head for support, and His right hand above for protection.

Concerning the first, there are three things which usually repel lovers: the stench of lust, the foulness of avarice, and the harshness of hatred, murmuring, and envy. Concerning the first: “Not in revellings and drunkenness, not in chambering and impurities” [Note: [Col. 0215] Rom. 13.]. Concerning the second: “Not pursuing shameful gain” [Note: [Col. 0215] I Tim. 3.]. And elsewhere: “Not for the sake of shameful gain” [Note: [Col. 0215] Tit. 1.]. Concerning the third: “Not in contention and emulation” [Note: [Col. 0215] Rom. 10.]. Of these it is likewise said: “Every head is sick and every heart sorrowful. From the sole of the foot even unto the crown of the head there is no soundness in it, but wound and bruise; the swollen sore has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil” [Note: [Col. 0215] Isai. 1.].

By the foot [Col. 0217A] is meant sensuality, which touches earthly things; by the heart, reason; by the head, affection. In sensuality is the wound of lust; in the heart, the bruise of avarice; in the head, the swollen sore of pride. By lust sensuality is defiled; by avarice reason is blinded; by pride devotion is extinguished. The first is not bound up with the bandages of chastity; the second is not healed with the medicine of charity; the third is not softened with the oil of humility. Against these three, the flower has three qualities as their remedy: sweetness in its scent, pleasantness in its appearance, gentleness in its touch. Its scent is chastity; its appearance, works of charity; its gentle touch, innocence and meekness. Concerning the first: “The scent of thy ointments is above all spices” [Note: [Col. 0217] Cant. 4.]. Concerning the second: “Behold, thou art fair, my friend; behold, thou art fair” [Col. 0217B] [Note: [Col. 0217] Cant. 1.]. Concerning the third: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” [Note: [Col. 0217] Cant. 2.].

Behold, she is supported with flowers; she must be surrounded with the fruit of apples. There are four fruits. The first is that of repentance. Hence: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” [Note: [Col. 0217] Matth. 3.]. The second is that of righteousness. Thus James: “The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace” [Note: [Col. 0217] Jac. 3.]. The third is that of contemplation. Thus: “He who abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit” [Note: [Col. 0217] Joan. 15.]. We abide in God, so far as human weakness is permitted, by persevering in contemplation; He abides in us by bestowing His grace upon us for this purpose. The fourth is that of blessedness. Hence: “That ye may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ibid.]. The first is thirtyfold, the second sixtyfold, the third hundredfold, the fourth infinite.

The first [Col. 0217C] is from that tree in which, finding no fruit, the Lord wished to cut it down [Note: [Col. 0217] Luc. 13.]. But the cultivator will dig around the root [Note: [Col. 0217] Ibid.], opening to the sinner the usefulness of his beginning; he applies dung [Note: [Col. 0217] Ibid.], reminding him of his sins, and thus the fruit of repentance is born. The second is from the olive tree. Hence: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” [Note: [Col. 0217] Psal. 51.]. Thus Paul: “The fruit of righteousness is charity, joy, peace, patience, goodness, long-suffering, and the rest” [Note: [Col. 0217] Gal. 5.]. The third is from a most beautiful tree. In Leviticus: “You shall take the fruits of the most beautiful tree and branches of palm trees” [Note: [Col. 0217] Levit. 23.]. Man is a beautiful tree in repentance, more beautiful in righteousness, and most beautiful in contemplation. In blessedness he is not only most beautiful, [Col. 0217D] but also forever most fruitful. The fourth is from the tree of life. Hence: “To him who conquers I will give to eat of the tree of life” [Note: [Col. 0217] Apoc. 2].

The Bride, supported by these flowers, will no longer complain of her poverty. This languor of love lifted the Bride’s heart toward that heavenly festival; yet she languished also in grief, because few travellers took the paths leading to it. Thus through Jeremiah she laments: “The ways of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the festival” [Note: [Col. 0217] Thren. 1.]. The ways of Zion are four: the first, of humility and obedience; [Col. 0218A] the second, of prudence; the third, of righteousness; the fourth, of wisdom. Concerning the first: “I ran in the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart” [Note: [Col. 0217] Psal. 118.]. Concerning the second: “O Wisdom, come to teach us the way of prudence” [Note: [Col. 0217] Offic. eccles.]. Concerning the third: “According to the blessing of Aaron upon thy people; and direct us in the way of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0217] Eccli. 36.]. Concerning the fourth: “Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful” [Note: [Col. 0217] Prov. 3.].

By the first travel those who despise themselves; by the second, warriors; by the third, lovers; by the fourth, explorers.
