Against the first: “The kindness and humanity of God our Saviour appeared” [Note: [Col. 0239] Titus 3]; against the second, there came “the Lord strong and the Lord mighty in battle” [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 23], “to free the poor from the powerful” [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 71]; against the third: “The grace of God and our Saviour appeared, that we may live soberly, piously, and justly” [Note: [Col. 0239] Titus 2]. Judgment was performed: he “also performed my cause” before the Father. For we owed him [Col. 0240D] the sinless man whom we took away from him in Adam, when Adam sinned. Likewise, we were guilty when, abandoning him, we clung to the devil.

We lost the way when we withdrew from his commandments. But he paid the debt, expiated the guilt, and restored the way to the kingdom: the first by being born, the second by dying, the third by rising and ascending. In the first coming he came to redeem; in the second he came to heal. “I,” he says, “shall heal the contrition of the people” [Note: [Col. 0239] Hos. 14]. In the third he shall come [Col. 0241A] to save. He heals contrition of the soul; he heals bodily weakness; he heals the whole person. Of the first: “Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” [Note: [Col. 0241] Church Office]; of the second: he healed lepers [Note: [Col. 0241] Luke 17]; of the third: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” [Note: [Col. 0241] Jer. 17]. For he healed those who were ill and oppressed by demons [Note: [Col. 0241] Matt. 4]. For he is “the one who heals the broken in heart” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 146]. Truly, “he himself bore our infirmities” [Note: [Col. 0241] Isa. 63]. Therefore “he sent his word and healed them” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 106], he who made the whole person sound on the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0241] John 7].

Therefore he came lovable. For he first loved us [Note: [Col. 0241] John 4]. For he “is the lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0241] II Macc. 14]. He also came hidden. For he is the treasure hidden in the field of the heart [Note: [Col. 0241] Matt. 13]. “If anyone opens to me, I shall enter in to him, and dine with him, and he with me” [Note: [Col. 0241] Rev. 3]. [Col. 0241B] Otherwise he will say: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” [Note: [Col. 0241] Luke 9]. In this he also instructs us in the form of discipline, because he came to teach the way of prudence. Hence we sing: “Give heed, you who rule Israel, who lead Joseph like a sheep” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 79].

In the third coming he shall be terrible: terrible through the sin of judgment and the jealous fire which shall consume adversaries. “For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” [Note: [Col. 0241] Heb. 10]. He is terrible and will swiftly appear to us [Note: [Col. 0241] Wisd. 6]. And who shall be able to consider the day of his coming? For he is like a refining fire and like fullers’ herb [Note: [Col. 0241] Mal. 3]. “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 111].

[Col. 0241C]

> What awareness, sinner, will be yours when you behold such things,  
> Or what groans will you utter?

He will see above him the angry Judge; below him hell devouring souls; around him the world burning; within him thought accusing, conscience bearing witness. There will occur an examination of sins, a reproach concerning the good things he did not do, and the pronouncement of a sentence of damnation. Hence that responsory for the dead ends in a threefold verse [Note: [Col. 0241] Church Office]. The first says this of the first: “I am made trembling, and I fear when the examination and the coming wrath shall arrive.” The second, of the second: “What then shall I, most wretched, say or do, when I bring no good thing before so great a Judge?” The third, of the third: “That day, a day of wrath, calamity, and misery, a day [Col. 0241D] great and exceedingly bitter.”

These three things were written upon the wall by the hand that appeared to Belshazzar: *Mene, Tekel, Peres*, that is, “he has numbered, weighed, divided” [Note: [Col. 0241] Dan. 5]. He numbered the sins, which are many; he weighed the good deeds, and they were found few; he divided the wicked from their homeland because of this. He shall be manifest, because “God shall come openly” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 49], and terrible to the wicked. In this coming he shall come for us if we are good, because he will be our advocate rather than judge; for “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who became [Col. 0242A] the propitiation for our sins” [Note: [Col. 0241] I John 2]. In this he comes to save us. Hence we sing: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” [Note: [Col. 0241] Church Office].

Thus we have how he redeemed us from death, from the devil’s power, and from the old manner of life. In order that we may hold fast to this, let us assent to the Apostle, who says: “Putting off the former manner of life, the old man who is corrupted according to the desires of error,” after the likeness of Christ “put on the new man, who according to God is created in righteousness and holiness of truth” [Note: [Col. 0241] Eph. 4]. First oldness is imposed; second, exposed; third, restored; fourth, put off. It is imposed upon the first parents, exposed in all living persons, put off by the predestined, restored to the reprobate. Upon the first, because of disobedience; [Col. 0242B] upon the second, because of propagation and original guilt; upon the third, through Christ’s mercy and human repentance; upon the fourth, for vengeance.

It should be noted, moreover, that there is oldness of guilt and oldness of punishment. The oldness of guilt was first imposed in the manner in which we still pursue it. First the devil suggested; second Eve took delight; third Adam then consented. In the same manner suggestion is still made through the devil: sensuality delights, reason consents. Against these three the Apostle gives these weapons: “Put on the armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day, having your loins girded in truth and your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” [Note: [Col. 0241] Eph. 6]. These are against the Gospel: “having put on the breastplate of righteousness, [Col. 0242C] by which Adam may be fortified; in all things taking the shield of faith, by which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one” [Note: [Col. 0241] ibid.], for repelling Satan. “For your wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the darkness of this world” [Note: [Col. 0241] ibid.]. Of the first: “Therefore be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” [Note: [Col. 0241] Rom. 8]. Of the second: “We are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die” [Note: [Col. 0241] I Pet. 5]. Likewise: “I find another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind. Unhappy man that I am! Who shall free me from this body of death?” [Note: [Col. 0241] Rom. 7]. Of the third: “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfil the desires of the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0241] Gal. 5]. [Col. 0242D] Likewise: “Those who are according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0241] Rom. 8]. Likewise: “Wherever the spirit went, the wheels went together, following it” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ezek. 1]. Behold, the oldness of guilt is imposed.

The oldness of punishment is likewise imposed: “Be subject” [Note: [Col. 0241] I Pet. 2]. For the tempter labours by devising evil in the heart, by slandering with the mouth, and by grieving that he is overcome by the flesh. These were imposed upon the serpent: “You shall go upon your breast; you shall eat earth [Col. 0243A] all the days of your life. The woman shall crush your head” [Note: [Col. 0243] Gen. 3]. A double punishment is imposed upon those who are tempted: that they neither do good without great pain nor avoid sins without the Spirit’s direction. Hence it was said to the woman: “In pain you shall bear your children; you shall be under your husband’s power” [Note: [Col. 0243] ibid.]. Upon the one who consents is imposed the punishment of shame. Hence it is said to Adam: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” [Note: [Col. 0243] ibid.]. Behold, both kinds of oldness are imposed.

It is also imposed thus: “When you have worked the earth, it shall not give its fruits; but it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” [Note: [Col. 0243] ibid.]. Adam worked the earth by propagating human nature. The earth brought forth thorns, namely sins, which prick inwardly; and thistles, that is, the miseries of the world, which afflict outwardly. Thus also the spirit cultivates the flesh [Col. 0243B] and produces the same things. Hear the thorns: “If I shall have been washed as with snow-water, and my hands shine as most clean, nevertheless you shall plunge me in filth, and my sins shall abhor me” [Note: [Col. 0243] Job 9]. Hear the thistles: “Man is born to labour, and the bird to fly” [Note: [Col. 0243] Job 5]. Behold oldness exposed.

Sensuality is the wife; the spirit is the husband, who is often deceived by her. For at one time she invites him to pride; at another she drags him into despair; at another into the disturbance of anger and sadness. The first is through prosperity, the second through adversity, the third through detected and reproved iniquity. The first was Eve, who persuaded her husband to aspire to God’s excellence; the second was Job’s wife, who provoked her husband against God to insulting speech. For Eve took of the fruit [Col. 0243C] and ate and gave it to her husband, thereby hoping for equality with God [Note: [Col. 0243] Gen. 3]. But Job’s wife said: “Bless God and die” [Note: [Col. 0243] Job 2]. The third was Tobias’s wife, who, when she brought in a bleating kid, Tobias said: “See lest perhaps it be stolen.” Then, angered, she said: “Now your alms and your prayers have appeared” [Note: [Col. 0243] Tob. 2]. The bleating kid is detected sin, reproved by the spirit. Hence sensuality grieves.

It is also restored, now through continuation, now through retribution alone. Through continuation, when punishment begins here and shall never cease, as in Herod, who “while living began to swarm with worms, and so expired” [Note: [Col. 0243] Acts 12]. Likewise: “He shall labour for ever and yet live to the end” [Note: [Col. 0243] Ps. 48]. Through retribution, as in the rich man, [Col. 0243D] who feasted splendidly every day and was buried in hell [Note: [Col. 0243] Luke 16]. “Sinners in Zion have been terrified; trembling has seized the hypocrites. For who among you can dwell with devouring fire? Or who among you can dwell with everlasting burnings?” [Note: [Col. 0243] Isa. 33].

There they will be charged with three things: namely, breach of faith, betrayal, and commission of theft. With breach of the faith which we promised in baptism; with betrayal, because we receive the devil into the heart, expelling Christ from his fortress; with commission of theft, because we conceal sin by not confessing it. [Col. 0244A] Of the first, because they made their first faith void, the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0243] I Tim. 5]; of the second: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God shall destroy him” [Note: [Col. 0243] I Cor. 3]. Of the third, Job says: “If, like a man, I concealed my sin and hid my iniquity in my bosom” [Note: [Col. 0243] Job 33]. Behold how oldness is imposed.

The oldness of guilt is also put off by the Lord, by forgiving past sins and turning us away from them through his grace; not by forgiving future sins, but by conferring the grace through which we avoid them. And the oldness of punishment is put off, so that it may be feared less here, as though by binding the tyrant; and at the end of the age, by utterly destroying it. It follows that we should put on the new man. There is a threefold newness: first, from the oldness of original guilt; second, from the oldness of actual guilt [Col. 0244B] or wicked conduct; third, from the oldness of corruption. The first is like that of the eagle; the second, of the hawk; the third, of the serpent. Of the first: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” [Note: [Col. 0243] Ps. 102]. Hence the Saviour came, renewing the old man. Of the second: “Does the hawk grow feathers, spreading its wings toward the south?” [Note: [Col. 0243] Job 39]; and: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” [Note: [Col. 0243] Eph. 4]; and: “Put on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God” [Note: [Col. 0243] Col. 3]. Of the third: the serpent passes through the opening of the rock, leaving its skin there. The skin is corruption; the rock is Christ; the opening is the wound in his hands and feet, the cavern is his side. Hence: “Come into the openings of the rock, into the caverns of the wall” [Note: [Col. 0243] Song 2]. Behold, “a great prophet shall come, and he himself shall renew Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0243] Church Office]. “I saw,” he says, “a new heaven and a new earth, and the sea [Col. 0244C] is no more” [Note: [Col. 0243] Rev. 21]. Nor only these. For he says: “Behold, I make all things new” [Note: [Col. 0243] ibid.], because “every creature shall be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” [Note: [Col. 0243] Rom. 8].

That this may quickly be fulfilled, with great longing the Church seeks the first coming of the beloved, saying thus: “O king of the nations and their desired one, and cornerstone, who make both one” [Note: [Col. 0243] Eph. 2], “come, save the man whom you formed from mud” [Note: [Col. 0243] Church Office]. Note that he is called king, desired one, and stone: king through wisdom, desired through benevolence, stone through patience. Through wisdom by which the Church is governed; through benevolence by which man is restored; through patience by which our weakness is strengthened. It is governed lest it walk disorderly; [Col. 0244D] restored in God’s will; strengthened in charity. Of the first, Jeremiah: “A king shall reign, and he shall be wise” [Note: [Col. 0243] Jer. 23]; of the second, another prophet: “The desired one of all nations shall come” [Note: [Col. 0243] Hag. 2]; of the third, Daniel: “A stone cut from the mountain without hands, which shattered Nebuchadnezzar’s statue” [Note: [Col. 0243] Dan. 2].

There are three kings. The first is king of those who labour; the second, king of those who die; the third, king of the nations. The first is the corrector of wrongs; the second, corrupter of souls; the third, their desired one. The first is a secular judge; the second, a solitary wild beast; the third [Col. 0245A] is the cornerstone. The first presents himself as a timely establisher of peace; the second, as an untimely destroyer of peace; the third makes both one. Of the first, the Jews say: “We have no king but Caesar” [Note: [Col. 0245] John 19]. Of the second, Solomon: “A ram, leader of the flock, and there is no king who can withstand him” [Note: [Col. 0245] Prov. 3]. Of the third: “But I have been established king by him over Zion, his holy mountain.” And he adds: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0245] Ps. 2].

Behold, the first is called king of those who labour, corrector of wrongs: a secular judge presenting himself as a timely establisher of peace; king of those who labour under imposed necessity; corrector of wrongs, so that the powerful may be restrained by severity. He is a secular judge, that he may judge in purity; presenting himself as an establisher of peace in integrity; through the necessity [Col. 0245B] of calamity, the severity of equity, the purity of truth, and the integrity of unity.

Let us therefore see that imposed necessity has temptation to sin as its head, the tribulation of pressures, and subjection to kings. For David mentions these three, saying: “You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back; you imposed men over our heads” [Note: [Col. 0245] Ps. 65]. Of the first, Boethius [Note: [Col. 0245] *The Consolation of Philosophy*, IV, 26, etc.]:

> What if you should wish to view  
> The abandoned night of the lands?  
> You would see tyrants in exile,  
> Whom wretched peoples fear grimly.

For the second, Job invites kings thus: “When I sat as a king with an army around me, I was [Col. 0245C] nevertheless a comforter of those who mourned.” And he added: “I broke the jawbones of the wicked, and took the prey from his teeth” [Note: [Col. 0245] Job 29]. In the third, David teaches kings to follow Christ, saying: “The works of his hands are truth and judgment” [Note: [Col. 0245] Ps. 110]. Hence Daniel the prophet: “Everything that you have done to us, you have done in true judgment” [Note: [Col. 0245] Dan. 3]. Of the fourth it is read that the people were gathered “as one man” to exact vengeance upon the sons of Benjamin, who had killed the Levite’s wife in rape [Note: [Col. 0245] Judg. 20]. And David: “When peoples are gathered together in one, and kings, to serve the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0245] Ps. 101].

The second is called king of the dying, corrupter of souls, solitary wild beast, presenting himself as an untimely distributor. He is king of the dying, whom he plunges into hell; corrupter of souls, which he sprinkles with the poison [Col. 0245D] of deceit; solitary wild beast, when he emerges from the shadow of deceit into open and violent temptation. He presents himself as an untimely distributor when he scatters those joined by the bond of charity. He plunges them in, that they may be afflicted forever; he sprinkles them, that the faint-hearted may be terrified; he scatters them, that those of one mind may be dissolved. These four properties are fittingly assigned to the four kings who fought against the five kings of Sodom [Note: [Col. 0245] Gen. 14].

To the first belongs Amraphel, which is interpreted “he said, that he might fall”; [Col. 0246A] Shinar, “their stench,” namely the stench of those in hell, who “like sheep are placed in hell; death shall feed upon them” [Note: [Col. 0245] Ps. 48]. The Wise Man declared that he was delivered from this, saying: “You delivered my body from destruction, from the snare of an unrighteous tongue,” and he adds, “from an unrighteous king” [Note: [Col. 0245] Ecclus. 51]. To the second belongs Chedorlaomer, who is called “a beautiful sheaf,” because he heaps up in a sheaf the blandishments of the world by which he deceives the unwary, because “he lies in wait that he may seize the poor, to seize the poor while he draws him” [Note: [Col. 0245] Ps. 10]. Hence Paul: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” [Note: [Col. 0245] II Cor. 11].

To the third belongs Tidal, king of the nations, who is called “knowing the yoke,” because under his yoke he violently drags the weak. Hence Isaiah: “Every violent plunder with tumult, and garment mingled with blood.” [Col. 0246B] And he adds: “For you have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod upon his shoulders, and the sceptre of his oppressor” [Note: [Col. 0245] Isa. 9]. To the fourth belongs Arioch, king of Pontus, who is called “drunken,” because as drunkenness dissolves a man, so the devil dissolves those firm in charity. Jeremiah laments this scattering, wrought in the city of Jerusalem, thus: “All her gates are destroyed; her priests groan; her virgins are squalid, and she herself is oppressed by bitterness” [Note: [Col. 0245] Lam. 1].

These four kings fought against the five kings of Sodom. In these four ways the devil is accustomed to attack our five senses. Sodom is interpreted “blindness,” or “the silence of cattle.” This is sensuality, in which, while the five senses dwell, they are blinded and become beastly. Lot too is taken captive; Lot is interpreted [Col. 0246C] “turning aside,” namely the human heart, which, while it bends itself toward the senses, is taken captive with them by these four. But Abraham, whose name is interpreted “exalted father,” brings them back, when God the Father turns heart and senses back to himself.

Of the third king it is said that he is king of the nations, their desired one, and the cornerstone making both one: king of the nations whom he predestined; their desired one—the nations whom he has inflamed with the spirit of knowledge; cornerstone upon which he founded the Church [Note: [Col. 0245] Matt. 16], in which he united Gentile and Jew. He reconciled them, so that, in praising the Creator, he might associate man and angel. Of the first: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be made conformed to the image of his Son” [Note: [Col. 0245] Rom. 8]. And the King says to those who shall be at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess [Col. 0246D] the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world” [Note: [Col. 0245] Matt. 25]. Of the second: “There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just Judge, shall render to me on that day; and not only to me, but to those who love his coming” [Note: [Col. 0245] II Tim. 2]. Hence the prophet: “He who is to come shall come, and shall not delay. There shall no longer be fear within our borders” [Note: [Col. 0245] Hab. 2], etc. Of the third: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner” [Note: [Col. 0245] I Pet. 2].

This stone is sometimes on high ground. At the bottom it is a foundation; [Col. 0247A] at the corner, a bond; on high, a reward. At the bottom, it is the foundation upon which the spiritual building is raised; the bond by which the raised building is strengthened; the reward by which the builder is recompensed. Concerning the foundation: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ” [Note: [Col. 0247] 1 Cor. 3.]. Concerning the first, the prophet says: “I will lay your stones in order, and found you upon sapphires” [Note: [Col. 0247] Isa. 54.]. And jasper is placed first in the foundation of the city of God. “The Most High himself founded it” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 86]. Concerning the corner, Job also says: “Who laid down the cornerstone, when the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?” [Note: [Col. 0247] Job 38]. Hear his strength: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength; the Lord is my support, [Col. 0247B] my refuge, and my deliverer” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 17]. “Upon one stone are seven eyes,” says the prophet [Note: [Col. 0247] Zech. 3]. Hence: “We sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone” [Note: [Col. 0247] Deut. 32]. On high is the stone cut from the mountain without hands [Note: [Col. 0247] Dan. 2]. He himself is our reward. Hence: “You have placed upon his head a crown of precious stone” [Note: [Col. 0247] Church Office]. It follows: “Who makes the two one” [Note: [Col. 0247] Eph. 2].

He made three unions. The first united Jew and Gentile; the second, divinity and humanity; the third, creature and Creator: Jew and Gentile in the Church, divinity and humanity in one person, creature and Creator in glory. In the first, brotherhood was made; in the second, loving humility was shown to us; in the third, the truth of the resurrection will appear. Paul shows united brotherhood when he speaks of the wild olive grafted into the good olive [Note: [Col. 0247] Rom. 11], that is, Jews and Gentiles in the one Church of Christians. Hence the same writer says: “All of us are one in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0247] Gal. 3]; and again: “Be careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 0247] Eph. 4]. Hence in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, my beautiful one is one” [Note: [Col. 0247] Song 8], etc. The Church shows divinity and humanity united when it says: “As a rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ” [Note: [Col. 0247] Athanasian Creed]. Concerning love it says: “With everlasting love I have loved you; therefore in mercy I have drawn you” [Note: [Col. 0247] Jer. 31]. The union of Creator and creature will come about when “there shall be one fold and one shepherd” [Note: [Col. 0247] John 10]. The truth of the resurrection will be when death is swallowed up in victory [Col. 0247D] [Note: [Col. 0247] 1 Cor. 15], when this corruptible thing puts on incorruption and this mortal thing immortality [Note: [Col. 0247] Ibid.]. Then we shall say: “The Lord has truly risen” [Note: [Col. 0247] Luke 24], namely, the head together with the body, “and has appeared to Simon,” that is, to every obedient person.

Since, therefore, the power of this king is so great, he must be invoked thus: “Come and save the human being whom you formed from clay” [Note: [Col. 0247] Church Office]. For God formed the human being; the devil deformed him; Christ re-formed him. He formed him from clay, deformed him with dung, and re-formed him with the purest gold: from the clay of earth, the dung [Col. 0248A] of guilt, and the gold of glory. Concerning the first: “Therefore the Lord God formed the human being from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life” [Note: [Col. 0247] Gen. 2]. Deformed through the devil’s suggestion, they became like the dung of the earth; in the course of time, “they rotted away like beasts in their dung” [Note: [Col. 0247] Joel 1]. Concerning the third, it is said that “Christ will re-form the body of our lowliness, making it like the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0247] Phil. 3], when the streets of Jerusalem are paved with pure gold [Note: [Col. 0247] Tob. 13].

## Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.

[CARD.] As though it said: The presence of his help was desired, and behold, he comes. He comes, I say, leaping because of his haste, as one who accelerates both step and course by a leap; he leaps upon the mountains, trampling the mountains beneath his foot; [Col. 0248B] and bounds over the hills, subjecting them to himself. By mountains he means the greater demons, and by hills the lesser. Hence Zechariah: “What are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel? A plain!” [Note: [Col. 0247] Zech. 4]. As though it were said: Who or how great are you, O great mountain, Satan, whose pride and presumption are humbled and levelled before Zerubbabel, by whom Christ was prefigured? Christ therefore leaps from mountain to mountain and bounds over the hills when, having subdued the lesser demons with a certain ease and crushed them beneath the foot of his power, he tramples down one of the greater demons after another, walking, as the Prophet says, “upon the asp and basilisk, and trampling down the lion and the dragon” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 90]. The Mother, speaking of her Son, shows that the great spirits cannot escape his prudence and [Col. 0248C] power:

## My beloved is like a roe or a young stag.

[THO.] This is a comparison he assigns in the preceding chapter, because leaping and passing over belong to the young stag and the roe; but it is also because of their keen sight, since unless it saw sharply, it could not distinguish, while running about, upon whom it should leap and whom it should pass over. In swiftness is the longing of one who leaps; in sight, the discernment of one who chooses. Thus in these two things let us consider mercy and judgment, saying with David: “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 200].

He is compared to a young stag. For although he was in the form of God [Note: [Col. 0247] Phil. 2], “a little child [Col. 0248D] has been born to us, a son has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0247] Isa. 9]. Or the stags are the patriarchs, from whom he was born according to the flesh. The roe takes its name in Greek from seeing; and Christ alone is he who sees or knows the Father, yet he will make others see as well, because it belongs to the nature of the roe to provide sight to others. By the young stag is meant the little one according to the flesh; by the roe, which sees keenly, incarnate Wisdom, whom our fathers awaited with longing and cried out to: “O Wisdom, 48 who came forth from the mouth of the Most High, reaching mightily from end to [Col. 0249A] end and disposing all things sweetly” [Note: [Col. 0249] Wis. 8], come to teach us the way of prudence [Note: [Col. 0249] Church Office].

There are four wisdoms. The first is called *metamorphosis*, the second *physis*, the third *hypothesis*, and the fourth *theos*. The first is a wise human being as a beast; the second, a human being as human; the third, a human being as spirit; the fourth, a human being as God. The first is written in the heart by the devil’s goad; the second, by the stylus of natural ability; the third, by the pen of the Holy Spirit; the fourth proceeds from the mouth of the Most High. The first descends to lower things; the second is occupied with middle things; the third investigates its own origin; the fourth reaches from end to end. The first destroys; the second instructs; the third builds up; the fourth sweetly orders all things. The first is to be avoided; the second tolerated; the third desired; the fourth both desired and [Col. 0249B] invoked thus: “Come to teach us the way of prudence.”

The first is to be avoided because it destroys, now through deformity, now through conformity: through the deformity of pleasure and the conformity of arrogance. For by following pleasure, a human being deforms the image of God in which he was made, “like horse and mule, which have no understanding” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 31]. By arrogance he conforms himself to his Creator, as though saying: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I shall be like the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0249] Isa. 14]. The second is to be tolerated because it instructs: “For whatever things were written were written for our instruction” [Note: [Col. 0249] 1 Cor. 10]. This is *physis*, which treats of visible and invisible natural things: “For the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are understood through the things that have been made, including [Col. 0249C] his eternal power and divinity” [Note: [Col. 0249] Rom. 1]. The third is to be desired because it builds up. For it removes iniquity, introduces fear, confers righteousness, keeps the commandments, and reveals hidden things.

Concerning the first, a certain poet says [Note: [Col. 0249] Horace, *Epistles* I.1, vv. 41–42]:

> Virtue is to flee vice; and the first wisdom  
> is to have been free from folly.

Concerning the second: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 110]. Concerning the third: “Blessed is the man who remains in wisdom and meditates upon righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0249] Sir. 14]. Concerning the fourth: “Who is wise and will keep these things and understand the commandments of God?” [Note: [Col. 0249] Jer. 9]. Again: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 50].

The fourth “reaches from end to end” [Note: [Col. 0249] Wis. 8]: from the end of heaven to the end of hell, through the middle [Col. 0249D] of the world, mightily casting the proud down from heaven, restraining the wicked in the world, and despoiling the greedy in hell. It orders sweetly: in heaven, by confirming the good angels; in the world, by redeeming sinners; in hell, by freeing the redeemed.

In another sense, it reaches from end to end: namely, from the end of the first creation to the end of the final dissolution, that is, by creating, re-creating, and restoring. It creates from primordial matter, re-creates from guilt, and restores from misery. In creating, it does so in weight, number, and measure: in weight, namely lightness and heaviness; in measure, namely increase and decrease; [Col. 0250A] in number, namely multitude and fewness. In re-creating, it does so in the measure of what is to be done, so that there may not be unmeasured and irrevocable progress; in the number of dispositions of mind and virtues, which are gathered from the deformity of folly into the form and beauty of wisdom; and in the weight of will and love, where it appears how greatly each thing is weighed in desiring, fleeing, and intending it. But this is the measure of souls and minds. Another measure is restrained, number is formed by another number, and weight is savoured by another weight.

In restoring, namely after the resurrection, it receives measure, number, and weight from him who is measure without measure: what is from that measure is equal to it, and it itself is not from elsewhere; who is number without number, by which all things are formed, while he himself is not formed; [Col. 0250B] who is weight without weight, to whom things are referred so that they may rest, and whose rest is pure joy, which is no longer referred to another. The creature will therefore then have a measure of being without number and without limit; a number of beauty, because “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0249] Matt. 13]; and a weight of love by which they love God without limit.

Again: “It reaches from end to end.” That is, from heaven to hell. There are three heavens and three hells. The first heaven is the highest state of created nature; the second, progress in virtue above nature; the third, the height of contemplation. The first hell is the infirm state of created nature; the second, the defect of iniquity below nature; the third, the depth of damnation. The first heaven and first hell are called end and end; the second [Col. 0250C] heaven and second hell, end and end; the third heaven and third hell, end and end. From one of these to another the Wisdom of God ranges, ordering all things, shutting hell against the righteous and opening heaven to them. For of him it is sung: “O Key of David, who shut and no one opens, who open and no one shuts: come and lead the captive out of bondage, and him who sits in darkness and the shadow of death” [Note: [Col. 0249] Church Office].

Through the sin of the first human being, the human spirit was prevented from returning to the kingdom. First it was bound in chains; second, consigned to prison; third, wrapped in darkness; fourth, thrust from the vision of God into the shadow of death: in the chains of guilt, the prison of bodily corruption, and the darkness of worldly misery. The shadow of death is, that is, certain infernal enclosures by which it was kept from the vision of God. Concerning the first David says: “The cords of sinners have entangled me” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 118]. And: “Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with the rope of a cart” [Note: [Col. 0249] Isa. 5]. Concerning the second David says: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 141]. And Job: “Am I a sea or a sea-monster, that you have surrounded me with a prison?” [Note: [Col. 0249] Job 7]. Concerning the third, Job says: “In darkness I made my bed, and again after darkness I hope for light” [Note: [Col. 0249] Job 17]. Concerning the fourth, Isaiah says: “Upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death a light has arisen” [Note: [Col. 0249] Isa. 9]. Therefore the oppressed ancient fathers, with all [Col. 0251A] earnestness, invoked the key that would unlock these troubles, saying: “O Key of David,” etc.

In Holy Scripture we read of four kinds of keys: the key of the kingdom, the key of knowledge, the key of death and hell, and the key of David. Of the first it is said to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0251] Matt. 16]; of the second: “Woe to you, Pharisees, who have taken away the key of knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0251] Matt. 23]; of the third, in the Apocalypse: “I am living and I was dead, and I have the key of death and hell” [Note: [Col. 0251] Rev. 1]; of the fourth: “O Key of David.” The first is priestly power and discernment; the second is the perfection of faith; the third is the hidden ordering of divine judgment; the fourth is Christ’s incarnation. The vicar of Christ uses the first, the Christian the second, and Antichrist the third. The fourth is our Lord Jesus Christ. The first, therefore, [Col. 0251B] determines ecclesiastical judgments; the second sends us toward invisible things; the third opens the king’s secret; the fourth “shuts and no one opens, opens and no one shuts” [Note: [Col. 0251] Rev. 3]. The first binds or absolves everyone from difficulty; the second draws us by the greatness of its gift; the third holds the combatant under uncertainty concerning the covenant; the fourth leads the captive out of the prison-house. The first brings in or leads out through the gates of the Church; the second brings into chambers and gardens of spices; under the third, the human being has sweated as a strong warrior; the fourth leads out the one sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

The first closes and opens—that is, it determines ecclesiastical judgments, which masters close or open by suspending or promoting persons. They close sinners who are within the Church by suspending them from certain sacraments [Col. 0251C] and imposing penance upon them; they open by absolving them. Again, they close by excommunicating persons from the Church, and open by absolving them. Thus, first, it determines ecclesiastical judgments; second, it burdens or releases by the greatness of its burden; third, it brings in or leads out at the gates of the Church. As a figure of those degraded from office, Noah shuts the window of the ark after sending out the raven [Note: [Col. 0251] Gen. 8]. Hence: “Give an account of your stewardship, for you will no longer be able to be steward” [Note: [Col. 0251] Luke 16]. And the Lord drove from the temple those selling and buying sheep and oxen, with a whip made of cords [Note: [Col. 0251] John 2]. On account of the shutting out of the excommunicated, the Lord shut the door from outside, namely that of the ark, lest the excommunicated floods enter. Hence in the Apocalypse: “Cast out the court which is outside” [Col. 0251D] [Note: [Col. 0251] Rev. 11]. And Lot shuts the door of his house behind him lest the Sodomites enter [Note: [Col. 0251] Gen. 19].

But conversely the key opens: by promotion, the gates of military service; by absolution, the gates of righteousness to those who do penance in the Church; and by receiving the excommunicated, the gates of the Church. Judith cries concerning the first opening: “You who are in the towers, open the gates; the almighty Lord has done a great work of power” [Note: [Col. 0251] Judith 1]. Concerning the second: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, and having entered through them I shall confess the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 117]. Concerning the third: “Zion, the city of our strength, shall have wall and outer wall set within it; open the gates, and let [Col. 0252A] the righteous nation enter” [Note: [Col. 0251] Isa. 26], that is, the nation made righteous from excommunication.

The second key, namely the key of knowledge—which is the perfection of knowledge—opens in three ways. A sinner opens his heart to the teacher; he opens it to God; and he opens it to his neighbour: to the teacher by confession, to God by devotion, to his neighbour by edification. The first brings you purity, the second sweetness to God, the third health to the neighbour. Concerning the first the Lord says: “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened” [Note: [Col. 0251] Church Office, in the rite of admitting baptism]. Concerning the second: “Open to me, my sister, my bride” [Note: [Col. 0251] Song 5]. Again: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I shall enter to him and dine with him, and he with me” [Note: [Col. 0251] Rev. 3]. Concerning the third: “Open, Lebanon, your forests” [Note: [Col. 0251] Zech. 11]. Lebanon means whiteness, that is, the heart of the righteous person, which is opened [Col. 0252B] when the virtues of the heart are shown to one’s neighbour for edification. And that strong woman “opened her hand to the needy” [Note: [Col. 0251] Prov. 31]. For this key draws me toward invisible things. Hence: “Seek him in simplicity of heart, for he is found by those who do not put him to the test; but he appears to those who have faith in him” [Note: [Col. 0251] Wis. 1]. It also draws us by the greatness of its gift. Hear the gift: “Whoever believes in him, even if he has died, shall live” [Note: [Col. 0251] John 11]. It leads into chambers and gardens of spices. “The faithful,” it says, “shall rest in love for him” [Note: [Col. 0251] Wis. 3], that is, those who have faith working through love. They shall rest in him by following his will; for they see that by this they will come to the chamber of peace and the garden of love, which is a gift and peace for God’s [Col. 0252C] elect—that is, the gift of peace.

The third key of God is that of death and hell. Death means the devil, as in the same Apocalypse: “Behold, a pale horse, and he who sat upon it was named Death, and hell followed him” [Note: [Col. 0251] Rev. 6]. Death is the devil; the pale horse is the soul possessed by him; hell is the soul which, by following him, makes itself worthy of hell. For he first brings death in the soul, second in the body, and third in the obstinacy of both: in the soul by thinking, in the body by acting, and in both by not repenting. First the soul becomes ugly, so that it is no longer said to her: “You are altogether beautiful, my friend” [Note: [Col. 0251] Song 4]; second, it becomes sick and cries: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed” [Note: [Col. 0251] Jer. 17]; third, it is dead, because “the soul that sins shall itself die” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ezek. 18]. This is the dead girl in her mother’s chamber [Col. 0252D] [Note: [Col. 0251] 3 Kings 3]. The first occurs by thinking, the second by taking delight, the third by consenting. This is the jar which the two women carried into the land of Shinar [Note: [Col. 0251] Dan. 1], in which wickedness sits: the person who is dead through deeds. He is the young man who had died, already outside the gate of the city [Note: [Col. 0251] Luke 7]. A very great eagle bears him, with great wings and a broad extension of its limbs, as is found in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0251] Ezek. 17]. The third is Lazarus, four days dead [Note: [Col. 0251] John 11]: acting in habitual sin, drawing others, taking delight, acting, and despairing. Hence the prophet: “What is it, Israel, that you are [Col. 0253A] in the land of enemies?” [Note: [Col. 0253] Baruch 3], etc.

This key is called the hidden judgment of God. It opens the king’s secret, because the reason why we are tested by God is not clear to us. “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” [Note: [Col. 0253] Rom. 11]. For the judgments of God are a great abyss [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 35]. Again: “O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments!” [Note: [Col. 0253] Rom. 12]. Under this key a person fights in uncertainty concerning the end—that is, it is doubtful whether he will conquer. “For no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred” [Note: [Col. 0253] Eccles. 9]. Yet under it he fights as a strong warrior, knowing that “no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” [Note: [Col. 0253] 2 Tim. 2], because there is no crown where there is no fight. Hence the Apostle: “I have fought the good fight” [Note: [Col. 0253] 2 Tim. 4]. The Lord opens this key when “he permits us [Col. 0253B] to be tempted by the devil, as Job was” [Note: [Col. 0253] Job 1]. Let the person who thinks he stands take care not to fall. “Let no temptation seize you except one that is human” [Note: [Col. 0253] 1 Cor. 10]. This opening is feared. “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ibid.]. This is confidence concerning the shutting.

The fourth key is the key of David, that is, Christ’s incarnation. It shut the womb of the Virgin, and no one opens it. According to Ezekiel: “This gate shall be shut; no one shall enter through it” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ezek. 44]. Again, it opened heaven to us and no one shut it [Note: [Col. 0253] Rev. 3]. Hence: “Having overcome the sting of death, you opened to believers the kingdoms of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0253] Hymn, *Te Deum*]. Thus it opens three things to us: our heart; its own secret; and heaven. The first, for understanding the commandments and the infusion of love; the second, for wonder and the firmness of [Col. 0253C] hope; the third, for receiving glory. Concerning the first: “May the Lord open your heart in his light and in his commandments” [Note: [Col. 0253] 2 Macc. 1], etc. And concerning the infusion of grace: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0253] Isa. 45]. Concerning the second: “Behold, I John saw a door opened in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0253] Rev. 4]. Again: “Heaven was opened, and the ark of God was seen in it” [Note: [Col. 0253] Rev. 11]. And: “Stephen saw the heavens opened” [Note: [Col. 0253] Acts 7]. And concerning Christ: “The heavens were opened over him” [Note: [Col. 0253] Matt. 3]. Concerning the third: “The foolish virgins said, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us’” [Note: [Col. 0253] Matt. 25]. And to blessed Mary: “Through you the gates of Paradise have been opened to us.” And the Lord gave hope to believers, having opened Paradise, which the first-created human had shut.

[Col. 0253D] “Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him” [Note: [Col. 0253] Isa. 40]. [Note: [Col. 0253D] He has already said this above, col. 45, with a few changes.] For in the first opening he shows his work; in the second he sets his reward before us; in the third he offers the promised purpose. Thus he shuts and opens: in opening heaven, he “will lead the captive out of the prison-house” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ezek. 52]; in opening his secret, the one sitting in darkness [Note: [Col. 0253] Luke 1]; in opening the heart, the one sitting in the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0253] Ibid.].

Behold, the gatherer comes; the comforter comes; the searcher comes: gatherer of the dispersed, comforter of those engaged in battle, searcher of good and evil. He made three gatherings: first he gathered believers; second, brethren; third, virtues—believers in the Church, brethren in the religious house, virtues in the conscience. Concerning the first: “The Lord, building Jerusalem, will gather the dispersed of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 146]. Concerning the second: “He will gather the lambs in his arm” [Note: [Col. 0253] Isa. 40]. Concerning the third: “He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 31]. Behold, he is a gatherer and also a comforter in battle.

He also assigns to us a place of instruction, a place of battle, and a place of healing: in the cloister, in the oratory, in the field, in the chapter-house. In the first the brother is taught; in the second battle is joined; in the third the wound is healed: the first in reading, the second in prayer, the third [Col. 0254B] in confession. Concerning the first it is said: “I will give you understanding and instruct you.” Concerning the second: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 143]. In the third: “He heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 146].

Concerning the gathering the prophet says: “I see a man standing upon a plastered wall, and in his hand a mason’s trowel” [Note: [Col. 0253] Amos 7]. That man is divinity; the trowel is humility; the mortar that binds the gathered stones is love. The trowel applies the mortar when Christ binds the fellowship of brethren with love. Hence: “The love of Christ has gathered us into one” [Note: [Col. 0253] Isa. 52]. Concerning consolation in battle: “The angel said to the man clothed in linen: ‘Go in among the wheels that are beneath the cherubim, and fill your hands [Col. 0254C] with coals of fire that are beneath the cherubim, and scatter them over the city’” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ezek. 10]. This man is Christ; the wheels are human modes of life, which are beneath the cherubim because angelic nature is higher than human. Christ enters among them because “he was made a little lower than the angels” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 8]. He filled his hands with fire because all his works were full of love; he cast it over the city when he inflamed the brethren with love.

Third, he will search with lamps. Hence a certain man saw a man with a measuring line in his hand, and it was said to him: “Where are you going?” And he answered: “To measure Jerusalem, how great its length and breadth may be” [Note: [Col. 0253] Zech. 2], that is, love, as the prophet says: “He will search Jerusalem with lamps” [Col. 0254D] [Note: [Col. 0253] Zeph. 1]. There are four such lamps: the first, that of the divine word; the second, that of good work; the third, that of reason enlightened by God; the fourth, the humanity of the Saviour. Concerning the first: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 118]. And: “You light my lamp, O Lord my God” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 17]. Concerning the second: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” [Note: [Col. 0253] Luke 12]. Concerning the third: “The lamp of your body is your eye” [Note: [Col. 0253] Luke 11]. And Job: “His lamp shone above [Col. 0255A] my head, and by its light I walked in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0255] Job 29]. Concerning the fourth: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” [Note: [Col. 0255] Ps. 131].

The first will search out those who despise the commandments. Hence: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” [Note: [Col. 0255] John 15]. The second will search out those sluggish in working. Hence: “I was hungry and you did not give me food” [Note: [Col. 0255] Matt. 25], etc. Solomon: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plough; therefore he shall beg in summer, and nothing shall be given him” [Note: [Col. 0255] Prov. 20]. Concerning the third: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0255] Rom. 1]. Concerning the fourth: “O Lord, those who forsake you shall be confounded; those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” [Note: [Col. 0255] Jer. 17].

The good also will be seen by God through these lamps. Concerning the first he will say: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” [Note: [Col. 0255] Ps. 17]. Concerning the second: “I was hungry and you gave me food” [Note: [Col. 0255] Matt. 25]. And: “Let her works praise her in the gates” [Note: [Col. 0255] Prov. 31]. Concerning the third it is said: “Those who instruct many unto righteousness shall shine like stars for everlasting ages” [Note: [Col. 0255] Dan. 12]. Concerning the fourth: “You who have followed me shall sit upon a seat, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, says the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0255] Matt. 19].

## My beloved is like a roe or a young stag.

[CARD.] Job’s words concerning Christ accord with this: “By his wisdom he struck the proud one, and by his hand acting as midwife the twisting serpent was brought forth” [Note: [Col. 0255] Job 26]. Thus Christ is like a roe in keenness of sight: he clearly sees the devil’s tricks, and the proud one cannot hide himself from his wisdom [Col. 0255C] because, as Solomon says in Proverbs, “Hell and destruction are before the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0255] Prov. 15]. He is also like a young stag, which kills serpents drawn out from their dens. For, by the midwifing hand of divine power, the devil—the twisting serpent—is brought forth from the minds of sinners wickedly pregnant with him. But because it had said, “Behold, he comes leaping,” in order to show the speed and haste of his coming, it immediately adds:

## Behold, he himself stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.

[THO.] The wall is our flesh, which he assumed. The windows are the senses of the body, through which life and death enter the soul. Hence Jeremiah: “Death has ascended through [Col. 0255D] your windows” [Note: [Col. 0255] Jer. 9]. For if we see “a woman so as to lust after her” [Note: [Col. 0255] Matt. 5], death enters our eyes. But if someone looks upon the beautiful world and praises the Creator, life enters through the windows of the eyes. Through these, therefore, the bridegroom looks and urges the bride to rise, leave bodily things, and seek incorporeal ones. “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” [Note: [Col. 0255] 2 Cor. 4].

What is said about gazing through lattices, which are narrow openings, means that the soul, as long as it is [Col. 0256A] in the body, cannot grasp God’s wisdom nakedly and openly. This wall may be called the bed of which the same woman says: “On my bed I sought by night him whom my soul loves” [Note: [Col. 0255] Song 3]: namely, in the Virgin’s womb, in which he lay hidden as if in a wall, and reclined as if upon the bed of our weakness. Nor is this his only bed. For Christ has three beds: the first in the Virgin’s womb, the second in the manger, the third on the gibbet of the cross. The first is adorned with flowers, the second honoured with gifts, the third made purple with wounds: with flowers of virtues, gifts of the Magi, wounds of nails. In the first, the fountain is visible; in the second, he was found humble; in the third, he appeared passible. Visible insofar as “he was seen on earth and conversed with human beings” [Note: [Col. 0255] Baruch 3]. Humble [Col. 0256B] because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0255] Phil. 2]; passible because “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example” [Note: [Col. 0255] 1 Pet. 2].

In the first, the bridegroom’s friend found the beloved; in the second, the Magus; in the third, the crucified thief. While he was in the first, “John leaped for joy” [Note: [Col. 0255] Luke 1]; at the second, the angel sang, the shepherd praised [Note: [Col. 0255] Luke 2], the Magus worshipped; in the third, the thief prayed. John leaped with joy; the angel sang, “Glory to God in the highest”; the shepherd praised at the sight of the miracle [Note: [Col. 0255] Ibid.]; the Magus worshipped with myrrh, frankincense, and gold [Note: [Col. 0255] Matt. 2]; the thief prayed that he might not be excluded from the kingdom.

In the first he lay between grace and law; in the second, between ass and ox; in the third, between thief and thief [Note: [Col. 0255] Luke 23]. Between grace and law, so that through Christ old things may be cast away and newness received: “putting off the old human being [Col. 0256C] with his deeds and putting on the new human being” [Note: [Col. 0255] Col. 3]—“that we may walk in newness of life” [Note: [Col. 0255] Rom. 6]. Between ass and ox, so that through Christ the simpler may be instructed by the wise; hence: “If anyone is caught in some offence, you who are spiritual instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” [Note: [Col. 0255] Gal. 6]. Hence: “The oxen were ploughing and the asses feeding beside them” [Note: [Col. 0255] Job 1]. Between thief and thief, to show how merciful Christ will be found toward the penitent, and how severe a judge toward the obstinate, at judgment.

Let us also prepare for him in ourselves three moral beds, as the woman says of Elisha: “Consider that this is a holy man who passes by us. Let us make for him a small upper room, and put in it a bed, a table, [Col. 0256D] a chair, and a lampstand” [Note: [Col. 0255] 4 Kings 4]. This upper room is our heart.

First, let us place a threefold little bed in it for our child, so that when he is sought there he may be found. The first is the virtue of humility; the second, patience in adversity; the third, purity of heart. The first is a bed of sorrow; the second, of pain; the third, of love. Of the first: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” [Note: [Col. 0255] Ps. 6]. Of the second: “May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain” [Note: [Col. 0255] Ps. 40]. Of the third: [Col. 0257A] “Our little bed is flowering” [Note: [Col. 0257] Song 1]. Hence it is that in these Songs the little bed is mentioned three times: “On my bed I sought by night him whom my soul loves” [Note: [Col. 0257] Song 3]. Again: “Sixty strong men surround Solomon’s little bed” [Note: [Col. 0257] Ibid.]. Again: “Our little bed is flowering” [Note: [Col. 0257] Song 1]. In the first, we express infant cries, as though in a manger; in the second, the pains Christ endured on the cross; in the third, our soul becomes one spirit with God, as humanity was joined to divinity in the womb of virginal purity.

Let us also make a table for the child. This table is a good purpose. Upon this table are set the three baskets of the chief baker, who was in prison with Joseph, from which the birds ate [Note: [Col. 0257] Gen. 40]. They are memory, understanding, and will; when we use these badly, the birds—that is, the demons—[Col. 0257B] feed upon them. But let the three branches of the vine be set upon it, from which the chief cupbearer offered drink to the king [Note: [Col. 0257] Ibid.]. From the first comes white wine, from the second reddish wine, from the third red wine. The first is the brightness of chastity; the second, the ardor of charity; the third, the shedding of blood in the Passion.

These are the three kinds of people in the prison, namely, of this world: the baker, that is, sinners deserving death; the cupbearer, that is, those reconciling themselves to God; Joseph, that is, those despising the world and having their citizenship in heaven [Note: [Col. 0257] Phil. 3]. On this table is served the dish of good will.

This good will is threefold. The first will is to benefit one’s neighbor; the second, to advance ourselves in good; the third, to advance by agreeing with the divine will. Of the first it is said to Peter: “Feed my sheep” [Note: [Col. 0257] John 21]. Of the second: “Eat rich foods and drink sweet wine” [Note: [Col. 0257] 2 Esdras 8]. Of the third: [Col. 0257C] “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” [Note: [Col. 0257] John 4]. The first is good, the second pleasing, the third perfect.

The divine will likewise is threefold: first, that a person be converted; second, that he be kindled; third, that he be made blessed. Of the first: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” [Note: [Col. 0257] Ezek. 33]. Of the second: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it burn?” [Note: [Col. 0257] Luke 12]. Of the third: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my minister may be” [Note: [Col. 0257] John 12]. This will is good, pleasing, and perfect: first in remission, second in promise, third in fulfillment: remission of sins; the promise of future goods; the bestowal of rewards.

Let us also make for this child the judge’s chair. Three judgments are considered in it. [Col. 0257D] First, that you should not presume to judge your neighbor; second, that you should accuse yourself of sins known to you; third, that you should leave unknown matters to be judged by God. Of the first: “Who are you, that you judge your brother?” [Note: [Col. 0257] Rom. 14]. “For in judging another, you condemn yourself” [Note: [Col. 0257] Rom. 2]. Again: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged” [Note: [Col. 0257] Luke 6]. Of the second: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” [Note: [Col. 0257] 1 Cor. 11]. Of the third: “But the one who judges me is the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0257] 1 Cor. 4].

Whoever sits in this chair ought to have the chair [Col. 0258A] of the teacher, the tribunal of the judge, and the throne of the king. First, a person ought to instruct himself, so that he may recognize the evil he must flee and the good he must do [Note: [Col. 0257] Titus 2]; behold, the teacher on his chair and the Church. Second, because of his sins he ought to judge himself deserving of eternal death [Note: [Col. 0257] Rom. 1]. Even concerning his good deeds, he should judge himself an unprofitable servant [Note: [Col. 0257] Matt. 25]: behold, the judge at the tribunal. Third, he should govern himself by suppressing vices and advancing virtues: behold, the man upon the throne. Of the first: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the chair of pestilence” [Note: [Col. 0257] Ps. 1]. Of the second: “All of you must stand before the tribunal of the judge” [Note: [Col. 0257] Rom. 14]. Of the third: “Upon a lofty throne I saw a man seated, whom a multitude of angels worship” [Note: [Col. 0257] Rev. 19].

It should be noted that there are three instruments by which [Col. 0258B] light is supplied: the small lamp, the lamp, and the lampstand. The first is commonly made of earth and is cheaper; the second, of ash, but it is fired by heat and becomes purer; the third, of silver and gold, is purer and more precious. The small lamp signifies the sentient flesh; the lamp, a simple conscience; the lampstand, understanding and wisdom. Of the first: “You light my lamp, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0257] Ps. 17]. Of the second, Job says: “The simplicity of the just is mocked; the lamp is despised in the thoughts of the rich” [Note: [Col. 0257] Job 12]. Of the third, in Revelation: “I shall come and remove your lampstand from its place” [Note: [Col. 0257] Rev. 2].

The first gives light for action; the second, for discerning good and evil and loving God; the third, for knowledge of heavenly things. Of the first: “Let your loins be girded” [Note: [Col. 0257] Luke 12], “and lamps burning in your hands” [Note: [Col. 0257] Matt. 25]. [Col. 0258C] Of the second: “The prudent virgins trimmed their lamps” [Note: [Col. 0257] Exod. 40]. As a figure of the third, the lampstand was placed in the tabernacle of Moses [Note: [Col. 0257] Ezek. 10]. For the first, Ezekiel saw a fiery man from the loins downward [Note: [Col. 0257] Ibid.]; for the second, he was like a flame of fire from the loins upward [Note: [Col. 0257] Rev. 1]. On account of the third, that man in Revelation had eyes like a flame of fire; or, if one prefers, all illumination is in the lampstand which in the tabernacle of Moses had seven branches [Note: [Col. 0257] Exod. 25], because of the Holy Spirit who gives sevenfold illumination [Note: [Col. 0257] Isa. 11].

For he illumines outwardly and inwardly: outwardly, by displaying visible signs; inwardly, by inspiring invisible grace. Outwardly he illumines in three ways: by word, miracle, and example. In the word, by the spirit of piety; in miracle, by the spirit of fear; [Col. 0258D] in example, by the spirit of fortitude. By word he teaches love of God and neighbor; by miracle, fear of the worker of wonders; by example, courage in suffering.

These branches are on the left of the central stem. Three others are on the right of the central stem. The first of these three is in the administration of lower things, and is called the spirit of knowledge; the second is in foreseeing snares and perplexity, and is called the spirit of counsel; the third is understanding of the invisible things of God, and is called the spirit of understanding. The central stem is in the contemplation [Col. 0259A] of God and delightful love, and is called the spirit of wisdom. Of the first: “He who ministers well shall acquire a good rank” [Note: [Col. 0259] 1 Tim. 3]. Again: “Priests who have ministered well are to be held worthy of double honor” [Note: [Col. 0259] 1 Tim. 5]. Hence that strong woman considered the paths of her household and did not eat the bread of idleness. Of the second: “Be prudent as serpents” [Note: [Col. 0259] Matt. 10]. And: “The sinews of Leviathan’s testicles are intertwined” [Note: [Col. 0259] Job 40]. Of the third: “The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen through the things that have been made” [Note: [Col. 0259] Rom. 1]. And he adds concerning the fourth: “His everlasting power also and divinity” [Note: [Col. 0259] Ibid.]. This is the central stem, namely the spirit of wisdom, from which the others rise.

Human flesh is the wall; the windows and lattices through which the sense of the flesh looks are human affections, through which he gained experience [Col. 0259B] of human needs, through which “he himself bore our infirmities and carried our pains” [Note: [Col. 0259] Isa. 53]. And he stands well, because he alone was in the flesh who did not experience the sin of the flesh. He also stood through the power of his divinity, he who fell through the weakness of the flesh. For he says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” [Note: [Col. 0259] Matt. 26].

There are five walls that obstruct sight. The first is concupiscence; the second, consent; the third, action; the fourth, habit; the fifth, contempt. Avoid the first and the others will cease; then there remains only the one sense of the flesh. Of it you may boast and say: “Behold, he stands behind our wall.” But you must take care that the bridegroom always finds your windows [Col. 0259C] open, and certain lattices of your confessions.

We may open the five windows for caution, compassion, example, material for praise, and a sign of contemplation. For caution, the window of the ark was opened, and the dove was sent out to see whether the flood had receded [Note: [Col. 0259] Gen. 8]. Thus through our senses we learn what we must avoid. For compassion, the bridegroom looked through our windows [Note: [Col. 0259] Song 2], because through bodily senses he experienced miseries in order to have compassion upon us. For example is signified by that window of the house-top through which Rahab the harlot let down the scouts of Jericho, telling them to go up into the mountain and look about [Note: [Col. 0259] Josh. 2]; from this let us take an example. For material of praise, when we simply contemplate creatures in order to praise the Creator [Col. 0259D] in them.

Our flesh is that harlot, which opens our senses to us, so that we may incline toward the mountains—that is, look to great persons—and take an example from them. “These fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows” [Note: [Col. 0259] Isa. 60]. For a sign of contemplation, when we lift our senses toward heaven, as a sign of devotion extending toward the heavenly things we contemplate. Hence Daniel prayed alone in his upper chamber, with windows open toward Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0259] Dan. 6]. Yet these windows are to be opened rarely and briefly.

[Col. 0260A] A threefold birth of the Lord must be considered. The first is in the world; the second, in the human heart; the third, in heaven. The first is from a mother; the second, in a brother; the third, from the Father. The first is humble; the second lovable; the third desirable. The first is humble, because through it we are reconciled to God [Note: [Col. 0259] Rom. 5]. The second is lovable, through which we are kindled in love. The third is desirable, in which we are made heirs of Christ [Note: [Col. 0259] Rom. 8].

Of the first: “He was made a curse for us, that he might free us from the curse” [Note: [Col. 0259] Gal. 3]. Of the second: “He first loved us” [Note: [Col. 0259] 1 John 4]. Of the third: “Who regenerated us unto an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance reserved in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0259] 1 Pet. 1]: incorruptible, because it will suffer no loss; undefiled, because there will be no sin there; unfading, because there [Col. 0260B] no one will suffer weariness. In the first: “The Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0259] John 1]. In the second: “And dwelt in us” [Note: [Col. 0259] Ibid.]. In the third: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” [Note: [Col. 0259] Ibid.].

In the first he became the instrument of reconciliation; in the second, the incentive of love; in the third, the evidence of the future inheritance. Of the first: “No one comes to the Father except through me” [Note: [Col. 0259] John 14]. Of the second: “I came to cast fire on the earth; and what do I will but that it burn?” [Note: [Col. 0259] Luke 12]. Of the third: “The works which I do themselves bear witness of me” [Note: [Col. 0259] John 5]. In the first, the day of his resurrection shone upon us; in the second, the day of ancient restoration; in the third, the day of eternal happiness.

This threefold birth is against a threefold loss. For man [Col. 0260C] lost in Paradise the glory of incorruption. Hence: “On whatever day you eat from the tree, you shall die by death” [Note: [Col. 0259] Gen. 2]. He lost also the prerogative of dignity: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” [Note: [Col. 0259] Ps. 48]. He also lost the abundance of fullness. Hence: “Cursed is the earth in your work; it shall not yield its fruit” [Note: [Col. 0259] Gen. 3].

Against this threefold loss the Lord made a threefold promise through the prophet. Against the first: “My dead shall live; my slain shall rise again” [Note: [Col. 0259] Isa. 26]. Against the second: “I shall give them in my city and within my walls a place and a name better than sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0259] Isa. 56]. Against the third: “No eye has seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you” [Note: [Col. 0259] Isa. 64].

He also gave [Col. 0260D] a threefold sign: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” [Note: [Col. 0259] Isa. 7]. Here, through the incorrupt Virgin, is given the sign of incorruption. Through the first birth: “And he shall be called Emmanuel” [Note: [Col. 0259] Ibid.], which means, “God with us”: behold the sign of recovered fullness and dignity. Through the second birth: “He shall eat butter and honey” [Note: [Col. 0259] Ibid.]: behold the sign of recovered fullness. Through the third birth this is given to us.

Because of these three births, three Masses are celebrated at the Nativity of the Lord. Because of the birth from the Father, the first is sung: “The Lord [Col. 0261A] said to me” [Note: [Col. 0261] Ps. 2]. Because of the birth in the brother, the second is sung: “Light shall shine upon us today” [Note: [Col. 0261] In the Introit of the Mass on the Nativity of the Lord]. Because of the birth from the mother, the third is sung: “A child is born to us” [Note: [Col. 0261] Isa. 9]. Of him it follows: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” [Note: [Col. 0261] Ibid.].

He was wonderful in his birth; counselor in preaching; God in the performance of miracles; mighty in the Passion; Father of the age to come in the resurrection; Prince of Peace in the resurrection, ascension, and sending of the Holy Spirit. Or, morally: Wonderful in conversion; Counselor in conduct; God in the remission of sins; Mighty in helping amid temptation; Father of the age to come in promise; Prince of Peace in reward. The first birth is marvelous [Col. 0261B] because it is contrary to nature; the second, beyond estimation because it is beside nature; the third, incomprehensible because it is above nature.

According to nature are things in which only lower causes operate, such as human birth. Contrary to nature are things in which higher causes operate in lower things, as when the she-ass spoke [Note: [Col. 0261] Num. 22] and violence is done to nature. In Christ’s birth higher and lower causes concurred. That he was born as a man from a mother was effected by lower causes; but that this was without a man’s seed was effected by higher causes. What occurs beside nature is where higher causes operate in lower things and yet no violence is done to nature, as in the remission of sins. What occurs above nature is where higher causes operate in higher things, [Col. 0261C] as in the eternal birth, which is that of the Son from the Father, and in the Trinity, and in the other matters which are to be wondered at rather than investigated by reason.

“Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.”

[CAR.] Another reading: “through the nets”; in this expression are marked the benefits of the coming Word of God. He says therefore: “Behold, he stands,” as though ready to help us and fight for us. He stands behind our wall. This is the wall toward which Hezekiah turned and wept [Note: [Col. 0261] 4 Kings 20], namely, the obstacle to divine vision and knowledge arising from the sin of the first parent. Behind this wall the Lord stands, assisting us and seeing us, although he is not seen by us; and he is the one looking through our windows.

For, looking upon the soul from [Col. 0261D] above, he illumines the windows of our senses by hidden inspiration, lest through them death enter the houses of our consciences, as Jeremiah says: “Death has climbed through our windows; it has entered our houses” [Note: [Col. 0261] Jer. 9]. He also gazes through the nets, and by his gaze makes all kinds of temptations which the devil spreads for our feet vanish away. For he is that king who sat on the throne of judgment, as Solomon says: “And by his gaze he disperses every evil” [Note: [Col. 0261] Prov. 20]. It follows:

“And my beloved speaks to me.”

[Col. 0262A] [THO.] He had come in order to instruct her. Therefore he calls and invites her from carnal things to spiritual, from visible things to invisible, from the Law to the Gospel. He comes, hastens, draws near, is present, looks, speaks. None of these things escapes the bride’s attentive care. He comes in angels, hastens in patriarchs, draws near in prophets, is present in the flesh, looks in miracles, speaks in apostles.

Or thus: He comes in affection; he hastens in zeal to show mercy; he draws near in zeal to help. He is present in present things. He looks toward future things; he speaks to all, teaching and “persuading concerning the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0261] Acts 19]. In these things we observe operative and cooperative grace. He comes by delaying, hastens by freeing, draws near by healing: behold operative grace. He is present by helping, looks by preserving, speaks by bringing to completion. He begins through contrition, frees [Col. 0262B] through confession, heals through satisfaction. He helps through good will, preserves the persevering person, and brings to completion through the consolation of things promised.

The bridegroom speaks, inviting the bride to the prize, instructing her for the race, and leveling the course. He invites to the prize by promising; instructs for the race by commanding; levels the course by forbidding—by promising the life of the apostles, commanding works of virtue, and forbidding stains of vice. Hear the promise: “The king shall say to those at his right hand: Come, blessed of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0261] Matt. 25], etc. Hear the command: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” [Note: [Col. 0261] Matt. 5]. Hear the prohibition: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged” [Note: [Col. 0261] Matt. 7].

Hence Paul says: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword,” [Col. 0262C] for uprooting the roots of vices [Note: [Col. 0261] Heb. 4]. “Living”: behold life. “Effective”: behold the work of virtues. “More penetrating than any two-edged sword”: for uprooting the roots of vices. This word, whether spoken or the Word who is the Son of God, reaches “to the division of soul and spirit” [Note: [Col. 0261] Ibid.]. By “soul” are signified carnal sins; by “spirit,” spiritual sins, between which the word of God discerns.

The spirit has three powers: the first is that by which temporal things are prudently administered; the second, that by which it contemplates heavenly things; the third, that by which it contemplates God. The animal nature likewise has three powers: the first is that by which it conceives temporal things; the second, that by which it desires what it has conceived; the third, that by which it wretchedly subjects itself to what it desires. Between these also the word of God discerns.

It is also “a discerner of joints and marrow” [Note: [Col. 0261] Ibid.]. Joints are correspondences and resemblances of things; it teaches us to distinguish between them, lest we be deceived by resemblance. For sometimes avarice imitates frugality, and laxity imitates seriousness, and so forth. But for these reasons God discerns the marrow of the spirit. The marrow of the spirit is devotions; the marrow of animality is carnal desires. Between these also the word of God discerns and causes us to discern. It is also a discerner of actions—namely, which is good and which evil—and likewise of intentions: namely, which is good, which evil, which discriminating, and which undiscriminating.

This beloved [Col. 0263A] is none other than the Son of God, through whom the Beloved speaks to us, while through him the Father’s will is revealed to us. For formerly he spoke through the patriarchs, afterward through the prophets; “but in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages” [Note: [Col. 0263] Heb. 1]. This Word of God is the Son of God. He does three things: removes guilt so that we may act well; confers grace; gives eternal life. The first levels the way; the second produces love; the third confers glorification. Hence: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0263] John 14]. Although the Apostle states them in reverse order: “Living,” behold life; “effective,” behold the work of virtues, as was said above.

There are three sons: the son of wrath, the son of adoption, and the son of grace. The first is begotten, the second reborn, the third only-begotten. The first is begotten of bloods and the will [Col. 0263B] of man [Note: [Col. 0263] John 1], and the will of the flesh. The second is reborn because he is born of God through the sacrament of penance and baptism. The third is the only-begotten of the Father and the son of the Virgin. Of the first the Apostle says: “By nature we are all children of wrath” [Note: [Col. 0263] Eph. 2]. Of the second: “You received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” [Note: [Col. 0263] Rom. 8]; for “he poured out the Holy Spirit into the children of adoption” [Note: [Col. 0263] Preface of the Mass for Pentecost]. Of the third it is read: Christ is the Son of God by nature, but the son of the Virgin by grace.

The first, having received his portion of the estate, went away to the farm to feed swine [Note: [Col. 0263] Luke 15]. The second earned his father’s blessing when, at his mother’s counsel, he prepared a dish for his father [Note: [Col. 0263] Gen. 27], killing and skinning two excellent kids. “Kill,” that is, “mortify your members which are upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0263] Col. 2]. Again: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden [Col. 0263C] with Christ in God” [Note: [Col. 0263] Ibid.]. “Blessed are the dead who die in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0263] Rev. 14].

Moses taught how to skin in this way: “When you offer a sacrifice to the Lord from cattle, you shall remove the skin” [Note: [Col. 0263] Lev. 4]. Hence: “I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” [Note: [Col. 0263] Song 5]. Again: “The guards of the walls took away my cloak” [Note: [Col. 0263] Ibid.].
