Joseph left this cloak in the hand of his adulterous mistress [Note: [Col. 0263] Gen. 39].

We ought to have a cloak, that is, a manner of life, which hides our sins from God; which gladdens those who look upon it; which scatters the currents of the age. The first was Rebekah’s, by which she hid herself from Isaac’s sight [Note: [Col. 0263] Gen. 24]; the second, Mordecai’s: “When Mordecai went out from the royal palace, from the king’s presence, he was clothed in a silk and hyacinth-colored cloak” [Note: [Col. 0263] Esther 8]. Hence “the whole city [Col. 0263D] rejoiced.” The third was Elijah’s cloak, which he left upon the ground when he ascended [Note: [Col. 0263] 4 Kings 2], at whose touch the Jordan was divided [Note: [Col. 0263] Luke 24].

Hear one cooking: “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus?” [Note: [Col. 0263] Ps. 38]. And: “My heart grew hot within me.” Again: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame” [Note: [Col. 0263] Song 8]. The third is sent by his father into Shechem, to see whether all was going well with his brothers [Note: [Col. 0263] Gen. 37].

Therefore the Father deprived the first of the spoils of gratuitous gifts and natural goods; he established for himself the second [Col. 0264A] as “a people acceptable, zealous for good works” [Note: [Col. 0263] Titus 2]; he “appointed the third heir of all things” [Note: [Col. 0263] Heb. 1]. The first is he through whom he made the bonds of hell; the second is he for whom he performed miracles; the third is he “through whom he also made the ages” [Note: [Col. 0263] Ibid.]. The first is the stench of filth; the second, the fragrance of righteousness; the third, “the brightness of glory and the image of substance.”

The first, producing the stench of sins through the vice of faintheartedness, is to be placed at the left with the kids. The second, fleeing the stains of sin through the aid of his strength, now has his citizenship in heaven and afterward will wander with the angels. The third, “bearing all things by the word of his power, having made purification of sins, sits at the right hand of majesty on high” [Note: [Col. 0263] Ibid.].

This is the Son of God, who commends his love to us, since through the Apostle he here shows in human fashion the reasons why he ought to be loved by us. These reasons are three: because he is rich, wise, and beautiful—rich in possession of all things, wise in the creation of all things, beautiful in the re-creation of humankind, both in divinity and in humanity; powerful in governing the world. “Whom he appointed heir of all things”: behold the first. “Through whom he made the ages”: behold the second. “Who, being the brightness of glory and the image of substance” [Note: [Col. 0263] Ibid.]: behold the third. “And bearing all things by the word of his power, making purification of sins”: behold the fourth.

Of the first: “The heavens are yours and the earth is yours” [Note: [Col. 0263] Ps. 88]. Of the second: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0263] Col. 2]. Of the third: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely” [Note: [Col. 0263] Song 1]. Of the fourth: “His power is an eternal power [Col. 0264C] which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one which shall not be destroyed” [Note: [Col. 0263] Dan. 7]. For lovers are accustomed to boast of these four things. Hence Virgil [Note: [Col. 0263] Eclogue 2], of the first:

> How rich in snow-white sheep, how abounding in milk!

Of the second:

> I sing what Dircaean Amphion was wont to sing  
> Whenever he called his cattle.

Of the third:

> Nor am I so uncomely: lately I saw myself upon the shore,  
> When the sea stood still beneath the gentle winds.

Of the fourth:

> A thousand of my lambs roam the Sicilian mountains.

There is yet further reason why you should love him: for our sake, though rich, he was made poor; though wise, he was reckoned foolish; though beautiful, he was disfigured; though powerful, he was made weak. Of the first: “Though Christ was rich, for our sake he became needy, that by his poverty we might become rich” [Note: [Col. 0263] 2 Cor. 8]. Of the second, this reproach was made against him: “You have a demon” [Note: [Col. 0263] John 7]. Of the third: “We saw him as a leper, struck by God and humbled; and he had neither form nor beauty” [Note: [Col. 0263] Isa. 53]. Of the fourth: “He became obedient unto death” [Note: [Col. 0263] Phil. 2].

He is rich in spiritual and heavenly riches. Of the first: “Do you despise the riches of the goodness, [Col. 0265A] forbearance, and patience of God?” [Note: [Col. 0265] Rom. 2]. Of the second: “Dwell in the land, and you shall feed upon its riches” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 26]. You shall possess both if you are poor—poor, I say, not in understanding, not in the habit of virtues, but rather in spirit than in understanding. Of this the poet says:

> O secure means of life,  
> The narrow household of the poor! O gifts of the gods  
> Not yet understood!

As has been said, Christ became needy for our sake, that through his poverty we might become rich [Note: [Col. 0265] 2 Cor. 8]. Look upon him: born without lodging, between ox and ass in a manger, wrapped in a cheap cloth, a fugitive, seated on an ass, naked on the cross. Behold the poor man: “Go, and do likewise” [Note: [Col. 0265] Luke 10].—“Therefore dwell in the land and feed upon its riches. For the meek shall inherit the land” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 36].

[Col. 0265B] This is the Lord’s inheritance, because we shall be “heirs indeed of God and coheirs with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0265] Rom. 8]—Christ whom the Father “appointed heir of all things” [Note: [Col. 0265] Heb. 1], who will bring us “into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance reserved in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0265] 1 Pet. 1].

He is wise, he “through whom he made the ages” [Note: [Col. 0265] Heb. 1]. Yet for our sake he was accounted foolish amid blows, spittle, and insults. And “he was reckoned among the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0265] Isa. 53], in order that we might be wise by reckoning ourselves foolish; for “God chose the foolish things of the world in order to confound the strong” [Note: [Col. 0265] 1 Cor. 1], or the wise: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent before yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0265] Isa. 5]. He is truly wise, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0265] Col. 2].

This wisdom “is drawn from hidden places,” says Job [Note: [Col. 0265] Job 28], that is, from the secret bosom of the Father. The wise Son is the glory of the Father. This “wisdom has built herself a house” in us, namely the human body; “she has hewn out seven pillars” [Note: [Col. 0265] Prov. 9], namely the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. This wisdom conquers malice. “For it reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” [Note: [Col. 0265] Wis. 8]. “It reaches from the end,” that is, from the beginning of good conduct, “to the end,” the final dissolution, “mightily,” by freeing from sins, helping in temptation, and bringing perseverance to completion; “it orders all things sweetly,” instructing you first to love God, second yourself, and third your neighbor.

Again, it acts “mightily” by casting down the proud from heaven, overcoming the evil one in the world, and despoiling the greedy one in hell. It “orders sweetly” by redeeming humanity in [Col. 0265D] the world, freeing it from hell, and bringing it back to heaven. This wisdom reaches everywhere because of its purity. Therefore, if you wish to possess this wisdom, feign foolishness. For to feign foolishness in the proper place is the highest prudence.

He is also comely, of whom it is said: “Being the brightness of glory” [Note: [Col. 0265] Heb. 1], that is, coeternal with the Father, as brightness is coeval with the sun or fire; “and the image of substance” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ibid.], that is, equal, just as the image of a thing is equal to the thing itself. Of him it is also said: “He is the brightness of eternal light and a spotless mirror” [Note: [Col. 0265] Office of the Church], into whom [Col. 0266A] angels desire to look [Note: [Col. 0265] 1 Pet. 1]. And in his humanity: “Beautiful in form above the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 44].

Therefore, if you wish to share in his glory, do not desire the beauty of this misery. For this beauty which you desire prevents you from being such a participant. Isaiah says: “He has neither form nor beauty” [Note: [Col. 0265] Isa. 53]. Yet by the things he accomplished in the world he was the brightness of that glory, of which it is said: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to persons of good will” [Note: [Col. 0265] Luke 2], namely, the manifestation of the name. For the man Christ merited through the obedience of the Passion not the name, but its manifestation. Thus it is said figuratively: “He gave him the name that is above every name” [Note: [Col. 0265] Phil. 2], that is, its manifestation.

At his birth there was glory in the lowest places, glory in the heights, glory in the highest. The first was in the world, the second [Col. 0266B] in heaven, the third upon the throne. The first was for the human race, the second for the angel, the third for God. Through the first shone upon us the day of new redemption; through the second, the day of ancient restoration; through the third, the day of eternal happiness. The day of new redemption is that by which human nature was redeemed; the day of ancient restoration, that by which the loss arising from the fall of the angels was repaired; the day of eternal happiness, in which the creature shall perpetually praise the Creator.

This is the first, of which it is said: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” [Note: [Col. 0265] John 1]. “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright in heart” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 96]. Of the second: “They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom and tell of your power” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 144]. Of the third: “The heavens declare the glory of God” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 18].

This threefold glory drives away a threefold shame. For there was shame in [Col. 0266C] the world, in heaven, and in hell. The first was when Adam sinned [Note: [Col. 0265] Gen. 3]; the second, when the angel became proud [Note: [Col. 0265] Isa. 14]; the third, which the devil endures forever. Of the first: “The shame of my face has covered me” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 43]. Of the second: “All who forsake you, O Lord, shall be put to shame” [Note: [Col. 0265] Jer. 17], namely, the evil angels. Of the third: “They have been put to shame, because God has rejected them” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 52], namely, by condemning them in hell.

The radiance, that is, the manifestation, of the aforesaid glory is the sun that has risen for us. But the same solar radiance was darkened for our sake in three ways; for the sun is darkened by the interposition of a cloud, by an eclipse, and by its natural setting. The first occurred in the Nativity, the second in the perversity of persecutors, the third in the Passion. Of the first: “I shall cover the sun with a cloud” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ezek. 32]. Again: [Col. 0266D] “The sun shall be darkened on the day of its rising” [Note: [Col. 0265] Amos 8]. Of the second, in Revelation: “The sun became like a sackcloth of hair” [Note: [Col. 0265] Rev.]. Haircloth is cheap and pricks with thorns; thus sinners accounted Christ cheap. They attacked him with thorns—that is, with argumentative objections. Of the third: “The sun shall set at noon” [Note: [Col. 0265] Amos 8].

These three darkenings are found in the sinner: the first in worldly anxiety, the second in temptation, the third in the commission of crime.

In the first: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0267] Phil. 2]; of the second: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0267] John 9]; in the third: “He became obedient to the Father unto death” [Note: [Col. 0267] Phil. 2]. Behold beauty. Power follows: “His power is an everlasting power which shall not be taken away” [Note: [Col. 0267] Dan. 7]; yet this too was weakened for our sake. “Father,” he says, “if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 26]. Likewise: “He began to be afraid and distressed” [Note: [Col. 0267] Mark 14]. You “say: I am rich, and need nothing” [Note: [Col. 0267] Rev. 3]. But:

> To attain your wish, be miserable.  
> [Note: [Col. 0267] Ovid, *Art of Love*.]

For he bears both you and what is yours.

He bore four things for us: he bore the deficiency of our weakness; he bore the burden of our iniquity; he bears the glory of resurrected flesh; he bears the devotion of our prayer [Col. 0267B]. He began to bear the first in the Virgin’s womb, the second on the gibbet of the cross, the third in the resurrection, and the fourth for as long as he remained in this misery. Of the first: “Surely he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our offences” [Note: [Col. 0267] Isa. 53]; of the second: “Leaving the ninety-nine in the wilderness, he came to seek one; and, having found it, he carried it back upon his shoulders” [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 18; Luke 15]. Hence: “Like an eagle provoking her young to fly and hovering over them, he spread out his wings and took them up; indeed, he carried them upon his shoulders” [Note: [Col. 0267] Deut. 32]. Of the third: “You carried him in your strength to your holy dwelling-place” [Note: [Col. 0267] Exod. 15], presenting before the Father’s countenance the glory of victorious flesh. Of the fourth: “Command these things to be carried by the hands of your holy angel to your sublime altar, in the sight of your divine majesty” [Note: [Col. 0267] Office of the Church]—“for we have an advocate [Col. 0267C] with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who became the propitiation for our sins” [Note: [Col. 0267] 1 John 2]. In the first, he became our companion; in the second, our servant; in the third, our forerunner; in the fourth, our messenger. Here he laboured for us. But behold, “he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” [Note: [Col. 0267] Heb. 1].

Four sittings ought to precede this sitting: first, the embracing of discipline with perseverance; second, diligence in judging; third, humility in exaltation; fourth, rest in weakness. The first is required lest one be fickle; the second lest one be prejudiced; the third lest one be proud; the fourth lest one be indiscreet in labours. We read that Christ fulfilled these. In the first, he sat among the teachers, listening to and questioning them [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 2]; and Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet [Col. 0267D; Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 10], and so forth. In the second, Jesus sat opposite the treasury, judging concerning the widow’s offering [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 21]. In the third, he sat upon the mountain, “and when he had sat down, he opened his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 5]. Therefore Christ says: “Sit in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 24]. In the fourth, weary from his journey, “he sat by the fountain” [Note: [Col. 0267] John 4]. Behold, “he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” [Note: [Col. 0267] Heb. 1]; hence: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men” [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 2 and Office of the Church], and so forth.

There is peace for persons of evil will, peace for persons of lukewarm will, and peace for persons of good will [Col. 0268A]. Of the first: “I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 72]; of the second, Hezekiah: “Only let there be peace in my days” [Note: [Col. 0267] 4 Kings 20]; of the third, the Apostle: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0267] Heb. 12]. The first sin confidently, because the Lord does not punish them; the second act negligently, because temptation does not often assail them; the third languish sweetly, because he reveals to them his glory. Of the first: “Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” [Note: [Col. 0267] Rom. 2]. Of the second: “Would that you were cold or hot!” [Note: [Col. 0267] Rev. 3]. Of the third: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0267] Song 2]. Such a beloved speaks to me, saying what follows: “Arise, hasten, my friend.”

[CARD.] “Behold, my beloved speaks to me.” This chapter [Col. 0268B] concerns the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, who, when the fitting time had come, is shown to have been assumed into heaven so that she might intercede for us with greater confidence. The mother therefore says of the Son: “Behold, my beloved speaks to me,” as though she said: My beloved so greatly desires to have mercy and spare humankind that he calls me to the kingdom, so that I may stir and urge him to show mercy. For behold, my beloved speaks to me and says:

> Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.

[THO.] All things are ordered by the succession of times. Since the beloved had first visited her upon the flowering bed, he now invites her to cultivate the vineyards and drive the beasts away from them—that is, to build churches [Col. 0268C] and defeat heretics. Thus he says: Arise from the bed of contemplation; nor will you therefore be separated from me, because you are my friend. Hasten to gather the faithful in the Church in a spirit of gentleness, because you are my dove. Come to restrain the Church’s adversaries, so that they may reverence your present manner of life, because you are beautiful in virtues. Or: because she obeys, she is a friend; because she acts simply, a dove; because she lives honourably, beautiful.

The bride is here commended in three respects: preaching, prayer, and contemplation. She is rightly called a friend who seeks the bridegroom’s gains by preaching, counselling, and ministering; a dove, because by groaning prayer she wins divine mercy for herself; beautiful, because, shining with heavenly desire, she clothes herself with the beauty of higher contemplation [Col. 0268D]. Here see Martha ministering [Note: [Col. 0267] John 12]; Lazarus groaning beneath the stone and demanding the glory of resurrection [Note: [Col. 0267] John 12]; Mary at leisure [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 10]. She is at leisure for the vineyards—that is, for revisiting, correcting, instructing, and saving souls. She is called friend by her affections, dove by her groanings, beautiful by the virtues in which she flourishes. She desires that he may be sweetly felt; she groans that sin may be forgiven; she flourishes that she may be found pleasing by him.

Arise, therefore, lest by abandoning sin you seem lukewarm. Hasten, lest the day of death overtake you. Come, lest you tire before reaching the goal. “How long, sluggard, will you sleep?” [Col. 0269A; Note: [Col. 0269] Prov. 6]. “Would that you were either cold or hot!” [Note: [Col. 0269] Rev. 3]. Hasten: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 20]. Come: “So run that you may obtain” [Note: [Col. 0269] 1 Cor. 9]. Therefore one must arise from sleep.

Sleep is threefold: the first is the sleep of cherishing iniquity; the second, of restoring weakness; the third, of contemplation. Of the first: “Arise, you who sleep” [Note: [Col. 0269] Eph. 5]; of the second: “If he sleeps, he will be safe” [Note: [Col. 0269] John 11]—this is said of Lazarus; of the third: “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch” [Note: [Col. 0269] Song 5]. The first is to be fled, the second allowed, the third desired. Hence, when the Lord found his disciples sleeping, he first rebuked them, saying: “Could you not watch with me one hour?” [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 26]. The second time he found them sleeping and was silent [Note: [Col. 0269] Ibid.]; the third time he said: “Sleep now and rest” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ibid.].

One must arise from the first; but in this sleep [Col. 0269B] some are overcome by drowsiness, some weighed down by sleep, and some suffer from lethargy. The first trifle with temptations; the second yield to temptations; the third, after yielding, wish to return. Of these it is said: the cock rouses those lying down and rebukes the drowsy; the cock reproves those who deny. This cock who rouses was Moses, the prophets, the apostles, the Fathers, and Christ. He rebukes the drowsy, lest, like Samson, they be caught in Delilah’s lap [Note: [Col. 0269] Judg. 16]; he rouses those lying down, that, like the paralytic, they may rise from the bed [Note: [Col. 0269] John 5]; he reproves those who deny, lest they rot like beasts in their dung [the text perhaps reads *ne putrescant*, “lest they rot”] [Note: [Col. 0269] Joel 1].

This cock does four things: he rouses those lying down, as in this place; he distinguishes the hours of the night; he recalls wanderers to the way; he announces the coming light. He distinguishes the hours of the night, which are three [Col. 0269C]. Night is the life of the sinner. The first hour is contrition, the second confession, the third satisfaction. Or, the life of every person is a night, whose hours the Prophet distinguishes: “I will show you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you: namely, to love mercy, do justice, and walk diligently with your God” [Note: [Col. 0269] Mic. 6]. He recalls wanderers; hence the Apostle: “See how carefully you walk, not as foolish persons but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil” [Note: [Col. 0269] Eph. 5].

The evil day is threefold: because of guilt—“Sufficient for the day is its own evil” [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 6]; because of temporal punishment—Jacob says, “My days have been few and evil” [Note: [Col. 0269] Gen. 48]; and because of the severe sentence at judgement—“The Lord will deliver him in the evil day” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 40]. The first [Col. 0269D] we ought to avoid; the second patiently endure, so that we may securely await the third. Some take away time, some redeem it, some purchase it. Those take it away who always live in iniquity; those redeem it who repent at some time; those purchase it who always live without crime. The days of the first fail; hence David: “My days have failed like smoke” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 101]. The second halve their days; hence: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 54]; and: “I said: In the middle of my days I go to the gates of hell” [Note: [Col. 0269] Isa. 38]. The third fulfil them [Col. 0270A]; hence it is said of Job: “He died full of days” [Note: [Col. 0269] Job 42].

Likewise, the cock announces the coming light, namely eternal light. There are four lights: the first is Christ; the second, a work; the third, an impious spirit; the fourth, the light above in heaven. Of the first: “I am the light of the world” [Note: [Col. 0269] John 8]; of the second: “Let your light shine before men” [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 5]; of the third: “Walk while you have the light” [Note: [Col. 0269] John 12]; of the fourth: “Everlasting light shall shine upon your saints, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0269] 4 Ezra 2]. The first is for instruction; the second for example; the third is a spiritual gift; the fourth: “The righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father” [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 13]. The first is for faith, the second for conversion, the third for understanding and discernment, the fourth for the vision of God. The first was among us, the second is among us [Col. 0270B], the third is for us, the fourth is above us.

Of these it is said: “The path of the righteous proceeds like a shining light, and grows unto the perfect day” [Note: [Col. 0269] Prov. 4]. There is the righteous person who lives by faith [Note: [Col. 0269] Hab. 1; Rom. 1]; the righteous person confident like a lion [Note: [Col. 0269] Prov. 28]; and the righteous person who is not saddened by whatever befalls him. The first is in Moses, the second in John, the third in the Saviour. The path of the first approaches, that of the second goes before, that of the third goes forth. It approaches like a lantern, goes before like a lamp, and goes forth like a shining light. For first Christ lay hidden under the letter in the Law; second, he was shown in John’s birth [Note: [Col. 0269] Luke 1]; third, he fully appeared in assumed human nature. For their transformation we ought to hold a lantern, a lamp, and a shining light: a lantern, by which the zeal of the novice may in part remain concealed; a lamp, by which the light of the strong may appear [Col. 0270C]; and a light by which God may be made known in contemplation.

Novices, therefore, hold the lantern in mouth, hand, and body: in prayer, action, and satisfaction. Thus the Lord says of the first: “When you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 6]; of the second: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet, and let not your left hand know what your right hand does” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ibid.]; of the third: “When you fast, anoint your head and wash your face” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ibid.]. Hence the poet:

> If skill lies hidden, it benefits; detected, it brings shame.  
> [Note: [Col. 0269] Ovid, *Art of Love* II, 313.]

Likewise:

> Believe me: he who has lain hidden well has lived well;  
> and each person ought to remain within his own fortune.  
> [Note: [Col. 0269] Id., *Tristia* III.iv.25.]

Similarly, the lamp of good works ought to be in the mouth [Col. 0270D], hand, and head: in preaching, action, and inspiration. Of the first: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 118]; of the second: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” [Note: [Col. 0269] Luke 12]; of the third Job says: “Who will grant that I might be as in former months, when God protected me, while his lamp shone above my head?” [Note: [Col. 0269] Job 29]. Therefore John was called “a burning and shining lamp” [Note: [Col. 0269] John 5], but also one that grows fat.

As a figure of the first, Ezekiel says of the living creatures: “And sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ezek. 1]; of the second [Col. 0271A]: “The likeness of the faces of the living creatures was like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ezek. 1]; of the third John says: “His eyes were like a flame of fire” [Note: [Col. 0271] Rev. 1].

Contemplatives hold the light. Light is threefold: by the first, wickedness is recognized; by the second, conscience is clear; by the third, joy arises in the heart. The first teaches the flight from sins; the second leads through the way of virtues; the third gladdens by the sight of rewards. Of the first it is said: “He who does evil hates the light” [Note: [Col. 0271] John 3]. Concerning this light it is said that the harlot woman, gazing more attentively in clear light before Solomon, recognized that the dead child was not the one she had borne [Note: [Col. 0271] 3 Kings 3]. For the dead son is the dead work of a sinner. Of the second: “They shall go in the light of your arrows, in the radiance of your flashing spear” [Note: [Col. 0271] Hab. 3]. Of the third it is said: “Light has arisen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart” [Col. 0271B; Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 96].

The first path of the righteous therefore proceeds up to the second; through the tainted day the second grows up to the third; through the affected day the third, by growing, leads unto the perfect day [Note: [Col. 0271] Prov. 4]. For there is a tainted day, an affected day, and a perfect day: tainted by the corruption of sins, affected by devotion to good things, and perfect by their consummation. The first, therefore, is tainted in three ways: by pleasure, vanity, and malice. Of the first Jeremiah says: “I have not desired the day of man; you know it” [Note: [Col. 0271] Jer. 17]. Of the second: “Man is like grass; his days, like the flower of grass, shall so flourish” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 102]. Of the third Paul says: “But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day” [Note: [Col. 0271] 1 Cor. 4].

The second day is affected [Col. 0271C] in three ways: by purity of conscience, holiness of righteousness, and sweetness of joy. Of the first: “Behold, now is the day of salvation, giving offence to no one” [Note: [Col. 0271] 2 Cor. 6]. Of the second: “Let us serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days” [Note: [Col. 0271] Luke 1]. Of the third: “Let this joyful day pass …” [abbreviation/reading uncertain: *p. s. v. d.*]. The third day likewise is perfect in three ways: first, because it will have no interruption of night or cloud; second, because of the greatness of its light; third, because of the full vision of God. Of the first: “Until the day breathes and the shadows decline” [Note: [Col. 0271] Song 2]. Of the second: Behold, the Lord will come, and all his saints with him, and on that day there shall be great light. Of the third: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” [Note: [Col. 0271] Hos. 6], and so forth, without the burden of corruption. We shall know the heavenly mysteries; by obedience we shall follow the footsteps [Col. 0271D] of his will, so that we may know the Lord, namely the three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—in one substance.

The cock, that is, the Apostle, therefore says: “The night has passed; the day, however, has drawn near” [Note: [Col. 0271] Rom. 13], and so forth. Likewise, the bride is called friend, dove, and beautiful. She is called friend as guardian of the soul; dove, as cultivating the loins; beautiful through conscience, by which she avoids the devil’s machinations. Let it therefore be said: Arise, friend, in whom wisdom through prudence conquers malice; hasten, dove, possessing continence [Col. 0272A], because, clean through abstinence of the flesh, you wear down pride; come, beautiful one, because the king has desired your beauty. Therefore, that you may be a friend, arise from the dunghill of sins; that you may be a dove, hasten toward the merits of virtues; that you may be beautiful, come to the joys of the blessed.

Thus she is a friend while, by fleeing malice, the love of God is set above the world; a dove while she meditates on heavenly things; beautiful while she lives angelically on earth. Of the first: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 96]; of the second: “I will meditate like a dove” [Note: [Col. 0271] Isa. 38]; of the third: “To live in the flesh beyond the flesh is nothing else than to lead an angelic life on earth.” Or otherwise: she is friend through knowledge, dove through understanding, beautiful through wisdom. Through knowledge, by which good things are distinguished from evil; through understanding [Col. 0272B], by which heavenly things are known; through wisdom, by which what is known is savoured. Good things are distinguished from evil lest love be undiscerning; heavenly things are known so that our expectation may become manifest; known things are tasted so that every other delight may be proved frivolous. Of the first: “See how carefully you walk” [Note: [Col. 0271] Eph. 5]; of the second: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0271] Rev. 21]; of the third: “You gave them bread from heaven, having every delight and every flavour” [Note: [Col. 0271] 2 Esdr. 9].

First, the friend must be a guardian of the soul against three things: lust, avarice, and pride. Against the first, she must oppose constancy in work; against the second, the solicitude of circumspection, by which we avoid desire for worldly things; against the third, truthful knowledge of oneself, by which we may grow [Col. 0272C] in humility—against the threefold adversary, namely flesh, world, and devil. Let us therefore do as Jacob did, who set three companies against Esau when he met him [Note: [Col. 0271] Gen. 33]. The first company was that of the maidservants with their sons: the maidservants are “my bodies” [*corpora mea*, apparently corrupt], and the sons are works, which we ought to oppose to lust, because idleness is the enemy of the soul. The second company was Leah with her sons; Leah is said to mean “laborious.” This is solicitous circumspection, which has children, namely manifold safeguards against the world’s desire. The third company was Rachel with her son Joseph; Rachel is said to mean “seeing the beginning.” For when we consider the beginning of our birth, we gain an increase of humility against pride; for Joseph is said to mean “increase.” This is the friend through wisdom, because [Col. 0272D] that wisest king Solomon fell away, conquered by these three enemies.

For he sacrificed to Astarte, goddess of the Sidonians, whose name means “hunting” [Note: [Col. 0271] 3 Kings 11]: those ruled by lust hunt after the attainment of their pleasure. He also sacrificed to Chemosh, god of the Moabites [Note: [Col. 0271] Ibid.]. This name means “assembly,” that is, avarice. Those ruled by avarice are called Moab, “from the father,” because in this they follow the father Adam, from whom all avarice proceeded. He sacrificed to Moloch, god of the Ammonites [Note: [Col. 0271] Ibid.], that is, to pride. Moloch [Col. 0273A] means “king,” for pride always desires to reign. Ammon, however, means “a people that crushes” or “a troubled people”; for those ruled by pride are always troubled and crush others.

Behold the friend; but the dove flies simply. One must also contemplate sublime things simply. Whoever wishes to attain them must consider three things: the disturbance of this world; then, being at peace in himself, he must make peace for others. This will be Noah’s dove, which went out to see the flood and found nowhere for its foot to rest, yet brought back to the ark an olive branch, the sign of peace [Note: [Col. 0273] Gen. 8]. Thus whoever considers the world finds in it nothing but disturbance. Yet he himself has peace with others and restores peace among those at discord [Col. 0273B]. This is Noah’s dove, and Noah means “rest.”

For we read of three doves: Noah’s dove, Christ’s dove, and David’s dove. The first considers the world’s disturbance; the second seeks our salvation; the third labours so that we may possess his Passion. The first, then, is Noah’s, whose name means “rest,” because it seeks a particular and momentary rest; the second is the Saviour’s, which seeks eternal salvation; the third is David’s—that is, “strong of hand”—because it works strongly to attain it. Of the first: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0273] Heb. 12]. Of the second: “For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose from Israel, and will make them rest upon his shoulder” [Note: [Col. 0273] Isa. 14]. Of the third: “Look to Jesus, the author and finisher [Col. 0273C] of faith, who, with joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame, and now sits at God’s right hand” [Note: [Col. 0273] Heb. 12].

This third dove is “among the lots” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 67]; *cleros* is Greek, *sors* Latin, “a lot.” There are two lots: temporal life and eternal life. Between them she sleeps, despising the one and loving the other. Or the lots are fear and desire; between them she sleeps, having a bed of hope and love. Love moderates desire, while hope soothes fear; but “the hinder parts of her back are in the paleness of gold” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ibid.]. This back is the body, pale from affliction. But this pallor is of gold, because it merits the eternal crown, which is compared to gold.

I find three doves opposed to these. The first is a dove which has a swelling in its throat; this one is fit to be sacrificed beside the altar. The second is one whose dung is sold in the camp because of the severity of famine. The third is a deceived dove, without a heart to walk the way of salvation [Col. 0273D]. The first is proud because of temporal peace: this is the swelling in the throat. The second, through God’s mercy, presumes upon eternal salvation; sinning more confidently, she draws others by her example—this is selling dung. The third is deceived because indiscreet in works, and has no heart when she fears to undertake the way of salvation.

She is also called beautiful. In her is pure beauty, which first overcomes the assaults [Col. 0274A] of the wanton flesh by praises and prayers; second, lest it grow old through lukewarmness, the affection warmed by the fervour of charity groans; third, the beloved brings her, abiding in the solitude of the secret heart, to his bed. In the first she avoids ugliness; in the second she provokes love; in the third she possesses brightness. The first is Judith, that is, “praising,” who killed the corrupter Holofernes [Note: [Col. 0273] Judith 13]. The second is Abishag the Shunammite, that is, “the father’s roar,” who warms the feet of David now old [Note: [Col. 0273] 3 Kings 2]. The third is Esther, that is, “hidden,” whom King Ahasuerus—that is, “his blessedness”—raises to be queen [Note: [Col. 0273] Esther 2].

But, on the other hand, I find a beauty that is reprehensible in its outward appearance. First, because by her appearance she seeks the flesh’s pleasure; second, vanity; third, in both she has obstinacy. Of the first: “A golden ring in her nostrils: a beautiful woman [Col. 0274B] and foolish” [Note: [Col. 0273] Prov. 11]. Of the second: “Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain” [Note: [Col. 0273] Prov. 31]. Of the third Job says: “I saw a fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty” [Note: [Col. 0273] ch. 5].

> Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.

[CAR.] As though he said: Arise from that ruin of the human race, concerning which it was said to humankind: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” [Note: [Col. 0273] Gen. 3]. Arise, I say, my friend, guardian of my soul and privy to the divine secrets. Arise, my dove, simple and not envious, illuminated by the Holy Spirit. Arise, my beautiful one, wholly beautiful, in whom there is no blemish. Everywhere in this pronoun *my*, moreover, distinction and significance of a kind [Col. 0274C] of singular pre-eminence are indicated. Arise and come to share in the kingdom, assumed into the palace of heaven; come, I say, because the fitness of the time now demands this.

> For now winter has passed; the rain has gone away and withdrawn; flowers have appeared in our land.

[THO.] Winter signifies the severity of the Law, rain the consolation of prophetic promise, and flowers evangelical truth. For winter’s harshness usually uproots evil weeds, while preserving beneath the earth the roots of good plants unspoiled so that they may grow in spring. So the Law’s severity punished sins, but preserved the sacraments, hidden under the letter, until the time of grace. And because the time [Col. 0274D] of grace has now come and the Law has yielded, the beloved cries: “For now winter has passed.” Rain, however, by its moisture opens the pores of the earth so that shoots may spring forth; so prophetic promise opened the hearts of the faithful, that they might conceive faith and hope. Finally, the flowers of evangelical utterances made truth manifest.

These things are also fulfilled spiritually in the restoration of a human being: winter signifies the sorrow of penitents, rain the tears of mourners, and flowers the first fruits of virtues. By the first, oldness begins to be renewed; by the second, the spirit is made drunk; by the third, it is made fruitful. Of the first: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” [Note: [Col. 0273] Eph. 4]. Of the second [Col. 0275A]: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 39]; and: “As rain and snow descend from heaven and make the earth drunk” [Note: [Col. 0275] Isa. 55]. Of the third: “And he gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ibid.]; and: “Let the earth bring forth green grass, making seed according to its kind” [Note: [Col. 0275] Gen. 1]. In the first the spirit becomes young; in the second it becomes full; in the third it will blossom. Of the first: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 402, evidently Ps. 102]. Of the second: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 62]. Of the third: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 91].

For these persons winter has passed, since they no longer need penitential work, to whom the kindness and humanity of God our Saviour have spiritually appeared. The rain has gone away and withdrawn. What need is there of rain—that is, tearful weeping—where “the rushing of the river makes glad” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 45]? In its land [Col. 0275B], that is, in the soul, an abundance of flowers rightly appears, in which rests the flower of the field and lily of the valleys [Note: [Col. 0275] Song 2].

Winter is threefold: the first is that of sloth, the second of penitence, the third of the sentence of damnation. “He commands the waters of snow to descend upon the earth, and the rains of winter”: the rains of winter are the teachings of a slothful teacher. Of the second: “The dedication feast was held in Jerusalem, and it was winter” [Note: [Col. 0275] John 10]. Jerusalem means “vision of peace”; *Encaenia*, “renewals.” For the sinner, seeing the peace which is above, hastens to be renewed in winter—that is, through penitence. Of the third it is said: “See that your flight does not occur in winter or on the sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0275] Matt. 24]. For those who at the judgement hear that sentence of damnation, “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” [Note: [Col. 0275] Matt. 25], would wish to flee in winter if they could.

The first will fall into [Col. 0275C] want; the second strive toward renewal; the third descend into calamity: into want of virtues, renewal of spirits, and calamity of torments. Hear of want: “The sluggard would not plough because of the cold; therefore he shall beg in summer, and it shall not be given to him” [Note: [Col. 0275] Prov. 20]. And Job: “He who fears frost, snow shall fall upon him” [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 6]. Hear of renewal: “Although our outer man is corrupted, yet our inner man is renewed from day to day” [Note: [Col. 0275] 2 Cor. 4]. Likewise: “If anyone is a new creature in Christ, the old things have passed away” [Note: [Col. 0275] 2 Cor. 5]. Hear of calamity. Job says: “In six tribulations he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you. In famine he will rescue you from death, and in war from the hand of the sword” [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 5]. These two are in this exile: famine, namely of the word of God, and war, in which one fights against temptation. The other [Col. 0275D] five will be assigned to the wretched at judgement; yet the Lord promises to deliver the righteous from them thus: “You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ibid.], so that you may not hear: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” [Note: [Col. 0275] Matt. 22]. “You shall not fear calamity when it comes” [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 5]. Of this it is said: “That day is a day of wrath, calamity, and misery” [Note: [Col. 0275] Zeph. 1]. “In famine and desolation you shall laugh” [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 5].

Behold two: this famine will be the hunger of seeing God, of which one shall never be satisfied; hence: “My servants shall eat, and you shall hunger” [Note: [Col. 0275] Isa. 65]. Desolation derives its name from laying waste [Col. 0276A], concerning which it is said: “With hands and feet bound, cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” [Note: [Col. 0275] Matt. 22]. There he shall be handed over to the torturers until he pays the whole debt. The seventh is: “You shall not fear the beast of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 5]. The beast of the earth is the devil, who says to the Lord: “I have gone around the earth and walked through it” [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 2]. He is rightly feared; and in hell, where he is, there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells.

Four things in winter delay the slothful person. He is delayed by frost, snow, wind, and hail. Frost pierces the feet; snow blots the road from the eyes; wind invisibly attacks the whole body; hail wounds the head. Let us therefore construct a kind of inner human being. Let his feet be the affections, his eyes the understanding, [Col. 0276B] his body the intention, and his head reason. The sharpness of frost is the rigor of discipline; white snow is the blandishment of worldly glory; the invisible wind is the hidden suggestion of Satan; hail is the chastisement of divine wrath.

First, therefore, in the slothful person the feet—that is, the affections—are pierced by frost—that is, by the severity of discipline—while, through fear of discipline, they are distracted in different directions. Hence it is said: “The slothful person wills and does not will” [Note: [Col. 0275] Prov. 13]. For he says: “There is a lion in the road” [Note: [Col. 0275] Prov. 26]; “I shall be killed,” because every discipline seems to him at present to be not of joy but of sorrow. Of such persons the prophet says: “You struck them, and they were not healed; you afflicted them, and they refused to receive discipline” [Note: [Col. 0275] Jer. 5]. This is the wretched Bosheth, lame in his feet, who would not follow David when he fled before Absalom [Note: [Col. 0275] II Kings 15].

Second, by snow—that is, by the brightness of worldly glory—the road to the kingdom is covered over, because the eyes of understanding are blinded. And therefore “they did not find the city of habitation” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 106]. For the way of sinners is dark to those who forsake the straight path and walk in ways of darkness. Those who have the whiteness of snow—that is, worldly glory—in their eyes are prohibited in the Law: “A priest who has a whiteness in his eye shall not minister in the tabernacle” [Note: [Col. 0275] Lev. 21]. These are Tobias, upon whose eyes, as he lay on his back, the warm droppings of a swallow fell, and he was blinded [Note: [Col. 0275] Tob. 2]. The swallows that fly on high are the rulers of the world; their droppings are temporal goods, which fall warm upon the eyes when, desiring them with excessive ardor, we lose our understanding of heavenly things.

Third, the wind of diabolical suggestion [Col. 0276D] invisibly insinuates itself into the whole body—that is, the intention—and overturns a good intention, if there is one. It sometimes does this to those who willingly follow temptation and play along with it; hence it is said: “Ephraim feeds on wind” [Note: [Col. 0275] Hos. 12]. At other times they provoke temptation: “Ephraim, a solitary wild ass” [Note: [Col. 0275] Hos. 8], “in desire drew the wind of his love.” This is the wind of which it is said: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind” [Note: [Col. 0275] Song 4]. And “a whirlwind came from the north.” This wind shook the four corners of the house and crushed Job’s children [Note: [Col. 0275] Job 1]. When the slothful person does not return in these three matters, [Col. 0277A] fourth comes hail, wounding the head: that is, God’s wrath, in vengeance, making reason foolish. “For this reason the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief.” They are the beasts of Egypt struck by hail [Note: [Col. 0277] Exod. 9]; and because beasts are irrational, “God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things which are not fitting” [Note: [Col. 0277] Rom. 1].

“For who,” O Lord, “has known the power of your wrath, and who can number your anger because of your fear?” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ps. 89]. These are the kings of the Philistines fighting against Israel, of whom more were killed by hailstones than by the sword [Note: [Col. 0277] Exod. 9]. Behold, you have winter: the winter of judicial sentence, and also the winter of sloth. In three respects the winter of penitence renews. For its cold, by consuming the worms of the seeds of the earth, kills them, ripens the soil, and thus produces shoots in abundance from the seed. [Col. 0277B] After its departure, the pleasant breath of spring arises.

These worms are the suggestions of carnal impulses; the seed is a good resolution in the heart; it bursts into a shoot when it is brought into action; the spring mildness is liberation from sin. The worms therefore gnaw the seed when impulses of the flesh hinder a good resolution. But winter consumes the worms when penitence restrains the movements of the flesh. Likewise, winter ripens the soil and thereby produces shoots better when penitence chastises the body, and thus applies itself more effectively to good works. After such a winter a more pleasing mildness of spring is obtained, when, after penitence, thanksgiving is rendered to God from a good conscience.

Hear of the worms and of the winter which consumes them: “Not in revelling and drunkenness, not in beds [Col. 0277C] and indecencies” [Note: [Col. 0277] Rom. 13]: behold the worms. “But put on the Lord Jesus, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ibid.]: behold winter. These are the firstborn of Egypt who were slain [Note: [Col. 0277] Exod. 12]. Hear of the shoots from winter—that is, from penitence: “Tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; testing, hope” [Note: [Col. 0277] Rom. 5]. This is he whose children, after the scourges, were restored more beautiful than before. Hear the more pleasing breath of spring—that is, of a good conscience—after winter, that is, penitence. First: “I was a blasphemer and a persecutor, but I obtained mercy” [Note: [Col. 0277] I Tim. 1], through penitence. “But by the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0277] I Cor. 15]. Thus Tobias, after blindness and poverty, is found to have praised God more abundantly than usual [Note: [Col. 0277] Tob. 2].

Blessed, therefore, is the person found in this state, [Col. 0277D] so as to say: “Winter has passed.” But far more blessed is the person who, after that last winter, will be able here to say: “Winter has passed,” and “the love of many shall not grow cold” any more [Note: [Col. 0277] Matt. 24]. The rain of tears has gone, because “God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints” [Note: [Col. 0277] Rev. 7, 21]. Flowers have appeared on the earth, that flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys may surround the bride.

Threefold is the rain: the rain of punishments, the rain of the Scriptures, and the rain of tears. The first kills, the second gladdens, the third cleanses: it kills the one [Col. 0278A] who loves iniquity [Note: [Col. 0277] Ps. 10]; it gladdens the one who seeks truth; it cleanses the one who desires healing. By the first one is punished; by the second instructed; by the third healed. Of the first: “He will rain snares upon sinners” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ibid.]. But this is the rain by which the flood inundated the earth and the human race perished; for it rained forty days and forty nights [Note: [Col. 0277] Gen. 5].

Of the second: “I will command my clouds that they rain not” [Note: [Col. 0277] Isa. 4]. With this rain Christ came, who “descended like rain upon fleece” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ps. 71]. “And let the clouds rain down the righteous one” [Note: [Col. 0277] Isa. 44]. Of the third: “He made lightning into rain” [Note: [Col. 0277] Jer. 51], because by threatening he moves sinners to tears. This is the voluntary rain which God sets apart for his inheritance; Mary Magdalene had it, and Christ himself. The first rain proceeds, the second has gone, the third retreats. The first proceeds from this [Col. 0278B] exile all the way to hell; the second has gone from the world to the kingdom; the third retreats—that is, returns into nothingness.

The first proceeds because the punishment begins here and will be without end; hence: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” [Note: [Col. 0277] Isa. 66]. The fire is the punishment by which they labor here, but it becomes more burning in hell. The second goes away—that is, it goes from this exile to the kingdom—because what we say here about God through the Scriptures, we shall know more certainly in the kingdom, since all shall be taught by God [Note: [Col. 0277] John 6]. “For what we now see through a mirror in an enigma, then we shall see face to face” [Note: [Col. 0277] I Cor. 15]. The third rain retreats—that is, returns into nothingness—because there shall be no more mourning, nor crying, nor any pain [Note: [Col. 0277] Rev. 21]. Behold, winter has passed, the rain has gone and retreated; it follows that flowers should appear [Col. 0278C] in our land.

The earth is threefold: namely, hostile land, foreign land, and our land. The first is in hell; the second in the world; the third in heaven. Of the first: “What is it, Israel, that you are in the land of enemies?” [Note: [Col. 0277] Baruch 3]; of the second: “You have grown old in a foreign land” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ibid.]; of the third: “As is the land of the living” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ezek. 26]. The first is the land of the dying, the second of the languishing, the third of the living. Of the first: “Before I go to the dark land, covered with the gloom of death and the shadow of death” [Note: [Col. 0277] Job 10]; of the second: “The earth mourned and languished” [Note: [Col. 0277] Isa. 33]; of the third: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” [Note: [Col. 0277] Isa. 38].

In the first land the flower withered; in the second the flower obeyed; in the third the flower appeared. It withered in the flames of Gehenna; it obeyed not only teachers but persecutors; it will appear to [Col. 0278D] God, angels, and human beings. Of the first: “Man: his days are like grass, and he blossoms like the flower of the field” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ps. 102]. Likewise: “In the morning may he flourish and pass away; in the evening may he fall, harden, and wither” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ps. 80]. May he flourish in youth and pass into old age; in the evening—that is, in decrepit old age—may he fall into death; may he harden into a clod and wither into Gehenna.

How those in the second land obey: “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake, not only to the good and gentle but also to the perverse” [Note: [Col. 0277] I Pet. 2], so that you may be “like a lily among thorns” [Note: [Col. 0277] Song 2]. How they will appear: [Col. 0279A] “Those who come shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” [Note: [Col. 0279] Ps. 125]. For all who see them shall know them, because these are the seed whom the Lord has blessed [Note: [Col. 0279] John 13]. The first wither because they flourished in the world by birth; the second by holiness; the third by blessedness. Concerning the first, “the grass has withered and the flower has fallen, because all its glory is like the flower of grass” [Note: [Col. 0279] Isa. 40], as it is said: “Son, you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things” [Note: [Col. 0279] Luke 16]. To the second it is said: “Our bed is flowering” [Note: [Col. 0279] Song 1]. Of the third: “The righteous person shall sprout like a lily and flourish forever” [Note: [Col. 0279] Hos. 14].

“Now indeed winter has passed; the rain has gone and retreated.”

[CARD.] For winter is the present life, in which the cold numbness of our mortality constrains us. The rains of winter are the innumerable miseries of this present life. [Col. 0280A] He therefore says: “Come,” because according to the decree of divine predestination winter has now passed for you and winter’s rains have withdrawn. “Come,” because the prerogative of your merits itself calls for this, concerning which it is added: “Flowers have appeared in our land.” This land is that field which had not yet flowered, and yet Isaac then smelled the fragrance of its flowers in his son [Note: [Col. 0279] Gen. 27]. This land is the blessed Virgin, who produced that sublime fruit of which Isaiah says: “On that day the house of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth sublime” [Note: [Col. 0279] Isa. 4]. In this land flowers appeared: namely, the beauty and fragrance of graces, virtues, and works. “Come” also, because it is time to reap what you have sown. This is what is said:

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0279]

[Col. 0279B] “The time of pruning has come” [Note: [Col. 0279] Song 2].

[THO.] The Lord mentions this time in the Gospel when he calls himself the true vine and his Father the husbandman, adding: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will take away; and every one that bears fruit he will prune, that it may bear more fruit” [Note: [Col. 0279] John 15]. Perhaps the time of pruning is that of which the Apostle says: “Putting off the old man with his deeds, put on the new” [Note: [Col. 0279] Eph. 4]. Explaining this elsewhere, he says: “Therefore, putting away all lying, speak truth, each one with his neighbor” [Note: [Col. 0279] Ibid.]. And afterward: “He who used to steal must steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands what is good” [Note: [Col. 0279] Ibid.].

“Flowers have appeared,” he says, “in our land.” By what process this has happened he shows when he adds: [Col. 0279C] “The time of pruning has come. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. The fig tree has produced its early figs. The flowering vines have given their fragrance.” This is the order of pruning. First comes reckoning; second, imputation; third, reappraisal; fourth, cutting away; fifth, assigning; sixth, disputation: reckoning, by recalling; imputation, by turning the cause back upon oneself; reappraisal, by judging oneself; cutting away, by judging oneself in the ears of one’s master; assigning; disputation, by seeking God’s will.

The first is so that one’s past life may be known; the second, so that one may not excuse oneself; the third, so that one may pronounce oneself worthy to be scourged by the Lord; the fourth, so that one may obtain pardon; the fifth, so that one may not produce a relapse; the sixth, so that God’s will may be fulfilled. In the first one gains contrition; [Col. 0279D] in the second humility; in the third fear; in the fourth God’s mercy; in the fifth diligence; in the sixth progress along the royal road. Behold the root of ascent to the flowers. For first comes pruning in confession; second, the groaning of the turtledove in tearful [Col. 0280B] prayer; third, the early fig is the flower of the fig tree, which is the beginning of good conduct, so that sweet fruit may afterward follow in the visitation of the Holy Spirit. Finally, the flowering vine—that is, the soul flourishing with inward glory—gives its neighbors the fragrance of its reputation.

That king reckoned when he said to the smiting angel: “It is I who have sinned; I have committed iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0279] II Kings 24]. The prophet reappraised thus: “All that you have done to us, O Lord, you have done in true judgment” [Note: [Col. 0279] Dan. 3]. James taught cutting away: “Confess your sins to one another” [Note: [Col. 0279] Jas. 5]. The Savior taught assigning: “If the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely watch and would not permit his house to be broken into” [Note: [Col. 0279] Luke 12]. Paul taught disputation, saying: “That you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God” [Note: [Col. 0279] Rom. 12].

[Col. 0280C] There are three times: the time of temptation, the time of struggle, and the time of pruning. The first was before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace. The first was when the devil reigned; the second when Moses showed the Law to the Israelite people; the third when Jesus Christ reigned. In the first the devil was king and lord; in the second, his power having been diminished through observance of the Law, he became a violent plunderer; in the third, his violence having been restrained through grace, he became a petty thief. Of the first: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses” [Note: [Col. 0279] Rom. 5]; of the second: “Every violent plundering with tumult, and garment mixed with blood, shall be for burning, the food of fire” [Note: [Col. 0279] Isa. 9]; of the third: “If the householder knew at what hour the thief would come,” [Col. 0280D] etc.

Thus, in the first Adam was tempted and conquered by the devil without any resistance; in the second Israel resisted, armed with observance of the Law; in the third the Christian guards himself against the deceit of the thief, enlightened by Christ’s grace. The first [Col. 0281A] is the empty time, the second the middle, the third the full. Under the first were slaves; under the second, hired laborers; under the third, sons. The first awaited a word of refreshment; the second the end of the work; the third the redemption of soul and body. Of the first two: “As a deer longs for shade and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work, so I have had empty months, and I have counted out laborious nights for myself” [Note: [Col. 0281] Job 7]. Of the middle: “While all things kept the middle silence, your almighty Word, O Lord, came from royal thrones” [Note: [Col. 0281] Wis. 18]. Of the last: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son into the world” [Note: [Col. 0281] Gal. 4].

Behold, this is the time of pruning, namely full grace. This is the pruning of the vine which Noah planted, and of which he became drunk and lay uncovered [Col. 0281B] in his tent [Note: [Col. 0281] Gen. 9]. For its sake the son of the householder went out to invite laborers into the vineyard [Note: [Col. 0281] Luke 20]. Noah—that is, Christ—was uncovered when, born of the Virgin, he appeared in our weakness. He was slain by the cultivators [Note: [Col. 0281] Ibid.], that is, by the scribes and Pharisees on the cross. He will go out to invite people into the vineyard when he appears at the final judgment.

There are three kinds of mysteries: one to be pruned at the beginning, another in the middle, a third at the end. The first thing is the wild vine (*labrusca*), that is, the woodland vine; the second is adulterous shoots; the third is the overabundance of branches. The wild vine is the malice of heretics; adulterous shoots are our sins; the overabundance of branches is human corruption. Of the first the Lord says through the prophet: “Judge between [Col. 0281C] me and my vineyard: I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes” [Note: [Col. 0281] Isa. 5]. Of the second, the book of Wisdom says that they are reed-like shoots. Of the third: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit my Father will uproot” [Note: [Col. 0281] John 15].

At the beginning of this time, the first pruning must be done by the prelate; the second concerns every Christian; the third will be done by Christ. Of the first it is said: “Remove the evil person from among you” [Note: [Col. 0281] I Cor. 5]; likewise: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” [Note: [Col. 0281] I Cor. 7]. Of the second: “Our old man was crucified with Christ, that the body of sin might be destroyed and that we might no longer be slaves of sin” [Note: [Col. 0281] Rom. 6]. Of the third: “This corruptible thing shall put on incorruption” [Note: [Col. 0281] I Cor. 15].

The first pruning of heretics [Col. 0281D] from the Church, which concerns prelates, is to be done thus: first, by the argumentation of words; second, by the flashing forth of miracles; third, by the punishment of the material sword. In the first, therefore, there is compelling reasoning; in the second, astonishment; in the third, threat. For the first the bishop has the *logion*, that is, the breastplate of judgment, upon his breast; for the second a golden plate shines upon his forehead; for the third there is a goad at the top of the pastoral staff. Elijah pruned the priests of Baal in this order. First he disputed with them before Ahab; second, he convicted them by the miracle of fire, namely the fire of the sacrifice; finally, he killed them with the sword. [Col. 0282A] For he cried out on behalf of the Lord’s vineyard: “A boar from the wood has laid it waste, and a solitary wild beast has devoured it” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 79]. For it was not theirs; rather, “their vineyard was of the vineyard of Sodom and of the suburbs of Gomorrah.” This is the first pruning, of the wild vine—that is, of heretics—which belongs to the prelate.

There follows the pruning of adulterous shoots—that is, sin—which concerns every Christian. This must be done according to its manner. For our sins are like diseases, of which there are three kinds. Some grow like a swelling; some like superfluous moisture; some like dead flesh. The physician cuts the first with iron, burns the second with fire, and consumes the third with a biting ointment. The first—that is, a swelling—is every vice [Col. 0282B] that exalts the heart. The second—that is, superfluous moisture—is desire for secular things which a person covets. The third—that is, dead flesh—is the vice of the flesh, in which the carnal person delights.

The hoe by which the swelling is pruned is remembrance of death. That by which superfluous moisture is pruned is the shame of confession. That by which dead flesh is pruned is penitential labor. Of the first: “O death, how bitter is your remembrance to a righteous man!” [Note: [Col. 0281] Sir. 3]. “For when a human being dies, he shall inherit serpents, beasts, and worms” [Note: [Col. 0281] Sir. 10]. And likewise, “the destruction of man and beast is the same” [Note: [Col. 0281] Eccl. 3]. Of the second: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be saved” [Note: [Col. 0281] Jas. 5]. For if you do not blush when you confess, confession perishes, or relapse is produced. Of this it is said: “Whoever is washed after contact with a dead person, if he touches a dead body, what profit is that washing?” [Note: [Col. 0281] Sir. 34]. Of the third: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is approaching” [Note: [Col. 0281] Matt. 3]. Hence the prophet: “Return to me with your whole heart, in fasting, weeping, and lamentation” [Note: [Col. 0281] Joel 2]. And the Apostle: “In all things let us present ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in fastings and many vigils” [Note: [Col. 0281] II Cor. 6].

The third pruning, namely of corruption, will be performed by God. For then the sinner will be sanctified. The one who is now in darkness will then see God, who is now hidden from us; the one who is now foul with bodily age will then be renewed. John saw the Church descending prepared in this order: “I saw,” he says, “the holy city Jerusalem [Col. 0282D] coming down from heaven, prepared by God, like a bride adorned for her husband” [Note: [Col. 0281] Rev. 21]. “Holy”: behold the first. “Jerusalem,” which means vision of peace: behold the second. “New”: behold the third. “Adorned”: behold the fourth.

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.”

[THO.] The voice of the preacher has been heard in the land, which began to be ours when it received the word of faith. Therefore, on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, the Psalm is sung: “The earth belongs to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 23]. The voice of the mother, announcing winter’s departure and spring’s arrival, suits those who know how to teach that “the night has passed, but the day [Col. 0283A] has drawn near” [Note: [Col. 0283] Rom. 13]. The voice of the turtledove, which expresses groaning, suits those who groan from longing for their homeland, saying: “We ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption as children of God, the redemption of our body” [Note: [Col. 0283] Rom. 8]. Or they groan for sins, as: “Be miserable and mourn” [Note: [Col. 0283] Jas. 4].

We find four commendable things expressed in Scripture concerning the turtledove, with its name given: it is said to be of modest simplicity; it is offered in sacrifice; it seeks a nest for itself and its young, lest it seem to wander; and its voice is recognized as a sign of spring. Of the first: “Your cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove” [Note: [Col. 0283] Song 1]. Of the second: “Whoever cannot find a lamb, let him offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” [Note: [Col. 0283] Lev. 12]. Of the third: “The sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest in which to place her young” [Note: [Col. 0283] Ps. 83]. [Col. 0283B] Of the fourth: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.”

The first belongs to Christ because of his innocent simplicity: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he was silent and did not open his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0283] Isa. 53]. Likewise: “He shall not be turbulent or anxious” [Note: [Col. 0283] Isa. 42]. The second belongs to the Passion: “He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” [Note: [Col. 0283] Phil. 2]. The third belongs to the Ascension: “I go,” he says, “to prepare a place for you” [Note: [Col. 0283] John 14]. The fourth belongs to preaching and to prayer, as he intercedes for us before the Father [Note: [Col. 0283] Heb. 9], because “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who became the propitiation for our sins” [Note: [Col. 0283] I John 2]. But let us examine each of these.

First, the turtledove is said to be of modest simplicity. Three things hinder this. For the shameless person, first, unashamed to sin, confidently works iniquity; he presumes to undertake something above himself and not belonging to him; and he neglects correction. Of the first: “You have acquired the forehead of a harlot” [Note: [Col. 0283] Jer. 3]. Likewise: “They were not ashamed before the faces of the elders” [Note: [Col. 0283] Lam. 5]. These proclaimed their sin as Sodom did; they are that Israelite who, before all Israel, went in to the Midianite prostitute [Note: [Col. 0283] Num. 25]. Of the second: “Do not seek what is too high for you, nor investigate what is beyond your strength” [Note: [Col. 0283] Sir. 2]. These are King Uzziah, who presumed the priestly office and therefore became leprous [Note: [Col. 0283] II Chron. 26]. Of the third: “Because you despised all my counsel and neglected my corrections, I also will laugh at your destruction” [Note: [Col. 0283] Prov. 1]. These are the sons of Eli, who did not receive [Col. 0283D] their father’s correction [Note: [Col. 0283] I Sam. 4].

As a figure of these three, the Psalmist joins together three Psalms among the Songs of Ascents, in which he says that he is free from them. The first is “Out of the depths” [Note: [Col. 0283] Ps. 120], in which he acknowledges and laments his sin thus: “If you mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” [Note: [Col. 0283] Ibid.]. In the second he removes presumption, saying: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up” [Note: [Col. 0283] Ps. 103]. In the third he shows himself gentle in receiving correction: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his gentleness” [Note: [Col. 0283] Ps. 131].

The Apostle exhorts us “to live soberly, justly, and piously [Col. 0284A] in this age” [Note: [Col. 0283] Tit. 2]: soberly with regard to the flesh, justly with regard to sensuality, and piously with regard to spirituality. Soberly, lest the flesh be intoxicated; justly, lest Eve—that is, sensuality—rule Adam, that is, the spirit; piously, lest anything other than God be sought in contemplation.

For these three things Leviticus teaches [Note: [Col. 0283] ch. 3] that three kinds of living creatures are to be sacrificed. It teaches that oxen are to be sacrificed among quadrupeds, turtledoves among birds that fly lower, and pigeons among birds that fly higher. The first sacrifice is that of the flesh, the second of sensuality, the third of the spirit.

The flesh is sacrificed in three ways. Some people’s flesh, whether they will or not, is sacrificed because it is scourged by God, yet they are not corrected. Others voluntarily suffer for Christ unto the shedding of blood. A third group is worn down by vigils and fasts, so that the spirit may contemplate more freely. The first is Ephraim’s heifer [Note: [Col. 0283] Hos. 10], trained to love threshing; the second is the red heifer, which is sacrificed at evening; the third is Samson’s heifer, in which the ploughmen receive from Samson the solution of a riddle extorted through vexatious affliction. This means that, through affliction of the flesh, reason and understanding merit to have heavenly secrets revealed to them by Christ more freely and more subtly. This is the sacrifice of quadrupeds, that is, of the flesh.

But if the flesh is afflicted outwardly, sensuality must be restrained inwardly. This is the sacrifice of the turtledove, which must restrain itself inwardly from corrupt habits, lest it desire worldly things too much. [Col. 0284C] Yet it ought to provide the body with what belongs to it—that is, to give it sensible satisfaction—and to be content in taking food. This is what Leviticus commands there: that it be sacrificed with its head bent back toward its body [Note: [Col. 0283] Lev. 1]. But lest the spirit become proud through the knowledge of heavenly things which it contemplates, it too is sacrificed when it is restrained from this presumption, by this law: as was said of the turtledove, it should turn its head back toward the body—that is, it should look upon its own misery in order to be humbled by it.

The nest is threefold: the nest of grace, the nest of conscience, and the nest of heavenly rest. In the first it begets young; in the second it desires to be buried; in the third it prepares an eternal dwelling for its young. It begets young—that is, inward affections and the fruits of works; it desires to be buried, so that it may sleep and rest [Col. 0284D] together in peace [Note: [Col. 0283] Ps. 4], and grow into God. In the third it prepares a nest for its young, so that they may rest in God.

Of the first: “When you walk along the way and find a bird’s nest, with the mother sitting above her young, you shall hold the young captive, but permit the mother to go free” [Note: [Col. 0283] Deut. 22]. This nest is God’s grace; the mother brooding over her young is the purity of the turtledove—that is, of the faithful soul. It creates young when, with confidence, it asks greater things of God, is bolder against the devil, and fears the curses of neighbors less. But lest vanity, pride, and so forth perhaps creep in, the young must be held captive [Col. 0285A] within. But the mother—that is, purity—must go forth freely: through the mouth, so that pure words may be spoken; through the hands, so that works may be pure; and likewise through the remaining senses.

Of the second: “In my little nest I shall die, and like a palm tree I shall multiply my days” [Note: [Col. 0285] Job 29]. Of the third: “The sparrow has found herself a house and the turtledove a nest in which to place her young” [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 83].

There follows concerning the voice of the turtledove: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” Our heart is here understood as the land—not “my” land but “our” land—because it ought to be common to God and to all human beings: to God through devotion; to a brother through love; to a neighbor through compassion; to oneself through the virtue of moderation. To God through devotion, that we may have delight in him; to a brother through love, that we may love him as ourselves; to a neighbor through compassion, that we may bear their burdens [Col. 0285B] [Note: [Col. 0285] Gal. 6]; to ourselves through the virtue of moderation, that we may restrain ourselves from vices. From this land which we possess, this voice is heard in that land which we await; this voice is the groaning of the heart.

There are two groanings of the turtledove, two of the dove, and one common to both. The groanings of the turtledove, which flies lower, are those of penitents; the groanings of the dove, which flies higher, are those of spiritual persons; the groanings of compassion belong to both. Behold five: the first is of suffering, the second of suffering beforehand (*propasio*), the third of compassion, the fourth from weariness of life, the fifth from the soul’s desire. The first is for iniquity; the second for temptation; the third for a neighbor’s need; the fourth for the sojourn in this misery; the fifth for longing for the homeland.

[Col. 0285C] Of the first: afflicted daily for our sins, let us with tears await our end.^56 Of the second: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 6]. Of the third, Mattathias: “Why was I born to see the evils of my people?” [Note: [Col. 0285] 1 Macc. 2]. Of the fourth: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged” [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 119]. Of the fifth: “When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 41]. For these five groans just enumerated above, God in turn bestows five graces. To those who groan with the groan of suffering, God gives grace by which he guards them as though they were his own possession. To those who groan for their sins, he gives grace by which in his goodness he forgives them their sins. To those who groan out of compassion, he gives the grace of generosity, by which they clothe and feed the poor. To those who groan from weariness of the present life, he gives grace by which they hope for and love the resurrection [Col. 0285D]. To those who groan from longing for their homeland, he gives grace by which God will appear to them.

As a figure of these five graces, we read in the Old Testament of five Annas; for *Anna* is interpreted “grace.” The first is the Anna of Elkanah, whose name means “God’s possession.” For God possesses the first group as his own, lest they fall; hence Paul says: “Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” [Note: [Col. 0285] Rom. 14]. The second is the Anna of Tobit, whose name means “the Lord’s good one.” For in his goodness he forgives sins to those who so groan; hence: “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, and to the soul [Col. 0286A] that seeks him” [Note: [Col. 0285] Lam. 3]. Hear of this goodness: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety of my sin” [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 35]. The third is the Anna of Raguel, whose name means “the Lord’s feeding.” For those who sigh out of compassion receive from God the grace by which they feed the poor, and hear at judgment: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” [Note: [Col. 0285] Matt. 25]. The fourth is the Anna of Joachim, whose name means “resurrection.” For those who sigh from weariness of this life receive from God grace by which they may be assured of the resurrection; hence the Apostle: “We do not wish you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve as do the rest, who have no hope; for the dead who are in Christ shall rise first. Then we who live, who remain, together…” [Note: [Col. 0285] 1 Thess. 4], etc. The fifth is Anna, daughter of [Col. 0286B] Phanuel, whose name means “appearance of God.” For those who groan in longing for their homeland will see God in his glory; hence: “His eyes shall see the king in his beauty” [Note: [Col. 0285] Isa. 33].

There follows concerning the voice of the turtledove. We mentioned above three lands: the land of the dying, the land of the sick, and the land of the living.
