Likewise there are three voices: the voice of the vulture, the voice of the turtledove, and the voice of lightning. In the first land the voice of the vulture is heard; in the second, the voice of lightning; in the third, the voice of the turtledove. The voice of the vulture seduces to the devouring of souls and bodies; the voice of lightning—by thunder—threatens the punishments of hell, and—by its flash—the brightness of things above. The voice of the turtledove is that of Christ, whom we have as advocate with the Father [Note: [Col. 0285] 1 John 2].

For in the first case: “Your adversary, the devil, goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour; resist him, firm in faith” [Note: [Col. 0285] 1 Pet. 5]. “For his mouth abounded in malice, and his tongue kept deceit” [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 49]. For the enemy said: “I will pursue and overtake; I will divide the spoils; my soul shall be filled. I will draw my sword; my hand shall slay them” [Note: [Col. 0285] Exod. 12].

There follows the voice of lightning. It says in thunder: “Cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” [Note: [Col. 0285] Matt. 22]. “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” [Note: [Col. 0285] Matt. 13]. For Christ, coming into the world, brought these things from above to us; hence: “From the throne proceed flashes of lightning, voices, and thunders” [Note: [Col. 0285] Rev. 4]. The flashes are the promise of brightness, the voices are prayer, and the thunders are threats.

Concerning the voice of the turtledove—that is, Christ—it is said: “We have with the [Col. 0286D] Father an advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous, who became propitiation for our sins” [Note: [Col. 0285] 1 John 2]; and not only for ours, but for those of the whole world. Hear the voice of this turtledove groaning for us: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me” [Note: [Col. 0285] John 17]. Thus he himself prays for us.

The time of cutting, that is, the time of harvest, has come.

**CARD.** The text is otherwise. Therefore, in return for the sowing of merits, receive sheaves of rewards. Come also because the need of the Church so requires, because the voice of the turtledove—that is, of the Church—has been heard in our land. As though he said: In our land, that is, in the solid stability [Col. 0287A] of our kingdom, the voice of the turtledove—that is, of the Church—has been heard; she has recognized the time of her coming to the Lord, crying out and requesting fitting help, because

The fig tree has put forth its early figs.

**[THO.]** The fig tree has put forth its early figs when the Synagogue brought forth the apostles; born of her, they supplied believers with the sweetest food of doctrine. Or, what seems better: by the early figs which the fig tree bears instead of flowers are signified the prophets, who touched upon the Savior’s coming at close range; he is compared to the true fig. The succeeding fruit, however, is called the apostles.

In the Gospel we read of four fig trees, which we set down here. The first was cursed by the Lord because of its barrenness; the second was that beneath whose shade Nathanael lay hidden; the third was spared being cut down at the gardener’s request; the fourth was that beneath which Zacchaeus was placed in order to see Christ. In the first are figured those who retain freedom to sin; in the second, those who, though they do not do good, nevertheless turn away from evil because of their horror of Gehenna; in the third, those who, already loving God, begin a good manner of life; in the fourth, those who cast themselves beneath themselves, because they have tasted heavenly sweetness. The first produces dryness; the second greenness; the third puts forth early figs; the fourth, sweetest fruits. The first despise; the second fear; the third already love; the fourth, casting themselves beneath themselves in solitude, deserve to receive Christ in the house of their heart, like Zacchaeus, whose name is interpreted “justified.”

Of the first Solomon says [Note: [Col. 0287] Prov. 48, apparently an erroneous citation]: “When the sinner comes into the depth of evils, [Col. 0287C] he despises.” Of the second: “The fear of the Lord drives out sin” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ecclus. 1]. Of the third: “Their sons are like young plants in their youth” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 143]. Of the fourth: “He shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has lifted himself above himself” [Note: [Col. 0287] Lam. 3].

We read in the Gospel that “a good tree cannot bear bad fruits, nor can a bad tree bear good fruits” [Note: [Col. 0287] Matt. 7]. From this we gather that there are both bad figs and good figs; hence the prophet says: “I see bad figs, very bad” [Note: [Col. 0287] Jer. 24]. And again: “I see good figs, very good” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ibid.]. We must first deal with the bad ones, so that, once evil is known, good may be possessed more sweetly.

Thus, of the tree are early figs—that is, figs that are early or unripe. And there are bad figs, figs very bad. In the first are external signs of miracles or of a good life; in the second are fleshly sins that delight; in the third is corruption of faith. The first is like a trick, the second like hay, the third like poison, which deceives human beings. Hay, because pleasure quickly passes; poison, because it infects human beings. Therefore, in the first they seek to appear [good]; in the second, to satisfy their desires; in the third, to destroy faith.

The first will say at judgment: “Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, and perform signs in your name?” [Note: [Col. 0287] Matt. 7]. Of the second Solomon says: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” [Note: [Col. 0287] Prov. 2]. Of the third Jeremiah says: “The sea-monsters bared the breast; they suckled [Col. 0288A] their young” [Note: [Col. 0287] Lam. 4].

Of these three Jeremiah says: “The children gather wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the fat, so as to make cakes for the queen of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0287] Jer. 7]. These children are evil people, corrupted in faith by others, as if by evil fathers; they gather wood while performing evil works. The evil fathers are those who have outward signs, who kindle the fire while they commend the evil works of the children, now by signs, now by persuasion. The women are those softened by fleshly pleasures, who present their own desires to others and thus, as it were, knead in fat. Cakes are so called from *placere*, “to please”; by making cakes in this way, they make offerings for diabolical pride, which is called queen by antiphrasis, because the devil wished through pride to reign in heaven.

Since signs have been mentioned because of the early figs, it should be known that there are four kinds of signs.

There is a good sign in a good person; a bad sign in a bad person; a good sign in a bad person; and a bad sign in a good person. The first is when a person appears outwardly good, either through religious observance or through miracles, and is such inwardly; hence David says: “Work with me a sign for good” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 85]. Through miracles Stephen performed great wonders and signs among the people [Note: [Col. 0287] Acts 6]. You have heard that from every tribe of the children of Israel twelve thousand were sealed with the sign of the living God, so that they might say: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 4]. Of such persons it is said in the Song of Songs: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are [Col. 0288C] those of doves, apart from that which lies hidden within” [Note: [Col. 0287] Song 1].

A bad sign in a bad person is when a person either does something outwardly, or something happens to him outwardly, from which he is perceived inwardly to be evil—like those “who set up their signs as signs.” Of these it is said: “From the heart come evil thoughts, namely thefts, adulteries, murders” [Note: [Col. 0287] Matt. 15].

A good sign in a bad person is when someone appears good by miracles, outward religious observance, or even worldly prosperity, though he is nevertheless bad; or when prosperity smiles upon him to his own harm. They appear good through miracles. Such are those who will say at judgment: “Lord, did we not perform signs in your name, and cast out demons in your name?” [Note: [Col. 0287] Matt. 7]. To them the reply will be: “I do not know you” [Note: [Col. 0287] Matt. 25]. Of such people it is said that they are whitewashed tombs, [Col. 0288D] inwardly full of dead men’s bones and every kind of uncleanness.

A bad sign in a good person is when misfortune happens to someone, and from it he appears evil to some who think he is being scourged by God for his sins—as Job’s friends thought concerning him—although that scourge was for good, because it served his merit. Such people say: “They have set me as a target for an arrow” [Note: [Col. 0287] Lam. 3]. For an arrow wounds the target at which it is aimed. Paul consoles such people thus: “Although that which is outward, our old human being, is being corrupted, yet that which is inward is renewed from day to day” [Note: [Col. 0287] 2 Cor. 4].

Behold the four signs of the good tree, like unripe figs. [Col. 0289A] There are good figs; there are very good figs.

By these figs a threefold faith is signified: there is a more rudimentary faith, a purer faith, and a firmer faith. The first existed before Christ’s incarnation; the second after the resurrection; the third at the sending of the Holy Spirit, after the ascension. The first was more rudimentary because of the newness of these things; the second purer through the forgiveness of sins; the third firmer because God gave the Holy Spirit more abundantly. For the first, second, and third alike are inspired by the sweetness of the Holy Spirit.

For the Holy Spirit was given to the first parents and their followers; hence: “The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters” [Note: [Col. 0289] Gen. 1], that is, over unformed matter. “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh”: according to some, that is, “I will take the Holy Spirit away from them.” Others [Col. 0289B] interpret it more mercifully thus: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings,” that is, “I will take away from them the spirit of my wrath, because they are flesh” [Note: [Col. 0289] Gen. 6], that is, weak; and therefore I shall spare them.

It was given after the resurrection for the forgiveness of sins; hence: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” [Note: [Col. 0289] John 20]. It was also given a third time after the ascension; hence: “The Holy Spirit proceeding from the throne [toward] the breasts of the apostles,” etc. In the first instance the Holy Spirit was sweet; in the second, sweeter; in the third, sweetest. His sweetness, therefore, a threefold sweetness, is here signified by the three kinds of figs: by his early [Note: [Col. 0289] Mic. 7] or unripe figs, the first, rudimentary faith; by good figs, the pure faith; and by very good figs, the firmer faith.

Of the first the prophet said: “My soul desired unripe figs” [Col. 0289C] [Note: [Col. 0289] Ibid.], namely, that those whom he rebuked might have at least the rudimentary faith of the ancient fathers. The second figs, that is, the good figs, were those from whose mass Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0289] ch. 38] made a poultice for King Hezekiah when he was ill, and he recovered from his sickness. The third, that is, the very good figs, were those of which we read: “The trees of the forest came to the fig tree and said to it, ‘Rule over us.’ But it said to them, ‘Can I forsake my sweetness and my most sweet fruits, in order to be promoted among the trees of the forests?’” [Note: [Col. 0289] Judg. 9]. The trees of the forest are the rulers of the world, sterile in good works. Those who had received the Holy Spirit did not wish to yield to them, whether for a price or at the inducement of dignities, so as to be moved away from faith in Jesus Christ; [Col. 0289D] for they had been strengthened in that sweetness of the Holy Spirit.

The flowering vines gave forth their fragrance.

**THO.** By the flower of the vine is signified the renown of the Church as it arose; planted in Jerusalem, it spread far and wide through its reputation. The flower of this vine is very pleasing, because the juice pressed from it both gives health to the user and provides delight. Or, morally: by the flower of the vine is expressed the beginning of spiritual joy, after which a fuller joy is awaited in heaven, just as fruit is awaited to come from a flower [Col. 0290A], namely wine that gladdens [Note: [Col. 0289] Ps. 103].

For the holy person has three kinds of joy: first, because he has left vanity and worldly joys; second, because he follows in Christ’s footsteps [Note: [Col. 0289] 1 Pet. 2]; third, because he will receive rewards. In the first, life is purified; in the second, it is justified;^57 in the third, it is made blessed. The first is true, because it tends toward blessedness, but not unmixed, because the dregs of temptation intrude. The second is unmixed, temptation having now been conquered, but not full because of the deficiency of this miserable life. The third is full, because there fullness of glory is found.

Christ encouraged the disciples concerning the first when he said: “Take courage, for I have conquered the world” [Note: [Col. 0289] John 16]. Of the second he says: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0289] John 8]; and, to assure them concerning the third, he added: [Col. 0290B] “But shall have the light of life” [Note: [Col. 0289] Ibid.].

Hear of joy true but not unmixed: “Count it all joy when you fall into diverse temptations,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0289] Jas. 1]. If it were not true, the Apostle would not invite us to it; but it is not unmixed, because it undergoes the disturbance of temptations. Hear of joy true and unmixed: “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0289] Matt. 5]. Hear of full joy: “Ask and you shall receive” [Note: [Col. 0289] Luke 11], “that your joy may be full” [Note: [Col. 0289] John 16].

The first joy, therefore, is that by which a person rejoices when he has left behind vain glory, which arises in a person. Concerning the joys in which the world rejoices:

There is glory which arises beneath you; glory which arises from you; glory which arises beside you; and glory which arises [Col. 0290C] within you. The first is from sins; the second, from bodily goods; the third, from temporal goods; the fourth is the Son of the eternal Father. Of the first: “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” [Note: [Col. 0289] Ps. 51]. And the poet:

> No glory in your sin is to be sought.

Yet we may glory in the destruction of sins; hence the Apostle: “Thanks be to God that you were once slaves of sin; but you obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine into which you were delivered” [Note: [Col. 0289] Rom. 6].

Of the second, by which we glory in bodily goods: “Let not the strong man glory in his strength; for all flesh is hay, and all its glory is like the flower of hay” [Note: [Col. 0289] Jer. 9; 1 Pet. 1]. But we may also rightly glory in our flesh if we suffer in it for Christ; hence the Apostle: “I will most gladly [Col. 0290D] glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” [Note: [Col. 0289] 2 Cor. 12]; and: “We glory in tribulations” [Note: [Col. 0289] Rom. 5]; and: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0289] Gal. 6].

They glory in temporal goods who glory in the abundance of their riches. But, “When the glory of his house has increased, do not fear; for the glory of his house shall not go down with him” [Note: [Col. 0289] Ps. 48]. Nevertheless, we may rightly glory in them by using them well, so that in all things God may be glorified.

Evil glory arises within you if you are proud of God’s gifts. [Col. 0291A] “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” [Note: [Col. 0291] 1 Cor. 4]. Therefore, “let the one who glories glory in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0291] 2 Cor. 10], because “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within, in golden fringes” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ps. 44].

Within you are three things in which you may rightly glory: a pure conscience, righteousness, and delight in future blessedness. Of the first the Apostle says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0291] 2 Cor. 1]. Of the second David says: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; glory, all you upright in heart” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ps. 31]. Of the third the prophet says: “When you have been weaned from milk, feast upon the sight of his glory. ‘Glory shall arise over you’” [Note: [Col. 0291] Isa. 60], namely, the Son of the eternal Father. Hence Isaiah says: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, [Col. 0291B] for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ibid.]. Truly the glory of the Lord has risen over you—and you cannot attain to it—for he was conceived without the seed of a carnal father, born without corruption of virginity, established and borne in the womb without injury to the womb.

Therefore, when they have a good opinion founded upon faith, it may truly be said: The flowering vines gave forth their fragrance. For the flower smells sweetly on the vine when good reputation gives off its fragrance in the Church.

The joys of the world are no less to be shunned than vanity. The wise person carefully considers them, so that, having recognized them, he may flee them more readily and love their opposites more fervently. Thus Solomon sent his ships to Tarshish, and from there they brought him gold, elephant tusks, monkeys, and leopards [Note: [Col. 0291] 2 Chron. 9]. Solomon, who is called wise, is every righteous person; Tarshish is called the examination of joy; the sea is the world; the ship is religious curiosity, which brings from Tarshish—that is, the examination of joy—gold, that is, worldly wisdom; silver, that is, eloquence; elephant tusks, that is, the powerful people of the world, who devour and consume others. The monkey is an animal full of mockery, by which are signified those who rejoice. Because the leopard is an animal marked with diverse spots, it signifies double-dealers and deceivers; or the peacock, that is, those who glory in the beauty of feathers, that is, of virtues.

Of the first: “Our gold has rusted” [Note: [Col. 0291] Jas. 5]. Of the second: “Your silver has been turned into dross” [Note: [Col. 0291] Isa. 1]. Of the third: “Do not all who work iniquity know, those who devour [Col. 0291D] my people as though eating bread?” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ps. 52]. Of the fourth the Lord complains, saying: “I have become a mockery to all my people, their song all day long” [Note: [Col. 0291] Lam. 3]. Of the fifth: “Who speaks truth in his heart, who has not dealt deceitfully with his tongue” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ps. 14]. Seeing these false joys, the Wise One loves true joys more greatly. And: “They speak peace with their neighbor, but evils are in their hearts” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ps. 27].

The unmixed joys by which they follow Christ’s footsteps are principally possessed in three ways: because they have conquered the world; because they have made their good purpose firm; [Col. 0292A] and third, because they attribute nothing to themselves but everything to the grace of God. The first is through purity of faith; the second, through knowledge of truth; the third, through heavenly inspiration. Of the first: “Everything born of God conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” [Note: [Col. 0291] 2 John 5]. Of the second David says: “Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples, because his mercy is confirmed over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ps. 116]. Of the third Paul says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0291] 1 Cor. 15].

These are the three apostles whom Jesus took up the mountain, and before whom he was transfigured [Note: [Col. 0291] Matt. 17]. To the first pertains James, whose name means “supplanter”; to the second, Peter, whose name means “firm”; to the third, John, whose name means “grace.”

Full joys likewise have three things: in the kingdom there shall be no fault, misery shall not be feared, and God’s presence shall be seen. These are the other three who were seen in the same Transfiguration. To the first pertains Moses, whose name means “saved from the waters of sins”; to the second, Elijah, whose name means “my God,” who destroyed the corruption of miseries; to the third, Jesus, whose name means “Savior,” in the vision of whom shall be the salvation of all.

Of the first: “Where is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? For the sting of death is sin” [Note: [Col. 0291] 1 Cor. 15]. Of the second: “A natural body is sown; a spiritual body shall rise. It is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it shall rise in glory” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ibid.]. “The Lord shall build Zion and shall be seen in his glory” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ps. 101]. “Blessed are the pure in heart, [Col. 0292C] for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0291] Matt. 5].

These three joys are the flowers of the vine: the first have the strength of medicine; the second give fragrance; the third give the flavor of fruit. For the first drive away serpents, that is, sins; the second anticipate the good things that are in the homeland; the third show things long desired. Of the first: “My beloved is to me a cluster of cyprus (henna) in the vineyards of En-gedi” [Note: [Col. 0291] Song 1], which means “the spring of the kid,” that is, of sin, which it washes away. Of the second: “I, like a vine, have borne the sweetness of fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ecclus. 24]. Of the third it is said as the Passion drew near: “I shall drink no more of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new in my kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0291] Mark 14].

The fig tree has put forth its early figs.

**[CARD.]** The flowering vines gave forth their fragrance; the fig tree [Col. 0292D] has put forth its early figs. Of these Nahum says [Note: [Col. 0291] ch. 3]: “All your fortifications are like fig trees with their early figs: if shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater.” The fortifications of the soul are virtues and the works of virtues; but if the wind of temptation shakes the virtues, good works fall like early figs into the mouth of the tempter and are devoured by him.

Flowering vines are easily harmed, as he says: “Its cluster shall be harmed as in the first flower” [Note: [Col. 0291] Job 15]. Flowering vines give fragrance when the beginnings of good works emit a sweet odor; but if excessive cold or heat touches the flowering vine, then, when the flower has been shaken off, the cluster perishes. Thus, prosperity or adversity in this age often causes the beginnings of good works to wither. Therefore, because both the fig tree that has put forth early figs and the flowering vines need help against the dangers mentioned above, for their assistance it is said to the Virgin:

Arise, my friend, my spouse, and come, my dove, into the clefts of the rock and the hollow of the wall.

**[THO.]** The bridegroom had come to the bride and had awakened her. He repeats his summons so as to add this: to show her the place to which she should come, namely, into the clefts of the rock. “And the rock was Christ” [Note: [Col. 0293] 1 Cor. 10]. Therefore she is led into the clefts of the rock when, rejecting temporal things, she is raised to the things above. This path, however, is shown to be undertaken through the clefts of the rock—not under the open sky, nor so as to suffer the burning of the sun, lest she become dark again.

By the hollows of the wall he meant the places of the angels who fell through pride and were left, as it were, empty; they are to be filled from among human beings, as from living stones, where Christ himself is the cornerstone. Or we may say that the guardianship of angels is the wall in Christ’s vineyard.

During the time and place of her pilgrimage, the Church has two consolations: from the past, remembrance of Christ’s Passion; from the future, the thought that she belongs to the lot of the saints and the confidence that she will receive it. Each of us may hollow out, wherever he wishes, the heavenly wall: now revisiting the patriarchs, now [Col. 0293C] greeting the prophets, now joining the senate of the apostles, now being admitted among the choirs of martyrs; and likewise surveying in the mind the ranks and dwellings of the blessed virtues. Hence, rejoicing and marveling in conscience, we burst forth into praise of God and thanksgiving. Thus the bridegroom desires to see our face—that is, our conscience—and to hear our voice; hence he says: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” [Note: [Col. 0293] Song 8]. This is concerning the wall.

We may hollow out the rock, namely, God himself, by contemplating him. Here two kinds of contemplation may be discerned: one concerning the state and glory of the heavenly city, the other concerning the majesty of the king himself. Through the clefts of the rock waters are usually drawn from pools; hence Jeremiah: “Leave the city and dwell [Col. 0293D] in the rock, inhabitants of Moab; be like a dove nesting at the topmost opening of a cleft” [Note: [Col. 0293] Jer. 48]. “And the rock was Christ” [Note: [Col. 0293] 1 Cor. 10]. The clefts are the wounds in his feet and hands, from which the blood came forth by which we are washed. There he wished the bride’s face—that is, her conscience—to be washed, that she might be presented to him clean. The wall is Christ’s flesh; the hollow is the wound in his side, through which he wishes her prayer to pass to his heart, because in such hollows a voice usually sounds more clearly.

We read of waters brought forth from a rock, of rocks from water, and of rocks to water. The first occurred when Moses struck the rock in the wilderness and [Col. 0294A] waters of divine grace flowed forth [Note: [Col. 0293] Exod. 17]. The second, when the children of Israel crossing over took twelve stones from the Jordan [Note: [Col. 0293] Josh. 4], that is, the apostles from the flowing divine grace. Others were brought from the place of the camp, that is, from the world, to God’s grace.

But now let us consider these things morally. The first place was in the wilderness, the second in the Jordan, the third in the camp. The first place is penitence; the second, the presumption of confidence; the third, the despair of distrust. The first stone is the strength of patience; the second, firmness in good; the third, obstinacy in evil. He set a good stone in the wilderness who said: “I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them; I did not turn my face away from those rebuking and spitting upon me” [Note: [Col. 0293] Isa. 50].

Good [Col. 0294B] stones must be gathered from the Jordan and placed in the place of the camp, and conversely, so that “on the day of good things you may not be forgetful of evils, nor on the day of evils forgetful of good things” [Note: [Col. 0293] Ecclus. 11]. Of the first: “I shall never forget your justifications, for by them you have given me life” [Note: [Col. 0293] Ps. 118]. Of the second: “For I know my iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0293] Ps. 50]. Of the third Pharaoh says: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” [Note: [Col. 0293] Exod. 5].

That first stone was strong for bearing our burdens, “because he himself bore our infirmities and carried our burdens” [Note: [Col. 0293] Isa. 53]. He carried our burdens either by having them in himself or by suffering for them. Now some burdens are necessary, some violent, and some voluntary. Necessary burdens were imposed upon us by the first parents, though necessary only by God. Violent burdens are now from God, now from the devil, in temptation or affliction. Voluntary burdens arise either by yielding toward temptation or by undertaking toil for sins.

There are five reasons for which God afflicts a human being: for sins, as Miriam, Moses’ sister [Note: [Col. 0293] Num. 12]; as the beginning of eternal punishment, as Herod [Note: [Col. 0293] Matt. 2]; for testing, as Job [Note: [Col. 0293] ch. 1]; for increase of the crown, as Paul [Note: [Col. 0293] Acts 9]; and for the glory of God, as the man born blind [Note: [Col. 0293] John 9].

Therefore, according to Isaiah, there are eleven burdens which we bear. The first is this: sometimes a burden is imposed upon us by the world; this is the burden of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0293] Isa. 13]. Babylon means “confusion” and signifies the world, the love of which cupidity makes burdensome in three ways: through labor, fear, and sorrow. For by labor a person attains what he desires; he possesses it [Col. 0294D] with fear; he loses it with sorrow.

There are three things a person desires in the world: first, eminence; second, gifts of body and soul, namely wisdom, beauty, and strength; third, things related to pleasure, namely an abundance of possessions, adornment, and a woman. He desires the first above himself, the second within himself, the third around himself: the first, that he may be beautiful; the second, that he may be glorious; the third, that he may be pleasure-loving.

Of these Solomon says [Note: [Col. 0293] Eccles. 1]: “I was king in Jerusalem”—behold the first. “God gave me wisdom”—behold the second. “I had riches beyond all the kings who were before me in Jerusalem”—behold the third. But first he said: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not investigate things greater than yourself” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ecclus. 3]. For the higher the rank, the heavier the fall. Therefore, one who desires high things ought to avoid ruin. From the first things people come into abasement; from the second, into weakness; from the third, into bitterness.

Nebuchadnezzar is our example of the first: “Is this not Babylon,” he says, “which I made for the glory and beauty of my kingdom?” [Note: [Col. 0295] Dan. 4]. And immediately he was changed into an ox. To those who desire gifts within themselves, the Apostle says: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you” [Note: [Col. 0295] 1 Tim. 1]; for one neglects it who either does not act by it or misuses it. Thus they fall into weakness: so Solomon’s wisdom was made foolish, Absalom’s beauty destroyed, Samson’s strength blinded.

Of the third things it is said concerning a woman: [Col. 0295B] “Her throat is smoother than oil, and her latter end^58 bitter as wormwood” [Note: [Col. 0295] Prov. 3]. Of riches: “Do not be high-minded, nor hope in the uncertainty of riches” [Note: [Col. 0295] Rom. 11; 1 Tim. 6]. Of adornment: “Not in costly clothing” [Note: [Col. 0295] Luke 7]. But see to what bitterness he came who first abounded in these things—namely, that prodigal son who afterward fed pigs [Note: [Col. 0295] Luke 15]. Behold what is desired in the world.

But see with how much labor these things are acquired: people labor in heart, labor in body, and labor in speech. In heart they labor in three ways: by desire, anxiety, and solicitude. By desire, through which they love a thing; by anxiety, through which they waver in hope whether they will acquire it; by solicitude, through which they arrange the method of acquiring it. Jeremiah removed this desire from himself when he said: “O Lord, I have not desired the day of man; you know it” [Note: [Col. 0295] Jer. 17]. Of the second David says: “My spirit was made anxious over me; my heart was troubled within me” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ps. 142]. Of the third the Lord says: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’” [Note: [Col. 0295] Matt. 6].

They also labor in body: private persons in daily work, soldiers in prowess of arms, clerics in the study of knowledge. Of the first: “All a person’s labor is for his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0295] Eccles. 6]. Of the second: “A man shall not be strengthened by his own might” [Note: [Col. 0295] 1 Sam. 2]. Against the third: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not premeditate how you shall answer” [Note: [Col. 0295] Luke 25].

But the fear of the world is not only concerned with things acquired by labor. For there is fear over the loss of one’s possessions; a second fear, over the disturbance caused by living creatures; [Col. 0295D] a third, over the disordering of the elements. The first arises from the loss of property, of carnal friends, and of the comforts of one’s own body. Job was afflicted in these three respects; hence he himself says: “And that which I feared has come upon me” [Note: [Col. 0295] Job 3.]; for he lost his substance, his children died, and he endured the anguish of the flesh. But he himself teaches what we ought to do in such a case: “The Lord,” he says, “gave; the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0295] Job 1.].

The second fear, namely that arising from the disturbance caused by living creatures, has three forms: the snares of evil persons are feared; [Col. 0296A] the savagery of beasts is feared; the infection of venomous creatures is feared. Daniel was tested in these three ways. For there were malicious men who contrived to tear him away from the king’s side; secondly, he was cast into the lions’ den; thirdly, he contended with a venomous dragon [Note: [Col. 0295] Dan. 6.]. But because he feared God, he was delivered from them all. Hence David rejoices that he has been delivered from these three things. Of the first: “He himself delivered me from the snare of hunters” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ps. 90.]; of the other two: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and shall tread down the lion and the dragon” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ibid.].

The third fear of the world arises from disturbances of the elements in three ways: in atmospheric phenomena, in earthquakes, and in storms at sea. Peter experienced atmospheric disturbances; hence: “When he saw the strong wind coming, he was afraid” [Note: [Col. 0295] Matt. 14.]. The Jews experienced an earthquake at Christ’s passion; Paul, storms at sea, he who was a day and a night in the depths of the sea. Of these David says, first concerning the storm at sea: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and feared, and the depths were troubled—the multitude of the sound of waters” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ps. 77.]. And of thunder: “The clouds gave forth their voice; the voice of your thunder was in the wheel. Your lightnings illuminated the world” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ibid.]. He adds concerning the movement of the earth: “The earth was shaken and trembled” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ibid.]. Concerning these things the three youths spoke, that they might be delivered from them: “Bless the Lord, seas and rivers”; and: “Bless the Lord, lightning and cloud”; and: “Let the earth bless the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0295] Dan. 3.].

But worldly sorrow depends on the first three things. For we grieve when the renown of our high estate is reduced to nothing, when the glory [Col. 0296C] of favors is humbled, and when pleasures are cast down into bitterness. Jeremiah laments these three. Of the first he says: “How does the city, once full of people, sit solitary? The mistress of nations has become as a widow; the princess of provinces has been made tributary” [Note: [Col. 0295] Lam. 1.]. Of the second: “How the gold has grown dim, how its finest color has changed!” [Note: [Col. 0295] Lam. 4.] Of the third: “Those who feasted luxuriously have perished in the streets; those nurtured in saffron garments have embraced dung” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ibid.].

This is the burden of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0295] Isa. 13.], that is, the confusion of the world. Jeremiah says of it: “Babylon was a golden cup; all nations drank of its wine and became drunk” [Note: [Col. 0295] Isa. 51.]. But that we may flee this burden, and the one that follows it, he says: “Go out from Babylon, and flee from the Chaldeans” [Note: [Col. 0295] Isa. 50.]. For the Chaldeans are said to be fierce. These are the demons, signified by [Col. 0296D] the Philistines when it is said: “The burden of Philistia.” For at times a burden lies upon us through the assault of unclean spirits. And this is called the burden of the Philistines, who are said to be “falling through drink,” and who signify those who, intoxicated by pride, fell from heaven.

In this fall we see a threefold burden: first he was proud; second, he envied; third, he seduced. He was proud against God, envied the first man, and seduced him. And thus he cast him down into this infirmity. First, therefore, he sinned against the humility of the Son; secondly, against the goodness of the Holy Spirit; thirdly, against the power of the [Col. 0297A] supreme Father. On account of the first, therefore, he is called one falling through drink; on account of the remaining two, he is called a twofold ruin. Thus through pride the heart became mountainous; through envy, venomous; through seduction, full of lurking places. In the first, one is exalted over one’s own goods; in the second, one is tortured by grief over another’s goods; in the third, one schemes evil against one’s neighbor. Of the first it is said: “Before ruin the heart is exalted” [Note: [Col. 0297] Prov. 16.]. Of the second: “How long shall I lay up counsels in my soul, grief in my heart all the day?” [Note: [Col. 0297] Ps. 12.] For perhaps David was at some time moved by such a passion. Of the third, Solomon, listing the seven things God hates, included among them “a heart devising most wicked thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0297] Prov. 6.].

Pride burdens the heart, burdens the hands, burdens the tongue: the heart through obstinacy, the tongue through insult, the hands through violence. [Col. 0297B] The first takes away the sabbath of the mind, that is, its rest; the second takes away from one’s neighbor the consolation of speech; the third, the bestowal of mercy. Of the first Jeremiah says: “Do not carry your burdens on the sabbath day” [Note: [Col. 0297] Jer. 17.], that is, on the day of the soul’s rest. Of the second Job says to his friends, who had come to console him but burst forth in insults against him: “You are all burdensome comforters” [Note: [Col. 0297] Job 16.]. Of the third Isaiah says: “Set free those who are broken, and break every burden” [Note: [Col. 0297] Isa. 58.], namely, the burden of violence.

The burden of envy also burdens in three ways: first, through hatred of one’s neighbor it leads to murder; secondly, it consumes the heart tortured by grief; thirdly, it afflicts the body with pallor and emaciation. John says of the first: “Whoever hates his brother [Col. 0297C] is a murderer” [Note: [Col. 0297] 1 John 3.]. Of the second a certain poet says:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which at once  
> Gnaws at its very author, tormenting his mind.

Of the third the same poet says:

> The envious man wastes away at another’s abundant prosperity.  
> [Note: [Col. 0297] Horace, *Epistles* I.2.57.]

Again, the same poet:

> The Sicilian tyrants devised  
> No greater torment than envy.  
> [Note: [Col. 0297] Ibid., v. 58.]

And Solomon says: “Anger kills the foolish man, and envy slays the little one” [Note: [Col. 0297] Job 5.].

The devil also burdens by seduction. And he sometimes burdens in three ways: at one time by affliction of bodies, at another by violent temptation, and at another he deceives fraudulently. He afflicts the body, as we read that an evil spirit from God afflicted Saul, and struck Job with a most grievous sore [Note: [Col. 0297] Job 2.]. That boy also, who sometimes cast himself into fire and often into water, was thrown upon the ground foaming [Col. 0297D] at the mouth. Hence David says: “He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation” [Note: [Col. 0297] Ps. 77.], and so forth.

He also tempts us violently, as he did Paul: “Lest,” he says, “the greatness of the revelations exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me” [Note: [Col. 0297] 2 Cor. 13.], so that he had to cry out: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me” [Note: [Col. 0297] Isa. 38.]. For the devil commands imperiously, saying: “Bow down, that we may pass over” [Note: [Col. 0297] Isa. 51.]. For the enemy says: [Col. 0298A] “I will pursue and overtake; I will divide the spoil; my soul shall be filled. I will draw my sword; my hand shall kill them” [Note: [Col. 0297] Exod. 15.]. And against these threats the Apostle warns us, saying: “Brothers, be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” [Note: [Col. 0297] 1 Pet. 5.]. And he cries out with Pharaoh: “Go to your burdens; you are idle through leisure” [Note: [Col. 0297] Exod. 5.].

He also tempts fraudulently, as he spoke to Eve in peaceable words with deceit: “Why did God command you not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?” And she: “Lest perhaps we die.” And he: “You shall by no means die” [Note: [Col. 0297] Gen. 3.]. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God” [Note: [Col. 0297] 1 John 3.]. And elsewhere: “For the angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light” [Col. 0298B] [Note: [Col. 0297] 2 Cor. 11.]. For he himself says: “I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab’s prophets” [Note: [Col. 0297] 3 Kings 22; 2 Chron. 18.].

Shechem, whose name means “labor,” that is, the devil, was the son of Hamor, that is, Asim, who was king of Eve—that is, who is said to mean “most evil”; because he was the son of the most evil Asim, that is, Lucifer, who fell first, he first violently carried off Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. And after he had violated her, he soothed her and spoke to her heart, that she might remain with him forever [Note: [Col. 0297] Gen. 34.]. So indeed the devil, after he has struck someone down by violent temptation, seduces him by fraudulent temptation, lest he wish to rise again from such a fall.

At times a burden lies upon us through a certain natural and unavoidable necessity. And this is the burden of Moab [Note: [Col. 0297] Isa. 15.], whose name is interpreted “from the father,” expressing that natural necessity which the father has transmitted to the son through generation: such as the unavoidable [Col. 0298C] necessity of eating, drinking, and sleeping. By this we are compelled, after spiritual food, to provide for the burdens of the belly.

This burden is considered in three stages: at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end. At the beginning is lowly conception; in the middle, labor and affliction; at the end, the dissolution of misery. The first is for coming into being; the second, for being sustained; the third, for dying. In the first, observe the foulness; in the second, the labor; in the third, the horror. Consider, therefore, the foulness of the first, and ask that woman with how great a stench she conceives, with what weariness, in the secret place of generation, she nourishes the child with her own blood, and with what pain she gives birth. Hear John speak of spiritual birth with respect to the first two: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will [Col. 0298D] of a man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” [Note: [Col. 0297] John 1.]. For those born carnally are born from man and flesh, that is, from woman. But they are nourished from bloods until birth. Concerning the pain of the woman giving birth, ask Eve, to whom it was said: “In pain you shall bear your children” [Note: [Col. 0297] Gen. 3.]. For there is no pain beyond the pain of a woman in labor: “For a woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0297] John 16.].

Of this beginning Job said: “Man born of a woman” [Note: [Col. 0297] Job 14.]; of the end: “Living for a short time” [Note: [Col. 0297] Ibid.]; of the middle: “He is filled with many miseries” [Note: [Col. 0297] Ibid.]. Again: [Col. 0299A] “Who comes forth like a flower” [Note: [Col. 0299] Job 14.]—behold, the first; “and is crushed” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ibid.]—the second; “and flees like a shadow” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ibid.]—the third.

In the middle, however, four things must be considered. For this burden consists in four things: food and drink; clothing; sleeping and waking; and natural weakness. The first is against want; the second against the severity of atmospheric conditions; the third for restoration; the fourth belongs to the course of life’s ages. This is the heavy yoke, or burden, upon the children of Adam, from the day of their coming out of their mother’s womb until the day of burial into the mother of all.

The first necessity, therefore, is to eat and drink. Hence: “All things wait upon you, that you may give them food in due season” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ps. 103.]; and: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ps. 127.]. But few are those who do not turn this necessity [Col. 0299B] into excess. For through such excess bellies are distended, hearts are dulled, and senses are made foolish. Of the first Paul says: “Food for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” [Note: [Col. 0299] 1 Cor. 6.]. Of the second the Lord says: “See to it that your hearts are not weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness” [Note: [Col. 0299] Luke 21.]. Of the third: “Wine causes even the wise to fall away” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ecclus. 19.].

There are those more attentive to their own pleasure than to the need of the poor, to whom it will be said at judgment: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 25.]. Therefore Job said: “If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it” [Note: [Col. 0299] Job 31.]. Such a one does not escape the fate of “that rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day” [Note: [Col. 0299] Luke 16.]. But what follows? “He was buried in hell” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ibid.]. Nor does that other man escape it, he who said: [Col. 0299C] “My soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, and drink” [Note: [Col. 0299] Luke 12.]. But what did he hear? “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and whose will be the things you have prepared?” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ibid.]

Let them hear the Lord saying: “Do not be anxious for your life, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ Look at the birds of heaven: they neither labor nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. And why are you anxious about clothing?” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ibid.] For the nations seek all these things. Clothing belongs to the burden of Moab; but let us see with how much labor it is acquired. For this reason, as the poet says:

> The restless merchant runs to the furthest Indies.

Wool is taken from the sheep; afterward it is drawn by women’s hands into thread; then it is woven; afterward dyed; then dried and sewn. Behold the labor. But consider its cost, its cut, and its color. In cost there is excess; in color, vain glory; in cut, pride. For first you seek it so that you may seem costly; secondly, so that you may seem splendid; thirdly, so that you may seem more elegantly shaped. But hear Paul: “Not in costly apparel” [Note: [Col. 0299] 1 Tim. 2.].

Oh, at what great expense a fine garment is sought! Hence the poet:

> Here is splendor of dress beyond one’s means.

And:

> [Col. 0300A] Sometimes another’s money-box is taken.

But such people disdain to labor more; hence Horace:

> Whenever Eutrapelus wished to harm someone,  
> He gave him costly garments. Happy now,  
> He will sleep until daylight; he will put a whore before  
> His honorable duty.  
> [Note: [Col. 0299] Horace, *Epistles* I.18.31.]

But why do you not expend these excesses upon the uses of the poor, so that it may be said to you at judgment: “I was naked, and you clothed me” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 25.]? As Job says: “If I despised the passerby because he had no garment, and the poor man without covering; if his sides did not bless me, and if he was not warmed with the fleeces of my sheep” [Note: [Col. 0299] Job 31.]. To such persons the Lord says: “Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, [Col. 0300B] how they grow: they do not labor or spin. Amen, I say to you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 6.].

Sleeping and waking, which alternate as causes of restoration, belong to the burden of Moab. Yet he permits them, as the Lord says to his disciples: “Sleep now and rest” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 26.]. And concerning waking: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ibid.]. Yet they are a burden, because some sleep immoderately and keep watch indiscreetly. To the former someone said: “Sleep what is enough.” But to the latter:

> Always be more wakeful; do not give yourself over to sleep.

Hear what Boethius says of these three things:

> Happier by far was the earlier age,  
> Content with its faithful fields,  
> [Col. 0300C] 59 Not ruined by idle luxury;  
> It was accustomed to break its late fasts  
> With the simple acorn.  
> Nor did it know how to mix  
> Bacchic gifts with flowing honey,  
> Or blend the bright fleeces of the Seres  
> With Tyrian dye.  
> Wholesome grass gave sleep,  
> The tallest pine trees gave shade,  
> And the gliding stream gave drink.  
> [Note: [Col. 0299] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book II, metre 5.]

Natural weakness likewise belongs to the burden of Moab, as it appears in the succession of ages. First, the infant needs nourishment from milk. As an adolescent, he needs a pedagogue, lest through the license of his age he wander from the good. Once made a man, he needs counsel; once made old, another’s support, because nothing remains in him but labor and pain. Hence David says: “The number of [Col. 0300D] our years is seventy years; and if in the strong, eighty years; and beyond that, labor and pain” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ps. 89.]. Hence also the poet:

> Many inconveniences surround an old man: either because  
> He seeks, yet miserably abstains from what he has found, and fears to use it;  
> Or because he manages every matter coldly and sluggishly,  
> Complaining about everything, praising the time when he  
> Was a boy.  
> [Note: [Col. 0299] Horace, *Art of Poetry*, v. 369.]

Behold, these things are considered in the middle period of a human being. At the last things, these must be considered: the miserable divorce of body and soul. We must also consider the failure of the body and the peril of the soul, when [Col. 0301A] its spirit goes forth and does not return into its earth [Note: [Col. 0301] Ps. 145.]. David signified these three things when he said: “You take away their spirit and they fail, and they return to their dust” [Note: [Col. 0301] Ps. 103.]. “You take away their spirit,” when it departs from the body. “They fail,” because in the separation of body and soul they cease to be. “They return to their dust,” when the body becomes worm, and the worm becomes dust.

Behold the body’s failure. But how great is the danger to the spirit, when “young lions, roaring to seize,” lie in wait for it [Note: [Col. 0301] Ibid.]! For who can deliver it from those roaring creatures prepared for prey? Only the Beloved, who bore these three burdens for us: the burden of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0301] Isa. 13.], because the world’s subjection was offered to him; the burden of Moab [Note: [Col. 0301] Isa. 15.], because he took the aforesaid defects into his incarnation. For he is [Col. 0301B] the rock, to whose clefts he invites the bride. But because the fourth burden, namely that of Damascus, which is called “the drinking of blood,” does not pertain to him but disturbs our consciences, he wishes us to be purified from it. Hence he says: “Show me your face.”

> Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears.

**[THO.]** As if he said: You who love rest in the secrecy of the mind, and delight in the clefts of the rock and in the hollow of the wall, come forth outside into good works, so that you may give an example to your neighbors; and make your voice heard, that you may invite others to the voice of confession, preaching, and praise. For while you show examples of good works and lead others to such a voice, you show [Col. 0301C] your face to me.

What face did he seek to see, if not that of the spiritual temple? As is read concerning the Maccabees, of whom it is written: “They adorned the face of the temple with golden crowns, and dedicated the altar to the Lord, and there was great joy among the people” [Note: [Col. 0301] 1 Macc. 4.].

There are four temples: the first is that of the human body; the second, the congregation of the faithful people; the third and fourth are the flesh and body of Christ. Of the first: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” [Note: [Col. 0301] 1 Cor. 6.] Of the second: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” [Note: [Col. 0301] 1 Cor. 3.] Of the third: “And the things which were concerning himself” [Note: [Col. 0301] Ibid.], and so forth. Of the fourth: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” [Note: [Col. 0301] John 2.].

The first has a bodily face; the second a moral face; the third a spiritual face; the fourth was formerly mortal, but is now immortal. [Col. 0301D] The first is a certain harmony of limbs; the second, the beauty of religion; the third, conscience; the fourth, in a human countenance, something divine breathing grace. The carnal person admires the first; one’s neighbor is edified by the second; God delights in the third; by the fourth the sinner is saved. Of the first: “He breathed into his face the breath of life” [Note: [Col. 0301] Gen. 2.]. Of the second: “Their faces were not ashamed” [Note: [Col. 0301] Lam. 5.]. Of the third: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears.” Of the fourth: “I did not turn my face away from those rebuking and spitting upon me” [Note: [Col. 0301] Isa. 50.].

These [Col. 0302A] four are represented by the four faces of Ezekiel’s living creatures [Note: [Col. 0301] ch. 1.]: the first by the face of an ox, which is a sluggish animal; the second by the face of a man, who is rational; the third by the face of an eagle, which, like an eagle, flies on high; the fourth by the face of a lion, which is compared to Christ because of its strength. The beauty of the first is deceitful and empty favor; to the second it is said: “You are beautiful and fair, daughter Jerusalem, terrible as an ordered army in battle array” [Note: [Col. 0301] Song 6.]; to the third: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0301] Song 1.]; of the fourth: “All the beauty of the Lord is exalted above understanding.”

These must be adorned with gold. It should be known that “gold” signifies the splendor of worldly vanity; [the second sense is uncertain in the supplied text]; thirdly, the splendor of heavenly wisdom; fourthly, the splendor of divinity. Of the first: “Babylon was a golden cup” [Note: [Col. 0301] Jer. 51.]. [Col. 0302B] Of the second: “The angel was girded about the breasts with a golden belt” [Note: [Col. 0301] Rev. 1.]. Of the third: “Your gold has rusted” [Note: [Col. 0301] Jas. 5.]. Of the fourth, the bride says: “His head is the finest gold” [Note: [Col. 0301] Song 5.].

The first is “a golden ring in her nostrils” [Note: [Col. 0301] Prov. 11.]; the second, the golden crown and the small golden crown which are upon the table of the bread of the presence [Note: [Col. 0301] Exod. 25.]; the third, the golden crown which Mordecai wore when he went out from the palace and from the presence of King Ahasuerus [Note: [Col. 0301] Esth. 8.]; the fourth, the crown which he had upon his head as he sat upon a white cloud, like the Son of Man [Note: [Col. 0301] Rev. 14.].

The first face, therefore—bodily beauty—has deceitful and vain favor: vain as regards voluptuous adornment, deceitful as regards the pretense of hypocrites. For the voluptuous strive to adorn [Col. 0302C] their faces with a harlot’s ornament, although the Apostle says: “Not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls” [Note: [Col. 0301] 1 Tim. 2.], because they cover everything with gems and gold. What madness it is to carry one’s wealth upon one’s body, “since all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” [Note: [Col. 0301] 1 Pet. 1.]! Behold the vain.

It is deceitful in hypocrites: “For they disfigure their faces, so that they may appear to men to be fasting” [Note: [Col. 0301] Matt. 6.]. These are whitewashed tombs [Note: [Col. 0301] Matt. 23.]. “The Lord will strike you, whitewashed wall,” says Paul [Note: [Col. 0301] Acts 23.]. This is the face that fools admire.

The second face is the beauty of religion, namely that of the temple which is the congregation of the faithful people. It is adorned with the golden splendor of charity, which is the golden crown and small golden crown upon the table of the bread of the presence [Note: [Col. 0301] Exod. 25.]. It has four corners: for charity is hard, strong, fiery, and unquenchable. Strong, to undergo death; [Col. 0302D] hard, to endure daily affliction; fiery, to kindle desire; unquenchable, to prevail over the waves of pleasures; strong, to hate temporal life; hard, to subdue animal nature; fiery, not to grow lukewarm in idleness; unquenchable, that steadfastness may not perish.

Of the first Paul says: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for Christ” [Note: [Col. 0301] Acts 21.]; for he had heard: “He who hates his life in this world keeps it unto eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0301] John 12.]. Of the second, the same Apostle says: “In all things we suffer tribulation, but are not distressed” [Col. 0303A] and so forth [Note: [Col. 0303] 2 Cor. 4.], unlike those who “gave all their precious things for food, to restore their soul” [Note: [Col. 0303] Lam. 1.], that is, their animal nature. Of the third: “Was not our heart burning within us” because of Jesus “while he spoke to us on the way?” [Note: [Col. 0303] Luke 24.] Otherwise, if you are lukewarm, “I will begin to vomit you from my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0303] Rev. 3.].

Of the fourth: when the children of Israel were led into captivity, they hid the sacred fire in the earth; but when they returned, they found nothing but thick water [Note: [Col. 0303] 2 Macc. 1.]. Therefore he says: “Wait, and you shall see the help of the Lord upon you.” The bride taught these four things in the Song of Songs when she said: “Love is strong as death” [Note: [Col. 0303] Song 8.]—behold the first; “jealousy is hard as hell” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ibid.]—behold the second; “its lamps are lamps of fire and flames” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ibid.]—behold the third; “many waters could not quench [Col. 0303B] charity, nor shall rivers overwhelm it” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ibid.]—behold the fourth.

Of charity so adorned it is rightly said: “You are beautiful and fair, daughter Jerusalem, terrible as an ordered army in battle array” [Note: [Col. 0303] Song 6.]. Hence it is rightly said: “This place is terrible; it is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0303] Gen. 28.]. It is truly terrible to the devil, when no entrance lies open to him. In this face, thus adorned, one’s neighbor is edified. Behold the golden crown of charity by which it is adorned. The first was the face of the ox; this is the face of man.

There follows the third face, of the third temple, which is the soul of the just person: its face is a clean conscience. It is adorned with the golden crown of wisdom, which also has four corners. For heavenly wisdom is shrewd, profound, strong, and sweet. It is shrewd, to overcome malice; profound, when [Col. 0303C] it foresees the straits of hell; strong, when it vigorously strives to seize heaven; sweet, when it peacefully orders the degrees of its affections.

Hence it is written of these four things: “Wisdom conquers malice, reaches mightily from end to end, and disposes all things: it conquers malice” [Note: [Col. 0303] Wis. 7.]—behold the first. It is shrewd because by wisdom’s counsel the soul has the means to flee its own malice, patiently endure that of its neighbor, and manfully resist the malice of the devil. Yet it should not merely endure its neighbor, but graciously pardon him. Behold the vengeance of wisdom, as the poet says:

> A noble kind of vengeance is to pardon the conquered.

“For wisdom conquers malice,” says the Wise Man [Note: [Col. 0303] Ibid.]. If malice confronts it, the soul says to itself: “Do not emulate [Col. 0303D] evildoers” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ps. 36.]. And you will say to your adversary: “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ps. 51.] Of evil spirits it is said: “They made the king glad in their malice” [Note: [Col. 0303] Hos. 7.].

Afterward it becomes profound and descends into hell. For wisdom reaches everywhere because of its purity. And, seeing the punishments of hell, it cries: “Deliver me, Lord, from eternal death.” Afterward it becomes strong, looks toward heaven, and cries: “Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0303] Mic. 4.]. Finally it becomes sweet when it tranquilly orders its affections. First it desires [Col. 0304A] the rest of the heavenly city; secondly, the fellowship of angels; thirdly, the vision of God. First it says: “In all things I sought rest, and I shall dwell in the inheritance of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ecclus. 24.]. Secondly, it rejoices because we shall be fellow citizens of the holy angels, and they our companions and fellow citizens. Hence the angel in the Apocalypse says to John, who wished to worship him: “See that you do not do this, for I am your fellow servant” [Note: [Col. 0303] Rev. 22.].

Because of these four things it is said: “Give me, O Lord, wisdom, the companion seated upon your thrones, by whose strength I may obtain the kingdom; which may be with me when I descend into hell, and labor with me, so that through it I may conquer the evil one, know what is pleasing before you, and according to your will order the degrees of my affections” [Note: [Col. 0303] Wis. 9.]. Or otherwise: “Come over to me, all [Col. 0304B] who desire me, and be filled with my generations” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ecclus. 24.].

There are four generations of wisdom: the first, by which the world is created and governed; the second, by which the human heart is built up; the third, by which malice is overcome; the fourth, by which the blessed person is enlightened to see God. In the first, the greatness of divine power is shown; in the second, the benevolence of the divine will; in the third, the obstacle of difficulty is excluded; in the fourth, the countenance of majesty is shown. We know the first by the instrument of the letter; the second by the teaching of the Holy Spirit; the third by the incontrovertible proof of the passion and resurrection; the fourth by the truest experience.

Of the first: “The Lord founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by prudence. By his wisdom [Col. 0304C] the deeps burst forth, and clouds grow thick with dew” [Note: [Col. 0303] Prov. 3.]. Of the second: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven columns” [Note: [Col. 0303] Prov. 9.]. Of the third: “Wisdom conquers malice” [Note: [Col. 0303] Wis. 7.]. Of the fourth: “I called wisdom my friend, and appointed her to be my light” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ibid.].

Hear of its brightness: “It is the radiance of eternal light, and a spotless mirror” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ibid.]. Again: “It is more beautiful than the sun, and, compared with every arrangement of the stars, is found to surpass the light” [Note: [Col. 0303] Ibid.]. In this face, so adorned, God delights, so as to say: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0303] Song 1.]. Beautiful because of purity of conscience; beautiful because of the crown of wisdom.

For this is the crown which Mordecai wore upon his head when he went out from [Col. 0304D] the palace and from the presence of King Ahasuerus [Note: [Col. 0303] 2 Macc. 1.]. Mordecai is said to mean “pure myrrh.” Impure myrrh is bitterness for sins; pure myrrh, bitterness from desire for the kingdom of heaven. Ahasuerus is said to mean “their blessedness”: he is God. He is keen in sight, when the contemplative soul goes forth in order to look upon its lower things. It returns from his presence crowned with the crown of wisdom.

Behold how the face of the temple of the human body, the face of the temple of the faithful people, and the face of the temple which is the soul of the just person are adorned, and with what crowns. It follows: “And they dedicated the altar to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0303] 3 Kings 8.]. This [Col. 0305A] altar is the heart of the just person; hence it has been said: “The offering of the just person makes the altar fat” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ecclus. 35.]. Therefore, one consecrated here must first renounce, secondly take root, and thirdly dedicate: renounce the vanity of the world, take root in charity, dedicate the altar—that is, the purity of the heart. The vanity of the world, lest one again be entangled in its pleasures; charity, lest one fall before the gusts of worldly air; purity of heart, that thereafter it may yield itself to divine uses.

Of the first: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” [Note: [Col. 0305] 1 John 2.]. Of the second: “Rooted and grounded in charity” [Note: [Col. 0305] Eph. 3.]. Of the third: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ps. 56.]. Of this altar it was said: “When you enter the land which the Lord will give you, build an altar to the Lord God from stones which iron has not touched” [Note: [Col. 0305] Deut. 27.]. These stones [Col. 0305B] are virtues. The iron of discord touches them when anger, envy, or something of that kind mingles itself with them. But let the cornerstone be placed upon them [Note: [Col. 0305] 1 Pet. 2], namely Christ, who is true peace—or our peace—“who made both one” [Note: [Col. 0305] Eph. 2.], as Jacob did: “For he erected a stone as a pillar, pouring oil upon it” [Note: [Col. 0305] Gen. 28.].

Of him it has elsewhere been said: There remains the adornment of Christ’s face, whose flesh we called a temple. His face is threefold: first, that of human condition; second, that of transfiguration; third, that of incorruption. 60 The first is adorned with comeliness; the second with splendor; the third with honor: with comeliness of fitting order; with splendor as a sign of the resurrection to come; with honor of glorious majesty. The first gives us a model of religious life; the second confidence in resurrection; the third joy in beholding him. Of the first: “I did not turn [Col. 0305C] my face away from rebukes and from those spitting upon me” [Note: [Col. 0305] Isa. 50.]; and: “They spat in his face and struck him with fists” [Note: [Col. 0305] Matt. 15.]. Then he was “beautiful in form beyond the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ps. 44.]. In this respect his face was like that of one going to Jerusalem. Of the second: “His face shone like the sun, and his garments like snow” [Note: [Col. 0305] Matt. 17.]. Of the third: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears.” This face is adorned with the crown of glory; hence: “You crowned him with glory and honor” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ps. 8.]. Of it it is said: “I saw a white cloud, and upon the cloud one like the Son of Man sitting, with a golden crown upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0305] Rev. 14.].

That we may see this face, we must be diligent, cautious, and afterward joyful: diligent in seeking, cautious in anticipating, [Col. 0305D] joyful in seeing him. Of the first: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ps. 104.]. Of the second: “Let us anticipate his face in confession” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ps. 94.]. Of the third Jacob says: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” [Note: [Col. 0305] Gen. 32.]. In beholding him it will truly be said: “There was great joy among the people” [Note: [Col. 0305] 1 Macc. 4.], through him who grants this, to whom belong honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

This face is at one time good, at another evil. The evil face is shown to oneself, to one’s neighbour, and to God: first, so as to [Col. 0306A] recognize the disease; second, to seek counsel; third, to receive a remedy—namely, the disease of iniquity, the counsel of satisfaction, and the remedy of forgiveness. Of the first: “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is ever before me” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ps. 50]. Of the second, the leper is told: “Go, show yourself to the priest” [Note: [Col. 0305] Matt. 8]. Of the third: “Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ps. 50].

Likewise a good conscience is shown to oneself, to one’s neighbour, and to God: to oneself for assurance, to one’s neighbour for edification, and to God for thanksgiving; for assurance amid tribulation, for edification in purity, and for thanksgiving for the consolation of benefits received. Of the first, Job says: “I have not sinned, and my eye shall remain amid bitter things” [Note: [Col. 0305] Job 17]. Of the second, the same writer: “I shall not abandon the righteousness which I have begun to maintain; for my heart does not reproach me throughout my whole life” [Col. 0306B] [Note: [Col. 0305] Job 27]. Of the third: “I will confess you, O Lord and King, and praise you, God my Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ecclus. 51].

He sought this voice of thanksgiving when he added: “Let your voice sound in my ears.” But he also sought the voice of prayer. Now one kind of prayer is useful, another useless. Of useless prayers, the first is unfruitful, the second undiscerning, the third sinful. It is unfruitful when what is asked with the mouth is not attended to in the heart; whence: “This people honours me with its lips, but their heart is far from me” [Note: [Col. 0305] Mark 7]. If I pray with the tongue, my spirit does not pray, and my mind is without fruit.

Prayer is undiscerning when, although both the petitioner and the person for whom prayer is made are good, what is asked is not good. Hence the Apostle says: “We do not know what we ought to pray for” [Col. 0306C] [Note: [Col. 0305] Rom. 8]; and the Lord says to the mother of the sons of Zebedee: “You do not know what you are asking” [Note: [Col. 0305] Matt. 20]. It is sinful when either the petitioner or the person for whom prayer is made is guilty; hence in Isaiah: “When you multiply your prayers, I shall not hear; for your hands are full of blood” [Note: [Col. 0305] Isa. 15].

Useful prayer is sometimes made with a modest disposition, sometimes with a pure disposition, sometimes with a generous disposition, sometimes with a devout disposition. Paul sets these forth in this order: “I desire,” he says, “that there be made in the Church supplications, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings” [Note: [Col. 0305] 1 Tim. 2]. Supplications are made for the forgiveness of sin, prayers for obtaining good, petitions for one’s neighbour, and thanksgivings to God. Of the first: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” [Note: [Col. 0305] Luke 15]. Of the second, Susanna says: [Col. 0306D] “God, you know what these men have maliciously contrived against me; and behold, I die although I have done none of these things” [Note: [Col. 0305] Dan. 13]. Of the third, Moses says: “Either forgive them this offence, or blot me out of your book which you have written” [Note: [Col. 0305] Exod. 32]. Of the fourth, the blessed Virgin says: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour, because he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0305] Luke 1].

Sometimes we are defiled by the corruption innate to us; and thus our face—that is, our conscience—becomes polluted. The Beloved wished it to be cleansed when [Col. 0307A] he said: “Show me your face.” This is the burden of Damascus [Note: [Col. 0307] Isa. 17], which is said to mean “drinking blood,” expressing that corruption innate in us. In a certain manner it drags us unwillingly toward sin. It is the law in our members, resisting the law of our mind. This natural movement of sin, in a kind of delight, almost absorbs the very power of reason. Yet some feel these impulses without consenting; they are attacked but not conquered, burdened but not overthrown.

There are three kinds of blood: moral blood, historical blood, and the blood of redemption. The first has its source in the tinder of sin; the second, in the law of Moses; the third, in the body of Christ. The first pollutes a person; the second sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh; [Col. 0307B] the third sanctifies for purity of conscience. Of the first it is said: “The man who flows with blood shall be unclean, and he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” [Note: [Col. 0307] Gen. 9]. Of the second: “For if the blood of goats or calves sanctifies the defiled unto the cleansing of the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0307] Heb. 9]. Of the third: “How much more shall the blood of Christ cleanse our consciences from dead works, to serve the living God?” [Note: [Col. 0307] Ibid.]

In the first is a heavy burden; in the second, an unendurable burden; in the third, a light burden: heavy for sinners because of future condemnation; unendurable for those under the Law because of the Law’s difficult observance; light for those who love, because of future recompense. Of the first David says: “For [Col. 0307C] my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed me down” [Note: [Col. 0307] Ps. 37]. Of the second: “This is what neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” [Note: [Col. 0307] Acts 15]. Of the third the Saviour says: “For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” [Note: [Col. 0307] Matt. 11].

The first blood, then, is the tinder of sin. At times it is drunk, at times shed, at times sprinkled. It is drunk when one consents to a suggestion; it is shed when one gives oneself over to the deed; it is sprinkled—that is, scattered upon another—when one corrupts one’s neighbour by example. Or it is drunk through delight in sin, shed through cruelty, and sprinkled through defaming one’s neighbour. Of the first Solomon says: “There are two daughters of the leech, which always say: Bring, bring” [Note: [Col. 0307] Prov. 30]. For the leech is the one who drinks this blood; [Col. 0307D] its two daughters are fleshly desire and spiritual desire, for these are never satisfied. Of the second: “They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them” [Note: [Col. 0307] Ps. 78]. Of the third: “Their blood has been sprinkled upon my garments, and I have defiled all my clothing” [Note: [Col. 0307] Isa. 63].

It does not seem pointless that, according to some, Adam was formed in the garden of Damascus. Paul, as he went to Damascus, was struck blind on the road [Note: [Col. 0307] Acts 9]. Damascus, Eliezer the servant of Abraham, when a new heir was born, was deprived of his lord’s inheritance [Note: [Col. 0307] Gen. 15]. For Adam drank this blood when he was seized by [Col. 0308A] the delight of sin, so as to transmit it to us. Paul, however, shed this blood, because he was going to Damascus in order to shed blood. Perhaps at some time Damascus committed some sin against Abraham by which he sprinkled others.

Paul complained of this draught of blood when he said: “The evil which I will not, this I do. For, indeed,” he says, “the willing is present to me, but I do not find the accomplishing of good” [Note: [Col. 0307] Rom. 7]. Nor should anyone be troubled that we made the division of animal blood fourfold there, but threefold here. For the principle here is one thing and there another: here it is according to higher matters, there according to lower matters. Nor is this surprising: for the will is threefold—the will of nature, the will of vice, and the will of grace. The will of nature resists vice, but is conquered unless aided by the will of grace. [Col. 0308B] It is at one time subjected, at another adjacent, at another set above. It is subjected so long as it lies beneath vice; adjacent so long as it struggles against vice; it is set above when vice is overcome. And it is God’s just judgment that the one who refused to obey his superior should be troubled by his inferior.

Historical blood, because it is wholly figurative, is left aside. But what is left aside in the blood of redemption is washed in the first. For when it is shed, it washes away sin; when it is drunk, it raises our hope toward the kingdom; when it is sprinkled, it makes us secure against danger. Of the first: “This is the cup of the New Testament, which shall be shed for you for the remission of sins” [Note: [Col. 0307] Matt. 26]. Of the second: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink [Col. 0308C] his blood, you shall not have abiding life in yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0307] John 6]. Of the third: “We know that the blood of the paschal lamb was sprinkled on the doorposts of the Egyptians, where the children of Israel were, and they were delivered from the danger of the Egyptians” [Note: [Col. 0307] Exod. 12]; whence the Apostle “sends greeting to the elect children of Pontus, Galatia, Asia, and Bithynia in the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0307] 1 Pet. 1].

“For your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.”

[THO.] Sweet is that voice which instructs one’s neighbour toward the good and raises itself in the praise of God, so that it may say with David: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0307] Ps. 118]. Lovely is that face which presents itself in such a manner as to deserve to see the face of the Creator, and says: “My face has sought you; [Col. 0308D] I shall seek your face, O Lord. Do not turn your face from me; do not in anger turn away from your servant” [Note: [Col. 0307] Ps. 26].

The bride’s voice is heard in the ears of her enemy, of her neighbour, and of her Beloved. In the first case it is sweet, in the second sweeter, in the third sweetest. The first is the voice of compassion, the second of consolation, the third of exultation and salvation. The first is sweet because of forgiveness; the second sweeter because of the promise of the kingdom; the third sweetest because it imitates the jubilation of the citizens above. The Lord thus invites us to the first: “Unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0309A] [Note: [Col. 0309] Matt. 18]. Of the second: “He shall not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” [Note: [Col. 0309] 2 Tim. 2]. Of the third: “Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us sing for joy to God our Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0309] Ps. 94].

By the first voice we ought to forgive the person who asks, the person who does not ask, and the person who does evil to us. In the first respect, the Lord forgave the thief when he said: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0309] Luke 23].
