In the second respect, he forgave Peter even though Peter did not ask: for he looked upon Peter, and Peter wept bitterly [Note: [Col. 0309] Matt. 26]. In the third respect, he not only forgave his crucifiers but prayed for them: “Father,” he says, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Note: [Col. 0309] Luke 23].

The second voice is addressed to the hard-hearted, the slothful, and the devout. It rebukes the first, rouses the second, and kindles the third. Of the first: “Woe to you, hard of heart,” and, “Because you have despised my counsel and neglected my corrections, [Col. 0309B] I too will laugh at your destruction” [Note: [Col. 0309] Prov. 1]. Of the second: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep?” [Note: [Col. 0309] Prov. 24]. Of the third: “Let us run toward the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who endured the cross for the joy set before him and now sits at the right hand of God” [Note: [Col. 0309] Heb. 12].

The third voice praises the Creator, so that praise may proceed from knowledge. For there is voice without knowledge; knowledge without voice; voice of knowledge; and knowledge of voice. Voice without knowledge belongs to the chatterer, who, when he cries out, does not understand what he says; hence Paul calls such persons “like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal” [Note: [Col. 0309] 1 Cor. 13]. Knowledge without voice belongs to those who are not eloquent, or who are too sluggish to utter what they know; hence Solomon says: “What profit is there in hidden knowledge and [Col. 0309C] hidden treasure alike?” [Note: [Col. 0309] Ecclus. 2]. Voice of knowledge belongs to those who know and express themselves well; hence: “Desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” [Note: [Col. 0309] Prov. 21]. Knowledge of voice is that which by divine power makes the tongue-tied eloquent and grants the grace of interpretation. Thus it happened to the apostles at the coming of the Holy Spirit, that they knew every kind of language [Note: [Col. 0309] Acts 2]; whence: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” [Note: [Col. 0309] Wis. 1].

Behold, the sweet voice. It follows: “Your face is lovely,” namely, your conscience.

There is a threefold beauty. The first is when it is without blemish; the second possesses a certain elegance of taste and adornment; the third is a grace of members and colour that draws to itself the affection of those looking upon it. [Col. 0309D] This threefold beauty is in the soul: 61 the first is present through the abolition of sin; the second through religious conduct; the third through the hidden inspiration of grace. Of the first Job says: “If you remove the iniquity which is in your hand, and injustice is not in your tent, then you shall be able to lift up your face without blemish” [Note: [Col. 0309] Job 11]. Of the second: “How beautiful you are in your sandals, daughter of the prince!” [Note: [Col. 0309] Song 7]. By the sandals, that is, the examples of the fathers, made of dead animals, are signified. After their example we conduct ourselves well and fortify the feet of our affections.

[Col. 0310A] Of the third: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, lovely as the moon, chosen as the sun?” [Note: [Col. 0309] Song 6]. The dawn leaves the night of vices; the moon illumines the darkness of sins; the sun penetrates, through contemplation, the hidden things of heaven. In the first beauty one merits reconciliation; in the second, familiarity; in the third, the revelation of heavenly secrets. Of the first: “When the wicked turns away from his wickedness which he has committed, and does judgment and justice, I shall not remember any of his iniquities” [Note: [Col. 0309] Ezek. 18]. Of the second: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: [Col. 0309] John 14]—behold familiarity. Of the third: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends, because I have made known to you everything [Col. 0310B] which I heard from my Father” [Note: [Col. 0309] John 15]—behold the revelation of heavenly secrets.

In the first, a person escapes the darkness of guilt; in the second, the darkness of invincible ignorance; in the third, the darkness of bodily mass. This is the fifth burden of Isaiah, namely the burden of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0309] Isa. 19], which is said to mean “darkness.” For sometimes, because our sins demand it, we bear this burden—the darkness of ignorance; sometimes, however, from necessity; sometimes through negligence. These are burdened from Egypt, but not with Egypt—that is, not with those who are the darkness of iniquity. Of them it is said: “Whoever does evil hates the light” [Note: [Col. 0309] John 3]. “Those who sleep, sleep by night”: and this is voluntary.

There are three darknesses: the first is that of guilt; the second, of [Col. 0310C] ignorance; the third, of bodily mass. The darkness of guilt is a certain confusion caused by sin, through which the inward person observes neither his fall nor how he may rise again. The darkness of ignorance is that by which a person, even if wishing to do good, does not know how. The darkness of bodily mass is that by which excessive sensual indulgence obstructs the spirit, so that it cannot know the heavenly secrets which it desires.

Of the first David says: “I said: Perhaps darkness will trample me” [Note: [Col. 0309] Ps. 138]. Of the second, the same writer: “They have not known nor understood; they walk in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0309] Ps. 81]; and Job: “There is no darkness and no shadow of death in which those who work iniquity may hide themselves” [Note: [Col. 0309] Job 34]. Of the third Job says: “In darkness I have spread my bed” [Note: [Col. 0309] Job 17].

Of the first Paul says: “Those who sleep, sleep by night; and those who are drunk, are drunk by night” [Col. 0310D] [Note: [Col. 0309] 1 Thess. 5]; and: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” [Note: [Col. 0309] John 12]. Therefore: “Arise, you who sleep; rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” [Note: [Col. 0309] Eph. 5]. Hence David exulted, saying: “For darkness shall not be dark to you, and night shall be illuminated as day” [Note: [Col. 0309] Ps. 138]. For Christ, Paul says, “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” [Note: [Col. 0309] 1 Cor. 4].

Of the second David exulted, saying: “For you light my lamp, O Lord my God; enlighten my darkness” [Note: [Col. 0309] Ps. 17]. The lamp is Christ, who through his teaching illumined human [Col. 0311A] ignorances. For Isaiah had said concerning these: “Woe to you who call evil good and good evil, sweet bitter and darkness light” [Note: [Col. 0311] Isa. 5]. Of the third Jeremiah lamented thus: “How in his wrath has the Lord covered the virgin daughter of Zion with gloom, cast down from heaven to earth the splendour of Israel?” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ibid.] But see how Isaiah, in the spirit, beheld the consolation to come for these darknesses: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come. For behold, darkness has covered the earth, and gloom the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0311] Isa. 60]. But behold the remedy: “The Lord shall arise over you, and his glory shall be seen in you, and the nations shall walk in your light” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ibid.].

Those who are in the first darkness labour under three things. They have delight in sin, abandon the fear of God, and do not [Col. 0311B] remember the horror of death. Of the first: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in most wicked things” [Note: [Col. 0311] Prov. 2]. Of the second: “For there is no change in them, and they have not feared God” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ps. 50]. Of the third David says: “Who is the man that shall live and not see death? Shall he deliver his soul from the hand of hell?” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ps. 88]. And the poet:

> Behold, death does not delay, and steals onward with every hour.

Those who are in the second darkness likewise suffer a threefold ignorance. A person does not know himself, does not know God, and does not know the devil: himself, that he is a sinner; God, that he is Creator; the devil, that he is a caviller. He is a sinner and therefore in need of repentance; God is Creator, bestowing mercy; the devil is a caviller through envy. Of the first: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth and follow the tracks of your flocks” [Col. 0311C] [Note: [Col. 0311] Song 1]. And the poet:

> From heaven descended Γνῶθι σεαυτόν—“Know or recognize yourself.”

Of the second: It is true that there are some who do not know, nor believe, that God exists; some know of him but do not acknowledge him; and some both know and acknowledge him, yet do not worship him with due reverence. Of the first David says: “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ps. 13]. Of the second Pharaoh: “Who is the Lord, that I should obey him? I do not know the Lord, and I shall not let Israel go” [Note: [Col. 0311] Exod. 5]. Of the third, Paul: “Though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” [Note: [Col. 0311] Rom. 1].

Those who are in the third darkness are also hindered by a threefold disadvantage from seeing the secrets of heaven that they desire. For they desire to see brightness, [Col. 0311D] peace, and the king: the brightness of the kingdom of heaven, the peace of human beings and angels, and the King of all kings. Of the first: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” [Note: [Col. 0311] Matt. 6]. The eye is intention. It is evil when it inclines more toward serving the flesh than the spirit; hence it is called “evil,” that is, unequal. “The whole body,” that is, the collection of virtues, it makes dark: namely, although a person may possess virtues, with such an intention he cannot see heavenly things. A collection of virtues is called a body, as one speaks of “the body of sin.” “But if your eye [Col. 0312A] is single,” that is, serving the spirit alone, “your whole body,” that is, the collection of virtues, “will be full of light” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ibid.], by beholding heavenly things. For the evil eye serves the flesh; the single eye serves the spirit alone; the multiple eye now serves the one, now the other.

Of the peace which they wish to see it is said: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us, to enlighten those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to direct our feet,” that is, our affections, “into the way of peace” [Note: [Col. 0311] Luke 1]—so that we may know the peace above. Of the third it is said: Our life is hidden, because neither our life nor Christ now appears to us so long as we labour in this bodily mass. But if you wish to see “through a mirror and in an enigma” [Note: [Col. 0311] 1 Cor. 13], hear John: “Whoever loves his brother is born of God and sees God” [Note: [Col. 0311] 1 John 2].

The first darkness is [Col. 0312B] that blindness with which the Sodomites were struck, when they could not find the door of Lot’s house [Note: [Col. 0311] Gen. 19]. The second darkness is that numbered among the plagues of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0311] Exod. 10]. The third darkness is the blindness suffered by that blind man to whom the Lord said: “What do you want me to do for you?” And he: “Lord, that I may see the light” [Note: [Col. 0311] John 18]—namely, that light above, in whatever manner I may love it on the way, so that afterwards I may possess it in the homeland.

Since, therefore, the bride was free from these, it is said to her: “Show me your face, for it is lovely” [Note: [Col. 0311] Song 2]. By his own aid we ought to turn this lovely face toward God, so that he too may show his serene face to us. David prayed for this, saying: “God of hosts, turn us, show us your face, and we shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ps. 79].

All bodily senses abound in the face. [Col. 0312C] Thus, for him to show us his face is to set forth full knowledge of himself. For he has his own senses. Hear of sight: “In every place the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0311] Prov. 15]. Of hearing: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ps. 10]. Of smell, it is said concerning Noah’s sacrifice: “The Lord smelled an odour of sweetness” [Note: [Col. 0311] Gen. 8]. Of taste: “Abraham compelled the Lord to enter in to him, that he might taste a little” [Note: [Col. 0311] Gen. 16]. Of touch the Prophet says: “The Lord sent his hand and touched my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0311] Jer. 1].

Thus he sees, because nothing is hidden from his wisdom. He hears, because the ears of his mercy are open to the prayers of suppliants. He smells, because through his justice he discerns the quality of merits. He tastes, when in his goodness he delights in the glory of the blessed. [Col. 0312D] His being touched consists in compassion for the misery of the afflicted. Accordingly, he sees through wisdom; hears through mercy; smells through justice; tastes through goodness; touches through compassion.

Let the bride therefore say to her Beloved: Show me your wisdom, that I may not wander; reveal your mercy, that I may not despair; teach me your justice, that I may not presume. Make your goodness known to me, that I may love you in your gifts; make your compassion known to me, that I may not be overcome by my evils. I beseech you, Lord, enlighten your face over your servant, so that, when I know it, [Col. 0313A] I may show mine more fully and securely, as you require.

For what is more pleasant to those who love, what can be sweeter, than to be cherished by mutual affection, delighted by mutual sight, delighted by mutual speech? Since the bride therefore desires to see him alone, all else is dreadful to her, all things are sordid, and those things which are merry in the world are wearisome. Thus, like a living creature, she is intent upon beholding the face of the heavenly King; as the Beloved said: “Show me your face” [Note: [Col. 0313] Song 2]. Certainly he sought to see her in exile, to see her in judgment, and to see her in the kingdom: in exile beautiful, in judgment precious, in the kingdom glorious. Let the bride, then, behold his face as rejoicing, judging, and reigning: rejoicing, that through it she may be pure; judging, that she may be secure; reigning, that through [Col. 0313B] him she may be glorious.

“Arise, hasten, my friend, my beautiful one, my dove, and come.”

[CARD.] You who will assist the Church by your prayers, in the manner which follows: “In the clefts of the rock, in the caverns of the wall, show your face” [Note: [Col. 0313] Ibid.]. The clefts of the rock are the wounds in Christ’s hands and feet. Of him the Apostle says: “And the rock was Christ” [Note: [Col. 0313] 1 Cor. 10]. The cavern of the wall is the wound in his side. Thus he says: “Show your face in the clefts of the rock, in the cavern of the wall” [Note: [Col. 0313] Song 2], as if to say: In my wounds, and among my wounds, present your face to intercede for sinners.

And because she assists not only through the beauty of her merits but also through the very sweetness [Col. 0313C] of her prayers, she is told: Together with the presentation of your face, “let your voice sound in my ears” [Note: [Col. 0313] Ibid.], for it has great power. “For your voice is sweet to me” [Note: [Col. 0313] Ibid.] in prayers; and it is sweet because your face is lovely, because, namely, the wondrous beauty of virtues is made known in your face. There follows, in the person of the Mother of the Lord:

“Catch for us the little foxes which destroy the vineyards.”

[THO.] The foxes are heretics; the vineyards are individual churches. Foxes destroy vineyards because through heretics churches are dried up from the freshness of faith. They are rightly called little, because, though proud within, outwardly they pretend humility. They are caught by the saints when, in disputations, they are convicted by true arguments.

For a wise man, his life is his vineyard, as are his mind and his conscience, because within himself [Col. 0313D] he leaves nothing uncultivated or deserted. There is the vine of virtue, the cluster of good work, and the wine of spiritual joy. The righteous person is a good vineyard: virtue is its vine, action its branch, the witness of conscience its wine, and the tongue its winepress of expression. The worst vine is the secret detractor and the flattering sycophant. These two must be caught by kindnesses and services, admonitions, and prayers poured out to the Lord for them; then they will not harm the vineyard already flowering.

The flower is a new manner of life: judgments are the future fruit; dress is more modest, speech less frequent, countenance more cheerful, glance more restrained, [Col. 0314A] gait more composed. This flower must fear the cold of the north wind. For if it reaches the interior, descends into the bosom of the mind, shakes the affections, occupies the paths of counsel, disturbs the light of judgment, and introduces freedom of spirit, immediately a certain stiffness of soul enters; freshness grows slack; weakness consumes strength; the horror of austerity increases. Fear of poverty troubles one; the mind is contracted; grace is withdrawn; the length of life is drawn out; reason is lulled to sleep; the spirit is extinguished; the fervour of the novice cools; wearisome torpor grows heavy; charity becomes cold; pleasure flatters; security deceives; habit calls one back; the law is ignored; right is rejected; what is lawful is proscribed; the fear of the Lord is abandoned; a hand is given to shamelessness; and that diabolical leap is presumed upon—[Col. 0314B] from the height into the abyss, from the pavement into the dungheap, from the throne into the sewer, from heaven into mud, from the cloister into the world, from paradise into hell.

But the vineyard is planted by the hand of the Lord, redeemed by blood, watered by the word, propagated by grace, and made fruitful by the Spirit. The foxes that gnaw at it are demons. At times they hide in the pits of valleys; at times they run about 62 on the plain full of crops; at times they climb up to the vineyards of the mountains. For in the ground of the human heart three things are found: the depth of the valley, namely the care of sustaining the flesh; the fruitful plain, the purpose of religious life; and the mountain vine, the taste of heavenly sweetness. In the first they deceive us by proposing the necessity of the flesh, because through it they lead us to drunkenness; in [Col. 0314C] the second they deceive us through respectability, because through it they draw us to dissipation; in the third they deceive us through usefulness, because through it they lead us to ambition for offices.

Against the first the Lord says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness” [Note: [Col. 0313] Luke 21]. Against the second the Apostle says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” [Note: [Col. 0313] 1 Cor. 15]. Against the third the Lord warns us to beware of those who “love the chief places at dinner and greetings in the marketplace, to be called Rabbi by men” [Note: [Col. 0313] Matt. 23].

In the first they defile their den. “Foxes,” he says, “have dens, and birds of heaven nests” [Note: [Col. 0313] Matt. 8]. “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hand of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes.” These are in the lower region; the second are in the middle; the third in the highest. In the second they burn the crops: these are those to whose tails Samson bound [Col. 0314D] burning torches, and, running about, they burned the crops of the Philistines [Note: [Col. 0313] Judg. 15], which is said to mean “falling through drink.” For when we fall through the draught of pride which this fox offers us in its tail—that is, at the end of its offering—we feel our virtues being burned up. In the third they gnaw, as in the present passage.

The great fox is the devil, signified under the person of Herod, who is called *pellicens*, that is, “deceiver”: “Go,” he says, “tell that fox” [Note: [Col. 0313] Luke 13]. He has his own servants, three little foxes: heretics, hypocrites, and flatterers. The first gnaw the roots, the second the trunks, [Col. 0315A] the third the flowers: the roots of faith, the trunks of virtue, the flowers of sweetness already tasted.

The first do so by unbelief, the second by ambition, the third through love of pleasing or of some other advantage. But do you wish to catch them? You will catch the first by increases of faith; the second by the frustration of their expectation; the third if you repel them from the favour of your familiarity. Thus your vineyard will be undisturbed by these foxes.

And this is the sixth burden of Isaiah, called that of the desert sea [Note: [Col. 0315] Isa. 21]. Persecutors abandoned by God are called a sea. Sometimes people are burdened by the persecution of evil persons, and this is the burden of the desert sea. The desert sea is the multitude of reprobate persons, who, abandoned by God under the weight of persecutions, oppress the holy Church. Moreover, a sea is those who are tossed by the varied tumults of passions [Col. 0315B] and vices, who never remain in the same condition. Of them David says: “Sinners have built upon my back; they have prolonged their iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0315] Ps. 128].

The desert sea is so called for three reasons: because of its rising waves, the mountains of sand hidden beneath its waters, and its deep pits that swallow waters into themselves in constant whirlpools. In the first a ship is submerged; in the second it is broken; in the third it is sunk into the abyss. These are the three kinds of persecutors: the first are rulers of the world, who pursue by tyranny; the second are heretics; the third, hypocrites. An example of the first was Cain against his brother Abel [Note: [Col. 0315] Gen. 4]; of the second, Ishmael against [Col. 0315C] Isaac [Note: [Col. 0315] Gen. 21]; of the third, Esau against Jacob [Note: [Col. 0315] Gen. 28]. In all these David declares himself steadfast thus: “Many who persecute me afflict me; yet I have not turned aside from your testimonies” [Note: [Col. 0315] Ps. 118].

Of the first the wicked said: “Come, let us unjustly oppress the righteous man” [Note: [Col. 0315] Wis. 10]. Of the second: “The lips of the harlot drip honey, and her throat is more shining than oil, but her end is bitter as wormwood” [Note: [Col. 0315] Song 6]. The Lord calls the third “whitewashed tombs” [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 23].

This accords with a threefold interpretation of the term: the first are called *mare* (“sea”) because they fill with bitter evil; the second *mare*, as though *malum remigio* (“an evil through rowing”); the third are called *mare*, as though *male animas irretiens* (“badly entangling souls”). But this sea is called deserted. For in the first case such a person is deserted; in the second, implanted; in the third, sown together: deserted by God, implanted by the devil, [Col. 0315D] and sown together with the counsel of the wicked.

The first occurs through reprobation, the second through instigation, the third through consenting to the wicked. For Judas was first abandoned by God: “Woe,” he says, “to that man through whom the Son of Man shall be betrayed” [Note: [Col. 0315] Luke 12]—behold, deserted by God through reprobation. “The devil put it into Judas’s heart” that he should betray him—behold, the devil was implanted through instigation. He came into the garden, having received a crowd from the chief priests, in order to betray him—behold the desert sea.

Thus the first burdens with the hand, the second with the tongue, the third with gesture and dress: with the hand, by scourging; with the tongue, by preaching; with dress and gesture, by feigning.

[Col. 0316A] By scourging the innocent, by preaching against the faith, by feigning holiness. The first prevail by enduring patiently; the second by resisting in word and knowledge; the third by mocking with prudence. Of the first: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” [Note: [Col. 0315] Jas. 1]; and: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 5]. Yet prayer must also be made for them: that God may give them a health-giving shame for their sin; that they may return to the fear of God; that they may have contrition of heart and body. Thus the prophet Jeremiah prays: “Let those who persecute me be put to shame, but let me not be put to shame; let them be afraid, but let me not be afraid; crush them, Lord God, with a double crushing” [Note: [Col. 0315] Jer. 17].

Of the [Col. 0316B] second it is said: “The lips of the harlot drip honeycomb, and her throat is more lustrous than oil; but her end is like wormwood” [Note: [Col. 0315] Song 6]. Of these Solomon says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” [Note: [Col. 0315] Prov. 1]; of the third: “Hypocrite, cast the beam out of your own eye, so that afterward you may cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” [Note: [Col. 0315] Luke 6]. All these are called foxes. The first are called foxes, as though *vulnerating most wickedly*; the second, foxes, as though *casting down the common people*; the third, foxes, as though *enticing by a serene countenance*. These, while destroying the vineyards—that is, souls or churches—burden them with the burden called “the wilderness of the sea”: “It destroys what it did not bear; it made riches for itself by judgment and not by justice, and in the midst of its days it will leave them, [Col. 0316C] and at its end it will be a fool” [Note: [Col. 0315] Jer. 17]. These are heretics: what Catholics have begotten in faith, they themselves cherish in their own error.

“Catch for us the little foxes,” etc.

[CARD.] She herself, indeed—as the preceding verse shows—having been called to heaven for the Church’s help, so that foxes may not harm the flowering vineyards, therefore arouses and invites the teachers to drive heretics out of the Church gathered from the Gentiles. She says: “Catch,” that is, rebuke and overcome, for us—for the glory and honor alike of my Son and of myself—the little foxes, which is to say, because they destroy the vineyards. Do this, for our vineyard has flowered. Foxes harm vineyards in bloom because they shake off and eat the blossoms.

[Col. 0316D] By foxes she means crafty heretics, who walk tortuously and perversely through Holy Scripture, and who pretend to be humble and little in order to do greater harm. They destroy by gnawing and corrupting in the vineyards, that is, in the churches: the flowers and shoots of virtues, namely the beginnings of holy works. For this reason she stirs zeal against the foxes, saying: “For our vineyard has flowered,” signifying the same thing by “vineyards” and “vineyard,” because all churches are one Church. But, in order to make those whom she arouses more attentive to this work, the Mother adds:

“My beloved is mine, and I am his; he feeds among [Col. 0317A] the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline.”

[THO.] As though she said: I steadfastly retain the friendship of my Beloved, because I perceive his benevolence towards me to be constant, and in his intimacy I perceive what he does. For he feeds among lilies. By lilies are signified souls which, while retaining the whiteness of chastity, emit a sweet fragrance to their neighbors through the reputation of a good name. Thus he feeds among lilies who delights in the chastity of souls. But the day will then breathe, and the shadows will decline, because eternal life will appear and the present life will end. Here are the shadows of night; there they will decline, that is, fail. Yearning for this, souls cry: “Return.”

The Bridegroom is said to feed among lilies because of truth, gentleness, and justice: namely, because through him the promises [Col. 0317B] have been fulfilled, iniquities remitted, and proud demons judged. Thus he appeared as one deservedly to be loved: true in himself, gentle for humankind, just for humankind. Therefore every soul ought to entrust itself to so faithful a rewarder, so merciful a pardoner, so just a defender.

Hear of the lilies: truth, gentleness, and justice—lilies springing from the earth, shining above the earth, pre-eminent among the flowers of earth, fragrant beyond the smell of spices. Truth is well called a lily: its fragrance animates faith and its radiance illumines understanding. Gentleness too is a lily, by reason of innocence’s whiteness and hope’s fragrance; justice also is a lily: “The righteous man shall blossom like a lily” [Note: [Col. 0317] Hos. 14].

Christ’s lilies are his [Col. 0317C] conception, birth, manner of life, utterances, miracles, sacraments, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension. His Mother’s incorruptible virginity made his birth white; innocence of life, his conduct; truth, his utterances; purity of heart, his miracles; the hidden mystery of mercy, his sacraments; willingness to suffer, his passion; freedom from the necessity of dying, his death; the fortitude of martyrdom, his resurrection; the fulfilment of promises, his ascension.

Among these are three lilies which we must have: innocence, continence, and patience. Therefore, if that lover of lilies comes in order to make the Passover among us, in the first there will be that renowned sweetness, in the second fragrant delight, and in the third great security. It is night; the Lord is day [Note: [Col. 0317] Jer. 46]—the day that illumines and breathes, which by the spirit of his mouth drives away the shadows. For shadows to decline is for them [Col. 0317D] to be annihilated. And by shadows he means the enigmas of Scripture, philosophy, sophistical quibbles, and convoluted arguments, which will cease.

In the angels the day is breathing, eternal brightness. In the first parents it was inspiring: “He breathed into his face the breath of life” [Note: [Col. 0317] Gen. 2]. Afterwards it became conspiring, because the serpent, Eve, and Adam conspired together [Note: [Col. 0317] Gen. 3]. Then it became expiring, because its brightness vanished and it became necessary for us to die abundantly. From then until Christ it became sighing; but from Christ it became breathing again; after judgment it will be breathing toward us.

[Col. 0318A] There are three lilies: marital chastity, widowed continence, and virginal integrity. The first is excused, the second cleansed, the third inborn. The first is excused by the sacrament, through hope of offspring and faith; the second is cleansed by renunciation of what has been experienced; the third is inborn in imitation of angelic purity. In the first the Bridegroom feeds upon fruit—that is, faith, hope of offspring, the sacrament—and upon abstention from permitted embraces. In the second he feeds upon gladness in fulfilling voluntary vows. In the third he feeds upon the fragrance of angelic purity.

Or, in one and the same lily, marital chastity is in the pallor of the root; widowed continence in the greenness of the stalk; virginal integrity in the whiteness of the flower. The first are in the root, which is in the earth, because they are mutually bound by the marital debt. Widows are in the stalk: on one side they cleave to the root, [Col. 0318B] because they share with the first the fact that they were once subject to corruption; on the other side they approach the flower, because they aspire to virginity. Virgins are in the flower, because in its whiteness they have purity, in its fragrance a good reputation, and in its golden color inward love of God.

The first lily is commended by Christ through a miracle; the second through an oracle; the third through a seal. The first, by the miracle performed when he was invited to the wedding at Cana of Galilee; the second, when he was presented in the Temple and received from the aged Simeon and the widow Anna an oracle concerning him; the third, when at Christ’s birth the modesty of his Mother was sealed by him. Among these he feeds until the day breathes.

There are three days: the first is temporal, the second [Col. 0318C] spiritual, the third heavenly. The first brings us calamity, the second pardon, the third the vision of God. Job cursed the first thus: “Let the day perish on which I was born” [Note: [Col. 0317] Job 3]. Of the second: “Day utters speech to day” [Note: [Col. 0317] Ps. 18]. Of the third: “His throne is like the day of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0317] Ps. 88].

The first is conspiring, expiring, and sighing. It conspires by deliberating to sin; expires by perpetrating what has been deliberated; sighs by mourning what has been perpetrated. The second day is inspiring by understanding heavenly things, and breathing again by delighting in them; the third will be breathing toward us by seeing God. In that day the shadows will decline.

There are three shadows: the first tempers light; the second mitigates heat; the third darkens light. The first comes from the interposition of a cloud, the second from the placing of some [Col. 0318D] body before it, the third at evening through the setting of the sun. The first was at Christ’s birth, the second at his passion, the third from the disturbance of our misery. For neither could the Blessed Virgin have borne the weight of the Godhead, nor could we have understood it, unless the first shadow tempered it; whence it is said to her: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” [Note: [Col. 0317] Luke 1]. This was through the cloud of Christ’s flesh placed between; whence it is said: “The Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0317] Isa. 18]; and John says: “I saw a white cloud, and upon the cloud the Son of Man sitting” [Note: [Col. 0317] Rev. 14].

Likewise, we could not bear either the heat of temptations or the devil’s devices unless the second shadow [Col. 0319A] intervened, Christ’s body being set before us in the Passion; whence: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders” [Note: [Col. 0319] Ps. 90]. “In your shadow we shall live among the nations.” The third shadow darkens the light of contemplation when the sun sets at evening, that is, when Christ withdraws from us.

This evening is threefold. The first comes from temptation, the second from worldly care, the third from the reflection of heavenly light. Of the first: “Weeping will tarry in the evening, and joy at morning” [Note: [Col. 0319] Ps. 29]. Of the second: “Man shall go out to his work and to his labor until evening” [Note: [Col. 0319] Ps. 103]; and Job: “If I lie down, I say, ‘When shall I rise?’ and again I await evening” [Note: [Col. 0319] Job 7]. Of the third: “Stay with us, Lord, for it is toward evening and the day is declined” [Note: [Col. 0319] Luke 24].

For this is the sense of the threefold interpretation of the name. According to [Col. 0319B] the first, *vespera* (“evening”) is called, as it were, “breathing woe” (*vae spirans*); according to the second, it is called “veiling the sphere”—that is, Christ, who is a sphere according to the philosopher, whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere. He is also called a sphere because of the perfection denoted by roundness. According to the third, *vespera* is “force taking away appearance,” or “taking away appearance”: namely, when a man returns from contemplation because of the weakness of his spiritual eyes, which are dazzled by excessive brightness.

The first have blind eyes, like Tobit from the dung of a swallow [Note: [Col. 0319] Tob. 2], that is, from the devil’s suggestion. The second have bleary eyes, like Leah, because of active works [Note: [Col. 0319] Gen. 29]. The third have eyes weakened by excessive brightness; whence: “My eyes are weakened, looking upward [Col. 0319C] on high” [Note: [Col. 0319] Isa. 38]. He who has such eyes: “His lamp shall not be put out in the night” [Note: [Col. 0319] Prov. 31], even if it is weakened.

Therefore, when the day breathes, the shadows will decline. Evening will not then hinder humankind, because he will shine like the sun in the kingdom of his Father [Note: [Col. 0319] Matt. 13], and the Lamb will be its lamp. Moreover, the shadow which now mitigates heat will here be particular, but there will become general, because “the sun will not fall upon them, nor any heat” [Note: [Col. 0319] Rev. 7]. But the shadow which tempers light will then be perfected, because “what we now see through a mirror in an enigma, then we shall see face to face” [Note: [Col. 0319] 1 Cor. 13], so that Solomon’s saying may be fulfilled: “The path of the righteous, like a shining light, goes forward and increases unto the perfect day” [Note: [Col. 0319] Prov. 4]. There we shall say: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” [Note: [Col. 0319] Ps. 117].

At times we are wearied [Col. 0319D] by a hidden vexation of the mind. This is the burden of Dumah. For *Dumah* is interpreted “silence.” Many are burdened by silence, and rest weighs upon those for whom it is pleasant to be weighed down. This burden is voluntary. There is a threefold silence that burdens and is blameworthy: the first is silence required by monastic observance; the second, silence in secret confession; the third, cessation from divine praise.

Oh, how burdensome regular observance is to many when they have complaints in their hearts—frivolities, rumors, displays, detractions, murmurings—which strive to come out. Frivolities that provoke laughter; rumors by which we marvel at some [Col. 0320A] novelty; displays by which a person exhibits himself in pride; detractions by which he harms his neighbor; murmurings by which he sets forth his own defect. Oh, how great is the burden of a heart in which frivolities play wantonly, rumors roam, displays make a din, detractions prepare revenge, and murmurings disturb the heart. For frivolities make a man excessively merry within; rumors, slow; displays, hidden and unknown; detractions, insulted and cast down. When a monk has such things in his heart and has no power to utter them, he can say with Elihu: “I am full of words, and my spirit constrains me. My belly is like new wine without a vent, which bursts new wineskins” [Note: [Col. 0319] Job 32].

Such a heart is the Dead Sea. These five are the five cities of Sodom, which is called the silence of beasts. For these are the five foolish virgins who knock at the door, and no one opens to them [Note: [Col. 0319] Luke 13].

The silence of confession burdens in three ways: first, because it seems hard to the sinner to depart from the habit of sinning; second, because of the worm of conscience; third, because of the shame of embarrassment. In the first he considers God merciful; in the second, a severe judge; in the third, his confessor insufficiently trustworthy: merciful, that he may pardon; judge, that he may punish; confessor insufficiently trustworthy, lest he make the sin public and disclose it. In the first he says within himself: “God is merciful; I shall do penance without confession. For he will not judge twice for the same thing, nor will a double [Col. 0320C] tribulation arise.” Or: “I shall give alms, because it is written: ‘Give alms, and all things are clean for you’” [Note: [Col. 0319] Luke 11]. Or: “I shall groan before God, for he himself says: ‘At whatever hour the sinner groans, I will remember none of his iniquities’” [Note: [Col. 0319] Isa. 43].

In the second he sets before himself the terror of the Judge, the horror of the word, and the pain of hell: terror, because he is dreadful and will appear swiftly, for the pillars of heaven fear his coming; horror of the word: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” [Note: [Col. 0319] Matt. 25]; pain of hell: “Where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” [Note: [Col. 0319] Matt. 8].

Regarding the third he thinks thus: perhaps my confessor is such a one as, being angry, will make public and disclose my iniquity. Hence I shall say: “All day my shame is before me, and the confusion of my face has covered me, because of the voice of one reproaching and [Col. 0320D] speaking against me” [Note: [Col. 0319] Ps. 43]. Or he will hinder my advancement, saying, “Do not promote him,” for “God is not before his eyes; his ways are in iniquity at all times” [Note: [Col. 0319] Ps. 9]. Or perhaps he will judge me contemptible in his heart, saying: “He is grievous even to behold, because his ways are unlike my ways and his thoughts unlike my thoughts.”

The third silence lies in three things: a person is too sluggish to preach, pray, or praise. The first is owed to one’s neighbor, the second to oneself, the third to God: to one’s neighbor for conversion, to oneself for one’s own benefit, to God for honor. Of the first it is said: [Col. 0321A] “Am I my brother’s keeper?” [Note: [Col. 0321] Gen. 4]. Yet he does not heed: “I will require your brother’s blood from your hand” [Note: [Col. 0321] ibid.]. Of the second he says: “Who is the Lord, that we should fear him?” [Note: [Col. 0321] Deut. 6]; or, “What does it profit us if we pray to him?” He does not heed: “The persevering prayer of the righteous avails much” [Note: [Col. 0321] Jas. 5]; nor Elijah’s example: “He prayed and drought came to pass; and he prayed again, and heaven gave rain” [Note: [Col. 0321] 3 Kgs. 18]. Of the third he says: “The Lord has no need to be praised by me, because he has no need of my goods” [Note: [Col. 0321] Ps. 15]. Yet he does not heed: “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises” [Note: [Col. 0321] Ps. 46].

Behold the burden of Dumah. In the first, it burdens because one does not speak where it would be useful to speak; in the second, because one does not speak where it would be good to speak; in the third, because one does not speak where it would be delightful to speak. Therefore those whom the Lord calls to fulfil this can say: “My Beloved is mine, and I am his”; but if they do not do so, they say: “My Beloved is mine, and I do not answer him.”

“My beloved is mine, and I am his.”

[CARD.] As though she said: “My only and most dear Beloved said to me: ‘Arise, make haste, for the flowering vineyards have given forth their fragrance’” [Note: [Col. 0321] Song 2]. And I, his uniquely chosen one, invite you to aid the flowering vineyard, so that he who feeds among lilies may feed and delight in us, until the day breathes and the shadows decline.

Lilies are accustomed to heal burned bodies. Therefore, in the great and terrible wilderness, by which this world is signified—as Moses says in Deuteronomy—there is “a serpent that burns with its breath” [Note: [Col. 0321] Deut. 8]. This serpent is the devil, “from whose mouth,” as [Col. 0321C] Job says, “lamps come forth like burning firebrands” [Note: [Col. 0321] Job 41]. The mouth of the devil, however, is heretics, who kindle their hearers’ minds with the burning heat of unbelief. They have, like a torch, a sweet smell but a dark light: sweet is what they exhale, but black is what they shine. For they smell sweet through a simulation of righteousness, yet burn darkly through the perpetration of wickedness.

Therefore the Mother of the Lord wills that the teachers of the Church heal minds burned by the poisons of unbelief proceeding from heretics as from the serpent’s mouth; and that in this manner they may be lilies in which God feeds, that is, in which he delights, until the day breathes—the light, namely, of everlasting life, which has no evening—and until the shadows decline, that is, until the errors, ignorances, and darkness of the present life pass away and fail. Having said these things against heretical perversity, the Mother turns to her Son, to implore the Son’s aid against Jewish unbelief, saying:

“Return; be like, my beloved, a roe and a young hart upon the mountains of Bethel.”

[THO.] Our Beloved bodily departed from us when, after the resurrection, he ascended into heaven. He will return when, at the end of the world, the bodies of human beings having been raised, he is manifested in judgment. Upon the mountains of Bethel he will appear like a roe and a young [Col. 0322A] hart, because he will come to judgment in the same form of humanity which he received from the Church, when in this world he was born from the lineage of the fathers, outwardly humble like a young hart.

An intemperate person makes this summons. Such a person, triumphing in himself and taking captive every sense of shame, brings forth neglect of the measure of propriety, the counsel of deliberation, modesty, and timeliness. He seeks not only the Beloved’s presence in his heart but also clemency at the judgment. For if, even with this moderation of mercy, there will be such equity in the judgment, severity in the Judge, sublimity in majesty, and unprecedented novelty in the appearance of things themselves, that the day of his coming cannot be conceived—what would it be if he came in that greatness, power, and purity of divinity, “to show his power against [Col. 0322B] a leaf driven by the wind,” and to pursue dry stubble [Note: [Col. 0321] Job 13]?

But for the children of grace there will appear a certain gentle vision of a man: a support of faith, a strength of hope, an argument for confidence. But what is a child of grace? If I find a soul which the Bridegroom is accustomed frequently to visit, and to which familiarity has given boldness, tasting has given hunger, and contempt for all things has given leisure, I should call that soul worthy. Carried by vows, drawn by desires, it overlooks merits; it closes its eyes to majesty and opens them to delight. Acting confidently in salvation, it securely calls him not “Lord” but “Beloved,” saying: “Return, my Beloved.”

Long deprivation compels it to call—the nurse of weariness, the tinder of suspicions, the fountain of impatience. For it claims for itself all that the Lord did in his humanity, and says: “The mortality of the one born is mine; the weakness of the little child is mine; the expiration of the Crucified is mine; the sleep of the Buried is mine; therefore I trust.”

Since we read of three advents of the Savior, we believe that the Bride desires the third when she says, “Return, my Beloved.” Of these three advents, the first was in flesh, the second in the heart, and the third will be in majesty. The ancient fathers desired the first; those ensnared by sins, the second; the righteous desire the third. The first desire for three things, likewise the second for three things, but the third for one thing. Hence come the seven vowel antiphons, which are sung before Christmas.

For in the first three are sought the three things desired by the ancient fathers: instruction, redemption, and liberation. Thus the first says: “O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High, come to teach us the way of prudence” [Note: [Col. 0321] Office of the Church; Prov. 9]. The second asks redemption thus: “O Adonai, come to redeem us with outstretched arm” [Note: [Col. 0321] ibid.; Jer. 27]. The third asks freedom thus: “O Root of Jesse, come to set us free; delay no longer” [Note: [Col. 0321] ibid.; Isa. 11].

These three pertain to the first [Col. 0322D] advent. But the following three refer to the second advent, which is in the heart and which the fathers ensnared by sins desire, on account of the three things for which they ask in these three: cleansing from the darkness of sins, illumination by grace, and salvation against temptation. Thus the first asks: “O Key of David, who shuttest and none opens, openest and none shuts, come and lead the captive out of the prison house, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death” [Note: [Col. 0323] ibid.; Rev. 3]. The second asks: “O Dayspring, splendor of eternal light, come and enlighten humankind” [Note: [Col. 0323] ibid.; John 1]. The third asks: “O King of glory, come and save the human being whom you formed from the mud” [Note: [Col. 0323] ibid.].

The seventh concerns the third advent, which will be in majesty. The righteous desire this advent, and therefore ask one thing, in accordance with the words: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek” [Note: [Col. 0323] Ps. 26]—namely, to be saved from this present misery. For in the foregoing was sought salvation from temptation; here, however, the salvation of the eternal homeland is sought. Thus it asks: “O Emmanuel, come to save us, O Lord our God” [Note: [Col. 0323] Office of the Church]. For Emmanuel means “God with us,” who will be with us perpetually in that [Col. 0323B] salvation in which we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our lowliness, making it conformed to the body of his glory. But in order that we may await him securely in the third advent, whenever we are troubled by some defect through which we can fall from righteousness into sin, let us invoke him thus: “Return; be like a roe,” etc.

For then there presses upon us the burden called Abisaia: “The burden in Arabia” [Note: [Col. 0323] Isa. 21]. Therefore it is necessary that we pursue this burden. At times we are burdened by the consideration of death and the horror of our final lot. This is the burden in Arabia; *Arabia* is interpreted “evening,” which is the end of day and the beginning of night, aptly signifying the hour of death, which lays no light weight of fear upon all mortals. [Col. 0323C] But who may rejoice to be exempt from this, when the Savior, willingly suffering, “began to fear and to be distressed” [Note: [Col. 0323] Mark 14]?

Evening, as we have said, is the end of day and the beginning of night. It expresses the fall of one who, after works of righteousness, begins works of darkness. This burden also is necessary. This evening is threefold, because this burden is threefold. The first evening is the hour when a person passes from prosperity into adversity; the second, when one falls from righteousness into iniquity; the third, when one descends from life into death.

Of the first David says: “At evening, morning, and noon I will declare” [Note: [Col. 0323] Ps. 54]. For evening is adversity in conception; morning, prosperity in its beginning; noon, prosperity in its fullness. Likewise Jacob says of this: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall seize prey; in the evening he shall divide food” [Note: [Col. 0323] Gen. 49]. In great prosperity he persecuted Christians—that is, in the morning he seized prey; in great adversity he preached God’s commands—that is, in the evening he shall divide food. Likewise, when the crowds followed the Lord through the wilderness, at evening the disciples said to Jesus: “Dismiss the crowds, that they may buy food” [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 9], as though saying: From the wilderness, in which evening is drawing on—that is, adversity is beginning.

Of the second evening: “Woe to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness until evening” [Note: [Col. 0323] Isa. 5]. Likewise: “In the evening you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’” [Note: [Col. 0323] Matt. 16]. In the hour of sin you say: “Christ’s blood will wash everything away.” Of the third it is said: “In the morning may he flourish and pass away; in the evening may he fall, grow hard, and wither” [Note: [Col. 0323] Ps. 89]. Likewise: Jesus supped with his disciples when evening had come, the hour of death being near [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 22].

The first, therefore, breaks; the second afflicts; the third touches. It breaks patience, afflicts conscience, and touches our pride: patience with pain, conscience with sorrow, pride with fear. Of the first David says to Joab: “Let not adversity break you, for the outcome of war is various” [Note: [Col. 0323] 2 Sam. 11]. We have an example of the second in Peter, whom, after his denial, “God looked upon, and he went out and wept bitterly” [Note: [Col. 0323] Matt. 26]. Of the third David says: “The pains of death surrounded me” [Note: [Col. 0323] Ps. 17]; and another says: “Fear of death troubles me.”

Let us therefore see [Col. 0324B] concerning the first, namely how great a burden it is for patience to be broken. When more deeply broken by adversity, a person avenges his anger: first upon himself, second upon his neighbor, third upon God. Sorrow agitates himself; he scourges his neighbor; he blasphemes God. Of the first the Apostle says: “The sorrow of the world works death.” Of the second we read of Herod that, while he teemed with worms, justly scourged by God, he went so mad with pain that at his death he had many of the nobler Jews killed, lest the Jews rejoice in his death. Of the third Elihu said, speaking against Job: “He who heaps blasphemy upon his sins, let him be restrained among us” [Note: [Col. 0323] Job 34].

The second evening burdens grievously when the sinner considers how great a sweetness of conscience he has lost, into how great an unpleasantness of conscience he has fallen, into how great an impurity of guilt he has fallen, and how great a severity of punishment awaits him. First, with Adam, he fell from the pleasantness of Paradise [Note: [Col. 0323] Gen. 3]; second, with him, he fell into the filth of this world; third, with him, he deserved the punishments of hell. Of the first Job said: “I, once prosperous, have suddenly been shattered” [Note: [Col. 0323] Job 16]. Of the second Jeremiah says: “My life has fallen into the pit; they laid a stone upon me” [Note: [Col. 0323] Lam. 3]; likewise: “Woe to us, for we have sinned, because the crown of our head has fallen” [Note: [Col. 0323] Jer. 13]. Regarding the third the Prophet says: “Who among you will be able to dwell with devouring fire, or who among you will dwell with everlasting burnings?” [Note: [Col. 0323] Isa. 33].

The third evening likewise burdens grievously if one considers the discord between body and [Col. 0324D] soul, the cruelty of the devil, and experience of an unfamiliar region: the discord by which the soul withdraws from the body its vegetative functioning; the devil’s cruelty, as he stands beside the dying and zealously investigates their sins; experience of the region, because the departing soul does not know into what region of unlikeness it is going.

Concerning the first, ask the Savior, who before the Passion “began to fear and to be distressed” [Note: [Col. 0323] Mark 14]; concerning the second, blessed Martin, who at his death saw a devil standing by him; concerning the third, Job, saying: “Leave me, that I may mourn my pain a little before I go to a land [Col. 0325A] dark and covered with the gloom of death” [Note: [Col. 0325] Job 10].

Therefore, if we fall into these three evenings, the Beloved withdraws from us. Hence we must cry: “Return, my Beloved.” Let him return, then, in the first evening, that he may sustain us in adversity; in the second, that he may protect us in temptation; and in the third, that he may reform the body of our lowliness, making it conformed to the body of his glory.

In the first, therefore, let him return like a roe, for the roe feeds upon high rocks. And in his return, let us feed upon lofty meditations, so that, refreshed by his heavenly consolation, we may be sustained by him in adversity. But in the second evening let him return like a young hart, which by its nimbleness leaps over thorn-bushes, so that in our temptations, through him who was born of sinners without sin, we may [Col. 0325B] flee sins. In the third evening let him return upon the mountains of Bethel, which is interpreted “house of God,” so that, as he stands by us in death, we may pass with him to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God. May he grant this, to whom are honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

“Return; be like, my beloved, a roe and a young hart, upon the mountains of Bethel.”

[CARD.] As though she said: “Return, my Beloved, upon the mountains of Bethel.” By mountains are indicated pride and exaltation. Bethel is interpreted “the house rising up.” This house is the Synagogue, which rose up against the Lord as an enemy, as he says through the prophet Micah: “Are not my words good to him [Col. 0325C] who walks uprightly? Yet, on the contrary, my people have risen up as an adversary” [Note: [Col. 0325] Mic. 2]. God is therefore asked mercifully to return to the Jewish people, who have risen against him as an adversary and whom he abandoned because of the pride of their unbelief; and to be like a roe and a young hart, which do not so abandon the places they leave that they do not sometimes return to them. It follows.

## Chapter III

“Upon my bed I sought by night him whom my soul loves.”

[THO.] The holy soul makes a little bed for herself when, fleeing the disturbances of the world, she prepares a secluded place in which to rest. There she seeks Him whom she loves, because, when she is free from worldly care, she does not cease, in that very search, from considering how she may attain to Him. [Col. 0325D] He seeks by night who lives in this world and thoroughly shakes off from himself the darkness of temporality. But because no one who seeks perfectly in this world finds, she adds: “I sought him and did not find him.” There are three causes that commonly frustrate seekers: namely, when one does not seek at the proper time, or not as one ought, or where one ought not. But she seeks at the proper time, because “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0325] II Cor. 6.]. Nor does the second cause hinder her. For she seeks with a burning heart and wholly untiringly. But perhaps the third hinders her, when He is sought where He ought not to be sought. For perhaps He ought to have been sought not in a little bed but in a bed—He for whom the world is narrow. Why do you seek the strong one in a bed, the great one in a little bed, the glorified one in a stable? For He who, in the glory of the resurrection, cast off every infirmity, girded Himself with power and clothed Himself with light as with a garment.

We find three beds in this Song: one here: “Upon my little bed I sought by night him whom my soul loves” [Note: [Col. 0325] Song 3.]; another there: “Behold Solomon’s bed; sixty mighty men surround it, of the mightiest of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0325] Ibid.]; a third there: “Our little bed is flowering” [Note: [Col. 0325] Song 1.]. This little bed is the conscience variously disposed. In the first lie the wounded, in the second the weary, in the third the refined. Wounded by sin; weary in battle; refined by holy leisure. The first is called dark by night, the second fortified with weapons, the third adorned with flowers. In the first lie penitents; in the second, [Col. 0326B] those at work; in the third, contemplatives. The first are in withdrawal, the second in progress, the third in ecstasy: in withdrawal from sins, in the progress of virtue, in the ecstasy of the mind.

Of the first: “Every night I shall wash my bed” [Note: [Col. 0325] Ps. 6.]; likewise: “May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain” [Note: [Col. 0325] Ps. 40.]. Of the second: “Jacob gathered up his feet upon his bed and died” [Note: [Col. 0325] Gen. 49.]. He gathers his feet upon his bed who examines his affections in his conscience; and thus he dies securely, because he dies to sin, not to God. Of the third: “Two shall be in one bed: the one shall be taken and the other left” [Note: [Col. 0325] Luke 17.]. For there are two contemplations. The first is that of philosophers, and these shall be left; the second, that of religious persons, and these shall be taken.

The first is dark by night. It has three darknesses: [Col. 0326C] the first of sin, the second of ignorance, the third of hell. The first causes anxiety and disturbance; the second, unsteady steps; the third, fear. Of the first: “He has placed me in darkness as the dead of old” [Note: [Col. 0325] Lam. 3.], and “My spirit was troubled within me” [Note: [Col. 0325] Ps. 142.]: “My heart within me was disturbed.” Of the second: “They have not known nor understood; they walk in darkness; all the foundations of the earth shall be shaken” [Note: [Col. 0325] Ps. 81]. Of the third the same author says: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me” [Note: [Col. 0325] Ps. 54.]. Because of these Job said: “In darkness I have spread my bed” [Note: [Col. 0325] Job 17.].

The second bed is covered with weapons, because “the life of man upon earth is warfare” [Note: [Col. 0325] Job 7.]. But the weapons [Col. 0326D] of our warfare are not carnal, but pleasing to God. Let us therefore put on the weapons of light [Note: [Col. 0325] Rom. 13].—“Stand, having your loins girded with truth, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0325] Eph. 6.], and the rest which follows.

The third bed is flowering [Note: [Col. 0325] Song 1.]. For flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys surround it [Note: [Col. 0325] Song 2.], concerning which enough has been said above. There are three flowers: purity in the heart, truth in the mouth, sincerity in work. Then the little bed flowers: if we think what is holy, if we speak what is true, if we do what is just. In these three the Lord lies: in the first as physician, in the second as advocate, in the third as beloved. In the [Col. 0327A] first as physician, because those in health have no need of a physician, but those who are ill; in the second He lies as advocate, that He may be a helper in tribulations; in the third as beloved, that He may say to us: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” [Note: [Col. 0327] Ps. 33.].

This is the order of seeking, unlike the bride, who, while still lying in the first bed, sought where the physician ought to have been sought. Therefore she adds: “I sought and did not find” [Note: [Col. 0327] Song 3.]. Thus, when we seek Him whom we desire and cannot find Him, we are weighed down by a great burden.

This is the burden of the valley of vision [Note: [Col. 0327] Isa. 22.]. It happens that we are burdened in five ways: by vanity, namely because we make progress in good. This is called the valley of vision. Vision is related to contemplation, the valley to humility or abasement. For some persons’ contemplation is [Col. 0327B] humble, and others’ abased: humble in the saints, abased in philosophers. For if virtue makes progress, humility must be preserved; if it burdens, it is vanity. If human favour at times exalts the saints, they return; but philosophers are given over to a reprobate mind. And this is voluntary.

But, that this beloved may more readily be found and seen, let us consider the kinds of vision, so that we may find that by which He is seen and in which lies the burden of the valley of vision.

There are three kinds of vision. One is through the eyes, by which the letters themselves are seen; another through the human spirit, by which things absent and things near are thought of while absent. The third is through the gaze of the mind, by which love itself is contemplated as understood. The first is manifest [Col. 0327C] to all, by which heaven and earth are seen and perceived with material eyes. Nor is it difficult to explain the second, by which absent bodies are thought of: for we can see heaven and earth and the things in them. Even while situated among them, we think of them; and sometimes, seeing nothing with the eyes of the body, we behold in the mind alone bodily images, either true, as we see the bodies themselves, or fictitious, as thought has been able to form them. For we think differently about what we know and differently about what we do not know.

But the third kind is that by which understood love is contemplated; and it contains those realities which have no images resembling themselves, which are not what it itself is. For love is not seen in one way when present in its form as it is, and in another when absent in some similar [Col. 0327D] image; but, so far as it can be conceived by the mind, it is seen more by one person and less by another. These are the three kinds of visions. The first is called bodily, because it is presented to the bodily senses; the second spiritual, because whatever is not body but is substance is now rightly called spirit; the third is called intellectual, from intellect.

According to the first vision Belshazzar saw a hand, and at once, through bodily sense, the image of the thing bodily done was impressed upon the spirit and remained in thought [Note: [Col. 0327] Dan. 5.]. It was seen in the spirit and was not understood; nor was it then understood when it was occurring and appearing bodily. According to the second vision, Peter saw in ecstasy a vessel full of various living creatures and heard the voice, “Kill and eat” [Note: [Col. 0327] Acts 10.]. But, restored to bodily sense, he beheld by thought in the same spirit the very thing which, seen in the spirit, memory had retained: all of which were not bodies but images of bodies. In the third vision, called intellectual, are seen those things that are not bodies and do not bear forms resembling bodies: such as the mind itself, the soul, affection, charity, joy, peace, faith, and other such things by which one approaches God—and God Himself, from whom are all things, in whom are all things, through whom are all things.

These are the three heavens of which it was said that Paul was caught up to the third heaven [Note: [Col. 0327] II Cor. 12.]. Behold, these three visions burden us. [Col. 0328B] The first burdens by astonishment and wonder; the second, in investigating its meaning; the third, if it signifies evil, by the weight of sorrow, but if good, burdens by the effort of considering how the thing may come to pass. Hear that Belshazzar experienced this burden. In the first vision he saw bodily a hand writing on the wall: *Mene, Thekel, Peres* [Note: [Col. 0327] Dan. 5.]. Hear the burden: for in astonishment his knees struck together. According to the second vision he was burdened in seeking the meaning, until he summoned Daniel; according to the third vision, when he had heard the meaning, he was burdened, being anxious, as one might expect, over the death of which he had heard. Hear another burden of those who see.

For some fall from their vision into covetousness. Another burden: some into vanity, others into astonishment, others into humility. The first bear the burden, namely [Col. 0328C] avarice; the second, vainglory; the third fear in conscience; the fourth merit grace. The first, so far as lies in them, debase the favour of divine generosity; the second attribute to the creature—that is, to themselves—what belongs to the Creator; the third render fear to the Lord; the fourth pay honour to majesty. The first do not heed the Lord’s word: “Freely you have received; freely give” [Note: [Col. 0327] Matt. 10.]. The second do not heed the Apostle saying: “What have you that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” [Note: [Col. 0327] I Cor. 4.]. The third say: “Enter not into judgment with thy servant, O Lord, because no living person shall be justified in thy sight” [Note: [Col. 0327] Ps. 142.]. The fourth cry: “I am a worm and no man” [Note: [Col. 0327] Ps. 21.].

Balaam represents [Col. 0328D] the first to us: led by avarice, he taught how the children of Israel should commit fornication [Note: [Col. 0327] Num. 22.]. Zedekiah designates the second, who struck the prophet Micaiah on the cheek, saying: “Has the spirit left me and spoken to you?” [Note: [Col. 0327] III Kings 22.] This is the same man who had made iron horns for himself [Note: [Col. 0327] II Chron. 18.]. The wife of Manoah shows the third; when she had seen the angel, she said in wonder and fear: “We shall die, because we have seen the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0327] Judg. 33.]; and Isaiah: “Woe is me, because I am a man defiled in the lips, because I have seen the King, the Maker, with my eyes” [Note: [Col. 0327] Isa. 6.]. Abraham figures the fourth. For after he saw three men coming along the way, while standing by the oak of Mamre, he said: [Col. 0329A] “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” [Note: [Col. 0329] Gen. 18.].

These three visions are considered in another way: let the first, then, be called imaginative vision, the second rational, the third intellectual. Imagination, therefore, is the first heaven; reason, the second; understanding, the third. In the first, then, is the vision of the valley; in the second, the vision of the hill; in the third, the vision of the mountain. To the first belong images and likenesses of all visible things; to the second, investigations of visible things; to the third belong apprehensions and contemplations of spiritual things themselves, even divine things.

Therefore, in the vision of the valley, first consider yourself, that you may learn to appraise your spirit. Examine, then, what you are, what you were, what you ought to have been, what you still can be: what you were by nature; what now you are [Col. 0329B] by fault; what you ought to have been through diligence; what you still can be through grace. Learn from your own spirit to know what you ought to judge concerning other spirits. Shape your spirit from consideration of the ark. First consider the gold laid over the wood by which the ark is covered, that is, wisdom by which our heart is governed; secondly, that it is placed beneath the mercy-seat; thirdly, that it is set between the two.

It is laid over the wood so that it may conceal the lust of the eyes and be to you a covering for your eyes, lest perhaps your eyes be opened and see vanity. It is placed beneath the mercy-seat in order to raise it on high and that lower knowledge may serve higher knowledge. It is placed between the mercy-seat and the wood in order that the two may be kept apart and it may suspend our heart from the love of lower things, lest perhaps it go after its lusts, like a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0329] Gen. 4.].

Behold, imagination, through which you have knowledge of yourself, now passes to the rational faculty, through which you may know the creation of things, and thus ascend through it to the intellectual faculty, where you may have knowledge of God. The rational faculty therefore first treats of the use of temporal things; secondly considers their nature; thirdly, the ordering of morals and virtues. The first is so that we may use them moderately for necessity; the second, so that the Creator may be known in creatures; the third, so that what is first may not be put last.

Of the first it is said in praise of the strong woman: “She considered the paths of her household and did not eat the bread of idleness” [Note: [Col. 0329] Prov. 31.]. Of the second: “The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are understood and seen through the things that have been made—His eternal power and riches also” [Note: [Col. 0329] Rom. 1.]. Of the third, in this Song: “He ordered charity in me” [Note: [Col. 0329] Song 1.].

Reason also considers how spiritual nature is created in order that it may exist; secondly, justified in order that it may be good; thirdly, glorified in order that it may be true. By creation, therefore, it is initiated into good; by justification, enlarged in good; by glorification, consummated in good. The goods of creation are for a beginning; the goods of justification, for advancement; the goods of glorification, for consummation. The first goods are gifts of the Creator and rewards of the creature. In the first, the rational creature [Col. 0330A] is initiated toward the perfection of future fullness; by the second it grows, advances, and is enlarged; in the last it is raised to glory and exalted in glory.

And this is full blessedness. Blessedness may be true yet false; true, yet neither secure nor full; true and secure, yet not full; or true and secure and full. Of the first: “My people, those who call you blessed, themselves deceive you” [Note: [Col. 0329] Isa. 3.]; and: “They called blessed the people to whom these things belong; blessed is the people whose God is the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0329] Ps. 143.]. Of the second: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor” [Note: [Col. 0329] Ps. 40.]. Of the third: “Now the Spirit says that they may rest from their labours” [Note: [Col. 0329] Rev. 14.]. Of the fourth: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0329] Matt. 5.], once their bodies too have been received. The first are those who live in prosperity; the second in charity; the third [Col. 0330B] are souls that, freed from the weight of their bodies, have already received the first robe; the fourth are angels and human beings after they have been rewarded with the splendour of both robes.

Concerning the third vision, namely that of understanding, Solomon says: “The sun rises and sets and returns to its place” [Note: [Col. 0329] Eccl. 1.]. The sun rises when the understanding of truth is inspired into the heart; likewise it sets when the ray of understanding is withdrawn. But it returns again to its place and is born anew there. The place of this sun is the mind, because understanding is born from Christ when grace is inspired. Therefore, its first birth pertains to the first vision, namely the spiritual; its rebirth, to the second, namely the rational; its circling toward the south, to the third, [Col. 0330C] namely the intellectual; and its turning toward the north means that, after all these visions, it considers from afar the punishment of Gehenna.

We said that the first is in the valley, the second on the hill, and the third on the mountain. Therefore, when the sun rises in the first, we become conscious within ourselves of vices and virtues. When it returns through the second, namely the rational, we know the Creator more fully through inspection of creatures. When it is at noon in the third vision, we contemplate the rewards of good merits, the joy of the heavenly citizens, and the hidden mysteries of divine secrets. But when we return from the south, we turn to the north, where we see the recompenses of evil merits, the end of malignant spirits, and of reprobate human beings. That vision which is at noon is itself on the mountain.

[Col. 0330D] “I sought him and did not find him.”

[THO. (so marked)] The human mind naturally dreams of and investigates the good. But because it seeks through nights, it does not find. By “nights” he means ignorance or worldly occupations which blind. Therefore, those who are ignorant or hindered by worldly business can indeed seek, but as long as they remain in that state they cannot find. For we shall not find unless we know and are freed from worldly affairs. And we are not freed when we take delight in them beyond measure.

There are three things that prevent this beloved from being found. First, He is sought unworthily; second, He withdraws Himself so that, not found, He may be sought more fervently; third, He is not sought for the purpose for which He ought to have been sought. In the first way Herod sought Him, namely in order to kill Him, and thus unworthily. In the second way the apostles sought after the resurrection. But He often withdrew Himself, and they sought more ardently. In the third way the women sought Him at the tomb in order to anoint Him, though He had already risen; and He was not to be sought in the tomb, which is the place of the dead, but above, which is the place of the living. Thus she sought because she was still in the dark little bed.

Behold, while she thus seeks and does not find, she suffers the grievous burden of anxiety. This is that tenth [Col. 0331B] burden of Isaiah called the burden of Tyre [Note: [Col. 0331] Isa. 23.]. For Tyre is interpreted “narrowness” or “disturbance.” This burden is considered especially in three things. The first is in the bitterness of penitence, the second in the labour of continence, the third in bodily sickness. There is also another narrowness of heart, caused by self-love. Opposed to it is the breadth of heart caused by love of God and neighbour.

Self-love proceeds from one’s own will. Whoever therefore loves his own will regards another’s will as a burden. Such a person is prompt toward everything that his own will suggests to him; toward everything that another’s will suggests to him he is sluggish and perverse. This burden too is voluntary. Great indeed is the burden of the bitterness of penitence, as the Saviour Himself testifies: “Broad,” He says, “is the way [Col. 0331C] that leads to death; but narrow is that which leads to life” [Note: [Col. 0331] Matt. 7.]. For the way of life is penitence, concerning which John the Baptist says [Note: [Col. 0331] Matt. 3.]: “Make straight in the wilderness the paths of our God.”

Likewise, the labour of continence is a grave burden and full of narrowness, as that most chaste woman—Susanna, I mean—testifies. For in keeping continence she chose death for herself rather than to lead a shameful life, saying: “I am hemmed in on every side: for if I do this, it is death to me; but if I do not do it, I shall not escape your hands. Yet it is better for me to fall into the hands of men than to forsake the law of my God” [Note: [Col. 0331] Dan. 13.]. But how great a burden the distress of bodily illness is, ask Saul. For he said [Col. 0331D] to his armour-bearer: “Draw your sword and stand over me, because distresses press upon me and my whole soul is still within me” [Note: [Col. 0331] I Sam. 31.].

The burden of Tyre is otherwise assigned, namely in three ways. Note that she said “I sought” three times. First, “Upon my little bed I sought by night”; second, “I sought and did not find”; third, “Through lanes and squares I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him” [Note: [Col. 0331] Song 7.]. And this corresponds to the threefold interpretation of this name. For Tyre is called narrowness, or tribulation, or strong; and also corresponds to the threefold state of religion.

For there are three kinds of people in religious life: there are perverse persons, penitents, and perfect persons. [Col. 0332A] The first are burdened with the burden of narrowness, the second with the burden of tribulation, the third with the burden of strength. The first burden comes from the worm of conscience, the second from penitence, the third from love. For the first threatens hell; the second washes away sin; the third incites one to seek the beloved, and, when it finds Him, the lover suffers faintness. Therefore the bride’s little bed is holy religious life. These three lie in it, though differently. For in religious life there are good and evil persons.

On account of the first there is the first inquiry, at night, and therefore He is not found; on account of the second there is the second inquiry, as though at dawn, and she does not find because they are not perfect; on account of the third there is the third, as though at noon, but He is not found at once, so that He may be sought with more burning desire. On account of the first it was said: “All her persecutors overtook her amid straits” [Note: [Col. 0331] Lam. 1.]; on account of the second: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and He will save the humble in spirit.
