Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them” [Note: [Col. 0331] Ps. 33.]; for the third it is said: “I love those who love me, and those who watch for me in the morning shall find me” [Note: [Col. 0331] Prov. 8.].

These lie differently in the little bed of religious life. For religion is severe to the perverse, merciful to penitents, best for the perfect. Concerning the perverse, we know that whatever goodness exists in severity is a burden to them. For it preserves propriety, chastens laxity, and the unlearned fears it. It is the ornament of old men, the rod of young men, adorns the persons of prelates, and gives colour to the beauty of virtues. The sweetness of the prelate draws the sinful disciple to penitence. Severity corrects; rectitude gives law to the offender. Thus neither does severity permit laxity, nor sweetness dissipation, nor rectitude transgression of the line of justice. Hence David says: “Sweet and upright is the Lord; therefore He will give a law to offenders in the way” [Note: [Col. 0331] Ps. 24.].

Indiscreet teachers make this burden heavier for the perverse. They display anger in place of severity, bitterness in place of sweetness, cruelty in place of rectitude; for anger disturbs the sinner, bitterness persecutes, cruelty afflicts. Some perverse persons are manifest, others hidden. The open ones defend their evils, pervert the goods of others, are incorrigible, slow to obedience, provoke humble brothers, and disturb silence. Such persons [Col. 0332D] Goliath represents, both by his great size and by the variety of his weapons; he challenged the children of Israel, trusting, that is, in his weapons [Note: [Col. 0331] I Sam. 17.].

The head of perversity is the intention of evil action; the left side, the left part; the legs, the end of the action; the body, the whole action; the helmet upon the head is commendation of the intention; the shield is excuse for the left-hand part. The two greaves are perseverance and obstinacy. The breastplate is open defence of the whole action.

The perversity of others is hidden. By their counsel these stir up brothers to anger and incite them to quarrels. They make Absalom rise against David, like Ahithophel [Note: [Col. 0331] II Sam. 15.]. Behold the burden of the perverse, namely narrowness, by which not only they themselves but others also are disturbed.

But the burden of penitents is the lighter, the more useful it is. A human being repents in three ways, and God has mercy in three ways. He waits for the sinner, consoles the despairing, and rejoices with the penitent. He recalls the sinner by the gift of grace; He consoles the despairing through hope of pardon; He strengthens the penitent from promises of glory. A person also has mercy upon another person in three ways. For a prelate has mercy upon a disciple, a disciple upon a prelate, and a disciple likewise upon a disciple.

A prelate has mercy upon a disciple when he kindly corrects the sinner with words, raises the despairing to hope by examples of mercy, and loves the corrected person after his misdeeds. A disciple likewise has mercy upon a prelate in three ways: when he does not resist his master when angry, does not speak ill of him when sinful, or endures him when perverse. [Col. 0333B] For David fled from Saul when he was angry. When Saul was relieving himself in the cave, David, though able to kill him, did not kill him. He endured the perverse man as long as he lived. A disciple also has mercy upon a disciple when he compassionately prays for one who sins, or corrects him alone, between himself and that person, or graciously forgives one who sins against him. Behold the burden of tribulation, namely of penitents, by which even their neighbour is burdened when, as has been said, he compassionately shares their suffering.

The burden of the perfect is the burden of strength arising from love. It is, as it were, at noon; yet the beloved withdraws Himself from such persons in order that He may be sought more fervently and the perfect person thereby become more perfect. For them religion is best. The distribution of possessions makes persons good; renunciation of the world, better; dwelling together in religion, best. For religion makes the evil person good, the good person better, and the better person best. And this occurs when God visits the ungodly, whence David says: “You visited the earth and made it drunk” [Note: [Col. 0333] Ps. 64.].

God visits bad earth, good earth, better earth, and best earth. He visits bad earth through fear; good earth through charity beginning; better earth through abundance; best earth through perfect charity. Therefore He visits bad earth when someone is pierced by fear of judgment; good earth through beginning charity when someone distributes his possessions; better earth through abundance when someone renounces the world, changes his habit, and keeps peace with the brothers. Yet if he is slandered, perhaps he suffers not lightly; but he is still lightly disturbed, becomes angry, and hates. These are the sons of the prophets who cried, “Death is in the pot” [Note: [Col. 0333] IV Kings 4.], whose food Elisha sweetened by adding flour. But perfect charity loves an enemy. What perfect charity is, and how the third burden of Tyre, namely that of strength, is found, is set forth in the following chapter.

“Upon my little bed by nights I sought him whom my soul loves.”

[CARD.] In this chapter, moreover, are signified the blindness of the Jewish people abandoned by the Lord and the concern of the blessed Virgin Mary for the salvation of that same people; and the words refer to the time of the Lord’s Passion. She says, therefore: Through the nights of my tribulation and sorrow, through the nights of my son’s passion and burial, through the nights of my people’s ignorance and error, I sought Him whom my soul loves upon my little bed—that is, in tranquillity of mind and quiet of contemplation, in which little bed I had been accustomed to rejoice with Him. For I sought there and did not find, because there was no rest and tranquillity in my mind, but rather pain and disturbance; and I said to myself in my mind:

“I shall arise and go about the city through lanes and squares; I shall seek him whom my soul loves. I sought and did not find.”

[THO.] This soul is not sluggish: it rises, goes about, and seeks. It rises from the bed, goes about the city, seeks through lanes and squares: from the bed of contemplation, the city of heavenly dwelling; the lanes of narrower conduct, [Col. 0334B] and the squares of more lenient conduct. It departs from the bed of contemplation; it enters the city of heavenly dwelling. It passes before the lanes of narrower conduct; it approaches the squares of more lenient conduct. It departs in order profitably to withdraw itself; enters in order to draw itself into the unity of charity; passes before in order to draw others toward the kingdom; approaches in order to draw them toward the higher life.

To the first, when He foretold His ascension, He said: “Because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart” [Note: [Col. 0333] John 16.], namely, because of my departure. But it is beneficial for you, “because I shall come to you and your heart shall rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0333] Ibid.]. To the second He says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am in the midst of them” [Note: [Col. 0333] Matt. 18.]. To the third He says: [Col. 0334C] “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” [Note: [Col. 0333] Matt. 16.]. To the fourth He says: “Whoever leaves father, mother, wife, or fields for my sake shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0333] Matt. 19.].

Through these paths she seeks strength not only in the body but also in the heart. For there are three kinds of strong persons: strong in wisdom, strong in body, and strong in spirit. Strong in wisdom are those who, though they have neither the affection of love nor bodily strength, nevertheless possess a certain knowledge by which, knowing their own weakness and their Creator’s kindness, they bend the severity of their spirit and compel the body to serve its Creator. These bear their brothers’ burdens by consolation and raise up the fallen by teaching. If they themselves fall, they quickly rise again.

Those are strong in body whom nature has made robust for enduring labours. Some can work but will not: these are Goliaths. Others can and will, like David. Those who can and will not are accused of theft, robbery, and falsehood. They are thieves because they withdraw themselves from the common need. They lie before God and men who are able but unwilling to render what they know they can render. They are robbers before God who violently withhold from the common life what they can and know how to contribute. Therefore they are thieves before their brothers, robbers before God, and liars before God and men.

Among those strong in spirit, some are strong, others stronger, others strongest. [Col. 0335A] Tobit was strong, Job stronger, Abraham strongest. Strength of spirit is tested by covetousness and carnality. Tobit did not yield to covetousness when he entrusted money to Gabael [Note: [Col. 0335] Tob. 9.]. Job lost his money but said: “The Lord gave, the Lord took away; as it pleased the Lord, so it was done” [Note: [Col. 0335] Job 1.]. Abraham voluntarily left what he possessed, obeying the Lord [Note: [Col. 0335] Gen. 22.]. Tobit entrusted, Job lost, Abraham left behind: the first money, the second property, the third house, land, and kindred. One in hope, the other patiently, the third willingly; the first by compassionating the needy, the second by enduring the persecutor, the third by obeying the one who commanded.

Thus some do not yield to covetousness, which consists in three things: love of possessing, grief at losing, and compulsion to surrender. But all three at once cast out their respective three. Tobit loved his son no more than he ought, and prayed for him while he was present; Job did not grieve beyond measure at his children’s death. At their death he shed tears; while they lived he offered holocausts for each of them. Abraham not only sent Ishmael away but also offered Isaac to God.

Abraham was most strong; yet Lawrence was stronger than the strongest. For Abraham left behind his own possessions; Lawrence scattered his own. Abraham offered his son to God; Lawrence offered himself for the Son of God. Abraham prepares the fire, binds his son, draws the sword; but hears the angel forbidding him to accomplish the deed. Lawrence, placed upon the fire, preached Christ, enraged his executioners with words, and sacrificed his flesh to God. This is the bride’s strength, which rises and goes about the cities.

[Col. 0335C] There are three cities in which the Beloved is sought: the city of the world, the city of the Church, and the city of God. Of the first it is said in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0335] ch. 10] that the man clothed in linen entered among the wheels that were beneath the cherubim, filled his hands with coals of fire, and cast them upon the city. Of the second: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband” [Note: [Col. 0335] Rev. 21]. Of the third, Ezekiel says: “He saw the structure of a city inclining toward the south” [Note: [Col. 0335] Ezek. 42].

In the first, we seek with Moses to see his back [Note: [Col. 0335] Exod. 33]; in the second, to see his side with Thomas [Note: [Col. 0335] John 21]; in the third, on Mount Tabor, to see his face, which shines like the sun, with Moses and Elijah [Note: [Col. 0335] Matt. 17]. His back [Col. 0335D] is what he endured in the world—namely calamity and misery. In the second, from his side charity and mercy flowed to us; in the third, his face shines like the sun in the glory of majesty. From the first we ought to rise; in the second, to go about; in the third, to seek through lanes and streets.

67 The prophet teaches thus how we must rise from the first: “Go out from Babylon, and flee from the Chaldeans” [Note: [Col. 0335] Isa. 40]. The Apostle teaches how we ought to go about the second: “That you may be able,” he says, “to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, [Col. 0336A] breadth, height, and depth” [Note: [Col. 0335] Eph. 3]. Tobit knew that one must seek in the third when he said: “Your streets, Jerusalem, shall be paved with gold, and through all your lanes alleluia shall be sung” [Note: [Col. 0335] Tob. 3].

The bride knew her Beloved as a lover of purity, a cultivator of unanimity, a comforter of the afflicted, and one who kindles the lukewarm. Therefore she rises from the bed of carnal pleasure; she goes about the city of charitable unity; she seeks the Beloved in the lane of rigid severity; she seeks him in the streets of relaxed weakness. In the first the Beloved does not dwell, because it is a brothel; in the second he has a little bed of quiet and peace; in the third, the dwelling-place of a tower; in the fourth, an infirmary for the sick.

Therefore he would not enter the first, because he would cry: “I am sunk in deep mire” [Note: [Col. 0335] Ps. 68]; and to the bride: “Your uncleanness [Col. 0336B] is abominable; I wished to cleanse you, and you were not cleansed from your filth” [Note: [Col. 0335] Ezek. 24]. There is the tomb of Lazarus, dead four days [Note: [Col. 0335] John 11]. Coming to the second, he rejoices, because “he makes those of one manner of life dwell in a house” [Note: [Col. 0335] Ps. 67], and he sings: “Behold, how good and delightful it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” [Note: [Col. 0335] Ps. 132]; and: “I beseech you to walk worthily of the calling by which you were called, with humility and gentleness, with patience bearing one another in charity, being eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 0335] Eph. 4]. For there is Solomon’s litter, which he paved in its midst with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0335] Song 3].

Coming to the third, he says: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” [Note: [Col. 0335] Luke 21]. There he finds the house which no storm shakes. Though wandering winds rage, clouds penetrate, rivers come, [Col. 0336C] winds blow, and strike against that house, it does not fall, because it is founded upon firm rock [Note: [Col. 0335] Luke 6]. For it is “the tower of David, built with battlements: a thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty” [Note: [Col. 0335] Song 4].

When he comes to the fourth, he cries: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep?” [Note: [Col. 0335] Prov. 24]; “Why do you stand here idle all day?” [Note: [Col. 0335] Matt. 20]; “Lift up the slack hands and strengthen the weak knees” [Note: [Col. 0335] Isa. 35]; “make straight paths for your feet, lest anyone who is lame go astray” [Note: [Col. 0335] Heb. 12].

As she seeks the Beloved through these dwelling-places, the bride cries: “I sought and did not find”—perhaps because she was insufficiently adorned with purity, and this with reference to the first; insufficiently formed by charity with reference to the second; insufficiently disciplined by seriousness with reference to the third; and, with reference to the fourth, sluggish [Col. 0336D] and languid. It was therefore necessary that those should meet her who would invite her to beauty, instruct her in love, strengthen her for labour, and animate her toward fervour.

Let the first, David, therefore come and invite her to beauty thus: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and the king has desired your beauty” [Note: [Col. 0335] Ps. 44]. Let John the Evangelist instruct her in love thus: “Let us love one another, because charity is from God” [Note: [Col. 0335] 1 John 4]. And where charity and love are, there is the gathering of the saints. Let Paul strengthen her for labour thus: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck” [Note: [Col. 0335] 2 Cor. 11]; as though to say: Here, by my example, endure labour. Let Isaiah animate the fourth sort toward fervour thus: “You faint-hearted, be strengthened; do not fear” [Note: [Col. 0337] Isa. 35]. And Solomon: “If you are diligent, your harvest will come like a spring, and poverty will flee far from you” [Note: [Col. 0337] Prov. 6]. These are the watchmen of the city. After the bride recognizes herself as less worthy of the Bridegroom, and hence of finding him, she asks them whether they have seen him. Hence follows:

> I will arise and go about the city through the lanes and streets, seeking him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.

[CARD.] As though she said: I considered these things within myself, upon my troubled bed. I shall arise, and I shall go about the city—not so much by the movement of my feet as by the progress of reflection—Jerusalem, through its lanes and streets. In the lanes, which [Col. 0337B] are narrower, is expressed the condition of those sinners whom fear of hell, shame before the world, or some worldly difficulty narrows and restrains, lest they sin altogether freely. But in the streets, which are broad, is marked the condition of those morals which, their reins broken and bridle cast off, continually spread themselves toward worse things.

The Blessed Virgin therefore says: I shall go about the city; and, considering both those who were preparing a cross for my Son with at least some fear and those who were doing so with none at all, I did as I had said in my mind: for I sought him among them and did not find him. For he was not with them through the devotion of faith. It follows:

> The watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loves?

[Col. 0337C] [THO.] The watchmen who guard the city are heralds of truth, who keep watch continually with devout concern for the guardianship of the holy Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, and who persist by the word of preaching lest it be corrupted by unbelievers. Thus they found the Gentile world anxiously searching out truth, and showed it what it was seeking: as Philip opened to the eunuch the light of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0337] Acts 8]; Peter filled Cornelius and his household with the grace they had so greatly desired [Note: [Col. 0337] Acts 10]; Paul made known to the Athenians the God whom they did not know yet worshipped [Note: [Col. 0337] Acts 17]. And the other apostles, sent by the Lord into other regions, instructed the Gentile world crying: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”

Why do you seek the strong man in a bed, the great one in a little bed, the glorified one in a stable? For every weak body puts off weakness in the glory of the resurrection. He girded himself with power; he clothed himself with light as with a garment. It is well said: “Have you seen him whom I love,” but “him whom my soul loves,” because, when we love something spiritually—God, an angel, the soul, virtues—it must be referred to the soul. But when we love something pertaining to the body, it should rather be called love of the flesh.

Night is Jewish unbelief; night is the disgrace of pagans; night is heretical perversity; night is the fleshly conduct of Catholics. Here the Bridegroom must be sought in prayers, followed in deeds, and found by faith. Good are those guards who, watchful in mind, sagaciously [Col. 0338A] investigate the enemy’s snares, forestall the counsels of the wicked, uncover traps, evade ambushes, scatter nets, and frustrate devices. These are lovers of the brethren and of the people of Israel [Note: [Col. 0337] 2 Macc. 15]. These are those who pray much for the people and for the entire holy city, Jerusalem.

Without the twofold endeavour, namely prayer and watchfulness, neither city nor bride nor sheep can be secure. These three are one; but it is a city by reason of its gathering, a bride by reason of love, and sheep by reason of gentleness. It is a city: keep watch for its protection. It is a bride: attend to its adornment. They are sheep: attend to their pasture. The protection of the city consists in three things: it is made safe from the force of tyrants, the fraud of heretics, and the temptations of demons. The bride’s adornment, however, lies in good works, conduct, and ranks of order. [Col. 0338B] The sheep’s pastures are the precepts of Scripture: there are vegetables of dispensations for the weak, and strong counsels for the healthy.

For this a man is needed who is strong, spiritual, and faithful: strong to repel injuries; spiritual to perceive snares; faithful, one who does not seek his own interests [Note: [Col. 0337] 1 Cor. 13]. When found and instructed by such persons, the bride finds and holds the Bridegroom: that she may consent to him for correction; be enlightened by him for knowledge; lean upon him for strength; be re-formed by him for wisdom; be conformed to him for beauty; be wed to him for fruitfulness; and enjoy him for delight with angels and saints in the kingdom.

This is “the burden of the beasts of the south” [Note: [Col. 0337] Isa. 30]. For sometimes we are burdened by charity—that is, when we desire to benefit others. [Col. 0338C] The south wind, which is a warm wind, signifies the Holy Spirit; hence in the Song: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind” [Note: [Col. 0337] Song 4]. Blessed is the soul over which the Holy Spirit presides and directs all its works, orders its thoughts, regulates its movements, and composes its conduct; hence: “Where the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” [Note: [Col. 0337] Ezek. 1]. These are the beasts of the south, and are therefore burdened by the south wind. This is the burden: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0337] Rom. 5]. Learn from Paul what it is to know this burden: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” [Note: [Col. 0337] 2 Cor. 11].

There are four kinds of beasts: beasts of the north, beasts of the west, beasts of the east, and beasts of the south. The first [Col. 0338D] are obstinate sinners; the second, sinners who are fearful; the third, the humble and devout; the fourth, fervent and wise prelates. The first are burdened with the burden of iniquity; the second with the burden of supplying the needs of the poor; the third with the burden of commanded obedience; the fourth with the burden of guarding the city.

Of the first: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts” [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 48]; and of these it is said: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” [Note: [Col. 0337] Joel 1]. Of the second: “You will save men and beasts, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 35]. These hear: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” [Note: [Col. 0337] Luke 11]. Of the third: “I have become like a beast [Col. 0339A] before you” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 72]. These recall: “Christ became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” [Note: [Col. 0339] Phil. 2]. Of the fourth: “All the beasts of the forests are mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 49]. These hear: “He who has ministered well will acquire a good joy [Vulg., rank]” [Note: [Col. 0339] 1 Tim. 3].

These are the beasts of the south. The south wind is the Holy Spirit, through whom Christ was incarnate; the prelate is imbued with Christ’s teaching; the subject is adorned with virtues. Of the first: “God will come from the south” [Note: [Col. 0339] Hab. 3]; of the second: “The queen of the south came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0339] Luke 11]; of the third, Job says: “Does the hawk take wing, spreading its wings toward the south?” [Note: [Col. 0339] Job 39].

Such a beast was Christ, who placed upon his own beast the man wounded by robbers. For he found him in the Sabbath, carried him to the inn, [Col. 0339B] and conveyed him to nourishment [Note: [Col. 0339] Luke 10]: from the Sabbath of worldly vanity, into the inn of ecclesiastical unity, to the nourishment of eternal refreshment. In the first he was blinded; in the second he was healed; in the third he was filled. Hear of the blind man: “Christ was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” [Note: [Col. 0339] John 1]. Of the healed man: “He himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows. And the Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all” [Note: [Col. 0339] Isa. 53]. Of the third: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 16].

Those who follow Christ thus working are guardians of the city; but they must guard purity, truth, and the city: purity of innocence; truth in fulfilling a vowed promise; and the city of religious unity. [Col. 0339C] The first in oneself, the second before God, the third for one’s subject. Of the first: “Guard innocence and behold equity” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 36]; of the second: “Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter—that is, the one keeping truth” [Note: [Col. 0339] Isa. 26]; of the third: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen” [Note: [Col. 0339] Isa. 62].

The first is done from necessity, the second from choice, the third from authority. In the first a person is bound by necessity; in the second, obligated by voluntary choice; in the third, compelled by obedience. Without the first, salvation is impossible; without the second, salvation was possible, but is no longer so once a promise has been made; without the third, it was possible, but is no longer so once absolution has been made by a superior. Of the first: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0339] Heb. 12]; of the second: “Make vows and fulfil them [Col. 0339D] to the Lord your God” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 75]; of the third: “No one takes this honour upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” [Note: [Col. 0339] Heb. 5].

Such a guardian is the good shepherd, who lays down his life for his sheep [Note: [Col. 0339] John 10]. He lays down, I say, his life for the sheep in the world, in the bedchamber, and in danger. In the world he administers; in the bedchamber he orders; in danger he sets himself in opposition. First, by handling temporal matters so that the brethren may have necessities; second, by forming them in conduct so that they may live according to rule; third, by resisting tyrants lest they carry them away. Of the first: “My life is always in my hands” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 118], while I labour for one subject to me; [Col. 0340A] of the second: “Brethren, as Christ loved us, we too ought to lay down our lives for our brethren” [Note: [Col. 0339] 1 John 3]; of the third: The good shepherd arose, who lays down his life for his sheep [Note: [Col. 0339] John 10], and deigned to die for his flock.

In the first, thieves and robbers insinuate themselves under the pretext of temporal matters; in the second, hired servants. In these three matters are good shepherds. To them the bride says: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” Him whom I choose, whom I love, whom I bind to myself: I choose him from among a thousand; I love him in my heart; I bind him to myself in my body. I choose him from among a thousand because he is “fairer in form than the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 44]. I love him in my heart because “he first loved us [Note: [Col. 0339] 1 John 4], and washed us in his blood [Note: [Col. 0339] Rev. 1]” from the stain of sins. I bind him to myself in my body because I hear: “You were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body” [Note: [Col. 0339] 1 Cor. 6].

[Col. 0340B]

> The watchmen who guard the city found me.

[THO. (sic)] As though it were said: I, not finding my Son in the lanes of Jerusalem, was found and afflicted with my Son by those who guard the city. For the watchmen—the scribes and Pharisees—who guard, that is, who have the office of guarding the city, found me. But, though found and afflicted by them, I did not find in those very rulers the Beloved whom I sought; for she asked them: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” Since, when questioned, they do not answer, it is apparent that Christ was not in them by knowledge. But where she found not the Beloved, and how great a concern she has for the salvation of her people, the following words [Col. 0340C] make clear. For she says:

> A little while after I had passed them by, I found him whom my soul loves.

[THO. (sic)] The seeker of truth ought to pass by the watchmen; that is, to mingle with and unite himself to the assemblies of faithful teachers, and to run through their writings and sayings in frequent meditation. Having done this a little, he will find the Beloved himself, because the Lord makes a shortened word [Note: [Col. 0339] Rom. 9], when he says: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” [Note: [Col. 0339] Mark 16].

Such a passage would be dangerous for us in coming to know God, should it happen that we lacked guardians. Therefore we must see who the guardians of the seeker are. There are five guardians: the person himself, the neighbour, the prelate, the angel, and God. Of the first: [Col. 0340D] “Guard yourselves against murmuring, which profits nothing” [Note: [Col. 0339] Wis. 1]. Of the second Cain said: “Am I my brother’s keeper?” [Note: [Col. 0339] Gen. 4]. Of the third: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen” [Note: [Col. 0339] Isa. 62]. Of the fourth it is said concerning Jerusalem: “Upon its walls I saw a guard of angels” [Note: [Col. 0339] Jer. 51]. Of the fifth: “Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 126].

The first seeks; the second gives assurance; the third shows; the fourth impels; the fifth presents himself. The first does so by circumspection; the second by example and admonition; the third by example and teaching; [Col. 0341A] the fourth by forestalling the devil’s devices; the fifth by granting a person grace and patience by which he may stand.

Likewise, there are four from whom the account of a person is required: the person himself, the devil, the neighbour, and the prelate. Hence the Lord says: “From the hand of every beast, and from the hand of man, I shall require the blood of your souls; from the hand of a man and his brother I shall require your souls” [Note: [Col. 0341] Gen. 9]. By beasts he means demons; by man, the sinner himself; by man [*vir*], the prelate; by brother, the neighbour. Of these she asks: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” Instructed by them, she adds: “A little while after I had passed them by, I found him whom my soul loves.”

First we go, second we pass over, third we pass beyond. We go from the world to the first little bed. We pass over from the first to the second; we pass beyond from the second to the third. In this third place the Beloved is found. This [Col. 0341B] is the threefold passage of the children of Israel on their way to the land of promise. First they crossed the danger of the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0341] Exod. 14]; second, the harshness of the desert [Note: [Col. 0341] Exod. 19]; third, the streams of Jordan [Note: [Col. 0341] Num. 13].

So Christ first passed from life to death; second, from death to incorruption; third, from the world to the Father. So we first pass from the world to mortification of the flesh; from mortification, as it were, to life—to religious observance; from religious life to contemplation, that we may see the Beloved’s face. For in all that Christ did, the perfect person is figured for us: in his passion, the sorrow of penitents; in his lying in the tomb, the rest of those absolved; in his resurrection, the life of the righteous; in his ascension, the progress of the perfect; [Col. 0341C] in his sitting at the right hand of the Father, the glory of the blessed. Here is found him whom my soul loves.

Otherwise: we go, pass over, and pass beyond. We go by investigating the incomprehensible things concerning Christ’s humanity; we pass over by following his footsteps; we pass beyond by contemplating his most exalted works. In the first he is understood; in the second he is sought; in the third he is found. The first belongs to the honour of our weakness; the second to the fervour of religious life; the third to the love of blessedness. In the first, “The Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0341] John 1]; in the second, “he dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0341] ibid.]; in the third, “we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” [Note: [Col. 0341] ibid.].

These things are shown to us in the Apocalypse in the man whom John saw amid seven golden lampstands: he “was clothed with a long robe, and girded at the breasts [Col. 0341D] with a golden girdle; and his head and hair were white as snow” [Note: [Col. 0341] Rev. 1]. These three belong to the first stage. For in that first stage we marvel at these three things: that he was born of a virgin, with the seal of virginity preserved; that he shone in the world by miracle; and that he rose again after conquering the sting of death.

Thus in the whiteness of the long robe is signified the integrity of virginity; in the golden girdle, the brilliance of miraculous wisdom; in the white head, the joy of the Lord’s resurrection; in the hairs hanging from the head, all those predestined to life, which comes from Christ [Col. 0342A] the head. Behold the first stage, in which we go and see the incomprehensible things that pertain to the honour of our frailty.

In the second stage we likewise follow in three things: if we are radiant in contemplation, fervent in action, and assiduous in prayer. In the first, that we may say with David: “To you I have lifted my eyes, who dwell in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0341] Ps. 122], just as blessed Stephen, looking into heaven, saw God’s glory and said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened” [Note: [Col. 0341] Acts 7]. In the second: “Whatever your hand can find to do, do it earnestly” [Note: [Col. 0341] Eccl. 9], as Jonathan, crawling on feet and hands, passed to the Philistines’ outpost [Note: [Col. 0341] 1 Sam. 14]. In the third: “Pray without ceasing” [Note: [Col. 0341] 1 Thess. 5], so that it may be said: “Your lips, bride, drip honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue” [Note: [Col. 0341] Song 4].

Corresponding to these three, it follows concerning the aforesaid man: “His eyes were like a flame of fire” [Note: [Col. 0341] Rev. 1], which [Col. 0342B] pertains to the brightness of contemplation; “his feet were like fine bronze, as though glowing in a furnace” [Note: [Col. 0341] ibid.], which pertains to fervour in labour; “and his voice was like the voice of many waters” [Note: [Col. 0341] ibid.], which denotes abundance and constancy in prayer. For waters signify abundance, and they clash with one another when prayers meet prayers. Behold, in these we follow Christ’s footsteps, which belong to the fervour of religious life, in which he is sought by us.

In the third stage we likewise find three great works of God: first, sweet kindness; second, severe power; third, joyful majesty. The first is for illumination through the sending of the sevenfold Spirit; the second, in judgment; the third, in the kingdom, [Col. 0342C] when he shone like the sun with his own brightness. With regard to the first, Zechariah saw seven eyes upon one stone [Note: [Col. 0341] Zech. 3]; of the second David says: “Unless you are converted, he has brandished his sword; he has bent his bow and made it ready” [Note: [Col. 0341] Ps. 7]; of the third: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall arise” [Note: [Col. 0341] Mal. 4].

These are the three things that follow concerning the aforesaid man: “In his right hand, seven stars” [Note: [Col. 0341] Rev. 1], that is, the sevenfold Spirit. Of the second it is said: “And a sword sharp on both sides was in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0341] ibid.], namely in judgment. Of the third: “And his face shone like the sun in its strength” [Note: [Col. 0341] ibid.]. For Christ shone like the sun in youth, like the sun in old age, and like the sun in strength. The first was in his birth; the second in his passion; the third in his resurrection, in which he began [Col. 0342D] according to the human nature to shine “like the sun in its strength,” that is, at midday.

Therefore, with the bride we must pass over, that he may first shine for us in youth, that is, in his nativity. “Let us pass over as far as Bethlehem, and see this word which has come to pass” [Note: [Col. 0341] Luke 2]. Let us go, pass over, and draw near. Let us go to the watch of the shepherds, pass over as far as Bethlehem, and draw near to the manger: first, that we may hear the word which was uttered; second, that we may see the Word which was made; third, that we may find the Word which was born. [Col. 0343A] The word uttered by the angel, the Word made by the Lord, the Word born from the Virgin’s womb. First: Christ is born; second: Christ’s nativity; third: Christ born. The first is made an example for us; the second, a miracle; the third, provision for our exile. In the homeland, he is salvation for all.

Therefore, first to keep watch is to watch over the flock of good thoughts. “Blessed,” says Wisdom, “is he who watches at my gates and keeps watch at the posts of my door” [Note: [Col. 0343] Prov. 8]. For God’s brightness shone around them [Note: [Col. 0343] Luke 2] by the light of grace; and the word is uttered in the heart, announcing and recalling the Word that was made, that is, Christ’s nativity. Thus let us go to the watch of the shepherds, that we may imitate them; let us pass over as far as Bethlehem—that is, the house of bread—that we may be refreshed.

It should be noted that there are three cities in which the Lord wrought great things: [Col. 0343B] Bethlehem, Bethany, and Bethphage. The first is called the house of bread; the second, the house of obedience; the third, the house of eating. In the first Christ was born; in the second Lazarus was raised by Christ; in the third Christ was placed upon an ass. Let us therefore enter the first, that, finding Christ born there, we may be conformed to him through humility. Let us enter the second, obeying Christ, that we who are dead through iniquity may be raised by him. Let us enter the third, that, rising above the weakness of our flesh, we may be refreshed there by worthily eating the bread we have found.

See how this bread becomes useful on the way. He himself is the lawgiver; he himself the giver of grace; he shines through truth; he pours charity into us. He is lawgiver, teaching how we ought to hold fast; giver of grace, by which we may advance; shining through truth, by which we may keep the way; [Col. 0343C] pouring in charity, by which we may taste and love this bread. Of the first: “For the lawgiver will give blessing” [Note: [Col. 0343] Ps. 83]; of the second: “The Lord will give grace and glory” [Note: [Col. 0343] ibid.]; of the third: “We saw him full of grace and truth” [Note: [Col. 0343] John 1]; of the fourth: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us by Christ himself” [Note: [Col. 0343] Rom. 5].

Nor is it without reason that ox and ass, shepherd and angel, come together at this nativity. For he was ox for tilling, ass for bearing, shepherd for guarding, angel for revealing: for tilling untrained hearts, bearing the burdens of our sins, guarding the gifts of virtues, and revealing the secrets of heaven. [Col. 0343D] Hear him as tiller: “The first account I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began to do and to teach” [Note: [Col. 0343] Acts 1]. Finally, Mary takes him for a gardener. Hear him as bearer: “Truly, he himself bore our infirmities” [Note: [Col. 0343] Isa. 53]. Hear him as guardian: “I am the good shepherd, and my own know me” [Note: [Col. 0343] John 10]. He laid down his life for his sheep, and deigned to die for his flock. Hear him as revealer: “I go to prepare a place for you, and I come to you” [Note: [Col. 0343] John 14], and the rest.

Therefore he was a cultivator in the conduct of his whole life, bore burdens in his passion, was a guardian in his resurrection, and a revealer [Col. 0344A] in his ascension. Let us therefore “pass over,” not merely to the watch of the shepherds, that we may hear the word uttered, or “as far as Bethlehem, that we may see the Word which was made” [Note: [Col. 0343] Luke 2], but as far as the manger, that we may find the word which was born: the serene word, the sweet word, the Word which is light, the Word which is dew—serene through gentleness, sweet through mercy, light through truth, dew through grace. Through gentleness, by which he was not disturbed against the one scourging him; through mercy, by which he forgave iniquity; through truth, by which he taught kindness; through grace, by which he watered the thirsty.

“He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and did not open his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0343] Isa. 53]: behold, gentleness. “Son, your sins are forgiven you” [Note: [Col. 0343] Luke 7]: behold, mercy. “He who follows me does not walk in darkness” [Col. 0344B] [Note: [Col. 0343] John 8]: behold, truth. “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” [Note: [Col. 0343] John 7]: behold, watering. On account of these last two, it is said in the prophet: “Your dew is the dew of light” [Note: [Col. 0343] Isa. 26]. For it does both: it waters and illumines, shines and makes fruitful. “In the drops of this dew, that which springs up shall rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0343] Ps. 64].

But one must know that there is dew of light; light of dew; dew without light; and light without dew. Dew of light exists when a certain sweetness and gracious delight spring forth from perfect truth. Light of dew exists when sweetness, through some share in delight, brightens the soul into the light of truth. Dew without light exists when abundant sweetness gladdens the soul, but subtle knowledge does not greatly enlighten it. Light without dew exists when knowledge is present, but is dry and parched, not watered by the dew of love.

Of the first it is said: “Light has arisen [Col. 0344C] for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart” [Note: [Col. 0343] Ps. 96]. Of the second: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” [Note: [Col. 0343] Ps. 33]. Of the third: “The heavens shall grow dark with dew” [Note: [Col. 0343] Deut. 33]. She signifies that she has the fourth when she cries to her father: “You have given me a southern land” [Note: [Col. 0343] Josh. 15], namely, a land near the sun: a land of light, but dry. It is indeed good, and southern, yet less pleasant because parched. Therefore I ask: join to it also watered land.

In the figure of the first, the children of Israel 69 first saw manna, saying: “Manhu,” that is, “What is this?” [Note: [Col. 0343] Exod. 15]; afterward they tasted it. With regard to the second, it was said of the strong woman: “She tasted and saw that her merchandise was good” [Note: [Col. 0343] Prov. 31]. She first tasted and from tasting saw. In the figure of the third, Isaac tasted the stew of his son Jacob [Note: [Col. 0343] Gen. 27], but did not see; [Col. 0344D] hence 16*: “They have zeal indeed for God, but not according to knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0343] Rom. 10]. In the figure of the fourth, the children of Israel saw the fruits of the promised land which the scouts brought back, but did not taste them [Note: [Col. 0343] Josh. 2]. These are those “who, though they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks” [Note: [Col. 0343] Rom. 1]. Of these two it was said: “Would that they were wise and understood, and foresaw their latter end!” [Note: [Col. 0343] Deut. 32].

> I held him and shall not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her who bore me.

[Note: [Col. 0345] [[Col. 0345] This note appears at the foot of columns 345 and 346, but the callout number (27*) has not been printed in the text.] Ibid.]

[Col. 0345A] [THO. (sic)] Our mother is Jerusalem, which is free, which is above, which is our mother [Note: [Col. 0345] Gal. 4]. Her house is that heavenly dwelling-place, whence: “I rejoiced in the things said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ps. 121]. Her chamber is eternal rest, where all shall feed and recline, and there shall be none to terrify them. For there shall be rest from labour, peace from temptation, and security from the torments of Gehenna. Hence Boethius [Note: [Col. 0345] *On the Consolation of Philosophy*]:

> Here shall be rest for your labours;  
> Here a harbour abiding in tranquil calm,
Here one refuge lies open to the wretched, namely, security. But “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” [Note: [Col. 0345] Eccles. 4]; much more difficult to break is the fourfold cord by which this man is held. For he is held in four ways: he is held by persistence, by service, by desire, by constancy. By the persistence of prayers, by the service of gifts; he is held by the desire of devotions, by the constancy of spirits. The first obtains healing of infirmity; the second, firmness of faith; the third, the consolation of the Holy Spirit; the fourth, the spiritual vision of God. In the first sense the Canaanite woman held him [Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 15]; in the second, the disciples travelling to Emmaus [Note: [Col. 0345] Luke 24]; in the third, the women who came and held his feet [Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 28]. In the fourth, Jacob says: “I will not let thee go unless thou bless me” [Note: [Col. 0345] Gen. 32].

In the first example, that of the Canaanite woman, we observe three stages among petitioners. There are those who cease asking at the first rebuff to their petitions; there are those who, at the second, fall away from the practice of devotions; there are those who, at the third, despairing, return to their sins, “like a dog returning to its vomit” [Note: [Col. 0345] II Pet. 1]. In these three ways the Lord tested her persistence. She cried out; the Lord did not answer: behold the first test. She cried more loudly, and the Lord answered: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 15]: behold the second. She fell to the ground and worshipped. He said: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ibid.]: behold the third. See how she humbles herself: “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ibid.]. Great humility. He calls her a dog, and she herself professes to be a very small dog. Behold the humble persistence of prayer by which the Lord is held, and by which she obtains healing of infirmity.

In the second example he is held by the service of gifts, because they constrained him and fed him: behold the service of gifts. “And therefore they recognized him in the breaking of the bread” [Note: [Col. 0345] Luke 24]: behold the strengthening of faith. Thirdly, the holy women held him by desire: “They held his feet,” he says, “by desire” [Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 28]. God’s feet within us are our affections. We hold these when we desire God, and obtain spiritual consolations, just as they afterwards received the Holy Spirit. Fourthly, Jacob held him by constancy, because he wrestled with him throughout the night [Note: [Col. 0345] Gen. 32].

[Col. 0346A] And the victor said: “I will not let thee go unless thou bless me” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ibid.]. Thus we conquer if we are constant in the night of God’s scourges and adversities, by which we contend with him. Nor is it surprising if we conquer him through constancy, because “from the time of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” [Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 11]. Nor did he conquer merely through constancy; he held on until he received the blessing—namely, that he should be called Israel, that is, “a man seeing God.”

But now the order of the words must be noted. For it is said thus: I sought; I found; I held; I shall bring in. “I sought,” she says: for he is sought with a certain devout curiosity; found by persistence in seeking; held by steadfastness of soul; brought in by a certain timely importunity. In the first he is inspired; in the second strengthened; in the third [Col. 0346B] confirmed; in the fourth one ventures because of love. The first, that he may begin sweetly; the second, that he may advance manfully; the third, that he may cling to the beloved inseparably; the fourth, that he may happily enjoy him.

Job sought with devout curiosity when he said: “Who will grant me that I may know and find him, and come even to his throne?” [Note: [Col. 0345] Job 23]. Samuel was persistent in seeking: he did not depart from the temple day or night. Therefore he deserved not only to find, but to be called by the Lord, who said: “Samuel, Samuel”; and he replied: “Speak, Lord, for thy servant hears” [Note: [Col. 0345] I Kings 3]. And Jacob—“to whom, because of the greatness of his love, the days seemed few” [Note: [Col. 0345] Gen. 29]—held firmly when he said: “I will not let thee go unless thou bless me” [Note: [Col. 0345] Gen. 32]; and accordingly he blessed him in that same place.

The bride wished to bring the beloved into her mother’s house by virtue of his authority, when he says that, from the time of John the Baptist, [Col. 0346C] “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” [Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 11]. On account of these four things the Gospel says: “Seek, and ye shall find” [Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 7]. “Seek” is said on account of the first; “and ye shall find,” on account of the second; “ask, and ye shall receive” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ibid.], on account of the third; “knock, and it shall be opened unto you” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ibid.], on account of the fourth.

It should be noted, however, that the beloved sometimes enters of his own accord; sometimes he is courteously brought in by the master of the house; sometimes he is forcibly drawn in. The first occurs when grace first pours itself into the heart; the second, when a person in whom grace has been poured works from it; the third, when amid adversities and temptations the beloved pretends to be going farther away. But in these [Col. 0346D] the man thus tested holds him manfully, by the patience of works and persistence of prayers.

In the first sense, he entered among the apostles, though the doors were closed [Note: [Col. 0345] John 20]; in the second, into the Pharisee’s house, because a certain Pharisee asked Jesus to eat with him [Note: [Col. 0345] Luke 7]. And the father of the dead girl brought him in, and he raised her [Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 7]. “If anyone,” he says, “opens to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” [Note: [Col. 0345] Rev. 3]. In the third sense, his disciples travelling to Emmaus constrained him—namely, Luke and Amaon [Note: [Col. 0345] Luke 24].

Then, as the beloved ascended into the house of the mother Church—that is, into the kingdom of heaven—the [Col. 0347A] apostles held him in affection and wonder; hence the angels say to them: “Men of Galilee, why do you marvel, looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, shall so come as you saw him ascending into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0347] Acts 1]. O great solemnity, in which the merciful one ascends. Captivity follows: first, from the world; second, from hell; third, from heaven. A solemn procession of angels meets him: from the world to the Father; from hell to blessedness; from heaven to the king’s feast. The first sings: “Nor will I leave you orphans,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0347] John 14]; the second: “My soul, like a sparrow, has escaped from the snare of the hunters” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 123]; the third: “Who is this that comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bosra?” [Note: [Col. 0347] Isa. 63].

There is a Galilean man, an empyrean man, a man who is God. The first is a Christian; the second, an angel; the third [Col. 0347B] is Christ, the man. “Galilean” means “one passing over.” The first passes from vice to virtue; the second inhabits the region of brightness; the third ascends from the world to the Father. The first flees the vanity of the world; the second consoles our weakness; the third “leads captivity captive” [Note: [Col. 0347] Eph. 4].

Of the first man it is said: “Men of Galilee, why do you gaze into heaven?” [Note: [Col. 0347] Acts 1]; of the second: “Behold, two men,” he says, “in white garments” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ibid.]; of the third: “Upon a high throne I saw a man, whom a multitude of angels worships” [Note: [Col. 0347] Rev. 3]. Of the passage of the first it is said: “Turn away from evil and do good” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 33], and “hating evil, cleaving to good” [Note: [Col. 0347] Rom. 12]. Hence Abraham is told: “Go forth from thy land, from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house” [Note: [Col. 0347] Gen. 12].

The second consoles [Col. 0347C] weakness: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth for ministry?” [Note: [Col. 0347] Heb. 1]. Thus the angel consoled Tobias; hence, “May the angel of God accompany you, and direct your journey well” [Note: [Col. 0347] Tob. 1]. The third “leads captivity captive” [Note: [Col. 0347] Eph. 4], for bands set free from captivity follow Jesus. For “he spread his wings and took him up, and bore him upon his shoulders” [Note: [Col. 0347] Deut. 32].—“Thou hast been a guide in thy mercy to the people whom thou hast redeemed, and hast borne them in thy strength unto thy holy dwelling-place” [Note: [Col. 0347] Exod. 15].

But concerning the first, it should be noted that there is one who migrates, one who emigrates, and one who transmigrates. He migrates away from the face of temptation; he emigrates from the sweetness of inward refreshment; he transmigrates to the splendor of contemplation. The first happens lest he lose grace; the second, that he may follow [Col. 0347D] the world’s folly; the third, that he may taste the joy above.

Hear the one who migrates: “Judah migrated because of affliction and the multitude of servitude” [Note: [Col. 0347] Lam. 1]; hence the prophet says: “Go out from Babylon and flee from the Chaldeans” [Note: [Col. 0347] Isa. 48]. Of the second: “God shall pluck thee out and shall make thee emigrate from thy tent” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 52]. Likewise: “God is my saviour, my helper; I shall not emigrate” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 61]. Hence: “Those who fed delicately have perished in the ways; those who were nurtured in saffron have embraced dung” [Note: [Col. 0347] Lam. 4].

[Col. 0348A] Of the third, Ezekiel was told: “Make for thyself vessels for transmigration” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ezek. 12]; hence: “Set your minds on things above, not on things below” [Note: [Col. 0347] Col. 3].—“For man shall come to a lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 63]; hence: “He will go before you into Galilee; there you shall see him” [Note: [Col. 0347] Mark 16].

But it should be noted that this transmigration has three vessels: in the first are waters; in the second, oil; in the third, kinds of spices. The water is that of tears, the oil of love, the spices of devotion. The first washes, the second enriches, the third gladdens. Of the first: “Elijah found at his head a vessel of water” [Note: [Col. 0347] III Kings 17]; of the second it is said: “The prudent virgins took oil in their vessels” [Note: [Col. 0347] Matt. 25]; of the third Jacob says to his sons: “Take with you, in your vessels, of the best fruits of the land” [Note: [Col. 0347] Gen. 43].

But it should be noted that the Chaldeans form three companies which hinder this transmigration. [Col. 0348B] The first is the concealment of sins; the second, indignation at subjection; the third, effeminate dissolution of life. The first blinds the heart so that it does not see the way; the second lifts it up in pride, so that it may fall more grievously; the third flatters it, so that it may not set out upon the way to the kingdom of heaven, which suffers violence [Note: [Col. 0347] Matt. 11].

Of the first Job says: “If, like a man, I have concealed my sin and hidden my iniquity in my bosom” [Note: [Col. 0347] Job 31].—“Yet there are no darknesses and no shadow of death where those who work iniquity may hide themselves” [Note: [Col. 0347] Job 4]. Therefore “destruction and unhappiness are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 13].

Those oppressed by the second company “go up to the heavens and down to the depths; and thus their soul wasted away in evils” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 106]; for [Col. 0348C] “before ruin the heart is exalted” [Note: [Col. 0347] Prov. 16]. Hence Saul went up into the mountains of Gilboa and there fell [Note: [Col. 0347] I Kings 28]. He was oppressed by the third who cried: “I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground” [Note: [Col. 0347] Ps. 68]. Such a person cannot walk, because his filth is upon his feet; “nor did she remember her end” [Note: [Col. 0347] Lam. 1]. Hence it was said to the Israelites going out to war: “Whoever is faint-hearted, and whoever has taken a wife, let him return to his house” [Note: [Col. 0347] Deut. 20].

Three things are opposed to these three companies: to the first, diligence in confession; to the second, obedience; to the third, the practice of virtues. The first shows the truth of the way; the second gives firmness; the third supplies the security of hope. Hence it is written: “Judas said to Simon his brother: Take men for thyself, and go into Galilee and free thy brothers” [Note: [Col. 0347] I Macc. 5]: behold these three things. For Judas is interpreted “confession,” while Simon means “obedient.” The men who are chosen are virtues. Therefore these go into Galilee when by these means a passage is made to the kingdom, and he frees his brothers from the three aforesaid companies by which those who journey are impeded.

Therefore the first wonders, the second rejoices, the third is glorified. The first wonders while gazing into heaven; the second rejoices on returning to heaven; the third is glorified while ascending into heaven. He wonders at our Christ, who bore his body on high to the royal palace of heaven; [Col. 0349A] he rejoices because Christ makes the country of earth and sky into one commonwealth; he is glorified as he presents before the Father’s face the glory of conquering flesh.

Likewise, this Galilean man wonders while looking upon the world, while looking upon hell, and while looking upon heaven. In the first he finds vanity; in the second, calamity; in the third, truth. 70 In the first he wonders that man follows the world’s illusion; in the second he wonders that he goes down to hell’s misery; in the third he wonders that he does not follow Christ into glory.

Solomon looked upon the world when he said: “I saw all things that are under heaven, and behold, vanity and all is vanity” [Note: [Col. 0349] Eccles. 1]. David likewise wondered, saying: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” [Note: [Col. 0349] Ps. 3]. Job saw hell when [Col. 0349B] he said: “Leave me a little, that I may lament my sorrow, before I go and return no more to the land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death” [Note: [Col. 0349] Job 10]. The same prophet wondered, saying: “Who among you can dwell with devouring fire, or who among you can abide with everlasting burnings?” [Note: [Col. 0349] Isa. 33]. Stephen looked upon heaven, saying: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at God’s right hand” [Note: [Col. 0349] Acts 7]. Jeremiah wondered, saying: “The ways of Zion mourn because there are none who come to the solemn feast” [Note: [Col. 0349] Lam. 1].

Likewise, this Galilean man wonders at the cloud, wonders at Christ, wonders at the angel: the cloud becoming bright, Christ ascending, the angel descending. The cloud becomes bright for knowledge of truth; Christ ascends to the place [Col. 0349C] of immortality; the angel descends to the place of mortality. Of the first: “I saw a white cloud, and upon the cloud one like the Son of Man sitting” [Note: [Col. 0349] Rev. 14]; of the second: “He ascended upon the cherubim” [Note: [Col. 0349] Ps. 17]; of the third Isaiah says: “One of the seraphim flew to me” [Note: [Col. 0349] Isa. 6]. Hence, after this ascension, the angel would not allow John to worship him [Note: [Col. 0349] Rev. 22].

From the first we have illumination; from the second, expectation; from the third, visitation: illumination toward truth, expectation toward reward, visitation for consolation. Hence the cloud gave light to the children of Israel, the ark of God passed over into the land of promise, and the angel prepared the way. Hence: “Behold, I send an angel who shall prepare the way before thy face” [Note: [Col. 0349] Mal. 3]. Hear of brightness: “The Paraclete Spirit shall teach you all things” [Note: [Col. 0349] John 14]. Hear the promise: “I go [Col. 0349D] to prepare a place for you, and I shall come again to you” [Note: [Col. 0349] Ibid.]. Of the third, the angel says: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, shall so come as you saw him going into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0349] Acts 1].

But let us see how Christ ascended. First he ascended by humility; second, by adversity; third, by truth; fourth, by brightness: by the humility of the Incarnation, the persecution of the Passion, the truth of the Resurrection, and the brightness of glorification. In the first he conquered the devil’s pride; in the second, the wantonness of Adam’s flesh; in the third, the power of hell; in the fourth, the misery of the world. Of the first: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0349] Phil. 2]; of the second: [Col. 0350A] “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example” [Note: [Col. 0349] I Pet. 2]; of the third: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon” [Note: [Col. 0349] Luke 24]; of the fourth: “Great is the mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, preached to the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” [Note: [Col. 0349] I Tim. 3].

Therefore, that we may imitate Christ by the same stages, we must ascend: first through humility, second through persecution, third through the truth of resurrection, fourth through brightness. A man humbles himself when he is ashamed of sin; he endures persecution when he is afflicted; he rises when he is absolved from sin; he shines when, if he glories, he glories in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0349] II Cor. 10]. In the first he is diminished; in the second he afflicts himself; in the third he advances; in the [Col. 0350B] fourth he is perfected. He is diminished as boasting is put aside; he afflicts himself by the abundance of tears; he advances in righteousness; he is perfected by the understanding of things above. Of the first David says: “I have been utterly humbled; Lord, give me life according to thy word” [Note: [Col. 0349] Ps. 118]; of the second: “I am afflicted and greatly humbled; I roared because of the groaning of my heart” [Note: [Col. 0349] Ps. 37]; of the third: “Teach me, Lord, thy statutes” [Note: [Col. 0349] Ps. 118]; of the fourth: “I have understood more than all my teachers, because thy testimonies are my meditation” [Note: [Col. 0349] Ibid.].

> A little after I had passed them by, I found him whom my soul loves; I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her that bore me.

[Col. 0350C] [CARD.] As if she said: “A little,” that is, a little later, after I had passed those who were in the lanes and streets, and after I had passed the watchmen, I found him whom my soul loves—in the faith of the Gentile centurion [Note: [Col. 0349] Matt. 8], and in the faith of the women [Note: [Col. 0349] Luke 24] who announced the Resurrection—and she adds: “I held him.” Of this holding Isaiah says to the Lord: “There is no one who rises up and holds thee” [Note: [Col. 0349] Isa. 64]; and the Lord says through Ezekiel: “I sought for a man who would set a hedge in place and stand opposed before me for the land, lest I destroy it; and I found none” [Note: [Col. 0349] Ezek. 22].

The Blessed Virgin therefore shows that the Lord was angry with his vineyard, namely the Jewish people, which had turned to bitterness and produced wild grapes when it ought to have produced grapes [Note: [Col. 0349] Isa. 5]. And [Col. 0350D] she says: “I held him,” lest he utterly destroy his vineyard; and she adds, “I will not let him go, but by the continual persistence of prayers I shall restrain his wrath.” For that the Lord is held by the prayers of saints he himself shows to Moses, saying: “I see that this people is stiff-necked; let me go, that my wrath may be angered against them” [Note: [Col. 0349] Exod. 32].

She says, therefore: “I will not let him go, but shall always hold him and persist in prayers, until I bring him to the Jewish people, my mother or begetter, and through faith he may dwell there, as in a house and as in a chamber.” The house signifies the condition of the active life: Martha received [Col. 0351A] the Lord into her house [Note: [Col. 0351] Luke 10]. By the chamber or bed is signified the repose of the contemplative life. Therefore, by these words both conditions of life—the contemplative and the active—are promised beforehand to the Jewish people who will believe. It follows.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0351]

> [Col. 0351A] I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not arouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.

[THO.] In this, indeed, he shows that after their conversion he will find among the Synagogue some persons of that perfection of which he finds many in the Church; and, since he likewise delights in their repose, he forbids them disturbance, [Col. 0351B] as he forbade it to the Church. He has truly been brought into the chamber of her that bore him, where he wishes to rest with the bride; therefore he commands that she not be awakened.

We know a threefold rest of the soul. It must first rest from sin; second, from human work; third, it will rest from this miserable exile. The first is for justification; the second, for contemplation; the third, for beatification. This is the threefold Sabbath whose observance is commanded in the Law. Of the first: “Thou shalt do no servile work therein” [Note: [Col. 0351] Lev. 23]. Servile work is sin. Of the second it is commanded absolutely: “You shall do no work therein” [Note: [Col. 0351] Exod. 12]; of the third: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0351] Exod. 20].

Christ also rested in these three Sabbaths. He entered on the Sabbath into the house of a certain Pharisee to eat with him [Note: [Col. 0351] Luke 7]. This is the refreshment of contemplation. Likewise, [Col. 0351C] on the Sabbath he lay in the tomb. This is the rest by which we die to sin. Likewise, on the Sabbath he rested from every work that he had accomplished [Note: [Col. 0351] Gen. 2], and this is blessedness.

Of the first, Jeremiah says: “Do not carry your burdens on the Sabbath day, nor bring them through the gates of Jerusalem, nor cast your burdens out of the city on the Sabbath day” [Note: [Col. 0351] Jer. 17]. By burdens or loads he means sins. Here he notes two things: sometimes sins are brought to the soul through the outward senses; this is, “Do not bring them through the gates of Jerusalem.” Sometimes they are first conceived in the heart and afterwards are committed to action through the senses. And this is what follows: “Do not cast your burdens out of your city on the Sabbath day.”

Of the first Job says: “I made a covenant with my [Col. 0351D] eyes, that I would not so much as think upon a virgin” [Note: [Col. 0351] Job 31]; concerning the second he subsequently adds: “If my eye has followed my heart, and a stain has clung to my hands” [Note: [Col. 0351] Ibid.].

Of the second Sabbath it is said through Ezekiel: “This gate shall be closed during the six days on which work is done; but on the Sabbath it shall be opened” [Note: [Col. 0351] Ezek. 46]. This gate is called the inward sense, which is closed when we work outwardly, but opened when, outwardly at leisure, we contemplate. Hence it is written: “Write wisdom in the time of leisure, and he who is reduced from activity shall receive it” [Note: [Col. 0351] Ecclus. 35].

Of the third Sabbath Isaiah says: “There shall be month [Col. 0352A] after month, and Sabbath after Sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0351] Isa. 66]. Sabbath after Sabbath will be when, in return for this rest from guilt, we rest from misery. Month after month will be when, in return for a multitude of virtues, a multitude of beatitudes is bestowed. For virtues are days, from which there is a collection just as a month is made from days; so it is also with beatitudes.

Hear “month after month”: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0351] Matt. 5]: behold the day on the way; “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0351] Ibid.]: behold the day granted to this person in the homeland; and so with the rest which follow. Those who in the first Sabbath abstain from one sin only in order to commit another are like the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0351] Num. 13]. Those who in the second contemplate in such a way that they do not delight in God are those of whom it is said: “Her enemies saw her and mocked at her Sabbaths” [Note: [Col. 0351] Lam. 1]. To those who aspire to the fourth without merits it is said: “See that your flight be not in winter or on a Sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0351] Matt. 24].

Those resting in the repose of the first Sabbath can be awakened for two reasons: first, lest they be sluggish in temptation; second, that they may advance in good, lest they think [Col. 0352C] it sufficient merely to have turned away from evil. In the first sense Peter was awakened by the angel when he was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains [Note: [Col. 0351] Acts 12]; in the second Elijah was awakened, sleeping beneath a juniper tree [Note: [Col. 0351] III Kings 19].

Those who rest in the second Sabbath are awakened for two reasons. The first is lest they be excessively saddened by the terror of contemplation, because sometimes they see the torments of hell, sometimes joys above; hence Job: “If I sleep, I say, ‘When shall I rise?’ and again I await the evening” [Note: [Col. 0351] Job 7]. Wishing to free himself from this error, he spoke thus. In the second kind of awakening, which is for the benefit of the brethren, the Lord was awakened while sleeping in the little boat [Note: [Col. 0351] Matt. 8].

Those who rest in the third Sabbath are sometimes awakened so that they may pray for us, as we do in the litanies. They will also be awakened in the resurrection, as Gregory says concerning the ten virgins. Of the second Sabbath it was said: “When it was evening on that day, the first of the Sabbaths, and the doors were shut, Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples and said: Peace be unto you” [Note: [Col. 0351] John 20]. In this Sabbath the doors are shut when, through the grace of contemplation, we restrain the outward senses; and thus God stands in the midst, declaring peace.

In the first Sabbath it is evening; in the second, morning; in the third, noon. In the first Jesus stands in the midst of his disciples, to fight against [Col. 0353A] vice; in the second he walks, for the perfection of virtues; in the third he rests, for delight. In the first the doors of the outward senses are shut; in the second the doors of the inward senses are open; in the third the gates of heaven are shut to the wicked. Hence: “They entered into the wedding, and the door was shut” [Note: [Col. 0353] Matt. 25]. To the good they are open; hence: “Its gates shall not be shut by day” [Note: [Col. 0353] Rev. 21].

Such persons ought both to make peace and to possess it—not merely worldly peace from adversity, but spiritual peace from every disturbance—a threefold peace: peace in the house, peace in one’s own heart, and peace in heaven. In the house, with one’s brother; in the heart, within oneself; in heaven, with the Creator. With one’s brother, freedom from detraction; within oneself, freedom from covetousness; with the Creator, freedom from murmuring: freedom from detraction against failings, from covetousness of pleasures, from murmuring at divine [Col. 0353B] scourges.

For there is one who tears apart his household, troubles his own heart, and provokes God to anger. These are the three difficult things spoken of by Solomon. The first is “a serpent upon the ground” [Note: [Col. 0353] Prov. 30], namely, one destroying the stability of God’s house; the second is “a ship in the sea” [Note: [Col. 0353] Ibid.], a heart tossed about through varied pleasures; the third is “an eagle flying to heaven” [Note: [Col. 0353] Ibid.], one provoking God to anger through pride.

The first destroys the household, for he says that the teaching of teachers is burdensome: “Hypocrisy,” he says, “is the religious life of the brothers”; the steward’s frugality is called intolerable avarice; the obedience of the simple is called foolishness. Behold, a wind came from the wilderness and shook the four corners of the house in which Job’s children were eating [Note: [Col. 0353] Chap. 1]. Such a person is unstable in thought, disordered in deed, and undisciplined in speech: in the first, imagining [Col. 0353C] pleasures; in the second, stretching out his hands to every unlawful thing; in the third, judging everything, ordering everything.

71 In him is found what was in the house of Micah: the ephod, that is, the religious garment; and the seraphim, which means “imagination”: this is in the heart; the graven image is in deed; and the molten image is in speech. These are found in the house of Micah, which means “what is here?” Therefore, “Into whatever house you enter, say: Peace to this house” [Note: [Col. 0353] Luke 10].

There are some who do not disturb the household, yet have no peace in their heart because they desire worldly things. When they possess what they desire, they rejoice beyond measure; they fear losing it, and grieve excessively over what they have lost. Hence the poet:

> They fear and desire, grieve and rejoice; nor do they behold  
> The breezes, shut up in darkness and a blind prison.

[Note: [Col. 0353] Vergil, *Aeneid* VI, 633.]

“Dig,” he says to Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0353] Chap. 8], “through the wall”; and he dug and found images of four-footed creatures, that is, earthly affections; of serpents, that is, the hidden poison of hatred and envy; and of birds, that is, ambition for dignities. To such persons the Apostle says: “Let the peace of God dwell in your hearts” [Note: [Col. 0353] Col. 3].

The third sort rise up against God because of scourges, on account of which “they spoke iniquity on high and so set their mouth against heaven” [Col. 0354A] [Note: [Col. 0353] Ps. 72]. They build the tower of Babel, which means “confusion,” in order to oppose God. Thus these disturb the beloved.

The bride desires peace in the house, lest a root of bitterness springing up above should hinder, and through it many be defiled. “But if you bite and devour one another, beware lest you be consumed by one another” [Note: [Col. 0353] Gal. 5]. We ought to be like the two cherubim upon the mercy-seat, looking toward one another so that we may bear one another’s burdens [Note: [Col. 0353] Gal. 6]. “And if a man be overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” [Note: [Col. 0353] Ibid.], and, with faces turned toward the mercy-seat, looking toward one another, let us do all things with God in view.

“Have peace, and the God of peace and love shall be with you” [Note: [Col. 0353] II Cor. 13]; likewise: “Pursue peace with all men, and holiness, [Col. 0354B] without which no one shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0353] Heb. 12]. Likewise, if we seek peace of heart, the heart ought to be like a golden urn in the ark, containing with it the rod of discipline and the tablets of the covenant [Note: [Col. 0353] Heb. 12], that is, the teaching of the divine law; and manna within itself, that is, the taste of heavenly sweetness—so that “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may keep your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0353] Phil. 4].

If we seek peace with God, we must be like goats’-hair coverings in the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0353] Exod. 26], exposing ourselves to the wind and hail of the severity of divine chastisement, so that in him you may have peace. For he thinks thoughts of peace and not of affliction: “You shall call upon me, and I will hear you, and I will restore your captivity from all places” [Note: [Col. 0353] Jer. 29].

Our captivity is threefold: the first under sin, [Col. 0354C] the second under the devil, the third under the present exile. The first has its place in the human heart; the second, in hell; the third, in the world. Therefore, if we patiently endure his scourges, he will restore our captivity from all these places; and may the God of peace, who brought from the dead the shepherd of all mercies, our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

We admire this peace in the bride, concerning whom it follows:

> I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the stags of the field, do not arouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.

[CARD.] Seeing the concern which the mother bears for the Church, the son repeats this verse, so that, as above he invited the impatient to patience and the hasty [Col. 0354D] to long-suffering, so also he may restrain and correct their impatience and haste. He then adds concerning the mother’s praises:

> Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a wisp of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and every powder of the perfumer?

[THO.] Whoever sees the holy conduct of the soul cries with wonder: “Who is this that comes up,” etc.? The holy soul lives in the wilderness of this world while, still exiled from the kingdom, it dwells among demons as among wild beasts. It always [Col. 0355A] labours to ascend, so that it may feel more and more the one whom it loves exceedingly. Such persons disdain visible things, raise themselves toward heavenly things, put off evil habits, despise worldly desires, and by hope tend toward things invisible. Those ascend through the wilderness who, while enduring temptations here, fear being forsaken.

They rightly ascend like a wisp of smoke, because they have the fragrance of good repute and subtlety of mind. This fragrance is of myrrh, which is the mortification of the flesh, and of frankincense, which is devotion in prayer. We make spices when we gather virtues into fragrance; when we examine each virtue lest some vice be hidden, lest anything remain uncultivated; we grind the kinds of virtues, as it were, into powder. Whoever thus examines the heart makes of that heart a little bed on which the bridegroom may rest. Hence follows: [Col. 0355B] “Behold the bed of Solomon.”

There are four wildernesses. The first is hell; the second, the world; the third, the austerity of one’s manner of life; the fourth, the heavenly homeland. Of the first, Ezekiel says: “I will cast thee into the wilderness, O Pharaoh, and all thy fish” [Note: [Col. 0355] Ezek. 29].
