Of the second, in Tobit: “He bound in the wilderness of Upper Egypt the demon who killed Sarah’s husbands” [Note: [Col. 0355] Tob. 8], that is, in the world. Of the third: “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness?” And it is the wilderness in which John the Baptist preached [Note: [Col. 0355] Matt. 3] and Christ fasted [Note: [Col. 0355] Matt. 4]. Of the fourth: “The Lord left the ninety-nine in the wilderness and came to seek that which had perished” [Note: [Col. 0355] Luke 15].

The first is to be execrated; the second fled; through the third one must ascend; the fourth must be attained. The first is full of horror; the second, of error; the third, of pain but also beauty; the fourth, of fruit but also love. The first is tormenting with punishments and monstrous with portents. The second is venomous with serpents and laborious with misery; the third is torn by thorns but beautiful with flowers; the fourth is fruitful and glorious with love. Hear the torments of the first:

> With fire, cold, worm, hunger, filth, scourging:  
> Horror with darkness, and fiery chains upon the limbs.

Of fire and the worm: “Their fire shall not be quenched, and their worm shall not die [Note: [Col. 0355] Isa. 66];” of frost: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth [Note: [Col. 0355] Matt. 22];” of hunger: “My servants shall eat, and you shall be hungry [Note: [Col. 0355] Isa. 65];” of stench: “Lightning and storm-wind are the portion of his cup [Col. 0355D] his [Note: [Col. 0355] Ps. 10];” of the scourge: “He handed him over to the torturers until he should pay the whole debt [Note: [Col. 0355] Matt. 18];” of horror: “Where,” he says, “there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells [Note: [Col. 0355] Job 10];” of darkness and bonds: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness [Note: [Col. 0355] Matt. 22].”

We said that the second [desert] is poisonous with serpents and laborious through misery, as it is said: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread [Note: [Col. 0355] Gen. 3].” Three kinds of serpents encountered the children of Israel in the desert: namely, the asp, which flatters with its face and stings with its tail. This is [Col. 0356A] the pleasure of the flesh, which smiles at the beginning but is bitter. The second is the *dipsas*, which is small and hides in the dust, and causes people to perish of thirst. This is vainglory, which, as it is written, is heavenly in origin and dwells in ashes. Many perish while thirsting for this. The third is the scorpion, which emits fire: this is anger and envy. By these the desert of the world is poisonous; but they made for themselves a serpent upon a pole, that is, Christ upon the cross: by looking upon him, those wounded by serpents were healed.

We said that the third, that is, the harshness of religious life, is torn by thorns, because through many tribulations one goes to God [Note: [Col. 0355] Acts 14]; but it is beautiful with flowers: “The wilderness shall rejoice, and the solitude shall exult on the way, and it shall blossom like the lily [Note: [Col. 0355] Isa. 35],” namely, with the flowers of virtues. Of the soul which thus flowers it is said: “Who is [Col. 0356B] this who ascends through the desert?” The fourth is abundant in fruit, in which all shall feed and recline, and there shall be none to frighten them [Note: [Col. 0355] Zeph. 3]. “They shall neither hunger nor thirst any more [Note: [Col. 0355] Apoc. 7].” It will also be glorious in charity: “O how glorious is the kingdom in which all the saints reign together with Christ [Note: [Col. 0355] Office of the Church].”

Into the first descend the guilty; from the second those newly converted have ascended; through the third the perfect ascend; to the fourth the blessed ascend. Of the first: “Let them go down alive into hell [Note: [Col. 0355] Num. 16].” Of the second: “Who is this who ascends through the desert?” Of the third: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn [Note: [Col. 0355] Song 6]?” In this desert, not to grow is to diminish; not to be perfected is to fail; not to advance is to fall back; not to ascend is to descend. [Col. 0356C] Of the fourth: “Christ, ascending on high, leads captivity captive [Note: [Col. 0355] Eph. 4].” “Like a little rod of smoke,” he says.

There are three rods: the first is that of kings, the second of shepherds, the third of high priests. By the first rebels are subdued; by the second sheep are threatened; by the third sons are ruled. The first is effective for casting out vices; the second for shaping conduct; the third for ordering virtues. The first was Joseph’s, by which the Egyptians were subjected to him and his dying father leaned upon it [Note: [Col. 0355] Gen. 47]; the second was Moses’, by which Moses’ serpents were swallowed [Note: [Col. 0355] Num. 21], and the Red Sea was divided [Note: [Col. 0355] Exod. 14]; the third is Aaron’s, by which he was shown worthy of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0355] Num. 17].

But it is called a little rod of smoke. Smoke provokes tears: this is compunction. Smoke is produced sometimes from earth, sometimes from [Col. 0356D] water, sometimes from fire. Earth is our body; from it compunction arises when we bewail the miseries which we endure in it. Compunction arises from water when we bewail the flowing course of our past life. It arises from fire when we sigh through love for the heavenly homeland. But it is called a rod made from the spices of myrrh and incense and every powder of the perfumer. This is the rod of discipline, which at its beginning has myrrh, by which we are chastened from the rottenness of vices while we afflict the flesh; secondly it has the incense of prayer and fragrance, while by prayer we reconcile God to ourselves [Col. 0357A] and by the example of our deeds give fragrance to our neighbors. It also has the perfumer’s powder, while through it, outwardly restraining ourselves from worldly things, we savor the things above [Note: [Col. 0357] Col. 3]. This rod of discipline, therefore, has bitterness at the beginning, fragrance afterward, and savor at the end: bitterness by mortifying the flesh; fragrance by prayer and by advancing one’s neighbor through example; savor by tasting heavenly blessedness. At first it is burdensome; secondly precious; thirdly delightful to the heart.

Likewise, in the first desert misery has its place; in the second, grace has failure; in the third, a fall has restoration; in the fourth, progress has blessedness. The first is the wilderness of the Dead Sea; the second, that in which Ishmael’s water-skin failed; the third, that in which the children of Israel were refreshed by the sweetness of heavenly food. [Col. 0357B] Of the fourth it is said that Moses drove his sheep to the inner parts of the desert and saw the vision of the burning bush [Note: [Col. 0357] Exod. 3], that is, of Christ incarnate and glorified, not consumed but strengthened by the fire of the Passion.

Or the desert may be called the generation of the ancient fathers, who under the old law lived uncultivated and, as it were, rude; from them the Blessed Virgin Mary ascended by being born, so that it may be said of her: “Who is this who ascends through the desert?” If you wish to hear her being born from the desert, hear how solemnly the Church sings: “Today the Blessed Virgin Mary was born, sprung from the seed of Abraham, from the tribe of Judah, illustrious from the stock of David.”

Seed is a portion of male flesh sown in the mother’s womb, so that from it childbirth may result. A tribe is a collection of persons from the same seed, [Col. 0357C] both those descending collaterally and those in a direct line. A stock is a collection of persons descending directly from someone. In the first is authority; in the second, prowess; in the third, distinction: the authority of fleshly descent, the prowess of manly excellence, the distinction of royal nobility. Authority, because in Abraham were the beginnings of faith; prowess, because the tribe of Judah, always adhering to Moses and first exposing itself to danger, was eminent; royal nobility, whose preeminence was in David. In the first is the beginning of good; in the second, the advancement of virtues; in the third, consummation.

O glorious birth, through which, passing over the angels, the Son of God took hold of Abraham’s seed; through which the lion from the tribe of Judah conquered and opened the seven seals; through which, by means of David, there came forth “a rod from the root [Col. 0357D] of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root [Note: [Col. 0357] Isa. 11].” O blessed seed, from which Paul glories that he was born, which Saul prophesies to all, and which human nature glories to have grasped the Son of God. For Paul says of the first: “They are Abraham’s seed, and so am I [Note: [Col. 0357] II Cor. 11].” Of the second: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed [Note: [Col. 0357] Gal. 3].” Of the third: “He took hold not of angels, but of the seed of Abraham [Note: [Col. 0357] Heb. 2].”

This is the seed through which peace is restored, the Church of the faithful is multiplied, and captivity is set free. 72 Peace is restored with humanity; the Church is multiplied in number and virtue; captivity is liberated from slavery. The first is so that God may be loved more; the second, [Col. 0358A] so that he may be praised more by more persons; the third, so that he may be honored more generously. For the Lord proposed these three things to Abraham. Of the first: “I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed [Note: [Col. 0357] Gen. 9].” Hence: “I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven, and it shall be the sign of a covenant between me and the earth [Note: [Col. 0357] Ibid.].” The bow is Mary, who shines among the saints like the rainbow among clouds. Of the second: “Look up at heaven and count the stars, if you can: so shall your seed be [Note: [Col. 0357] Gen. 15].” Of the third: “Know beforehand that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own; and they shall subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years [Note: [Col. 0357] Ibid.]. But in the fourth generation they shall return here.” For this is according to our present purpose.

The first generation is Abraham’s, the second Judah’s, the third [Col. 0358B] David’s, the fourth Christ’s and Mary’s. For in this generation the wretched were freed from slavery to the devil. Our own case is at issue: we are strangers, subjected to slavery, afflicted by scourges. Yet through this birth we shall be freed: strangers, driven from the delightfulness of paradise; slaves, under the devil’s power; afflicted by the world’s calamity; freed by the birth of the Blessed Virgin.

In the first we were wanderers and fugitives over the earth: wanderers, following concupiscence; fugitives, fleeing misery; or wanderers, following the world’s vanity; fugitives, avoiding religious austerity. In the second, we were encircled by the cords of sins. In the third, in Egypt, we were oppressed by the labors of straw, brick, and mud. In the fourth, when morning watch came—that is, the birth of the Virgin, who comes forth like the rising dawn—we were raised up, so that at judgment [Col. 0358C] we may be fully acquitted.

In the first, with the prodigal son we departed into a far country. Hence David: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged [Note: [Col. 0357] Ps. 119]!” “For as long as we are in this body, we are away from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0357] II Cor. 6].” Hence: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land [Note: [Col. 0357] Ps. 136]?” In the second, we are Ishmael, son of Hagar, whose name means “slavery,” she who serves with her children, bringing forth into slavery [Note: [Col. 0357] Gal. 4]. “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin [Note: [Col. 0357] John 8]”—“But now, freed from sin, you have become servants of God. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness [Note: [Col. 0357] Rom. 6].” We serve with children when, by the example of another’s wickedness, we subject ourselves to the devil; we bring forth into slavery when, by the example of our own depravity, we subject others to the devil. [Col. 0358D] In the third, we are Israel serving

in straw, mud, and brick. By straw we have bodily frailty. By mud, which is mixed from water and dust, we have disturbance of the soul. By brick, which once broken cannot by any skill be made solid again, we have the irreparable dissolution of body and soul in death.

But this birth remedies these things, as the prophet says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root [Note: [Col. 0357] Isa. 11].” For the rod of virtue shall remove the constriction of calamity; the flower has freed slaves by taking away sin’s uncleanness; and the good spirit shall lead back [Col. 0359A] the strangers into the right land [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 142].”

This birth was from the tribe of Judah. This tribe was praiseworthy, victorious, and authoritative. Praiseworthy, because the Blessed Virgin was to be born from it; victorious, because through it death was to perish; authoritative, because human nature was assumed from it by the Son of God. Through the first, the world received a new flower; through the second, hell conceived pain; through the third, heaven dripped with honeyed sweetness. Jacob prophesied these three things to his son Judah. Of the first: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you [Note: [Col. 0359] Gen. 49].” Of the second: “Your hand upon the necks of your enemies [Note: [Col. 0359] Ibid.].” Of the third: “The sons of your father shall worship you [Note: [Col. 0359] Ibid.].”

Hear of the flower: “I shall be like dew; Israel shall blossom like the lily [Note: [Col. 0359] Hos. 14].” Hence: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters”—of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0359] Song 2]. [Col. 0359B] Hence: “Flowers have appeared in our land [Note: [Col. 0359] Ibid.].” Of the second: “Pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia [Note: [Col. 0359] Exod. 16],” that is, the devil, who is called “double ruin.” Of the third: “The heavens dripped at the presence of the God of Sinai, at the presence of the God of Jacob [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 67].” Hence the heavens were made honey-flowing throughout the whole world.

And morally: if we have been born from Judah, which means “confession,” we can advance through these three things: so that a person may first be praiseworthy, secondly victorious, and thirdly authoritative. First, fleeing sin, he is born like a flower from a dungheap; secondly, by manfully resisting the sting of temptation; thirdly, by holy meditations he penetrates heaven and takes part in the divine council. First, he approaches virginal purity; secondly, he frees himself from the prison of hell; thirdly, [Col. 0359C] he enters the royal palace. By the first he becomes more beautiful; by the second, more powerful; by the third, more exalted.

Of the first: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 44].” Of the second: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one [Note: [Col. 0359] Ibid.].” Of the third: “Aim prosperously, proceed, and reign [Note: [Col. 0359] Ibid.].” So that it may be said: “The queen stood at your right hand in golden raiment, surrounded by variety [Note: [Col. 0359] Ibid.].”

Judith proceeded in this order: first, she made herself beautiful by more elegant clothing; secondly, she cut off Holofernes’ head; thirdly, by offering his head in the Temple she won for herself the glory and remembrance of lasting fame [Note: [Col. 0359] Judith 10]. Thus Joseph was first adorned with a variegated garment; secondly, he manfully endured prison rather than lie [Col. 0359D] with his adulterous mistress; thirdly, when exalted, he was made second after the king [Note: [Col. 0359] Gen. 39 and following].

In the figure of this birth of the Blessed Virgin, “Judah begot Zarah [Note: [Col. 0359] Matt. 1],” whose name means “rising.” Judah pitched camp east of the tabernacle; hence Balaam: “A star shall arise from Jacob [Note: [Col. 0359] Num. 24].” By these three things he deserved to be preferred to the others: because Judah freed Joseph from the hands of his brothers; because by these three he was the first to cross the Red Sea; because David led a return from Hebron to Jerusalem. For these merits the tribe was worthy of the birth of the Blessed Virgin, who was also illustrious from the stock of David.

For she was illustrious by royal descent, illustrious by abundance of grace, illustrious by the conception of Christ, illustrious by glorification. [Col. 0360A] In the first she was founded in humility; in the second, flourishing in virginity; in the third, gilded in charity; in the fourth, radiant in joy. By the first she was honorable to human beings; by the second, beloved by angels; by the third, pleasing to God; by the fourth, visible in the kingdom of heaven. For the first it is said: “Illustrious from the stock of David”; for the second: “Whose glorious life gave light to the world”; for the third: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, and the earth was illuminated by his glory [Note: [Col. 0359] Apoc. 18],” that is, Mary by her Son; for the fourth:

> O with what glorious light you shine,  
> Royal offspring of David’s stock,  
> Virgin Mary, seated on high.

Therefore whoever wishes to imitate this Blessed Virgin must first be from the seed of Abraham, whose name means [Col. 0360B] “exalted father”; secondly, from the tribe of Judah, whose name means “confession”; thirdly, from the stock of David, whose name means “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance.” First, the seed of true contrition must be infused into him by the Exalted Father; secondly, he must confess his sins; thirdly, he must be strengthened in charity; fourthly, with the Blessed Virgin he must be made radiant by spiritual understanding.

For the first it is said: Abraham, father and servant of blessed seed, is the first way of believing, because “He who does not believe is already judged [Note: [Col. 0359] John 3] [Note: [Col. 0359] Jas. 5].” Of the second: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be saved [Note: [Col. 0359] Isa. 35],” because in confession all things are washed. Of the third: “Lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 58].” Hence David: “I shall keep my strength for you [Note: [Col. 0359] John 1].”

Fourthly, let us be made radiant [Col. 0360C] with the Blessed Virgin, and by the same stages: first by descent, because we were created by God; secondly by the infusion of grace, because we were re-created through the Holy Spirit; thirdly by the conception of Christ, when Christ dwells in the lodging of our heart; fourthly when we shall be remade in blessedness. First, therefore, we are illuminated by reason, by which we naturally distinguish the use of things; secondly by inspiration, by which we recognize ourselves as sinners; thirdly by spiritual understanding, by which we sigh for heavenly things; fourthly at the resurrection, when we shall see God.

First, “[He] enlightens every person coming into this world 15*.” Of the second: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 12].” Of the third: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come [Note: [Col. 0359] Isa. 60].” Of the fourth: “The righteous shall shine [Col. 0360D] like the sun in the kingdom of their Father [Note: [Col. 0359] Matt. 33].” For the fourth Ambrose says:

> O with what glorious light you shine,  
> Royal offspring of David’s stock,  
> Virgin Mary, seated on high,  
> Above all the heaven-born beings of the sky.

These four things are found in Solomon’s palanquin. For he says: “Solomon made himself a palanquin of the woods of Lebanon; he made its pillars of silver, its back of gold, its ascent of purple [Note: [Col. 0359] Song 3].” By the woods of Lebanon are meant the ancient fathers: they set their roots as far down below as their branches rise on high. This loftiness is humility. By silver, virginity; by gold, the conception of Christ; by the purple ascent, the glorification of Christ or of her.

“Who is this who ascends through the desert, like a little rod of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and incense, and every powder of the perfumer?”

[CARD.] The Blessed Virgin indeed ascended, because “she set ascents in her heart [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 83].” She ascended from virtue to virtue, advancing outwardly in her works. She ascended through the desert—that is, through the world, which she regarded as a desert; for, despising the world and its desires, she clung to spiritual delights. She ascended like a little rod because of the uprightness of her intention and work, the grace of humility, the firmness of perseverance, and the attenuation of her flesh. A little rod is straight and firm, [Col. 0361B] slender and lowly.

This rod is called one of smoke because smoke is swift, comes from the heat of fire, moves onward, and as it ascends vanishes from human sight. And the Blessed Virgin was swift in helpful service: she went up into the hill country to Blessed Elizabeth [Note: [Col. 0361] Luke 1], in order to minister to her and to the son who was to be born from her. She was swift because, with light running and a light leap, like an *iditum*—that is, one leaping across—she leapt over every thorn and pit of vices. Enkindled by the ardor of the Holy Spirit, she thus advanced in grace by ascending and thus ascended in glory, so that, as if vanishing, she surpasses all human knowledge.

And because the foregoing commendation might seem insufficient for the praise of this little rod, its fragrance is added: “From the spices of myrrh and incense, and every [Col. 0361C] powder of the perfumer.” For the Blessed Virgin poured out upon the Church the fragrance of all virtues; she possessed all the spices of virtues. Hence it is said: “From the spices of myrrh and incense and every powder of the perfumer,” which the perfumer has and knows how to make—namely, Jesus Christ, the giver of all virtues. By myrrh, with which dead bodies are embalmed, fasting and other mortifications of the flesh are signified. By sweet-smelling incense, the fragrance of prayers is signified. By every powder of spices—for spices are ground so that they may be reduced to powder, and when reduced to powder may be crushed—are signified all virtues seasoned with patience and humility. It follows:

[Col. 0361D] “Behold Solomon’s bed; sixty strong men surround it, from among Israel’s strongest men, all holding swords and most skilled in warfare.”

[THO.] Solomon means “peaceful.” He is Christ. Therefore we make him a bed when we cease from worldly care and rest in the desire for him alone. Now ten multiplied by six makes sixty. By ten, therefore, understand the Decalogue; by six, the whole time in which all things were made. Thus by the sixty strong men we understand all the perfect members of the Church. While they fulfill the Decalogue in the six days, they surround Christ’s bed, because they fortify by words and examples the holy mind in which he rests, and thus repel enemies from it, holding [Col. 0362A] swords while they fulfill the word of God, and being most skilled in warfare while they teach others to beware; and by the sword, “which is the word of God [Note: [Col. 0361] Eph. 6],” wisdom conquers malice [Note: [Col. 0361] Wis. 7]. By the hands with which the swords are held, works are signified.

> The virtue of preserving what has been gained is no less than that of seeking it;  
> There is danger in the one, but in the other there is the work of skill.

It is good to prepare the bed of conscience; better to bring in the bridegroom; best to preserve the world when he has been brought in: to prepare it with fragrant flowers, to bring in the bridegroom with caresses, and to preserve the world with watchmen and swords—by the flowers of virtues, the caresses of prayers and services, the watches of circumspection, and the swords of the divine word and rebukes. “Prepare,” he says, “your hearts for the Lord [Note: [Col. 0361] I Sam. 7]”: behold how they prepare the bed. “And serve him alone”: behold how he is drawn by services [Col. 0362B] and prayers. “And he will free you from our sins”: behold how he is guarded. 73 Hear also the poet:

> First, labor to find what you wish to love,  
> You who now, a new soldier, first come into arms.  
> The next labor is to win by entreaty the one you have found and pleased;  
> The third is that love may endure for a long time.

Hear the first: “Create a clean heart in me, O God [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 50]”; the second: “Renew a right spirit within me [Note: [Col. 0361] Ibid.]”; and the third: “Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me [Note: [Col. 0361] Ibid.].”

“Sixty strong men,” he says: this is said on account of the perfection of six and ten, by which the number is multiplied. Six is the first perfect number, whose parts when added multiplicatively make six; and it signifies the perfection of keeping God’s commandments, so that we may neither go beyond them through presumption nor fall short through negligence. Ten consists of seven and three. Seven is a virgin number, because below the first boundary it neither begets nor is begotten; and it signifies the incorruption of the mind. Three signifies the three things through which a teacher ought to advance: teaching in words, gravity of morals, and integrity in enduring sufferings. Hence the Apostle: “In all things show yourself an example of good works, in teaching, in gravity, in integrity [Note: [Col. 0361] Titus 2].”

Likewise, he ought to instruct those subject to him in three things: purity of heart, sincerity of works, and soundness of words. Hence the Apostle: “Let not the sun go down upon [Col. 0362D] your anger [Note: [Col. 0361] Eph. 4].” Behold purity of heart. “Let him who stole steal no more, but rather let him labor, so that he may have something to give to one suffering need [Note: [Col. 0361] Ibid.].” Behold sincerity of work. “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth [Note: [Col. 0361] Ibid.].” Behold soundness of words.

Among Israel’s strongest men David had thirty mighty men. But three were stronger than these: Abishai, Sobochai, and Jonathan. The first is called “the sacrifice of my father,” on account of repentance; the second, “dense,” on account of frequency in prayer and almsgiving; the third, “gift of the dove,” on account of the grace of good will. But the three mightiest who guarded [Col. 0363A] his bed were Eleazar, Shemaiah, and Jashobeam. These also guard our beds according to the interpretation of their names. Eleazar means “the Lord’s help,” against despair; Shemaiah, “obedient to the Lord,” against Adam’s disobedience; Jashobeam, “becoming foolish,” against Satan’s pride. For a person ought to regard himself as foolish and lacking wisdom. Thus, whoever trusts in the help of the Most High, whoever is obedient, whoever is humble, is strong to guard the bed.

There are three beds of Solomon: the first, of married persons; the second, of the continent; the third, of virgins. Although the first render one another their due, they endeavor to preserve themselves from sin. The second, having experienced marriage, endeavor thereafter to abstain. The third, despising both, strive [Col. 0363B] to devote themselves to God alone. The first are in the thirtyfold state, the second in the sixtyfold, the third in the hundredfold. This follows from the method of counting.

At the lower joint of the left thumb say ten; at the second, twenty; at the third, thirty, where the tip of the thumb and first finger touch, because married persons thus embrace one another with a gentle kiss. Continue by counting the fingertips: at the tip of the second finger, thirty-one; of the third, thirty-two; of the fourth, that is, the little finger, thirty-four. Descend through the joints of the little finger: at the first, thirty-four; at the second, thirty-five; at the lower one, thirty-six. Returning by the three lower joints to the first finger, at the lower joint of the second finger say thirty-seven; at the lower joint of the next, thirty-eight; at the lower joint of the first, thirty-nine. Ascend to the second joint of the first, saying forty. Ascend to the third joint of the first, saying fifty. There remain the four [Col. 0363C] middle joints of the two middle fingers, which are the enclosure. At the first of them, namely the higher joint of the larger finger, say sixty: there is the entrance of the enclosure in which the continent dwell. At the second of those four say seventy; at the third, eighty; at the fourth, ninety. Behold, the enclosure is completed. Since there are no more joints on the left hand, one must count the hundredfold on the right, and thus pass from left to right. This is the number assigned to virginity.

In thirty is the fruit of married persons, because it is multiplied from three, which is half of six—the perfect number—and ten, which is perfect. Their perfection is half-full insofar as they abstain from unlawful things. In sixty is the fruit of the continent, which is made from six and ten, both perfect numbers, because there is a double perfection in the continent: they avoid unlawful things and also abstain from lawful ones. In one hundred is the fruit of virgins. The hundredfold is worthier, since it is perfect through ten and six, because it contains them beneath itself; it is multiplied by ten taken into itself and is square. Therefore married persons and the continent are after the first boundary; virgins, however, are in the second and sigh toward the third, namely the thousandfold, which is solid, because ten times ten are a thousand—that is, because it is God, who is solid, that is, stable, while all other things are movable. Hence Boethius [Note: [Col. 0363] Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*]:

> Remaining stable, he grants all things to be moved.

[Col. 0364A] David had thirty mighty men: these guard the first bed. The three stronger men guard the second: namely Abishai, whose name means “my father is superfluous”; Sobochai, “turning me”; and Jonathan, “gift of the dove,” that is, God’s grace. For avoiding superfluities, turning oneself to God, and retaining God’s grace guard continence. These three are said to guard the sixtyfold, because three times twenty are sixty. The three mightiest guard the third: Eleazar, “God’s help”; Shemaiah, “obedient”; and Jashobeam, “becoming foolish” and humble. These three things are useful for guarding virgins.

“All holding swords.” There are six swords: the first is material; the second spiritual. Hence Peter: “Behold, here are two swords [Note: [Col. 0363] Luke 22].” And the sword [Col. 0364B] is the word of God: “The word of God is living and effective and sharper than every two-edged sword [Note: [Col. 0363] Heb. 4].” Passion too is a sword: “A sword shall pierce your own soul [Note: [Col. 0363] Luke 2].” Chastisement of the flesh is also a sword: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one [Note: [Col. 0363] Ps. 44].” Action too is a sword: “Two-edged swords in their hands [Note: [Col. 0363] Ps. 174].”

The first sword strikes through ecclesiastical censure; the second, through secular power; the third, through the teacher; the fourth, through the persecutor; the fifth, through the Lord; the sixth, through the spirit. The first strikes in order to give life; the second, to chastise by example; the third, to heal; the fourth, to put to death; the fifth, to awaken; the sixth, to cut off superfluities. First the prelate strikes the rebel against the Church; secondly, the judge the thief; thirdly, the preacher the sinner; fourthly, the tyrant the innocent; fifthly, the Lord the servant [Col. 0364C] who is on pilgrimage; sixthly, the spirit the flesh that is lustful.

“And most skilled in warfare,” he says. Those who fight the devil are skilled; those who fight the world, more skilled; those who fight their own body, most skilled. For the devil is sometimes caught by cunning; the world can be overcome by patience; but the wantonness of the flesh always thrusts itself upon us. Therefore greater vigilance must be applied, so that we may be most skilled in warfare. Hence follows:

“Each one’s sword upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night.”

[THO.] (Thus.) The elect who have already reached perfection bear the sword—that is, the rigor of conversion—upon their thigh, by which they break the appetite of the flesh, [Col. 0364D] lest the enemy whom they fear in the night of this world, approaching through softness, presume to defile the bed.

We read of the sword upon the thigh, in the mouth, in the hand, and in the heart. Let us likewise carry it upon the thigh, to cut off fleshly pleasures; in the mouth, to cut off superfluous speech; in the hand, to cut off disorderly works; and in the heart, against unlawful thoughts. The Lord too will carry it in these ways at judgment: upon his thigh, to remove our corruption; in his mouth, in pronouncing sentence by approval or condemnation; in his hand, in separating sheep from goats; in his heart, by showing the wound in his side through which [Col. 0365A] he was wounded for us.

The terror of the night is temptations arising from ignorance; the arrow flying by day, sins committed knowingly; the business that walks in darkness, slight sins committed knowingly; the terror of the night, slight sins of ignorance; the attack and the noonday demon, grave sins committed knowingly. There are four temptations: the first is the terror of the night; the second, the arrow flying by day; the third, the business that walks in darkness; the fourth, the noonday demon. The first terror of the night is adversity which presents itself to one who is converting, and on whose account he fears to convert. The second is vainglory arising from human praises: when the arrow of reputation flies in the day of a commendable life. The third is ambition for dignities: perhaps one who does not care for praises desires honors; and this is [Col. 0365B] the business that walks in darkness, because ambition blinds them. The fourth is the noonday demon [Note: [Col. 0365] Ps. 90], which exists among the imperfect. By a falsely good thing the devil deceives them. The wise do not fail to recognize the devil’s wiles, because he calls good what is not good. The first hinders conversion; the second wounds religious life; the third exchanges reward for evils; the fourth hurls one down through error.

Likewise, prelates are guardians of the Church, or each person is guardian of his own soul. Although “night” is understood in many ways, here it is understood as consent to temptation. Hence: “May a dark whirlwind possess that night [Note: [Col. 0365] Job 3].” Of guardians: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set guardians [Note: [Col. 0365] Isa. 62].” Terror of the night is sometimes produced by one’s own deficiency, sometimes by another’s act. Against the first we need a staff; against the second, a sword: a staff by which we may be guided and a sword by which we may be defended.

Jacob says of the staff: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies [Note: [Col. 0365] Gen. 32].” In fear produced by one’s own deficiency we fear loss, stumbling, and falling: loss of the way, stumbling at a stone, falling into a pit. The way is the rigor of discipline under which we serve as soldiers. “And the rock was Christ [Note: [Col. 0365] I Cor. 10].” The pit is the failure of despair. The first fear lest they stray from the way that leads them into the harbor of their desire; the second lest they strike their foot against the stone; the third lest, with Daniel’s accusers, they be cast into the lions’ den. The first say: “My soul is filled with evils [Note: [Col. 0365] Ps. 87].” The second: “My life has drawn near to hell [Note: [Col. 0365] Ibid.].” The third: [Col. 0365D] “I have been counted with those who descend into the pit [Note: [Col. 0365] Ibid.].” Therefore against these three one must have the staff of governance, by which the way may be felt out, the stone touched, and the pit discovered.

Therefore let the watchman standing at the crossroads feel out the road, touch the stone, detect the pit, and cry: “Let us live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this world” [Note: [Col. 0365] Titus 2.]. Tamar was at a crossroads when Judah had intercourse with her, and by her begot Perez and Zerah [Note: [Col. 0365] Genesis 38.]. Tamar is interpreted “bitterness,” Judah “confession,” Perez “division,” Zerah “rising.” Therefore, when the soul sits at the crossroads—[Col. 0366A] namely, between the road to the left and that to the right—it is in bitterness. On the one hand it fears to sin because of the punishment of hell; on the other it fears to undertake the narrow way that leads to life [Note: [Col. 0365] Matthew 7.], fearing that its own weakness will prove inadequate. But Judah joins with her when it hastens to the remedy of confession. Then it begets Perez when it is separated from the evil way; it begets Zerah when grace rises within it so that it may keep to the way. Therefore the watchman cries: “Broad is the way that leads to death, and many enter by it” [Note: [Col. 0365] Ibid.]. For this is the way by which a certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho [Note: [Col. 0365] Luke 10.], that is, from the vision of peace into the failing of the world; and Shimei, who had cursed David, fled by it, leaving Jerusalem and pursuing his runaway servant [Note: [Col. 0365] 2 Kings 16]. Shimei means “my hearing”; his servant is [Col. 0366B] the flesh. Although the flesh ought to hear and obey the spirit, the spirit hears it; and while it flees outside Jerusalem—that is, outside the vision of peace—the spirit follows it. Hence it is slain, because the king had said to it: “On whatever day you go out from Jerusalem, you shall surely die.” Thus do those flee who fear to undertake the narrow way. But it is written: “He who fears the frost, snow shall fall upon him” [Note: [Col. 0365] Job 6.]. But the way to the right “is narrow, which leads to life, yet few enter by it” [Note: [Col. 0365] Matthew 7.]. Yet this gives us great comfort: Christ suffered upon it, “leaving us an example, that we should follow his footsteps” [Note: [Col. 0365] 1 Peter 2.]. Let us therefore go by him; and thus, fleeing the loss of the way, we shall escape this terror of the night.

But the stumbling-block of the stone still lies before my eyes. “And the rock was [Col. 0366C] Christ” [Note: [Col. 0365] 1 Corinthians 10.]. On the way we have struggled, relaxing the rigor of discipline. We strike against the rock, 74 by incurring grievous sin; we slip into the pit when we fall into despair. This rock is good to the good, but hard to the wicked. For to the wicked it is first a rock of offense, second of scandal, third of crushing: offense in the world, scandal at judgment, crushing in hell; in the world through sin, at judgment through sentence, in hell through everlasting misery. Of the first and second it is said: “A stone of offense and a rock of scandal” [Note: [Col. 0365] 1 Peter 2.]. Of the third: “Those who stumble upon him are dashed to pieces; but he upon whom he falls will be crushed” [Note: [Col. 0365] Matthew 21.]. He shall fall upon the one to whom it will be said: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” [Note: [Col. 0365] Matthew 25.]. For this is the stone [Col. 0366D] cut from the mountain without hands, which shattered Nebuchadnezzar’s statue [Note: [Col. 0365] Daniel 2]. When it is touched by a prelate, it gives forth this sound: “Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to each according to his works” [Note: [Col. 0365] Revelation 22]. It also renders to the good according to their works. Meanwhile, it is strength for the weak, richness of devotion, sweetness for the perfect: strength by which they may prevail against the adversary; richness by which they may love sweetly; sweetness so that they may relish the things above. Of the first it is said: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” [Note: [Col. 0365] Psalm 103]. And: “Come, my friend, into the clefts of the rock, into the cave of the wall” [Col. 0367A] [Note: [Col. 0367] Song of Songs 2.]. Of the second, Job says: “I washed my feet in butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil” [Note: [Col. 0367] Job 29]. Likewise: “That he might suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone” [Note: [Col. 0367] Deuteronomy 32]. And of the third: “He satisfied them with honey from the rock” [Note: [Col. 0367] Psalm 80]. Otherwise, if they stumble at this stone, it remains for them to fall into the pit.

But first they open this pit, second they dig it, third they fall into it. They open it when others imitate the offense of sinners; they dig it when one declines from evil to worse; they fall into it when they are caught in such things at death. David shows this in one verse: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the hole that he made” [Note: [Col. 0367] Psalm 7.]. Therefore, first they are handed over to a judge, second to an exactor, third to a torturer: to a judge who passes judgment concerning their sins; to an exactor who enforces [Col. 0367B] what has been judged; to a torturer who wrings out by scourges what has been exacted, until they pay the entire debt to the last farthing. It should be noted that there are four farthings. For man consists of four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. In fire is understood charity, which is the first farthing; in air, the grace of God or human life, which is the second farthing; in water, the washing away of sin, which is the third farthing; in earth, which is the body, the fourth and last farthing. There, therefore, he will pay because he sinned against charity, which is the first; and because he received the grace of God in vain [Note: [Col. 0367] 2 Corinthians 6], or lived wickedly, which is the second farthing; and because after baptism he defiled himself, which is the third farthing. He acted wickedly in the body: this is the fourth and last farthing.

Behold the terror of the night arising from one’s own defect. There is another terror of the night arising from another’s deed. The terror of the night is threefold: for there is fear of illusion, stratagem, and attack—illusion by phantoms, stratagem by robbers, attack by beasts. Phantoms disturb; robbers carry away; beasts devour: they disturb the soul, carry away one’s substance, and devour the human body. These are three enemies. Of the first: “The beast shall enter its hiding-place and remain in its den” [Note: [Col. 0367] Job 32]. Of the second: “If the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely watch and not permit his house to be broken into” [Note: [Col. 0367] Luke 22]. Of the third: “For I, your servant, have killed both lion and bear” [Note: [Col. 0367] 1 Kings 17]. First, the apostles were troubled when, seeing Christ walking upon the waves, they thought that it was a phantom [Note: [Col. 0367] Matthew 14]. Phantoms are [Col. 0367D] worldly pleasures; thieves are those who take away the treasure of virtues; beasts devour through the severity of scourges. Therefore you must have a sword against these things. Against the first, the sword of discernment upon your thigh, and then dreams and phantoms of the night will retreat far away. Against the second, the sword of vigilance in your hand, and then you will store up treasures for yourself in heaven, where thieves neither break in nor steal [Note: [Col. 0367] Matthew 6]. Thus against the third you will be most skilled for war, and you will not fear the beast of the earth.

“Behold Solomon’s bed: sixty strong men surround it,” etc.

[Col. 0368A] [CARD.] Angels, Christ’s holy companions, insert this verse and the following one, describing with what zeal angels serve and attend upon the Blessed Virgin. Thus it says: “Behold Solomon’s bed: sixty strong men, of the strongest of Israel, surround it, all holding swords and most skilled in war. Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.” The bed of Solomon—that is, of Christ, the true peacemaker—is said to be the Blessed Virgin, in whom the Son of God, the Deity inclining its head, rested as upon a bed. Hence she herself says: “He who created me rested in my tabernacle” [Note: [Col. 0367] Sirach 24]. But since, as the Apostle says, “All heavenly spirits are ministering spirits, and are sent for those who shall inherit salvation” [Note: [Col. 0367] Hebrews 1], and not only the lesser [Col. 0368B] spirits are sent to minister to human beings, but also the higher spirits of the order of Seraphim, who, because of the ardor of charity, are called a flame of fire or burning fire—whence the Psalmist says: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers” a flame of fire or “burning fire” [Note: [Col. 0367] Psalm 103]—this passage shows that angels not of lower but of higher rank were appointed for the protection and service of the Blessed Virgin. For it says that sixty strong men, chosen from the strongest of Israel, surround this bed. Angelic spirits, strong among the strongest of spirits, surrounded the Blessed Virgin with diligent protection and reverent service; because they behold God in continual contemplation, they are denoted by the name Israel. These sixty strong men are called so not because of their number, but because of the mystery of the number.

[Col. 0368C] For that number consists of six and ten; six signifies perfection. Ten likewise, which bears the image of the king and contains within itself the number ten as a price, designates the angelic nature, created in the image of God. More explicitly, it possesses, as it were, a certain coinage: the three natural powers of intellect, will, and memory, adorned with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. This interpretation agrees with the fact that, by the ten drachmas in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0367] Luke 15], the nine orders of angels and human nature are signified. Therefore, by the sixty strong men are signified those spirits who are known to excel the rest in the subtlety of their natural faculties, the abundance of spiritual graces, and a more express likeness to the Creator, with a certain perfection. Their strength, prudence, and readiness of service [Col. 0368D] are shown when it says: “All holding swords, and most skilled in war,” and in what follows. The swords signify the power to overcome malignant spirits. Their being called most skilled in war shows their prudence in resisting every assault of demons. And when it says, “Each man’s sword is upon his thigh,” it shows how unencumbered and ready they are for battle; for men about to fight, while awaiting an adversary, customarily hold a drawn sword upon their thigh. Why these strong men surround this bed is shown when it says: “Because of the terrors [Col. 0369A] of the night”—namely, in order to repel not merely grave temptations, but also that brief and slight temptation signified in the Psalm by the terror of the night, where it says: “You shall not fear the terror of the night” [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 90]. For by the ministry of angels every temptation was so repelled from the Blessed Virgin that, after the conception of her Son, she is believed not even to have sinned venially. It follows:

“Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon: he made its pillars of silver, its reclining-place of gold, its ascent of purple; he paved the middle with charity, for the daughters of Jerusalem.”

[THO.] There are three litters. The first is the Church, the second the soul, the third Mary. The first bears Christ by sustaining the unity of the sacraments; the second [Col. 0369B] by bearing the sweet yoke of his commandments; the third by conceiving him in her womb. The woods of Lebanon are incorruptible. From these Solomon made himself a litter, because Christ made the Church from saints who will remain forever. He made its pillars of silver, because he appointed in it preachers who support it; they are silver because they instruct others by the brilliance of speech. He made the reclining-place of gold, because God, while shining forth in the hearts of the perfect, showed them through contemplation the power of his divinity. And this reclining-place is golden because wisdom is better than all riches. Its ascent is purple because one reaches it through many tribulations, and sometimes through the shedding of blood. But because we are weak, we cannot attain it through labors, [Col. 0369C] the following comforts us: “He paved the middle with charity, for the daughters of Jerusalem.” The daughters of Jerusalem are called weak because they do not struggle against vices manfully, as males do.

That litter is the soul of the righteous, which is said to bear Christ by bearing his sweet yoke. For *ferculum* is so called from *ferre*, “to bear”; it is made from the woods of Lebanon. Lebanon is interpreted “whitening.” Its woods are incorruptible; and as far upward as they extend their branches, so deeply do they fix their root in the earth. This litter is said to be made of three materials: wood, silver, and gold. The wood is works in their performance; silver, virtues in their habitual possession; gold, wisdom and knowledge in ordering, and sweetness in tasting.

[Col. 0369D] Therefore let our works be incorruptible—that is, without the admixture of sin. Let them have root, excluding hypocrisy and negligence; let them possess cheerfulness, excluding compulsion and sadness. Of the first, Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0369] ch. 1]: “My soul has hated your calends and new moons. For your hands are full of blood.” Of the second: “Rooted and founded in charity” [Note: [Col. 0369] Ephesians 3]. Of the third: “Not from sadness or necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver” [Note: [Col. 0369] 2 Corinthians 9]. Because of the first, leaven is forbidden in sacrifice; because of the second, fat is offered; because of the third, oil is poured over it. Of the first: “Purge out [Col. 0370A] the old leaven” [Note: [Col. 0369] 1 Corinthians 5]. Of the second: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 62]. Of the third: “That he may make the face cheerful with oil” [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 103].

The silver pillars are the four cardinal virtues: justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance. They have a different use in the homeland than on the way. There justice is to submit oneself to God; prudence, to set none equal to or greater than him; fortitude, to cleave to him inseparably; temperance, to take delight in nothing harmful. Here, however, justice is to render to each what is his, or mercy toward the needy; prudence, to foresee snares; fortitude, to stand firm in adversity; temperance, to impose a measure upon excess. In the first we are upright; in the second cautious; in the third steadfast; in the fourth sober. Christ invited us to these. To the first: [Col. 0370B] “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another” [Note: [Col. 0369] Matthew 7]. To the second: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” [Note: [Col. 0369] Matthew 10]. To the third: “Be strong in war” [Note: [Col. 0369] Hebrews 11]. To the fourth: “See that your hearts are not weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness” [Note: [Col. 0369] Luke 21].

The golden reclining-place follows. It should be understood that first we must turn aside, second bow down, third recline: turn aside from evil, bow down in humility, recline by leaning upon Christ. We turn aside so that we may be clean; we bow down so that we may not be proud; we recline so that we may be secure. And thus let us make for Christ a golden reclining-place, which is wisdom. It must have three things: knowledge for the ordering of works and virtues; understanding for the knowledge of heavenly things; taste, so that we may perceive their sweetness. Hence David: [Col. 0370C] “The unfolding of your words gives light”—knowledge of lower things—“and gives understanding to little ones.” For knowledge of higher things, and that I might taste them, “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 118]. Likewise, there is an ivory reclining-place, a silver one, and a golden one: the first in the Virgin’s womb; the second in a brother’s heart; the third in the Father’s bosom. The first is ivory because of the whiteness of virginity; the second silver because of the brightness of innocence and gentleness; the third gold because of the splendor of divinity. In the first Christ rested through the Incarnation; in the second through purity of heart; in the third through his eternal birth from the Father.

“He made its ascent purple,” he says. Ezekiel was shown [Col. 0370D] a building whose ascent had eight steps. I believe that these are the same steps of this litter which Peter enumerates in his Catholic Epistle: “Supply,” he says, “in your faith virtue; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, abstinence; in abstinence, patience; in patience, godliness; in godliness, brotherly love; in brotherly love, charity” [Note: [Col. 0369] 2 Peter 1]. Behold, he has arranged ascents from virtue to virtue [Note: [Col. 0369] Psalm 83]. Here he calls virtue steadfastness, godliness toward God, brotherly love toward one’s neighbor, and charity; 75 patience in the practice of these things. This is the step and the color by which this whole ascent is purple. Purple is a royal garment; [Col. 0371A] distinguished persons wear it, and it signifies distinguished ascents. They say that there is red purple, *scandicina* purple [reading uncertain], and white purple. Red is martyrdom in the litter of the Church; *scandicina* is humility in the litter of the soul; white is virginity in the litter of Mary. But because not all can attain the exercise of virtue, or reach the summit of virtues or the taste of wisdom, though they can nevertheless love God and neighbor, it follows: “He paved the middle with charity, for the daughters of Jerusalem.”

Solomon also made another litter—the glorious Virgin who bore him in her womb—from the woods of Lebanon. Mount Lebanon is a royal tribe in Israel. Its woods are the Fathers descended from David, from whom this litter was made, because Mary was born from them. Hence: “Mary, sprung [Col. 0371B] from royal offspring, arose from the tribe of Judah, illustrious from David’s stock” [Note: [Col. 0371] Church Office]. Nor is there any doubt that Wisdom built itself a house in her and cut out seven pillars [Note: [Col. 0371] Proverbs 9], that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. But of these she has four formed pillars. The first is immunity from sin; the second incomparable humility; the third privileged virginity; the fourth fertility contrary to nature. The first is silver tested by fire, because in her the fire of the Holy Spirit effected the cleansing away of sin. The second is silver beaten with hammers, adapting itself to receive the form of any vessel. The third is white silver, which is an evidence of virginity. The fourth is silver which, impressed in the Virgin’s womb, became the coinage of our misery and sufficed for the redemption of all. The first [Col. 0371C] is disciplined reasoning under divine overshadowing; the second rubbed clean of the rusty chaff of self-abasement; the third polished with the file of sobriety; the fourth adorned with the electrum of divinity and humanity. By the first was broken the cord by which the human race was dragged. At the second was dashed down the pride by which the heart of demons had been lifted up before their fall. By the third was weakened the tinder of sin, through which “I find no good in myself—that is, in my flesh” [Note: [Col. 0371] Romans 7]. By the fourth the curse of our earth was excluded, namely: “Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to you” [Note: [Col. 0371] Genesis 3]. For our earth has yielded its fruit [Note: [Col. 0371] Psalm 66].

The golden reclining-place follows. It is the flesh assumed in the Virgin, in which the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily [Note: [Col. 0371] Colossians 2]. Gold is more precious than other [Col. 0371D] metals, and that flesh than all creatures: more precious in the womb than all who have been begotten; in the world than all creatures; in heaven than the angels. First, because no defilement of intercourse intervened; second, because in the resurrection Christ’s flesh blossomed anew more gloriously than every creature; third, because, sitting at the Father’s right hand, it ascended above the cherubim. The first is a sign of remission, the second of incorruption, the third of the vision of God.

“He made its ascent purple,” he says. This ascent, as has been said, is patience, which is called purple [Col. 0372A] because blood is often shed in it. It has three steps. First we must be pacified, second patient, third peacemakers: pacified from previous murmuring; patient, so that we endure without disturbance; peacemakers, making peace among those who are in strife. Through this purple ascent we can touch the woods of Lebanon by imitation and feel the pillars from afar; but another purple must color the ascent if we are to reach the reclining-place—namely, Christ’s blood. For he too ascended: having become the high priest of good things to come, he entered once into the holy places through his own blood [Note: [Col. 0371] Hebrews 9]. But because the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the weak—can neither expressly imitate the religious life of the Fathers, nor touch the perfection of the pillars, nor [Col. 0372B] attain the consummation of the reclining-place, he paved the middle with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem, so that they may at least arrive through love of God and neighbor.

Daughters of Jerusalem are called neither weaker nor more blessed. The first are so called because of the weakness of their sex; the second because women’s love is more vehement; the third because women, not laboring like men, have rest. Of the first, as here: “He paved the middle with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem”; of the second: “Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0371] Song of Songs 5]; of the third: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I languish for love” [Note: [Col. 0371] Song of Songs 2]. He paved the litter of the Church with charity, that they may be founded in charity; he inflamed the litter of the soul in the middle with charity, that they may be fervent; he strengthened the litter of Mary in the middle with charity, [Col. 0372C] that they may be secure. Of the first: “Rooted and founded in charity” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ephesians 3]; of the second: “Lamps of fire and flames” [Note: [Col. 0371] Song of Songs 8]; of the third: “Charity never fails” [Note: [Col. 0371] 1 Corinthians 13].

“King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon; he made its pillars of silver, its reclining-place of gold, its ascent of purple; he paved the middle with charity, for the daughters of Jerusalem.”

[CARD.] In this verse the privileges of the Blessed Virgin are commended through the construction of the litter. Therefore King Solomon—that is, Christ—made himself a litter, or throne, by which he is conveyed into human knowledge, when he prepared the Blessed Virgin for his Incarnation and made her his mother. He made this [Col. 0372D] litter from the woods of Lebanon. Lebanon is interpreted “whiteness” or “incense,” because the Lord joined together the Virgin’s holiness from the fragrance of good works and the brightness of virtues. He made the pillars of this litter silver. The strength of the litter lies in its pillars; these pillars were four, and silver, indicated by the properties of silver. For silver gives a sweet sound, shines, is white, and has value as a price. Therefore, by the four silver pillars are signified in the Mother of the Lord: the sweet sound of prayer in her petitions before the Lord; the splendor of holiness for the illumination of human beings; the whiteness of virginity in [Col. 0373A] the mother; and the preciousness of motherhood in the virgin.

Christ also made himself a golden reclining-place in the litter, for he flooded the Virgin’s mind with the fullness of wisdom, which is signified by gold, and so illuminated her by divine knowledge that it may fittingly be said that he rested the head of his divinity in her. The Lord also made an ascent of purple, for purple is the emblem of royal dignity; and through the assumption of flesh Christ ascended and entered this seat and declared himself to the world as king. For in his Passion, with the blood of the flesh he had assumed, he wrote upon his thigh and upon his garment: “King of kings and Lord of lords” [Note: [Col. 0373] Revelation 17]. His entrance into the Virgin’s womb is called an ascent, after the likeness of Isaiah’s saying: “The Lord ascended upon a light cloud” [Col. 0373B] [Note: [Col. 0373] Isaiah 10]; and he calls the holy flesh of Christ a light cloud, not weighed down by any burden of sin. The Lord is rightly said to have ascended in descending into the Virgin: for, by descending through the bending down of divinity, he then ascended in human hearts through knowledge.

The ensuing words, “He paved the middle with charity, for the daughters of Jerusalem,” where another translation reads, “Below it he made a pavement of charity from the daughters of Jerusalem,” are to be understood thus. For *lithostrotus*, or *Gabbatha*, which is read in the Lord’s Passion, means “a raised slope.” Therefore “the middle,” or “pavement,” signifies the seat itself in the litter, which is as it were a slope in comparison with the height of the pillars. Thus, when Christ made himself a seat in the litter, he [Col. 0373C] paved—or levelled and laid—the parts which were between the seat and the wooden structure of the litter with charity, preparing them for sitting, as a horse is saddled when a seat is prepared on it. Christ therefore paved the seat of the litter with charity, because he remains, sits, or rests only in charity. The Lord made and arranged this litter in this way for the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, for the salvation of faithful souls. It follows:

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of his heart’s joy.”

[THO.] The mother of Christ is the Blessed Mary. She crowned him with a diadem when he assumed flesh from her, [Col. 0373D] and this on the day of his betrothal and on the day of his heart’s joy. For when he joined his divinity to our humanity in our flesh, although he endured the Passion, he rejoiced exceedingly in our redemption. But since a diadem is assumed for glory, whereas he had not glory but humiliation in the flesh, how did he receive a crown? Because we who are his members shall be crowned by this; and since he is the head, the crown of the members, because of the unity of the body, is attributed to Christ the head.

A threefold going forth is commanded to Abraham by the Lord: “Go forth,” he says, “from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” [Note: [Col. 0373] Genesis 12]: from your land, that is, from carnal pleasure; from your kindred, [Col. 0374A] that is, from unstable thought; from your father’s house, that is, from worldly manner of life. The children of Israel made this threefold departure when they went to the promised land: first from Egypt, second from the Red Sea, third from the wilderness. First, lest they should serve in the mud and brick of their flesh; second, lest they be submerged in wavering thought; third, lest they waste away in the poisonous vanity of the world. The first was difficult, for Pharaoh says: “You shall not go out” [Note: [Col. 0373] Exodus 3]. Of the second he says: “Go, sacrifice, but do not go farther away” [Note: [Col. 0373] Exodus 8]. Of the third: “Go, but leave your cattle behind” [Note: [Col. 0373] Ibid.]. Fourth, they are compelled to depart when the firstborn die. First the devil prevents us from leaving the will of the flesh. Immediately he tempts us not to go farther—that is, not to persevere. Then he seeks to make us leave behind our cattle—that is, beastly appetites—for him. [Col. 0374B] Finally God kills the firstborn—that is, thoughts—and thus we go forth. But the waves of the sea meet us—that is, the flux of worldly thoughts—which we cross with the rod of Moses, that is, discipline. These thoughts are the people Amalek, which is interpreted “licking blood”; but they perish if we first kill their king, namely Agag, which is interpreted “meditation.” Then we must depart from the wilderness of the world, where there are poisonous serpents of worldly vanity, if we look upon the serpent on the wood—that is, Christ on the cross. In order that Christ might help these departures, he too departed three times: first from heaven, second from the Virgin’s womb, third from the tomb.

Therefore, because through sin we transgress, first let us go forth, second enter in, third undertake, [Col. 0374C] fourth engage, fifth advance, sixth return. First let us go forth from the flesh, the world, and kindred; second, let us enter the field; third, undertake battle; fourth, engage while holding the enemy; fifth, advance to triumph. Thus “Abraham went, advancing and progressing toward the south” [Note: [Col. 0373] Genesis 12], and Isaac went on, advancing and growing, until he became great [Note: [Col. 0373] Genesis 26]. Sixth, let us return to our homeland, that is, to paradise with Christ. Solomon is interpreted “peacemaker.” Thus we ought to go forth so that we may behold and receive him: peaceful in the world, patient on the wood, at peace in judgment, peace itself in the kingdom.

“In the diadem,” he says. We read of three crowns of Christ: the first fleshly, [Col. 0374D] the second thorny, the third golden. Two are evident; concerning the third, the Apocalypse says: “I saw,” it says, “an angel coming down from heaven, and a golden crown upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0373] Revelation 14]. The first is of warfare, the second of insult, the third of glory. His mother crowned him with the first, his stepmother with the second, his Father with the third. In the first let us behold him so that the scourges may terrify us; in the second, so that we may endure mockery; in the third, so that rewards may draw us. Through the first he gave us consolation; through the second he teaches us contrition; through the third he invites us to blessedness.

Likewise, there are three crowns pertaining to us: the first signifies holiness, the second justice, the third glory. The first is the cutting [Col. 0375A] of the hair, which signifies perfection in us; hence of Aaron: “The crown upon his head was like the sun.” Of the second Paul says: “There is laid up for me a crown of justice” [Note: [Col. 0375] 2 Timothy 4]; of the third David says: “You have crowned him, Lord, with glory and honor” [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 8]. The first is in exile, the second will be at judgment, the third in the kingdom. The first is a sign, the second a testimony, the third a reward: a sign of grace, a testimony of warfare, a reward of victory.

“On the day of his betrothal,” he says. There is a marriage begun, a marriage perfected, and a marriage consummated: the first in betrothal, the second in union under the testimony of the Church, the third in consummation. In this order Christ joined the Church to himself. He first betrothed her, but this betrothal was made threefold, as the prophet Hosea says: 76 [Col. 0375B] “I will betroth you to myself forever; I will betroth you in justice and judgment, in mercy and compassions, and I will betroth you in faith” [Note: [Col. 0375] Hosea 2]. The first was made under circumcision, the second under the Law, the third under grace. The first through Abraham, the second through Moses, the third through Christ. The first was made “forever,” for steadfastness; the second “in justice,” because of equity, and “in judgment,” because of severity; “in mercy,” because of love, and “in compassions,” because of action; the third “in faith,” for knowledge of the Trinity.

This can also be said morally of the soul, in reverse order. First it must be betrothed in faith, so that it may believe; second in judgment, so that it may examine its sins; and in justice, so that it may punish what it has examined; in mercy, [Col. 0375C] so that God may forgive its sins; and in compassions, so that the soul itself may give alms; third, forever, so that God may preserve it in goodness. The first was made at the beginning of night, the second at midnight, the third in the day. Hence it is said, “on the day of his betrothal.” Behold the marriage announced, perfected in the Passion, consummated in the coming of the Holy Spirit.

“And on the day,” he says, “of his heart’s joy”—that is, in the Passion. For although he endured pains, he nevertheless rejoiced in our salvation. There is joy of the flesh, joy of the heart, and joy of soul and body. The first concerns temporal things, the second spiritual things, the third heavenly things. Of the first: “They rejoice when they have done evil” [Note: [Col. 0375] Proverbs 2]. Of the second: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep festival” [Note: [Col. 0375] Introit, Fourth Sunday of Lent]. Of the third: “In their land they shall possess double; everlasting joy shall be [Col. 0375D] theirs” [Note: [Col. 0375] Isaiah 61].—“There was not such great joy, in the First Book of Kings, from yesterday and the day before yesterday” [Note: [Col. 0375] 1 Kings 4]. Nor is this surprising, because God came into the camp. Therefore David, rejoicing, invites all who seek the Lord to this joy, saying: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” [Note: [Col. 0375] Psalm 104].

There are those who seek him with the Magi at the manger; there are those who seek him with Mary and Joseph in the Temple; and there are [Col. 0376A] those who seek him with the women at the tomb. The first seek with gifts; the second with tears and groans; the third with spices: with the gifts of gold, myrrh, and incense; with tears and groans in petition for reconciliation; with the spices of devotion. The first are those newly converted; the second, those who return after a fall; the third, those who sigh because they are so long delayed from the kingdom.

The first come with gifts of myrrh, incense, and gold: myrrh of satisfaction, incense of prayer, gold of wisdom and discernment. But this myrrh is threefold. The first is contrition in the heart; the second, confession by the mouth; the third, in the hand—that is, in deed. The first is bitter, the second more bitter, the third most bitter. Of the first: “I shall recall to you my years in the bitterness [Col. 0376B] of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0375] Isa. 38.]. This is the myrrh of which it is said: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall abide between my breasts” [Note: [Col. 0375] Cant. 1.]. Of the second: “I shall speak in the bitterness of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0375] Job 10.]. Hence: “His lips dripping with first myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0375] Cant. 5.]. Of the third: “You will rebuke me and revive me” [Note: [Col. 0375] Psal. 37.].—“Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” [Note: [Col. 0375] Isa. 38.]. Likewise: “My hands dripped myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0375] Cant. 5.].

By incense we have signified prayer. But that prayer may be pure, the incense must first be burned with the fire of charity, as in a censer; in the heart it must send forth smoke from tears and from confession and utterance of the mouth. It must give forth the fragrance of incense by the offering of good works. Of the first two the Apostle says: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray [Col. 0376C] also with the mind. I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” [Note: [Col. 0375] I Cor. 14.]. “With the spirit,” that is, with the breath of the mouth. Of the second, the same says: “I desire men in every place to pray, lifting up pure hands” [Note: [Col. 0375] II Tim. 2.].

Behold myrrh; behold incense; gold follows—namely, the wisdom to order one’s life. Hence: “Desirable treasure” [Note: [Col. 0375] Prov. 21.] rests in the mouth of the wise. Likewise: “From the north gold will come” [Note: [Col. 0375] Job 32.], that is, from sinners, through God’s mercy, wisdom. To the convert this gold grants three things: caution, strength, and foresight—caution against the devil’s cunning, strength against the wantonness of the flesh, and foresight for ordering one’s senses against the world’s deceit. Hence: “Wisdom conquers malice” [Note: [Col. 0375] Sap. 7.], that is, the devil’s cunning. “She reaches from the end,” that is, from the beginning of conversion, “unto the end,” the final dissolution, “mightily,” against the wantonness of the flesh, [Col. 0376D] “and orders all things sweetly” [Note: [Col. 0375] Sap. 8.], ordering one’s senses against the world’s deceit.

For the first, John saw “an angel girded at the breasts with a golden girdle” [Note: [Col. 0375] Apoc. 1.]. For the second, the prophet saw another girding his loins with refined gold [Note: [Col. 0375] Dan. 10.]. For the third, John says: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, and on his head a golden crown” [Note: [Col. 0375] Apoc. 14, 20.]. Behold the first, who seek with gifts; to them it is said: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0375] Psal. 104.]. It should be noted that those who sought [Col. 0377A] with gifts found him appeased. But since, as the poet says:

> It is no lesser virtue to preserve what has been won than to seek it,

care must be taken that, through negligence or by entangling themselves in the crowd of worldly affairs, they do not become like Mary and Joseph, who lost him in the crowd [Note: [Col. 0377] Luc. 2.]. Thus they will have to seek him again with tears and groans.

With tears, I say—three kinds of tears. The first are for their loss; the second, for the difficulty of finding him; the third, for shame. They are for the loss of him whom they have lost; for the difficulty of finding him whom they have sought for so long; and for shame because they departed from him. To the first it is said: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.” But these say: “Woe to us, because we have sinned, [Col. 0377B] because the crown has fallen from our head” [Note: [Col. 0377] Thren. 5.]; and Job says: “Our harp has been turned to mourning, and our joy into the voice of those who weep” [Note: [Col. 0377] Job 30.].

There follow tears over the difficulty of finding him. Thus she says: “Upon my bed I sought by night him whom my soul loves” [Note: [Col. 0377] Cant. 3.]. But why “by night”? Because they did not heed: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come” [Note: [Col. 0377] Isa. 60.]; yet they cry with Job: “Why do you hide your face and consider me your enemy?” [Note: [Col. 0377] Job 13.]. Here Job seems to lament when he says: “Who will grant that I might be as in former months, according to the days when God was with me, when I washed my feet with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil, when God was secretly in my tent?” [Note: [Col. 0377] Job 29.].

But they adopt sound counsel, saying: “I will rise and go about [Col. 0377C] the city; through streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves” [Note: [Col. 0377] Cant. 3.]. By the squares, that is, among the way of life of those who live in the world; by the streets, that is, by the narrow way of religious persons. But he is not found in the squares, where sensual people are, where the wise glory in doing evil, and where philosophers rule over others and are lovers of the world. Hence Job says: “Wisdom is drawn out of hidden places; it is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” [Note: [Col. 0377] Job 28.]—behold the sensual; “the deep says, ‘It is not in me’” [Note: [Col. 0377] Ibid.]—behold the wise and philosophers; “and the sea says, ‘It is not with me’” [Note: [Col. 0377] Ibid.]—behold the lovers of the world. But it is found in the street, namely, in the narrow way of religious persons.

A religious life exists if there is purity in the heart, truth in the mouth, and sincerity in deed: [Col. 0377D] purity, that one may think what is holy; truth, that one may speak what is true; sincerity, that one may do what is just. Of the first: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he himself will sustain you” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psal. 54.]. Of the second: “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue” [Note: [Col. 0377] Cant. 3.]. Of the third: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works” [Note: [Col. 0377] Matth. 5.]. Thus Mary and Joseph found Jesus not among the crowd of lovers of the world, but in the Temple among the doctors of the Law [Note: [Col. 0377] Luc. 2.].

The third kind is groaning, even after he has been [Col. 0378A] found, out of shame; so that it may be said: “All day my shame is before me” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psal. 43.]. Thus the Lord, having compassion on Peter’s shame because he had denied him, called him by name, saying: “Tell his disciples and Peter: he will go before you into Galilee” [Note: [Col. 0377] Marc. 16.]. Thus Job says, as if from shame: “By the hearing of the ear I heard you, but now my eye sees you; and therefore I reproach myself and do penance in ashes and dust” [Note: [Col. 0377] Job 42.].—“A little while after I had passed by,” she says, “I found him whom my soul loves” [Note: [Col. 0377] Cant. 3.].

For first she went, second she passed, third she passed beyond. She went, groaning for the loss of him lost; she passed, weeping for the difficulty of finding him; she passed beyond, crying from shame before the face of him found. To these it is said: “Seek the Lord, and be strengthened” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psal. 104.]. Hence the bride says: “I held [Col. 0378B] him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house” [Note: [Col. 0377] Cant. 3.]. Thus seek his face always with the groaning women, because they are delayed from the kingdom.

There are four faces of the Lord, as it was said: “Each had four faces, and each four wings” [Note: [Col. 0377] Ezech. 1.]. The first is that of human birth; the second, of worldly affliction; the third, of glorified humanity; the fourth, of divine majesty. In the first, the bridegroom was “beautiful in form above the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psal. 44.]; in the second: “We saw him as leprous, and struck by God, and humbled” [Note: [Col. 0377] Isa. 53.]; in the third: “He ascended into heaven, beautiful in his robe” [Note: [Col. 0377] Isa. 63.]; in the fourth, “angels desire to look” [Note: [Col. 0377] I Petr. 1. Sap. 7.], because “he is the brightness of eternal light and a spotless mirror” [Note: [Col. 0377] Sap. 7.].

In the first he is to be sought [Col. 0378C] by conforming ourselves to Christ’s humanity; in the second, by imitating his Passion; in the third, having put off the old man, we are to hold fast to newness of life; in the fourth, if we continually sigh to behold God’s majesty. Of the first: “Show your face, and we shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psal. 79.]. This is the face of Joseph, of whom it is said: “Joseph was fair of face and beautiful in appearance” [Note: [Col. 0377] Gen. 39.].
