Christ taught us to seek this face when he said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” [Note: [Col. 0377] Matth. 11.].

Of the second it is said: “They spat in his face and struck him with blows” [Note: [Col. 0377] Matth. 26.]. This was the face of David, which he changed before King Achish, while saliva ran down his beard [Note: [Col. 0377] I Reg. 21.]. Jesus invited us to imitate this when he said: “Whoever wishes to come [Col. 0378D] after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” [Note: [Col. 0377] Matth. 16.].

Of the third, it was said at the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor: “His face was like the sun, and his garments white as snow” [Note: [Col. 0377] Matth. 17.]; likewise: “His face was set as he went to Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0377] Luc. 9.]. This was the face of Moses, of whom it was said: The face of Moses became radiant while the Lord looked upon him [Note: [Col. 0377] Exod. 34.]. For in the resurrection the Lord looked upon Christ, so that this face might be sought. The Apostle invites us thus: “Putting off, according to [Col. 0379A] your former manner of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desire of error, put on the new man” [Note: [Col. 0379] Ephes. 4.], “who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him” [Note: [Col. 0379] Coloss. 3.]. For “as Jesus rose through the glory of the Father, so may we walk in newness of life” [Note: [Col. 0379] Rom. 6.].

The fourth face is that of divine majesty, of which it is said: “You shall see his face in a cloud” [Note: [Col. 0379] Job 33.]. Likewise: “John saw an angel descending from heaven, and his face was like the sun” [Note: [Col. 0379] Apoc. 18, 20.]. For God is “the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” [Note: [Col. 0379] Joan. 1.]. The Apostle proclaims it to us thus: “Seek the things that are above; set your minds on the things that are above, not on those below” [Note: [Col. 0379] Col. 3.].

Behold, “those four faces belonged to one”; it follows: “and [Col. 0379B] four wings to one,” of which it continues: “Two wings of each were joined together, and two covered their bodies” [Note: [Col. 0379] Ezech. 1.], namely fear and repentance, because fear of hell and the affliction of repentance protect bodies from sins. The two wings joined to the spirit are hope and love. The first two are those of a hen; the other two, those of an eagle. The first two shade from temptations; the other two lift upward. Of the first: “He shall overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you shall hope” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psal. 90.]; hence: “How often have I wished to gather your children?” [Note: [Col. 0379] Matth. 23.]. Of the others: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and be at rest?” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psal. 54.]. Likewise: “As an eagle provokes her young to fly, hovering above them” [Note: [Col. 0379] Deut. 32.].

You seek to see his face, and he seeks yours. Hence: “Show me your face” [Note: [Col. 0379] Exod. 33.]. This face is conscience variously disposed. For as there are four faces of God, so there are four faces of the bride. The first corresponds to Christ’s first face: as Christ was born without sin, so our conscience should strive to be cleansed from every defilement of sin. Hence Job: “If you remove the iniquity that is in your hand” [Note: [Col. 0379] Job 11.], etc.

The second corresponds to the second: sharing the suffering Christ’s pain with compassion. Hence: “Our face has swollen with weeping” [Note: [Col. 0379] Job 16.]. The third corresponds to Christ’s third face, so that by cleaving to him in newness, our conscience may glory. Therefore each of them walked before its own face, not falling backward to the ground like the guards of the tomb. The fourth face corresponds to the fourth. Hence, of [Col. 0379D] the same living creatures [Note: [Col. 0379] Ezech. 1.]: “Their faces and their wings were stretched upward,” looking toward God. To stand before him will be tranquility; to behold him, brightness; to desire him, happiness; to see him, incomparable delight. To live with him will be eternity.

Go forth, daughters of Jerusalem.

[CARD.] And this is the word of the Lady to the young women. As though she said: Since the litter was made on account of the daughters of Jerusalem, for the display of Solomon, therefore, O daughters of Jerusalem, go forth to see, and behold King Solomon, who made a litter [Col. 0380A] in a diadem, in the honor of pure flesh. His mother, the Virgin, crowned him with it and prepared him for the crown of victory, by supplying him from her own flesh with pure flesh in which he would conquer the devil. This, I say, she did on the day of his betrothal—that is, on the day of his Incarnation, when in the Virgin’s womb the nuptials of the divine and human natures, or of Christ and the Church, took place—and on the day of the joy of his heart.

For that day on which Christ became man with human beings was a day of joy to him; for he himself says through Solomon: “My delights are with the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0379] Prov. 8.]. This verse can also be expounded of Mother Synagogue, and of the day on which she crowned Christ with a crown of thorns—the day on which the nuptials of Christ and the Church were ratified. That day was for Christ a day [Col. 0380B] of joy in his heart; for though he suffered in the flesh, he nevertheless rejoiced in his heart for the redemption of the human race. It follows:

## CHAPTER IV. How beautiful you are, my beloved; how beautiful and lovely you are! Your eyes are doves’ eyes, apart from that which is hidden within.

[THO.] Since we explained this above, we do not repeat it. But because “apart from that which is hidden within” has been added, let us see how it is joined to what precedes. She is beautiful because she disdains to embrace temporal things; and if anything in this world sometimes pleases her, she nevertheless abhors following her own desires. But far more beautiful and honorable is the fact that she strives to preserve the desire of her heart unblemished, because she keeps within her mind the brightness of eternal blessedness.

“Drink water from your own cistern, and distribute your waters in the streets,” says Solomon [Note: [Col. 0379] Prov. 5.]. Here the twofold beauty of the soul is indicated: the first is brightness; the second, charity. The first pertains to the contemplation of heavenly things; the second, to concern for outward things. The first is water that falls from heaven; the second springs from the ground, because its concern is directed outward. For outwardly it is occupied with the neighbor’s salvation, its own benefit, and God’s honor. Therefore, with reference to this latter, he repeats for the third time: “Behold, how beautiful you are, my beloved; behold, how beautiful and lovely!” This is not done elsewhere in this Song; and it is “apart from that which is hidden within,” that is, apart from that beauty called brightness.

Therefore outwardly she is [Col. 0380D] beautiful in three things: in speech, in work, and in the moderation of discipline. There are four ways in which she is beautiful in speech: namely, in confession, prayer, preaching, and the praise of God. Of these David says: “Confess to the Lord and call upon his name; proclaim his works among the nations. Sing to him and chant psalms to him; recount all his wonders” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psal. 104.].

She is also beautiful in the work of repentance, the work of mercy, and the work of piety. Of the first: “Do penance” [Note: [Col. 0379] Matth. 3.]; of the second: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” [Note: [Col. 0379] Luc. 11.]; of the third: “Honor the Lord from your substance” [Note: [Col. 0379] Prov. 3.]. She is likewise beautiful in the moderation of discipline, [Col. 0381A] whence Job says: “Whenever I laughed at them, they did not believe it, and the light of my countenance did not fall to the ground” [Note: [Col. 0381] Job 29.].

This beauty is apart from that which is hidden within. Some, however, conceal themselves badly, like the servant who hid his lord’s money in a napkin [Note: [Col. 0381] Luc. 19.]. Others conceal themselves well, and this for three reasons. The first who conceals fears being wounded by the arrow that flies by day [Note: [Col. 0381] Psal. 90.]; the second fears to give what is holy to dogs and to scatter pearls before swine [Note: [Col. 0381] Matth. 7.], lest he see them trampled underfoot; the third sees ineffable things which it is not permitted a human being to speak [Note: [Col. 0381] II Cor. 12.]. The first does so because of weakness; the second because of the value of the thing; the third because of incomprehensibility. The first fears lest vanity steal something from him; the second, lest the thing be made cheaper because of unclean vessels; the third fears to presume upon great things lest he fail.

To the first it is said: “Do not consent if sinners entice you” [Note: [Col. 0381] Prov. 1.]. The second says: “Since you have made yourselves unworthy of the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0381] Act. 13.]. The third says: “It is good to conceal the secret of a king” [Note: [Col. 0381] Tob. 12.]. The first is careful to remove the foreskin from his fruits; the second hesitates to put new wine into old wineskins; the third ascends Mount Sinai alone to the Lord.

Of the first, who is careful to remove the foreskin, the Law says: “When you enter the land which the Lord will give you, and plant fruit trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins. In the fourth year you shall consecrate them for praise to the Lord. In the fifth year you shall eat of them” [Note: [Col. 0381] Lev. 19.]. The land is our heart. [Col. 0381C] In the first year we enter the land when we dispose our heart to act rightly. In the second year we plant fruit trees, when we establish virtues in the heart; from these later we gather the fruits of works. In the third year we remove foreskins, when we remove from our works the excrescences of vainglory. In the fourth year we consecrate them to the Lord for praise, when we give him thanks for the goods gathered. In the fifth year we eat of them, when we take delight in them in our conscience.

The second fears to put new wine into old wineskins [Note: [Col. 0381] Luc. 5.], that is, to disclose the savor of higher things to sinners, who are unclean vessels. For there are vessels of wrath; there are old wineskins, that is, persons grown old in malice. To these the Apostle says: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new [Col. 0381D] lump, as you are unleavened” [Note: [Col. 0381] I Cor. 5.]. These are unworthy. There are also earthen and wooden vessels. The earthen are the carnal; the wooden, those excessively intent upon temporal things. These are excluded from sacrifices, because they need lesser things. Hence the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, as to carnal persons” [Note: [Col. 0381] II Cor. 3.].

There are also bronze vessels: namely, those troubled only by venial sins. Of the first it is said that they should be broken, namely through repentance, because they are for dishonor. But the bronze vessel will be scoured through some light satisfaction, and thus will be fit for use in sacrifices [Col. 0382A]. There are also silver vessels: namely, the innocent, who are admitted because they are for honor. And there are golden vessels: namely, those perfect in wisdom. Of them the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” [Note: [Col. 0381] I Cor. 2.].—“Not only in a great house are there gold and silver vessels, but also wooden and earthen ones” [Note: [Col. 0381] II Tim. 2.].

The third ascends Mount Sinai alone to the Lord, having his heart raised to God. For his heart is land raised toward God; hence in the Law: “That land is not like the land of Egypt,” because it is not a dark land in which waters are led for irrigation, in the manner of a garden—that is, from the earth, which are carnal desires—but “it is mountainous,” because raised upwards, and level, that is, without the thorns of vices, “awaiting rain from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0381] Deut. 11.], namely the voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance [Note: [Col. 0381] Psal. 67.], that is, devotion and grace. “And the Lord visits it always” with the sweetness of heavenly things; “and his eyes are upon it from the beginning of the year to its end” [Note: [Col. 0381] Deut. 11.], because “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” [Note: [Col. 0381] Psal. 33.], that he may delight in them, while they look simply upon him. Thus it follows: Your eyes are doves’ eyes, etc.

The prophet foretold this visitation of the Lord thus: “The Lord will bring a scorching wind rising from the desert; it will dry up the veins of death and lay waste its fountain, and it will plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel” [Note: [Col. 0381] Ose. 13.]. How necessary this visitation was, to calm the troubled world! For Daniel saw [Note: [Col. 0381] Cap. 7.] four winds of heaven fighting upon the great sea. The first is the whirlwind wind; the second, the shaking wind; the third, the dew wind; the fourth, the scorching wind. The first is that of fault, punishment, and ignorance in flight; the second rushes in from sin; the third is Christ’s Incarnation; the fourth is the love and activity of the incarnate Word. The first infects the human race; under the second the faint-hearted fail; in the third the strong advance; the fourth restores what has been scattered.

The first is the north wind from the north, that is, far from rest; the second, the west wind from the west, that is, fierce with zeal; the third, the east wind from the east, from that which is good and, as it were, dewily refreshing what is burned; the fourth, from the south, namely the south wind laying low the north wind’s burning. The first brings a whirlwind, cloud, and fire. Hence: “A whirlwind wind came from the north, and a great cloud, and enveloping fire” [Note: [Col. 0381] Ezech. 1.]. The whirlwind is the confusion of sin; the cloud, the darkening of understanding; the fire, the affliction of calamity. Through the first, man departed from God; through the second, he did not understand God; through the third, he languishes on earth.

Of the first: “They were confounded because God despised them” [Note: [Col. 0381] Psal. 52.].—“He has forsaken,” he says, “God his maker, and has departed from God his savior” [Note: [Col. 0381] Deut. 32.]. Wretched Adam, you have forsaken the God who begot you and have forgotten God your creator. Through the second: “They forgot the Lord who saved them” [Note: [Col. 0381] Psal. 105.].—“For when man [Col. 0383A] was in honor, he did not understand; he became like horse and mule, which have no understanding” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psal. 48.]. And therefore, “they did not know or understand; they walk in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psal. 81.]. Thus they have fallen into the third, because “man is born for labor and the bird for flying” [Note: [Col. 0383] Job. 5.]. Hence: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” [Note: [Col. 0383] Gen. 3.]. Thus David cries: “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psal. 114.].

But that God might aid us, from its midst came something like the appearance of electrum, that is, from the midst of the fire: namely, Christ in divinity and humanity. He is the turning, fiery sword before the gates of paradise [Note: [Col. 0383] Gen. 3.]; these are the veins of death through which death came. The shaking wind follows, namely the west wind fierce with zeal. Thus in Job: “A wind came from the region of the desert and struck the four [Col. 0383B] corners of the house, which fell and crushed Job’s children” [Note: [Col. 0383] Job 1.].

The Church, which is our house, has four corners. The first is advancing justice; the second, instructing truth; the third, inflaming charity; the fourth, restraining discipline. Through the first one ascends to heaven; through the second one knows the reward; through the third one loves what one knows; through the fourth one preserves the way. Of the first: “Teach me the way of your justifications, and direct me in the way of justice” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psal. 118.]. Of it: “Each of them walked before its own face” [Note: [Col. 0383] Ezech. 1.]. Of the second: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? He who,” he says, “speaks truth in his heart, who has not worked deceit with his tongue” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psal. 14.]; and: “I am the way, [Col. 0383C] the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0383] Joan. 14.]. Of the third it is said: “God is charity, and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” [Note: [Col. 0383] I Joan. 4.]. We dwell in this if we live “rooted and grounded in charity” [Note: [Col. 0383] Ephes. 3.]. Of the fourth: “My son, hear the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother, that grace may be added to your head” [Note: [Col. 0383] Prov. 1.].

Behold the four-cornered house. Hear the four corners: “He walks in justices”—behold the first. “And speaks truth”—behold the second. “He casts away avarice and calumny, and shakes his hands free from every gift”—behold the third. “He stops his ears lest he hear bloodshed, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil” [Note: [Col. 0383] Isa. 33.]—behold the fourth. The wind shakes the first corner through the vice of lukewarmness; the second through falsehood; the third through avarice and hatred; [Col. 0383D] the fourth through the wandering of the senses. Of lukewarmness it is said to the angel of Laodicea: “Because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you from my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0383] Apoc. 3.]. Hear the corner of truth shaken: “He did not stand in the truth” [Note: [Col. 0383] Joan. 8.]; and: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psal. 5.]. The third is shaken when charity departs; hence in the Apocalypse: “I have something against you, because you have forsaken your first charity” [Note: [Col. 0383] Apoc. 2.]. The fourth corner is shaken when discipline is scattered; hence Solomon: “They will rise in the morning and will not find me, because they have hated discipline” [Note: [Col. 0383] Prov. 1.].

Behold, from [Col. 0384A] the house of the righteous there came to be the furnace of Babylon. But the angel comes and makes the middle of the furnace like a standing wind of dew. Therefore Isaiah says: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth open and bring forth the Savior” [Note: [Col. 0383] Isa. 45.]. Christ is dew from heaven, rain from the cloud, and a shoot from the earth: dew licking, rain pouring in, shoot coming forth. Dew from heaven, that is, coming from the sweet-flowing serenity of the Father; rain from the cloud, pouring into the Virgin with serene fruitfulness; the shoot coming forth from the Virgin’s bridal chamber, being born in assumed humanity.

But note: heaven distills dew, the cloud rains, and the earth brings forth. Heaven brings forth the reconciler, the cloud the Just One, the earth the Savior. Heaven is the seat of majesty; the cloud, the obscurity of prophetic proclamation; the earth, the Virgin’s womb. Of the reconciler it is said: [Col. 0384B] “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who became the propitiation for our sins” [Note: [Col. 0383] I Joan. 2.]. Of the Just One: “A nation shall see your Just One,” etc. Of the Savior: “We await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0383] Philipp. 3.].

By the first we are formed; by the second conformed; through the third re-formed. We are formed in God’s image; conformed to the image of Christ crucified; we shall be re-formed to the image of Christ glorified. Of the first: “God formed man in his own image and likeness” [Note: [Col. 0383] Gen 1.]; of the second: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be made conformable to the image of his Son” [Note: [Col. 0383] Rom. 8.]; of the third: “He will reform the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0383] Phil. 3.].

[Col. 0384C] These are the three men of whom Samuel spoke to Saul: “When you come to the oak of Tabor, you will find three men: one carrying three kids, another three loaves of bread, and the third a flask of wine” [Note: [Col. 0383] I Reg. 33.]. The first “will dry up the veins of death”; the second “will lay waste its fountain”; the third “will plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel” [Note: [Col. 0383] Ose. 13.]. Tabor means “coming light,” namely Christ, to whose oak we come when we embrace with him those things which he accomplished on the cross.

Therefore the first kid heals original sin; the second, actual sin; the third, temporal misery. These indeed are the three veins of death. The first is sacrificed at the announcement of Samson; the second is slain with the Paschal lamb; the third is alleged by the brother of the prodigal son never to have been received from his father. Of the first Manoah says to [Col. 0384D] the angel: “Wait here until I make for you a kid from the goats” [Note: [Col. 0383] Judic. 13.]. Samson means “their sun,” that is, Christ, who was born in the likeness of sinful flesh [Note: [Col. 0383] Rom. 8.] and thus cleansed us from original sin. Of the second it is said: “According to which rite you shall also take a kid” [Note: [Col. 0383] Exod. 12.]. For the innocent one was slain as though guilty, and thus freed the human race from temporal misery. Of the second it is said: “You never gave me a kid, that I might feast with my friends” [Note: [Col. 0383] Luc. 15]. For he himself associated with sinners in order to draw them from actual sin, and bestowed upon them the feast of teaching.

[Col. 0385A] Behold, thus the first, reconciling us to the Father, dried up the veins of death. The second brings three loaves, through which he will lay waste the fountain of death; for this is refreshment to man and desolation to the devil.

The first bread is that of the Eucharist; the second, that of teaching; the third, that of angelic refreshment. The first gives life; the second gives strength; the third gives blessedness. The first gives life from sin; the second gives strength in goodness; the third gives blessedness in the kingdom. Of the first: “The bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” [Note: [Col. 0385] Joan. 6.]. And: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven, and I give life to the world” [Note: [Col. 0385] Ibid.]. Of the second: “Bread strengthens the heart of man” [Note: [Col. 0385] Psal. 103.]. In the strength of this bread Elijah went as far as Mount Horeb, the mountain of God [Note: [Col. 0385] III Reg. 19.]. Of the third: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0385] Luc. 14.]. Of these it is said: “Friend, lend me three loaves” [Note: [Col. 0385] Luc. 11.]; and: “You who inhabit the land of the south, [Col. 0385B] meet the fugitive with bread” [Note: [Col. 0385] Isa. 21.].

The third gives wine of joy, by which he will plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel [Note: [Col. 0385] Ose. 13.], because in the joy of Christ’s resurrection the righteous who were held in hell returned from misery. But this misery is threefold. The first purifies; the second intoxicates; the third gladdens. The first purifies from the filth of sin; the second intoxicates with love of God; the third gladdens with the joy of heaven. The first the Samaritan pours upon the man wounded by robbers; with the second Noah was intoxicated and lay uncovered in his tent; the third Melchizedek offered to Abraham returning from battle. Of the first: “He will wash his robe in wine and his mantle in the blood of grapes” [Note: [Col. 0385] Gen. 49.]. Of the second: “The king brought me into the wine cellar” [Note: [Col. 0385] Cant. 2.]; and: [Col. 0385C] “Eat, friends, and be intoxicated, beloved ones” [Note: [Col. 0385] Cant. 5.]. Of the third: “That you may bring bread out of the earth, and wine may gladden the heart of man” [Note: [Col. 0385] Psal. 103.].

The first grants us honorableness; the second, fragrance; the third, honor: the honorableness of religious life, the fragrance of a life of good repute, and the honor of a glorious life. Concerning the first the Apostle says: “Let us live soberly, justly, and piously in this age” [Note: [Col. 0385] Tit. 2.]. And likewise: “As in the day, let us walk honorably” [Note: [Col. 0385] Rom 13.]. Of the second, the same says: “Let us look upon Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who endured the cross for the joy set before him” [Note: [Col. 0385] Hebr. 12.], so that we may say: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God” [Note: [Col. 0385] II Cor. 2.]. Of the third: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him” [Note: [Col. 0385] Joan. 12.]. Of these three Wisdom says: “I, like a vine, brought forth the sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers are the fruits [Col. 0385D] of honor and honorableness” [Note: [Col. 0385] Eccli. 24.].

This is the dew wind, namely the east wind, beneficially dew-refreshing what has been burned. The scorching wind follows, namely the south wind, the incarnate Word. For Christ burned us with his charity. First, he destroyed the oldness of sin; second, he made the garden of the heart fruitful with the fruit of virtues; third, he freed us from the torrent of our mortality. This is the south wind which, with reference to the first, is said to lay low the north wind’s burning. Hence in Job: “Does the hawk take wing, spreading its wings to the south?” [Note: [Col. 0385] Job 39.]. With reference to the second it is said: The south wind [Col. 0386A] increases the seeds of the earth. Hence: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and its spices shall flow” [Note: [Col. 0385] Cant. 4.]. With reference to the third it is said: The south wind tempers breezes. Hence: “Turn back, O Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south” [Note: [Col. 0385] Psal 125.]. May you transfer from the torrent of this mortality the vessels—that is, the saints—to the kingdom of blessedness. Amen.

How beautiful you are, my beloved, how beautiful you are!

[CARD.] In this chapter the Son dwells upon the praises of his mother and commends her by manifold praise. He says, therefore: How beautiful you are, my beloved, in those virtues which crown the soul; how beautiful you are also in those things which adorn the soul. Afterwards he praises her part by part, saying:

Your eyes are doves’ eyes; your hair is like a flock of goats which have climbed Mount Gilead.

[Col. 0386B] [THO.] Just as preachers are understood by the eyes, because they show the way to others, so the eyes are signified by the hair, because they too contribute ornament to the Church. The bride’s hair is rightly compared to goats, because, while attending to the precepts of the Law, they contemplate heavenly things: they are clean animals and feed in high places. Gilead, moreover, is interpreted “heap of testimony,” by which we understand the multitude of martyrs who, by their suffering, bore witness to Christ. This flock therefore ascends from Mount Gilead, because they raise themselves toward eternal things all the more as they know that the holy martyrs bore witness more bravely.

Our head is the soul; the hairs are the thoughts by which the head is adorned. The goat has three qualities [Col. 0386C] on account of which it is compared to hair: it stinks in steep places, climbs in search of pasture, and sees keenly. These correspond to the three kinds of thoughts. For there are thoughts of temporal things, of spiritual things, and of heavenly things. The first are signified by its smell, the second by the steep height, the third by keen sight. Heavenly thoughts are ruined by pride; spiritual thoughts are stained by pleasure; temporal thoughts are darkened by dust. Thus there are five heavenly thoughts, leading to occasion of destruction; spiritual thoughts, to occasion of falling away; temporal thoughts, to occasion of advancement: destruction in Gehenna, falling away from grace, advancement in life.

The first hairs are Absalom’s, through which he perished [Note: [Col. 0385] 2 Kings 18.]. The second are Samson’s, which he lost through pleasure [Note: [Col. 0385] Judges 16.]; the third, Joseph’s, which he cut when he came out of prison [Note: [Col. 0385] Genesis 41.], because [Col. 0386D] perhaps they had been darkened by the dust of the prison. “Which ascend,” he says, “from Gilead.” Some ascend Mount Gilboa, which is interpreted “slippery,” and there proud persons die, like Absalom. He had precious hair, namely thoughts of heavenly things; but because he became proud on account of them, he perished. He raised the hairs of pride on high and hung in the oak of obstinacy—for an oak is hard. Joab, that is, the devil, came and pierced his heart with three spears: first, he despises his neighbour; second, he exalts [Col. 0387A] himself; third, he forgets God.

Samson fell away from the grace of spiritual thoughts while he delighted in lying in Delilah’s lap [Note: [Col. 0387] Judges 16.]. For the Philistines—that is, the devils—shaved off the seven locks of his head, that is, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Joseph, however, though in prison he brushed the light dust from the hairs by thinking of temporal matters, shaved his head when he went out; and thus, coming to God’s service, he emptied himself of those thoughts, and so advanced.

Some descend from Mount Gilead, which is called “heap of testimony,” like Joseph. Some descend, while others ascend Mount Gilboa. Hear of the righteous ascent: “Gilead is mine,” that is, heaping up his sins in confession; “and Manasseh is mine” [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 59.], namely, that which gives concupiscences to oblivion, [Col. 0387B] because Manasseh means “forgetfulness”; “and Ephraim is the strength of my head.” Ephraim means “sanctification.” For after forgetfulness one rightly ascends to the fruit of virtues. “Judah,” he says, “is my king” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ibid.], because confession is what Judah signifies; it rules us, as necessary in all things.

Hear of the descent from Gilgal: “They rise up to the heavens” through contemplation, while they possess grace; when that is lost, “they go down even to the depths,” because they pass from brightness into forgetfulness of God. And how? I shall explain. “Their soul languished in evils” [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 106.], in the poisonous corruption of wickedness. “They were troubled” by the confusion of abundant vices, “and they reeled like a drunken man” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ibid.], holding no certainty of the way, that is, of discipline. “And all their wisdom was swallowed up” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ibid.], because the heavenly savour is exchanged for the wisdom [Col. 0387C] of the flesh. Behold, these fall into decline; but “they cried to the Lord in their tribulation, and he delivered them from their necessities” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ibid.].

Hear how they ascend Mount Gilboa: “I will ascend,” says Satan, “above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0387] Isaiah 14.]. But by so ascending he came to eternal destruction.

Yet it must not be passed over that Laban, who means “whitening,” that is, the world, overtook Jacob, that is, the supplanting of vices, on this mountain. But since he found nothing of his own with him, they made a covenant with one another that neither would cross over to the other; and as testimony to their agreement they set up a heap of stones, with one name accepted by both. This stone is Christ [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 Corinthians 10.], but many stones are said to have been laid there because there are many matters in which we have Christ’s testimony.

[Col. 0387D] For Christ ascended three mountains, and thus gave us a threefold testimony: first, concerning contempt for worldly things; second, concerning the glory of bodies rising again; third, concerning the glory of angels. He ascended the mountain from which the devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world [Note: [Col. 0387] Matthew 4.], which he despised. Second, he ascended Mount Tabor [Note: [Col. 0387] Matthew 17.], interpreted “coming light,” and there was transfigured before his disciples, showing the future glory of the resurrection. Third, from the Mount of Olives [Col. 0388A] he ascended to the Father [Note: [Col. 0387] Acts 1.], because through love we are to ascend; there his face shone like the sun.

For he has four faces, whence it is said: “Four faces to each one, and four wings to each one” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ezekiel 1.]. The first is that of human birth; the second, of worldly calamity; the third, of glorified humanity; the fourth, of divine majesty. In the first he was “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 44]; in the second, “we saw him as leprous, struck by God, and humbled” [Note: [Col. 0387] Isaiah 53]; in the third, “he ascended into heaven, beautiful in his robe” [Note: [Col. 0387] Isaiah 63]; in the fourth, “the angels desire to look” [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 Peter 1], because “he is the splendour of eternal light and a spotless mirror” [Note: [Col. 0387] Wisdom 7].

In the first, he must be sought by conforming ourselves to Christ’s humility; in the second, by imitating his Passion; in the third, after putting off the old man, let us hold fast [Col. 0388B] to newness of life; in the fourth, if we continually long to see the heavenly majesty. Of the first: “Show your face, and we shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0387] Psalm 79]. This is Joseph’s face, whence “Joseph was beautiful in face and handsome in appearance” [Note: [Col. 0387] Genesis 39]. Christ taught us to seek this face as follows: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” [Note: [Col. 0387] Matthew 11].

Of the second it is said: “They spat upon his face” [Note: [Col. 0387] Mark 15]. This was David’s face, which he altered before Achish the king [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 Kings 21]. Of the third: “He was transfigured on Mount Tabor; his face was like the sun” [Note: [Col. 0387] Matthew 17]. Likewise: “His face was set as he went to Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0387] Luke 9]. This was Moses’ face. Moses’ face became splendid when the Lord looked upon him. Of the fourth Elihu says: “You shall see his face in joy” [Note: [Col. 0387] Job 33]. For the sake of this John saw [Col. 0388C] “an angel descending from heaven, and his face was like the sun” [Note: [Col. 0387] Revelation 18, 20].

And just as the bridegroom has four faces, so the bride has four faces, that is, four dispositions of conscience. The first corresponds to Christ’s first, so that we may be humbled with him. Of this Job says: “If you put away the iniquity that is in your hand, etc., then you will be able to lift up your face without stain” [Note: [Col. 0387] Job 11]. The second corresponds to the second, that we may sympathize in grief with Christ who suffers; whence: “My face was swollen from weeping” [Note: [Col. 0387] Job 16]. The third corresponds to the third: if, cleaving to Christ glorified, we walk in newness of life [Note: [Col. 0387] Romans 6] and our conscience glories in him, and, following him, we do not look back. Thus it is said of the living creatures: “Each one walked before its own face” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ezekiel 1]. The fourth corresponds to the fourth if we desire to see God’s [Col. 0388D] face in the kingdom; thus it is said of the same beings: “Their faces and their wings were stretched upward” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ibid.].

Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing.

[THO.] Just as the more fragile people still given to the Church are signified by the hair, so the more perfect persons fit to govern the Church are signified by the teeth: the former excel in number, the latter in strength. The latter inwardly nourish with the word; the former adorn the Church with good works [Col. 0389A]. Peter was a tooth when he was told: “Rise, kill, and eat” [Note: [Col. 0389] Acts 10]. They were also called eyes above, because they see the Church’s secrets before others; they are teeth because they rebuke the wicked with the word of truth and bring them back to the members of the holy Church; they are teeth because they prepare the bread of doctrine for the weaker.

These teeth are compared to a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing, because they have been cleansed at the font of baptism and stripped by the renunciation of their possessions. There are teeth of serpents and teeth of sheep. The former bite poisonously in order to kill; the latter press gently in order to give life. Of the former it is said in the Apocalypse that the dragon John saw had three rows of teeth in its mouth [Note: [Col. 0389] Revelation 12]. For teeth are ordinarily distinguished thus: some are biting teeth, others canine teeth, others jaw-teeth [Col. 0389B] or molars. The first bite, the second tear, the third chew the cud. They bite by word, tear by deed, and chew by hatred.

They bite by blasphemy, insult, and harsh rebuke; they tear by detraction; they chew by devising harm. [79] They bite in order to confound; they tear in order to diminish their goods; they chew in order to seek an opportunity for injury—so that they may confound them and thus deprive them of reason; diminish their goods, so that they may be held cheap; and seek an opportunity, so that they may be wholly destroyed. The Jews used these teeth against Stephen when they gnashed their teeth at him. “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” [Note: [Col. 0389] Psalm 56]. They also used them against Christ and bit him when they said: “You have a demon” [Note: [Col. 0389] John 7]. They tore him when they said: “This man is not [Col. 0389C] from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0389] John 9]. They chewed when the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council, saying: “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs” [Note: [Col. 0389] John 11].

Of the first the Apostle says: “If you bite and devour one another, beware lest you be consumed by one another” [Note: [Col. 0389] Galatians 5]. Of the others Job says: “I broke,” he says, “the molars of the wicked man, and plucked the prey from his teeth” [Note: [Col. 0389] Job 29].

The teeth of sheep likewise bite, tear, and chew the cud. They bite by rebuke, tear by threatening, and chew by instruction: by rebuking vices, threatening the punishments of hell, and teaching heavenly blessedness. These are the teeth of the ass’s jawbone [Note: [Col. 0389] Judges 5], by which Samson—whose name means “their sun,” that is, Christ, who is the Sun of righteousness—[Col. 0389D] slew the Philistines, whose name means “double ruin,” or “tormenting by drink”: namely, the demons. These teeth, that is, teachers, are like sheep that have come up from the washing, because first they washed themselves and then preached to others.

This washing is accomplished in seven ways. Sins are washed away by baptism, repentance, the Eucharist, martyrdom, giving alms, converting a sinner, and forgiving what has been committed against oneself. There are also molar teeth: the interior senses, by which we chew the cud—that is, distinguish our actions and conduct—namely [Col. 0390A] what is good, what evil, what true or false, what advantageous or disadvantageous. Concerning these we are instructed in Leviticus about acceptable burnt offerings: “After the skin has been removed,” that is, without glorying in its outward conversion, “they shall cut the limbs into pieces,” that is, discern them; “they shall put on the fire” of charity, “after the wood has been arranged upon the pile,” that is, holy thoughts which, like wood, feed the fire of love; “they shall arrange the limbs that have been cut upon it” [Note: [Col. 0389] Leviticus 1], that is, distinct works among charitable thoughts. Jeremiah says of these: “He broke my teeth by number” [Note: [Col. 0389] Lamentations 3]. It is also said of them that Moses did not lose his teeth [Note: [Col. 0389] Deuteronomy 34], because he always examined his own actions.

Hear the teeth that chew the cud. They turn over within themselves their own sins and those of others, past, [Col. 0390B] present, and future, so that they may make satisfaction for the past, free themselves from the present, and guard against the future. In this, circumspection ought to come first, reason to follow, and deliberation to come after. Circumspection sets the matter before one; reason makes a judgment; deliberation adds counsel. To circumspection it is said: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” [Note: [Col. 0389] 1 Corinthians 11]. To deliberation it is said: “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” [Note: [Col. 0389] Ecclesiasticus 32].

Circumspection answers to these words: “I will recall to you all my years in the bitterness of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0389] Isaiah 38]. Reason: “I have done judgment and justice” [Note: [Col. 0389] Psalm 118]. Deliberation: “What shall I return to the Lord for all that he has returned to me?” [Note: [Col. 0389] Psalm 115]. These teeth, chewing the cud both for themselves and others, are like a flock of shorn sheep which lay down their fleeces in shearing, and which [Col. 0390C] likewise lay aside their former way of life, as shorn sheep lay aside their fleece.

It should be noted that these teeth are preachers for the Church. First they are shorn, second they are beaten, third they are stretched. They are shorn by abandoning their old manner of life; beaten by worldly persecution; stretched by tireless long-suffering. They are shorn according to the sentence of the Apostle Peter: “Putting aside all malice and all deceit and hypocrisies and envies, like newborn infants desire the rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow unto salvation” [Note: [Col. 0389] 1 Peter 2]. They are beaten with the three boys in the furnace of fire, but have consolation because the angel of the Lord makes the middle of the furnace [Note: [Col. 0389] Daniel 3], etc. They are stretched with Jacob, to whom the days seemed few because of the greatness of his love [Col. 0390D] [Note: [Col. 0389] Genesis 29].

Let us take an example from below. Paul was shorn when he abandoned his former way of life, temporal property, and kindred. Hear of his former conduct. Paul says: “I was a blasphemer and a persecutor, but I obtained mercy” [Note: [Col. 0389] 1 Timothy 1]. Hear of temporal property: “The things which were gain to me have become losses to me for Christ, for whose sake I have counted all things loss and considered them as dung, that I might gain Christ” [Note: [Col. 0389] Philippians 3]. Hear of the kindred he abandoned: “But Paul grew stronger and strengthened [Col. 0391A] the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0391] Acts 9], from whom he had been born.

These are the three things by which Lazarus was hindered in the tomb from rising [Note: [Col. 0391] John 11]. His feet and hands were bound with bands, he was wrapped with a cloth, and covered with a stone. The bands were the love of temporal goods, preventing him from giving them away. The cloth was love of carnal friends, preventing him from departing from them. The stone was hardened conduct, by which he remained obstinate. Behold what teachers are shorn of; it follows that they are stretched and made intent. Regarding the first, the Apostles said to Jesus: “Behold, we have left all things”; regarding the second, “and have followed you” through sufferings and many tribulations; “what therefore shall there be for us?” [Note: [Col. 0391] Matthew 19]. As though they said: Through long-suffering we await from you a reward for these things.

Hear therefore how Paul was beaten [Col. 0391B]. He was shorn by a word, beaten by danger, stretched by the scourge: by a word of mockery, by the danger of fear, by the scourge of suffering. Was not this a mocking word: “Paul, your much learning has brought you to madness” [Note: [Col. 0391] Acts 26]? Of danger he himself says: “Danger at sea, danger among false brethren,” etc. Hear the beating of the scourge: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck” [Note: [Col. 0391] 2 Corinthians 11]. Behold how he was beaten; hear how he was stretched.

He was stretched in patient prayer, in bearing his infirmity; stretched in continual persecution; stretched in awaiting rewards. Of the first: “There was given to me an angel of Satan to strike me with fists, concerning which I asked the Lord three times” [Note: [Col. 0391] 2 Corinthians 12]. And it follows: “I will gladly glory in my infirmities” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ibid.]. Thus he urged us [Col. 0391C] to pray without ceasing [Note: [Col. 0391] 1 Thessalonians 5]. Hear how he was stretched in persecution: “Who,” he says, “shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress?” [Note: [Col. 0391] Romans 8], etc. Hear him stretched in expectation: “But what we do not see, we hope for; through patience we await it” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ibid.].

Nor was he alone. The ancient fathers were likewise stretched, modern persons are stretched, and all are stretched. The first because they awaited Christ’s first coming; the second, his second; the third, his third. The first awaited him to free them from hell; the second, to absolve them from sins; the third, to glorify them in the kingdom. Of the first David rejoiced as though it had already happened, saying: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he inclined to me and brought me out of the pit of misery and from the mire of dregs” [Col. 0391D] [Note: [Col. 0391] Psalm 39]. Hence another prophet says: “If he delays, wait for him, because he who is coming will come and will not delay” [Note: [Col. 0391] Habakkuk 2]. Of the second it is said: “Against you we have sinned, O expectation of Israel and their saviour in the time of tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0391] Jeremiah 14]. And: “Lord, have mercy on us, for we have waited for you; be our arm in the morning and our salvation in the time of tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0391] Isaiah 33]. For the third Jacob says: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0391] Genesis 49]. And Jeremiah: “It is good to wait in silence for the salvation of God” [Note: [Col. 0391] Lamentations 3].

Behold, these are the flock of shorn sheep, the flock of beaten sheep, the flock of stretched sheep. It follows: “Which have come up from the washing.”

[Col. 0392A] There are four washings from which we ascend. The first is baptism; the second, the Lord’s blood; the third, confession; the fourth, the heavenly fountain. The first washes, the second frees, the third raises up, the fourth restores. It washes from sin, frees from hell, raises from daily falling, and restores by freeing from the misery that is in this exile. In accordance with these four, we assign four interpretations to the name *lavacrum* (“washing”): with reference to the first, it is called a washing that washes away guilt; to the second, a washing that washes in blood; to the third, a washing that washes the raw or wounded; to the fourth, a washing that washes away torments.

Of the first the prophet says: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” [Note: [Col. 0391] Zechariah 13]. Of the second: “In the blood of your covenant [Col. 0392B] you redeemed your bound ones from the pit in which there was no water” [Note: [Col. 0391] Zechariah 10]. Of the third Jeremiah says: “Who will give waters to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep over the slain of my people?” [Note: [Col. 0391] Jeremiah 9]. For this is tearful confession, of which it is said: “Confess your sins to one another” [Note: [Col. 0391] James 5]. And likewise: “He who is washed after touching a dead person, if he touches a dead person again, what profit is that washing?” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ecclesiasticus 34]. Hence Christ also says: “He who is clean needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” [Note: [Col. 0391] John 13]. As though he said: You have been washed in baptism and are therefore clean. But since you cannot live without sin, at least sin of thought, you need daily to wash your feet—that is, your affections—in confession. “For the righteous man falls seven times” [Note: [Col. 0391] Proverbs 24], but through this he rises stronger.

[Col. 0392C] The fourth washing is called “the fountain of gardens, the well of living waters flowing impetuously from Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0391] Song of Songs 4]. And Sedulius:

> A harvest gladdened by the heavenly fountain  
> Is cleansed when its thorns have been removed.

From the first, therefore, a person rises cleaner; from the second, safer; from the third, stronger; to the fourth he rises more glorious. The first accordingly has four effects: it releases guilt, remits punishment, weakens the tinder of sin, and gives grace. These were figured in what befell the children of Israel in the Red Sea. Their enemies were drowned in it: behold, sins remitted. They were freed from the labour of mud and brick: behold, the punishment of sin remitted. Those who previously had not dared resist under the Egyptians [Col. 0392D] fought bravely in the wilderness against uncircumcised kings: behold, the tinder of sin weakened. In the wilderness they ate manna from heaven [Note: [Col. 0391] Deuteronomy 8]: behold, grace.

The second washing occurs through Christ’s blood. It should be noted that there are three kinds of blood: the blood of the burnt offering, Christ’s blood, and the blood of martyrdom. By the first human flesh was washed; by the second conscience is cleansed; by the third a crown is acquired. Paul says of the first and second: “If the blood of goats and calves sanctifies the defiled for cleansing of the flesh, how much more shall Christ’s blood [Col. 0393A] cleanse our consciences to serve the living God?” [Note: [Col. 0393] Hebrews 9]. Of the third the Church sings: “Holy men poured out their glorious blood for Christ, and therefore deserved crowns of triumph; for, made red by flowing blood, they are richly endowed with brightly gleaming laurels.” The first was historically poured out in the court; the second was figured in the red heifer; the third in the red-dyed skins of rams in the tabernacle.

The third washing occurs through tearful confession. It is first bitter, second shameful, third harsh: bitter in contrition, shameful in utterance, harsh in satisfaction. Thus it has Hezekiah’s bitterness, the shame of the woman with the issue of blood, and John the Baptist’s harshness. Of the first it is written: “I said, in the midst of my days, I shall go to the gates [Col. 0393B] of hell” [Note: [Col. 0393] Isaiah 38]. Of the second, the woman, not daring to approach Christ, said while standing behind him: “If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0393] Matthew 9]. Of the third it is said that John the Baptist was clothed in camel hair, with a leather belt around his loins [Note: [Col. 0393] Matthew 3].

The fourth washing is the heavenly fountain. It drives away lack, takes away sorrow, and expels misery. For the first it grants an abundance of every good; for the second, joy; for the third, eternal life. Of the first: “Whoever drinks from this water shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0393] John 4]: behold eternal life. Thus in the first Christ washed us “through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly” [Note: [Col. 0393] Titus 3]. In the second: “The saints [Col. 0393C] washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” [Note: [Col. 0393] Revelation 7]. In the third, “he who has been washed” [Note: [Col. 0393] John 13] says: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” [Note: [Col. 0393] Song of Songs 5]. In the fourth Christ will wash us when he has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the blood of Jerusalem from its midst, in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning [Note: [Col. 0393] Isaiah 4].

Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing.

[CAR.] The flocks of shorn sheep are those who, laying aside the burdens of possessions as though they were fleeces, left everything for Christ. The more they withdrew themselves from the world, the more freely they could understand the sacred Scriptures; nor could the darkness of sins cast an obstacle before them. [80] For, frequently washed by tears of repentance and devotion, [Col. 0393D] they ascended from virtue to virtue, that they might see the God of gods in Zion [Note: [Col. 0393] Psalm 83], which is interpreted “mirror”; that is, that with the eye of a pure heart they might behold God in the mirror of the Scriptures.

The Virgin’s teeth—that is, her understanding and diligence—are therefore likened to all these who, like the Lord’s flock, chewed the cud in the pastures of sacred Scripture. By these she plucked, crushed, chewed, ruminated, and incorporated into her soul, as though green herbs, the teachings of sacred Scripture. It follows:

All bearing twin offspring, and none among them is barren.

[Col. 0394A] [THO.] Christ’s sheep bear twin offspring because through their preaching love of God and neighbour, or faith and works, is produced. Thus none among them is barren, because they are fruitful in works, affections, and virtues. A sheep suffers a threefold barrenness: of milk, of lamb, and of fleece. The first comes from lack of pasture; the second from corruption of the womb; the third from frequent contact with briars: pasture of doctrine, the womb of obstinate wickedness, and frequent association with evil persons. These sheep, however, are not barren; they yield the milk of simplicity, the lamb of gentleness, and the fleece of good conduct.

Of the first: “Desire milk, that by it you may grow unto salvation” [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Peter 2]. Of the second, the Law commands a lamb to be offered by a woman who has given birth [Note: [Col. 0393] Leviticus 14]. Of the third the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in [Col. 0394B] sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” [Note: [Col. 0393] Matthew 7]. Or: milk is simple teaching—“I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0393] 2 Corinthians 3]; the lamb is patience and innocence—“Like a lamb before its shearer, he was silent and did not open his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0393] Isaiah 53]; the fleece is necessary provision—“He was warmed by the fleeces of my sheep” [Note: [Col. 0393] Job 31].

But among those who come up from the washing, some ascend from pride, some from concupiscence, some from charity. Those ascending from pride have three steps: fear, sorrow, and love. Those ascending from concupiscence of the flesh have three: patience, mercy, and compunction. From ignorance: knowledge, meditation, and contemplation. From charity: temperance, prudence, and fortitude.

Adam [Col. 0394C] was first created in charity, but fell into pride [Note: [Col. 0393] Genesis 3], then into concupiscence, and afterwards into ignorance. Therefore, where he first fell, from there he first ascended—that is, from pride—and there trampled the serpent’s head, that is, pride. In the second place he trampled the serpent’s belly, that is, concupiscence; in the third, the serpent’s breast, that is, ignorance. Ascending through charity, from which he had fallen, he crushed the whole coiled serpent. When he first began to return, he broke its tail, by which we have persisted in evil until repentance.

Since, therefore, these falls of Adam were the root of human ruin, it was necessary that a man should come who would be the root from which charity might sprout anew in us. This was none other than Christ, who would kindle charity in us anew and become a sacrifice [Col. 0394D] for the Church. Therefore the ancient fathers invoked him with great longing, saying: “O root of Jesse, who standest as a sign for the people, before whom kings shall keep silence, whom the nations shall entreat: come to deliver us with outstretched arm; do not delay any longer” [Note: [Col. 0393] Office of the Church, from Isaiah 11 and 52.]. Jesse means “fire” or “sacrifice of an island,” so that through Jesse’s root charity may be kindled in the Church, for which sacrifice is offered. For she is like an island shaken by the waves of tribulation.

There is a fourfold root: the root [Col. 0395A] of a dried-up tree; the root out of thirsty ground; the root sent forth toward the moisture of water; and the root of Jesse. The first is the evil will of the sinner; the second, the good will of the penitent; the third, the will touched by the grace of devotion; the fourth, the Virgin’s Son. The first revives when a basket of dung is put about it; the second languishes from the intensity of desires; the third grows green and buds because of the greatness of spiritual joys; the fourth stands as a sign for peoples. Over the first preachers will open their mouths; over the second, those who pray will open their mouths; over the third, those who praise will open their mouths; over the fourth kings will keep their mouths shut. For God’s commandments will be preached to the first; their desires will be obtained for the second; spiritual gifts will be increased for the third; [Col. 0395B] the nations will entreat the fourth. And so: “Come to deliver us; do not delay any longer.”

Of the first it is said: “Leave the tree this year, until I dig around its root and put on dung” [Note: [Col. 0395] Luke 13]. Of the second: “He shall come forth like a shoot before him, and like a root out of thirsty ground” [Note: [Col. 0395] Isaiah 53]. Of the third: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which sends forth its roots toward moisture” [Note: [Col. 0395] Psalm 1; Jeremiah 17]. Of the fourth we have it here. Therefore preachers will open their mouths over the first, and it will hear God’s commandments and revive when a basket of dung is put about it.

There are four kinds of dung found in the divine page: human dung, [Col. 0395C] ox dung, beast dung, and dove dung. The first is the sin of prelates; the second, of the wealthy; the third, of the lustful; the fourth, of the unlearned. Since the first are teachers, they sin knowingly; the second, presumptuously; the third, shamelessly; the fourth, simply. Of the first Ezekiel says [Note: [Col. 0395] Chapter 4]: “Son of man, make bread and bake it in human dung.” Of the second Solomon says: “The sluggard is stoned with ox dung” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ecclesiasticus 22]. Of the third: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” [Note: [Col. 0395] Joel 1]. Of the fourth, it is read in the Book of Kings that, because of famine, dove dung was sold [Note: [Col. 0395] 4 Kings 6].

For the first, while preaching to others, fall thereby into vain glory and pride. The second, like oxen labouring for temporal things and then giving alms from them, more presumptuously seek wealth by evil means. The third, [Col. 0395D] like beasts bearing the burden of penitence, shamelessly fall into lust. The fourth, because they are unlearned, sin through ignorance. Of the first: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” [Note: [Col. 0395] Romans 2]. Of the second the Apostle says: “If I spend all my substance in feeding the poor, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” [Note: [Col. 0395] 1 Corinthians 13]. To the third it is said: “Put on the Lord,” that is, Christ, “and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” [Note: [Col. 0395] Romans 13]. To the fourth, the same Apostle says: “I fear lest, just as the serpent [Col. 0396A] deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0395] 2 Corinthians 11].

The first, therefore, should be shown how the devil fell through pride; the second, how that rich man in purple of the Gospel perished; the third, how Sodom was overwhelmed; the fourth, how Eve was deceived. Behold, the basket of dung has been placed about this root. Let it therefore pass to the second root, namely the good will of penitents, and it will be from thirsty ground when the dry heart—that is, one without devotion—desires devotion.

Thus let it proceed in this order: first, hardness must be broken; second, it must be crushed on account of sin; third, good must be distinguished from evil, so that, while one is occupied with good alone, the devotion one desires may be attained. Isaiah teaches this [Col. 0396B] order thus: “The earth shall be broken with breaking; the earth shall be crushed with crushing; the earth shall be shaken with shaking” [Note: [Col. 0395] Isa. 24.]. It shall therefore be broken as in a trough by a hammer; crushed as in a mortar by a pestle; shaken as in a sieve through the openings of its holes. It shall be broken in the trough of impending condemnation; it shall be crushed in the mortar of self-reproach by the hammer of fear and the pestle of compunction; it shall be shaken in the sieve of continual meditation through the holes of discernment. For thus apothecaries customarily reduce their spices to powder. Hear the trough of condemnation: “Cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” [Note: [Col. 0395] Matt. 25.]. Hear the hammer of fear: “The fear of death troubles me, because in hell there is no redemption” [Col. 0396C]. Hence the same Isaiah adds [Note: [Col. 0395] Ch. 24.]: “Who shall escape the terror, the pit, and the snare of the Lord?” The terror of dying, the pit of hell, the snare of judgment. Of the first: “My heart is troubled within me, and the fear of death has fallen upon me” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 54]; of the second: “That thou mayest give him rest from evil days, until a pit be dug for the sinner” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 93]; of the third: “He shall rain snares upon sinners” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 10]. Hear the mortar of self-accusation: “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 105]. David teaches the pestle: “What you say in your hearts, be compunct in your beds” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 4]. Hear the sieve of constant meditation: “I meditated by night with my heart; I was exercised, and I searched my spirit” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 76]. Hear the openings of discernment: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Abstain yourselves from every appearance of evil” [Note: [Col. 0395] I Thess. 5.]. Behold the useless coarseness remaining around the sieve—that is, sin. “Hold fast that which is good.” Behold the fine powder which passes through the sieve’s openings. Having tasted this powder, one feels the sweetness of the devotion that one desired. Therefore it now ceases to be a root from the thirsty earth; and, that it may lay aside its languors, it becomes the third root, one sent forth toward moisture.

The third root is that which is sent forth toward moisture: namely, the will imbued with devotion. First it has the water of purity; second, the dew of grace; third, gladness in devotion; fourth, charity in edification. It has the water of purity, by which the moistened root produces shoots of good works; the dew of grace, by which it brings the harvest of virtues to maturity; gladness in devotion, by which, in tasting heavenly joys, it affects the conscience with a certain newness of glory; charity in edification, by whose example, as by a certain arrow of love, it pierces the neighbor’s heart with holy emulation. Job shows this sequence as follows: “My root is spread out beside the waters” [Note: [Col. 0397] Job 29.]. Behold the first. “And dew shall remain in my harvest” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ibid.]. Behold the second. “My glory shall always be renewed” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ibid.]. Behold the third. “And my bow shall be renewed in my hand” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ibid.]. Behold the fourth. For the bow is renewed in the hand when one works from [Col. 0397B] inward devotion according to the commandments of the New and Old Law, which are signified by the bow. From it, too, the arrow of emulation is sent by example toward the neighbor’s heart. Of the first: “I will pour upon you,” says the Lord through the prophet, “clean water, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ezek. 36.]. Of the second, the Lord says through the prophet Hosea [Note: [Col. 0397] Ch. 14.]: “I shall be as dew; Israel shall blossom as the lily.” And he adds: “And his fragrance shall be as Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ibid.], namely, the fragrance of good reputation which kindles neighbors to love. Hence the Bride: “I am wounded by charity.” For this wound of love was made by the root of Jesse, that is, the kindling of charity—which is called *Jesse*, or “the sacrifice of the island,” that is, of the Church, which is buffeted by the adversities of the world as an island by the waves of the sea. [Col. 0397C] For this reason it is said of him: “Who stands as a sign for the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0397] Isa. 11.], namely, as the sign of the cross.

There are four signs of the root of Jesse. The first is the sign of miracles; the second, of sacraments; the third, of peoples; the fourth, of those glorified. The first is of God incarnate; the second, of God regenerating; the third, of God dying; the fourth, of the living God. Through the first we are enlightened unto faith; through the second we are regenerated from sins; through the third we are freed from the devil; through the fourth we are crowned in glory. Of the first Nicodemus says: “No one can perform these signs which thou doest, unless God be with him” [Note: [Col. 0397] John 3.]. And the Lord: “These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons” [Note: [Col. 0397] Mark 16], etc. Of the second, [Col. 0397D] in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0397] Ch. 5.]: “Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive the book and to loose its seven seals,” that is, to open the mysteries. Of the third, it is said in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0397] Ch. 9] to the man clothed in linen, that he should imprint the wooden *tau* upon the foreheads of believers—that is, the sign of the cross. Of the fourth, in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0397] Ch. 7.]: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the sign of the living God.” And from every tribe of the children of Israel twelve thousand were seen to be sealed [Note: [Col. 0397] Ibid.]. For they possessed a certain distinguishing token of the future resurrection in glory. [Col. 0398A] In the first sign, therefore, Christ walked [81]; in the second he lay; in the third he stood; in the fourth he sat.

He walked, drawing us toward the kingdom. He sat with us, humbling himself through participation in the sacraments; he stood on the cross, fighting manfully for us; he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, judging us. The Apostle invites us to the first, saying: “He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” [Note: [Col. 0397] I John 2.]. He shows us the second when Christ was baptized by John [Note: [Col. 0397] Matt. 3], and when he lay in the manger [Note: [Col. 0397] Luke 2], humbling himself for us. Of the third, in the Apocalypse: “I saw upon Mount Sion a Lamb standing, as though slain” [Note: [Col. 0397] Apoc. 5.]. Of the fourth, in Daniel: “Thrones were set, and the Ancient of Days sat” [Note: [Col. 0397] Dan. 7.]. Thus he shall sit when he comes to judge, bearing [Col. 0398B] the sign and truth of the glorious resurrection. For he shall have “written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords” [Note: [Col. 0397] Apoc. 19.]. The sign of the cross is called the sign of peoples because through it the love of Christ has gathered us into one, that we might be “his people and the sheep of his pasture” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 94]. “Over him,” he says, “kings shall shut their mouths” [Note: [Col. 0397] Isa. 52]. Indeed, orators shall shut their mouths over him; philosophers shall shut theirs, and kings as well. Orators, because they have no ingenious argument to allege against him; philosophers, because they do not know the truth that is above nature; kings, because they humble their imperious power before him. Of the first, the Pharisees spoke as though posing an insoluble question: “Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not?” And he answered: “Render therefore to Caesar the things which are Caesar’s, [Col. 0398C] and to God the things which are God’s” [Note: [Col. 0397] Matt. 22]. And Scripture further says: “No one dared question him” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ibid.]. Of the second, Pilate, not knowing what he said, asked: “What is truth?” [Note: [Col. 0397] John 18.] Yet Christ himself knew; for he said of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0397] John 14.]. Of the third: the royal official, whose son was sick at Capernaum, held his peace and did not reproach him [Note: [Col. 0397] John 4.]. Moreover, Tiberius Caesar, hearing of his miracles, commanded that he be worshipped among the gods. It follows: “The nations shall entreat him” [Note: [Col. 0397] Isa. 11.]. It should be noted that the Jews themselves curse, the nations entreat, and Christians pray. The Jews imprecate condemnation; the nations beg remission of sins; Christians pray for salvation. Of the first they say: “He is guilty of death” [Note: [Col. 0397] Matt. 26]; and: “Crucify, [Col. 0398D] crucify him” [Note: [Col. 0397] Luke 23]. Second, the nations entreat, saying: “Come to deliver us; delay no longer” [Note: [Col. 0397] Office of the Church]. Third, Christians pray, saying: “Come to save us, O Lord our God” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ibid.].

“All with twin offspring, and none barren among them.”

[CARD.] What is said in this place is referred to three rewards, namely, the eyes, hair, and teeth, all of which have twins—twin fruits or offspring—because the intellect and affection of the Blessed Virgin, signified by the eyes; the contemplation of heavenly things, [Col. 0399A] signified by the hair; and also natural ability and diligence, denoted by the teeth, bore fruit both in the Virgin herself through merit and in us through example. In all these things—eyes, hair, and teeth—no act was barren or without reward, because, after she conceived her Son, she was so wholly endowed with charity that it may piously be believed of her that every movement of reason in her was fruitful and meritorious. This belongs to her as a unique privilege. It follows.

“Thy lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and thy speech is sweet.”

[THO.] The Bride’s lips are compared to scarlet, because the Church never ceases to proclaim the price of the Lord’s blood by which she was redeemed. Rather, she sings: “Far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0399] Gal. 6.]. Nor does he merely say “scarlet,” but “a scarlet ribbon.” A ribbon is customarily used to bind the hair. Therefore, if her hair denotes the faithful, the ribbon which binds them and joins them to the head, which is Christ, signifies the teaching of truth. It gathers them to their head, Christ, lest they flow away into unlawful things. “And thy speech is sweet,” because nothing so draws back the wanton as the mercy of the Lord’s Passion preached to them. We have Christ’s blood in our hands. There are many kinds of blood: the blood of desire, the blood of guilt, the blood of punishment, the blood of compunction, and the blood of redemption. Of the first: “The life of the soul is in the blood” [Note: [Col. 0399] Lev. 17]. Of the second: [Col. 0399C] “You shall not eat flesh with blood” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ibid.]. Of the third: “His blood shall be upon his own head” [Note: [Col. 0399] Lev. 20]. Of the fourth, Gregory says: “The tears of penitents are a certain blood of the soul.” Of the fifth: “He washed us from our sins in his blood” [Note: [Col. 0399] Apoc. 1.]. The first suggests; the second offends; the third punishes; the fourth implores; the fifth obtains. The first suggests poison; the second offends God; the third punishes the guilty; the fourth implores mercy; the fifth obtains pardon. The first suggests lightly; the second offends miserably; the third punishes servilely; the fourth asks humbly; the fifth obtains universally.

For these five, five kinds of animals are commanded to be sacrificed in Leviticus. The first is the ox, a large-bodied animal, whose blood signifies the appetite [Col. 0399D] of the flesh; it must be shed, lest that appetite reach the point of sin. If it reaches it, there follows the goat, a foul-smelling animal, whose blood signifies the stench of sin and must be shed, lest it be committed further. There follows the sheep, an innocent animal, whose blood is shed against the rock, lest one be punished by the scourge of God’s wrath. Fourth there follow birds, which fly high, whose blood signifies tears sent up to God. The blood of the aforesaid animals is poured out at the door of the tabernacle, because they are not yet near to God; but that of the birds is poured out beside the altar, because tears make us draw near to God. Note that there are three altars. The Church is called an altar, as in: “When you enter the land which the Lord will give you, you shall make an altar to the Lord of stones untouched by iron” [Note: [Col. 0399] Deut. 27]—that is, of peaceful persons, not schismatics. Christ too is called an altar. Hence the Apostle: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no power to eat” [Note: [Col. 0399] Heb. 13], that is, those who serve the flesh. Our heart also is an altar. Hence: “The offering of the righteous makes the altar rich” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ecclus. 35], that is, the heart. This blood of tears must be poured out upon the altar which is the Church, because it must be shed in the faith of the Church; and upon the altar of the heart, because it must flow forth from the heart. Or “beside the altar” denotes the eastern region, that is, Christ, who is the sun of righteousness; or the knowledge of God; and the crop of the throat, that is, pride; and the feathers, that is, levity of conduct, because [Col. 0400B] when we behold the loftiness of God, we lay aside our pride and shed the blood of tears for these things. There is also the blood of redemption, namely Christ’s: “In the blood,” he says, “of thy covenant thou hast redeemed thy prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” [Note: [Col. 0399] Zech. 9.]. This is signified by the scarlet ribbon. But to signify the same thing, we find a scarlet cord in the house of Rahab the harlot, by which she let down the spies of Jericho [Note: [Col. 0399] Josh. 2.]. Likewise, when the hand of Zarah was born, it was bound with a scarlet silken cloth [Note: [Col. 0399] Gen. 38.]. In these three Christ’s blood is signified, but for distinct purposes. A ribbon binds, a cord draws, and a cloth adorns. It binds the dissolute, draws back those turned away, and adorns the righteous: the dissolute, lest they depart from their head, Christ; those turned away, lest they descend into hell; and the righteous, that they may rejoice at judgment. Some have the ribbon, some the cord, some the cloth: the ribbon in the mouth, the cord in the heart, the cloth in the body. Teachers have it in the mouth, spiritual persons in the heart, martyrs in the body: teachers in preaching, spiritual persons in the will, martyrs in the shedding of blood. For preachers it is said:

“And thy speech is sweet.” Rahab the harlot, namely our flesh, which is in Jericho—that is, in the world; for Jericho means “moon,” on account of instability—has a house, that is, a manner of life. This house has two upper rooms: the lower, sensuality; and the upper, spirituality. In it are hidden two spies, namely reason and affection. Affection invites one to the Passion; reason orders how it is to be done. But [Col. 0400D] in it the king of Jericho, that is, the devil, seeks them, so that what he cannot achieve through the flesh he may achieve through vain glory. But they are hidden in worthless flax-straw, because they protect themselves by humility; at last they descend by the scarlet cord [Note: [Col. 0399] Josh. 2], fleeing to the Passion of Christ.

This cord is threefold, because “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” [Note: [Col. 0399] Eccles. 4], and this by reason of three effects: it remits sins, excludes temptations, and opens the kingdom to the righteous. Hear again its threefold effect: it split rocks, tore the veil, and despoiled hell—softening hard hearts, dissolving the enmities between God and humankind, [Col. 0401A] and drawing the righteous out of hell. Hear yet again its threefold effect: it brought trembling to the earth, fear to the underworld, and astonishment to heaven. Of the first: “The earth trembled and was still” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 75]. Of the second: “Lift up your gates, O princes. Who is this King of glory?” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 23]. Of the third, the angels say: “Who is this that comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bosra?” [Note: [Col. 0401] Isa. 63]. There is also the scarlet with which Christ was clothed in the Passion. In these four scarlets is signified the blood of the paschal lamb, set upon the four parts of Israelite houses [Note: [Col. 0401] Exod. 12]: namely, on the lower threshold and the upper—that is, upon sensuality and devotion—and on the left doorpost, that is, work, and on the right, that is, speech. That on the left, that is, in work, redeems us: namely, the scarlet on Zarah’s hand. That on the lower threshold, that is, in sensuality, washes us: [Col. 0401B] this is the scarlet with which Christ was clothed in the Passion. That on the right doorpost, that is, in speech, bears us: this is the scarlet ribbon. And that on the upper threshold, that is, in devotion, adorns us: this is Rahab’s cord in the upper chamber. How it is to be worthily received is added: with roasted flesh, unleavened bread, and wild lettuces [Note: [Col. 0401] Ibid.]. Of this scarlet David says to the daughters of Israel: “Who clothed you in scarlet with delights” [Note: [Col. 0401] II Kings 1]—that is, Saul, whom they lamented. He wished the man to be a scarlet cord to whom he said: “Make for thyself two silver, hammered trumpets, with which thou shalt summon the people when the camp must move” [Note: [Col. 0401] Num. 10]: namely, for proclaiming the purple of the Lord’s Passion and the scarlet of mutual love in Christ. “Two trumpets,” he says, for the utterance of the breath conceived; “silver,” [Col. 0401C] for displaying chastity and innocence; “hammered,” for enduring the Passion of Christ which we proclaim; “with which thou shalt summon the people,” for the mutual overcoming of enemies: the breath which the Holy Spirit infuses by inspiration; innocence, with which God adorns us when he remits sins; love, with which the Holy Spirit kindles souls; and the overcoming of enemies, by whom God permits us to be tempted.

First it should be noted that there is a bronze trumpet, a silver trumpet, and a horn trumpet. The first is cast; the second hammered; the third thoroughly drawn out. The first is prophetic, the second apostolic, the third angelic.
