The first is cast because, inflamed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, it was the herald of heavenly counsel; the second is the preaching of the holy [Col. 0401D] Gospel; the third was the Angel of great counsel. Hear the cast trumpet: “And sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ezek. 1.]. Of the first, second, and third: “With three hammered instruments and the sound of a horn trumpet” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 27]. Of the first: “As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from of old” [Note: [Col. 0401] Luke 1]. Of the second: “They declared the works of God and understood his deeds” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 63]. Of the third: “The Lord has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant” [Note: [Col. 0401] Luke 1]. Of the first it is said: “Sound [Col. 0402A] the trumpet in Sion” [Note: [Col. 0401] Joel 2]; of the second: “Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the day of your solemnity” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 80]; of the third: “Let the saving trumpet resound for the victory of so great a king” [Note: [Col. 0401] In the chant *Exsultet*, etc.]. The first sounds with a low voice, the second with a high one, the third with a very high one. The first is under the harshness of the Law, the second under grace, the third promises glory. The first, because “the deep gave forth its voice” [Note: [Col. 0401] Hab. 3], and “deep calls unto deep” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 41]. The hearts of the prophets are called “deeps” because of the profundity and obscurity of their sayings. God’s floodgates are inspirations. The second is high-pitched, therefore, because “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 18]. The third is very high-pitched, because “the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave forth his voice” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 17]. For the first announces the mysteries somewhat obscurely, as concerning [Col. 0402B] baptism: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David, for washing the sinner and the menstruating woman” [Note: [Col. 0401] Zech. 13]. The second openly declares that Christ has come. Hence: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ has appeared to all men, instructing us” [Note: [Col. 0401] Titus 2]. The third most openly calls us to glory. Hence: “Pass over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my generations” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ecclus. 24].

The seven trumpets which the seven angels sounded in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0401] Apoc. 8] signify the first; at the sound of the first of these, hail and fire mingled with blood came to pass. Gideon’s trumpets bore the figure of the second; at their sound the apostles fled. The seven trumpets by which the walls of Jericho fell were a figure of the third.

[Col. 0402C] These bronze trumpets are, as it were, discolored, lacking perfect brightness. Isaiah was a bronze trumpet when he threatened the straits of the lower world; Ezekiel was one when he set forth the misery of the world; John the Baptist was one when he called to repentance. The first strikes us with horror, the second with sorrow, the third with ardor: horror, that we may flee it; sorrow, that we may love the world less; ardor, that we may wash away sins. For Isaiah says: “The moth shall be spread beneath thee, and worms shall be thy covering” [Note: [Col. 0401] Isa. 14]. Ezekiel: “A whirlwind wind came from the north, and a great cloud, and enveloping fire” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ezek. 1]. John: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” [Note: [Col. 0401] Matt. 3]. Behold, for example, [Col. 0402D] the first of the seven trumpets of the Apocalypse, at whose sound comes the hail of worldly tribulation, mingled with the blood of guilt and the fire of eternal damnation. But because the time of grace has now come, we are commanded to make two silver trumpets—namely Peter and Paul—because “Peter the apostle and Paul the teacher of the nations, they taught us thy law, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0401] Office of the Church]. First they must be trumpets; second, silver; third, hammered. Trumpets, so that by the breath of teaching they provide nourishment; silver [Col. 0403A] so that they may be bright through simplicity, chastity, and innocence; hammered, so that amid the hammer of affliction and the anvil of penitence they may possess perfect righteousness. Of the trumpet it is said: “Sound the trumpet in Sion” [Note: [Col. 0403] Joel 2], as if to say: “Feed the flock of the Lord that is among you” [Note: [Col. 0403] I Pet. 5]. They possessed the brightness of silver through simplicity, chastity, and innocence: simplicity, that they might be “the silvered wings of a dove” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ps. 67]; innocence, that they might be “silver from electrum” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ezek. 1]—as though from the silver of humanity and the gold of divinity, namely Christ, “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0403] I Pet. 2]; chastity, that they might be like the silver cup in which Joseph customarily divined [Note: [Col. 0403] Gen. 44], he who refused the fornication of his mistress the harlot [Note: [Col. 0403] Gen. 39]. Of simplicity: “Be simple as doves” [Note: [Col. 0403] Matt. 10]. [Col. 0403B] Of innocence: “Innocent in hands and clean of heart” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ps. 23]. Of chastity: “Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and immodest acts” [Note: [Col. 0403] Rom. 13]. The first are lilies of the valleys [Note: [Col. 0403] Song 2]; the second, a lily among thorns [Note: [Col. 0403] Ibid.]; the third, like a heap of wheat surrounded with lilies [Note: [Col. 0403] Song 7]. Behold, these are “like two twin fawns of a roe” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ibid.], “which feed among the lilies until the day breathe and the shadows decline” [Note: [Col. 0403] Song 2]. They are hammered, formed between hammer and anvil through their own suffering, compassion for their neighbor, and the endurance of insults. Hear Paul, hammered: “In perils from my own nation, in perils from robbers, in perils from rivers, in perils among false brethren. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck” [Note: [Col. 0403] II Cor. 11]. And Peter too was seen handed over to prison, beaten with scourges, [Col. 0403C] subjected to insults, and finally crucified. Behold the trumpets; behold, silver; behold, hammered. Hence there were cups, globes, and lilies on the tabernacle’s lampstand [Note: [Col. 0403] Exod. 25]: cups, to administer the drink of doctrine; lilies, of simplicity, chastity, and innocence; globes, round by the craft of the lathe, signifying perfection of righteousness. To them he says: “Thou shalt summon the people when the camp must move” [Note: [Col. 0403] Num. 10].

For these trumpets first call the people back, second summon them together, third urge them onward. They call them back from error to truth; summon them to unanimity; urge them toward heavenly happiness. The first, that they may have firmness of faith; the second, that they may have charity; the third, that they may attain the brightness of the kingdom. [Col. 0403D] Hear Peter calling them back: “Putting away all malice, all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and all detractions, as newborn infants desire rational milk without guile, that by it you may grow unto salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” [Note: [Col. 0403] I Pet. 2], so that he may say: “You were once as wandering sheep, but now you have been converted to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ibid.]. Hear Paul calling them back: “The night is far spent, but the day is at hand. Let us therefore cast off [Col. 0404A] the works of darkness and put on the armor of light, that we may walk honorably in the day” [Note: [Col. 0403] Rom. 13]; having done which, he may say: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0403] Eph. 5]. Hear Peter summoning them: “Supply in your faith virtue; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, self-restraint; in self-restraint, patience; in patience, piety; in piety, love of the brethren; and in brotherly love, charity” [Note: [Col. 0403] II Pet. 1]. Hear Paul also summoning them: “I beseech you to walk worthily of the calling wherewith you have been called, with humility and meekness, with patience bearing one another in charity” [Note: [Col. 0403] Eph. 4]. Hear Peter urging them toward eternal happiness: “Blessed be God, who has regenerated us unto a living hope, unto an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and [Col. 0404B] unfading, reserved in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0403] I Pet. 1]. Incorruptible, because it shall not suffer loss; undefiled, because sin shall not be there; unfading, because no one there shall suffer weariness. Hear Paul also urging them: “If you have risen with Christ,” he says, “seek the things that are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God; set your mind on things above, not on things upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” [Note: [Col. 0403] Col. 3]. It follows:

“When the camp must move.” It should be noted that there are three kinds of camps: the camp of the Egyptians, the camp of the Israelites, and the camp of angels. Of the first it is said: “The Lord looked down upon the camp of the Egyptians” [Note: [Col. 0403] Exod. 14]; of the second: “He who is leprous shall go forth [Col. 0404C] outside the camp” [Note: [Col. 0403] Lev. 13]; of the third Job says: “They are the camps of God” [Note: [Col. 0403] Job 36]. The first are to be removed, the second moved, the third approached. The first are the camps of the world, the second those of the desert, the third those of heaven. The first wage war in order to plunder; the second, in order to reach the homeland; the third, in order to admit those who arrive. Therefore let us leave the first, choose the second, and sigh after the third. Having abandoned the first, then, let us serve as soldiers in the second, in which we must have unanimity of hearts, foresight for the future, refuge in Christ against temptations, and, in doing good, a heart set on high.

Of these four Solomon says: “Four things are least upon the earth, and are themselves wiser than the wise: the ‘locust,’ which has no king and yet [Col. 0404D] flies all in companies” [Note: [Col. 0403] Prov. 30]—this is unity of hearts; “the ant, which labors in summer for the means by which it may live in winter” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ibid.]—this is foresight; “the little hare, a weak people, which makes its bed in the rock” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ibid.]—behold refuge in Christ; “the lizard, which walks with its hands and dwells in the king’s house” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ibid.]—behold good work and the heart lifted on high. Of the first: “There was one spirit and one faith among them” [Note: [Col. 0403] Acts 4]. Of the second: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider [Col. 0405A] her ways, and learn wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0405] Prov. 6]. Of the third: “Be unto us, O Lord, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy” [Note: [Col. 0405] Office of the Church]. Of the fourth: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0405] Phil. 3]. Of works: “While we have time, let us work good toward all, especially toward those of the household of faith” [Note: [Col. 0405] Gal. 6]. Gideon’s people held these trumpets in their hands: that is, they practised the works of the apostles, though the commandments had not yet been promulgated. They struck the jars together—that is, their bodies—and they were broken, and they revealed shining lamps, namely the charity of the heart. Behold all things “terrible as an army drawn up in battle order” [Note: [Col. 0405] Song 6]. It follows:

“The horn trumpet,” which is Christ for three reasons. Horn, while not contracting the softness of flesh, is born from flesh. It is an instrument whose sound drives the wolf away [Col. 0405B] from the sheep; under heat it is bent according to the craftsman’s will. This horn is Christ, who was born of flesh, yet did not contract from it any defilement. This is our protection against the devil; love made him accommodate himself to our misery. Of the first: “He came in the likeness of sinful flesh” [Note: [Col. 0405] Rom. 8], he “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0405] I Pet. 2]. Of the second it is said: “The good shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep” [Note: [Col. 0405] John 10], and who deigned to die for his flock. Of the third: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0405] Phil. 2], like Elisha, who stretched himself to the measure of the boy, the son of the Shunammite [Note: [Col. 0405] IV Kings 4]. At the sound of this trumpet the walls of Jericho fell—that is, the strength of the world. [Col. 0405C] Hence: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” [Note: [Col. 0405] John 16]. This trumpet invites us to imitate him, to spiritual resurrection, and to participation in the kingdom: first, that we may journey confidently; second, that we may live sweetly; third, that we may reign with him happily. Of the first: “He who wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” [Note: [Col. 0405] Matt. 6]. Of the second: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” [Note: [Col. 0405] Matt. 11]; “He who thirsts, let him come and drink; and from his belly shall flow living waters” [Note: [Col. 0405] John 7]. Of the third: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” and the other good works that follow thence, down to: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0405] Matt. 5]. To this may [Col. 0405D] Jesus Christ bring us, to whom be honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

“Thy lips are like a scarlet ribbon [or, according to another reading, a scarlet cord], and thy speech is sweet.”

[CARD.] As though he said: Thy lips, by prayers poured out to God, bind and fasten human thoughts to their head, Christ, as a ribbon binds the hair, lest they flow away or depart from him. It is called a scarlet cord—that threefold cord—which, together with the preaching of the Trinity, mingles a word concerning the scarlet of the Passion. “And just as this preaching [Col. 0406A] binds our thoughts in Christ and preserves them in him, so too does the intercession of the Blessed Virgin, because her speech is sweet in prayers. It follows:

“As a fragment of pomegranate, so are thy cheeks, apart from that which lies hidden within.”

[THO.] By the cheeks modesty is truly signified, because in blushing a sudden flush usually suffuses us. The pomegranate, however, because it is rose-coloured, fittingly signifies the Lord’s Passion. Therefore, because the Church is not ashamed of Christ’s cross, but rejoices in sufferings and insults for Christ, and is accustomed to bear the banner of His cross upon her face, she is rightly said to bear cheeks like a pomegranate. And it is well said, “like a fragment of a pomegranate,” because in it the part [Col. 0406B] of redness that was visible is seen, and the part of whiteness that lay hidden within is revealed. Thus, when she confesses the Lord’s Passion, she displays this redness. She displays the pomegranate’s whiteness when, assailed by pressures, she preserves purity of heart. And just as the many seeds of a pomegranate cannot be seen unless it is broken, so neither can the virtues of the Church be seen unless she is tested by tribulations.

The soul is compared to a pomegranate because of its imitation of Christ’s Passion. Christ was a pomegranate for this reason: a pomegranate has pallor in its rind, redness in the appearance of its seeds, and hidden whiteness within. Likewise Christ, in the humanity He assumed, had the pallor of our weakness; when this was broken in the Passion, the redness of blood appeared. But within was hidden the whiteness of divinity. In such flesh [Col. 0406C] He visited the earth; with blood He made it drunk; from divinity He enriched it with virtues.

But this earth is threefold: there is the earth of the blessed Virgin’s womb; there is the earth of the Church militant; and there is the earth of the Church triumphant. In the first He assumed flesh; in the second He endured tribulation; in the third He received blessedness. He visited the first by bringing blessing: “You have blessed, O Lord, Your land” [Note: [Col. 0405] Ps. 84]. He visited the second by bringing reconciliation and peace. Hence the prophet: “There shall be peace in the land when He comes” [Note: [Col. 0405] Mic. 5]. He visited the third by leading captivity back: “Christ, ascending on high, leads captivity captive” [Note: [Col. 0405] Eph. 4].

He visited the first, that is, the blessed Virgin, with the angelic greeting; He made her drunk with the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit; [Col. 0406D] He enriched her manifoldly by His incarnation. The greeting was angelic, so that His coming might be instituted; the overshadowing, so that the fuel of sin in her might be extinguished and grace increased; His incarnation, so that through her the whole world might be enriched. But because this “has become wonderful, and I cannot attain to it” [Note: [Col. 0405] Ps. 138], I pass to the second, namely the Church militant, following and reverencing this counsel of the poet:

> Follow from afar, and ever reverence her footsteps.

Lord Jesus, was it not enough for You to descend from Hebron into Shechem unless You also descended from Shechem into Dothaim [Note: [Col. 0405] Gen. 37]? Hebron means “eternal vision,” that is, [Col. 0407A] the heavenly homeland. From there He came into Shechem, which means “shoulder,” or “labour”: that is, into the Virgin’s womb, where He undertook our labours. From there He came into Dothaim, that is, “defect,” namely of death. I would know, Lord,

> What mercy conquered You,  
> That You should bear our crimes?  
> [Note: [Col. 0407] Hymn, *Jesu nostra*, etc.]

“I,” He says, “have indeed seen the affliction of My people who are in Egypt, and I have come down to deliver them” [Note: [Col. 0407] Exod. 3]. Truly, mercy conquered Him. “Joseph saw his brother, and all his inward parts were moved” [Note: [Col. 0407] Gen. 43]; and entering the Virgin’s chamber, He wept, where He took upon Himself our tears and pains. You came well, Lord, because “You have executed my judgment and my cause” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 5].

In three matters we had a legal dispute with the devil; in three matters a case with God. For, as we have said, he sowed enmities [Col. 0407B] between God and humanity; he broke the covenants between creature and Creator; he established a great chaos between this exile and the heavenly homeland. Hence Isaiah: “The roads are laid waste; the traveller has ceased from the paths” [Note: [Col. 0407] Isa. 33]. Behold the chaos. “The covenant has been made void” [Note: [Col. 0407] ibid.]: behold the broken covenant. “He has cast down cities; he did not regard human beings” [Note: [Col. 0407] ibid.]: behold the enmities. By this written bond the devil held us liable to eternal death. But Paul did not conceal how He executed judgment: “He blotted out the handwriting [83] of the decree, which was against us, and took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross” [Note: [Col. 0407] Col. 2].

God the Father had a cause against us in three respects: namely, that we should restore to Him the sinless human being [Col. 0407C] whom we took from Him in Adam; that we should make satisfaction to Him for the injury, because, abandoning God, we followed the devil; and that we should repair the road to the kingdom, which our negligence had destroyed. But because “I am poor” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 24] and He “has no need of my goods” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 15], He paid the debt without sin by being born of a Virgin: “What He did not seize, He then paid” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 68]. He expiated guilt in the Passion by shedding His blood: “Truly He Himself bore our infirmities and carried our pains” [Note: [Col. 0407] Isa. 53]. He repaired the road to the kingdom by rising from the dead, because “the crooked places became straight and the rough places level paths” [Note: [Col. 0407] Luke 3].

Again, by paying the debt He dissolved the enmities, because “a righteous man was found, and in the time of wrath he became reconciliation” [Note: [Col. 0407] Office of the Church]. Thus God restored peace, reconciling the lowest things with the highest; namely, [Col. 0407D] by expiating guilt He renewed the covenants. Hence the rejoicing Peter says: “Blessed be God, who has regenerated us unto the hope of life, unto an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance reserved in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0407] 1 Pet. 1]. Truly incorruptible, because it will suffer no decay; undefiled, because there will be no sin there; unfading, because no one there will suffer weariness. By repairing the way to the kingdom He dispersed the chaos, when “He shattered the gates of bronze and broke the iron bars” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 106].

[Col. 0408A]

> Penetrating the bars of hell,  
> Redeeming His captives.  
> [Note: [Col. 0407] Hymn, *Jesu nostra*, etc.]

“And He led them into the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 106]. You have heard how God visited the earth of the Virgin and manifoldly enriched her. But how did He visit the earth of the Church? He visited it in the Passion; He made it drunk with water and blood; He manifoldly enriched it with the gift of grace.

He visited it in the Passion so that we might order our life by His example. For “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example” [Note: [Col. 0407] 1 Pet. 2]. And this was through the insult of speech, the harshness of death, and the shame of the cross. Through the insult of speech, that He might free us at judgment “from the harsh word” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 90], such as “Hail, King of the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0407] John 19] and “He has a demon” [Note: [Col. 0407] Luke 7]. Through the harshness [Col. 0408B] of death, that He might free us from penal hell. Hence the prophet: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0407] Lam. 1]. Through the shame of the cross, that He might glorify us in the kingdom. Hence Paul: “For the joy set before Him, He endured the cross, despising shame, and now sits at the right hand of God. By His example let us run the contest set before us, looking to the author of faith” [Note: [Col. 0407] Heb. 12], because it was we who deserved to suffer, not He. “We indeed receive what is due for our deeds; but what has this man done?” [Note: [Col. 0407] Luke 23]. We suffer these things deservedly, “because we have sinned and acted wickedly” [Note: [Col. 0407] Dan. 9].

Therefore let us gladly endure insult in speech, harsh suffering, and every kind of shame, so that we may say with Paul: “We are cursed, and we bless; [Col. 0408C] we suffer persecution, and we endure it; we are reviled, and we entreat; we have become like the refuse of this world” [Note: [Col. 0407] 1 Cor. 4]. Lord God, see whether it is the tunic of Your Son or not [Note: [Col. 0407] Gen. 37], which hangs upon the cross for us, so that You may say to the sluggish and those who flee repentance: “A savage beast,” that is, death, “has devoured my son” [Note: [Col. 0407] ibid.]. And behold, He meets us upon the gallows, lest He meet us at judgment, saying: “My people, what have I done to you? Or wherein have I grieved you? Answer Me” [Note: [Col. 0407] Mic. 6].—“O man, who are you, to answer God?” [Note: [Col. 0407] Rom. 9]—“If you desire to contend with Him, you cannot answer Him one thing out of a thousand” [Note: [Col. 0407] Job 9]. But You, good Jesus, who came for this purpose, answer for me.

It follows how He made it drunk with blood, namely in a threefold manner. For that blood brought redemption to the imprisoned, washing to the stained, and anointing to the sick: redemption to the imprisoned: “The Lord sent redemption to His people” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 110]. Truly, “with the Lord is mercy, and with Him abundant redemption” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 129]. As the prophet says: “In the blood of Your covenant You redeemed the bound ones through Your death from the pit in which there was no water” [Note: [Col. 0407] Zech. 9]. To the stained it brought washing, as in the Apocalypse: “He first loved us” [Note: [Col. 0407] 1 John 4] “and washed us from our sins in His blood” [Note: [Col. 0407] Rev. 1], “that He might cleanse for Himself an acceptable people, [Col. 0409A] zealous for good works” [Note: [Col. 0409] Titus 2]. It brought anointing to the sick, because “He sent His Word and healed them” [Note: [Col. 0409] Ps. 106].

> Whom the sacred blood anointed,  
> Poured forth from the Lamb’s body.  
> [Note: [Col. 0409] Hymn, *Lustra sex*, etc.]

But He also washed in water, as being that man of whom He Himself said to the disciples: “As you enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you” [Note: [Col. 0409] Mark 14]. There He also gave the pattern of our progress: that first we should be washed by the jar of water, and afterwards be refreshed in the upper room of devotion, as Job says: “Before I eat, I sigh” [Note: [Col. 0409] Job 3].

So that this washing might suffice for the whole world, four streams flowed from His body, like the four rivers from Paradise, which water the whole earth: namely, Christ’s Passion—blood; water from His side; [Col. 0409B] the water of sweat; and the water of tears:

> Earth, sea, stars, and world  
> Are washed by this stream.  
> [Note: [Col. 0409] Hymn, *Lustra sex*, etc.]

In His tears He indicated to us a threefold weeping, for He wept three times. First, at Lazarus’s tomb [Note: [Col. 0409] John 11]: behold tears of contrition. Second, “seeing the city, He wept over it” [Note: [Col. 0409] Luke 19]: behold tears of compassion. Third, when the Passion was imminent, “He went up alone upon the mountain to pray,” when “He entered into agony” [Note: [Col. 0409] Luke 22]: behold tears of devotion. Thus it is found concerning Jeremiah: “Streams of water ran down from my eyes” [Note: [Col. 0409] Jer. 3].

It follows how He enriched it with the gift of wisdom, by which we may preserve what has been bestowed; for:

> It is no lesser virtue to preserve what has been gained than to seek it.  
> (Ovid, *Art of Love* II.13)

[Col. 0409C] And Wisdom herself cries out, that we may approach her: “Pass over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my offspring” [Note: [Col. 0409] Sirach 24]. There are three generations of wisdom: secular prudence, literal knowledge, and heavenly wisdom.

Behold how He brought blessing to the earth of the Virgin and reconciliation and peace to the earth of the Church militant. It follows how He led captivity back to the earth of the Church triumphant. He visited it in the Ascension, when the Lord “ascended on high” [Note: [Col. 0409] Eph. 4], returning, that is, to His own place. He made it drunk with the delight of joy, because the realms of heaven rejoiced at the return of the Only-begotten. He manifoldly enriched it by repairing the ruin of the angels, as it is written: “The ruins of Jerusalem shall be rebuilt.” He enriched it [Col. 0409D] by the exaltation of glorified flesh, presenting before the Father’s face the glory of victorious flesh. He enriched it by joining angels and human beings in love, because He makes the homeland of earth and heaven a single commonwealth. To this pomegranate the bride is compared:

> Like a fragment of a pomegranate are your cheeks, apart from that which lies hidden within.

[CAR.] For a fragment of pomegranate shows redness and whiteness. But a woman’s appearance and beauty reside in her cheeks. Therefore the Mother of the Lord is called beautiful because of the redness of modesty and the whiteness [Col. 0410A] of innocence, apart from that which lies hidden within, known to God alone and revealed to no one. For how great the beauty of the blessed Virgin is, He alone knows who gave it. It follows:

> Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements; a thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty.

[THO.] It was said above that the neck signifies teachers: Christ is the head, and the Church is the body. Therefore nourishment of doctrine passes from Christ the head through the neck—that is, the preachers—to the body, that is, the Church. Hence in the Gospel, “He gave bread to His disciples; the disciples set it before the crowds; and they ate and were satisfied” [Note: [Col. 0409] Mark 8].

This neck is aptly compared to a tower. For if the city of Jerusalem is the Church, rightly within it is the tower of the constancy of teachers. [Col. 0410B] This tower, that is, constancy, was constructed by David, that is, Christ of the strong hand. The battlements by which this tower is defended are Holy Scripture, or the sacraments of the Church, or miracles performed by them. The thousand shields hanging from the tower are the thousand protections of the divine dispensation, which the Lord has supplied for their use, lest they be conquered. “All the armour of the mighty” is that which Paul enumerates when he says: “Stand, with your loins girded in truth” [Note: [Col. 0409] Eph. 6], and the rest which follows there.

And it is rightly called the tower of David, not of Solomon, because strength is needed in war; Solomon’s tower, however, has its use in peace. This tower is called constancy. The shields are different kinds of patience. But because they are said to be a thousand, it is easier to discuss the kinds of each than each individual example of the kinds.

[Col. 0410C] Therefore we set forth four shields: the first is iron, the second bronze, the third silver, and the fourth gold. The first is obstinacy; the second, pretence; the third, innocence; the fourth, charity. The first belongs to rebels; the second to hypocrites; the third to the meek; the fourth to those who love. Saul bore the first, and upon the mountains of Gilboa he fell beneath it [Note: [Col. 0409] 1 Sam. 31]; Goliath bore the bronze one, and David killed him [Note: [Col. 0409] 1 Sam. 17]; Joshua had the silver one, and, helped by it when it was raised, he and his companions burned the city [Note: [Col. 0409] Josh. 8]; the Maccabees had the golden one [Note: [Col. 0409] 1 Macc. 6], and they scattered the strength of the nations.

Those who possess the first shield are asses under bodily affliction; a harlot under imposed shame; an asp under verbal correction; a lurking bear when it comes to vengeance. Of the first: “You struck them [Col. 0410D] and they were not healed; You afflicted them, and they refused to receive discipline” [Note: [Col. 0409] Jer. 5]. Of the second: “The forehead of a harlot woman has become yours” [Note: [Col. 0409] Jer. 3]. Of the third: “Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp stopping its ear” [Note: [Col. 0409] Ps. 75]. Of the fourth: “He became to me like a lurking bear” [Note: [Col. 0409] Jer. 3], as Jeremiah says: “Cursed be their anger,” because it is stubborn, “and their indignation” [Note: [Col. 0409] Jer. 36], because it is hard. “Let not my soul enter into their counsel.” Job’s friends laid this charge upon him, saying: “What man is there like Job, drinking mockery like water?” [Note: [Col. 0409] Job 34].

[Col. 0411A] Saul had this shield: he endured Samuel’s rebukes and did not cease from evil; and therefore, on the mountains of Gilboa—that is, of pride—that shield was cast down. The second, namely bronze, is the shield of hypocrites. It seems to have a golden colour but is not gold, just as hypocrites seem to suffer from charity what they suffer from vanity. And this occurs for three reasons. First, that they may avoid an impending disadvantage. Hence Satan says of Job: “Skin for skin; and all that a man has he will give for his life” [Note: [Col. 0411] Job 2]. The second is when they show compassion for some temporal gain, namely because they suppose godliness to be gain, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0411] 1 Tim. 6]. The third is when they suffer for human praise, like those who “disfigure their faces, that they may appear to men to fast” [Note: [Col. 0411] Matt. 6].

[Col. 0411B] This was Goliath’s shield. “A bronze shield,” it says, “covered his shoulders” [Note: [Col. 0411] 1 Sam. 17]. In him was the whole confidence of the Philistines, for he was thought strong and his shield invincible. The third shield is called silver. This is natural innocence: that is, when a person has a good and balanced constitution of humours. Yet this is not virtue in itself; formed by charity, it becomes virtue. Joshua had this shield. When he was attacking the city of Ai and the men of that city were pursuing him, he raised it aloft. When his companions who were lying in ambush saw it, they ran up and assisted him [Note: [Col. 0411] Josh. 8].

For some cast this shield down to earth when they direct their innocence toward earthly advantages. Others raise it on high, having it in order to spend it in God’s service; then the other virtues join themselves to it, and, as it were, companions coming out of ambush, run up and help to conquer. Job possessed this when he said: “He who is mocked by his friends, as I am, shall call upon God and He will hear him” [Note: [Col. 0411] Job 12].

[Col. 0411C] The fourth shield is gold, namely patience, which is possessed through charity alone. It bears Christ’s image in itself, gives brightness to neighbours, and terror to adversaries, as we can observe here: “The sun shone upon the golden shields” [Note: [Col. 0411] 1 Macc. 6]: behold the image of the true Sun, that is, Christ. “And the mountains shone from them” [Note: [Col. 0411] ibid.]: behold brightness for neighbours. The mountains are the powerful people of this world, who, seeing the power of religious persons, are enlightened. “And the strength of the nations was scattered” [Note: [Col. 0411] ibid.]: behold terror to adversaries, who see that they can do nothing against [Col. 0411D] the patient, though they “can kill the body, but have nothing they can do to the soul” [Note: [Col. 0411] Luke 12].

These say with Job: “May He who has begun to crush me Himself finish it; may He loose His hand and cut me off” [Note: [Col. 0411] Job 6]. Again: “If He scourges, let Him kill me at once” [Note: [Col. 0411] Job 9]. And Habakkuk: “Let rottenness enter into my bones and bubble beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation and go up to our girded people” [Note: [Col. 0411] Hab. 3]. Such shields hang upon the tower which is the bride’s neck.

It should be known, however, that there are three towers: the first, of virginity; the second, of martyrdom; the third, of humility. All who are continent together constitute one city, in which [Col. 0412A] virginity rises above the rest like a tower. Likewise, all who endure tribulation seem to be one city, in which martyrdom is raised as a tower. Likewise, all who share humility constitute a kind of city, in which a tower is raised—namely, love of one’s own lowliness. The first is against lust; the second against unbelief; the third against pride. [84] But lest anyone presume that these shields of patience suffice for eternal life without grace, the Apostle says: “I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0411] Rom. 8].

Therefore it must be noted what are the sufferings of the first time. There are sufferings of the first time; sufferings of this time; sufferings of the future time; and sufferings of no time. The first are temporal misery; the second [Col. 0412B] voluntary penitence; the third are the flame of purgatory; the fourth, the distress of infernal torments. The first came through the transgression of the first parent; the second effect reconciliation; the third supply for penitence’s imperfection; the fourth entail eternal condemnation.

Under the first: “Every creature groans and labours in birth until now” [Note: [Col. 0411] ibid.]. Among these Job groans, discovering a defective beginning, a miserable exile, and a sad end: the first in being born, the second in living, the third in dying. “Man,” he says [Note: [Col. 0411] Job 14], “born of woman”: behold the first. “Living for a short time”: behold the second. “Is filled with many miseries”: behold the third. And he adds [Note: [Col. 0411] ibid.]: “He comes forth like a flower”: behold the first. “And is crushed”: behold the second. “And flees like a shadow”: behold [Col. 0412C] the third. These are groaned over by those afflicted with continual miseries, oppressed with more grievous tribulations, and suspended in desire for heavenly glory. Regarding the first, Job said: “Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived” [Note: [Col. 0411] Job 3]. Regarding the second, he said: “Why did You bring me forth from the womb? Would that I had been consumed, so that no eye might see me” [Note: [Col. 0411] Job 10]. Regarding the third, he said: “Why is light given to the wretched, and life to those who are in bitterness of soul, who wait for death and it does not come, as though digging for treasure, and rejoice exceedingly when they find the grave?” [Note: [Col. 0411] Job 3]. These are the sufferings of the first time.

The sufferings of this time are voluntary penitence, [Col. 0412D] concerning which it is said: “Afflicted in heart because of our sins, let us await our end with tears.” Its order is this: first we must renounce evil works; second, wash the heart by tearful confession; third, raise to the Lord the face—that is, the conscience—which was formerly bowed down by sin; fourth, show ourselves steadfast in good purpose; fifth, consign the hardships of penitence to forgetfulness through love of heavenly things. Hence Job: “If you remove the iniquity that is in your hand” [Note: [Col. 0411] Job 11]: behold the first. “And injustice is not in your tent” [Note: [Col. 0411] ibid.]: behold the second. “Then you shall be able to lift up your face [Col. 0413A] without spot” [Note: [Col. 0413] Job 14]: behold the third. “And you shall be steadfast and shall not fear” [Note: [Col. 0413] ibid.]: behold the fourth. “You shall also forget misery” [Note: [Col. 0413] ibid.]: behold the fifth.

He shows what fruit follows from penitence, adding: “Then at evening the noonday brightness shall arise, and when you think yourself consumed, you shall rise like the morning star” [Note: [Col. 0413] ibid.]. This sense occurs in the Law, where it is said: “If there is a bronze vessel, it shall be scoured and washed with water” [Note: [Col. 0413] Lev. 6], and you shall be clean. Bronze is resonant. Therefore the bronze vessel is the penitent in prayer; it is scoured in satisfaction and washed with water in tearful confession. One is clean through perseverance in innocence; and thus the sufferings of purgatorial fire need not be feared.

Oh, how much more advantageous it would be to burn now in such a flame than to blaze miserably in purgatorial [Col. 0413B] fire, in which the Lord will be “like a refining fire, cleansing silver; and He shall cleanse the sons of Levi in a spirit of burning” [Note: [Col. 0413] Mal. 3]. If, therefore, you undergo the sufferings of penitence in this way, the prophet’s words shall be fulfilled in you: “When you walk through fire, you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not blaze upon you; for I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0413] Isa. 43].

There wood, hay, and straw shall be burned [Note: [Col. 0413] 1 Cor. 3]: that is, light sins, which are venial, like straw; or somewhat more serious sins, like hay; and the most serious, though still venial, like wood. There “the day of the Lord shall test what sort each person’s work is, because it shall be revealed by fire. If anyone’s work burns, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” [Note: [Col. 0413] ibid.]. Oh, how [Col. 0413C] much safer it would be now to build gold, silver, and precious stones [Note: [Col. 0413] ibid.]: namely, charity in the heart, innocence in conduct, and the radiance of good work in exemplary display. For such persons do not fear purgatorial fire.

The first sufferings, then, as we have said, came into the world through the transgression of the first human being; the second effect reconciliation. These three make up for the imperfection of the first. But much more urgently must those sufferings be avoided which entail eternal condemnation. Do you think Job saw these when he said: “Let me alone, that I may weep for my pain, before I go to the dark land covered by death’s gloom” [Note: [Col. 0413] Job 10], where there will be perpetual fire and perpetual cold, because they shall pass from snowy cold into excessive heat [Note: [Col. 0413] Job 24]; where perpetual worms [Col. 0413D] shall gnaw the wretched, because “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” [Note: [Col. 0413] Isa. 66]; where there will be eternal hunger and thirst. Hence: “My servants shall eat, and you shall hunger; My servants shall drink, and you shall thirst” [Note: [Col. 0413] Isa. 65]. There will be continual stench, because “fire and sulphur and a stormy blast are the portion of their cup” [Note: [Col. 0413] Ps. 10]. There will be the scourges of torturers, because there the sinner shall be delivered “to the torturers until he pays the whole debt” [Note: [Col. 0413] Matt. 18]. There will be intolerable horror, utter darkness, and continual weeping. Hence: “Cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” [Note: [Col. 0413] ibid.]. There the limbs of the dissolute shall be bound with fiery chains.

[Col. 0414A] It is therefore better to labour now in order to avoid these things than to endure them without end. In all these things He rebukes us, that we may return to Him, as is found in Job: “Do not reject His rebukes; for He wounds and heals; He strikes, and His hands make whole” [Note: [Col. 0413] Job 5]. And as he continues:

“In six tribulations He shall deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you,” which he enumerates thus: “In famine He shall deliver you from death, and in war from the hand of the sword; you shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and shall not fear calamity when it comes; in devastation and famine you shall laugh, and you shall not fear the beast of the earth.”

Let us therefore begin the exposition from the beginning: “In famine,” he says, “He shall deliver you from death, and in war from the hand of the sword.” This famine is the desire to please God. It will deliver you from the death [Col. 0414B] by which those perish who strive to please the world. This war is that of temptations. In it we are delivered from the hand of the devil’s sword, lest we be wounded. For the enemy said: “I will pursue and overtake; I will divide the spoils; my soul shall be filled. I will draw my sword; my hand shall kill them” [Note: [Col. 0413] Exod. 15].

The devil pursues when he wearies us with suggestions; he overtakes us when we consent; he divides the spoils when we offer our members as instruments of sin to the suggestion; his soul is filled when, giving ourselves to idleness and pleasures, we comply with his will; he draws his sword when we are held in despair; his hand kills when we remain obstinate unto death. It follows: “You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue,” [Col. 0414C] lest slanderers have any evil thing to say against you. Or at judgment: “Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire” [Note: [Col. 0413] Matt. 25]. It follows: “You shall not fear calamity,” namely when unexpected scourges of God come, as upon Job. It follows: “In devastation and famine you shall laugh.” Devastation is so called from laying waste. For then the wretched shall be devastated, because “fire shall go before Him and burn His enemies round about” [Note: [Col. 0413] Ps. 96], and they shall be handed over to the pains of hell for torture. Then famine will be when they desire to die and death flees from them [Note: [Col. 0413] Rev. 9]. It follows: “You shall not fear the beast of the earth.” The beast is called, as it were, *vastia*, from laying waste: namely, the devil, the author of torments. All these “sufferings are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0413] Rom. 8].

[Col. 0414D] Glory is called past, present, and future. The past was in Paradise; the present is in the human heart; the future shall be in the kingdom. The first consisted in the temperance of the first state; the second, in a pure conscience; the third, in the cessation of this misery’s affliction. The first passed away and became old, because the first parents “changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay” [Note: [Col. 0413] Ps. 105]. Thus “all flesh became hay, and all its glory like the flower of hay” [Note: [Col. 0413] Isa. 40]. Job sighed for its renewal when he said: “Our glory shall always be renewed, and the bow in our hand shall be restored” [Note: [Col. 0413] Job 29].

[Col. 0415A] Of the second, which is in the heart—namely, conscience—it is said: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0415] 2 Cor. 1]. In accordance with this: “Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0415] 2 Cor. 10]. Of the third: “I shall be satisfied when Your glory appears” [Note: [Col. 0415] Ps. 16]. The first, therefore, is born from us; the second is revealed to us; the third shall be revealed in us. The first is born from us through the sufferings of the first time; the second is revealed in us through the cloud of the sufferings of this time, which will in some measure be made manifest through the sufferings of future time: “Fire shall test what sort each person’s work is” [Note: [Col. 0415] 1 Cor. 3]. The third shall be revealed in us when, these sufferings having ceased, there remain in the wretched sufferings of no time—that is, unending sufferings.

The first, therefore, are not worthy of future glory; the third [Col. 0415B] are worthy of future glory; the fourth are wholly unworthy of future glory. The second, however, are not equal to future glory, namely because they cannot suffice to merit it unless the grace of God assists them. And that which is now hidden from us shall be revealed after judgment—though the cloud of our ignorance still keeps it concealed—when whoever is in Christ is already made manifest. Hence it is written: “After the tabernacle was completed, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the Lord filled that tabernacle” [Note: [Col. 0415] 3 Kings 8]. This tabernacle was Christ’s body: completed in the Passion; covered by the cloud in the guarding of the tomb; filled with grace in the Resurrection.

[Col. 0415C]

> Your neck [or, according to another reading, *cervix*, “nape”] is like the tower of David, built with battlements. A thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty.

[CARD.] The neck of the blessed Virgin signifies the loftiness of her exalted state. On account of it she is called the tower of David, which Christ David built and raised in Jerusalem—that is, in His Church—so that she might be a defence and refuge for sinners. This tower was built with battlements. These battlements are virtues and graces, dignities and prerogatives, purity of intentions and holiness of works, the power of prayers and the merits of deeds, through which the blessed Virgin protects the penitent sinner and overcomes the enemy.

A thousand shields hang from it, all [Col. 0415D] the armour of the mighty. The shields are virtues that repel the darts of the tempter: namely, virtues by which the assaults of temptation are resisted. Prudence is a shield repelling the snares of the devil. Likewise fortitude is a shield resisting the attacks of adversities. Temperance is a shield repelling the fiery darts of carnal desires. But the armour of the mighty is the works of virtues, by which the devil is attacked and defeated as with sword and spear: such as works of justice, piety, and mercy, prayers, and alms. He therefore says that a thousand shields and all the armour [Col. 0416A] of the mighty hang from her, for she supplies us with help for our defence and for attacking enemies, and with examples of every virtue. It follows:

> Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a doe, which feed among lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline.

[THO.] The same preachers who above were denoted by the names of eyes, teeth, and neck are now expressed by the term breasts. They are rightly called eyes, because they perceive the hidden mysteries of the sacraments; teeth, because, by reproving the wicked, they mortify them and convey them, once chewed, into the body of the Church; neck, because they minister to the Church, as it were, a vital breath, by preaching eternal joys. They are aptly called breasts because they pour into those still little in Christ the milk of the saving word [Col. 0416B]. They are like young roes because, with the pure eyes of their heart, they discern what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided. Young roes have great strength in the swiftness of their feet and the keenness of their eyes. By them are signified those who show the unlearned the way of knowledge and virtue. They are fittingly twins, because they are begotten in one faith and from one mother, the Church. They feed among lilies—that is, among the flowers of the sacred Scriptures—until the day breathes forth, that is, until the end of the age. For after that day has breathed forth, of which David says, “One day in thy courts is better than a thousand” [Note: [Col. 0415] Ps. 83], there will no longer be a place for teaching; but the shadows will decline—that is, when the darkness of this world has been consumed, “the righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father” [Note: [Col. 0415] Matt. 13].

The bride’s two breasts [Col. 0416C] are compassion and rejoicing-with-others. The first concerns evils, the second goods. One must have compassion for one’s neighbour in four matters: poverty, sickness, temptation, and affliction—poverty among those lacking, bodily sickness, temptation by suggestions, and affliction by persecutors—giving, first, assistance; second, consolation; third, counsel; fourth, aid. Job enumerates, concerning the first, the works of mercy which he performed: “If I ate my morsel alone,” he says [Note: [Col. 0415] Job 31], etc. Concerning the second: We command that the sick be visited. Concerning the third, Paul says: “Let no temptation take us except such as is human” [Note: [Col. 0415] I Cor. 10]. Concerning the fourth, Job says: “The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me” [Note: [Col. 0415] Job 29].

Yet poverty is fourfold. The first is poverty of possessions; the second, of understanding; the third, of fruitfulness; the fourth, of spirit. Of the first: “You always have the poor with you” [Note: [Col. 0415] Matt. 26]. Of the second: “You say, ‘I am rich and have become wealthy,’ while you are wretched and poor” [Note: [Col. 0415] Rev. 3]. Of the third: “Let thy mercies quickly come before us, for we have become exceedingly poor” [Note: [Col. 0415] Ps. 78]. Of the fourth: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0415] Matt. 5]. The first is burdensome, the second shameful, the third culpable, the fourth glorious. The first is to be endured, the second supplied, the third fled from, the fourth embraced. The first is to be endured through patience; the second supplied through wisdom; the third fled from [Col. 0417A] because of its barrenness; the fourth embraced because it leads to blessedness. And this is concerning the breast of compassion.

There follows concerning the breast of rejoicing-with-others, which concerns heavenly goods. There are three things in which we ought to rejoice with our brother: if he is freed from sins, at the progress of religious life, and at the expectation of eternal salvation. Of the first it is said: “Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma which I had lost” [Note: [Col. 0417] Luke 11]. For there is joy among the angels over one sinner doing penance [Note: [Col. 0417] Luke 15]. And concerning the prodigal son: “It was fitting,” he says, “to rejoice and feast, because this my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” [Note: [Col. 0417] Ibid.]. Of the second the Apostle says: “I thank God that you were once slaves of sin, but you obeyed from the heart that form [Col. 0417B] of teaching into which you were delivered” [Note: [Col. 0417] Rom. 6]. Of the third: “I rejoiced at those things which were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord’” [Note: [Col. 0417] Ps. 121]. He says, “We shall go,” not “I shall go,” because he rejoices at his neighbour’s salvation as at his own.

These breasts are like young roes, which are swift; this pertains to the swift and cheerful activity of compassion. They see keenly, which pertains to the discerning inspection of rejoicing-with-others.

“They feed among lilies.” The lily has a fragrance, which is found in the work of compassion; it has delightfulness in appearance, which is found in rejoicing-with-others, until the day of eternal brightness breathes forth and the shadows of this misery and darkness decline. Again, the swiftness of young roes pertains to the prompt fulfilment of obedience; their keen sight [Col. 0417C] to contemplation of oneself, of the angel, and of God. But we ought to hold, wipe, and inspect the mirror in which we see these things. For it is the reason of the human heart which we must hold, lest, falling to earth, it cling there through love; wipe, lest it be soiled in the useless dust of thoughts; inspect, lest it turn the eye of its intention toward vain pursuits.

In this mirror there are, as it were, three heavens: for the dignity of the human spirit is one thing, that of the angelic spirit another, and the excellence of the divine Spirit another. The human spirit is subject to guilt and punishment; the angelic is free from both; but the divine Spirit, which made both, surpasses them beyond all comparison. This is to ascend to three heavens. We may distinguish the knowledge of God which can be had here by three degrees, and, according to the threefold distinction of those degrees, divide it among [Col. 0417D] three heavens. For God is seen in one way through faith, known in another through reason, and perceived in another through contemplation. The first vision belongs to the first heaven, the second to the second, the third to the third. The first is below reason, the second alongside reason, the third above reason. Men can ascend to the first and second, but not to that which is above reason except in an ecstasy of the human mind.

I believe that these two young roes are Peter and Paul, who were strong in swiftness of course and keenness of sight. For they were swift to aid [Col. 0418A] their neighbour and obey God. They were strong in keenness of sight through the knowledge of God and the illumination of miracles. Hear their obedience: “Come after me,” says the Lord. “And they, leaving their nets and boat, followed him” [Note: [Col. 0417] Matt. 4]. And Paul: “Lord, what dost thou wish me to do?” [Note: [Col. 0417] Acts 9]. Hear their keen sight: “These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands shining before the Lord, that by this keenness of sight they might explore the world” [Note: [Col. 0417] Office of the Church]. Of them it is written: “Joshua sent two spies to Jericho” [Note: [Col. 0417] Josh. 2]. They not only explored, but lamented and implored. They explored the devil’s devices; they lamented human folly; they implored spiritual benefits for human beings: first, that they might detect the cunning of demons; second, that they might bring follies back [Col. 0418B] into harmony with good conduct; third, that they might obtain wisdom for men. First, that they might detect when the angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light [Note: [Col. 0417] II Cor. 11]; second, that the spiritual belly might sound like a harp for Moab, and the inward parts for the wall of baked brick [Note: [Col. 0417] Isa. 16]; third, that Wisdom might build herself a house in us and send servants and maidservants to call to the citadel and the walls of the city [Note: [Col. 0417] Prov. 9].

Paul taught us to explore when he said: “Do not believe every spirit” [Note: [Col. 0417] I John 4], for “the angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light” [Note: [Col. 0417] II Cor. 11]. Peter likewise had explored the devil’s snares in Simon Magus when he said: “May thy money perish with thee” [Note: [Col. 0417] Acts 8]. Paul lamented when he said: “I say weeping, [they are] enemies [Col. 0418C] of the Crucified One, whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame” [Note: [Col. 0417] Phil. 3]. And Peter: “The Lord looked upon him, and he went out and wept bitterly” [Note: [Col. 0417] Matt. 26]. Paul implored when he said: “I pray that your charity may abound more and more in understanding and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0417] Phil. 1]. And Peter: “The grace of the Lord be with all of you, those who are in Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0417] I Pet. 5].

If we are true explorers, we ought to explore hell, explore the world, explore our heart, and explore heaven.

Thus in hell we see intolerable straits; in the world, deceitful allurements; in the heart, manifold fantasies; in heaven, incomparable delights. The damned are afflicted by the first; fools are left behind by the second; the prudent are drawn by the third; the eternally blessed are delighted by the fourth [Col. 0418D]. He had explored hell who said: “Let me alone a little, that I may bewail my sorrow before I go to the land of darkness, covered with the gloom of death” [Note: [Col. 0417] Job 10]. He had explored the world who said: “Everything that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life” [Note: [Col. 0417] I John 2]. And the heart, he who said: “In the night I meditated with my heart” [Note: [Col. 0417] Ps. 76], etc. And heaven, he who said: “To thee have I lifted up my eyes, who dwellest in the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0417] Ps. 122].

In this order the spies of Jericho proceeded [Note: [Col. 0417] Josh. 2]. First they entered the house of Rahab, which [Col. 0419A] is called pride, namely hell; second, they hid in flax-stalks, that is, in the birth of the world; third, having opened the window—that is, having inspected the heart—they hung in it a scarlet cord, namely the remembrance of Christ’s blood; fourth, they went up into the mountainous country, namely by looking upon heaven. First they were spies of Egypt: “By the life of Pharaoh,” he says, “you are spies” [Note: [Col. 0419] Gen. 42]. Second, spies of Jericho. Third, spies of Laish [Note: [Col. 0419] Judg. 18], which is interpreted “for itself.” Fourth, spies of Tarshish [Note: [Col. 0419] III Kings 10], which is interpreted “the exploration of joy,” in that they were explorers. Second, they are the bride’s eyes: hence, “Thy eyes are doves’ eyes” [Note: [Col. 0419] Cant. 1]. In that they were lamenters, they are two springs, namely Jor and Dan, which make the Jordan; in that they were implorers, they are two trumpets by which the people were summoned [Col. 0419B] with a knowing blast, namely prayer and preaching.

In them there was a commendable pattern of mutual love, an example of edification, the strength of constancy, and the expectation of devout hope. For the first, they were “two cherubim above the mercy-seat, looking at one another with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat” [Note: [Col. 0419] Exod. 25]. Hence: “Glorious princes of the earth, how they loved one another in their life; so in death they were not divided” [Note: [Col. 0419] Office of the Church]. Therefore let us love one another, because “charity is from God” [Note: [Col. 0419] I John 4]. For the second, they were Obdab, which means “my father is protection,” and Besdechel, which means “in the shadow of God” [names uncertain as printed]. Hence Paul: “I planted, Apollos watered” [Note: [Col. 0419] I Cor. 3]. Hence: “When you enter the land which the Lord will give you, build an altar to the Lord of stones which iron has not touched” [Note: [Col. 0419] Deut. 27]. For the third [Col. 0419C] they were the two pillars in Solomon’s porch: Boaz, meaning “in strength,” and Jachin, meaning “firmness” [Note: [Col. 0419] III Kings 7]. Hence: “Who shall separate us from the charity of God? Tribulation, or distress?” [Note: [Col. 0419] Rom. 8], etc. Hence: “Be strong in battle.” For the fourth, they were two twin kids of the roe, which feed among lilies. Hence the Apostle: “Forgetting what is behind, I stretch forth to those things which are before, toward the prize of the heavenly calling” [Note: [Col. 0419] Phil. 3]. Behold the explorers. There are also lamenters.

It should be noted that there are shepherds who do not hesitate, by their bad example, to provoke their subjects to sin; there are those who neglect to devote themselves to their subjects; and there are those who labour to call their subjects back from error [Col. 0419D]. The first laugh, the second sleep, the third mourn. The first despise God’s wisdom; the second have received God’s grace in vain; the third await God’s mercy. Of the first it is said: “They shall eat the sins of my people, and shall lift up their souls to their iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0419] Hos. 4]. These laugh—or rather, they mock the Lord. Hence the prophet: “Feed the flock of slaughter, whose owners killed them and did not grieve; they sold them, saying, ‘Blessed be God; [Col. 0420A] we have become rich’” [Note: [Col. 0419] Zech. 11]. These likewise despise God’s patience. Hence the Apostle: “Dost thou despise the riches of God’s goodness, longsuffering, and patience?” [Note: [Col. 0419] Rom. 2]. These are the leaders whom the Lord commanded to be hanged on the gallows because they caused the people to sin. These are the elders who wished to violate Susanna [Note: [Col. 0419] Dan. 13], of whom Jeremiah says: “May the Lord make thee like Ahab and Zedekiah, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the furnace of the Chaldeans” [Note: [Col. 0419] Jer. 29]. Hence Isaiah: “Every head is sick and every heart sorrowful” [Note: [Col. 0419] Isa. 1].

To the second it is said: “You took what was fat, clothed yourselves in the wool, and ate the milk; what was weak you did not strengthen” [Note: [Col. 0419] Ezek. 34]. These sleep, and would that they slept between the midst of the lots [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 67]. But they are those men of whom it is said: “While men slept, [Col. 0420B] the enemy came and oversowed tares” [Note: [Col. 0419] Matt. 13]. Let them therefore hear: “He who keeps Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep” [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 120]. Hence the Lord rebukes the sleeping Peter, saying: “Simon, dost thou sleep? Couldst thou not watch one hour with me?” [Note: [Col. 0419] Matt. 26]. Let them hear that to shepherds keeping night watches over their flock an angel appeared, announcing Christ’s birth [Note: [Col. 0419] Luke 2]. Let them hear David: “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids” [Note: [Col. 0419] Ps. 131]. These receive God’s grace in vain, as the Apostle says: “See that you do not receive God’s grace in vain” [Note: [Col. 0419] II Cor. 6]. Such persons are like that servant who hid his lord’s money [Note: [Col. 0419] Luke 19], not attending to Daniel’s saying: “Those who have instructed many unto righteousness shall shine like stars unto everlasting eternities” [Col. 0420C] [Note: [Col. 0419] Dan. 12]. They have not, like the faithful and prudent servant, distributed in due season the measure of wheat to their fellow servants [Note: [Col. 0419] Luke 12]. Let them hear Solomon: “A hidden treasure and hidden knowledge: what profit is there in either?” [Note: [Col. 0419] Ecclus. 41]. The philosopher says: “Knowledge is a noble possession,” etc.

The third strive to call sinners back from their follies. Hence Paul: “Arise, thou who sleepest, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten thee” [Note: [Col. 0419] Eph. 41; evidently Eph. 5]. And Peter: “I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” [Note: [Col. 0419] I Pet. 2]. These mourn out of compassion. Hence, between the porch and the altar the priests wept, saying: “Spare, O Lord, spare thy people” [Note: [Col. 0419] Joel 2]. Hence the Lord, “seeing the city, [Col. 0420D] wept over it” [Note: [Col. 0419] Luke 19]. And David wept over Saul and Jonathan his son [Note: [Col. 0419] II Kings 1]. And the Lord says to Samuel: “How long wilt thou mourn for Saul?” [Note: [Col. 0419] I Kings 16]. These await God’s mercy, who says: “I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction” [Note: [Col. 0419] Jer. 29]. Otherwise we lament the Church as desolate, saying: “We have become her princes like rams, finding no pasture” [Note: [Col. 0419] Lam. 1]. And Isaiah: “All are dumb dogs, unable to bark” [Note: [Col. 0419] Isa. 56]. Such teachers, who [Col. 0421A] mourn from compassion, are like Joseph, who severely afflicted his brothers so that they might be punished as they had sinned in selling him; and, entering the chamber of his heart, he wept because through compassion he could not restrain himself [Note: [Col. 0421] Gen. 43]. There follows concerning implorers.

The first implore pardon, the second righteousness, the third their homeland. The first is the body of mercy, the second of grace, the third of glory; the first is for penitents, the second for pilgrims, the third for those who sigh; the first gives holiness, the second fruitfulness in virtues, the third the blessedness of glory. Of the first: “Have mercy on thy city Jerusalem, the city of thy rest” [Note: [Col. 0421] Ecclus. 36]. Of the second: “Fill Zion with thy ineffable powers” [Note: [Col. 0421] Ibid.]. Of the third: “And [fill] [Col. 0421B] thy people with thy glory” [Note: [Col. 0421] Ibid.]. By the first, live soberly; by the second, righteously; by the third, devoutly. Of these three the Lord says: “Seek and you shall find; ask and you shall receive; knock and it shall be opened to you” [Note: [Col. 0421] Luke 11]. Seek pardon and you shall receive mercy; ask for righteousness and you shall receive an abundance of virtues; knock through perseverance, and God will open to you the gate of the kingdom.

Those who are in the first degree are “the two cherubim looking toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat” [Note: [Col. 0421] Exod. 25]. Those in the second are two silver trumpets which gather the people by their blast [Note: [Col. 0421] Num. 10]. Those in the third are the two sons of brightness who stand before the ruler of the whole earth. The first are the two olive trees, namely those imploring mercy; the second are the two lampstands shining before the Lord through righteousness; [Col. 0421C] the third have power to shut heaven with clouds and open its gates, that they may bring people into glory.

It should be known, moreover, that sometimes superiors implore for inferiors, sometimes inferiors for superiors, and sometimes equals for equals. The first is from humility, the second from usefulness, the third from brotherly charity. In the first manner Moses implored for the people of Israel, saying: “Either blot me out of the book of life, or forgive them this offence” [Note: [Col. 0421] Exod. 32]. In the second the people prayed for Jonathan, saying: “As the Lord lives, not a hair of his head shall fall, because today he has worked with God” [Note: [Col. 0421] I Kings 14]. In the third, the Shunammite woman implored Elisha for her son, saying: “As the Lord lives, and as thy soul lives, I will not [Col. 0421D] leave thee” [Note: [Col. 0421] IV Kings 4].

Therefore, in imitation of these persons, explore, lament, implore. Be an explorer of the heart’s secrets; a lamenter over the stench of discovered filth; an implorer of the aid of the merciful God. For by the first you will have knowledge of yourself; in the second you will endure shame for God; in the third you will receive consolation from God. If, then, you wish to become an explorer of the heart, do not fear this saying: “The heart of man is perverse and miserable; and who has known it?” [Note: [Col. 0421] Jer. 17]. But hear: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” [Note: [Col. 0421] Isa. 46]. Detect, therefore, sin in your heart [Col. 0422A] and say: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” [Note: [Col. 0421] Ps. 50]. For Laban, whose name means “whitening,” that is, the devil, searches Jacob’s baggage and Rachel’s tent and will not find his idols; rather, the seeker’s anxious effort will be deceived [Note: [Col. 0421] Gen. 31].

Therefore endure shame for sins for a moment, lest you suffer it eternally. For a moment, that you may say: “The shame of my face has covered me” [Note: [Col. 0421] Ps. 43]. Not eternally, but say: “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped; I shall not be confounded for ever” [Note: [Col. 0421] Ps. 30]. It follows that you implore God’s help: help for the strengthening of faith; help for the removal of sin; help to endure tribulation; help to receive the vision of God. For the first, say the Gospel’s words: [Col. 0422B] “Lord, help my unbelief” [Note: [Col. 0421] Mark 9]; for the second: “Help us, O God our Saviour, and for the glory of thy name deliver us” [Note: [Col. 0421] Ps. 78]; for the third: “The Lord is a refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations which have found us exceedingly” [Note: [Col. 0421] Ps. 45]; for the fourth: “The stream’s rush makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0421] Ibid.], in which there shall be no shadow of worldly vanity, but the day of supreme truth shall breathe forth.

“Thy two breasts, two twin young roes which feed among lilies, until the day breathes forth and the shadows decline.”

[CAR.] The two breasts of the blessed Virgin, from which, as it were, the sweetness of the milk of kindly aid is drawn, are the dispositions of piety and mercy. Like roes, with keen light they consider both how much help another needs [Col. 0422C] and, through such consideration, they range about; and through swift aid they run quickly to help, like young roes. Because of the various modes of assistance, they are signified by young roes, which are distinguished by a beautiful variety. They are also called twins, that is, companionable and alike, because the benefits of mercy and piety are very much like one another and proceed, as it were, from one source. They die and fail among the ungrateful; they are nourished and flourish in those who, because of the whiteness and fragrance of good works, are likened to lilies.

These breasts of the blessed Virgin do not cease to offer their milk throughout this present life, until the day breathes forth—that is, until that day comes which will breathe the spirit of life and the life of glory into bodies refashioned from [Col. 0422D] dust—and until the shadows of present misery decline and fail. There follows in the person of the Virgin:

“I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hills of Lebanon, and I will speak to my bride.”

[THO.] In myrrh is expressed the mortification of the flesh or the endurance of sufferings for piety’s sake; in incense, the devotion of prayer rising on high. But the mountain of myrrh and the hill of incense are the loftiness of mind of those who both conquer the flesh and ardently raise themselves to the love of heavenly things. To this mountain [Col. 0423A] and hill the Lord goes, because he deigns often to visit and dwell in the hearts of those who pursue virtues. This is plainly to say: “I shall frequent the hills and glorify them by pious devotion and illumination. And I shall speak to my bride” with instruction, consolation, and promise—and this by inward inspiration.

Again, he says, “I will go for myself.” He goes for himself because singular love admits no partner into its secret. The bridegroom is God; the bride is the soul: a bride because she has received the pledge of gifts of grace; a bride because she is joined to him in chaste love; a bride because she is made fruitful with the offspring of virtues. Every soul has received a pledge from this bridegroom. But there is a common pledge and a special pledge. It is common because we have been born, because we feel, because we understand, [Col. 0423B] because we discern. It is a special pledge because we have been reborn, because we have received the remission of sins, because we have received the charisms of virtues; and whatever good each person has is for that person a pledge.

“I will go for myself,” he says, “to the mountain of myrrh.” Myrrh, which is bitter, signifies death. Lebanon, which is interpreted “whitening,” signifies purity of heart. This is the way by which the bridegroom comes to the bride: namely, the mountain of myrrh and the hills of Lebanon. For first, by abstinence he kills the concupiscence of the flesh; then, by purity of heart, he wipes away the mind’s ignorance; finally, coming as on the third day to converse with the bride, he kindles the soul with his desire. He rightly said “mountain of myrrh,” because in affliction we ought to be constant; and “hills of Lebanon,” because in success in virtues we ought to be humble. On the mountain of myrrh we receive strength against the concupiscence of the flesh; on the hills of Lebanon, illumination of the mind against ignorance; in conversation with the bride, charity against ill will. Power pertains to the Father, wisdom to the Son, charity to the Holy Spirit.

“I will speak,” he says, “to my bride.” God speaks to the soul in two ways: differently to the harlot and differently to the bride; differently to the ugly and differently to the beautiful; differently to the sinful woman and differently to the justified. He rebukes the ugliness of the former; he praises the beauty of the latter. By rebuking he shakes the former with fear; by praising he kindles the latter to love. He speaks to the former when he shows her her stains; to the latter, when he recalls the gifts which he has bestowed. “I will speak,” he says, [Col. 0423D] “to my bride.”

Again, three things are set forth: the mountain of myrrh, the hill of Lebanon or incense, and conversation with the bride. To the first the Beloved comes, enduring the calamity of the world; to the second, interceding with the Father for us; to the third, bringing preaching. In the first, by his example, he invites us to the bitterness of suffering; in the second, he sets before us the pattern of prayer; in the third, he teaches us the way of salvation. Hear the first: “Surely he himself bore our infirmities and carried our offences” [Note: [Col. 0423] Isa. 53]. Of the second: “He prayed for transgressors [Col. 0424A] that they might not perish” [Note: [Col. 0423] Ibid.]. For the third, the ancient Fathers cried: “Come to teach us the way of prudence” [Note: [Col. 0423] Office of the Church].

He came first to the valley of myrrh, second to the hill of myrrh, third to the mountain of myrrh: to the valley, by taking on the weakness of our flesh; to the hill, by enduring tribulations and mockery; to the mountain, by bearing the Passion. The valley to which he came was the Virgin’s humility; the hill, the holiness of the righteous; the mountain, the loftiness of martyrdom. Therefore he came to the valley of Mary, to the hill of John the Baptist, and to the mountain of Calvary: to the first through the Incarnation; to the second through conformity to an austere manner of life; to the third through the Passion. Of the valley it is said: “Joseph was sent from the valley of Hebron”—which means “eternal vision”—[Col. 0424B] “to visit his brothers” [Note: [Col. 0423] Gen. 37]. Of the hills it is said: “The hills shall be girded with exultation” [Note: [Col. 0423] Ps. 64]. Of Christ the mountain, who ascended Mount Calvary, it is said: “The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be above the summit of the mountains, and all hills shall flow unto it” [Note: [Col. 0423] Isa. 2].

Therefore, to this Mount Calvary, which is called the mountain of myrrh because of the bitterness of Christ’s Passion, the Beloved came—for man, for the angel, and for himself. “I will go for myself,” he says, so that it may be understood wholly as something acquired, that is, for advantage. He came to man for necessity, to the angel for delight, and to himself for exaltation: for necessity, that man might be redeemed; for delight, that the angelic ruin might be repaired; for exaltation, that the Beloved might be exalted. Of the first the ancient Fathers cried: “Come to redeem us with an outstretched [Col. 0424C] arm” [Note: [Col. 0423] Office of the Church]. Because of the second, at Christ’s birth there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” [Note: [Col. 0423] Luke 2]. For the third David said: “I will exalt thee, O Lord, because thou hast received me” [Note: [Col. 0423] Ps. 29]. And: “I will exalt thee, my God and King, and will bless thy name for ever and ever” [Note: [Col. 0423] Ps. 144].

It should be noted that there is first myrrh, choice myrrh, and most excellent myrrh. The first belongs to the sick, the second to the righteous, the third to martyrs. The first consists in the distress of penitential satisfaction; the choice myrrh is not penitential, but an austerity freely undertaken for the sake of more fervent religious devotion, amid the beauty of virtues; the most excellent is in the experience of suffering. Of the first: “The bridegroom’s lips dripping first myrrh” [Col. 0424D] [Note: [Col. 0423] Cant. 5]. For the bridegroom’s lips are called the lips of the sinner confessing his sins in bitterness of soul. Of the second: “Like choice myrrh I gave sweetness of fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0423] Ecclus. 24]. Of the third: “My hands distilled myrrh, and my fingers were full of most excellent myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0423] Cant. 5].

This threefold myrrh is not simple but compounded. The first is compounded with the astringency of wine; the second with gold and incense; the third with the sweetness of spices. The wine of the first is austerity in penance; the gold of the second is the splendour of charity [Col. 0425A]; incense is the fragrant aroma of prayers. The spices of the third are an abundance of heavenly savour. As a figure of the first, the Jews gave the Lord wine mixed with myrrh to drink [Note: [Col. 0425] Mark 15], so that myrrh signifies contrition of heart and wine the austerity of outward penance. As a figure of the second, the Magi offered the Lord gold, incense, and myrrh [Note: [Col. 0425] Matt. 2]. Of the third it is said: “Myrrh and stacte and cassia [come] from thy garments, from ivory houses” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 44].

There are hills of the devil; there are hills of the world; there are hills of Lebanon, or of incense, which are the same thing. The first are those who imitate the devil in pride; the second, those who are elevated in worldly dignities and power; the third follow Christ in righteousness. Of the first Isaiah says: “Every mountain and hill shall be humbled” [Note: [Col. 0425] Isa. 40].
