Of the second Habakkuk says: [Col. 0425B] “The hills of the world are bowed down by the paths of his eternity” [Note: [Col. 0425] Hab. 3]. Of the third: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 71]. And David: “The hills shall be girded with exultation” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 64].

Christ comes to the first to grant humility; to the second, to remove inequity; to the third, to teach truth: humility in respect of himself, equity of judgment, and truth for knowing the way of faith, charity, and hope. Humility in respect of himself is obtained through confession; equity of judgment is dictated by reason; truth for knowledge of the way is gained under the guidance of prudence. The first hills lift themselves up in pride when the head is raised, the tongue loosened, and the hand extended: the head is raised in order to scorn, the tongue loosened in order to revile, the hand extended in order to oppress. [Col. 0425C] But confession cuts off the head—that is, foolish thought, which is the beginning of sin—in contrition; the tongue, in the utterance of sin; the hand, in satisfaction.

All this is signified by that deed of Judas Maccabaeus. For Demetrius, whose name means “excessively persecuting,” that is, the devil, sent Nicanor, whose name means “standing lamp,” that is, exaltation of heart, against Judas, whose name means “confession.” Nicanor commanded elephants whose bones lack joints, because pride is inflexible. But Judas killed him and cut off his head, tongue, and hands [Note: [Col. 0425] II Macc. 15].

But in the sinner’s heart there are three scruples which repress confession: fear, pain, and shame. Fear causes despair because of the magnitude of sin; pain because of the austerity of penance; shame because of disgracefulness. Therefore, when one recalls the shameful things one has done, one rightly blushes to confess; when one considers their multitude, one rightly groans in pain; when one considers their magnitude, one rightly languishes in fear. These scruples must be polished away like a stone. In the polishing of stones three things are used: oil, a stone, and a hand. Oil is poured out, the stone is rolled over it, and one hand is moved by drawing the other. Therefore the oil of kindness softens harshness. Persistence in penance, like a stone, wears away the scruples of sins. The purity of conscience, like a hand [Col. 0426A], wipes away stains. This is the oil of the Spirit, this is the cornerstone, this is the right hand of God the Father.

The first softens, the second presses, the third draws. Thus first God softens pain, second presses down fear of mind, third extends the right hand through the works of his hands. This is concerning the first hills. Second, he invites to equity; and this happens thus: first one must consult reason, second separate the just from the unjust, third render to each person what is his. Consult, then, Solomon judging the harlot women [Note: [Col. 0425] III Kings 3]. First he commanded that a sword be brought, second that the infant be divided, third that to each her portion be given. This is concerning the second hills.

Third, he invites to truth, that they may hold the way of faith, hope, and charity; that they may know what they ought to believe, love, and [Col. 0426B] hope, lest in faith there be the scruple of error, in hope the deficiency of fear, and in charity the obstacle of rancour. Therefore faith should be fortified by the practice of good work; hope by the desire of eternity; charity by the service of active giving. Because of faith concerning hidden things, Rahab the harlot hid the spies of Jericho [Note: [Col. 0425] Josh. 2]; because of charity, she made with them a covenant for her salvation [Note: [Col. 0425] Ibid.]; because of hope, she placed the scarlet cord in the window [Note: [Col. 0425] Ibid.]. These are the hills of Lebanon, or of incense, to which he descends. Incense is a drop which first lies hidden in the tree because of faith, second is burned by fire because of charity, and third sends smoke upward because of hope.

“And I will speak,” he says, “to my bride.” He addresses the foolish woman differently, the unwary differently, and the honourable woman differently. He rebukes the first, instructs the second [Col. 0426C], praises the third. Concerning the first he says: “Under the apple tree I raised thee up; there thy mother was corrupted, there thy mother that bore thee was violated” [Note: [Col. 0425] Cant. 8]. Concerning the second: “If thou knowest not thyself, O fairest among women, go forth and follow after the tracks of the flocks” [Note: [Col. 0425] Cant. 1]. Concerning the third: “Behold, thou art beautiful, my friend; behold, thou art beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ibid.]. To this one he says: “And I will speak to my bride.” What he will say, however, he adds: “Come from Lebanon, bride, where I shall lie down at noon” [Note: [Col. 0425] Cant. 4].

“I will go to the mountain of myrrh,” etc.

[CARD.] Amid her praises, as though touched by a pain of heart at the presence of her Son’s Passion while recounting his praises, she exclaims: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh.” By myrrh she means the bitterness of compassion in the Passion of her Son; and she calls it a mountain of myrrh because no greater bitterness of pain could have been in a mother’s heart. But after the pain she adds something concerning the consolation of pain, saying: “I will go to the hill of incense.” The fragrance of incense signifies the sweet odor of the Lord’s Resurrection; she calls the consolation of this odor the hill of incense, and declares that she will go to it to assuage her pain. Yet by calling one a mountain of myrrh and the other a hill of incense, since a hill is smaller than a mountain, she seems to suggest that consolation did not then correspond to grief. For she fully saw and experienced her dying Son and the grief of his death; but although she saw him rising, she did not then yet fully see the glory of the risen one. It follows:

> You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.

[THO.] Every soul is either turned away from God or turned toward God. Of souls turned away, one is defeated and another is most remote. Of souls turned toward him, one is near and another nearest. The soul that is remote is ugly, but not wholly so; the one that is most remote is wholly ugly. Likewise, the soul that is near is beautiful, but not wholly so; the one nearest is wholly beautiful.

We have heard what the bridegroom said; let us hear by what path the bride must come: “Come from Lebanon, bride. You shall come and pass over Mount Sanir, or Seir.” Seir is interpreted “rough” or “hairy”; Sanir, “night-bird” or “stench.” Seir is the concupiscence of the flesh. Seir has a mountain, a plain, and a valley: weak in the valley, strong on the plain, unconquerable on the mountain. On the mountain is the appetite of the flesh in necessity; on the plain, the appetite of the flesh in satiety; in the valley, the appetite of the flesh in pleasure. When the flesh receives only as much support as is needed to prevail, Seir is on the mountain; when it seeks strength for nourishment, Seir is on the plain; when it demands delights for wantonness, Seir is in the valley.

On the mountain it is unconquerable, when support is necessary for those living in this exile; on the plain it is strong, because bodily vigor is sometimes useful for the soul’s progress; in the valley it is weak, because fleshly pleasure is always superfluous. In the valley it is forbidden; on the plain it is permitted; on the mountain it is rewarded. In the valley it serves; on the plain it fights; on the mountain it reigns. In the valley is luxury; on the plain, temperance; on the mountain, frugality. In the valley, with grace assisting, it is easily trampled down; on the plain, it is conquered with difficulty; on the mountain, our daily weakness continually supplies it with strength, so that it may not be overcome.

Whoever cuts away superfluities tramples Seir in the valley; whoever diminishes something of necessities conquers Seir on the plain; whoever grants nature only what is necessary for support, when Seir is on the mountain, renders obedience to its exactor. If Sanir is read, it conveys the same judgment: for it is interpreted “stench” or “night-bird,” because the pleasure of the flesh comes both foully and secretly. Hermon is interpreted “his anathema.” Whose “his”? Namely, the devil’s, who was first separated from God. The anathema of the accursed one is the person who is separated from him.

It should be noted that some are Mount Hermon, others the plain, and others the valley. The valley consists of those who have already been separated from the devil by faith, but still lie in desires through their carnal life. The plain consists of those who hold a middle condition: they neither descend to the depths through pleasure nor can rise to the heights through spiritual conduct. The mountain consists of those who are not only separated from the devil by faith, but are raised up against the devil through eminence of virtue and steadfastness of mind.

By the dens of lions is understood a slumbering cruelty, that is, fleshly pleasure: first it pleases through experience, next it torments through conscience, and third it will scourge through hell. The leopard is of varied color; it signifies the heretic or hypocrite, or those devoted to varied vices and proud lovers of this age. Again, from the passage, “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you,” the meaning is: not only in the more eminent members of the elect, whom I have enumerated above, are you beautiful, but also in those who are little and frail. You shine with the beauty of virtues and lack the stain of vices.

Lebanon, according to Hebrew etymology, means “whiteness”; according to Greek etymology, “incense.” He therefore exhorts her to come to him. For when the Lord sees a faithful soul made bright by good works and offering him the incense of pure prayer, delighted by her devout endeavors, he encourages her to persist in what she has begun. For the third time he commands the bride to come from Lebanon, because in his elect he requires progress in good action, saving speech, and pure thought. Or certainly: come through the best life which you practice while living in the body; come, when released from the body, to receive the soul’s everlasting life; come a third time, when the body has been restored, to behold the perfect joys of the Resurrection—for then you will be crowned perfect.

For then you will be crowned. But whence? “From the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” Amana, Sanir, and Hermon are mountains of Cilicia and Judaea, providing lairs for lions, leopards, and other wild beasts. These are the proud hearts of unbelievers, in which unclean spirits have their seat. Lions are demons because of pride; leopards, because of the varied arts of their malicious cruelty.

Again, from the passage, “I will go for myself to the mountain of myrrh”: myrrh is bitter and therefore signifies sufferings.

Myrrh has a plain, a hill, and a mountain: the plain of harsh discipline, the hill of inward compunction, and the mountain of the shedding of blood. On the hill it marshals its forces; on the plain it fights; on the mountain it triumphs. It marshals an army, fights against the enemy, and triumphs in order to receive a reward: an army of virtues; the enemy, namely the devil; the reward, namely the glory of angels. These are the three kinds of martyrdom.

On the plain there are three things: continence in youth, generosity in poverty, and sobriety in abundance. Likewise, on the hill there are three: contrition for sin, compassion for one’s neighbor, and anxiety of desire. On the mountain we conquer in three ways: if we endure the reproach of insult, the disgrace of humiliation, and the harshness of suffering. Christ marshaled his forces on the hill, preaching in the world; he fought on the plain, resisting the devil who tempted him; through death he triumphed on Mount Calvary.

The Lord came to the hills of Lebanon, interpreted “whiteness,” through the Resurrection. Thus he showed us the threefold glorification of the body: brightness, subtlety, and agility. First, on Mount Tabor through the Transfiguration, when “his garments became white as snow” [Note: [Col. 0427] Matt. 17]; second, on Mount Zion, when he entered among the disciples while the doors were shut [Note: [Col. 0427] John 20]; third, on the Mount of Olives, whence he ascended to the Father [Note: [Col. 0429] Acts 1].

Thus, coming, he says to the bride the following four things: first, “You are wholly beautiful”; second, “Come from Lebanon”; third, “You will be crowned”; fourth, “You have wounded my heart.” First he praises, second he calls, third he invites, fourth he recalls. First he praises purity; second he calls her to her homeland; third he invites her to the crown; fourth he reminds her of his beneficence. First he praises purity, that she may be joyful; second he calls her to her homeland, that the pilgrim may return to her city; third he invites her to the crown, that he may draw her by rewards; fourth he recalls his beneficence, that she may render thanks to him. Yet third he says: “Come from Lebanon.” Lebanon means whiteness, which may pertain both to good and to evil.

[Col. 0429B] There is a threefold whiteness in evil: pleasure, vanity, and duplicity. The first belongs to carnal persons, the second to the proud, and the third to hypocrites. Of the first Moses says: “If whiteness appears in the wound, it is leprosy” [Note: [Col. 0429] Lev. 13]. Of the second: “Whoever has a white spot in his eye shall not minister in the tabernacle” [Note: [Col. 0429] Lev. 21]. Of the third, the Lord calls hypocrites “whitewashed tombs” [Note: [Col. 0429] Matt. 23].

There is also a threefold whitening in good: continence, innocence, and wisdom. Of the first and second: “Whiter than snow, brighter than milk” [Note: [Col. 0429] Lam. 4]. Of divine wisdom it is said: “She is the brightness of eternal light” [Note: [Col. 0429] Wis. 7]. From the threefold evil he calls us sinners in order to convert us to the threefold good. He calls the bride that she may advance to better things. “You will be crowned,” he says; but he adds for what victory she ought to be crowned: “from the summit of Amana,” that is, the devil, who is the head of all evils.

His heads are three: the first pride, the second suggestion, the third the tinder of sin, or original sin. The first cast him down from heaven; the second cast Adam from Paradise; the third defiles every human being in the world. Of these David says: “You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters” [Note: [Col. 0429] Ps. 73]. You shattered the heads of the dragon in the waters, namely of baptism.

Sanir is called “stench,” namely that of the flesh, whose summit is the pride of the flesh. Hermon is called “anathema,” that is, separation, whose summit is worldly arrogance; we ought to be separated from it. The dens of lions are hidden ferocity; the mountains of leopards, the variety of manifest wickedness. Therefore the soul that has conquered all these things will be crowned.

> You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.

[CARD.] The Son returns to continue the praise of his mother, saying: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved,” because in every sense of the body you preserve the purity of virginal integrity; “and there is no blemish in you,” because in no bodily instrument of the senses has the stain of carnal concupiscence adhered. Or thus: you are wholly beautiful in mind and body, and there is no blemish in you that could repel or hinder you from offering to the Lord an acceptable whole burnt-offering from yourself.

Therefore: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon; come, you will be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” Lebanon indeed means whiteness, and Lebanon is also the fragrant tree of incense. Thus the Blessed Virgin is called to come from merits to the crown, and it is said to her: “Come from Lebanon; come from the brightness of virtues. Come from Lebanon; come from the fragrance of sweet-smelling good works, to receive your reward for them. Come, you will be crowned” for manifold victory, since you have triumphed over the summit of Amana, the peak of Sanir, and Hermon.

For she triumphs over the malice of the devil, signified by the summit of Amana; over worldly wisdom, denoted in the peak of Sanir; and over heretical perfidy, signified by the peak of Hermon. Amana is interpreted “tooth of watchfulness,” and signifies the whole company of demons, who gnaw a person with the tooth of temptation and are ever vigilant for his overthrow, as Job says: “By night my bone is pierced with pains” [Note: [Col. 0429] Job 30]. As if he said: by night, when I do not guard myself, my bone—that is, the strength of my virtue—is pierced by temptations, which are causes of pains. And he adds: “Those who eat me,” namely the tempters, “do not sleep, but in their multitude my garment is consumed” [Note: [Col. 0429] Ibid.], namely the adornment of good conduct.

Peter agrees with this statement, saying: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil goes about seeking whom he may devour” [Note: [Col. 0429] 1 Pet. 5]. The head of this company, signified by Amana, is that prince of demons whose head the Blessed Virgin crushed [Note: [Col. 0429] Gen. 3].

Sanir is interpreted “night-bird,” which flies and sees by night and is blinded by the sun. These are the philosophers and wise persons of this world, blind to the light of divine wisdom, but keenly seeing worldly wisdom and malice. Of them Jeremiah says: “They are foolish and senseless children; they are wise to do evil, but they have not known how to do good” [Note: [Col. 0429] Jer. 4]. The Blessed Virgin triumphs over these, and is crowned for this victory because she bore Wisdom, through whom the wisdom of this world is proved foolishness [Note: [Col. 0429] 1 Cor. 1].

She is likewise crowned from the peak of Hermon, that is, over the leaders of heretics, because she destroyed all heresies throughout the whole world. Hermon means “anathema” or “separated.” These are heretics, concerning whom Hosea, under the name Ephraim, says to Judah—that is, to faithful and Catholic persons: “Ephraim is a partner of idols; leave him. Their banquet is separated” [Note: [Col. 0429] Hos. 4]. As if he said: heretical perfidy shares in idolatry; therefore you, a Catholic person, leave him, lest you share with heretics. For their banquet is separated: the faithless doctrine and false religion of heretics have been anathematized.

She is also crowned from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards because she takes away from the devil what is signified by them. The dens signify the torpor and softness of luxury. By lions are understood the proud, wrathful, and powerful persons of this age; yet luxury so softens them, as lions, that they grow sluggish and wither in the dens of their lusts. Thus of the harlot woman it is said in Proverbs: “For she has cast down many wounded, and even the strongest have been slain by her” [Note: [Col. 0431] Prov. 7].

The leopard, which is of diverse color and marked by certain spots or blotches, signifies those who mingle evil with good works. Because of their differing color the Lord rebukes them through Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0431] Chap. 12], saying: “Is my inheritance a bird of diverse colors to me?” Although such people ought to be humbled by the evil work that is contaminated by their good work, they nevertheless rise into pride precisely from that good work. This pride is expressed by mountains when it says, “from the mountains of leopards.” And because the Blessed Virgin assists both these and those signified by lions, she is said to be crowned from the dens of lions and from the mountains of leopards. It follows:

> You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart.

[THO.] By the recollection of his wounded heart he wished to express the greatness of the love he has toward the Church. He rightly calls her his sister and bride: his bride, because he joined her to himself by the covenant of the heavenly bridal chamber; his sister, because he deigned to become man and naturally to be her brother. It may also be understood according to what Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0431] Chap. 53]: “But he was wounded for our iniquities.” And for what cause this happens, he himself adds: “With one of your eyes, and with one lock of your neck.”

Above, by many eyes we signified many teachers, and by many hairs many subjects. Now, by one eye is understood the unity of teachers, and by one lock the unity of subjects—as though he said: The whole form of your body appears beautiful to me. That which beyond all else kindles me to love you is that you are shown to possess unity of faith and love both in subjects and in prelates; this brought me to receive a wound for your life.

Love was the cause of this wound, by which many are wounded in imitation of Christ; not only this, for I see some wounded, others bound, others sick, and others failing. Love wounds, love binds, love makes one sick, love brings about failure. Hear of love wounding: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride.” Hear of love binding: “I will draw them with cords of Adam, with bonds of love” [Note: [Col. 0431] Hos. 11]. These bonds of love are God’s benefits: namely, the goods of nature, grace, and glory. He created nature, bestowed grace, and promised glory. Behold a threefold cord: the gifts of creation, the goods of justification, and the rewards of glorification. “A threefold cord is not easily broken” [Note: [Col. 0431] Eccl. 4]; yet this one was broken.

The Lord also added a restoration of the bonds of love: he bestowed good things upon us and bore our evils for us; by both he made us indebted to himself. Hear of love becoming sick: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell him that I am sick with love” [Note: [Col. 0431] Cant. 8]. Hear of love bringing failure: “My soul has failed for your salvation” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 118].

See what these stages do in distorted desires. In the first, desire pierces the affection; in the second, it binds thought; in the third, it dissolves action. Thus affection is taken captive in the first, thought in the second, action in the third; in the fourth, which nothing can satisfy, it exceeds the limits of human capacity. Here it brings failure and causes one to despair altogether. The first stage, then, is when the mind cannot resist its desire; the second, when it cannot forget; the third, when nothing else can please it; the fourth, when nothing can satisfy it.

In the first, love is unconquerable; in the second, inseparable; in the third, exclusive; in the fourth, insatiable. It is unconquerable when it yields to no other affection; inseparable when it never departs from memory; exclusive when it admits no other companion; insatiable when it cannot be satisfied. In the first stage is marked love’s excellence; in the second, its intensity; in the third, its violence; in the fourth, its surpassing quality among human affections.

The first stage can be good; the second is always evil; the third is not only evil but begins to be bitter; the fourth is worst of all. That first stage in the love of God is precious when it is unconquerable; the second more precious, when ardent affection begins to be inseparable; much better when it cannot delight in any thing other than God; highest when nothing can satisfy its desire.

In the first: “Many waters could not quench it, neither shall rivers overwhelm it” [Note: [Col. 0431] Cant. 8], because it is unconquerable. In the second, the soul sets her beloved as a seal upon her heart [Note: [Col. 0431] Ibid.], because she cannot forget. In the third: “If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as nothing” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ibid.], because he cannot delight in another thing. In the fourth: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ibid.], because whatever a person can do or endure for God is too little for it.

In the first, unconquerable love says: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 17]. In the second, inseparable love says: “May my tongue cleave to my palate if I do not remember you” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 136]. In the third, exclusive love says: “My soul refused consolation; I remembered God and was delighted” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 76]. In the fourth, insatiable love says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 115].

In the first, the unconquerable lover says: “Who shall separate us from the love of God?” [Note: [Col. 0431] Rom. 8]. In the second: “Love never fails” [Note: [Col. 0431] 1 Cor. 13], because it is inseparable; whence: “My soul has clung after you” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 62]. In the third: “I count all things as dung, that I may gain Christ” [Note: [Col. 0431] Phil. 3]. In the fourth: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain,” because it desires “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0431] Phil. 1].

In the first stage one loves from the heart; in the second, from the whole heart; in the third, from the whole soul; in the fourth, with all one’s strength. In the first: “I have hidden your words in my heart” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ps. 118]. In the second: “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ps. 9]. In the third: “My soul has desired to long for your justifications at all times” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ps. 118]. In the fourth: “I will not fear what man may do to me” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ps. 55].

In the first comes betrothal; in the second, marriage; in the third, union; in the fourth, childbirth. Of the first it is said: “I will betroth you to myself forever” [Note: [Col. 0433] Hos. 2]. In the second: “There is a wedding at Cana of Galilee” [Note: [Col. 0433] John 2]. Of the third: “Whoever clings to God is one spirit” [Note: [Col. 0433] 1 Cor. 6]. Of the fourth: “We conceived, labored, and gave birth to spirit” [Note: [Col. 0433] Isa. 26].

In the first, waiting for the return of the beloved, she cries: “Come, my beloved; be like a roe or a young hart” [Note: [Col. 0433] Cant. 2, 8]. In the second the bride is invited and it is said to her: “Come from Lebanon, my sister, my bride.” In the third she herself says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” [Note: [Col. 0433] Cant. 8]. In the fourth she says: “My little children, whom I labor again to bring forth until Christ be formed in you” [Note: [Col. 0433] Gal. 4].

Christ was wounded for the bride in body, heart, and head: in body by nails, in heart by a lance, in head by thorns. First, that he might be afflicted; second, that he might be killed; third, that he might be mocked. Of the first: “I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them” [Note: [Col. 0433] Isa. 50]. Of the second: “He delivered his soul unto death” [Note: [Col. 0433] 2 John 3]. Of the third he himself says: “All day long my enemies reproached me” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ps. 101]. Again: “For your sake I bore reproach; shame covered my face” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ps. 68]. Again: “The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ibid.]. Hence the Jews said to him, crowned with thorns: “Hail, King of the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0433] Matt. 27].

In the first, “he bore our pains”; in the second, “he carried our infirmities” [Note: [Col. 0433] Isa. 53]; in the third, he displayed discipline. The pains are of weakness and punishment; the infirmities are of guilt; the discipline is that of our peace: “The discipline of our peace,” he says, “was upon him” [Note: [Col. 0433] Isa. 50].

Let us imitate him. We have the body as an instrument, the heart as a dwelling, and the head as the breathing-place: the instrument of labor, the dwelling of love, the breathing-place of the vital breath. Therefore, in the first let us be wounded by the nails of fear; in the heart by the lance of compunction; in the head by the thorns of disciplined rigor. Of the first: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ps. 118]. As a figure of the second: “David struck his own heart because he cut off the hem of Saul’s cloak” [Note: [Col. 0433] 1 Sam. 24]. Of the third: “Hedge your ears with thorns” [Note: [Col. 0433] Sir. 20].

Let us be wounded in body lest we be afflicted through the dissolution of our works; wounded in heart lest we be killed by wanderings of thought; wounded in head lest the devil mock us because of curiosity. Christ was wounded by one of the eyes. There are two eyes in the soul: one looks inward to order temporal matters; the other upward to know heavenly things. By the second human beings ascend even to heaven; by the first they descend even to the depths.

We know that the seven locks shaved from Samson’s head are interpreted as the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Among these, the spirit of wisdom is preeminent, because whatever the other gifts accomplish, this one leads to savor and delight. Such a lock, which causes a person to delight in God, wounds the bridegroom’s heart with love. This lock is born in the head of spiritual affection; it descends through the neck of reason to adorn the body of sensuality. For first that divine savor is born in affection; second it passes through reason, by which it is examined and ordered whether it comes from God; third it descends to sensuality, which is adorned by it when, having tasted that savor, it forgets the customary use by which it gives sensation to the body.

This wound does not impose on God the burden of suffering, but manifests the intensity of the love which he has toward us. The sickness of this wounded one is for us a medicine, instruction for war, and a token of love. Hence it is fittingly said in the Book of Kings: “Elisha fell sick, and the king of Israel came down to him” [Note: [Col. 0433] 4 Kgs. 13]. “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor man,” whose Lord “turned all his bed in his sickness” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ps. 40]. He comes down to the one who is conformed to the likeness of his death, who learns from him to be a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness.

This king of Israel has war against Syria, which means “exalted,” that is, against pride. He comes with a bow, that is, with earnest zeal and an inclined affection. Its two arms bend toward one another when profession and consummation look toward one another through continual conduct, like a string reaching strongly from end to end. Or we may understand the first horn as the original condition of nature, the other as nature’s final glorification. These look toward one another through the string, namely grace, which restores the state of nature and confers glory. The upper horn bends when that higher glory inclines itself to our capacity, so that we may contemplate it. Thus, in lower things there is discerning discipline; in higher things, expectant devotion.

When, therefore, the bow has been thus drawn taut by grace—that is, the string—it shoots spiritual arrows, which wound in various ways. There are four such arrows:

The first wounds the devil; the second, the person turned away from God; the third, the devout person; the fourth, Christ. The first, that the defeated enemy may be troubled; the second, that he may be recalled; the third, that he may be inflamed; the fourth, that Christ might die for us. King Ahab was killed by the first [Note: [Col. 0433] 3 Kgs. 22], of which it is said: “Send forth your arrows, and you shall trouble them” [Note: [Col. 0433] Ps. 143]. The second and third are those which Jonathan shot as a sign for David to understand [Note: [Col. 0433] 1 Sam. 20], namely, that his father—that is, the devil—was to be fled.

Of the second Job says: “The arrows of the Lord are fixed in me, whose indignation drinks up my spirit” [Note: [Col. 0433] Job 6]. Of the third: “Jonathan’s arrow never went backward” [Note: [Col. 0433] 2 Kgs. 1]. And: “Sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” [Note: [Col. 0435] Ps. 119]. Again: “They shall go in the light of your arrows, in the brightness of your flashing spear” [Note: [Col. 0435] Hab. 3].

Of the fourth it is said: “They set me as a target for the arrow” [Note: [Col. 0435] Isa. 49]. This is the arrow by which Judas Maccabaeus was killed in defense of his people [Note: [Col. 0435] 1 Macc. 9]. Of the first wound it is said: “Have you not struck the proud one, wounded the dragon?” [Note: [Col. 0435] Isa. 51]. Of the second: “Do not reject the Lord’s corrections. For he wounds and heals; he strikes, and his hands make whole” [Note: [Col. 0435] Job 5]. Of the third: “I am wounded with love.” Again, she says: “The watchmen of the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; they took away my cloak” [Note: [Col. 0435] Cant. 5]. Of the fourth: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride.”

But in this place the wound is under discussion by which the enemy is wounded. “Open for me the eastern window,” Elisha says, “and shoot an arrow against Syria, and you shall strike it at Aphek” [Note: [Col. 0435] 4 Kgs. 13]. The one who shoots an arrow against Syria and toward the east directs his affection and thought to strike that proud one of whom it is said: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning” [Note: [Col. 0435] Isa. 14]. “You shall strike him,” he says, in affection—that is, in wrath, with the fervor proceeding from love. For Elisha calls this shot a shot of salvation.

Note here a double stroke: that of the arrow, which is made from afar, concerning which Jonathan, Saul’s son, said to the boy who bore his weapons: “The arrow is beyond you” [Note: [Col. 0435] 1 Sam. 22]; and that of the rod, which is made nearby, concerning which the prophet now speaks when he says: “Strike the ground with the javelin; and he struck three times and stopped” [Note: [Col. 0435] 4 Kgs. 13].

Strike in Syria the suggestion which the proud enemy sends against you. Strike the earth: the pleasure which arises from your flesh. For this is near to you, that is far off. Good is the eastern window, through which death does not enter, but the enemy is struck. To strike Syria is to kill worldly arrogance by divine revelation. He strikes the earth who chastises his flesh. Three times, if he restrains the soul’s threefold vice. For it is irascible, concupiscible, and rational. In the first he restrains the fury of anger; in the second, lust; in the third, fervor. But you ought to strike five or six or seven times [Note: [Col. 0435] Ibid.]: five times, by restraining the obstinacy of the five senses; six times, through good action; seven times, through the welcome repose of the mind.

> You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.

Or, according to another translation: “You have struck us in heart,” namely the whole Trinity.

[CARD.] Therefore he says: “You have wounded my heart with the wound of love,” for “with one”—that is, in the unity—“of your eyes,” namely affection and understanding, which in you are so one that affection desires nothing other than what understanding judges ought to be desired. “You have wounded [me] with one lock of your neck,” that is, with the unity of your thoughts, which cling so closely to their head, Christ, that nothing other can be said except the words of the Psalm: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek” [Note: [Col. 0435] Ps. 26].

Thus the Lord says that he has been wounded by love and struck in heart by one of the eyes and one lock of the neck of his mother, because this unity prevails in her heart; and no forgetfulness erases its remembrance, just as it cannot happen that the wound of the heart is not continually felt. The Lord calls his mother sister and bride: sister because of the fellowship of human nature; bride because of the unshaken steadfastness of faith. For when, in the time of the Passion, the faith of the apostles was shaken and faltered, she, like a bride, steadfastly clung to her bridegroom without wavering in faith. She also, like a bride more intimate with her bridegroom, obtains a greater share in the bridegroom’s goods.

How greatly the heavenly bridegroom desired her is shown in Ecclesiasticus, where it says: “The beauty of a woman gladdens a man’s countenance and surpasses every desire of man” [Note: [Col. 0435] Sir. 36]. A woman’s beauty humbles a powerful man and softens one who is stern and severe. The Lord so desired and chose the beauty of this woman that she carried his desire to such an excess that the Almighty was humbled to our weakness, and he who is the life of the living was softened unto death.

Of this bride Ecclesiasticus says: “Her husband is not like the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0435] Ibid.]; and shortly after: “There is help corresponding to him: a pillar and rest” [Note: [Col. 0435] Ibid.]. Let us therefore consider how this bride is opposed to the first bride. The first bride was formed from the side of her husband [Note: [Col. 0435] Gen. 2], but the bridegroom of this bride was formed from her flesh. Hence Ecclesiasticus says to the Lord: “Renew signs and change wonders” [Note: [Col. 0435] Sir. 36].

For it was a wonder to form a woman from a man’s side; the changing of wonders is that a man was formed from a woman’s flesh alone. Moreover, when the flesh of the woman was formed from the man’s bone, it was a sign that human nature would be weakened through woman. But an innovation of signs took place when man was made from woman’s flesh, signifying that through this generation human nature would return from weakness to strength.

This too should be noted: the first bride was made as a help for the man, when the Lord said, “Let us make a help like him” [Note: [Col. 0435] Gen. 2]; but woman is a weak help to man. Here, however, it says: “Her husband is not like the sons of men,” because Christ was not a son of men but the Son of Man, surpassing all human beings in dignity. And he is called the bride’s help according to him—that is, according to the bridegroom—who is the bride’s help, pillar—or support—and rest.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0437]

[Col. 0437A] “Your breasts are beautiful, my sister, my bride; your breasts are more beautiful than wine.”

[THO.] As in the eyes are signified teachers contemplating heavenly things; in the neck, those more perfect persons who pour spiritual grace into others; and in the teeth, those who rebuke the perverse: so in the breasts are denoted those who bring the weak—still black with the soot of sins—to the beauty of righteousness. He calls her bride because she receives from him and bears children for him; sister because she does the same work with him. Again, the bridegroom is the food of angels, insofar as “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” [Note: [Col. 0437] John 1]; the bread of spiritual persons, insofar as “the Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ibid.]; and the milk of little ones, insofar as “he dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ibid.]. The bride’s breasts are more beautiful than wine; that is, the sweetness of evangelical teaching is more beautiful than the severity of legal observance.

[Col. 0437B] Grace is the mother of all who serve Christ. She has a breast, an udder, and a nipple. Of the first, as here: “Your breasts are beautiful.” Of the udder, in what follows: “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine.” Of the third, Isaiah says: “You shall suck the nipple of kings” [Note: [Col. 0437] Isa. 60]. From the first milk is drawn; from the second richness is poured out; from the third honey is received. Hence *mamma* [breast] is so called as though “flowing by the hand”; *uber* [udder] as though “an anointing shower”; *mamilla* [nipple] as though “flowing with honey.” The first caresses, the second consoles, the third sweetens the one who sucks it. It caresses by promise, consoles by devotion, and sweetens by receiving the ineffable sweetness of heavenly glory.

Of the first it is said: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0437] 1 Cor. 3]. Of the second: “You have anointed my head with oil” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ps. 22]. Of the third Solomon says:

[Col. 0437C] “Eat honey, my son, because it is good” [Note: [Col. 0437] Prov. 24].

At the first breast the weak drink; at the second the strong are satisfied; at the third the perfect are made drunk. Thus Isaiah says: to the first, “that you may drink milk” [Note: [Col. 0437] Isa. 66]; to the second, “that you may be satisfied from the abundance of your consolation” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ibid.]; to the third, “that you may feast from the entrance of the glory of the nations” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ibid.]. These are made drunk by the abundance of God’s house.

The breasts are beautiful, the udders more beautiful, and the nipples most beautiful: beautiful through the whiteness of milk, more beautiful through the brightness of oil, most beautiful through the material of honey—that is, through the variety of flowers from which it is made. This is the whiteness of innocence, the brightness of conscience, and the variety of excellent flowers through the recollection of the beatitudes. The first is: “Innocent in hands and pure in heart” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ps. 23]. The second says: “This is our glory: the testimony

[Col. 0437D] of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0437] 2 Cor. 1]. The third frequently recalls: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0437] Matt. 5]. The first is from “a pure heart” [Note: [Col. 0437] 1 Tim. 1]; the second, from “a good conscience” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ibid.]; the third, from “unfeigned faith” [Note: [Col. 0437] Ibid.].

From the breast flow “the blessings of the deep lying beneath”; from the udder, “the blessings

[Col. 0438A] of the breasts and of the womb”; from the nipples, “the blessings of heaven above.” Jacob gave these blessings to his son Joseph [Note: [Col. 0437] Gen. 48]. From the breast flow truth and mercy; from the udder there is given to us abundance from the richness of the earth and from the dew of heaven; from the nipple, riches and glory. From the breast come truth in confession and mercy in remission. The earth is the body; heaven is the soul. Therefore, from the udder we receive from the richness of the earth zeal for bodily action; from the dew of heaven, an abundance of devotion; and from the nipple, riches—namely, the expectation of perpetual incorruption—and the glory of the divine vision.

But let us speak briefly about breasts without distinguishing the names. There are three kinds of breasts: those of a brute animal, those of a woman, and those of the Virgin. The brute animal is the carnal prelate;

[Col. 0438B] the woman, the spiritual teacher; the Virgin, the mother of the Savior.

For even carnal prelates have breasts of preaching. Hence Paul says: “What then? Provided that in every way, whether from pretext or from truth, Christ is proclaimed” [Note: [Col. 0437] Phil. 1]. Peter instructed spiritual persons, saying: “Feed the Lord’s flock which is among you: not for shameful gain, nor as lording it over the clergy, but becoming from the heart an example to the flock” [Note: [Col. 0437] 1 Pet. 5]. Of the Savior’s mother it is said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked!” [Note: [Col. 0437] Luke 11].

From the first breasts they give milk made from the juices of herbs; from the second, milk from human food; the third are full of the dew of heaven. The juices of herbs come by the gift of earth, human food by art, and the dew of heaven by the coming of the Holy Spirit. The first milk is made from the herb

[Col. 0438C] of the earth, because carnal prelates teach people to avoid earthly pleasures, since they neither have spiritual understanding nor know how to instruct spiritually. The second is made from human food prepared by art—that is, from the spiritual understanding of Scripture, by which people are taught to relish the things above. The third milk is from the Holy Spirit, by which the King of glory is nourished.

Samuel was weaned from the first [Note: [Col. 0437] 1 Sam. 1]; there no feast was held, but calves were offered—namely, the mortification of the flesh—and other things as well, namely purity of mind and a flask of wine, that is, the fervor of charity. Isaac was weaned from the second, and a great feast was made [Note: [Col. 0437] Gen. 21], which his father did not make at his birth. When we are first converted, we are then born; there is no place then for a feast of joy, but for sorrow. Yet it is said, “that you may drink

[Col. 0438D] milk.” Nor is there a feast when we are separated from this first milk, as Samuel was. But when we are separated from the second, like Isaac, then a feast must be made, so that, having been torn away from milk, they may feast from the entrance into his glory—that is, from the third milk.

The breasts of the blessed Virgin Mary were made fruitful by the dew of heaven; by them the Savior’s infancy was reared.

[Col. 0439A] But after the weaning of infancy, his mature age was offered for us upon the cross through grace. In his figure it was said: “After Samuel was weaned, his mother Hannah offered him in the tabernacle, with three calves, three measures of flour, and a flask of wine” [Note: [Col. 0439] 1 Sam. 1]. Samuel means “God’s petition.” He is Christ, who says: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” [Note: [Col. 0439] John 14]. Hannah means grace, namely blessed Mary, full of grace, who is said to offer Christ; for from her he assumed flesh, which he offered for us upon the gibbet of the cross. And this was after weaning, that is, after the laying aside of infancy.

Thus, according to the historical account, she offered flesh, she offered bread, she offered wine: flesh that was cooked upon the gibbet of the cross; bread formed in the Virgin’s bakery;

[Col. 0439B] wine pressed between death and life, at the moment of resurrection. Flesh, of which it is said: “The Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0439] John 1]. Bread, made from grain, of which it is said: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone” [Note: [Col. 0439] John 12]. Wine, of which it is said: “I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new in my kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0439] Matt. 26].

The flesh is Christ’s presence. The bread is God’s power and grace. The wine is eternal joy. Through the first, the famine of our old nature was removed. The second supplies us consolation on the way. The third will be our reward in the homeland. Of the first: “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom

[Col. 0439C] I am the first” [Note: [Col. 0439] 1 Tim. 1]. Of the second: “As a mother consoles her children, so I shall console you” [Note: [Col. 0439] Isa. 51]. Of the third: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting-places” [Note: [Col. 0439] Ps. 149].

Again in the Song of Songs: “His hands are rounded and golden, full of hyacinths” [Note: [Col. 0439] Song 5]. Rounded, because, as with a lathe, they scrape away the roughness of sins through perfect works. Golden, because they direct one’s path through wisdom. Smooth, because they lead to the serenity of heaven.

There is a young calf. There is a fattened calf. There is a most tender calf from the herd. The first produces horns and hoofs [Note: [Col. 0439] Ps. 68]: David brought it in his hand to be sacrificed at Bethlehem [Note: [Col. 0439] 1 Sam. 16]. The second is that which the good father killed for his returning son [Note: [Col. 0439] Luke 15]. The third is that which Abraham prepared for the angels beneath the oak of Mamre [Note: [Col. 0439] Gen. 18].

[Col. 0439D] Christ was a young calf because of his freedom from sin; fattened because of the usefulness of his graces; most tender because of the weakness he assumed. As young, he renewed us from the oldness of sins; as fattened, he nourished us with Eucharistic food; as most tender, he bore us back to paradise in strength. As young, he produces four hoofs against four habitual faults. He produces horns against spiritual wickednesses. Hear the four faults: vanity, pleasure, malice, and excessive worldly anxiety. These

[Col. 0440A] are the four horns in Zechariah which sold the children of Israel [Note: [Col. 0439] Zech. 1]. These are the four kings against the five kings of Sodom [Note: [Col. 0439] Gen. 14]. These are the four bearers who carried the dead young man outside the gate [Note: [Col. 0439] Luke 7].

But Christ removed these through himself: the first by his own abasement; the second by the affliction of his flesh; the third by love; the fourth by renunciation of the world. Of the first: “I do not seek my own glory” [Note: [Col. 0439] John 8]. Of the second: “I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them” [Note: [Col. 0439] Isa. 50]. Of the third: “Because of the exceeding charity with which God loved us, when we were dead in sin he made us alive together in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0439] Eph. 20]. Of the fourth: “My kingdom,” he says, “is not of this world” [Note: [Col. 0439] John 18]. These are the four craftsmen who broke the horns.

He also produces horns against the powers of the air. He had a figure in Moses, who had horns on his forehead, tablets in his hand, and brightness in his face [Note: [Col. 0439] Exod. 32]. By the first he defeated the powers of the air; by the second he taught God’s commandments; by the fourth he invited people by the example of good conduct.

Hear concerning the fattened calf how the good father received and enriched his son [Note: [Col. 0439] Luke 15].

[Col. 0440B] First he saw him from afar through inspiration; second, he ran to meet him, seeking contrition of heart; he kissed him through confession; he fell upon his neck, imposing satisfaction. He ordered the first robe to be brought—that is, the justification of the soul; sandals to be put on his feet, that he might be fortified against temptation; and a ring on his hand

[Col. 0440C] for the perfection of works. He produced music and dancing for thanksgiving.

The calf was killed for him beneath the oak of Mamre, that is, on the cross. But, strengthened thereby, he passed through the flaming and turning sword; he surpassed the cherubim and entered the gates of paradise. That flaming and turning sword is temporal punishment, through which one must return to paradise; the cherubim is the fullness of knowledge, namely charity, through which we must enter the gates of paradise. These gates are two-leaved: our obstinacy and God’s hardening; they are opened to us by this calf, namely through God’s mercy and our repentance. Behold what the flesh cooked upon the gibbet of the cross accomplishes.

There follows the bread formed in the Virgin’s womb. Which of us has a friend to whom he may say: “Friend,

[Col. 0440D] lend me three loaves” [Note: [Col. 0439] Luke 11]? For there are three loaves of God: the bread of sinners, the bread of converts, and the bread of the perfect. The first preserves the sinner from falling into despair; the second preserves the convert so that he may advance in good work; the third consoles him so that he may attain perfection. Abraham gave the first to Hagar and Ishmael when he dismissed them into the desert [Note: [Col. 0439] Gen. 16]; Elijah requested the second from the woman in Zarephath of Sidon [Note: [Col. 0439] 3 Kings 17]; the angel brought the third to Elijah beneath a juniper tree [Note: [Col. 0439] 3 Kings 19].

Of the first: “I am stricken as grass,

[Col. 0441A] and my heart is dried up, because I have forgotten to eat my bread” [Note: [Col. 0441] Ps. 101]. Of the second: “That oil may make the face cheerful, and bread strengthen the heart of man” [Note: [Col. 0441] Ps. 103]. Of the third: “You who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread” [Note: [Col. 0441] Isa. 21].

Therefore the Most High Father gives the first to Hagar and Ishmael as they flee. They say that Ishmael compelled Isaac to worship his idols. Sarah is the Spirit; Isaac, the works of the Spirit; Hagar—that is, servitude—is the flesh; Ishmael, the works of the flesh. The idols of the flesh are lofty rank, superfluity of riches, and immoderate pleasure. Hence the prophet says: “Son of man, dig through the wall” [Note: [Col. 0441] Ezek. 8]. He dug through it and saw images painted of birds—behold rank; of four-footed creatures—behold superfluity; of serpents—behold pleasure. These are the idols for which the flesh and its works are cast away. But lest they despair, the Most High Father gives them the bread

[Col. 0441B] of hope and a skin of the water of tears [Note: [Col. 0441] Gen. 21].

Of the second it is read that the prophet said: “Make me a little hearth-cake”; but the woman replied, “I have only a little oil in a jar and flour in a vessel” [Note: [Col. 0441] 3 Kings 17]. But through the prophet these things increase.

Behold, the prophet’s presence is at hand. Oil in the jar, flour in the vessel: the first is counsel, the second assistance, the third service. Counsel is against folly, assistance against heaviness, service for seeking God’s will. Of the first: “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed you shall not repent” [Note: [Col. 0441] Prov. 13]. Of the second and third: “That oil may make the face cheerful, and bread strengthen the heart of man” [Note: [Col. 0441] Ps. 103]. For God loves a cheerful giver [Note: [Col. 0441] 2 Cor. 2].

There is the bread of the perfect, namely consolation. “In the strength of that food

[Col. 0441C] one goes as far as Horeb, the mountain of God” [Note: [Col. 0441] Exod. 3]. But sometimes a crowd of foolish thoughts pursues these people; sometimes a crowd of demons attacks them; sometimes the weariness of the way overtakes them. Yet by the consolation of this bread they are refreshed: by the first they continue onward; by the second they fight bravely and conquer; by the third, cheered, they complete their course.

The first are the cows that draw the ark. The cows look back, yet continue onward, saying, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0441] Isa. 2]. Again: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” Jonathan signifies the second: crawling on feet and hands, he crossed to the Philistine outpost [Note: [Col. 0441] 1 Sam. 14]—that is, with affections and works—and defeated them, as though saying: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind, and blow through my garden.” Elijah signifies the third:

[Col. 0441D] wearied, he lay beneath a juniper tree and asked that he might die, saying: “Why is light given to the wretched, and life to those who are in bitterness of soul?” But the angel brought him bread and thus strengthened him [Note: [Col. 0441] 3 Kings 19]: “Arise, hasten, my friend, for winter has already passed, the rain has gone and departed.” Then, encouraged, like “Issachar, a strong ass, he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he put his shoulder to bearing” [Note: [Col. 0441] Gen. 49],

[Col. 0442A] crying: “He who walks in righteousness and speaks truth; who casts away avarice gained by extortion,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0441] Isa. 33]. And this concerns the first. Concerning the second: “The height of rocks is his stronghold” [Note: [Col. 0441] Ibid.], namely, of virtues. Concerning the third: “Bread is given to him” [Note: [Col. 0441] Ibid.].

There follows the wine. There is wine from the vineyard of Sodom [Note: [Col. 0441] Deut. 32]; wine from the vineyard which the Lord transplanted from Egypt [Note: [Col. 0441] Ps. 79]; wine from the vineyard for which Naboth died [Note: [Col. 0441] 3 Kings 21]; and wine from the vineyard of Soreth. These vineyards are joys. Wine from the vineyard of Sodom is joy in worldly prosperity. Hence: “Woe to you who now laugh, for you shall mourn and weep” [Note: [Col. 0441] Luke 6]; and: “I judged laughter to be error, and I said to joy: Why are you vainly deceived?” [Note: [Col. 0441] Eccl. 2]. The other three are the three shoots which rose from the head of Pharaoh’s cupbearer [Note: [Col. 0441] Gen. 40]. First, penitents rejoice,

[Col. 0442B] because they have escaped from the darkness of Egypt; second, those rejoice who are worthy to suffer reproach for Christ; third, the souls of the saints rejoice, who have followed Christ’s footsteps.

And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.

[THO.] The fragrance of the Church’s ointments is the renown of spiritual charisms, concerning which it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0441] Rom. 10]. When Mary Magdalene anointed the Lord with nard as a type of the Church, it is written: “And the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” [Note: [Col. 0441] John 12]. This mystically signified that the whole world would be filled with the devout services that the Church performs toward her redeemer.

By the sweetest fragrance of spices is indicated the renown of the saints.

[Col. 0442C] There are precious ointments, more precious ointments, and most precious ointments: the first for healing, the second for easing, the third for strengthening. They are for the healing of pain, the easing of sickness, and the strengthening of numbness: pain of the body, sickness of the inward parts, and numbness of the head when the brain is disturbed.

Let us therefore posit a certain inward person, to whom these things are assigned. Let him have a body: a collection of virtues as though limbs; inward parts: affections; and a head: intentions. For just as one body is formed out of many sins—whence Paul says, “that the body of sin may be destroyed” [Note: [Col. 0441] Rom. 6]—so, conversely, one body is formed out of many virtues. Likewise Isaiah speaks of these inward parts: “My belly shall sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for a wall of baked brick” [Note: [Col. 0441] Isa. 16]. Likewise, concerning the head of intentions:

[Col. 0442D] “Every head is sick, and every heart sorrowful” [Note: [Col. 0441] Isa. 1].

The body of virtues suffers pain through temptation; the inward parts of affections grow sick through lukewarmness; the head of intention is numbed through error. Against the pain of temptation, let us make a precious ointment from three ingredients: affliction, conciliation, and propitiation—affliction by penitential works, conciliation by almsgiving, propitiation by prayers. Penitential works are undertaken so that

[Col. 0443A] no place may be found for the adversary [Note: [Col. 0443] Eph. 4]; almsgiving, so that a needy witness may stand by us in our case [Note: [Col. 0443] Jer. 22]; and prayers, so that the judge may become our advocate [Note: [Col. 0443] Ps. 24]. With this ointment the women came to anoint Christ’s body at the tomb [Note: [Col. 0443] Mark 16]. This the angel of Tobit did when he said: “Prayer with fasting is good, and almsgiving is better than acquiring treasures of gold” [Note: [Col. 0443] Tob. 12].

We have affection toward ourselves, toward our neighbor, and toward God. Toward ourselves, that we may hate ourselves for our sins and glory in the Lord for our good deeds. If we scorn this, our affection toward ourselves languishes. Toward our neighbor, that we may sympathize with him in his needs and rejoice with him in his goods. But if we rejoice in his evils and envy his goods, our affection toward him languishes. Toward God, that we may love

[Col. 0443B] him as Father, honor him as God, and fear him as Lord. But if we forget this, our affection toward God languishes.

Against these things, however, let us make the ointment with which Mary anointed Christ’s feet [Note: [Col. 0443] John 12]; for Christ’s feet are our affections. The first ingredient is remembrance of eternal condemnation. This causes affection to return toward ourselves when we consider that in hell there is no redemption. The second is Christ’s passion: when we consider that “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example” [Note: [Col. 0443] 1 Pet. 2], affection returns toward our neighbor. The third is when we remember the Creator’s benefits; through this affection returns toward God: “I shall cry,” he says, “to God Most High, to God who has dealt well with me” [Note: [Col. 0443] Ps. 56]. This second ointment is more precious than the first against the sickness of the inward parts.

Let us also make the third against numbness of the head, that is, error of intention. Its first ingredient is confidence in the Lord; the second, faithful love of God; the third, desire for eternal or heavenly peace. The Prophet sets down these three in one short verse: “Those who trust in the Lord shall understand truth”

[Col. 0443C] [Note: [Col. 0443] Wis. 3]—behold the first. “And the faithful shall abide with him in love” [Note: [Col. 0443] Ibid.]—behold the second. “For grace and peace are for God’s elect” [Note: [Col. 0443] Ibid.]—behold the third. Through this ointment we have an anointing from the Holy One which teaches us concerning all things [Note: [Col. 0443] 1 John 2]. “When you fast,” he says, “anoint your head” [Note: [Col. 0443] Matt. 6], namely with this ointment, so that it may produce a sound intention. Mary poured this out upon the Lord’s head.

The fragrance of the first is above certain spices; the fragrance of the second, above many spices; but the fragrance of this third is above all spices. Spices are virtues. Some of them, such as prudence and temperance, prevent temptations from coming. But it is greater to resist them bravely when they come [Note: [Col. 0443] 1 Pet. 5]; this is done by the first ointment, and therefore its fragrance is above certain spices. Likewise, there are many virtues which rightly order our affections—such as justice, faith, and hope—and this is a great thing; but the middle ointment repairs what is disordered, which is greater, and therefore its fragrance is above many spices. But because the third ointment wholly reforms the person

[Col. 0444A] into love of God, no virtue is comparable to it; therefore its fragrance is above all spices.

But so that we may know both the physician and the effect of the ointments, hear John in the Apocalypse: “I saw a mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow upon his head, and his face like the sun,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0443] Rev. 10]. When the Son of God came into the world, he was seen in filthy garments [Note: [Col. 0443] Zech. 3], in linen garments [Note: [Col. 0443] Ezek. 9], clothed with a cloud [Note: [Col. 0443] Rev. 10], and clothed with light [Note: [Col. 0443] Ps. 103]. The first signifies that he came “in the likeness of sinful flesh” [Note: [Col. 0443] Rom. 8]; the second, that he was born without stain from the virgin chamber; the third, that divinity was hidden in mortal flesh; the fourth, that he shone above all other human beings with spiritual glory.

By the first we cleanse out the old leaven: “He condemned sin in the flesh through sin” [Note: [Col. 0443] Ibid.]. By the second,

[Col. 0444B] the flower of the field and lily of the valleys invited us to virginity. By the third, after overcoming death’s sting, he opened the kingdoms of heaven to believers. By the fourth, at his birth he was “fair in beauty above the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0443] Ps. 44]; at his resurrection the Father heaped delight and exultation upon him [Note: [Col. 0443] Ibid.].

For the first, Jesus the high priest was seen in Zechariah in filthy garments [Note: [Col. 0443] Zech. 3]; for the second, in Ezekiel, “clothed in linen, with a writer’s inkhorn at his loins” [Note: [Col. 0443] Ezek. 9]; for the third, as in this passage: “I saw a mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0443] Rev. 10]; for the fourth: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having great authority, and the whole earth was illuminated by his glory” [Note: [Col. 0443] Rev. 18].

Behold what the maker of ointments is like. Hear what

[Col. 0444C] effect the ointments which he prepared for the bride have. In the first of the aforesaid forms he saw sweetness; in the second, delight; in the third, usefulness; in the fourth, happiness: sweetness in his sending forth, delight in the bestowal of charisms, usefulness in redemption, happiness in recompense. Through the first, lost humanity is called back to the heavenly kingdoms; through the second, it was stripped by robbers; through the third, the captive is set free; through the fourth, the wretched are made blessed.

Of the first it is said: “Today the King of heaven deigned to be born for us from a virgin, so that he might call lost humanity back to the kingdom of heaven.” Of the second, the day of the ancient preparation has dawned. Of the third, the day of the new redemption has dawned. Of the fourth, the day of eternal happiness has dawned.

[Col. 0444D] Of the first: “The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works” [Note: [Col. 0443] Ps. 144]. Of the second: “Jerusalem, arise and stand on high, and see the joy that shall come to you from your God” [Note: [Col. 0443] Bar. 5]. Of the third: “You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver” [Note: [Col. 0443] Isa. 52]. Of the fourth: “Behold, a great prophet shall come, and he himself shall renew Jerusalem.”

Let us first, therefore, consider the filthy garments. There are defilements to which human frailty is subject; others by which purity is darkened; and others by which holiness is stained. The first are slight venial sins, the second graver venial sins, the third

[Col. 0445A] mortal sins. Of the first: “No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day.” Hence Job says: “If I should be washed as with snowy waters and my hands should shine as most clean, yet you would plunge me into filth, and my sins would abhor me” [Note: [Col. 0445] Job 9]. Of the second: “Her filthiness was upon her feet, and she did not remember her end” [Note: [Col. 0445] Lam. 1]. Of the third: “They sinned against him, and they are not his children in their filthiness” [Note: [Col. 0445] Deut. 32], and “Let the one who is filthy become still more filthy” [Note: [Col. 0445] Rev. 22]. Again: “Lebanon is ashamed and has become foul” [Note: [Col. 0445] Isa. 33].

Hear of Christ’s filthy garments: “Their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I defiled all my clothing” [Note: [Col. 0445] Isa. 63]. Hence, “we saw him as a leper, struck by God and humbled.” He was seen secondly in white garments. Hence Ezekiel: “Behold, a man clothed

[Col. 0445B] in linen garments” [Note: [Col. 0445] Ezek. 10].

He came to give color, to polish, and to inflame: to give color through whiteness, to polish through rigor, and to inflame through ardor; through the whiteness of innocence and chastity, the rigor of enduring hardship, and the ardor of charity. Hence: “The glory of Lebanon is given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon” [Note: [Col. 0445] Isa. 35]. Lebanon means “whitening,” Carmel “knowledge of circumcision,” and Pharon [Sharon] “kindling.” For the first he was seen in linen garments [Note: [Col. 0445] Ezek. 10]; for the second he marked the foreheads of the nations with Tau [Note: [Col. 0445] Ezek. 9], which is the sign of the cross; for the third he filled his hands with live coals [Note: [Col. 0445] Ezek. 10], which he scattered over the city.

In the first, he was a man flourishing in chastity; in the second, eager for fruits; in the third, languishing with love. Therefore the bride says, of the first: “Strengthen me with flowers”; of the second: “Surround me with apples”; of the third: “For I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0445] Song 2]. He was made flourishing through chastity, innocence,

[Col. 0445C] and spiritual joy. First, under the Law the priest is commanded to clothe himself in close-fitting linen [Note: [Col. 0445] Exod. 28]. Of the second, the strong woman “sought wool and linen, and worked according to the counsel of her hands” [Note: [Col. 0445] Prov. 31]. Of the third: “You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen” [Note: [Col. 0445] Deut. 22].

He polishes, as it were, by three instruments: a hammer, an axe, and a finer tool of iron. The hammer is fear of divine judgment; the axe, satisfaction; the finer instrument, watchfulness. Through the first the world is abandoned; through the second humanity is reconciled to God; through the third beauty is acquired. Of the first: “Unless you are converted, he shall brandish his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared it” [Note: [Col. 0445] Ps. 7]. Of the second: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” [Note: [Col. 0445] Matt. 4]. Of the third:

[Col. 0445D] “Keep your heart with all watchfulness, for life proceeds from it” [Note: [Col. 0445] Prov. 4]. And: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” [Note: [Col. 0445] Matt. 24]. Of these three, in Kings: “When the house was being built, neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in it” [Note: [Col. 0445] 3 Kings 6].

Likewise, he makes persons languish in three ways. First, the soul languishes because it considers itself unworthy of the love of him by whom it is loved; second, because it fears that the love may be broken off for some reason; third, because its desire is delayed. Of the first she cries: “Daughters of Jerusalem,

[Col. 0446A] tell my beloved that I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0445] Song 2]. Of the second: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0445] Ibid.]. Of the third: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women loved you exceedingly” [Note: [Col. 0445] Song 1]. And therefore, because I desire thus and cannot attain my desire by myself: “Draw me after you” [Note: [Col. 0445] Ibid.].

He was also seen clothed in a cloud, but a threefold cloud: a white cloud, a light cloud, and a glorious cloud. In the first respect, the flower of the field was born from the virginal lily [Note: [Col. 0445] Song of Songs 2]; in the second, he was in mortal flesh without the burden of sin; in the third, at the resurrection he was glorified in an immortal body. In the first, he announced the rewards of the good and the wicked; in the second, he knows how to erase the stains of sinners; in the third, he will make bright the bodies of the blessed.

Concerning the first, in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0445] Ch. 14]: “I saw a white cloud, and upon the cloud [Col. 0446B] one like a Son of Man sitting, with a golden crown on his head, and he had a sickle in his hand.” The golden crown is the reward of the good; the sickle, the reward of the wicked. Concerning the second: “The Lord has mounted upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence” [Note: [Col. 0445] Isa. 18]. Egypt means darkness, namely the heart of sinners; the idols are sins; the wasting heart is contrition of heart. Concerning the third it is said: “Simon son of Onias [is] like a shining rainbow among clouds of glory” [Note: [Col. 0445] Ecclus. 50]. Hence it is said: “Simon son of Onias shines like the morning star in the midst of a cloud, and shines like the full moon in his days, and like the shining sun; thus he shone in the temple of the Lord, and like a shining rainbow among clouds of glory” [Note: [Col. 0445] Ibid.].

He was the morning star in the midst of cloud, the moon at the full, the sun [Col. 0446C] emerging from cloudiness, the shining rainbow among clouds of glory. The first was at the bringing forth of his birth; the second, at the infusion of grace; the third, at his own resurrection; the fourth, at the general regeneration. The star was the messenger of light; the moon, the abundance of graces; the sun, the glory of the risen body; the rainbow, the distinction of merits in the kingdom.

Concerning the first: “A star shall arise out of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0445] Num. 24]. Hence: “Today light shall shine upon us.” Hence, when the tabernacle had been completed, “the cloud covered it, and the glory of the Lord filled it” [Note: [Col. 0445] Exod. 40]. It was completed when “the fullness of time had come” [Note: [Col. 0445] Gal. 4]. The cloud covered it when “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0445] John 1]. The glory of the Lord filled it because “we saw his glory, [Col. 0446D] glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” [Note: [Col. 0445] Ibid.].

The moon was full in the infusion of grace; for in himself he possessed fullness, but to others he gave by measure; and through his teaching the Church shines as the moon does by the sun. Hence it is added: “Full of grace and truth” [Note: [Col. 0445] Ibid.]. In the resurrection the sun emerged from the cloudiness of our mortality. Hence: “After the sun, formerly in cloudiness, shone forth, a great fire was kindled” [Note: [Col. 0445] 2 Macc. 1]. For then he set his tabernacle in the sun: that is, his assumed flesh in the brightness of immortality.

[Col. 0447A] Hence in the Apocalypse: “I saw an angel coming down from heaven, and the whole earth was illuminated by his glory” [Note: [Col. 0447] Rev. 18]. It follows: “And a rainbow was upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0447] Rev. 10], that is, the distinction of rewards. The rainbow has five colors: black, green, red, saffron-yellow, and white. In black is the crown of the prophets; in green, that of the apostles; in red, that of the martyrs; in saffron, that of the confessors; in white, that of virgins. For the prophets prophesied in obscurity; the apostles bore witness to Christ with great power; the martyrs became red through shed blood; the confessors grew pale through continual discipline; virgins blossomed through chastity.

But it should be noted that the rainbow is found upon the angel’s head, around the throne, and in the clouds of heaven. In the first are signified the crowns prepared from eternity. In the second, the time when they shall be offered [Col. 0447B] to the righteous at judgment. In the third, the time when they shall be crowned in the glorified body. Concerning the first, here: “And a rainbow upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0447] Ibid.]; concerning the second, in the Apocalypse: “And a rainbow around the throne” [Note: [Col. 0447] Rev. 4]; concerning the third, to Noah: “I shall set my bow in the clouds of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0447] Gen. 9].

All these things which our perfumer has wrought are ointments of the Bride, prepared by him: the first, namely, of repentance; the second, of grace; the third, of glory. The first stings but heals; the second anoints and strengthens; the third makes bright and gladdens. The fragrance of the first is beneath spices; the fragrance of the second comes through spices; the fragrance of the third is above all spices. David was first anointed at Bethlehem [Note: [Col. 0447] Matt. 2], secondly at Hebron [Note: [Col. 0447] 2 Sam. 5], thirdly at Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0447] Mark 16]. And lest perhaps the Bride should seem to have borrowed from elsewhere, [Col. 0447C] he adds whence the ingredients from which these ointments are made are gathered: “Garden.”

> How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments above all spices.

[CARD.] For what is more beautiful in the eyes of an afflicted sinner than pity and mercy, which are signified in the Virgin’s breasts? These breasts are more beautiful to sinners than the austerity of severity signified in wine. The ointments of the blessed Virgin are compounds of spiritual charisms and accumulated richnesses of virtues, which enrich her as though they were her own substance, delight us with fragrance, and by the pleasure of their scent invite us to run in the course of good works. The fragrance of these ointments surpasses all [Col. 0447D] spices in both fragrance and power. For these ointments possess greater fragrance before the Lord, and greater power against the devil, than the virtues of any saints whatsoever, which are signified by spices. After the power of the ointments, the power of the prayers of the blessed Virgin is added when it is said:

> Your lips, O bride, drip a honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.

[THO.] A honeycomb is honey in wax; honey in wax is the spiritual [Col. 0448A] sense of the divine utterances in the letter. A honeycomb drips when it has more honey than its casing can contain. So too is Holy Scripture: it is contained in a brief verse, though a manifold page is filled from it. The lips of the Bride are the teachers, in whom the honeycomb drips when they explain many things from the Scriptures to those subject to them.

“Milk and honey are under your tongue.” In milk is signified the instruction of little ones; in honey, teaching suited to the more perfect. The Apostle says of milk: “You have become those who need milk, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0447] Heb. 5]. Solomon says of honey: “Have you found honey? Eat what is sufficient for you” [Note: [Col. 0447] Prov. 25]. She has honey and milk under her tongue when she rightly discerns what should be offered to little ones and what to those who are greater. She has them on her tongue when she speaks them suitably. “The fragrance,” he says, “of your garments is like the fragrance [Col. 0448B] of incense.” The garments of the Church are her works. Hence in the Apocalypse: “The wife of the Lamb prepared herself, and it was granted her to clothe herself in shining white linen” [Note: [Col. 0447] Rev. 19]. For linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

In incense are signified the desires and prayers of the saints; for not only voices and affections are prayers, but all the good works that we perform, so that that saying of the Apostle may be fulfilled: “Pray without ceasing” [Note: [Col. 0447] 1 Thess. 5]. We fulfill this even while sleeping.

We find fire in the tongue; we find honey also, and milk also. Of the first it is said: “There appeared to the apostles divided tongues as of fire, and the Holy Spirit sat upon each of them” [Note: [Col. 0447] Acts 1]. There is fire for testing, fire for illuminating, and fire for raising up. The first is for testing our repentance: it searches kidneys and hearts [Note: [Col. 0447] Rev. 2]. The second is for illuminating our ignorance, because it illuminates the hearts of the disciples by invisible power [Note: [Col. 0447] Acts 1]. The third is for raising us up, so that our hearts may be fixed where true joys are [Note: [Col. 0447] Luke 12]. The fourth is for instructing the human tongue, so that it may speak the mighty works of God [Note: [Col. 0447] Acts 2].
