The first is the fiery bush that appeared to Moses [Note: [Col. 0447] Exod. 3]; the second, the pillar of fire that led the children of Israel through the byways of the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0447] Exod. 13]; the third, the fiery chariot that raised Elijah to the heights of heaven [Note: [Col. 0447] 4 Kings 2]; the fourth, that of which it is said: “There appeared divided tongues as of fire” [Note: [Col. 0447] Acts 1]. The first was experienced by the three youths in the furnace [Note: [Col. 0447] Dan. 3]. Seek [the discussion]. Through the second is given “every good gift and every perfect gift, coming down from the Father of lights” [Note: [Col. 0447] Jas. 1]. Seek [the discussion]. [Col. 0448D] The third is the chariot of charity, having four ardors. Seek [the discussion]. The fourth is that which appeared to the apostles in fiery tongues [Note: [Col. 0447] Acts 1].

It should be noted, moreover, that there are tongues which perished; tongues which obeyed; tongues which opened; and tongues which appeared. The first perished through the merit of pride; the second obeyed divine power; the third opened the secrets of grace; the fourth appeared as a sign of the glory of miraculous eloquence. The first were among the Babylonians; the second obeyed in human beings and beasts; the third were [Col. 0449A] in prophets and apostles; the fourth were in the form of fire.

Of the first the Lord says: “Come, let us confuse their languages” [Note: [Col. 0449] Gen. 11]. These are the tongues of murmurers, detractors, flatterers, deceivers, and boasters. These, indeed, are viperine; the second are milky; the third honey-flowing; the fourth fiery. 92 The viperine tongues arise from the vice of perverse speech; the milky from the simplicity of devout prayer; the honey-flowing from the sweetness of preaching; the fiery from the ardor of rebuke. Concerning the first: “He shall suck the head of asps, and the viper’s tongue shall kill him” [Note: [Col. 0449] Job 20]. Concerning the second and third: “Milk and honey are under your tongue.” Concerning the fourth: “There appeared to the apostles divided tongues as of fire” [Note: [Col. 0449] Acts 1].

Likewise note that among the tongues of teachers, some are sluggish or slow, others lukewarm, [Col. 0449B] others dry. They are slow through negligence; lukewarm through lack of charity; dry because they lack wisdom. Conversely, some are fervent, some swift, some healing: fervent through charity, swift through the prompting of the Spirit, healing through consolation. Concerning the first: “There appeared to the apostles divided tongues as of fire” [Note: [Col. 0449] Ibid.]. Concerning the second: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” [Note: [Col. 0449] Ps. 44]. Concerning the third: “The tongue of your dogs [is] from the enemy by him” [Note: [Col. 0449] Ps. 67]. Likewise: “But even the dogs came and licked his sores” [Note: [Col. 0449] Luke 16].

Likewise, there are four fiery tongues: the tongue of the sinner, the tongue of the one being beaten, the tongue of the judge, and the tongue of the preacher. The first is the tongue of the world; the second, of the rich man placed in hell; the third, of Christ; the fourth, of the apostle. Concerning the first: [Col. 0449C] “The tongue is set among our members, which defiles the whole body and sets on fire the wheel of our birth, itself set on fire by Gehenna” [Note: [Col. 0449] Jas. 3]. Concerning the second: “Send Lazarus, that he may cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame” [Note: [Col. 0449] Luke 16]. Concerning the third: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar; his lips are full of indignation, and his tongue is like a devouring fire” [Note: [Col. 0449] Isa. 30]. Concerning the fourth: “There appeared to the apostles divided tongues as of fire” [Note: [Col. 0449] Acts 1].

It follows: “And [the Holy Spirit] sat upon each of them.” Christ sits, the disciple sits, and the Holy Spirit sits. Christ sits judging in truth; the disciple, in tranquility; the Holy Spirit, in purity of heart. Christ distinguishes merits; the disciple awaits gratuitous gifts; the Holy Spirit pours in [Col. 0449D] charisms. Concerning the first: “The Lord sat opposite the treasury” [Note: [Col. 0449] Mark 12]. Concerning the second: “Sit in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” [Note: [Col. 0449] Luke 24]. Likewise: “The Holy Spirit filled the whole house where the apostles were sitting” [Note: [Col. 0449] Acts 1].

The second of these is to rest. The Holy Spirit rests in the chamber of humility, in the bed of tranquility, at the door of fear: of humility, by which a person humbles himself; of tranquility, by which he maintains peace; of fear, by which he fears losing the Holy Spirit. Concerning the first: “Be subject to the Lord, and pray to him” [Note: [Col. 0449] Ps. 61]. Concerning the second: “His place was made in peace, [Col. 0450A] and his dwelling in Zion” [Note: [Col. 0449] Ps. 75]. Concerning the third it is said: “When you pray, enter into your chamber; and when the door is shut, pray to your Father, who sees in secret” [Note: [Col. 0449] Matt. 6]. Likewise: “Now the door is shut, and my children are with me in bed; do not trouble me now” [Note: [Col. 0449] Luke 11]. Hence it is said: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, unless upon the humble and quiet man, who fears my words?” [Note: [Col. 0449] Isa. 66]. And of Christ it is said: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding” [Note: [Col. 0449] Isa. 11], etc.

Likewise, the incarnation of Christ is in the hands of this passage; for this verse addresses Mary thus: “Your lips, O bride, drip a honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue.” Three things are set forth in the Virgin: lips, tongue, and garment. In the lips, the kiss; in the tongue, speech; in the garment, adornment. The kiss [Col. 0450B] of the Father, the speech of the Son, the adornment and fragrance of the Holy Spirit. The kiss by which the Father is reconciled; the speech by which the Word and Son of God preaches and is preached; the adornment of virtues by which the Virgin is beautified through the overshadowing Holy Spirit.

Under her tongue—that is, beneath her womb—is honey, the divinity, and milk, namely the flesh assumed without sins. In the lips, where the kiss is, is the dripping honeycomb: that is, the incarnate Word, reconciling in himself by the Father’s kiss the lowest things to the highest. In the fragrance of the garment of humanity, from the incense of divinity, the Son is signified, who will refashion the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory. Honey and milk were under your tongue: incarnate in the womb; the dripping honeycomb was in the lips, preaching and preached in the world.

Morally, three things are set forth:

[Col. 0450C] A dripping honeycomb in the lips; honey and milk under the tongue; fragrance in the garments. The first is in the mouth; the second in the heart; the third in the body. The first, in the mouth, is grace of speech; the second, in the heart, constancy and wisdom; the third, in the body, the beauty of holy conduct. Grace of speech, so that you may soften the hard, according to Solomon’s saying: “A gentle answer breaks anger” [Note: [Col. 0449] Prov. 15]. And: “A good word is above the best gift” [Note: [Col. 0449] Ibid.]. Conscience, so that you may become secure; for a troubled conscience always anticipates dreadful things. Wisdom, so that you may have delight in things above: “Set your minds on things above” [Note: [Col. 0449] Col. 3]. Beauty of conduct, so that you may present yourself as a mirror to others, “that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0449] Matt. 5].

We have said much about speech, wisdom, and conscience; therefore let us pass [Col. 0450D] to the fragrance of the garment. A garment is praiseworthy in four respects:

In the value of its material, in the workmanship of its nature, in the brilliance of its color, and in the sweetness of its fragrance. The material of garments is threefold. It is sometimes made from the hair of animals, or from wool; sometimes from the bark of plants, as a linen garment is made through much rubbing; sometimes from the entrails of worms, as a silk garment. Of the first two it is said that the strong woman “sought wool and flax, and worked with the counsel of her hands” [Note: [Col. 0449] Prov. 31]. [Col. 0451A] Of the third: “Purple and fine linen are her clothing” [Note: [Col. 0451] Ibid.]. For purple is a silk garment.

The first, therefore, is experience in labors; the second, patience in tribulations; the third, almsgiving, when we withhold from our belly—as though from its entrails—that by which the needy person may be refreshed. Concerning the first: “Whatever your hand finds able to do, do it earnestly” [Note: [Col. 0451] Eccl. 9]. Concerning the second: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0451] Matt. 5]. Concerning the third: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” [Note: [Col. 0451] Luke 11].

This garment is also praiseworthy in the workmanship of its weaving, which is threefold. For you ought to do good: first, for God’s honor, whence: “Honor the Lord from your substance” [Note: [Col. 0451] Prov. 3]. Secondly, for your own benefit, whence: “Be gracious to your own soul, pleasing [Col. 0451B] to God” [Note: [Col. 0451] Ecclus. 30]. Thirdly, it should be done for the peace of one’s neighbor: “Pursue peace with all men, and holiness” [Note: [Col. 0451] Heb. 12]. Of these three things it was said of the strong woman: “She made herself a coverlet” [Note: [Col. 0451] Prov. 31]. For *stragulata* is said as though *triangulata*, “triangular,” because of these three things; or *stragulata* derives from *stratus*, “a bedcovering.” Behold the workmanship of this garment.

It is praised for the brilliance of its color when it appears pure as an example to people: “Let your light shine before men” [Note: [Col. 0451] Matt. 5]. This is the Lord’s garment in the Transfiguration, white as snow [Note: [Col. 0451] Mark 9]. Here it is praised for fragrance, not just any fragrance but that of incense. Incense gives a good scent when it is gathered from its tree; a better one when it is warmed by the sun; the best when it is burned by fire. The first is when we set apart from ourselves some temporal goods [Col. 0451C] for feeding the poor; the second, when we imitate the sun of righteousness; the third, when we are burned by the fire of tribulations.

Here Isaac perceives the fragrance of the garments and cries: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is as the fragrance of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” [Note: [Col. 0451] Gen. 27]. Or incense may be prayer, by which every good manner of life is made fragrant.

> Your lips, O bride, drip a honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.

[CARD.] A honeycomb is honey in wax, and it signifies divinity in flesh. Therefore the lips of the mother of Jesus Christ, in her prayers, drip the greatness of the Son, who was heard because of his reverence, so that she may be worthy to be heard in favor of so great a Son. And it is added: “Honey and milk are under your tongue,” where the preposition “under” is understood comparatively.

For honey, which draws its origin from heaven, denotes the angelic nature. Milk, which is born from flesh, denotes in holy people the whiteness of a pure life; and all these are lower in prayer than the tongue of the mother of Christ. To the effective power of her prayers there is added the fragrance of her garments, that is, the fragrance of the merits in which she shines adorned; and that fragrance is like the fragrance of incense—that is, like the fragrance of fervent and sweet-smelling prayer. For she intercedes for sinners no less by merits than by prayers. It follows.

[Col. 0452A]

> A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.

[THO.] The garden is the Church, which produces many shoots of spiritual works, subsequently enumerated under the various names of spices. The fountain is that which makes fruitful by spiritual teaching, watering the minds of believers as beds of spices. Hence it is written: “Deep water is a man’s words from his mouth, and a flowing torrent the fountain of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0451] Prov. 18]. It is enclosed because the Church is fortified by the Lord’s protection, lest demons or perverse people break in freely. The fountain is sealed because the word of faith, protected by the evangelical seal, cannot be disturbed by any agitation of those who err. Whoever endeavors to break the seal of the living fountain is in error.

There are four gardens: the garden [Col. 0452B] is the heavenly homeland, paradise, the Church militant, and the virginal womb. The first is of beatitudes; the second, of delights; the third, of sacraments; the fourth, of graces. Concerning the first: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride”; concerning the second, it is found: “Garden is interpreted as paradise”; concerning the third: “I went down into my garden”; concerning the fourth: “Let my beloved come into his garden.”

In the first, the seed of wisdom was sown, but it rose to the summit of pride, reached the ear of angelic ruin, and produced the fruit of eternal damnation. Wisdom from which it departed is threefold: first, to know the Creator; second, to love him; third, not to turn away from him. See how it fell into threefold folly: first, not to know the Creator; [Col. 0452C] second, to despise him; third, not to wish to return to Christ.

Hear its wisdom: “You were the seal of resemblance, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty” [Note: [Col. 0451] Ezek. 28]. Hear how it rose in pride: “I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0451] Isa. 14]. Hear its fall: “How have you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who arose in the morning? You have fallen to the earth, you who wounded the nations” [Note: [Col. 0451] Ibid.]. Hear the fruit of its damnation: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” [Note: [Col. 0451] Matt. 25].

This garden has the violets of confessors, the roses of martyrs, the lilies of virgins, and the gold of angels. There, indeed, the mud of confessors is turned into imperishable red pigment; the blood of martyrs into the royal dignity of purple; the purity of virgins into the whiteness of lilies; the gold of angels retains [Col. 0452D] perpetual brightness. This garden is enclosed by the unconquerable power of God: “For his power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom, one which shall not be destroyed” [Note: [Col. 0451] Dan. 7]. “Evil,” he says, “shall not come to you, and the scourge shall not draw near your tent” [Note: [Col. 0451] Ps. 90].

In it is the fountain of blessedness. Hence Augustine: “There the blessed life shall be drunk at its fountain, for with you, O Lord, is the fountain of life.” It is sealed with the seal of future predestination, so that none may enter except the predestined. For those whom he predestined, mercy also called; and those whom mercy called, grace also justified; [Col. 0453A] and those whom grace justified, glory also magnified.

The second garden is paradise. In it God sowed the commandment of obedience, and with the plant of disobedience came the fruit of misery. “For he grew fat, became gross, and spread abroad” [Note: [Col. 0453] Deut. 32]. He grew fat because of the pleasant place; he became gross because of the benefit of his condition; he spread abroad because of the gift of grace. Therefore he kicked back through the vice of disobedience.

“Thus he went in the counsel of the ungodly, stood in the way of sinners, and sat in the seat of pestilence” [Note: [Col. 0453] Ps. 1]. He went by consenting, stood by defending, sat by teaching. In one who goes, levity is marked; in one who stands, obstinacy; in one who sits, pride. In the first: “The prodigal son went into a far country” [Note: [Col. 0453] Luke 15]; in the second: “He attached himself to one of the citizens” [Note: [Col. 0453] Ibid.]; in the third: “He fed swine” [Note: [Col. 0453] Ibid.].

The commandment was made concerning the life of the soul; the permission, concerning the life of the body; the prohibition, against the life of the soul. The commandment binds; the permission aids; the prohibition is violated. To the commandment they owe obedience; to the permission, temperance; from forbidden things, flight. But here they broke the commandment through disobedience, rejected what was permitted, and burn for forbidden things. Hear the commandment: “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, do not eat” [Note: [Col. 0453] Gen. 2]. Hear the disobedience: “She saw that the tree was beautiful to behold and good for eating, etc.” [Note: [Col. 0453] Ibid.]. Hear the misery: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” [Note: [Col. 0453] Ibid.].

In this garden are trees of different kinds. There is also that fountain which is divided into four rivers, signifying the four virtues; I pass over their names and interpretations, since they are known. But both that garden is enclosed and the fountain sealed by angelic guard, [Col. 0453C] namely by a Cherub having a revolving sword [Note: [Col. 0453] Ibid.].

The third garden is the Church militant, in which grow the sacraments of the Christian faith. They are seven: nativity, baptism, passion, resurrection, descent into hell, ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit. These are the seven seals in the Apocalypse, which no one is worthy to open except the Lamb who was slain [Note: [Col. 0453] Rev. 5].

In this garden the word of God is sown. The seed is the word of God; hearing sprouts, faith grows, hope rises, charity bears fruit: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing is through the 93 word of God” [Note: [Col. 0453] Rom. 10]. Likewise: “Faith, hope, and charity, these three, remain” [Note: [Col. 0453] 1 Cor. 13]. This garden is enclosed by the wall which is Christ: “The city of our strength, Zion the Savior; in it there shall be set a wall and a bulwark” [Note: [Col. 0453] Isa. 26]. Likewise, “by your impregnable wall,” etc.

[Col. 0453D] In it is the fountain of baptism; hence the prophet: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” [Note: [Col. 0453] Zech. 13]. This fountain is sealed with that seal by which the firstborn of Egypt die and Israel is delivered [Note: [Col. 0453] Exod. 12], namely the passion of the Lord, without which baptism is of no benefit. “For all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” [Note: [Col. 0453] Rom. 6].

The fourth garden is the womb of the blessed Virgin. In it grow integrity, singularity, and usefulness: integrity of virginity, singularity of fruitfulness, usefulness for human [Col. 0454A] need. It is privileged virginity in the world, fruitfulness without a male, and human need delivered from the bond of sin. This garden is enclosed by the wall of humility: “For the Lord has regarded the humility of his handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0453] Luke 1]. And: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” [Note: [Col. 0453] Jas. 4].

She herself is the fountain of grace: “Hail, full of grace” [Note: [Col. 0453] Luke 1]. This fountain is sealed with the seal of the whole Trinity: lest she should be corrupted by violence, the Father guarded her by power; lest she should be deceived by fraud, the Son guarded her by wisdom; lest she should be accounted hateful, the Holy Spirit guarded her by benevolence. On this seal, moreover, are written: power, wisdom, benevolence.

Isaiah, who knew heavenly secrets, did not keep silent concerning this garden of our Virgin—whence it received irrigation, whence it received seed, and what it brought forth [Col. 0454B]—saying: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth open and bring forth the Savior” [Note: [Col. 0453] Isa. 45]. Behold, the Lord gives goodness, and our earth gives its fruit. For behold: heaven gives dew, cloud rains, earth brings forth. From heaven comes the Holy Spirit; in the cloud lies hidden the Son of God; the earth is the Virgin’s womb. Heaven gives dew by infusing grace into the Virgin; the cloud rains by granting virginity the power to bear; the earth brings forth the power of God and the wisdom of God. In the first, the Virgin was made gracious; in the second, mighty; in the third, fruitful. In the first it is said: “Hail, Mary, full of grace” [Note: [Col. 0453] Luke 1]; in the second: “The Lord is with you”; in the third: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.”

A great [Col. 0454C] mystery is declared today: the Father exposed the Son; the mother, contrary to nature, provided the material of flesh; the Holy Spirit wove a garment in the Virgin’s bridal chamber; the Son of God put on the garment woven. The Father exposed him so that he might be our redemption; the mother, contrary to nature, provided the material of flesh without union with a man; the Holy Spirit wove it with wonderful craftsmanship; the Son of God put on the woven garment, so that there might be a union of divinity and humanity.

Concerning the first: “After the fullness [of time] had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law” [Note: [Col. 0453] Gal. 4]. He was truly exposed, whence he cried: “Why have you forsaken me?” [Note: [Col. 0453] Matt. 27]. Behold, Abraham led his son to be sacrificed [Note: [Col. 0453] Gen. 22].

Concerning the second, namely that the mother provided the material [Col. 0454D] of flesh: she was that strong woman who “sought wool and flax and worked with the counsel of her hands” [Note: [Col. 0453] Prov. 31]. Since wool comes from the body, it does not know the body’s suffering; flax is drawn out by rubbing in weaving. In the wool, Christ’s flesh did not experience the suffering of guilt; in the flax, it endured the suffering of punishment. Thus the mother provided the material, the Holy Spirit the color, and the Son the fragrance.

Concerning the third: the Holy Spirit wove the garment in the Virgin’s bridal chamber. For he is the craftsman of all things, possessing every power and beholding all things: a craftsman because he has knowledge of all things; power because he has might over all things; beholding all things [Col. 0455A] because he surveys the hidden conscience. This was Joseph’s long robe and many-colored garment [Note: [Col. 0455] Gen. 37]: long, for perseverance; many-colored, for the variety of virtues.

The Holy Spirit colored it with three colors. For the garment was snow-white, red-pigmented, and rose-colored: snow-white because it had no contagion of sin; red-pigmented because it was livid through affliction; rose-colored through the shedding of blood. This was “without seam, woven from above throughout” [Note: [Col. 0455] John 19]: without seam, because it was not from the union of male and female; woven from above, because it was made by God’s ordination.

His mother clothed him with these garments: namely, Esau’s exceedingly good garments, which she had with her, and she put the skins of kids around his neck and hands [Note: [Col. 0455] Gen. 27]. Esau, hairy, [Col. 0455B] is corrupt human nature; the exceedingly good garment is Christ’s flesh, clean from the corruption of sin when assumed. But because the kid signifies sin, he is clothed in the skins of kids. He was born “in the likeness of sinful flesh” [Note: [Col. 0455] Rom. 8].

He who put it on imparted fragrance: by which the sluggish might awaken, the devout be stirred, and the dead rise again—those sluggish to patience, the devout to the reality of love, the dead to the glory of incorruption. Concerning the first, Job: “A tree has hope: if its root has grown old in the earth and its trunk has died in the dust, at the scent [of water] it comes to life again” [Note: [Col. 0455] Job 14]. “We shall run,” he says, “in the fragrance of your ointments.” Concerning the second: “Your fragrance has stirred eternal desires within me,” says John. Hence: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell [Col. 0455C] the beloved that I languish with love.” Concerning the third: “My fragrance is unmixed balsam” [Note: [Col. 0455] Ecclus. 24]. Hence: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” [Note: [Col. 0455] Rom. 6]. And in his members: “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat” [Note: [Col. 0455] Rev. 7], because an inestimable fragrance is in his garments.

Therefore, when Isaac had perceived the fragrance of the garments, he said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is as the fragrance of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” [Note: [Col. 0455] Gen. 27]. The Virgin’s womb is the field, full of the angelic salutation, full of the infusion of grace, full of the conception of Christ. At that time Isaac had gone out to meditate in the field, and Rebecca, whose name means “patience,” met him. For in the Virgin’s womb he assumed that by which he endured death for us.

[Col. 0455D] But now let us apply the dew, the rain, and the grass to our own benefit. Dew is threefold, because grace is threefold. There is temporal grace, spiritual grace, and heavenly grace. The first is an instrument for action, the second an increase of virtues, the third supplies nourishment for eternal life. The first gives capacity for acting, the second supplies usefulness, the third bestows immortality. Under Gideon, the first descended upon the fleece [Note: [Col. 0455] Judith 6.]; the second was squeezed out into the bowl; the third watered the threshing-floor. Concerning the first, Paul says to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace which is in you [Col. 0456A] [Note: [Col. 0455] 1 Tim.].” Again: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty [Note: [Col. 0455] 1 Cor. 15.].” Again: “See that you do not receive the grace of God in vain [Note: [Col. 0455] 2 Cor. 6.].” This is the dew of which it is said: “In the morning manna appeared like dew upon the ground.” With some it rotted, with others it remained sound [Note: [Col. 0455] Exod. 16.]. Of the second it is said: “The grace of God has appeared, instructing all people [Note: [Col. 0455] Titus 2.].” Of this the prophet says: “I shall be like dew; Israel shall blossom like the lily [Note: [Col. 0455] Hos. 14.].” Of the third it is said: “From his fullness we have all received glory in the homeland in place of grace on the way [Note: [Col. 0455] John 1.].” Again, of this it is said: “May God give you of the richness of the earth and an abundance of the dew of heaven [Note: [Col. 0455] Gen. 27.].” And Job: “Dew shall remain upon my harvest [Note: [Col. 0455] Job 29.].” The first labours outwardly; the second orders the inward affection; the third [Col. 0456B] rewards these two. For the first, it is said of the valiant woman: “From the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard [Note: [Col. 0455] Prov. 31.].” For the second, of the same woman: “She considered the paths of her household and did not eat the bread of idleness [Note: [Col. 0455] Ibid.].” For the third, of the same: “She shall not fear cold for her household, etc.; for all her household are clothed in double garments [Note: [Col. 0455] Ibid.].” The first is Martha serving with much solicitude; the second is Mary sitting at the Lord’s feet, hearing his word and pondering it in her heart with great diligence; the third is Wisdom inviting to God’s reward. To the first it is said: “Whatever your hand can find to do, do it earnestly; for there is neither work nor calculation nor knowledge nor wisdom in the underworld, to which you are hastening [Note: [Col. 0455] Eccles. 9.].” [Col. 0456C] The second seeks what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God. The third cries: “To the one who conquers I shall give to eat from the tree of life which is in the paradise of my God [Note: [Col. 0455] Rev.].” The clouds rained down the Just One [Note: [Col. 0455] Isa. 45.], because the prophets, obscurely like clouds, foretold Christ. Yet Christ himself, incarnate, was a cloud; hence Elijah’s servant on Carmel saw a cloud rising from the sea like the footprint of a man [Note: [Col. 0455] 3 Kings 18.]. Again: “The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt [Note: [Col. 0455] Isa. 19.].” Again: “I saw a mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud [Note: [Col. 0455] Rev. 10.].” Heaven gave dew, the clouds rain, because, although the works of the Trinity are undivided, grace is nevertheless attributed to the Holy Spirit and mercy to Christ. By mercy the wretched person is helped; by grace the person who has been helped acts rightly [Col. 0456D].

This cloud flashes, rains, and thunders: it flashes by enlightening toward faith; it rains through the exhortation of words; it thunders through threats. By enlightenment it leads to faith; by exhortation, to suffering; by threats, setting before us the calamity of hell. Hence the Apocalypse: “From the throne proceeded flashes of lightning and voices, etc. [Note: [Col. 0455] Rev. 4.].” The first is by miracle, the second by persuasions, the third by threats. This rain of mercy washed, softened, and drenched the Virgin’s earth. It washed it, in order to extinguish in her the tinder of sin; it softened it [Col. 0457A], so that, forgetting the hardness of astonishment, she might yield to the angelic words; it drenched it, so that, casting aside thirst for worldly desires, the divine shoot might grow strong in her from love. Of the first: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you [Note: [Col. 0457] Luke 1.].” Therefore it is said to her: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.” In the second, hear her hardness: “She was troubled at the angel’s saying and considered what sort of greeting this might be [Note: [Col. 0457] Ibid.].” But hear her softness: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word [Note: [Col. 0457] Ibid.].” And therefore she now runs in the fragrance of your ointments. Hear the third: “As rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there, but drench the earth, soak it, and make it germinate, so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth [Note: [Col. 0457] Isa. 55.].” Hence it is said: “You are a garden enclosed, [Col. 0457B] my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.” The garden is enclosed so that thirst for earthly desire may not reach her; the Holy Spirit is the fountain, because he intoxicates her with devotion. Its outflows are those of paradise, because Christ came forth from her womb, he who leads us to paradise.

But in us too this fountain of mercy pours forth three streams: namely, tears of lower compunction, tears of compassion, and tears of higher compunction. The first are for the commission of sins, the second for a neighbour’s affliction, the third for desire of eternal life. These are the three miraculous waters for the children of Israel in the desert. The first are the waters of Marah, which received sweetness when wood was laid upon them [Note: [Col. 0457] Exod. 15.]; the second are the waters from the rock, which flowed out when struck by the rod [Note: [Col. 0457] Exod. 17.]; the third are the waters of the Jordan, [Col. 0457C] which afforded the children of Israel a path for entering the promised land [Note: [Col. 0457] Josh. 3.]. The first came forth from Christ’s body through sweat; the second from his side through the piercing of the lance; the third from his eyes through the pouring forth of tears. Drenched by this water, our earth germinated the Saviour.

But it should be noted that there is the earth of the wicked, the earth of the righteous, and the earth of the blessed. The first germinates a pale shoot, the second a green one, the third a white one. Pale, because it produces eternal misery; green, because it produces the vigour of virtues; white, because it produces eternal joy. Of the first, in Leviticus: “The fruits which germinate shall be unclean to you [Note: [Col. 0457] Lev. 19.].” Hence it is said: “And it shall devour the earth with its produce [Note: [Col. 0457] Deut. 32.].” Of the second: “Let the earth [Col. 0457D] bring forth green grass, bearing its own seed [Note: [Col. 0457] Gen. 1.].” “I went down,” he says, “into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys, and to observe whether the vines had flowered and the pomegranates had budded [Note: [Col. 0457] Song 6.].” Again: “Our bones shall spring up like grass [Note: [Col. 0457] Isa. 66.].” Of the third: “The righteous shall blossom like the lily [Note: [Col. 0457] Hos. 14.].” And of these three: “As the earth brings forth its shoot [Note: [Col. 0457] Isa. 61.].” See the first: “And as a garden makes its seed germinate [Note: [Col. 0457] Ibid.].” See the second: “So the Lord God shall make praise and glory spring up before all nations [Note: [Col. 0457] Ibid.].” See the third: when “the branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth sublime, and joy to those who have been saved [Col. 0458A] from Israel [Note: [Col. 0457] Isa. 4.],” through the grant of our Lord Jesus, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

My sister is a garden enclosed.

[CAR.] “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.” Under the figure of the enclosed garden and sealed fountain, the Lord commends his mother, calling her an enclosed garden. For at the beginning the Lord planted a garden of delight, namely Paradise, in which he placed the tree of life [Note: [Col. 0457] Gen. 2.]. We lost the use of it because that garden was not enclosed. Hence Job says of Satan: “He did not shut the doors of the womb that bore me, nor remove evils from my eyes [Note: [Col. 0457] Job 3.].” It is as though he said: Satan opened the gates of Paradise, from which humankind came forth as though from a womb’s offspring. Had he not opened those gates, [Col. 0458B] evils would have been removed from my eyes. But as a remedy for so great an evil, the Lord made another paradise: the womb of the blessed Virgin, in which he planted the tree of life, when the Son of God, who is life, assumed flesh from her. But the Lord so enclosed this paradise that no malignant enemy had access to it. 94 Yet not merely once, but again she is called an enclosed garden, and this repetition is a confirmation of the truth. The whole Trinity enclosed this garden: the power of God the Father fortified the Virgin against the violence of the devil; the wisdom of the Son, against the enemy’s deceit; the goodness of the Holy Spirit, against that same enemy’s malice.

Isaiah also speaks of the enclosing and fortification of this garden: “The city of our strength is Zion; the Saviour shall be set in it as a wall [Col. 0458C] and a rampart [Note: [Col. 0457] Isa. 26.].” As though he said: O Zion, that is, O Church, I announce to you that the city of strength shall be ours. And what that city is, he shows in the following words: “The Saviour shall be set in it as a wall and a rampart,” namely, shall be set there. Observe that it is said: “The Saviour shall be set in it as a wall.” For if the Saviour is set in it, he is enclosed within it; and if he is set as a wall, he encloses it.

This description of the city therefore applies especially to the blessed Virgin. For the Saviour was enclosed in her through the mystery of the Incarnation, and he himself enclosed her as a wall through the office of defence. Christ himself is figured by Gideon, whose name is interpreted “going about in the womb.” For Christ, in the Virgin’s womb, was circumscribed with respect to his human [Col. 0458D] nature, while nevertheless, through the uncircumscribed nature of his divine power, he encompassed all things. The rampart of this city—which is our refuge and strength of defence—was the continual and watchful guardianship of angels, of which it was said above: “Sixty mighty men, of the mightiest of Israel, surround Solomon’s bed [Note: [Col. 0457] Song 3.].” She too is called a sealed fountain—that is, a fountain marked with a seal. The seal of this fountain was virginal chastity; through that seal Christ came forth without rupture, like a stream of our salvation. Hence in Ecclesiasticus the Son says of himself: “I came forth from paradise like a river-channel [Col. 0459A] (*dioryx*), and like an aqueduct [Note: [Col. 0459] Ecclus. 24.].” He calls the Virgin’s womb paradise, since the Holy Spirit poured such abundance of graces into it that her womb became for the Son of God a paradise of delights and a garden of pleasure. From this paradise came forth a river-channel, *dioryx*, which is interpreted “a remedy of generation.” For the Virgin’s childbirth was a remedy for human generation. Having designated the Virgin by the enclosed garden and the sealed fountain, he proceeds to commend both the garden and the fountain, saying:

“Your outflows are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchards: henna with nard; nard and saffron; reed and cinnamon with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloe with every perfume.”

[Col. 0459B] [THO.] This is the Church which, watered by the heavenly fountain, has brought forth from itself a paradise—not of trees of just any kind, but of pomegranates with the fruits of orchards. Pomegranates are red with a blood-coloured hue: that is, the martyrs, who, after the washing of the fountain—that is, baptism—have also been baptized in their own blood. The fruits of orchards, however, signify the works of virtues in general, or virtuous persons themselves. Henna (*cyprus*) is an aromatic tree in Egypt. Its seed, whiter than coriander seed, is cooked in oil and pressed, and from it is made a royal perfume called *cyprus*; it signifies heavenly grace and patience arising from charity. Nard, which signifies remembrance of Christ’s passion, indicates the works of holy women. [Col. 0459C] Saffron, which is golden in colour, signifies those same persons who abound in greater charity. For nard, because it is hot in nature, designates those who burn with love for the Passion. The reed, which is cassia, has a strong, purple bark and cures disorders of the inner organs. It is small; it signifies those who are strong for enduring Christ’s sufferings and humble in spirit. Cinnamon is a low-growing shrub, exceptional in fragrance, twice as excellent as reed for medicinal uses, and signifies the perfectly humble. Since it is bronze- and ash-coloured, it signifies those who say: “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes [Note: [Col. 0459] Gen. 18.].” *Cinnamomum* is Greek; in Latin, “spotless.” “With all the trees of Lebanon”: these are tall trees, and they signify those in the Church who are of greater merit. Myrrh and aloe express continence of the flesh [Col. 0459D], because bodies of the dead anointed with them do not decay. These are the first perfumes of which the Apostle says: “Though I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but have not charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal [Note: [Col. 0459] 1 Cor. 13.].” This is fittingly joined with myrrh and aloe, because it belongs to the chaste.

There are four sendings forth from heaven: first the devil was sent forth, second a good angel, third the Son of God, fourth the Holy Spirit. The devil, that he may not be admitted; the angel, that he may be sent beforehand; Christ, that he may remit; the Spirit, that he may infuse. The devil was sent forth lest he be admitted [Col. 0460A] to presumptuous exaltation; the angel, that he might be sent beforehand to the Virgin Mary; Christ, that he might remit both actual and original guilt; the Spirit, that he might infuse charity into the heart. In the first the world is brought to death; in the second Mary is fortified in advance; in the third the world is purified; in the fourth a human being rejoices in the Lord. Of the first: “Through the devil’s envy death entered into the world [Note: [Col. 0459] Wis. 2.].” Of the second: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you [Note: [Col. 0459] Luke 1.].” Of the third: “Who is this who even remits sins [Note: [Col. 0459] Luke 5.]?” Of the fourth: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but joy and peace in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0459] Rom. 14.].”

There was also a sending forth from the Virgin’s womb. From her Christ was sent forth into the world, that he might pardon, bestow, and repay: pardon guilt to sinners, bestow gifts upon people, and repay glory to those who live well. Of the first: “Woman, your sins are remitted to you [Note: [Col. 0459] Luke 7.].” Of the second: “He led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings [Note: [Col. 0459] Eph. 4.].” Of the third he says to the innkeeper: “Take care of him; and whatever you spend beyond this, when I return I shall repay you everything [Note: [Col. 0459] Luke 10.].” There are sendings forth from the human heart, when a good reputation proceeds from inward goods. Of the species enumerated here, some bring health, some pertain to preserving health, and some to delight. Contrition of heart is a species with three outflows, which bring health to the soul: the outpouring of tears; shame and prayer expressed by the mouth; and the satisfaction of penitence. Hence the prophet says: [Col. 0460C] “Return to me with your whole heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning [Note: [Col. 0459] Joel 2.].” Spiritual concern has three outflows that pertain to the preservation of health: careful examination of one’s works, just dispensation, and the savoury devotion of these things. The first is against sin; the second, that good may be ordered; the third, that it may be loved. Hence: “Blessed is the man who dwells in wisdom and in understanding meditates upon God’s providence [Note: [Col. 0459] Ecclus. 14.].” Contemplation has three outflows: remembrance of God and of the eternal inheritance to be received; a certain confident expectation in these meditations; and a certain sweetness of spirit. Hence: “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. My memory is unto generations of ages [Note: [Col. 0459] Ecclus. 24.].” These meditations are like a [Col. 0460D] delightful paradise. The Holy Spirit is sent from heaven in order that such consolations may be had and the devil’s wiles detected.

But it should be noted how often he was given. The Holy Spirit was given three times: first before the Passion, second after the Resurrection, third at Pentecost. First, to repress the devil’s power; second, for the remission of sins; third, for the bestowal of virtues. Of the first: “He gave his disciples power to tread upon scorpions [Note: [Col. 0459] Luke 10.].” Of the second: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them [Note: [Col. 0459] John 20.].” Of the third: “Suddenly there came [Col. 0461A] from heaven a sound, and it filled the whole house [Note: [Col. 0461] Acts 2.]” with the powers of the Holy Spirit. Thus in the first the devil is resisted, in the second sin is forgiven, in the third the heart is anointed with grace. In the first one confronts him as he comes; in the second one takes away the thing from him who possesses it; in the third one mocks him as he flees. Thus in the first there is watchfulness against deceit; in the second, a remedy for evil; in the third, possession of good. Accordingly, in the first he is given by word alone; in the second by breath and word; in the third by a visible sign, an audible sound, and the operation of fullness.

Concerning the word: there are three words by which we oppose the devil: a word of rebuke, a word of prayer, and a word of admiration. By the first he is resisted; by the second he is cast out; by the third he is captured. Of the first: when Satan stood at the right hand of Jesus the high priest, it was said to him: “May the Lord rebuke you, [Col. 0461B] Satan [Note: [Col. 0461] Zech. 3.].” Of the second, the Lord says: “This kind is not cast out except by fasting and prayer [Note: [Col. 0461] Matt. 17.].” Of the third, it is read that Solomon shut demons in a vessel by adjuration. This scorpion draws some people into hardness of heart. For *scorpius* (“scorpion”) is said to be as it were *sine cordis pietate*, “without compassion of heart.” It draws some into hypocrisy through pretence. Hence it is also said to be as it were *scoria pietatis*, “dross of piety.” It begrudges religion to others; hence again it is said to be as it were *sugillans corda piorum*, “bruising the hearts of the devout.”

The Holy Spirit was given a second time, not by word alone but by breath. The breath of the Holy Spirit does three things. First, through tearful contrition it removes hardness of heart; second, it renews by forgiving guilt; third, it restores one who is as though dead to life. Of the first: “His spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow [Note: [Col. 0461] Ps. 147],” namely, waters [Col. 0461C] of tears. Of the second it is said here: “He breathed on them, saying: Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them [Note: [Col. 0461] John 20.].”—“For the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters [Note: [Col. 0461] Gen. 1]” of tears, that they might obtain this remission. Thus renewal was accomplished. Hence: “Renew a right spirit within my inward parts [Note: [Col. 0461] Ps. 50.].” Again: “Send forth your Spirit and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth [Note: [Col. 0461] Ps. 103.].” Of the third, the prophet says: “Come, spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain ones, that they may live again [Note: [Col. 0461] Ezek. 37.].” So he “breathes into the face of man the breath of life, and man became a living soul [Note: [Col. 0461] Gen. 2.].”

The first gift of the Holy Spirit pertains to subjects, the second to priests, the third to prelates: to subjects who wage battles; to priests who forgive sins; [Col. 0461D] to prelates to whom the mysteries of heaven are revealed. Of these three it is said: “Moses and Aaron were among his priests; Samuel among those who call upon his name [Note: [Col. 0461] Ps. 98.].” Moses represents the person of prelates, Aaron that of priests, and Samuel that of subjects. Here occurs the “ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard—the beard of Aaron—which descends to the hem of his garment [Note: [Col. 0461] Ps. 132.].” The head on which is the ointment of the Holy Spirit is Christ. The right beard is the prelate; the left beard, the priest; the garment, the Church. [Col. 0462A] Its hem is the subjects. Therefore the grace of the Holy Spirit descends from Christ the head to the prelates; from the prelates to the priests; and from the priests to the subjects. In the figure of subjects, “the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson, so that he might fight with the Philistine [Note: [Col. 0461] Judg. 14.].” In the figure of priests, the Lord took from the spirit of Moses and gave it to the men who ministered to the people in his place [Note: [Col. 0461] Exod. 18]. In the figure of prelates, Elijah’s spirit was given to Elisha, that he might reveal in prophecy heavenly secrets on Elijah’s behalf.

But let us now pass to the fact that at Pentecost the Spirit was given by an audible sound, by fire as a visible sign, and by the office of fullness: the first for instruction, the second for enkindling, the third for perfection; for instruction in religion, enkindling of love, and perfection of ministry. [Col. 0462B] Therefore we find: “The Holy Spirit is mobile, keen, subtle [Note: [Col. 0461] Wis. 7.].” Mobile for subjects, keen for priests, subtle for prelates: for subjects, lest they be sluggish for battles; for priests, that they may cleanse sins; for prelates, that they may understand heavenly secrets. He was mobile when he rushed upon Samson to fight the Philistines [Note: [Col. 0461] Judg. 14], and when he leapt upon David [Note: [Col. 0461] 1 Kings 10]. Hence: “When you hear the sound of one marching at the top of the pear trees, then you shall go out to battle [Note: [Col. 0461] 2 Kings 5.].” Hear “keen”: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he himself shall convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment [Note: [Col. 0461] John 16.].” Hear “subtle”: “But the Paraclete, the Spirit whom the Father shall send in my name, shall teach you all truth [Note: [Col. 0461] John 14.].” Again: “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and [Col. 0462C] daughters shall prophesy [Note: [Col. 0461] Joel 2.].” Thus the spirit of prelates perceives all things, even the depths of God [Note: [Col. 0461] 1 Cor. 2.].

It should be noted that on the first day the Holy Spirit was given in fire. There are three fiftieths: the first, of psalms; the second, of days; the third, of years. The first is for the remission of sins; the second, for the infusion of grace; the third, for the reception of grace. This is the year of jubilee. Therefore there is a fire which reaches the fiftieth, one which does not touch it, and one which consumes it. The first is the fire of charity; 95 the second, of diabolical instigation; the third, of divine punishment. The fire of charity reaches the first fiftieth, because in it the Holy Spirit was given. The fire of diabolical instigation does not touch the second, because it is contrary to love. Hence the fire of Nebuchadnezzar’s furnace [Note: [Col. 0461] Dan. 3] rose forty-[Col. 0462D]nine cubits; it did not reach the fiftieth, in which the youths were placed and saved. For those who unjustly aspire to the third, the fire of divine punishment is prepared—those who, because of their false hope, already reckon themselves among the fiftieth. Hence, at Elijah’s prayer, fire consumed the companies of fifty [Note: [Col. 0461] 4 Kings 1.].

There is also another distinction of sendings. An angel was sent, the Word of God was sent, and a mere human being was sent. The first came from heaven, the second from the Father’s throne, the third was a man sent by God. The first, whose name was [Col. 0463A] Gabriel [Note: [Col. 0463] Luke 1]; the second is Emmanuel [Note: [Col. 0463] Matt. 1]; the third is John [Note: [Col. 0463] John 1]. The first came for ministry, the second for assistance, the third for testimony: for ministry, to speak the King’s secret with the Virgin; for assistance, to show mercy to humankind; for testimony, to bear witness to the light [Note: [Col. 0463] Ibid.]. Hear the secret: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you [Note: [Col. 0463] Luke 1.].” And the assistance: “Our Lord is refuge and strength, a helper in the troubles which have found us exceedingly [Note: [Col. 0463] Ps. 45.].” Again: “We shall give thanks to him, because he has shown us his mercy.” And the testimony: “Behold the Lamb of God [Note: [Col. 0463] John 1.].”

These were sent miraculously. The heavenly city sent the first; virginity bore the second; barrenness begot the third. The first was a messenger of returning blessedness; [Col. 0463B] the second, to perform works of charity; the third, to bear witness to truth. From the first we have joy; with the second we work righteousness; through the third we return to penitence. Of the first David says: “I rejoiced at the things said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0463] Ps. 121.].” Of the second: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? The one who walks without stain and works righteousness [Note: [Col. 0463] Ps. 14.].” The third says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near [Note: [Col. 0463] Matt. 3.].” An angel is called a messenger. These three are found called angels in theology. Of the first: “The angel Gabriel was sent [Note: [Col. 0463] Luke 1.].” Of the second: “His name shall be called Angel of Great Counsel [Note: [Col. 0463] Isa. 9.].” Of the third: “Behold, I send my angel, who shall prepare your ways [Note: [Col. 0463] Mal. 3.].” These three were figured [Col. 0463C] in the three whom Abraham saw coming down the road: he saw three and worshipped one [Note: [Col. 0463] Gen. 18.], for Gabriel and John were not to be worshipped, but Christ alone.

But these must be sent to us in a moral sense. Therefore, first Gabriel—that is, “strength of God”—is made in us; second, Emmanuel, so that the Lord may be with us; third, John, that is, “grace of the Lord.” Therefore, first let us have the power of strength; second, the presence of God; third, the grace of the Lord. The first is for destroying sins; the second, as refuge in tribulations; the third, as help for action. For in the figure of the sinner it was said to blind Tobit: “Be of strong heart; it is near that you shall be healed by the Lord [Note: [Col. 0463] Tob. 5.].” And: “Be strong in battle [Note: [Col. 0463] Heb. 11.].” Of the second: “The Lord of hosts is with us [Note: [Col. 0463] Ps. 45.].” Hence: “Our Lord is refuge and strength [Note: [Col. 0463] Ibid.].” Of the third: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me [Note: [Col. 0463] Ps. 120.].” Hence Paul says: “I laboured more than all of them—yet not I, but the grace of God with me [Note: [Col. 0463] 1 Cor. 15.].”

There is threefold proof that John was sent by God: first, from his conception; second, from the conversation; third, from the comparison. The conception was miraculous, the conversation gracious, the comparison virtuous. The first was signified by an angelic announcement; the second by the mothers’ conversation; the third [Col. 0464A] by comparison with Elijah’s manner of life. Of the first, the angel says: “Elizabeth shall bear a son, and his name shall be called John.” Of the second: “Mary went into the hill country and greeted Elizabeth.” Of the third: “He himself shall go before in the spirit and power of Elijah [Note: [Col. 0463] Luke 1.].”

Let us now consider the conception. Gabriel becomes the bearer; Zachariah, the unbeliever. Each parent is elderly: the one a bearer of the new birth, the other unbelieving toward the future event. Old age surpasses the limits of nature. The new grace is made known through the angel; Zachariah becomes mute; old age blooms again. Of the first: “You shall call his name John.” Of the second: “You shall be silent and unable to speak.” Of the third: “Elizabeth your kinswoman has conceived her son in her old age [Note: [Col. 0463] Ibid.].”

And morally: through the first, let us see what has been conceived in us; through the second, what is cut away; through the third, what is put to death. Newness of grace is conceived; superfluous speech is cut away; inveterate iniquity is put to death. The first, so that an affection of devotion may be conceived in us; the second, so that in us may be found the effect of prayer, divine praise, and preaching; the third, so that growth in virtues may blossom anew in us. Of the first Paul says: “His grace in me was not empty [Note: [Col. 0463] 1 Cor. 15.].” Hear the affection: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell the beloved that I languish with love [Note: [Col. 0463] Song 5.].” Of the second: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth. But if any is good, let it build up those who hear; and let old things depart from your mouth [Note: [Col. 0463] Eph. 4.].” Hence it is said to the bride: “Let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet [Note: [Col. 0463] Song 2.].” Of the third: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, [Col. 0464C] as you are unleavened [Note: [Col. 0463] 1 Cor. 5.].” And to the bride: “Winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared in our land [Note: [Col. 0463] Song 2.].” Winter is malice in the heart; rain is softness in the flesh; flowers are virtues in action. Behold the miraculous conception.

The gracious conversation follows. It is truly grace where Mary greets, Elizabeth prophesies, and John leaps for joy: Mary greets the mother of the Forerunner; Elizabeth prophesies the advent of the Redeemer; John leaps in the presence of his Redeemer. Of the first: “She came into Zachariah’s house and greeted Elizabeth.” Of the second: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” Of the third: “The child leapt for joy in my womb [Note: [Col. 0463] Luke 1.].”

And morally: Elizabeth means “house of God,” Mary “star of the sea,” John “grace,” and Jesus “saviour” or “saving.” The house of God is sincerity of heart; [Col. 0464D] the star of the sea is the truth of special understanding. Thus Elizabeth, that is, the house of God, conceived John when purity of heart receives an infusion of graces. Mary, that is, the star of the sea, conceived Jesus when special understanding both believes Christ glorified and hopes that it will reach his brightness in the life to come. In the first, the Lord found the hearts of the disciples clean receptacles, infused with the gifts of charisms. Hence the bride says: “The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress [Note: [Col. 0463] Song 1.].” Behold the house of God. But hear of the gifts of charisms infused: “Our bed [Col. 0465A] is flowering [Note: [Col. 0465] Song 1.].” Of the second: “May the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus our Lord [Note: [Col. 0465] Phil. 4]!” Hence, of the bride: “Who is she who comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed for battle [Note: [Col. 0465] Song 6.].” She comes forth like the dawn when she beholds the purity of conscience; she is fair as the moon when, by example, she offers benefit to her neighbour; she is chosen as the sun when she both hopes for and sees Christ’s brightness. Thus far concerning the conversation.

The comparison follows: “He shall go before,” he says, “in the spirit and power of Elijah, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people [Note: [Col. 0465] Luke 1.].” In the spirit is prophecy; in power, perfect righteousness among the people; example and teaching. The first is that by which the Lamb of God is shown; the second [Col. 0465B] that by which he is praised by Christ; the third that by which a neighbour is converted. Of the first: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world [Note: [Col. 0465] John 1.].” Of the second: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen [Note: [Col. 0465] Luke 7.].” Of the third: “That he may turn the hearts of fathers toward their children [Note: [Col. 0465] Luke 1.].”

Morally, we possess the spirit of prophecy when we foresee future things, both good and evil; perfect righteousness when we do not do to others the evils we do not wish done to ourselves. Third, we convert our neighbour from his malice. In the first, the misery of hell and the blessedness of heaven are considered; in the second, adversity is willingly endured; in the third, the neighbour’s benefit is sought. Of the first: “It is better for you to enter life blind than, having two eyes, to be cast into Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0465] Matt. 18.].” Hence the bride says: “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0465] Song 1.].” [Col. 0465C] Of the second: “If someone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also [Note: [Col. 0465] Matt. 5.].” And the bride: “The sons of my mother fought against me [Note: [Col. 0465] Song 1.].” Of the third: “If a person has been caught in any fault [Note: [Col. 0465] Gal. 6.],” etc. The bride invites such persons thus: “Eat, my friends, and drink; be intoxicated, beloved ones [Note: [Col. 0465] Song 5.].” Behold the comparison.

It follows: “Whose name was John [Note: [Col. 0465] John 1.].” John means “the grace of God.” Rightly is this name given to him spiritually by the angel [Note: [Col. 0465] Luke 1.], since the grace of the whole Trinity is in some measure revealed to him at his baptism, now by sight, now by hearing. Hence this three-syllable name remains unchanged in every case in the singular number. For he saw the Son in the flesh, the Holy Spirit in the dove, and heard the Father in the voice [Note: [Col. 0465] Matt. 3.].

For the sake of these persons, he recognized a threefold grace. [Col. 0465D] For there is the grace of adoption, the grace of incarnation, and the grace of operation. The first belongs to the Father, the second to the Son, the third to the Holy Spirit. By the first the Father calls us to an inheritance; by the second the Son assumed our weakness; by the third the Holy Spirit leads us to the city. By the first we are heirs and children of the Father; by the second, co-heirs and companions of Christ; by the third the Spirit of counsel governs us. Of the first Paul says: “He who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace” [Note: [Col. 0465] Gal. 1.]; of the second: “The grace of God has appeared [Col. 0466A] to all people, instructing us” [Note: [Col. 0465] Titus 2.]; of the third: “There are varieties of graces, but one Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0465] 1 Cor. 12.]. Of the first and second: “Heirs indeed of God, and co-heirs indeed of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0465] Rom. 8.]; of the third: “Your good Spirit will lead me into the upright land” [Note: [Col. 0465] Ps. 142].

It follows: “This man came to bear witness concerning the light” [Note: [Col. 0465] John 1.]: that he might dispel, wash away, and atone for. He might dispel darkness, wash away foulness, and pay for captivity: the darkness of the Mosaic law, the foulness of both actual and original guilt, and the captivity of human nature. He did the first by teaching and miracles, the second by the water of baptism, the third by the shedding of blood. Of the first, by word and miracles: “Jesus began to do and to teach” [Note: [Col. 0465] Acts 1]. “The night has gone before, but the day has drawn near” [Note: [Col. 0465] Rom. 13]. Of the second: “I shall pour [Col. 0466B] clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your iniquities” [Note: [Col. 0465] Ezek. 35]. Of the third: “By the blood of your covenant you redeemed your bound ones from the pit in which there was no water” [Note: [Col. 0465] Apoc. 5; Jer. 3].

Three bore witness to this light. The Father bore witness, Peter bore witness, and John bore witness: the Father, that he was the Son; Peter, that he was the Christ; John, that he was the Lamb. The Lamb, who might wash; the Christ, who might anoint; the Son, who might bring in. He might wash by the laver of mercy, anoint with the oil of gladness, and bring into the kingdom of glory. Of the first: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” [Note: [Col. 0465] John 1]. This adverb *behold* is demonstrative. Of the second: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” [Note: [Col. 0465] Matt. 16]—“that he may make the face cheerful with oil” [Note: [Col. 0465] Ps. 103]—Peter says. *You* is a demonstrative pronoun. *Christ* is called “anointing.” [Col. 0466C] Of the third it is said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” says the Father [Note: [Col. 0465] Matt. 3], who carried the hundredth sheep upon his shoulders back to the flock [Note: [Col. 0465] Luke 15]. *This* is a demonstrative pronoun.

In a moral sense: John means grace, Peter firmness, while Father is a name of love. Therefore, if we are able with John to bear witness to Christ, we must be absolved from sins by his grace, persevere steadfastly in the anointing of devotion, and walk in love. Thus let a clean conscience bear witness to Christ; let our steadfastness cling to him firmly; let the intensity of love follow him continually and ardently, so that with Jesus we may rejoice in the glory of the true light. Amen.

[Col. 0466D] Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruit of orchard-trees; henna with nard, nard and crocus, calamus and cinnamon with every tree of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes with all the choicest perfumes.

[CARD.] In these words the fruitfulness of the garden is displayed. For the shoots and products of the Virgin are called a paradise with every kind of fruit and tree, aromatic herb, and perfume. By the paradise the Church is signified; by the herbs and trees, the faithful within the Church. Their virtues are denoted by the fruits, their works by the perfumes, and the sacraments are likewise denoted. All these are said to be sent forth or proceed [Col. 0467A] from this garden, because all the faithful are from the Church: all virtues of the faithful produce flowers or fruits in no other way. Nor do the perfumes of the sacraments avail unless the root of all, faith, is formed in the mystery of the Incarnation, through which both God became the son of a woman and the woman was made the mother of God.

Therefore, by the fruits of pomegranates, in which many seeds are enclosed beneath a single rind, are prefigured the fruits of associations or congregations in the Church; but by the fruits of orchard-trees are signified the 96 merits of individual persons. By henna, which is a white and fragrant tree, chastity is signified; by nard, humility; by crocus, which changes into its own colour the things with which it is mixed, just as leaven draws kneaded flour into its own savour, charity [Col. 0467B] is expressed, for it is the form of all virtues. Calamus, which is purple in colour and represents the blood of the Passion, signifies compassion, which conforms a human being to the likeness of Christ’s death. By ash-coloured cinnamon remembrance of death is expressed; by myrrh and aloes are shown the greater and lesser mortification of the flesh.

Thus in the herbs we have either the virtues themselves or those distinguished by those virtues. We have also, in the herbs, the lesser persons; but in the trees of Lebanon and the other trees, those who rise to higher things in virtue and merit. It follows:

> A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon.

[THO.] This fountain is heavenly teaching, which rises [Col. 0467C] in the enclosed garden of the Lord—that is, the primitive Church—in order to water other gardens, that is, Churches born from it. It is also called a well: a well because the fountain is not open to everyone, but to spiritual persons and also to the lesser ones; to the greater, however, it is open through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. Living waters are those which continually flow from springs; these are not cisterns filled by snow or rain, but flow with force from Lebanon. *Lebanon* is interpreted “whitening.” This is the Church, which is white through its life. Of these streams it is said: “He who believes in me, streams shall flow from his belly” [Note: [Col. 0467] John 7]. Living waters are said to flow with force because, when the apostles preach them, no one can resist them; yet in preaching they gave up their lives.

This fountain is manifold. It washes, waters, and gives drink to what is unclean, dry, and thirsty. Since our uncleanness is threefold, the fountain that washes it away is threefold. The first is that of original guilt, the second that of actual guilt, the third that of our corruption. The fountain of baptism washes away the first; the fountain of tearful confession, the second; the fountain of heavenly blessedness, the third. Of the first: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” [Note: [Col. 0467] Zech. 13]. Of the second: “Who will give waters to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” [Note: [Col. 0467] Jer. 9]. Of the third, Boethius:

> Grant, Father, that the mind may ascend to the august seat;  
> Grant that it may behold the fountain of the Good.

[Col. 0468A] “I shall pour,” says the Lord through the prophet, “clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” [Note: [Col. 0467] Ezek. 36]. This is the fountain of kids; the second, the fountain of gardens; the third, the fountain of lambs. In the first kids—that is, sinners—are washed, that they may become clean; by the second gardens—that is, those striving after virtues—are watered, that they may become fruitful; by the third lambs—that is, the innocent and meek—are given drink, that they may be made drunk with the abundance of God’s house [Note: [Col. 0467] Ps. 35].

The second fountain waters our dryness. For this fountain goes out from paradise and waters the whole earth. In our garden we have a valley, a plain, and a hill. The dry valley is penitence without an outpouring of tears; the dry plain is a known need of one’s neighbour without compassion; the dry hill is endurance [Col. 0468B] of tribulations with murmuring; the dry mountain is knowledge of heavenly things without devotion. But Caleb gave Achsah, his daughter, the lower and upper watering-place [Note: [Col. 0467] Judg. 1], that is, of mountain and valley; and where these two are, there are also the two intermediate places. This fountain first waters the valley, as David says: “I shall water my bed with my tears” [Note: [Col. 0467] Ps. 6]. It waters the plain: “Their soul shall be like a watered garden” [Note: [Col. 0467] Jer. 31]. For the garden nourishes that by which it feeds others, and this is compassion. It waters the hill of adversities, whence the prophet says: “The Lord shall water the torrent of thorns” [Note: [Col. 0467] Joel 3], which is the onrush of tribulations. It waters the mountains too: “Watering the mountains from his upper regions” [Note: [Col. 0467] Ps. 103].

Accordingly, if penitence has an outpouring of tears, one’s neighbour receives compassion, the afflicted person exultation, and the contemplative devotion, [Col. 0468C] the watering will be complete: the valleys will abound in grain, the plains will be filled with plenty, the hills will gird themselves with exultation, and there will be “the mountain of God, a rich mountain” [Note: [Col. 0467] Ps. 67].

The third fountain gives drink. There are three thirsty persons: the penitent thirsts in order that he may be able to endure labours for God; the advancing person thirsts to savour the things above; the perfect person thirsts to see God. Of the first the Lord will say: “I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” [Note: [Col. 0467] Matt. 25]. To the Samaritan woman, concerning the second: “Give me drink” [Note: [Col. 0467] John 4]. Concerning the third: “I thirst” [Note: [Col. 0467] John 19], he said on the cross.

The first fountain is that of which Rebecca, whose name is interpreted “patience,” gave drink to Damascus and the camels [Note: [Col. 0467] Gen. 24]; the second is that which God gave Samson after the Philistines had been killed [Note: [Col. 0467] Judg. 15]; the third is at the gate of Bethlehem, interpreted “house of God,” and David thirsted for it [Note: [Col. 0467] 2 Sam. 23]. Of the first it is said: “You who thirst, come to the waters” [Note: [Col. 0467] Isa. 55]. Of the second: “He who thirsts, let him come and drink; a river of living waters shall flow from his belly” [Note: [Col. 0467] John 7]. Of the third: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” [Note: [Col. 0467] Ps. 41].

There is dead water, weak water, and living water. The first is grace by which a person breaks out into pride; the second, grace by which a person is afraid to act through sloth; the third is grace by which one acts well through wisdom. The first is the Dead Sea, in which no creature can live; it is the water of Jericho, which Elisha healed by casting in salt [Note: [Col. 0467] 4 Kings 2]. [Col. 0469A] The second is the water of Marah, from which the children of Israel could not drink because of its bitterness, unless wood—that is, the cross—was laid upon it [Note: [Col. 0469] Exod. 15]. The third is from the fountain at the gate of Bethlehem, from which David desired to drink [Note: [Col. 0469] 2 Sam. 23].

Therefore Elisha—that is, “My God is Lord”—heals the first by applying the salt of wisdom; Moses—that is, “saved from the waters”—heals the second by confession of Christ’s cross; the third is carried to David, namely, “desirable in sight,” that is, Christ, through the exploit of the three mighty men: Eleazar, that is, “the strength of my God”; Shammah, that is, “obedient to the Lord”; and Jashobeam, that is, “coming to his senses,” who chooses the foolish things of the world with Christ in order to confound the wise.

It should be noted that the soul sometimes thirsts for God, sometimes thirsts toward God, sometimes thirsts in God, and sometimes thirsts according to [Col. 0469B] God. He thirsts for God who says: “My soul has desired you in the night, and likewise my spirit within my breast” [Note: [Col. 0469] Isa. 26]. The soul thirsts toward God when it says: “My soul thirsted toward God, the living fountain” [Note: [Col. 0469] Ps. 41]. The soul thirsts in God when it says: “My soul thirsted in you” [Note: [Col. 0469] Ps. 62]. The soul thirsts according to God when it says: “My soul has desired to long for your justifications at every time” [Note: [Col. 0469] Ps. 118].

The soul thirsts for God when it desires to experience how sweet the Lord is; the soul thirsts toward the Lord when it desires to be raised above itself and to see the king in his beauty; the soul thirsts in God when, in ecstasy of mind, it desires wholly to pass into God; the soul thirsts according to God when it abandons its own will or judgment, so that it may say: [Col. 0469C] “I have not come to do my own will” [Note: [Col. 0469] John 5].

In the first, God enters the mind and the mind returns to itself; in the second, it rises above itself and is lifted to God; in the third, the mind is raised to God and passes wholly into him; in the fourth, the mind goes out for God’s sake and descends below itself. In the first the mind enters into itself; in the second it passes beyond itself. In the first it enters by meditation; in the second it ascends by contemplation; in the third it is brought in by jubilation; in the fourth it enters by compassion.

A fountain is grace openly offered to many; a well is grace manifest only to spiritual persons. There are three wells, as we have already said, which Isaac’s servants dug [Note: [Col. 0469] Gen. 26]. They call the first “contentions,” the second “enmities,” the third “abundance.” From the first is drawn the water of worldly [Col. 0469D] prudence; from the second, that of literal knowledge; from the third, that of heavenly wisdom. Of these waters Job says: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters, and those who dwell with them” [Note: [Col. 0469] Job 26].

Giants are notable above other human beings in three respects. First, because they are born from the earth—hence they are said to derive their name from Greek *gē* (γῆ), “earth”; second, because they are great; third, because they are strong. The first seek earthly things; the second lofty but philosophical matters; the third pursue heavenly things vigorously. The first treat earthly matters for earthly ends; the second heavenly matters for earthly ends; the third heavenly matters for heavenly ends. The first seek temporal advantage; the second the vanity of glory; [Col. 0470A] the third heavenly sweetness. The first seek the things upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0469] Col. 3]; the second, “although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God” [Note: [Col. 0469] Rom. 1]; the third savour the things above [Note: [Col. 0469] Col. 3], that is, the waters which flow with force from Lebanon, that is, which come from the brightness of heavenly glory.

> A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon.

[CAR.] Having treated the garden more fully, he adds concerning the sealed fountain. It is said to be the fountain of gardens, that is, the fountain from whose stream the gardens are watered. For when the Son said of himself in Ecclesiasticus, “Like an aqueduct I came forth from paradise” [Note: [Col. 0469] Ecclus. 24], he added, “I shall water the garden of my plantations” [Note: [Col. 0469] Ibid.]. Therefore she herself is the fountain, the Son the stream; the garden of plantations, planted with the herbs and [Col. 0470B] trees mentioned above, is the Church, watered by the river that flows from the sealed fountain.

She herself is also, because of the unfathomable depth of graces heaped up in her, a well of living waters—that is, graces springing up into eternal life. In granting benefits to human beings, these graces flow abundantly, powerfully, and with force, such that our adversaries, evil spirits, cannot resist them. They flow from Lebanon, that is, from the Virgin herself, who says of herself in Ecclesiasticus: “Like Lebanon not cut down, I filled my dwelling with fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0469] Ibid.]. For she gave birth to her Son without cutting, with her virginity unimpaired, just as Lebanon, the tree of incense, gives out a fragrant vapour. Observe that she says, “I made my inheritance fragrant” [Col. 0470C]—as if to say: I brought him forth without injury, he who would dwell bodily in me, while I dwelt spiritually in him.

The following passage concerns this flowing and rushing force of the waters flowing from Lebanon:

> Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.

[THO.] In the north and the south are signified two temptations of the Church. In the north, which is a cold wind, is understood the severity of the world when it terrifies; in the south, which is warm, the flattery of the world when it deceives. The Lord showed that the Church is wearied by this twofold temptation in the parable of the good seed, explaining it thus: “Those who fell upon rock are they who receive the word with joy, but they have no root. For when [Col. 0470D] persecution arises, they are immediately scandalized on account of the word. And those which fell among thorns are they who receive the word, but are choked by the deceitfulness of riches and become unfruitful” [Note: [Col. 0469] Matt. 13].

The south wind is the Holy Spirit; the north wind is the evil spirit; they contend, as it were, for the salvation and damnation of a human being. For the north wind, perceiving our inward disposition from outward signs, is first swift in devising evil, second importunate in temptation, third heavy in obstinacy. In the first respect it is called *aquilo* [north wind], as though *swift as eagles* (*aquilis ocior*); hence Jeremiah: “Our persecutors were swifter [Col. 0471A] than the eagles of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0471] Lam. 4]. In the second respect it is called *aquilo*, as though “far from rest” (*a quiete longe*); hence: “They devised iniquities in their heart all day; they prepared battles” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 139]. In the third it is called *aquilo*, as though “binding waters with a burden,” namely by freezing them into obstinacy; hence the prophet says: “They hardened their face above rock” [Note: [Col. 0471] Jer. 5].

Of the first: “He stretches out the north over the void” [Note: [Col. 0471] Job 26]; of the second: “A whirlwind wind came from the north” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ezek. 1]; of the third: “From the north every evil shall be opened” [Note: [Col. 0471] Jer. 1]. When the Holy Spirit expels him, he takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself [Note: [Col. 0471] Luke 11]. For there are seven good spirits, seven wicked ones, and seven more wicked ones.
