The good spirit of wisdom is opposed by the wicked spirit of foolishness; more wicked is the spirit of simulated wisdom. The good spirit of understanding is opposed by the evil spirit of stupidity; more wicked is the simulation of learning. The good spirit of counsel is opposed by the wicked spirit of imprudence; more wicked is the simulation of foresight. The good spirit of fortitude is opposed by the wicked spirit of cowardice; more wicked is weakness under the shadow of deceptive strength. The good spirit of knowledge is opposed by the wicked spirit of ignorance; more wicked is the usurpation of knowledge. The good spirit of piety is opposed by the wicked spirit of impiety; more wicked is false piety. The good spirit of fear is opposed by the wicked spirit of rashness; more wicked is the deceit of feigned religion.

Since the north wind is evil and the beginning of evil, it should be noted that there is evil which defiles, evil which troubles, and evil which torments: namely sin, the devil, and hell. Against this threefold pestilence—[Col. 0471C] of guilt, conflict, and punishment—David prays for threefold mercy in three psalms. The first: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 50]; the second: “Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me down” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 55]; the third: “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul trusts in you” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 56].

This verse shows the north wind’s threefold temptation: “Let not the tempest of water overwhelm me,” namely the violent temptation of adversities; “nor let the deep swallow me,” namely the fraudulent deception of impiety; “nor let the well press its mouth upon me” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 68], namely the perilous thing of despair.

But the south wind, coming against the three things mentioned above, does three things: it moderates the swiftness of evil, extinguishes importunity, and melts obstinacy, according to the threefold interpretation of its name. In the first sense *auster* [south wind] is said to mean “tempering breezes”; in the second, “laying low the burning heat of the north wind”; in the third, “increasing the seeds of the earth,” or “removing barrenness.” Against the first the south wind gives the sinner a fountain of tears; against the second, the fruit of virtues; against the third, that a person may go wholly into God.

Of the first: “Turn, O Lord, our captivity like a torrent in the south” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 125]; of the second: “Does the hawk become feathered, spreading its wings toward the south?” [Col. 0472A] [Note: [Col. 0471] Job 39]; of the third: “He led me by the southern way, and behold, a gate facing south” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ezek. 40]. Against evil design he appeared in the form of a dove [Note: [Col. 0471] Matt. 3]; against the heat of importunity, in a cloud [Note: [Col. 0471] Matt. 17]; against the coldness of obstinacy, in fire [Note: [Col. 0471] Acts 2].

Thus the south wind, when it comes, refreshes the garden of our heart. If it finds the heart bright as heaven, it advances it further; if dark as an abyss, it brings it back to brightness; if firm in constancy like earth, it makes it firmer; if slippery as water, it restores it to solidity. For “the Lord has done whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all abysses; bringing clouds forth from the end of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 134]. The first regions of the earth are good works; the middle regions are indifferent works, such as eating, and so forth; the extremities of the earth are sins. From these latter follow: clouds, that is, the darkness of shame; lightning, the terror of majesty; and rain, the tears of compunction.

Thus the Holy Spirit works in us: first we are ashamed through remembrance of sins; second, we are shaken by terror; third, we are pierced with compunction in weeping. I see a cloud over myself whenever “the shame of my face has covered me” [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 43]. I receive lightning whenever the terrors of the Lord wage war against me [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 87]. Rain falls whenever I can water my bed [Note: [Col. 0471] Ps. 6]. After such rain winds are brought forth from the treasuries, because after weeping comes the consolation of the Holy Spirit; for winds are called his gifts which console. By these the firstborn of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0471] Exod. 12] are struck down—from man, that is, the arrogance [Col. 0472C] of holiness, to cattle, that is, the pride of vanity.

Four of the seven winds pertain to the intellect, three to the affection. To the intellect belong wisdom, understanding, discernment, and knowledge; to the affection, confidence, love, and fear. From those four arise the affections of the three, because understanding comes first, and then being affected by what has been understood. The spirit of wisdom blows from the south; the spirit of understanding, from the east; the spirit of counsel, from the north; the spirit of knowledge, from the west.

The treasury from which these proceed is divided into four storehouses. The first is fashioned in the western part, from the historical sense; the second is raised in the northern region, from the moral sense; the third, furnished from allegory, stands in [Col. 0472D] the east; the fourth, from anagogy, in the south. In the western one is stored the silver of eloquence; in the northern, varied and innumerable gems of virtues; in the eastern are contained purple, fine linen, and the other royal ornaments in the sacraments of the Church; in the southern is kept the gold of heavenly wisdom. In the first faith is taught; in the second action is instructed; in the third devotion is exercised; in the fourth contemplation of heavenly things begins.

Through history we learn what has been done; through morality we know what ought to be done; [Col. 0473A] through allegory we understand how the sacraments of the Church were foretold in the figures of preceding things. Through anagogy, “we behold the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made” [Note: [Col. 0473] Rom. 1]. Let us therefore make a certain inner person, whose bones are the natural powers, such as chastity and sobriety; these, without charity, are not virtues and thus are dry bones. Let sinews of fortitude be laid upon them, lest they lie scattered; let the work of piety be put on over them, to nourish the flesh of the poor. Or the sinews are discernment, which joins virtues together; the flesh is sensuality, which covers bones and sinews while applying its senses to them. Let the skin of honourable conduct be stretched over all through fear. The human being has been formed, [Col. 0473B] but does not yet live until charity informs these things—namely, the Holy Spirit, who comes from the four winds mentioned above through understanding.

Therefore, when the north wind rises, the south wind comes—that is, the Holy Spirit—and blows through the garden of our heart. But first it breathes upon, second it blows toward, third it blows through. It breathes upon, and phantasms flee; it blows toward, and charisms come; it blows through, and spices flow: the phantasms of wicked suggestions, the charisms of spiritual graces, the spices of heavenly delights. Hear of the breathing upon: when Christ appeared to his disciples after the resurrection, he breathed on them, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0473] John 20]. He adds how the phantasms flee: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” [Note: [Col. 0473] Ibid.].

Likewise, through the blowing toward, charisms come: diverse voices sound together, and they proclaim God’s mighty works [Note: [Col. 0473] Acts 2], because to one is given kinds of tongues, to another discernment of spirits, to another interpretations of utterances [Note: [Col. 0473] 1 Cor. 12], and so forth. “One and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” [Note: [Col. 0473] Ibid.]. Here hear of the blowing through: “Blow through,” he says, “my garden, and its spices shall flow”—that is, hear the bride flowing with the spices of heavenly delights. “Who,” she says, “is this who comes up through the desert, abounding in delights?” [Note: [Col. 0473] Cant. 8].

But the bride herself, desiring at the coming of the Holy Spirit to be filled with his grace and to have the fervour of charity kindled in her members, so that through him love of God and neighbour may increase and discernment of spirits may be acquired, cries:

> “Come, Creator Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful [Col. 0473D] [Note: [Col. 0473] Invocation to the Holy Spirit].”

There are four spirits: the spirit of the flesh, the spirit of the world, the spirit of the devil, and the Spirit of God. The first is an unclean spirit; the second, a vain spirit; the third, a wicked spirit; the fourth, the Holy Spirit. The first defiles; the second mocks; the third devises fraud; the fourth comes to help. The first kindles desire; the second makes a person slippery; the third empties the heart of the imprudent of virtues; the fourth fills the hearts of his faithful. The first extends the impulses of desire; the second spreads the veil of favour; the third stretches the snares of error; [Col. 0474A] the fourth kindles the fire of his love.

Of the first the Apostle says that some are puffed up by the spirit of their flesh [Note: [Col. 0473] Col. 2]; of the second: “We have not received the spirit of this world” [Note: [Col. 0473] 1 Cor. 2]; of the third: “An evil spirit of God troubled Saul” [Note: [Col. 0473] 1 Sam. 16]; of the fourth: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful and withdraw from desires that are without understanding” [Note: [Col. 0473] Wis. 1].

Thus the first spirit is the spirit of impurity, the second the spirit of falsehood, the third of iniquity, the fourth the Spirit of truth. The first stains through gluttony and lust; the second deceives through vainglory; the third grieves at guilt forgiven and grace bestowed; the fourth fulfils his promises. Of the first it is said: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a human being” [Note: [Col. 0473] Luke 11], and so forth; of the second: “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources” [Note: [Col. 0473] John 8]; [Col. 0474B] of the third: “He takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself” [Note: [Col. 0473] Luke 11]; of the fourth: “When I have been taken up, I shall send you the Spirit of truth” [Note: [Col. 0473] John 16].

But because discernment of spirits is not given to everyone, it is necessary to consider carefully “that one should not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God” [Note: [Col. 0473] 1 John 4]. This unclean spirit pollutes in pleasure, consent, and deed. Thus John, in the Apocalypse, saw three unclean spirits coming out from the dragon’s mouth in the likeness of frogs [Note: [Col. 0473] Apoc. 16]. For a frog lives in a marsh, touches the earth with its belly, and makes frequent leaps with its feet. One lives in a marsh who delights in lust; one touches the earth with the belly who consents; one leaps with the feet when one acts.

This unclean spirit defiles: first through the flow of thoughts; second by kindling desire; [Col. 0474C] third through the effect of deeds; fourth through the excess of conduct. Thus it often cast the boy into fire, often into water, dashed him to the ground, and caused him to foam [Note: [Col. 0473] Mark 9]. It casts him into water through the flow of thoughts; into fire when it kindles desire; it dashes him to the ground through the perpetration of deeds. It causes foaming through the multitude of excesses. For foam arises from an excess of humours.

It follows:

The lying spirit: it lies by invention, lies by proclamation, lies by promise. It lies by proclamation because it instructs others to lie; it lies by promise because it does not render what was promised. First it was cast out; second, man was infected; third, man was deceived. Of the first: “When he speaks [Col. 0474D] a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father” [Note: [Col. 0473] John 8], that is, the father of lying. In the second case it says: “I shall be a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab’s prophets” [Note: [Col. 0473] 2 Chronicles 21]. In the third, it lied to Eve when it said: “Why did God command you not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?” And she: “Lest perhaps we die.” And he: “By no means shall you die. For God knows that, on whatever day you eat, you shall be like gods” [Note: [Col. 0473] Genesis 3].

It lies to its neighbour, it lies to itself, it lies to God. It lies to its neighbour when it asserts truth as falsehood, or falsehood as truth; it lies [Col. 0475A] to itself when it disguises its sin; it lies to God when it takes no care to fulfil a vow. It was lying to its neighbour when Daniel said to it: “You too have rightly lied against your own head” [Note: [Col. 0475] Daniel 13]. For the shameless elders were lying in order to put Susanna to death. Of the third David says: “Unjust witnesses rose up against me, and iniquity lied to itself” [Note: [Col. 0475] Psalm 26], just as Adam lied when he excused his sin [Note: [Col. 0475] Genesis 3], as did Ananias and Sapphira, who concealed the money [Note: [Col. 0475] Acts 5]. It lies to God. Hence Job: “Does our God need falsehood, that you should speak deceits for him?” [Note: [Col. 0475] Job 13]. Thus the children of Israel lied, who returned in heart to Egypt [Note: [Col. 0475] Exodus 16].

The spirit of wickedness, as has been said, devises deceits, strips the souls of the imprudent of their virtues, and lays snares. It devises deceits, as the serpent [Col. 0475B] corrupts Eve’s understanding along with that of her children [Note: [Col. 0475] Genesis 3]. It strips the souls of the imprudent of virtues, and thus despoils the man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho [Note: [Col. 0475] Luke 10]. It lays snares, so as thus to cast man, with feet and hands bound, into outer darkness [Note: [Col. 0475] Matthew 22]. In the first case he loses the way; in the second, he loses the grace of his Lord; in the third, he endures the forced services of his adversary.

Of the first the prophet says: “The roads have been laid waste; the traveller on the path has ceased” [Note: [Col. 0475] Isaiah 33]. For Dan becomes a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path [Note: [Col. 0475] Genesis 49]. For he is that evil spirit of God which troubled Saul [Note: [Col. 0475] 1 Samuel 16]. Of the second: “The enemy stretched out his hand over all Jacob’s precious things” [Note: [Col. 0475] Lamentations 1]. Hence the same writer: “The stones of the sanctuary were scattered at the head of every street” [Note: [Col. 0475] ibid.], because Nebuzaradan, commander of the army, carried the vessels of the Temple to Babylon [Note: [Col. 0475] 2 Kings 25]. This the wicked [Col. 0475C] spirit did. Hence: “He takes with him seven spirits more wicked than himself” [Note: [Col. 0475] Luke 11]. This wicked spirit is called sevenfold because it deprives one of sevenfold grace.

Of the third: “In this path in which I walked they hid a snare for me” [Note: [Col. 0475] Psalm 141]. Hence Job says of Behemoth: “The sinews of his testicles are intertwined” [Note: [Col. 0475] Job 40]. This spirit so hardens a man that he opens neither his mouth for prayer and confession nor his ears for preaching. Of it the Lord says in the Gospel: “Deaf and dumb spirit, come out of him” [Note: [Col. 0475] Mark 9].

Behold, the earth is empty and void, and darkness is upon the face of the deep [Note: [Col. 0475] Genesis 1]. With regard to the unclean spirit, darkness is upon the face of the deep; with regard to the vain spirit, the earth is empty; with regard to the wicked spirit, the earth is void: dark because of the gloom of gluttony and lust; empty because of the vanity of the world; void because virtue has been lost. But “the Spirit of the Lord was borne over these waters” [Note: [Col. 0475D] ibid.], because against the unclean spirit he sets the clean Spirit, against the vain spirit the Spirit of wisdom, against the wicked spirit the upright Spirit. The first, to remove the uncleanness of the unclean spirit; the second, to remove from the vain spirit the folly of the world; the third, to bring about righteousness.

He sets the first against the unclean spirit because “the Spirit reaches everywhere by reason of its purity” [Note: [Col. 0475] Wisdom 8]; the second against the vain: “for the Spirit of wisdom is kindly” [Note: [Col. 0475] Wisdom 1]; the third [Col. 0476A] against the wicked: for he is the princely Spirit. Hence: “Strengthen me with a princely Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0475] Psalm 50]. For he is the Spirit of truth.

Therefore the Holy Spirit comes in this order: first he breathes, second he instructs, third he empties, fourth he forestalls. He breathes prevenient grace; he instructs those who are fighting to flee evil and choose good; he empties the presumptuous confidence of the arrogant; he forestalls the faithless security of the sluggish. The first, that the heart may be pierced with compunction; the second, that one who has been pierced may be justified; the third, that prevenient grace may not be imputed to merits; the fourth, that the flight of grace may be feared. Of these four it is said: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” [Note: [Col. 0475] John 3]. He breathes where he wills when grace is bestowed; you hear his voice when our wickedness is instructed [Col. 0476B]; but it does not know whence it comes, because your conscience has no knowledge of what proceeds from [98] merits; nor whither it goes, because you do not know to what end your righteousness comes. It follows:

“Fill the hearts of your faithful.”

First he supplies, second he fills, third he completes. He supplies what our weakness cannot do; he fills what wickedness has emptied; he completes, so that holiness may persevere in us. The first, that a man may be stronger for acting; the second, that he may be richer in virtues; the third, that he may be more long-suffering. Of the first David says: “Strengthen me with a princely Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0475] Psalm 50]. But “the Holy Spirit helps our weakness. For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself prays for us with unutterable groanings” [Note: [Col. 0475] Romans 8], so that “what our ability [Col. 0476C] does not obtain may be granted us through his intercession” [Note: [Col. 0475] Office of the Church]. Of the second: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak” [Note: [Col. 0475] Acts 2]. Of the third: “Your good Spirit shall lead me into the right land” [Note: [Col. 0475] Psalm 142]. It follows:

“And pour out in them the fire of your love.”

This fire first consumes, second kindles, third burns. It consumes healthfully, kindles sweetly, burns blessedly. The first is in converts, the second in the righteous, the third in saints and angels. In the first, sin begins to depart; in the second, the mind begins to transcend itself; in the third, angel and human being, stripped of this mortality, rejoice. The first was in Mary Magdalene; the second in John the Evangelist; the third affects the burning seraphim [Col. 0476D]. “Our God is a consuming fire” [Note: [Col. 0475] Deuteronomy 4]. Hence: “Many sins have been forgiven her, because she loved much” [Note: [Col. 0475] Luke 7]. Of the second: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will but that it burn?” [Note: [Col. 0475] Luke 12]. In accordance with this it is said: “I love those who love me; and those who watch for me in the morning shall find me” [Note: [Col. 0475] Proverbs 8]. Of the third: “You make your angels spirits, and your ministers burning fire” [Note: [Col. 0475] Psalm 103]. With this fire the angels burn continually. Hence: “Charity never fails” [Note: [Col. 0475] 1 Corinthians 13], because what is possessed on the way is possessed in the homeland.

[Col. 0477A] Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.

[CAR.] As though she were saying to the wicked spirit signified by the north wind: Arise, do not press upon the Church in order to crush her; rather, withdraw and yield, conquered by him who has been foretold to you. But you, south wind—that is, the inspiration of the Holy Spirit—blow through my garden, that is, through my mother, steadfastly; breathe into her an abundance of graces, so that from her remedies of benefits may flow abundantly and unfailingly to the weak. It follows in the mother’s voice:

CHAPTER V—Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his trees.

[THO.] Let the Lord come into his Church, that he may preserve her immaculate and fruitful in the harvest of faith. [Col. 0477B] For as long as I can say, “I shall love you, O Lord, my strength” [Note: [Col. 0477] Psalm 17], he will deliver me from my enemies and set me upon the heights of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0477] ibid.], that he may eat the fruit of his trees. Hence he says to his disciples: “I have food to eat which you do not know” [Note: [Col. 0477] John 4].

This may also be said in the voice of the perfect, who know how to serve God with sincere devotion: “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his trees.” As though it were plainly said: Let the gracious Lord come, that he may restore the reward to us. There is a garden of vegetables, a garden of fruit trees, a garden of nuts, and a garden of spices. Of the first, Sedulius says:

> Some worship vegetables, and throughout soft gardens  
> water their dry divinities.

Of the second, in this place: “Let my beloved come into [Col. 0477C] his garden.” Of the third: “I went down into my garden to see the fruits of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0477] Song of Songs 6]. Of the fourth: “My beloved went down into his garden, to the bed of spices” [Note: [Col. 0477] ibid.].

In order that we may eat the first, it is first cut with iron; the second is put into a pot; the third is cooked in fire. The second, namely the fruit, is peeled; the third, namely the nut, is separated when its shell is broken; the fourth, namely the spice, is crushed in a mortar. The first are penitents; the second are those who cast off the outward favour they receive, as the peel of a fruit; the third are those who willingly endure the breaking afflictions; the fourth are those who, imbued with heavenly savour, do not feel the sufferings inflicted on them, and thence diffuse a good fragrance among others.

The first are cut, judging their sins when they say: “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0477D] Psalm 105]. They are placed in the pot of discipline, to whom it is said: “All discipline seems to one undergoing it not to be joy but sorrow; yet afterwards it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0477] Hebrews 12]. They are cooked in the fire of which it is said: “Burn my reins and my heart” [Note: [Col. 0477] Psalm 25].

See how the second attributes to God the glory of favour, namely, casts the peel away from himself: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” [Note: [Col. 0477] Psalm 113]. And: “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0477] 2 Corinthians 10]. See how the third constrains [Col. 0478A] the shell: “Although our outer old man is corrupted, yet the one within is renewed from day to day” [Note: [Col. 0477] 2 Corinthians 4]. Hear how the fourth are insensible through heavenly sweetness: “The stones of the torrent were sweet to him.”

The first still await the Lord; the second call him; by the third he is now received; in the fourth he is now fed. The first do so through shame; the second from a pure conscience; the third through patience; the fourth through wisdom. The first say with the centurion: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” [Note: [Col. 0477] Matthew 8]. The second say with Cleophas and Ammon: “Stay with us, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0477] Luke 24]. The third, rejoicing with Zacchaeus, receive him into their house [Note: [Col. 0477] Luke 19]. The fourth have the great furnished upper room, where he eats the Passover with his disciples [Note: [Col. 0477] Mark 14].

Or, if it please you, understand these four gardens in one man. In the first, man begins, as though he were a lowly vegetable, to account himself humble; in the second, as the peel of a fruit, he separates temporal goods from himself in works of mercy; in the third, like the shell of a nut, he breaks himself in affliction; in the fourth he sprinkles his neighbours, as it were with spices of spiritual life, with fragrance. In the first he hears the Lord saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0477] Matthew 11]. In the second he hears: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” [Note: [Col. 0477] Luke 14]. In the third he hears: “Whoever hates his life in this world preserves it unto eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0477] John 12]. In the fourth he hears: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy, and no one shall take your joy [Col. 0478C] from you” [Note: [Col. 0477] John 16].

When the beloved comes, he eats of these four fruits. This garden is the womb of the Blessed Virgin. O blessed and pleasant garden, adorned with the threefold flower of miracle! O blessed fruit, gathered and preserved by most devout persons, and presented to the highest King in his court!

To behold the beauty of this garden and the worthiness of the aforesaid persons, the Church thus invites us: “Behold the miracle of the Mother of the Lord: a Virgin conceived, knowing no union with a man.” At the offering of the Saviour four venerable persons come forth: Joseph, Mary, Anna, and Simeon. Joseph bears the governance of the world; Mary displays the miracle; Simeon utters the oracle; holy Anna receives the desired [Col. 0478D] breath. The governance is he who teaches the way of truth; the miracle is fruitful virginity; the oracle is the weakness that shall die in Christ; the spectacle is the divinity in charity. The first removes error from the pilgrim; the second brings wonder to nature; the third proclaims the Redeemer; the fourth shows the Saviour.

Of the first: “Give heed, you who rule Israel, you who lead Joseph as a sheep” [Note: [Col. 0477] Psalm 79]. Of the second: “Behold the miracle.” Of the third: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many” [Note: [Col. 0477] Luke 2], and so forth. Of the fourth: “Now dismiss your servant, O Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” [Note: [Col. 0479A] Luke 2].

Joseph bears the governance of the world which directs those sailing on the sea, travelling on land, and flying in the air. Those sail upon the sea who roll about in the shifting pleasures of the flesh; those walk upon land who prosper in earthly goods; those fly in the air who, raising their hearts on high, delight in heavenly things. But “whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps” [Note: [Col. 0479] Psalm 134]. In the first, he saved Peter walking upon the sea [Note: [Col. 0479] Matthew 14]. In the second, he converted Paul wandering as he went to Damascus [Note: [Col. 0479] Acts 9]. In the third, he received Elijah ascending through the air [Note: [Col. 0479] 2 Kings 13].

For he is the angel in the Apocalypse who set his right foot upon the sea, his left upon the land, and lifted his hand to heaven, [Col. 0479B] swearing that time would be no more [Note: [Col. 0479] Revelation 10]. With the first foot he treads down the pleasure of the flesh; with the second, the vanity of the world. With his uplifted hand he summons and draws the one ascending; he swears that time shall be no more—that is, delay or the motion of mutable things—because in heaven there is no change, nor shadow cast by the alternation of things [Note: [Col. 0479] James 1]. To the first he cries: “Arise, hasten, my beloved” [Note: [Col. 0479] Song of Songs 2]. To the second it is said: “Come from Lebanon, bride, and you shall be crowned” [Note: [Col. 0479] Song of Songs 4], that is, from the whiteness of the world; for Lebanon means “whitening.” The third cry: “Draw me after you” [Note: [Col. 0479] Song of Songs 1]. Joseph bears this one, who is called “increase,” namely, growing in virtues.

Mary displays the miracle. Her miracle is threefold. [Col. 0479C] First she is greeted by the angel; second, the tinder of sin is extinguished in her; third, virginity is made fruitful. The first is wrought by the angel, the second by the Holy Spirit, the third by the Son of God. Of the first: “The watchmen of the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; they took away my cloak.” The watchman of the city, that is, of the Church, is the angel, the Holy Spirit, and the Son of God. The angel struck her with a certain astonishment of disturbance. For she was troubled at his saying, and considered what sort of greeting this might be [Note: [Col. 0479] Luke 1]. The Holy Spirit wounded her with the love of Christ and took away her cloak, that is, the veil of ignorance.

Of the second: “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0479] Song of Songs 2]. Of the third: “Your womb is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies” [Note: [Col. 0479] Song of Songs 7]. These three miracles which we set forth are to be imitated by us. First, then, let us cultivate familiarity with angels; second, let us flee the tinder of sin according to the capacity of our weakness; third, let us glorify and bear Christ in our heart and body through the merit of chastity [Note: [Col. 0479D] 1 Corinthians 6]. We seek the first through devout prayer, the second by fighting temptation, the third by vehement love.

For the wife of Manoah acted in this order. First, seeing the angel; second, she spoke to him, saying: “Wait, that we may prepare for you a kid from the goats” [Note: [Col. 0479] Judges 13]. [Col. 0480A] Third, she conceived Samson, whose name means “their sun.” Mary, or the holy soul, is called the wife of Manoah, whose name means “rest from rest,” that is, from God the Father, in whom we shall rest eternally if we rest temporarily from sin. The goats are sins. The kid, which is the leader of the goats, is the tinder of sin which we sacrifice to God when we subject the tinder of sin to ourselves. When this has been done, we conceive the Sun of righteousness.

Let us have the first through devout prayer. Hence, because Tobias had an angel familiar to him, the angel said: “When you fasted and prayed, I presented your prayers to God” [Note: [Col. 0479] Tobit 12]. Of the second Paul says: “I find another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind. Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0479] Romans 7]. But in order that [Col. 0480B] in the third place we may conceive through the merit of chastity and love of Christ, let us say: “Our bed is flowering” [Note: [Col. 0479] Song of Songs 1], because of chastity, because of love. Christ says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: [Col. 0479] John 14].

Simeon utters the oracle: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many, and for a sign that shall be contradicted; and a sword shall pass through your own soul” [Note: [Col. 0479] Luke 2]. For the fall of damnation; for the resurrection of restoration; for the sign of testing; the sword of the Passion shall pass through.

The fall is threefold. The first was from heaven into this darksome air; the second from Paradise into the world; the third from the world into hell. The first was of angels, [Col. 0480C] the second of the first-created humans, the third of the obstinate. Of the first: “When Michael fought with the dragon, there was a great fall in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0479] Revelation 12]. Of the second the prophet says: “He himself shall repair the ruins of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0479] Isaiah 51]. And David: “He shall judge the nations; he shall fill up the ruins” [Note: [Col. 0479] Psalm 109]. Of the third Solomon says: “Before ruin the heart exalted itself” [Note: [Col. 0479] Proverbs 24]. Likewise: “The fear of the Lord is a fountain of wisdom, that one may turn aside from the ruin of death” [Note: [Col. 0479] Proverbs 12].

The first is irreparable, the second curable, the third irremediable. Of the first it is said: “Their place was found no more in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0479] Revelation 20]. Of the second: “The Lord lifts up all who fall and raises all who are cast down” [Note: [Col. 0479] Psalm 145]. Of the third, Job says: “He who descends into hell shall not ascend again, nor shall he return any more to his own place” [Note: [Col. 0479] Job 17].

[Col. 0480D] Therefore Christ, who is the wisdom of the Father, became a cause of fall to the first, because they did not hesitate to seek equality with this wisdom; to the second, because they refused to acquiesce in the counsel of wisdom; to the third, because they refused to walk after Christ, wisdom. For the first said: “I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne” [Note: [Col. 0479] Isaiah 14]. To the second it is said: “Because you despised my counsel and neglected my corrections, I too shall laugh at your destruction” [Note: [Col. 0479] Proverbs 1]. To the third it is said: “Whoever follows [Col. 0481A] me does not walk in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0481] John 8]. The middle group, as has been said, can rise again. Hence it was said: “He is set for the resurrection of many” [Note: [Col. 0481] Luke 2].

There is a spiritual resurrection, a particular resurrection, a general resurrection, and a special resurrection. The first is of the predestined; the second is of those inspired; the third is of all; the fourth is of the blessed. The first is through the infusion of grace; the second is for testing; the third is for the restoration of nature; the fourth is for recompense. Of the first: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above” [Note: [Col. 0481] Colossians 3]. Of the second: “The deaf hear, the dead rise” [Note: [Col. 0481] Matthew 11]. Of the third: “We shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be changed” [Note: [Col. 0481] 1 Corinthians 15].

99 Of the fourth: “One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, another the glory of the stars; so is the resurrection [Col. 0481B] of the dead” [Note: [Col. 0481] ibid.]. It follows: “And for a sign that shall be contradicted” [Note: [Col. 0481] Luke 2].

The sign is threefold: there is the sign of the living God, the sign of the righteous person, and the sign of the life-giving wood. The first is the display of a miracle; the second, the outward discipline of a religious person; the third, the instrument of suffering. And this is the sign of testing. In the first, Christ is proved to be God; in the second, a righteous man; in the third, a strong man.

As a figure of the first John says: “I saw an angel having the sign of the living God” [Note: [Col. 0481] Revelation 7]. Hence: “These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons” [Note: [Col. 0481] Mark 16], and so forth. And Nicodemus: “No one can do these signs which you do unless God is with him” [Note: [Col. 0481] John 3]. Of the second: “From every tribe of the children of Israel, twelve thousand sealed” [Note: [Col. 0481] Revelation 7], namely, with the sign of religious life. And: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, is marked [Col. 0481C] upon us” [Note: [Col. 0481] Psalm 4], that is, the brightness of Christ’s religious life, he who is called the countenance of God. And Isaiah: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law” [Note: [Col. 0481] Isaiah 8]. Of the third it is said: “Mark Tau upon the foreheads of the men who have not gone astray” [Note: [Col. 0481] Ezekiel 9]. And the doorposts of the Israelites in Israel were marked with the blood of the lamb [Note: [Col. 0481] Exodus 12]. This sign of the cross shall be in heaven when the Lord comes for judgment.

First it was contradicted when they said of him: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” [Note: [Col. 0481] Matthew 12]. Second, thus: “Why does your master eat with publicans and sinners?” [Note: [Col. 0481] Matthew 9]. And: “This man is a drinker of wine” [Note: [Col. 0481] Matthew 11]. Third, as Paul says: “They are enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame” [Col. 0481D] [Note: [Col. 0481] Philippians 3].

It follows: “A sword shall pass through your own soul” [Note: [Col. 0481] Luke 2]. This sword of the Passion went, passed through, and passed completely through. It went as far as the soul of the Saviour; it passed through to the soul of his mother; it passed completely through the soul of the Virgin. In the first, Christ gave up his own soul; in the second, the martyr rendered up his soul in return; in the third, Mary held her soul suspended. He gave it up in suffering; the martyr rendered it in return for the recompense of suffering; Mary suspended it from every consolation.

See how she saw Jesus scourged, smeared with spittle, pierced with nails, pierced through with a lance; and thus, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit [Note: [Col. 0481] Matthew 26, 27]. [Col. 0482A] See the one rendering in return: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I shall take the cup of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0481] Psalm 115]. Hence Stephen first repaid to the Saviour the death which the Saviour deigned to suffer for all. Mary, suspending her soul, could say: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0481] Lamentations 1]. And: “I am black but beautiful, because the sun has discoloured me” [Note: [Col. 0481] Song of Songs 1]: black through the cruelty of grief, beautiful through charity; the Sun of righteousness has discoloured me.

It follows, the desired spectacle which Simeon received. O blessed widow who saw the spectacle! O blessed old man who saw salvation, bore the light, acknowledged glory: the salvation of all whom he predestined, the light of the nations whom he enlightened by faith, the glory of the Israelites from whom he took flesh. [Col. 0482B] Hence he himself says: “Now dismiss your servant, O Lord, in peace” [Note: [Col. 0481] Luke 2]. Of the first: “Because my eyes have seen your salvation” [Note: [Col. 0481] ibid.]. Of the second: “A light for the revelation of the nations” [Note: [Col. 0481] ibid.]. Of the third: “And the glory of your people Israel” [Note: [Col. 0481] ibid.].

O in how great a peace his spirit rested, as he said: “Now dismiss your servant, O Lord, in peace.” Why? “Because my eyes have seen your salvation.” Did he not bear the light of which it was said: “The old man bore the child, but the child guided the old man”? Therefore he was the light when the old man was guiding him; he acknowledged the glory of Israel. Hence it was said: “Simeon received weakness in his hands, but inwardly acknowledged majesty.” For Israel means “seeing God.” Glory, therefore, belongs to those who see the Lord: [Col. 0482C] here “through a mirror and in an enigma,” in the homeland “face to face” [Note: [Col. 0481] 1 Corinthians 13].

Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his trees.

[CARD.] For the mother, hearing herself called a garden and remembering also that fig tree which, because it did not feed Christ seeking fruit upon it, was cursed by him and withered [Note: [Col. 0481] Matthew 21], invites her beloved to come and eat, and to delight in the fruit of the trees—that is, in the works of virtues which he planted in her. But he, invited, is immediately present; and he commends himself for the good refreshment, saying:

I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.

[THO.] “I come very often,” he says, “into [Col. 0482D] my Church, and I never cease to do this throughout her time of pilgrimage: that I may correct the erring, help the weak, strengthen those doubtful in faith, and feed upon the fruits of those who do good.” By myrrh are signified those who have ended their lives in martyrdom, or those who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. By spices are signified all who are distinguished by the renown of good works. He gathers when he cuts off martyrs and other perfect people from this life, as though with a certain sickle of death, and brings them to the storehouses of heavenly blessedness. “Many are called, but few are chosen” [Note: [Col. 0481] Matthew 20].

[Col. 0483A] The Lord calls the wicked, he calls the weak, he calls the righteous: the first to repentance, the second to steadfastness, the third to glory; to repentance, by which they may purify themselves; to steadfastness, by which they may persevere; to glory, by which they may receive rewards. Of the first, through the prophet: “Return to me, and I shall return to you” [Note: [Col. 0483] Zechariah 1]; and: “Why will you die, house of Israel?” [Note: [Col. 0483] Ezekiel 33]. Of the weak: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I shall refresh you” [Note: [Col. 0483] Matthew 11]. Of the third: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Note: [Col. 0483] Matthew 25].

He calls because the first die in their sins, the second are burdened by the difficulty of the way, and the third await him with great longing. Among the first, some refuse and do not excuse themselves; some refuse and excuse themselves; some neither excuse themselves nor refuse. [Col. 0483B] The first have no fear; the second have servile fear; the third filial fear. The first do not excuse themselves because they regard this exile as the highest happiness; the second excuse themselves before God, reckoning him merciful beyond measure; the third neither refuse nor excuse themselves, knowing that God will be judge and generous rewarder. The first say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” [Note: [Col. 0483] 1 Corinthians 15].

The second put forward as excuses pleasure of the flesh, curiosity of the senses, worldly occupation, and worldly rank: like those invited to the wedding, of whom one said, “I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come” [Note: [Col. 0483] Luke 14]: behold, the pleasure of the flesh. Another said, “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them” [Note: [Col. 0483] ibid.]: behold, curiosity, or worldly occupation. The third said, “I have bought a farm, [Col. 0483C] and I must go out and see it” [Note: [Col. 0483] ibid.]: behold, worldly rank or vanity.

Those who neither excuse nor refuse themselves say: “What then shall I, most wretched man, say or do, if I bring no good work before so great a judge?” To the righteous it is said: “I have gathered my myrrh.” As though he said: In return for the abasement of humility, I give a crown; in return for sorrow of heart, joy; in return for the shame of suffering, praise and glory. Thus it is read in Isaiah: “I shall give,” he says, “a crown for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0483] Isaiah 61]. Thus he gathers the myrrh of bitterness.

“But you shall also gather spices of sweetness,” when the poor in spirit and the humble shall be blessed, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0483] Matthew 5]. The meek—that is, the gentle—shall possess the earth: now that of the heart, then that of the body, or likewise that of the heavenly homeland, when the peacemakers shall be blessed, shall be children of God, and those pure in heart shall see God [Note: [Col. 0483D] ibid.]. See also the spices stored in the cellars, namely faith, hope, and charity. Faith shall pass into certainty; hope shall attain what it expects; charity shall not be emptied, but shall grow into its perfection—that is, into everlasting love of God and neighbour.

Again, we have heard the bridegroom, we have heard the bride, we have heard the garden: the bridegroom by whom the bride is aroused; the bride who is invited; the garden to which she is called. [Col. 0484A] In the first, namely the bridegroom, we have generosity; in the bride, kinship; in the garden, pleasantness: generosity by which the bridegroom shares his joys; kinship by which she is called sister and bride; pleasantness where myrrh and spices are named.

He is truly generous who gives to the needy, gives to those who labour, and gives to sinners: to the needy, refreshment; to those who labour, consolation; to sinners, forgiveness; refreshment of food, consolation in tribulations, forgiveness of sins. Abraham fittingly prefigured this when he received three men in hospitality [Note: [Col. 0483] Genesis 18]. As a figure of the first, he gave them food; for the second, he placed them beneath the shade of an oak; for the third, he washed their feet with water.

Hence Samuel also says to Saul: “When you come before the oak of Tabor, three men shall meet you: [Col. 0484B] one carrying three kids, another three loaves of bread, and a third a flask of wine” [Note: [Col. 0483] 1 Samuel 10]. In the kids is understood remission of sins; in the loaves, refreshment; in the wine that gladdens, consolation. Of the first: “He heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds” [Note: [Col. 0483] Psalm 146]. Of the second: “He gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him” [Note: [Col. 0483] ibid.]. Of the third: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord, who consoles us in all our tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0483] 2 Corinthians 1].

But it should be observed that this threefold bread signifies that bread which came down from heaven; for it accomplishes three things: it restores the failing, strengthens the one already sound, and satisfies the hungry. It restores unto grace, strengthens for battle, and satisfies by granting a taste of wisdom. The five loaves, with which he fed the crowd in the wilderness, signify the first [Note: [Col. 0483] Matthew 14]. [Col. 0484C] Hence he says: “If I dismiss them fasting, they will faint on the way” [Note: [Col. 0483] Mark 8]. Of the second: “Bread strengthens the heart of man” [Note: [Col. 0483] Psalm 103]. In its strength Elijah walked as far as Horeb, the mountain of God [Note: [Col. 0483] 1 Kings 19]. Of the third: “Break your bread for the hungry, and [receive] wanderers” [Note: [Col. 0483] Isaiah 58], and so forth. The priest Ahimelech gave this bread to David when he was hungry and fleeing from Saul [Note: [Col. 0483] 1 Samuel 21]. Behold refreshment.

It follows: consolation. This is the flask of wine. Wine taken moderately produces three things: namely, it makes one subtle, bold, and cheerful, namely, against the three tribulations of man.

It must be keen-witted against the devil’s devices, bold against the darts of temptations, and cheerful in accepting the scourges brought upon it. Thus, in the first there must be diligence; in the second, boldness; in the third, joy. Of the first wine it is said: “Your eyes are more beautiful than wine” [Note: [Col. 0483] Gen. 49], that is, Christ’s disciples possess greater subtlety than others—a subtlety compared with wine. Isaiah reproaches the Jewish people concerning the second as follows: “Your wine is mixed with water” [Note: [Col. 0483] Isa. 1], that is, your boldness is mixed with faintheartedness. Of the third: “Wine gladdens the heart of man” [Note: [Col. 0483] Ps. 103].

Behold consolation. Forgiveness follows, signified in three kids, because a kid signifies sin. These are three because there is original sin, actual sin, and the debt of eternal death. The first is broken at Christ’s birth; the second is destroyed by repentance; the third is remitted by Christ’s Passion. The first is the kid sacrificed by Manoah to the angel at the announcement of Samson [Note: [Col. 0485] Judg. 13]; the second, that which Judah promises on account of intercourse with Tamar [Note: [Col. 0485] Gen. 38]; the third, by whose blood Joseph’s garment is dyed by his brothers [Note: [Col. 0485] Gen. 37]. Hence: “Their blood was sprinkled upon my garments” [Note: [Col. 0485] Isa. 63].

Hear the first broken: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise,” says David [Note: [Col. 0485] Ps. 115]. Hear the second destroyed: “Our old man was crucified with Christ, that the body of sins might be destroyed, so that we should no longer serve sin” [Note: [Col. 0485] Rom. 6]. For it is destroyed with Christ when, conforming our sins to his Passion, we wash them away by repentance. Hear the third: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell” [Col. 0485B; Note: [Col. 0485] Hos. 13], says he who, by dying, destroyed our death and, by rising, restored life [Note: [Col. 0485] Ecclesiastical Office]. “For now, as John says, there shall be no more death, nor mourning, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” [Note: [Col. 0485] Rev. 21].

O how generous is he who restores what was lost, grants what is freely given, and preserves what has been entrusted. In the first see the Lord’s pardon; in the second, a friend’s goodwill; in the third, an advocate’s care. In the first, the fugitive is called back; in the second, something is given to one who possesses; in the third, what has been given is retained. The first is represented to us by the father receiving his son [Note: [Col. 0485] Luke 15]; the second, by the man who went into a far country and entrusted his goods to his servants [Note: [Col. 0485] Luke 19]; the third, by the woman who hid leaven in measures of flour [Note: [Col. 0485] Matt. 13].

The woman is divine Wisdom [Col. 0485C]. She hides the leaven—that is, she preserves wisdom in the purity of conscience. But what that father did for the prodigal son must not be passed over. First he saw him from afar; second, he ran to meet him; third, he fell upon his neck; fourth, he received him with a kiss; fifth, he gave him the first robe together with a ring and shoes; sixth, the fatted calf is killed; seventh, music and dancing are heard.

The first four belong to the first point. He saw him from afar through foreknowledge; he ran to meet him through prevenient grace; he fell upon his neck through repentance; through the kiss he gave confidence in pardon. The three that follow belong to the second point, that is, freely granted gifts. The father gave him shoes for the protection of his feet—that is, of his affections—lest through desire they touch earthly things [Col. 0485D]. He also gave the first robe, that is, the justification of the soul, that it might be adorned with virtues. He also gave a ring on his hand, so that he might possess perfection in works.

Behold how he restores what was lost and grants what is freely given. There follows how he preserves what has been entrusted. First, in adversity he gives patience; second, in prosperity he preserves the harmony of virtues, lest they fall into discord through pleasure, vanity, and pride; third, he pours in his love, that it may flow out again in love of neighbor through showing mercy to that neighbor [Col. 0486A].

The first is effected by the fatted calf [Note: [Col. 0485] Prov. 15], that is, Christ’s flesh, the spiritual food which strengthens one for endurance. The second is music (*symphonia*), said to derive from *syn*, “together,” and *phonos*, “song”; this signifies the harmony of virtues. The third is the dance, which has two pipes: an upper one, through which it receives the breath from above, and a lower one, through which it sends back its sound, “like drops dripping upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0485] Ps. 71]. For love of God and neighbor accomplishes much in preserving virtues.

To such a one it is said: “Come into my garden.” Behold the generosity of the beloved. Relationship follows, namely: “my sister, my bride.” The Church is the Bridegroom’s sister: first animal, second spiritual, third royal; first through kinship, second through religious life, third through adoption. For first Christ, together with the persons of the Church, is born from parents of the same stock; second, religious persons live in the household, of one mind and one way of life; third, they are crowned in the kingdom [Col. 0486B].

First she is a little sister; second, mature; third, perfect. For first she brings little benefit to her neighbor; second, she does God’s will; third, she attains the inheritance. Of the first: “My little sister has no breasts” [Note: [Col. 0485] Song 8]; of the second: “Whoever does the will of my Father, he is my brother and sister and mother” [Note: [Col. 0485] Mark 3]; of the third, it is said here: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride.” Of the first the Apostle says: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0485] 1 Cor. 3]; of the second: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0485] Rom. 8]; of the third: “We shall indeed be heirs of God, and co-heirs with Christ” [Col. 0486C; Note: [Col. 0485] Ibid.].

Every human being has three sisters. The first is the temptation of corruption, the second reason, the third wisdom. The first pricks, the second leads, the third feeds: it pricks so that a person may thus be tested; it leads because a person is enlightened; it feeds so that a person may be drawn toward heavenly things. Of the first: “I said to corruption, ‘You are my father,’ and to worms, ‘My mother and my sister’” [Note: [Col. 0485] Job 17]. This is Miriam, Moses’ sister, who murmured against him [Note: [Col. 0485] Num. 12]. Of the second: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken to?” [Note: [Col. 0485] Song 8]. For we speak with reason when we consult it. This is Sarah, to whom Abraham said as he went down into Egypt: “Say, I pray, that you are my sister” [Note: [Col. 0485] Gen. 12]. Of the third: “I said to wisdom: ‘You are my sister’” [Col. 0486D; Note: [Col. 0485] Prov. 7]. This is Martha, who ministers [Note: [Col. 0485] Luke 10], and Lazarus, one of those reclining at table, whom she feeds [Note: [Col. 0485] John 11].

The bride is admitted for the begetting of children, for rest in the bed, and for knowledge of secrets. In the first she is industrious, in the second beautiful, in the third delightful: industrious, that the number of believers may increase; beautiful, without the cosmetic of temporal things; delightful, through the taste of heavenly things. Of the first the Apostle says: “The woman shall be saved through the bearing of children” [Note: [Col. 0485] 1 Tim. 2]. This is that strong woman who “planted a vineyard from the fruit of her hands” [Note: [Col. 0485] Prov. 31]. To her the Bridegroom comes down into “my garden” [Col. 0487A], to see the fruits of the valleys, and to observe whether the vines have flowered and the pomegranates have budded. She meets him as an honored mother, saying: “I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope” [Note: [Col. 0487] Sir. 24]. As though she said: “I bear for you those who love, fear, know, and hope.”

She is also beautiful. Hence it is said to her: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish in you” [Note: [Col. 0487] Song 4]—namely, no blemish of temporal anxiety. For she is the woman of whom the Apocalypse says: “I saw the holy city Jerusalem descending like a bride adorned for her husband” [Note: [Col. 0487] Rev. 21]. Thus she approaches her Bridegroom for rest in the bed, so that she may say: “While the king was at his table, nard of myrrh gave forth its fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0487] Song 1].

She is also admitted to knowledge of secrets, as through Paul, John the Evangelist, the prophets, and spiritual persons who, with unveiled face, behold the glory of God [Col. 0487B]. Hence she is delightful: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness, abounding in delights?” [Note: [Col. 0487] Song 3]. This is “the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet” [Note: [Col. 0487] Rev. 12]. Behold the affinity for which the Bridegroom calls her thus: “Come into my garden,” to the heavenly pleasantness, “where I have gathered my myrrh with my spices”—that is, where I have graciously received the bitterness of repentance and prepared for myself the spices of heavenly sweetness.

“**I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.**”

[THO.] (Thus.) The honeycomb is those who understand the Scriptures and explain them to others. Those are called honey who gladly taste the meals of the word set before them and desire them insatiably [Col. 0487C]. In wine are understood strong and eminent preachers of heavenly things; in milk, hearers still weak. Therefore, when the Lord sees the children of the Church fervent in these pursuits, he eats wine with honey, delighting, as in a sweet banquet, in their perfections; and he invites others to similar refreshment when he adds: “Eat, friends, and drink; become drunk, dearly beloved.”

Isaiah says: “The Lord will make upon Mount Zion a banquet of rich foods, a banquet of vintage wine, of rich foods full of marrow, of clarified vintage wine” [Note: [Col. 0487] Isa. 26]. These are the four affections which we have toward the two spies of Jericho [Note: [Col. 0487] Josh. 2], namely, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The first affection is the banquet of rich foods, which we have toward Christ’s humanity, here called the honeycomb [Col. 0487D]. The banquet of rich foods full of marrow is the affection we have toward Christ’s divinity, here called honey. The banquet of vintage wine is the affection toward the Holy Spirit on account of the consolation of the simple, here called milk. The banquet of clarified vintage wine is affection toward the Holy Spirit on account of the abundance of charisms which he grants to the more perfect.

Toward Christ’s humanity we have three affections: first toward his birth, second toward his Passion, third toward his resurrection [Col. 0488A]—first, humility; second, compassion; third, exultation. Humility, by which “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0487] Phil. 2]; compassion, by which “he became obedient to the Father even unto death” [Note: [Col. 0487] Ibid.]; exultation, by which “every creature, groaning and travailing, is delivered from the bondage of corruption.” By his birth we are formed; to his Passion we are conformed; by his resurrection we are re-formed.

We are formed when we hear that “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” [Note: [Col. 0487] Jas. 4]. We are conformed because “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example that we should follow in his footsteps” [Note: [Col. 0487] 1 Pet. 2]. We shall be re-formed when he reforms the body of our humility, making it conformed to the body of his glory. Behold the banquet of rich foods, in which we shall eat the honeycomb.

Let us eat honey, and there will be for us a banquet of rich foods full of marrow [Col. 0488B]. This is the affection toward Christ’s divinity, which is threefold. For we are moved toward him because of his condescension, because of his love by which he reconciled us to the Father, and because of his generosity, because he made us co-heirs of the heavenly kingdom.

Let us drink milk. This is the banquet of vintage wine: affection toward the Holy Spirit on account of the consolation of the simple, which is threefold. For the simple are moved toward him because of three kinds of milk: that of doctrine, innocence, and simplicity. Of the first: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0487] 1 Cor. 3]. Of the second: “Like newborn infants, desire rational milk without deceit” [Note: [Col. 0487] 1 Pet. 1]. Of the third: “that you may drink from milk.” Of this threefold milk Isaiah says: “A man shall nourish a cow of oxen and two sheep, and shall eat butter because of the abundance of milk” [Col. 0488C; Note: [Col. 0487] Isa. 7].

Oxen are commonly understood as teachers; therefore the milk of the cow of oxen is the doctrine of the simple. There follow two sheep: one gives the milk of innocence, the other that of simplicity. From these butter is eaten, that is, the richness of devotion in the Holy Spirit, without which he would not remain in us. As is said in the Book of Wisdom: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” [Note: [Col. 0487] Wis. 1]. This is against simplicity. “And he will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” [Note: [Col. 0487] Ibid.]; this is against doctrine. “And he will be reproved by the iniquity that comes upon him” [Note: [Col. 0487] Ibid.]; this is against innocence.

Let us also drink the wine of clarified vintage, namely, affection toward the Holy Spirit. This is threefold [Col. 0488D], because wine does three things: it warms, gladdens, and intoxicates. So too the Holy Spirit: he warms by coming, gladdens by visiting, and intoxicates by pouring himself in more abundantly. Of these it is said:

> Come, Creator Spirit,  
> Visit the minds of your people;  
> Fill with heavenly grace  
> The hearts which you have created.  
> [Note: [Col. 0487] Pentecost hymn.]

He warms toward love, gladdens toward devotion, and intoxicates toward the sleep of the senses of the outward person. Of the first: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall blaze” [Col. 0489A; Note: [Col. 0489] Ps. 38]. Of the second: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0489] Rom. 14]. Of the third: “We are intoxicated by the abundance of your house” [Note: [Col. 0489] Ps. 35].

Likewise, the honeycomb is Christ’s flesh, which we eat; honey is the sweetness of eternal salvation, which we await. It should be noted that some eat the honeycomb without honey; some with honey that is not their own; and some with their own honey. The first are hidden heretics, who eat Christ’s body but do not believe eternal salvation comes from it. The second are Christians in sin who receive it and believe that salvation is in it; indeed it is, but not for them. The third are good Christians, who receive it and place their own salvation in it [Col. 0489B].

Wine signifies blood, for it is made from wine. By milk, which is white and nourishes little children, are understood the washing away of sins and the nourishment of virtues, effected through Christ’s blood, but also through Christ’s body. Yet it is more commonly attributed to the blood because it is liquid, and wounds are washed with it—namely with wine—as it is written: “He first loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” [Note: [Col. 0489] Rev. 1]. The same division is found in it as in the honeycomb: some drink wine without milk, namely those who believe that remission of sins and nourishment of virtues are in it; and some drink with milk that is not their own; some with their own milk, as was said.

It should be noted that he says “the honeycomb,” but not “my honeycomb,” whereas he says “my honey,” because the body is Christ’s; but the salvation which proceeds from it is ours [Col. 0489C]. The honeycomb is Christ’s assumed flesh; honey is divine Wisdom incarnate; milk is Christ’s manner of life in the flesh and his teaching; wine is the miracles he performed. Hence John says: “The Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0489] John 1], namely God: this by the Incarnation; “and dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0489] Ibid.], by teaching and good conduct; “and we saw his glory,” by the display of miracles; “full of grace,” by the sending of the Holy Spirit; “and truth,” by the resurrection. Therefore: “The Word was made flesh,” in whom “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.”

It should be noted that there is a spoken word, an enacted word, and an immortal Word. The first is received by the ear; the second is perceived by the eyes [Col. 0489D]; the third is conceived in the womb. By the first the mystery of the Incarnation was foretold; by the second it was obscurely foretold and revealed; the third, however, is “The Word was made flesh.” The first was inspired in the prophets under the Law; the second revealed to the just between Law and grace; the third, under grace, “dwelt among us.” By the first we believe that Mary would be born of a mother; by the second we perceive grace poured into the brother; in the third, “we saw his glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father” [Note: [Col. 0489] Ibid.].

The first we saw full of ambiguity [Col. 0490A]; the second we saw full of evident necessity; the third we saw “full of grace and truth.” Of the first it is said: “When the Word is announced to her, the Virgin trembles at the light.” Of the second: “Let us go and see the Word which has been made” [Note: [Col. 0489] On the Ecclesiastical Office]. Of the third: “The Word was made flesh.”

Hear the first: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” [Note: [Col. 0489] Isa. 11]. The second was that the angel announced it, the star appeared, and brightness shone around the shepherds [Note: [Col. 0489] Luke 2]. The third—“The Word was made flesh”—was for three reasons: first, that he might raise up fallen human nature; second, that by our weakness he might temper the light of divinity; third, that by honorable conduct he might form our life.

Of the first: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0489] Phil. 2]. Behold his abasement. Hear his exaltation: “For this reason God also exalted him” [Col. 0490B; Note: [Col. 0489] Ibid.]. Again: “He sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” [Note: [Col. 0489] Heb. 1]. But this concerns Christ; hear of us: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” [Note: [Col. 0489] 1 Pet. 1]. Therefore he cries: “Shake yourself from the dust; arise, sit down, Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0489] Isa. 52]. Shake yourself from the dust of worldly vanity; rise from the stench of carnal pleasure; sit down, that you may judge the desert of your iniquity; loose the bonds from your neck, lest you be held by the snare of despair. Behold our abasement.

Hear our exaltation: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” [Note: [Col. 0489] John 12]. For he “will reform the body of our humility, making it conformed to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0489] Phil. 3]. In the first he will form us [Col. 0490C], in the second he will reform us, in the third he will conform us.

Of the second, in which he tempers the light of divinity: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun” [Note: [Col. 0489] Ps. 18], namely because “he dwells in inaccessible light” [Note: [Col. 0489] 1 Tim. 6]. Hence he says: “Turn your eyes away from me, because they have made me flee” [Note: [Col. 0489] Song 6]. “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice” [Note: [Col. 0489] Song 2]. The wall is our flesh. He is seen through windows and lattices: neither wholly seen nor wholly hidden. Thus Christ appeared through windows, namely through miracles, and through his lattices, through the inspiration of grace by which he inwardly formed us in the image of the Trinity—through memory, understanding, and will.

The third reason was that he might conform us to himself through his manner of life [Col. 0490D]. “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” [Note: [Col. 0489] Rom. 8]. Take heed, therefore, that “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example that you should follow in his footsteps” [Note: [Col. 0489] 1 Pet. 2], thus: “Be imitators of God, as dearly beloved children, and walk in love as Christ loved you” [Note: [Col. 0489] Eph. 5]. “For the grace of God has appeared to all people,” etc.: “Let us live soberly, justly, and piously in this age” [Note: [Col. 0489] Titus 2]: soberly in relation to ourselves, justly toward our neighbor, piously toward God.

For these reasons “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [Col. 0491A; Note: [Col. 0491] John 1]. This Word dwelt in our sufferings; dwelt with the just and sinners; dwelt with those who love him. The first dwelling is singular, the second general, the third spiritual. For the first is in the misery of human flesh, the second in the Church, the third in a pure conscience. Of the first: “Salvation is near to those who fear him” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ps. 84], etc. Of the second: “Behold the tabernacle of God with men, and he dwelt among them” [Note: [Col. 0491] Rev. 21]. Again: “She dwelt among the nations and found no rest” [Note: [Col. 0491] Lam. 1]. And the prophet: “Make your ways and your works good, and I will dwell with you in this place” [Note: [Col. 0491] Jer. 7, 18]. Of the third Paul says: “I will gladly glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” [Note: [Col. 0491] 2 Cor. 12].

“Rabbi, where do you dwell?” says Nathanael [Note: [Col. 0491] John 1]. And he replies: “Come and see” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ibid.], as though he said: See whether your conscience is pure [Col. 0491B], for I dwell in such persons. For a pure conscience does three things: it ministers holiness, imparts virtue, and illuminates through truth. The first provides restraint from sins; the second, experience of perfect religious life; the third, illumination for beholding the glory of heavenly things.

Of the first it is said: “But you dwell in the holy place, O praise of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ps. 21]. And Wisdom herself: “In the holy dwelling-place, before him, I ministered” [Note: [Col. 0491] Sir. 24]. Of the second it is said: “That the power of Christ may dwell in me.”

“Virtue is difficult, I confess, but it strives toward lofty things,” says the poet [Note: [Col. 0491] Ovid]. The same author:

> Virtue grows amid adversities.  
> [lacuna]  
> The same author:
>
> Set your minds to the great work of virtue.

[Col. 0491C]

> [lacuna]  
> Patience rejoices in hardships. Do you wish to know how he dwells in the virtuous person?
>
> Is there a seat of God, etc.; and therefore he says:
>
> [lacuna]  
> Virtue is lavish of life.

Again:

> Burning virtue has carried a few across to heaven.

Of the third: “His place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ps. 75]. Zion is the Church, which contemplates heavenly things and leads life in peace.

> Happy is the man who has been able to lead a tranquil life  
> And steadily close his day with a joyful end.

Again: “The Lord chose Zion; he chose her for his dwelling” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ps. 131]. But if there should be there “a lair of dragons and pastures of ostriches” [Col. 0491D; Note: [Col. 0491] Isa. 34], namely creeping things beyond number, he will not dwell there. For “perverse thoughts separate from God” [Note: [Col. 0491] Wis. 1]. And “Wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ibid.]. Therefore, “let their habitation become desolate, and let there be none to dwell in their tents” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ps. 68].

Or thus: “He dwelt among us,” because in the Virgin; “he dwelt among us,” because in a just person; “he dwells among us,” because in the holy congregation. The first is through the Incarnation [Col. 0492A], the second through inspiration, the third through mutual love. Of the first: “The young man shall dwell with the virgin” [Note: [Col. 0491] Isa. 62]. And: “As the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ps. 86]. And: “In the holy dwelling-place before him” [Note: [Col. 0491] Sir. 24], etc.

Second, he dwells in a heart cleansed from vices. Otherwise he will say: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” [Note: [Col. 0491] Matt. 8]. For Wisdom does not dwell in a body subject to sins. “I will gladly,” says the Apostle, “glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” [Note: [Col. 0491] 2 Cor. 12]. Of such a person Christ said: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: [Col. 0491] John 14].

He dwells in the congregation, as we have already said: “Make your ways good, and I will dwell with you in this place” [Note: [Col. 0491] Jer. 7, 18]. You are “the mountain in which the Lord is well pleased” [Col. 0492B; Note: [Col. 0491] Ps. 77]. Therefore let us love one another, “that glory may dwell in our land” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ps. 84].

“We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” [Note: [Col. 0491] John 1]. There is the glory of one degenerating from the Father, the glory of one regenerated by the Father, and the glory of the Only-begotten from the Father. The first is that of the proud, the second of the pleasure-seeking, the third of the blessed. In the first the devil was glorified; in the second, the foolish man; in the third, man was glorified in Christ. For the devil said: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0491] Isa. 14]. Wretched man, “what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” [Note: [Col. 0491] 1 Cor. 4].

Of the second it is said that “the devil showed Christ all the kingdoms of the world and their glory” [Note: [Col. 0491] Matt. 4]. Of the third it says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” [Col. 0492C; Note: [Col. 0491] Ps. 18]. It should be noted that the glory of the Only-begotten from the Father is threefold. First is purity of conscience; second, the truth of miracles; third is called eternal happiness. The first is the testimony of good conduct; the second is the true proof of the divine promise; the third is the consummation of our perfection. Of the first: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0491] 2 Cor. 1]. Of the second: “Did I not tell you that, if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” [Note: [Col. 0491] John 11]. Of the third: “I will give salvation in Zion and my glory in Jerusalem, Israel” [Note: [Col. 0491] Isa. 46].

We have seen the first in conscience, the second in the Church, and we shall see the third in the homeland. In the first we saw him “full of grace” [Note: [Col. 0491] John 1]; in the second, “full of truth” [Note: [Col. 0491] Ibid.]; in the third, “from his fullness we have all received” [Col. 0492D; Note: [Col. 0491] Ibid.]. This fullness is threefold: the fullness of redemption, the fullness of resurrection, and the fullness of majesty. In the first we received the abundance of graces; in the second we shall receive wholeness of body and soul; in the third, ineffable joy. In the first one is made white by righteousness; in the second firm through immortality; in the third resplendent with divine brightness.

Of the first: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law” [Col. 0493A; Note: [Col. 0493] Gal. 4]. Of the second: “We shall all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age” [Note: [Col. 0493] Eph. 4]. Of the third: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and the whole earth was full of his majesty” [Note: [Col. 0493] Isa. 6].

Therefore, we possess the honeycomb of Christ’s human flesh; we possess the honey of his divinity; we possess the milk of Christ’s preaching and manner of life; we possess the wine of his miracles or love. Our Solomon invites us to enjoy these things, where he subsequently adds: “Eat, friends, and become drunk.”

“**Come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.**”

[CARD.] As though he said: As one comes into his garden to delight there after his labors, so I, after those who had made me labor through their iniquities, came to delight in the merits and virtues of the Blessed Virgin [Col. 0493B]. In this garden I gathered and collected in abundance myrrh with my spices. What these spices are, she herself specifies in Ecclesiasticus, where she joins cinnamon and balsam with myrrh, saying: “Like cinnamon and balsam I gave forth fragrance; like choice myrrh I gave sweetness of scent” [Note: [Col. 0493] Sir. 24].

That choice myrrh signifies the bitter mortification of the flesh without a wound—produced by a soul wounded by no scar of sin. Such myrrh the Lord gathered in the Blessed Virgin, who, although she had no wound of sin, took care to mortify herself in many ways and gave fragrance like cinnamon [Col. 0493C]. For just as cinnamon, the more slender it is, is the better and more fragrant, so she, made slender and thin by abstinence, was both more acceptable to God and more fragrant to the world.

Balsam signifies the fragrance and reputation of holiness. She gave the fragrance of uncorrupted balsam, as she says in Ecclesiasticus: “My scent is unmixed balsam” [Note: [Col. 0493] Ibid.]. Balsam is indeed corrupted if mixed with milk or oil; similarly holiness is corrupted when it is practiced for the oil of empty glory, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” [Note: [Col. 0493] Ps. 140], that is, my mind. The holiness of life is likewise corrupted when it is practiced to acquire the milk of worldly delight. Of this Solomon says that milk drips from the lips of a harlot [Note: [Col. 0493] Prov. 5], under whose name John describes the world’s condemnation in the Apocalypse: “Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot, who sits upon many waters” [Col. 0493D; Note: [Col. 0493] Rev. 17].

In this garden the Lord also says that he found the sweetness of refreshment: “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey.” Here he shows that the Virgin pleased him in a twofold life, namely the contemplative and the active. For strained honey signifies the sweetness of pure contemplation; but the honeycomb, which outwardly displays rough wax while concealing honey in its cells, signifies the active life [Col. 0494A]. Though it appears rough in its works, it contains in each cell of its works the sweetness of rewards.

What the Lord drank in this refreshment he shows by saying: “I have drunk my wine with my milk.” For he who, on account of human iniquities, was inwardly so touched by grief that he prepared for the world a flood of eternal punishment, after he drank milk from the Virgin was as one made drunk by wine and gladdened in heart. As if forgetful of the sorrow produced by the world’s evils, he turned from punishments to the benefits of mercy. It follows:

“**Eat, friends, and drink, and become drunk, dearly beloved.**”

[THO.] That is, you who are my friends by doing what I command you are dearly beloved by embracing one another with whole love. I therefore beseech you: fill our hearts with the deeds of the saints as with choice foods [Col. 0494B]. For not only after eating honeycomb and honey, after drinking wine and milk, are we to rejoice in the wondrous virtues of the good, imitate them, dispel the torpor of our minds by recalling them, and rise more vigorously to the love of heavenly things. We read that Christ set before us three banquets: the first at the approach of his Passion, the second at the Ascension, the third after the general resurrection has been celebrated.
