The first was when he ate the Passover with his disciples; the second, when eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem; the third he promised his soldiers: “I appoint for you a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0493] Luke 22]. In the first we eat in order to acquire strength against labors [Col. 0494C]; in the second, to satisfy hunger; in the third, for love. The first is of bodies, the second of spirits, the third of angels. In the first servants partake; in the second friends eat; in the third the dearly beloved become drunk.

In the first, three matters must be considered: what, when, and how much we eat—namely, the kind of food, the time, and the measure—lest we take anything unlawful, outside the proper time, or beyond measure. Adam ate unlawfully in Paradise and was expelled [Note: [Col. 0493] Gen. 3]; Jonathan ate outside the proper time and was cursed by his father [Note: [Col. 0493] 1 Sam. 14]; the people of Israel ate beyond measure at the graves of lust and were killed [Note: [Col. 0493] Num. 11]. Adam transgressed the Lord’s command; Jonathan broke what the multitude of the people observed; Israel was deceived by the fullness of food. Thus transgression deserved expulsion [Col. 0494D], neglect of a vow the curse due to a crime, and surfeit death.

Religious persons ought to observe three things concerning food: manner, measure, and number. Manner means that we use the foods set before us moderately; measure, that what is set before us should suffice for sustenance, not pleasure; number, that they should be refreshed by some of the things set before them, lest the flesh fail through excessive abstinence or grow wanton through satiety. There are four measures: the first of avarice, the second of pleasure, the third of stewardship, the fourth of necessity. The first is excessive frugality, the second superfluity, the third generosity, the fourth sufficient equality [Col. 0495A]. Avarice takes away from necessity; pleasure exceeds necessity; stewardship mercifully adds to necessity; necessity requires what is due to need.

There follows the banquet of spirits. In the spirit there are three tables, three senses of Scripture: the historical, the mystical, and the moral. The first is for the simple, the second for teachers, the third common to both. At the first there is coarser food, at the second subtler, at the third sweeter. The first feeds by miracles, the second by figures, the third by words. The reality of miracles strengthens faith, the fulfilment of figures hope, moral teaching charity. Upon these tables Moses sets mixed bread [Note: [Col. 0495] Exod. 25.], the apostles barley bread [Note: [Col. 0495] John 6.], Elijah bread baked under ashes [Note: [Col. 0495] III Kings 17.]. Barley bread belongs to the observances of the Law; mixed bread, to tears; ash-baked bread, to sins.

[Col. 0495B] Three dishes of flesh are set upon this table: lamb, ram, and cow. Abel sets forth a lamb [Note: [Col. 0495] Gen. 4.], Abraham a ram [Note: [Col. 0495] Gen. 15.], Joshua a cow [Note: [Col. 0495] Josh. 5.]. The lamb, silent before its shearer [Note: [Col. 0495] Isa. 53.], is Christ humble in his Passion, and ourselves patient in tribulation. The ram, caught by its horns among the brambles, is Christ on the cross by his hands, and ourselves by works of obedience. The ram leading the flock is Christ leading the people by life, and prelates leading the congregation by example; the cow slain outside the camp is Christ [102] outside Jerusalem, and ourselves, mortified outside the vanity of the world. In the lamb is simplicity of heart; in the ram, strength in action; in the cow, the milk of preaching. Let us be like those who fly as clouds [Note: [Col. 0495] Isa. 60.], prudent as serpents and simple as doves [Note: [Col. 0495] Matt. 10.]. Let there not be a cloud without rain, a serpent without prudence, or a dove without simplicity. Let the dove lack gall, the serpent venom, and the cloud dryness, so that simplicity may be without bitterness, prudence without malice, and teaching without vanity.

Some fish are set forth from the sea, some from a river, some from a pool. Those from the sea are secular persons; those from the river, teachers; those from the pool, cloistered persons. Let them have scales—that is, austerity of life—and fins—that is, the wings of contemplation. Tobias goes down to the river, Christ to the world, and the wise or righteous person to tears: Tobias to wash his feet, Christ to wash away sins, the righteous person to cleanse carnal affections. Tobias finds the fish by casting out its entrails; Christ finds the devil by exposing his malice; the righteous person does so through confession, casting out the hidden things of the breast.

[Col. 0495D] Tobias has material salt with which the fish is seasoned; Christ has the mystical salt of prudence by which the devil is guarded against; the righteous person has the moral salt of wisdom by which the convert is instructed. Behold the spiritual banquet at which friends eat. There follows the eternal banquet at which the dearest ones are made drunk. That banquet is nothing other than participation in heavenly joys. Its dishes are as numerous as the kinds of blessedness, as in the Gospel: “They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” [Note: [Col. 0495] Matt. 7]. It will be good in the brightness of bodies, pressed down in subtlety, [Col. 0496A] shaken together in greatness, and overflowing in the vision of God.

It should be noted that one measure is flowing, another outflowing, another through-flowing, another overflowing. It is flowing when grace is poured into one’s neighbour; outflowing when what has been poured in is shared with one’s neighbour; through-flowing when one perseveres in it unto death; overflowing when God is seen face to face. Hence: “I shall be satisfied,” he says, “when thy glory shall appear” [Note: [Col. 0495] Ps. 16]. And: “Our soul shall be like a watered garden” [Note: [Col. 0495] Isa. 58]. Whoever wishes to be refreshed and made drunk must first be watered with the water which Rebecca gave to Damascus [Note: [Col. 0495] Gen. 24]; second, may be refreshed with that which was given to the prophet as ash-baked bread [Note: [Col. 0495] IV Kings 4]; third, made drunk with the wine made from water at the wedding feast [Note: [Col. 0495] John 2]. The first was served from Rebecca’s pitcher, the second [Col. 0496B] from the pitcher of the woman of Zarephath, the third from the vessel in which water was changed into wine. These vessels are fittingly assigned to the blessed Mary, who gave us to drink, that we might eat and be made drunk, the water of grace, the bread of flesh assumed in her, and the wine of eternal joy.

Therefore, that we may assign them suitably, let us hear what Damascus said: “Therefore the maiden to whom I shall say, ‘Give me drink,’ and who shall say, ‘Drink, my lord, and I will give your camels drink also’: she is, O Lord, the one whom thou hast prepared for the son of my lord” [Note: [Col. 0495] Gen. 24]. O venerable maiden! O happy vessel! O saving water! O truly venerable maiden, who carries such a vessel! Happy vessel, which contains such water! Saving water, which waters the whole earth! The first is the Virgin Mary; the second, the royal chamber of her womb; the third, the grace of God.

[Col. 0496C] The first is she whom thou hast prepared, O Lord, for the son of my lord; the second is that in which the Son of God assumed flesh; the third is “the rush of the river” which “makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0495] Ps. 45]. None is more virginal than the first, none more fruitful than the second, none more watering than the third. Of the first: “This is she who knew not a bed in transgression, having fruit in the visitation of holy souls” [Note: [Col. 0495] Wis. 3]. From the second is born “the living bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world” [Note: [Col. 0495] John 6]; the third is “a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing mightily from Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0495] Song 4]. Therefore the Blessed Virgin was “like a lily among thorns” [Note: [Col. 0495] Song 2], because she was pure among sinners. Our vessel was like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies, because the Virgin’s womb was fruitful while her virginity remained unharmed.

[Col. 0496D] That water was a fountain going out of Paradise and watering the whole earth—that is, the depths of the human heart. But let us now speak of our maiden, considering what virginity consists in. First there must be bodily integrity; second, purity of heart; third, humility; fourth, charity. The first closes the entrance against vices; the second strengthens the resolve; the third makes one subject to inferiors; the fourth perfects merit.

The first was Noah’s ark, coated with bitumen so that not even a small crack might be open to admit water [Note: [Col. 0495] Gen. 6]; the second was [Col. 0497A] the column in the middle of the ark which supports the entire structure; the third was the haircloth covering over the tabernacle which concealed the other ornaments [Note: [Col. 0497] Exod. 26]; the fourth was the ark gilded within and without with most precious gold [Note: [Col. 0497] Exod. 25], so that it shone within and without—that is, appeared inwardly to God and outwardly to human beings.

The prophet speaks of what the Blessed Virgin Mary possessed first, namely bodily integrity: “This gate shall be shut and shall not be opened, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it” [Note: [Col. 0497] Ezek. 44]. She herself testifies that she possessed the second, namely the inward resolve of virginity: “How shall this be, since I know not a man?” [Note: [Col. 0497] Luke 1]. Of the third she says: “The Lord has regarded the humility of his handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0497] ibid.]. Concerning the fourth, under her figure the bride cries: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved [Col. 0497B] that I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0497] Song 2].

How greatly bodily integrity pleases God is shown in the Apocalypse: “These,” he says, “are they who have not defiled their garments, and therefore, clothed in white robes, follow the Lamb wherever he goes” [Note: [Col. 0497] Rev. 7]. Hence the bridegroom says to the bride: “My sister, my bride, is a garden enclosed; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” [Note: [Col. 0497] Song 4]. In praise of this integrity John the Evangelist is said to be as free from the pain of death as he was untouched by corruption of the flesh. Hence the bridegroom says: “I am a flower of the field and a lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0497] Song 2]. The flower of the field is the rose, because of the difficulty of virtues; the lily of the valleys, because of humble chastity. Hence the ark of the Lord is said to have been made of *setim* wood, which is likened to the white thorn: white because of chastity, thorny because of the austerity of [Col. 0497C] the religious life. For the bridegroom loves such a one as has neither spot nor wrinkle: the spot of lustful foulness, the wrinkle of deceitful duplicity. This is enough concerning bodily integrity; now concerning serenity of mind,

[lacuna]

“that there may be a sound mind in a sound body,” as the poet says [Note: [Col. 0497] Horace]. Hence: “Thy eyes are those of doves” [Note: [Col. 0497] Song 1], “apart from what lies hidden within” [Note: [Col. 0497] Song 4]; for “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” [Note: [Col. 0497] Ps. 44]. This is the good resolve called the column in the middle of the ark. Hence in the Song: “Thy neck is like a tower of ivory” [Note: [Col. 0497] Song 7].

Now humility should follow virginity as its guardian. Certainly the devil was cast out of heaven, not because he had lost virginity, but because he had lost humility. This is the haircloth covering which conceals the whole glory [Col. 0497D] of the tabernacle. Therefore the bride says: “I am black, but beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0497] Song 1]: black in humility, beautiful in chastity. And why does she go on, “Because the sun has darkened me” [Note: [Col. 0497] ibid.]? That is, because of the love of Christ. In charity virginity is perfected, without which no virtue exists. Hence, when Solomon made the litter, after the other adornments he said: “He paved its midst with charity” [Note: [Col. 0497] Song 3].

For these four qualities virginity is denoted in Scripture by the lily: humility is understood in the paleness of the root; bodily integrity in the greenness of the stalk; inward virginity in the whiteness of the leaves; charity in the golden grains. In these [Col. 0498A] consists perfect virginity. Behold what a venerable maiden she is. No less happy is the vessel of the womb, which sends out water, sends out flour, and sends out the joy of wine. The first waters the dryness of the arid land; the second gives the hungry person fullness; the third gives immortality to the corruptible. By the first the threshing-floor of the heart is watered; by the second we are strengthened on the way; by the third we shall rejoice in our homeland.

The water, then, is from the vessel which Rebecca brought; from the vessel of the woman of Zarephath flour was taken, and ash-baked bread made, by which the prophet was healed; the fourth was the vessel in which wine was made from water. These are the outpourings of this vessel: “Thy outpourings are a paradise” [Note: [Col. 0497] Song 4]. Let us first therefore consider the water, namely the outpouring of grace. “A fountain,” he says, [Col. 0498B] “went out of Paradise and was divided into four rivers” [Note: [Col. 0497] Gen. 2].

The first is the Nile, called Gehon, that is, “earthly”; the second, the Ganges, that is, Phison, called “the opening of the mouth”; the third, the Tigris, because of the swiftness of that animal; the fourth, the Euphrates, called “good fruitfulness.” This is the fourfold grace flowing from Paradise—that is, from the vessel of the Virgin’s womb. The first river, then, is the grace of bodily conduct; the second is the grace of interpreting literal knowledge; the third is the grace by which both actual and criminal guilt are swiftly remitted; the fourth is the grace by which the fruit of spiritual virtues grows.

Peter invited us to the first, namely bodily conduct, saying: “Having [Col. 0498C] your conduct good among the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0497] I Pet. 2]. Hence Paul: “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” [Note: [Col. 0497] I Cor. 9]. Hence: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0497] I Cor. 15]. The Holy Spirit conferred the second upon the apostles when he gave them the spirit of wisdom and understanding, and so forth, likewise so that they knew every kind of language. Hence: “The apostles spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God” [Note: [Col. 0497] Acts 2].

By the Tigris, which is swift, the third grace is signified: namely, swiftness of forgiveness. Was not this grace swift for Mary Magdalene, reclining at the Lord’s feet? Was it not swift for Peter, weeping after his denial? Was it not swift for the thief hanging on the cross? And all received a sign of such swift grace. For after the resurrection the first appearance was made to Mary [Col. 0498D] [Note: [Col. 0497] John 20]. Peter was summoned to Galilee [Note: [Col. 0497] Mark 16] by his own name. To the thief it was said: “Today thou shalt be with me in Paradise” [Note: [Col. 0497] Luke 23]. Behold the great swiftness of this river of grace.

The fourth is the Euphrates, called good fruitfulness from *eu*, “good,” and “fruit.” Morally, this fruit is threefold: the fruit of righteousness, the fruit of patience, and the fruit of wisdom. The first grows in religious life, the second in tribulation, the third in heavenly conduct. The first is possessed in the constancy of circumspection, the second in the difficulty of labour, the third in the abundant sweetness [Col. 0499A] of delight. Of the first it is said: “The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace” [Note: [Col. 0499] Jas. 3]. Likewise: “The fruit of righteousness is charity, peace, patience” [Note: [Col. 0499] Gal. 5]. Of the second the Gospel says: “The seed which fell upon good ground: these are they who hear the word in a good and excellent heart and bear fruit in patience” [Note: [Col. 0499] Luke 8]. Of the third: “Blessed is the man who shall abide in wisdom, and who shall meditate upon righteousness and think in understanding upon the providence of God”; and it concludes: “lest he ever cease to bear fruit” [Note: [Col. 0499] Ecclus. 14].

The bride invited the bridegroom to these three fruits. To the first she says: “Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat the fruits of his apple trees.” Of the second she says: “I will climb into the palm tree and take hold of its fruits” [Note: [Col. 0499] Song 7]. This palm is the cross [Col. 0499B] of the Saviour, which the person who exposes himself to tribulations climbs. He takes hold of its fruit when, triumphing over the enemy, he acquires patience. For the third: “I sat under his shadow whom I desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0499] Song 2].

Of the person who acquires the fruit of wisdom it is said: “The water of wisdom shall give him drink” [Note: [Col. 0499] Ecclus. 15]. Of the patient person it is said: “And he shall be established in it,” through grace, “and shall not be bent,” through the violence of adversity [Note: [Col. 0499] ibid.]. Concerning the fruit of righteousness it follows: “And it shall hold him fast,” lest he expose his senses to wandering among worldly things; “and he shall not be confounded” [Note: [Col. 0499] ibid.] at the judgment where he must render an account of his own acts [Note: [Col. 0499] Rom. 14]. Behold the four rivers of Paradise which go out from Rebecca’s vessel, namely from the womb of our Virgin. O happy water, which gives the body [Col. 0499C] capacity for action; knowledge to the heart; truth to the tongue; purity from sin; and abundance of spiritual fruits! O blessed Virgin, give me water from thy vessel, that I may drink and know that thou art she whom the Lord prepared for the Son of my Lord.

This is the outpouring of water. There is also another outpouring, of bread: namely bread made from the little flour which was in the vessel of the woman of Zarephath. It should be noted that the woman is called Shunammite, that is, miserable or scarlet; she is called Zarephathite, that is, “burning”; Mary is called miserable because in her Christ assumed our misery. Scarlet is red in colour. She too is called scarlet, because from her was assumed the blood which washed our filth away. She is also called burning, because [Col. 0499D] in her was baked the bread which refreshed our need.

First, lest under such consolation we should be swallowed up by more abundant sorrow [Note: [Col. 0499] II Cor. 2]; second, so that, driven from Paradise because of the leprosy of sin, we may return to the camp with Mary, Moses’ sister [Note: [Col. 0499] Num. 12]; third, lest we fail on the way. The first was a work of condescension, [103] the second of compassion, the third of love. Of the first: “O wonderful exchange, Creator of the human race” [Note: [Col. 0499] Office of the Blessed Virgin], etc. Of the second Paul says: “For we have not a high priest who cannot have compassion upon our infirmities” [Note: [Col. 0499] Heb. 4]. Of the third: “He gave them manna from heaven [Col. 0500A] containing every delight of sweetness” [Note: [Col. 0499] Wis. 16]. He himself became for us a sacrifice of fine flour.

But the sacrifice is threefold: a sacrifice from the oven, a sacrifice from the frying pan, a sacrifice from the griddle. It was from the oven because he was baked and formed in the Virgin’s womb; from the frying pan because he set himself as a wall against the devil for the human race; from the griddle because he was roasted on the cross for the whole world. The first was that he might make us conformed to himself; the second, that he might protect us; the third, that he might redeem us. Of the first: “Those whom he foreknew, he predestined to be made conformable to the image of his Son” [Note: [Col. 0499] Rom. 8]. Of the second: “Thou hast protected me from the assembly of the wicked, from the multitude of those who work iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0499] Ps. 63]. Of the third: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, because cursed is everyone who hangs upon [Col. 0500B] a tree” [Note: [Col. 0499] Gal. 3].

This bread, then, was made from the little flour taken from the vessel of our Virgin. It was ash-baked bread—not, however, the sort that is not turned over. He was little through humility; ash-baked because he bore our iniquity upon himself; turned over because he laid down our iniquity, and his and our infirmity. Hear that he was little: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” [Note: [Col. 0499] Isa. 9]. And ash-baked: “Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our burdens” [Note: [Col. 0499] Isa. 53]. And turned over: “Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more” [Note: [Col. 0499] Rom. 6].

He also was *versatus*, *conversatus*, and *reversatus*: he was placed in the Virgin’s womb, dwelt in the world, and was turned back at the moment of death. Of the first:

> The banners of virtues gleam;  
> [Col. 0500C] God dwells in the temple.  
> [Note: [Col. 0499] Office of the Church]

Of the second: “After this he was seen upon earth and conversed with men” [Note: [Col. 0499] Baruch 3]. Of the third:

> The angels tremble as they behold  
> The mortal order reversed.  
> [Note: [Col. 0499] Office of the Church]

This is the vessel which brings fullness. There follows the vessel which gives immortality: this is the manifold vessel in which water is changed into wine. Yet they are called six because of perfection: “We shall all come to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0499] Eph. 4].—“Fill the vessels with water,” he says [Note: [Col. 0499] John 2], as though he said: In my vessel, human misery was assumed by my Son, which afterward shall be changed into glory.

Let us therefore consider the defect of the water by which the human race was infected, and the perfection of wine made from water. In the first was humanity’s expulsion from Paradise; in the second, the corruption of guilt and labour; in the third, the restoration of the human race. Of the first: “Eve took and ate” [Note: [Col. 0499] Gen. 3]; of the second: “In sorrow thou shalt bear thy children” [Note: [Col. 0499] ibid.]; of the third he says: “Draw now and carry it to the steward” [Note: [Col. 0499] John 2]. This is immortality from Mary’s vessel.

Therefore, ministers, be watered from Rebecca’s vessel; friends, eat from the vessel of the woman of Zarephath; dearest ones, be made drunk from the vessel of the wedding feast. The first is so that you may invite others to the gifts of grace; the second, so that [Col. 0501A] you may be steadfast in the virtue of patience; the third, so that you may rejoice in the attainment of glory. In the first say: “He who thirsts, let him come and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters” [Note: [Col. 0501] John 4]. In the second: “Give us this day our daily bread” [Note: [Col. 0501] Matt. 6], so that bread may strengthen the heart of man [Note: [Col. 0501] Ps. 103], the bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world [Note: [Col. 0501] John 6]. In the third, let those who “shall be made drunk by the abundance of the house of God” [Note: [Col. 0501] Ps. 35] say: “The king has brought me into the wine-cellar; he has ordered charity within me” [Note: [Col. 0501] Song 2]. Hence follows:

> Eat, friends; drink, and be made drunk, dearest ones.

[CARD.] Christ, richly refreshed in his garden, invites all his friends to the refreshment of this garden. It could indeed have seemed that the Lord had appropriated to himself alone everything that might delight in this garden, since he had added to each item a pronoun signifying possession, [Col. 0501B] saying, “my myrrh,” “my honeycomb,” “my wine,” and so of the rest. But although he has certain special delights in the Virgin—as one who knows her prerogatives, which our mind cannot comprehend—nevertheless each of us, according to the measure of grace received from the Lord, finds in the Blessed Virgin something to eat and something to drink; finds that from which to be nourished and strengthened in good; finds that by which he may be made drunk, so that he no longer even recalls the things he formerly loved in the world.

He therefore says: O friends, eat and delight in the fruits of this garden; drink and be made drunk with the wine of that vineyard which the vine bore that says: “I have borne as a vine the sweetness of fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0501] Ecclus. 24]. There follows, in the mother’s voice:

> [Col. 0501C] I sleep, and my heart watches.

[THO.] As though the Church said: With the makers of persecutions ceasing for a time, I have begun to enjoy a little rest in the Lord even in this present life; and with all my desire I do not cease to keep watch for that rest which knows no end. “And my heart watches,” because the freer I am from assaults outwardly, the more deeply I see inwardly: “For he is the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0501] Ps. 94].

There are four watches. The first is nocturnal; the second, morning; the third, midday; the fourth, evening. Of the first: “In the fourth watch of the night the Lord came to the disciples, walking upon the sea” [Note: [Col. 0501] Matt. 14]. Of the second: “Those who watch for me in the morning shall find me” [Note: [Col. 0501] Prov. 8]. Of the third: “O God, my God, from the dawn I watch for thee” [Note: [Col. 0501] Ps. 62]. [Col. 0501D] Of the fourth: “Abraham sacrificed a three-year-old cow, a ram, and a goat” [Note: [Col. 0501] Gen. 15].

The first is of contrition; the second, of confession; the third, for guarding virtue; the fourth, against temptation. The first is for healing; the second for continuation; the third for caution; the fourth for protection. The first is for healing, so that sin may be cured through contrition; the second for continuation, so that confession may carry forward the resolve of contrition; the third for caution, by which virtue is guarded; the fourth for protection, so that the conscience may be defended against temptation.

Hence, of the first: *vigilo* (“I keep watch”), that is, “I inspect the humps of vices” [Col. 0502A]; of the second: *vigilo*, that is, “I turn my life by the light of the eye”; of the third: *vigilo*, that is, “I flourish by the light of the eye”; of the fourth: *vigilo*, that is, “I circle the places of the way.” Of the first: “Arise in the night, at the beginning of thy watches”; of the second: “Pour out thy heart like water before the face of the Lord thy God”; of the third: “Lift up thy hands to him”; of the fourth: “He will have mercy on thee” [Note: [Col. 0501] Lam. 2].

Of the first, namely the nocturnal watch, it is said: “There were shepherds in that country, etc., keeping the watches of the night over their flock” [Note: [Col. 0501] Luke 2]. And: “In the fourth watch of the night Jesus came to his disciples, walking upon the waters” [Note: [Col. 0501] Matt. 14]. Night lasts as long as a person remains in sin. But night has four watches: first, when a person recalls his sin; second, when he grieves to have committed it; third, when he hates [Col. 0502B] sin; fourth, when he abominates sin. In this watch the Lord comes walking upon the waters in order to heal: “He heals the contrite of heart” [Note: [Col. 0501] Ps. 146]; for this is done for healing. In this watch one must rise from sin.

The second watch is the morning watch, in which we keep watch concerning confession, because with confession itself there rises in us a certain brightness of conscience, like a kind of morning light. Hence Wisdom: “Those who watch for me in the morning shall find me” [Note: [Col. 0501] Prov. 8].

It should be noted that in the first our heart is confounded; in the second, poured out; in the third, spread abroad; in the fourth, infused. It is confounded by shame, poured out in confession, spread abroad in preaching, infused with spiritual consolation. It is commanded to be poured out like water.

[Col. 0502C] Some pour it out like oil, others like honey, others like wine, others like milk, others like water. When oil is poured out, some of its substance always remains in the vessel because of its fatness. These are those who confess some of their sins and conceal others. Those pour it out like honey who confess everything but retain their delights, as a vessel retains honey. Those pour it out like wine who retain its scent, as a wine vessel does—that is, when they gladly listen to the recounting of things which incite to sin. Those pour it out like milk who retain the colour of sin, as a vessel retains the whiteness of milk—that is, when they gladly look upon the delights of the world.

The third watch is the midday watch for the keeping of virtues. Ish-bosheth did not observe it, sleeping at midday with the woman whom he had made a doorkeeper—that is, the spirit [made] the flesh [a doorkeeper]. [Col. 0502D] Since she kept watch badly, robbers took away his head [Note: [Col. 0501] II Kings 4]. This serves for caution, lest the devil steal something from our good things. Hence: “Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” [Note: [Col. 0501] I Pet. 5].

But because “unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain” [Note: [Col. 0501] Ps. 126]—“lift up thy hands to him” [Note: [Col. 0501] Lam. 2]. Hands are to be lifted in the offering of sacrifice, as Christ lifted his on the cross: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 0501] Ps. 140]. They are to be lifted in prayer: “I will,” says the Apostle, “that men should pray in every place, [Col. 0503A] lifting up pure hands,” as Christ did in praying [Note: [Col. 0503] I Tim. 2]. They are also to be lifted in the giving of alms: “Let us lift up,” he says, “our hearts in our hands to God” [Note: [Col. 0503] Lam. 3]: the heart for loving, the hands for giving, the tongue for correcting. Thus Christ, with uplifted hands, “was carried into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0503] Luke 24], to give alms by bestowing the Holy Spirit upon us.

The fourth watch is the evening watch, namely against temptations. Hence the Lord says: “Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation” [Note: [Col. 0503] Matt. 26].—“If the master of the house knew,” he says, “at what hour the thief would come, he would surely watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” [Note: [Col. 0503] Matt. 24]. Abraham kept this watch [Note: [Col. 0503] Gen. 15] when he sacrificed the ram—that is, pride—the goat—that is, lust—and the cow—that is, sloth of the flesh. “And when the sun had set,” that is, when Christ had set from the heart [Col. 0503B] through the violence of temptation, “a great horror seized him” [Note: [Col. 0503] ibid.], because he saw a smoking furnace—that is, hell—and a shining lamp—that is, the brightness of the blessed, for the flight of temptations.

But, to return to the beginning, by sleep I understand nothing but forgetfulness of temporal concerns; by waking, the contemplation of heavenly things. In sleep memory withdraws and flees from worldly acts. In waking it nourishes the solitude of the heart, that it may attend more freely to heavenly things. Hence David: “Behold, I fled afar off and remained in solitude” [Note: [Col. 0503] Ps. 54].

If we consider the flight by which John the Baptist, to take one example, made himself a stranger to worldly affairs; the withdrawal by which he reduced to nothing the blandishments of spiritual phantasms; and the solitude by which he sought to please God alone by his service, the heavenly life of any saint will shine forth, as in a mirror, in our subject. Did not flight from worldly affairs make him a stranger to them? For:

> While yet young he sought  
> The caves of the desert, fleeing the crowds of citizens,  
> Lest even a slight hunger might have power  
> To stain his life.

Did he not teach how spiritual withdrawal crushes phantasms, when, eating locusts—that is, pride—he consumed wild honey [Note: [Col. 0503] Matt. 3], namely when the bitterness of sufferings became sweet to him? Did he not strive to please God alone, who exulted for God alone in his mother’s womb [Note: [Col. 0503] Luke 1]?

Therefore, if we desire to be his imitators, let us know that flight is withdrawing one’s person from the dwelling-place of secular people; [Col. 0503D] withdrawal is committing vices in the heart to oblivion; solitude is devoting one’s care to God alone.

Beginning, then, with flight, let them know that some flee sins, some imminent danger, some the way of salvation because it is a harsh road, and some the exile of this world. The first do so to gain purity; the second with a view to the useful purpose of prudent provision; the third through the vice of faintheartedness; the fourth through desire for eternal happiness.

Of the first it is said: “Flee fornication” [Note: [Col. 0503] I Cor. 6]—not only that of the flesh but also that of the spirit. And the prophet says: “Go forth from Babylon, and flee [Col. 0504A] from the Chaldeans” [Note: [Col. 0503] Isa. 48]. Likewise: “Flee from the midst of Babylon” [Note: [Col. 0503] Jer. 50]. He did not say “from the beginning” or “from the end,” but “from the midst.” The beginning of Babylon is suggestion; the middle, deliberation and delight; the end, action. No one can prevent being tempted: where there is no suggestion, there is no struggle; where there is no struggle, there is no crown. Nor does he say, “from the end of Babylon,” because one who has fallen into the deed is already wounded. Therefore he can no longer flee; he can be carried by others’ hands. Flee delight, and suggestion will not harm you; let action not follow, and save your souls anew. They were saved in baptism, but were lost again through sin. Now we are saved anew through grace and the labour of repentance.

Hence it was said to Abraham: “Go forth from thy land, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house” [Note: [Col. 0503] Gen. 12]: from thy land, that is, from carnal desire; from thy kindred, that is, from thy thought; from thy father’s house, namely from the world which was the possession of the devil. Hence: “Ye are of your father the devil” [Note: [Col. 0503] John 8]. Or [the father is] Adam, who, cast out of Paradise, had his house in the [Col. 0504B] world. Therefore you, says the prophet, “who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread” [Note: [Col. 0503] Isa. 21]. Joseph fled sin when, leaving his cloak in his mistress’s hand, he escaped naked [Note: [Col. 0503] Gen. 39]. Thus, by fleeing sin, he flees hell.

The second flee imminent danger in prudent provision. Hence the Lord says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” [Note: [Col. 0503] Matt. 3]. Thus Paul was “let down in a basket through the wall” [Note: [Col. 0503] II Cor. 11], that he might preserve himself for the benefit of the brethren. Hence he says: “I am constrained by two things: to remain in the flesh for your sake [Col. 0504C] is good, but to be dissolved and be with Christ is much better” [Note: [Col. 0503] Phil. 1]. Thus Christ fled into Egypt [Note: [Col. 0503] Matt. 2], because his hour had not yet come.

The third flee the way of salvation because it is harsh. Hence David: “Whither shall I go from thy spirit, and whither shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present” [Note: [Col. 0503] Ps. 138]. And the poet [Note: [Col. 0503] Ovid]:

> Whither do you flee, Enceladus? To whatever shores you come,  
> You shall always be beneath Jupiter.

> To save your body, you will endure sword and fire;  
> To be sound in mind, will you refuse to endure anything?

And Horace [Note: [Col. 0503] Ep. I.ii.32]:

> Men rise from the night to murder other men;  
> Will you not wake to save yourself?

Such was Jonah when he said: “I flee from the face of God of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0503] Jonah 1]. But do not take account of the fact that, cast into the sea and swallowed by the whale, he attained harbour. It is a miracle and therefore must be drawn into the sequel. John the Evangelist also, “having cast away the linen cloth, fled naked” [Note: [Col. 0503] Mark 14]. Therefore let those who hate God flee from his face [Note: [Col. 0503] Ps. 67]. David says: “Flight has perished from me, and there is none to seek my soul” [Note: [Col. 0503] Ps. 141].—“See,” he says, “that your flight be not in winter or on the Sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0503] Matt. 24]: in winter, when it is said, “Go, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” [Note: [Col. 0503] Matt. 25]; on the Sabbath, when it is said, “Come, ye blessed [Col. 0505A] of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0505] Matt. 25]. The prophet says: “O Lord, let those who forsake thee be confounded; those who depart from thee shall be written in the earth” [Note: [Col. 0505] Jer. 17].

The fourth flee the misery of the world. Perhaps they would not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal might be swallowed up by life, says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0505] II Cor. 5]. But whoever wishes to flee the world must leave riches behind, as in the fable [Note: [Col. 0505] Horace, *Ep.* I.vii.28]:

> By chance a thin little fox had crept through a narrow crevice  
> Into a bin of grain; after feeding, it tried  
> To go out again with its body full. A weasel, seeing  
> It from afar, said: “If you wish to escape from there,  
> You must return lean through the narrow opening through which you entered lean.”

Hence the Apostle: “We brought nothing into this world, and it is certain that we can carry nothing out” [Note: [Col. 0505] I Tim. 6]. And, that we may flee the world perfectly, let us heed John the Evangelist: “I heard,” he says, “the voice of one [Col. 0505B] eagle flying through the midst of heaven and crying with a loud voice: ‘Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth!’” [Note: [Col. 0505] Rev. 8].

The first woe is because of guilt, the second because of temporal misery, the third because of the punishment of hell. Therefore, that we may flee these three, we must be winged with Ezekiel’s living creatures: “Their faces and their wings were extended above” [Note: [Col. 0505] Ezek. 1.]. Elijah fled the misery of the world when he was taken up in a fiery chariot [Note: [Col. 0505] 4 Kings 2.], as Christ himself did when ascending into heaven. Hence the bride: “Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” [Note: [Col. 0505] Song 8.]. This concerning flight. What follows concerns withdrawal.

It should be noted that some neither flee nor withdraw; some flee but do not withdraw; some withdraw but do not flee; and some both withdraw and flee, as has already been said.

[Col. 0505C] The first, then, neither withdraw nor flee, because they are fixed in the mire of the depth of this age [Note: [Col. 0505] Ps. 68]. Hence the prophet: “Moab was fertile from his youth, and he rested upon his dregs; he has not been poured from vessel into vessel, nor has he gone into exile. Therefore his taste has remained in him, and his smell has not changed” [Note: [Col. 0505] Jer. 48.]. These are like Sodomites, proclaiming their sins. “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment descend to hell” [Note: [Col. 0505] Job 21.].

The second flee, but do not withdraw: these are those who flee bodily into religious life, but in whose heart the world flourishes. Hence the Lord: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” [Note: [Col. 0505] Matt. 15.]. For in these are found the things which the tribe of Dan found in Micah’s house, namely the carved and molten *seraphim* [Col. 0505D] [Note: [Col. 0505] Judg. 17.]. But concerning them it has already been said in this work: “These,” says the Lord, “come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” [Note: [Col. 0505] Matt. 7.]; hence the prophet: “Man shall cast away the idols that he made in order to worship moles and bats” [Note: [Col. 0505] Isa. 2.].

These are two kinds of vice in religious life: blind love of earthly things and blind ambition for offices. The first is the mole, which does not come into the light but always lives beneath the earth; the second the bat, which flees the light and flies by night. These are the children of Israel who go through the desert yet return in heart to [Col. 0506A] Egypt, from which they flee [Note: [Col. 0505] Exod. 16.]. These are Bel, the god of Acharon, golden outwardly but muddy within [Note: [Col. 0505] Dan. 14.].

The third withdraw but do not flee: their bodily manner of life is in the world, but their spirit dwells in heaven. They endure in the world the reproaches of the perverse, yet receive from heaven the consolations of angels. Again, it is said of them: “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among daughters” [Note: [Col. 0505] Song 2.]. These are like Solomon’s temple, golden within and stony without. To these the Apostle says: “Be without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world” [Note: [Col. 0505] Phil. 2.].

The fourth are those who withdraw in spirit and flee bodily from human dwellings, saying: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.” Again: “My heart and my flesh have exulted [Col. 0506B] in the living God” [Note: [Col. 0505] Ps. 83.]. Why? Because: “The sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest in which to place her young” [Note: [Col. 0505] Ibid.]. And the bridegroom: “Do not awaken her or make her rise until she herself wills it” [Note: [Col. 0505] Song 2.]. John was awake when he said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” [Note: [Col. 0505] John 1.]. And when, at the baptism, the whole Trinity shone upon him. It follows: “And I remained in solitude” [Note: [Col. 0505] Ps. 54.]. For it profits little to be in solitude unless one perseveres in it.

There is a threefold solitude: local solitude, good and spiritual solitude, and singular solitude. The first pertains to the discipline of the senses; the second, to the contemplation of heavenly things; the third, to obstinacy in one’s own will. Of the first: “Wandering in deserts and in caves and in caverns of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0505] Heb. 11.]; [Col. 0506C] of the second: “I have watched and become like a solitary sparrow on the roof” [Note: [Col. 0505] Ps. 101.]. Such a man keeps Sabbath in this way: he neither transmits to the heart the external senses’ perceptions, nor sends out through the windows of the senses the inner thoughts. Hence in Jeremiah, as has already been said: “Do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day, nor bring them in through the gates of Jerusalem, and do not cast them out from charity, etc., on the Sabbath day” [Note: [Col. 0505] Jer. 17.].

John practised this Sabbath, or solitude, well when he recognized the Christ who was to come, pointed him out with his finger, and baptized in the Jordan. The herald recognized the Judge; the lamp pointed out the Light; the soldier baptized the King: the Judge whom he proclaimed, the Light by whom he kindled Christ, the King in whose service he was a soldier.

[Col. 0506D] In such repose the Lord grants the necessities and consolation of life, angelic encouragement, and a manifestation of his own exultation: the first for support in temporal life, the second for the spirit’s delight, the third as an indication of infused blessedness. Of the first: “Elijah slept, and, awakening, found bread and water” [Note: [Col. 0505] 3 Kings 17.]; of the second: “Jacob saw angels ascending and descending” [Note: [Col. 0505] Gen. 28]; of the third: “Joseph saw the sheaves of his brothers worshipping his sheaf” [Note: [Col. 0505] Gen. 41.].

“Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my immaculate one.”

[Col. 0507A] [THO.] The beloved knocks at our door when the Lord stirs us toward perfection in the virtues, when he admonishes us concerning the joys promised to those who gain the kingdom. “Behold,” he says, “I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him” [Note: [Col. 0507] Rev. 3.].

We open to the Lord when he knocks in two ways: either when we open our heart to receive an increase of that love of his which we do not possess; or when, by preaching, we open the heart to receive fear or love of God and neighbour. The Lord knocks a third time when he warns us to depart from this life. “My sister,” he says, “because you have been made co-heir of my kingdom; my friend, because, having departed from the yoke of slavery, you have been made privy to my secrets; my dove, because you have been enlightened by the gift of my Spirit; my immaculate one, because you have been withdrawn from busy [Col. 0507B] acts to divine contemplation.” Rightly, then, he asks that that be opened which he first opened for us.

For we read of four openings of Christ: the first was made over him, the second by him, the third in him, the fourth through him. In the first, “the heavens were opened over him” [Note: [Col. 0507] Matt. 3.]. In the second, when teaching the crowds, “he opened his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0507] Matt. 5.]. In the third, one of the soldiers opened his side [Note: [Col. 0507] John 19.]. In the fourth, “he opened the understanding of his disciples, that they might understand the Scriptures” [Note: [Col. 0507] Luke 24.].

When he opened his mouth, the bride became immaculate, because he instructed her in confession. When he opened the understanding, she became a dove, so that she might have simplicity in her faculties. When his side was opened, she became a sister, because then he made her co-heir of eternal glory. When the heavens were opened, he made her his friend, because he made her a participant in heavenly secrets [Col. 0507C].

The beloved’s immaculate one is she who rejoices in the washing away of sin. The dove is she who has done every good thing with simplicity. The first has no blemish; the second has no wrinkle. The friend is she who does everything with fervent love. Hence it is said: “Let all that is ours be done in charity” [Note: [Col. 0507] 1 Cor. 16.]. The sister is she who imitates Christ, conforming herself to him in the sufferings of the assumed flesh, hearing that saying of the Apostle: “Those whom he foreknew, he predestined to be made conformable to the image of his Son” [Note: [Col. 0507] Rom. 8.].

The immaculate one opens by receiving the beloved unto purity of knowledge; the dove, unto tranquillity of heart; the friend, unto the sweetness of love; the sister, unto thanksgiving. To the first he says when he comes: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish in you” [Note: [Col. 0507] Song 4.]; of the second it is said: “Here [Col. 0507D] is truly an Israelite, in whom there is no guile” [Note: [Col. 0507] John 1.]; to the third he says: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God anointed you” [Note: [Col. 0507] Ps. 44.]; to the fourth he says: “She has become like a merchant ship, bringing her bread from afar” [Note: [Col. 0507] Prov. 31.].

By God’s agency, our conscience is opened four times: first to the priest, second to one’s neighbour, third to God, fourth to God, man, and angel. First in confession; second in disclosure; third in thanksgiving; fourth in judgment, when an account is rendered. The first opening purifies, the second builds up, the third gives grace, the fourth examines. In the first, the key of David [Col. 0508A] closes by abstinence, and no one opens without God’s pleasure [Note: [Col. 0507] Rev. 3.]. He opens by grace, and no one closes against his good will. Of the second: “May the Lord open our heart in his law and in his commandments” [Note: [Col. 0507] 2 Macc. 1.]. Of the third it is said that “Daniel three times a day bent his knees, with the windows open toward Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0507] Dan. 6.]. Of the fourth: “The books were opened; judgment sat” [Note: [Col. 0507] Dan. 7.]. The books are consciences.

Hear the first: “I have sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea, and I am not worthy to see the height of heaven.” Hear the second: “I am conscious of nothing” [Note: [Col. 0507] 1 Cor. 14], and the same person: “I believe that I too have the Spirit of God” [Note: [Col. 0507] 1 Cor. 7.]. Hear the third: “You know, Lord,” says Hezekiah, “how I have walked uprightly and done what is good in your sight” [Note: [Col. 0507] Jer. 18]. Hear the fourth: “Do not judge before the time,” says the Apostle, “until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the consciences of hearts” [Col. 0508B] [Note: [Col. 0507] 1 Cor. 4.].

These are the four gates in the building shown to Ezekiel. The first is toward the west: through it no entrance is shown, because sin goes out through it, not in. The second is toward the north, from which all evil comes: through it your conscience enters into your neighbour’s heart, which is toward the north. The third is toward the south: through it you enter when you fervently give thanks to God for the benefits granted you. The fourth is toward the east: through it there will be entrance when all consciences are opened.

Sometimes God is said to open our heart; sometimes we open it. Thus God opened the door of the ark, [Col. 0508C] while Noah opened the window when he wished [Note: [Col. 0507] Gen. 8.]. The door signifies an exit from the ark—that is, from the heart—through action; the window, an exit through thought. The door is below, the window above. The door is below because action pertains to the body; the window is above because thought pertains to the soul. Hence birds went out through the window, but beasts and human beings through the door.

We leave through the door, by action, in four ways. Some actions are carnal, pertaining to the body’s use; others spiritual, pertaining to instruction of the mind. Both good people and evil people go out to each kind. Those who go out to earthly actions in order to fulfil pleasure are the unclean animals which go out of the ark. Those who handle them for necessary use [Col. 0508D] are clean animals. Those, however, who undertake the governance of the Church—which is a spiritual action—and leave the secret place of the mind not from ambition but obedience, are like Noah. But those who do this for their own glory are like Cain.

Likewise, we open our heart to contemplation in four ways. First, when we consider every creature as it is in itself and find all things vanity, because as it came into being from nothing, so, insofar as it is in itself, it shows that it tends toward nothing. The second way is when we consider what [Col. 0509A] the same creature is by the Creator’s gift, and see in it the likeness of divine reason: although in itself mutable, by God’s gift it is such that it is not wholly reduced to nothing. The third way is when we consider how God uses the ministry of creatures to fulfil his judgments, whether in mercy 105 or in judgment. In this kind, we hear every creature speaking to us with three voices. The first says, “Receive”; the second, “Render”; the third, “Flee.” Receive a benefit; render what is owed; flee punishment. The first is the voice of one serving; the second, of one warning; the third, of one threatening.

The fourth way is when we consider creatures in respect of how a human being can use them to fulfil the pleasure of carnal desire, and think in them not of aid for weakness but of the delight of lust. [Col. 0509B] Those who go out in this manner are like the raven, which did not return [Note: [Col. 0509] Gen. 8.]. The remaining three pertain to the dove’s departure [Note: [Col. 0509] Ibid.].

In this chapter four words of the bridegroom should be noted: sister, friend, dove, immaculate one. “Open, sister, because the ‘lover of the brethren’ [Note: [Col. 0509] 2 Macc. 15] comes to you; my friend, because ‘you loved righteousness and hated iniquity’ [Note: [Col. 0509] Ps. 44]; ‘with everlasting charity I have loved you’ [Note: [Col. 0509] Jer. 31]. Dove, open, because you have lived in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart; the Holy Spirit shall come upon you” [Note: [Col. 0509] Luke 1]. “My immaculate one: the ‘Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world’ [Note: [Col. 0509] John 1], comes to you, because ‘you are wholly beautiful, and there is no blemish in you’” [Note: [Col. 0509] Song 4.].

Therefore, blessed soul, if you have performed the commanded opening, lest the devil occupy an empty vessel through poisonous suggestion, [Col. 0509C] ask from him who commanded the opening an outpouring of the Holy Spirit, saying:

“Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle within them the fire of your love” [Note: [Col. 0509] Invocation of the Holy Spirit].

At this petition manna rains down for you from heaven, namely the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the Son promised, the Father sent forth, and the Spirit himself remitted. He promised it to the world, sent it forth from heaven, and remitted guilt to those bound by sins. Hear the Son’s promise: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you. When I have been taken up” [Note: [Col. 0509] John 16], etc. The Father sent it forth: “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the Father give the good Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0509] Matt. 7] to those who fear him, or who ask him. Hear the Spirit: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you remit, they shall be remitted to them” [Note: [Col. 0509] John 20.].

For he comes not only [Col. 0509D] to justify sinners, to enrich the poor, and to kindle them intensely and eagerly. Hence the first cry, “Come, Holy Spirit”; the second, “Fill the hearts of your faithful”; the third, “And kindle within them the fire of your love.” We find that the ancient fathers prayed for these three things. For the first, in Ezekiel we find: “Come, spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live” [Note: [Col. 0509] Ezek. 37.]. For the second, David: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0509] Ps. 103.]. For the third, the bride: “Arise, [Col. 0510A] north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and its spices shall flow” [Note: [Col. 0509] Song 4.]. Of the first it is said: “Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0509] Ezek. 37.].

It should be noted that these bones were dry, disjointed, and scattered: dry because without the richness of devotion; disjointed because without the affection of heavenly religious life; scattered through the dissipation of both action and thought. Of the first: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0509] Acts 7]. Stiff-necked against obedience; uncircumcised in heart because of the filth of superfluous thoughts; uncircumcised in ears, since they willingly lend their hearing to foolishness.

Hear of the disjointed: “Whoever does not love remains in death” [Note: [Col. 0509] 1 John 3].—“If you bite and devour one another, [Col. 0510B] take care lest you be consumed by one another” [Note: [Col. 0509] Gal. 5]. But hear this: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” [Note: [Col. 0509] Acts 4]. Likewise, they had one spirit and one faith. The Apostle says: “Would that those who trouble us were cut off!” [Note: [Col. 0509] Gal. 5]. Those are scattered bones who are always wandering and never steadfast, so that they can say: “My bones have been scattered beside hell” [Note: [Col. 0509] Ps. 140.].

The Holy Spirit comes at times to rebuke, at times to instruct, at times to kindle: to rebuke the world, to instruct the ignorant, to kindle the lukewarm. He rebukes the world concerning sin, judgment, and righteousness [Note: [Col. 0509] John 16]; he instructs the ignorant concerning what is the way, the truth, and the life [Note: [Col. 0509] John 14]; he kindles the lukewarm where charity is subtle, mobile, and keen. Therefore, if he comes to you for the first purpose, do not resist; if for the second, [Col. 0510C] do not extinguish him. Of the first: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0509] Acts 7]. Of the second, the Apostle: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” [Note: [Col. 0509] Eph. 4]. Of the third, the same Apostle: “Do not despise prophecies. Do not extinguish the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0509] 1 Thess. 5].

First, then, he comes to rebuke the world concerning sin, which it committed; concerning righteousness, which it did not maintain; concerning judgment, which it feared. Concerning sin, because those who sin against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven in this age or in the age to come [Note: [Col. 0509] Matt. 12]. Concerning righteousness, because “he shall withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding, and shall be rebuked by iniquity coming upon him” [Note: [Col. 0509] Wis. 1]. Concerning judgment, because he shall judge concerning the spirit of judgment and the spirit of error.

But perhaps someone is more anxious about tomorrow’s food than about the coming of the Holy [Col. 0510D] Spirit; about filling sheepfolds than about his filling the hearts of the faithful; about setting fire to an enemy’s house than about kindling the fire of the Holy Spirit. Yet the Holy Spirit does not fill the belly but the mind; he does not bring bodily riches but heavenly delights; he seeks not vengeance upon an enemy but brotherly love. It follows.

He comes to instruct concerning what is truth, way, and life [Note: [Col. 0509] John 14]. Concerning truth: “When I have been taken up, I shall send you the Spirit of truth” [Note: [Col. 0509] John 16]. Concerning way and life: “If [Col. 0511A] we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.” And Ezekiel’s living creatures went wherever the impulse of the Spirit was. “When the living creatures moved, the wheels also moved with them, because the spirit of life was in the wheels” [Note: [Col. 0511] Ezek. 1.].

The Spirit therefore proceeds, showing the way by which we are to flee, by which we are to walk, and by which we are to arrive. Let us flee sin; let us walk only through the advances of virtues; let us arrive at the kingdom. “For those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” [Note: [Col. 0511] Rom. 8]. Let us therefore follow the first way, saying with Ezekiel: “The Spirit seized me by a lock of my hair, set me in the temple of Jerusalem, and I saw there the abominations which the children of Israel commit and which must be fled” [Note: [Col. 0511] Ezek. 8]. Behold the first way.

Of the second way, by which we may advance, it is said to the prophet: “Go out, for the Lord is passing by: a great and strong wind overthrowing and breaking rocks; but the Lord is not in the spirit” [Col. 0511B] [Note: [Col. 0511] 3 Kings 19]. And Job: “When the spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh stood up” [Note: [Col. 0511] Job 4]. That is, because of my sins I recoiled from the presence of the Spirit. Of the third: “He took me and led me to a high mountain, and showed me the structure of a city sloping toward the south” [Note: [Col. 0511] Ezek. 40]. This is the way by which we shall arrive at the kingdom.

It follows that he may kindle charity, which is mobile, subtle, and keen: mobile, because it now comes and now withdraws from the soul; subtle, so that one tempted may perceive the devil’s phantasm; keen, whence “The Holy Spirit proceeding from the throne penetrated the breasts of the apostles with invisible power” [Note: [Col. 0511] Church Office for Pentecost].

This building has four gates, which were shown [Col. 0511C] to the prophet: the eastern gate, the southern gate, the northern gate, and the western gate. Through these four come four winds, concerning which it is said: “Come, Spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live” [Note: [Col. 0511] Ezek. 37]. From the west, then, comes the spirit of fear; from the north, the spirit of counsel and fortitude; from the east, that of knowledge and understanding; from the south, that of piety and wisdom.

From the west, so that one who has fallen may return through fear of God; from the north, so that one tempted may prevail by counsel against deceitful schemes and by fortitude against violent temptations; from the east, so that by knowledge one may perceive temporal things and by understanding heavenly things; from the south, so that through piety one may love, and through wisdom may savour the things above.

Hear the first wind, from the west, namely fear: “Fear God and keep [Col. 0511D] his commandments” [Note: [Col. 0511] Eccl. 12]. For whoever has forsaken the fear of the Lord cannot be justified. Hear the wind from the north, namely counsel and fortitude. The Lord says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” [Note: [Col. 0511] Matt. 10]. He says “prudent” on account of counsel. For fortitude he says: “Be strong in battle” [Note: [Col. 0511] Church Office for the Holy Apostles]. Of the third wind, namely knowledge: “Blessed is he who finds wisdom, and he who abounds in prudence” [Note: [Col. 0511] Prov. 3]. Of the fourth wind, namely piety and wisdom, it is said: “Seek the things above; savour the things above, not those upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0511] Col. 3].

[Col. 0512A] Therefore it is fittingly said of these: “Come, Spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.” Let the dry bones, then, grow fat through mercy; let the disjointed be joined through heavenly concord; let the scattered be recalled through the harmony of deeds and thoughts. Of the first: “Let oil not fail from your head” [Note: [Col. 0511] Eccl. 9], and: “You have made my head fat with oil” [Note: [Col. 0511] Ps. 22]. That oil, I say, which was poured upon the man wounded by robbers [Note: [Col. 0511] Luke 10]. Of the second, the Apostle: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 0511] Eph. 4], so that it may be “good and delightful for brethren to dwell together in unity” [Note: [Col. 0511] Ps. 132]. Of the third it is said: “I shall show you the way of wisdom; I shall lead you through the paths of equity” [Note: [Col. 0511] Prov. 4]. Behold, the Holy Spirit comes from the four winds and breathes upon the slain, and they live.

[Col. 0512B] Very often the entrance of the Holy Spirit is impeded. For we hear that some impediment confronts each of these four winds. John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw angels standing upon the four corners of the earth, and they held the four winds so that they should not blow” [Note: [Col. 0511] Rev. 7], the winds already mentioned. Against the wind of fear stands faithless sanctity; against the wind of counsel and fortitude, rashness and faintheartedness; against knowledge and understanding, the darkness of ignorance; against the spirit of piety and wisdom, weariness and forgetfulness of God. Behold the coming of the Holy Spirit. It follows:

“Fill the hearts of your faithful.” Some have a soul empty of the grace of the Holy Spirit; some have [Col. 0512C] little grace; some have it, but not continuously. He fills the first, supplies the second, and completes the third: the first, lest they come into a desert; the second, that they may labour toward perfection; the third, that they may attain perfection.

The first is that man wounded by robbers [Note: [Col. 0511] Luke 10], who, though he had no oil, nevertheless had it poured upon him. To these the Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” [Note: [Col. 0511] Matt. 11]. Again: “Whoever thirsts, let him come and drink” [Note: [Col. 0511] John 7]; again: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but have received the spirit of adoption” [Note: [Col. 0511] Rom. 8].

The second are that woman who had a little oil and borrowed empty vessels from her neighbours; and she poured in as many as her son supplied [Note: [Col. 0511] 4 Kings 4], because works and grace grow together. Of these the Apostle says: “See that you do not receive the grace of God in vain” [Note: [Col. 0511] 2 Cor. 6], lest [Col. 0512D] you be that wicked servant who did not put his lord’s money out at interest [Note: [Col. 0511] Luke 19]. For to these the Lord will say: “Conduct business” [Note: [Col. 0511] Ibid.], etc.

The third are the prudent virgins who, while all were asleep, preserved their oil. Therefore they entered with the bridegroom into the wedding feast [Note: [Col. 0511] Matt. 25]. Hence the Apostle: “O Timothy, guard the good purpose” [Note: [Col. 0511] 1 Tim. 6]. And he himself concerning himself: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit unto that day” [Note: [Col. 0511] 2 Tim. 1].

Of the first it is said: “The earth was void and empty, and darkness was upon the face of the abyss” [Note: [Col. 0511] Gen. 1]: void because of sins, empty without [Col. 0513A] the fruit of virtues, and darkness was upon the face of the abyss, upon the fleshly heart, so that they could not know God. But “the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters” [Note: [Col. 0513] Gen. 1], in order to confer grace. To the second he says: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” [Note: [Col. 0513] Ibid.]: increase in virtues among yourselves; multiply through teaching and example among your neighbours; fill the earth, that is, earthly people, with the promise of glory.

Behold, now the Holy Spirit has come and filled the hearts of the faithful. But that his coming may be celebrated perfectly, he kindles within them the fire of his love: first, that they may meditate willingly; second, that they may resolve joyfully; third, that they may desire ardently. Let them meditate willingly on heavenly things, resolve joyfully upon acts of service, and desire ardently to see in heaven the mighty works of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore open by vomiting out sin; [Col. 0513B] open so that you may understand and keep his commandments; open so that you may see the blessedness of heaven. In the first, the Holy Spirit will come when he finds purity in the heart; in the second, he will fill the hearts of the faithful because he will find his will done there; in the third, he will kindle the fire of his love, granting eternal happiness. For the first, Noah opened and sent out the raven [Note: [Col. 0513] Gen. 8]; for the second it is said: “May the Lord open your heart in his law and in his commandments” [Note: [Col. 0513] 2 Macc. 1]; for the third, Daniel, bending his knee three times daily, prayed in his chamber with the windows open toward that heavenly Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0513] Dan. 6]. May Jesus Christ our Lord lead us there.

“I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.”

[CARD.] Here she shows in herself the two lives which the Son had signified through honey and honeycomb. Therefore she says: “Thus, being at rest from the cares [Col. 0513C] of this age, I sleep in the bosom of my beloved, in contemplation of God; but because I languish with love, through love of neighbour, my heart keeps watch for works of charity.” Yet what she says, “my heart keeps watch,” can be referred to that concern which she even now bears for the Church: for although in herself she sleeps and rests, she is nevertheless devoutly concerned for us, in prayers to her Son and in defences against the enemy. It follows.

“The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister, my dove, my immaculate one.” In this chapter the mother speaks concerning the conception of the Son; and these words correspond to the angelic salutation to the Virgin and the Virgin’s answer to the angel. She says, therefore: This is the voice of my beloved [Col. 0513D] knocking and saying to me, “Open to me.” This word accords with the word of Isaiah: “Let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0513] Isa. 45].

But how was the earth of the virginal womb opened so that it brought forth the Saviour, when the Virgin herself conceived and gave birth? Hence we have in Ezekiel: “This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it” [Note: [Col. 0513] Ezek. 44]. For she knew no intercourse with a man. And it is added: “The Lord God of Israel has entered through it, and it shall be shut for the prince” [Note: [Col. 0513] Ibid.]. For although the Lord God entered the world through the gate of the virginal womb, the gate nevertheless remained shut for him and in honour of him, who [Col. 0514A] came forth from the Virgin’s closed womb.

Yet the following words will explain in what sense this saying, “Open to me,” and that saying of Isaiah, “Let the earth be opened,” are to be understood. The mother therefore says: This is the voice of my beloved, the Son of God the Father, knocking at me through the angel Gabriel speaking to me. “Open to me, my sister,” namely one who will be conformed and akin to me and a sharer in the eternal inheritance. There follow words corresponding to the angelic salutation: “my friend,” that is, one privy to my secrets, freed from the yoke of slavery to sin and from the curse—which is signified in the angel’s salutation by “Hail.” There follows: “my dove,” that is, “full of grace”; for fullness of spiritual grace is signified by the dove. “My immaculate one,” and therefore “blessed among women” [Note: [Col. 0513] Luke 1], of whom none was [Col. 0514B] without blemish: for she also is cursed who does not bear children; and the statement that she should bear in pain is spoken because of the curse of childbearing. Thus the latter has the blemish of sterility, the former the blemish of corruption.

Having said this, the cause 106 is added for which the Son of God wished to become incarnate, as though he said: Therefore I knock, that you may open to me:

“Because my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night.”

[THO.] The head of Christ is God, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0513] 1 Cor. 3]. The locks are the thoughts gathered together in the minds of the faithful: they do not flow down scattered, but are bound together by discipline. But the dew and drops of the night, which descend from above in darkness and cold, are the minds of the wicked, dark and blind indeed, [Col. 0514C] and always desiring the things that are on earth. When we love him less than we ought, and when many, what is worse, are held by no affection of charity toward him, Christ’s head is full of dew; and when the wicked render hatred to God’s servants in return for love, his locks are wet with drops of the night.

When, therefore, such a storm presses in, the beloved rightly rouses his beloved from the sweet sleep of contemplation, commands her to apply herself to the word of preaching, and through frequent exhortation to warm, enlighten, and open to him the hearts of the wicked, which were shut against him. One dew is useful, another useless. The dew of night, of which this passage speaks, is cold and therefore useless. The dew of dawn is lukewarm and therefore barren. This dew does three things: it cools, moistens, and makes fruitful. It cools the burning [Col. 0514D] of temptation, moistens the dryness of devotion, and makes fruitful the barrenness of virtue.

Against the cooling of this dew the king of the Chaldeans kindled the furnace—that is, the world—which he inflamed with these four things: naphtha, tow, pitch, and vine-prunings [Note: [Col. 0513] Dan. 3]. The first is the malice of envy and brotherly hatred; the second, the vanity of the world; the third, pleasure of the flesh; the fourth, the wickedness of apostasy. For naphtha is the dregs of oil, or olive-stones which remain dry when the oil—that is, charity—has been pressed out. Of this John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” [Note: [Col. 0513] 1 John 3]. By this Cain was condemned [Note: [Col. 0513] Gen. 4]; by this the devil kindled the furnace of the world when he envied [Col. 0515A] and hated Adam’s prosperity [Note: [Col. 0515] Gen. 3].

By tow, which burns easily, is signified the vanity of the world, namely that which passes easily. By this the devil inflamed Adam, saying: “On whatever day you eat, you shall be like gods” [Note: [Col. 0515] Ibid.]. By pitch is signified the pleasure of the flesh, whence: “Whoever touches pitch shall be defiled by it” [Note: [Col. 0515] Sir. 13]. By this the devil inflamed the world when Adam saw that the tree was beautiful to behold and sweet to eat, and took of its fruit and ate [Note: [Col. 0515] Gen. 3].

*Mal­leoli* are knotted, barren stocks cut from vines. This is the wickedness of apostasy. Hence the Lord: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Without me you can do nothing” [Note: [Col. 0515] John 15]. By this the devil inflamed the world when Adam, by transgressing the commandment, departed from God [Note: [Col. 0515] Gen. 3].

[Col. 0515B] Or otherwise. The flame of this furnace—that is, of the world—is threefold. The first is that of vices, the second of temptations, the third of temporal afflictions. In the first many sinners are entangled; in the second many, by the grace of God, struggle manfully; in the third, tribulations are manfully overcome by spiritual men. Again, we find that the Lord appeared in three fires. Concerning the first it is said: “A whirlwind came from the north, and a great cloud and enfolding fire; and from its midst there was, as it were, the appearance of electrum—that is, from the midst of the fire” [Note: [Col. 0515] Ezek. 1.]. Concerning the second it is said: “The angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace” [Note: [Col. 0515] Dan. 3.]. Concerning the third, in the Apocalypse John saw a man among seven golden candlesticks, as though in a furnace of blazing fire [Note: [Col. 0515] Apoc. 1.].

Who, therefore, could stand [Col. 0515C] in this furnace, where there was the command of a proud king, the execution of cruel ministers, and the kindling of the four things mentioned above, unless the angel of the Lord had descended into the furnace [Note: [Col. 0515] Dan. 3.]—that is, Christ? I do not mean the angel of evil counsel, namely the devil; nor the angel of delegated counsel, namely Gabriel; but the Angel of great counsel, namely Christ. But let us hear how he shook off the flame: the proud king, that is, the devil, by humility; the ministers by love; the four things mentioned above by creation. Against the first: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0515] Phil. 2.]. Against the second: “Because of the exceeding love with which he loved us, when we were dead in sin, he made us alive together in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0515] Eph. 2.]. Against the third: “We have an advocate [Col. 0515D] with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who became the propitiation for our sins” [Note: [Col. 0515] I John 2.]. For he is the one “who prays greatly for the people and for the whole holy city of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0515] II Macc. 15.].

This one brings a threefold dew: that of mercy, grace, and glory. The first came upon the fleece, and from the fleece [Note: [Col. 0515] Judg. 6.], that is, from the Virgin. The second came into the basin [Note: [Col. 0515] Ibid.], that is, into the hearts of the apostles. The third came from the basin onto the threshing-floor [Note: [Col. 0515] Ibid.], that is, into the universal Church. The first cleanses, the second makes fruitful, the third gladdens. It cleanses from the dregs of sins; it makes fruitful with the shoot of virtues; [Col. 0516A] it gladdens by contemplation of things above. The first purifies a person, the second magnifies him, the third makes him joyful. Of the first: “May the Lord give you abundance from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0515] Gen. 27.]; of the second: “I shall be like dew; Israel shall blossom like a lily” [Note: [Col. 0515] Hos. 14.]. Of the third it is said: “Dew shall remain in my harvest, and my glory shall always be renewed” [Note: [Col. 0515] Job 29.].

These three dews extinguish or cool the three burnings of the Chaldeans, concerning which the following is said. The burning of temptations has three hopes. There are some who are always wearied by temptations and sometimes fall, sometimes rise again; there are those who always labor and do not fall; there are those who tempt and do not fall, but are so spiritual that they do not even feel the temptation itself. These are the three youths in the furnace [Col. 0516B] of the Chaldeans: namely Ananias, whose name means “the grace of the Lord”; Azarias, whose name means “the help of God”; and Misael, who is called “the touching of God.” But the fourth among them was like the Son of God, who made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing dew [Note: [Col. 0515] Dan. 3.].

And thus the first, if he falls, rises again, because he is Ananias: that is, the dew of God’s grace comes to his aid, so that he may say, “You have tested me by fire” [Note: [Col. 0515] Ps. 16.], as silver is tested; for there is the voice of the Lord cutting through the flame of fire. The second does not fall, because he is Azarias—that is, the help of God—and says: “You have tested me by fire, and no iniquity has been found in me” [Note: [Col. 0515] Ibid.], because he who was like the Son of God made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing dew [Note: [Col. 0515] Dan. 3.]; and he cries: “When you walk through fire, you shall not be burned, because I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, [Col. 0516C] your Savior” [Note: [Col. 0515] Isa. 43.]. The third does not even feel it, because he is Misael, that is, the touching of God. He says: “You delivered, Lord, my heart from destruction, from the pressure of the flame that surrounded me, and in the midst of fire I was not scorched” [Note: [Col. 0515] Ecclus. 51.], because he made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing dew. The fourth was with them, like the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0515] Dan. 3.].

Secondly, it was said that dew moistens dryness. There is a threefold dryness, as we have already said: contrition without tears, compassion without mercy, contemplation without devotion. But the dew of divine grace moistens contrition with tears, compassion with works of mercy, and contemplation with devotion. In the first, God gives of the richness of the earth [Note: [Col. 0515] Gen. 27.]; in the third, abundance from the dew of heaven [Note: [Col. 0515] Ibid.]. Of the [Col. 0516D] middle we do not doubt when it possesses the dew of heaven, as Job says: “Dew shall remain in my harvest” [Note: [Col. 0515] Job 29.].

Thirdly, it was said that dew makes fruitful. It makes virginity fruitful; it makes the human mind fruitful; it makes the Church of God militant fruitful: virginity by the incarnation of divinity, the human mind by the shoot of virtue, the Church by sacraments. The first is for redemption, the second for renewal, the third for regeneration. Of the first it is said: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One” [Note: [Col. 0515] Isa. 43.].
