Of the second the prophet says: “I shall be like dew; Israel shall blossom [Col. 0517A] like a lily, and his root shall break forth like Lebanon; his branches shall spread, his glory shall be like the olive tree, and his fragrance like Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0517] Hos. 14.]. The third is the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Sion [Note: [Col. 0517] Deut. 4.]: namely, from under the anathema—that is, separation—which “Hermon” signifies, of Gentilism or Judaism, into the contemplative Church, which “Sion” signifies.

Thus, at Gideon’s request, dew first descended upon the fleece [Note: [Col. 0517] Judg. 6.], that is, into the Virgin’s womb, by the grace of the Holy Spirit. It was squeezed from the fleece into the basin, that is, into the human heart, because by means of the Virgin’s womb the grace of God came to us. Thirdly, it descended onto the threshing-floor, that is, the Church militant. The first dew was evil, because it was of the night and therefore cold. But this dew is good, and from the head. The Son of God, about to come in the flesh in order to free humanity from evils, asks that the bridal chamber of the virginal womb be opened to him. Opened, I say, not through the pollution of intercourse, but through the affection of love. But he adds why he comes: because his head—that is, God, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0517] I Cor. 3.]—is full of the dew of night, which is cold and falls in darkness. This is the love that existed under the Law: blind, since it did not understand spiritually; and cold, because God was loved more for the love of temporal things than through the ardor of charity.

The locks hanging from the head are the faithful who cleave to God in faith, and who are full of drops of night, because they loved one another not so much with the affection of charity as with that of carnality. Therefore David promised that he himself would come in the flesh and water the world with a stronger dew, prophesying thus: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece, and like drops upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ps. 71.]. Just as it had been [Col. 0517C] promised by God, foreseen by the prophets, and desired by the world, so today we see it fulfilled.

> A mighty order of the ages is born anew;  
> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.  
> (VIRGIL, *Eclogue* IV, 5.)

Thus the world, constrained by the languor of old age, might blossom anew with a kind of spiritual youth when the flower descended from the root of Jesse. For the world languished through pride, diabolical suggestion, and dissolution of life: first, so that man might despise his Creator; second, so that he might obey the devil; third, so that he might corrupt his own good nature. Therefore Isaiah reproaches them thus: “Woe to the sinful nation, a people heavy with iniquity, an evil seed, wicked children” [Note: [Col. 0517] Isa. 1.].

Accordingly, the Lord descends [Col. 0517D] “like rain upon the fleece,” because, in order to restrain pride, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0517] Phil. 2.]. In order to remove the devil’s yoke, “he became obedient to the Father” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ibid.]; in order to restrain dissolution of life, he endured “death, even death upon a cross” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ibid.]. Let us therefore consider Christ’s love, Mary’s dignity, and our benefit: the love by which he endured unworthy things for us; the dignity by which the blessed Virgin brought forth such a one for us; the benefit by which he bestowed upon us both spiritual and eternal goods. Therefore we owe Christ love, Mary honor, and ourselves [Col. 0518A] astonishment.

Hear the first concerning Christ: “Because of the exceeding love with which God loved us, when we were dead in sin, Christ made us alive” [Note: [Col. 0517] Eph. 2.]. Hear Mary’s dignity: “You alone were chosen in the female sex in the world, and deserved to carry the holy Lord in your womb” [Note: [Col. 0517] Office of the Church.]. Hence:

> Nor was she seen to have one like her before, nor one to follow.

Hence: “For you are blessed, O holy Virgin Mary, and worthy of every praise, because from you arose the Sun of righteousness, Christ our God” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ibid.]. Hear the benefit he bestowed upon us, at which we ought to marvel: namely, that he who is the giver of all things labored so greatly for the salvation of the nations. “Lord, what is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ps. 8.] For whose sake you descended “like rain upon the fleece, [Col. 0518B] and like drops falling upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ps. 71.].

We read that the Lord descended like dew [Note: [Col. 0517] Judg. 6.], descended like snow, descended like a downpour [Note: [Col. 0517] Ps. 71.]. Of the first: “He descended like rain upon the fleece” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ibid.]. Of the second, we read that dew descended upon Gideon’s fleece [Note: [Col. 0517] Judg. 6.]. Of the third: “As rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again” [Note: [Col. 0517] Isa. 55.], and so forth. The fourth is found here: “He descended like rain upon the fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ps. 71.].

Rain makes fruitful; late dew pours itself forth; snow is white and cold; a downpour descends with force. In the rain, therefore, we have the fruitfulness bestowed upon the Virgin by her Son; in dew, serenity of character; in snow, white and cold, incomparable virginity bestowed from heaven; in the downpour, the usefulness of graces. [Col. 0518C] Concerning the rain we have: “The Lord rained upon one city, and upon another he did not rain” [Note: [Col. 0517] Amos 4.]. The land rained upon was holy Mary, made fruitful from heaven. “Glorious things are said of you, city of God” [Note: [Col. 0517] Ps. 86.]. The city not rained upon is Eve, concerning whom the Church cries: “Look, Lord, for the city once full of divinity has been made desolate.” For she received the curse of the proud. Hence: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you” [Note: [Col. 0517] II Kings 1.].

But in the city of Mary we have the temperate and latter rain upon the earth. Hear of the fruitful rain: “As rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth and drench it and make it spring forth, so shall my word be that goes [Col. 0518D] forth from my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0517] Isa. 55.]. Snow also, which is virginity, descends from heaven. Hence: “He commands the snow to descend upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0517] Job 36.]. Hence Jerome: “To live in the flesh apart from the flesh is not an earthly life but a heavenly one—not so much human as angelic.” Hence the poet [Note: [Col. 0517] Virg., *Ecl.* IV, 6.]:

> Now the Virgin returns; the Saturnian reigns return.

This rain inundates the earth, intoxicates it, and makes it spring forth. It inundates by the irrigation of grace, intoxicates by love, and makes it spring forth in the Incarnation itself. “He gives seed to the sower” [Note: [Col. 0517] Isa. 55.]. Seed is the word [Col. 0519A] preached to one’s neighbor; seed is the example of a good life which another imitates; seed is the beginning from which virtues spring. The first establishes, the second instructs, the third builds. It establishes truth, instructs one’s neighbor, and builds a spiritual edifice. Of the first: “The seed is the word of God” [Note: [Col. 0519] Luke 8.]. Of the second: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation” [Note: [Col. 0519] Ps. 125.].

It should be noted that this dew descends upon the fleece, descends upon the threshing-floor, descends upon the earth. Of the first we have the fleece of Gideon [Note: [Col. 0519] Judg. 6.]; of the second, that when the fleece had been dried, dew descended onto the threshing-floor [Note: [Col. 0519] Ibid.]; of the third, we read that manna descended for the children of Israel like dew upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0519] Exod. 16.]. The fleece, therefore, is called the blessed Virgin; the threshing-floor, religious life; the earth, the Church. Thus it descended into the Virgin’s fleece, giving fruitfulness; into the threshing-floor of religious life, producing [Col. 0519B] the soul’s immortality; and into the earth of the Church, producing the truth of faith. Therefore it first brought about conception in the Virgin; secondly, conformity of character in religious life and relief against temptation; thirdly, illumination of faith in the Church.

Of the first: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One” [Note: [Col. 0519] Isa. 45.]. Again: “May God give you of the richness of the earth and abundance of the dew of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0519] Gen. 27.]. Of the second: “The angel of the Lord, who descended into the furnace, made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing dew” [Note: [Col. 0519] Dan. 3.]. Of the third: “Your dew is the dew of light,” says the prophet [Note: [Col. 0519] Isa. 26.], namely, unto the light of faith in Christ.

It should therefore be noted that the Lord descends into some in order to convert them as though by a kind of force; into others by a grace of sweetness; into still others as persons established in the excellence of contemplation. [Col. 0519C] Upon the first he descends “like drops falling upon the earth”; upon the second he descends with a certain serenity, “like rain upon the fleece” [Note: [Col. 0519] Ps. 71.]; upon the third, “like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Sion” [Note: [Col. 0519] Ps. 132.]. Thus the first are converted, drawn by a certain force; the second delight within themselves in good knowledge; the third dwell with Paul in heavenly places.

In the first let us observe Paul, because he was drawn forcibly; in the second, Mary, how greatly she delights to sit at the Lord’s feet [Note: [Col. 0519] Luke 10.]; in the third, Stephen, who amid the stones and insults of persecutors beholds the Father with the Son in heaven [Note: [Col. 0519] Acts 7.]. Therefore, if you open your heart to God, our head—that is, God—will now be full of dew and drops, not of night [Col. 0519D] but of light, according to the saying: “Your dew is the dew of light” [Note: [Col. 0519] Isa. 26.]. Mary opened her womb to her Son, and he filled the whole world with grace. Open your mouth and heart in confession, and receive the drops of mercy; open your conscience in devotion, and the fruitful rain of charity will descend into you, and thus there will be in you an abundance of the dew of light.

## My head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night.

[CARD.] As if he said: My head—namely that head of which Isaiah says, “Every sick head is [Col. 0520A] full of dew” [Note: [Col. 0519] Isa. 1.]—for captains and prelates among the people are full of night-water and the irrigation of vices, which, because of the darkness of ignorance, like nocturnal drops of dew, are scarcely felt. The locks too are said to be full of drops of night. By the locks, which are twisted hairs hanging from the head, are signified the lesser people, who hang from prelates as from a head, yet are twisted away from their teaching. They too are full of drops of night: that is, of vices, which rain down abundantly when the light of grace has departed and the darkness of malice has arisen.

Then follows the response of the Virgin Mother to the voice of him knocking through the angel, when it is added:

## I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?

[Col. 0520B] [THO.] As though she plainly said: I have abandoned the affairs of the lowest things; on what grounds should I resume them? For one who girds himself for the office of preaching, just as he provides for those subject to him in spiritual things, so they are obliged to him in temporal things. Therefore, because she has shunned all temporal things, she says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again?” For the tunic signifies temporal action. Hence the Savior, speaking of the last judgment, says: “Let him who is in the field not return to take his tunic” [Note: [Col. 0519] Matt. 24.].

“I have washed,” she says, “my feet; how shall I defile them?” As if she said: My thoughts, by which I was once accustomed to touch the earth, I have now washed with the frequent tears of secret compunction; and, as far as is possible for mortals, I have made them worthy of a heavenly entrance. So that I may say: “Our feet [Col. 0520C] stood in your courts, O Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0519] Ps. 121.]; that is, even though I have not yet deserved to enter the walls of the heavenly city, yet by inward affection I have tasted certain of its joys.

There are five tunics. The first is the corruption of creatures; the second, the connection of virtues; the third, the ordering of character; the fourth, the spiritual activity of teachers; the fifth, that of the blessed. The first is the sackcloth of our mortality, which is cut apart in the Passion. We read four times that Christ laid aside his garments: first, at the supper, but he took them up again; second, when bound to the pillar, but they were restored to him; third, when mocked by the soldiers, and they were restored to him; fourth, when crucified, and he did not take them up again. Because of the second and fourth, altars are stripped on the fifth day before the day of the Resurrection, [Col. 0520D] and dust is also shaken out as if with a scourge of rods, in token of Christ’s scourging.

The second is the first robe with which the returning prodigal son is clothed [Note: [Col. 0519] Luke 15.]; the third is the fragrant garments with which Jacob, clothed by them, is blessed by his father [Note: [Col. 0519] Gen. 28.]; the fourth is the filthy garment in which Jesus the high priest is clothed in Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0519] ch. 3.]; the fifth is the hyacinth-blue tunic in which Aaron, entering the Holy of Holies, is adorned [Note: [Col. 0519] Lev. 8.].

Hear of the first: “Every creature groans and labors in childbirth even until now” [Note: [Col. 0519] Rom. 8.]. Hear of the second: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience” [Note: [Col. 0519] Gal. 5.], and so forth. Of [Col. 0521A] the third: “In all things we suffer tribulation, but are not distressed; we are brought into perplexity, but not forsaken; we suffer persecution and endure it; we are humbled, but not confounded; we are cast down, but do not perish” [Note: [Col. 0521] II Cor. 4.]. Of the fourth: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” [Note: [Col. 0521] II Tim. 4.], mingling times with times, blandishments with terrors. Of the fifth: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” [Note: [Col. 0521] Matt. 13.].

Of the first: “He who has a tunic, let him sell it and buy a sword” [Note: [Col. 0521] Luke 22.]; that is, let him not hesitate to spend his corruptible life for the sword—that is, the word of God. Of the following two it is said: “He who has two tunics, let him give one to him who has none” [Note: [Col. 0521] Luke 3.]; that is, one who shines in virtues and character should at least instruct those who lack these in character. Of the fourth the Lord says concerning judgment: “Whoever is in the field, let him not return [Col. 0521B] to take his tunic” [Note: [Col. 0521] Matt. 13.]. The fifth is that with which Jesus the high priest, when the filthy garment has been removed, is clothed [Note: [Col. 0521] Zech. 3.].

Of the first it is said that the Lord made tunics of skins for the first parents [Note: [Col. 0521] Gen. 3.], which were made from dead animals as a sign of our corruption. The second is Joseph’s embroidered, long robe [Note: [Col. 0521] Gen. 37.], that is, one of many virtues together with perseverance. The third was the little tunic which Hannah made for her son Samuel [Note: [Col. 0521] I Kings 2.]: that is, grace—for “Hannah” means grace—for one asking God, which “Samuel” signifies; it is the form of character, small in comparison with virtues. Of the fourth it is said that Peter “girded himself with his tunic” [Note: [Col. 0521] John 21.] so that he might go freely across the waters to Christ, because spiritual actions bind teachers lest they be [Col. 0521C] soaked by the waves of worldly vanity.

For teachers ought to defend those subject to them, show the way by example, and instruct them from the Scriptures in the knowledge of God. Thus they ought to be girded, closely girded, and apron-girded: girded with the belt of patience, closely girded with the girdle of penitence, apron-girded with the linen cloth of chastity; girded for battle, closely girded for the road, apron-girded for the table; first in order to resist, second in order to walk, third in order to serve: to resist the adversary, to walk so as to draw near to heaven, to serve one subject to them.

Thus Peter girded himself with a sword when he cut off Malchus’s ear [Note: [Col. 0521] Matt. 26.]. He closely girded himself when he walked upon the waters. He apron-girded himself when he came out of prison. “Gird yourself,” the angel says to Peter [Note: [Col. 0521] Acts 12.]. Of the first: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” [Note: [Col. 0521] Ps. 44.]; of [Col. 0521D] the second, Paul: “Stand, having your loins girded in truth” [Note: [Col. 0521] I Pet. 1.]; of the third: “Let your loins be girded” [Note: [Col. 0521] Luke 12.].

The fifth tunic is Christ’s seamless tunic [Note: [Col. 0521] John 19.], which we shall possess when this corruptible thing puts on incorruption and this mortal thing immortality [Note: [Col. 0521] I Cor. 15.]. We wish to be stripped of the fourth so that we may be able to put on this one.

Feet are our affections. For just as bodily feet carry the outward person, so our affections carry the inward person. These often need washing, [Col. 0522A] because sometimes they are burned by heat, sometimes weakened by cold, sometimes struck against a stone, sometimes defiled by mud, sometimes sprinkled with dust. The first are burned by the flame of anger, hatred, and envy; the second grow numb with the chill of negligence; the third strike against the stone, Christ, through hesitation in faith; the fourth are defiled by fleshly pleasure; the fifth are sprinkled with the dust of vain glory.

Of the first Solomon says: “Can a man walk upon burning coals, and his soles not be burned?” [Note: [Col. 0521] Prov. 28.] Of the second, in the Gospel: “See that your flight does not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” [Note: [Col. 0521] Matt. 24.]; for in winter the numbness of negligence binds the feet. Of the third: “Lest at any time you strike your foot against a stone” [Note: [Col. 0521] Ps. 90.]. Of the fourth Jeremiah says: “Her filth is upon her feet, and she did not remember [Col. 0522B] her end” [Note: [Col. 0521] Lam. 1.]. Of the fifth he says: “Shake the dust from your feet as a testimony” [Note: [Col. 0521] Mark 6.].

From the first, because they are burned, the shoe—that is, dead works—must be removed so that they may be cooled. Hence Moses and Joshua are told: “Remove the shoe from your feet, for the ground on which you stand is holy” [Note: [Col. 0521] Exod. 3.], that is, the house of religious life. The second, because they are cold, must be protected with a shoe made from the skins of dead animals—that is, from examples of our predecessors. Hence of the paschal lamb it is said: “You shall eat with shoes upon your feet” [Note: [Col. 0521] Exod. 12.]. The third must be anointed with richness, whence Job says: “I washed my feet with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil” [Note: [Col. 0521] Job 29.]. Christ gave the butter of mercy before the Passion; [Col. 0522C] after the Resurrection, when he sent the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0521] Acts 2.], he gave the oil of grace.

The fourth must be washed with water. Hence the Lord washed the feet of his disciples, and Peter said: “Not only my feet, but also my hands and head” [Note: [Col. 0521] John 13.]; that is, not only my affections, but also my hands—that is, my works—and my head—that is, the wandering of my senses. But it is difficult to wash the affections completely. Thus Ezekiel was led “into water up to the ankles,” namely washed from the contact of earthly things; “and up to the knees,” which bend, so that the stiffness of pride might be washed away; “and up to the loins,” so that there might be a washing away of carnal pleasures; but not up to the heart, because of the difficulty of washing the affections that are in the heart. This is why he could not cross over [Note: [Col. 0521] Ezek. 47.]. From the fifth, dust must be shaken off, as we have said: [Col. 0522D] “Shake the dust from your feet” [Note: [Col. 0521] Mark 6.].

Nevertheless, all these things are called washing in a general sense. Taking occasion from the stripping off of this tunic, let us consider also the tunic which we call good conduct; and that one which we believe will be the glorification of the saints, in which “the righteous shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds; they shall judge nations and reign forever” [Note: [Col. 0521] Wisd. 3.]. For there is a tunic in which the vain shine; there is a tunic in which the righteous shine; there is a tunic in which the saints shine. [Col. 0523A] The first shine in the world, the second in the bosom of the Church, the third in heaven; the first by display, the second by miracles and conduct, the third by the vision of God.

Of the first: “They have turned night into day, and after darkness I hope again for light” [Note: [Col. 0523] Job 17.]. They turn night into day when they seek splendor from their sins. Of the second: “Let your light shine before men” [Note: [Col. 0523] Matt. 5.]; of the third: “Everlasting light shall shine upon your saints, O Lord.” The first run about in a dunghill, the second among reeds, the third in a fig-orchard and olive-grove. The first are like ashes, the second like sparks, the third like pupils of the eye. The first endure disgraceful sufferings; the second shall judge nations; the third have obtained the promises. The first go down alive into hell; the second overcome unto the kingdom above; the third [Col. 0523B] reign forever.

Thus the vain shine in three ways in that tunic which must be put off: by the natural power of reason, worldly cunning, and boastful display. Of the first it is said: “He enlightens every person coming into this world” [Note: [Col. 0523] John 1.]; of the second: “Your light shall be taken away from the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0523] Job 38.]; of the third Job says: “If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly” [Note: [Col. 0523] Job 31.].

The first, namely reason, sometimes shines above the head, sometimes below the head, sometimes in the head. It is below the head when a person treats of temporal matters; in the head when he treats of spiritual matters; above the head when he has his conversation in heavenly things. Of the first it is said of the strong woman: “She considered the paths of her house and did not eat the bread of idleness” [Note: [Col. 0523] Prov. 31.]; likewise, “Her lamp shall not be extinguished in the night” [Col. 0523C] [Note: [Col. 0523] Ibid.]. For we are in night when we deal with temporal matters. Of the second: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” [Note: [Col. 0523] Eccl. 2.]. Of the third Job says: “Who will grant me that I may be as in former months, according to the days in which God guarded me, when his lamp shone over my head and by his light I walked in darkness?” [Note: [Col. 0523] Job 29.]

But woe to us, because this light of reason, having abandoned spiritual things, wholly entangles itself in temporal affairs. Hence: “How the gold has grown dark, how its finest color has changed!” [Note: [Col. 0523] Lam. 4.] Hence we cry concerning temporal things: “O Key of David, who shuts and no one opens” [Note: [Col. 0523] Apoc. 3.], come and bring forth the bound man from the prison-house [Note: [Col. 0523] Jer. 52.], sitting in darkness and the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0523] Ps. 87.]. Concerning spiritual things: “O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0523] Ecclus. 24.], come to teach us [Col. 0523D] the way of prudence [Note: [Col. 0523] Isa. 40.]. Concerning heavenly things: “O Dayspring, come and enlighten the person whom you formed from clay.”

They also run about like ashes in a dunghill, because while they shine outwardly, they glitter like straw. But when they are harassed by the fire of tribulation, the straw vanishes into the ashes of sorrow. Then the ashes of sorrow, turning toward the desire for temporal goods, rot as it were upon a dungheap. Hear of straw: “My God, make them like a wheel, and like straw before the face [Col. 0524A] of the wind” [Note: [Col. 0523] Ps. 82.]. Job says of ashes: “I repent in ashes and dust” [Note: [Col. 0523] Job 42.]. Ashes in the heart are sorrowful compunction for sins; dust is the lowly outward affliction of the body. Yet these ashes are not dissolved into a dungheap, but are formed into the purest glass of a pure conscience. Again Job says: “I have become like ashes and dust” [Note: [Col. 0523] Job 30.]. Of the dungheap of temporal goods it is said: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen” [Note: [Col. 0523] Ecclus. 22.]. The oxen are preachers; temporal things are dung, because with Paul they account them as dung [Note: [Col. 0523] Phil. 3.].

Thus the vain shine; the winds also shine; and they shall shine when they are saints. The truly pure shine; they shine securely: first from a clean conscience, second through justice, third in glory; first in the chamber of the heart, second in judgment, third on the throne [Col. 0524B] of the kingdom. Of the first: “Your dew is the dew of light” [Note: [Col. 0523] Isa. 26.], namely illuminating grace. Of the second, the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” [Note: [Col. 0523] I Cor. 4.]. Of the third: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” [Note: [Col. 0523] Matt. 13.].

It should be noted that the righteous now shine inwardly, shine outwardly, and shine above. They shine inwardly by knowledge of themselves and of God; outwardly by conduct; above by the performance of miracles. In the first they have the delight of a good conscience; in the second, imitation of Christ; in the third, they produce wonder. David prayed for the first: “Enlighten my eyes, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0523] Ps. 12.]. This is the woman who lights a lamp and overturns the whole house, seeking the drachma [Col. 0524C] that she had lost [Note: [Col. 0523] Luke 15.], namely knowledge of God and of herself; otherwise it is said to her: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and follow the tracks of your flocks” [Note: [Col. 0523] Song 1.]. And concerning knowledge of God: “Have I been with you so long, and have you not known me?” [Note: [Col. 0523] John 14.]

But in order that you may know God as prudent virgins, trim your lamps [Note: [Col. 0523] Matt. 25.]. Thus you will be the candlestick 108 in the tabernacle, in which there were seven lamps: namely, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. O lamp of conscience, having within it the light of faith, the oil of mercy, and the fire of love! O blessed conscience, which can say truly with Job: “By the hearing of the ear I heard you, but now my eye sees you. Therefore I rebuke myself and repent in ashes and dust” [Note: [Col. 0523] Job 42.]. Behold how [Col. 0524D] the righteous shine through knowledge of themselves and of God, and through the delight of conscience. It follows how they shine through good conduct.

Not only by the tongue, but also by the hand and by the body: by the tongue in preaching, by the hand in working, by the body in suffering. Thus they shine by word, example, and martyrdom. Hence John is called “a burning and shining lamp” [Note: [Col. 0523] John 5.]: burning in fearless rebuke, shining everywhere by proclaiming the word of God [Note: [Col. 0523] Matt. 3.]; shining when clothed in a leather girdle and camel’s hair [Col. 0525A] [Note: [Col. 0525] Matt. 3.]; shining when beheaded for righteousness’ sake [Note: [Col. 0525] Matt. 14.]. Hear him shining with his tongue: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” [Note: [Col. 0525] Ps. 118]. And in work: “Let your loins be girded, and let burning lamps be in your hands” [Note: [Col. 0525] Luke 12]. And concerning the body: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” [Note: [Col. 0525] Ps. 131], namely, the flesh in which he suffered for us.

Because of the word it is said: “Those who are righteous shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who have instructed many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting ages” [Note: [Col. 0525] Dan. 12]. For the brightness of the hands it is said to the man clothed in linen in Ezekiel: “Enter into the midst of the wheels which are above the cherubim, fill your hands with coals of fire, and cast them upon the city” [Note: [Col. 0525] Ezek. 10], that is, with good works, displaying fervour or [Col. 0525B] light. For the warfare of the martyrs Gideon took sounding trumpets in the right hand and lamps enclosed among jars in the left [Note: [Col. 0525] Judg. 7]. The trumpet is the voice of preaching; the jar is the frailty of the flesh; and the lamp within the jars is called the brightness of a good will.

Because the saints endured mockeries and stripes, and moreover bonds and prisons, they therefore “shine and run to and fro like sparks among reeds” [Note: [Col. 0525] Wis. 3]. Sparks consume a bed of reeds; the reed, white within and green without, is the vanity of the world. Therefore the flaming sparks run to and fro—that is, the saints, kindled by charity, reduce the world’s vanity to truth. Hence it is said of Ezekiel’s living creatures: “And sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze” [Note: [Col. 0525] Ezek. 1]. These sparks consume sin and illuminate unto righteousness. Hence their appearance [Col. 0525C] was like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps.

Let us therefore run to and fro, run together, and run to meet, like sparks. Let us run to and fro by investigating sins; let us run together by giving thanks for God’s benefits; in the first let us be consuming sparks, in the second let us be burning, and in the third let us be shining. The Lord commanded us to run abroad when he said, “Go into the whole world” [Note: [Col. 0525] Mark 16]; and to consume when he said to Peter, “Kill and eat” [Note: [Col. 0525] Acts 10]. The Apostle taught us to run together: “Bear one another’s burdens” [Note: [Col. 0525] Gal. 6]. Again: “If a man is overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” [Note: [Col. 0525] Ibid.]. Let us run to meet God by rendering him praise and [Col. 0525D] glory for his benefits. Hence: “I will sing to the Lord, who has repaid me with good things, and I will sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High” [Note: [Col. 0525] Ps. 12].

These shall judge the nations. Hence: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” [Note: [Col. 0525] II Cor. 6]. Again: “You shall sit upon the heavens, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0525] Matt. 19]. Behold, we have: “The righteous shine like sparks among reeds” [Note: [Col. 0525] Wis. 3]. It follows: The righteous shall shine and run about like pupils of the eye in a fig orchard, in a vineyard, and in an olive grove. The pupil is the wholly luminous part of the eye; likewise the saints shall be wholly luminous in body and soul. The fig is the sweetness of the Father; oil, the mercy of the Son; wine, [Col. 0526A] the love of the Holy Spirit. The fig orchard consists of those who perceive the sweetness of the Father’s gentleness; the oil grove, of those who have received the sweetness of Christ’s mercy; the vineyard, of those who shall possess more abundantly the charity of the Holy Spirit. Among these the saints shall run about, giving thanks to God for all these things.

The first, therefore, are clothed with the tunic of vanity; the second, with the tunic of religious devotion; the third, with that of immortality. The first is that of which the Apostle said: “Hating even the defiled garment which is carnal” [Note: [Col. 0525] Jude 23]. The second was Joseph’s many-coloured, long robe [Note: [Col. 0525] Gen. 37]; the third was Christ’s seamless tunic [Note: [Col. 0525] John 19]. Wretched Adam was stripped of this third; Joseph was stripped of the second by his brothers; the bride glories that she has stripped off the first. But because it is of little use for the tunic of vanity to be put off unless the inward affections are washed, she adds: “I have washed [Col. 0526B] my feet; how shall I defile them?” The feet are the affections, which ought to be clean, straight, beautiful, and fiery: clean, that they may possess purity; straight, that they may maintain equity; beautiful, that they may delight in contemplating things above; fiery, that they may possess charity.

Of the first it is said that the Lord washed the disciples’ feet [Note: [Col. 0525] John 13]. Again: “Shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against those who did not receive you” [Note: [Col. 0525] Mark 16]. Of the straight feet it is said: “Their feet were straight feet, and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf’s foot” [Note: [Col. 0525] Ezek. 1]. Of the beautiful: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things!” [Note: [Col. 0525] Rom. 10]. Ezekiel also says of these that he saw a man and a sapphire-like work beneath his feet [Note: [Col. 0525] Ezek. 1]. Sapphire has the colour of heaven; for heaven is beneath the feet, because [Col. 0526C] by contemplating the things above heaven the affection penetrates there. Of fiery feet John says in the Apocalypse, concerning the man whom he saw amid seven golden lampstands: “His feet,” he says, “were like fine bronze, as though burning in a furnace” [Note: [Col. 0525] Rev. 1].

But because we cannot possess such feet without divine operation, it follows: “My beloved put his hand through the opening”; that is, by his operation he penetrated my heart, in order thus to form my affections. “But my belly trembled at his touch,” because my frailty regarded itself with suspicion, as unworthy and insufficient to receive so great a gift.

## “I have stripped off my tunic; how shall I put it on?”

[Col. 0526D] [CARD.] Indeed, in answer to the angel’s other utterance, “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” [Note: [Col. 0525] Luke 1], the Virgin replies: “I have stripped off my tunic.” As though she said: I have entirely stripped myself of every worldly entanglement and care; how shall I put it on again?—that I might involve myself in cares and, like one who is married, think upon the things of the world and how I may please a husband; especially since I have washed my feet, and how shall I defile them? As though she said: By my purpose of virginity I have washed my feet and affections from every carnal act and from its desire; how shall I defile them in [Col. 0527A] union with a man? This is what she herself said to the angel: “How shall this be, since I know not a man?” [Note: [Col. 0527] Luke 1]. Thereupon the manner of the Lord’s incarnation is set forth, as the Virgin says:

## “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.”

[THO.] The beloved puts his hand through the opening when the Lord kindles us to works of virtue by hidden inspiration; likewise, when he recalls to our memory the work which he has wrought in us; likewise, when he admonishes us concerning the work which he has wrought for us. Nor is it surprising, when we remember him incarnate, scourged, and dead, if the belly of our conscience trembles. Hence: “I considered your works and was afraid” [Note: [Col. 0527] Eccl. 8].

By the name “belly” is also understood [Col. 0527B] the softness and weakness of those who shrink from taking up the burden of teaching, whether because they do not believe themselves fit for it or because they love repose. The bridegroom sometimes puts his hand to the head, sometimes to the mouth, sometimes to the belly. The bridegroom’s hand is the operation which he works in us. Here the head is understood as the human soul; the mouth is the instrument of utterance; the belly is the softness of the flesh. God works three times in each person, to pluck their souls from corruption, as is said in Job [Note: [Col. 0527] Job 33].

Therefore the beloved puts his hand to the head, that something may be divinely inspired in us; to the mouth, that what has been inspired may be proclaimed; to the belly, that the flesh may perform what has been inspired and proclaimed. The first sending of the hand to the head serves three purposes: first, flight and choice; second, the correction and [Col. 0527C] instruction of one’s neighbour; third, beholding the examination at the final judgment.

Of the first it is said to Ezekiel: “Behold, a hand was sent to me, and in it was a scroll; and written in it were lamentation, a song, and woe” [Note: [Col. 0527] Ezek. 1]. For we ought to flee woe, that is, the torment of hell; we ought to choose the song, that is, the glory and praise of the blessed. But sin, that is, lamentation, is an impediment to both, because it must be mourned. Woe must be fled, because in hell there is no redemption; the song must be chosen, because glorious is the kingdom in which all the saints rejoice with Christ; sin must be lamented, because “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Note: [Col. 0527] Matt. 5].

The second sending is for the correction and instruction of one’s neighbour through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. Hence Ezekiel: “The hand seized [Col. 0527D] me by the lock of my head” [Note: [Col. 0527] Ezek. 8]. Behold, in the lock is the infusion of grace: “And he set me in the temple,” where the people’s instruction is customarily carried out, “and I dug through the wall, and there appeared a varied depiction of images” [Note: [Col. 0527] Ibid.], that is, error, on account of which correction was required.

At the judgment these three things shall occur: the examination of the sins which a person has committed; the reproach of the good things which he has not done; and the pronouncement of the sentence of condemnation. This is the hand which Belshazzar saw writing on the wall [Note: [Col. 0527] Dan. 5], namely [Col. 0528A] these words: “Mene,” that is, “he has numbered”—what? Sins. Hence it is said: “I became trembling and afraid when the examination and the coming wrath shall arrive.” “Tekel,” that is, “he has weighed” good deeds, and few have been found. Hence it is said: “What then shall I, most wretched one, say or do, when I bear no good thing before so great a judge?” “Peres,” that is, “he has divided from the kingdom”; this shall occur through the pronounced sentence of condemnation: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” [Note: [Col. 0527] Matt. 25]. Hence it was said: “That day is a day of wrath, calamity, and misery” [Note: [Col. 0527] Zeph. 1].

God’s hand is sent twice to the mouth: first, to cleanse it of loquacity; second, to confer the grace of eloquence. For the first, the hand was sent to Isaiah, touched his lips with a coal, and cleansed them [Note: [Col. 0527] Isa. 6]. For the second, the hand was sent to Jeremiah; hence he says: [Col. 0528B] “The Lord sent his hand and touched my mouth, and made me a prophet among the nations” [Note: [Col. 0527] Jer. 1].

Concerning the third: The Lord sends his hand to the belly, that the flesh may do what has been inspired and proclaimed. The belly is human weakness; the opening is a narrow aperture, signifying the straits of our mortality, through which the beloved sent his hand—that is, he accomplished salvation by enduring sufferings. Therefore, when he touched our misery by assuming flesh and suffering in it, rightly the belly—that is, our weakness—trembled.

We tremble in three ways at the arrival of a great person: through fear of condemnation, admiration for a magnificent work, and reverence for majesty. Of the first: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me” [Note: [Col. 0527] Ps. 54]. Of the second: “Exult [Col. 0528C] before him with trembling” [Note: [Col. 0527] Ps. 2]. Of the third: “Dominions adore; powers tremble” [Note: [Col. 0527] Preface of the Mass].

There are three openings: the opening of the rock, the opening of the asp, and the eye of the needle. In the first Moses stood when he saw the back parts of the Lord passing by [Note: [Col. 0527] Exod. 33]. Of the second Isaiah says: “The child shall rejoice over the opening of the asp” [Note: [Col. 0527] Isa. 11]. In the third, a comparison is made between a camel and a rich man [Note: [Col. 0527] Mark 10]. In the first, Christ’s true humility is recognized; in the second, the devil’s cunning is detected; in the third, pride is subdued by poverty.

When the beloved sends his hand through the opening—that is, when he accomplishes our salvation through the wound in his side—rightly the belly, that is, our weakness, trembles on account of sin. When he sends his hand into the openings of asps, casting demons out from possessed bodies, the belly [Col. 0528D] trembles in admiration of the miraculous work. When he sends his hand to the opening of the belly, humbling the proud, the belly trembles as it humbles itself in reverence for the divine majesty.

The belly of the soul is memory: at the first trembling it conceives sorrow; at the second it gives birth to virtue; at the third it brings forth the fruit of works and the delight of devotion. Of the first Jeremiah says: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain” [Note: [Col. 0527] Jer. 4]. Of the second Isaiah: “My belly shall sound for Moab like [Col. 0529A] a harp” [Note: [Col. 0529] Isa. 16]. For the strings of the harp are the virtues sounding together in the soul. Of the third it is said in this work: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies” [Note: [Col. 0529] Song 7]. In the wheat fruit is signified; in the lilies, the delight of devotion. All these things are worked by the hand of the Lord sent through the opening to the belly.

God the Father and the Son are called the beloved. Hence in the Song of Songs the king of virtues is likewise called “Beloved from beloved.” The hand of the beloved is God’s operation, because the Father worked all things through the Son [Note: [Col. 0529] John 5]. Accordingly, God the Father sent his hand into the Son. But to some he sent it through an opening, as through a window, or as through a door. He who is sent through an opening is somewhat manifest; through a window, more manifest; through a door, wholly manifest.

Christ was sent through the opening when God appeared in the flesh through incomparable [Col. 0529B] teaching, the revelation of the mysteries of Scripture, and endurance in tribulations. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “Stand in the opening of the rock, and when I pass by you shall see my back parts” [Note: [Col. 0529] Exod. 33]. He appeared through the window when he was more fully believed to be God, working wonders [Note: [Col. 0529] Ps. 85]. Hence Noah opened the window of the ark and received the dove with an olive branch [Note: [Col. 0529] Gen. 8]. Through the door God appeared wholly in the glory of the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0529] John 20]. Hence it is said: “A door was opened in heaven, and the ark of God was seen in heaven.”

The bride opened these three; for she says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows and peering through the lattices.” A lattice is an opening in a door. “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved, but he had turned aside and passed on.” Many saw the sending through the opening. Through the door [Col. 0529C] the blessed shall see. Nebuchadnezzar and his ministers perceived it through the window in the furnace of the three children: “For the angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace” [Note: [Col. 0529] Dan. 3].

This furnace is the world, in which the king of the Chaldeans, namely the devil, held the human race captive; he had set this furnace ablaze with vices—namely naphtha, tow, pitch, and bundles of vine-stalks. The first is the malice of envy and fraternal hatred; the second, the world’s vanity; the third, pleasure of the flesh; the fourth, the iniquity of apostasy. Naphtha is the dregs of oil, or olive stones left dry after the oil has been pressed out—that is, after charity has been abandoned. John says of this: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” [Note: [Col. 0529] I John 3]. Cain was condemned by it [Note: [Col. 0529] Gen. 4]. By this the devil set the furnace 109 of the world ablaze when he saw and [Col. 0529D] hated Adam’s prosperity [Note: [Col. 0529] Gen. 3].

Tow, which burns easily, signifies the world’s vanity, which quickly passes away; namely, its threefold form: covetousness, calamity, and mortality. Hence Solomon: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” [Note: [Col. 0529] Eccl. 1]. Therefore, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity?” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ps. 4]. By this the devil set the world ablaze; for he said to Adam: “In whatever hour you eat, you shall be like gods” [Note: [Col. 0529] Gen. 3].

Pitch signifies pleasure of the flesh: “He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” [Note: [Col. 0529] Sir. 13]; therefore [Col. 0530A] turn away from your pleasures. By this the devil set the furnace of the world ablaze when he saw that the tree was beautiful, took from it, and ate. The vine-stakes are useless trunks cut away from vineyards: this is the iniquity of apostasy. Hence the Lord: “I am the vine and you are the branches; without me you can do nothing” [Note: [Col. 0529] John 15]. By this the devil set the furnace of the world ablaze when Adam departed from God through transgression of the commandment.

Morally understood: three children were placed in this fire—Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael [Note: [Col. 0529] Dan. 3]. The first is called “God’s help,” the second “God’s grace,” the third “God’s touching.” The first, namely Hananiah, signifies those who sometimes fall and sometimes rise again, because with him is the voice of the Lord cutting off the flame of fire, [Col. 0530B] so that he may say: “You tested us by fire, as silver is tested” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ps. 65]. The second, namely Azariah, signifies those who bravely resist temptations and never fall, so that they may say: “You tested me by fire, and no iniquity was found in me” [Note: [Col. 0529] Mal. 2]. And the angel who descended into the furnace says to him: “When you walk through fire, you shall not be burned, because I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0529] Isa. 43]. Mishael signifies those who are spiritual, so that they do not feel the temptations surrounding them, but rather say: “You have delivered my body from destruction” [Note: [Col. 0529] Sir. 51], etc.

Or otherwise: the flame of this furnace, that is, of the world, is threefold. The first is the flame of vices; the second, of temptations; the third, of temporal afflictions. Many sinners are enveloped in the first; many in the second [Col. 0530C] struggle bravely through God’s grace; in the third, temporal temptations are surpassed by spiritual persons. Thus we find that the Lord appeared in three fires. Of the first it is said: “A storm wind came from the north, and a great cloud and enfolding fire; and from its midst something like the appearance of electrum, that is, from the midst of the fire” [Note: [Col. 0529] Ezek. 1]. Of the second: “The angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace” [Note: [Col. 0529] Dan. 3]. Of the third John saw in the Apocalypse “a man among seven lampstands, clothed in a long robe, and his feet like fine bronze, as though in a burning furnace. His eyes were like a flame of fire” [Note: [Col. 0529] Rev. 1].

There descended the Angel of Great Counsel; and let us see how he shook off the flame [Note: [Col. 0529] Dan. 3]: the proud king, namely the devil, by humility; his ministers by love; the four things mentioned above by prayer. Hear of humility: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0529] Phil. 2]. For he—that is, the meekest one—appeared [Col. 0530D] thus to his people [Note: [Col. 0529] Num. 12]. And of love: “Because of the exceeding charity with which God loved us, when we were dead in sins, Christ made us alive together” [Note: [Col. 0529] Eph. 2]. “For this is the lover of his brothers and of the people of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0529] II Macc. 15]. And of prayer: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0529] I John 2]. “For he is the one who prays greatly for the people and for the whole holy city [Col. 0531A] Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0531] II Macc. 15].

Likewise: “He made the middle of the furnace like a blowing wind of dew” [Note: [Col. 0531] Dan. 3]. Hence: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind” [Note: [Col. 0531] Song 4]; and the prophet: “The Lord brought a scorching wind from the desert, and it dried up the veins of death” [Note: [Col. 0531] Hos. 13]. These add a threefold dew: that of mercy, grace, and glory. But hear the order: first, into the fleece from the fleece—that is, from the Blessed Virgin into the shell. From the shell, that is, from the hearts of the Apostles, into the threshing-floor, that is, into the universality of the Church. Hear of the fleece: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you” [Note: [Col. 0531] Luke 1]; and of the shell, the Apostle says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0531] I Cor. 15]; and of the threshing-floor: “From his fullness we have all received grace for grace” [Note: [Col. 0531] John 1].

The first cleanses, the second makes fruitful, the third [Col. 0531B] gives joy. It cleanses from the dregs of sins, makes fruitful with the shoot of virtues, and gives joy through contemplation of heavenly goods. The first purifies a person; the second magnifies; the third gladdens. Of the first it was said: “The kindness and humanity of God our Saviour appeared” [Note: [Col. 0531] Titus 3]. Behold the dew of mercy, of which Isaac said to his son: “May God give you from the fatness of the earth and an abundance of the dew of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0531] Gen. 27]. Of the second it was said: “The grace of God appeared to all men, teaching us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires” [Note: [Col. 0531] Titus 2], etc. Hence the prophet: “I shall be as dew; Israel shall blossom as a lily” [Note: [Col. 0531] Hos. 14]. Of the third Job says: “Dew shall remain in my harvest, and my glory shall always be renewed” [Note: [Col. 0531] Job 29]. If any grow proud, because of this grace it shall be said to them: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor [Col. 0531C] rain come upon you” [Note: [Col. 0531] II Sam. 1].

The first dew, that of mercy, belongs to Azariah, whose name means “the Lord’s help”; the second belongs to Hananiah, whose name means “the grace of God”; the third to Mishael, whose name means “the touching of God.” For this one first touches him lying in the manger, second hanging upon the cross, and third reigning on the Father’s throne. In the first he is humbled for us; in the second he labours for us; in the third he reigns for us. Consider him humble in the manger: born from a woman’s womb, having no place in the inn, lying with ox and ass, wrapped in a cheap little cloth. Secondly, it touches him labouring on the cross—that is, scourged and struck with fists. Thirdly, it touches him as the Apostle describes him: O gentle, wise, beautiful, powerful one, as in the passage: “In many and various ways God formerly spoke [Col. 0531D] to the fathers through the prophets” [Note: [Col. 0531] Heb. 1]. I remember having expounded this elsewhere in this work. Hear of him as rich: “Whom he appointed heir of all things” [Note: [Col. 0531] Ibid.]; and as wise: “Through whom he also made the ages” [Note: [Col. 0531] Ibid.]. Of the first: “You have subjected all things under his feet” [Note: [Col. 0531] Heb. 2]; of the second: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0531] Col. 2]. Hear of him as beautiful: “Who, being the brightness of glory and the image of his substance” [Note: [Col. 0531] Heb. 1]; and as powerful: “Upholding all things by the word of his power” [Note: [Col. 0531] Ibid.]. “For his power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” [Note: [Col. 0531] Dan. 7].

And because he conquered the devil: “For you have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the sceptre of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian” [Note: [Col. 0531] Isa. 9]. Christ overcame all these things, as on the day of Midian, namely when Gideon defeated the Midianites [Note: [Col. 0531] Judg. 7]. His men had trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left, among which were shining lamps. Therefore they sounded the trumpets of preaching and prayer; they shattered the jars, namely through the martyrdom of the body; and shining lamps appeared in miracles.

It should be noted that the trumpet has three sounds: low, middle, and high. It has a low sound in prayer, a middle sound in praise, and a high sound in preaching. He had the low sound of prayer when he went up alone onto the mountain to pray: “When you pray,” he says, “enter into your chamber and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” [Note: [Col. 0531] Matt. 6]. [Col. 0532B] He had the middle sound when, at Lazarus’s tomb, he said: “Father, I give you thanks because you always hear me” [Note: [Col. 0531] John 11]. He had the high sound when he said: “Now the axe has been laid to the root of the tree” [Note: [Col. 0531] Matt. 3]. Hence it is said: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature” [Note: [Col. 0531] Mark 16].

He held this trumpet in his right hand, because we ought to preserve what pertains to heaven; the jars in his left, because we ought to set aside our bodies as temporal things for martyrdom. Thus shining lamps shall appear: namely miracles, or our bodies glorified in the resurrection. Those who now oppose us, seeing them, shall be troubled with terrible fear, saying: “These are they whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach. We fools considered their life madness. Behold how they have been reckoned [Col. 0532C] among the children of God” [Note: [Col. 0531] Wis. 5].

Behold, the beloved appeared through the opening by preaching and living religiously, and through the window by working miracles. He shall appear through the door, to be seen gloriously by the good after judgment. Therefore, when he is seen through the opening, our belly—that is, our weakness—trembles at his touch, because in his suffering humanity it sees things unworthy of him. When he sends his hand through the window, human nature wonders, because it sees unfamiliar things. When he is seen through the door, every saved person shall rejoice, because in his vision he shall know unknown things, since then the body shall be made firm through immortality.

Therefore the bride, inflamed with love of heavenly things, that she may more readily attain them, adds: “I arose to open to my beloved,” so that by receiving him I may later deserve [Col. 0532D] to enjoy his fellowship in the palace of his kingdom. May he himself bring us there, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## “I arose to open to my beloved; my hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh.”

[THO.] (Thus.) We open to the Lord when we receive his coming in the heart through love. We open when, by preaching, we turn hard hearts so that they receive him. We arise for this work, so that we may first fulfill in deed what we preach [Col. 0533A]. The fingers signify discernment, by which works are directed, because no limbs are more flexible or divided into more distinct joints. By this we are admonished that whenever we correct others, we should first shape our own conscience with diligent discernment.

Myrrh signifies continence of flesh and hands. Thus the bride’s hands drip with myrrh when they devote themselves to works of continence; and her fingers are full of the finest myrrh when, examining herself with watchful discernment, she finds that she lives continently with a view to eternal recompense.

The fitting order is this: first the sinner rises, second the righteous person opens, third the perfect person drips. The sinner rises by loosing the yoke of wickedness; the righteous person opens the gates of righteousness; the perfect person drips the myrrh of patience. The first rises from the body, the second in [Col. 0533B] love, the third in fragrance: from the body of perversity, in the love of holiness, in the fragrance of blessedness. Of the first: “Shake yourself from the dust; arise, sit down, Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck” [Note: [Col. 0533] Isa. 52]. Of the second: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered through them, I will give thanks to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0533] Ps. 117]. Of the third: “Myrrh and drops and cassia flow from your garments, from ivory houses” [Note: [Col. 0533] Ps. 44].

The first is Lazarus, the second Zacchaeus, the third Stephen. Lazarus means “helped,” because he was raised from the tomb. Zacchaeus, “justified,” which came to pass when he appeared rejoicing and received Christ into his house. Stephen is, as it were, a standing sanctuary: after Christ he was the first to drip myrrh, receiving the stones raining down upon him with all cheerfulness, and among them devoutly praying for his enemies. The more bitter the myrrh, [Col. 0533C] the finer it is. One sort is bitter, another more bitter, another most bitter. It is bitter to the sinner in satisfaction; more bitter to the righteous person, in zeal for religion; most bitter to the perfect person, in enduring suffering. The first says: “I shall recount to you all my years in the bitterness of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0533] Isa. 38], and: “I shall speak in the bitterness of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0533] Job 10]. Of the second Ezekiel says: “I went away bitter in indignation” [Note: [Col. 0533] Ezek. 3]. Of the third: “O death, how bitter is your remembrance!” [Note: [Col. 0533] Sir. 41]. But when it is endured for God, “behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” [Note: [Col. 0533] Isa. 38].

The first is tested, the second more tested, the third most tested. Or it is tested in vessels, more tested in hands, most tested in fingers: in the vessels of the heart through resolve, in the hands through action, in the fingers through prudently discerning works. There are fingers of God’s right hand and fingers of the human right hand. We read of five fingers of God: “With three he measures the mass of the earth;” with the fourth, “he weighs the mountains in a balance”; with the fifth, “the hills in scales” [Note: [Col. 0533] Isa. 40].

[Col. 0533D] The earth’s mass is threefold: vanity, pleasure, and malice. This earth is our heart. Against vanity is the finger called the spirit of knowledge. Pharaoh’s magicians spoke of it when Moses produced gnats: “This is the finger of God” [Note: [Col. 0533] Exod. 8], that is, the spirit of knowledge [Note: [Col. 0533] Isa. 11], so that we cannot deceive Moses. Against pleasure is the second finger, namely the spirit of fear [Col. 0534A] [Note: [Col. 0533] Ibid.]. Hence the Lord gave Moses stone tablets written by God’s finger [Note: [Col. 0533] Exod. 24], because that writing restrained those given to pleasure by fear of punishment. Against malice is the spirit—or finger—of piety [Note: [Col. 0533] Isa. 11]. Of this the Gospel says [Note: [Col. 0533] John 8], when the malice of the Jews condemned the adulterous woman, the Lord wrote with his finger on the ground: “Write these men as condemned” [reading uncertain].

The fourth finger is that of fortitude [Note: [Col. 0533] Isa. 11], the fifth the spirit of counsel [Note: [Col. 0533] Ibid.]. With the fourth “he weighs the mountains in a balance”; with the fifth, “the hills in scales.” These are two kinds of demons. Some harm human beings violently: these are proud mountains, which the Lord weighs in the balance of fortitude by casting them out. Others harm them deceitfully: these are hills, because they abase themselves under an appearance of humility, lest they seem to be mountains. The Lord weighs these in the scales [Col. 0534B] of counsel, by which we weigh—that is, examine carefully—whether they are good or evil; and thus the fifth finger 110 casts them out. Of the fourth it is said: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has indeed come upon you” [Note: [Col. 0533] Luke 11]. Of the fifth: “The Lord put his finger into the ears of the deaf man, and he was healed” [Note: [Col. 0533] Mark 7].

The hands of human beings are two: the right and the left. In the right hand are works of justice; in the left, works of mercy. Each is adorned with five fingers; for each activity, if it is to be ordered, requires discernment. And as there are five fingers on a hand, so we may assign five stages in discernment: the first is judgment, the second deliberation, the third arrangement, the fourth dispensation, the fifth moderation. For first one must judge what is lawful and what is unlawful. [Col. 0534C] But since not all lawful things are advantageous, we rise secondly to deliberation, where we learn what is beneficial. Once this is known, it remains to ask in what manner or order we should act. Once the order has been arranged, we often resort, according to varying circumstances, to the grace of dispensation. Finally, one must impose a suitable measure. By judgment we separate lawful from unlawful things; by deliberation, useful from useless things; by arrangement, we reduce appropriate things to order; by dispensation, according to the outcome of affairs, we yield to the opportunity of the times; by moderation, we preserve modesty in all things. Of the first the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” [Note: [Col. 0533] 1 Cor. 11.]. Of the second: “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” [Note: [Col. 0533] Ecclus. 32.]. Of the third: [Col. 0534D] “The man is gracious who has mercy and lends; he orders his words with judgment” [Note: [Col. 0533] Ps. 111.]. Of the fourth: “Here moreover it is required among stewards that one be found faithful” [Note: [Col. 0533] 1 Cor. 1.]. Of the fifth: “Let your moderation be known to all people” [Note: [Col. 0533] Phil. 4.].

These fingers belong to the right and the left hand. First we must rise to build a house; secondly, to open it; thirdly, to minister in it: the first through a collection of virtues, the second through devout desire, the third through the performance of works. Of the first it is said [Col. 0535A] to the Church: “You shall not build me a house, but your son who comes forth from your womb” [Note: [Col. 0535] 2 Par. 17.]. Of the second: “May the Lord open our heart in his law and in his commandments” [Note: [Col. 0535] 2 Macc. 1.]. Of the third: “Work while it is day” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ecclus. 51.].

David was intent on building the house when he said: “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ps. 131.]. Woe to you who take care to found houses that will perish, yet refuse to be even a humble dwelling for Christ, saying that reproach of the Prophet: “The time for building the house of the Lord has not yet come” [Note: [Col. 0535] Hag. 1.]! Rather cry out with David: “Woe to me! For the ark of the Lord is in skins, while I dwell in houses of cedar” [Note: [Col. 0535] 1 Par. 17.], and so forth. He clothed himself in the dead flesh of our frailty, while I am clothed [Col. 0535B] in vainglory. Therefore recall the manger of the stable, the enclosure of the virginal womb, and the stone of the tomb; and see that you do not offer, in place of a manger, a house of commerce [Note: [Col. 0535] John 2.]; in place of the virginal enclosure, a brothel of pimps [Note: [Col. 0535] Nahum 2.]; or in place of the tombstone, a den of robbers [Note: [Col. 0535] Matt. 21.]. Rather cry out: “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord.”

In the manger is the house of humility; in the Virgin’s womb, the house of chastity; in the tombstone, the house of disciplined religious life. Pride is driven from the first; lust is cast out from the second; sensual wandering flees from the third. The Prophet expressed the first for us thus: “I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor clothing” [Note: [Col. 0535] Isa. 3.]. A physician removes [Col. 0535C] sins; bread is the refreshment of teaching; clothing is the exemplary display of religious conduct—so that the Lord of this house may say: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” [Note: [Col. 0535] Matt. 11.]. And of bread: “You who have no money, hasten, buy, and eat” [Note: [Col. 0535] Isa. 55.]. And of clothing: “Arise, arise, put on your strength, Zion. Put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, holy city” [Note: [Col. 0535] Isa. 52].

The bride possessed the house of chastity, of which she says: “Our bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress” [Note: [Col. 0535] Song 1.]. Behold: beams in the house, ceilings in the chamber, a flower in the bed. In cedar is loftiness; in cypress, sweetness of fragrance; in the flower, delight. The first belongs to the angel, the second to God, [Col. 0535D] the third to the person himself. For virginity is akin to angels; purity is fragrant to God; and to the chaste person the consciousness of chastity is delightful.

Of the house of discipline it is said to the woman pouring out oil: “Shut the door upon yourself and upon your son” [Note: [Col. 0535] 4 Kings 4.]. And the man from whom three loaves were requested in the Gospel said: “My door is now shut, and my children are with me in my bed; do not trouble me” [Note: [Col. 0535] Luke 11.]. And the Lord says: “But when you fast, enter your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” [Note: [Col. 0535] Matt. 6.].

[Col. 0536A] David marked these three houses when he said: “Myrrh and stacte and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ps. 44.]. Myrrh has a bitter taste; stacte is a substance which removes the swelling of a wound; cassia grows in waters, rises high, and gives forth fragrance. Thus chastity is preserved through the bitterness of myrrh; the swelling of pride is humbled through stacte; cassia grows in waters—that is, discipline in tearful compunction. It stretches upward, namely in the love of God. It is fragrant in conduct. Of this the Prophet says: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into your house” [Note: [Col. 0535] Isa. 52.]. Our senses have gone wandering from the house of discipline, roaming through the curiosities of the world; they are needy because they bring back from there no benefit with them, and they hunger, desiring the word [Col. 0536B] of teaching. Hence it is said of the strong woman: “She considered the paths of her house and did not eat the bread of idleness” [Note: [Col. 0535] Prov. 31.]. The first path is that by which one comes to humility; the second, that by which we preserve chastity; the third, that by which we walk according to the regularity of discipline.

Many transfer themselves to the house of pride, abandoning the house of humility; others to the house of unchastity, abandoning the house of chastity; a third group, having despised the house of discipline, to the house of wandering. The house of Hezekiah was a house of pride when he displayed his treasures to the Chaldeans [Note: [Col. 0535] Ezek. 27.]; likewise the tower of Babel, which means “confusion,” and therefore their languages were scattered [Note: [Col. 0535] Gen. 11.]. Potiphar the eunuch’s wife was making a house of chastity into a house of lust when she tried to take Joseph [Note: [Col. 0535] Gen. 39.]. Dinah went out from the house of discipline [Col. 0536C] and was therefore violated [Note: [Col. 0535] Gen. 34.].

In the house of pride are the idols which Rachel carried away from Laban’s house [Note: [Col. 0535] Gen. 31.], Laban being interpreted “whitening.” In the house of pleasure are idols—namely Adonis, for whom the women wept in the temple [Note: [Col. 0535] Ezek. 8.]. In the house of curiosity are the idols which the tribe of Dan found in Micah’s house. These are what prevent the house of the Lord from being built: the vanity of the world, the pleasure of the flesh, and idleness. The first is the house of the proud; the second, the bed of the self-indulgent; the third, the sleep of the slothful. Hence David: “If I enter into the tent of my house” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ps. 131.]. Behold the first. “If I ascend upon the bed of my couch” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ibid.]. Behold the second. “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ibid.], behold the third. “And rest to my temples” [Note: [Col. 0535] Ibid.], which is the cause of sleep. [Col. 0536D] For first we rest from good work through sluggishness; afterward we doze, now falling and now rising; thirdly we sleep by taking delight in sin. David removes these things from himself in order to build God’s house.

The tent or house is worldly prosperity. Hence it is said to Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” [Note: [Col. 0535] Gen. 12.]; hence Job says: “They dwell in houses of clay and have an earthly foundation” [Note: [Col. 0535] Job 4.]. Of sleep it is said: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” [Note: [Col. 0535] Eph. 5.]; [Col. 0537A] likewise: “Arise, hasten, my friend” [Note: [Col. 0537] Song 2.]. The bed is that of which it is said: “Take up your bed and walk” [Note: [Col. 0537] Matt. 9.]; likewise: “Not in beds and acts of unchastity” [Note: [Col. 0537] Rom. 13.]. I shall give none of these things to myself, “until I find a place for the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ps. 131.].

There is a threefold place: a place in the heart of those who love, a place in the congregation of the faithful, and a place of those being reborn. The first is in the human heart, the second in the world, the third in heaven. In the first are the sweetness and ardour of love; in the second, the bond of unanimity; in the third, joy in the security of eternal blessedness. Of the first we have this passage; of the second: “Truly the Lord was in this place, and I did not know it” [Note: [Col. 0537] Gen. 28.]; likewise: “This place is terrible; this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ibid.]; of the third: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place” [Note: [Col. 0537] Eccl. 1.]. Hear [Col. 0537B] the ardour of the first: “Was not our heart burning within us?” [Note: [Col. 0537] Luke 24.]—concerning Jesus. Of unanimity: “Bearing with one another in love, diligently preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 0537] Eph. 4.]. Of the third: “Rejoice in the Lord, saints and righteous; the Lord has chosen you as his inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ps. 32.].

Behold three places: “Lord, if you wish, let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” [Note: [Col. 0537] Matt. 17.]. Elijah is interpreted “making the sun,” and signifies ardour. In the first: “Wisdom has built herself a house and hewn out seven pillars” [Note: [Col. 0537] Prov. 9.]; in the second: “This place is terrible; this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven”; in the third: “The sparrow found herself a house, and a nest in which to place her young” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ps. 83.].

Let us therefore speak of the house that Wisdom built in our hearts. It has seven pillars: “The spirit [Col. 0537C] of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0537] Isa. 11.]. The spirit of knowledge produces foresight in governing temporal matters; the spirit of fortitude, constancy in adversity; the spirit of fear makes one careful not to offend God’s mercy; the spirit of understanding gives knowledge of spiritual things; the spirit of counsel removes perplexity and causes one to do good according to the rule of discernment; the spirit of piety causes one to show mercy to those in need and render to God the worship owed to him; the spirit of wisdom enables one to taste and desire heavenly glory.

Of the first it is said: “He who ministers well will acquire a good rank” [Note: [Col. 0537] 1 Tim. 3.]. That one may not desire temporal things beyond measure, nor grieve beyond measure over what has been lost, it says: “Let us so pass through temporal goods [Col. 0537D] that we do not lose eternal ones.” Of the spirit of fortitude it is said: “Be strong in battle” [Note: [Col. 0537] Heb. 11.]; likewise: “Brethren, be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power” [Note: [Col. 0537] Eph. 6.]. Of the spirit of fear it is said: “He who fears the Lord will do good” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ecclus. 15.]; likewise: “Fear God and keep his commandments: this is the whole duty of man” [Note: [Col. 0537] Eccl. 12.]. Of the spirit of counsel it is said: “Do not believe every spirit, but test whether they are from God” [Note: [Col. 0537] 1 John 4.]. And concerning being pulled in two directions, the Apostle says: “I am constrained by two things,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0537] Phil. 1.].

[Col. 0538A] Of the spirit of understanding: “Give me understanding, and I shall live” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ps. 118.]; likewise: “I will give you understanding and instruct you” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ps. 31.]. Of the spirit of piety it is said: “Exercise yourself in piety; for bodily exercise is useful for a little, but piety is useful for all things” [Note: [Col. 0537] 1 Tim. 4.]. Likewise: “All who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” [Note: [Col. 0537] 2 Tim. 3.]. Of the spirit of wisdom it is said: “Seek the things above, not the things that are [on earth]” [Note: [Col. 0537] Col. 3.], and so forth.

Behold the seven pillars in the house of the heart. It should be noted that some sinners are ashamed to receive Christ into this house on account of their sins. Others, although sinners, receive him joyfully; a third group, as good people, receive him confidently. The first render reverence to God; the second hope for pardon from his coming; the third trust because [Col. 0538B] they have a good conscience. The first say with the centurion: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” [Note: [Col. 0537] Matt. 8.]; the second joyfully receive Christ with Zacchaeus into their house; the third prepare a great furnished upper room in which he may eat the Passover with his disciples [Note: [Col. 0537] Luke 22.].

Hear how the centurion opened to him: he possessed humility and sincerity of faith, and therefore obtained healing for his servant. Of the first: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; only say the word, and my servant shall be healed” [Note: [Col. 0537] Matt. 8.]. Likewise: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ibid.]. Of the third: “And the servant was healed in that hour” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ibid.].

Hear how Zacchaeus opened: “He received him joyfully into his house” [Note: [Col. 0537] Luke 19.]. But how does he set his smallness straight? [Col. 0538C] He raises himself above the folly of the world, extends a hand to the needy, and corrects his errors. For thus it is read: “He was small in stature” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ibid.]—this is the first; “He climbed into a sycamore tree” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ibid.], which is called the foolish fig, namely the world—this is the second; “I give half of my goods to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ibid.]—the third; “And if I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ibid.]—the fourth.

The third is a great furnished upper room. But hear also how this is opened. It should be noted that it is an upper room, it is large, and it is furnished: an upper room, lest God endure hail and rain; large, lest its inhabitant endure cramped conditions; furnished, lest he find hardness instead of delights. Hail and rain come from the importunity of worldly disturbance; cramped conditions, from a perverse will; delights, from the usefulness of affection. [Col. 0538D] Of the first: “That there may be a tabernacle for shade by day from the heat, and for security and shelter from whirlwind and rain” [Note: [Col. 0537] Isa. 4.]. In the second: He commands us to consider how great my will is—namely, its length, breadth, height, and depth. In the third: “May all the glory of the king’s daughter be within, clothed about in fringes of gold and in varied colours” [Note: [Col. 0537] Ps. 44.].

But the bride says what ought to precede the opening: “My hands distilled first myrrh, choice myrrh, most approved myrrh.” [Col. 0539A] The first is in repentance and confession; the second, in an austere manner of life; the third, in suffering inflicted upon one. 111 Of the first: “Her lips distilling first myrrh.” Of the second: “Like choice myrrh I gave forth the sweetness of fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0539] Ecclus. 24.]. Of the third: “My fingers are full of most approved myrrh.”

Accordingly, one ought to open one’s hand, open one’s tongue, and open one’s heart: the hand for giving alms, the tongue for praise and preaching, the heart for devotion. Of the first: “She opened her hand to the needy” [Note: [Col. 0539] Prov. 31.]. Of the second: “Open your mouth, and the Lord will fill it” [Note: [Col. 0539] Ps. 80.]. Of the third: “May the Lord open your heart in his law and in his commandments” [Note: [Col. 0539] 2 Macc. 1.]. To him be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0540A] “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch.”

[CARD.] As though she said: My beloved, God the Father, sent his hand—that is, his Son—through the opening, that is, through my ear. Hence the Church sings of her: “You shall conceive God through the ear, and shall bear a man.” And my inward parts, out of reverence for so great a guest, trembled at his touch: that is, when he touched me and separated flesh from my flesh, which he formed and fitted to himself as a human body. But since in the voice of the one knocking the words “Open to me” come first, the Blessed Virgin adds: “I arose to open to my beloved,” and, after some intervening matter, adds:

## BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0539]

[Col. 0539B] “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved; but he had turned aside and passed on.”

[THO.] The soul opens the bolt of its door to the bridegroom when it makes its heart worthy of divine implantation. It opens the bolt when, kindled by sudden inspiration toward the desires of heavenly things, it strives to open more widely the bosom of the mind, so as to receive a taste of that same heavenly sweetness.
