The bridegroom had first put his hand through the opening; therefore, being vehemently kindled, she now enjoys his blessed embrace not through the narrowness of the opening, but with the door fully opened. Yet, since he cannot be possessed fully in this life, she adds: “But he had turned aside and passed on.” This is what David says: “Let man draw near to the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0539] Ps. 63.]. And Solomon: “I said, ‘I shall become wise,’ but wisdom withdrew [Col. 0539C] farther from me” [Note: [Col. 0539] Eccl. 7.].

Nor did she say simply “the door,” but “the bolt of the door.” For she had shut and barred it when her heart was lifted on high, lest some plotter should enter, according to Solomon’s saying: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it” [Note: [Col. 0539] Prov. 5.]. There is a threefold door: the first of discipline, the second of circumspection, the third of solitude. Of the first: “Hear, my son, the discipline of your father” [Note: [Col. 0539] Prov. 1.]. Of the second: “Blessed is the man who remains in wisdom, meditates on justice, and in his understanding considers God’s circumspection” [Note: [Col. 0539] Ecclus. 14.]. In the third was the one who said: “I kept watch and became like a solitary sparrow upon the roof” [Note: [Col. 0539] Ps. 101.].

These three were in the tabernacle. The first was at the entrance of the court; the second at the entrance to the holy place; the third gives access to the Holy of Holies. The first is shut [Col. 0539D] against the robber, the second against the thief, the third against the trader: against the robber, who is evident; against the thief, who is hidden; against the trader, who is importunate. For the robber carries off those who wander; the thief deceives the unwary; the trader steals away repose.

He wished the first to be shut who said: “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth and a watch around my lips” [Note: [Col. 0539] Ps. 140.]. Hence the Lord shut the door of the ark from outside. Of the second: “When you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut your door, pray to your Father” [Note: [Col. 0539] Matt. 6.]. Hence the woman, at the prophet’s command, as she poured out oil, shut the door upon herself and her son [Note: [Col. 0539] 4 Kings 4.]. Of the third in the Gospel: “Which of you has a friend?” The friend said to the petitioner: “Do not trouble me; my door is already shut and my children are with me in bed” [Note: [Col. 0539] Luke 11.]. This is the door at which Peter kept knocking after escaping from prison, where the other apostles were [Note: [Col. 0539] Acts 12.].

The same doors can fittingly be opened. The first is opened for purity, the second for truth, the third for glory. [Col. 0540C] The first, that the received sinner may be purified; the second, that the purified person may be instructed; the third, that the instructed person may contemplate. Job opened the first when he said: “My door stood open to the traveller” [Note: [Col. 0539] Job 31.]. Abraham had opened the second: while standing in the doorway of his tent, he saw three and worshipped one [Note: [Col. 0539] Gen. 18.]. John saw the third open: “I saw,” he says, “a door opened in heaven, and behold, a throne was set there” [Note: [Col. 0539] Rev. 4.].

The bolt of the first door is fervour; of the second, fear; of the third, love: the fervour of religious life, fear of diabolical deception, love for knowing heavenly blessedness. The first is opened to the contrite, the second to the person already instructed, the third to the beloved: to the contrite, that he may enter the court, where the animals were found and where the flesh also may be sacrificed; to the person already instructed, that he may enter the holy place, where was the table of the offering—that is, apostolic teaching—so that he may be instructed there; to the beloved, that he may come out and be seen by us from the couch that is the Holy of Holies. When this has occurred, the sight, beheld for a moment in a mirror and in an enigma [Note: [Col. 0539] 1 Cor. 13.], turns aside and [Col. 0541A] passes beyond us.

First he came to us, then he turned aside, and thirdly he passed on. He came through the Incarnation; he turned aside in order to make us desirous of incorruption; he passed on to call us to the kingdom. In a moral sense: he came for our consolation; he turned aside so that we should not grow lukewarm through security; he passed on to show that “we do not have here a lasting city” [Note: [Col. 0541] Heb. 13.].

We still have something to say concerning the door. Solomon made a door in the porch, in the temple, and in the oracle. The door of the porch is prophetic speech; the door of the temple is Christ; the door of the oracle is entrance into the heavenly homeland. But, in the porch of renunciation, morally understood, the door is knowledge of the world; in the temple of conduct, knowledge of oneself; in the oracle of contemplation, knowledge of him.

For when you consider the downfall of the world—how one is placed amid the uncertainty of riches [Note: [Col. 0541] 1 Tim. 6.], amid the slippery descent of pleasures, [Col. 0541B] amid the danger of dignities—you approach the door of the porch. When, however, you consider the frailty of your own flesh, the rising of childhood, the brief moment of youth, and the evening of old age, you hasten to pass through the door of the temple. But when you consider the goodness of God, who lacks nothing, and blessedness which needs nothing, and draw near to behold the goodness of his chosen ones and rejoice in the gladness of his people [Note: [Col. 0541] Ps. 105.], you prepare to enter through the special door of the oracle.

It should also be noted that, at the equinox, the sun, by straight lines of rays, illuminated the ark of the covenant through those three doors. Thus the sun of understanding, by the direct ray of consideration, penetrating the clouds of thoughts that move through the air of meditation, illuminates through the aforesaid doors the ark—that is, [Col. 0541C] the conscience. This occurs at the equinox, that is, when nights and days are equal. Morally, nights and days are prosperity and adversity, losses and gains, sadness and joy, purity and disturbance of mind, the light of contemplation and the darkness of temptation. When the mind weighs these matters, it balances days and nights as though under an equal measure.

It should be noted, moreover, that this beloved passes through the good and passes on to the perfect. He is the man of whom the woman says: “This is a holy man of God, who passes by us. Let us make him a small upper room, and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that, when he comes to us, he may remain there” [Note: [Col. 0541] 4 Kings 4.]. Nothing happens on earth without cause. Since there have been three wretched expulsions, this man passes through us in order to repair them by three praiseworthy [Col. 0541D] sendings forth. For he cast the devil out of heaven, Adam out of Paradise, and at judgment he casts the sinner out from the fellowship of the blessed. The first was because of pride, the second because of disobedience, the third because of hardness of heart. He therefore came so that the first might be restored, the second relieved, and the third avoided: the first restored by the number of the blessed, the second relieved by forgiveness of sins, the third avoided by keeping the commandments. Of the first David says: “He shall judge among the nations; he shall fill up the ruins” [Note: [Col. 0541] Ps. 99.]. Of the second: “He sent his word and healed them; he delivered them from their destructions” [Note: [Col. 0541] Ps. 106.]. Of the third: [Col. 0542A] “You have given those who fear you a sign, that they may flee from before the bow” [Note: [Col. 0541] Ps. 59.].

The bride invites him to the first thus: “Come, my dove, into the clefts of the rock and into the hollow of the wall” [Note: [Col. 0541] Song 2.]. Of the second she herself says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” Against the third: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke.”

For this purpose three sendings from heaven occurred. An angel was sent forth, the Holy Spirit was sent into, and Christ was received: the angel was sent to the Virgin’s ear; the Spirit was sent into her mind; Christ was received into her womb. The angel was sent to the ear in order to reveal God’s counsel; the Spirit was sent into the mind so that, overshadowing the Virgin, he might give her consolation; Christ was received into the womb to bring aid to a shipwrecked world. Of the first it is said [Col. 0542B]: “The angel Gabriel was sent by God into a city of Galilee” [Note: [Col. 0541] Luke 1.]. Of the second: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Note: [Col. 0541] Ibid.]. For the Holy Spirit came to her, arrived in her, and came upon her: he came with the vow of chastity, arrived with the virtue of humility, came upon her with the mystery of the Incarnation. Of the third: “The holy thing that shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” [Note: [Col. 0541] Ibid.].

Behold, the Virgin’s womb is an upper room. O upper room, which, as on a spring day, was surrounded by violets of the woodland glades, rose-flowers, and lilies of the valleys. In it humility gives fragrance, charity burns, virginity flowers: humility in the violets, charity in the roses, virginity in the lilies. O chamber delightful in affections, serene in character, full of grace. Let us therefore place a little bed in this upper room, [Col. 0542C] so that the Virgin may say: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0541] Song 1.].

We too ought to make him an upper room—that is, our heart. Therefore prepare your hearts for God, so that you may say: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” [Note: [Col. 0541] Ps. 107.]. Let us then put in it a bed of tranquillity and peace, a table of devotion, a chair of self-judgment, and a lampstand of contemplation: peace, that he may be found free from worldly disturbance; devotion, that he may be satisfied with the sweetness of heavenly delight; self-judgment, that a person may accuse himself without excuse; contemplation, for the knowledge of heavenly things.

This man is not found in the bed unless he is free from sin. Hence: “On my bed I sought by night him whom my soul loves; I sought and did not find him” [Note: [Col. 0541] Song 3.]. [Col. 0542D] Because “You have turned his whole bed in his weakness; may the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0541] Ps. 40.], so that afterward he may say: “Our bed is flowering, and he shall dry up my veins.” “A little while after I had passed by, I found him whom my soul loves.” On this day—that is, today—true peace came down.

Concerning his threefold peace, seek elsewhere. This little bed alleviates languor, restores pain, and ministers sleep: the languor of temptation, the pain of satisfaction, and sleep of forgetfulness of the world. For when this man comes to this bed, he lightens guilt, alleviates oppression, [Col. 0543A] and takes away worldly anxiety. In the first, the sick man on the pallet is healed [Note: [Col. 0543] Mark 2.]; in the second, the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho is strengthened [Note: [Col. 0543] Luke 10.]; in the third, the Lord commanded the disciples to give themselves to sleep, saying: “Sleep now and take your rest” [Note: [Col. 0543] Mark 17.]. Of the first: “I perform healings today and tomorrow” [Note: [Col. 0543] Luke 13.]. Of the second: “For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” [Note: [Col. 0543] Matt. 11.]. Of the third it is said: “Forget your people and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty, for he is the Lord your God, and you shall worship him” [Note: [Col. 0543] Ps. 44.].

The Blessed Virgin also set a table for this man. For “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has set her table” [Note: [Col. 0543] Prov. 9.]. She calls her son to this table when she says: “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruits of his orchard.” And he himself says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I shall enter to him and dine with him” [Note: [Col. 0543] Rev. 3.]. She knew herself filled from that table when she said: “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue.” Truly honey, because throughout the world the heavens have become honey-flowing. Indeed, the heavens are read to be manna-flowing, dew-flowing, and honey-flowing: manna-flowing for the ancient Fathers in the desert; dew-flowing at the fulfillment of the Law; honey-flowing at the beginning of the year of favour. 112 The first was in the promise of the prophets, the second in the conception, the third in the nativity. Of the first: “I shall rain manna upon you from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0543] Exod. 16.]; of the second: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above” [Note: [Col. 0543] Isa. 45.]; of the third in Job: “Let not the hypocrite see the streams of the torrent of honey and butter” [Note: [Col. 0543] Job 20.].

Let us set this table for this man: [Col. 0543C] “When you sit at a great table, carefully consider what is set before you” [Note: [Col. 0543] Prov. 23.]. At it you shall dine with this man and say: “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, and drink deeply, beloved ones.” The Blessed Virgin also prepared a chair for him, because “Solomon made himself a palanquin of the woods of Lebanon, its pillars of silver” [Note: [Col. 0543] Song 3.], and the other matters which we applied to the Blessed Virgin. The Son of God sat on the chair in the Incarnation.

But we too must raise up within ourselves a chair of self-judgment, upon which we must judge our works, thoughts, and words justly, lest, if we judge badly, we fall backward from the chair like Eli the priest and die with broken necks [Note: [Col. 0543] 1 Kings 4.]. But we have spoken elsewhere about the threefold judgment.

The Blessed Virgin also raised a lampstand of four lamps. For she was called a star: “A star shall arise out of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0543] Num. 24.]. She was called moon, dawn, and sun: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” [Note: [Col. 0543] Song 6.] She was a star for the erring, a moon for those asleep in their pleasures, a dawn for penitents, and a sun for those who love perfectly: a star for the erring, to lead them back to the way; a moon for those asleep in sins, to obtain pardon for them; a dawn for penitents, to lighten their penance; a sun for those who love, [Col. 0544A] to lead them to the heavenly light.

Hear concerning the star. *Maria* is interpreted “star of the sea,” which leads to the way; hence: “Rejoice, Virgin Mary: you alone have destroyed all heresies throughout the whole world.” Those asleep at night cry to the moon thus: “When you receive our vows, excuse our faults by your prayers.” Penitents cry to the dawn thus: “Holy Mary, help the wretched, aid the faint-hearted, comfort the weeping”: the wretched, whose hearts are contrite; the faint-hearted, weighed down by outward penance; the weeping, bathed in tears of compunction. She was the sun; hence: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun” [Note: [Col. 0543] Ps. 18.], Christ assuming flesh in her. Does not she shine like the sun, whose glorious life gave life to the world? Does she not lead lovers to heavenly brightness, she whose glorious life illuminates all the churches?

Behold, the man—that is, Christ—passes [Col. 0544B] through us. You therefore have the Blessed Virgin as an upper room, and also her little bed. We have her womb; you also have a spiritual table, her refreshment with Christ; you have a chair, namely Solomon’s palanquin. You also have a lampstand, if you enlighten in the Church those who err, those who sin and repent, and the righteous who praise God.

“I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved; but he had turned aside and passed on.”

[CARD.] In these words are shown both the devout obedience of her who opens and what was pleasing in her to him who entered. She says, therefore: “I arose to open to my beloved,” who was knocking and saying, “Open to me.” She then rose to the height of such dignity that she deserved to conceive the Son of God, when, after the angel’s many and exceedingly great promises, she said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0543] Luke 1.]. She then opened to her beloved when she consented that the beloved should enter and be conceived in her, namely when she said: “Let it be done to me according to your word” [Note: [Col. 0543] Ibid.].

And because the inward will of the heart ought to unlock—or confirm—the consent of the mouth, as it were a bolt, she, opening her mind to the consent of her mouth, opened the door in order to express that consent, saying: “Let it be done to me according to your word.” But he had indeed already turned aside and passed on. For unless the Lord had already entered and turned aside within her through indwelling grace, she could neither have risen nor opened the door, because, as the Apostle says to the Philippians: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to [Col. 0544D] his good will” [Note: [Col. 0543] Phil. 2.].

Yet the Blessed Virgin makes a certain interpolation between these words, because things which happened together could not be spoken together. She says, therefore: “My hands distilled myrrh; my fingers are full of most approved myrrh.” The hands signify works; the fingers, discernment in works. Most approved myrrh is the most perfect mortification of the flesh and fleshly pleasures. How the Holy Spirit conformed her to the divine will, however, she shows when she adds:

“My soul melted when my beloved spoke; I sought him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me.”

[Col. 0545A] [THO.] Because I received the voice of the beloved through the opening of secret compunction, whatever was cold within me grew warm. Everything hard was softened, so that nothing is sweet to me except to dissolve into tears; and since I could not hold fast the one who appeared to me by his grace, it delights me to pursue him with tears, and thus, by melting, I poured out my soul within me. But she says: *I sought and did not find.* For whenever a chaste soul either desires to go forth to the Lord, or, while placed in the flesh, to be raised by a foretaste of future blessedness, it does not immediately obtain this, and says groaning: *I sought and did not find.*

“Soul” is understood in three ways, and we call the first animal life, the second the life-giving spirit, the third temporal life. [Col. 0545B] Besides these, “soul” is said of something so beloved that the prophet David says: “My eye, my soul, and my belly are troubled in anger” [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 30.]. Since we speak elsewhere of this, we are silent about it here, as it does not belong to the present contemplation. Of the first: “They gave all their precious things for food, to restore the soul” [Note: [Col. 0545] Lam. 1.]; of the second: “Man became a living soul” [Note: [Col. 0545] Gen. 2.]; of the third: “He who hates his soul in this world preserves it unto eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0545] John 12.].

The first has the hardness of obstinacy; the second, that of sluggishness; the third, that of lukewarmness. Of the first Jeremiah says: “You struck them, and they were not healed; you crushed them, and they refused to accept correction; they made their face harder than rock and were unwilling to return” [Note: [Col. 0545] Jer. 5.]. Of the second Isaiah says: “We know that you are hard, and that [Col. 0545C] your brow is bronze and your neck an iron sinew” [Note: [Col. 0545] Isa. 48.]. Of the third: “The Lord reproved the unbelief of the disciples and hardness of heart” [Note: [Col. 0545] Mark 16.].

The first impedes conversion, the second knowledge, the third devotion. Against these three the beloved speaks three words: against the first, a word of threat; against the second, of instruction; against the third, of promise. Of the first melting: “He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great deep” [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 77.]; of the second, Gideon shattered the pitchers and burning lamps appeared [Note: [Col. 0545] Judg. 7.]; of the third, Mary Magdalene broke the alabaster vessel, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment [Note: [Col. 0545] Mark 14.]. Of the first: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” [Note: [Col. 0545] Luke 6.]; of the second: “Whoever wishes to come [Col. 0545D] after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” [Note: [Col. 0545] Matt. 16.]; of the third: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0545] Matt. 5.].

At the first word, the soul melts into the fluidity of water; at the second, into the softness of wax; at the third, into the beauty, fragrance, and taste of an aromatic substance. The first—that is, the obstinate—promise themselves impunity, despise God’s goodness, and take no account of God’s forbearance: impunity, lest they suffer in hell; goodness, by which God gives them beauty so that they may be converted; forbearance, by which they are patiently [Col. 0546A] awaited by God so that they may repent. Hence: “Do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of God’s goodness and forbearance? Do you not know that his goodness leads you to repentance?” [Note: [Col. 0545] Rom. 2.]

At this voice the soul of the obstinate person melts, so as to say: “My heart was inflamed, and my reins were disturbed” [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 72.]. Nor is this surprising, because “the word of the Lord inflamed him” [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 104.], so that they may flow into water—that is, into a flood of tears for their sins: “He shall send forth his word and melt them; his spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow” [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 147.]. Behold how the first soul is melted into the fluidity of water.

It follows how the second is melted into the softness of wax: namely, through the word of instruction, by which the heart is softened for understanding God’s commandments: “Speak, [Col. 0546B] Lord, for your servant hears” [Note: [Col. 0545] 1 Sam. 3.]—“For my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall blaze” [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 38.]. By this, “my heart became like wax melting in the midst of my belly” [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 21.], so that God’s commandments may be written upon it and I may understand them. For “the unfolding of your words gives light and grants understanding to the little ones” [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 118.].

It should be noted that we paint upon wax, write upon it, and seal it. First, so that we may retain the memory of the fathers; second, the commandments of God, so that we may know them; third, we stamp the image of the king. In war, boldness is useful against the enemy, as are the memory of the ancient fathers and the assistance of prayers. Thus Judas Maccabaeus says: “Do not fear the attack of enemies; remember how the fathers were saved” [Note: [Col. 0545] 1 Macc. 4.], etc. We write; hence: “Hear, Israel, the commandments [Col. 0546C] of God, and write them in your heart as though in a book” [Note: [Col. 0545] Baruch 3.]. We also stamp the image of the king, that is, of Christ, when we form his image in our heart, so that we may say: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, is stamped upon us” [Note: [Col. 0545] Ps. 4.].

There is a threefold image of Christ. The first is that of corruptible flesh; the second, that of glorified humanity; the third, that of divinity. We ought to stamp the first upon our heart, that we may suffer with him; the second, that we may long for his likeness; the third, that we may see it in the kingdom. Of the first: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be made conformable to the image of his Son” [Note: [Col. 0545] Rom. 8.]. Of the second: “With unveiled face we shall behold the glory of God, so that we may be transformed into the same image from glory to glory” [Note: [Col. 0545] 2 Cor. 3.]. Of the third: “Putting off the old man [Col. 0546D] with his deeds, let us put on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him” [Note: [Col. 0545] Eph. 4.].

The image to which we are renewed is: the Father, memory; the Son, understanding; the Holy Spirit, goodness. This image was re-formed in that man, but is re-formed in the knowledge of God. Behold the melting into the softness of wax.

There follows the third melting, into the beauty, fragrance, and taste of an aromatic substance. For an aromatic substance is beautiful in a garden, fragrant in a mortar, and savoury when prepared in an electuary: in the garden of religious life, in the mortar of tribulation, in an electuary [Col. 0547A] compounded from virtues. It is beautiful in the ordering of morals, fragrant in patient endurance of suffering, and savoury through a foretaste of heavenly sweetness in contemplation.

Hear the teaching concerning beauty: “In all things,” says the Apostle, “present yourself as an example of good works—in doctrine, gravity, and integrity” [Note: [Col. 0547] Titus 2.]. Hear what is fragrant: “Three times I was beaten with rods,” says Paul, “once I was stoned” [Note: [Col. 0547] 2 Cor. 11.], etc. Hear what teaches taste: “If you have risen with Christ, relish the things that are above” [Note: [Col. 0547] Col. 3.].

These three meltings come from the beloved. The bridegroom expresses the manner of a lover:

> Who flees to the willows and wishes himself to be seen first.  
> [Note: [Col. 0547] Vergil, *Eclogues*.]

He appeared first at the tomb, perhaps without having been called. Behold: though sought and called, he is not found. Perhaps he sought rather this order: first that he be sought, second inquired after, third acquired, [Col. 0547B] fourth sought again. Let him be sought when absent, inquired after when hidden, acquired when found, and sought again when estranged. The first is through action; the second through prayer; the third through long-suffering; the fourth through his mercy and goodness.

He himself teaches the first three degrees in the Gospel: “Seek,” he says, “and you shall find; ask and you shall receive; knock and it shall be opened to you” [Note: [Col. 0547] Matt. 7.]. The first is through action, the second through prayer, the third through perseverance in virtues, the fourth through humble supplication. The Lord performed the first for us by his incarnation; the second through the Law, the prophets, and apostolic teaching; the third through the distress of his passion; the fourth through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Of the first it is said: “He came to seek the sheep that [Col. 0547C] had strayed” [Note: [Col. 0547] Luke 15.]; of the second: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners” [Note: [Col. 0547] Luke 5.]; and: “Many are called, but few are chosen” [Note: [Col. 0547] Matt. 22.]; of the third: “He became obedient to the Father unto death” [Note: [Col. 0547] Phil. 2.]; of the fourth David says: “Seek again your servant, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0547] Ps. 118.].

Likewise, let the absent one be called; let the hidden one be invoked, that is, called within; let the found one be summoned, that is, called to you; let the estranged one be called, that is, called again. In the first case, let him be called with an audible voice; in the second, with sweet affection; in the third, with purity of conscience; in the fourth, with abundant satisfaction.

*My soul melted when the beloved spoke.*

[CARD.] As though she said: After my beloved spoke to me through the angel, my soul grew warm and melted, so that, like metal melted by heat, it might receive whatever form the craftsman, the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0547D] wished. The following words, however, refer to different times; for what follows—*I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me*—looks to the time when Christ’s parents sought him among relatives and acquaintances. Thus his mother says: *I sought and did not find him*; and when I found him in the temple, seated among the teachers, I called him and said: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I were seeking you in sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0547] Luke 2.]. Yet he did not answer me as a mother, to satisfy maternal [Col. 0548A] affection, but said: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in those things which are my Father’s?” [Note: [Col. 0547] Ibid.] She also says that he did not answer her because she did not understand the word of the one answering. Hence the Gospel immediately adds: “And they did not understand the word which he spoke to them” [Note: [Col. 0547] Ibid.].

But the passage that follows refers to the time of the Lord’s passion, namely:

*The watchmen who went about the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak.*

[THO.] The watchmen of the Church are the teachers, to whom this responsibility has been entrusted: that they defend her from depraved teaching and kindle her toward love. They find the bride wearied by seeking the beloved, strike and [Col. 0548B] wound her, because they find the soul distressed by heavenly love and kindle it still further by their example and teaching. And while they extinguish in her whatever earthly thing they discover still remaining, making her as though insensible to lower things, they seem to strike and wound her—namely, by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

These same watchmen are those of the walls, that is, of the virtues; they strip the bride of her cloak, that is, of her worldly covering, so that she may freely see the beloved. For this cloak is the same as the tunic mentioned above. There are three cities treated in theology: the first, Babylon; the second, Sion; the third, Jerusalem. The first is called confusion, the second a watchtower, the third the vision of peace. The first is hell; the second, the Church militant; the third, the Church triumphant. The first lacks watchmen; the second [Col. 0548C] has them; the third has no need of them.

The first lies open, so that whoever wishes may enter: “Broad is the way that leads to death” [Note: [Col. 0547] Matt. 7.].

> Easy is the descent to Avernus:  
>   
> [lacuna]  
>   
> But to retrace one’s step and escape to the upper air—  
> this is the task, this is the labour.  
> [Note: [Col. 0547] Vergil, *Aeneid* 6.126.]

The second is shut, lest the devil contrive anything within it. “The Lord has strengthened the bars of your gates” [Note: [Col. 0547] Ps. 147.]—“Narrow is the way that leads to life” [Note: [Col. 0547] Matt. 7.].

> We undertake difficult things; but no virtue exists save difficult virtue.  
> [Note: [Col. 0547] Ovid.]

The third is secure, because there it fears neither thief nor robber. “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where rust and moth do not destroy, and where thieves do not break in or steal” [Note: [Col. 0547] Matt. 6.].

Sion, therefore, has [Col. 0548D] three watchmen: a prelate, an angel, and God. Of the first: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set watchmen; all day and all night they shall never be silent” [Note: [Col. 0547] Isa. 62.]. Of the second: “And upon the walls, the guardianship of angels.” Of the third: “Unless the Lord guards the city, he watches in vain who guards it” [Note: [Col. 0547] Ps. 126.]. The first strikes, the second wounds, the third strips off the cloak. The first strikes by rebuke; the second wounds by visitation; the third strips off the cloak by removing imitation of worldly conduct.

But note the order of the words: they found, wounded, [Col. 0549A] struck, and took away the cloak. They found her at the wall of solitude; they struck her with the staff of correction; they wounded her with the sword of separation; they stripped her of the cloak of worldly conduct. They found her at the wall of solitude, lest she grow weary through delay; with the staff of correction, lest the flesh become wanton; with the sword of separation, lest the spirit consent to the flesh; they stripped her of the cloak of worldly conduct, so that she might be unencumbered for action.

First, they found her at the wall of solitude. Solitude is threefold: the first is that of vicious singularity; the second is abandonment amid the straits of tribulation; the third is meditation upon heavenly desire. Of the first: “Woe to the one who is alone, because if he falls, he has no one to raise him up” [Note: [Col. 0549] Eccles. 4.]. The devil was the first such solitary person. Of the second: “Wandering in deserts” [Note: [Col. 0549] Heb. 11.]. [Col. 0549B] And Christ in his passion: “I looked around, and there was no helper” [Note: [Col. 0549] Isa. 63.]; and: “I became like a pelican of the wilderness” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 101.]. Of the third: “I became like a solitary sparrow upon the roof” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ibid.]. In this solitude was Mary Magdalene, seeking the Lord: “Lord,” she says, “if you have taken him away, tell me, and I will take him away” [Note: [Col. 0549] John 20.].

Second, they struck with the staff of correction. Hence: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 22.]—“The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 140.]. “I,” says the Lord, “rebuke and chastise those whom I love” [Note: [Col. 0549] Rev. 3.]. “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” [Note: [Col. 0549] 2 Tim. 4.]—“Correct the disorderly, console the faint-hearted, support the weak” [Note: [Col. 0549] 1 Thess. 5.]. Jeremiah: “You struck them and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept correction; they hardened their faces above the earth and were unwilling [Col. 0549C] to return” [Note: [Col. 0549] Jer. 5.].

Third, they wounded with the sword of separation. Of this he said: “I did not come to bring peace, but a sword” [Note: [Col. 0549] Matt. 10.]. This is “the living and efficacious word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” [Note: [Col. 0549] Heb. 4.]. I have called this sword the Word not uttered, but incarnate. Fourth, they took away the cloak of worldly conduct.

This cloak is threefold: the first of pleasure, the second of vanity, the third of malice. The first was that which Joseph, fleeing, left in the hand of his adulterous mistress [Note: [Col. 0549] Gen. 39.]; the second, that which John the Evangelist left in the hands of the Jews: “But he,” it says, “casting away the linen cloth, fled” [Note: [Col. 0549] Mark 14.]. The third was that which, [Col. 0549D] when Elijah ascended to heaven, remained on earth [Note: [Col. 0549] 4 Kings 2.].

The finding by the watchmen removes desolation; the staff’s blow makes a bruise; the wounding sword pours out blood; stripping off the cloak makes one ready for action: it removes the desolation of solitude; creates the bruise of contrition; pours out the blood of spiritual desire for virtuous action; and prepares one for action. The finding by the watchmen removes desolation, so that one may say: “Blessed are you, Lord God, because you have helped and comforted me” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 85.]; and: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in [Col. 0550A] my heart, your consolations made my soul glad” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 93.].

The staff makes a bruise. There is a bruise from bodily injury, and a bruise of envy. Hence: “Wound and bruise and swelling sore” [Note: [Col. 0549] Isa. 1.]. And there is a bruise of spiritual anguish; Christ was the first to have this bruise, and by his bruise we have been healed [Note: [Col. 0549] Isa. 53.]. The sword pours out the blood of spiritual desire, for the life of the soul is in the blood. Thus David says: “I poured out my soul within me” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 41.]. The stripping off of the cloak makes one ready. Thus, once Joseph had left it behind, he was swifter in flight; John, having left the linen cloth, was freer in escape; Elijah, having left his cloak on earth, was readier to ascend into heaven.

We rightly said that the watchmen of the city, namely the Church, are the apostles, according to: “Upon the walls of Jerusalem I have set [Col. 0550B] watchmen” [Note: [Col. 0549] Isa. 62.], especially Peter and Paul. They found the bride—that is, the Church—wandering; struck her when she resisted; wounded her, though obstinate, with the arrow of love; and stripped her, though grown old, of the cloak of her former conduct.

Of the first it is said: “I have wandered like a sheep that has perished” [Note: [Col. 0549] Ps. 118.]. But in contrast: Peter the apostle and Paul, teacher of the nations, taught us your law, O Lord. She resisted, according to: “May you be his disciple; we are disciples of Moses” [Note: [Col. 0549] John 9.]. But she was struck, according to: “Strike your son with the rod, and you shall save his soul from death” [Note: [Col. 0549] Prov. 23.]. She was obstinate, so as to say: “But neither have we heard that there is a Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0549] Acts 19.]. But once wounded she says: “I am wounded by love.” She had grown old, to whom it was said: [Col. 0550C] “Put off the old man with his deeds” [Note: [Col. 0549] Col. 3.]. Hear her stripped: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?”

Therefore, that knowledge may be enlightened against error, let Peter and Paul come as two lights of knowledge. For this reason Solomon is read to have made for God in the temple cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high, their wings five cubits long [Note: [Col. 0549] 3 Kings 6.]. It was fitting that Christ, who came to show us mercy, should appoint men of mercy; that, to those who fell through Adam’s folly, he who teaches man knowledge should assign knowledgeable men, so that through them he might enable them spiritually to understand the Law—he who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it [Note: [Col. 0549] Matt. 5.].

These two cherubim were made of [Col. 0550D] olive wood, because these are men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not passed into oblivion [Note: [Col. 0549] Ezek. 33.]. They are called the fullness of knowledge because they did not seek knowledge through fanciful arguments, but “knowledge of God more than holocaust” [Note: [Col. 0549] Hos. 6.]. They are said to be ten cubits high because, spiritually both teaching and fulfilling the ten articles of the Law, they will receive with you individual denarii.

Therefore, in the cherubim we have knowledge; in the olive wood, mercy; in the ten cubits, observance of the Law: knowledge, that [Col. 0551A] we may have knowledge of God and of ourselves; mercy, that compassion for our neighbour may be in us; observance of the Law, that the fulfilment of God’s commandments may advance in us. Of the first: “The lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” [Note: [Col. 0551] Mal. 2.]. And elsewhere: “My people perished because they lacked knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0551] Hos. 4.]. For this purpose the Spirit of knowledge was given to the apostles.

Of mercy Job says: “Compassion grew up with me, and came forth with me from my mother’s womb” [Note: [Col. 0551] Job 31.]. Thus they were made men of mercy. Of the Law: “Great peace is for those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” [Note: [Col. 0551] Ps. 118.].

Of knowledge: there is knowledge followed by punishment; there is half-full knowledge; and there is full knowledge. The first knows God’s will but does not abandon iniquity. The second, though occupied with temporal matters, nevertheless retains purity. The third pursues God’s will. The first is pagan, because pagans do this; the second political, because states order temporal matters justly; the third apostolic, because apostolic men obey the divine will.

Of the first: “It would have been better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” [Note: [Col. 0551] 2 Pet. 2.]. Likewise: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” [Note: [Col. 0551] Luke 12.]. Whoever adds this knowledge adds labour also. Of the second Paul says: “I know how to be hungry and how to be satisfied, and how to abound and suffer want” [Note: [Col. 0551] Phil. 4.]. Likewise: “Priests who know well should be held worthy of double honour” [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Tim. 5.]. Of the third, the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who speaks [Col. 0551C] with you, perhaps you would have asked him to give you living water” [Note: [Col. 0551] John 4.].

The prophet complains of this knowledge: “There is no mercy, no truth, and no knowledge of God in the land” [Note: [Col. 0551] Hos. 4.]. Likewise Peter: “Supply in your faith virtue, and in virtue knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0551] 2 Pet. 1.]. And Paul: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Cor. 2.]. Again: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit” [Note: [Col. 0551] 2 Tim. 1.].

O Peter, where is that word by which you denied the Lord, saying to the maidservant: “I do not know what you are saying” [Note: [Col. 0551] Matt. 26.]? You too, Paul, when you were keeping the garments of those stoning Stephen, and when you did not cease to persecute Christ and his members, then knew something other than Jesus Christ crucified. And he says: “I acted ignorantly in unbelief” [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Tim. 1.]. [Col. 0551D] “The Lord,” says Peter, “permitted me to fall so that I might raise up the fallen.” “God,” says Paul, “permitted me to err so that I might lead the erring back to the way.”

Perhaps these are prefigured when Samuel said to Saul: “You will find two men leaping over great pits.” For they leapt over great pits when they passed from sin to righteousness, from the snares of the devil to Christ’s free way, from fear of eternal death to confidence. This is the cloak which they took away from the bride. “Upon you [Col. 0552A] who are upon the earth shall come terror, pit, and snare” [Note: [Col. 0551] Isa. 24.]: the snare of diabolical seduction, the pit of obstinacy, and the terror of final examination; the snare, that one may fall into temptation; the pit of obstinacy, that one may come to despair; terror, that one may be ready for final condemnation.

Of the snare: “They prepared a snare for my feet” [Note: [Col. 0551] Ps. 56.], etc. But there is a remedy, because “our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of hunters” [Note: [Col. 0551] Ps. 123.], etc. Of the pit: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the pit which he made” [Note: [Col. 0551] Ps. 7.]. Likewise: “Foxes have dens, and birds of heaven have nests” [Note: [Col. 0551] Matt. 8.]. Of terror: “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth” [Note: [Col. 0551] Ps. 111.], etc.

These men found the bride wandering. Hence Peter: “You were once like wandering sheep” [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Pet. 2.]. And Paul, after enumerating many [Col. 0552B] sins: “Such were some of you, but you have been washed, sanctified, and justified” [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Cor. 6.]. Peter struck her: “Putting away all malice, all deceit, and hypocrisies” [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Pet. 2.], etc. And Paul: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you so that you do not obey the truth?” [Note: [Col. 0551] Gal. 3.] Peter wounds her: “God has regenerated us unto a living hope, unto an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance kept in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Pet. 1.]. And Paul: “Relish the things that are above” [Note: [Col. 0551] Col. 3.]. Peter strips her: “Having your conduct good among the nations” [Note: [Col. 0551] 1 Pet. 2.]. And Paul: “I beseech you to walk worthily of the calling by which you were called, with humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love” [Note: [Col. 0551] Eph. 4.].

[Col. 0552C] *The watchmen who guard the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak.*

[CARD.] As though she said: The high priests, scribes, and Pharisees, who by their office ought to have guarded the city, when they had seized the guardian—my Son—found me in him. By striking him they struck me; by wounding him they wounded me, because the sword of his passion passed through my soul. They also took away the cloak of joy and gave in its place the spirit of mourning [Note: [Col. 0551] Isa. 61.]. It follows:

> I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love.

[Col. 0552D] [THO.] The Bride rightly languishes with love when, struck and wounded by the sword of the Spirit, she has put off the garment of carnal desire; for insofar as the soul is perfected in God, it becomes weak and infirm in worldly things. Nor is it surprising that the perfected soul languishes, when the Apostle calls those who have left the world dead: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0551] Col. 3.].

*Daughters of Jerusalem.* The daughters of Jerusalem are citizens of the heavenly homeland; there are daughters of Babylon, daughters of Judah, daughters of Sion, and daughters of Jerusalem. Of the first: “O wretched daughter of Babylon” [Col. 0553A] [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 136.]; of the second: “The daughters of Judah rejoiced” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 96.]; of the third: “That I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Sion” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 72.]; of the fourth, in this place.

The first lies in the confusion of sins; the second purifies herself in confession; the third is in contemplation; the fourth enjoys the vision of God. For the first means confusion; the second, confession; the third, contemplation; the fourth, vision of God. The first laughs in error; the second is bruised by sorrow; the third languishes with love; the fourth rejoices in honour. To the first it is said: “Beauty is deceitful and vain” [Note: [Col. 0553] Prov. 31.]; the second says: “I am black, but beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0553] Song 1.]; to the third it is said: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ibid.]; to the fourth it is said: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend” [Note: [Col. 0553] Song 4.], as was said.

The first sits in confusion, as though beside the rivers of Babylon. There are four [Col. 0553B] rivers of Babylon: hatred of one’s brother, the heat of carnal pleasure, forgetfulness of God, and worldly sorrow. These are the four rivers of hell, as is read in the poets: the first is Styx, which means hatred; the second Phlegethon, called burning; the third Lethe, called forgetfulness; the fourth Cocytus, that is, lamentation. According to their meanings, these are the aforementioned rivers of Babylon.

Sometimes a person is above the rivers, sometimes beneath the rivers, and sometimes in the rivers. Those are above the rivers who resist temptations; those are in the rivers who are overcome; those are beneath the rivers who delight to lie in temptations. The first says: “The waters have entered even unto my soul” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 68.]; the second: “I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ibid.]; the third: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ibid.].

[Col. 0553C] “In the willows” of these rivers “we hung up our instruments” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 136.]. We hang our instruments upon the willows, that is, upon barren things, when we are ashamed to preach to others what we ourselves do not do. There are five kinds of barrenness: first, of action; second, of speech; third, of thought; fourth, of affection; fifth, of intention. Of the first: “Their days failed in vanity” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 77.]; of the second: “Each one spoke vain things to his neighbour” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 11.]; of the third: “Woe to you who devise useless things” [Note: [Col. 0553] Mic. 2]! Of the fourth: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 4.] Of the fifth: “Their heart is vain” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 5.].

The first is in Babylon’s suburb, the second about its gate, the third within its walls, the fourth about the middle of the city, the fifth in the city’s innermost part. Barrenness of works is outside, because it is seen by human beings; barrenness of speech is beside the gate, because through speech, as through a gate, we disclose inner things; the other three are in the city because no one can see them. Behold the five barrennesses.

Likewise there are five instruments: the first, teaching of truth; the second, kindling of the will; the third, obtaining grace; the fourth, gladness of conscience; the fifth is jubilation, by which we give thanks to God for inward sweetness. Of these instruments, the first [Col. 0554A] is an instrument of instruction, the second of exhortation, the third of devotion, the fourth of exultation, the fifth of jubilation. To the first belongs teaching the unlearned; to the second, reproving the negligent; to the third, supplicating the Lord; to the fourth, rejoicing in the Lord; to the fifth, rising into the greatness of wonder.

He promised to sing upon the first instrument who said: “My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 13]. He sang upon the second who said: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life” [Note: [Col. 0553] Jas. 1.]. Upon the third: “At every time bless God, and ask him to direct your ways” [Note: [Col. 0553] Tob. 4.]. Upon the fourth: “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 94.]. Upon the fifth: “God is wonderful in his saints” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 67.]—“Grace is in the hands of the saints.”

The daughter of Babylon laughs in error, [Col. 0554B] not hearing: “Laughter shall be mixed with my sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy” [Note: [Col. 0553] Prov. 14.]; and likewise: “I considered laughter an error, and said to joy: Why are you vainly deceived?” [Note: [Col. 0553] Eccles. 2.]; likewise: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you too shall mourn” [Note: [Col. 0553] Luke 6.]; likewise James: “Let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0553] Jas. 4.]. “Charm is deceitful, and beauty vain” [Note: [Col. 0553] Prov. 31.], namely outward beauty. “A beautiful and foolish woman is a golden ring in her snout” [Note: [Col. 0553] Prov. 11.]. And Job: “I saw a fool firmly rooted, and immediately cursed his beauty” [Note: [Col. 0553] Job 5.]. But the poet also says [Note: [Col. 0553] Ovid]:

> Beauty is a fragile good; and by however many years it advances,  
> it grows less and is itself consumed by its own passage of time.

The daughters of Judah purify themselves in confession, according to: “Confess your sins to one another” [Note: [Col. 0553] Jas. 5.]; and: [Col. 0554C] “Let all things be washed in confession, for confession is the second plank after shipwreck.” They humbly say: “I have sinned beyond the number of the sand of the sea, and I am unworthy to see heaven because of the multitude of my iniquities.”

They cleanse that threefold leaven of which the Apostle speaks: “Purge out the old leaven—not,” he says, “with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness” [Note: [Col. 0553] 1 Cor. 5.]. The old leaven is the devil’s suggestion, which begins in thought, passes into delight, breaks forth into consent, and reaches the act: this is sinning within oneself. The leaven of malice is when we sin against our neighbour by plotting something against him through anger, hatred, or envy. The leaven of wickedness is that by which we sin against [Col. 0554D] God: by pride, blasphemy, or unbelief. Therefore, “Let us come before his face in confession” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 94.], etc.

She was once among the daughters of Babylon; but, groaning, she turned back. Hence she is bruised by sorrow, because “weeping, she wept in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks” [Note: [Col. 0553] Lam. 1.]. Thus she cries: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch” [Note: [Col. 0553] Ps. 6.], mindful of that Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Note: [Col. 0553] Matt. 5.].

Therefore, afflicted daily for our sins, let us await our end with [Col. 0555A] tears, lest perhaps, overtaken by the day of death, we be unable to find a place for repentance and pardon. Though she is in sorrow, she rejoices in hope, because she has carried out judgment and righteousness in herself in this world, and therefore will not be judged at the judgment. Hence: “The daughters of Judah rejoiced, because of, etc.” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 96.]. Therefore she confidently speaks what follows: “I am black, but beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0555] Song 1.]: black through satisfaction, beautiful through love; black through remembrance of sins, beautiful through hope of future goods; black in human judgment, beautiful through the visitation of angels.

The third are the daughters of Zion, which is interpreted “watchtower”; for, as it was said, “These are upon the watchtower; they languish with love,” to them it is said: “Behold, you are fair, my friend; behold, fair” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ibid.]. Here it should be noted [Col. 0555B] that some are in the mirror and on the watchtower: some neither in the mirror nor on the watchtower; some on the watchtower but not in the mirror; some in the mirror but not on the watchtower. The first are good before God and human beings; the second evil before God and human beings; the third evil before God but good before human beings; the fourth good before God but evil before human beings. The first advance by example; the second infect; the third deceive; the fourth despise themselves. They are in the mirror when they consider themselves inwardly; on the watchtower when they appear outwardly. Of the mirror it is said: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” [Note: [Col. 0555] Eccl. 2.]; of the watchtower: “Let your light shine before human beings” [Note: [Col. 0555] Matt. 5.]. Of the second it is said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who have taken away the key of knowledge: you yourselves did not enter, nor did you allow others to enter” [Note: [Col. 0555] Luke 11.]; of the third: “They come to you in [Col. 0555C] sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” [Note: [Col. 0555] Matt. 17.]; of the fourth: “When you pray, enter your chamber; and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” [Note: [Col. 0555] Matt. 6.].

Again, it should be noted that there are four mirrors. In the first we consider our own iniquity; in the second, our condition; in the third, the punishments of hell; in the fourth, the blessedness of heaven. The first draws us to mourning; the second invites us to humility; the third instils fear in us; the fourth inflames us to love. In the first we lay aside self-confidence; in the second pride; in the third boldness; in the fourth sloth. They lay aside self-confidence who, looking upon their sins, see that they vainly trust in their own strength and rejoice in the multitude of their sorrows; with Job they have to say: “Behold, there is no help for me in myself” [Note: [Col. 0555] Job 6.]. Again: “Against a leaf carried away by the wind you display your power, and you pursue dry stubble” [Note: [Col. 0555] Job 13.]. Adam was a tree created by God: a leaf when he fell through the wind of suggestion; stubble when he was cast out of paradise. Of the first Isaiah says: “I shall take away the ornaments from your feet, and the crescents, and the mirrors” [Note: [Col. 0555] Isa. 3.]. The feet are our affections, from which the grace to recognize sins is withdrawn. Of the second James says: “If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he shall be compared,” he says, “to a man considering the face of his birth in a [Col. 0556A] mirror” [Note: [Col. 0555] Jas. 1.]; of the third the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” [Note: [Col. 0555] 1 Cor. 13]—not only blessedness, but also the punishments of hell. Of the fourth, in the Book of Wisdom: “Wisdom,” he says, “is the brightness of eternal light and a spotless mirror” [Note: [Col. 0555] Wis. 7.]. For by Wisdom herself we contemplate heavenly things.

The first, as was said, draws us to mourning; whence: “Woe to us, because we have sinned, because the crown of our head has fallen” [Note: [Col. 0555] Lam. 5.]; again: “They have putrefied and become corrupt” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 37], etc.; again Job: “Though I should be washed as with snowy waters and my hands should shine as the cleanest, yet you will plunge me into filth, and my sins will abhor me” [Note: [Col. 0555] Job 9.]; again: “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 105.]. In the second mirror we see our [Col. 0556B] condition, and it invites us to humility, since in it we see a base beginning, a miserable exile, and a sad ending. Thus Job: “A human being born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” [Note: [Col. 0555] Job 14.]. Hear the base beginning: “Who comes forth like a flower,” namely, born of woman, “and is crushed,” because he is filled with many miseries, “and never remains in the same state” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ibid.]. Behold the miserable exile: “And he flees as a shadow” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ibid.], namely, living for a short time. Behold, you have the sad and hasty ending. And these things lead to humility; hence: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes? When a human being dies, he shall inherit serpents, beasts, and worms” [Note: [Col. 0555] Sir. 10.].

In the third we see the punishments of hell, by which it instils fear in us. These are inflicted by fire and frost, worm, hunger, stench, and scourging. There is also [Col. 0556C] horror, with darkness and fiery chains upon the limbs. Of fire and stench: “Fire, sulphur, and the blast of storms are the portion of their cup” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 10.]; of chains, darkness, and frost: “Having bound his hands and feet, cast him into the outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” [Note: [Col. 0555] Matt. 22.]; of the worm: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” [Note: [Col. 0555] Isa. 66.]; of hunger: “My servants shall eat, and you shall hunger” [Note: [Col. 0555] Isa. 65.]; of horror: “Where there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells” [Note: [Col. 0555] Job 10.]. Seeing this, one rightly cries: “The fear of death troubles me” [Note: [Col. 0555] Sir. 40], etc. Job had seen these things when he cried: “Leave me a little, that I may lament my sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0555] Job 10], etc.

The fourth mirror, because in it we see heavenly blessedness, inflames us to love. For they see how the souls [Col. 0556D] of the saints rejoice in heaven, who have followed Christ’s footsteps; and how glorious is the kingdom in which all the saints rejoice with Christ. Therefore they cry: “My heart grew hot within me, and in meditation” [Note: [Col. 0555] Ps. 38], etc., because there nothing is lacking to those who love God in truth. Of these mirrors it is said that Moses made the bronze basin from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0555] Exod. 30.]. The tabernacle is the heavenly homeland, at whose door—that is, entrance—the women keep watch, that is, the holy souls. From their aforesaid mirrors Moses—that is, [Col. 0557A] “saved from the waters,” namely God without sin—makes as it were a bronze vessel: that is, one strong and dark-coloured, signifying weeping; four-sided, because it derives from four mirrors. In it the priests who are about to sacrifice—that is, those subduing their flesh—wash themselves in the tears that flow from the first side, namely the remembrance of sins; and from the second side, namely the misery of our condition; and from the third, namely fear of Gehenna; and from the fourth, namely love of the homeland.

These things have been said concerning the daughter of Zion, who is on the watchtower. But she also, as was said, languishes with love: she languishes in defect, in effect, and in affection—in the defect caused by sin, in the performance of good, and in the desire for God. She languishes in defect because she has offended her beloved; in effect because she is unable to suffer as much as she would wish for her beloved; in [Col. 0557B] affection because the blessedness for which she longs is delayed.

**115.** First, with this languor he languished who said: “All that you have done to us,” etc.; secondly, he languished who said: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 115.] And Job: “May he who began himself to crush me release his hand and cut me down” [Note: [Col. 0557] Job 6.]; and Habakkuk: “Let rottenness enter into my bones and bubble up beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation, that I may go up to our armed people” [Note: [Col. 0557] Hab. 3.]. With the third languor he languished who said: “My soul thirsted for the living God: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 41.] Again: “My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 83.].

First Mary Magdalene languished when she lay at Christ’s feet, where “many sins were forgiven her because she loved much” [Note: [Col. 0557] Luke 7.]. [Col. 0557C] Secondly, she languished when she prepared spices to anoint the Lord and laboured with such anxious care to seek him. Thirdly, she languishes when, having found him in the appearance of a gardener, she said: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” [Note: [Col. 0557] John 20.]. Hence great joy followed when the Lord said: “Mary”; and she: “Rabboni, which means Teacher” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ibid.]. Behold, for a time her languor was relieved. But she languished still more after the Ascension.

To this woman it is said: “Behold, you are fair, my friend; behold, you are fair; your eyes are doves’ eyes” [Note: [Col. 0557] Song 1.]. She is called fair twice because she is fair in affection and fair in effect: in affection, by loving; in effect, by acting—loving God and neighbour; performing works of mercy [Col. 0557D] for her neighbour, works of virtue in herself, and works of piety toward God. Again, she is fair in progress and fair in ecstasy: in progress of virtue, ascending from virtue to virtue [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 83.]; in ecstasy of mind, contemplating heavenly things. Again she is told: “In your splendour and your beauty, attend prosperously; go forth and reign” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 44]—humbling yourself in it. Go forth in contemplation, emulating the daughters of Jerusalem; and reign by attaining their peace, to whom you now say: Announce to my beloved that I languish with love. For they already enjoy the vision of peace [Col. 0558A] of which it is said: “In peace, in the selfsame place, I shall sleep and rest” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 4.]. They rejoice in honour, to whom the Bridegroom says: “You are altogether fair, my friend” [Note: [Col. 0557] Song 4.], because they are fair without fault and fair without misery forever.

Those labouring in the world follow their form and endeavour, that they may enjoy their joy. The first remain upon the dunghill like the unskilled; the second walk at a slow pace, fettered by temptations; the third run, yet are still hindered by corruptions; the fourth ascend with Christ, freed from the bonds of the flesh. The first say: “I sit as a queen, and am not a widow, and shall not see mourning” [Note: [Col. 0557] Rev. 18.]; the second: “Draw me after you” [Note: [Col. 0557] Song 1.]; the third: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ibid.]; the fourth: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0557] Song 2.].

[Col. 0558B] The first are obstinate, continually looking back toward Sodom with Lot’s wife [Note: [Col. 0557] Gen. 19.], hardened into a stone statue. The second, ashamed of their sins, seek to touch the hem of the Saviour’s garment from behind, with the woman suffering from a flow of blood [Note: [Col. 0557] Matt. 9.]. The third, ardent with love, find him in the appearance of a gardener with Mary Magdalene [Note: [Col. 0557] John 20.]. The fourth, entering Jerusalem with the queen of Sheba, hear the wisdom of Solomon [Note: [Col. 0557] 3 Kgs. 10.], that is, of the true Peacemaker. The first are excluded from the heavenly solemnity; the second are admitted momentarily; the third visit it frequently; the fourth possess it continually. Of the first: “The ways of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemn feast” [Note: [Col. 0557] Lam. 1.]; of the second: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of our solemnity” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 80.]; of the third: “Appoint a [Col. 0558C] solemn day amid the thickly gathered throngs,” that is, gatherings, “up to the horn of the altar” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 117.], that is, Christ’s kingdom. The fourth rejoice with Christ, in whose solemnity the angels rejoice and praise the Son of God together.

These are the four horses which the prophet Zechariah saw [Note: [Col. 0557] Ch. 6.]: one was black, another variegated, another red, another white. The black horse signifies the first, who are black with the rust of temptations; the third, which is red, signifies the third, who are inflamed with charity; the fourth, white, signifies the fourth, now made radiant in the incorruption of the first robe. Of the first: “His face has been blackened beyond coals, and they are not recognized in the streets” [Note: [Col. 0557] Lam. 4.]. Of the second Paul says: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are [Col. 0558D] unleavened” [Note: [Col. 0557] 1 Cor. 5.]. They are unleavened because clean from sin. Yet they still need to be purged from leaven, that is, from the imminent temptation. Concerning the third David says: “My heart was inflamed, and my reins were changed” [Note: [Col. 0557] Ps. 72.]. Concerning the fourth it is said in Revelation: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain, crying: ‘How long, Lord, do you not avenge our blood upon those who are on the earth?’ And white robes were given to each of them” [Note: [Col. 0557] Rev. 6.]. These are they who fly with Christ to the kingdom.

[Col. 0559A] “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, announce to him that I languish with love.”

[CAR] At this point a woman is introduced speaking to the women who seek the Lord at the tomb, saying: “I adjure you, daughters of the heavenly Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that for love of him I languish from sorrow at his Passion.” They, however, are introduced as replying and asking:

“What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest of women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?”

[THO.] “Beloved from beloved” is understood as Son from Father, just as light from light, God from God. For as there is one brightness and one divinity of Father and Son, so there is one love, as John says: “Everyone who loves him who begot also loves him who is born of him” [Col. 0559B] [Note: [Col. 0559] 1 John 5.]. There is beloved from beloved; beloved from a beloved woman; and beloved in the beloved. From the beloved Father, from the beloved mother, in the beloved brother. From the beloved, begotten eternally; from the beloved woman, assuming flesh temporally; in the beloved, building a spiritual temple for himself. Of the first: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” [Note: [Col. 0559] Ps. 2.]; of the second: “The Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0559] John 1.]; of the third: “And dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0559] Ibid.]. Hence: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” [Note: [Col. 0559] 1 Cor. 3.].

If one asks what the beloved from beloved is like, he is found merciful and sweet; from the beloved woman, obedient and humble; from the beloved, glorious and wonderful. Of the first: “The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works” [Note: [Col. 0559] Ps. 144.]; of the [Col. 0559C] second: “He emptied himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death” [Note: [Col. 0559] Phil. 2.]; of the third: “A wise son is the glory of his father” [Note: [Col. 0559] Prov. 13.]. And he is “beloved by God and human beings, whose memory is in blessing” [Note: [Col. 0559] Sir. 45.].

He is merciful because his mercy goes before us, accompanies us, and follows us. Of the first: “My God, his mercy shall go before me” [Note: [Col. 0559] Ps. 58.]; of the second: “My truth and my mercy are with him” [Note: [Col. 0559] Ps. 88.]; of the third: “His mercy shall follow me all the days of my life” [Note: [Col. 0559] Ps. 22.]. Behold: first it precedes, second it accompanies, third it follows. It precedes in order to show the way; it accompanies in order to draw us out on the way from the pit of misery and the mire of filth [Note: [Col. 0559] Ps. 39.]; it follows in order to foresee the snares of robbers. In the first, by inspiring good will; [Col. 0559D] in the second, by forgiving sins; in the third, by freeing from temptations. Hence David: “He shall fulfil the desire of those who fear him,” by preparing it; “and he shall save them,” by forgiving their sins; “the Lord guards all who love him” [Note: [Col. 0559] Ps. 144.], by defending them from temptations.

Again, this beloved is sweet in works of repentance, sweet in ordering the affections, and sweet in the tasting of things above. Of the first it is said: “For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” [Note: [Col. 0559] Matt. 11.]; of the second: “O Wisdom, who have come forth from the mouth of the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0559] Office of the Church], etc.; of the [Col. 0560A] third: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” [Note: [Col. 0559] Ps. 33.].

From the beloved woman he is obedient. There are three degrees of obedience: obedience rendered through fear; obedience rendered for advantage; and obedience rendered through love—through fear of the scourge, for the advantage of gain, through love of God and neighbour. The first is a slave’s; the second a hired servant’s; the third a son’s. The first springs from murmuring; the second from worldly desire; the third from charity. The first is an ass’s; the second a hawk’s; the third a dog’s. For an ass does not obey unless beaten; a hawk returns to its master when enticed by food; but a dog follows its master even when struck and driven away by him. In the first, the slave obeys until the scourging stops; in the second, the hired servant until he receives payment; [Col. 0560B] in the third, the Son is obedient to the Father unto death [Note: [Col. 0559] Phil. 2.].

Again, obedience may be good, better, or best. Good obedience is rendered to a superior; better obedience to an equal; best obedience to an inferior. By the first fault is pardoned; by the second goodwill is gained; by the third grace is accumulated. Of the first Paul says: “Children, obey your parents” [Note: [Col. 0559] Eph. 6.]; of the second: “Bear one another’s burdens” [Note: [Col. 0559] Gal. 6.]; of the third: “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake” [Note: [Col. 0559] Rom. 13.].

Again, the beloved has from the beloved woman the quality of being humble according to the flesh. Why did he humble himself? His supreme cause was mercy. Yet from this four causes arise: he humbled himself in order to blot out our sins; to relieve the shame of the human condition; to remove the scourges of hell; and to confer upon us [Col. 0560C] spiritual gifts on the way and eternal gifts in the homeland. Of the first: “He shall put away our iniquity and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” [Note: [Col. 0559] Mic. 7.]; of the second: “He shall reform the body of our humility, conformed to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0559] Phil. 3.]; of the third: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” [Note: [Col. 0559] Hos. 13.]; of the fourth, concerning spiritual gifts on the way: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” [Note: [Col. 0559] Eph. 4.]. In the homeland: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” [Note: [Col. 0559] 1 Cor. 2].

Likewise we too ought to humble ourselves for these four reasons. Mary Magdalene humbled herself for guilt, lying at Christ’s feet [Note: [Col. 0559] Luke 10.]; Abraham, for the [Col. 0560D] misery of his condition, when he said: “I shall speak to the Lord, though I am dust and ashes” [Note: [Col. 0559] Gen. 18.]; Job, for [an uncertain cause], saying: “Blessed be the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0559] Job 1.]; David, on account of benefits conferred, saying: “I have praised, and I shall become still more lowly in my own eyes before the Lord, who chose me as king” [Note: [Col. 0559] 2 Sam. 6.].

Perhaps they inquire more ardently into the beloved’s quality because perhaps they had heard what is said here: “God is glorious in his saints, wonderful in his majesty.” God is burdensome to his saints, abundant, and glorious: burdensome when he draws out; abundant when he gives; glorious when he rewards. [Col. 0561A] He draws them out of the abyss of vices; he gives gifts of charisms; he repays with gifts or joys of the blessed. He is burdensome to sinners, abundant to those who love him, glorious to those who reign with him.

David experienced him as burdensome when he said: “Your arrows are fixed in me” [Note: [Col. 0561] Ps. 37.], and added: “For my iniquities have passed over my head; as a heavy burden they have weighed upon me” [Note: [Col. 0561] Ibid.]. But he was drawing him out, for he says: “He drew me out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth” [Note: [Col. 0561] Ps. 39.]. Hear him as abundant: “You open your hand and fill every living thing with blessing” [Note: [Col. 0561] Ps. 144.]. Behold, he gives as he gave to the apostles, for he gave them gifts of charisms. Hear him as glorious: “O how glorious is the kingdom in which all the saints rejoice with Christ!” For here he repays; hence: “You [Col. 0561B] are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint a kingdom for you” [Note: [Col. 0561] Luke 22.].

In the first he washes away our foulness; in the second he supplies our want; in the third he relieves our lowliness: the foulness of carnal love, the want of divine consolation, the lowliness of the human condition. Of foulness: “Her filthiness is on her feet, and she did not remember her end” [Note: [Col. 0561] Lam. 1.]; again: “Your uncleanness is abominable; I wished to cleanse you, and you have not been cleansed from your filth” [Note: [Col. 0561] Ezek. 24.]. Of want: “You say, ‘I am rich and need nothing,’ though you are wretched, poor, blind, naked, and miserable” [Note: [Col. 0561] Rev. 3.]; of lowliness: “See, Lord, and consider, for I have become lowly” [Note: [Col. 0561] Lam. 1.]. Therefore he is burdensome in order to change foulness into cleanliness; abundant, to change want into abundance; glorious, to [Col. 0561C] turn lowliness into glory.

Let us therefore first see to whom he is burdensome. He is burdensome to the damned, to the wicked, and to the righteous: to the damned for eternal affliction, to the wicked for correction, to the good for increase of glory. The first have the burden of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0561] Isa. 13.], which is called confusion; the second, the burden of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0561] Isa. 19.], which is called darkness; the third, the burden of the beasts of the South [Note: [Col. 0561] Isa. 30.], namely, of the Holy Spirit. Of the first: “Each shall bear his own burden” [Note: [Col. 0561] Gal. 6.]. Hence Pharaoh said: “Go to your burdens” [Note: [Col. 0561] Exod. 5.]; of the second: “Food, a rod, and a burden for the ass” [Note: [Col. 0561] Sir. 33.]; hence the Apostle: “Bear one another’s burdens” [Note: [Col. 0561] Gal. 6.]; of the third: “For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” [Note: [Col. 0561] Matt. 11.].

[Col. 0561D] [Lacuna.] For a burden that is well borne becomes light. For the damned the burden is the affliction of bodily scourging, the worm of conscience, and despair of pardon. This is what Joab did when he captured the city of Rabbah: he made the people of that city pass under threshing-sledges, drags, and iron carts [Note: [Col. 0561] 1 Chr. 20.]. The threshing-sledges strike with blows; the drags prick with teeth; the carts crush bones. Of these it is said: “For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I shall not turn him back, because they threshed Gilead with iron carts” [Note: [Col. 0561] Amos 1.]. Damascus means “drinking of blood,” namely the demons [Col. 0562A] who thirst for our blood; Joab means “adversary,” that is, the devil. He is David’s—that is, Christ’s—minister, because by Christ’s command he punishes the wicked. Rabbah means “immense”: it is this world, which is great. The devil captures it when he draws worldly people to himself and, as has been said, punishes them. Behold, he is burdensome to the damned.

He is also burdensome to the wicked: first, by divine punishment; secondly, in separation from pleasure; thirdly, in penitential satisfaction. The first is done so that one may be converted; the second, so that one may be cleansed; the third, so that one may be reconciled. Thus the Lord threatened through the prophet: “Strike your hand and stamp your foot, because those who are far off shall die by pestilence; those who are near shall fall by the sword; and those who are shut up within shall die by hunger” [Note: [Col. 0561] Ezek. 6.].

[Col. 0562B] Those far from the Church are the despairing; those near are believers entangled in sin; those within are unlearned persons wandering astray, because they perish through hunger for God’s word. Thus the first perish through the pestilence of despair; the second through the sword of diabolical deception; the third through famine of preaching. That pestilence was prefigured in the Egyptians who perished with swelling blisters [Note: [Col. 0561] Exod. 9.]. Of the second it is said: “I shall draw my sword; my hand shall slay them” [Note: [Col. 0561] Exod. 15]. Of the third: “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” [Note: [Col. 0561] Lam. 4.].

He is also burdensome in separation from pleasure. Pleasure first seizes, secondly kisses, thirdly embraces. It seizes when it presents worldly glory to our senses; it kisses when it inflames desire; it embraces when it ensnares the desiring person. You find these three [Col. 0562C] things in Solomon’s foolish woman [Note: [Col. 0561] Prov. 7.]. For he says: “She seized the young man.” Behold the first. “And she kissed him.” Behold the second. “Let us enjoy the embraces we desire.” Behold the third.

He is also burdensome in penitential satisfaction. In this, iron cuts, fire burns, and dust consumes.
