Iron cuts open the scar of repeated sin; fire burns the flowing humour of perverse pleasure; dust consumes the rotten flesh of inveterate sin. Of the first: “Rule them with a rod of iron” [Note: [Col. 0561] Ps. 2.]. Of the second: “Who among you can dwell with devouring fire?” [Note: [Col. 0561] Isa. 33.] Of the third: “Let him put his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope” [Note: [Col. 0561] Lam. 3.]. Christ applied this dust when he raised Lazarus, dead four days. For he said: “I confess to you, Father”; because of bitterness [Col. 0562D] “he groaned in spirit and wept,” and prayed: “I give thanks to you, Father, because you always hear me” [Note: [Col. 0561] John 11.]. Behold how he is burdensome to sinners.

He is also burdensome to the saints. This must be borne courageously, for the poet says [Note: [Col. 0561] Ovid.]:

> Bear it as a burden: strive with head held upright;
>
> for if you allow your sinews to bend, you will fall.

Although this burden has much bitterness, it also has much consolation. For Christ’s yoke is sweet and his burden light [Note: [Col. 0561] Matt. 11.]. It has bitterness [Col. 0563A] in the heart, in the hands, and in the mouth: in the mouth, when Christ’s sufferings are preached to others; in the hand, when others are invited to martyrdom by the example of one’s own suffering; in the heart, when Christ’s sufferings are pondered inwardly. Of the first: “His lips dripping with choicest myrrh.” Of the second: “My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh.” Of the third: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall lodge between my breasts.” Behold bitterness in the myrrh; consolation in the bundle, namely because it is small. Hear the bitterness: “The saints endured mockeries and scourges, and moreover chains and prisons” [Note: [Col. 0563] Heb. 11.]. Hear the consolations: “If they have suffered torments before human beings, their hope is immortal forever.” — “Going forth they went and wept, scattering [Col. 0563B] their seeds; but returning they shall return with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 125.]. Hence it was said in the Law: “When you offer to the Lord the firstfruits of your crops, you shall bring a sheaf to the priest, who shall lift the bundle before the Lord, that it may be for you” [Note: [Col. 0563] Lev. 23.], etc. Behold, he is burdensome to the saints.

It follows how he is abundant in giving. For he gives temporal goods, spiritual goods, and eternal goods: temporal goods by which we are sustained; spiritual goods by which we are helped; eternal goods by which we are made blessed. The first lest the flesh fail; the second that the spirit may advance; the third that glory may suffice for us. Of the first: “Who gives their food to cattle and to the young ravens that call upon him” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 146.]. Again: “Who gives food to every [Col. 0563C] flesh” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 135.]. Of the second: “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” [Note: [Col. 0563] Eph. 4.]. Of the third: “The Lord will give grace and glory” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 83.]; and: “You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 60.].

Again, he gives the Son, gives the Holy Spirit, and will give himself: the Son to be leader in battle, the Spirit to direct us by counsel, himself as the reward. He is leader in battle so that we may follow him to the kingdom; he gives the Spirit to direct us by counsel, so that through him we may be consoled amid tribulations; and he gives himself in the kingdom, so that we may enjoy his vision. Of the first: “A child is born to us” [Note: [Col. 0563] Isa. 9.]. Of the second: “I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth” [Note: [Col. 0563] John 14.]. Of the third he promised: “I shall be their Lord forever” [Note: [Col. 0563] Wis. 3.].

Of these three things it is said to the angel [Col. 0563D] of Pergamum: “To the one who conquers, I shall give hidden manna,” that is, the Holy Spirit; “and I shall give him a white stone,” that is, Christ in flesh clean from sins; “and upon the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it” [Note: [Col. 0563] Rev. 2.], that is, the Father who is above the stone, because the Father is greater than the Son according to his humanity. For it is new that the Father is in one person of God and man, namely the Father in the Son, bounded together [*conterminato*; sense uncertain], which we shall not understand until we receive it. Behold, he is abundant.

[Col. 0564A] He is also glorious: glorious in himself, glorious in the Son, glorious in the saint. In himself through sovereignty; in the Son through office; in the saint through service—through the sovereignty of majesty, through the office of weakness which he fulfilled, through the service which the saint rendered in works. Of the first: “The nations shall fear your name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ps. 101.]. Again: “The Lord has built Zion, and he shall be seen in his glory” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ibid.]. Of the second: “A wise son is the glory of his father” [Note: [Col. 0563] Prov. 13.]. Of the third: “Glorify and bear the Lord in your body” [Note: [Col. 0563] 1 Cor. 6.].

You have heard him burdensome; you have heard him abundant; you have heard him glorious. Let us see the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne [Note: [Col. 0563] Isa. 6.], and the saints coming to meet him at the solemn feast, that they may see the majesty of the Trinity. Hence [Col. 0564B] they sing: “In the beginning was the Word” [Note: [Col. 0563] John 1.]. There comes “a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet” [Note: [Col. 0563] Rev. 12.]: the blessed Virgin, radiant with the sun, who gave birth. Hence we sing to her: “For you are blessed, holy Virgin Mary, and most worthy of all praise, because from you arose the Sun of righteousness, Christ our God” [Note: [Col. 0563] In the Office of the Blessed Virgin].

The morning stars follow: the rejoicing sons of God, namely the angels, praising the King upon golden harps and saying: “Holy, holy, holy” [Note: [Col. 0563] Rev. 4.]; and all the angels praise the holy Lord, saying: “Praise and honour befit you, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0563] Ibid.]. The prophets also come to meet him; drunk with the Spirit, preparing the way for the King, they announced future things beneath the covering of speech and offer the King a book sealed with seven seals to be opened [Note: [Col. 0563] Rev. 5.]. Hence: [Col. 0564C] “Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist” [Note: [Col. 0563] Matt. 11.].

There also appears a crown of twelve stars, namely the apostles. Wise with dove-like simplicity, they enriched the world’s dryness with heavenly dew. Hence: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” [Note: [Col. 0563] Isa. 60.] Behold the choir of martyrs with its purple banner: carrying the pomegranate, they offer the King its grains glittering with rosy colour, its rind cast away; for they “have come out of great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” [Note: [Col. 0563] Rev. 7.]. The golden urn follows, that is, the confessors, shining outwardly through good works and inwardly possessing manna, that is, the sweetness of devotion; tablets of understanding; and the rod of discipline. Hence: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in [Col. 0564D] your hands” [Note: [Col. 0563] Luke 12.]. Lastly virgins are offered to the King, who have not defiled their garments, crying: “Our bed is flowery,” in which the flower of the field and lily of the valleys may rest.

Thus God has in Mary lodging; in the angels, service; in the prophets, a mirror; in the apostles, preaching; in the martyrs, suffering; in the confessors, discipline; in the virgins, purity of life. From the beloved he was glorious and wonderful: now to the Gentiles and Jews, now to the apostles, now to the angels—first by the performance of miracles, second in the Resurrection, third in the [Col. 0565A] Ascension. Of the first it is said: “Today we have seen wonderful things” [Note: [Col. 0565] Luke 5.]. Of the second: “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me” [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 138.]. Of the third: “Men of Galilee, why do you marvel, gazing into heaven?” [Note: [Col. 0565] Acts 1.]

“What is your beloved, that you have so adjured us?”

[CARD.] As though they said: “O fairest of women, you who, kindled by love for your beloved, have so adjured us, answer us: how lovable he is, how desirable, how beautiful in both natures. Tell us what your beloved from beloved is like—what he is like, namely in divinity, according to which he is from the Father, beloved from beloved—and tell us also what your beloved is like according to the beauty of assumed humanity.” To this she replies:

[Col. 0565B] “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.”

[THO.] White, because “appearing in the flesh, he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0565] 1 Pet. 2]. Red, because “he washed us from our sins in his own blood” [Note: [Col. 0565] Rev. 1]. And rightly first white, then red: for first he came into the world free from the blood of sin, then, bloodied by his passion, he departed from the world. Chosen from among thousands, because one from the human race, through whom the world might be reconciled, was assumed by God. He alone among mortals was worthy to hear from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Note: [Col. 0565] Matt. 17]; that is, in whom I found no fault to offend me, and the full weight of every virtue in which I might delight. Hence in Ecclesiastes: “One man out of a thousand I found” [Col. 0565C] [Note: [Col. 0565] Eccl. 7].

Christ was white from the Virgin, red from the cross, chosen from among thousands by the Father. White from the Virgin, because from her was born he “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0565] 1 Pet. 2]. Red upon the cross, by which the devil was conquered and the world redeemed by Christ’s blood [Note: [Col. 0565] Rev. 5]. Chosen from among thousands by the Father, he alone being worthy to open the book and loose its seven seals [Note: [Col. 0565] Ibid.]. In the first he came without sin; in the second he washed us from sin; in the third he showed by what instruments—that is, sacraments—we are to guard ourselves from sin. By the first he teaches us to be white through the cleanliness of purity; by the second, patient through the ardour of charity; by the third, steadfast [Col. 0565D] in faith and the knowledge of truth.

It should be noted that there are four kinds of whiteness. The first is illusory, as in enchanters; the second superficial, as in painters; the third inborn and changeable in its subject, as in human beings who, though often born white, turn black; the fourth inborn, but incapable of being separated from its subject, as in pearls. The first is worldly vanity in the lover of the world; the second hypocrisy in the pretender; the third virtue in the religious person; the fourth brightness in the blessed.

Moses forbids us the first when he says: “The priest who has a white film in [Col. 0566A] his eye shall not offer sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 0565] Lev. 21]. He has a white film in his eye who gladly contemplates worldly things outwardly and takes delight in them inwardly. Hence the owl, because it has excessive whiteness in its eyes, cannot see in daylight. The second deters us when, in the Gospel, he calls hypocrites whitewashed tombs [Note: [Col. 0565] Matt. 23]. Solomon invites us to the third, saying: “Let your garments always be white, and let oil not fail from your head” [Note: [Col. 0565] Eccl. 9]. By this we are white, yet we sometimes fall away from it; whereas Christ is on the way, but without falling. Of the fourth: “Individual white robes were given to them” [Note: [Col. 0565] Rev. 6]. Again, in the same book: “To the one who conquers I will give a white stone” [Note: [Col. 0565] Rev. 2]. Yet this whiteness should not be without redness, so that it may shine more pleasantly, and the ardour of charity may give form to the whiteness of virtue.

[Col. 0566B] But there is scarlet red, rose-red, and purple-red. Scarlet is more ardent; rose-red more pleasant; purple more precious. Scarlet is more ardent because it resembles fire; rose-red more pleasant because it is mixed from both whiteness and redness; purple more precious because royal clothing is honoured by its splendour. Scarlet signifies the ardour of temporal sufferings; rose-red, the whiteness of virtues mingled with love of things above; purple, the royal dignity of martyrs.

Of the first David says: “You tested me with fire, as silver is tested” [Note: [Col. 0565] Ps. 63]. Of the second: “He stored up joy and exultation upon him” [Note: [Col. 0565] Sir. 15]. Of the third: because they shed their blood for love of Christ, therefore they shall reign with Christ [Col. 0566C] for ever [Note: [Col. 0565] Ezek. 33]. Again: “By your blood you made us a kingdom and priests for God” [Note: [Col. 0565] Rev. 1]. Hence: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” [Note: [Col. 0565] 1 Pet. 2].

As a sign of the first, Christ in his passion was clothed in a scarlet cloak, whence he was called red. As a sign of the second, the angel appeared at the tomb in red and white: “For his appearance was like lightning, and his garments like snow” [Note: [Col. 0565] Matt. 28]. For there was redness in him because of charity, whiteness because of purity; the mixture of these produces pleasantness. But in order that this mixture might come about, Christ in his passion is recorded as clothed not only in scarlet but also in a white garment. He was also clothed in purple [Note: [Col. 0565] Rev. 17], so that in that purple might be fully expressed the dignity which, after his ascension, he was to receive from the Father and impart to his martyrs with royal honour [Col. 0566D].

The Beloved is said to be chosen from among thousands, but also chosen from tens, from hundreds, and from thousands—that is, perfect in every respect. For these three numbers signify a threefold perfection in the Church: in ten, the perfection of virtue; in a hundred, that of virginity; in a thousand, that of understanding truth. In ten is the perfection of virtue, because it is produced from two and five, which are the seven virtues. This is the first perfection, because ten is the first boundary [Col. 0567A] among numbers. In a hundred is the perfection of virginity, because one passes from the left hand to the right, counting by fives all the joints and tips on the surface of the left hand, and thus the final five is reckoned on the right. For virginity, fleeing the left hand—that is, the care of the world—seeks the right hand, that is, the life of angels. This number is multiplied from ten, because virginity is empty if it is not founded upon virtues. In a thousand is the perfection of understanding truth. It is multiplied from ten and a hundred, because strength of virtues and purity of chastity are necessary for understanding the truth of things above.

This Beloved is chosen from tens, for he not only possesses perfection of virtues, but is also called [Col. 0567B] the Lord of virtues. Hence: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 23]. He is also chosen from hundreds, because he is not only perfect in virginity but was also born of a Virgin. Hence: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” [Note: [Col. 0567] Isa. 7]. He is likewise chosen from thousands, because he is not only perfect in understanding truth, but is called Truth itself.

117 Hence: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0567] John 14]; again: “We saw him full of glory and truth. And from his fullness we all received” [Note: [Col. 0567] John 1]. Therefore he was worthy to open the book and loose its seven seals [Note: [Col. 0567] Rev. 5], namely: birth, baptism, passion, descent into hell, resurrection, ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit. The closed seals were the obscure prophecies in which these things lay hidden; the book which [Col. 0567C] he opened was the Scripture which he fulfilled.

His birth lay hidden beneath this seal, Malachi chapter 4: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall arise.” Baptism, beneath this passage of Zechariah chapter 13: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David,” and, “for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman.” Passion, beneath this passage of Isaiah chapter 53: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he is silent.” Descent into hell, beneath this passage of Hosea chapter 13: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell.” Resurrection, beneath this passage of Judges chapter 16: “Samson slept until midnight,” and, “At midnight Samson arose from the city of Gaza and carried away the gates of the city.” Of the ascension David says: “God ascended with jubilation, and the Lord [Col. 0567D] with the sound of the trumpet” [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 46]. The sending of the Holy Spirit lay hidden beneath this: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created” [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 103].

By these seals the Father, who commands the deliverances of Jacob, saved us through his Son [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 43]. For the Son, by assuming flesh, restored the dignity of humankind, which through the fall of the first man [Note: [Col. 0567] Gen. 3] “was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 48]. Through baptism he washed away the impurity of both actual and original human guilt, whose righteous acts were like a menstrual cloth [Note: [Col. 0567] Isa. 64], because they rotted like [Col. 0568A] beasts in their heart [Note: [Col. 0567] Joel 1]. Through his passion he reconciled us to the Father, because, offering himself upon the cross and atoning for our guilt, he supplied for our poverty: “For by nature we were children of wrath” [Note: [Col. 0567] Eph. 2]. By his descent into hell he freed the righteous from the power of darkness, so that those “sitting in darkness and the shadow of death” might see the Father’s face [Note: [Col. 0567] Ps. 106]. Through the resurrection he gladdened humankind, because he assured us that this corruptible body shall put on incorruption and this mortal body immortality [Note: [Col. 0567] 1 Cor. 15], although “all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass” [Note: [Col. 0567] 1 Pet. 1]. By his ascension he gave us who believe hope of returning from this exile to our homeland, for “we seek the city to come,” because “we have no enduring city here” [Note: [Col. 0567] Heb. 13]. By sending the Holy Spirit he instructs us in true [Col. 0568B] discipline, understanding, and love of righteousness. “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, withdraw from thoughts devoid of understanding, and be rebuked by approaching iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0567] Wis. 1].

These seals are contained under the number seven, which is a virgin number, because below the first limit it stands alone: it neither begets nor is begotten—that is, it neither multiplies another nor is multiplied by another—signifying that Christ alone, a virgin and born of a Virgin, was worthy to open them. Again, it exceeds six, the first perfect number, by one, because Christ alone surpassed all the perfect in righteousness; and therefore he was chosen from among thousands, so as to be worthy to open the seals [Note: [Col. 0567] Rev. 5].

Or thus: in the Apocalypse one reads, “From the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand sealed” [Note: [Col. 0567] Ibid.], and the rest that follows. From among all [Col. 0568C] the thousands of the children of Israel, Christ alone, of the tribe of Judah, was chosen to open these seals by which they were sealed but which were still closed. The first seal, namely Christ’s birth, is opened to us if we follow the purity and simplicity of that child, so that we may be like newly born infants, desiring rational milk without deceit [Note: [Col. 0567] 1 Pet. 2]. The seal of baptism is opened to us if through confession we wash our sins, namely, if we confess our sins to one another and pray for one another that we may be saved [Note: [Col. 0567] Jas. 5]. The seal of the passion is opened to us if, for sins washed in confession, we make satisfaction through the harshness of penance, so that we crucify our flesh with its vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0567] Gal. 5]. The seal of the descent into hell is opened to us if, often recalling the punishments of hell, we carefully [Col. 0568D] guard ourselves lest we fall into temptations and the devil’s snare [Note: [Col. 0567] 1 Tim. 6]. The seal of the resurrection is opened to us if, abandoning worldly conduct, we live to God as dead to the world, so that, putting off the old person with his deeds, we may walk in newness of life [Note: [Col. 0567] Col. 3]. The seal of the ascension is opened to us if, cleaving to Christ, we seek and set our minds on the things above [Note: [Col. 0567] Ibid.], so that, in this pilgrimage being present only in body, we may dwell in that eternal homeland in thought and longing. The seal of the sending of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0569A] is opened to us if the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us [Note: [Col. 0569] Rom. 5], so that we love God more than ourselves—that is, with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind—and our neighbour as ourselves [Note: [Col. 0569] Matt. 22]. Therefore Christ alone opens the book of the heart, that we may understand these things; he looses the seals, that we may do them.

“My beloved is white and red, chosen from among thousands.”

[CARD.] As though she said: My Beloved is utterly pure in the whiteness of divinity, and according to his humanity is red with the blood of his passion. He is chosen from among thousands as “beautiful in form” and beautiful “beyond the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0569] Ps. 44], because, as Job says, “man does not know its price” [Note: [Col. 0569] Job 28]. Next she describes the head [Col. 0569B] and limbs of her Beloved; and the Mother of the Lord answers those who inquire, saying:

“His head is finest gold; his locks are like raised palm branches, black as a raven. His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed in milk and sitting beside fullest flowing waters.”

[THO.] The Apostle says: “The head of a woman is a man; the head of a man is Christ; the head of Christ is God” [Note: [Col. 0569] 1 Cor. 11]. This head is finest gold, because, as gold surpasses other metals, so the highest Divinity excels all that he has made. His locks are likened to raised palm branches, that is, the companies of saints awaiting the sweetness of the heavenly reward. Hence: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” [Note: [Col. 0569] Ps. 91]. These locks are said to be black as a raven, because, though they await heavenly sweetness through God’s mercy, [Col. 0569C] yet they confess that of themselves they are black—that is, sinners and unworthy.

His eyes are called like doves on account of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, who is signified by the dove. Thus John saw the Lamb having seven horns, which he explains as follows: “These are the seven spirits sent into all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0569] Rev. 5], that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. They sit beside streams of water because whatever blemish spiritual eyes detect in themselves they wash away with the waters of spiritual grace; or they sit beside fullest flowing waters because through God’s grace they discern the devil’s contrivances. They are washed in milk because, nourished by the simple teaching of Scripture, they see their sins and are cleansed from them so as to be pure.

The head of the Beloved—that is, of Christ—compared to gold is his divinity; his locks compared to raised palm branches are the unity of the faithful depending upon him; the eyes of his Beloved, the doves, are the unity of divine [Col. 0569D] understandings and purity and simplicity. Of the first: “The head of Christ is God” [Note: [Col. 0569] 1 Cor. 11]; of the second: “Not a hair from your head shall perish” [Note: [Col. 0569] Luke 21]; of the third: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine” [Note: [Col. 0569] Gen. 49].

A golden head is sometimes mixed with silver, producing electrum; sometimes joined with gems, producing an ornament; sometimes set by itself and precious by its own nature. In the first [Col. 0570A] it takes on pallor; in the second it has a variegated colour; in the third it possesses, like the sun, innate splendour from itself. Of the first: “The rear parts of his back are in the pallor of gold” [Note: [Col. 0569] Ps. 67], because “he emptied himself, assuming our mortality” [Note: [Col. 0569] Phil. 2]. Of the second it is said: “A rainbow upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0569] Rev. 10], because of the variety of colours. For it has the redness of gold, that is, divinity; and the greenness of a gem, that is, humanity now glorified. Of the third: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” [Note: [Col. 0569] Matt. 13], as if from the brightness of divinity.

In the first is good gold, in the second better, in the third best—not because it admits any degrees in itself, but because it benefits us by diverse effects. The first was good when, joining himself to the silver of our humility, he illuminated [Col. 0570B] our darkness by the light of his grace [Note: [Col. 0569] 1 Cor. 4], we who were once darkness but now light in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0569] Rom. 9]. The second is better, because in the manner of his resurrection “he will reform the body of our lowliness, configuring it to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0569] Phil. 3]. The third is best, for it is of such immeasurable brightness and beauty that, although angels behold it continually, they desire still further to gaze upon it [Note: [Col. 0569] 1 Pet. 1]. Hence the Lord says: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory I had before the world existed” [Note: [Col. 0569] John 17].

Morally, this threefold gold is in the human being. The first is good: discipline in outward bearing; the second better: purity of love in the affections; the third best: the savour of heavenly things together with understanding. As a figure of the first, Daniel [Col. 0570C] saw an angel with his loins girded with fine gold [Note: [Col. 0569] Dan. 10]. In the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0569] ch. 1], as a figure of the second, one girded at the breasts with a golden belt. As a figure of the third, in the same book [Note: [Col. 0569] ch. 14], an angel was seen: “And a golden crown upon his head.” Again, as a figure of the first, the ark of the Lord was gilded outside; as a figure of the second, inside; as a figure of the third, within it was a golden vessel containing manna—that is, the sweetness of things above—and the tablets of the Testament [Note: [Col. 0569] Heb. 9], namely, understanding of those same things.

Jeremiah laments the loss of the first in the children of Israel, saying: “The renowned children of Zion, clothed in pure gold—how have they been reckoned as earthen vessels?” [Note: [Col. 0569] Lam. 4]. Of the second, in the Apocalypse, to the angel of Laodicea: “I counsel you to buy from me gold refined and pure by fire, that you may become rich” [Note: [Col. 0569] Rev. 3]. Again, of the third Jeremiah says: “How the gold has grown dim, the [Col. 0570D] finest colour changed!” [Note: [Col. 0569] Lam. 4]. The first shines for others’ eyes, the second for one’s own, the third for divine eyes. By the first a neighbour is enabled “to turn away from evil” [Note: [Col. 0569] 1 Pet. 3]; in the second a person sees in himself so as to incline toward the Creator; in the third “the Son of Man has somewhere to lay his head” [Note: [Col. 0569] Matt. 8]. For there “Solomon made for himself a golden couch” [Note: [Col. 0569] Song 3], in which he may rest.

From this head depend the locks, that is, the faithful who follow their head in obedience; they are said to resemble raised palm branches, that is, branches or palm fronds lifted on high. For the palm has four features in which we ought to imitate it. Below it has roughness; above, smoothness. Below its trunk is thinner; above, thicker. We ought to live our temporal life, which is lower, in the roughness of penance; our spiritual life, which is higher, in gentleness of conduct. Likewise below we ought to be thinner, lest we desire earthly things too much; above, thicker, pouring out our hearts toward things above, so that we may set our minds on “the things above” [Col. 0571A] [Note: [Col. 0571] Col. 3].

Hear concerning the first, the harshness of temporal life: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” [Note: [Col. 0571] Gal. 5]; again: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0571] Col. 3]. The Apostle says: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery” [Note: [Col. 0571] 1 Cor. 9]. Hear of gentleness of conduct in [Col. 0571B] spiritual life: “Putting away all malice, all deceit, pretences, envies, and every slander, like newly born infants desire rational milk without deceit” [Note: [Col. 0571] 1 Pet. 2]. The Apostle says: “We are cursed, and we bless” [Note: [Col. 0571] 1 Cor. 4], etc. Hear of thinness, that is, the rejection of temporal things: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” [Note: [Col. 0571] 2 Tim. 2].—“Command the rich of this age not to think highly of themselves, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” [Note: [Col. 0571] 1 Tim. 6].—“If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 61]. Hear of thickness above, that is, a heart enlarged upward: “Set your minds on the things above” [Note: [Col. 0571] Col. 3]. Again: “Hope in him, all the assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him: God is our helper for ever” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 61].

Again, the palm has four things: shoulder-blades, that is, branches, which are like shoulder-blades; the crowns of victors; the beauty of flowers; and the sweetness of dates. In the shoulder-blade it invites us to battle; in the victor’s crown, to victory; in the beauty of flowers, it shows the glory of resurrection; in the sweetness of dates, the delight of seeing God present.

Of the first: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 44]; and, “Be strong in battle and fight against the ancient serpent” [Note: [Col. 0571] Heb. 11]. Of the second: “Everything born of God shall live for ever” [Note: [Col. 0571] 1 John 5]. Again: “To the one who conquers I shall give the crown of life” [Note: [Col. 0571] Rev. 2]. Of the third: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” [Note: [Col. 0571] Matt. 13], when “the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 91]. Of the fourth: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for [Col. 0571D] they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0571] Matt. 5], namely when “we shall be like him,” when “we shall see him as he is” [Note: [Col. 0571] 1 John 3].

These locks are said to be black as a raven, namely so that a person, however righteous, may confess himself a sinner for the sake of humility. The raven has four notable features in theology: blackness; rapacity; it lives on carrion; and it has an ugly, delaying cry, namely *cras*, “tomorrow,” which it always postpones until tomorrow. Its blackness signifies the sorrow of present misery, which came from Adam’s rapacity, because he regarded it as a thing to be seized [Col. 0572A] when he wished to be like God [Note: [Col. 0571] Phil. 2]. He also fed on carrion when he fulfilled his will by eating from the forbidden tree [Note: [Col. 0571] Gen. 3]. Thus from immortal he became a corpse—that is, flesh given to worms. He had an ugly and delaying voice when he deferred confession, when he excused himself by saying: “The woman whom you gave me gave me from the tree, and I ate” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ibid.]. This blackness signifies in us: when we grieve our theft of pride; the corpse of pleasure; and delay in confession.

There are three kinds of blackness. The first is that of sin: “Their faces were blackened beyond coals, and they were not recognized in the streets” [Note: [Col. 0571] Lam. 4]. The second is that of affliction, as here: “Black as a raven.” The third is that of humility, 118 whence: “I am black, but beautiful” [Note: [Col. 0571] Song 1].

As figures of these, we read of three ravens. The first, leaving [Col. 0572B] the ark, found a corpse and disdained to return [Note: [Col. 0571] Gen. 8], because one who feeds on pleasures despises the unity of the Church. This raven therefore feeds on the blackness of pleasures and remains in the flood. The second grows black through affliction of the flesh and merits salvation from God. For it brought meat to Elijah [Note: [Col. 0571] 3 Kgs. 17], whose name means “My God is the Lord,” and “the Lord is salvation.” The third grows black through humility and, as it were, brings the refreshment of bread to Christ, who was humbled for us. This is the raven that brought bread to the first hermit, Paul, whose name means “little” or “quiet,” that is, humble, like Christ.

It follows: “His eyes are like doves, washed in milk; and they sit beside fullest flowing waters.” In Scripture we find the eyes of the Beloved understood in four ways. His eyes are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which [Col. 0572C] illuminate our hearts. Hence the prophet says: “Upon one stone, seven eyes” [Note: [Col. 0571] Zech. 3]. And John saw the standing Lamb having seven eyes [Note: [Col. 0571] Rev. 5]. His eyes are also divine approval. Hence: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 33]. His eyes are prophets and apostles. Hence: “My eyes fail because of want” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ps. 87]. His eyes are also the contemplative and circumspect. Hence: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine” [Note: [Col. 0571] Gen. 49]; and: “There was stature in the wheels, and height, and a fearful appearance, and the whole body was full of eyes” [Note: [Col. 0571] Ezek. 1]. These eyes see the height by contemplating the heavenly things they should desire; the terror of hell which they should flee; and they foresee the snares of the adversary, so that they may have stature—that is, steadfastness in good. These things are in the wheel, that is, in human life, which is turning because transitory.

[Col. 0572D] Here the discussion concerns these eyes of circumspection, which are compared to doves washed in milk because of their simple gaze. They are washed in milk—that is, cleansed from sins by simple teaching—and, in order to look about themselves, they sit beside fullest flowing waters. These streams are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by whose grace we foresee approaching dangers. Of them: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink. Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” [Note: [Col. 0571] John 7]. These are full in the forgiveness of sins; fuller in imparting love of God [Col. 0573A] and neighbour; fullest in careful circumspection lest one fall away from them.

Or the streams are divine Scripture: full in morality, in which we see how we ought to live; fuller in allegory, in which we learn the things done for us; fullest in anagogy, in which we consider the heavenly things we await as reward. Of these streams it is said: “The river of God is filled with waters” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ps. 64], etc. In these rivers we look about ourselves, so that, like a dove recognizing a hawk, we may recognize the approaching enemy. Our enemy is threefold: flesh, the world—that is, the tyrant of the world, the devil. Hence Paul says: “Your struggle is not only against flesh and blood” [Note: [Col. 0573] Eph. 6]: behold the first; “but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of [Col. 0573B] this world’s darkness” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ibid.]: behold the second; “against spiritual forces of wickedness in heavenly places” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ibid.]: behold the third. The first fights through pleasure, the second through malice, the third through suggestion. The first seeks to stain sobriety, the second to break the firmness of faith, the third to obscure the knowledge of God. The first is conquered by flight, the second by voluntary suffering, the third by manly resistance.

This is what was said to David: “When you hear the sound of one walking in the tops of the pear trees, then go out to battle” [Note: [Col. 0573] 2 Kgs. 5]. For the Lord walks at the bottom of the pear trees, moderating our sensuality so that it does not fall into fleshly pleasure; in the middle, when through patience he preserves in us faith and reason against the rulers of the world; at the top he walks when he gives us [Col. 0573C] strength and understanding against the devil’s suggestion. Hence: “Circle around behind” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ibid.], so that you may discover his deception.

Of the first: “Flee fornication” [Note: [Col. 0573] 1 Cor. 5]. Of the second: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation” [Note: [Col. 0573] Jas. 1]. Of the third: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” [Note: [Col. 0573] Jas. 4]. In the first, flesh desires against spirit and spirit against flesh. “For the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” [Note: [Col. 0573] Matt. 26]. Weak, I say, through the fall by which it draws down the spirit. Would that it were weak, so that the spirit might be stronger, according to the Apostle. “For when I am weak,” he says, “then I am strong. For power is perfected in weaknesses” [Note: [Col. 0573] 2 Cor. 12]. See how it is weakened: “Put to death,” he says, “your members which are upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0573] Col. 3].—“For those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh [Col. 0573D] with its vices and desires” [Note: [Col. 0573] Gal. 5]. Again: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery” [Note: [Col. 0573] 1 Cor. 9]. Because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” [Note: [Col. 0573] Wis. 9]. Therefore, “we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live” [Note: [Col. 0573] Rom. 8].

See wherein we are debtors: “Food, a rod, and a burden for an ass; bread, discipline, and work for a servant” [Note: [Col. 0573] Sir. 33].—“Those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those according to the Spirit, on the things which belong to the Spirit and [Col. 0574A] perceive them” [Note: [Col. 0573] Rom. 8].—“Wherever,” he says, “the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ezek. 1], not wherever the impulse of the flesh was.

For the flesh has its own impulses. First comes thought, then delight, then consent, afterward the act, then delight in the deed, then persistence, afterward despair, and thus obstinacy, and so eternal death. This is Delilah—that is, “the little poor woman” or “the thirsty woman”—who troubles Samson, whose name means “their sun,” that is, the spirit, even to the raising of his eyes and his death [Note: [Col. 0573] Judges 16.]. The spirit, too, has its own impulses. First it grieves over sin; second, it hates it; third, it abominates it; fourth, it confesses it. It makes satisfaction by works of mercy, acts by loving its neighbour, and burns with desire for God. Those who follow the impulses of the flesh go down alive into hell; those who follow the impulses of the spirit say: “Come, [Col. 0574B] let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0573] Micah 1.]. The latter ascend even to heaven; the former descend even to the depths.

This is the wrestling of Hercules with Antaeus. Hercules is said to mean “glorious in strife,” that is, the spirit; Antaeus, “against God,” that is, the flesh. Whenever, in the contest, Antaeus could touch the earth, he renewed his strength, because the flesh is strengthened by earthly things. Seeing this, Hercules—that is, the spirit—lifted him from the ground between his arms and killed him there, because the spirit, by withdrawing earthly things from the flesh, compels it to die to sin. Feeling this conflict, the Apostle cries: “I find another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind. Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0573] Romans 7.].

Hercules shows us this threefold conflict: first, by fighting [Col. 0574C] Antaeus; second, when he laboured by supporting heaven; third, by fighting the robber named Cacus. Christ taught us to fight against the flesh when he fasted in the wilderness; against the rulers of the world, when he endured persecution from the Jewish people; against demons, when he was tempted by the devil. Likewise John the Baptist waged the first war, clothed in “camel’s hair and with a leather girdle about his loins” [Note: [Col. 0573] Matthew 3.]; the second, when he rebuked Herod for adultery [Note: [Col. 0573] Matthew 14.]; the third, when he could have been called Christ, but rejected vain glory, not consenting to the devil who suggested it.

And the Saviour says: “In my name they shall cast out demons” [Note: [Col. 0573] Mark 16] from the heart. Behold the third conflict. “They shall speak with new tongues” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ibid.], against the earthly [Col. 0574D] ruler. Behold the second. “They shall take up serpents” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ibid.] from the flesh—that is, sensual pleasures. Behold the first. As it has been said: the first enemy is conquered by flight, because “he who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” [Note: [Col. 0573] Ecclesiasticus 13.]. The second will be conquered by patient endurance, just as “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example that you should follow his footsteps” [Note: [Col. 0573] I Peter 2]; because “like a lamb before its shearer he was silent and did not open his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0573] Isaiah 53].

Therefore, according to Paul, “let us run to the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, for the joy set before him, [Col. 0575A] endured the cross, despising shame, and sits at the right hand of God” [Note: [Col. 0575] Hebrews 12.]. Behold the reward of war. Therefore, “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life” [Note: [Col. 0575] James 1.]; for there is no crown where there is no combat. And: “He shall not be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” [Note: [Col. 0575] II Timothy 2.]. Therefore the saints, “having experienced mockings and scourges, moreover also chains and prisons,” etc., “were stoned, were sawn apart, were tempted, died by the slaughter of the sword” [Note: [Col. 0575] Hebrews 11.].

Christ foretold this conflict to his disciples: “Thus indeed you shall have tribulation in the world, but the world shall rejoice, and you shall be sorrowful. Yet your sorrow shall be turned into joy” [Note: [Col. 0575] John 16.]. Therefore “the disciples went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus” [Col. 0575B] [Note: [Col. 0575] Acts 5.]. Thus Paul fought when he said: “In all things we suffer tribulation, but are not distressed; we are reduced to perplexity, but not forsaken; we suffer persecution, but are not abandoned; we are cast down, but do not perish, always bearing about in our bodies the mortification of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Christ also may be manifested in us” [Note: [Col. 0575] II Corinthians 4.].

Behold Hercules—that is, the spirit—bearing heaven, because for desire of the heavenly kingdom he gladly endures these things, hearing: “Blessed are they who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0575] Matthew 5.]. Behold John eating wild honey, namely the sweetness of joy amid tribulation. According to that saying of the Apostle: “rejoicing in tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0575] Romans 12]; and: “Count it all joy when you fall into various temptations” [Note: [Col. 0575] James 1.]. So also [Col. 0575C] Stephen, when the stones of the torrent were sweet to him [Note: [Col. 0575] Acts 7.].

Behold, this enemy is conquered by endurance; the second, however, by manly resistance. Against the first, temperance is required; against the second, fortitude and justice; but against this one, fortitude and prudence are necessary. For the devil sometimes fights fiercely or violently, sometimes deceitfully. Therefore let us oppose fortitude to violence and prudence to fraud, so that we may say with David: “I, your servant, slew both lion and bear” [Note: [Col. 0575] I Kings 17.]. For the devil is a violent lion and a deceitful bear. Hence: “Your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Resist him, strong in faith” [Note: [Col. 0575] I Peter 5.].

To conquer, let us have boldness against the adversary, remembrance of the victorious Fathers, [Col. 0575D] and the aid of prayers, as Judas Maccabaeus said: “Do not fear the attack of the enemies; remember how our fathers were saved, and now let us cry out to heaven, and our God will have mercy on us” [Note: [Col. 0575] I Maccabees 4.]. Concerning the first, see that you do not say: “There is a lion in the road” [Note: [Col. 0575] Proverbs 26], “I shall be killed.” Concerning the second, remember how Samson—that is, Christ—seeking a wife—that is, the Church—killed the lion—that is, the devil—and found in its mouth a swarm of bees—that is, the Fathers who were in hell, [Col. 0576A] and ate honey: that is, by the sweetness of love he brought them forth and incorporated them into himself [Note: [Col. 0575] Judges 14.]. Thirdly, let us cry to heaven: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the lion’s mouth” [Note: [Col. 0575] Psalm 21].

The Saviour says: Be strong in battle and fight with the ancient serpent, and you shall receive the eternal kingdom. Here Hercules fights with the serpent Hydra, whose one severed head gives rise to two others; because, when we repel one power of the devil, we sometimes feel many others raised up by the devil in its place. Against the bear the Lord says: “Be prudent as serpents” [Note: [Col. 0575] Matthew 10]; since “if the master of the household knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” [Note: [Col. 0575] Luke 12]. For that thief, through winding byways and frauds, agitates tranquil hearts. Therefore, “do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from [Col. 0576B] God” [Note: [Col. 0575] I John 4.]—“for the angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light” [Note: [Col. 0575] II Corinthians 11.]. Hence Joshua said to the angel appearing to him: “Are you one of ours or of our adversaries?” [Note: [Col. 0575] Joshua 5.] For he often proposes a good beginning in order to impose a very bad end.

Hence we must say that verse of Virgil [Note: [Col. 0575] Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 48.]:

> Either the Achaeans, shut in, are concealed in this timber;
>
> Or some deceit lies hidden in the horse. . . .
>
> Is Ulysses thus well known?
>
> [lacuna]
>
> Whatever it is, I fear the Danaans even when they bring gifts.

This is the combat in which Hercules fights with Cacus the robber, who is said to derive his name from *kakos*, “evil.” Cacus dragged cows by their tails into his cave, so that the tracks of their entrance could not be found, because the devil brings a good beginning to a bad conclusion. But Hercules [Col. 0576C] hears the oxen lowing—that is, the affections of the spirit crying out—and frees us by killing Cacus, that is, the evil one. He tempts not only secular people but also religious persons, because “Satan shall swallow up a river and not marvel, and he is confident that Jordan shall flow into his mouth.” This one hides in a cave because he loves a dark heart, a vain heart, a slippery heart: dark through ignorance, vain through worldly glory, slippery through negligence, fickleness, and inconstancy. Hence the Lord says to Job: “He sleeps in the shadow” [Note: [Col. 0575] Job 40.]. Behold the dark heart. “In the secret places of reeds” [Note: [Col. 0575] Ibid.]. Behold the vain heart. “In moist places” [Note: [Col. 0575] Ibid.]. Behold the slippery heart.

But it is slippery through negligence with regard to watchfulness, through fickleness with regard to dissipation, and through inconstancy by a change of good resolution. Therefore, against this one, “see how carefully you walk” [Note: [Col. 0575] Ephesians 5.].

> I shall recount what the cautious fox once answered the sick lion:
>
> [Col. 0576D] “Because the footprints alarm me:
>
> All point towards you; none lead back.”

There is another war which the Saviour waged for us in the flesh. Hence the Church sings thus [Note: [Col. 0575] Hymn for Good Friday.]:

> Tell forth, O tongue, the battle  
> Of the glorious contest,  
> And concerning the trophy of the cross  
> Declare the noble triumph, etc.

The battle is threefold. The first is ruinous, the second fruitful, the third glorious. The first is that of the devil and his members against God and their neighbours; [Col. 0577A] the second, that of the righteous person against vices; the third, that of Christ against the devil and his members. The first is damnable, the second praiseworthy, the third noble. The first is that of the devil against Michael and his angels; the second, of Joshua against the Amalekites; the third, of Gideon against the Midianites.

Of the first: “There was a great battle in heaven: the dragon fought with Michael and his angels” [Note: [Col. 0577] Revelation 12.]. Of the second: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war” [Note: [Col. 0577] Psalm 143.]. And Paul: “Thus I run, not as though uncertain; thus I fight, not as beating the air” [Note: [Col. 0577] I Corinthians 9.]. Of the third: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” [Note: [Col. 0577] Psalm 23.].

Of these three the Bride spoke in the Song of Songs. Of the first: “The sons of my mother fought against me” [Note: [Col. 0577] Song of Songs 1.]. Of the second: “Behold Solomon’s bed: [Col. 0577B] sixty mighty men from among the mightiest of Israel surround it, all holding swords and chosen for wars” [Note: [Col. 0577] Song of Songs 3.]. Of the third: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which is built with bulwarks” [Note: [Col. 0577] Song of Songs 7.]. The tower is Christ; hence: “Be for us, O Lord, a tower of strength before the enemy” [Note: [Col. 0577] Psalm 60.].

Therefore, in the first:

> Lament, O tongue, the battle  
> Of the ruinous contest;

in the second:

> Lament, O tongue, the battle  
> Of the fruitful contest;

in the third:

> Tell forth, O tongue, the battle  
> Of the glorious contest, etc.

The first is against the Church. In it three kinds of people fight: tyrants, heretics, and schismatics. Tyrants fight by violence, heretics [Col. 0577C] by worldly learning, schismatics by malice of heart. Tyrants seek temporal advantage; heretics break the truth of faith; schismatics scatter heavenly unity. Of the first Jeremiah says: “How does the city once full of people sit alone? And her enemies have become her head; her foes have grown rich” [Note: [Col. 0577] Lamentations 1.]. Of the second: “How has the Lord in his fury covered the rod of the daughter of Zion with darkness?” [Note: [Col. 0577] Lamentations 2.] Of the third: “How has gold become dim! The finest colour changed!” [Note: [Col. 0577] Lamentations 4.]

Of the first Ezekiel says: “A whirlwind came from the north”; of the second, “and a great cloud”; of the third, “and a fire enfolding” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ezekiel 1.]: this is battle. Hence it is said in Revelation: “The woman was in labour, about to give birth, and the dragon pursued her so as to devour her [Col. 0577D] son; and she fled into the wilderness and bore a male child, and the earth helped her” [Note: [Col. 0577] Revelation 12.]. The dragon is the devil; the woman, the Church; her son, a good work, which the devil devises to destroy; therefore the earth is the Virgin Mary, whence: “You have blessed your land, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0577] Psalm 84.]. Or the earth is the flesh which Christ assumed from her, by which the Church is helped lest it fall.

But this battle is ruinous for the devil; hence: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer? You have fallen to earth, you who wounded the nations” [Note: [Col. 0577] Isaiah 14.]. And: “A thousand shall fall at your side [Col. 0578A] and ten thousand at your right hand” [Note: [Col. 0577] Psalm 90.]. Therefore:

> Lament, O tongue, the battle  
> Of the ruinous contest.

The second war is that of the righteous person with vices. In it some vices attack violently, some creep in gently, and some insinuate themselves deceitfully. The first come in the guise of a raider, the second in the role of an innkeeper, the third in the form of a robber. The first wound with a dart, the second intoxicate with a cup, the third ensnare with a net: with the dart of disobedience, the cup of unchastity, the net of deceit. Of the first the Apostle says: “In all things take up the shield of faith, by which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ephesians 6.]. Of the second: “Babylon is a golden cup; the nations drank of her wine and were made drunk” [Note: [Col. 0577] Jeremiah 51.]. Of the third: “Sinners shall fall into his net” [Note: [Col. 0577] Psalm 140.].

Of the first it is said: “With men who work iniquity I shall not share fellowship [Col. 0578B] with their chosen ones” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ibid.]. Of the second: “But let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ibid.]. Of the third: “In this way by which I walked, the proud hid a snare for me” [Note: [Col. 0577] Psalm 141.].

The first fight violently, such as anger, hatred, and envy. The second fight gently, such as gluttony, lust, and vainglory. The third fight deceitfully, such as an erroneous opinion in faith, singularity arising from one’s own will, and presumptuous hope of pardon. Of the first Paul says: “These are the things that wage war against the soul” [Note: [Col. 0577] I Peter 2.]—“wraths, quarrels, dissensions, envies, jealousies, contentions” [Note: [Col. 0577] Galatians 5.]. Of the second, the same writer says: “Not in feasting and drunkenness, not in beds and unchastities” [Note: [Col. 0577] Romans 13.]. Of the third: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve, so your minds may be corrupted from the charity [Col. 0578C] of Christ which is in Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0577] II Corinthians 11.].

In all of these fortitude is necessary: against the first, the arms of justice are required; against the second, the arms of temperance; against the third, the arms of prudence. The arms of justice prevent offence to God or neighbour; the arms of temperance prevent the spirit’s defilement; the arms of prudence prevent reason’s deception. “For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0577] II Corinthians 10.]. He proposes the same things to us thus. Of the first: “Clothed with the breastplate of justice” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ephesians 6.]. Of the second: “Your feet shod with preparation for the Gospel of peace” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ibid.]. For just as footwear protects the feet against the stones of the earth, so temperance protects human affections against earthly pleasures. Of the third he likewise says: “In all things taking the shield of faith” [Note: [Col. 0577] Ibid.].

This war is fruitful. [Col. 0578D] For justice has its fruit, temperance its own, and prudence its own. Of the first Paul says: “The fruit of justice is charity, peace, patience, goodness, kindness” [Note: [Col. 0577] Galatians 5.]. Of the second: “She who has not known a bed in transgression shall have fruit in the visitation of her soul” [Note: [Col. 0577] Wisdom 3.]. Of the third the Bride says to the Bridegroom: “Let us go out into the field; let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers bear fruit” [Note: [Col. 0577] Song of Songs 7.].

The field is heavenly unity; the vine, charity which roots itself in the earth and proceeds from faith to works; [Col. 0579A] the flower is hope that iniquity may be remitted. Thus we go out into the field of heavenly unity when we consider whether the shrub of singularity grows within it. We rise for the vineyards when we cut off from faith the branches of error. We see whether flowers bear fruit when we take care whether this is a hope such as is followed by growth in virtue. Therefore:

> Tell forth, O tongue, the fruitful battle,

by admonishing one’s neighbour through preaching, so that by fighting he may gain the fruit of virtue.

The third battle follows. It was, first, burdensome; second, skilfully contrived; third, glorious: burdensome when Christ fought, skilfully contrived when he conquered, glorious when he triumphed. In the first he recovered our inheritance; in the second he frustrated Satan’s cunning; in the third he led captivity captive [Col. 0579B] [Note: [Col. 0579] Ephesians 4.]. It was burdensome because “he himself bore our infirmities” [Note: [Col. 0579] Isaiah 53.]; it was skilfully contrived because:

> The order of our salvation  
> Required this work:  
> That the art of the many-formed traitor  
> Might be deceived by art;  
> And that the worthy author of salvation,  
> By the reward of victory,  
> Might open his homeland to his own.  
> [Note: [Col. 0579] Hymn for Passion Sunday.]

Hence on Palm Sunday mention is made of three kinds of wood: namely, the cross, the olive, and the palm. In the first he waged battle; the olive signifies victory, for oil floats upon it; in the palm, which was given to triumphant men, we receive the triumph. Of the first it is said that he bore his cross himself [Note: [Col. 0579] John 19]; of the second, that the Hebrew children, bearing olive branches, came out to meet [Col. 0579C] the Lord [Note: [Col. 0579] Matthew 21]; of the third: “The crowds come forth with flowers and palms.”

Was it not burdensome when he had the cross for a shield, nails in his hands for a dart, a wound in his side for a sword, and thorns on his head for a helmet? O mercy of the Father, who gave up the Son so that he might blot out our iniquity! O generous Son, so that the creature might be redeemed by the Creator! O one who suffered with us, so that the glorious one might relieve our shame! Of the first: “For the zeal of my people I struck him”; of the second: “I repent that I made man” [Note: [Col. 0579] Genesis 6], that is, punishment holds me because I made man; of the third: “He was counted among the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0579] Isaiah 53.].

Man needed this aid, because “every head is sick and every heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown [Col. 0579D] of the head there is no soundness in him” [Note: [Col. 0579] Isaiah 1.]. Perversity of works produced sickness in the feet and hands; infirmity, drawing unlawful thoughts to itself, makes the heart sorrowful; and lukewarmness of charity and hidden truth make the head sick. Of the first: “Their feet are swift to run to evil, and their hands are full of blood” [Note: [Col. 0579] Romans 3.]. Of the second: “A heart devising most wicked thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0579] Proverbs 6.]. Of the third: “My iniquities have gone over my head” [Note: [Col. 0579] Psalm 37.].

But in order that Christ might repair these things, he was pierced in hands and feet, side and head: by nails, lance, and thorns. Of the first: “They pierced my hands and my feet” [Note: [Col. 0579] Psalm 21.]. [Col. 0580A] For the second: “The servants of Abraham dug a well” [Note: [Col. 0579] Genesis 26.]. For the third, the son of the Shunammite woman said: “My head aches, my head aches” [Note: [Col. 0579] IV Kings 4.].

From the first came ointment; from the second, a washing; from the third, nourishing and shining oil. The first, from feet and hands:

> Which the sacred blood anointed,  
> Poured from the body of the Lamb.

From the side came blood and water:

> Earth, sea, stars, and world  
> Are washed by that stream.  
> [Note: [Col. 0579] Hymn for Passion Sunday.]

From the head came oil, whence: “Your name is poured-out oil” [Note: [Col. 0579] Song of Songs 1.]. The first was a wave of blood; the second, blood and water; the third, a tear. Behold the burdensome battle.

It was skilfully contrived in its victory, [Col. 0580B] because infirmity was set out as bait, while divinity lay hidden as the hook. Life was dying, so that death itself might die. The greedy one seized, but hell disgorged the prey which the wicked one had devoured. Behold the skilfully contrived battle, showing how the Creator and Redeemer of the world saw indeed that “there is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0579] Proverbs 21.].

> For Christ, the unconquered Lion,  
> Having conquered the dragon, rises;  
> Obedient, from the sacrifice  
> A victor, through the heights of the world,  
> He raises up his sons.  
> [Note: [Col. 0579] Hymn for the Ascension.]

The glorious battle in triumph follows. Therefore:

> Tell forth, O tongue, the battle  
> Of the glorious contest.

O how glorious was the triumph, when, at the Ascension, with captivity set free, companies follow Jesus to [Col. 0580C] the homeland! Angels come to meet the risen one, wondering at his power. Christ himself

> Presents before the Father’s face  
> The glory of his victorious flesh.  
> [Note: [Col. 0579] Ibid.]

Thus:

> Tell forth, O tongue, the battle  
> Of the glorious contest,  
> And concerning the trophy of the cross  
> Declare the noble triumph  
> [Note: [Col. 0579] Hymn for Good Friday.]

so that with him we may deserve to attain eternal glory.

## His head is finest gold

[CARD.] For, as the Apostle says: “The head of every man is Christ, but the head of Christ is God the Father” [Note: [Col. 0579] I Corinthians 11.], who begets from himself a coeternal Son, just as finest gold produces from itself a radiance [Col. 0580D] equal to itself. Or, by the head of Christ his mind may be understood; and his head is called finest gold because in his mind “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0579] Colossians 2.].

It follows: His locks, like lofty palm branches, black as a raven. In the locks, which grow from the head, are signified thoughts proceeding from the mind. Lofty palm branches reach upward; the palm also signifies victory; blackness signifies obscurity; and the raven desires to incorporate corpses into itself. Therefore Christ’s locks—that is, his thoughts—are compared to [Col. 0581A] lofty palm branches because his thoughts were upright and directed upward, and he always thought of victory over the enemy of the human race. His thoughts were also, because of their depth, unsearchable and obscure, as is signified by blackness, just as the Apostle says to the Romans: “How incomprehensible are the judgments of God, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0581] Romans 11.] His thoughts are also called raven-like, for they were occupied with incorporating sinners, who resemble corpses, into himself.

It follows: His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, and sitting beside full-flowing waters. In this verse his eyes are praised in many ways. For in doves simplicity and innocence are understood: sitting beside streams of water, they look upon waters which are presently [Col. 0581B] flowing, those which have already flowed away, and those which are flowing toward them. Likewise the Lord’s dove-like eyes, through simplicity and innocence, keenly contemplate the present, the past, and the future alike. The Lord’s eyes are also compared to doves steeped in milk because his gaze is suffused with the sweetness of loving-kindness and mercy. And these eyes see so subtly, like doves, because they rest beside the fullest streams of divine Wisdom, beside the waters of saving wisdom. For his created wisdom, as far as is permitted, approaches uncreated Wisdom.

It follows:

> His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers.  
> His lips are lilies dripping first myrrh.

[Col. 0581C] [THO] As the Lord’s words which he spoke are signified in lilies, so modest gentleness and severity of countenance are signified in his cheeks, because it is written: “The wisdom of a man shines in his face” [Note: [Col. 0581] Ecclesiastes 8.]. Therefore the cheeks are beds of spices, which, being arranged becomingly and in order, offer to those beholding them the favour of fragrance and affection. Thus Christ incarnate enlightened those present by the sweetness of virtues and teaching, and drew those absent to himself by fame. The perfumers who planted these beds are the prophets, who inserted into the sacred pages the hidden mysteries of his future incarnation, and the apostles, who inserted there the deeds he performed in the present.

His lips are called lilies because they promise the brightness of the heavenly kingdom, dripping myrrh because they preach that one reaches it through contempt for present pleasures. But this myrrh was first present in his passion, which preceded the others: he first preached it and endured it. Again, his lips were lilies when, in his own person, he preached God, who is signified inwardly by the golden colour of the lily, and man, who is signified outwardly by the whiteness of the flowers. The inward affection of the mind is customarily discerned in the cheeks. Therefore the cheeks of the beloved are called those in which it may be discerned how great is the love held inwardly.

[Col. 0582A] Cheeks are notable in three respects: if they are pale, if red, and if bearded. In paleness we understand fear; in redness, love; in a beard, honour. For God is to be feared as Lord, loved as Father, and honoured as God. Hence he himself says: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? If Father, where is my love? If God, where is my honour?” [Note: [Col. 0581] Malachi 1.]

Again: in paleness, sparingness of food; in redness, the modesty of one who loves; in the beard, manly strength and constancy. Sparingness of food is required so that the flesh may be subdued and not grow wanton; the modesty of one who loves, so that he may not presume; manly strength, so that he may correct vices in others and take up in himself the arduous path of virtues. Of the first: “See that your hearts are not weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness” [Note: [Col. 0581] Luke 21.]. Of the second, it was said to the sons of Zebedee, who presumptuously sought Christ’s love: “You do not know what you ask” [Note: [Col. 0581] Matthew 20.]. Of the third: “Enter by the narrow gate” [Note: [Col. 0581] Matthew 7.].

These cheeks are like beds of spices. A bed is first ploughed, [Col. 0582B] second sown, third watered: it is ploughed with ploughshares, sown with spices, and watered now with waters from above, now with lower waters—with the ploughshares of contrition, the spices, that is, natural and gratuitous gifts, and the waters of visiting grace. Of the first: “Judah ploughed; Jacob shall break his furrows” [Note: [Col. 0581] Hosea 10.]. Of the second follows: “Sow in justice” [Note: [Col. 0581] Ibid.]. Again: “Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field?” [Note: [Col. 0581] Matthew 13.] Of the third: “Watering the mountains from his upper chambers” [Note: [Col. 0581] Psalm 103.].

The threshing-floor of the heart is ploughed, first by recalling one’s sins: “I will recall for you all my years in the bitterness of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0581] Isaiah 38.]; then by grieving after recollection: “My sorrow is always before me” [Note: [Col. 0581] Psalm 37.]; then, after sorrow, by confession: “Confess your sins to one another” [Col. 0582C] [Note: [Col. 0581] James 5.]. It will then be sown with spices.

There are three kinds of spices. The first are natural goods; the second, gratuitous and active goods; the third, gratuitous and spiritual gifts. The first are those with which the human race was created, such as the five senses and human intelligence. The second are works of virtues, such as the work of humility and the practice of almsgiving. The third are the invisible grace of charisms. The first are instruments; the second, merits; the third, the cause of meriting.

As a figure of these, we read that the camels of the Israelites carried spices into Egypt [Note: [Col. 0581] Genesis 37.]. For some are carried into Egypt, some are bought, and some are freely given. Some—namely the first—are carried into Egypt by those who misuse natural gifts, when they are expended on works of darkness, [Col. 0582D] for Egypt has that meaning, namely by camels, that is, by the proud. To these the Apostle says: “See that you do not receive the grace of God in vain” [Note: [Col. 0581] II Corinthians 6.].

The second are bought in order that Christ may be anointed with them, because, when we perform works of virtue, we buy them by labour. With these we anoint Christ when we augment his faith by works, because “faith without works is dead” [Note: [Col. 0581] James 2.]. Hence: “The holy women bought spices so that, coming, they might anoint Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0581] Mark 16.]. The third are given freely to us, so that we may be anointed with them. Hence: “You have an anointing [Col. 0583A] from the Holy One” [Note: [Col. 0583] I John 2.]. Namely, this anointing itself teaches us about all things. Of these gifts: “Freely you have received; freely give” [Note: [Col. 0583] Matthew 10.].

With these Joseph commanded his servant physicians to anoint Jacob his dead father, so that, by their fragrance, his body might remain incorrupt and be carried from Egypt to the land of his fathers [Note: [Col. 0583] Genesis 50.]. For *aroma* (“spice”) is so called as though filling the breezes with its spreading fragrance. This Joseph is Christ; his physician-servants are the apostles, to whom he commands that they anoint their father—that is, the human race from which he was born according to the flesh—by preaching the grace of the Holy Spirit over it, until, incorrupt and free from sins, they come from the Egypt of this world to the heavenly homeland. Behold, these beds are winged and planted with spices.

[Col. 0583B] “By perfumers,” he says. There are three perfumers: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Father planted the first spices, by bestowing the gifts of nature in the first creation; the Son the second, by displaying the works of the virtues through example and preaching; the Holy Spirit the third, through the infusion of the seven gifts. These beds are watered with waters from springs, that is, with outward tears, which flow openly, as it were from the surface of the earth, in remembrance of sins. They are watered with waters from wells, that is, with deep groanings of the heart, because of our dwelling in this misery; they are watered with waters from heaven, by sighing for desire of the homeland. Of the first: “Every night I shall wash my bed with my tears” [Note: [Col. 0583] Ps. 6]; of the second: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged!” [Note: [Col. 0583] Ps. 119]; of the third: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” [Note: [Col. 0583] Ps. 41].

Likewise, they are watered with waters from the [Col. 0583C] earth, waters from rain, and waters of dew. The first are the tears of penitents; the second, the devotion of prayers; the third, confident expectation of future joys. Of the first: “Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” [Note: [Col. 0583] Jer. 9]. Of the second: “I shall give you the early rain” [Note: [Col. 0583] Jer. 5]; of the third, Job: “Dew shall remain upon my harvest” [Note: [Col. 0583] Job 29]. The first soften the earth’s dryness; the second bring the germinating seed forth into greenness; the third advance it to ripeness. The first are more troubled, the second warmer, the third richer. The first are more troubled through shame for sins; the second warmer, because by the heat of love and the moisture of devotion they make the spices grow; the third richer, because from the sweetness of heavenly delight they bring them [Col. 0583D] to maturity.

The bridegroom’s lips too are called lilies, because the lily has a golden colour within, whiteness in its petals, and fragrance in both. In the gold, the lips preach divinity; in the white petals, humanity without sin; in the fragrance, the wonderful sweetness of miracles. Or, in the gold is the wisdom of the soul; in the whiteness, the chastity of the body; in the fragrance, graceful eloquence proceeding from both. For our speech ought to begin from wisdom, issue from a clean mouth, and contain within itself the fragrance of edification. Of the first: “Let our speech be seasoned with salt” [Col. 0584A] [Note: [Col. 0583] Col. 4], that is, wisdom; of the second: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances” [Note: [Col. 0583] Ps. 11]; of the third: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but whatever is good, that it may give grace to those who hear” [Note: [Col. 0583] Eph. 4]. Let them not be insulting, which belongs to the proud; nor vain, which belongs to braggarts; nor indecent, which belongs to the lustful; nor useless, which belongs to the idle.

Such lips distil the first myrrh, namely Christ’s bitterness at his entry into this misery; they distil the second, namely harshness in his manner of life; and they distil the third, namely pain in his Passion. The first is commended for bitterness, because at his entry into this misery Christ experienced your bitterness; the second for fragrance, because of holy conduct; the third for the incorruptibility which [Col. 0584B] our flesh will have through the present Passion. Again, we read of a first myrrh, as here: myrrh compounded with vinegar and gall; and chosen myrrh in an anointing. The Magi offered the first to the child [Note: [Col. 0583] Matt. 2]; the Jews offered the second on the cross; with the third Joseph, a noble councillor, anointed the dead man in the tomb [Note: [Col. 0583] Matt. 27]. Of this Wisdom says: “I, like choice myrrh, gave forth the sweetness of fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0583] Ecclus. 24]. He received the first with gold and incense; of the second, “when he had tasted it, he would not drink” [Note: [Col. 0583] Matt. 27]; with the third he was anointed and wrapped in a linen cloth [Note: [Col. 0583] ibid.].

The first was joined with the gold of divinity and the incense of prayer, that is, of our propitiation; for “he became propitiation for our sins” [Note: [Col. 0583] 1 John 2], amid the bitterness of our weakness. Of the second, “when he had tasted it, he would not drink,” because it was the bitterness of envy and resentment. With the third he [Col. 0584C] was wrapped in clean linen, that is, received in the pure conscience of one grieving devoutly over his Passion. Or, as regards us, the beloved’s lips distil myrrh in the bitterness of confession; the second myrrh is the labour of satisfaction; the third, remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. Of the first, as here; of the second: “My hands distilled myrrh”; of the third: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he shall abide between my breasts” [Note: [Col. 0583] Song 1].

Or thus: let the term “first” distinguish it not from another myrrh but from other kinds, so that this may be said: the beloved’s lips distil knowledge of repentance, the first myrrh; they distil knowledge of God’s commandments, the second; they distil the grace of his bounty, the third. For the beloved’s lips first deal with doing penance; second, they teach men to know [Col. 0584D] God’s commandments; third, they promise the grace of spiritual goods on the way and eternal goods in the homeland. Of the first, as here; of the second: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” [Note: [Col. 0583] Mal. 2]; of the third, it is said in the Psalm: “Grace is poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever” [Note: [Col. 0583] Ps. 44].

“His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers.”

[CARD.] The perfumers, who compound spices of spiritual sweetness and [Col. 0585A] delights in the conscience, are the seven spirits who are before the throne, as John says [Note: [Col. 0585] Rev. 5], namely: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0585] Isa. 11]. These perfumers planted in orderly fashion the spices of graces and virtues in the natural powers of the soul of Jesus Christ, as though in beds. In these consists the beauty of that soul, just as the beauty of the face is seen in the cheeks. It follows: “His lips are lilies, distilling the first myrrh.” What is more beautiful, what sweeter in fragrance, than a lily? Yet how do lilies distil myrrh? This is what the Psalmist says: “His words were softened beyond oil, and yet they are arrows” [Note: [Col. 0585] Ps. 54]. Therefore the lips of the Lord, like lilies, [Col. 0585B] sweetly [suavem, “sweet”] produce a fragrance by promising the glory of eternal blessedness; but they distil most bitter myrrh when they say: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross” [Note: [Col. 0585] Matt. 16]; and again: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, brothers and sisters, children, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” [Note: [Col. 0585] Luke 14]. It follows:

“His hands are turned, golden, full of hyacinths.”

[THO.] Rightly, after the lips, the Church praises the hands, so that deeds may follow words. For what he taught in words, he demonstrated in virtues. Thus, after preaching on the mountain, descending into the valley he cleansed a leper by the mere touch of his hand [Note: [Col. 0585] Matt. 8]. His hands are also rightly called turned [on the lathe], because of their readiness in working: “For he has done all things whatsoever he willed” [Note: [Col. 0585] Ps. 113]. All other works require the careful application of a rule and keen inspection by the eyes lest they become crooked; but one who turns work on a compass requires no such things. “For he spoke, and they were made” [Note: [Col. 0585] Ps. 148]. Divinity is expressed by gold; therefore his hands are called golden, so that the virtues which he performed may be understood as divinely wrought. They are said to be full of hyacinths, which are sky-coloured, so that he may adorn with gems of this sort the vessels of election which he prepares for glory; that is, he may gladden the hearts of his own with desire, expectation, and hope of heavenly glory.

The beloved’s hands are turned, that they may lack the scruple; they are golden, lest they be without a rudder; they are full of hyacinths, so that there may be, for heavenly desire, freedom from the [Col. 0585D] scruple of ambition and avarice, the rudder of wisdom, and heavenly desire in expectation of eternal life.
