There are three works which the beloved works in us: works of penitence, works of mercy, and works of piety. Hence Job: “Three times God works with each person, that he may draw their souls away from corruption and enlighten them with the light of the living” [Note: [Col. 0585] Job 3]. Therefore works of penitence ought to be free from the scruple of murmuring; works of mercy, from the scruple of vain glory and temporal reward; works of piety, from the scruple of presumption. Of the first: “Keep yourselves from murmuring, [Col. 0586A] which profits nothing” [Note: [Col. 0585] Wisd. 1].—“Neither murmur, as some murmured and perished by the destroyer” [Note: [Col. 0585] 1 Cor. 10].—“Why does a living man murmur, a man on account of his sins?” [Note: [Col. 0585] Lam. 3]. Of the second, Paul: “I do not seek glory from you or from men; God knows. Nor was I ever an occasion of avarice to you; God is witness” [Note: [Col. 0585] 1 Thess. 2]. Of the third, the mother of the sons of Zebedee: “Lord, say that these two sons of mine may sit in your kingdom, one at your right hand and the other at your left” [Note: [Col. 0585] Matt. 20].

In the first works sin is lamented; in the second the neighbour is consoled; in the third God is honoured. Of the first: “Turn to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning” [Note: [Col. 0585] Joel 2]. Of the second, Job: “The blessing of one about to perish came upon me, and I consoled the heart of the widow” [Note: [Col. 0585] Job 29]. Of the third: “Honour the Lord from [Col. 0586B] your substance and from the first fruits of all your crops” [Note: [Col. 0585] Prov. 3]. By the first, God is rendered appeased; by the second, grateful; by the third, a member of the household. Of the first: “I afflicted you; I shall afflict you no longer” [Note: [Col. 0585] Nah. 1]. Of the second: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” [Note: [Col. 0585] Matt. 25]. 121 Of the third: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: [Col. 0585] John 14]. Of these Job says: “Three times God works with each person” [Note: [Col. 0585] Job 33].

They are called golden hands because of the wisdom by which works are guided. Hence: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” [Note: [Col. 0585] Prov. 21]. They are not called gilded, lest they be made by the outward counsel of worldly prudence; but golden, that they may be guided by the counsel of heavenly wisdom. Therefore they must have a beginning of good intention, a middle of fitting endurance, [Col. 0586C] and an end of perseverance:

> Lest the beginning conflict with the middle, or the middle with the end.

Otherwise there will result that monster of Horace, concerning which he says [Note: [Col. 0585] Horace, *Ars Poetica* 1]:

> If a painter should wish to join a horse’s neck  
> To a human head, and clothe the gathered limbs  
> With varied feathers everywhere, so that a woman  
> Fair above ends foully in a black fish—  
> Would you, my friends, admitted to the sight, restrain your laughter?

Therefore, lest works become monstrous, they should be guided by the counsel of wisdom. “Do everything,” he says, “with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” [Note: [Col. 0585] Ecclus. 32]. So did that strong woman, who worked by the counsel of her hands [Note: [Col. 0585] Prov. 31]. Therefore one must offer rightly at the beginning, distribute rightly in the middle, and complete with cheerfulness at the end. Offer rightly, that is, with good intention; distribute rightly, with discernment; complete with cheerfulness, [Col. 0586D] that is, with devotion. “If you offer rightly,” he says, “but do not distribute rightly, you have sinned.” And: “God loves a cheerful giver” [Note: [Col. 0585] 2 Cor. 9].

One must work by this rule. This is that golden rule which Achan son of Carmi took from the accursed things of Jericho, but hid away [Note: [Col. 0585] Josh. 7]. Jericho signifies the world. This rule is taken from there, because we often learn in worldly studies the means by which we wisely direct divine works. But those steal and hide it who refuse to act according to the knowledge granted them by God. With this gold we can despoil the Egyptians and enrich the Hebrews.

[Col. 0587A] By this wisdom we ought to work: that we may sustain our own weakness; secondly, for the neighbour’s benefit; thirdly, that an enemy may be reconciled; fourthly, that the love of God may be acquired and preserved. These are the four golden rings at the four corners of the ark, by which the ark itself is carried. This ark is our soul, which is raised to heaven by these rings, that is, by these works. Behold, we have seen hands turned, that is, free from the scruple of ambition and avarice; we have seen them golden, lest they lack the rudder of wisdom; we have seen them full of hyacinths, in which love for the heavenly homeland shines. But of these hyacinths some have scarcity, some abundance, some fullness: scarcity, those who are rarely in this desire; abundance, those who are frequently so; fullness, those who are so continually.

Balaam had the first when he said: “May [Col. 0587B] my soul die the death of the righteous, and may my last end be like theirs” [Note: [Col. 0587] Num. 23]. The second was had by him who said: “My soul desired you in the night, but with my spirit in my inmost heart” [Note: [Col. 0587] Isa. 26], etc. The third by him who said: “Lord, before you is all my desire” [Note: [Col. 0587] Ps. 37]. His hands were full of hyacinths.

For adornment, hyacinth is sometimes placed with a golden colour, sometimes with white, sometimes with blue-grey, sometimes with red. With gold, in those who act wisely, as here; with white, in preachers and speakers—thus in the Law the high priest wore a hyacinth-coloured tunic over the close-fitting garment [Note: [Col. 0587] Lev. 8]; with blue-grey and red, in penitents and martyrs—thus in the tabernacle hyacinth-coloured skins were placed over goats’-hair coverings and over reddened ram skins [Note: [Col. 0587] Exod. 35]. Sometimes it is joined with twisted fine linen, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet [Note: [Col. 0587] ibid.], that is, in contemplatives, who ought to have within themselves twisted fine linen, namely chastity and innocence; purple, which is royal dignity, because they govern their affections well, or because they delight to behold the King in his beauty; and twice-dyed scarlet, namely love of God and neighbour. Hence the veil before the ark hung of twisted fine linen, purple, hyacinth, and twice-dyed scarlet.

The beloved’s hands are Christ’s works: turned, because free from sins; golden, because they are from the power of divinity; hyacinth-coloured, because, though he performed many works of our weakness, they were marked out by divine miracles. Or the fullness of hyacinths in him was the fullness of grace, which he possessed [Col. 0587D] without measure.

We read that Christ had a golden back, golden hands, and a golden head. Of the first: “The hinder parts of his back are in the paleness of gold” [Note: [Col. 0587] Ps. 67]. Of the second, here. Of the third: “His head is the finest gold.” This gold is divinity; Christ’s back is humility or humanity; the hinder parts of the back are our mortality; the hands are works; the hyacinths are miracles. In the first, therefore, it was pale; in the second, adorned; in the third, finest and splendid. The first came from suffering our death; the second, from the showing of miracles; the third, from the purity of his own nature. In the first he redeemed us in humility; in the second he strengthened [Col. 0588A] us in faith; in the third he will make us blessed by his brightness.

Hear of the pale gold: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0587] Phil. 2]. Hear of that adorned with hyacinths: “The works,” he says, “which I do bear witness concerning me” [Note: [Col. 0587] John 5]. Hear of that which is finest and splendid in its own nature: “That city,” he says, “does not need sun or moon to shine in it, because the glory of God will illuminate it, and the Lamb will be its lamp” [Note: [Col. 0587] Rev. 24].

There is gold in us also: pale in our temptations; adorned with hyacinths, that is, with works of virtue; splendid in its own nature, that is, in the splendour of his majesty, in which he must be seen by us. In the first he sympathizes with our weakness; in the second he rejoices in our profit; in the third he will make us, eternally glorified, devoted to his majesty. Hear him sympathizing: “How often I wished to gather [Col. 0588B] your children” [Note: [Col. 0587] Luke 13], etc. Hear him rejoicing: “See King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of his heart’s gladness” [Note: [Col. 0587] Song 3]. Hear those devoted to majesty: “I saw the Lord seated upon a high throne, and the whole earth was full of his majesty” [Note: [Col. 0587] Isa. 6].

“His hands are turned, golden, full of hyacinths.”

[CARD.] Turning on the lathe is more ready and swift than other crafts; it observes the rule of justice and rounds off its work most beautifully. In the same way Christ’s works are well-rounded; and although they are done with a certain readiness and swiftness of action, they nevertheless do not depart from the rule of justice. The Lord’s hands are golden because of the wisdom of acting, which is signified [Col. 0588C] by gold; and full of hyacinths, a stone of sky-like colour, because everything that he did in the body proceeded from the fountain of wisdom and shone fully with a heavenly intention. Subsequently the beloved is praised for the virtue of chastity, when it is said:

“His belly is ivory, marked out with sapphires.”

[THO.] The beloved’s belly indicates the frailty of his humanity, by which he showed himself conformed to us; ivory indicates the beauty of chastity, by which he remained in the flesh immune from the corruption of fleshly sin; sapphires express the sublimity of the heavenly virtues by which he shone in the flesh. We read of the belly of the prophet, the belly of the bride, and the belly of the bridegroom—that is, of the beloved. Of the first: “My belly will sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick” [Note: [Col. 0587] Isa. 16]. [Col. 0588D] Of the second: “My belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies” [Note: [Col. 0587] Song 7]. Of the third, here.

The first is spiritual, the second material, the third singular. For the first is the understanding of the heart; the second, the Virgin’s womb; the third, in Christ, is the weakness of our humanity. In the first Christ was announced; in the second incarnate; in the third he performed many works. Of the first: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” [Note: [Col. 0587] Isa. 7]. Of the second: “A woman shall encompass a man” [Note: [Col. 0587] Jer. 31] in the womb of her bosom. Of the third: “I have shown you many good works; for which of them do you wish to kill me?” [Note: [Col. 0587] John 10].

The first is compared to a harp because of its resonance; the second to a heap of wheat because of its fruitfulness; the third to ivory because of [Col. 0589A] coolness, strength, and whiteness. The first conceives by grieving over a neighbour’s sin; it labours by deliberating how it may rescue him; it gives birth by rebuking with a free voice. Hence: “My belly shall sound for Moab like a harp.” By Moab, who was born of incest, we understand any unclean sinner; by a wall of unbaked brick, anyone prone to sin; by a wall of baked brick, anyone obstinate. To such people the prophet’s belly sounds like a harp, namely by rebuking sins from below. Hence: “My harp has been turned into mourning” [Note: [Col. 0589] Job 30].

A harp is first turned into the mud of stench, second into the mourning of sorrow, third into the sport of love: into the mud of stench through unlawful speech; into mourning of sorrow through confession or rebuke; into the sport of love [Col. 0589B] through joy and exultation. Of the first, Job: “They take up tambourine and harp; they rejoice at the sound of the instrument” [Note: [Col. 0589] Job 21]. Of the second, again: “My harp has been turned into mourning.” Of the third, David: “Praise him with tambourine, psaltery, and harp” [Note: [Col. 0589] Ps. 150].

In the first, Nebuchadnezzar invites men to worship the statue; in the second, David drives the demon from Saul; in the third, David dances before the ark of the Lord. Of the first: “When you hear the sound of the harp and psaltery and every kind of instrument, fall down and worship the statue which King Nebuchadnezzar has set up” [Note: [Col. 0589] Dan. 3]. Saul says, of the second: “Find for me someone who plays the harp well” [Note: [Col. 0589] 1 Sam. 16], and David was brought to him. Of the third: when the ark was brought from the house of Obed-edom to Jerusalem, David played the harp [Col. 0589C] with the singers [Note: [Col. 0589] 2 Sam. 6].

This belly is the human understanding, while the inward parts are the inner things of the heart. Hence: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name” [Note: [Col. 0589] Ps. 102]. For this belly conceived the incarnation of the Saviour by foreseeing it; laboured by considering within itself the benefit of that incarnation; and gave birth by announcing it.

The second belly, that of the Saviour’s bride—that is, the Virgin—conceived when the Holy Spirit overshadowed her; it did not labour, because that conception was without a man’s seed; and therefore she gave birth without pain in Christ’s nativity. Hence she is compared to a heap of wheat, because the grain of wheat fell into her earth, died, and brought forth much fruit.

The third belly, that is, the Saviour’s humanity, conceived by sharing the sorrow of [Col. 0589D] our misery; laboured through his Passion by redeeming us; and gave birth through his resurrection by leading our mortality onward to immortality. Of the first: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0589] Lam. 1]. Of the second: “By the blood of your covenant you redeemed your prisoners from the pit” [Note: [Col. 0589] Zech. 9]. Of the third: “Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him” [Note: [Col. 0589] Rom. 6].

Here he is compared to ivory because of the strength which he had amid every pressure of tribulation; because of coolness, since fleshly wantonness did not inflame him; [Col. 0590A] and because of whiteness, since in him there was complete innocence. Of the first: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” [Note: [Col. 0589] Ps. 23]. Of the second: “You will not give your holy one to see corruption” [Note: [Col. 0589] Acts 13], namely corruption of the flesh both as decay and as lust. Of the third: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0589] 1 Pet. 2].

The first belly is varied with strings; the second is surrounded by lilies; the third is marked out with sapphires. The first is varied with the strings of virtues, yet so that this variety may be harmonious, and the low notes may accord with the high, the high with the highest. The low notes are fortitude and temperance: fortitude against the pressure of tribulation; temperance against unlawful motions of the heart and fleshly wantonness. The high notes are prudence and justice: prudence against the snares of demons; justice toward one’s neighbour. The highest are faith, hope, and charity. [Col. 0590B] The first are low, because they sound more humbly: a person treats of these within himself. The second are high, because they are raised toward the neighbour or the devil. The third are highest, because they rise to God. If one of these is lacking, the others will not produce a pleasing sound, because where one virtue is absent, the others too are absent. The Apostle James: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” [Note: [Col. 0589] Jas. 2]. Therefore let them harmonize in a prophet or preacher, so that he may say with Paul: “Lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” [Note: [Col. 0589] 1 Cor. 9].

The second belly, namely that of the Blessed Virgin, is surrounded by lilies, because in her heart she had charity, that is, the golden colour in the lily; she had virginity, namely the lily’s whiteness; she had humility before human beings, angels, and God, that is, the [Col. 0590C] lily’s fragrance. Or she had several lilies: one before childbirth, one in childbirth, one after childbirth, because she was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth.

The third belly was marked out with sapphires. Sapphire has the colour of heaven. Three sapphires mark out Christ’s humanity: the first in heavenly conduct, the second in contemplation, 122 the third in the display of miracles. As a figure of the first, Ezekiel saw a man, and beneath his feet a work like sapphire stone [Note: [Col. 0589] Ezek. 1]. Those who can say, “Our manner of life is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0589] Phil. 4], sustain Christ’s feet as he walks in them. Of the second, Jeremiah: “Her Nazarites were whiter than snow, that they might shine in it, more beautiful than sapphire” [Note: [Col. 0589] Lam. 4]. For those are more beautiful [Col. 0590D] than sapphire who contemplate not heaven alone, nor angels alone, but God himself. Of the third, it is said here: “His belly is marked out with sapphires,” that is, his humanity adorned with many miracles.

In the first he instructed the disciples when he preached to them on the mountain [Note: [Col. 0589] Matt. 5]; in the second, when he was transfigured before his disciples on Mount Tabor [Note: [Col. 0589] Matt. 17]; in the third, when before them he gave sight to the blind and cleansed lepers [Note: [Col. 0589] Luke 7], etc.

We ought to possess this threefold moral belly: the first in remembering sins, the second in bringing virtues to fruit, the third in the gladness of devotions. [Col. 0591A] The first, then, conceives in remembrance of sins, labours in contrition, and gives birth in confession. Hence the prophet: “Lord, from fear of you we have conceived, laboured, and given birth to a spirit of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0591] Isa. 26]. The second conceives by gathering the words of teachers within itself, labours by deliberating how to act, and gives birth by committing the matter to effect. Thus that woman of the Apocalypse had conceived, who went into the wilderness labouring to give birth, and the dragon pursued her [Note: [Col. 0591] Rev. 12]. For the dragon pursues those who strive to bear fruit. That third belly of devotion conceives in desire, labours in sighing, and will give birth in reward. They glory in all these things, because “their glory is from childbirth, womb, and conception” [Note: [Col. 0591] Hos. 9], although the prophet takes this in the contrary sense concerning evildoers.

The first is varied with strings: for it has low notes within itself in the sorrow of groans, high notes with the priest in confession, and highest notes with God in prayer. The [Col. 0591B] second is surrounded by lilies: within itself it has the golden colour, namely love of God and neighbour; in its petals, whiteness, namely chastity of body; around itself, a good fragrance, namely a good reputation among neighbours. The third is marked out with sapphires, because it displays heavenly conduct in its works: when it prays, when it praises God aloud, and when it is glorified amid tribulation.

“His belly is ivory, marked out with sapphires.”

[CARD.] As if he were saying: His belly is not like the belly of other human beings, in whom the devil crawls through luxury, as it was said to the serpent [Note: [Col. 0591] Gen. 3], “You shall crawl on your breast and belly”; rather, his belly is ivory. For just as its whiteness is born with ivory, so the whiteness of virginity in the flesh was born with [Col. 0591C] Christ’s flesh. And because sapphire is of heavenly colour, this belly is fittingly said to be marked out—that is, beautifully distinguished—with sapphires: that is, with certain conformities to the angelic nature, which is denoted by sapphire. For holy angels possess virginity and the incorruptibility of that virginity. In angels, moreover, every movement is subject to the divine will. Therefore this belly was marked by this manifold beauty and distinguished from other bellies. For in Christ’s flesh virginity was incorruptible, and in his flesh there was no motion at variance with God’s good pleasure.

But another translation does not merely liken the purity of Christ’s flesh to angelic purity; it places it above that purity, [Col. 0591D] saying: “His belly is an ivory casket upon a sapphire stone.” It follows:

“His legs are marble columns, founded upon golden bases.”

[THO.] The Lord’s legs signify the courses of his incarnation, by which he deigned to come to save us. They are rightly called columns of marble, because they are both strong and straight. For what is stronger than marble? What straighter than a column? David beheld this strength when he said: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” [Note: [Col. 0591] Ps. 18]. Of his straightness he said: “The Lord is righteous in all his ways” [Note: [Col. 0591] Ps. 144]. Hence on the cross his legs were not broken and his garments were not torn [Note: [Col. 0591] John 19]. The golden bases upon which they are founded are the counsels of the divine promise, by which all things were provided from eternity: the incarnation of the Savior; his will to come from heaven to earth, dwell upon earth, descend into hell, rise from the tomb, and return to heaven. They are firm as marble, straight as columns, aligned with the rule of divine justice; founded upon the golden bases of divine providence.

The legs sustain the whole framework of the body by their strength, and are therefore compared with marble columns. These are the prelates who bear the burden of the Church. Those who are marble columns ought to be straight, strong, and smooth: straight in judgment, firm in battle, smooth and free from roughness; in judging subjects, in fighting tyrants, free from the roughness of sins. Of the first: “Judge rightly, sons of men” [Col. 0592B; Note: [Col. 0591] Ps. 57]; of the second: “Be strong in battle, and fight against the ancient serpent” [Note: [Col. 0591] Heb. 11]. And: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” [Note: [Col. 0591] Matt. 10]; of the third: “A bishop must be blameless, hospitable, not violent, not given to wine” [Note: [Col. 0591] 1 Tim. 3], etc. Likewise, a priest who has a blemish shall not minister in the tabernacle of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0591] Lev. 21].

We know that there are three kinds of columns: some wooden, some metal, some marble. Wooden ones were used in Noah’s ark; metal ones in Moses’ tabernacle; marble ones in Solomon’s temple, as here. The first are subject to two dangers, the second to one, the third to none. For wood rots in water and is burned by fire; bronze, however, is not damaged by water but is melted by fire; marble is corrupted neither by fire nor by water. Fire and water are the two temptations of the world: prosperity through water, adversity through fire. Prosperity causes rotting through pleasure; adversity melts through tribulation. The former therefore affects carnal persons, the latter breaks the faint-hearted.

Thus wooden columns are carnal and faint-hearted prelates; bronze ones are not carnal, but are faint-hearted; marble ones are neither carnal nor faint-hearted. The first, namely the wooden, often perish by the elements of fire and water. Such is the Gospel boy [Note: [Col. 0591] Matt. 17], who was often thrown by the demon into water and frequently into fire. He was also often dashed to the ground, because the demon makes such people incline toward earthly pleasures. And it makes him foam: foam arises from an excess of humors—that is, from superfluous thoughts—and makes him overflow into idle words, unrestrained laughter, and wanton deeds. “This kind is not cast out except by fasting and prayer” [Col. 0592D; Note: [Col. 0591] ibid.]: by fasting against the pleasure of prosperity, by prayer against the adversity of tribulation.

Prelates of the second kind, compared to bronze columns, do not rot in the waters of pleasure, but are melted by the fire of adversity. Nadab and Abihu prefigured them: they escaped the waters of the Red Sea, but perished by fire [Note: [Col. 0591] Num. 3]. Peter too was saved while walking upon the waters [Note: [Col. 0591] Matt. 14], but at the fire he denied [Note: [Col. 0591] Matt. 26]. But the third kind of prelates, understood in the marble columns [Col. 0593A], are neither dissolved by the water of pleasure nor melted by the fire of tribulation. They can cry: “We passed through fire and water, and thou didst bring us into refreshment” [Note: [Col. 0593] Ps. 65]. To them the Lord says through the prophet: “When you walk through the waters, the rivers shall not overwhelm you; when you pass through fire, you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not burn in you” [Note: [Col. 0593] Isa. 43].

Such columns are founded upon a golden base, that is, charity. For, according to the Apostle, they are “rooted and founded in charity” [Note: [Col. 0593] Eph. 3]. Founded upon such a base, they ought to cultivate the soil by uprooting the thorns of their own hearts and of others’ hearts; they must have boldness against tyrants, and in both matters the moderation of discernment. Thus, in Solomon’s temple, the bases had lions, oxen, and cherubim carved upon them [Col. 0593B; Note: [Col. 0593] 3 Kings 7], which signifies fullness of knowledge. Without this base, preaching is without usefulness; firmness of faith is weakness; almsgiving is without fruit; bodily suffering is without recompense. Hence the Apostle: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am become as sounding bronze or a tinkling cymbal. And though I have all faith so as to remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. And though I distribute all my goods as food for the poor, and give up my body so that I burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” [Note: [Col. 0593] 1 Cor. 13].

There are also columns of the soul, namely the virtues. These columns are cut, carved, and polished. They are cut when virtues are separated from vices by the tool of discernment; they are carved when the hands put into practice the good things [Col. 0593C] which the mind conceives. Thus Solomon made projecting carvings in the temple. For carvings project when the thoughts of the mind appear outwardly in example and deed. They are polished when they are struck by tribulation. In this polishing they acquire gentleness and evenness: gentleness when they are not made bitter by anger; evenness when pride is uprooted, that pride which thinks no one its equal. Of evenness: “I know how to be humbled and how to abound; everywhere and in all circumstances I have learned to be full and to hunger, to suffer need and to abound” [Note: [Col. 0593] Phil. 4]. He shows gentleness, saying: “If it be possible, so far as depends on you, being at peace with all men” [Note: [Col. 0593] Rom. 12]. Likewise: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” [Note: [Col. 0593] ibid.]. Beneath these columns is placed the base of patience [Col. 0593D], which supports the burden of the spiritual building.

In Scripture we find three kinds of bases: bronze, silver, and gold. Bronze denotes strength; silver, brightness together with strength; gold, splendor together with strength and brightness. Strength is in work, brightness in speech, splendor in the mind. Whoever preserves patience in these three bears the structure of virtues firmly, as though on a golden base. Moses used these three in constructing the tabernacle. The boards set around it signify spiritually the order of virtues; the two tenons in each board [Note: [Col. 0593] Exod. 36] are [Col. 0594A] the disposition of the mind and the performance of the deed. The two bases beneath each board are perseverance in patience and long-suffering in prosperity and adversity.

There are three other kinds of bases, now found in our buildings: wooden, stone, and painted. But these are more fragile than the foregoing, for the wooden is burned by fire, the stone is broken by frost, and the painted bears nothing but is supported by something else. These can readily be discerned in our heart. When we are kindled by the torches of anger or the flames of lust, the strength of the base of patience or abstinence in us—that is, the wooden base—is destroyed. But when charity grows cold within us [Note: [Col. 0593] Matt. 24] and the mind is divided among various desires, the stone base is split into parts by the frost of temptation. The painted base is feigned patience. It possesses likeness, not reality; color, not strength.

But in heavenly blessedness there are four orders of columns, distinguished by four colors [Col. 0594B]. The first order is saffron-colored, the second red, the third sky-blue, the fourth violet. The first is like saffron, the second a rose, the third a lily, the fourth a violet. These four varieties of color signify four orders of the blessed: the first are angels, the second martyrs, the third virgins, the fourth confessors. These columns are founded upon one golden base, which is everlasting charity; and charity never fails [Note: [Col. 0593] 1 Cor. 13].

“His legs, marble columns, founded upon golden bases.”

[CARD.] Another translation says: “His shins are marble columns.” By the shins, strong as marble columns [Col. 0594C] and bearing the entire compacted frame of the body, are signified the two virtues, namely courage and perseverance, which bear and support the whole structure of virtues and holy works. To be sufficient to support this building, these columns are founded upon golden bases: charity and wisdom, signified by gold. Courage is founded in wisdom, lest it rush headlong. Perseverance is founded in charity; otherwise it fails and does not stand. It follows:

“His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as the cedars.”

[THO.] So that he need not labor through a description point by point, he comprehends the whole in brief. Just as Mount Lebanon is renowned and distinguished by its abundance, so Christ rightfully surpasses all those born of earth by the loftiness of his grace [Col. 0594D]. That mountain is fertile in trees; he exalts the saints and roots them so that they are not moved by the wind of temptation. And all the beauty of forests yields to the beauty, strength, loftiness, and fragrance of cedars. So too the Beloved: “Fairer in form than the sons of men; grace has been poured upon thy lips; therefore God has blessed him” [Note: [Col. 0593] Ps. 44]. The Beloved, then, is chosen as the cedars, because he surpasses in singular dignity the grove of the Church in which he was born. His appearance is like Lebanon, which produces outstanding trees; and like the cedar, because among his chosen ones he created himself, as he willed, like the tree of life in the midst of paradise [Note: [Col. 0593] Gen. 2].

[Col. 0595A] We read of four mountains on which the appearance was changed: on the first the appearance of the angel was emptied; on the second the appearance of Christ was compared; on the third it was darkened; on the fourth it was raised. It was emptied because of pride, compared because of manifold grace, darkened through distress, raised from glory to glory: because of the proud aspiration to what was unlawful; because of the manifold grace of fruitfulness and loveliness; through the distress of the Passion; from the glory of the Passion to the glory of the Father’s acknowledgment. The first mountain is on the sides of the north; the second, Mount Lebanon; the third, Calvary; the fourth, the Mount of Olives. Of the first: “I shall sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north. I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0595] Isa. 14]. Of the second: “His appearance is like Lebanon.” Of the third: “We saw him [Col. 0595B] as leprous, struck by God, and humbled” [Note: [Col. 0595] Isa. 53]; likewise: “He has neither appearance nor beauty” [Note: [Col. 0595] ibid.]. Of the fourth: “All the beauty of the Lord has been exalted above the stars.”

When Lucifer fell from the first mountain [Note: [Col. 0595] Isa. 14], his beauty was emptied. Another prophet says of him: “You were the seal of resemblance, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty” [Note: [Col. 0595] Ezek. 28]. On this mountain the appearance of those is emptied who despise the lowliness of their subjects, resent equality with their peers, and envy the loftiness of their superiors. Of the first, the poet says [Note: [Col. 0595] Lucan, *Pharsalia* I]:

> One commands, the other threatens.

Of the second and third:

> Nor can Caesar now endure a superior,  
> Nor Pompey an equal.

Of the first, Christ says: “See that you do not despise one of [Col. 0595C] these little ones” [Note: [Col. 0595] Matt. 18]. In the second, he did not reject equality when paying the tax; for he said: “You will find a stater in the fish’s mouth; pay it for me and for yourself” [Note: [Col. 0595] Matt. 17]. Of the third, he did not refuse to say: “The Father is greater than I” [Note: [Col. 0595] John 14]. Indeed, he was subject to his inferiors, namely his putative father Joseph and Mary. Indeed, he bent down to wash the disciples’ feet [Note: [Col. 0595] John 13].

Hear something greater: there are those who resent being subject to their superiors; secondly, they strive to make themselves their equals; thirdly, they even strive to surpass them. Thus Absalom, when he was in Jerusalem, first resented being subject to his father [Note: [Col. 0595] 2 Kings 13]. Secondly, he reigned in Hebron, now as if equal to his father, but this did not suffice. Thirdly, he wished to reign alone when he drove his father from Jerusalem, and thus perished [Note: [Col. 0595] 2 Kings 18]. So Saul was killed on the mountains of Gilboa—which means “slippery” or “descent” [Col. 0595D] [Note: [Col. 0595] 1 Kings 31]. Behold: pride, born in heaven, descended to earth, because, as it is said, “It is heavenly in origin and dwells in ashes.” Hence: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” [Note: [Col. 0595] Ecclus. 10]. Thus, brothers, “the heart is exalted before ruin” [Note: [Col. 0595] Prov. 16]. See that “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” [Note: [Col. 0595] Jas. 4]. Job thought thus when he said: “Why does your heart lift you up, and why, as though thinking great things, do you hold your eyes fixed?” [Note: [Col. 0595] Job 15]. The Lord says through David: “He who practises pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” [Note: [Col. 0595] Ps. 100], because, as it is written:

[Col. 0596A]

> . . . God breaks every proud person.

On the second mountain, which is treated here, the comparison of the Beloved is made for four reasons: his height, breadth, fruitfulness, and pleasantness. His height is in miracles; his breadth, in charity; his fruitfulness, in spiritual pastures; his pleasantness, in mystical trees. Of miracles: “The blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed” [Note: [Col. 0595] Luke 7]. Of charity: “Because of the exceeding charity with which he loved us, when we were dead in sin Christ made us alive together” [Note: [Col. 0595] Eph. 2]. “For he first loved us, and washed us from our sins in his blood” [Note: [Col. 0595] Rev. 1]. By the fruitfulness of his pastures he refreshes us at the spiritual table.

There are three tables at which we are refreshed on this mountain, and three outside this mountain. Of the tables outside this mountain [Col. 0596B], the first is that of man, the second that of the flesh, the third that of the devil. The first serves necessity, the second excess, the third deadly drunkenness. At the first, according to Paul, “Let him who is weak eat vegetables” [Note: [Col. 0595] Rom. 14], lest his heart be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness [Note: [Col. 0595] Luke 21]. At the second there is offered wine “from the vineyard of Sodom and the suburbs of Gomorrah” [Note: [Col. 0595] Deut. 32]. At the third, “their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” [Note: [Col. 0595] ibid.].

The first has this lesson: “Not in revelries and drunkenness” [Note: [Col. 0595] Rom. 13]. The second: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” [Note: [Col. 0595] 1 Cor. 15]. At the third: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” [Note: [Col. 0595] Prov. 2]. At the first one lives from the labors of one’s hands: “‘You shall eat,’ he says, ‘the labors of your hands; [Col. 0596C] blessed are you, and it shall be well with you’” [Note: [Col. 0595] Ps. 127]. Hence it adds: “Your children, like young olive trees around your table” [Note: [Col. 0595] ibid.]. At the second table sat the rich man clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting every day; but Lazarus waited for the crumbs that fell from his table [Note: [Col. 0595] Luke 16]. Such was Herod’s table, whence:

> The drunken luxury of the tyrant’s table was filled with a virgin’s sober blood.

Of the third: “Let their table become a snare before them” [Note: [Col. 0595] Ps. 68]; and Paul: “You cannot be partakers of Christ’s table and the table of demons” [Note: [Col. 0595] 1 Cor. 10].

There are three tables on this mountain at which the Lord, or Beloved, refreshes us. The first was in the Law, the second in the Gospel, the third in heaven. Moses speaks of the first in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0595] ch. 25], where it is said to have been placed in the tabernacle near the entrance; upon it were twelve loaves of presentation bread made of fine flour, and upon each a golden dish with a handful of incense. Of the second the Apostle says: “You cannot share in the table of Christ and of demons.” Of the third Christ says: “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” [Col. 0596D; Note: [Col. 0595] Luke 22]. The first therefore showed refreshment but did not provide it; the second satisfies, the third glorifies. The first was in the letter, the second in the spirit, the third in vision. The first teaches, the second aids, the third brings to completion.

Or again: the first is in the Law, the second in the Gospel, the third in heaven [Col. 0597A]. The first is Moses’ table, the second Christ’s, the third God’s. The first was in figure, the second in truth, the third will be in glory. The first teaches, the second perfects, the third glorifies. We can also make other divisions of these tables, drawn from Scripture, in this way: the first table is under the Law, the second under grace, the third in glory. The first is shown by Moses in Exodus, the second in the Gospel, the third in the kingdom. The first was the table of presentation in the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0597] Exod. 25]; of the second it is said: “You cannot share in the table of Christ and the table of demons” [Note: [Col. 0597] 1 Cor. 10]; of the third: “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0597] Luke 22]. The first is in the letter, the second in the spirit, the third in vision. The first displays, the second gives a taste, the third satisfies. At the first the paschal lamb is eaten under the cloud of a figure; at the second, under a sacrament; at the third, openly.

Of the first it is said: “You shall eat it in the same house” [Col. 0597B; Note: [Col. 0597] Exod. 12]. Of the second: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” [Note: [Col. 0597] Ps. 33]. Of the third: “I shall be satisfied when thy glory appears” [Note: [Col. 0597] Ps. 16]. The middle table is that of our own time. At it the bride invited the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple trees.” For the Blessed Virgin said this to her incarnate Son. She had within herself a threefold fruit: the fruit of her womb, the fruit of her mind, and the fruit of prayer. The first is Christ’s incarnation, the second virtuous devotion, the third devout prayer. Of the first the angel says: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” [Note: [Col. 0597] Luke 1]. And she herself says: “I, like a vine, have borne the fruit of sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers are the fruit of honor and uprightness” [Note: [Col. 0597] Ecclus. 24]—namely [Col. 0597C] Christ. For she was the vine, Christ the cluster; the flowers were the violet of humility, the rose of charity, and the lily of virginity.

> O chamber of the Word of God,  
> Delightful in affections,  
> Serene in conduct,  
> Full of grace.

Of the second it is said: “Hearken, divine fruits, and bear fruit like a rose planted beside streams of water” [Note: [Col. 0597] Ecclus. 39]. Hear the divine fruits: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, peace, patience, goodness, kindness” [Note: [Col. 0597] Gal. 5], etc. These proceed from the rose of charity and grow beside the streams of God’s grace. Of the third the Church sings: “Through you we have shared in the fruit of life.” These are the three fruits [Col. 0597D] which the scouts of the children of Israel brought from the holy land: the cluster on the vine, that is, Christ on the cross; the fig, that is, the sweetness of devotion; and pomegranates, that is, the fruit of Mary’s prayer. For as the outer rind is pale, so the Church is bruised with tribulation. Within are many purple grains: the faithful hidden within her, who by the prayer of the Blessed Virgin shall be clothed in royal purple in the kingdom.

These three are signified when it is said: “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb”—that is, the sweetness of prayer—“honey and milk are under your tongue” [Note: [Col. 0597] Song 4]. Under the tongue is the heart, in which is honey, namely the sweetness of devotion. Again, beneath the tongue is the womb, in which is milk: that is, Christ’s flesh, taken from the ancient fathers as milk is taken from animals.

According to another consideration, we read in the divine page of five tables [Col. 0598A]: the first, the poor person’s; the second, the world’s; the third, the devil’s; the fourth, the rich man’s; the fifth, the Father’s. The first is of necessity, the second of vanity, the third of iniquity, the fourth of truth, the fifth of consummation. Nature sets the first, avarice the second, unbelief the third, grace the fourth, life the fifth. The first restores strength, the second provokes, the third chokes, the fourth satisfies, the fifth completes. At the first sit beasts, at the second serpents, at the third dogs, at the fourth birds, at the fifth heirs. Of the first, the Gospel says: “Even the little dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ tables” [Note: [Col. 0597] Matt. 15]. Of the second, Isaiah says [Col. 0598B]: “Babylon’s table is a golden cup in it” [Note: [Col. 0597] Jer. 51]. Of the third the Apostle says: “You cannot partake of the table of demons and of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0597] 1 Cor. 10]. Of the fourth: “My son, if you sit at a rich man’s table, attend diligently to what is set before you” [Note: [Col. 0597] Prov. 23]. Of the fifth: “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0597] Luke 22].

The poor man whose table is the first is the human race. On it are set bread, broth—or salt—and drink. Of the first, David says: “I have forgotten to eat my bread” [Note: [Col. 0597] Ps. 101]. Broth is the same as salt. Hence in Ezra [Note: [Col. 0597] 1 Ezra 4]: “Do you suppose that we are forgetful of the salt which we eat in your court?” The water is that which Abraham put in a skin and laid upon Hagar’s shoulders [Note: [Col. 0597] Gen. 21].

At the second table, where serpents sit, five things are set out. It is the vanity of the world, and serpents always urge vain things. Boethius numbers these five in the *Consolation of Philosophy*: human favor, riches, dignities, glory, and power. The first attracts air, that is, favor; the second, sand, that is, covetousness; the third, sparks, that is, the desire for power; the fourth, gems, that is, the glory of riches; the fifth licks the limbs, signifying the pleasure of lust. Serpents sit at this table, because they never cease creeping in order to climb to higher things.

At the fourth table—which is the devil’s—three things are set out [Col. 0598C]: *seneciae*, husks, and *quisquiliae*. A *sene* is an unclean animal; hence: “*Seneciae* are any unclean foods.” Others say *senencias* or *sinantias*. A *sinantia* is a kind of membrane in the mouth which unclean creatures are accustomed continually to chew. A husk is a kind of legume with broad pods, but empty within. *Quisquiliae* are the sweepings of hemp and flax. *Seneciae* are the foods of gentiles who eat things sacrificed to idols; husks are the foods of Jews who cling to the outer covering; *quisquiliae* are the foods of heretics, namely erroneous opinions. These are the unclean dogs who sit at this table.

At the fourth table, which is the rich man’s table, three things are set out: the fatted calf, the good things of the earth, and the marrow of wheat. The calf is that which the father killed for the son returning from a far country [Note: [Col. 0597] Luke 15]. The good things of the earth are readings; hence Isaiah—or rather Leviticus 26—says [Col. 0599A]: “You shall eat the very oldest of old stores, and, when new things come in, you shall cast away the old.” The very oldest of old stores are the natural and moral precepts, which we eat by observing and proclaim by preaching. You shall cast away the old things—that is, the legal observances—when new things come in, that is, the grace of the Gospel. The marrow of wheat is the most purified flour placed in sacrifices; this is prayer.

The Lord sets these three against three others: against the flesh, against the world, and against the devil. Against the incitements of the flesh he gives us the fatted calf, that is, the flesh and blood of Christ. He sets reading against the world, which invites us to its wanderings. But let us say to it: “Get behind me, Satan” [Note: [Col. 0599] Mark 8]. Against the devil he sets prayer, for the devil never ceases to trouble all religious persons [Col. 0599B], but they have recourse to the remedy of prayer. At this rich man’s table sit birds, namely holy people who hope to fly from this fourth table to the fifth. This rich man is Christ, both rich and poor in one: rich because he is God, poor because he is man. At this table sit those who fight against the devil, the world, and the flesh, that they may be able to attain the fifth and final table.

The final table, the fifth, is the Father’s table. At it sit heirs. At this table only one thing is set out, namely the vision of God, and not many things. Hence Martha was told: “But one thing is necessary” [Note: [Col. 0599] Luke 10], and no more. And David: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek,” namely, “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” [Note: [Col. 0599] Ps. 26].

[Col. 0599C] Fourthly, we said that this mountain possesses the pleasantness of trees. It has pleasantness in the green freshness of leaves, the varied color of flowers, and the coolness of shade. These trees are virtues: their leaves are green in words of edification; the variety of flowers smiles in works of virtue; in their shade the heat of vices is tempered. Of the first: “Its leaf shall be green, and in the time of drought it shall not be anxious” [Note: [Col. 0599] Jer. 17]. Of the second: “Flowers have appeared in our land” [Note: [Col. 0599] Song 2]. Of the third: “You shaded my head in the day of battle” [Note: [Col. 0599] Ps. 139].

On the third mountain, namely Calvary, we said that his appearance was darkened. Do you wish to see the darkness? Look upon the blasphemy of the Jews, the disgrace of the thieves hanging around him, the crown of thorns upon his head, the piercing by nails in his hands, the narrow opening of the wound in his side [Col. 0599D]. Behold, “he has neither appearance nor beauty” [Note: [Col. 0599] Isa. 53]. Behold, according to the Apocalypse: “The sun became like a sackcloth of hair” [Note: [Col. 0599] Rev. 6]; and the prophet’s saying: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood” [Note: [Col. 0599] Joel 2]. For darkness came upon the earth during his Passion.

Of the fourth mountain we said that through death the Lord’s appearance was raised. For from it your magnificence was raised above the heavens; from it all the beauty of the Lord was exalted above the stars. Therefore angels marvel, saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe” [Note: [Col. 0599] Isa. 63]. Behold, his appearance [Col. 0600A] is like Lebanon. It follows: “Chosen as the cedars.” The cedar is compared to the Beloved for its height and incorruptibility, its straightness, and its fragrance. For height: while others are sons by adoption, he alone is the Son of the Father by nature. For incorruptibility: neither did Christ’s body decay in death, nor did any stain cling to him. For straightness: according to the rule of justice he will render to each according to his merits. For fragrance: while others draw people by good conduct, he does so both by conduct and by promises.

Of the first: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” [Note: [Col. 0599] John 1]. Of the second: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0599] 1 Pet. 2]. And of his flesh: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” [Note: [Col. 0599] Ps. 15]. Of the third: “The Lord is righteous and loves righteous deeds; his face beholds equity” [Col. 0600B; Note: [Col. 0599] Ps. 10]; and: “Let my judgment come forth from your countenance” [Note: [Col. 0599] Ps. 16]. Of the fourth: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what the Lord has prepared for those who love him” [Note: [Col. 0599] 1 Cor. 2].

“His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as the cedars.”

[CARD.] As if to say: Why do I range through individual details? His appearance is like Lebanon, which is interpreted “whitening”; as if to say: His appearance is known from this, that he is the whitening of all saints, through whom all saints are made beautiful and clean. His appearance is also like Lebanon because, just as Mount Lebanon surpasses other mountains in breadth, height, and fertility in trees, so Christ is distinguished above the sons of men. And he is chosen above all others as the cedar, a tree which surpasses all the beauty of forests in abundance, beauty, strength, height, [Col. 0600C] and fragrance, because the Spirit was not given to Christ by measure. It follows:

“His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable.”

[THO.] If above we understood words in the lips of the Beloved, then in His most sweet throat we ought rightly to understand the inward savor of those same words. Hence: “They shall pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of Your sweetness, and shall exult in Your righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0599] Ps. 144]. Peter had already tasted the remembrance of the abundance of God’s sweetness, and, pouring it forth, said: “Desire the rational milk without guile, that by it you may grow unto salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” [Note: [Col. 0599] 1 Pet. 2]. Again, as the lips signify the words that He spoke, so the throat signifies the inward and hidden disposition of compassion. But [Col. 0600D] He also showed the fruit of His own throat when, after the Resurrection, He breathed upon the disciples, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0599] John 20]. “And He is altogether,” he says, “desirable.” The whole Christ is God and man—that is, Word, soul, and flesh—because He is desirable not only by reason of the unchangeable majesty of His eternal divinity, but also by reason of the glorified substance of His assumed humanity. Above all because, when He ascended into heaven in order to transfer us to His glory, He promised that He would return, saying: “If I go and prepare a place for you, I come again and will receive you to Myself, [Col. 0601A] that where I am, you also may be” [Note: [Col. 0601] John 14].

There are three throats: the first fleshly, the second rational, the third spiritual. The first is that of the pleasure-lover, the second of the teacher, the third of the Beloved. For the pleasure-lover tastes first in order to satisfy the flesh; the teacher second, in order to distinguish; the Beloved third, in order to relish the things above. The first brings death; the second distinguishes between life and death; the third excludes death. Of the first Job says: “Can anyone taste that which, when tasted, brings death?” [Note: [Col. 0601] Job 6]. Of the second: vinegar was offered to Christ, “and when He had tasted it, He would not drink” [Note: [Col. 0601] Matt. 27]. Of the third: “Whoever eats of this bread shall not taste death for ever” [Note: [Col. 0601] John 6].

It is written in the Law: “An animal that chews the cud and does not have a cloven hoof is unclean” [Note: [Col. 0601] Lev. 11]. Likewise, that which has a [Col. 0601B] cloven hoof and does not chew the cud is unclean; but that which chews the cud and has a cloven hoof is clean [Note: [Col. 0601] Ibid.]. The first are the fleshly, namely the unclean, because with fleshly taste they chew over their pleasures, but do not divide the hoof, since they do not distinguish between good and evil, lawful and unlawful. The second are the rational, who divide the hoof—that is, by a kind of rational taste distinguish good from evil—but do not chew the cud, because they do not delightfully chew over the good which they distinguish from evil by reason. The third are the spiritual, who, by rational taste distinguishing good from evil, divide the hoof and chew the cud, while they sweetly turn over in their heart, delighting in it, the good which they have discerned.

Because of fleshly taste, honey is forbidden by the Law to be added to God’s sacrifice; [Col. 0601C] because of the third taste, that is, the spiritual, salt is commanded to be added to every sacrifice; because of the middle taste, that is, the taste of discernment, it is commanded that the victim’s skin be removed, its limbs cut into pieces—that is, its thoughts—and its blood poured upon the ground—that is, its thoughts. For we must separate the skin, that is, the manner of life of the flesh; then cut the limbs into pieces, that is, examine in the heart whether thoughts are fleshly or spiritual; and pour the blood, that is, fleshly appetite, upon the ground.

The first throat has sweetness in speech, a sweet flavor in inward delight; but bitterness follows in condemnation. Hence Solomon: “The lips of a harlot drip honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood” [Note: [Col. 0601] Prov. 5]. [Col. 0601D] In the lips dripping honeycomb are pleasurable words; in the smoothness of the throat, inward and savory delight; in the bitterness of wormwood, eternal condemnation.

The second throat, namely that of discernment, must first recognize the nature of a thing; second, weigh whether its use is good or bad; third, once it has known the good use, adopt it for itself. Hence Solomon: “When you sit at the table of a rich man, carefully consider what is set before you”—that is, consider the nature of the thing—“and put a knife to your throat” [Note: [Col. 0601] Prov. 23], that is, consider with the sharpness of discernment the use of the thing, and know [Col. 0602A] that you ought to prepare such things for yourself: that is, take the foreknown use of the thing into the service of your Lord, namely God, who gives you all things.

*Guttur*, “throat,” is so called from tasting and grinding; for food is first ground by the teeth, then tasted, and afterward conveyed into the stomach. It is ground by speaking, tasted by delighting, and conveyed into the stomach by entrusting it to memory. Some grind but do not taste, like hypocritical preachers; and some fleshly people taste but do not grind, namely those who are devout but inconstant. Some both grind and taste, and convey it into the stomach, as those who persevere in devotion do.

Herod chewed the cud but did not taste, when he said: “Go and inquire diligently concerning the child, so that I also, when I come, may adore Him” [Note: [Col. 0601] Matt. 2]. Balaam ground and tasted when he said: “Let my soul die [Col. 0602B] the death of the righteous” [Note: [Col. 0601] Num. 23]; but he did not transmit it to the stomach, because shortly afterward he gave counsel for their death. Stephen chewed the cud, tasted, and conveyed it into the stomach of memory, because even while he was being stoned he both preached and prayed [Note: [Col. 0601] Acts 7].

The throat is sweet, sweeter, and sweetest. Thus the third throat is sweet in those who are devout for a moment, sweeter in those who are so more frequently, and sweetest in those who possess a continual taste; and this is the Beloved. It follows:

“And He is altogether desirable.” There is a man who is altogether hateful; there is a man who is desirable in some respect; and there is a man who is altogether desirable. The first is devoid of every virtue; the second is endowed with many virtues; the third is furnished with every grace. The first is an obstinate sinner; the second is a lover of God and of the brethren; [Col. 0602C] the third is the Savior. Of the first: “I have hated the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0601] Ps. 118]. Of the second, David is said by interpretation to mean “desirable in appearance.” Of the third the prophet says: “The Desired One of all nations shall come” [Note: [Col. 0601] Hag. 2], that is, Christ.

For He is desirable in body, desirable in soul, desirable in divinity: in body, in which the Bridegroom is “beautiful in form above the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0601] Ps. 41]; in soul, in which He possessed the fullness of graces; in divinity, by which He is “King of kings and Lord of lords” [Note: [Col. 0601] 1 Tim. 6]. In the first He endured the Passion for us; in the second He showed great charity toward us; in the third we shall receive the recompense for our labor. Of the first Isaiah says: “We desired Him as the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity” [Note: [Col. 0601] Isa. 53]. Of the second: “My soul has desired [Col. 0602D] You in the night” [Note: [Col. 0601] Isa. 26]; and: “O Lord, Your memorial is in the desire of the soul” [Note: [Col. 0601] Ps. 134]. Of the third: “O Lord, before You is all my desire, and my groaning is from You” [Note: [Col. 0601] Ps. 37], etc.

Likewise, He was desirable in exile, desirable in hell, desirable in judgment, and desirable in the kingdom: in exile to sinners, in hell to the righteous who awaited Him, in judgment to those who love Him, and in the kingdom to those who exult. To sinners, that they might be justified; to the righteous, that they might be delivered; to those who love Him, that they might be transferred securely to the right hand away from the harsh word; to those who exult, [Col. 0603A] because they shall enjoy the vision of God. Hence the first say: “Come, Lord, and do not delay. Forgive our sins” [Note: [Col. 0603] Office of the Church]. The second: “Come to deliver us, O Lord God of hosts.” Of the third Paul says: “There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just Judge, shall render to me on that day; and not only to me, but also to those who love His appearing” [Note: [Col. 0603] 2 Tim. 4], “into which angels desire to look” [Note: [Col. 0603] 1 Pet. 4].

David reveals the reasons why He is desirable, saying: “O Lord my God, You are exceedingly magnified” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 103]. Why? Because “You have put on praise and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ibid.]. From the truth of Sacred Scripture we gather that Christ is great, magnificent, and magnified: great in the essence of divinity; magnificent in the creation [Col. 0603B] of worldly variety; magnified in the advancement of assumed humanity. In the first, because He is incomprehensible; in the second, because He is beyond estimation; in the third, because He is incomparable. In the first He puts on praise through faith; in the second He puts on beauty through the ordering of the world; in the third He is clothed with light as with a garment through the Resurrection. The first comes about through miracle, the second through the governance of the world; through the third He became a glorious spectacle to men and angels.

Hear that He is great: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 77]. Hence: “I fill heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0603] Jer. 23]. And that He is magnificent: “All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” [Note: [Col. 0603] John 1]; and: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0603] Gen. 1].—“Who alone performs great wonders” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 71]. [Col. 0603C] Hear that He is magnified: “The Lord is magnified, because He dwells on high” [Note: [Col. 0603] Isa. 33].—“Go, and do likewise” [Note: [Col. 0603] Luke 10].

Therefore be great in the gathering of spiritual goods, magnificent in outward action, that you may be magnified in eternal recompense. Therefore be great: first by hoping, second by aspiring, third by sighing, fourth by breathing again. The first comes about because a man is aroused by the heavenly calling; the second because desire is kindled; the third because desire is delayed; the fourth because, contemplating heavenly goods, he delights in them.

Hear the calling from which hope comes. The Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” [Note: [Col. 0603] Col. 3]. [Col. 0603D] The same says: “Those whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son; and those whom He predestined, He also called; those whom He called, He also justified; and those whom He justified, He also magnified” [Note: [Col. 0603] Rom. 8]. The Bridegroom called the bride: “Arise, hasten, my friend, and come” [Note: [Col. 0603] Song 2].

From this comes hope. “Hope does not confound” [Note: [Col. 0603] Rom. 5]. From this a man advances and aspires to the things above, because his desire is kindled. Hence: “My heart was inflamed” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 72]; and: “Your name and Your memorial are in the desire of the soul” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 134].—“My soul has desired [Col. 0604A] You in the night, and also my spirit within me” [Note: [Col. 0603] Isa. 26].—“Was not our heart burning within us,” concerning Jesus, “while He spoke to us on the way?” [Note: [Col. 0603] Luke 24]. Led by this desire, the Bride said: “Let Him kiss me with the kiss of His mouth” [Note: [Col. 0603] Song 1].

They sigh because of delay, because “hope deferred afflicts the soul” [Note: [Col. 0603] Prov. 13]. Hence David: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 41]. And the Bride: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell the Beloved that I languish with love.” Likewise David: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged!” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 119]. Behold why they sigh: “I remembered God,” David says, “and was delighted” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 76], because “at Your right hand are delights unto the end” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 15]. Why? “For the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest where she may lay her young” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 83]. For there “in peace I shall sleep and rest [Col. 0604B] in the selfsame” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ps. 4]. Hence the Bride: “I sleep, but my heart watches.” “I adjure you,” says the Bridegroom, “do not stir her up or awaken her until she herself wills it” [Note: [Col. 0603] Song 8]. She herself also says: “Under the shadow of Him whom I desired I sat, and His fruit was sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0603] Song 2]. Hence men cry out concerning her in admiration: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her Beloved?” [Note: [Col. 0603] Song 8].

On account of these four things it is said of Joseph: “A growing son” [Note: [Col. 0603] Gen. 49]. Joseph, whose name means “increase,” is the one who is increased by hoping; “growing,” while aspiring to the things above; likewise growing while sighing in desire; and beautiful in appearance in the meditation of heavenly things, and therefore breathing again. Thus this greatness results. Hence it is said of Job: “That man was great among all [Col. 0604C] the men of the East” [Note: [Col. 0603] Job 1].

Here it must be known that some are great among those of the West, some among those of the North, some among those of the East, and some among those of the South. The first, because in falling they entangle themselves in great crimes; the second, because they weary others with great temptations; the third, because they advance in virtues; the fourth, because they burn more than others in heavenly things.

The first great one in the West was the devil. Hence he himself says: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.”—“How have you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, you who rose in the morning?” [Note: [Col. 0603] Isa. 14]. Of the second it is said: “A storm wind came from the north, and a great cloud” [Note: [Col. 0603] Ezek. 1]. Of the third: “That man was great among all the men of the East.” Likewise, of the same man: “He was simple and upright, [Col. 0604D] fearing God and departing from evil” [Note: [Col. 0603] Job 1]: simple, seeking no pride or boastfulness from good works; upright, practicing no fraud or malice against his neighbor; fearing God, lest through his sins grace might be diminished in him; departing from evil, punishing in himself daily even slight sins through repentance.

Isaac was great among those of the South; of him it is said: Isaac went toward the south. And not long afterward: “Isaac went on growing and advancing, until he became great” [Note: [Col. 0603] Gen. 26]. He went by hoping; he grew by aspiring; he advanced by overcoming; he became great [Col. 0605A] by restoring. Behold, you have become great; see to it that you are magnificent. For Christ Himself was magnificent in the creation of the world: “For in the beginning He created heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0605] Gen. 1]. He created heaven for the angels. Your heaven is your soul; adorn it with the aforesaid virtues. Your earth is your body; by adorning it with good works, you will be magnificent.

For the earth often drinks the rain coming upon it, and, bringing forth vegetation suitable in its seasons, receives blessing from God from those by whom it is cultivated. But that which brings forth thorns and briers is reprobate and near to a curse; its end is in burning. Let this heaven be adorned with virtues; let this earth be fruitful in good works; and thus you will be magnificent. Moreover, let a man be munificent, magnificent, and wonder-working. Munificent, [Col. 0605B] by aiding the poor and needy from his labors and resources; magnificent, by crucifying his flesh with its vices and lusts through virtues; wonder-working, by laying down his life for his brethren. In the first he supplies his neighbor’s need; in the second he produces benefit for his own soul; in the third he possesses perfect charity. Of the first: “Break your bread for the hungry” [Note: [Col. 0605] Isa. 58], etc. Of the second: “Rend your hearts, and not your garments” [Note: [Col. 0605] Joel 2]. Of the third: “No one has greater charity than that a man lay down his life for his friends” [Note: [Col. 0605] John 15].

The first stores up treasures for himself in heaven; the second merits the renewal of incorruption; the third, with Christ, the glory of immortality. Therefore, in that the Bridegroom has been magnified, He is in some measure desirable—He into whom [Col. 0605C] angels desire to look—and whom, if we now wish to advance in virtues, all of us will not cease to praise and bless in the kingdom.

“His throat is most sweet.”

[CARD.] Because He has the words of eternal life, and is altogether desirable, since He is He into whom angels desire to look, at last the Virgin concludes her discourse and says:

“Such is my Beloved, and this is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.”

[THO.] The more devoutly the Church, or any soul, loves God, the more intimately it has Him as a friend. For one who, still because of weakness of mind or consciousness of sin, keeps God’s commandments in servile fear has not yet been able to attain that apostolic perfection by which he deserves to hear: “I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard from My Father I have made known to you” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ibid.].

Having set forth the description of the Beloved, and showing from the matters included in that description that He is worthy of love, he adds three terms full of mystery: namely, Beloved, friend, daughters of Jerusalem. In the first is shown that He is worthy to be loved by her; in the second, she rejoices because she is loved by Him; in the third, she invites devout souls to love Him, that they may thus be loved by Him. For *dilectus* (“beloved”) is so called as though “worthily chosen”; *amicus* (“friend”) as though “guardian of the soul”; and daughters [Col. 0606A] of Jerusalem, as though daughters of the vision of peace.

He is therefore Beloved: that is, worthily chosen by God to be sent into the world; by angels to render Him service; by human beings to bear His sweet yoke; into the world, to manifest His power, justice, and mercy—His power in miracles, His justice in merits, His mercy toward the afflicted. His power in miracles, to call back unbelievers; His justice in merits, to terrify sinners and kindle the righteous; His mercy toward the afflicted, to strengthen the fainthearted. Of the power of miracles He says: “If you do not believe My words, at least believe the works” [Note: [Col. 0605] John 10]. Of the justice of tribulations: “These shall go,” He says, “into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0605] Matt. 25]. Of mercy toward the afflicted: “I have seen,” He says, “I have seen the affliction of My people [Col. 0606B] who are in Egypt; I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them” [Note: [Col. 0605] Exod. 3].

Thus the Beloved sent into the world manifested the Father: “Father,” He says, “I have made Your name known to the men whom You gave Me” [Note: [Col. 0605] John 17]. Behold the Beloved, that is, the One worthily chosen by God. He is also Beloved, that is, worthily chosen by angels, to whom they render service, so that He might restore the angelic fall. Hence the prophet: “He Himself will restore the ruins of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0605] Zech. 12].

They rendered Him service at His birth, announcing Him to the shepherds: “There was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying, Glory to God in the highest!” [Note: [Col. 0605] Luke 2]. They rendered service also in His childhood, appearing to Joseph in dreams; service in His temptation, carrying Him away from the pinnacle of the Temple; service in His Passion, when the strengthening angel was present [Col. 0606C] with Him; service in His Resurrection, when two angels appeared in white garments; service in His Ascension, when two men stood in white garments, saying: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?” [Note: [Col. 0605] Acts 1].

For He is Beloved, that is, worthily chosen by human beings to bear His sweet yoke, in order that He might lighten the yoke of the first parent’s disobedience. Hence: “You have overcome the yoke of his burden and the sceptre of his oppressor” [Note: [Col. 0605] Isa. 9]. The righteous man bears His threefold yoke: namely, the yoke of discipline, the yoke of modesty, and the yoke of patience—of regular discipline, of modesty amid insults, and of patience under scourges. The first makes gentle, the second humble, the third prepares rest. Hence He says: “Take My yoke upon you, and learn of Me, because I am gentle and humble [Col. 0606D] of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” [Note: [Col. 0605] Matt. 11].

Behold how He is Beloved, that is, worthily chosen for us to love. He is also friend, the guardian of the soul. For in three ways He knows us as a friend, as David says: “The Lord guards you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul. May the Lord guard your going in and your coming out” [Note: [Col. 0605] Ps. 120]. Behold, “guards” is said three times. First, He guards from every evil, lest you be deceived by suggestion or corrupted by another’s example; second, He guards your soul lest it be infected by the vice of pleasure or excessively terrified; third, He guards your going in [Col. 0607A] lest, when you begin to suffer scourges for Christ, you yield; and your coming out, so that when you depart from the world through inflicted death, you may even rejoice in that death.

Thus He is friend, that is, guardian of the soul, in order to guard you in both small and great virtues. For there is a small virtue, a lesser one, and a least one. The small virtue is not to be deceived by suggestion; the lesser is not to be corrupted by another’s example; the least is not to be infected by the vice of the will. There is also a great virtue, a greater, and a greatest. Great is not to fear threats; greater is not to yield to scourges; greatest is not merely to endure inflicted death manfully, but even to rejoice in it.

But He shows to whom He is such when He adds: “Daughters of Jerusalem,” that is, daughters of the vision of peace. There are three daughters of Jerusalem. The first is the righteous soul which delights in the love of God; the second is the Church militant, which [Col. 0607B] is still in pilgrimage; the third is the blessed soul which now enjoys rest. The first sees peace in purity of conscience; the second when it lacks persecution; the third because it is free from every calamity. The first has peace with respect to vices; the second from tyrants, schismatics, and heretics; the third from the corruption of old age.

The first is figured in the leper cleansed by God [Note: [Col. 0607] Matt. 8]; the second in the little boat laboring at sea, which the Savior aids [Note: [Col. 0607] Ibid.]; the third in the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor, in which God’s glory is manifested while the disciples stand by [Note: [Col. 0607] Mark 9]. The daughter of Jerusalem sees the first peace within herself, the second around herself, the third above herself. For there will be rest for the body from labor, peace for the soul from temptation, and security for both from the devil’s power. Rest from labor: for now the Spirit says, [Col. 0607C] “That they may rest from their labors” [Note: [Col. 0607] Rev. 14]. Peace for the soul from temptation: “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 4]. Security for both from the devil’s power, because: “The enemy shall profit nothing against him, and the son of iniquity shall not add to harm him” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 88].

Of these the philosopher says [Note: [Col. 0607] Boethius]:

> Come hither, all you captives  
> Whom deceiving earthly desire, dwelling in minds,  
> Binds with wicked chains, dwelling in earthly minds.  
> Here shall be rest from your labors;  
> Here a harbor remaining in tranquil calm;  
> Here the one open refuge for the wretched.

The Beloved, that is, the One worthily chosen by the Father, is He who, as the Angel of Great Counsel, descended to you by the grace of consolation into the prison of this world. The friend, namely the guardian of the soul, is He who, clothed in the cloud of flesh, [Col. 0607D] provided refreshment against the heat of temptations; who formed us by word and example, and invited us to rewards by miracles. John saw such a one in the Apocalypse, saying: “I saw a mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0607] Rev. 10].

O truly prudent steward, true friend, faithful physician! The first, because He forestalls the malice of the enemy; the second, because He provides angelic protection for His sheep; the third, because He offers Himself in this exile as a saving victim, and in the kingdom as grace and [Col. 0608A] glory. For our enemy is the angel of death; the guardian is an angel who improves his own lot [reading uncertain]. The first is the devil; the second is the good spirit created by God; the third is the Son of God. The first did not so much descend as was cast headlong from heaven to his own confusion; the second descends for man’s consolation; the third descends for the redemption of the human race. The first, indeed, is cast headlong; the second is sent by God; the third is predestined by God.

Of the first: “How have you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” [Note: [Col. 0607] Isa. 14], etc. Of the second: “Jacob saw a ladder and angels ascending and descending” [Note: [Col. 0607] Gen. 28].—“For they are all ministering spirits, sent for ministry” [Note: [Col. 0607] Heb. 1]. Of the third: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having great authority, and the whole earth was illuminated by his glory” [Note: [Col. 0607] Rev. 18]. This One was predestined by God. [Col. 0608B] Hence Paul: “Who was predestined Son of God in power” [Note: [Col. 0607] Rom. 1].

126. But for what purpose this friend descended, He Himself says: “I descended into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys and to inspect whether the vines had flowered and the pomegranates had budded” [Note: [Col. 0607] Song 6]. The nuts in the garden of the Church are those who struggle under the heaviness of sufferings; the fruits of the valleys, those who restrain themselves in humility; the vines, those fervent in charity; the pomegranates, those united in unanimity. The first follow their friend, namely Christ, manfully; the second bear fruit abundantly; the third love ardently; the fourth live together harmoniously.

Of the first: “The saints suffered mockings and scourges, moreover also bonds and prisons” [Note: [Col. 0607] Heb. 11]. Of the second: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that [Col. 0608C] He may exalt you in the day of visitation” [Note: [Col. 0607] 1 Pet. 5]. He also answers: “Neither have I walked in great matters nor in wonders above me” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ps. 130].—“For he who has lowered his eyes shall be saved, and he who has been humbled shall be in glory” [Note: [Col. 0607] Job 22]. The third say: “Was not our heart burning within us,” concerning Jesus, “while He spoke to us on the way?” [Note: [Col. 0607] Luke 24]. Likewise: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame” [Note: [Col. 0607] Song 8]. The fourth are guarded by Him “who makes those of one manner dwell in a house” [Note: [Col. 0607] Isa. 67]. These are “careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 0607] Eph. 4]. Thus it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” [Note: [Col. 0607] Acts 4].

The animals of Ezekiel are read to have possessed these four properties. They were strong, because “where the impulse was, there they went; nor did they turn back when they went” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ezek. 1].
