They were humble: [Col. 0608D] “For when there was a voice above the firmament that was over their heads, they stood and lowered their wings” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ibid.]. They burned with charity, because “their appearance was like burning coals of fire, and like the appearance of lamps” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ibid.]. Likewise: “And sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ibid.]. They went unanimously, because “when the living creatures went, it was like the sound of an army camp, like the sound of a multitude” [Note: [Col. 0607] Ibid.].

But I find these four things also in the angel set before us, namely our friend. And when I see them in anyone, I can say: [Col. 0609A] “Such is my Beloved.” “I saw,” he says, “a mighty angel” [Note: [Col. 0609] Rev. 10], on account of patience, because “He became obedient to the Father unto death” [Note: [Col. 0609] Phil. 2]. It follows: “Clothed with a cloud” [Note: [Col. 0609] Rev. 10], on account of humility, because “He emptied Himself, becoming obedient unto death” [Note: [Col. 0609] Phil. 2]. “A rainbow on His head” [Note: [Col. 0609] Rev. 10], on account of the unanimity by which in Christ we are all one [Note: [Col. 0609] Gal. 3], because the Father presents a holy Church having neither spot nor wrinkle [Note: [Col. 0609] Eph. 5]. For He Himself is the living bread from many grains, which are the faithful in the Church. The rainbow is upon His head, having many colors because of the various crowns of the saints. “And His face was like the sun” [Note: [Col. 0609] Rev. 10], because of charity appearing outwardly. “His feet were like pillars of fire” [Note: [Col. 0609] Ibid.], because of charity hidden inwardly.

Therefore He is called mighty on account of patience. [Col. 0609B] Hence He is called: “The mighty God, Father of the world to come” [Note: [Col. 0609] Isa. 9]. For He was mighty on the cross, mighty in hell, mighty in rising again: on the cross, where He did not fear death; in hell, where He bound Satan; in rising again, where He utterly trampled death down. Hence in Job: “If strength is sought, He is most strong” [Note: [Col. 0609] Job 9]. In the first He was “Issachar, a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries” [Note: [Col. 0609] Gen. 49].—“Truly He Himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” [Note: [Col. 0609] Isa. 53]. In the second He was “the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” [Note: [Col. 0609] Ps. 23]. In the third He was that mighty Samson who, after killing the lion, found in its mouth a swarm of bees [Note: [Col. 0609] Judg. 14].—“Go therefore, and do likewise” [Note: [Col. 0609] Luke 10].

In accordance with the first, be strong by mortifying the flesh; in accordance with the second, by resisting the devil; in accordance with the [Col. 0609C] third, by rising from eternal death through love of the Spirit. Hear, concerning the first, what is said of the strong woman: “She girded her loins with strength and strengthened her arm” [Note: [Col. 0609] Prov. 31]; concerning the second: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in [Col. 0610A] faith” [Note: [Col. 0609] 1 Pet. 5]; concerning the third: “Who shall find a strong woman? Her worth is far off and from the uttermost bounds” [Note: [Col. 0609] Prov. 31]; likewise: “Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she shall laugh on the last day” [Note: [Col. 0609] Ibid.].

It follows: “Clothed with a cloud” [Note: [Col. 0609] Rev. 10]. O blessed cloud, which guides those who wander, offers grace to those who labor, corrects sinners, and lifts heavenward those who sigh! It guides by the will, so that penitents may endure hard and bitter things; it offers grace, so that they may present the gifts of virtues; it corrects, lest they be lifted up by prosperity; it raises them by removing the weight of earthly burden. The first is signified by the cloud which gave guidance to the children of Israel; the second by the cloud in which the Holy Spirit appeared at the Transfiguration; the third by the cloud signifying the apostles, which drenched the earth; the fourth by the cloud which, when the Lord ascended, rendered Him splendid [Col. 0610B] service.

Of the first: “It was for them a covering by day and a light of stars by night” [Note: [Col. 0609] Wis. 10]. The second cloud offers grace; hence: “We saw Him full of grace and truth. And of His fullness we have all received grace for grace” [Note: [Col. 0609] John 1]. In this cloud the Holy Spirit appeared at the Transfiguration. Of the third: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” [Note: [Col. 0609] Isa. 60]. Of the fourth: “And a bright cloud received Him from their eyes” [Note: [Col. 0609] Acts 1].

When I see these clouds in anyone, I recognize in them the image of Christ, namely my Beloved, and cry out:

“Such is my Beloved, and He is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.”

“Such is my Beloved.”

[CARD.] Namely, such as I have described; and He is my friend, [Col. 0610C] who has revealed His secrets to me and knows mine. Therefore, once the question concerning the Beloved’s character and beauty has been resolved, the daughters of Jerusalem, desiring to know where her Beloved is and where He may be found—because she had said above, “I adjure you, if you find my Beloved”—accordingly add their question:

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 0609]

[Col. 0609D] “Where has your Beloved gone, O most beautiful of women? Where has your Beloved turned aside? And we will seek Him with you.”

[THO.] When the daughters of Jerusalem hear the description of the beloved which they had so earnestly sought, they add the question of where he has gone; for this too must be learned within the unity of holy Church—especially in the hearts of what sort of persons, and in what manner of life, the Lord is usually found. The Church is called the fairest also among women, because, although her beauty is great throughout the world in particular churches, as in women made fruitful by a spiritual flower, yet, gathered together from all these as from her own members, she is believed to be far more beautiful [Col. 0610D].

But God’s grace is often withdrawn from a soul. If one asks why this happens, it is unknown—where he has gone or turned aside, that is, whether it occurs for advantage or disadvantage. Here another kind of knowledge is sought, namely that which follows: “and we will seek him with you.” The beloved goes away in five ways. First, by withdrawing protection, when he exposes a person to tribulation; second, when he withdraws a grace which may be absent without danger to the soul, such as knowledge, kinds of tongues, interpretations of utterances, or the spirit of prophecy; third, when he withdraws the grace of strength; fourth [Col. 0611A], by withdrawing the sweetness of devotion; fifth, by ascending into heaven through the removal of his bodily presence.

Of the first Christ says in his Passion: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” [Note: [Col. 0611] Matt. 27.] Of the second, Elisha, when the Shunammite woman came to him: “Her soul,” he says, “is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden it from me” [Note: [Col. 0611] 4 Kings 4.]; of the third: “The spirit of the Lord departed from Samson,” after his seven locks had been shorn [Note: [Col. 0611] Judg. 16.]; of the fourth David says: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 50.]; of the fifth Christ says: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come” [Note: [Col. 0611] John 16.].

The first departure causes anxiety in the one left behind; the second shows a person his weakness; in the third he loses his strength; in the fourth he loses much sweetness; from the fifth he awaits the consolation of the Holy Spirit. Of these five Job says: “Who will grant me that I might be as in former months, according to the days in which God guarded me?” [Note: [Col. 0611] Job 29.] Behold the first: “When his lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked in darkness?” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ibid.] Behold the second: “According to the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tent, and my servants were around me?” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ibid.] For God is in the tent of the heart when virtues are possessed inwardly; servants are around it when those virtues are outwardly committed to action. Behold the third: “When I washed my feet with butter?” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ibid.]—that is, my affections with the richness of devotion. Behold the fourth: “And the rock poured out for me streams of oil?” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ibid.]—“Now the rock was Christ” [Note: [Col. 0611] 1 Cor. 10.], [Col. 0611C] especially established in the Resurrection; he poured out streams of oil, that is, he gave human beings the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

First, the beloved withdraws himself so that a person, placed and tested in tribulations, may deserve more abundantly; second, that he may be made humbler; third, that he may rise again stronger; fourth, that he may seek more eagerly the sweetness he has tasted beforehand; fifth, that he may give believers hope of eternal blessedness.

We read of his threefold bending down: he bent down by descending from heaven, he bent down in writing, and he bent down in dying. Of the first: “He bowed the heavens and came down” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 17.]; of the second: “Again Jesus, bending down, wrote with his finger upon the ground” [Note: [Col. 0611] John 8.]; of the third: “Having bowed his head, he gave up the spirit” [Note: [Col. 0611] John 19.]. In the first he changed the exalted to humility; in the second he taught the cruel compassion; in the third he taught the disobedient to persevere [Col. 0611D] in obedience unto death. For in the first Christ “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0611] Phil. 2.]; concerning the second he cries: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” [Note: [Col. 0611] Matt. 5.]; in the third, “he became obedient to the Father unto death” [Note: [Col. 0611] Phil. 2.].

Likewise we too, brethren, ought to bow down our eyes, lest our brows savor of pride; secondly, to incline our ears, in order to receive instruction from Christ’s Passion; thirdly, to incline our heart, so that it may be prepared also to render obedience to one who is lower [Col. 0612A]. Of the first it is read in Job: “He who has bowed down his eyes shall be saved, and he who has been humbled shall be in glory” [Note: [Col. 0611] Job 22.]; of the second David says: “I shall incline my ear to a parable; upon the psaltery I shall unfold my proposition” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 48.]; of the third the same man said: “I have inclined my heart to perform your ordinances forever, for the sake of recompense” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 118.].

We also read of a threefold resting-place of the beloved: for he reclined in the bridal chamber, reclined in the manger, and reclined in a dwelling-place—in the bridal chamber of the Virgin, in the manger of the ass and ox, and in the dwelling-place of the heart. Of the first it is said that Solomon made for himself a golden resting-place in his litter [Note: [Col. 0611] Cant. 3.]. Of the second, that “Mary and Joseph laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn” [Note: [Col. 0611] Luke 2.]. Of the third [Col. 0612B], by contrast, it is said: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” [Note: [Col. 0611] Matt. 8.]. Some interpret this literally of the Lord’s cross, but morally of the human heart. In the first, divinity rested; in the second, human weakness; in the third, God’s loving-kindness. In the first: “He was made a little lower than the angels” [Note: [Col. 0611] Heb. 2.]; in the second, he was prefigured as the future food of the faithful beasts; in the third: “A lamp for the soul sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” [Note: [Col. 0611] Ps. 106.].

Morally, the beloved has these three places of reclining in us. In the place of the virginal bridal chamber, we conceive him when we begin to possess purity of conscience. When, laboring well in the works of virtue, we receive him while retaining the simplicity of the ass—that is, so that in our works we admit neither sensual pleasure, nor vanity, nor malice [Col. 0612C]. We bring him into the heart if we offer him the frequent delight of devotion. Behold the beloved’s bending down; after this comes the turning aside of which we have begun to speak. Yet it is more to turn aside than merely to go away. To go away is to go somewhere and depart from somewhere; to turn aside is, after leaving, to hide oneself as though in some place where one is difficult to find. But it should be noted that the beloved does not withdraw or turn aside from anyone by inflicting evil upon him or taking away a good from him, but by not bestowing his grace upon him, or by not sustaining the grace already bestowed.

He who thus turns aside must be sought with the bride. There are some who knowingly do not seek where he is; some who unknowingly seek where he is; and some who knowingly seek where he is. The first are perverse persons; the second are deceived in religion by their own singularity; the third are discerning religious persons. The first, “when they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0611] Rom. 1.]. The second, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to God’s righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0611] Rom. 10.]. The third cry with the bride: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you rest at noon” [Note: [Col. 0611] Cant. 1.]. The first deserve punishment; [Col. 0613A] the simplicity of the second will at some time deserve to receive counsel; the third will reap in their homeland the reward—namely, the beloved whom they seek with the bride in every devotion.

[CAR.] “Where has your beloved gone, O fairest among women? Where has your beloved turned aside, that we may seek him with you?” They therefore propose two questions; but the fairest among women does not answer the first, namely, “Where has your beloved gone?” For where Christ went when he emerged from the tomb, and where he rested during those continuous forty days in which he appeared in turn to his disciples, he himself knows, but Scripture does not tell. But to the second question, namely, “Where has your beloved turned aside?”, she answers as follows:

## CHAPTER VI.—My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.

[Col. 0613B]

[THO.] This garden is the Church; it is also the faithful soul; and it is rightly called his own. He himself made it, cultivated it, sowed it with the fragrant plants of virtues, watered it with the fountain of his grace so that it should not fail, and enclosed it with the wall of his protection so that it should not be profaned by strangers. In it he sowed the grain of mustard seed—that is, the word of God, small in humility but ardent in charity—which later grows and stretches the branches of virtues on high, so that the birds of heaven, that is, the angels, may rest in them, delighting in the progress of human beings. In this garden he suffered, was seized, crucified, buried, and rose from death. He wished to be thought a gardener by Mary Magdalene [Col. 0613C] [Note: [Col. 0613] John 20.]. In this garden too he planted the virtue of patience, contempt for death, hope of blessed rest, and desire for blessed immortality.

And it is fittingly said that he “went down,” not that he entered. For this garden is in the valley of tears, whereas his own place is lofty; hence: “The Lord is high, and looks upon lowly things; and he knows lofty things from afar” [Note: [Col. 0613] Ps. 137.]. Therefore he went down into it in order to make us ascend. Hence in Exodus Moses ascended the mountain [Note: [Col. 0613] Exod. 19.], but the Lord came down in order to make us ascend.

“To the bed of spices,” he says. The bed of spices is the mind of the faithful which has been instructed in the discipline of right faith, turned over by the digging of diligence, and cleared of the superfluous weeds of vices. He also adds what he comes to do there: “to pasture in the gardens and [Col. 0613D] gather lilies.” He pastures in the gardens because he delights in the devout labors of the saints and in spiritual fruits; he gathers lilies when he leads the just from this life, perfected in the whiteness of their merits, and conveys them elsewhere.

There are three descents of the beloved. The first is from heaven; the second, from the gibbet of the cross; the third, from the throne of the kingdom. The first was into the Virgin’s womb; the second, into the tomb, and from the tomb into hell; the third, upon the Mount of Olives. From there he will ascend when he comes to judgment. The garden into which he descends is the universal Church. In it are three beds of spices to which he descends. The first [Col. 0614A] we know to be that of the Virgin; the second, that of the tomb; the third, that region of the air in which all will meet him at judgment. The spices of the first are spiritual; those of the second material; those of the third incorruptible. The first is the fullness of grace; the second, the anointing of Christ’s body; the third, the glorification of bodies and souls. Of the first it is said: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices” [Note: [Col. 0613] Cant. 4.], because the blessed Virgin was full of grace [Note: [Col. 0613] Luke 1.]. Of the second it is said that the holy women bought spices in order to come and anoint Jesus [Note: [Col. 0613] Mark 16.]. Of the third: “Make yourself like, my beloved, a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” [Note: [Col. 0613] Cant. 8.].

He descended to the first in order to scatter seeds; to the second, in order to take pasture; to the third, in order to gather lilies: the seeds of preaching, the pasture of captivity to be liberated [Col. 0614B], and the lilies of glorified flesh. Of the first: “The sower went out to sow his seed” [Note: [Col. 0613] Luke 8.]; of the second: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell” [Note: [Col. 0613] Hos. 13.]; and: “I have food to eat which you do not know” [Note: [Col. 0613] John 4.]; and: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover” [Note: [Col. 0613] Luke 22.]; of the third: “He shall blossom like a lily” [Note: [Col. 0613] Hos. 14.].

Morally too, the soul of the just person is a bed of spices, that is, of virtues. In it seeds are scattered, he himself feeds, and lilies are gathered.

There are three seeds which the beloved scatters in it. The first is the word of instruction, that is, preaching; the second is the casting down of the body in tribulation; the third is the humble beginning of charity. Of the first: “The seed is the word of God” [Note: [Col. 0613] Luke 8.]; of the second: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation” [Note: [Col. 0613] Ps. 125.]; of the [Col. 0614C] third: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed” [Note: [Col. 0613] Matt. 13.]. This grain is small when it is sown, but it grows to become greater than all herbs. So charity, founded in humility, rises above all the shoots of virtues. From the first arises knowledge of the divine will; from the second will arise the glory of incorruption; from the third, perpetual love among human beings and angels. Of the first: “The word of God was spread throughout the whole region” [Note: [Col. 0613] Acts 13.]; of the second Paul says: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” [Note: [Col. 0613] 1 Cor. 15.]; the third is the seed which fell into good soil and produced a hundredfold fruit [Note: [Col. 0613] Luke 8.].

The Lord figures this threefold seed in three parables. The first is the seed which falls now into good soil [Col. 0614D] and produces a hundredfold fruit, now into bad soil, because there are those who make progress in the word of God and those who fall away from it. The second is that of which he says: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, has died, it remains alone; but if it has died, it bears much fruit” [Note: [Col. 0613] John 12.]. For there are some who are a grain of wheat falling into the ground when they mortify themselves, yet do not die because they expect from this temporal advantage or human praise. The third is that which a man sowed in his field, and the enemy oversowed weeds [Note: [Col. 0613] Matt. 13.]. For there are those in whom the Lord sows [Col. 0615A] the good beginning of charity, but the devil brings them to the point of turning it toward the use of vanity.

Behold what the beloved sows in this bed. In it he feeds on three pastures. First he feeds on works of mercy; second, on pure virginity; third, on sweet devotion. Of the first he says: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat” [Note: [Col. 0615] Matt. 25.]; of the second: “He who feeds among lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline” [Note: [Col. 0615] Cant. 2.]; of the third, in the Apocalypse: “If anyone opens to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” [Note: [Col. 0615] Apoc. 5.].

These three were prefigured in the three meals which the Lord celebrated with his disciples after his Resurrection. He ate with those going to Emmaus, who compelled him to accept hospitality [Note: [Col. 0615] Luke 24.]; this pertains to works of mercy. He ate with [Col. 0615B] the fishermen on the shore a portion of roasted fish and a honeycomb [Note: [Col. 0615] Ibid.]; this concerns the purity of virginity. In the roasted fish, mortification against the lust of the flesh is signified; in honey, which does not arise from intercourse but from the pure flowers of virginity, pure refreshment. He dined with his disciples when about to ascend to heaven, commanding them not to depart from Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0615] Ibid.]. For in Jerusalem, whose name means “vision of peace,” the devout remain while they contemplate peace, and this devotion is Christ’s refreshment.

In this bed he also gathers lilies when, by a certain spiritual intimacy, he draws to himself those beautiful in virtues. There are three lilies: the first of innocence, the second of virginity, the third of perfection. Of the first: “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among daughters” [Note: [Col. 0615] Cant. 2.]. For as [Col. 0615C] a lily is among thorns, so is the innocent person, who is peaceable, “with those who hate peace” [Note: [Col. 0615] Ps. 119.]. Of the second: “You who feed among lilies, surrounded by choirs of virgins”; of the third: “I shall be like dew, and Israel shall blossom like a lily” [Note: [Col. 0615] Hos. 14.]. That this lily signifies perfection is taught by the following text: “Its root shall burst forth like Lebanon, and its branches shall spread” [Note: [Col. 0615] Ibid.]—that is, its virtues shall grow until they receive the perfection of glory. Hence it follows: “And his glory shall be like that of the olive tree” [Note: [Col. 0615] Ibid.].

Hear of the first: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent,” he says, “in hands and pure in heart” [Note: [Col. 0615] Ps. 23.]. Behold, he gathers this; he gathers the second also. For he says: “These follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and they are without stain [Col. 0615D] before God” [Note: [Col. 0615] Apoc. 14.]. Hear how he gathers the third too: “If you wish,” he says, “to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me” [Note: [Col. 0615] Matt. 19.].

This lily is fourfold, for perfection is fourfold: there is the perfection of prelates, the perfection of contemplatives, the perfection of clerics, and the perfection of those who fear. These four have four signs. The sign of prelates is to lay down their life for their sheep [Note: [Col. 0615] John 10.]; that of contemplatives, to follow Christ and leave all things; that of clerics is continence [Col. 0616A]; and that of those who fear is to desire death and endure life patiently. To the first it is said: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” [Note: [Col. 0615] John 10.]; to the second: “Set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0615] Col. 3.]. But they themselves also say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0615] Phil. 3.]; to the third it is said: “Not in reveling and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies” [Note: [Col. 0615] Rom. 13.]. The fourth say: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0615] Phil. 1.].

Christ descends into this garden in order to remain with us. Therefore, desiring him, they say: “O Emmanuel, our leader and lawgiver, expectation of the nations and their Savior, come and save the human being whom you formed from clay” [Note: [Col. 0615] Proper of the Third Sunday of Advent, at Vespers.]. Blessed be God, who, so that we may find consolation in this exile, sends us so many comforters from heaven. Michael was sent [Col. 0616B] to Daniel [Note: [Col. 0615] Dan. 10.], Raphael to Tobit [Note: [Col. 0615] Tob. 3.], Gabriel to Mary [Note: [Col. 0615] Luke 1.], and Emmanuel to the whole human race.

The first was to Daniel as a chief captain; through the second, light was restored to Tobit; the third became Mary’s messenger; the fourth became our leader. The first is called the standard-bearer of mysteries; the second, Tobit’s light-bearer; the third, Mary’s bearer of salvation; the fourth, the Christians’ lawgiver. Michael is the chief captain of those who fight; Raphael, the physician of the sick; Gabriel, the manifestation of those who wait; Emmanuel, the expectation of the nations. Michael is the guide of souls to paradise; Raphael, the physician of infirm souls; Gabriel, the strength of the robust; Emmanuel, their Savior. The first, to gladden the soul which the devil deformed; the second, to heal the soul which the devil rendered shapeless [Col. 0616C]; the third, to strengthen the soul which the devil weakened; the fourth, to save the human being whom he formed from clay.

But if we consider the matter morally, these are the stages by which the soul itself advances, as is clear from the meanings of the names. Michael means “Who is like God?”; Raphael, “God’s medicine”; Gabriel, “God’s strength”; Emmanuel, “God with us.” First the sinner raises himself to admiration of divine magnificence; second, he runs to healing through the satisfaction of repentance; third, he receives strength in doing good works; fourth, he ascends to fellowship with Christ, who is here called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.”

Of the first: “A human being approaches a lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0615] Ps. 63.], so that he may say with the Apostle: “O [Col. 0616D] man, who are you to answer back to God?” [Note: [Col. 0615] Rom. 9.] And Job: “If he should wish to contend with him, he could not answer him one thing out of a thousand,” because “he is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has resisted him and had peace?” [Note: [Col. 0615] Job 9.]

Having therefore seen this greatness, in accordance with the second he cries: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” [Note: [Col. 0615] Ps. 6.]; and: “Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” [Note: [Col. 0615] Ps. 40.]. For this angel heals from vices; and this is the leper whom Christ healed [Note: [Col. 0615] Matt. 8.]. He heals hands from the cessation of good work, and this is the man whose withered hand Christ restored in the synagogue [Col. 0617A] [Note: [Col. 0617] Matt. 12]. He heals ears so that they may not be stopped against hearing divine words; and the Lord restored hearing to the deaf man [Note: [Col. 0617] Mark 7.]. He heals the mouth so that it may open for divine speech; and the Lord healed the mute man [Note: [Col. 0617] Ibid.]. He heals the eyes of the heart for the task of contemplation; hence the Lord also healed the eyes of the man blind from birth [Note: [Col. 0617] John 9.].

Three things prevent these eyes from seeing heaven: vanity, which is the dimness of the eyes. Thus Job says: “My eyes have grown dim” [Note: [Col. 0617] Job 16.]. But the dimness had fallen away when he said: “By the hearing of the ear I heard you, but now my eye sees you” [Note: [Col. 0617] Job 42.]. Worldly anxiety: these are the films which fell from Tobit’s eyes [Note: [Col. 0617] Tob. 11.]. The pressure of tribulation: these are like the scales which fell from Paul’s eyes [Note: [Col. 0617] Acts 9.].

Such a person, healed like Tobit, now receives heavenly things, and the angel Gabriel—that is, [Col. 0617B] God’s strength—comes to meet him. He therefore becomes strong, not with the strength of which it is said: “A man shall not be strengthened by his own strength” [Note: [Col. 0617] 1 Kings 2.], but with that of which it is said: “I shall keep my strength for you” [Note: [Col. 0617] Ps. 58.].

We ought to be strong with a threefold strength: in laboring, in enduring, and in resisting. In laboring, when works of repentance are done; 128 in enduring, when affliction is inflicted; in resisting, when temptation is imminent. As a figure of the first: “Who shall find a strong woman? She has worked according to the counsel of her hands” [Note: [Col. 0617] Prov. 31.]. Job laments that he does not fully possess the second when he says: “Neither is my strength the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze” [Note: [Col. 0617] Job 6.]. The Lord preached the third to his own, saying: “Be [Col. 0617C] strong in battle.” These are the three mighty men who brought David water from the spring that is at the gate of Bethlehem. This strength brings Emmanuel, that is, brings it about that God is with him.

God is with us in three ways: temporally, spiritually, and eternally. Temporally through the Incarnation; spiritually through the infusion of grace; eternally through glorification. The first, that he might fight for us; the second, that he might adorn us; the third, that he might glorify us. He fought in order to restore to us the inheritance of our homeland; he adorned us with the robe of innocence; he will glorify us with the crown of glory. As a figure of the first, David fought with Goliath [Note: [Col. 0617] 1 Kings 17.]; as a figure of the second, the good father clothed the prodigal son with the first robe [Note: [Col. 0617] Luke 15.]; as a figure of the third, the golden crown and little crown hung above the table of the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0617] Exod. 25.].

First, therefore, he is with us [Col. 0617D] through the Incarnation, to fight for us, lest perhaps the enemy say: “I have prevailed against him” [Note: [Col. 0617] Ps. 12.]—“For those who afflict me have multiplied; many rise up against me” [Note: [Col. 0617] Ps. 3.], so that I must cry: “Attack those who attack me. Take hold of weapon and shield, and rise up to help me” [Note: [Col. 0617] Ps. 34.]. And: “My enemies have trampled me down all day, because …” [Note: [Col. 0617] Ps. 55.], etc. But “the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior” [Note: [Col. 0617] Jer. 20.]—“horns are in his hands” [Note: [Col. 0617] Hab. 3.]. For there is no other who fights for us except [Col. 0618A] you, our God [Note: [Col. 0617] 2 Esdr. 4.].

That you may also teach us to fight “through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left,” he explains when he adds: “through glory and dishonor, through evil report and good report” [Note: [Col. 0617] 2 Cor. 6.]. Through glory on the right, so that one may not be lifted up; through dishonor on the left, so that one may be humbled by it; through evil report on the left, so that the conscience may not be disturbed by it; through good report on the right, so that the conscience may be cheerful.

In the second way Emmanuel is with us, when he adorns us with the robe of innocence. This robe is first purchased, secondly firmly guarded, and thirdly, one clothed in it serves the Lord: it is purchased by the fruit of repentance, guarded by watchful circumspection, and serves the Lord by obedience and devotion.

As a figure of these three stages of innocence, we read of three linen cloths, which signify the whiteness of innocence [Col. 0618B]. The first is read of as sold, the second as cast away, the third as wrapping Christ’s flesh. Of the first it is said concerning the strong woman: “She made linen cloth and sold it” [Note: [Col. 0617] Prov. 31.]. Therefore, one must labor, not be idle, in order to purchase this; hence Solomon: “Hand in hand, the wicked shall not be innocent” [Note: [Col. 0617] Prov. 11.]. Of the second it is said: John was “clothed with a linen cloth upon his naked body,” but did not guard it well, because “casting away the linen cloth, he fled” [Note: [Col. 0617] Mark 14.]. For both he and all the others sinned in Christ’s Passion; hence Christ himself says: “All of you will suffer scandal because of me this night” [Note: [Col. 0617] Matt. 26.]. David proposed that he would guard this firmly when he said: “Judge me, Lord, because I have walked in my innocence; and, trusting in the Lord, I shall not be weakened” [Note: [Col. 0617] Ps. 25.].

In the third [Col. 0618C] Joseph, that noble councillor, is shown to have offered service and devotion to God, when it is said: “Joseph wrapped the body of Jesus in a clean linen cloth” [Note: [Col. 0617] Matt. 27.]. Of this David says: “The innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor—he shall receive blessing from the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0617] Ps. 23.].

Thirdly, Emmanuel will be with us when he crowns us with the crown of glory. But Christ himself first becomes a crown for us; secondly, it is given to the soldier; thirdly, the soldier is crowned. He is a crown in the Resurrection; it is given to the soldier in the consummation of a good life; he will be crowned with it once the examination of judgment is finished. Of the first it is said: “You shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a diadem in the hand of our God” [Note: [Col. 0617] Isa. 62.]; of the second: “He magnified him in the sight of kings and gave him a crown of glory” [Col. 0618D] [Note: [Col. 0617] Office of the Church.]; of the third: “The Lord crowned him with glory and honor” [Note: [Col. 0617] Ps. 8.], etc.

It should be noted that he is called leader, lawgiver, expectation of the nations, and their savior. He is leader, to foresee the way for us; lawgiver, to restrain transgressions; expectation, to supply for our incapacity; savior, to advance the just to blessedness. He foresees the way in which the devil lays snares for us; the transgressions by which God’s wrath is aroused; the incapacity by which the sinner falls into despair; and he advances the just to blessedness, the fullness prepared for the just [Col. 0619A].

Thus the leader provides for the way. Sometimes Satan makes it dark, poisonous, and ruinous: dark by cunning, poisonous by envy, ruinous by cruelty; the first after the manner of a robber, the second after that of a serpent, the third after that of a lion. Of the first: “In this way in which I walked, they hid a snare for me” [Note: [Col. 0619] Ps. 141.]. “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers” [Note: [Col. 0619] Luke 10.]. Of the second: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path” [Note: [Col. 0619] Gen. 49.]. Of the third Solomon says: “There is a lion in the way; I shall be killed” [Note: [Col. 0619] Prov. 26.].

But against the dark way he is leader; hence: “You were a leader in mercy to the people whom you redeemed” [Note: [Col. 0619] Exod. 15.]. Against the poisonous way: “You transplanted a vine out of Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it. You were the guide of its journey before it” [Note: [Col. 0619] Ps. 79.]. Against [Col. 0619B] the ruinous way, the leader made the path level; hence the Church sings: “For your name’s sake you will be my guide and nourish me.”

He is also called lawgiver. He gave three laws: the first to the first parents in paradise; the second to those walking in the wilderness; the third to those dwelling in the promised land. The first prevents sin; the second finds the sinner; the third comes to the help of the sinner. The first was violated by disobedience; the second punishes wrongdoing bodily; the third is fulfilled by repentance. The first is: “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, do not eat” [Note: [Col. 0619] Gen. 2.]. Hear how it was violated: “The woman took and ate, and gave to her husband” [Note: [Col. 0619] Gen. 3.]. The second found the sinner when they sinned concerning the golden calves, but punishes thus: “Tooth for tooth, eye for eye” [Note: [Col. 0619] Exod. 21.]. The third comes seeking thus: “I did not come to call the just, but sinners” [Note: [Col. 0619] Luke 5.]. Thus it is given: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another” [Note: [Col. 0619] John 13.].

Thirdly, he is called expectation of the nations, consolation of those who weep, and refreshment of minds: of nations, which he might cleanse; of those who weep, whose punishment he might lighten; of minds, which he might anoint with grace. He cleanses them so that they may be more fitting to receive Christ; lightens them so that they may be more ready to serve God; anoints them so that they may be more eager to love. Of the first: “He washed us from our sins in his blood” [Note: [Col. 0619] Apoc. 1.]—“that he might cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works” [Note: [Col. 0619] Titus 2.]. Of the second: “He sent me to announce to the meek, that I might console those who mourn” [Note: [Col. 0619] Isa. 61.]. These are readier, because “the Lord lifts up all [Col. 0619C] who have fallen and raises up all who are cast down” [Note: [Col. 0619] Ps. 144.]. Of the third: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” [Note: [Col. 0619] Ps. 44.]—“For the Lord loves a cheerful giver” [Note: [Col. 0619] 2 Cor. 9.].

Fourthly, he is called Savior; hence: “Come and save the human being whom you formed from clay” [Note: [Col. 0619] Office of the Church.]. God formed the human being; the devil deformed him; Christ reformed him: he formed him from clay, the devil deformed him with the dung of guilt, and Christ reformed him in the depths of humility, in order to change clay into solidity. According to the first: “This corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal immortality” [Note: [Col. 0619] 1 Cor. 15.]. According to the second: [Col. 0620A] “Freed from sin, we shall become servants of God” [Note: [Col. 0619] Rom. 6.]—“in holiness and righteousness before him all our days” [Note: [Col. 0619] Luke 1.]. According to the third: “He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dungheap, that he may seat him with princes and make him possess a throne of glory” [Note: [Col. 0619] 1 Kings 2.].

“My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to pasture there in the gardens and gather lilies.”

[CARD.] As if she said: My beloved came down from heaven and, taking flesh in me, came into his garden, this world, but especially to the bed of spices. For although he was everywhere and with all by power, essence, and presence, yet in a certain singular manner he was with those who, by their small number and by the fragrance of their life, are signified by a bed of spices; for the sake of conferring or increasing grace he came down to them. He came down into this garden, namely the world, to feed in individual gardens and delight in the consciences of individual people, and there gather lilies of purity in which he might rest.

Yet in this garden Christ found thorns and a cross instead of lilies. For this garden, namely the world, in which the Lord placed as many plants as there are persons, is that vineyard mentioned in the Gospel, to which the heir came and was cast out by the cultivators [Note: [Col. 0619] Matt. 21.]. But at present the Virgin passed this over in silence, because she had recounted the event, and could not repeat it without bitterness, and because it was not unknown to the women. Yet she gives the reason why she had previously adjured the women in this manner: she was impelled to it by the special prerogative of love, which she shows in these words.

“I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, he who feeds among the lilies.”

[THO.] I prepare for my beloved a welcome feeding in beds of spices, that is, in the pure hearts of the faithful. And my beloved is for me, who feeds among the holy desires of chaste minds. He repays this return for his grace by fulfilling those same desires of his faithful ones whom he has brought forth. He will fulfil them by leading them from this paradise of holy delight and gathering them into the secret chambers of the heavenly dwellings,

[Col. 0620C] where they shine with the twofold appearance of the lily, that is, golden and gleaming white. Among friends there is usually much graciousness in giving and receiving gifts. Hence the bride rejoices that she trusts a return will be made to her by her beloved. It is as though the beloved said: “I shall descend to the garden-bed so that I may ascend to the king’s palace. I have fed in the gardens so that I may sit in the kingdom at the rich man’s table. I gathered lilies so that he may gather me into the joyous joys of heaven.”

The beloved descended beneath himself, descended beneath man, descended beneath an angel. Beneath himself, when in the unity of his person he united a creature to himself; [Col. 0621A] beneath man, when he rendered obedience to Mary and Joseph, endured the injury of a judge and the abuse of persecutors; beneath an angel, when he assumed flesh liable to death. For in the first case, “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0621] John 1]; in the second, he was “as a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” [Note: [Col. 0621] Psalm 21]; in the third, whereas an angel owes nothing to death, he himself paid death’s debt: “He was made a little lower than the angels” [Note: [Col. 0621] Heb. 2].

Therefore, if you are to ascend through these descents, you must first ascend above yourself, secondly above the world, and thirdly above heaven. If you wish to ascend above yourself, first rise above the pleasure of your flesh, secondly above your own will, thirdly above human reason. If you do not ascend, [Col. 0621B] the first will draw you into pain; the second will make you powerless over yourself; through the third you will fall into error.

Therefore first ascend above pleasure, because “he who delicately nourishes his servant from youth will afterward find him rebellious.” For pleasure carries punishment, while necessity produces a crown. Hear the poet:

> Rare use often commends pleasures.

And:

> Despise pleasures: pleasure bought with pain harms.

David saw the pain of pleasure: “In the morning,” he says, “it flourishes and passes away; in the evening it falls, grows hard, and withers” [Note: [Col. 0621] Psalm 89]. In the morning it flowers in being born; it passes from childhood into adolescence, from adolescence into youth, from youth into manhood, from manhood into old age, from old age into decrepitude; [Col. 0621C] from decrepitude, in the evening—that is, at the end—it falls into destruction. Then it hardens into a corpse and at last dries into dust. Let man therefore reflect, because “the death of man and that of beast is the same, and the condition of both alike” [Note: [Col. 0621] Eccles. 3]. See, then, that you do not rot like a beast in its dung [Note: [Col. 0621] Joel 1], lest perhaps it be said to you: “He was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” [Note: [Col. 0621] Psalm 48].

Secondly, ascend above your own will, according to the saying, “Turn away from your own desires” [Note: [Col. 0621] Ecclus. 18], and, “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” [Note: [Col. 0621] John 5]. For it is a great thing to rule one’s self and one’s own spirit. Hence Solomon: “The patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his spirit than a conqueror of cities” [Note: [Col. 0621] Prov. 16]. And the poet [Note: [Col. 0621] Ovid]:

[Col. 0621D]

> If you persist in doing what you wish,  
> You will hear what you do not wish.

And another [Note: [Col. 0621] Horace]:

> Rule your spirit; unless it obeys, it rules.  
> Restrain it with reins; crush it with whips.

Restrain it with reins, lest it rush into what is forbidden; crush it with whips, lest it grow sluggish toward what is good. Hear the philosopher:

> Let him who wishes to be powerful tame fierce spirits.  
> For though the remotest land should tremble beneath your laws  
> and farthest Thule be subject to you,  
> yet not to be able to conquer black cares  
> and drive away miserable complaints—that is not power.

Hence the same author elsewhere:

[Col. 0622A]

> You would rule more widely by mastering  
> your greedy spirit than if you joined Libya  
> to distant Gades, and each Carthaginian  
> were subject to one man.

Therefore, if you do not wish to follow your own will, yield to Solomon: “Do everything,” he says, “with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” [Note: [Col. 0621] Ecclus. 32]. One’s own will is that which disagrees with the divine will. Therefore, that it may be understood what one’s own will is, consider the threefold will. There is the will of the Father, the will of the Spirit, and the will of the flesh. The will of the Father is that we do good; the will of the Spirit, that we obey; the will of the flesh, that we fulfil its desires. The Father’s will must be honoured; the Spirit’s will must be done; the flesh’s will must be directed. When, therefore, the will [Col. 0622B] is thus regulated, it is not called one’s own.

He also ascends above reason, by not following lower causes, lest you set your reward here, but rather above; so that you may understand that your reward is God himself. Therefore, “We lift up our hearts unto the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0621] Office of the Church]. Hence David says: “To you have I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0621] Psalm 122]. And Jeremiah: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands unto the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0621] Lam. 3]. Therefore, he who thus ascends, despising lower things, thinks in silence upon higher things. Hence: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has lifted himself above himself” [Note: [Col. 0621] ibid.].

He also ascends above the world by despising it: “For all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride [Col. 0622C] of life” [Note: [Col. 0621] 1 John 2]. And because the world is such, you who are religious should not wonder if the world hates you: “For if you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” [Note: [Col. 0621] John 15]. Look therefore upon it and say with that religious man: “O unclean world, why did we love you?” You will easily conquer the world if you are sons of God. For he himself said: “Take courage: I have conquered the world” [Note: [Col. 0621] John 16]. Accordingly, “Whatever is born of God conquers the world” [Note: [Col. 0621] 1 John 4].—“Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from this age” [Note: [Col. 0621] James 1].

Behold, you have ascended above the will of the flesh. You have also ascended above the world, if indeed you have trampled underfoot its abundance of possessions and its delight in doing evil. For in these two things the love of the world consists. Persevere in this state, [Col. 0622D] and nothing remains except that you ascend above heaven, where the beloved will repay you for having offered him spices, fed him, and presented lilies. For in return for these he will give spices whose fragrance will bring perpetual incorruption. In return for feeding, we shall sit at table, where we shall receive the fullness of the divine vision. In return for lilies, we shall obtain the fellowship of saints and angels. For in the first case, “The body that is sown animal shall rise in glory” [Note: [Col. 0621] 1 Cor. 15]. In the second: Lord Jesus, we shall be satisfied “when your glory appears” [Note: [Col. 0621] Psalm 16]. In the third: “We shall no longer be strangers and sojourners, but [Col. 0623A] fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” [Note: [Col. 0623] Eph. 2]. Then, Lord, “all the sons of God shall rejoice, and the morning stars shall praise you together” [Note: [Col. 0623] Job 38]. There, from God’s fullness, we shall all receive grace for grace [Note: [Col. 0623] John 1], that is, your glory.

> I am for my beloved, and my beloved is for me, who feeds among the lilies.

[CARD.] As though she said: “I belong to my beloved.” She says “I” in a singular, significant, and antonomastic sense. She likewise adds: “My beloved is for me”; and she says “for me” likewise in a singular, significant, and antonomastic sense. But observe that she did not say what she is to her beloved, or what her beloved is to her, because that “what” is so great that words fail in explaining it. Yet she adds, “who feeds among the lilies”; and “my lilies” must be supplied, for Christ himself feeds and finds especial delight among the virgin’s lilies: her life and [Col. 0623B] purity of flesh.

There follows the voice of the Son, recounting the mother’s praises and saying:

> You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and fair as Jerusalem, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.

[THO.] Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.” This is the heavenly homeland, which abides in the highest tranquillity. The soul or the Church imitates it through integrity in worldly activity, sweetness in divine praise, and the tenderness of mutual love. She is sweet and fair as Jerusalem in those of whom Isaiah writes: “As the new heavens and the new earth which I make to stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your seed and your name stand” [Note: [Col. 0623] Isa. 66].

She is terrible as an army drawn up in battle array when, through the fixed intention of good prayer, she repels within herself every attack of the demonic army; when, through preaching, she shatters every weapon of wandering doctrine; when, through good examples, she leads the life of sinners back to the path of truth. She is terrible when each believer remains in the calling in which he was called: namely, when rulers furnish their subjects with a model in word and deed; when the continent cleanse themselves from every defilement of flesh and blood; when married people so use this world that they do not neglect to give alms. These are the three men who shall be saved: namely Noah, Daniel, and Job.

The bride is praised in four respects. First she is called beautiful; second, sweet; third, fair; fourth, terrible. She is [Col. 0623D] beautiful to the member of the household, sweet to the subject, fair to the beloved, terrible to the adversary: beautiful to the household member through works, sweet to the subject through manners, fair to the beloved through affections, terrible to the adversary through virtues; through just works, ordered manners, the affections of desire and love, and ordered virtues. First she instructs her neighbour for action; second she draws the subject to love for her; third she receives the beloved; fourth she repels the adversary.

The beloved himself instructed us in this. Of the first he says: “He who believes in me shall also do the works that I do” [Note: [Col. 0623] John 17]. And to subjects he says: “Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0623] Matt. 11]. And of the third: “I give you thanks, Father, because you always hear [Col. 0624A] me” [Note: [Col. 0623] John 11]. Of the fourth likewise, when tempted by the devil, he says: “Get behind me, Satan” [Note: [Col. 0623] Matt. 4].

Hear beauty in labour: “These hands,” he says, “have laboured for all the things needful to me and to those who were with me” [Note: [Col. 0623] Acts 20]. Again: “Night and day, labouring with our hands, lest we burden any of you” [Note: [Col. 0623] 1 Thess. 2]. Hear sweetness in manners: “My little children, with whom I travail again until Christ be formed in you” [Note: [Col. 0623] Gal. 4]. Hear fairness in devotion: “Forgetting what is behind, I stretch forth to what lies before, toward the prize of the high calling” [Note: [Col. 0623] Phil. 3]. Hear terribleness in virtue: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of my Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0623] Acts 21]. Hence he said confidently: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” [Col. 0624B] [Note: [Col. 0623] 2 Tim. 4]. How terrible in virtue he was when he said: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned” [Note: [Col. 0623] 2 Cor. 11], and so forth.

Likewise, this friend is beautiful in justice, sweet in humility, fair in obedience, terrible in the severity of her seriousness. The beauty of justice is perfected by three degrees: the first is to submit oneself to a superior; the second, not to prefer oneself to an equal; the third, to serve an inferior. The first begins, the second advances, the third completes. Elisha submitted himself to a superior in serving Elijah; Paul did not prefer himself to an equal, when he conferred advocacy upon Peter disputing with Simon; Mary served an inferior when she went into the hill country and served Elizabeth, her kinswoman. Therefore “the Lord regarded the humility of his handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0623] Luke 1], because she [Col. 0624C] fulfilled perfect justice: a mistress serving a handmaid, a queen serving her soldier, the mother of the living God serving the mother of a mortal man. Behold, beautiful justice.

She is also sweet in humility. There are three degrees of this humility: the first sufficient, the second abundant, the third perfecting. The first is to submit oneself to a superior and not prefer oneself to an equal; the second is to submit oneself to an equal and not prefer oneself to an inferior; the third is to be subject to an inferior. The apostles fulfilled the first in submitting themselves to Christ; they fulfilled the second by ministering to one another; Christ fulfilled the third when he submitted himself to John to be baptized by him. Behold how the friend is sweet in humility.

She is also fair in obedience. Obedience consists in three things: humility of heart, patience [Col. 0624D] in action, and perseverance in good work. Christ fulfilled the first when “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0623] Phil. 2]; the second, when “he was found in form as a man” [Note: [Col. 0623] ibid.], in which condition he showed patience by enduring many things; the third, when “he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” [Note: [Col. 0623] ibid.]. Behold how she is fair in obedience.

But she is called fair as Jerusalem, which is interpreted “vision of peace.” For in the heavenly Jerusalem there is peace, because all there obey their Creator. Hence: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” [Note: [Col. 0623] Matt. 5].

This friend is terrible in the severity of seriousness. The religious person’s severity is fourfold: the severity of abstinence, the severity of discipline, the severity of patience, and severity in prayer or rebuke. Abstinence is from food; discipline is from outward levity in the members; patience ensures that unbecoming movements of the limbs caused by pain do not appear in outward signs; rebuke prevents one from being excessively lax and soft. Of the first: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with feasting and drunkenness” [Note: [Col. 0625] Luke 21]. Hence the poet [Note: [Col. 0625] Lucan, *Pharsalia* IV]:

> Learn how little is needed to prolong life:  
> for besieged peoples, a river and Ceres suffice.

And the same author on stern Cato [Note: [Col. 0625] Lucan, *Pharsalia* II.386]:

> For him, a feast was to conquer hunger;  
> a great household, to keep winter out with a roof;  
> costly clothing, to draw a rough toga  
> over his limbs, in the manner of the Roman Quirite.

[Col. 0625B] The philosopher Boethius also commends this severity [Note: [Col. 0625] Boethius II, 5, 1]:

> Most happy was the former age,  
> content with faithful fields  
> and not ruined by idle luxury.  
> It knew neither how to mix Bacchic gifts  
> with liquid honey,  
> nor to blend shining fleeces of silk  
> with Tyrian dye.  
> Health-giving grass bestowed sleep,  
> the flowing stream gave drink,  
> and the tallest pine gave shade.

John the Baptist possessed this severity when he ate locusts and wild honey and wore a leather belt about his loins [Note: [Col. 0625] Matt. 3]. Of the severity of discipline it is said: “Lay hold of discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry” [Note: [Col. 0625] Psalm 2]. As Saint Benedict says: “Lest buffoonery [Col. 0625C] find fuel.”—“A fool,” he says, “raises his voice in laughter” [Note: [Col. 0625] Ecclus. 21]. Therefore we must restrain the outward man. For not only inward but outward discipline must be observed.

Do you wish to have a model of outward discipline? Look upon the beloved’s eyes closed in death; his ears enclosed by the thorny crown; his tongue uttering, “It is finished” [Note: [Col. 0625] John 19]; his hands and feet fastened with nails. There is also the severity of patience, so that pain may not draw you into womanish howlings, like the beloved, who “was led as a lamb to the slaughter and did not open his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0625] Isa. 53]. Again: “He shall not be turbulent, nor cry out, nor shall his voice be heard abroad” [Note: [Col. 0625] Isa. 42]. There is also the severity of rebuke. Hence the Apostle: “Rebuke the unruly, comfort the faint-hearted, support the weak” [Note: [Col. 0625] 1 Thess. 5]. Again: “Reprove, entreat, [Col. 0625D] rebuke” [Note: [Col. 0625] 2 Tim. 4]. Whoever is arrayed with such severity is terrible to enemies, like an army drawn up in battle array, which has no opening through which an enemy may enter.

Or thus: You are beautiful in charity, sweet in will, fair in work, terrible in temptation: in charity, by which the soul lacks crime and original sin; in will, by which it obeys its Creator; in work, by which it strives outwardly to offer service to God; in temptation, by which it manfully resists the devil. But you are fair as Jerusalem, that is, in likeness to Jerusalem, [Col. 0626A] because you now in some measure bear its image. For your manner of life is in heaven. Hence: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0625] Rev. 21]. Jerusalem descends from heaven when the faithful imitate true peace on earth, and their whole manner of life is already in heaven.

Or: beautiful among married people, sweet among the continent, fair among prelates, terrible among martyrs. It will also be like an army drawn up in battle array if martyrs are placed in front, prelates in the second place, the continent in the third, and married people at the end: so that they may have from martyrs an example of suffering passion; from prelates, the word of preaching; from the continent, love of chastity; and from married people [p. 130], abstinence and generosity in almsgiving; and thus may be found stable in faith and [Col. 0626B] effective in work.

> You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and fair as Jerusalem, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.

[CARD.] As though he said: “O my friend, you are beautiful in the intention of your mind, sweet in speech, fair in works. You are to me like Jerusalem, that is, a vision of peace, making peace between God and man. You are terrible to evil spirits, like a tower built with ramparts, as was said above, and because you are like an army drawn up in battle array. For all the ordered hosts of saints follow her as a queen, according to their respective states, proper dignities, and merits, so that beneath her and with her they may fight for us against the enemy.” And it continues:

> Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.

[THO.] It is as though it were openly said: “I gave you dove-like eyes, by which you may know the mysteries of the Scriptures, separate virtues from vices, recognize the paths of righteousness by which you might come to me, or simply look upon me. But see that you do not seek here to behold my majesty: ‘For no man shall see me and live’ [Note: [Col. 0625] Exod. 33]. Therefore turn your eyes away from me, because while, established in the flesh, you journey away from eternal goods, you cannot know me perfectly. Therefore do not seek on the way the reward that shall be given to none of the living except in the homeland.”

Some turn their eyes away from truth, some from vanity, some from majesty. Of the first: “The turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity of fools [Col. 0626D] shall destroy them” [Note: [Col. 0625] Prov. 1]. Of the second: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” [Note: [Col. 0625] Psalm 118]. Of the third, as here: “Turn your eyes away from me, because they have made me fly away.” The first turning-away is one of blindness, the second of seriousness, the third of weakness. That of blindness casts into a pit; that of seriousness makes justice stable in us; that of weakness restrains the boldness of excessive desire.

Of the first: “They have neither known nor understood; they walk in darkness; therefore all the foundations of the earth shall be moved” [Note: [Col. 0625] Psalm 81], that is, the firmness of the heart. For one who does not see retains no stability in his heart. Of such persons it is written in Proverbs: “I called and you refused; I stretched out my hand and there was none to look” [Note: [Col. 0627] Prov. 11]. Nor is this surprising, because “the eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0627] Prov. 17]. Yet let them hear that “he who is ignorant shall be ignored” [Note: [Col. 0627] 1 Cor. 14]. They “wandered in a wilderness, in a waterless place; they found not the way to an inhabited city” [Note: [Col. 0627] Psalm 106]. Hence the Prophet prayed: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” [Note: [Col. 0627] Psalm 12]. When these fall, they do not add that they may rise again [Note: [Col. 0627] Psalm 40]. For they do not fall upon their faces so as to see where they fall; rather, they fall backward with those who guarded the Lord’s tomb, so that they may not see where they fall.

The second turn their eyes away from vanity and walk securely; and thus “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” [Note: [Col. 0627] Prov. 1]. Nor is this surprising, because “the eyes [Col. 0627B] of a wise man are in his head” [Note: [Col. 0627] Eccles. 2], by which he takes care lest he must lament with the prophet: “My eye has afflicted my soul because of all the daughters of my city” [Note: [Col. 0627] Lam. 3]. Job had guarded against this when he said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think of a virgin” [Note: [Col. 0627] Job 31]. Eve did not possess such eyes when she saw the tree, which was beautiful to look upon and pleasant for eating. Hence the eyes of both were opened, and they saw that they were naked [Note: [Col. 0627] Gen. 3]. Opened, I say, to see vanity, not truth. And they saw that they were naked outwardly of garments, inwardly of virtues. Why? Because they did not turn their eyes away from vanity.

The third, after their presumption, turn their eyes away from majesty. For they have learned by experience that “he who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” [Note: [Col. 0627] Prov. 25]. And: “The beast that touches the mountain shall be buried beneath stones” [Note: [Col. 0627] Exod. 19; Heb. 12], since not even the angels themselves can comprehend his greatness. For he ascended above the cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds [Note: [Col. 0627] Psalm 17]. “Cherubim” means “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore he ascended above the cherubim because no fullness of knowledge can comprehend him: “For the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy, and there is no end to his greatness” [Note: [Col. 0627] Psalm 144].

Therefore, the first turn their eyes away from the beloved so as, forgetting him, not to make remembrance of him; the second turn their eyes from vanity lest they lose the highest truth; the third turn their eyes away from him lest they presumptuously search out majesty. Indeed, after their presumption, they turn away [Col. 0627D] eyes struck back by his incomprehensible brightness.

Accordingly, Christ flies away from the first, flies toward the second, and flies away from the third. He flies away—that is, outside them—through deprivation of grace; he flies toward them—that is, to them—through the conferring of grace; he flies away from them not through deprivation of grace but through the incomprehensibility of his own exaltation.

The eyes of the first are darkened by a threefold cloud: one of pleasures, another of iniquities, another of fantasies. The first is smoky, the second malicious, the third troubled. Of the first: “How in his wrath has the Lord [Col. 0628A] covered the virgin daughter of Zion with darkness?” [Note: [Col. 0627] Lam. 2]. For the virgin is darkened when what is pure is defiled. Of the second: “Bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0627] Psalm 134]. The end of the earth—that is, of the heart—is malice. Of the third: “You have set a cloud before yourself so that prayer may not pass through” [Note: [Col. 0627] Lam. 3]. The first cloud, smoky as it is, blinds; the second, that is, the malicious cloud, poisons; the third, which is of fantasies, troubles those who pray.

Against these three are three other, good clouds: the first of thunder, the second of rain, [Col. 0628B] the third of day. The cloud of thunder is terrible, because it threatens and terrifies; the cloud of rain is moist, because it waters and teaches; the cloud of day is bright and mild, because it illumines and refreshes. The cloud of thunder drives away the cloud of pleasure; the cloud of teaching, the cloud of iniquity; the cloud of day, the cloud of fantasy. Of the first: “The clouds gave forth their voice” [Note: [Col. 0627] Psalm 67]. And it follows: “The voice of your thunder in the wheel” [Note: [Col. 0627] Psalm 76]. Of the second the Lord says through the prophet: “I will command my clouds that they rain not” [Note: [Col. 0627] Isa. 5]. Of the third: “A bright cloud received Jesus from the eyes of his disciples in his ascension” [Note: [Col. 0627] Acts 1].

By the first cloud, the first are roused; by the second, the second are made fruitful; by the third, the third are illumined. Therefore, through the terror of the first, the first lift their eyes so as to be delivered from sins; in the second, the second rejoice in virtues, [Col. 0628C] and so their eyes are raised upward; in the third, the third contemplate Jesus ascending into heaven. For the eyes of contemplatives are lifted up to him.

As a figure of the first lifting-up, Jacob, whose name means “supplanter,” returning to his own land, lifted up his eyes and saw his brother Esau, whose name means “hairy,” that is, “sinner,” coming to meet him [Note: [Col. 0627] Gen. 33]. As a figure of the second, Isaac, whose name means “laughter,” lifted up his eyes when he had gone out to meditate in the field and saw Rebecca, whose name means “patience,” coming to him [Note: [Col. 0627] Gen. 24]. As a figure of the third, Abraham, while he stood by the oak of Mamre at the entrance of his tent in the very heat of day, lifted up his eyes and saw three men coming down the road; he ran to meet them, fed them, and worshipped them [Note: [Col. 0627] Gen. 18].

Abraham, whose name means “father of many nations,” that is, the spirit, lord of thoughts, stands at the entrance of his tent—that is, while contemplating, he is not hidden in the flesh—and saw three men, that is, the three persons in the Trinity. He meets them with desire, worships them with humility, and feeds them with devotion and love.

It is worthy of inquiry why the bride is rebuked for her contemplation when the ancient Fathers so greatly glory in the divine vision. Thus Isaiah: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” [Note: [Col. 0627] Isa. 6]. Jacob likewise: “I saw the Lord face to face, and [Col. 0629A] my soul was saved” [Note: [Col. 0629] Gen. 32]. But it is one thing that we are forbidden to search out majesty, another that we are permitted to know Christ’s humanity. For there it says: “He who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” [Note: [Col. 0629] Prov. 25]. Here the angel says: “He will go before you into Galilee; there you shall see him” [Note: [Col. 0629] Mark 16]. Therefore, turning our eyes away from majesty, we turn them toward knowing the benefits of his humanity.

Therefore, first let us inquire, secondly seek, thirdly acquire. Let us inquire with what love he embraces us; let us seek, so that he may be found; let us acquire, so that, having been found, he may be possessed. Let us inquire through continual meditation; let him be sought as an indweller in a pure conscience; let him be acquired through desire and indwelling. Of the first: “Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” [Note: [Col. 0629] Psalm 33]. Of the second: “Seek the Lord while he may be found” [Note: [Col. 0629] Isa. 55]. Of the third: “His acquisition is better than trade in silver and gold” [Note: [Col. 0629] Prov. 3].

We have all already inquired through faith; but let us see how he is sought and acquired. The Gospel parable teaches thus: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man seeking fine pearls; when he found one precious pearl, he went away, sold all that he had, and bought it” [Note: [Col. 0629] Matt. 13]. We read in the Gospel of three parables especially assigned to Christ. In the first there is the pearl which is sought; in the second, the coin found in the fish’s mouth [Note: [Col. 0629] Matt. 17]; in the third, the treasure hidden in the field [Note: [Col. 0629] Matt. 13]. The pearl was in the nativity, the coin in the passion, the treasure in restoration.

[Col. 0629C] In the first, the wise woman lights a lamp in order to find the drachma she had lost [Note: [Col. 0629] Luke 15]; in the second, Christ carries back to the flock the sheep that had strayed [Note: [Col. 0629] Matt. 18]; in the third, the prodigal son is preached, who by living luxuriously squandered his goods [Note: [Col. 0629] Luke 15]. Let us therefore light a lamp, that we may seek the pearl: a lamp for the feet, a lamp for the hands, a lamp for the head. The first, that we may know; the second, that we may discern works; the third, that we may grasp heavenly things. Of the first: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” [Note: [Col. 0629] Psalm 118]; of the second: “Burning lamps in your hands” [Note: [Col. 0629] Luke 12]; of the third: “Who will grant me that I might be as in months past, when God was with me, when his lamp shone over my head?” [Note: [Col. 0629] Job 29].

By this the precious thing is sought: precious [Col. 0629D] in the mother’s womb, more precious in the brother’s heart, most precious in the Father’s bosom. Hence Solomon: “A most welcome jewel is the expectation of one who waits; wherever it turns, it understands wisely” [Note: [Col. 0629] Prov. 17]. It is welcome to converts, more welcome to the just, most welcome to saints. Again, it is welcome when touched, more welcome when carried, most welcome when seen. In touch it gives health; when carried, security; in sight, brightness: health from the sickness of sins; security from the snares of enemies; brightness in the knowledge of things above.

Of the first: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” [Note: [Col. 0629] Jer. 27]. Again: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” [Note: [Col. 0629] Psalm 40]. Hence that woman with a flow of blood: “If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be healed” [Note: [Col. 0629] Matt. 9]. And he: “Someone touched me, for I perceive power has gone out from me” [Note: [Col. 0629] Mark 5]. Hence: “The whole crowd sought to touch him” [Note: [Col. 0629] Luke 6], because it did not yet have pure faith.

And it should be noted that at one time we touch Christ’s feet, at another his head, at another his breast. His feet, when we are devout toward his humanity; his head, when we long to behold his divinity; his breast, when we know the truth concerning both. Mary Magdalene touched his feet [Note: [Col. 0629] Luke 7]; his head, the woman who [Col. 0630B] poured ointment upon the head of him reclining at table [Note: [Col. 0629] Matt. 26]; his breast, John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0629] John 13]. He touched his feet who said, “Do you think I shall endure?” [Latin *Putas durabo?*, reading uncertain], Job his head: “In my flesh,” he says, “I shall see God my saviour” [Note: [Col. 0629] Job 19]; his breast, he who said: “My Lord and my God!” [Note: [Col. 0629] John 20].

At times Christ touches us. He touches the bier, he touches the belly, he touches the mouth, he touches the ear. The bier, that he may raise one lying dead in sins; the belly, that he may stir the memory toward spiritual love; the mouth, that he may invite it to the grace of preaching, praising, and working; the ear, that he may summon it to obedience. Of the first: “He touched the bier of him who lay dead, the only son of his mother” [Note: [Col. 0629] Luke 7]. Of the second the bride says: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch” [Note: [Col. 0629] Song 5]. Of the [Col. 0630C] third, Jeremiah: “The Lord put forth his hand and touched my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0629] Jer. 1]. And Isaiah: “The angel touched my mouth with a burning coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs” [Note: [Col. 0629] Isa. 6]. Of the fourth: “The Lord touched the ears of the deaf man” [Note: [Col. 0629] Mark 7]. And: “The Lord healed the ear of the servant which Peter had cut off” [Note: [Col. 0629] Luke 22].

The first says: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” [Note: [Col. 0629] Eph. 5]. The second says: “I remembered God and was delighted” [Note: [Col. 0629] Psalm 76]. The third says: “Evening and morning and noon I will recount and proclaim, and he will hear my voice” [Note: [Col. 0629] Psalm 54]. Thus Christ touches and is touched; he heals sin, is carried, and renders one secure. [p. 131] Hence: “An old man carried a child, but the child guided the old man; therefore he went securely.” Therefore, that you may go securely, “glorify and carry God in your body” [Note: [Col. 0629] 1 Cor. 6].

Thirdly, he makes sight bright. Hence in the Apocalypse: “I saw an angel coming down from heaven, and the whole earth was illumined by his glory” [Note: [Col. 0629] Rev. 18], so that, with unveiled face, we may behold the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0629] 2 Cor. 3]. He who finds this pearl goes away, sells all he has, and buys it [Note: [Col. 0629] Matt. 13]. He goes away by fleeing sin; sells by abandoning the desire for temporal things; buys by denying himself. Of the first:

[Col. 0631A] “Go out of Babylon and flee from the Chaldeans” [Note: [Col. 0631] Isa. 48]. Of the second: “Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0631] Matt. 19], so that you may say: “The things that were gains to me have become losses for Christ’s sake” [Note: [Col. 0631] Phil. 3]. Of the third he says: “Hasten, buy, and eat” [Note: [Col. 0631] Isa. 55]. Behold, thus you have turned your eyes from vanity, since you have left the world. You have turned them from majesty, and therefore investigated the essence. You have turned them toward Christ’s humanity and found the pearl.

Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of sheep that have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none among them is barren. Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within you.

[THO.] (Thus.) Do not repeat what has been said. For since these sections have already been treated above in full [Col. 0631B], either they should be passed over in silence, or dealt with briefly, lest they seem to have been introduced idly by so wise a man. In the bride’s hair is signified the manifold loftiness of her thoughts; in her teeth, the most steadfast firmness of her speech. For the latter assist lips and tongue in speaking, while the former grow imperceptibly from the brain and do not hurt when cut. One should not grieve, but rejoice, at the cutting away of superfluous thoughts. Thus Moses’ teeth, though he was already old, were neither altered nor loosened [Note: [Col. 0631] Deut. 34.]; and no razor came upon Samuel’s head, because he was a Nazirite—that is, consecrated to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0631] I Kings 1.].

Hair is aptly compared to a flock of goats, because a goat was sacrificed under the Law for sins [Note: [Col. 0631] Lev. 4], and our thoughts are compared to goats when we sacrifice their wanderings to God through compunction [Col. 0631C]. Again, the goat feeds on high places, and the thought of the righteous delights in heaven. When they ascend Gilead, which means “heap of testimony,” the righteous are shown to have renounced the world by the visible display of many virtues.

Teeth are compared to sheep—that is, to teachers—because of the whiteness of virtues and innocence. They are fittingly said to have come up from the washing, because no unclean speech proceeds from their mouth. As the Apostle says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth; but if any speech is good for the building up of the edifice, let it give grace to those who hear” [Note: [Col. 0631] Eph. 4.]. They are all said to bear twins because of the love of God and neighbour which they preach; or because of the teaching of the Old and New Testaments; or because of the salvation of soul and body.

The cheeks are compared to the rind of a pomegranate [Col. 0631D]. In the cheeks is signified the modesty of the preacher; in the red colour of the rind, the Passion of the Saviour. It follows: “apart from what is hidden within you,” because in preachers Christ’s Passion appears outwardly, while inwardly strength and devotion lie hidden.

Morally: in the hair is thought; in the teeth, the discernment of thoughts; in the redness of the cheeks, ardour in good things and shame in evil things. The order is fitting. A person ought first to turn over in his heart both his good and evil thoughts; second, as it were with certain teeth, to judge them after considering them, separating good from evil [Col. 0632A]; third, to blush over evils, as on the left cheek, and to direct himself through good things, as on the right cheek, toward greater ardour.

Concerning the recollection of evils it is said: “I shall recount to you all my years in the bitterness of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0631] Isa. 38.]. Concerning good things: “I remembered God and was delighted” [Note: [Col. 0631] Ps. 76.]; concerning the second point: “For if we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” [Note: [Col. 0631] I Cor. 11.].
