But because we are not sufficient to make this separation without God, we ask David that he may supply our insufficiency: “Let my judgment come forth from your face,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0631] Ps. 16.]. See how he separated what he had judged: “I hated and abhorred iniquity, but I loved your law” [Note: [Col. 0631] Ps. 118.].

Concerning evils, see the blush of the left cheek: “All day my shame is before me [Col. 0632B], and the confusion of my face is always against me” [Note: [Col. 0631] Ps. 43.]. See the ardour arising from good things: “My heart grew hot within me” [Note: [Col. 0631] Ps. 38.], etc.; and, “My heart was inflamed” [Note: [Col. 0631] Ps. 72.], etc. Jeremiah also says concerning these things: “Let us search our ways,” by remembering them, “and seek,” by discerning them, “and return,” by blushing [Note: [Col. 0631] Lam. 3.].

But let us note carefully that the devil strives to tear away the hair of good thoughts and leave evil thoughts behind; to break the teeth of discernment; and to make blushing cheeks shameless. A figure of the first occurred when Hanun, who is called king of Rabbah, shaved half the beard and half the hair of David’s messengers [Note: [Col. 0631] II Kings 10]. Hanun, whose name means “their sorrow”—that is, the devil—king of Rabbah, which means “dry,” that is, of hell, shaves half the beard and half the hair of the messengers of David, whose name means “strong of hand,” that is, of Christ. Thus he removes good thoughts from those who proclaim the Lord’s name [Col. 0632C], while leaving evil thoughts behind.

Jeremiah says of the breaking of teeth: “He broke my teeth by number” [Note: [Col. 0631] Lam. 3.]. Of the shamelessness of the cheeks, the same prophet says: “The faces of the old men did not blush” [Note: [Col. 0631] Lam. 5.]. And another prophet: “The forehead of a harlot has been made yours” [Note: [Col. 0631] Jer. 3.].

Three things are to be noted concerning the hair: that it is likened to a goat, that it comes up from Mount Gilead, and that it is fixed in the head. The goat is foul-smelling and climbs on high. So a person who reviews his thoughts ought, before God, however righteous he may be, to regard himself as a sinner, and to ascend in heart to God’s mercy; yet from Mount Gilead—that is, from the height of a pure conscience, from the heap of virtues bearing testimony for him. The hair is fixed [Col. 0632D] in the head. For our thoughts ought to cling inseparably to God, who is our head.

Hear one who regards himself as a foul-smelling goat: “My wounds have putrefied and become corrupt because of my foolishness,” he says [Note: [Col. 0631] Ps. 37.], etc. Hear the heap of testimony: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0631] II Cor. 1]; likewise: “We are reviled, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and endure it” [Note: [Col. 0631] I Cor. 4]. “We are perplexed, but not forsaken” [Note: [Col. 0631] II Cor. 4], etc. Hear thoughts fixed in the head: “Cast your thought upon the Lord [Col. 0633A], and he will nourish you” [Note: [Col. 0633] Ps. 54]. “To you, Lord,” he says, “I have lifted up my soul” [Note: [Col. 0633] Ps. 85]. Such persons look upward, because “their reward is with God, and therefore their thoughts are with the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0633] Wis. 5].

Fixing their hearts there, they are like the living creatures that did not turn when they went [Note: [Col. 0633] Ezek. 1], because at the height of their thoughts is hope of that eternal blessedness, which holds them like an anchor. Hence the Apostle says: “We who flee to hold fast the hope set before us have the surest consolation, which we have as an anchor of the soul, safe and firm, entering even within the veil” [Note: [Col. 0633] Heb. 6].

Notice also that there are three things in the teeth: first, they are compared to sheep; second, they are said to come up from the washing; third, they all bear twins. In three things we have the signification of the sheep [Col. 0633B]: in simplicity, wool, and milk. Therefore, those who, after the manner of teeth, bite sins both their own and others’, should take from sheep simplicity: innocence with respect to crimes; from wool, generosity in temporal goods; from milk, instruction in spiritual matters. In the first, that one may be “innocent in hands and clean in heart” [Note: [Col. 0633] Ps. 23]; in the second, that one may give in simplicity [Note: [Col. 0633] Rom. 12]; in the third, that one may preside with diligence [Note: [Col. 0633] Ibid.].

Joseph showed himself such a one to his brothers in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0633] Gen. 45]. He was innocent, rendering no evil for evil. He possessed the generosity of wool when he gave them grain and had their money returned in their sacks [Note: [Col. 0633] Gen. 44]. He showed the instruction of milk when he said to them: “Do not be angry on the way” [Note: [Col. 0633] Gen. 45].

Second, one must come up from the washing. This washing is threefold: the first takes place in baptism; the second [Col. 0633C] in confession; the third in the pouring forth of tears. In the first we are washed from the infection of original leprosy; in the second, from the daily corruption of sins; in the third, from the blindness of obstinacy. The first occurs in the Jordan, the second in the Sheep Pool, the third in the pool of Siloam. Jordan is interpreted “descent,” signifying humility; *probatica*, “of the sheep,” signifies innocence and simplicity; Siloam, “sent,” signifies the kindness and humanity of the Saviour who was sent.

In the first Naaman the Syrian is healed [Note: [Col. 0633] IV Kings 5; Luke 4]; in the second, the paralytic lying on a bed [Note: [Col. 0633] Mark 2]; in the third, the man blind from birth [Note: [Col. 0633] John 9]. Naaman means “beauty.” Syria is “the pride of the king,” whose soldier he was. The king of pride is the devil; before baptism we were his soldiers. Paralysis means “dissolution”; and whenever we are entangled in worldly and carnal sins [Col. 0633D], we lie paralysed—that is, dissolved—upon a bed. The third was blind from birth: so those who remain continually in the habit of sinning are blinded by their obstinacy.

The first, therefore, is healed in the Jordan, that is, in humility, which Christ’s humility bestowed. The second is healed in the Sheep Pool, because Christ’s innocence and simplicity have cleansed our sins. The third is healed in Siloam, which means “sent,” because the kindness and humanity of Christ, sent to us, healed the blindness of our obstinacy. In such persons we find no barrenness, because they bear twins [Col. 0634A] through love of God and neighbour.

The cheeks too are said to be red like the rind of a pomegranate. There are three causes of redness in the face: shame, burning by the sun, and an abundance of blood. The first redness arises from shame at sin; the second from the ardour and longing of love; the third, in martyrdom, from the shedding of blood. Of the first David said: “Let all my enemies be greatly ashamed and troubled” [Note: [Col. 0633] Ps. 6]. Of the second Jeremiah says concerning the Nazirites: “More ruddy than ancient ivory” [Note: [Col. 0633] Lam. 4]. Of the third the Church sings [Note: [Col. 0633] Hymn from the Office of Martyrs]:

> For, red with flowing blood,  
> they encircle their temples with shining laurels.

Therefore Wisdom says: “I am like a plantation of roses in Jericho” [Note: [Col. 0633] Ecclus. 24]. These are the pomegranates [Col. 0634B] hanging on the priestly garment with golden bells [Note: [Col. 0633] Exod. 28], that is, with divine praise in the mouth of the wise person. These appear outwardly; but besides these, the roots of virtues are inward: hidden contemplations, sweet desires, and holy devotions.

Turn your eyes away from me, because they have caused me to fly away.

[CAR.] As though it were said: You have been promised: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you [Note: [Col. 0633] Luke 1]” and will illumine your eyes to see me more fully than others do. Yet do not believe that you see me fully while on the way; instead, turn your eyes away from me—that is, from the incomprehensibility of my majesty. For the power of the Most High is so great that it “will overshadow you” [Note: [Col. 0633] Ibid.], just as the sun overshadows and strikes back the eyes, preventing them from seeing it in its orb [Col. 0634C]. Therefore, I say, turn your eyes away, because they—that is, the imperfection of those unable to comprehend me—have caused me to fly away, so that you cannot comprehend me well. As is read in Proverbs: “Do not raise your eyes to riches which you cannot possess, for they will make themselves wings like eagles and fly to heaven” [Note: [Col. 0633] Prov. 23]; and in the Psalm: “Man comes to a deep heart, and God shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0633] Ps. 63].

Accordingly, after certain praises of the mother have been repeated—praises which the preceding Scripture contains and the exposition explains—it is added:

Sixty are queens, and eighty concubines, and maidens without number.

[THO.] Queens and concubines alike indeed approach the king’s throne and bear the king’s children, but [Col. 0634D] not both alike ennoble their heads with the royal diadem. Both acquire souls for God through preaching and baptism, but they differ greatly from one another. Those are queens who serve God with the intention of obtaining the kingdom. Those are concubines who acquire souls for Christ for the advantage of fleshly comforts and occasions of pleasure. Hence the Apostle says: “Whether through pretext or through truth, provided that Christ is proclaimed, I rejoice in this and shall rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0633] Phil. 1].

The queens are designated by the number sixty, on account of knowledge of the Decalogue and perfection of good work, signified by the number six [Col. 0635A]. Again, five multiplied by twelve makes sixty. These rule the five senses and shape their life according to the twelve apostles, so that with them they may receive a crown in the kingdom.

The number eighty, which is divisible by four, is taken in an evil sense on account of the pleasures of temporal things, because the course of this world is conducted through four seasons, or because the world is divided by four regions: east, west, north, and south. The maidens are those newly reborn in Christ, not yet capable of preaching. As though not yet fit for the royal tone, they attend the faithful in the queen’s ministry by watchful service, because they faithfully obey the commands of holy Church. Hence above: “The maidens loved you exceedingly” [Note: [Col. 0635] Song 1]. Their number is without number, because the total number of citizens of the heavenly homeland surpasses [Col. 0635B] the measure of our estimation.

**132.** Three classes of women are enumerated: queens and concubines, and maidens. Queens bear children to the king in marriage; concubines bear without marriage; maidens, because of their age, are not suited to childbearing. Queens bear children for royal honour; concubines for temporal consolation; maidens are intent upon the queen’s service.

Queens are spiritual preachers; concubines are carnal preachers; maidens are lesser persons who emulate the life of spiritual people. Queens benefit others by word and example; concubines benefit them by word but corrupt them by example; maidens attend to the words and examples of the good. Of the first the Apostle says [Col. 0635C]: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” [Note: [Col. 0635] II Cor. 11]. Of the second Solomon says: “You will be delivered from the strange woman, who softens her words”—namely, by preaching—“and abandons the guide of her youth,” that is, Christ, by acting wickedly, “and forgets the covenant of her God” [Note: [Col. 0635] Prov. 2], which she promises in word but does not fulfil in deed. Of the third: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you” [Note: [Col. 0635] Ps. 44].

Of queens Paul says: “A woman shall be saved through childbearing, if they remain in faith and love” [Note: [Col. 0635] I Tim. 2]. Of concubines, the same Apostle says: “Let us not be like the many who adulterate the word of God” [Note: [Col. 0635] II Cor. 2]. Of maidens: “The maidens loved you exceedingly”; and, “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” [Note: [Col. 0635] Song 1].

Bathsheba, whom David took as wife, made queen, and who bore him a wise son, namely Solomon [Note: [Col. 0635] II Kings 11], prefigured these queens [Col. 0635D]. Bathsheba means “sevenfold” or “well of abundance.” Those filled with the sevenfold Spirit and abounding in knowledge beget peaceful sons—which is the meaning of Solomon.

Such queens please David, for they are praiseworthy in four respects: in glory, beauty, companionship, and childbearing. Their beauty is outward, their glory inward; their companionship is that of the maidens, and their childbearing that of converts. Of beauty: “The king shall desire your beauty” [Note: [Col. 0635] Ps. 44]. Of glory: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed about with golden fringes,” that is, works of charity, “arrayed in varied colours” [Note: [Col. 0635] Ibid.], namely, virtues. Of companionship: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you” [Note: [Col. 0635] Ibid.]. Of childbearing: “Sons have been born to you in place of your fathers” [Note: [Col. 0635] Ibid.].

“Who,” he says, “shall find a strong woman?” [Note: [Col. 0635] Prov. 31]. Behold, you have found her. But what is the purpose of her strength? Because “her price is from afar, even from the uttermost boundaries” [Col. 0636A] [Note: [Col. 0635] Ibid.]—that is, from heaven, which is the highest boundary. “The heart of her husband trusts in her” [Note: [Col. 0635] Ibid.].

Concubines, however, sometimes bear children like the king, sometimes like their mother, and sometimes degenerate children: like the king in virtue, like the mother in pleasure, degenerate in unbelief. The first are wise and strong men; the second are soft and effeminate; the third are heretics. In figure of these, the prophet Hosea took as wife a prostitute, namely Gomer [Note: [Col. 0635] Hos. 1]. Hosea means “saviour,” that is, Christ. By the prostitute he first begets a son like himself, and therefore he was called Jezreel, that is, “seed of God” or “son of God.” Second, the prostitute bears a daughter like herself, because she is pleasure-loving; therefore she is called “Without Mercy,” because in following her mother she deserves to be deprived of God’s mercy. Third, she bears a degenerate son, because he degenerates in this: that he surpasses his mother in unbelief; therefore he is called “Not My People” [Note: [Col. 0635] Ibid.].

The first are built up by their mother’s word; the second are corrupted by her example; the third are led astray because they think their mother wholly estranged from God. To the first it is said [Col. 0636C]: “Do what they say.” To the second: “But do not do what they do” [Note: [Col. 0635] Matt. 23]. To the third: “Even the sea-monsters have uncovered their breasts and nursed their young” [Note: [Col. 0635] Lam. 4]. The first are conformed to the king: “For those whom he foreknew, he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” [Note: [Col. 0635] Rom. 8]. Of the daughter who resembles her mother it is said: “Wretched daughter of Babylon” [Note: [Col. 0635] Ps. 136]. She is wretched because she resembles her mother. Hence the poet [Note: [Col. 0635] Juv. VI, 239]:

> Do you expect a mother to hand down honourable conduct,  
> or manners other than those she herself possesses?  
> Indeed, it is advantageous to produce a filthy little daughter  
> for a filthy old woman.

“When the living creatures went, the wheels beside them went also; and when they were lifted up from the earth, the wheels following them were lifted up likewise” [Note: [Col. 0635] Ezek. 1]. These living creatures are prelates; the wheels are the lives of people [Col. 0636D]. Therefore, when prelates walk through earthly things, people’s lives conform to them; and when they are raised to heavenly things, the wheels likewise are raised. Of the last it is said: “Woe to the sinful nation, to the people burdened with iniquity, to the evil seed, to wicked children!” [Note: [Col. 0635] Isa. 1].

The task of maidens in the Church is to observe the life of religious persons; to refresh themselves with the teaching of masters, as with bread; to recollect their sins in bitterness; and frequently to bathe themselves in tears, so that at last they may be among the number of queens and approach the king’s bed. So Ruth, who is called “inspired,” a Moabitess, in the field [Col. 0637A] of Boaz, which means “in strength”—that is, in the Church of Christ, who is the mighty God—gathered ears after the reapers: that is, she observed the life of religious people. She refreshed herself with the teaching of masters as with bread. This is what Boaz said to her: “Eat bread with our servants.” And he added: “Dip your morsel in vinegar” [Note: [Col. 0637] Ruth 2]. This means that, in her refreshment, she ought to recollect her sins in bitterness. “And drink,” he says, “the water from our bundles” [Note: [Col. 0637] Ibid.]: this means that she ought to bathe herself in tears. Thus, growing, she sometimes becomes a queen, so that by preaching she may bear children to the king.

Morally, the king is our spirit; the queen, reason; the concubine, sensuality; and the maidens, holy meditations. Reason bears children to the king—that is, to the spirit—namely knowledge of truth [Col. 0637B] and discernment in actions and deliberations. The concubine—that is, sensuality—also bears children to the king when it directs the outward senses, which it gives life to, toward good uses. Although the maidens do not bear children, they assist in nourishing those who are born and serve the queen.

Queen Esther [Note: [Col. 0637] Esther 15] approached trembling before King Ahasuerus; and because she was delicate and almost fell to the ground from fear, she had two maidens in her service. One—hope—supported her head, that is, the higher power of reason, which is contemplation of God. The other—fear—supported her garments, lest they trail on the earth; that is, lest a good ordering of morals and works incline itself toward earthly things.

Concubines are sometimes good together with their children: namely, when movements of sensuality direct the outward senses to good uses. These are the concubines who bore Jacob good sons, that is, the patriarchs. There are also concubines who are evil with their children, and they must be cast out. Hence it is said of Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant [Col. 0637C]: “Cast out the maidservant and her son” [Note: [Col. 0637] Gen. 21]. For Hagar, whose name means “servitude”—that is, sensuality, which ought to serve reason—was proud against her mistress; and Ishmael played shamefully with his brother Isaac [Note: [Col. 0637] Gen. 23], because the wanderings of the senses often overthrow good uses.

Maidens also serve the queen when holy meditations nourish devout affections. Hence Abishag the Shunammite, whose name means “my father’s laughter” or “joy,” warmed David’s feet [Note: [Col. 0637] II Kings 2].

The fact that queens are placed under the number sixty and concubines under eighty is significant. Sixty has two divisions beneath it. Sixty is divided into thirty and thirty: this is the first. Again, thirty is divided into fifteen and fifteen; but fifteen cannot be divided. These are the two divisions suffered by the righteous. First, they grieve because they are still separated from the kingdom; second, they suffer when the soul is separated from its body.

Eighty, however, has four divisions: first into forty and forty; second, forty into twenty and twenty; third, twenty into ten [Col. 0638A] and ten; fourth, ten into five and five. But five is not divided. In these understand the two divisions already mentioned, together with two others suffered by the unrighteous: one by which they are divided from God’s grace, the other by which they are divided from the fulfilment of their desire. But the maidens are without number because of the multitude of thoughts, which cannot be comprehended under a number.

One is my dove, my perfect one; she is one to her mother and chosen by her who bore her.

[THO.] (Thus.) She is one, because there is not one Church before the Law, another under the Law, another under grace, another from the circumcision, and another from the uncircumcision. Rather, as there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all [Note: [Col. 0637] Eph. 4], so the Catholic Church is one, dispersed throughout the whole [Col. 0638B] world.

She is called a dove because the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove [Note: [Col. 0637] Matt. 3], in order to show both his simplicity and the simplicity of the one upon whom he descended, which he also bestowed upon the Church. She is called perfect because she is gathered from all peoples and made perfect by receiving all divine gifts. The mother and begetter of the present Church is that one of whom the Apostle says: “The Jerusalem which is above is free; she is our mother” [Note: [Col. 0637] Gal. 4]. For “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” [Note: [Col. 0637] Jas. 1]. She is chosen by her mother and approved by the heavenly Church because of her unity.

Note that the bride is called one, called a dove, called perfect, and called chosen. She is one when she begins [Col. 0638C]; a dove when grace increases; perfect when the world is wholly despised; chosen when the entire mind is directed toward God.

To say nothing for the present of philosophical unities, so far as the present subject is concerned: there is a spiritual one, a singular one, and an eternal one. The first is by gathering into one; the second by union; the third by eternal unity. The first is in faith; the second comes about in the Virgin; the third in the Trinity. Of the first: “Whoever clings to God becomes one spirit” [Note: [Col. 0637] I Cor. 6]. Of the second: “As rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ” [Note: [Col. 0637] Athanasian Creed]. Of the third: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and these three are one” [Note: [Col. 0637] I John 5].

By the first, we are gathered together as living stones to build God’s temple; by the second, we are raised up; by the third, we shall be brought to completion [Col. 0638D]. Of the first: the love of Christ gathered us into one; of the second: the Lord raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant; of the third it is said that God will perfect and establish us. Again, we ourselves groan, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling which is from heaven.

By the first unity, then, the bride is called one: namely, by the gathering of the faithful, like stones for building the Lord’s temple. It is first founded with rough and unpolished stones, namely humility. Then stones, carved in patience, are set in place; polished stones, in gentleness, are laid upon them; they are bound together, as it were with cement, by charity; and finally the temple is built up through diligent preservation of peace. Thus the Apostle taught how to build, saying: “I beseech you to walk worthily, with humility and gentleness, with patience bearing with one another in charity, diligently preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 0639] Eph. 4].

Christ likewise acted thus: “See that you make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” [Note: [Col. 0639] Exod. 25]. Thus the bride is one; she is also a dove through good simplicity. This occurs in three ways: if she invites others to peace; if, when injuries are inflicted upon her, she does not retaliate; and if she exalts others in God’s grace. Of the first: “Pursue peace with all men and holiness, without which no one shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0639] Heb. 12]. Of the second: “Not rendering evil for evil [Col. 0639B], nor curse for curse, but on the contrary blessing” [Note: [Col. 0639] I Pet. 3]. Of the third, as the Apostle says: “It is best to strengthen the heart by grace” [Note: [Col. 0639] Heb. 13]; and, “See that you do not receive the grace of God in vain” [Note: [Col. 0639] II Cor. 6]; and, “Blossom, flowers, in grace” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ecclus. 39].

Hence we read in Scripture of three doves. The first brought an olive branch to the ark as a sign of peace during the flood; the second was offered in sacrifice under the Law; the third appeared over the Lord at his baptism. Concerning these doves, against the Simoniacs, it is said that the Lord, having made a whip of cords, drove from the temple those who sold sheep, oxen, and doves [Note: [Col. 0639] John 2]. Here the sheep signifies simplicity, the ox the labour of preaching, and the dove the sacraments of the new grace. Hypocrites sell the first; hirelings, the second; Simoniacs, the third, and are worse [Col. 0639C] than the rest. Because they sell the dove, they are cast out of the temple, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “Cast out the court which is outside” [Note: [Col. 0639] Rev. 11], namely by a whip made of the cords of sins. Hence David says: “The cords of sinners have encircled me” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 118]. Thus this dove is not one among them.

Again, the bride is perfect when the world is perfectly despised, in the order taught by the Lord: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0639] Matt. 19]. The first stage, then, is in the intention; the second in the act; the third in advancement; the fourth in the outcome: in the intention of the will, in the act of relinquishment, in the advancement of giving away, and in the outcome of the reward hoped for. For, as Gregory says [Col. 0639D]: “To will with the mind is to go; by willing, good is already loved.” By relinquishing, we utterly despise the world. By giving away, we love our neighbour when we provide from our own resources for his need. Then, by hoping that we shall have rewards in heaven, we lay up treasure and raise our heart on high.

Thus the holy martyrs, “going, went and wept, sowing their seed; but coming, they shall come with rejoicing” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 125].

The bride is also chosen by her mother—that is, “the Jerusalem which is above, which is our mother” [Note: [Col. 0639] Gal. 4]—whose head is Christ, who has chosen her [Col. 0640A]. It should be known, however, that there is election of predestination, election of grace, and election of assumption. The first preserves the human being’s free will; the second advances one to dignity; the third leads one to blessedness. Of the first the Apostle says: “As he chose you before the foundation of the world” [Note: [Col. 0639] Eph. 1]. Of the second, the same Apostle Paul says: “Chosen not by men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0639] Gal. 1]. Of the third David says: “Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up; he shall dwell in your courts” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 64]. Again: “Holy and righteous ones, rejoice in the Lord: God has chosen you as his inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0639] Office of the Church]. By the first the Lord foreknew us; by the second he calls and justifies us [Note: [Col. 0639] Rom. 8]; by the third he will glorify us in his heavenly glory.

Humanity is praised not in one person alone, but in unanimity among brethren. Thus the Apostle says: “Unanimous in one Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0639] Phil. 1]. But it should be noted that in prayer some are faint-hearted, whereas they ought first to be great-hearted; second, of one mind; third, long-suffering.

Three things make people faint-hearted in prayer: impurity of conscience, the loftiness of the petition, and the severity of the one who asks. The first was Judas, who despaired because of the guilt of his conscience. The second was Ahaz, king of Israel, to whom it was said: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord”; and he said: “I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test” [Note: [Col. 0639] Isa. 7]. The third was the woman with the issue of blood, who, not daring to touch Christ, “touched the fringe of his garment” [Note: [Col. 0639] Matt. 9].

For the first had heard: “God does not hear sinners” [Note: [Col. 0639] John 9]. The second had heard: “Do not seek what is higher than you [Col. 0640C], nor search into what is greater than you” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ecclus. 3]. The third had heard: “When you stretch out your hands in prayer, I shall not hear; your hands are full of blood” [Note: [Col. 0639] Isa. 1]. Therefore, as it is written: “Whoever is faint-hearted, and whoever has taken a wife, let him return to his house” [Note: [Col. 0639] Deut. 20]. You who are faint-hearted, do not be afraid. Do not attend to severity; rather attend to him who “saves from faintness of spirit and storm” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 54], who cries: “I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction. You shall call upon me, and I shall hear you” [Note: [Col. 0639] Jer. 29].

Having heard these things, those who were faint-hearted become great-hearted. Three things make people great-hearted in prayer: hope of pardon, hope of grace, and hope of glory. Hope of pardon produces purity of conscience; hope of grace enables one securely to ask for lofty things; hope of glory, setting severity aside, kindles one through the giver’s benevolence. Of the first: “Hope in him, all you assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 61], etc. Thus, by cleansing your conscience, you will have boldness in asking. Of the second: “Hope in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land, and you shall be fed by its riches” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 36]. Of the third: “Let all who hope in you rejoice; they shall exult forever, and you shall dwell in them” [Note: [Col. 0639] Ps. 5].

These hear: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it shall be done for you” [Note: [Col. 0639] Mark 11]. “The prayer of faith,” says James, “shall raise up the sick person” [Note: [Col. 0639] ch. 5]. But if [Col. 0641A] we have become great-hearted, we must be of one mind.

In three respects we are of one mind: in simplicity, in mortality, and in faithfulness. The first is against duplicity, the second against one’s own will, the third against unbelief. The first, lest one be deceitful toward one’s neighbour; the second, lest one be seditious among the saints; the third, lest one be divided from God through heresy. Because of these three things the Bridegroom says of the bride: “My dove is one; my strength is one; she is one to her mother.” Of simplicity David says: “He who speaks truth in his heart, who has practised no deceit with his tongue [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 14].” For a double-minded person is scarcely steadfast in all his works. Of the second: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together as one [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 132]!” Again [Col. 0641B] he says: “Who makes those of one disposition dwell in a house [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 112].” Of the third: “There was one spirit and one faith among them [Note: [Col. 0641] Church Office].” Again: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul [Note: [Col. 0641] Acts 4].” They are also of one mind in prayer, because they ask for one thing. “But one thing is necessary [Note: [Col. 0641] Luke 10].”—“One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 26].” Meanwhile, therefore, let there be in us “one spirit, one faith, one baptism [Note: [Col. 0641] Eph. 4].” One spirit in earthly concord, one faith in the Church, one baptism in the cleansing of conscience.

But since momentary unanimity profits little, perpetual long-suffering must be present. Therefore, if we behold Christ as long-suffering in enduring worldly tribulation, long-suffering in his Passion, long-suffering in expectation, [Col. 0641C] we too ought much more to be long-suffering in prayer. Prayer, therefore, ought to have depth, long-suffering, breadth, and height: depth in contrition, breadth in love, length in expectation, height in awaiting recompense. Hear of depth: “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; O Lord, hear my prayer [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 129]”; and of breadth: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved [Note: [Col. 0641] Jas. 5]”; and of long-suffering: “Pray without ceasing,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0641] 1 Thess. 5]. “For the continual prayer of the righteous person is very powerful,” says James [Note: [Col. 0641] ch. 5]. And David: “Let my prayer be directed like incense before you [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 140].” The same author: “Let the evening prayer ascend to you, O Lord, and let your mercy descend upon us [Note: [Col. 0641] Antiphon for the First Sunday of Advent, at Vespers].” Hear of height [Col. 0641D]: “For you, my God, have heard my prayer; you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name [Note: [Col. 0641] Ps. 60].” Of the same matter Solomon says: “The end of prayer is better than its beginning [Note: [Col. 0641] Eccles. 7].” Thus, “when you stand to pray, if you ask anything in this manner, believe that you will receive it [Note: [Col. 0641] Mark 11].”

Therefore, that prayer may be heard, let the faint-hearted hasten to mercy; the great-hearted to temperance; the united in heart to obedience; the long-suffering to patience: to mercy, lest he fall into despair; [Col. 0642A] to temperance, lest he fall into self-exaltation; to obedience, that he may fulfil not only the command of a master but also that of a brother; to patience, lest he fail through weariness. Let the faint-hearted therefore say: “O Lord, when you are angry, you will remember mercy [Note: [Col. 0641] Hab. 3].” Let the great-hearted beware lest what was said to the two sons of Zebedee be said to them: “You do not know what you are asking [Note: [Col. 0641] Mark 10].” Let those who are of one mind look to Christ, who “became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted him [Note: [Col. 0641] Phil. 2].” But because “hope deferred afflicts the soul [Note: [Col. 0641] Prov. 13],” let the long-suffering hear: “He who perseveres unto the end shall be saved [Note: [Col. 0641] Matt. 10],” and the Apostle: “Do not grow weary, fainting in your souls. For you have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin [Note: [Col. 0641] Heb. 12].”

This unanimity, moreover, exists not only [Col. 0642B] in prayer but also in compassion. Here it must be observed that *propasio* (the first involuntary stirring of passion) is one thing, *compassio* (compassion) another, and *passio* (suffering) another. In *propasio*, the vehemence of the first suggestion must be avoided; in compassion, life is born; in suffering, the constricting anguish of beneficial affliction rages. The first is material for the exercise of virtue; through the second forgiveness is obtained; the third, however, is followed by the glory of the heavenly kingdom. In the first, a person triumphs because he quickly recognizes the suggestion; in the second, he bestows a benefit on his neighbour; in the third, he repays Christ who suffers in return.

He invites you to the first when he says: “With every vigilance guard your heart [Note: [Col. 0641] Prov. 4],” etc.; “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them [Note: [Col. 0641] Prov. 1].” In this conflict Agag was slain, that is, the suggestion so called—namely the king of Amalek [Note: [Col. 0641] 1 Sam. 15]—whose name means “a people [Col. 0642C] bound.” Mercy, which follows, is called compassion: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful [Note: [Col. 0641] Luke 6].” Again: “I desired mercy and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings [Note: [Col. 0641] Hos. 6].” Of suffering he says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake [Note: [Col. 0641] Matt. 5].” Therefore in the first there is the dove; in the second, the perfect one; in the third, she is one to her mother and beloved by her begetter, the Church above the heavens. May Jesus Christ bring us to her: “to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen [Note: [Col. 0641] Rom. 16].”

Sixty are queens, eighty concubines, and young women without number. Nevertheless, my dove is one.

[CARD.] By queens and concubines are signified the souls of prelates [Col. 0642D], because alike they approach the bed, alike they beget, but they are not alike crowned. Queens serve from a true regard for the heavenly kingdom; concubines, however, serve from regard for temporal things and on the pretext of teaching. Of the fruit of both the Apostle rejoices, saying to the Philippians: “What then? Provided that in every manner, whether from truth or from occasion, Christ is proclaimed, in this I rejoice and shall rejoice [Note: [Col. 0641] Phil. 1].” Yet we should note [Col. 0643A] that concubines are more numerous than queens. By the young women, moreover, is indicated the inexperienced and, as it were, innumerable multitude of those souls which are renewed through faith, still dependent upon the breasts of their teachers. Of them Christ says that, although the multitude of the souls mentioned is so great, yet my dove is one, full of grace beyond the rest; and she herself is one to her mother, namely to heavenly grace, because she can uniquely say: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty [Note: [Col. 0643] 1 Cor. 15]”; and she herself is chosen by her mother. For among all daughters she is pre-elect to her mother—the Church, whether militant or triumphant. Therefore all rise up to praise her. This is what follows:

[Col. 0643B] The daughters saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her.

[THO.] Great is the praise of Catholic unity, which both Grace, the mother who bore her, chose for eternity, and the daughters whom she herself bore and nourished for God through the Spirit. As soon as they saw her—that is, as soon as they learned the chastity of her life and heard the gifts of the inheritance promised to her—they deservedly do not cease to call her blessed. The queens and concubines also exalt her with just praises: that is, the heavenly ones who are truly participants in her kingdom, and those who cleave to her in name alone but are earthly in hope and mind, acknowledge her worthy of everlasting praise.

The daughters saw; the queens saw; the concubines saw. The daughters sigh in emulation of her; the queens rejoice with her over her perfection; [Col. 0643C] the concubines are gnawed by the worm of conscience. The daughters sigh for her, recognizing their own weakness; the queens rejoice with her, hastening together toward blessedness; the concubines are gnawed by the worm of conscience because they see themselves prepared for condemnation. Hence the young women cry: “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments [Note: [Col. 0643] Song 1].” Thus Ruth, whose name is said to mean “inspired,” cries to her mother-in-law Naomi, whose name means “beautiful”: “Wherever you go, I too shall go; wherever you remain, I too; as the Lord lives, only death shall separate you and me [Note: [Col. 0643] Ruth 1].” The queens say: “I rejoiced at the things said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 121].” The concubines are gnawed by the worm of conscience, [Col. 0643D] their own conscience bearing witness to them and their thoughts accusing one another; hence certain ones who return cry: “O Lord, do not remember our former iniquities [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 78].” Some despair with Cain, saying: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for [Note: [Col. 0643] Gen. 4].” Others, with Judas, run to the noose, saying: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood [Note: [Col. 0643] Matt. 27].”

The order is fitting: first they see, second they proclaim her most blessed, third they praise. They see her “without spot or wrinkle [Note: [Col. 0643] Eph. 5]”; they proclaim most blessed her who is [Col. 0644A] now filled with heavenly refreshment; they praise her as exalted above human condition to heavenly joys. She has neither spot nor wrinkle, being purified by sacrifices; she is filled, satiated with heavenly bread; she is exalted to joys, made glad, that is, by the wine of gladness. These are the three things of which Samuel said to Saul: “When you come to the oak of Tabor, three men going to Bethel will meet you: one carrying three kids, another carrying three loaves of bread, another a flask of wine [Note: [Col. 0643] 1 Sam. 10].” Tabor means “coming light”; the oak is the cross of Christ through which light came; the three men are three classes of persons: beginners, those advancing, and the perfect; or Daniel, Job, and Noah. In the three kids is the threefold sacrifice by which the bride is purified, because kids were sacrificed under the Law. The first sacrifice is [Col. 0644B] contrition, the second justification, the third jubilation. Of the first: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 50]”; of the second: “Offer a sacrifice of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 4]”; of the third: “The sacrifice of praise will honour me [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 49].” Thus the bride first slays the old person in herself through repentance. Then she walks in newness of life through righteousness [Note: [Col. 0643] Rom. 6]. Finally, she praises God through ineffable joy.

The bride is called most blessed when satiated with three loaves, concerning which the Gospel says: “Friend, lend me three loaves [Note: [Col. 0643] Luke 11].” The first is that of teaching [134], the second of tears, the third of divine consolation. The first is from the table of presentation [Note: [Col. 0643] Num. 8]; of the second David says: “My tears became bread for me day and night [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 41]”; of the third: “Man ate the bread of angels [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 77].” [Col. 0644C] For the first she is proclaimed blessed; for the second, more blessed; for the third, most blessed.

The flask of wine is joy, by which she inwardly touches Christ, already with him tasting the joys of the heavenly homeland. These, set aflame with vehement love, recline at supper upon the Lord’s breast with John [Note: [Col. 0643] John 13]. For the first touch is to touch the hem of his garment—that is, his faith or manner of life—with the woman suffering from haemorrhage [Note: [Col. 0643] Luke 8]; and by this we are healed from the blood of guilt. The second touch is to touch his feet—that is, his affections—with Mary Magdalene. The third is to recline at supper upon his breast with John: that is, to taste heavenly joys; and for this she is praised.

These matters can be understood of the Blessed Virgin. It should be noted, however, that the concubines [Col. 0644D] can be understood as those who still weep over the enormity of their sins, who do not yet judge themselves worthy to approach the embraces of the King; the daughters are those who contemplate in this pilgrimage; the queens are those who already enjoy the vision of God. Therefore, to assign individual words to each: the concubines praise, the daughters see, the queens proclaim. The concubines do so as they have received it by instruction; the daughters as they prove it by the evidence of contemplation; the queens as they have learned it by experience. The concubines praise because “she rose in the night and gave prey to her household and provisions to her maidservants [Note: [Col. 0643] Prov. 31]”; the daughters, because “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within, in golden fringes [Note: [Col. 0643] Ps. 44]”; the queens, [Col. 0645A] because “she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom [Note: [Col. 0645] Matt. 12].”

Behold, the concubines praise her as blessed, the daughters see her as more blessed, the queens proclaim her most blessed. The concubines, therefore, praise her in respect of her conception, praise her in respect of her fruit, praise her in respect of her childbirth. In respect of conception, because it was without the foulness of lust; in respect of the fruit, because he was free from original necessity; in respect of childbirth, because it was without difficulty. In conception, Aaron’s rod blossomed without human cultivation [Note: [Col. 0645] Num. 17]; in the fruit: “A scorching wind will come from the desert region, and it will dry up the veins of death [Note: [Col. 0645] Hos. 13]”; in childbirth: the bush was seen burning without damage from the burning [Note: [Col. 0645] Exod. 3]. In the first, virginity is praised; in the second, newness; in the third, sublimity. Virginity which conceived and did not wither; newness which lay hidden in the woman when created; subtlety by which the Creator went forth from the womb and did not open the gate.

[Col. 0645B] Of the first Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son [Note: [Col. 0645] Isa. 7].” Of the second the prophet says: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man [Note: [Col. 0645] Jer. 31].” Of the third Ezekiel says: “This gate shall be shut and shall not be opened; no man shall enter through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it. The man shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord [Note: [Col. 0645] Ezek. 46].” Therefore the concubine, seeing these great deeds of the bride in her delivery, does not cease to praise, and rightly so; for she weeps because she sees that she cannot attain that place. Against the first, therefore, she blushes; against the second, she considers herself worthless; against the third, she wastes away. She blushes to be propagated from corruption. Hear her shame: “All day long my shame is before me,” says David [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 43]. Hence the same says: “I am a worm and not a man [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 21].”

[Col. 0645C] Of corruption Job says: “To corruption I said: You are my father; and to worms: my mother and my sister [Note: [Col. 0645] Job 17].” Hear of the second: “The snares of death overtook me [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 17].” Again: “The cords of sinners have encircled me [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 118].” Of humility: “Do you think it worthy to open your eyes upon one such as this? [Note: [Col. 0645] Job 14].” Of the third, hear of the toil of misery: “Like a flower he comes forth and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and does not remain in the same state [Note: [Col. 0645] ibid.].” Again: “Man is born for labour, and the bird for flying [Note: [Col. 0645] Job 5].” And: “You have made his soul waste away like a spider [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 38].” Behold how she wastes away through the labour of present misery.

These three things are figured in Rebecca. For when Isaac, having gone out to meditate in the field, met her [Note: [Col. 0645] Gen. 24], see what she did: first she covered [Col. 0645D] her face with a veil; second, she dismounted from the camel; third, she led Deborah, whose name means “bee,” at her side. By covering her face, she was ashamed; by dismounting from the camel, she was humbled; by having Deborah at her side, she was wearied by the sting of misery. But while she is exercised in such things, she is received by Isaac, whose name means “laughter,” and is brought into his mother’s chamber; thus she becomes his bride. For these concubines, while exercised in such things, deserve in the course of time to become brides of Christ.

The faithful bride is customarily praised in three respects: [Col. 0646A] for piety, for fear, and for labour. For piety, by which a father’s anger is tempered toward little ones; for fear, by which reverence is rendered to the bridegroom; for labour, by which the pleasure of the flesh is subdued and the riches of the house furnished. Such was the Blessed Virgin: pious, reconciling to her Son the people subject to God; reverent, honouring her Son with due honour; industrious, subduing the flesh and furnishing the virginal chamber for her Son with the riches of virtues. In the first she recalled God’s people to their inheritance; hence she says: “I took root among an honoured people, and in the portions of my God is his inheritance [Note: [Col. 0645] Sir. 24].” As if she said: “I acquired for them the inheritance of my God.” Of the second she herself says: “I am the mother of fair love and fear [Note: [Col. 0645] ibid.].” Of the third: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all [Note: [Col. 0645] Sir. 31].”

[Col. 0646B] Solomon set forth these three praises in his treatment of the strong woman [Note: [Col. 0645] Prov. 31]. Of the first he says: “Her children rose up and proclaimed her most blessed; her husband too praised her.” Of the second he says immediately afterwards: “The woman who fears the Lord shall be praised.” Of the third he adds there: “Her works praise her in the gates,” that is, she is praised because of them. Behold, the handmaids, or concubines, have praised her. It follows:

The daughters saw, but differently; for of the daughters some go forth, some draw near, some go beyond. They go forth with the riches of virtues; they draw near with the spices of spiritual love; they go beyond into the amazement of admiration. Of the first: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all.” Of the second: “Myrrh and stacte and cassia from your garments [Col. 0646C] [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 44],” etc. For Mary was the King’s garment and an ivory house [Note: [Col. 0645] ibid.]. Of the third: “The daughters ran upon the wall [Note: [Col. 0645] Gen. 49].” The wall is the firmness and loftiness of virtues, through which we are more ready for seeing heavenly things. The first imitate Mary from afar; the second emulate her at close hand; the third, in thought and longing, live in that eternal homeland. The first are honoured by the abundance of fruits; the second, in joy and exultation; the third rejoice in newness. Of the first: “Virgins shall be brought to the King after her [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 44].” Of the second: “Her companions shall be brought to you; they shall be brought in joy and exultation [Note: [Col. 0645] ibid.].” Of the third: “They shall be brought into the temple of the King [Note: [Col. 0645] ibid.],” which is heavenly blessedness, where they enter in mind with Mary.

The first [Col. 0646D] imitate her by receiving from her strictness and discipline; the second receive the honey-sweetness of devotion; the third taste the wisdom of heavenly things. Mary is indeed the ark of which Revelation says: “Heaven was opened, and the ark of God was seen in it [Note: [Col. 0645] Rev. 11].” In it were the rod, manna, and tablets of the covenant [Note: [Col. 0645] Heb. 9]. Therefore the rod signifies discipline, manna the sweetness of devotion, and the tablets of the covenant wisdom. She herself stood at God’s right hand, surrounded with variety [Note: [Col. 0645] Ps. 44]. Truly with variety, for she is the rainbow of diverse colours of which John speaks in the same [Col. 0647A] Revelation: “He who sat upon the throne was like the appearance of jasper and sardius [Note: [Col. 0647] Rev. 4],” namely Christ. Jasper is green in colour, and in it is divinity; sardius is red, the humanity that suffered for us. Then it is added: “And around the throne was a rainbow like an emerald in appearance [Note: [Col. 0647] ibid.].” An emerald is green in colour. Yet the rainbow has more colours than this one, which signify something in the Blessed Virgin: it has blackness, pallor, greenness, whiteness, and redness. In blackness is signified her care for sinners; in pallor, for those who suffer; in greenness, for those striving after virtues; in whiteness, for virgins; in redness, for those fervent in charity. For the first, that she may obtain pardon for them from her Son; for the second, patience; for the third, [Col. 0647B] the grace of advancement; for the fourth, humility; for the fifth, piety. Concerning the first she says: “I am black, but beautiful [Note: [Col. 0647] Song 1]”; concerning the second: “Because the sun has discoloured me [Note: [Col. 0647] ibid.]”; concerning the third, in this place, that she was like an emerald in appearance; concerning the fourth: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters [Note: [Col. 0647] Song 2]”; concerning the fifth: “Your lips are like a scarlet thread [Note: [Col. 0647] Song 4].”

Again, the rainbow signifies peace, announces rain, and radiates in many forms from the presence of the sun. In the first respect, through her peace was obtained for humankind; in the second, through her the rain of grace was poured forth; in the third, she is glorious in the vision of God. On account of the first, the Bridegroom kissed her with the kiss of his mouth—of his mouth [Note: [Col. 0647] Song 1]. On account of the second, she was “a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing mightily from Lebanon [Note: [Col. 0647] Song 4].” [Col. 0647C] On account of the third, the Bridegroom says to her: “Come, my chosen one, and I shall set my throne in you, because the King has desired your beauty [Note: [Col. 0647] Church Office].” Such did the daughters see her. It follows:

The queens proclaimed her most blessed—not with just any blessedness. For there are different kinds of blessedness: false blessedness, true blessedness, secure blessedness, and full blessedness. The first deceives; the second begins; the third attains; the fourth receives. The first deceives through vain delight; the second begins through virtue and action; the third attains the divine promise; the fourth receives glorification of body and soul. Of the first it is said, after David has enumerated many temporal prosperities: “They called blessed the people to whom these things belong [Note: [Col. 0647] Ps. 143].” Of the second he immediately adds: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God [Note: [Col. 0647] ibid.].” And the Lord said to Simon Peter: [Col. 0647D] “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0647] Matt. 16].” Again: “Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he comes, finds watchful [Note: [Col. 0647] Luke 12].” Of the third, John the Evangelist says: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0647] Rev. 14].” And why they are blessed he adds: “From now on, the Spirit says, let them rest from their labours [Note: [Col. 0647] ibid.].” Of the fourth the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth [Note: [Col. 0647] Matt. 5],” that is, the body. For then they shall be glorified in soul and body. With this blessedness the queens proclaimed Mary most blessed.

[Col. 0648A] The daughters of Zion saw her.

[CARD.] Those whom he earlier called young women proclaimed her most blessed in their praises, and the queens and concubines praised her. The Son himself also takes up her praises with wonder, saying:

Who is this who comes forth like the dawn rising, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in battle?

[THOM.] The converted Synagogue marvels at the Church, so greatly exalted. She comes forth like the dawn rising, because after the darkness of ignorance the rising of the true light is now clearly shown in her to the world, while her heralds cry: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near [Note: [Col. 0647] Rom. 13].” Beautiful as the moon, because, illuminated by the Sun of righteousness, she has flooded the night of this age with the light of heavenly knowledge and evangelical conduct. [Col. 0648B] Chosen as the sun, because she has begun to make bright the image of her Creator, walking in all righteousness, holiness, and truth [Note: [Col. 0647] Eph. 4], and truly giving thanks to him, because “the light of your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us [Note: [Col. 0647] Ps. 4].”

Again, beautiful as the moon, because in the night of this life she now appears despised by the world, now bright; now full of the whiteness of virtues, now dishonoured by the vices of the wicked; after the manner of the moon she waxes and wanes. Chosen as the sun on the day of future blessedness, when she shall shine in the vision of unchangeable light, when all “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father [Note: [Col. 0647] Matt. 13].” Terrible as an army arrayed in battle, because the more perfectly both the Church and every faithful soul establishes in itself the order of virtues, the more terrible it becomes to the powers of the air.

[Col. 0648C] Again, dawn puts night to flight; the moon illumines night; the sun makes day bright; the terror of armies drives enemies away. Dawn puts night to flight by washing away guilt; the moon illumines night by removing ignorance; the sun makes day bright by revealing the righteousness of the saints; the terror of armies drives enemies away by restraining their savagery. Again, she is dawn for her own profit, moon for her neighbour’s edification, sun by restoring in herself God’s image, terrible as an army arrayed in battle by fortifying herself against the adversaries’ [135] contrivance.

But there is a threefold dawn, distinguished according to the threefold etymology of this name. The first is that of mercy, by which we recognize sin in order to flee it; the second is that of grace, by which [Col. 0648D] we see good in order to do it; the third is that of the glory of contemplation, in order that we may love and seek it. The first is called *aurora*, that is, *aura oriens*, “a rising breeze,” that is, moderation, because in it we restrain ourselves from vices. Of it Moses says: “It came to pass in the morning watch [Note: [Col. 0647] Exod. 14],” etc. The second, namely that of grace, is called *aurora*, “increasing dew,” because the dew of grace increases in us so that we may do good. Thus Gideon, rising early, found the fleece full and squeezed it into a bowl [Note: [Col. 0647] Judg. 6], that is, it came from the Virgin into the human heart. The third is called *aurora* as though *avium hora*, “the hour of birds,” because in it, contemplating the glory of heaven, we praise God at dawn like birds. Thus the Lord says to Job: [Col. 0649A] “Who set free the cornerstone, when the morning stars praised me and all the sons of God shouted for joy [Note: [Col. 0649] Job 38]?”

The first is dawn rising, the second dawn ascending, the third dawn advancing. The first rises from sin to holiness; the second ascends from virtue to virtue; the third advances as far as knowledge of God. Of the first Paul says to the sinful soul: “Awake, you who sleep; arise from the dead, and Christ will illuminate you [Note: [Col. 0649] Eph. 5].” It is also said of her: “Who is this who comes forth like the dawn rising?” And blessed Cecilia, as dawn was rising, said: “Come, soldiers of Christ, cast away the works of darkness [Note: [Col. 0649] In her Life].” Of the second, namely the ascending dawn, the angel said to Jacob: “Let me go, for the dawn is already rising [Note: [Col. 0649] Gen. 32].” For when the Lord has granted ascent toward virtues, while the mystical struggle goes on, so as to test her desire, he pretended to go farther, saying: “Let me go, for the dawn is already rising.” But the soul, inflamed with desire, answers: “I will not let you go unless you bless me [Note: [Col. 0649] ibid.],” that is, until you advance me to the third dawn, so that:

> Let the dawn advance its course,  
> Let the whole dawn come forth:  
> The whole Son in the Father,  
> And the whole Father in the Word.  
> [Note: [Col. 0649] Church Office]

When I have seen him in that dawn—that is, in the hour of birds—with the birds of heaven, namely the angels and the saints of this world, may I worthily praise, bless, and proclaim him: that I may give glory and proclamation, honour and praise, blessing and thanksgiving. Hence the elders in Revelation gave [Col. 0649C] “glory and honour and blessing to him who sits upon the throne [Note: [Col. 0649] Rev. 5].” And rightly, because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights [Note: [Col. 0649] Jas. 1],” as he himself says: “Without me you can do nothing [Note: [Col. 0649] John 15].”—“Truly, without you we can do nothing, O Lord. For our salvation is in your hand; give us sustenance, that we may be able to live. May your mercy look upon us, that we may securely serve our King and Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0649] Church Office].” Behold, this is of dawn as regards one’s own profit. It follows:

Beautiful as the moon, as regards the edification of one’s neighbour. As dawn puts darkness to flight, so the moon illumines the neighbour’s night. There is a threefold night: the night of guilt, the night of ignorance, and the night of human or [Col. 0649D] worldly adversity. Of the first Paul says: “You are not children of night or of darkness [Note: [Col. 0649] 1 Thess. 5].” Of the second: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near [Note: [Col. 0649] Rom. 13].” Of the third: “Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived [Note: [Col. 0649] Job 3].” She illumines the first, so that a person may see and abhor his own foulness; the second, lest he fall into error; the third, so as to reveal the recompense of worldly life or adversity. Through the first illumination the neighbour shines with purity; through the second, with knowledge of God; through the third, with the glory he awaits. Of the first: “You were once darkness, but now light [Col. 0650A] in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0649] Eph. 5].” Of the second: “The path of the righteous is like a shining light: it goes forth and increases unto the perfect day [Note: [Col. 0649] Prov. 4].” Of the third: “With unveiled face we behold the glory of God, so that we may be transformed into the same image from glory to glory [Note: [Col. 0649] 2 Cor. 5].”

The first light proceeds from purity, the second from truth, the third from the majesty of God contemplated. The soul teaching its neighbour receives these brightnesses from Christ, as the moon receives them from the sun. Through the first it is beautiful; through the second more beautiful; through the third most beautiful. For when it performs the first, it is in the new moon; when the second, in the half-moon; when the third, in the full moon. This accords with the threefold interpretation of the name. In the first sense it is called *luna*, namely, cleansing (*luens*) night—that is, guilt; in the second it is called *luna*, “light of night,” because [Col. 0650B] it illumines the erring person; in the third it is called *luna*, “light making the night pleasant.” For when the righteous person endures the adversities of this world, he finds much delight in the rewards which he expects from them: this is the moon’s increase.

But sometimes it wanes: for sometimes, according to the vicissitudes of times, it is turned toward loss and diminution; sometimes it is darkened by a cloud; sometimes it undergoes eclipse. Morally speaking, the first happens through weakness, because after labour our frailty grows lukewarm from weariness; the second through worldly concern, which prevents the teacher from being free to attend to an abandoned brother; the third through the teacher’s vicious manner of life, which causes his teaching to be despised. Of the first: “He made the moon for the seasons [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 103],” through whose alternation the moon waxes and wanes. Of the [Col. 0650C] second: “A fool changes like the moon [Note: [Col. 0649] Sir. 27],” while he entangles himself too deeply in worldly concern. Of the third: “The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood [Note: [Col. 0649] Joel 2].” For the moon is turned into blood when the life of a teacher is stained by sin.

The chosen soul is as the sun, reforming within itself the image of the true Sun—that is, of the Creator—which was deformed in Adam, so that it may say: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 4]. This, moreover, is the image of God. The Father is called memory, the Son understanding, the Holy Spirit will. Therefore receive from the Father memory, that you may say: “I remembered God and was delighted” [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 76]. From the Son, understanding, saying with David: “I have understood beyond the aged” [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 118], and: “Give me understanding, and I shall live” [Col. 0650D] [Note: [Col. 0649] Ibid.]. From the Holy Spirit, will, that you may say: “I have desired to do your will, O my God” [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 39]. Therefore remember, lest you forget and it be said to you: “You have forgotten the Lord your Creator” [Note: [Col. 0649] Isa. 51]. Understand, lest you be deceived and hear: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand” [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 48]; and: “He was unwilling to understand, so as to do good” [Note: [Col. 0649] Ps. 53]. Have will, lest you appear hard, among those of whom it is said: “They hardened their faces harder than rock” [Note: [Col. 0649] Jer. 5].

Likewise, God is compared to the sun because he courses around the fabric of the world: in this is signified power, namely the Father; he has brightness, in which is wisdom, namely the Son; he has heat, in which is benevolence, [Col. 0651A] namely the Holy Spirit. Therefore, in the circuit by which the one God created all things is power; in the brightness by which he illumines all is wisdom; in the heat by which he lights and quickens all is benevolence. And this is according to the threefold derivation of the name *sol*, “sun.” In the first sense it is called *Sol*, as though *solus*, “alone,” because “he alone is truly mighty” [Note: [Col. 0651] I Tim. 6]. In the second, it is called *Sol* from *solon*, which means “common,” because wisdom commonly “enlightens every human being coming into this world” [Note: [Col. 0651] John 1]. In the third, it is called *Sol*, as though “illuminating the paths of all,” by quickening all and seeing all: “For she is the artificer of all things, possessing every power, and overseeing all things” [Note: [Col. 0651] Wis. 7], and elsewhere: “The spirit proceeds, illuminating all things in its circuit, and returns to its circles” [Note: [Col. 0651] Eccl. 1]. Therefore, if you have within yourself [Col. 0651B] power to resist temptations, wisdom by which to recognize deceit, and benevolence by which to love God—likewise, if you remember God, if you understand, and if you will what you remember and understand—you are chosen as the sun.

But because the devil does not cease to assail the righteous, you must be terrible as an army drawn up in battle order. The soul has its own order, and the Church likewise has hers: the soul in its affections, the Church in the persons who serve in warfare. For each is a bride. The order of the soul is that it should first love what is above it; second, what it itself is; third, what is beside it; fourth, what is beneath it. First is God; second, the human being himself; third, the neighbour; fourth, one’s own body. Therefore it ought to love God more than itself; itself, secondly; its neighbour as itself, thirdly; and its body less [Col. 0651C] than neighbour and self.

The Church’s order is that it waits for the weary, bears the weak, strengthens the faint-hearted, restrains the rash, and appoints the strong beforehand: the weary, who have long borne the burden and heat of the day [Note: [Col. 0651] Matt. 20]; the weak both in body and character; the faint-hearted through fear; the rash through recklessness; the strong through charity. It waits for the weary out of compassion; bears the weak through a sustaining dispensation of compassion; strengthens the faint-hearted by promise; restrains the rash by discernment; appoints the strong beforehand, making them secure through expectation of reward.

Of the first: “Being compassionate one toward another; for if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” [Note: [Col. 0651] Rom. 8]. Of the second: “Bear one another’s burdens” [Note: [Col. 0651] Gal. 6]. And Paul: “I became weak to the weak, in order that I might gain the weak” [Note: [Col. 0651] I Cor. 9]. To the third it is said: “What eye has not seen, nor ear [Col. 0651D] heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, are the things which God has prepared for those who love him” [Note: [Col. 0651] I Cor. 2]. To the fourth it is said: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God” [Note: [Col. 0651] I John 4]. To the fifth it is said: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint for you a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0651] Luke 22].

The young Amalekite, whom David found weary on the road and refreshed, bore the figure of the first [Note: [Col. 0651] I Kings 30]. The man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, wounded by robbers, bears the figure of the weak [Note: [Col. 0651] Luke 10]. [Col. 0652A] The people of Israel, exhausted by hardships in the wilderness and wishing to return to Egypt, figures the faint-hearted [Note: [Col. 0651] Exod. 16]. Asahel, in pursuing Abner too impetuously and being slain by him, figured the rash in relation to Joab [Note: [Col. 0651] II Kings 2]. David fighting Goliath figured the strong [Note: [Col. 0651] I Kings 17]. And by fighting the Philistines and bringing two hundred foreskins, he won for himself Michal, daughter of King Saul, in marriage [Note: [Col. 0651] I Kings 18].

We believe that these same words were spoken prophetically of the Blessed Virgin. For she was dawn in her birth, beautiful as the moon in Christ’s conception, chosen as the sun in her Assumption, and terrible as an army drawn up in battle order in the conduct of her life. Nearly the same is said and understood of her as is said in the Book of Wisdom concerning Simon son of Onias: “Like the morning star amid a cloud, and like the full moon in his days he shines; and [Col. 0652B] like a sun shining forth, so he shone in the temple of the Lord; and like a rainbow shining among clouds of glory” [Note: [Col. 0651] Ecclus. 50].

For she was the morning star in her birth, the full moon in Christ’s conception, the shining sun in her Assumption, and the rainbow shining among clouds of grace in the holy conduct of her life; or, indeed, among the saints at the general resurrection. We read of several stars. There is the evening star, there are stars of the night, and there is the morning star. The first was Eve; the second, the glorious life of the ancient Fathers; the third was Mary. The first was in the beginning, but was extinguished when it fell, introducing the night of guilt and punishment. The second shone in the night of adversity through the virtue of patience. The third shone by grace amid the cloud of the Mosaic law.

The first is called *vesperus*, “evening,” as though “breathing woe.” For this is the star called wormwood in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0651] Apoc. 8], on account of the bitterness of the misery it brought. The second are called stars of the night. Hence: “She was for them a covering by day, and a light of stars by night” [Note: [Col. 0651] Wis. 10]. The third is called Lucifer for three reasons, according to a threefold interpretation. For she bore within herself the light, namely the incarnate wisdom of God; hence she is called *Lucifer*, as though “bearing light.” Likewise, by giving birth to Christ, whom the Law and Prophets had obscurely foretold, she illumined their cloud, blind with obscurity; hence she is called Lucifer, “bearing light to the blind.” Whence [Note: [Col. 0651] Office of the Church]:

> Bring forth light to the blind.

Likewise, being full of grace [Note: [Col. 0651] Luke 1], she bore light to those who came after her—that is, an abundance of grace. Hence she is called Lucifer [Col. 0652D] as though “fruitful in light,” she whose “glorious life gave light to the world” [Note: [Col. 0651] Office of the Church].

She was like the full moon in the conception: full in the angelic salutation, full in the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, full in the incarnation of divine wisdom. In the angelic salutation she was full of joy; in the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, full of grace; in the incarnation of divine wisdom, full of the remedy by which human infirmity might be healed. For the first reason it was fitting that this be sung to her: “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God” [Note: [Col. 0651] Isa. 61]. Of the second: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you” [Note: [Col. 0651] Luke 1]. Of the third [Col. 0653A] we cry: “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments; therefore the young maidens loved you exceedingly” [Note: [Col. 0653] Song 1].

It should also be noted that, when the moon is first illuminated, philosophers call it διτόμος (*ditomos*), from δύο, “two,” and τόμος, “division”: namely, when it has two horns. This was so in the angelic salutation: when the Virgin was first illumined, she was divided from others—that is, chosen above others—having love of God and neighbour as two shining horns. Hence: “You alone among the female sex have been exalted for ever” [Note: [Col. 0653] Office of the Church]. When it truly advances in growth, it is called *amphicircos*, from ἀμφί, “around,” and *circos*, “circle,” because, not yet wholly illuminated, it is surrounded by a certain circle of brightness. This occurred in the Virgin through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, by whom she was surrounded with every spiritual gift for her [Col. 0653B] preservation. When full, it is called πανσέληνος (*panselēnos*), from πᾶν, “all,” and σελήνη, “brightness,” and νύξ, “night”: as though “wholly shining in the night.” This took place in Christ’s incarnation, because then she received within herself the perfect light of wisdom. 136 It should also be known that the moon illumines the blindness of night and obscures the brightness of the other stars. Yet it continually suffers within itself the obscurity of a certain little cloud.

It illumines the blindness of night—that is, the unbelief of unbelievers—whence: “Her renowned life illumines all the Churches” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ibid.]. It obscures the brightness of the other stars because, however religious other holy women may have been, in comparison with the Blessed Virgin their merits have little brightness, since many daughters gathered riches, but this one surpassed them all. This moon, that is, the Blessed Virgin, suffers the obscurity of a little cloud—not, I say, of guilt, since she was made immune from sin, but of punishment, which she endured in compassion with her Son for those things which he endured in this exile. Hence it was said to her: “A sword shall pierce your own soul” [Note: [Col. 0653] Luke 2], that is, the Passion.

Likewise: “Like a sun shining forth, so he shone in the temple of the Lord.” There is a threefold temple of the Lord: the Blessed Virgin, the Church militant, and the heavenly homeland. Of the first it is said: “Temple of the Lord, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0653] Office of the Church]. Of the second: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” [Note: [Col. 0653] I Cor. 3]. Of the third the prophet says: “Do you think that I shall see your holy temple?” [Note: [Col. 0653] Jonah 2]—understood mystically. [Col. 0653D] In the first she shone as the sun by conceiving Christ; in the second by giving birth to him; in the third by following him: in the first, through purity of conscience; in the second, through the revelation of the prophets; in the third, through her Assumption. Through purity of conscience, because she was “full of grace” [Note: [Col. 0653] Luke 1]. Through the revelation of the prophets, because the woman in childbirth bore him whom the prophets had foretold. Through her Assumption, when the holy Mother of God was exalted above the choirs of angels into the heavenly kingdoms.

This sun sometimes shines in the temple, sometimes in the face, sometimes in the shield: in the temple of the heart, in the face of conduct, in the shield of adversity to be endured. In [Col. 0654A] the first, through purity of conscience; in the second, through the revelation of the Prophets; in the third, through the virtue of patience. Of the first, this is said morally: “As a shining sun, so he shone in the temple of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ecclus. 50]. As a figure of the second, in the Apocalypse an angel was seen, “and his face was like the sun” [Note: [Col. 0653] Apoc. 10]. Of the third it is said in the Book of Maccabees: “The sun shone upon the golden shields, and the mountains gleamed from them” [Note: [Col. 0653] I Macc. 6].

It follows: “Like a rainbow shining among clouds of glory” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ecclus. 50]. There is a threefold cloud, or mist, which here is taken as the same thing: clouds of whirlwind, clouds of air, and clouds of heaven. Of the first: “A storm-wind came from the north, and a great cloud” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ezek. 1]. Of the second: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ps. 17]. Of the [Col. 0654B] third: “I shall place my bow in the clouds of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0653] Gen. 9]. The first are the impiety of heretics; the second, the hardness and obscurity of the Law and the Prophets; the third, the revealed manifestation of the Gospel and the holy Fathers. The first envelop dust; the second send forth thunder and hail; the third pour out the early and latter rain. The first, the dust of impious blindness; the second, thunder as a threat of eternal condemnation and hail of temporal affliction; the third, rain of operative and co-operative grace. Of dust: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ps. 1]. Of thunder: “The moth shall be spread beneath you, and worms shall be your covering” [Note: [Col. 0653] Isa. 14]. Of hail: “Tooth for tooth, eye for eye” [Note: [Col. 0653] Deut. 19]. [Col. 0654C] Of rain: “God shall set apart a willing rain for his inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ps. 67].

In these three clouds a threefold bow is placed. For “bow” signifies a snare; hence: “They bent their bow, a bitter thing, to shoot the blameless in secret places” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ps. 63]. Likewise, “bow” signifies the day of judgment; hence: “You have given those who fear you a sign, that they may flee from the face of the bow” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ps. 59]. Likewise, “bow” signifies divine Scripture; hence: “He stretched his bow and made it ready, and in it he prepared instruments of death” [Note: [Col. 0653] Ps. 7]. The first is of deception, the second of confusion, the third of splendour. The first is in the first cloud, that of heretical perversity; the second in the second, that of sorrow; the third shines in the third, that of glory.

The bow, therefore, is called a snare, because it strikes [Col. 0654D] unexpectedly; it is also called the day of judgment because “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye,” just as a bow suddenly strikes, “judgment shall take place” [Note: [Col. 0653] I Cor. 15]. It is also called Scripture, because, as a string bends wood, so the grace of the New Testament bends the hardness of the Law and the Prophets.
