This bow is placed in the clouds of heaven, that is, in the Scriptures, and is the sign of the covenant between God and humankind; and they are called clouds of glory because they promise it.

Likewise human bodies are called clouds; hence: “The Lord ascends upon a light cloud” [Note: [Col. 0653] Isa. 19]. But among these clouds, some are bodies in hell, some bodies in exile, some bodies in the kingdom. [Col. 0655A] Bodies in hell are clouds of boundless blindness; bodies in exile, clouds of temporal misery; bodies in the kingdom, clouds of glory. In these clouds God places three bows, which we see appearing in clouds as one bow under three colours. For the bow has a saffron colour, a red colour, and a green colour. The saffron colour is placed in the clouds of infernal bodies, to signify the pallor of eternal death; red is placed in the bodies of this exile, to signify the affliction of temporal burning; the green colour or bow is placed in the clouds of the kingdom or heaven, to signify in those who rise again the fresh greenness of eternal joy. Therefore the first shows fear, the second pain, the third hope and love. Such a [Col. 0655B] bow is the Blessed Virgin: at the general resurrection she will shine among resurrected bodies, which will be clouds of glory, and she herself will shine more brightly as a rainbow.

> Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle order?

[CARD.] The Lord has summed up both generations, namely that of Christ and that of the Blessed Virgin, in one phrase, when by the dawn he signified the Blessed Virgin, who arose from the darkness of the Synagogue and bore Christ, the true sun. This is the dawn of which the angel said to Jacob in Genesis: “Let me go, for now the dawn is rising” [Note: [Col. 0655] Gen. 32]. For by Jacob wrestling with the angel are signified the holy Fathers, who, wrestling with the Lord in prayers [Col. 0655C] and tears, strove with such urgency, as by a kind of victory, to wrest and obtain from the Lord the incarnation of his Son. But to their company the Lord answers [Col. 0656A]: “Let me go, for now the dawn is rising”; as if to say: Let the urgency of your wrestling now cease, because dawn is now rising, light is now being born—namely, the Blessed Virgin, who will bear for you the true Sun.

Thus the Blessed Virgin shone like the dawn in her birth. But she came forth as the dawn in order to become the moon, concerning which Ecclesiasticus says: “The moon in all things in its season, an indication of time and a sign of the age” [Note: [Col. 0655] Ecclus. 43]. For the Blessed Virgin, among all nations at the time of her appearing, is an indication of that time of which Galatians says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a Virgin” [Note: [Col. 0655] Gal. 4]. And she is the sign of the age, marking every age past and future. Appropriately it is then added of her: “From the moon you have made a sign of God” [Col. 0656B] [Note: [Col. 0655] Ecclus. 43], for from her arises all our festivity.

It follows: “A luminary which wanes at its full” [Note: [Col. 0655] Ibid.]; but it grows wonderfully at its full, which cannot at all be understood of the material moon. For it does not first diminish and afterwards grow, but the reverse; nor does it diminish in completion, but after completion. Therefore this order of words properly describes the Blessed Virgin. For when she heard the great promise that she would be Mother of God, she humbled herself even to being a handmaid; and in this self-abasement she conceived and became the full moon.

She was likewise chosen as the sun, because, as the sun—that is, Christ—was chosen from thousands of men [Note: [Col. 0655] Song 5], so the Blessed Virgin was chosen from thousands of women. For as it was said of Christ: “As an apple-tree [Col. 0656C] among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons” [Note: [Col. 0655] Song 2], so it is said of the Blessed Virgin: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” [Note: [Col. 0655] Ibid.].

# BOOK TEN

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655C] “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valley, to observe whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had budded.”

[THO.] This garden is the Church, in which there are nuts, [Col. 0655D] that is, the righteous. The life of the righteous is rightly compared to nuts, because just as they keep the sweetness of their spiritual fruit in their innermost core, so that they cannot make known to their neighbours outwardly how great it is; likewise, as the nut has a most bitter husk and is encased in a very hard shell, but, once the harsh and hard layers are removed, a most sweet fruit is found, so every correction and the labour of continence by which the holy Church is exercised seems bitter indeed for the present, but produces a most sweet fruit in the future, according to the Apostle’s saying: “All discipline seems at the present time to be not of joy but of sorrow; yet afterwards it will yield, to those exercised by it, the most peaceable fruit of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0655] Heb. 12].

The fruits of the valley are the fruits of humility; hence the valleys will abound [Col. 0656C] in grain. Therefore the bride goes down to the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley when teachers turn their eyes from the height of secret rest and contemplation to consider the state of the Church, so that they may see who are advancing in good and who need [Col. 0656D] help. She observes whether the vine has flowered when she examines whether the hearts of those whom she instructs have been made drunk with the newness of virtues. She observes whether the pomegranates have budded when she attends to whether there are any found who imitate the Lord’s Passion. Hence Peter says to Christians: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought” [Note: [Col. 0655] I Peter 4].

A prelate, conforming himself to Christ in all things, as Christ descended in three ways, likewise makes it his aim to descend in three ways. Christ descended through the Incarnation; he descended through compassion; he will descend for the examination of the final judgment. Of the first: “He descends like rain upon the fleece” [Note: [Col. 0655] Ps. 71]. Of the second: “Bow your heavens and descend; touch the mountains and they shall smoke” [Note: [Col. 0655] Ps. 143]. Of the third: “The Lord shall descend from heaven with a command, with the trumpet of God, and with the [Col. 0657A] voice of the archangel” [Note: [Col. 0657] I Thess. 4].

The first descent took place in the womb; the second takes place in the heart; the third will take place in the air. Of the first: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” [Note: [Col. 0657] Isa. 7]. Of the second: “I shall gladly glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” [Note: [Col. 0657] II Cor. 12]. Of the third: “We shall meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0657] I Thess. 4].

The first was in our infirmity; the second takes place in purity of heart; the third was in royal majesty. For in the first, “he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” [Note: [Col. 0657] Isa. 53]. Of the second: “God does not dwell in a body or heart subject to sins” [Note: [Col. 0657] Wis. 1]. Of the third: “The king shall say to those at his right hand: Come, blessed of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0657] Matt. 25].

In this manner, therefore, the Church descends through its prelates [Col. 0657B] into its garden—that is, to examine the life of the righteous. First it descends from pride to humility; second, from contemplation to action, because of compassion for its neighbour; third, from the summit of virtues to watchfulness over itself. In accordance with the first, the king of Nineveh descended from his throne and clothed himself in sackcloth when he heard Jonah’s preaching [Note: [Col. 0657] Jonah 3]. In accordance with the second, Christ descended from the mountain into the valley to the crowds, in order to benefit them, after delivering a discourse to the greater ones on the mountain [Note: [Col. 0657] Matt. 8]. In accordance with the third, Jacob saw angels ascending and descending [Note: [Col. 0657] Gen. 28].

The first descent exalts the humbled person; the second reconciles one’s neighbour to oneself; the third forestalls the demons’ snares. Of the first it is said: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0657] Luke 14]. [Col. 0657C] Of the second: “Who do you think was neighbour to the man who fell among robbers?” [Note: [Col. 0657] Luke 10]. And the answer was: “The one who showed mercy to him” [Note: [Col. 0657] Ibid.]. Because of the third: “The living creatures went and returned” [Note: [Col. 0657] Ezek. 1]. They went to the summit of virtues; they returned to guard against the demons’ snares.

But because that descent brought us many benefits, we may also distinguish its descents in this way. There are three descents of Christ: the first of presence, the second of benevolence, the third of vengeance. The first was his self-presentation, the second compassion, the third the punishment of sinners: a presentation of humility, compassion of brotherhood, punishment of equity. Of the first: “Lord, bow your heavens and descend; touch the mountains and they shall smoke” [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 143]. Of the second: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, [Col. 0657D] and I have descended to deliver them” [Note: [Col. 0657] Exod. 3]. Of the third, concerning those building the tower of Babel, it is said: “Come, let us descend and confuse their tongues” [Note: [Col. 0657] Gen. 11].

Likewise, there is a descent of sickness and guilt; and there is a descent of compassion and mercy; and 137 there is a descent of benevolence. The first is guilt, the second mercy, the third benevolence. The first belongs to the wicked, the second to the righteous, the third to Christ. Of the first: “I shall be like those descending into the pit” [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 142]. Of the second: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing [Col. 0658A] work upon great waters, these have seen the works of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 106]. Of the third: “He bowed the heavens and descended” [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 17].

Here the second is discussed when it says, “I went down into the garden of nuts.” The first descends into the pit of toils, into the pit of failings, into the pit of darkness. Into the pit of toils, when one labours in temptation; into the pit of failings, when one falls away from good through despair; into the pit of darkness, when, in despair, one consigns God to forgetfulness. The first is the pit of misery [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 39]; the second, the lions’ den into which Daniel was cast [Note: [Col. 0657] Dan. 6]; the third, Jeremiah’s pit [Note: [Col. 0657] Jer. 38]. Thus Joseph descended into Egypt [Note: [Col. 0657] Gen. 37]. First he descended from Hebron, which is interpreted “eternal vision,” into Shechem, which is called “toil”; second, into Dothan, which is called “failing”; third, into Egypt, which is called “darkness.”

[Col. 0658B] There follows the descent of compassion. He descends in order to have compassion on three classes: first, those who suffer want; second, those harassed by distress; third, those burdened by affliction. Want is poverty; distress, tribulation; affliction, temptation. He descends, therefore, to restore those poor in virtues, to strengthen the afflicted, and to comfort the tempted: the first by fear, the second by righteousness, the third by hope. David mentions these three. The first thus: “Fear God, all you his saints, for there is no want to those who fear him [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 33].” And Tobit: “You will have many good things, if you fear God [Note: [Col. 0657] Tob. 4];” likewise: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.” The second: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 33].” [Col. 0658C] For the righteous person will not be troubled, whatever may happen to him. The third: “The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants, and none of those who hope in him shall offend [or: be condemned; *delinquet* is uncertain in construction] [Note: [Col. 0657] Ps. 33].”

With regard to the first: “When Christ had come down from the mountain, he fed the crowd [Note: [Col. 0657] Matt. 8].” For the second he says to Moses: “Go down into Egypt and say to Pharaoh: Let my people go, that it may sacrifice to me in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0657] Exod. 7].” For the third he says: “Go down from the mountain: your people has sinned [Note: [Col. 0657] Exod. 32].” Good, therefore, is the descent that satisfies the needy, strengthens the afflicted, and comforts the tempted. Thus he brought with him those three evangelical loaves, of which it is said: “Friend, lend me three loaves [Note: [Col. 0657] Luke 11].”

These are Elijah’s three loaves. The first, against the want of famine, the woman of Zarephath offered him [Note: [Col. 0657] 3 Kings 17]; the second, an angel under the shade of a juniper tree, while he was fleeing [Col. 0658D] Jezebel [Note: [Col. 0657] 3 Kings 19], that is, the instability of temptations; the third, an angel brought him so that by its strength he might climb the steep heights of Mount Horeb [Note: [Col. 0657] 3 Kings 19].

The third descent is that of benevolence, by which he descends into the garden of the heart and finds fruit there. The fruits are a true estimation of oneself; the vineyard, delight; the pomegranates, religious conformity of conduct. Yet the fruits are those of the valley, which is humility; the flower of the vine is uprightness. In the seeds of the pomegranate is vanity. Of the first: “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes [Note: [Col. 0657] Gen. 18].” Of the second: “All good things came to me with her, and innumerable uprightness through her hands [Note: [Col. 0659] Wisd. 7].” Of the third: “May God the Father grant you to think the same thing toward one another, so that, being of one mind, with one mouth you may glorify the Lord [Note: [Col. 0659] Rom. 15].”

But it should be noted that there are fruits *of valleys* (*vallium*), fruits *of low valleys* (*convallium*), and fruits *of ramparts* (*vallorum*). The fruits of valleys are in the inward humility of the heart; those of low valleys, in the outward display of example through deeds; those of ramparts are surrounded, as it were, by a rampart of many virtues. David possessed the first when he said: “I am a worm and not a man [Note: [Col. 0659] Ps. 21].” The second, when before all he humbled himself by dancing before the ark of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0659] 2 Kings 6]. The third, when his wife Michal rebuked him, yet, strong in humility, he did not on that account abandon it.

Hear the first: “Whom are you pursuing, O king? One dog and one flea [Note: [Col. 0659] 1 Kings 24].” Hear the second: “Unless he humbles himself like [Col. 0659B] this little child, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0659] Matt. 18].” Hear the third: “I beseech you to walk worthily of the calling to which you were called, with humility [Note: [Col. 0659] Eph. 4]”—but with what sort of humility? Namely, one strong in virtues; hence he adds: “And meekness, with patience, bearing with one another in charity, being diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace [Note: [Col. 0659] ibid.].”

The root of the vine is meditation; the vine itself, the ordering of the affections; the branch, devotion; the leaves, exhortation; the flowers, action; the fruit, eternal recompense. Of the third: “As the earth brings forth its shoot, and as a garden makes its seed spring up, so the Lord God will give righteousness and praise before all nations [Note: [Col. 0659] Isa. 61].”

The Church is called a garden of nuts, that is, of prelates, who are said to possess nuts for the following reason. [Col. 0659C] A nut has four things that pertain to prelates: outwardly, a base and bitter husk; secondly, a shell; thirdly, a skin; and fourthly, a kernel. In Christ, the husk was humility and the bitterness of his manner of life; the shell, his flesh, strong against the incentives of lust; in the skin, the soul; in the kernel, divinity. Or: in the husk, the bitterness of the Passion; in the shell, the cross; in the skin, the weakness of the flesh; in the kernel, the sweetness of divinity.

The Church is the garden of this nut. In prelates, however, the husk is abasement, the shell power, the skin will, the kernel knowledge: abasement, lest he be proud; power, lest there be weakness in him; will, that affection may be in him; knowledge, that he may be discerning. Hear of abasement: “We have become as the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all things even until now [Note: [Col. 0659] 1 Cor. 4].” Of power: “God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be [Col. 0659D] tempted above that which you are able [Note: [Col. 0659] 1 Cor. 10].” Of will: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to good will [Note: [Col. 0659] Phil. 2].” Of knowledge: “Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0659] Ps. 118].”

First, therefore, let us consider the husk, that is, the abasement of prelates. First a prelate ought to abase himself from temporal goods; secondly, from the favor of human praise; thirdly, from the pleasure of the flesh: first, lest he be avaricious; secondly, lest he be proud; thirdly, lest he be lustful. In a figure of these three, “Jesus cast out of the Temple those selling oxen and sheep and doves [Note: [Col. 0659] John 2].” Those sell oxen [Col. 0660A] who labor in the Church so that, being avaricious, they may heap up money; those sell sheep who wish to appear simple and religious so as to procure empty glory for themselves; those sell doves who sell spiritual things, so that from what they acquire they may more abundantly satisfy their luxury.

Concerning the avarice of prelates the Lord says through the prophet: “Feed the flock destined for slaughter, whose possessors killed them and did not grieve, and sold them, saying: Blessed be God, we have become rich [Note: [Col. 0659] Zech. 11].” And another prophet: “Woe to him who gathers evil avarice to his house, so that his nest may be on high, and he thinks himself delivered from the hand of evil [Note: [Col. 0659] Hab. 2].”

There are others who vainly glory in God’s gifts and therefore wish to be honored by everyone. Of these the Lord says: “They love the first places at supper, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called by men, Rabbi [Note: [Col. 0659] Matt. 23].” To them the Apostle says: [Col. 0660B] “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it [Note: [Col. 0659] 1 Cor. 4]?” To them Isaiah says: “Where will your glory be left, lest you bend beneath the bond and fall among the slain [Note: [Col. 0659] Isa. 10]?”

But what of glory in clothing? For they wish to appear in the streets: some on mules, some on caparisoned horses with golden bells, in silken, splendid, varied garments, in sable furs bought with the tears of the poor, the pennies of widows, and the sins of the rich. Woe, miserable man, who strives to glory in sheep’s hair, mouse skins, worms’ entrails, the juice of roots, and the weight of metals. Be ashamed, for through the Apostle these things are forbidden even to women, to whom they are more readily permitted. “Not with braided hair,” he says, “or gold, or pearls; not in costly apparel [Col. 0660C] [Note: [Col. 0659] 1 Tim. 2].” Where, then, is your boasting? It is excluded.

Others take delight in reveling and drunkenness, and thus invite their subjects to love of the world. Of them the Lord says through the prophet: “They will eat the sins of my people, and they will lift up their souls to its iniquity [Note: [Col. 0659] Hos. 4].”—“For when the living creatures moved, the wheels beside them moved also; but when they were lifted up from the earth, the wheels following them were lifted up also [Note: [Col. 0659] Ezek. 1].” The wheels are the lives of subjects; the living creatures drawing the wheels are teachers.

The Apostle excuses himself from vanity: “We do not speak,” he says, “as if wishing to please men, nor seeking glory from men, neither from you nor from others; God knows [Note: [Col. 0659] Eph. 6].” And from avarice: “Neither were we ever among you [Col. 0660D] under a pretext of avarice; God is witness [Note: [Col. 0659] 1 Thess. 2].” And from pleasure of the flesh: “I chastise my body,” he says, “and bring it into slavery, lest, after I have preached to others, I myself should be found reprobate [Note: [Col. 0659] 1 Cor. 9].”

Observe, therefore, how the priests of Bel were slain by Daniel on account of avarice, because at night they stole the offerings presented to their god [Note: [Col. 0659] Dan. 14]. Their footprints were discovered in the dust—that is, the lives of the priests in temporal goods. Observe Nadab and Abihu, namely the sons of Aaron, slain by the Lord on account of vain glory [Note: [Col. 0659] Num. 3], because they sacrificed not with the fire of the altar—that is, not [Col. 0661A] with love of God—but with earthly fire, that is, love of human praise. See also the shameless elders condemned by Daniel because of the pleasure of the flesh, since they wished to corrupt Susanna [Note: [Col. 0661] Dan. 13].

Therefore take upon yourselves the form of the four living creatures, so that the wheels—that is, the lives of the faithful—may follow you. They have the form of an ox, because they slaughter themselves, as it were like a nut’s husk, by casting off wealth, vanity, and pleasure; the form of a lion, by stoutly resisting vices and tyrants; the form of a man, by rationally offering a good will to God; the form of an eagle, by investigating heavenly things through divine knowledge.

“Three things,” says Solomon [Note: [Col. 0661] Prov. 30], “go well, and a fourth proceeds happily,” namely “a cock girded about the loins.” These are cast down in the manner of the husk, restraining the instability [Col. 0661B] of luxury; and, like the cock, they first strike themselves with the wings of correction, then sing by preaching to others. The second is “the lion, which fears no encounter with any beast.” These are strong like the shell, manfully bearing tribulations and resisting tyrants. The third is “the ram,” leader of the sheep, “and there is no king who can resist him.” These, armed with the two horns of the Old and New Testaments, govern their subjects through knowledge. The fourth is “that which proceeds happily,” namely, one appearing foolish when he has been raised on high, who, even if he acts, nevertheless does not act from good will: this is the casting off of the husk.

There follows the power of the shell. This power is nothing other than the strength of a teacher, which he possesses in imitation of Christ, who was mighty [Col. 0661C] in deed and word. A teacher ought to possess threefold strength: that of a giant, of a strong lion, and of a strong ass—the giant’s for fighting, the lion’s for trampling down, the ass’s for carrying: for fighting against vices, trampling down the schemes of tyrants, and carrying the burdens of brothers.

Of the first it is said: “Judas Maccabeus put on armor like a giant and protected the camp with his sword [Note: [Col. 0661] 1 Macc. 3].” Of the second it is said here: “The lion, strongest of beasts, fears no encounter with any animal [Note: [Col. 0661] Prov. 30].” And in Samson’s riddle: “What is stronger than a lion? What is sweeter than honey [Note: [Col. 0661] Judg. 14]?”—“The righteous is confident as a lion [Note: [Col. 0661] Prov. 28].” Of the third: “Issachar, a strong ass lying down between the boundaries, saw that rest was good and the land excellent, and put his shoulders under the burden [Note: [Col. 0661] Gen. 49].”

The Apostle equipped the giant [Col. 0661D] when he said: “Brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against the spirit of wickedness in the heavenly places [Note: [Col. 0661] Eph. 6].” Hear the lion, namely Stephen: “Stiff-necked, and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0661] Acts 7].” Hear the strong ass: “I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them; I did not turn my face away from those reproaching and spitting [Col. 0662A] upon me [Note: [Col. 0661] Isa. 50].” For thus “he himself bore our infirmities and carried our pains [Note: [Col. 0661] Isa. 53].”

There follows the skin of the will. All these things must be done with good will. For it is the seat of charity. This will ought to agree with the divine will; hence: “I have desired to do your will, O my God [Note: [Col. 0661] Heb. 10].” It begins from fear; hence: “He will do the will of those who fear him [Note: [Col. 0661] Ps. 144].” It is completed in peace, because “On earth, peace to men of good will [Note: [Col. 0661] Luke 2].” This is the fine flour offered in sacrifice, because it ought to be pure of the bran of sin, enriched with the oil of charity, and fragrant with the incense of prayer.

There follows the kernel, which has the form of the heart. Within it has the sweetness of knowledge and wisdom, which a prelate ought to possess, lest perhaps he hear that saying of the prophet: “My people has fallen silent because it lacked [Col. 0662B] knowledge. Since, therefore, you have rejected knowledge, I too will reject you, that you may not perform the priesthood for me [Note: [Col. 0661] Hos. 4].” And another: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts [Note: [Col. 0661] Mal. 2].” Therefore, while he both guards and improves himself and governs his subjects,

> He stirs his own wings and looks back upon those of his offspring.

But there are some who neither know nor preach, of whom Isaiah says: “Their watchmen are all blind, all mute dogs unable to bark [Note: [Col. 0661] Isa. 56].” There are some who do not know, yet preach: “They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness.” Hence the Lord says: “They are blind guides of the blind; and if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit [Note: [Col. 0661] Matt. 15].”

There are some who know but do not [Col. 0662C] preach, and even allow their subjects to mingle with perverse heretics. To them it is said in the Law: “You shall not allow your beast to mate with an animal of another kind [Note: [Col. 0661] Lev. 19].” There are some who both know and preach, but by living badly corrupt by their example. Hence in the Law: “You shall not sow your field with diverse seed [Note: [Col. 0661] Lev. 25].” There are some who preach and know, and live outwardly honorably, but seek glory alone. Hence: “This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me [Note: [Col. 0661] Matt. 15].” And in the Law: “You shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen [Note: [Col. 0661] Deut. 22].”

**138** But those who preach well ought to be proficient in three things: to restrain the rashness of the disorderly through rebuke; to cut away the temptations of the weak through discerning diligence; and through entreaty and consolation to smooth the harsh dispositions [Col. 0662D] of the unformed. Hence the Apostle: “Argue, entreat, rebuke [Note: [Col. 0661] 2 Tim. 4].” Thus the pastoral staff is curved at its beginning, to draw; sharp at its end, to prick; straight in the middle, to govern.

> Draw with the first part; govern with the middle; prick with the lowest.

Hence the prophet: “What do you see, Amos?” “I see a mason’s trowel, plastering a wall [Note: [Col. 0661] Amos 7].” The mason is Christ; the trowel, namely the instrument, is the teacher; the mortar is charity; the stones, the faithful; the wall, the Church or religious order. This trowel therefore has a handle, that is, rebuke, by which it restrains the disorderly [Col. 0663A]; it has a point, by which it casts hard little stones out of the mortar—that is, keenness of intellect, by which it expels movements of the soul that impede charity; it has a flat surface, by which it smooths rough things—that is, consolation, by which it reforms uncultivated dispositions.

This man ought to have the eight vestments of Aaron [Note: [Col. 0663] Exod. 28]. In abasement, linen breeches of continence; a close-fitting linen garment of innocence; a belt for restraining temptation. Those who possess the strength of the shell should have the ephod, in order to bear the burdens of those below, and the *logion*, or breastplate of judgment, in order to do this discerningly. Those who possess the will of the skin should have sandals—the meditation upon dead fathers—with which they protect their feet, that is, their affections, from dust, that is, earthly love; and a hyacinth-colored tunic, which has the color of heaven, that is, heavenly conduct, [Col. 0663B] by which they conform themselves to heavenly things. Those who possess the knowledge of the kernel should have on their head a two-horned mitre, that is, knowledge of the New and Old Testaments, which has two tails, that is, love of God and neighbor; and a golden plate on the forehead, on which are written *he*, *ioth*, *ede*, and *vau*, interpreted: “This is the beginning of the Passion of life.” He has this plate upon his forehead, that he may always think upon Christ’s Passion; the two-horned mitre upon his head, that he may examine the Old and New Testaments with reason; the two tails at its top, that they may commend to memory the love of God and neighbor.

“They descend to see the fruits of the valley,” etc. Here three things are enumerated about which prelates ought to be concerned: the fruits of the low valleys, flowering vineyards, and germinating pomegranates. In the fruits are signified those who [Col. 0663C] humble themselves because of their weakness; in the vineyards, those who go down from virtue to virtue; in the pomegranates, those who contend for Christ unto the shedding of blood.

The first concern, then, is for the weak. But there is accidental and bodily weakness; accidental and spiritual weakness; and common and natural weakness. The first is such as an acute fever; the second, such as hatred and envy; the third is corrupted nature. The first arises from the corruption of humors; the second from an assaulting temptation; the third from the infirmity of nature, by which the body continually suffers weakness. The soul is prone to sin. Of the first: “I was sick and you visited me [Note: [Col. 0663] Matt. 25].” Of the second: “He who is weak, let him eat vegetables [Note: [Col. 0663] Rom. 14].” Of the third: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak [Note: [Col. 0663] Ps. 6].”

A prelate ought to assist the first [Col. 0663D] with temporal benefits; relieve the second through exhortation to confession and prayer; and promise glory to the third because of bodily weakness. Against proneness to sin he should employ caution. Of the first, Job says: “I was an eye to the blind, a foot to the lame, a father to the poor [Note: [Col. 0663] Job 29].” Of the second, James says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another that you may be saved [Note: [Col. 0663] Jas. 5].” Of the third, as regards the body: “This corruptible thing shall put on incorruption, and this mortal thing immortality [Note: [Col. 0663] 1 Cor. 15].” As regards proneness to sin: [Col. 0664A] “My son, guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds [Note: [Col. 0663] Prov. 4].”

There are some from whom, because they are negligent, no medicine is sought; others, being desperate, rage against the Lord; and thirdly, some humble themselves because of their weakness. Of the first David says: “My sores have putrefied and become corrupt because of my foolishness [Note: [Col. 0663] Ps. 37].” Of the second: “You struck them and they were not healed; you afflicted them, and they refused to receive correction [Note: [Col. 0663] Jer. 5].” The third say: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak [Note: [Col. 0663] Ps. 6].”

Of the first: “Her filth is on her feet, and she did not remember her end [Note: [Col. 0663] Lam. 1].” Of the second: “She has been cast down exceedingly, having no comforter [Note: [Col. 0663] ibid.].” Of the third: “See, O Lord, my affliction, for my enemy has been lifted up [Note: [Col. 0663] ibid.].” Therefore the prelate [Col. 0664B] should first make the first man see his weakness by revealing it to him; second, lead the second back to hope; third, promise glory to the third for his humility. Let him therefore say to the first: “You say: I am rich and need nothing, though you are wretched and poor and blind and naked and miserable [Note: [Col. 0663] Rev. 3].” To the second: “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him [Note: [Col. 0663] Lam. 3].”—“He who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities [Note: [Col. 0663] Ps. 102].” To the third: “He who exalts himself shall be humbled [Note: [Col. 0663] Luke 44],” and that saying of Job: “He who has lowered his eyes shall be saved, and he who has been humbled shall be in glory [Note: [Col. 0663] Job 22].”

“And I should see,” he says, “whether the vineyards had flowered.” A vineyard has three things: an ugly vine, a medicinal flower, and the pleasure of wine. In the ugly vine is the abasement of one’s own body; in the medicinal flower, [Col. 0664C] the fragrance of virtue; in the wine of pleasure, the gladness of devotion. In the first appear those who despise the world; in the second, those ascending from virtue to virtue [Note: [Col. 0663] Ps. 83] and killing serpents; in the third, those rejoicing in heavenly things.

The first was Christ, when “we saw him as a leper and struck by God, humbled [Note: [Col. 0663] Isa. 53].” The second: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root [Note: [Col. 0663] Isa. 11].” The third, “on the day of the gladness of his heart [Note: [Col. 0663] Song 3],” that is, at the resurrection. The first “wandered about in sheepskins, in goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy [Note: [Col. 0663] Heb. 11].” To the second the Lord says at the Ascension: “These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons, they shall speak in new tongues, they shall take up serpents [Note: [Col. 0663] Mark 16].” Of the third: “Rejoice in the Lord [Col. 0664D] and exult, O righteous, and glory, all you upright in heart [Note: [Col. 0663] Ps. 31].” The prelate observes these: the first with admiration, congratulating the progress of the second, and delighting in the third.

There follows: “And whether the pomegranates had germinated.” In the Scriptures we read of four kinds of things that germinate: virgin earth, spiritual earth, the verdant lily, and the pomegranate. Of the first: “Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth open and bring forth the Savior [Note: [Col. 0663] Isa. 45].” Of the second: “Let [Col. 0665A] the earth bring forth green grass [Note: [Col. 0665] Gen. 1].” Of the third: “The righteous shall germinate like a lily [Note: [Col. 0665] Office of the Church].” Of the fourth it is said here: “Whether the pomegranates had germinated.”

The first earth, then, is Mary; the second, the Church; the third is righteousness; the fourth is the red suffering of martyrs. The first brings forth the Savior; the second, green grass; the third, a fragrant flower; the fourth, fruit like itself. The first is the food of the faithful; the second, the splendor of confessors; the third, the adornment of virgins; the fourth, the purple of martyrs.

These four are so called according to four interpretations of the word *germen* (“shoot”). According to the first, it is called *germen*, that is, “bearing a new harvest.” The new harvest was Christ, born of a virgin; hence it was said: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0665] Isa. 43].” According to the second, *germen* means “begotten from the root in the mind.” For confessors, like [Col. 0665B] a shoot, come forth from the root of faith and from its mind, that is, from its inner depths, because faith concerns not visible things but hidden ones; hence Paul calls it “the proof of things not seen [Note: [Col. 0665] Heb. 11].” According to the third, *germen* means “begotten from pure dew,” that is, the order of virgins. For virginity comes from grace, which is pure dew, as if making people clean. According to the fourth, *germen* derives from *GE*, meaning “earth,” and *Radice*, “root,” and *MEta*, “boundary,” and *Nescia*, “ignorant,” as though “ignorant of the boundaries of an earthly root.” For the root of the human body is the pleasure of intercourse, and this has a boundary, that is, an end. But martyrs, who are these shoots, pass beyond those boundaries when, despising these things, they seek heavenly things.

Pomegranates, then, germinate in themselves when they possess faith, the root, the shoot [Col. 0665C] of the martyrs, and glorification, the fruit; they germinate in others through the example of preaching, word, and miracle. There is a shoot of the devil, a shoot of the righteous, and a shoot of the Lord. Thus it should be known that there are three shoots: a deadly shoot, a fruitful shoot, and a saving shoot. The first is iniquity, the second purity, the third humility. The first came from the root of the serpent; the second sprouted from the good olive; the third was put forth by the root of Jesse. The first seduces, the second leads onward, the third brings to the end: the first to sin, the second through the stages of virtues, the third to the kingdom.

The first shoot germinates, flowers, and bears fruit: the shoot of iniquity, the flower of worldly vanity, the fruit of eternal calamity. Hear of the shoot: “It shall not give its fruits, but it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you [Note: [Col. 0665] Gen. 3]”: thorns, which penetrate more deeply, namely temptation of the soul; thistles, which prick outwardly, the itching of the flesh. Hence in Leviticus: “The fruits which germinate shall be unclean to you [Note: [Col. 0665] Lev. 19].” But hear the end: “And it shall devour the earth with its shoot [Note: [Col. 0665] Deut. 32].”

Hear of its flower: “In the morning it passes away like grass; in the morning it flourishes and passes away [Note: [Col. 0665] Ps. 89].” Likewise: “His days shall bloom like the flower of the field [Note: [Col. 0665] Ps. 102].” Likewise: “He comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees like a shadow [Note: [Col. 0665] Job 14].” Likewise: “All its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass has dried up [Col. 0666A] and the flower has fallen [Note: [Col. 0665] Isa. 40].” Of the fruit it is said: “A bad tree cannot bear good fruits. Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles [Note: [Col. 0665] Matt. 7]?” These are the tares that shall be bound in bundles to be burned, because “you will destroy their fruit from the earth [Note: [Col. 0665] Ps. 20].”

There follows the shoot of the righteous. This shoot is purity; its flower, the delight of conscience; its fruit, charity together with the other virtues. Hence: “The righteous shall germinate like a lily [Note: [Col. 0665] Office of the Church].” Likewise: “I shall be like dew; Israel shall germinate like a lily [Note: [Col. 0665] Hos. 14].” Likewise: “Your bones shall germinate like grass [Note: [Col. 0665] Isa. 66].” Hear of the flower: “Bear fruit like a rose planted beside streams of water [Note: [Col. 0665] Ecclus. 39].”—“For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience [Note: [Col. 0665] 2 Cor. 1].” Hear of the fruit: “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience [Note: [Col. 0665] Gal. 5].”

But the shoot of the Lord germinated in the Nativity, flowered in the Resurrection, [Col. 0666B] and bore fruit in the Ascension. It offered the use of its fruit in confession of the Father—or rather, it flowered at the Nativity, fully flowered in the Passion, and flowered again in the Resurrection. Of the first: “A flower shall rise from his root [Note: [Col. 0665] Isa. 11].” Of the second: “The flower of Lebanon has withered [Note: [Col. 0665] Nah. 1].” Of the third: “And my flesh has flowered again [Note: [Col. 0665] Ps. 27].”

Behold, “the shoot of the Lord is in magnificence [Note: [Col. 0665] Isa. 4],” in the Resurrection. Yet it was also in magnificence before the Passion, and in the Resurrection after the Passion: first, in activity; second, in victory; third, in resurrection. In activity, by which he worked miracles and created all things; in victory, by which he subjected the devil; in resurrection, by which he glorified his flesh. Of the first: “How magnified are your works, O Lord [Note: [Col. 0665] Ps. 91].” Of the second: “They shall speak of the magnificence of the glory [Col. 0666C] of your holiness, and they shall recount your wonders [Note: [Col. 0665] Ps. 144].” Of the third: “O Lord my God, you are exceedingly magnified [Note: [Col. 0665] Ps. 103].” Of this he says: “Now I shall arise, says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0665] Ps. 11].” Likewise: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above [Note: [Col. 0665] Col. 3].”

Behold, the shoot of the Lord was in magnificence in the Resurrection, and in glory in the Ascension. For in it hell was made poorer, the world more flourishing, the heavenly city more wealthy, humankind more joyful, and the angel more glad. Hell was poorer because Tartarus disgorged the prey that it had wickedly devoured. The world was more flourishing, because:

> Behold, at the joys of the world’s rebirth  
> all gifts rejoice to return with their Lord.

The heavenly city was wealthier, because Christ presents before the Father’s [Col. 0666D] face the glory of his victorious flesh. Humankind becomes more joyful, because he has carried upward to the palace of heaven that body of ours which he had borne. The angel becomes more glad, for the kingdoms of heaven rejoiced at the return of the Only-begotten, because he made the homeland of sun and pole a single commonwealth.

Hear likewise of the glory: “Angels go before; captives accompany; apostles follow: the angels in wonder, the captives because of their liberation, the apostles in devotion.” In wonder, because mortal nature has been changed into immortality; joyful because of their liberation, because [Col. 0667A] they enter the region of unlikeness; in devotion, awaiting the promise of the Holy Spirit. Of the first: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I am sick with love [Note: [Col. 0667] Song 5].” Of the second: “On my bed, through the nights, I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him. A little while after I had passed by, I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, that I might bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me [Note: [Col. 0667] Song 3].” Of the third: “The angels tremble as they behold the reversal of the condition of mortals.”

The apostles say: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh [Note: [Col. 0667] Song 1].” The captives say: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance [Note: [Col. 0667] ibid.].” The angels say: “My beloved is to me a cluster of cypress [Note: [Col. 0667] ibid.].” This is the new glory of our king. If anyone is passed over by this new glory, here

[Col. 0667B] [lacuna]

the devil, condemned to many barren years, had glory in heaven; Adam in paradise; humankind in the world. But this threefold glory grew old, because the devil fell from heaven, Adam was cast out of paradise, and humankind was made miserable in the world. Behold: “The shoot of the Lord is in glory [Note: [Col. 0667] Isa. 4].” And: “Seek the things that are above [Note: [Col. 0667] Col. 3].”—“As I shall be exalted,” he says, and adds: “And now I shall be lifted up [Note: [Col. 0667] Isa. 33].”

This is his excellence. This excellence is threefold: eminence, preeminence, and coeminence. It consists in the eminence of heaven, the preeminence over the angel, and coeminence with the exalted Father. In the eminence of heaven, whose brightness he enjoys; in preeminence over the angel, whom he surpasses in dignity; in coeminence with the exalted Father, to whom [Col. 0667C] he is equal in majesty. Of the first: “Who alone possesses immortality and inhabits inaccessible light [Note: [Col. 0667] 1 Tim. 6].” Of the second: “Having become so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs [Note: [Col. 0667] Heb. 1].” Of the third it is said: “Equal glory, coeternal majesty [Note: [Col. 0667] Office of the Church].”

Let us therefore consider the abundance of the city, the joy of its citizens, and the power of its king: its abundance, because there will be no lack there; its joy, because all will have toward the Lord and toward one another a pleasing affection; its king’s power, because he will be perfect in all things. Hear of abundance: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house [Note: [Col. 0667] Ps. 64].” And of joy: “As the dwelling of all those who rejoice is in you [Note: [Col. 0667] Ps. 86].” Hear of the king’s power: “God shall be all in all [Note: [Col. 0667] Eph. 1].”

Behold the sublime fruit of the land. Therefore, “set your minds on the things above [Note: [Col. 0667] Col. 3],” that is, on the fruits of that land which its explorers brought with them: namely, a cluster, pomegranates, and figs [Note: [Col. 0667] Num. 13]. From the cluster is pressed wine that gladdens the heart of man [Note: [Col. 0667] Ps. 103], that is, heavenly joy. A pomegranate contains many red seeds under one rind: this is the loving unanimity of the citizens above. The sweetness of the fig is the delight of the divine vision; hence there will be exultation for those who have been saved from Israel.

It should be noted, however, that at the end there will be reproach, exultation, and exaltation: reproach [Col. 0668A] at the condemnation of the wicked; exultation over the proclamations of the good; exaltation at the right hand of the Father, unto equality with the angels. Of the first: “I was hungry and you did not give me food [Note: [Col. 0667] Matt. 25],” etc. Of the second: “I was thirsty and you gave me drink. I was a stranger and you received me [Note: [Col. 0667] ibid.],” and the other works of mercy. Of the third: “His right hand shall embrace me,” says the bride in the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 0667] Song 8]. “There they shall all be like the angels of God [Note: [Col. 0667] Matt. 22].”

“I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the low valleys, and to observe whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had germinated.”

[CARD.] Another translation reads thus: “I went down into the garden of the walnut-tree, to look in the budding of the stream, to see whether the vine had blossomed and the pomegranates had come into flower.” These are the words of the Blessed Virgin. For the Son had first expressed wonder at His mother’s going forth [Col. 0668B]. Her movement, moreover, concerns a progress from the active life and her return to the contemplative. Thus she says of her active life: “I went down into my garden of walnut-trees.” As if she said: I, who by contemplation had ascended to divine things, descended to lower things by considering what is being done in the Church.

For the Church is signified by a garden of walnut-trees, because of the patience of the saints and the fruit of patience, which is signified in the walnut: beneath its bitter husk and hard shell it contains a sweet kernel. So patience, through the bitterness of sufferings and the strength of steadfastness, reaches the sweetness of rewards. “I went down,” she says, “to see the fruits of the valleys,” by which the fruits of humility are signified. Or, according to another reading: “I went down [Col. 0668C] to look in the budding of the stream,” namely, that I might observe what, and how much, the stream of Jesus Christ’s blood had put forth.

“I went down to see whether the vine had blossomed,” that is, Christ; or whether the vineyard had blossomed, that is, whether charity had produced flowers—charity which, like a vineyard, cheers the mind by its fruit. Joel laments its barrenness and the languor of piety, saying: “The vine is confounded, and the fig tree has withered” [Note: [Col. 0667] Joel 1.]. “I went down to see whether the pomegranates had budded,” or “whether the pomegranate-trees had come into flower,” that is, whether pomegranates had been formed out of flowers. As if she said: I went down to consider whether the beginnings of the Church had reached those fruits which are signified in pomegranates.

For by pomegranates is signified the Church of God, differentiated into diverse ranks or orders or communities, according to the conformity and distinction [Col. 0668D] of ranks, offices, or graces. But while the blessed Mother turns her eyes to consider these things for the sake of our aid, and turns away from the sweetness of contemplation, she is troubled in this concern; finally, turning away from it and recognizing herself, she says:

> I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.

[THO.] Thus the Church spoke to the Synagogue. The Synagogue replies to the Church: “I did not know the gifts of spiritual grace with which she was enlightened by the Lord, because the inward concern of my mind troubled [Col. 0669A] me on account of the old Testament being superseded by the new,” that is, by the four Gospels. It calls them chariots because they bore Christ’s name through the four regions of the world. They are said to be Aminadab—that is, Christ—because Aminadab means “willing.” For whatever Christ did and suffered in the world, He did and suffered willingly, not under compulsion. He is called the charioteer of the chariots because He guided them as they enlightened the world by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

There are three things which the soul complains that it does not know: the lowest, the middle, and the highest. The first is the burden; the second, the way; the third, the goal. The burden is what is carried; the way, what is sought; the goal, that toward which one tends. The first occurs when a person is ignorant of himself; the second, when the progress of virtues is not known; the third [Col. 0669B], when what is above is not understood. Of the first: “They did not know”; of the second: “nor did they understand”; of the third: “they walk in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0669] Psal. 81.]. Of the first: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks” [Note: [Col. 0669] Cant. 1.]. Of the second: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they found not the way to a city of habitation” [Note: [Col. 0669] Psal. 106.]. Likewise: “The bird has not known the path, nor has the eye of the vulture beheld it” [Note: [Col. 0669] Job 28.].

The wise of the world do not understand the third, because “their foolish heart was darkened; professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” [Note: [Col. 0669] Rom. 1.].—“They profess that they know God, but deny Him by their deeds” [Note: [Col. 0669] Tit. 1.]. The soul’s first ignorance is set in the humility of the fruits of the valleys; the second in the flowering vineyard [Col. 0669C]; the third in the budding of the pomegranates.

Through ignorance of himself, a person does not see himself as a sinner; he loves his present exile and disguises his own advantage. Against these things Job says: “Show me my crimes and sins” [Note: [Col. 0669] Job 13.]. Against the second: “Do you display your power against a leaf carried by the wind, and pursue dry stubble?” [Note: [Col. 0669] Ibid.]. Against the third: “I am to be consumed like rottenness, and like a garment eaten by moths” [Note: [Col. 0669] Job 15.].

From ignorance of the way arise singularity among religious, heretical perversity among teachers, and impurity of life among the simple. The first, even while doing good, do not know what is advantageous or disadvantageous; the second, what is true or false; the third, what is good and evil. The first have a crooked way [Col. 0669D], the second a dark one, the third a muddy one. To the first it is said: “Make straight the paths of our God” [Note: [Col. 0669] Matth. 3.]; of the second: “Let their way be darkness”; and for the third is added, “and slippery” [Note: [Col. 0669] Psal. 34.]. To the first it is said: “Not knowing the righteousness of God and wishing to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” [Note: [Col. 0669] Rom. 10.]. To the second: “You err, not knowing the law or the Scriptures” [Note: [Col. 0669] Matth. 22.]. To the third: “You were once wandering like sheep” [Note: [Col. 0669] I Petr. 2.].

Those who do not know eternal life are not drawn by longing, enticed by sweetness, or consoled by knowledge: by the longing of love, the sweetness [Col. 0670A] of devotion, and the knowledge of the divine vision. The first do not say with David: “Lord, all my desire is before You” [Note: [Col. 0669] Psal. 37.]; nor with the Bride: “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” [Note: [Col. 0669] Cant. 1.]. Nor do the second say: “I remembered God and was delighted” [Note: [Col. 0669] Psal. 76.]. The third say with Jacob: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” [Note: [Col. 0669] Gen. 32.]. But why this ignorance has come about, he adds its cause: “because my soul troubled me.”

There are five reasons for seeking knowledge: that the seeker may know, may be known, may build up, may be built up, or may gain profit. The first is curiosity; the second vanity; the third charity; the fourth prudence; the fifth gain. Of the first: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil” [Note: [Col. 0669] Gen. 3.]. [Col. 0670B] Of the second: “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” [Note: [Col. 0669] I Cor. 8.]. And the poet [Note: [Col. 0669] Pers. Sat. I, 27.]:

> Your knowledge is nothing unless another knows that you know it;  
> but it is pleasant to be pointed out with the finger and called: “That is he.”

Of the third: “This I pray, that your charity may abound more and more in all understanding and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0669] Philip. 1.]. Of the fourth: “My people have perished because they had no knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0669] Isai. 5.]. Of the fifth, the poet:

> Everyone wishes to know; no one wishes to pay the fee.

The first belongs to philosophers, the second to poets, the third to shepherds, the fourth to advancing Christians, the fifth to hirelings.

The soul of the ignorant is disturbed by a threefold whirlwind. The first is the continual assault of temptations; the second, the adversity of tribulations; [Col. 0670C] the third, concern for temporal things. The first wraps one in smoke; the second in wood and stones; the third in dust. The first shakes, the second crushes, the third blinds the eyes. Of the first it is said: “You cursed the sceptres of his warriors, who came as a whirlwind to scatter me” [Note: [Col. 0669] Habac. 3.]. Of the second Job says: “He will crush me in a whirlwind and multiply my wounds, even without cause” [Note: [Col. 0669] Job 9.]. Of the third Job says: “Let a dark whirlwind possess that night” [Note: [Col. 0669] Job 3.].

This is said according to a threefold interpretation of this word. In the first sense, *turbo* means a swelling that presses upon good; in the second, *turbo* means “one grinding cities”; in the third, a whirlwind that troubles the eyes. David had experienced these three whirlwinds. Of the first he said: “Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled” [Note: [Col. 0669] Psal. 6.]. [Col. 0670D] Of the second: “And my soul is greatly troubled” [Note: [Col. 0669] Ibid.]. Of the third: “My eye is troubled by anger” [Note: [Col. 0669] Ibid.].

Thus the first whirlwind is set against the first ignorance, the second against the second, the third against the third. A person can scarcely live without some one of these whirlwinds. But some resist them well. Therefore, against the first a person ought to be cautious; against the second, steadfast; against the third, temperate: cautious through knowledge, steadfast through excellence, temperate through self-restraint. The first, lest he be deceived; the second, lest he be broken by adversity; the third, lest prosperity exalt him.

Of the first: “A storm-wind came from the north, and a great cloud”—that is, blindness—“and enveloping fire” [Note: [Col. 0671] Ezech. 1.], namely, the heat of vices. But if you are cautious, in its midst is the appearance of electrum—that is, Christ helping you. Hear the cautious man, Paul: for a whirlwind assailed him when he said, “There was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me” [Note: [Col. 0671] II Cor. 12.]. Again: “I find,” he says, “another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” [Note: [Col. 0671] Rom. 7.]. Yet he was not blinded by this whirlwind. Hear how he knew himself: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0671] Ibid.]. For He is “a shelter by day from the heat, and for security and [Col. 0671B] concealment from whirlwind and rain” [Note: [Col. 0671] Isa. 4.].

Hear also the steadfast man against the third whirlwind—for the whirlwind of tribulations rushed upon him when he said: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked” [Note: [Col. 0671] II Cor. 11.]. But hear his steadfastness: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword?” [Note: [Col. 0671] Rom. 8.]. And because Job was steadfast, the Lord adds that Job spoke; and He called him out of the whirlwind under which he had not succumbed. Hear the strong man: “If He scourges, let Him kill at once; and even if He kills me, I shall hope in Him” [Note: [Col. 0671] Job 9.].

Again, hear Paul, temperate amid the whirlwind of temporal affairs: “These hands have laboured for what was necessary for me and for those who were with me” [Note: [Col. 0671] Act. 20.]; and: “Apart from those things which are outward, my daily [Col. 0671C] pressure: concern for all the Churches” [Note: [Col. 0671] II Cor. 11.]. Behold the whirlwind of temporal concern. Yet in these matters he was so temperate that he did not consign heavenly things to forgetfulness; for he was caught up even to the third heaven [Note: [Col. 0671] II Cor. 12.]. And the same man says: “Seek the things above; set your minds on the things above, not on things upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0671] Coloss. 3.].

Through such temperance Elijah was taken up into heaven [Note: [Col. 0671] IV Reg. 2.], because he was temperate in handling temporal affairs, namely in bearing concern for Israel. Hence, when the Lord took Elijah up to heaven in a whirlwind, his cloak was left upon the earth: that is, his intercourse with secular affairs.

Christ endured the first whirlwind when tempted by the devil; the second when crucified by the Jew; the third when, by preaching, He bore concern for the Church. [Col. 0671D] Hear the second: “The Lord kills and makes alive; He brings down to hell and brings back” [Note: [Col. 0671] I Reg. 2.]. Hear the third: “Raising the needy from the dust” [Note: [Col. 0671] Ibid.]. Hear the first: “And lifting the poor from the dungheap” [Note: [Col. 0671] Ibid.]. For what end? “That he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory” [Note: [Col. 0671] Ibid.].

Thus the Lord begins to lift us to heaven through the whirlwind when we are cautious against the first; He raises us from the earth when we are strong against the second; He lifts us to heaven when we are temperate against the third [Col. 0672A], so that worldly concern may not hinder us from knowing heavenly things.

**140.** But why the soul troubled him, he adds the cause, namely: “because of the chariots of Aminadab.” I believe these are the chariots seen by the prophet Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0671] Zach. 6.]. The souls of the saints who reign with Christ are free from these disturbances. Hence it is written: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them” [Note: [Col. 0671] Sap. 3.].

There are souls of the reprobate, souls of penitents, and souls of the righteous. The first are in the hand of the devil; the second are in their own hand; the third are in the hand of God. The first are touched by the torment of conscience; the second by the torment of penitence; the third are not touched by the torment of malice. Of the first: “The souls of the wicked [Col. 0672B] raged against me, and my heart was weighed down over them” [Note: [Col. 0671] Offic. Eccl.]. Of the second: “Every soul that is not afflicted on this day shall perish from among its people” [Note: [Col. 0671] Lev. 23.]. Of the third: The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.

The first appeared to the eyes of the wise to die; the second appeared to the eyes of the pleasure-loving to die; the third appeared to the eyes of fools to die. The first endure the scourges of demonic cruelty; the second are tested in the furnace; the third are in peace.

But there is the hand of the devil, the hand of man, and the hand of God. The devil’s hand afflicts bodily, strikes spiritually, and tortures eternally. Of the first it was said to Satan concerning Job: “Yet do not put your hand upon him” [Note: [Col. 0671] Job 2.]. Of the second David says: “Deliver my soul, O God, from the sword, my only one from the hand of the dog [Col. 0672C]” [Note: [Col. 0671] Psal. 21.]. Of the third he likewise says: “Rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me” [Note: [Col. 0671] Psal. 30.].

Again, there is an idle hand of man, a working hand of man, and an affectionate hand of man. The first delights in idleness; the second does good; the third is lifted up. The first has deficiency, the second progress, the third affection. Of the first: “The sluggard hides his hand in his bosom and does not bring it to his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0671] Prov. 1.]. Of the first and second: “A slack hand brings poverty, but the hand of the diligent obtains riches” [Note: [Col. 0671] Prov. 10.]. Of the second: “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it earnestly” [Note: [Col. 0671] Eccle. 9.]. And that strong woman “put forth her hand to strong things, and worked by the counsel of her hands” [Note: [Col. 0671] Prov. 31.]. Of the third: “I spread out my hands to You” [Note: [Col. 0671] Psal. 67.]. Again: “Thus will I bless [Col. 0672D] You in my life, and in Your name I will lift up my hands” [Note: [Col. 0671] Psal. 62.].

A person is in God’s hand by creation, governance, and protection: by creation, through which the universe was made; by governance, through which He directs our paths; by protection, through which calamity does not approach the righteous. The first is so that God may be known from the variety of things; the second, so that we may walk in truth; the third, so that we may live in blessedness. Of the first: “Your hands made me and fashioned me wholly round about [Col. 0673A]” [Note: [Col. 0673] Job 10.]. Of the second: “For there Your hand will lead me, and Your right hand will hold me” [Note: [Col. 0673] Psal. 138.].

But in governing, God afflicts, heals, and lifts up. He afflicts through penitential satisfaction, heals through the remission of fault, and lifts up to contemplation. Of the first: “Have pity on me, at least you, my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me” [Note: [Col. 0673] Job 19.]. Again: “Keep Your hand far from me, and let not Your terror frighten me” [Note: [Col. 0673] Job 13.]. Of the second: “He wounds and heals; He strikes, and His hands heal” [Note: [Col. 0673] Job 5.]. Of the third Ezekiel says: “A hand took me by the lock of my head and lifted me between heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0673] Ezech. 8.].

Of God’s protection it is said: “He protected me in the shadow of His hand” [Note: [Col. 0673] Isai. 49.]. Hence: “His left hand is under my head, and His right hand shall embrace me” [Note: [Col. 0673] Cant. 2.]. On account of these three it is said: [Col. 0673B] “His hands are rounded, golden, full of hyacinths” [Note: [Col. 0673] Cant. 5.]: rounded with respect to creation, golden with respect to governance, full of hyacinths with respect to protection. For what is rounded is easily moved to act; gold signifies wisdom; and hyacinth, which has the colour of heaven, suggests the blessedness of heaven. Therefore “the torment of malice does not touch them” [Note: [Col. 0673] Sap. 3.].

Those who are in the devil’s hand are touched by a threefold torment of conscience: shame, oppression, and exclusion. Shame for sins; oppression by pains; exclusion from the number of the blessed. Shame for sins, because their sins will be open to all; oppression by pains, because these continually grow stronger; exclusion from the number of the blessed, at whose glory they will waste away. Of the first [Col. 0673C] it is said: “The Ancient of Days sat down; the books were opened” [Note: [Col. 0673] Dan. 7.], that is, consciences, because then the secrets of our heart will be made manifest. Of the second: “Cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” [Note: [Col. 0673] Matth. 22.]. Of the third: “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away; the desire of sinners shall perish” [Note: [Col. 0673] Psal. 111.]. Behold, these are touched by the torment of conscience.

The second are touched by a threefold torment of penitence: contrition of repentance, bodily suffering, and rushing temptation. In the first they suffer weakness, in the second pain, in the third fear. The first was the portico “in which lay a multitude of the infirm” [Note: [Col. 0673] Joan. 5.]. Of the second Job says: “May He who began crush me; may He loose His hand and cut me down; and this would be my consolation, that in afflicting me with pain He should not spare me” [Note: [Col. 0673] Job 6.]. [Col. 0673D] Of the third: “Fear and trembling came upon me” [Note: [Col. 0673] Psal. 54.].

The third are not touched by the torment of malice, which is threefold. There is the malice of one’s neighbour, the malice of the devil, and the malice of one’s own heart. The first attacks, the second inflames, the third torments. The first leads to bodily punishment, the second draws toward Gehenna, the third infects the soul. Of the first: “Do not emulate evildoers, nor envy those who commit iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0673] Psal. 36.]. Of the second: “Restore my soul from their malice [Col. 0674A], my only one from the lions” [Note: [Col. 0673] Psal. 34.]. Of the third: “Your mouth abounded in malice, and your tongue contrived deceits” [Note: [Col. 0673] Psal. 49.].

The righteous do not fear these three torments, because against the first they are in a safe place, against the second in a pleasant one, and against the third on high ground. Therefore, in the first they do not fear temporal death; in the second, the pain of hell; in the third, the deceit of thoughts. Against the first it is said: “The righteous shall live for ever” [Note: [Col. 0673] Sap. 5.]. Against the second: “And their reward is with the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0673] Ibid.]. Against the third: “And their thought is with the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0673] Ibid.].

It follows: “They seemed, in the eyes of fools, to die” [Note: [Col. 0673] Sap. 3.]. But, as has been said, the first seemed to the eyes of the wise to die in three ways: spiritually, temporally, and eternally. Spiritually through iniquity; temporally through the separation [Col. 0674B] of body and soul; eternally through eternal damnation. The first makes one impious; the second is the divorce of body and soul; the third makes one subject to perpetual calamity. Of the first death Paul says: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” [Note: [Col. 0673] I Tim. 5.]. Of the second: “Abraham died, and the prophets died” [Note: [Col. 0673] Joan. 8.]. Of the third: “Whoever believes in me shall not die for ever” [Note: [Col. 0673] Joan. 11.].

The second seemed to the eyes of the pleasure-loving to die, because they flee bodily pleasure, abandon their own will, and reject the vanity of the world. In the first the flesh is mortified; in the second the spirit is humbled; in the third the world is rejected. In the first sensuality is oppressed; in the second the spirit’s loftiness is restrained; in the third worldly delight is checked. Of the first [Col. 0674C] the Apostle says: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0673] Coloss. 3.]. Of the second: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0673] Ibid.]. Again: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of Him who sent me” [Note: [Col. 0673] Joan. 6.]. For those are dead with Christ who, as Christ emptied Himself, humble their own loftiness. Of the third Paul says: “Brothers, I die daily for your glory” [Note: [Col. 0673] I Cor. 16.], that is, I abandon worldly glory, so that, leaving it by my example, you too may seek the glory of God. Again: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” [Note: [Col. 0673] I Joan. 2.]. These are those whom the world, retaining them, has shuddered at. To the pleasure-loving they seem to die, because the latter judge it impossible to live in this manner and not to die. For they hear them crying: “For Your sake we are put to death [Col. 0674D] all day long” [Note: [Col. 0673] Rom. 8.].

The third seemed to the eyes of fools to die. For they do not believe that another life succeeds this one, that anyone rises from the underworld, or that a body putrefies in the earth. In the first they attend to this: “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither, for this is our portion and this our lot” [Note: [Col. 0673] Sap. 2.], and not to this: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God” [Note: [Col. 0673] Psal. 86.]. In the second, to this: “Who has returned from the dead?” [Note: [Col. 0673] Sap. 2.], and not to this: “Many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep [Col. 0675A] rose with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0675] I Cor. 15.]. In the third, to this: “The death of man and beast is the same, and the condition of both is equal” [Note: [Col. 0675] Eccle. 3.], and not to this: “The corruptible shall put on incorruption and the mortal immortality” [Note: [Col. 0675] I Cor. 15.].

Again, the first are subject to the devil’s power. There are there an untiring torturer, intolerable torture, and endless wailing. The first, because they were not wearied in perpetrating iniquity; the second, because they did not wash away sin by the severity of penitence; the third, because they sinned with laughter and merriment. Of the first: “The master handed the servant over to the torturers until he should pay the whole debt” [Note: [Col. 0675] Matth. 18.]. Of the second: “They are not in the labour of men, nor are they scourged with men” [Note: [Col. 0675] Psal. 72.]. Of the third: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you also shall mourn” [Note: [Col. 0675] Luc. 6.], when, according to the prophet, [Col. 0675B] “there shall be a cry from the first gate and a wailing from the second” [Note: [Col. 0675] Soph. 1.].

The second are tested in the furnace when inwardly pricked by pain, outwardly afflicted by punishment, and made ashamed by confession. Of the first: “I was turned in my misery while the thorn is driven in” [Note: [Col. 0675] Psal. 31.]. Of the second: “Let rottenness enter into my bones, and let it boil beneath me” [Note: [Col. 0675] Habac. 3.]. Of the third he says: “Shame of face has covered me” [Note: [Col. 0675] Psal. 43.].

But the third are in peace. That peace has forgetfulness of present evils, delight in heavenly goods, and the vision of the divine majesty. By the first they lack pain; by the second they are affected with sweetness; by the third they rejoice in God’s love. Of the first: “The sun shall not fall upon them, nor any heat” [Note: [Col. 0675] Apoc. 7.]. Of the second: “How great is the multitude of Your sweetness, O Lord, which [Col. 0675C] You have hidden for those who fear You” [Note: [Col. 0675] Psal. 30.]. Of the third: “They shall rejoice before You as those rejoice at harvest, and as victors exult when the spoil is taken” [Note: [Col. 0675] Isai. 9.]. These say: “In peace, in the selfsame place, I shall sleep and rest” [Note: [Col. 0675] Psal. 4.].—“Four chariots,” he says, “were going forth from between two mountains, and the mountains were of bronze” [Note: [Col. 0675] Zach. 6.]. I take these mountains to be angelic blessedness and divine loftiness.

In the first chariot were red horses, in the second white, in the third black, in the fourth dappled. The first is martyrdom; the second virginity; the third cloistered religious life; the fourth preaching. The first, namely martyrdom, has four wheels: the first is the inward desire to suffer; the second actual outward suffering; [Col. 0675D] the third the preservation of faith; the fourth exclusion from purgatorial fire. Of the first Paul says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0675] Philip. 1.]. He displayed the second by being beheaded. Of the third the same man says: “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith” [Note: [Col. 0675] II Tim. 4.]. On account of the fourth it is said: “The sun shall not fall upon them, nor any heat.”

There are two red horses: in the body, the appearance of purple suffering; in the soul, the fervour of perfect charity. Of the first: “Flowers of roses surrounded her,” that is, the purple of martyrs. Of the [Col. 0676A] second: “Charity never fails” [Note: [Col. 0675] I Cor. 13.].

The second chariot is virginity. Its first wheel is integrity; its second, purity of heart; its third, humility; its fourth, constancy of purpose. You may see these in the Blessed Virgin. Of the first the prophet says: “This gate shall be shut” [Note: [Col. 0675] Ezech. 46.]. Of the second: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Note: [Col. 0675] Luc. 1.], and thus she was pure in heart. Of the third: “The Lord has looked upon the humility of His handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0675] Ibid.]. Of the fourth: “How shall this be, since I know not a man?” [Note: [Col. 0675] Ibid.], which perhaps she had resolved in her purpose.

This chariot is drawn by two horses: the desire to possess in the homeland, in the body, the distinguished sign of virginity—namely whiteness—and the desire to follow the Lamb wherever He goes. Of both it is said: “Clothed in white robes, they follow the Lamb wherever He goes” [Note: [Col. 0675] Apoc. 14.].

The third chariot [Col. 0676B] is cloistered religious life. Its first wheel is silence; its second, disciplined bearing both in clothing and in body; its third, solitude in the cloister; its fourth, obedience rendered to one’s superior. The first, lest one offend in speech; the second, lest one appear undisciplined; the third, lest one covet secular things upon seeing them; the fourth, lest one retain one’s own will. Of the first: “In the hands of the tongue are death and life” [Note: [Col. 0675] Prov. 18]. Of the second: “Do not abandon your mother’s discipline” [Note: [Col. 0675] Prov. 1.]. Of the third: “Pure and undefiled religion before God 141 and the Father is this: to keep oneself undefiled from this world” [Note: [Col. 0675] Jac. 1.]. Of the fourth: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” [Note: [Col. 0675] Eccle. 4.].

Its two horses are black: groaning for sins and grief over present evils. Of the first: “I have laboured [Col. 0676C] in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed” [Note: [Col. 0675] Psal. 6.]; of the second: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged!” [Note: [Col. 0675] Psal. 119.].

The fourth chariot is preaching. Its first wheel is knowledge of the Scriptures; its second, ability in utterance; its third, the example of an honourable life; its fourth, authority imposed by superiors. Of the first: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0675] Mal. 2.]. Of the second Moses complains: “I am,” he says, “of more impeded speech than yesterday and the day before” [Note: [Col. 0675] Exod. 4.]. Of the third: “In all things show yourself an example of good works” [Note: [Col. 0675] Tit. 2.]. Of the fourth: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” [Note: [Col. 0675] Rom. 10.].

The two horses drawing it are dappled, because now they suffer with their neighbour, now they render honour to God. These [Col. 0676D] are called Aminadab, which means “willing,” because Christ grants these things to human beings by grace, not as a debt. These chariots disturb the newly converted soul, which formerly thought it knew something, but now sees in itself the three aforesaid ignorances which it did not previously know.

> I did not know: my soul was troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab.

[CAR.] As if she said: “Formerly I did not know and did not notice that my soul was troubled.” This is what the Lord [Col. 0677A] says to Martha: “You are anxious and troubled about many things” [Note: [Col. 0677] Luc. 10.]. But my soul was troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab, whose going forth, progress, and fruit of labour I anxiously considered.

These are the evangelical chariots, the chariots of Aminadab—that is, of Jesus Christ, who is signified by Aminadab because it is interpreted “my willing one.” For He Himself, willingly and not compelled, became obedient to the Father unto death [Note: [Col. 0677] Phil. 2]. By the ministry of these chariots there are walnut-trees in the garden, fruits of the valleys, the vineyard blooms, and pomegranates bud.

These are the chariots of which Zechariah says: “I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots going forth from between two mountains; and the mountains were of bronze” [Note: [Col. 0677] Zach. 6.]. This [Col. 0677B] is evangelical preaching, which goes forth from between the two Testaments. They are called mountains because of the height of their spiritual understanding, and bronze because of the sound of preaching.

They are called four chariots because of the diversity of teachers, like horses drawing a chariot, of whom the same prophet says: “In the first chariot were red horses; in the second chariot, black horses; in the third chariot, white horses; in the fourth chariot, dappled and strong horses” [Note: [Col. 0677] Ibid.]. Therefore, by the red horses are signified those who, reddened in their own blood, were martyrs in body and soul. By the black horses, because black is a dark colour, are shown those who are dark in their knowledge of divine mysteries because those mysteries are profound. The white horses signify those who retain the whiteness of virginity [Col. 0677C] in both mind and body. By dappled horses we may understand those who were martyrs in soul but not in body, and those who, uncorrupted by any error, were virgins in mind, though they did not preserve virginity in the flesh.
