There follows the Son’s utterance:

> Return, return, Shulamite; return, return, that we may behold you.

[THO.] Return to acknowledgment of your Creator, from whom you had turned away. Return to the peace of kinship; return, that we may behold you. Return to purity of faith. Return, return, through perfection of works to the love of the Lord, that with rejoicing eyes and souls we may see the hope of your chastity which we have desired. [Col. 0677D] I do not know whether the name *Sunamite* is found elsewhere; it seems to be the designation of one of the noble women, whether a proper name or derived from another word, who at that time was distinguished by the glory of wisdom, beauty, or virtue. Bede says this, although the name *Sunamite* occurs in many other places; perhaps he had not read them. But if *Sunamite* means “despised” or “captive,” it suits the Synagogue well.

There are four returns. The first is from secular affairs to the religious life; the second, from a fall to former grace; the third, from the contemplative life to the active; the fourth, from love of temporal life [Col. 0678A] to the palm of martyrdom. The first is so that one returned from sin may make satisfaction; the second, lest one remain in despair; the third, that one may give thanks for benefits bestowed on him by God; the fourth, that through greater merit one may obtain a greater reward. In the first, a sinner is called one “returning” (*revertens*), as though “turning as a guilty person” (*reus vertens*); in the second, “returning,” as though “turning again” (*iterum vertens*); in the third, “returning,” as though “turning back” (*retro vertens*); in the fourth, “returning,” as though “holding the true thing” (*rem veram tenens*).

We find these four in the Apostle Peter. In the first, he returned to the Lord’s call, when he saw Peter and Andrew and called them [Note: [Col. 0677] Matt. 4]. In the second, after his denial, when “the Lord looked upon Peter, and, going out, he wept bitterly” [Note: [Col. 0677] Matt. 26]. In the third, in prison after the angelic vision, when it is said: “But Peter, coming to himself, said: Now I know truly that the Lord has sent [Col. 0678B] his angel and delivered me from the hand of Herod” [Note: [Col. 0677] Acts 12]. In the fourth, at Christ’s meeting with him, when he saw Christ coming toward him and said: “Lord, where are you going?” “I am coming,” he said, “to Rome to be crucified again” [Note: [Col. 0677] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*].

The order of the first return is this. First, on some occasion, we are called by the Lord; second, we are justified; third, we are glorified. “For those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified” [Note: [Col. 0677] Rom. 8]. Thus he called Peter. Second, by “leaving the nets and the boat” [Note: [Col. 0677] Matt. 4], he justified him; third, because “he followed him” [Note: [Col. 0677] Ibid.], he glorified him.

Thus we too, brothers, are called by the Lord when any occasion is presented; we are justified by leaving not only sins but also earthly things; we are glorified by following [Col. 0678C] Christ through the increase of virtues. “Whoever wishes to come after” Christ at his call, “let him deny himself,” by leaving earthly things; “let him take up his cross,” by advancing in virtues; “let him follow” him [Note: [Col. 0677] Matt. 16].

We find this progress in Job: “If you return,” he says [Note: [Col. 0677] Job 22], “to the Almighty, he will give you flint in place of earth,” that is, strength in place of the rejection of earthly things; “golden torrents in place of flint,” that is, gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are called golden because of charity. But so that you may forestall the second return by not falling into temptation, he adds [Note: [Col. 0677] Ibid.]: “And the Almighty shall stand against your enemies, and silver shall be heaped up for you,” namely, the divine utterances.

But one who suffers a fall after such gifts of God should look to Peter, when, that is, after his fall [Col. 0678D] he returned. For first the cock crowed; second, the Lord looked upon Peter; third, he went out; fourth, he wept bitterly. The cock crows to one who has fallen through the inward vision of the Holy Spirit, or outwardly through the rebuke of the Teacher; the Lord looks upon Peter, giving him contrition of heart; he goes out through confession; he weeps bitterly through penitential satisfaction and tearful prayer.

“When the cock crows,” he says, “hope returns,” namely, hope of rising again; “the Lord looked,” and health is restored to the sick, namely, the will to repent; when he goes outside through confession, the thief’s sword is sheathed—that is, the devil’s—so that he may not have [Col. 0679A] the power to compel; when he weeps bitterly, faith returns to the fallen person, enabling him to recover his first grace. Thus he says, while weeping, that saying of the prophet: “I will go and return to my former husband, because it was then better with me than now” [Note: [Col. 0679] Hos. 2].

By these two degrees of return the Sunamite, that is, the captive woman, is addressed. For it is a great thing to be held by secular concerns, and a great thing to suffer a fall by returning to former sins.

The third return is from the contemplative life to the active life. This happened to Peter when the angel appeared to him in prison [Note: [Col. 0679] Acts 12]. But it should be noted that he was in prison, that the doors were shut, that he was bound with chains, and that he was guarded by soldiers. The prison is the depth of evils; the shut doors are despair, which prevents the sinner from going out to confession; [Col. 0679B] the chains are obstinacy, when God withdraws his grace so that the soul is not free to do good; the guarding soldiers are the continual assaults of temptations. The depth of evils is such that the sinner despises; despair obstructs confession so that he may remain in sin; freedom to do good is impeded, so that he may consign God to forgetfulness; the persistence of temptations is at hand, so that it may entice by flatteries.

On the other hand, note that “the angel of the Lord stood by, and a light shone in the dwelling. The angel struck Peter’s side and awakened him” [Note: [Col. 0679] Ibid.]. This is the Angel of Great Counsel, that is, Christ. He stands against the depth of evils; the light against the enclosure of the mighty; the striking of the side against the chains; the awakening against the soldiers’ guard. Against the depth of evils, he shows the evils he suffered for us, so that the sinner may no longer despise; [Col. 0679C] the light is set against the enclosure of the mighty, so that, when heavenly things are shown to him, he may lay aside despair and go out; the striking of the side is set against the chains, so that his heart, softened and its obstinacy laid aside, may become free for doing good; the awakening is set against the soldiers’ guard, so that by divine warning he may flee enticing temptations.

But after he has been led out, the angel withdraws in brightness, so that, having seen heavenly things, he may return to the knowledge of his own weakness and profit others. Of the first: “Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners” [Note: [Col. 0679] Heb. 12]. Of the second: “But I said in the excess of my mind: I am cast away from before your eyes” [Note: [Col. 0679] Ps. 30]. And: “My eyes are weakened, looking on high. Lord, I suffer violence; [Col. 0679D] answer for me” [Note: [Col. 0679] Isa. 38]. Of the third: “I will take away from you the heart of stone and will give you a heart of flesh” [Note: [Col. 0679] Ezek. 11]. And Job: “God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me” [Note: [Col. 0679] Job 23]. Of the fourth the Lord says to the paralytic: “Take up your bed and walk” [Note: [Col. 0679] Mark 9]. And: “See that your hearts are not weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness” [Note: [Col. 0679] Luke 21]. “In this manner the living creatures went and returned” [Note: [Col. 0679] Ezek. 1].

In the fourth return, a person returns from love of temporal life to the palm of suffering. Here too the following order should be noted: first, we ought to contemplate Christ’s passion in our hearts; [Col. 0680A] second, to honor it because of such condescension; third, to seek his will; and, having known it, to devote ourselves to it in affection. We contemplate it in order to imitate his patience; honor it lest we be found ungrateful; seek his will lest the devil contrive anything in us; devote ourselves to it in affection lest we be found lazy servants.

Thus Peter first saw Christ coming toward him; second, he adored him; third, he said, “Lord, where are you going?” fourth, the answer was given: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.” Of the first Paul says: “Let us look to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, with joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame” [Note: [Col. 0679] Heb. 12]. Of the second: “Let all the earth adore you, O God, and sing to you” [Note: [Col. 0679] Ps. 65]. Of the third we say: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” [Note: [Col. 0679] Matt. 6]; and Paul says: [Col. 0680B] “Lord, what do you want me to do?” [Note: [Col. 0679] Acts 9]. Christ himself says: “Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” [Note: [Col. 0679] Matt. 26]. Fourth, the Apostle desired it when he said: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0679] Gal. 6]. And blessed Andrew says: “O good cross, long desired, receive the disciple of him who hung upon you” [Note: [Col. 0679] Antiphon for the feast of St. Andrew].

Of this return the prophet said: “Come, and let us return to the Lord, for he himself has seized us and will save us” [Note: [Col. 0679] Hos. 6], etc. In the first two cases it is said: “Return, return, Sunamite.” In the latter two it is said: “Return, return, that we may behold you.” For, by returning from the contemplative life to the active, and from love of temporal life to the palm of martyrdom, while attending to the things above [Note: [Col. 0679] Col. 3], we are beheld by the Lord.

[Col. 0680C]

Return, return, Sunamite; return, return, that we may behold you.

[CAR.] *Sunamite* is interpreted “mortified” or “scarlet,” and signifies the Blessed Virgin, who, as her Son died, died with him through compassion for her Son, as though reddened with the scarlet of suffering. Therefore, seeing her troubled from the repose of contemplation, the Son calls her back to the tranquillity of contemplation. And because she had said that she was troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab, he says “return” four times because of the four chariots, or because of the four wheels in one chariot; or because she had said that she had gone down for four purposes: namely, to see the garden of nuts and the fruits of the valleys, to see the flowers of the vine, and the buds of the pomegranates.

And although [Col. 0680D] he ought to have said, “Return, that you may behold me with the eye of contemplation,” or “us,” namely the whole Trinity, he says, “Return, that we may behold you,” because, just as a person cannot look upon the material sun unless the sun itself looks upon and illuminates him, so no soul can contemplate the true Sun unless he himself beholds and enlightens it. But when the angels hear that the whole Trinity desires to behold her, they answer. Yet, to show that the three persons are one God, when the three say “that we may behold you,” they answer in the singular, as to one person.

## Chapter VII.—What will you see in the Sunamite, except choirs of camps?

[Col. 0681A]

[THO.] As if he were plainly saying: You indeed grieve that the Synagogue had remained turned away for so long, and pray that it may return to me; and you delight to behold her countenance adorned for me. But know that the time is near in which you will see in her nothing of her former unbelief 142 and turning away, but only works of virtues and spiritual contests. What then will you see in the Sunamite except choirs of camps? That is, the warfare of peace: for in choirs the voices of singers sound together, while in camps the hands of armed men fight. What then will you see in her except choirs of the elect, who with one heart and soul proclaim the praises of their Creator? And these same choirs are camps, because by serving the Creator they repel the battle-lines [Col. 0681B] and rout their enemies, namely, the devils.

Three names are set before us: Sunamite, choirs, and camps. In the first is signified the order of those who mourn; in the second, of those who praise; in the third, of those who fight. The first is the order of the weak, the second of the righteous, the third of the strong. The first seek remission; the second stir devotion; the third overcome temptation. The first have their place in the chamber, the second in the temple, the third in the field: in the chamber of secret compunction, in the temple of the religious congregation, in the field of manifold unrest.

To the first James says: “Be miserable and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into voices of weeping” [Note: [Col. 0681] Jas. 4]. [Col. 0681C] To the second: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise befits the upright” [Note: [Col. 0681] Ps. 32]. To the third it is said: “Put on the armor of faith, that you may be able to resist in the evil day” [Note: [Col. 0681] Eph. 6].

Thus the children of Israel mourned, burdened with mud and brick in Egypt; they sang praise to the Lord after crossing the Red Sea; they fought their adversaries in the wilderness. Thus too Christ first wept over the city and wept at Lazarus’s tomb; second, he received praises from the Hebrew people; third, he fought on the gibbet of the cross.

Therefore perfect mourning consists in three things: confessing with the mouth, weeping with the eyes, and carrying the cross with the body. In confession there are three persons: those accusing themselves, those bearing witness, and those judging. The first is the accused person, the second the prelate, the third God. The accused person is humbled, the prelate has compassion, [Col. 0681D] God is appeased. For the accused suffers shame, the prelate helps through prayer, and God remits punishment. This is the shame that brings glory. Likewise: “The persistent prayer of a righteous man has great power” [Note: [Col. 0681] Jas. 5]. The accused person says: “I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0681] Ps. 31]. From this follows: “And you forgave the impiety of my sin; therefore every holy person shall pray to you for this” [Note: [Col. 0681] Ibid.].

There follow tears: tears of contrition, tears of devotion, and tears for the blessedness that is desired. The first are for washing, the second for anointing, the third for watering. By the first guilt is washed away; grace accompanies the second; the third are followed, as it were, by the refreshing dew of glory from this misery. The first have the groaning of toil, the second the bread of consolation, the third the sigh of future refreshment. Of the first: “Every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears, because I have labored in my groaning” [Note: [Col. 0681] Ps. 6]. Of the second: “My tears have been my bread day and night” [Note: [Col. 0681] Ps. 41]. Of the third: “Before I eat, I sigh; and like overflowing waters, so is my roaring” [Note: [Col. 0681] Job 3].

The perfection of mourning is in carrying the cross. There are three crosses: the first, that of the despairing thief; the second, of the one praying and saying, “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0681] Luke 23]; the third is Christ’s. The first deserved the cross and did not profit by it; the second deserved it and did profit by it; the third did not deserve it but did profit by it. [Col. 0682B] Therefore the first is the devil’s cross, the second that of the righteous person, the third Christ’s. The first is of malice, the second of penitence, the third of justice.

Each has four dimensions. In the devil’s cross there are height, by which he “exalts himself above everything that is worshiped” [Note: [Col. 0681] II Thess. 2]; depth, despair, of which it is said: “When a sinner comes into the depth of evils, he despises” [Note: [Col. 0681] Prov. 18]; breadth in carnal matters; and length in obstinacy. In the cross of the righteous person, depth is humility, length the persistence of labor, height contemplation, and breadth prayer, which embraces both enemy and friend. Therefore the cross has the depth of fear, the height of hope, the breadth of charity, and the length of perseverance. On the first cross I am tortured; toward the second I strive; for the third I sigh. I fear the first, seek the second, [Col. 0682C] desire the third. In the first is punishment; in the second, punishment and pardon; in the third, glory. Therefore I fear punishment, seek pardon, and desire glory. Job possesses the depth of the Lord’s cross, David its height, Paul its breadth, Naboth its length. These things have been said concerning the Sunamite, that is, those who mourn perfectly. There follows the matter of choirs: as has been said, these choirs have a place for psalmody in the temple or tabernacle.

There are three tabernacles: the material, the mystical, and the moral—namely, the tabernacle of Moses, the tabernacle of Christ, and the tabernacle of every righteous person. Moses’ tabernacle was a structure fittingly made from diverse adornments; Christ’s tabernacle is the Church; the righteous person’s tabernacle is every faithful soul. Thus one is made from incorruptible shittim wood [Note: [Col. 0681] Exod. 25], another from tireless saints, [Col. 0682D] the third from virtues. Moses erected his in the wilderness, Christ in the world, the righteous person in the soul. Moses placed the ark in his tabernacle, Christ his own flesh in his, and the righteous person conscience. Moses’ ark is overlaid within and without with pure gold [Note: [Col. 0681] Ibid.]; Christ’s flesh is overlaid within with divinity and without with the splendor of miracles. The righteous person’s conscience shines inwardly with the radiance of purity and outwardly with works of charity.

Therefore, in Christ’s tabernacle, which is the Church, choirs have their place in praising God, to stir devotion and give thanks. The Apostle teaches how they ought to praise God: [Col. 0683A] “Speaking,” he says, “to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” [Note: [Col. 0683] Eph. 5]. Psalms belong to good works; hymns to the praise of God; spiritual songs to rejoicing in heavenly things. Of the first Paul says: “While we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” [Note: [Col. 0683] Gal. 6]. Of the second David says: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise befits the upright” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ps. 32]. Of the third, the same David says: “I rejoiced at the things said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ps. 121].

You praise God well if there is harmony in conduct just as in voices: that through example you may be in harmony with your neighbor, through will with God, and through obedience with your master.

It should be known that there are three kinds of sounds: those made by striking, by blowing, and by singing. Striking belongs to the lyre, [Col. 0683B] blowing to the organ, singing to the voice. The work of the hands corresponds to the striking of the lyre; the devotion of the mind, to the blowing of the organ; exhortation in speech, to the singing of the voice. Strike, then, the strings of the lyre with the hand of good works, that you may be in harmony with your neighbor through the example of mortified flesh. Fill the organ of the heart with breath—that is, with the spirit of holy inspiration—that you may render to God the sweet sound of devout affection. Likewise, that you may be in harmony with your master, sing the new song, the song of obedience. Do not sing with Lucifer in heaven or with the first man in paradise, but sing in the temple with Christ. For the devil’s song is cupidity; the first man’s song is pleasure; Christ’s song is charity. The devil began in heaven the antiphon of pride, saying: “I will set my seat [Col. 0683C] in the north; I will be like the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0683] Isa. 14]; the antiphon of suggestion in paradise, and of despair in hell.

There follows the matter of camps.

There are three kinds of camps: the camps of the Egyptians, of the Israelites, and of the angels. Of the first: “The Lord looked upon the camps of the Egyptians” [Note: [Col. 0683] Exod. 14]. Of the second: “Whoever is leprous shall go outside the camp” [Note: [Col. 0683] Deut. 23]. Of the third Jacob says: “These are the camps of God” [Note: [Col. 0683] Gen. 32]. The first are camps of the world, the second of the wilderness, the third of heaven. The first wage war in order to plunder, the second in order to reach their homeland, the third in order to guard us. Let us therefore leave the first, choose the second, so that we may come to the third.

In the second camps we must have unity of hearts, provision for the future, weakness in the face of temptations, refuge in Christ, and, by doing good works, a heart directed upward. Of these four Solomon says [Note: [Col. 0683] Prov. 30]: “Four things are smallest on the earth, and they are wiser than the wise”: namely, “the locust, which has no king and all flies in bands”—this is unity of hearts; “the ant, which labors in summer, whence it may live in winter”—behold provision; “the little hare, a weak people, which makes its bed in the rock”—behold refuge in Christ; “the stellio, which dwells in the king’s house and walks with its hands”—behold good work and a heart [Col. 0684A] lifted upward.

Of the first: “There was one spirit and one faith in them.” Of the second: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider its ways and learn wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0683] Prov. 6]. Of the third: “Be for us, Lord, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ps. 60]. Of the fourth: “Our citizenship is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0683] Phil. 3]. And concerning works: “While we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” [Note: [Col. 0683] Gal. 6].

From these camps we shall pass to the camps of the angels, where we shall rest in body and soul, praise the Creator with the angels, and see God face to face [Note: [Col. 0683] I Cor. 13]. Of the first: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ps. 83]. Of the second: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages upon ages they shall praise you” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ibid.]. Of the third: “The God [Col. 0684B] of gods shall be seen in Zion” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ibid.].

What will you see in the Sunamite, except choirs of camps?

[CARD.] Of these camps it was said above: “Terrible as an army arrayed in battle” [Note: [Col. 0683] Song 6]. In her, indeed, choirs of camps are seen: namely, the blessed battle-line of saints joined to her, who with her fight for us against the enemy. Hence she is called the vessel of camps in Ecclesiasticus, where, under the name of the moon, it is said of her: “The vessel of camps on high, shining in the firmament of heaven, the hope of heaven, the glory of the stars” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ecclus. 43]. There follows:

How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince!

[THO.] First he marvels at the beauty [Col. 0684C] of her steps, that is, the constancy of her works, by which she might set forth beforehand examples of virtues to those whom she wished to instruct. Hence David says: “Perfect my steps in your paths” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ps. 16], that is, direct my actions in the narrow way by which one comes to life. These steps are in sandals when they are fortified by the examples of our predecessors. Of them the Apostle says: “Your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” [Note: [Col. 0683] Eph. 6].

He calls her the daughter of the prince, namely, of him concerning whom it is written: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; clothed about with variety in golden fringes” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ps. 44]. There is a prince of heaven, a prince of the world, and princes of the earth. The first is Christ, the second the devil, the third Peter and Paul. The first is [Col. 0684D] prince of angels, the second prince of demons, the third are princes of the apostles. Of the first Ezekiel says: “This gate shall be shut for the prince; the prince shall sit in it, that he may eat bread before the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0683] Ezek. 44]. Of the second Christ says: “For the prince of this world comes, and he has nothing in me” [Note: [Col. 0683] John 14]. Likewise it was said of Christ: “In Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” [Note: [Col. 0683] Luke 11]. Of the third the Church sings: “Glorious princes of the earth, how they loved one another in their life; so too in death they were not separated” [Note: [Col. 0683] Office of the Church]. David also says of them: [Col. 0685A] “The princes of the peoples have gathered together with the God of Abraham” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ps. 46].

This Bride is daughter of the first prince, stepdaughter of the second prince, and little sister of the third princes. She is daughter of the first prince because he regenerated her by the sacraments; she is stepdaughter of the second prince because he adulterated her mother, namely, the Synagogue; she is little sister of the third princes because with them she was born of the same father, Christ, and reborn through grace of the same mother, the Church. Of the first it is said in this passage: “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince!” Likewise David says of the same: “Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ps. 44]. She is rightly called the stepdaughter of the second, with whom her mother committed fornication. Therefore in this Song the Bridegroom says to her: “Under the apple tree [Col. 0685B] I raised you up; there your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated” [Note: [Col. 0685] Song 8]. For when Eve, the first parent, ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, the devil, under the apple tree, corrupted her by seducing her [Note: [Col. 0685] Gen. 3]. Under that same tree Christ raised her up when he redeemed her through the wood of the cross: let this be understood as a simple reference. Of the third, 143 it is also said in this Song: “Our little sister has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken to?” [Note: [Col. 0685] Song 8].

But now let us treat of these princes according to the threefold interpretation of this name. The first is called *princeps*, as though “first head” (*primum caput*); the second *princeps*, as though “beginning of captivity” (*principium captivitatis*); the third, *principes*, as though “those taking primacy” (*primatum capientes*). The first is the first head insofar as he is God; the second [Col. 0685C] insofar as he is God-man; the third insofar as he is man. Of the first the Apostle says: “God is the head of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0685] I Cor. 11]. Of the second: “Christ is the head of man” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ibid.]. Of the third: “Man is the head of woman” [Note: [Col. 0685] Eph. 5]. Behold the prince, namely the first head.

The devil is called prince, namely, the beginning of captivity, because he was the first to fall from heaven, the first to seduce humankind in paradise, the first to make humankind captive in hell; for through the devil’s envy death entered into the world. The apostles are called princes, namely, those taking primacy, as the Lord says to them: “Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions” [Note: [Col. 0685] Luke 10]; and: “Heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cast out demons; freely you have received, freely give” [Note: [Col. 0685] Matt. 10]. Hence they were called princes of the Churches, triumphant leaders in war.

Because of these things which they did, it was said of Peter and Paul: “Glorious princes of the earth, how they loved one another in their life; so in death they were not separated.” Therefore let us praise glorious men, so that, while we recall their distinctions, we may have consolations in this vale of tears, and, through their imitation, may become glorious, charitable, and strong: glorious on earth, charitable in life, strong in the straits of suffering. Through imitation, I say, for they themselves were glorious princes of the earth. They were glorious, more glorious, most glorious: glorious in [Col. 0686A] conduct, more glorious in love, most glorious in suffering. Glorious in conduct in the eyes of the Church; in love in the secret place of conscience; in suffering in the sight of the divine majesty. In the eyes of the Church, because they became the Church’s ornament; in the secret place of conscience, because they became like fragrant ointment; in the sight of the divine majesty, because they became the foundation of faith. They became the Church’s ornament because they adorned the face of the temple with golden crowns; like fragrant ointment because they were two breasts fragrant with the finest ointments. They became the foundation of faith because “its foundations are in the holy mountains” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ps. 86].

There are three ornaments of the Church: the first, that of princes; the second, that of prelates; the third, that of subjects. The first is of those who possess secular power; the second of those who hold ecclesiastical dignity; the third of those who are subject in truth. There are three things in the ornament of princes: to restrain the tyrant, free the oppressed, and console the wretched. Of the first Job says: “I broke the jaws of the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0685] Job 29]. Of the second: “And from his teeth I took away the prey” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ibid.]. Of the third: “When I sat as king with the army around me, I was nevertheless the comforter of mourners” [Note: [Col. 0685] Ibid.].

Likewise, there are three things in the ornament of prelates. They ought to have knowledge for instruction, continence that they may be pure, and boldness against persecutors. Of these three Solomon says [Note: [Col. 0685] Prov. 30]: “There are three things that walk well”: first, “the ram,” the leader of the sheep, having two horns, namely, the Old and [Col. 0686C] New Testaments; second, “the cock girded about the loins”; third, “the lion, which fears no encounter.”

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0685] Ibid.], there are four things in the adornment of religious persons. They ought to have concern to acquire virtues by which they may live hereafter; to frequent the company of religious persons; to do works with their hands by which they may ascend into heaven; and to place their refuge in Christ. These “are four things smallest on the earth, and they are wiser than the wise”: first is “the ant, which labors in summer, whence it may live in winter”; second, “the locust, which has no king and all flies in bands”; third, “the stellio, which walks with its hands and dwells in the king’s house”; fourth, “the little hare, a weak people, which makes its bed in the rock.” This is [Col. 0686D] true religion.

But there is counterfeit religion, shadowed religion, and manifest religion: counterfeit through hypocrisy, shadowed through humility, manifest through evident conduct. The first is the god Bel of Accaron, golden without and muddy within [Note: [Col. 0685] Dan. 14]; the second is Solomon’s temple, stone without and gold within [Note: [Col. 0685] III Kings 7]; the third is the ark of the covenant, overlaid with the purest gold within and without [Note: [Col. 0685] Exod. 37]. “Therefore the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their adornment” [Note: [Col. 0685] Gen. 2].

In the first adornment Mordecai stood in the sight of King Ahasuerus [Col. 0687A] [Note: [Col. 0687] Esth. 6]. In the second adornment Aaron was clothed in priestly garments [Note: [Col. 0687] Exod. 28]. In the third Judith the widow offered the head of the tyrant Holofernes [Note: [Col. 0687] Judith 13]. Behold the ways in which Peter and Paul became glorious princes of the earth. For in these things they became the ornament of the Church. There follows:

“*They loved one another in their lifetime, whereby they became fragrant ointment*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Office of the Church]. Its fragrance produces the trampling down of temporal things, love among brethren, and steadfastness in love: first, that we may rule earthly things; second, that we may be united in brotherhood; third, that no adversity may separate us. With reference to the first: “*They were glorious princes of the earth*”; with reference to the second: “*They loved one another in their lifetime*”; with reference to the third: “*In death they were not separated*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ibid.].

The steps of the righteous [Col. 0687B] ought to be straight, firm, and beautiful: straight through justice, firm through constancy, beautiful through the gracefulness of life. They are straight against loss, firm against falling, beautiful against scandal to the brethren. Of the first the Apostle says: “*Make straight paths for your feet, lest any who is lame go astray*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Heb. 12]. Likewise: “*Their feet were straight feet*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ezek. 1]. Of the second it follows: “*The sole of their foot was like the sole of a calf*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ibid.], that is, firm; for an ox plants its foot firmly. Of the third: “*How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Isa. 52]!

It should be noted that this uprightness is threefold. First, it ought to be in intention; second, in distribution; third, in the ordering of virtues. Of the first David says: “*How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright of heart*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ps. 72]! Hear such an upright man: “*That man was simple and upright, fearing God and withdrawing from evil*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Job 1]. Of the second: “*The path of the righteous is straight for walking*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Isa. 26].—“*If you offer rightly,*” he says, “*but do not divide rightly, you have sinned*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Gen. 4, according to the LXX]. We offer rightly by a good intention; we divide rightly by observing the proper distribution. Of the third: “*If you rise early to the Almighty, if you walk pure and upright, he will immediately awaken for you*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Job 8]. But what fruit results? “*The generation of the upright shall be blessed*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ps. 111], he says.

We find three things that hinder firmness of step and cause falling: difficulty of ways, the weight of burdens, and the force of winds. In the first are worldly impediments; in the second, impediments of sin; in the third, vainglory arising from good things. Of the first, in the [Col. 0687D] Book of Wisdom: “*We have walked difficult paths*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Wis. 5]. Of the second: “*My iniquities have passed over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ps. 37]. Of the third: “*A wind rushing from the desert region crushed Job’s children*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Job 1].

There are three difficulties on the way: roughness, softness, and length—roughness of tribulations, softness of pleasures, and length of weariness. Against the first the Apostle says: “*Do not be conformed to this age*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Rom. 12]. Of the second: “*We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution [Col. 0688A] and endure it*” [Note: [Col. 0687] I Cor. 4]. Against the third: “*Let us not fail while doing good, for in its season we shall reap if we do not fail*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Gal. 6].

The first walk through fire, the second through water, the third through the wilderness. Of the first and second: “*We passed through fire and water, and you led us out into refreshment*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ps. 65]. Of the third: “*They wandered in a waterless wilderness; they did not find the way to an inhabited city*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ps. 106]. Some perish in fire, like Nadab and Abihu, by fire from heaven [Note: [Col. 0687] Num. 26]. Others are drowned by water, like the Egyptians in the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0687] Exod. 14]. Others die in the wilderness through weariness of the long way [Note: [Col. 0687] Num. 26]. Some endure fire well, like the three boys in the furnace [Note: [Col. 0687] Dan. 3]. Others escape from the waters, as Peter walked upon the waters at the Lord’s call [Note: [Col. 0687] Matt. 14]. Others bear wilderness well, like Joshua and Caleb [Col. 0688B] in reaching the promised land [Note: [Col. 0687] Num. 26]. Of the first: “*When you pass through fire, you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not burn in you*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Isa. 43]. Of the second: “*When you walk through waters, rivers shall not overwhelm you*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ibid.]. Because of the third it is said: “*The living creatures went and returned*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ezek. 1].

There follows the weight of burdens, of which there are four.

There is a burden that destroys one’s step; a burden that presses down; a burden that obstructs; and a burden that draws upward. The first is the burden of sins; the second, of temptations; the third, bodily weakness; the fourth, Christ’s sweet yoke. Of the first: “*Release those who are broken, free, and break every burden*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Isa. 58]. Of the second: “*Come to me, all you who [Col. 0688C] labor and are burdened*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Matt. 11]. Of the third: “*A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam, from the day of their coming forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial, into the mother of all*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ecclus. 40]. Of the fourth: “*For my yoke is sweet and my burden light*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Matt. 11].

There follows the wind of vainglory. The wind of vainglory likewise hinders one’s steps. It is that wind which, coming from the desert region, shook the four corners of the house and crushed Job’s children [Note: [Col. 0687] Job 1]. That desert is hell, whose king is the devil, from whom vainglory has its beginning. Hence it is said to Pharaoh: “*Behold, I will cast you into the wilderness*” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ezek. 29]. That house is the ordered life of a human being. Its four corners are these: works of justice; purity of conscience; the gift of knowledge; and grace of speech, for the praise of God and [Col. 0688D] the benefit of one’s neighbor. By the first a person merits; by the second one lives securely; by the third the other things are governed; by the fourth God is praised and one’s neighbor edified.

The first is set against the north, the second against the south, the third toward the west, the fourth toward the east: against the north, lest the ardor of action grow lukewarm in the cold of the north; toward the south, that conscience may be fervent in charity; against the west, lest the night of ignorance rushing in deceive the ignorant; toward the east, that the sun of justice may begin through preaching to shine upon one’s neighbor [Col. 0689A]. Of the first: “*Arise, north wind*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Song 4]. Of the second: “*Come, south wind, and breathe through my garden*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ibid.]. Of the third: “*Your word is a lamp to my feet*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 118]; for the preacher’s word is God’s word. Of the fourth, in Genesis: “*He divided the light from the darkness*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Gen. 1]. For light is knowledge and darkness ignorance.

Whoever boasts vainly of these four gifts of God has his steps shaken by an evil wind. The Pharisee boasted of the first when he said: “*I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Luke 18]. Of the second, when he said: “*I am not like other men—robbers, adulterers*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ibid.]. Elihu boasted of the third when he said: “*My belly is like new wine without a vent, which bursts new wineskins*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Job 32]. Of the fourth, when he said: “*I am full of words, and the spirit of my belly constrains me*” [Col. 0689B] [Note: [Col. 0689] Ibid.]. Behold the straight; behold the firm. There follows the beauty of steps.

Three things make feet ugly: mud, dust, and disease. Mud defiles; dust dries; disease swells. Mud, that is, carnal pleasure, defiles them; the dust of anger, envy, and worldly desire dries them; the wind of pride swells them. These feet are our affections, which sometimes incline toward pleasure, sometimes toward anger, envy, and covetousness, and sometimes toward self-exaltation. That the steps in these may be beautiful, let them have footwear made from the skins of dead animals—that is, let them be protected by examples drawn from the lives of the ancient Fathers. Against pleasure take Daniel’s chastity; against anger, envy, [Col. 0689C] and desire, take Job’s charity; against self-exaltation take David’s humility.

Of the first feet it is said: “*I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Song 5]. Of the second the Lord says: “*Shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Mark 6]. Of the third David says: “*Let not the foot of pride come upon me*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 35].

It should be noted, moreover, that she is called the daughter of a prince. For the soul of the righteous person is, first, the daughter of a priest; second, the daughter of a prince; third, the daughter of a king. First, she is the daughter of the priest of Midian [Note: [Col. 0689] Num. 25]. Of the second it is said: “How beautiful in sandals is the daughter of a prince, daughter of a king!” Of the third: “*All the glory of the king’s daughter is within*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 44].

The priest’s daughter is for sacrifice; the prince’s daughter for ruling; the king’s daughter for governing or directing: for sacrificing [Col. 0689D] her flesh through the absolution of sins; for ruling the motions of temptation; for governing the order of virtues. First, that she may be reconciled; second, that the servant may not rule; third, that order may not be dissolved. Of the first: “*I beseech you to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Rom. 12]. To the second it is said: “*He who delicately nourishes his servant from his youth will afterward find him rebellious*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Prov. 21]. And: “*Let no temptation seize you except a human one*” [Note: [Col. 0689] I Cor. 10]. Of the third, the poet says:

[Col. 0690A] … *Rule your mind; unless it obeys, it commands.*

We are taught to order the virtues in the Catholic Epistle: “*Be all of one mind, patient in faith, lovers of brotherhood, merciful, modest, humble*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Jas. 5]. Thus it is said to those who rule: “*The kingdom of God is within you*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Luke 17].

*The joining of your thighs is like necklaces fashioned by an artisan’s hand.*

[THO.] (Thus.) In the thighs of the Church is understood her singular and spiritual generation, which is accomplished through the ministry of the word and the washing of regeneration. The joining of the two thighs is the concord of two peoples—namely, Jew and Gentile. From these, united in one faith, comes the universal Church [Col. 0690B]. This joining is compared to necklaces because Catholic faith is manifested by the testimony of good works. These necklaces, however, were fashioned by the hand of an artisan, because the works of virtue, by which the Church is built as one from two peoples, are established by the ineffable generosity of our Creator. For he is the cornerstone who made both one [Note: [Col. 0689] Eph. 2].

The joining of the thighs is rightly praised after the bride’s sandaled steps, because the harmonious union of believing peoples is accomplished through the ministry of preachers. The head of a human being signifies the divine nature; the thighs, the human; the body, the Church; and the joining, Christ’s holiness. From the head, all the senses are diffused to the other members; the body is the gathering of members into one [Col. 0690C]; a necklace, to which the joining is compared, is made from metal and a precious stone; but there are two thighs.

For from the head—that is, from divinity—life is diffused into every animate creature, and grace into every believer. The Church, however, is made complete as a body from believers as from members. The necklaces to which the joinings are compared are fitted together from the metal of human flesh and the jewel of divine wisdom. The duality of the thighs signifies our twofold defect, namely guilt and punishment. By this joining, therefore, human nature, compared to thighs, is absolved from sins, restored from misery, and freed from eternal death. This is mercifully granted by Christ, who is the joining; the Church is renewed by the sacraments; and from the head of divinity our desire shall be fulfilled.

As David says of all these things: “*Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities, who redeems your life from destruction*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ps. 102]—these concern the first. “*Who crowns you with mercy and compassion*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ibid.]—behold, the second. “*Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ibid.]—behold, the third. “*Who satisfies your desire with good things*” [Note: [Col. 0689] Ibid.]—behold, the fourth.

In this joining three things are joined: flesh, soul, and divinity. For through our first parents a threefold division was made in Paradise: first, from justice; second, from grace; third, from glory—[Col. 0691A] from justice by sinning; from grace, by which a person could persevere in good; and from glory, which is free from death’s sting. In the first division, man ceased to be beautiful; in the second, he became poor; in the third, miserable—he who had ceased to be beautiful. The first man covered his private parts with a leaf because, being poor, he hid himself lest he be seen stripped by God of virtues. He was miserable when he was cast down from Paradise into this valley of tears.

Jeremiah lamented this threefold misfortune when he said: “*How the gold has grown dim, how the finest color has changed*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Lam. 4]—behold, lost beauty. “*The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ibid.]—behold, poverty. “*The illustrious sons of Zion, clothed at first in gold—how are they reckoned as earthen vessels, the work of the potter’s hands?*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ibid.] For as a potter’s vessel is fragile [Col. 0691B], so is human nature through misery.

To represent these three divisions, when Abraham sacrificed a three-year-old she-goat, a cow, and a ram, he divided the flesh in two [Note: [Col. 0691] Gen. 15]. The goat is a foul-smelling animal. Its flesh is divided to express the division from justice, and it is sacrificed so that satisfaction may thus be made for it. The cow is suited for plowing and for gaining profit for its owner; it is sacrificed to express the second division. The ram is called king of the sheep and makes the flock secure by its protection. Its flesh is divided to signify the third division, and it is sacrificed for recovery.

Thus the first parents: first sinned; second, were separated from Paradise; third, were reconciled through this joining, as David says: “*They defiled his covenant*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 54]—behold the first. “*They were divided from the anger of his face*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ibid.]—behold the second. “*And his heart drew near*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ibid.]—behold the third.

These necklaces, to which the joinings are likened, were fashioned by the hand of an artisan—that is, by the working of God, who is the highest artisan. Or, “by the hand of an artisan” means through Christ, who is called the artisan’s hand, that is, the Father’s hand, because through him the Father created all things. Christ is aptly compared to a necklace, because the metal of a necklace is worked by the striking of hammers. A jewel possesses power and brightness in itself. Thus three things came together in Christ: flesh bruised in the Passion; a soul in which he had love for us; and the brightness of divinity, by which he promised us his vision [Col. 0691D]. This accords with the three interpretations of *monile* (“necklace”).

According to the first, *monile* is so called because it softens vicious motions. This is what it does in women through recollection of its meaning, and what Christ does for us by his Passion. According to the second, *monile* means “admonishing of the law,” namely the law that is to be observed between husband and wife. Likewise, Christ’s love for us in his soul invites us to keep his law. According to the third, *monile* means “moving joy by brightness.” Women rejoice in it; and we ought to be moved to joy by the impressed brightness of divinity.

The first, therefore, is opposed to the first division, namely, from justice [Col. 0692A]; the second to the second, namely, from grace; the third to the third, namely, from glory. In the first, Christ expiated our iniquity; in the second, he restored our old condition; in the third, he shall refashion our lowliness. Of the first: “*Christ bore our sins in his body upon the tree, that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness*” [Note: [Col. 0691] I Pet. 2]. Of the second: “*Because of the great charity with which he loved us, when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Eph. 2]. Of the third: “*He refashioned the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Phil. 3]. It follows: *fashioned by an artisan’s hand.*

There is an artisan who makes art, an artisan who works upon art, and an artisan who works by art. The first acts for the sake of art [Col. 0692B], the second from art, the third by means of art. The first is an inventor, the second a teacher, the third a worker. This artisan is Christ, who from eternity devised the art by which man might be restored; in time he taught how man might be restored; in flesh he wrought the means by which man might be restored.

This thigh signifies our flesh, which is sometimes without a joining, namely when it is loosened to wantonness. At other times it has a joining, namely when pleasure is restrained. This joining is the region of the loins, which is sometimes commanded to be covered by breeches, sometimes girded by a belt, and sometimes compared to necklaces. The first belongs to the order of the married, the second to the order of the continent, the third to the order of virgins: the first for decency, the second against weakness, the third for devotion [Col. 0692C]. The first is so that the indecency of marital intercourse may not appear; the second, that virtues may prevail over vices; the third, that there may be devotion in tasting heavenly sweetness.

For the first, Aaron is commanded to be clothed around his private parts with linen breeches. For the second it is said: “*Let your loins be girded*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Luke 12]. For the third: “*The joining of your thighs is like necklaces fashioned by an artisan’s hand.*” Of the first the Apostle says: “*We ought to surround our weaker members with greater honor*” [Note: [Col. 0691] I Cor. 12]. Of the second, to Job: “*Gird up your loins like a man*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Job 40]. Of the third: “*We know that, if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, in heaven*” [Note: [Col. 0691] II Cor. 5].

That these thighs—that is, our flesh—may possess their joinings, the soul sometimes permits them to attend to their own necessity; sometimes makes them serve the soul’s usefulness; sometimes the soul itself conforms itself within the flesh to angelic purity [Col. 0692D]. In the first case it gives the flesh a sword, that it may defend itself against the vice of excess; in the second it causes it to waste away through discipline, fasts, and vigils; in the third it suspends it from every earthly work in honor of the Lord’s Incarnation.

Of the first: “*Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Ps. 44]. For the second: “*The sinew in Jacob’s thigh withered*” [Note: [Col. 0691] Gen. 32]. As a figure of the third, Damascus, Abraham’s servant, placed [Col. 0693A] his hand under his master’s thigh when he swore to him [Note: [Col. 0693] Gen. 24], signifying that the flesh is to be honored above the works of human beings, because Christ was to be born from it. He is this necklace, made of the metal of humanity and the jewel of divinity, to which the joining of the thighs—that is, the presentation of our flesh—ought to be compared.

*How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince! The joining of your thighs is like necklaces fashioned by an artisan’s hand.*

[CARD.] These are the words of the Son, who again rises to praise his mother and shows why she is deservedly desirable to behold. For she was clothed in fine linen and shod in hyacinth-blue. Therefore her steps are said to be beautiful in sandals. For her thoughts and deeds shone with the beauty of spiritual devotion and intention [Col. 0693B], like feet in hyacinth-colored shoes. And because she was clothed in the fine linen of chastity and bound with the girdle of virginity, the joining of her thighs is said not merely to be chaste or beautiful, but also to admonish chastity. Therefore it is compared to necklaces, called *monilia*, as though “admonishing chastity.” For by her example she reminds and invites us to the purity of continence.

These necklaces are said to have been fashioned by an artisan’s hand. For the Holy Spirit, the artisan, fashioned in her thighs this joining, this purity, this prerogative of chastity, so that through the descending dew of heavenly grace she possessed no tinder of carnal desire. Hence, concerning the prerogative of her virginity, it is said:

*Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking cups.*

[THO.] The navel, the most fragile member of our body, signifies the weakness of our mortality. Our navel, then, becomes a turned bowl, never lacking cups, when, admonished by the consciousness of our mortality, we offer our neighbors the cup of the saving word, so that for such mercy the mercy of heavenly blessedness may be given in recompense. This may also be understood generally of the cup of almsgiving, concerning which the Judge will say: “*I thirsted, and you gave me drink*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Matt. 25].

A *crater* is a large cup with two handles; hence the poet [Note: [Col. 0693] Vergil, *Aeneid* I.722]:

> But when the first repose after the feast has come, and the tables have been removed,
>
> [Col. 0693D] they set out great mixing-bowls and crown the wines.

It is aptly called “turned,” because just as a turned vessel is finished more quickly than others, so mercy ought to be performed more promptly than other works for those who need earthly or heavenly cups. Hence Solomon: “*Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I shall give to you,’ when you can give at once*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Prov. 3].

The navel is more prone to lust in women; in men it too is a weaker part; and in all who are born it is the superfluous flesh by which they adhere to their mother. The first signifies lust in the soft [Col. 0694A] and effeminate; the second, continence wavering in temptation; the third, superabundance of food and clothing among lovers of the world. Of the first the Lord says to Job concerning Behemoth: “*His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Job 40]. Of the second: “*Ezekiel saw a man who from the navel upward was like fire, and from the navel downward like fire*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ezek. 8]. This is the fire of tribulation adhering to the navel—that is, to weakness; the other fire above is charity kindling. Of the third, in the same book, concerning Oholibah: “*On the day of your birth your navel was not cut*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ezek. 23].

The first navel attacks chastity, the second strength, the third frugality. The first casts one into filth; the second changes one into hay; the third makes one poor: into foul-smelling filth, into rotting hay, poor in abundance of virtues. Adam fell into filth when he saw his wife naked; they desired one another and covered themselves with loincloths. He was changed into hay when cast out of Paradise, whence: “*Do you display your power against a leaf driven by the wind, and pursue dry straw?*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Job 13]. He saw himself poor when he said: “*I heard your voice,* Lord, *in Paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Gen. 3].

Against the first the Apostle says: “*Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the fornicator sins against his own body*” [Note: [Col. 0693] I Cor. 6]; and: “*God will judge fornicators and adulterers*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Heb. 13]. Against the second: “*When I am weak, [145] then I am stronger*” [Note: [Col. 0693] II Cor. 12]. [Col. 0694C] Against the third: “*I know how to be hungry and to be full, to abound and to suffer want*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Phil. 4].

There are three causes why the loins of prelates are not turned cups: first, corruption of the flesh; second, frequent indulgence in worldly pleasure; third, the devil’s contrivance.

These are the three things that drive a person out of his house: smoke, dripping water, and a bad wife. The bad wife is the desire of the flesh, of which David says: “*My loins are filled with illusions*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ps. 37]; and the Apostle: “*I find no good in myself, that is, in my flesh*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Rom. 6]. Dripping falls from the roof of a house and stains garments: this is desire coming from the world, which stains good conduct—that is, the loincloth which Jeremiah hid in the Euphrates River [Col. 0694D] and which rotted [Note: [Col. 0693] Jer. 15], namely continence turned into pleasure. Hence in the Catholic Epistle: “*Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life*” [Note: [Col. 0693] I John 2].

Smoke is the devil’s suggestion, which, like smoke, blinds the human senses. Thus of Behemoth: “*His strength is in his loins*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Job 40]; and of the same: “*The sinews of his testicles are entwined*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Ibid.]. But prelates are told: “*Let your loins be girded*” [Note: [Col. 0693] Luke 12]. For in this way a prelate is stronger, more beyond reproach, and more discerning: stronger against temptation, [Col. 0695A] more beyond reproach for preaching, and more discerning for contemplation of heavenly things.

For the first Judith [Note: [Col. 0695] ch. 8] put sackcloth upon her loins; hence: “*Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Gal. 5]. For the second John had a leather belt around his loins [Note: [Col. 0695] Matt. 3]; hence the prophet says to his servant: “*Gird your loins and take your staff in your hand*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Jer. 1]; hence Paul says: “*I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become rejected*” [Note: [Col. 0695] I Cor. 9]. For the third Elijah had his loins girded; hence the Lord says to Job: “*Gird your loins like a man, and I shall speak with you*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Job 38]; and Paul says: “*Putting off the old man according to your former way of life, put on the new man, who is renewed [Col. 0695B] in the knowledge of God*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Eph. 4].

It should be noted that lust and abundance promise life, whereas weakness is a messenger of death. There are three messengers of death: accident, sickness, and old age. Accident announces doubtful death, sickness serious death, old age certain death. Accident announces hidden death, sickness apparent death, old age present death. From the uncertainty of death fear ought to follow; from the severity of sickness, sorrow; from the certainty of old age, not obstinacy but humility and affliction.

Bowls or cups are usually made from three materials: clay, wood, and metal. The first is fragile, the second carveable, the third malleable. From the first a cup is formed by fingers; from the second, by tools; from the third, by hammers. The first cup signifies the simple, who, judging themselves lowly, incline their head to their master’s [Col. 0695C] command. The second signifies those who discipline themselves by afflictions and cut away from their flesh not only what is unlawful but also what is lawful. The third signifies those who willingly endure the hammers of suffering.

Of the first David says: “*I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you*”; and it follows: “*You held my right hand and led me according to your will*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 72]. Of the second: “*They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, oppressed, afflicted*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Heb. 11]. Of the third: “*The saints experienced mockeries and scourges, moreover bonds and prisons; they were stoned, sawn apart, tested, and died by the slaughter of the sword*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ibid.].

But one must see how each is formed. First it is trodden under foot; second it is formed on the wheel; third [Col. 0695D] it is hardened in fire: by the feet of discipline, the wheel of circumspection, and the fire of charity. Of the first it is said: “*The righteous shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 140]. Of the second: “*Blessed is the man who remains in wisdom, meditates in justice, and in understanding considers the providence of God*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ecclus. 14]. Such a person says: “*How many iniquities and sins have I? Show me my crimes and offenses*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Job 13]. Having seen them, he cries with Job: “*Though I be washed with snow-water and my hands shine as most clean, yet you shall plunge me into filth, and my garments shall abhor [Col. 0696A] me*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Job 9]. Of the third: “*Who shall separate us from Christ’s charity? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword?*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Rom. 8].

The second, wooden cup is first cut down, second carved, third turned. It is cut down when a person is separated from the world; it is carved by making satisfaction for sin; and it is turned by cutting away much even from things permitted. It is cut down with the axe of fear; carved with the coarser tools of sorrow; turned with the finer tools of fervor. Of the first: “*Already the axe has been placed at the root of the tree*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Matt. 3]. Of the second: “*Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near to you*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ibid.]. Of the third: “*Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Matt. 19].

The third cup is of metal. First it is tested by fire; second it is struck with hammers; third it is rubbed with iron filings. By the fire of voluntary discipline: “*You tested us by fire as silver is tested*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 65]. By hammers of inflicted suffering: “*I gave my body to those striking me and my cheeks to those plucking them*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Isa. 50]. By the iron filings of insult: “*I did not turn my face away from those reproaching and spitting upon me*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ibid.]. By fire, that it may cast off dross; by hammers, that it may receive form; by filings, that it may shine in brightness. It casts off the dross of worldly conduct, receives the form of the Savior, and gains the brightness of renowned religious life. Of the first: “*Putting off the old man with his deeds, according to the former way of life*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Eph. 4]. Of the second: “*Put on the new man in knowledge of the Son of God, according to the image of him who created him*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ibid.]. Of the third: “*Let your [Col. 0696C] light shine before men*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Matt. 5].

The first cup gives the drink of water; the second, mead; the third, myrrhed wine: the drink of tears; the mead of devotions; myrrhed wine because it offers now the joys of heavenly things, now the bitterness of sufferings. Of the first: “*I mixed my drink with weeping*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 101]; and: “*You shall give us drink in tears by measure*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Ps. 79]. Of the second: “*Do not mourn and do not weep, for the day is sanctified to the Lord. Eat rich food and drink mead*” [Note: [Col. 0695] II Esdr. 8]. Mead is made from wine and honey. Of the third: “*They gave the Lord myrrhed wine to drink*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Mark 15].

The first sometimes lacks water; the second never lacks cups; the third sometimes interrupts its taste of heavenly sweetness. The first lacks water because it is sometimes anxious about temporal things; the second never lacks cups because it is stripped of every anxiety; the third interrupts its taste because it is impeded by the bitterness of suffering. Of the first the prophet complains: “*Who will give waters to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Jer. 9]. The Apostle exhorts the second: “*Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice*”; and it follows: “*Be anxious about nothing*” [Note: [Col. 0695] Phil. 4]. Of the third, Christ first said: “*Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had before the world was made*” [Note: [Col. 0695] John 17], tasting, that is, heavenly sweetness. [Col. 0697A] But afterward, as the Passion intensified, he began to fear and be distressed, saying: “*My soul is sorrowful unto death*” [Note: [Col. 0697] Matt. 26]. Behold the interruption of taste.

The bride’s navel, therefore, is every righteous person who considers his own weakness so as through it to become stronger, according to the Apostle: “*For when I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful*” [Note: [Col. 0697] II Cor. 12]. First, as has been said, he cuts himself off from the world; second, he makes satisfaction for sin; third, he cuts away something from what is lawfully allowed him. Such a person never lacks cups, because he offers either preaching to the sinner, the abundance of almsgiving to the poor, or devotion to God; and thus he never lacks cups.

*Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking cups.*

[CARD.] By the navel is signified the weakness of carnal desire [Col. 0697B], whence Job says that the strength of Behemoth is in the navel of his belly [Note: [Col. 0697] Job 40]. But in this Virgin the navel so withered and hardened that it was like dry wood, possessing none of the moisture of carnal desire. And, as if by a turning-work, her navel was cut round, within and without, from every inward and outward temptation. Nor does this bowl need the cups from which he drinks who cries on the cross, “*I thirst*” [Note: [Col. 0697] John 19].

Rather, from this bowl he drank wine and milk. For, together with the milk of virginal brightness, he found the mortification of his own flesh, which has an austere taste, mixed into wine, so that he might delight alike in both. It follows:

*Your belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies.*
[THO.] The belly signifies the condition of our mortality [Col. 0697C]. Therefore our belly is like a heap of wheat when, mindful of our frailty, we prepare in this present life the fruits of good works by which we may continually be refreshed. It is rightly called a heap of wheat, and not an abundance of wheat, so that the virtues’ growth rising on high may be denoted. And just as a heap is broad at its base and narrower at its summit, so our good works: the better they are, the fewer are those who perform them. This heap is rightly said to be surrounded by lilies, so that we may perform the good things we do for the sake of beholding eternal brightness.

We have said that the Bride sometimes signifies the Virgin Mary, sometimes the soul walking in righteousness, and sometimes the Church militant. The first has a material belly, the second a spiritual one, [Col. 0697D] the third a sacramental one. The first belly is immaculate virginal flesh; the second, pure intention; the third, inviolable unity. Of the first: “Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the breasts which thou hast sucked [Note: [Col. 0697] Luke 11]!” Of the second, the prophet says: “My belly shall sound for Moab like a harp [Note: [Col. 0697] Isa. 16].” Of the third: “Our belly hath cleaved unto the earth [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 43].” The first has fruitfulness, the second fullness, the third capacity: fruitfulness, by which “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us [Note: [Col. 0697] John 1]”; fullness, by which “the living bread which came down from heaven” satisfies [Note: [Col. 0697] John 6]; capacity, [Col. 0698A] by which it contains all who come to it from the four quarters of the world.

Hear of its fruitfulness: “Behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb and shalt bear a son, and he shall be called the Son of the Most High [Note: [Col. 0697] Luke 1].” Hear of its fullness: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread shall not taste death for ever [Note: [Col. 0697] John 6].” Hear of its capacity: “Many shall come from east and west, and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0697] Matt. 8].”

Thus, in the first was sown the grain of wheat; the second is satisfied from the fat of wheat; the third is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies. Of the first: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone [Note: [Col. 0697] John 12].” Of the second: “He fed them from the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock [Note: [Col. 0697] Ps. 80].” Of the third, in the [Col. 0698B] present chapter: “Thy belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies.”

Now, in order that the grain sown in the first womb may make the second, it must first be ground after it has been sown, and have its bran removed. It was sown in the Virgin through the assumption of flesh; ground on the cross through the pains of the Passion; stripped of bran in the Resurrection through shedding the condition of our mortality. Hear of its sowing: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we should have been as Sodom and made like Gomorrah [Note: [Col. 0697] Isa. 1].” Hear of its grinding: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me [Note: [Col. 0697] Isa. 63].” Hear of its removal of bran: “Christ, rising from the dead, dieth now no more; death shall have no more dominion over him [Note: [Col. 0697] Rom. 6].”

From this bread the spiritual belly is satisfied: “Make me first,” says Elijah, “a cake baked under the ashes;” [Col. 0698C] afterward thou shalt make one for thyself and thy son [Note: [Col. 0697] II Kings 17]. We make bread because in it we hope to have refreshment: a little cake, when we consider his humility; a cake baked under ashes, when we behold his Passion. But because we ought to love God more than ourselves, let us first make it for him—namely, by assigning him honour in all these things and returning thanks. Then let us make it for ourselves, seeking in these things our own benefit: conforming ourselves to his humility, enduring sufferings, and aspiring to the glory of the Resurrection.

It should be noted, moreover, that this spiritual belly is satisfied with bread, food, and drink: bread, namely the saving sacrifice; food, namely the understanding of the Scriptures; drink, namely Christ’s blood and the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0698D] “That bread is the living bread which came down from heaven [Note: [Col. 0697] John 6].” Of food, that is, the understanding of Scripture, Ezekiel says: “Son of man, eat this scroll; and it shall be sweet as honey in thy mouth, and it shall make thy belly bitter [Note: [Col. 0697] Ezek. 3].” For the understanding of Scripture sounds sweet in preaching; but in the recollection of sins and of the punishment of hell which it presents, it troubles the soul. Of the drink of blood the Saviour said: “Drink ye all of this, for this is the cup of the New Testament [Note: [Col. 0697] Matt. 25].” There is also a drink, namely the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which they are made drunk with the abundance of God’s house.

Having such a [Col. 0699A] belly, the Lord seeks them with the torrent of his delight; whence: “He that thirsteth, let him come and drink; rivers of living water shall flow from his belly. But this he said concerning the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive [Note: [Col. 0699] John 7].” David desired to be filled with these things when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise thee with lips of exultation [Note: [Col. 0699] Ps. 62].”

The third, sacramental belly has great capacity, receiving all the faithful within itself; whence it is written: “O Israel, how great is the house of the Lord, and how vast the place of his possession [Note: [Col. 0699] Baruch 3]!” Truly great, because it conceives those returning, labours to bring forth those who toil, and gives birth to those passing on.

146 Those returning are those returning to the unity of the Church; those who toil, those working for their own benefit and that of their neighbours; those passing on, those passing from the world to the Father. It conceives that they may be nourished, labours [Col. 0699B] that they may merit, and gives birth that they may be rewarded. Of conception Job says: “I should not have endured as an untimely birth, or as those conceived who did not see the light [Note: [Col. 0699] Job 3].” For people are conceived in the womb of mother Church when they return to her. They do not see the light when, failing to receive the light of grace, they return to sins. The Church labours in those who toil. Whence: “There were pains as of a woman in labour [Note: [Col. 0699] Ps. 47].” In those passing from the world to the Father, the Church gives birth, as is sung in the Church: “That the mother may bear them into a new infancy [Note: [Col. 0699] Office of the Church].”

Thus the grain of wheat—that is, Christ—was sown in the first belly; the second is fed by his fatness. From the same grain the heap of wheat—that is, the multitude of saints—has grown in the third. It follows: “Surrounded by lilies”: both the first and the second belly, but never the third, are [Col. 0699C] surrounded by lilies. And this is according to the lily’s threefold colour. For in its leaves it has whiteness, in its stalk greenness, and in its interior grains a golden colour. The first colour is beautiful, the second precious, the third regal: beautiful because of its brightness; precious because it gives vigour to churches; regal because golden colour confers honour in an emperor’s crown.

Therefore the first belly shines with lilies, that is, with the whiteness of virginity; the second is precious in the greenness of virtue; the third is regal, desiring to reign with angels. The lily, prince of chastity—that is, Christ, who says, “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys [Note: [Col. 0699] Song 2]”—adorned the first belly. The lily adorns the second, of which it is said: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among [Col. 0699D] the daughters [Note: [Col. 0699] Ibid.].” Lilies adorn the third, of which it is said: “Flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys surrounded her [Note: [Col. 0699] Office of the Church].” These surround it in hope now, but then in reality: the belly, that is, the unity of the Church, shall be surrounded.

There is a belly full of stench; a belly full of swelling; a belly full of pain; a belly full of fear; a belly full of love: of the stench of carnal pleasure; of the swelling of pride; of the pain of tribulation; of fear of the Lord’s rebuke; of the love of pure affection. Pleasure defiles the soul; tribulation disturbs the mind; rebuke awakens the sluggard; affection helps one’s neighbour for God’s sake. Of the first: “Our belly hath cleaved [Col. 0700A] to the earth [Note: [Col. 0699] Ps. 43].” Of the second, Elihu: “My belly is as new wine without a vent, which bursts new bottles [Note: [Col. 0699] Job 32].” Of the third, Jeremiah: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain”—that is, the perceptions of my troubled heart are disturbed within me [Note: [Col. 0699] Jer. 4]. Of the fourth, the Bride: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch [Note: [Col. 0699] Song 5].” Of the fifth: “My belly shall sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick [Note: [Col. 0699] Isa. 16].”

Three notable bellies are read of in the Gospel. The first is that in which Jeremiah was sanctified [Note: [Col. 0699] Jer. 1]; the second, that in which John was sanctified [Note: [Col. 0699] Luke 1]; in the third, Christ the sanctifier [Note: [Col. 0699] Ibid.]. In the first Jeremiah was sanctified and conceived according to nature; in the second John was sanctified and conceived contrary to nature; [Col. 0700B] Christ, conceived above nature, sanctified the third. But that third belly, of the blessed Virgin, is first commendable, secondly marvellous, and thirdly praiseworthy: commendable in modesty, marvellous in virtues and chastity, praiseworthy in fruits and innocence—modesty by which virtue is restrained; chastity by which it is adorned with miracles; innocence by which its fruit is given colour.

Of these three things we read in the Song of Songs. Of the first: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch”; for she says: “How shall this be, since I know not a man [Note: [Col. 0699] Luke 1]?” Of the second: “His belly is ivory, set with sapphires [Note: [Col. 0699] Song 5].” Ivory, that is, most chaste, because the elephant is a most chaste animal. Hence: “Thou shalt indeed bear a son, and shalt suffer no loss of virginity.” “It is set [Col. 0700C] with sapphires,” that is, with heavenly miracles; for sapphire has the colour of heaven. For it was a miracle that she conceived without a man, gave birth without pain, and remained a virgin [Note: [Col. 0699] Office of the Church]. Of the third: “Thy belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies.” Christ was the grain of wheat ground upon the cross; Christ was the heap when, with his members, he suffered martyrdom. They too were surrounded by the lilies of innocence, just as Christ “did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth [Note: [Col. 0699] I Pet. 2].” But also the Virgin’s womb, from which Christ, our head and beginning, proceeded, was surrounded by these lilies. Hence Damascene: “The Holy Spirit shall overshadow thee [Note: [Col. 0699] Luke 1].” For he made her chaste from every sin, gave her power to conceive without a man, and extinguished in her the tinder [Col. 0700D] of sin.

For praise of this womb, ivory, lily, and wheat are set forth: ivory for solidity, lily for pleasantness, wheat for fertility. It had solidity, by which it was inviolable; pleasantness, by which it was delightful; fertility, by which it was desirable. It was inviolable because after giving birth it remained an untouched virgin; delightful when the rod of Jesse flowered; desirable because it bore God and man.
