Hear of its solidity: “Jesus entered into a certain village [Note: [Col. 0699] Luke 10].” This village was the womb of the blessed Virgin. For in it was the tower of virginity, the wall of solidity, and the ditch of humility. In it were “Martha, anxious about much serving, [Col. 0701A] and Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet and hearing his word [Note: [Col. 0701] Luke 10].” Behold, in Mary the contemplative and the active life: active, in nourishing the little Christ; contemplative, in keeping all his words and pondering them in her heart.

Hear of its pleasantness; for pleasantness is perfected in three things: virginity must be beautiful, sweet, and delightful. Hence the Church sings of the Bride: “Thou hast become beautiful and sweet in thy delights [Note: [Col. 0701] Office of the Church].” For she was beautiful in purity, sweet in character, delightful in devotion: in purity, by which she turned sinners aside; in character, by which she won the good to herself; in devotion, by which she invited her beloved. Hear of the beautiful one: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun [Note: [Col. 0701] Song 6]?” Hear of the sweet one: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved [Col. 0701B] among the daughters [Note: [Col. 0701] Song 2].” Hear of the delightful one: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights [Note: [Col. 0701] Song 8]?”

This belly was fertile in three things: namely wheat, wine, and oil. Hence: “They are multiplied by the fruit of wheat, wine, and oil [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 4].” And Isaac said of Jacob: “I have established him in wheat, wine, and oil [Note: [Col. 0701] Gen. 27].” Wheat is Christ’s own flesh; wine, his blood; oil, mercy enriching the heart. The first is bread that strengthens the human heart; the second is wine that gladdens the human heart; the third is oil that enriches the heart with devotion. Of the first two: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood hath eternal life [Note: [Col. 0701] John 6].” Of the third, David: “He anointed me with the oil of his mercy [Note: [Col. 0701] Ps. 88].” Of this womb the woman in the Gospel cried out: [Col. 0701C] “Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the breasts which thou hast sucked [Note: [Col. 0701] Luke 11],” O Christ!

“Thy belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies.”

[CARD.] This is suitably understood of the carnal belly. For the womb of the blessed Virgin had heaped up in itself the wheat by which the dove must be fed and the Church nourished. She bore him in her womb, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0701] Col. 2].” This belly is said to be surrounded by lilies, namely by the whiteness and fragrance of virginal purity. Her spiritual belly too—that is, her mind—is compared with a heap of wheat: for, since she kept all the words and pondered them in her heart, she then heaped up the wheat of the holy Gospel which she afterward presented to the apostles for rumination. It follows:

[Col. 0701D] “Thy two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe.”

[THO.] Although this chapter has been carefully treated above, at least its fitting order should be considered—namely, the breasts after the belly. For after spiritual children are born from the womb of mother Church, it is necessary that their infancy be nourished with the milk of breasts—that is, of teachers—namely, preaching, until as time advances they become stronger and are refreshed with the bread of wisdom. These breasts are rightly called two, because those coming from Jews and Gentiles are nourished by them. They are also rightly compared to two fawns of a roe, [Col. 0702A] because they are filled with the milk of the Old and New Testaments. The fawns are rightly called twins because the two Testaments flowed from the same author. He is compared to a roe because it is a clean animal, remarkable in sight and in speed, dividing the hoof, chewing the cud, and armed with horns.

The saints have a divided hoof in discernment; they chew the cud in uttering what they have discerned; they have keen eyes for contemplating heavenly things; they are swift in their course—that is, in virtues—hastening toward what they have contemplated; and with the horns of faith they stand raised against the world. These breasts pertain to the revealing of Christ’s Incarnation. From one milk is expressed, namely the lowliness of his humanity; from the other wine, namely the loftiness of his divinity. Mother Church possesses these, and is compared to a roe because of purity, [Col. 0702B] for divinity does not feel the thorns of pains.

There are four who draw milk and wine from them, namely the four evangelists, signified to us by the two breasts and the two fawns, which make four. By their lightness the fawns pass through thickets. One fawn is compared to the first breast because Christ’s humanity leapt over the thickets of sins; the other fawn is compared to the remaining breast because divinity does not feel the thickets of pains.

But let us turn to those four evangelists who press the breasts. I believe that they are here set before us for imitation, so that we may derive something for our profit from the form of their bodies, the progress of their works, and the outcome of marvels: from the form of their bodies, that those beginning the journey may be adorned in character; from the progress of their works, that they may prepare the steps by which they are to go; from the outcome of marvels, that they may know him whom they are to see as marvellous in the kingdom.

The form is fourfold: that of an ox, a lion, a man, and an eagle. Luke bears the form of the ox, because he treated Christ’s sacrifice; Mark that of the lion, because he treated the Resurrection; Matthew that of the man, because he treated the Incarnation; John that of the eagle, because he treated divinity. Christ too possessed these forms and taught them to us: that of an ox, by dying for us; that of a lion, by rising mightily from the dead; that of a man, by being born to care for us; that of an eagle, by showing us through the Ascension the way to the kingdom.

Therefore he teaches us to have, from the ox’s form, the sacrifice of the flesh; from the lion’s, strength; from the man’s, discernment; [Col. 0702D] from the eagle’s, contemplation: sacrifice of the flesh, to destroy sin; the lion’s strength against the onset of temptations and adversities; the man’s discernment, lest anything be done rashly; the eagle’s ascent, “seeking the things above, setting our minds on the things above [Note: [Col. 0701] Col. 3].” Of the first: “I beseech you to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God [Note: [Col. 0701] Rom. 12].” And: “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected [Note: [Col. 0701] I Cor. 9].”—“For Christ our Passover has thus been sacrificed [Note: [Col. 0701] I Cor. 5].”

Of the second: “The righteous is confident as a lion [Note: [Col. 0701] Prov. 28].” For the lion, the strongest of animals, fears the encounter of no animal [Note: [Col. 0703] Prov. 30]. And: “When a strong, armed man guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are in peace [Note: [Col. 0703] Luke 11].” Of the third: “Your rational service [Note: [Col. 0703] Rom. 12].” And: “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed thou shalt not repent [Note: [Col. 0703] Ecclus. 32].” Hence it is said: “Their feet were straight feet [Note: [Col. 0703] Ezek. 1],” so that even in doing good one may keep measure. Hence the poet [Note: [Col. 0703] Horace]:

> Let the wise man who seeks virtue itself beyond what is enough  
> be called mad, and the just man unjust.  
> There is measure in things; finally, there are fixed limits  
> beyond or short of which right cannot stand.

And let him remember Jacob’s saying: “If I make my flocks labour too much in walking, they will all die in one day [Note: [Col. 0703] Gen. 32].” In the third [case] let us say: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands unto God [Note: [Col. 0703] Lam. 3].” And: [Col. 0703B] “To thee have I lifted up my eyes, who dwellest in the heavens [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 122],” so that thou mayest transfer me from this night to thy brightness. Hear the philosopher:

> Alas! Near the bounds of night, Orpheus saw his Eurydice, lost her, and died.

This fable concerns all of you who seek to make the mind your guide toward the day above. For whoever, overcome, turns his eyes toward the Tartarean cavern will lose whatever excellence he draws onward, while he looks upon the underworld.

The progress of works follows. If we carefully reconsider Ezekiel’s first vision, we shall find that these living creatures walked, ran, flew, and stood [Note: [Col. 0703] Ezek. 1]. They walk in progress, run in affection, fly in withdrawal, and stand in ecstasy: in the progress of merits, the affection of desires, withdrawal from worldly things, and ecstasy in heavenly things. They advance in merits through pain; in desires through love; from worldly things by despising them; in heavenly things by wondering at them.

It should be noted that while they walk, the wheels follow; while they run, they imitate the spirit; while they fly, their faces are lifted up; while they stand, punishments are remitted. Of the first: “When the living creatures walked, the wheels likewise walked beside them.” Of the second: “Whither the impulse of the spirit was, thither they went.” Of the third: “Their faces and their wings were stretched out above.” Of the fourth: “When there came a voice above the firmament which was over their heads, they stood and let down their wings.”

The walking living creatures are any saints advancing both themselves and others by the example of their works. The wheels are human lives. Hence: “A wheel appeared in the midst of a wheel,” like the life of those below formed from the life of those above. [Col. 0703D] These experience sometimes tranquillity, sometimes disturbance: “The appearance and work of the wheels was like the appearance of the sea,” which is sometimes calm, sometimes troubled.

For our life is like a wheel, having noon in its upper part, north in its lower, west on its descending side, and east on its ascending side. Thus our life was at noon in Adam; when temptation had been completed, it fell into the west; it descended into the north, subject to worldly misery; it began to ascend through the east in Christ’s Incarnation. So too we descend from the noon of divine love through the [Col. 0704A] west by committing sin. We fall into the north by remaining obstinate. We ascend through the east by rising through the gift of grace. We shall arrive at noon, existing at the summit of virtues;

147 namely, through the example and admonition of prelates, who are the thunders of God that inspire fear; whence: “The voice of thy thunder is in the wheel [Note: [Col. 0703] Ps. 76].”

Hear one descending from noon through west into north: “How hast thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, thou that didst rise in the morning! Thou hast fallen to earth, thou that didst wound the nations [Note: [Col. 0703] Isa. 14].” Hear the ascent from north through east to noon: “Who among you,” he says, “shall be able to dwell with devouring fire [Note: [Col. 0703] Isa. 33]?” Or, “Who among you shall dwell with everlasting burnings [Note: [Col. 0703] Ibid.]?” Behold, these are in the north: “He who walks in righteousness [Col. 0704B] and speaks truth, who rejects gain from oppression and shakes his hands free from every bribe [Note: [Col. 0703] Ibid.].” These ascend through the east: “This man shall dwell on high [Note: [Col. 0703] Ibid.].” Behold, arrival at noon.

Here one says, “I glory, exalted”; another, falling, says, “I descend, mortified”; another, obstinate, says, “Buried beneath the axle, I am worn down”; another, exalted anew, says, “Again I am borne to the stars.” Of this wheel Solomon says: “Remember thy Creator before the silver cord is broken, and the golden band returns, and the pitcher is shattered over the fountain, and the wheel is broken over the cistern; and the dust returns to the earth from which it was taken, and the spirit returns to God who gave it [Note: [Col. 0703] Eccl. 12].”

The silver cord is the little rope by which we are drawn toward good, that is, the eloquence of preaching; it will be broken at the coming of the Judge, [Col. 0704C] because then no one will be preached to. The golden band is the glory of the Resurrection, which fled from us in Adam but will return in the Resurrection. The pitcher is our heart. The fountain is heavenly joys, whose water is not under the earth but above it. We draw that water—that is, heavenly joys—when we long for them. But then the pitcher will be shattered over the fountain, when we receive those joys in full and no longer sigh for them.

The wheel is our temporal life. The cistern, which has waters in the depths of the earth, is the world; its waters are muddy, namely worldly pleasures. These are drawn out of the world’s cistern by a wheel-mechanism while human life labours in seeking them. But this wheel, which is over the [Col. 0704D] cistern, will be broken when, by dying, a human being is no longer occupied in acquiring the world’s delights. Then the dust of our flesh will return to the earth, but the spirit of the righteous to God.

These are the wheels that follow the walking living creatures: that is, the lives of ordinary persons follow the good works of teachers. Thus much concerning those who walk in the progress of merits and whom the wheels follow. But when they run in the affection of desires, they imitate the spirit—not just any spirit, but the Holy Spirit.

“For where the impulse of the spirit was, thither they went [Note: [Col. 0703] Ezek. 1].” There is an evil spirit, a human spirit, [Col. 0705A] and a divine Spirit. The first obstructs, the second runs, the third directs: it obstructs by the error of falsehood; runs by the love of holiness; directs by the brightness of truth. On account of the first David asked for the Spirit by which he could rule the malignant spirit: “Strengthen me,” he says, “with a princely Spirit [Note: [Col. 0705] Ps. 50].” On account of the second, for the Spirit by which he might be sanctified: “Take not thy Spirit from me [Note: [Col. 0705] Ibid.].” On account of the third, for the Spirit by which he might be directed: “Renew,” he says, “a right Spirit within me [Note: [Col. 0705] Ibid.].”

This human spirit is drawn in different directions, now by the evil spirit, now by the Holy Spirit. For the first is the evil spirit of God that tormented Saul: “I will go forth,” he says, “and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets [Note: [Col. 0705] III Kings 22].”

For this reason the human spirit cries: “Hear me speedily, O Lord; my spirit faileth [Note: [Col. 0705] Ps. 142].” [Col. 0705B] But conversely the Holy Spirit teaches it toward truth: “I will give you,” he says, “the Spirit of truth, and he shall teach you all truth [Note: [Col. 0705] John 14].” Comforted thereby, the human spirit cries: “Thy good Spirit shall lead me into the right land [Note: [Col. 0705] Ps. 142].” These are those who run by imitating the Spirit of God: “For those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God; for those who are according to the spirit have their minds on the things of the spirit [Note: [Col. 0705] Rom. 8].”

But those who fly by withdrawing from worldly things lift up their faces—that is, their consciences. It should be noted that this face sometimes descends to the depths, sometimes remains about the middle, and sometimes is raised to the height: to the depths, bending toward sins; about the middle, doing good things; to the height, considering [Col. 0705C] God’s mighty deeds. The first, that it may see how guilty it is; the second, that it may return through good works; the third, that it may delight in the future reward.

Of the first face it is said: “Their faces are blackened more than coals, and they are not known in the streets [Note: [Col. 0705] Lam. 4].” Hence it is said in Job: “If thou remove the iniquity that is in thy hand, and there be no injustice in thy tent, then thou shalt be able to lift up thy face without stain [Note: [Col. 0705] Job 11].” Of the second: “Each of them walked before its own face, or before its face [Note: [Col. 0705] Ezek. 1].” Of the third: “Their faces and their wings were stretched out above [Note: [Col. 0705] Ibid.].” And in Job: “Thou shalt abound in delights upon the Almighty, and shalt lift up thy face to God [Note: [Col. 0705] Job 22].”

Of those who stand in ecstasy in heavenly things it is said: “When a voice came over the [Col. 0705D] firmament, they stood and lowered their wings [Note: [Col. 0705] Ezek. 1].” And behold three things: a voice arises; they stand; they lower their wings. The voice is revelation; standing, consideration; lowering, humility: revelation of heavenly secrets; consideration of merits and rewards; humility in awareness of their own poverty.

Hear revelation: “Abraham at the oak of Mamre saw three and adored one [Note: [Col. 0705] Gen. 18].” Hear consideration of merits and rewards: “Lord God,” Abraham says, “what wilt thou give me [Note: [Col. 0705] Gen. 15]?” Hear humiliation: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes [Note: [Col. 0705] Gen. 18].” Hear it [Col. 0706A] more clearly in the Apostle: “I know such a man caught up to the third heaven [Note: [Col. 0705] II Cor. 12]”—behold revelation; “what is present, momentary and light, worketh in us beyond measure in sublimity an eternal weight of glory [Note: [Col. 0705] II Cor. 4]”—behold consideration of merits and rewards; “the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us [Note: [Col. 0705] Rom. 8]”—behold humility arising from awareness of one’s own poverty.

Behold, we have set something before you concerning the form of bodies and the progress of works. What follows concerns the outcome of marvels: “This,” he says, “was the vision darting to and fro in the midst of the four living creatures: the brightness of fire, and lightning coming forth from the fire [Note: [Col. 0705] Ezek. 1].” Behold the brightness of fire; behold its heat; behold its flash. This is the outcome of marvels. In brightness is heavenly clarity; in heat, the vehemence of charity; in the flash, terror of fire or of hellish punishment. [Col. 0706B] These move to and fro among the four living creatures when, in the spirit of brightness, they foresee future joy, the sweetness of charity, and the horror of hellish fear which must be fled.

The Apostle presumed the first when he said: “He shall reform the body of our humility, configured to the body of his brightness [Note: [Col. 0705] Phil. 3].” Of the second: “Charity never fails [Note: [Col. 0705] I Cor. 13].” Of the third, David: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me [Note: [Col. 0705] Ps. 54].” Behold how the evangelists draw milk from the aforesaid breasts, that they may feed us by their teaching, the example of their works, and their manner of life.

“Thy two breasts are like twin fawns of a roe.”

[CAR.] This verse is repeated to confirm the praise, [Col. 0706C] but since it has been explained above, there is no need for the explanation to be repeated. Then, in the praises of the Virgin, there is added for the consolation of sinners:

“Thy neck is like an ivory tower.”

[THO.] Because the voice proceeds through the neck and food enters through it, teachers are fittingly signified by it: with the voice of exhortation they strengthen the children of the Church and restore them with the nourishment of life. This neck is like an ivory tower because the Church’s teachers furnish the adornment, strength, and beauty of their lives, by which they show themselves white as ivory to all, and defend the city of God like a tower from the enemy’s assault.

The neck is Christ; the head, divinity; the body, the Church. Through the neck the word is uttered; food is conveyed to the body; saliva is swallowed. Thus through Christ the Word of the Father—who himself is that Word—is manifested to the world. The food of life, that is, his own flesh, is offered by himself to the faithful. Saliva—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—is given for the anointing of the inward person, first from heaven after the Ascension and daily through inspiration. [Col. 0706D]

This tower, which is Christ, insofar as it is a tower has strength and height; insofar as it is ivory, beauty. It has strength in power, height in pre-eminence, beauty in grace. It has strength in our human nature, strength in divinity, and strength in works: the first [Col. 0707A] in tribulation, the second in incorruptibility, the third in defending his inheritance. The first extends to the gibbet of the cross; the second suffers no failure; by the third he protects us against the adversary. Of the first: “Mighty God, Father of the age to come [Note: [Col. 0707] Isa. 11].” Of the second, Job: “If strength be sought, he is most mighty [Note: [Col. 0707] Job 9].” Of the third: “When a strong, armed man guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are in peace. But if one stronger than he comes,” that is, Christ, “he takes away all his arms [Note: [Col. 0707] Luke 11].”

Hear the first strength: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me [Note: [Col. 0707] Isa. 63].” Hear the second: “Who hath measured the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in a balance and the hills in scales [Note: [Col. 0707] Isa. 40]?” Hear the third: [Col. 0707B] “As a shepherd he shall feed his flock; in his arm he shall gather the lambs, and in his bosom shall lift them; he himself shall carry those with young [Note: [Col. 0707] Ibid.].”—“I will love thee, O Lord, my strength [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 17],” says David.

This tower, Christ, is also high: high in knowledge, higher in grace, highest in essence—high in knowledge of cognition, higher in the grace of holiness, highest in essence by which he is equal to the Father. By cognition he penetrates all things, even the hidden things of the heart; by holiness he is holier than all and sanctifies all. He is equal to the Father because no one surpasses him in greatness. Of the first height: “The Lord is high, and he regardeth the humble, and knoweth the lofty from afar [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 137].” And Isaiah: “Cease from man, whose spirit is in his nostrils, for he is accounted high [Col. 0707C] [Note: [Col. 0707] Isa. 2].” Of the second, Job: “It is higher than heaven: what wilt thou do [Note: [Col. 0707] Job 11]?” Heaven sometimes means the soul of the righteous and sometimes angels, all of whom he surpasses both in holiness and in other respects. Of the third: “I, Wisdom, dwell in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud [Note: [Col. 0707] Ecclus. 27].”

We do not say this in order to posit degrees in God by means of those three matters mentioned; rather, it is because a difference is displayed in those who receive his gifts. For it is high that God, by purifying, knows our conscience; higher that he pours in his grace; highest that he will show us the presence of his majesty.

He has beauty in humanity, beauty in divinity, and beauty in operation: in humanity, elegance of form; in divinity, [Col. 0707D] eternal brightness; in operation, creation, re-creation, and restoration. Of the first: “Beautiful in form above the sons of men [Note: [Col. 0707] Ps. 44].” Of the second: “He is the brightness of eternal light and the spotless mirror [Note: [Col. 0707] Wis. 7].” Of the third, Boethius [Note: [Col. 0707] *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, metre 9]:

> The Most Beautiful himself, beautiful—
Bearing the world in mind, and shaping it after a like image.

This threefold beauty is derived from ivory, that is, from the elephant. First, because it is a most chaste animal, and Christ is without fault; second, because its bone is white, since eternal brightness is signified by whiteness; [Col. 0708A] third, because, on account of its size, it is an imposing beast, and Christ is wondrous on account of his works. Let us construct a certain interior human being, to whom we may assign these things: let his head be intention, his body a collection of virtues, his neck chastity. For if intention is without charity, it should rather be called opinion than intention. And virtues without charity are not virtues, but natural powers. This neck is compared with an ivory tower, as charity possesses strength, height, and beauty: strength against the engines of battering-rams; height, so that a missile cast down from above may wound the adversary more severely; beauty, lest it seem a brothel or a dung-heap. The battering-rams are, namely, the assaults of temptations; the missiles, alms and prayers; the brothel or dung-heap, [Col. 0708B] lust and other sins. Therefore let it possess the strength of constancy, the height of desire, and the beauty of chastity and innocence.

Hear of its strength against battering-rams: “Who shall separate us from the charity of God, says Paul: tribulation, or distress? or persecution? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or the sword?” [Note: [Col. 0707] Rom. 8.] Behold how mighty the battering-rams are. Hear of stones coming down from above: “Charity is kind, patient, merciful.” [Note: [Col. 0707] I Cor. 13.] Hear of the dung-heap removed from it, so that it may be beautiful: “Charity does not behave improperly, is not puffed up, is not envious, is not ambitious, does not seek its own.” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ibid.]

We read of an ivory tower, as here; of an ivory house in the Psalm: “Myrrh, and stacte, and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses.” [Note: [Col. 0707] Psal. 44.] Of an ivory throne, [Col. 0708C] in the Third Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0707] Cap. 10.]: “Solomon made for himself a great throne of ivory.” The tower belongs to those who fight; the house, to those who live in peace; the throne, to kings. In the ivory tower are those who, preserving innocence against vices, fight manfully; in the ivory house, those who fashion and order their innocent habits in peace; on the throne are those who, living innocently, daily judge their own actions and affections.

The first say: “Be to us, O Lord, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy.” [Note: [Col. 0707] Psal. 60.] The second say: “We walked in the house of God with one accord.” [Note: [Col. 0707] Psal. 54.]—“Who makes those of one manner of life dwell in a house.” [Note: [Col. 0707] Psal. 67.] The third: “I have done judgment and justice.” [Note: [Col. 0707] Psal. 118.] The Apostle strengthens the first, saying: “Brethren, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of [Col. 0708D] his might. For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ephes. 6.] To the second he says: “I beseech you to walk worthily, with humility and meekness, with patience, bearing one another in charity, being eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” [Note: [Col. 0707] Ephes. 4.] To the third he says: “Test all things; hold fast what is good; abstain from every kind of evil.” [Note: [Col. 0707] I Thess. 5.] And David: “If indeed you speak justice, judge uprightly, sons of men; [Col. 0709A] for in your hearts you work iniquities upon the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Psal. 57.]

“Your neck is like an ivory tower.” Christ was a wooden tower, a stone tower, and an ivory tower: wooden in the weakness of the flesh; stone in the solidity of the resurrection; ivory in the joy of the ascension. In the first he joined the head to the body through the sincerity of faith; in the second through the truth of incorruption; in the third, in the assumption, through the reception of glory. Hence he himself says: “I go to prepare for you a place in the homeland. And I shall come again to you, and your heart shall rejoice.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Joan. 14.] “I go to prepare for you a place in the homeland, and I shall come again to you, and lead you out of this misery; and your heart shall rejoice, when you sit at the right hand in glory.”

At this ascension the whole world throughout the earth exults. Nor [Col. 0709B] is it surprising, because his triumph is far, incomparably more glorious: after he had taken up what belongs to the people, the apostles accompany him, the captives attend him, angels meet him, and the throne of the exalted Father receives him. The peoples with fervour; the apostles with love; the captives with honour; the angels with astonishment; the Father’s throne with splendour. All do this with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

Hear the people’s speech: “I shall arise and go about the city through lanes and streets; I shall seek him whom my soul loves.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Cant. 3.] But they sing, exhorting one another: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Coloss. 3.], etc. Again: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Mich. 4.] But because we are weighed down by bodily mass, he has compassion on us. “For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our infirmities.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Hebr. 4.], etc. Hear now that he has ascended: “Christ, appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle [Col. 0709C] not made with hands, entered once for all into the Holy Places, having obtained eternal redemption.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Hebr. 9.]

He was High Priest, as though making a bridge by which we might ascend to heaven after him. That bridge was the cross; the bridge was his own body. The cross, because through the wood we were saved and through the holy cross delivered; the body, because “like an eagle stirring up her young to fly and hovering over them, he spread his wings and took him up and bore him on his shoulders.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Deut. 32.]—“You were a leader, O Lord, in mercy to the people whom you redeemed, and you bore them in your strength to your holy dwelling-place.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Exod. 15.]

Thus the apostles accompany him, lovingly recalling his promise: “You are those who have remained with me in my trials, and I appoint for you a kingdom.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Luc. 22.] Therefore they follow him thus: [Col. 0709D] “Draw us after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Cant. 1.] And from love they cry: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I languish with love.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Cant. 5.] Thus the apostles rejoice at Christ’s ascent; and “they returned to Jerusalem with joy, and were of one mind in prayer,” [Note: [Col. 0709] Act. 1.] inviting us to unanimity in prayer.

It follows: “The captives accompany him with honour, crying: [Col. 0710A] Let us all give thanks to the judge of our salvation, because he has borne our body on high to the royal court of heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Offic. Eccles.] And giving thanks, they say: “You saved us from those who afflicted us, and put to shame those who hated us.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Psal. 43.] Again: “You have magnified and honoured your people.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Offic. Eccles.] Hence: “A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves; I held him, and I shall not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Cant. 3.]

The angels meet him with astonishment. Hence [Note: [Col. 0709] Hymn. Eccl.]:

> The angels tremble as they behold  
> The changing lot of mortals.

Hence they say: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra? This one, beautiful in his robe, advancing in the greatness of his strength?” [Note: [Col. 0709] Isai. 63.]

[Col. 0710B]

> Therefore there is joy for them,  
> Because that splendid one triumphs,  
> Worthy of majesty;  
> He makes the homeland of heaven and earth  
> One commonwealth.  
> [Note: [Col. 0709] Hymn. Eccl.]

The Father himself received him with splendour. Nor is this surprising, for he is “beautiful in form above the sons of men”; [Note: [Col. 0709] Psal. 44.] and: “All the beauty of the Lord is exalted above the stars and raised among the clouds.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Offic. Eccle.] Hence [Note: [Col. 0709] Offic. miss.]:

> Presenting before the Father’s countenance  
> The glory of his victorious flesh.

Then the Father himself sings: “My son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Luc. 15.] Therefore, “it was fitting to rejoice and feast,” [Note: [Col. 0709] Ibid.] because “the kingdoms of heaven rejoiced at the return of the Only-Begotten.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Offic. Eccle.]—“Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance and the ends of the earth for your possession.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Psal. 2.]

Christ himself likewise says: “Father, I have made known your name to the people [Col. 0710C] whom you gave me; but now I come to you.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Joan. 17.] His prayer accompanies his rejoicing: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you gave me.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Ibid.] Behold, because “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who became the propitiation for our sins.” [Note: [Col. 0709] I Joan 2.]—“Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach; for we do not have here a lasting city, but seek the one that is to come,” [Note: [Col. 0709] Hebr. 13.] where he goes to prepare a place for us. [Note: [Col. 0709] Joan. 14.]

It should be noted that there is a place of warfare, a place of misery, a place that is the throne of justice, and a place that is the seat of glory. Into the first comes a condemned man, so that he may perish eternally, and so that he may exercise himself in imitating Christ’s warfare; in the second is the condemned man, in order that he may perish eternally; to the third he shall come, in order to present his [Col. 0710D] works to the judge; to the fourth, in order to occupy the seat of glory. Christ came to the first to restore humankind; to the second to separate his elect from him; to the third to judge the living and the dead; he goes to prepare the fourth for us.

He was in the place of warfare, and found man “in a place of horror and vast solitude.” [Note: [Col. 0709] Deut. 32.] Peter says of hell: “One of you must receive the lot of this ministry: from which Judas fell away, and went to his own place,” [Col. 0711A] [Note: [Col. 0711] Act. 1.] that is, to hell. Of judgment: “Silver has the beginning of its veins, and gold has a place where it is smelted,” [Note: [Col. 0711] Job 28.] namely judgment. Of the fourth: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells.” [Note: [Col. 0711] Psal. 25.] Again: “His place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Sion.” [Note: [Col. 0711] Psal. 75.] Christ goes there to prepare a place for you. There is that ivory tower of which we are now speaking.

It should also be noted that there is a tower of defence, a tower of watchfulness, and a tower of delightful habitation. In the first, a person is defended; in the second, our fruit is surveyed; in the third, the breath of the life-giving breeze is taken in. These three are found in this Song. Of the first: “Your neck is like [Col. 0711B] the tower of David, built with battlements; a thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty.” [Note: [Col. 0711] Cant. 4.] Hence: “Be to us, O Lord, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy.” [Note: [Col. 0711] Psal. 60.] Of the second: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.” [Note: [Col. 0711] Cant. 7.] Hence: “You who are in the towers, open the gates; the Lord Almighty has done a great work of power.” [Note: [Col. 0711] Offic. Eccl.] Of the third: “Your neck is like an ivory tower.” Ivory is white, cold, and strong: white because of the joy of the glorified body; cold against the heat of temptations; solid and strong against worldly corruption. This is Christ, who joins us to our head: in the first through faith; in the second through hope; in the third through sight. May he lead us to it.

[Col. 0711C] “Your neck” (or, according to another translation, “your nape”) “is like an ivory tower.”

[CARD.] As if he said: Your nape—that is, the eminence of your loftiness—is like a tower, a refuge for the wretched; and this tower is ivory. For it has the whiteness of chastity and the steadfastness of constancy. Nor are whiteness and firmness alone signified by ivory, but also this: ivory is the bone of the elephant, an animal naturally hostile to the dragon; and the Blessed Virgin likewise has perpetual warfare with our enemy, that she may bestow on us the aid of her defence. It follows:

“Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.”

[THO.] These eyes are preachers, because they learn in secret the mysteries [Col. 0711D] of the Scriptures which they may speak openly, so as to nourish the children of the Church. They are rightly compared with pools constructed at the gate of the city of Heshbon. He calls that city “daughter of the multitude” because of the abundance of its inhabitants: just as those pools, when citizens flowed to them, were accustomed to provide an unceasing supply of water, so teachers do not cease to provide their hearers with the flowing stream of doctrine.

But Heshbon, which is called “the girdle of sorrow,” is the Church: she who once possessed temporal joys now mourns them because of sins, with tears, [Col. 0712A] her loins restrained from the pleasures of the world. At its gate—that is, at its entrance—is that Sheep Pool, the pool for sheep, in which the priests washed the flesh of sacrificial victims: that is, baptism, in which those who enter the Church must be washed, so as to sacrifice their own flesh through penitence. Into it the angel descended, and one person was healed. [Note: [Col. 0711] Joan. 5.] Because Christ was baptized first, and after him the people of the Church were baptized in unity of faith, they were healed from sins.

This city was once that of Sihon, king of the Amorites—that is, of the devil, who is king of those who embitter; for this is what “Amorite” signifies. This pool signifies four pools. The first is legal, the second initiatory, the third sacramental, the fourth moral. The first is the text of the Mosaic Law; the second, baptism; the third, [Col. 0712B] Christ’s body; the fourth, human affection. In the first, observers were washed by temporal punishment; in the second, sinners from original fault; in the third is the regenerating power of the sacraments; in the fourth daily offence is washed away.

In the first is historical water: the five porticoes are the five books of Moses. “In these lay a multitude of the sick,” [Note: [Col. 0711] Ibid.] namely those inveterate in sins; for sickness is a long-standing disease; “of the blind,” because they lacked spiritual understanding; “of the lame,” because they relied on works alone; “of the withered,” because they lacked grace; “waiting for the movement of the water,” namely the holy Fathers, who awaited the coming of Christ—that is, the Angel of Great Counsel—who would descend into the great pool by coming into the world. Thus the water—that is, the letter—would be moved into spiritual understanding, or the severity of the Law into grace; and thus one would be healed, that is, all believers would become one in Christ.

The second pool is baptism, which we have called initiatory because it is the beginning of all the sacraments and all the faithful are initiated in it. Its water is material, but sanctified. Into it the Angel of Great Counsel descends, since he was baptized by John. It has five porticoes, namely the five acts observed in the rite of baptism. Or, according to some: the giving of salt, the anointing of the ears, entry into the church, the anointing of shoulders and breast, and triple immersion in water.

The first is exorcism, that is, the adjuration by which the devil is expelled, who held many in sickness, [Col. 0712D] that is, in the habit of sinning; and this is the sign that a multitude of sick persons is healed there. The second act is catechesis, that is, instruction concerning what Christians must hold, in which the blind are healed. The third is the profession of faith and renunciation of Satan; in this the lame are healed, because they do not walk rightly in faith. The fourth is the anointing with chrism and oil; in this the withered are healed, namely those who had been without God’s grace. The fifth is immersion in water; in this their desire is fulfilled, who awaited the movement of the water—that is, the transformation of historical meaning into spiritual understanding, or of severity [Col. 0713A] into mercy.

In these five acts are comprised five benefits in baptism. Five kinds of people are understood in them. In the sick, the sickness of nature—that is, the tinder of sin—is weakened; in the blind, original fault, by which the human race was blinded, is remitted; to the lame, strength in virtues is given; upon the withered, outward sanctification is bestowed by grace. For those awaiting the movement of the water, the kingdom of heaven is opened, so that the water of our corruption may be transformed into the water of incorruption. Of water: “The rush of the river gladdens the city of God.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Psal. 45.]

The third pool is Christ’s body. It has the material water which came forth from his side [Note: [Col. 0713] Joan. 19.] and the blood which washes perfectly. We have called it [Col. 0713B] sacramental, because many other sacraments receive their efficacy from it. Into it descended the Angel of Great Counsel, that is, the Son of God, assuming human flesh. And the water of our guilt was moved, in exchange for which we received the water of grace. It has five porticoes, namely the five wounds of feet, hands, and side. In these lay a multitude: the sick, through corruption of nature; the blind, through the darkness of ignorance; the lame, through unrestrained wandering; the withered, through deprivation of grace; and those awaiting the movement of the water, that is, the washing away of guilt and the reformation of punishment. They were subject to guilt and punishment through corruption of nature; they did not know their sickness through the darkness of ignorance; through unrestrained wandering they despaired of a remedy; the washing away of guilt and reformation [Col. 0713C] of punishment were what had been promised through the prophets.

Of the first Isaiah says: “Every head is sick, and every heart sorrowful.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Isai. 1.] But in this pool, “Truly he himself bore our infirmities.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Isai. 53.] Of the second: “They are blind, and leaders of the blind”; [Note: [Col. 0713] Matth. 15.] and: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Rom. 11.] But through the water of this pool they are illumined by him who “enlightens every person coming into this world,” [Note: [Col. 0713] Joan. 1.] as it is written in the prophet: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Isai. 35.] David knew his own weakness when he said: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Psal. 6.]

Of the third Paul says: “Lift up the feeble knees; make straight paths for your feet, lest one who is lame go astray.” [Col. 0713D] [Note: [Col. 0713] Hebr. 12.]—“Be of good courage,” he says, “for it is near that you shall be healed by God.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Tob. 5.] Of the fourth David complains: “My days have failed like smoke, and all my bones have dried up like fuel”; [Note: [Col. 0713] Psal. 101.] and: “I have been struck down like grass, and my heart has dried up”; [Note: [Col. 0713] Ibid.] and: “My days have declined like a shadow, and I have dried up like grass.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Ibid.] But he brought the anointing of grace, who said: “The Spirit of God is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to proclaim good news to the meek.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Isai. 61.] Thus “you have an anointing from the Holy One, and it teaches us concerning all things.” [Note: [Col. 0713] I Joan. 2.] Therefore you have to cry after him: [Col. 0714A] “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Cant 1.]

Of the fifth: through the water of this pool, which was moved as it came forth from his side, the water both of guilt and of punishment was moved. Therefore the Prophet says: “I saw water coming forth from the temple on the right side, and all to whom that water came were saved.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Ezech. 47.] Of these waters—namely, of guilt and punishment—David says: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Psal. 68.]

Of this transformation of our misery it was said: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth”—that is, soul and body—“and the sea is no more,” [Note: [Col. 0713] Apoc. 21.] that is, the bitterness of guilt and punishment.

The fourth pool is the human heart, which we have called moral. It has its waters, that is, its affections. It sometimes has porticoes, [Col. 0714B] namely the five senses. It sometimes has muddy waters, that is, shameful affections; at other times clear waters, namely holy affections. These, when they arise within, are sometimes carried through the senses to outward things; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not what enters the mouth defiles, but what proceeds from the heart. For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries,” [Note: [Col. 0713] Matth. 15.] etc. At other times they flow inward from outward things through the same senses. Hence the prophet says: “Death entered through our windows and came into our house, to destroy there our little ones.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Jer. 9.]

In its porticoes lies a multitude of sick, blind, lame, withered, and waiting people: sick through faint-heartedness; blind through the vanity of the world; lame because they spare the spiritual foot and lean [Col. 0714C] upon the carnal foot; withered because they do good without devotion; waiting for the movement of the water because they sin yet await an opportunity for pardon. They are faint-hearted because they fear the harshness of religion; blind through the world’s vanity, which they consider supreme blessedness; they lean upon the carnal foot because they delight to descend into the vileness of mud; they do good without devotion because of servile fear or love of praise. They await the movement of the water—that is, pardon for sins—knowing that God is merciful.

The first “trembled with fear where there was no fear.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Psal. 52.] Of the second David says: “The light of my eyes itself is not with me.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Psal. 17.]—“They have become old and have limped from their paths.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Psal. 37.] Of the fourth Job says: “If the Lord holds back [Col. 0714D] the waters, all things shall dry up; if he sends them forth, they overturn the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Job 12.] Of the fifth: “The deep surrounded me, and the sea covered my head.” [Note: [Col. 0713] Jon. 2.] “Do you think I shall see your holy temple when these waters have been moved?”

The angel of the Lord descends into this pool and moves the water whenever Christ inspires our heart and converts foolish affections into good ones. As was said of evil affections, these sometimes arise within and are carried through the senses outward; hence [Note: [Col. 0713] Isa. 26.]: “O Lord, through fear of you we conceived,” namely in the heart, “and brought forth” the deliberation to act, [Col. 0715A] “and gave birth to the spirit” of salvation in action. And at other times faith arises outwardly and is borne inwardly; hence: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Joan. 20.] For he first saw outwardly, from which faith was born inwardly.

We read of four waters miraculously moved: Mara, through the casting in of wood, changed bitterness into sweetness; [Note: [Col. 0715] Exod. 15.] the Jordan, at the passage of the Ark from the desert into the land of promise, reversed its course; [Note: [Col. 0715] Judic. 6.] the waters of Jericho, when Elisha poured in salt, turned corruption into health; [Note: [Col. 0715] IV Reg. 2.] and the Lord changed water into wine. [Note: [Col. 0715] Joan. 2.] The first water changed its taste, the second its course, the third its effect, the fourth its appearance. The first is the assault of tribulations; the second the flow of affections; the third the corruption of morals; the fourth the misuse of graces.

[Col. 0715B] Of the first: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Psal. 68.] Of the second: “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters; the God of majesty has thundered; the Lord is upon many waters.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Psal. 28.] Of the third: “Rescue me and deliver me from many waters and from the hand of the children of strangers.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Psal. 143.] Of the fourth: “Your silver has become dross; your wine has been mixed with water.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Isa. 1.]

In the movement of the first, those sick through faint-heartedness are healed. For when they remember that Christ hung on the wood for them, tribulation, formerly bitter, begins to grow sweet. Hence: “Consider him who endured such contradiction against himself, lest you grow weary and faint in your souls.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Hebr. 12.] Again: “Say to the faint-hearted: Do not fear.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Isa. 35.]

In the movement of the second, the blind are healed. For when they see the ark—that is, the Lord’s flesh—passing from the desert of this world into the land of promise, that is, the heavenly homeland, they lift up their eyes after it, looking to things above and casting away the film of worldly vanity. First, the waters which were going to the Dead Sea stand still—that is, the thoughts which led to hell; secondly, they rise into a great mountain—that is, they grow into an affection of charity; thirdly, they turn as far as Zarthan, [Note: [Col. 0715] Josue 3.] which is interpreted “their tribulation,” because charity grows so greatly that they desire to suffer for Christ. Behold, the prophetic saying is fulfilled: “The eyes of the blind shall be opened,” [Note: [Col. 0715] Isa. 35.] as the Apostle says: “May God the Father give you the illumined eyes of your heart, that you may know what is [Col. 0715D] the hope of his calling.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Ephes. 1.]

In the movement of the third water, the lame are healed. For Elisha, whose name means “the salvation of my God,” that is, Christ, casts salt into the corrupt waters, namely the salt of word, example, and miracle. Those who were corrupt in their habits, by which they walked badly, seeing and hearing these things, conform themselves to him and take up sound habits, as though abandoning a weak foot and cleaving to a stronger one, so that they may say: “My foot stood in the straight way,” [Note: [Col. 0715] Psal. 25.] as Isaiah says: “Then the lame shall leap like a stag.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Isa. 35.]

In the movement of the fourth water, the withered are healed, seeing that Christ, full of grace and truth, in all that he graciously did, sought not worldly [Col. 0716A] but God’s favour. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you,” [Note: [Col. 0715] I Tim. 4.] which he would do if he expected human favour from it. Hence: “See that you do not receive the grace of God in vain.” [Note: [Col. 0715] II Cor. 6.] Those who used to do good without devotion, now doing it devoutly, are no longer dry, as they attend to the evangelical saying: “When you fast, anoint your head,” that is, your soul, “and wash your face,” [Note: [Col. 0715] Matth. 6.] that is, your conscience.

“Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.”

[CARD.] The “daughter of the multitude,” not of one father only, is called the sinful soul, which is not Christ’s daughter but the daughter of as many demons as the vices by which it is defiled. The gate of this daughter is the gate of the eyes, through which those who plunder the soul frequently enter, as is said above: “My eye has plundered my soul.” [Note: [Col. 0715] Thren. 3.] But when the sinful soul repents, pools—that is, supplies of water and tears—are at this gate. These pools are said to be in Heshbon, which is interpreted “girdle of sorrow,” that is, sorrow that encircles, to be understood intransitively. For the sorrow of penitence encircles a person and restrains the discharge of sins, just as rue encircles a wounded person and restrains the flow of blood. Isaiah laments the absence of this girdle [Note: [Col. 0715] Cap. 5.]: “There is no plaster to apply, no bandages, no oil.”

The Blessed Virgin is therefore commended in this verse for the grace of tears: namely, because her eyes overflowed with tears of devotion as abundantly as [Col. 0716C] the eyes of a sinner overflow with tears of penitence. [Note: [Col. 0715] Offic. Eccles.] Thus he says: Your eyes, in the abundance of tears of devotion and love, are like pools—that is, abundant waters—existing in Heshbon, that is, in the sorrow of penitence which restrains the wounds of sin lest they flow. And these pools are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude—that is, in the eyes of the sinful soul which, in repentance, bewails having been the daughter of many vices. Again, consolation for sinners is added in the praise of the Virgin.

“Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.”

[THO.] Because odours and stenches are usually discerned by the nose, it signifies the dispensers of God’s word, who above, for particular reasons, are signified in the breasts, neck, [Col. 0716D] and eyes of the Church. For they ought to possess discernment, which is the mother of virtues, so that they know how to distinguish who walks sincerely and who falsely, lest vice conceal itself under the appearance of virtue. Those who have this grace are rightly compared with the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus, because they occupy a most lofty place, foreseeing for others. Therefore they are on Lebanon, a high mountain; and because they steadfastly endure adversities for the Church, they are a tower.

Damascus means “drinking of blood,” that is, the devil, who thirsts for our blood—that is, for our life. Or Damascus signifies carnal people, against whom the tower—that is, the strength of preachers—is set. [Col. 0717A] “The mountain of God is a rich mountain,” [Note: [Col. 0717] Psal. 67.] whoever lifts his heart upward to God, having much devotion within it. But Damascus, called “drinking of blood,” is opposed to this mountain: that is, the devil, who thirsts for the blood of our souls.

First he labours to make the affection languish; second, to darken the eye of reason; third, to weaken the body. He makes affection languish so that it does not feel heavenly sweetness; he darkens the eye so that it does not understand truth; he weakens the body so that it may plead its own frailty. Through the first charity grows cold; through the second blind simplicity errs; through the third impunity increases sin.

Of the first, the Lord says: “Because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many shall grow cold.” [Note: [Col. 0717] Matth. 24.] “Iniquity” is said emphatically of the devil. By contrast, concerning this charity the Law commands that fire should burn continually on the altar, [Note: [Col. 0717] Lev. 6.] that is, charity in the heart. Of the second the Lord says to Abimelech, when he sinned by taking Sarah from her husband: “I know that you did this with a simple heart; and therefore I spared you.” [Note: [Col. 0717] Gen. 20.] Such persons are “a deceived dove, without a heart.” [Note: [Col. 0717] Ose. 7.] Of the third the Apostle admonishes: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0717] Colos. 3.]—“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” [Note: [Col. 0717] Matth. 26.]

Therefore the devil urges you to nourish your servant—that is, your body—delicately, so that afterwards you may find him rebellious. Against these things, therefore, affection must be made weak, reason illumined, and the weak body aided. If, therefore, you are a mountain, be Mount Lebanon, which means “whitening,” so that by meditating upon heavenly sweetness you may acquire the burning of devotion. [Col. 0717C] Have a nose: seek from God the spirit of discernment for the illumination of reason. Be a tower: remember the punishments of hell, and thus acquire the strength of patience.

Of these Jeremiah says: “From on high he sent fire into my bones,” [Note: [Col. 0717] Thren. 1.] concerning the first. “And he instructed me,” [Note: [Col. 0717] Ibid.] concerning the second. “He turned against me and turned his hand all day long,” [Note: [Col. 0717] Thren. 3.] concerning the third. Of the first David says: “In my meditation fire shall blaze,” [Note: [Col. 0717] Psal. 38.] that is, through meditation on heavenly things. Have the burning of the affections. Of the second: “Give me understanding, and I shall live.” [Note: [Col. 0717] Psal. 118.] Of the third: “Let rottenness enter into my bones and boil beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation and go up to our girded people.” [Note: [Col. 0717] Habac. 3.]

[Col. 0717D] The nose smells through the nostrils. We find three kinds of nostrils: the nostrils of the devil, of the sow, and of the human being. From the first comes smoke; in the second is a ring; in the third is spirit. Concerning the first, the Lord says of Behemoth: “Smoke goes forth from his nostrils” [Note: [Col. 0717] Job 41.]. Concerning the second, Solomon says: “A golden ring in the nostrils of a beautiful but foolish woman” [Note: [Col. 0717] Prov. 11.]. Concerning the third, Isaiah says: “Cease from man, whose spirit is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted” [Note: [Col. 0717] Isa. 2.].

From the first proceeds smoke—that is, the devil’s craftiness for deception; in the second is [Col. 0718A] a golden ring—that is, the wisdom of the flesh for pleasure; in the third is spirit for the discernment of good and evil. Of the first it is said in Genesis: “The serpent was more crafty than all the animals of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0717] Gen. 3.]. And the Apostle says: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, so your minds should be corrupted from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” [Note: [Col. 0717] II Cor. 11.].

Of the golden ring in the second nostrils: “I will destroy,” he says, “the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” [Note: [Col. 0717] I Cor. 1.]; and: “They are wise in doing evil, but they have not known how to do good” [Note: [Col. 0717] Jer. 4.]; and: “The wisdom of the flesh is death” [Note: [Col. 0717] Rom. 8.]. Such people, “professing themselves to be wise, became fools” [Note: [Col. 0717] Rom. 1.]. Of the spirit in the third nostrils: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and who abounds in prudence” [Note: [Col. 0717] Prov. 3.]. Hence it is written in the Law [Col. 0718B]: “A priest shall not serve in the tabernacle if he has a broken foot; if [the] nose [is defective, text incomplete]” [Note: [Col. 0717] Lev. 21.], and so forth. Therefore the Church also prays: “Grant us, O Lord, we beseech you, ever by your mercy the spirit to think what is right and to do it” [Note: [Col. 0717] Offic. Eccles.].

Again: the first nose is like the opening of a furnace, the second like the skin of a drum, the third like the tower of Lebanon. The opening of a furnace gives off smoke; the skin of a drum, when greased, gives a worse sound; the tower of Lebanon surpasses the smoke of the furnace in height. The furnace gives off smoke when Satan kindles temptations. The greased drumskin sounds worse when the one wise according to the flesh, fattened by pleasures, sings psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs more poorly.

The first is so because, “While the wicked is proud, the poor is set on fire” [Note: [Col. 0717] Psal. 9.]. The second because, “God is not in [Col. 0718C] his sight; his ways are defiled at all times” [Note: [Col. 0717] Ibid.]. The tower exceeds the smoke in height when the discerning person raises his heart upward and there finds help amid temptations. Hence: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame” [Note: [Col. 0717] Psal. 24.].

Again, the nose clears the moisture of the head, supplies the soul with breath [150], and possesses discernment of smells. It clears the moisture of the head—that is, it cleanses from sins the soul which is our head. It gives breath to the soul, so that it may go out and at one time be occupied in arranging temporal affairs, and at another be free within for meditating on heavenly things. It has discernment of smells because it considers within itself whether it acts fittingly or unfittingly in all these matters.

Of the first the Apostle says: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened” [Note: [Col. 0717] I Cor. 5.]. Of the second, with respect to outward administration, it is said: “He who has ministered well shall acquire good joy” [Note: [Col. 0717] I Tim. 3.]; with respect to meditation David says: “I remembered God and was delighted” [Note: [Col. 0717] Psal. 76.]. Of smell—that is, discernment—it is said: “Diligently know the condition of your flock” [Note: [Col. 0717] Prov. 27.], and so forth; and the poet says:

> First discern what is shameful, what useful, and what neither.

Again, according to another:

[Col. 0719A]

> … See what burdens they refuse,  
> What their shoulders can bear.

The nose signifies for us the fragrance of heavenly goods, perceived by him who said: “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” [Note: [Col. 0719] Cant. 1.]. But this fragrance, like a tower, must be firm in the rigor of one’s conduct: Lebanon in the brilliance of example or miracles, for Lebanon means “whitened”; facing Damascus, which means “drinking blood,” in the ardor of fruitful charity.

To take one example: such was blessed Benedict, who preferred to suffer the evils of the world rather than receive its praise, choosing to be wearied by labors for God rather than exalted by the favor of this world. His miraculous life—behold Lebanon; his religious way of life—behold the tower; his fruitful institution, which faces [Col. 0719B] Damascus. His glorious end also indicates his perseverance in these things: his miraculous life, in that he raised the dead; his religious life, in that he endured hard and harsh things; his fruitful institution, in that he taught men to flee from and despise the world’s prosperity; his glorious end, in that he laid aside the burdens of this present misery.

The first was in order to give light to unbelievers; the second, that he might become an example to those languishing in sins; the third, that he might provide a pattern for beginners; the fourth, that he might become a joy to the heavenly spirits. In the first he was a lamp set upon a lampstand, so that he might give light to those in the house [Note: [Col. 0719] Matth. 5.]. “For the path of the righteous, like a shining light, goes forward and increases unto the perfect day” [Note: [Col. 0719] Prov. 4.], so that even unbelievers might say: “For we have seen wonderful things [Col. 0719C] today” [Note: [Col. 0719] Luc. 5.].

In the second he says with the Apostle: “I beseech you to present your bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God” [Note: [Col. 0719] Rom. 12.]. Again: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” [Note: [Col. 0719] Matth. 10.]. Thus they too may answer: “Let us run to the contest set before us, looking to its author” [Note: [Col. 0719] Hebr. 12.], and so forth.

In the third he says: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0719] I Cor. 3.]. Again: “I beseech you to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called” [Note: [Col. 0719] Ephes. 4.]. Thus those now formed may answer: “The king brought us into the wine-cellar; he set charity in order within me” [Note: [Col. 0719] Cant. 2.].

In the fourth: “The glory of Lebanon has been given to him” [Note: [Col. 0719] Isa. 35.], on account of the brightness of life, which is what Lebanon signifies; Carmel, on account of the cutting away of sins; Sharon, on account of fervor of life. [Col. 0719D] And the angels cry: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your lord” [Note: [Col. 0719] Matth. 25.].

This Benedict was not only blessed (*benedictus*), but holy and blessed (*beatus*). Blessed, because “he gave him the blessing of all nations” [Note: [Col. 0719] Eccli. 44.]; holy, because “he sanctified his tabernacle in him” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psal. 45.]; blessed, as it is written: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psal. 31.]. In the first respect, “he instructed peoples to render service to God”; in the second, he prepared [Col. 0720A] a lodging; in the third, now secure, he approached his reward.

But let us now pursue these matters: “He gave him the blessing of all nations.” There are nations to whom the Lord gives the blessing of sufficiency; others to whom he gives the blessing of fullness; and others to whom he gives the blessing of sweetness. The first lies in sufficiency of goods; the second in abundance of virtues; the third in the sweetness by which glory is tasted beforehand.

Of the first it is said: “The Lord blessed the house of Egypt because of Joseph” [Note: [Col. 0719] Gen. 39.]. Again, Satan says to the Lord concerning Job: “You have blessed the works of his hands” [Note: [Col. 0719] Job 1.]. Of the second: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence” [Note: [Col. 0719] Jer. 19.]. Again: “The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous” [Note: [Col. 0719] Prov. 10.]. Of the third: “Lord, you have gone before him with blessings [Col. 0720B] of sweetness” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psal. 20.].

These are the blessings of all nations. By these Benedict was blessed and blessed, because he had perceived the fragrance of heavenly things. Even small and few temporal things were sufficient for him. Nor is there any doubt that there was in him an abundance of virtues; and the sweetness that is in the homeland was both tasted beforehand and prepared beforehand. He was also holy, because “the Most High sanctified his tabernacle in him” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psal. 45.].

There is a threefold sanctification. The first is when something is consecrated for divine uses; the second, when someone is renewed from sin and established in good things; the third, when by a certain privileged grace one dwells with God. Of the first it is said: “Moses sanctified the tabernacle and all its vessels” [Note: [Col. 0719] Exod. 30.]. Of the second: “Sanctify them today and tomorrow; [Col. 0720C] for on the third day majesty shall appear among them” [Note: [Col. 0719] Exod. 19.]. Again: “Therefore the priests and Levites were sanctified, who carried the ark of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0719] I Par. 15.]. Of the third: “You dwell in the holy place, O praise of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psal. 21.]. Such a holy man was this Benedict.

He too is now blessed, in three ways. First, because he is secure from the horror of hell; second, because he will stand in judgment without fear; third, because he will see the King in his beauty. Of the first, Job says: “In six tribulations he shall deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you” [Note: [Col. 0719] Job 5.]. Of the second: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance; he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” [Note: [Col. 0719] Psal. 57.]. Of the third, as has been said: “His eyes shall see the King in his beauty” [Note: [Col. 0719] Isa. 33.].

Such persons desire the world’s evils more than its prosperity, because they possess a nose like the tower of Lebanon when it smells [Col. 0720D] heavenly things. They face Damascus when, discerning the devil’s devices, they despise the world’s delights. It should be noted that the world’s evil is threefold: evil is called sin; evil is called voluntary penance; and evil is called any worldly affliction. The first must be wholly avoided, the second voluntarily embraced, the third patiently received. The first defiles; the second washes; the third, if patiently endured, prepares merit.

Of the first it is said: “They are wise in doing evil” [Note: [Col. 0719] Eccli. 21.]; [Col. 0721A] again: “He who does evil hates the light” [Note: [Col. 0721] Joan. 3.]. Of the second: “Every buyer says, ‘It is bad, it is bad’; but when he has gone away, then he boasts” [Note: [Col. 0721] Prov. 20.]. Again, in Leviticus: “If anyone knows that he has acted well or ill, and has not fulfilled his vow, let him offer a lamb” [Note: [Col. 0721] Lev. 27.].

Of the third it is said: if there is evil, it is inflicted sometimes by God, sometimes by a human being, sometimes by the devil: by God for testing or correction; by a human being for vengeance; by the devil, to draw one into despair. Of the first: “Is there evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” [Note: [Col. 0721] Amos 3.]. Of the second, Samson says: “Had you not ploughed with my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle; therefore I will do you evil” [Note: [Col. 0721] Judic. 14.]. For the third, he tempted Job with scourges; therefore it is said there: “When Job’s three friends heard of all the evil that had happened [Col. 0721B] to him, they agreed to come to him and console him” [Note: [Col. 0721] Job 2.]. Job endured every evil here, yet, like the tower of Lebanon—that is, strong with joy—he endured all things against Damascus, that is, against the devil.

But it should be noted that this tower sometimes faces Tyre, which means “disturbance”; sometimes Damascus, which is “drinking blood”; sometimes Babylon, which is “disturbance”; sometimes Jerusalem, which is “vision of peace.” First, that it may flee the world’s folly; second, that it may beware the devil’s illusion; third, that it may avoid hell’s confinement; fourth, that it may prepare itself for peace and glory.

Of the first: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” [Note: [Col. 0721] I Joan. 2.]. Of the second: “We do not [Col. 0721C] ignore the devices of the devil; for the angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light” [Note: [Col. 0721] II Cor. 11.]. Of the third: “Who among you can dwell with devouring fire?” [Note: [Col. 0721] Isa. 33.]. Of the fourth: “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” [Note: [Col. 0721] Psal. 86.], to which may Christ bring us—“to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen” [Note: [Col. 0721] Rom. 16.].

Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which faces Damascus.

[CARD.] Damascus is interpreted “drinking blood,” and signifies the devil, who thirsts to drink the blood of sinners. Against his snares is set the nose—that is, the discernment of the Blessed Virgin—which perceives his malice and foresees it from afar as from a watchtower. Hence she is compared to a tower, from which the assaults of enemies are seen at a distance. Thus she looks from afar [Col. 0721D] against the enemy, and, like a tower, strongly opposes herself on our behalf. She is called the tower of Lebanon, as though situated on Mount Lebanon, which is interpreted “whiteness,” in order to show that by the whiteness of virginity, as though by a foot, she can crush the serpent’s head [Note: [Col. 0721] Gen. 3.]. It follows:

Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like the king’s purple bound to channels.

[THO.] The head of the bride is the mind of the faithful soul. For as the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind; and therefore thoughts, which come forth innumerably from the human mind at every hour and moment, are fittingly represented by the hair. So too [Col. 0722A] it is with the Church: although the multitude of believers differs in merits, nevertheless they are one heart and one soul [Note: [Col. 0721] Act. 4.].

On Carmel Elijah prayed and obtained rain [Note: [Col. 0721] III Reg. 18]. Hence the bride’s head is like Carmel, because the hearts of the elect are elevated above ordinary conduct and provide the Lord an ascent within themselves through daily advances in virtue. Carmel is called “knowledge of circumcision.” This aptly suits the Church, which circumcises rather her head—that is, her mind—than her flesh. The king’s purple is Christ’s Passion. The hair is likened to it because the thoughts of the righteous frequently meditate upon the Lord’s Passion, emulate it, and are strengthened by faith in the holy Cross.

The channels that receive the king’s purple are the inner hearts of Christ’s faithful. The wool cast into channels, to be afterward used as the king’s adornment, is the humility of the faithful conscience, which through sufferings progresses day by day toward the raiment of the eternal King.

The bride’s head is the soul of the righteous. It is compared to Carmel on account of its interpretation, on account of victory, and on account of the rain obtained. On account of its interpretation, because Carmel is called “knowledge of circumcision”; on account of the victory which Elijah had over the priests of Baal in the time of tribulation; and on account of the rain obtained in a time of drought. Likewise in the soul: first, there must occur in it the circumcision of sins; second, the defeat of temptations; third, the outpouring of rain—that is, of grace. Christ invites us to the first in his circumcision, to the second in his Passion, and to the third in the sending of the Holy [Col. 0722C] Spirit.

As a figure of this, Jacob, coming from Mesopotamia, first crossed the river Roboch—that is, flowing sins; second, he wrestled with the angel; third, he received the blessing [Note: [Col. 0721] Gen. 32.]. Thus a person must first be circumcised from sin; but first he must be cut, second cut to pieces, third circumcised. He is cut in the heart by inward grief; cut to pieces in the body by the pain of penance; circumcised by excluding occasions of sin through the rigor of discipline. Of the first: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” [Note: [Col. 0721] Joel 2.]. Of the second: “You have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with joy” [Note: [Col. 0721] Psal. 29.]. Of the third: “Laying aside every burden and the sin that surrounds us, let us run to the contest set before us” [Note: [Col. 0721] Hebr. 12.]. This is concerning the interpretation.

[Col. 0722D] There follows the reason of victory. Let us see what Elijah did. First, by preventing the sacrifice of the priests of Baal, he overcame them; second, by fire from heaven he offered his own sacrifice; third, he killed the defeated men. In the same way, after circumcision, we must courageously overcome the station of the priests of Baal—that is, the devil’s temptations—by fighting; second, in the fire from heaven—that is, in the fervor of charity—we must offer God a sacrifice of praise for victory; third, by despising the world, we must extinguish defeated temptations with the sword of prayer.

Of the first Solomon says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” [Note: [Col. 0721] Prov. 1.]. Of the second: [Col. 0723A] “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” [Note: [Col. 0723] Psal. 49.]. As a figure of the third, Samuel, whose name means “God’s petition”—that is, the sword of prayer—killed Agag, king of Amalek. Agag means “meditation,” and is king of Amalek, that is, the beginning of licking pleasures, which is what Amalek is interpreted to mean. This is concerning the reason of victory. There follows the reason of the rain obtained.

Let us see, then, what Elijah did after these things: “He bent down to the ground, put his face between his knees, and said to his servant: ‘Look toward the sea.’ But he looked and said: ‘There is nothing.’ And Elijah said: ‘Return seven times.’ The seventh time: ‘Behold, a little cloud rises from the sea like a man’s footprint’” [Note: [Col. 0723] III Reg. 18.]. Morally, the face [151] is our conscience, because through it we are known to God.

[Col. 0723B] The knees, which are flexible, signify humility. Therefore, after the circumcision of sins and the victory over temptations, the conscience ought to think humbly of itself. It sends its servant, namely reason, to look toward the sea—that is, toward the bitterness of sufferings; that is, reason examines what consolation it may obtain or receive from God after enduring the aforesaid bitterness. But because human reason can see nothing without sevenfold grace, it says: “There is nothing.” Therefore Elijah says: “Return seven times,” that is, seek sevenfold grace.

Thus on the seventh occasion—that is, with the aid of sevenfold grace—it sees a little cloud rising from the sea: divine help which brings rain, that is, God’s grace, like [Col. 0723C] a man’s footprint, so that by it one may live not brutishly, but in it, like a human being—that is, a rational animal—advance from virtue to virtue.

Allegorically, the face between the knees is the Wisdom of the Father, humbled in our flesh by being born and dying. The servants are the prophets, who looked toward the sea—that is, foresaw in the Spirit the bitter sufferings of Christ. Yet even then the fullness of rain—that is, glory—was not possessed, except when the cloud rose from the sea: that is, when, after the Resurrection, the Savior’s flesh passed from the world to the Father and sent us the sevenfold Spirit. “Which rises like a man’s footprint,” so that in himself he might show us the manner of spiritual ascent after him. It follows: The hair of his head is like the king’s purple bound to channels.

If the head is the soul, then the hairs that hang from it are rightly called thoughts. These hairs are sometimes like the king’s sackcloth, sometimes like the king’s purple, and sometimes like the king’s crown. They are like the king’s sackcloth when they meditate upon the humility of Christ’s Incarnation; like the king’s purple when they reconsider the shedding of blood in his Passion; like the king’s crown when they wonder at the glory and honor of the Resurrection [Col. 0724A] and Ascension.

They consider the humility by which “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0723] Philipp. 2.]; the shedding of blood in the Passion, by which “he became obedient to the Father unto death” [Note: [Col. 0723] Ibid.]; and the glory and honor of the Resurrection and Ascension, by which he reigns with the Father and has written on his garment, “King of kings and Lord of lords” [Note: [Col. 0723] Apoc. 19.].

The first garments, therefore, are yellow, the second red, the third golden. Yellow, when through humility we despise ourselves, judging ourselves to be mud; red, when we desire to become sharers in Christ’s sufferings; golden, when we aspire to the glory of his Resurrection. Hear of the yellow garments: “Remember, I beseech you, that you have made me like mud and will bring me back into dust” [Note: [Col. 0723] Job 10.].
