Hear of the red garments: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” [Col. 0724B] [Note: [Col. 0723] II Tim. 2.]—“In the blood of your covenant you redeemed your prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” [Note: [Col. 0723] Zach. 9.]. Hear of the golden garments, namely when they consider that all the streets of the heavenly Jerusalem will be paved with pure gold, when “he will reform the body of our lowliness, configured to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0723] Phil. 3.].

These hairs are like the king’s purple bound to channels. There are channels in which this purple, while still fresh, is dyed; others in which, when darkened, it is washed; and others in which, when old, it is renewed. It was still fresh while hidden in Christ’s body; it is darkened by the smoke of sin; it has grown old through forgetfulness. The first channels are the Savior’s wounds; the second, the sinner’s eyes; the third, the preacher’s tongue. Therefore it is dyed in the first by the flow from the wounds; washed in the outpouring of tears; and renewed in preaching.

[Col. 0724C] It was dyed when blood and water came forth [Note: [Col. 0723] Joan. 19.]. It was washed after Peter had heard, “Take all of you from this; this is my blood” [Note: [Col. 0723] Marc. 14.]; he immediately denied him, but washed it away, for “having gone out, he wept bitterly” [Note: [Col. 0723] Matth. 26.]. Hear Paul renewing it: “For if the blood of goats or calves sanctifies the defiled, how much more shall the blood of Christ cleanse our consciences to serve the living God?” [Note: [Col. 0723] Hebr. 9. Hebr. 9.]. Such ought to be the hairs of our head.

Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like the king’s purple bound to channels.

[CARD.] Carmel is interpreted “knowledge of circumcision.” The king’s purple is dyed in certain channels; and, because it is called bound to them, the freshness of the dye is signified. The meaning, therefore, is this: Your head, [Col. 0724D] that is, your mind, is wisely circumcised; and your hairs, that is, your thoughts, are dyed in remembrance of the blood of the Lord’s Passion. Your thoughts are affected as though they saw fresh blood flowing from the wounds. A bundle of myrrh remained between her breasts [Note: [Col. 0723] Cant. 1.] until she was assumed into the joy that swallowed up every sorrow. It follows:

## BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0725]

[Col. 0725A] How beautiful you are, and how lovely, most dear one, amid delights! Your stature is likened to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters.

[THO.] Above she was called beautiful and lovely, but “terrible as an army arrayed in battle order” [Note: [Col. 0725] Cant. 6.]; here, however, she is beautiful and lovely, but amid delights. This seems discordant: that she should be terrible and delightful—which is true of carnal delights. But spiritual delights and terror, that is, severity of conduct, agree very well. It is fitting that the soul should be most dear to God when he sees it occupied with heavenly delights. The more a pure mind tastes the food of the heavenly life, the more it is kindled with love of it; and the more ardently it loves heavenly things, the more perfectly it is loved by their very author.

Hence follows: [Col. 0725B] Your stature is likened to a palm tree. Stature is the uprightness of good action in one who, rejecting earthly things, raises his whole self to heavenly delights. Victors were accustomed to be crowned with palms; and therefore she is compared to a palm, because she fights in order to be granted heavenly delights. And your breasts are like clusters. Breasts are likened to clusters because teachers proclaim great things to the great and small things to the small. Thus breasts are likened to clusters because through them the children of the Church are taught in both small and great things. Hence the Apostle’s saying: “Whether we are carried away in mind, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for ourselves” [Note: [Col. 0725] II Cor. 5.].

For the soul to be perfect, it must have, in the outward person, the form of religious life, and, in the inward person, the nourishment of the spirit through righteousness from above. Accordingly, in this place the soul is called beautiful, lovely, [Col. 0725C] and most dear. A person is called beautiful when powerful to one beholding him: this belongs to the outward person. He is called lovely from the loveliness of the heart: this belongs to the inward person. Thus the soul is outwardly beautiful through maturity of conduct, inwardly lovely through purity of heart, and above most dear through the sweetness of delights. Through the first it is dear; through the second dearer; through the third most dear. Through the first it is pleasing to human beings; through the second akin to angels; through the third approved by the Beloved.

Hear these three things: “Beloved,” he says, “by God and human beings, whose memory is in blessing. He made him like unto the glory of the saints” [Note: [Col. 0725] Eccli. 45.], namely the angels, to whom such a person will be like in glory. Hear how it is pleasing to people in this same Song: “The daughters saw her and called her most blessed; queens and concubines [Col. 0725D] praised her” [Note: [Col. 0725] Cant. 6.]. She is akin to angels: thus John the Evangelist, on account of the purity of heart and body by which he was a virgin, saw angels appearing to him so familiarly and frequently in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0725] Apoc. 8.]. Because of kinship in purity, Tobias called the angel brother, saying: “Brother Azariah, where shall we stay [Col. 0726A] tonight?” [Note: [Col. 0725] Tob. 6.].

Purity consists in rejection of worldly pleasure, love of mercy, lamentation for sin, and prayerful seeking of heavenly goods. Hence the angel says to Tobias: “When you left your meal and secretly buried the dead, and prayed with tears, I offered your prayers to God” [Note: [Col. 0725] Tob. 12.]. In leaving the meal is signified rejection of pleasure; in burial of the dead, mercy; in tears, washing away sin; in prayer, desire for good.

Hear how she is approved by the Beloved: “Come,” he says, “my chosen one, and I shall place my throne in you, because the king has desired your beauty.” Again, this soul is most dear, most bright, and most dear: most dear by difficulty, most bright by truth, most dear by variety. By difficulty, because few attain through the arduous [Col. 0726B] way to this sweetness of delights. By truth, because beyond all others it sees heavenly blessedness. By variety, because above others it presents a beloved loveliness to the Beloved. Of the first: “Arduous is the way that leads to life, and few enter by it” [Note: [Col. 0725] Matth. 7.]. Of the second: “With unveiled face we shall behold the glory of God, that we may be transformed into the same image from glory to glory” [Note: [Col. 0725] II Cor. 3.]. Of the third: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed around in golden fringes with variety” [Note: [Col. 0725] Psal. 44.].

And because it stretches upward like a palm tree, it follows: Your stature is likened to a palm. The palm has slenderness below, breadth above, and permanence in its leaves. Whoever wishes to have this stature should likewise be more restrained in lower things, more abundant in higher things, and more constant in holy utterances, so that first he may free the soul from worldly anxiety; second, dissolve the chill of faint-heartedness; third, overthrow Satan’s devices.

Of the first: “Do not be anxious,” says the Lord, “for your soul, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall wear” [Note: [Col. 0725] Luc. 12.]. Hence Boethius [Note: [Col. 0725] *De consolatione philosophiae*, book I, metre 2]:

> Alas, how the mind, sunk in a headlong deep,  
> Grows dull and, abandoning its own light,  
> Strives to go into outward darkness!  
> Whenever driven by earthly blasts,  
> How harmful care grows without measure!

And the philosopher Crates of Thebes had a treasure; and whenever he wished to pursue philosophy, his thought returned to the treasure. Therefore, taking his treasure, he carried it to the sea [Col. 0726D] and, throwing it into the waters, said: “I shall drown you, lest you drown me.”

Of the second David says: “I waited for him who saved me from faintness of spirit and the storm” [Note: [Col. 0725] Psal. 54.]. Hence it is said in this Song: “Arise, [Col. 0727A] north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” [Note: [Col. 0727] Cant. 4.]. When this is fulfilled, it is said: “Charity has been poured forth into your hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to you” [Note: [Col. 0727] Rom. 5.].

Of the third: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold”; hence it adds: “You, O Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever” [Note: [Col. 0727] Psal. 11.], that is, from demons by divine utterances, lest their devices prevail against us. Again: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” [Note: [Col. 0727] Matth. 26.]. Therefore the evil spirit of God left Saul when David played before him [Note: [Col. 0727] I Reg. 18.]. On account of the first, Christ cast the crowd out of the bedchamber when he raised the little girl. As a figure of the second, he healed a certain man’s withered hand; on account of [Col. 0727B] the third, he healed a demoniac.

Again, there is another aspect of the palm’s stature. It has roughness at the base of its trunk; victors are crowned with its branches as a sign of triumph; and at its summit are very sweet fruits. The first is in tribulation, the second in expectation, the third in reward. In the first one fights outwardly against adversaries and inwardly against demons and vices; in the second one walks in righteousness; in the third one will enjoy heavenly delights.

Of the first it is said: “Without, fightings; within, fears; and without the sword kills, while at home there is death like it” [Note: [Col. 0727] II Cor. 7.]. The children of Israel fought inwardly when their hearts returned to the pots of meat [Note: [Col. 0727] Exod. 16.], and outwardly when they fought Amalek [Note: [Col. 0727] Exod. 17.]. Of the second Isaiah says: “He who walks in righteousness and speaks [Col. 0727C] truth” [Note: [Col. 0727] Isa. 33.]. “I shall not abandon my righteousness which I have begun to hold, for my heart does not reproach me in all my way” [Note: [Col. 0727] Job 27.]. Hear one walking in righteousness: “He who speaks truth in his heart, who has not dealt deceitfully with his tongue, nor done evil to his neighbor, nor accepted reproach against his neighbors: the wicked one is brought to nothing in his sight” [Note: [Col. 0727] Psal. 14.].

Hear of the third: “The streets of Jerusalem shall be paved with pure gold, and the Sun of righteousness shall arise for those who fear my name” [Note: [Col. 0727] Mal. 4.], because, as Isaiah says, “The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see the salvation of our God” [Note: [Col. 0727] Isa. 40.]. Behold, these are the delights which the righteous will have in the kingdom, and which already, in a certain manner, they enjoy on this path through devotion.

[Col. 0727D] But because they ought not merely to enjoy these things for themselves, but to teach others toward them, it follows: And your breasts are likened to clusters. It should be noted that in this Song the bride’s breasts are compared to fawns among lilies, to a vineyard in clusters, and to fragrant ointments. Of the first: “Your two breasts are like twin fawns of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline” [Note: [Col. 0727] Cant. 4.]. Of the second, in this place; of the third: “Your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments” [Note: [Col. 0727] Cant. 1.].

In this order neophytes ought to be led to the stature of the palm. Through the first, as in infancy, they should be formed in chastity; through the second, afterward, as in adolescence, invited to the fervor of charity; through the third, as in mature age, they should be brought to the fragrance of ointments—that is, the sweetness of heavenly delights. Hence Aaron, when advanced to the priesthood [152], was first clothed in linen garments, then girded with a belt, and third anointed with precious ointment.

We acquire the first by avoiding occasions that incite lust; the second if, like a cluster, we are pressed in the winepress of discipline; the third if we prepare ointment from a mixture of various virtues. Of the first, Paul says to Timothy: “Avoid young women” [Note: [Col. 0727] I Tim. 5.]; and “Flee fornication” [Note: [Col. 0727] I Cor. 6.]; and “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is lust” [Note: [Col. 0727] Ephes. 5.]. Behold the occasions of lust.

[Col. 0728B] Of the second: “Hedge your ears with thorns and make doors for your mouth” [Note: [Col. 0727] Eccli. 28.]. This discipline gives a person inward rest. This is what is meant by Lamech, whose name means “striking,” begetting Noah, whose name means “rest” [Note: [Col. 0727] Gen. 5.]. But Lamech also killed Cain while he was hiding in the leaves of shrubs [Note: [Col. 0727] Gen. 4.], that is, the soul hiding or remaining in the levity of dissipation. Noah too, when the flood rose, entered the ark and shut its door [Note: [Col. 0727] Gen. 6.]; so, when temptation assails us from without, we ought to flee to the ark of the heart and close the doors—that is, the outward senses.

Of the third, Paul prepared fragrant ointments when he said: “But the fruit of the Spirit is joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, self-control” [Note: [Col. 0727] Galat. 5.]. These are the ointments which [Col. 0728C] breathe forth heavenly delights, signified in the fruit of the palm.

How beautiful you are, and how lovely, most dear one, amid delights! Your stature is likened to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters.

[CARD.] As though it were said: How beautiful you are in motherhood, how comely in virginity, and wonderful in both. For such is the rainbow of which Ecclesiasticus says: “Look upon the rainbow, and bless him who made it; for it is exceedingly beautiful in its splendour” [Note: [Col. 0727] Ecclus. 43]. For it shines with two colours, each of which lends beauty to the other: it has the green of water, which is the mother of many living creatures; and the red of fire, which is virgin, because it produces no living creature. With these two colours the blessed Virgin shines beautifully, like the rainbow of heaven [Col. 0728D]. Of this rainbow it is said to Noah: “I will set my rainbow in the clouds of heaven, and I will remember my covenant which I made with you” [Note: [Col. 0727] Gen. 9]. For she herself has been assumed into the heavenly places, so that the Lord may remember the mercy which he promised beforehand to the human race. She is called “most beloved in delights,” namely because, like a woman of refinement, disdaining every other food, she desires that food alone: whoever eats it is always hungry, always satisfied, and never disgusted by it.

Her stature—that is, the uprightness of good intention and the directness of holy action—is compared with the palm, so that, just as the palm, namely the triumphant tree of the Lord’s cross, is terrible to evil spirits, so the blessed Virgin, by the merit of her uprightness, may terrify and drive out evil spirits [Col. 0729A]. Her breasts too are compared with clusters; in this is shown the Virgin’s wonderful prerogative of merit. For she earned no less merit by drawing milk from her breasts for the nourishment of her Son than the martyrs, figured by clusters, earned by shedding their blood in martyrdom; for the reward of every work is weighed according to the root of charity. Having commended the Mother’s beauty, he declares by these intercessions how much she can accomplish with him: in the time of wrath she was able to restrain the sword of vengeance. Therefore he says:

> I said: I will climb the palm-tree and seize its fruits;  
> and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine. [Col. 0729B]

[THO.] It was said of the Lord: “My beloved went down into his garden” [Note: [Col. 0729] Song 6]. Behold, he himself says: “I will climb the palm-tree.” This palm is the soul or the Church. Yet he descends into it when he sends down heavenly grace from above; he ascends when he reveals ever more fully to believers the knowledge of his majesty. He seizes its fruits in order continually to make them fruitful through his touch by a fuller blessing. “And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine,” because they preach to others what they know; at times they are made drunk with a more excellent gift of wisdom.

There are five steps in ascending the cross. First, the world is conquered; second, the sinner is healed; third, the bitterness of repentance is sweetened; fourth, grace is bestowed; fifth, one enters the kingdom [Col. 0729C]. In the first, Moses struck the sea with his rod [Note: [Col. 0729] Exod. 14], that is, Christ destroyed the world by the cross. Hence he says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” [Note: [Col. 0729] John 16]; and: “Everything born of God conquers the world” [Note: [Col. 0729] 1 John 5]; and: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” [Note: [Col. 0729] Gal. 6].

In the second, a serpent was suspended upon the wood, and those who had been wounded were healed by looking upon it [Note: [Col. 0729] Num. 21]. “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” [Note: [Col. 0729] Ps. 40].—“Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” [Note: [Col. 0729] Jer. 27]. In the third, when wood was placed in Marah—that is, the wood of the cross—the waters were sweetened. “The stones of the torrent were in the desert” [Note: [Col. 0729] Office of the Church]; and: “Things which my soul formerly refused to touch have now become, in my distress, my food” [Note: [Col. 0729] Job 6]. In the fourth, Moses struck the rock with his rod and waters flowed out [Note: [Col. 0729] Exod. 17], that is, Christ upon the cross, and from it grace came forth for us. “I washed my feet in butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil” [Col. 0729D; Note: [Col. 0729] Job 27]. Again: “Tribulation produces patience; patience, proof; proof, hope. And hope does not confound, because the charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0729] Rom. 5].

In the fifth, the ark borne upon wooden poles—that is, the flesh of Christ borne upon the wood of the cross—crossed the Jordan [Note: [Col. 0729] Josh. 3], namely beyond the world into the land of promise, that is, into the kingdom of heaven. “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” [Note: [Col. 0729] John 12].

By the name of palm is also signified the victorious tree of the cross. For this is one noble tree [Col. 0730A]; no forest produces one like it in leaf, flower, and fruit. A good tree provides shade by its leaves, adornment by its flowers, and nourishment by its fruit. Its leaves, then, are the words uttered by Christ on the cross; its flowers are the blood shed for us upon the cross; its fruit is the Lord hanging upon the cross. The leaves are therefore a shade against the heat of vices; the blood provides the adornment of spiritual goods; the fruit, which is Christ, provides nourishment. For “here he is food for the journey; in the kingdom he will be the bread of angels” [Note: [Col. 0729] Office of the Church].

The leaves are words, whence David says: “Its leaf shall not fall” [Note: [Col. 0729] Ps. 1]. And the poet [Note: [Col. 0729] Horace, *Ars Poetica*, 60]:

> As forests change their leaves with the declining years,  
> the first leaves fall; so the old generation of words perishes.

Of the flower of blood Solomon says: “The almond tree shall blossom [Col. 0730B], the locust shall grow fat, and the caper-berry shall be scattered” [Note: [Col. 0729] Eccl. 12]. Of the fruit, which is Christ, it is said to the blessed Virgin: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” [Note: [Col. 0729] Luke 1].

The leaves—that is, the words uttered by Christ on the cross—are seven. To the thief he says: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” [Note: [Col. 0729] Luke 23]. To his mother: “Behold your son” [Note: [Col. 0729] John 19]. To the Father: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” [Note: [Col. 0729] Luke 23]. Again, to the Father: “Eli, Eli, lama sabacthani,” that is: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” [Note: [Col. 0729] Matt. 27]. Again, to the same Father, concerning those who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Note: [Col. 0729] Luke 23]. He also said: “I thirst” [Note: [Col. 0729] John 19]. Finally: “It is finished” [Note: [Col. 0729] ibid.]. By these seven he instructed us, as it were, through a threefold and fourfold way [Col. 0730C].

In the threefold way, by the first word he sets before us his mercy; by the second he shows the narrow way; by the third, a secure dwelling-place: mercy in which we may trust; a rough way by which we may flee to him; a heavenly dwelling in which we may remain safe. Hear now concerning the first. In the first he teaches us to pour out prayer in tribulation; and he grants us consolation amid tribulation and, after tribulation, reward. Thus he says: “From whatever tribulation they cry out to me”—behold prayer—“I shall hear them”—behold consolation—“and I shall be their Lord for ever” [Note: [Col. 0729] Zech. 10]—behold recompense. Thus the thief prayed: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0729] Luke 23]. From the Lord’s regard he received consolation [Col. 0730D]; from the promise he now possesses recompense.

In the second word, hear the harshness of the way. As though he said: See him crowned with thorns, pierced by a lance, fastened with nails, smeared with spittle, struck with blows, flowing with blood, pale in death. In the third word, namely, “Woman, behold your son,” he invites us to humble ourselves and to have compassion on our neighbour. As though he said to his mother: I present myself to you as vilely treated; and you, as for your neighbour, should have compassion upon me. Abraham possessed these things when he called himself dust and ashes and was anxiously scrupulous in pleading for doomed Sodom [Col. 0731A; Note: [Col. 0731] Gen. 18].

In the third: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” [Note: [Col. 0731] Luke 23]. He warns us in tribulation to cast all our care upon him and to hope for help from him alone, casting all our care upon him. David says: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he himself will sustain you” [Note: [Col. 0731] Ps. 54]. Behold that threefold way.

The fourfold way follows, in which, as it were in the cross, is seen what the Apostle calls “the length, breadth, height, and depth” [Note: [Col. 0731] Eph. 3]. In the Lord’s cross there was the wood hidden in the earth into which the cross was fixed; this was the depth, in which faith concerning hidden things is understood. This is received in the saying: “Eli, Eli, lama sabacthani,” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” [Note: [Col. 0731] Matt. 27]. Christ asked a question, not because he did not know, but in order to provide us with a model of what we ought to ask and what we ought to keep silent about in doubtful matters [Col. 0731B]. For some things we must ask, because it is useful to know them. Thus Job says [Note: [Col. 0731] ch. 29]: “The cause which I did not know, I investigated diligently.” Yet some things we must leave to faith alone: “He who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” [Note: [Col. 0731] Prov. 25]. Thus this word establishes faith for us in the depth.

The breadth is the crossbeam, that is, charity, which extends itself even to loving enemies. This is shown in the saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Note: [Col. 0731] Luke 23]. The length is the upright wood, which shows us perseverance in longing for heavenly things; this is in the saying: “I thirst” [Col. 0731C; Note: [Col. 0731] John 19]. Of the breadth of charity it is said: “Do good to those who hate you” [Note: [Col. 0731] Matt. 5]. Of this perseverance: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0731] Matt. 24]. The height of the cross is the tablet placed at its summit, on which is written: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0731] John 19]. In this is signified the reward which we shall receive if we climb this palm—that is, the cross—and persevere. We have this in the saying: “It is finished” [Note: [Col. 0731] John 19].

For Scripture shows this. Jesus is called Saviour; Nazareth means flower, or holiness, or shoot of purity. Our bodies will bloom again in incorruption; we shall be holy in everlasting charity; we shall be pure because we shall no longer be able to sin. These are the seven trumpets, at whose sound the walls of Jericho fell [Col. 0731D; Note: [Col. 0731] Josh. 6]. See how great this noble tree is in leaf; and not only in leaf, but also in flower and fruit. This is the leaf carried away by the wind; this is the flower by which the cold of the north wind is beaten back; this is the fruit which, when eaten, is found whole. This leaf, therefore, is instruction; the flower is medicine. In the fruit we have the physician: the leaf teaches both knowledge of sin and the art of creation; the flower of blood accomplishes healing; the fruit—that is, Christ—provides the cure. Of the first: “You have the words of eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0731] John 6]. Of the second:

> [Col. 0732A] What sacred blood anointed,  
> poured forth from the body of the Lamb.  
> [Note: [Col. 0731] Hymn for the Lord’s Passion]

Of the third: “He has seized us and will heal us; he will strike us and cure us” [Note: [Col. 0731] Hos. 2].

Therefore this flower is exceedingly medicinal: it cleansed the sick, freed prisoners, and raised the dead. It washed the human race from sin, drew the fathers out of hell, and brought the dead out from their tombs. Of the first: “He first loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” [Note: [Col. 0731] Rev. 1]. Of the second: “By the blood of your covenant, you redeemed your prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” [Note: [Col. 0731] Zech. 9]. Of the third, it is clear that, when blood was shed upon the cross, “the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose” [Note: [Col. 0731] Matt. 27]. Christ is like the pelican, who drew his own blood from his side [Col. 0732B] and, sprinkling his dead young with it, thus brings them to life.

After this flower we ought to seize the fruit of the palm. It should be noted that this palm has three fruits, because the utility of the cross is threefold. The first is the justification of sinners; the second is Christ, who is our food for the journey; the third is the promised joy. By the first we are prepared; by the second we are separated; by the third we shall be restored. We are prepared to keep God’s commandments, separated from misery, and restored in glory. Of the first it is said: “Prepare your hearts for the Lord, serve him alone, and he will deliver you from the hands of your enemies” [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 Sam. 7]. The second will occur at the judgment, when this fruit—namely Christ [Col. 0732C]—will separate the sheep from the goats [Note: [Col. 0731] Matt. 25]. The third will occur in the kingdom, when he will restore “the body of our lowliness, made conformable to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0731] Phil. 3], when the day of ancient restoration and everlasting blessedness shall shine forth. Therefore, that we may seize these fruits, let us climb this palm.

It should be noted that the utility of the cross is sevenfold, because human oldness is sevenfold. There are four bodily abominations and three corruptions of the soul. Hence the prophet says: “They have become corrupt and abominable” [Note: [Col. 0731] Ps. 13]. They are corrupt in mind, abominable in body. For in the body we misuse the four elements: fire in the eyes by curiosity; air in the tongue by variety and talkativeness; earth in the hands by wickedness; water in the emission of seed by lust. These are what expel a brother from the cloister [Col. 0732D]. Hence the prophet says: “He went out in order to see” [Note: [Col. 0731] Ps. 40]: behold curiosity. “He spoke vanity” [Note: [Col. 0731] ibid.]: behold talkativeness. “His heart gathered wickedness to itself” [Note: [Col. 0731] ibid.]: behold wickedness. He went outside through lust. In the mind one is corrupted by a threefold corruption: in natural reason through pride; in concupiscence through avarice; in anger through envy. [“153” appears to be an intrusive page or line number.]

There are, however, four dimensions in the cross: breadth, length, height, and depth. And in its title there are three distinctions: Jesus, Nazarene [Col. 0733A], King of the Jews. Breadth of mercy was in Christ’s passion; length of life, in the resurrection; height of glory, in the ascension; depth of wisdom, in the hidden power by which he accomplished all these things and by which he will judge at the last. Just as the depth of the cross was hidden and the other parts visible, so the depth remains hidden by which the Lord Jesus performed the aforesaid things. But when he judges at the end, hidden things will then be made manifest, as it is written: “The Lord shall be known as one who executes judgments” [Note: [Col. 0733] Ps. 9].

In the passion was contempt of self; in the resurrection, contempt of the world; in the ascension, love of God; in hidden power, fear. Contempt of self excludes talkativeness; contempt of the world, curiosity; love of God, wickedness; fear, lust. What follows concerns the three distinctions [Col. 0733B]. In Jesus is understood faith, without which no one is saved; in Nazarene, hope—for Nazareth is interpreted “flower,” from which fruit is hoped for; in King of the Jews, charity, which makes kings and priests. Faith enlightens reason, which pride had blinded, and excludes pride. Hope lifts up concupiscence, which avarice had bent down, and excludes avarice. Charity moderates and orders anger, which envy had corrupted, and excludes envy. Thus, by the power and efficacy of the holy cross, we are stripped of our oldness and clothed with Christ’s newness.

But first we must climb above the world; second, above our own heart; third, we must climb upon the palm—that is, by mortifying our flesh [Col. 0733C] through the gallows of the cross. Hence, when Christ drew near to his passion, he marked out for us this threefold ascent. He went up into the upper room, to teach us to ascend above our heart. He mounted an ass, a foolish animal, to teach us to trample worldly folly. He ascended the gallows also, to teach us to tame the flesh. The first is: “He shall sit solitary and keep silence, because he has raised himself above himself” [Note: [Col. 0733] Lam. 3]. As a figure of the second, Zacchaeus climbed the sycamore tree, which is called the foolish fig [Note: [Col. 0733] Luke 19]. Concerning the third, Christ said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” [Note: [Col. 0733] John 12]. Thus, by climbing this tree, we purchase its fruit.

According to legal experts, some fruits are already gathered, some hanging, and some yet to be gathered. The first have already been gathered; the second are hanging [Col. 0733D]; the third are yet to be gathered. Again, expenses are incurred in acquiring fruits, gathering them, and preserving them. Upon the cross we expend our flesh, and so acquire the first; at the judgment we shall gather the second; after the judgment we shall preserve the third. The first is sweet; the second medicinal; the third splendid in beauty. The first soothes; the second pardons; the third shines. It soothes the conscience, pardons wickedness, and shines through God’s presence. Hear the soothing one: “The judgments of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart” [Note: [Col. 0733] Ps. 18]. Hear the healing—that is, pardoning—one: “For you who fear my name the Sun of righteousness shall rise [Col. 0734A], and healing shall be in his wings” [Note: [Col. 0733] Mal. 4].—“He heals those broken in heart” [Note: [Col. 0733] Ps. 146]. Hear the shining one: “That city has no need of sun or moon to shine in it, because the Lamb shall be its lamp and the glory of God shall illuminate it” [Note: [Col. 0733] Rev. 21]. Of this third it is said: “Isaac sowed in that land and found a hundredfold in that year” [Note: [Col. 0733] Gen. 26]. And the Lord: “Whoever loses his life for my sake shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0733] Matt. 19].

> And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine;  
> and the fragrance of your mouth like apples.  
> Your throat like the finest wine, worthy for my beloved to drink,  
> and for his lips and teeth to chew.

[THO.] (Thus.) Truly the breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, because, after the Lord’s passion and resurrection, the apostles possessed greater knowledge of doctrine and grace than before [Col. 0734B], since “he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” [Note: [Col. 0733] Luke 24], and they received the sevenfold Spirit.

In the fragrance of the mouth we understand the renown of speech; in the throat, the very office of a voice dedicated to God; and these are understood both in the soul and in the Church. The first concerns those absent; the second, the instruction of those present. This finest wine is the Gospel, worthy for the beloved to drink, because the first Redeemer himself preached the Gospel. His lips and teeth are the preachers, who discuss the Gospel among themselves and preach it to others.

Here three things are compared to three: breasts to a cluster, the mouth to a fragrant apple, and the throat to finest wine. By breasts the lesser are nourished; by the mouth interior fragrances are emitted [Col. 0734C]; by the throat flavours are distinguished. First infancy is nourished; second ignorance is instructed; third the difference of flavours is possessed. First strength is given to the weak; second knowledge to the ignorant; third the will is prepared in the unwilling. For if you have the will without the two preceding things, it is said to you: “It is vain for you to rise before daylight” [Note: [Col. 0733] Ps. 126]. If you have the others without that, it is said to you: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain” [Note: [Col. 0733] ibid.].

The first, therefore, is the gift of the Father, who fills the breasts for strength; the second, of the Son, who opens the mouth so that it may emit the fragrance of doctrine; the third, of the Holy Spirit, who pours a heavenly flavour into the throat for the preparation of the will. The first grace thus offers breasts that are compared with the cluster because of their effect. For the cluster [Col. 0734D] is first trodden under foot, second pressed in the winepress, third its must is expressed. Thus the new person must be nourished. First, let him be trodden under foot through humility; second, let him be in the winepress, that he may endure the harshness of discipline; third, let the sweetness of must be expressed, that the spirit, to which the flesh had previously resisted, may possess the sweetness of rest. Hence the Lord says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” [Note: [Col. 0733] Matt. 11]—behold the first; “Take my yoke upon you” [Note: [Col. 0733] ibid.]—behold the second; “And you shall find rest for your souls” [Note: [Col. 0733] ibid.]—behold the third.

Moreover, by his own example he instructed us in this. First he was humbled [Col. 0735A] in the Virgin by assuming flesh; second, he endured discipline by suffering upon the cross; third, he attained rest by lying in the tomb, or by rising from the dead. Hear Isaiah foreseeing him in these three: “We saw him,” he says, “leprous and struck by God and humbled” [Note: [Col. 0735] Isa. 53]—behold the first. And he adds: “The discipline of our peace was upon him” [Note: [Col. 0735] ibid.]—behold the second. “Of our peace” [Note: [Col. 0735] ibid.]—behold the third. And Ezekiel suggests this in the living creatures: “When the voice came,” he says, “they stood above the firmament and lowered their wings” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ezek. 1]—behold humility. Again: “Hear the sound of wings striking one against another” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ezek. 3]—behold discipline. “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ezek. 1]—behold, after the flesh has been conquered through discipline, the spirit of tranquillity.

We read of a cluster of the vine: the cluster brought by the scouts upon a pole from the land of promise; the cluster of Cyprus [Col. 0735B]. The first cluster, that is Christ, gives us the wine of saving doctrine; the second pours out wine, that is, the blood of our redemption; the third pours out the wine of sevenfold grace or the joy of the resurrection. The first is of the vineyard, that is, of the Church; the second, from the land of promise, that is, from heaven—for he who comes from heaven is above all, namely the Son of Man who came down from heaven; the third is from Cyprus, which is interpreted “mourning” or “sorrow,” because through the sorrow of the passion he came to the joy of the resurrection. The first urges; through the second the sinner rises; through the third the dead person will rise again. It urges on sloth; one rises to pardon [Col. 0735C]; one rises again to glory.

The wine of the first is Christ’s teaching, of which he says: “Those who drank wine sang against me” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ps. 68], that is, those who heard my teaching mocked me. The wine of the second is that which the Samaritan poured upon the man wounded by robbers [Note: [Col. 0735] Luke 10]. The wine of the third is that which gladdens the heart of man [Note: [Col. 0735] Ecclus. 40]. Of the first, David says: “I mingled my drink with tears” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ps. 101]; for when Nathan the prophet rebuked him concerning Bathsheba [Note: [Col. 0735] 2 Sam. 12], he took the drink of instruction and wept. Of the second, Christ says: “Drink all of this; for this is the blood which shall be given for you for the forgiveness of sins” [Note: [Col. 0735] Matt. 26]. Of the third: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ps. 35].

Although we find many fragrances in this Song [Col. 0735D], we find three belonging to the bride: the fragrance of the mouth, the fragrance of garments, and the fragrance of ointments. The first is found here; of the second: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense”; of the third: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices” [Note: [Col. 0735] Song 4]. The fragrance of the mouth is the knowledge of preceding Fathers, conveyed to us through writings; the fragrance of garments is the renown of former conduct handed down to our times; the fragrance of ointments is the richness of devotion derived from contemplating heavenly joy.

Of the first Paul says: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God among those who perish and among those who are saved, who everywhere makes manifest [Col. 0736A] through us the fragrance of his knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0735] 2 Cor. 2]. Of the second, when Isaac perceived the fragrance of the garments, he said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like that of a full field which the Lord has blessed” [Note: [Col. 0735] Gen. 37]. Of the third: “My fragrance is unmixed balsam” [Note: [Col. 0735] Ecclus. 21].

The first fragrance illuminates the eyes of the heart; the second reforms religion in the outward person; the third raises the heart to heavenly things. Of the first, in Revelation: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see” [Note: [Col. 0735] Rev. 3]. Of the second: “Put on the new man” [Note: [Col. 0735] Eph. 4]; and: “See how our fathers were saved.” Of the third: “Your fragrance has stirred eternal desires within me.” The fragrance of the mouth is compared with an apple; the fragrance of garments is equated with incense; the fragrance of ointments surpasses spices: with the apple because of flavour; with incense because of burning; above virtues—that is, spices—because of the sweetness of devotion [Col. 0736B].

For knowledge, if it has fragrance, must also have the flavour of divine love, by which it conquers every evil. Thus wisdom must grow so that the fragrance of one’s conduct, having strength through fervour, may act courageously from the beginning of one’s way of life to its end. One must also attain such perfection in devotion as to accomplish all things in the sweetness of the spirit. Hence it is morally said: “Wisdom conquers evil” [Note: [Col. 0735] Wis. 7]—this is the first; “she reaches mightily from end to end” [Note: [Col. 0735] Wis. 8]—this is the second; “and orders all things sweetly” [Note: [Col. 0735] ibid.]—this is the third. Therefore wisdom is followed by:

> Your throat is finest wine,

that is, discretion within wisdom. It should be noted that when we are refreshed by any food or drink [Col. 0736C], it is first touched by the lips, second ground by the teeth, third tasted by the palate, fourth distinguished by the throat. The lips of the heart are the first meditation; the teeth, the repeated reconsideration of meditation; the palate, appetite; the throat, discretion. First the meditation of good occurs; second, as though chewing with teeth, the wise person repeatedly brings it back to memory; third, as though tasting with the palate, he desires it; fourth, he is refreshed by discerning, as by a throat of discretion, lest an angel of Satan transform himself into an angel of light, or by perceiving what is good, what is better, and what is best.

Hence in Revelation: “If anyone opens the door to me, I will enter to him and dine with him, and he with me” [Note: [Col. 0735] Rev. 3]. For we open to the Lord when we receive good meditations; he enters us when we reconsider them; he dines with us [Col. 0736D] when, at his giving, we desire them; we dine with him when, according to the wisdom bestowed upon us, we delight in his love as in a most sweet feast. This is the wine worthy for the beloved to drink, when we are thus worthily refreshed in his love. It is chewed by his lips and teeth when, as stated, we conceive it by meditation and frequently reconsider what has been conceived within ourselves with delight. These are the beloved’s lips and teeth, which wholly and frequently, with much love and wisdom, perform their functions in his service.

> I will climb the palm-tree and seize its fruits,  
> and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine;  
> and the fragrance of your mouth like the fragrance of apples.

[Col. 0737A] [CARD.] As though he says: I said—that is, I disposed from eternity—that I would climb the palm-tree, namely the triumphant tree of the cross, and seize its fruits: the fruits of victory, namely the resurrection and ascension, and the faith of the apostles. And then, amid the straits of death, in the hour of my indignation against those who crucified me, when I should meditate “in my spirit, hard in the heat of the day,” as Isaiah has it [Note: [Col. 0737] ch. 27]—when, that is, my spirit, embittered in the heat of the passion, was thinking of the punishments and vengeance due to evildoers—then, I say, your two breasts were like clusters of the vine. For I remembered that I had assumed flesh from you, that I had sucked milk from your breasts; I remembered [Col. 0737B] the mystery of my incarnation. This remembrance, like a draught of wine, would make me forget my present wrath and indignation, lest I hasten to vengeance. And the fragrance of your mouth—that is, of your prayers and petitions—will be delightful to me, like the fragrance of apples. And your throat—that is, prayers proceeding from the throat—will be like finest wine, which is accustomed to console and relieve the pains of those afflicted.

Or thus: “Your throat is like finest wine.” The throat separates foods, retaining the good and vomiting up the bad. This is the virtue of discerning spiritual prayers, which, like wine, expels dregs through its heat, so that the finest wine may remain clarified and freed from sediment. Therefore the Virgin’s discretion in prayer is commended: she asks only that which is asked with discernment, that which is good, devout, pure, and purged of every stain. But when she hears these words from her Son, she takes up a word from his mouth and adds:

> Wine worthy for my beloved to drink,  
> and for his lips and teeth [154] to chew.

As though she says: This wine—that is, this my word of petition, compared with finest wine—is worthy for my beloved to drink, namely that it may please him and he may delight in it. This same wine is worthy of his lips; it is worthy for his teeth to chew. The lips receive the drink and perceive its flavour. Therefore this word is said to be worthy of Christ’s lips because it is fitting that his gracious favour receive it, and that it taste good and please the divine [Col. 0737D] will or goodness. And just as the finest wine is swallowed without difficulty and with pleasure, so she rightly declares that her petitions are to be admitted by her Son with every ease and delight. Yet because the taste of that which is drunk quickly passes, while the flavour of that which is chewed remains long, she adds of that wine that it is worthy for his teeth to chew: thus she shows that the Son delights in his Mother’s petitions not perfunctorily, but as in a sweetness pleasing to affection. Finally, why the Son especially delights in her, he shows by adding:

> I am for my beloved,  
> and his turning is toward me.

[Col. 0738A] [THO.] As though she said: I devote to my beloved the whole service and offering of my devotion; and his turning is toward me, so that in the meantime, in this mortal life, the presence of his regard may always help me, lest I fail through labour, lest I carry lamps without oil—that is, good works without charity—and that at the end he may lead me with him into the immortal joys of the heavenly bridal chamber.

Or this may be the voice of the Church awaiting his advent in the flesh. For the beloved had said: “I will climb the palm-tree,” namely in order to redeem the human race upon the cross. Therefore the rejoicing Church cries: “I am for my beloved, and his turning is toward me,” that is, he who has so often deigned to make himself invisibly present to me will deign visibly to appear in our flesh.

When the bride—that is, the soul—hears herself praised by the bridegroom, she shows in thanksgiving that she is wholly devoted to the beloved in her will, saying: “I am for my beloved, and his turning is toward me,” namely, I offer myself devoted to him with my whole will [Col. 0738B]. There are four kinds of human will: dry, upright, devout, and blessed. Dry in the reprobate, upright in beginners, devout in those making progress, blessed in the perfected. The first are moistened by no dew of grace; the second, abandoning former foulness, are converted so as to live uprightly; the third, by the practice of constant prayer, are raised from heaven into the love of doing good; the fourth, thinking of almost nothing but God, repose in him.

There are three things that prevent those first three good wills from ascending from virtue to virtue. Between dry and upright will there is a great fixed chasm, so that those wishing to cross cannot do so: namely, perverse intention. Between upright and devout will lies ingrained habit; between devout and blessed will, bodily affliction [Col. 0738C]. Of the first, the Wise Man says: “Perverse thoughts separate from God” [Note: [Col. 0737] Wis. 1]; how much more perverse wills? Of the second: “How good the God of Israel is to those who are upright in heart!” [Note: [Col. 0737] Ps. 72]. Of the third it is said concerning one who lovingly and earnestly loves God: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: [Col. 0737] John 14]. The Church says devoutly: “May we live in your light” [Note: [Col. 0737] Office of the Church]. Of the fourth: “Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, finds so doing, because he will set him over all his goods” [Note: [Col. 0737] Matt. 24]—the one found above all the world’s goods, as though trampling and rejecting them. Uprightness therefore tramples perverse intention [Col. 0738D]; devotion, ingrained habit; and blessed will kills bodily affection. Offering these things to the beloved, she can confidently rejoice in his turning toward her, and add: “And his turning is toward me.”

The first man, because he was overthrown in paradise, was turned away from his Beloved; but afterwards he was mercifully turned back, and at last he will be seen returning. On account of the first it is said that the strong man armed, entering his adversary’s house, overthrows it [Note: [Col. 0737] Luke 11.]; that is, the devil overthrows the human heart. By the first he incurred God’s wrath; by the second he lost God’s presence; by the third he returned to grace; by the fourth he will enter into glory. [Col. 0739A] On account of the first David cries: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury, nor chasten me in thy wrath” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 6.]; of the second: “Thou hast turned thy face away from me, and I was troubled” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 29.]; of the third: “The grace of God has appeared to all men, instructing us” [Note: [Col. 0739] Titus 2.]; of the fourth: “The Lord will give grace and glory” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 83.]. Thus the overthrow came through the devil’s suggestion; the turning-away through the iniquity of the first man; the turning-back when he came to be incarnate in the world; the return when he shall come for judgment. Of the first, as was said: “The strong man armed overthrew his adversary’s house” [Note: [Col. 0739] Luke 11.]; of the second David says: “Turn not thy face away from me; decline not in anger from thy servant” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 26.]; of the third: “Turn, O Lord, a little, and be entreated concerning thy servants” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 89.]; of the fourth: “Be ye like [Col. 0739B] men awaiting their lord, when he shall return from the wedding” [Note: [Col. 0739] Luke 12.]. Likewise these things occur in the inward person: he is overthrown through temptation; the Beloved is turned away through evil action; he is turned back through confession and prayer; he returns through satisfaction. Concerning the first, you have heard how the elder priests, who ought to have governed the people, overthrew their own judgment, being captivated by Susanna’s beauty [Note: [Col. 0739] Dan. 13.]; of the second: “Thou hast turned thy face away from me, and I was troubled” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 29.]; of the third: “Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul; save me for thy mercy’s sake” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 6.]; of the fourth the prophet says in the person of the Lord: “Return to me, and I will return to you” [Note: [Col. 0739] Mal. 3.]; and the Lord says: “I go to prepare a place for you, [Col. 0739C] and I shall come again to you” [Note: [Col. 0739] John 14.].

It should be noted that the Beloved’s turning-away is sometimes anger, sometimes justice, and sometimes mercy. It is anger because he is offended beyond measure; justice, so that sin may be punished by the pain of a deserted heart; mercy, so that he may be sought more ardently by the one left behind, and thus that person’s merit may be increased. Therefore David said of the first: “Decline not in anger from thy servant” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 26.]; another prophet of the second: “All that thou hast done to us, O Lord, thou hast done in true judgment, because we have sinned against thee” [Note: [Col. 0739] Dan. 3.]; of the third: “It is through the Lord’s mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions have not failed” [Note: [Col. 0739] Lam. 3.]. Earlier the Bride said, “His turning is toward me,” not “into me.” For the divine [Col. 0739D] nature was not changed into human nature, but toward human nature. Hence he says through the prophet: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” [Note: [Col. 0739] Zech. 1.]. She had herself been turned toward him: first in the righteous, secondly in the patriarchs, thirdly in the prophets. In the righteous, because they believed that he would come; in the patriarchs, because they foresaw the manner of his coming; in the prophets, because they promised the benefit of the one who was to come. Behold, Isaiah announces him as though already repentant and turned toward our flesh, saying: “Exult and praise, O dwelling-place of Zion, because great [Col. 0740A] in thy midst is the Holy One of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 12.]. Behold, he has turned toward us: “Therefore seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 55.]. Seek him, because “he came to seek the sheep that was lost” [Note: [Col. 0739] Luke 15.]; while he may be found, because he himself is the woman who lights a lamp in order to find the drachma which she had lost [Note: [Col. 0739] Ibid.]; call upon him, “because he himself came to call not the righteous but sinners to repentance” [Note: [Col. 0739] Luke 5.]; while he is near, because “the Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 144.].—“Let the wicked man forsake his way” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 55.], because “the grace of God has appeared to all men, instructing us that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and godly in this age” [Note: [Col. 0739] Titus 2.]. And thus: “O Lord, thou wilt be propitious to our ungodlinesses” [Col. 0740B] [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 64.]. And: “Let the unrighteous man forsake his thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 55.], because he thinks “thoughts of peace and not of affliction” [Note: [Col. 0739] Jer. 29.]; and therefore “cast thy thought upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 54.]; and: “Let him return to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 55.], because he cries to us: “Return, Shunammite, return, that we may look upon thee”; “and he will have mercy on him” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ibid.], because “we have received thy mercy, O God, in the midst of thy temple” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 49.].—“And to our God” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 55.], because “God came into the camp” [Note: [Col. 0739] 1 Sam. 4.]. Hence there was such great joy from yesterday and the day before yesterday [Note: [Col. 0739] Ibid.], “because he is abundant in pardoning” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 55.]. Therefore, O Lord, “according to the multitude of thy mercies blot out my iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0739] Ps. 50.]. Yet he is not only abundant, but humble; not only humble, but little; not only little, but strong; not only strong, but great. Therefore first, exult, dwelling-place of Nazareth: [Col. 0740C] because humble in thy midst is the Holy One of Israel; exult and praise, dwelling-place of Bethlehem, because little in thy midst is the Holy One of Israel; exult and praise, dwelling-place of Jerusalem, because strong in thy midst is the Holy One of Israel; exult and praise, dwelling-place of Zion, because great in thy midst is the Holy One of Israel. Humble, that he may be received gently; little, to propitiate; strong, to preach; great, to reward. Humility is in Nazareth, that it may be firm and pure; nativity in Bethlehem, that it may be fruitful; strength in Jerusalem, that it may be peaceful and serene; greatness in Zion, that it may be glorious in brightness. For Nazareth is said to mean flower, or holiness, or a shoot of purity; Bethlehem, house of bread; Jerusalem, vision of peace; Zion, watchtower. [Col. 0740D] Hear of the humble one: “He emptied himself” in Nazareth, “taking the form of a servant” [Note: [Col. 0739] Phil. 2.], whence he says: “Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0739] Matt. 11.]. Hear of the little one in Bethlehem: “Made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” [Note: [Col. 0739] Phil. 2.]; for there “he was made a little lower than the angels” [Note: [Col. 0739] Heb. 2.], because there “a little child is born to us, a son is given to us” [Note: [Col. 0739] Isa. 9.]. Hear of the strong one in Jerusalem: “He became” there “obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” [Note: [Col. 0739] Phil. 2.]; for there was “the strong Lord, [Col. 0741A] mighty God, mighty in battle” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 23.]. And hear of the peaceable one: because he was led like a lamb to the slaughter [Note: [Col. 0741] Acts 8.]. And hear of the great one in Zion: “Wherefore God also exalted him and gave him a name which is above every name” [Note: [Col. 0741] Phil. 2.].—“Bearing all things,” says the Apostle, “by the word of his power, and making purification of sins, he sat down at the right hand of Majesty on high” [Note: [Col. 0741] Heb. 1.]. Hear of the humble one in Nazareth: the blessed Virgin says, “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0741] Song 1.]. Nard is a lowly, fragrant herb; this is my humility assumed by him; humility gave forth its fragrance. But happy is the city of Nazareth. “Glorious things are spoken of thee, city of God” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 86.]; for in it the humble one dwelt in the Virgin, in Bethlehem the youth with the Virgin, in Jerusalem Christ with the human being, in [Col. 0741B] Zion God in light. The first was effected through Gabriel the messenger; the second, by birth in the manger; the third, by Christ’s office of redemption and preaching; the fourth will be upon the Father’s throne. Of the first: “Nevertheless his salvation is near to those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 84.]. Of the second: “The young man shall dwell with the virgin, and thy sons shall dwell in thee” [Note: [Col. 0741] Isa. 62.]. Of the third: “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 124.]; likewise: “Make your ways and your pursuits good, and I will dwell with you in this place” [Note: [Col. 0741] Jer. 7.]. Of the fourth: “He dwells in inaccessible light” [Note: [Col. 0741] 1 Tim. 6.]. Therefore, in the first, “The Lord made known his salvation” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 97.]; in the second, “He revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ibid.]; in [Col. 0741C] the third, “He remembered his mercy and his truth to the house of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ibid.]; in the fourth, “All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of God” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ibid.]. The first, Gabriel announcing it; the second, an angel and a shepherd praising it together; the third, Christ submitting himself to suffering; the fourth, he himself reigning with the Father. “Therefore exult and praise, dwelling-place of Nazareth, because humble in thy midst is the Holy One of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0741] Isa. 12.]. O blessed city, in which flowering virginity was made Christ’s chamber; holiness descended from heaven; in assumed flesh freedom from sin was found; in all these, fragrant humanity gave forth sweetness of scent! Of the first the Bride says: “Our bed is flowering” [Note: [Col. 0741] Song 1.]; of the second: “When the Holy of Holies shall come, our city shall be destroyed” [Note: [Col. 0741] Dan. 9.]; of the third: “Who did no sin, [Col. 0741D] neither was guile found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0741] 1 Pet. 2.]; of the fourth: “Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0741] Matt. 11.]. Therefore the Bride found the humble one in Nazareth when she said: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” Behold, we have how his turning was made toward me. First it was made “that I may bewail a little my sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0741] Job 10.]; secondly, that “my sorrow may be turned into joy” [Note: [Col. 0741] John 16.]. First, that we may be pure and secure; secondly, that we may live with Christ, never again to die. Of the first [Col. 0742A] it is said: “Turn to me with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning” [Note: [Col. 0741] Joel 2.]. Of the second it is said: “Turn us, O God our Saviour, and turn away thy wrath from us” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 84.]; of the third: “O God, when thou turnest, thou shalt give us life, and thy people shall rejoice in thee” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ibid.]. Hence: “Thou hast turned my mourning into joy for me; thou hast torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 29.]. May our Lord Jesus Christ bring us to it, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

*I am my Beloved’s, and my Beloved is mine.*

[CARD.] What is above has been expounded; but here is added: “And his turning is toward me.” As though she said: I pleased my Beloved so greatly that his turning from being angry to being appeased was toward me. For he directed himself toward me when he turned from anger to mercy. It follows:

*Come, my Beloved; let us go forth into the field; let us lodge in the villages; let us rise early for the vineyards.*

[THO.] The holy Fathers, desiring Christ’s coming in the flesh for the salvation of all, say as it were: “Awaken thy power and come, that thou mayest save us.” They desired him who is invisible with the Father to appear visibly in the field of the Church, according to the prophet’s words: “The Lord shall go forth from his holy place” [Note: [Col. 0741] Isa. 26.]. They also wished to lodge with him in the villages—that is, to entrust the word of faith also to the pagans—but, since without thee we can do nothing, come with us so that we may do it more safely. What she adds, [Col. 0742C] “Let us rise early for the vineyards,” is as though she plainly said: Since the night of ancient unbelief has now departed and the light of the shining Gospel begins to appear, let us rise for the vineyards—that is, let us devote our labour to establishing churches for God throughout the world. There are three kinds of field into which the Beloved goes forth.

**155.** There is a flowering field, a pasture field, and a field for sowing. The first is that in which flowers for delight spring up, such as rose-gardens and violet-beds; the second, that in which brute animals feed upon grasses and fruits; the third, that in which some seed is sown. The first is the Virgin’s womb; the second, the Church; the third, the human heart. The first flowers with the flower of virginity and grace; the second is pasture through the bread of the Eucharist; the third is a field for sowing through the word of teaching. Is it not flowering, of which [Col. 0742D] it is written: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” [Note: [Col. 0741] Song 2.], and again: “A flower shall arise from his root” [Note: [Col. 0741] Isa. 11.]? Truly flowering, for it lacks neither flowers of charity, lilies of chastity, nor violets of humility. The second is pasture, for it has pastures of which it is said: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0741] John 6.]. Therefore “eat, friends, and be intoxicated, beloved ones” [Note: [Col. 0741] Song 5.], because “we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” [Note: [Col. 0741] Ps. 94.]. The third is for sowing: “The seed [Col. 0743A] is the word of God” [Note: [Col. 0743] Luke 8.], which is sown in the field of our heart. Let us therefore see to it that the seed falls upon good ground, not upon rock, lest, lacking the moisture of grace, it wither in temptation; not among the thorns of riches, lest choked by them it fail; nor beside the way of worldly vanity, lest it be devoured and perish through the birds of heaven, that is, the powers of the air [Note: [Col. 0743] Ibid.]. His going forth is threefold: first, from the Father into the field of the Virgin; second, from his mother into the field of the Church in pilgrimage; third, from present calamity, and he frequently returns to the field of our heart. Of the first: “His going forth is from the height of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0743] Ps. 18.], because his going forth is from the Father and his return is to the Father. Of the second: “Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with thy Christ” [Note: [Col. 0743] Hab. 3.]; of the third: “His going forth [Col. 0743B] is prepared as the dawn” [Note: [Col. 0743] Hos. 6.], and: “He shall come to us as the early and latter rain upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0743] Ibid.]. The Bride’s going forth is likewise threefold: first from worldly vanity, secondly from fleshly pleasure, thirdly from fleeting thought. Abraham was commanded: “Go forth from thy land, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house” [Note: [Col. 0743] Gen. 12.]. From the house, that is, from the world, of the father, that is, the devil: “You are of your father the devil” [Note: [Col. 0743] John 8.]. From thy land, that is, from the flesh: “For God formed man from the mud of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0743] Gen. 1.]. From thy kindred, that is, from foolish thought: “A wicked and perverse generation” [Note: [Col. 0743] Matt. 17.]. Therefore, going out from the world, let us enter the Virgin’s field through faith, that we may believe in Christ’s true incarnation; hence: [Col. 0743C] “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the crown with which his mother crowned him” [Note: [Col. 0743] Song 3.], that is, in the flesh which he assumed from her. Going out from fleshly pleasure, let us enter with the Beloved into the field of the Church, that with him we may see and with him endure his passion; hence the Apostle: “Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” [Note: [Col. 0743] Heb. 13.]. Going out from foolish thought, let us enter with the Beloved into the field of the heart, that we may experience his sweet mercy; hence: “Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room” [Note: [Col. 0743] Joel 2.]. The sensual person is in the bed, the secret one in the chamber—that is, [they go forth] from the secret pleasure of thoughts. In the first going forth the Beloved entered the Virgin’s womb; hence in Genesis: “When the day had now declined, [Col. 0743D] Isaac went out to meditate in the field; and behold Rebecca was coming upon a camel. When she saw him, she dismounted from the camel, and Isaac loved her exceedingly” [Note: [Col. 0743] Gen. 24.]. This field is the Virgin’s womb, entered by Isaac, whose name means laughter or joy—that is, Christ—and there Rebecca, whose name means patience, met him. For there he assumed that by which, suffering for us, he had voluntary patience; hence: “He became obedient to the Father unto death” [Note: [Col. 0743] Phil. 2.], and: “He was offered because he himself willed it” [Note: [Col. 0743] Isa. 53.]; this is what it means that he loved her. But Deborah also, her nurse, whose name means bee—that is, stinging temptation—[Col. 0744A] came with her. For Christ too was tempted, now by the Jews, now by the devil. This is Rebecca’s nurse, that is, the nurse of patience. For temptation nourishes patience; hence the Apostle: “Tribulation works patience” [Note: [Col. 0743] Rom. 5.]. This happened when the day had already declined, that is, at the end of the age. In the second going forth he entered the field of the pilgrim Church; hence Ruth is said to mean “inspired”: “She went to reap in the field of Boaz” [Note: [Col. 0743] Ruth 2.], whose name means “in strength.” And Boaz—that is, Christ—entered that same field, that is, the Church; and conversing with Ruth, he showed her much kindness, that is, Christ shows it to every believer divinely inspired, and afterwards took her as his wife [Note: [Col. 0743] Ibid.]. In the third going forth he frequently enters the field of our heart [Col. 0744B] amid our calamity, or the field of the tomb; but now he is buried in the righteous person’s heart through secret love. Hence Sarah, whose name means “my princess,” and Abraham, whose name means “exalted father”—that is, the soul and Christ—are buried in the double cave: “For we have been buried with him through baptism into death” [Note: [Col. 0743] Rom. 6.]. For our heart is a double cave, in which Christ and the soul ought to be hidden. In the first, the conscience ought to rejoice because here it is without guilt, and in the future it will be hidden from the calamity of hell; hence: “Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy countenance from the disturbance of men” [Note: [Col. 0743] Ps. 30.]. Secondly, it ought to rejoice in the sweetness of eternal life, which is hidden in heaven; hence: “How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, [Col. 0744C] O Lord, which thou hast hidden for those who fear thee!” [Note: [Col. 0743] Ibid.]; and: “For ye are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0743] Col. 3.]. These caves are in the field which Abraham, whose name means “exalted father,” that is, God, bought from Ephron, whose name means “dust of sorrow,” that is, from the devil, who offers us the dust of sins to lick; he is called a Hittite, that is, “terror,” because his end is to be feared. Therefore that field is ourselves, whom the devil possessed. But God the Father gave his Son for us as a redemption: “For ye were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your hearts” [Note: [Col. 0743] 1 Cor. 6.].

The Beloved went out into the first field to meditate, into the second to reap, into the third to bury: [Col. 0744D] to meditate upon our salvation; to reap fruits of righteousness; to bury the Beloved in the secret place of conscience. Of the first: “I,” he says, “think thoughts of peace and not of affliction” [Note: [Col. 0743] Jer. 29.]; of the second: “Look,” he says, “upon the regions, for they are already white for harvest” [Note: [Col. 0743] John 4.].—“Send labourers into thy harvest” [Note: [Col. 0743] Matt. 9.]. Likewise of the third: when Mary Magdalene anointed Christ’s feet [Note: [Col. 0743] John 11.], the Beloved said: “She did it for my burial” [Note: [Col. 0743] Matt. 26.]. For first we wash the feet of divine mercy with tears; secondly, we anoint them with devotion; thirdly, by loving intensely we [Col. 0745A] bury them in the secret affection of the heart. This is concerning the going forth into the field.

It follows: *Let us lodge in the villages.* There are three villages of celebrated memory in which the Beloved remained: namely, Bethlehem, where he was born; Nazareth, where he was brought up; and Jerusalem, where he was crucified and raised. Bethlehem means “house of bread”; Nazareth, “flower,” “holiness,” or “shoot of purity”; Jerusalem, “vision of peace.” Let us also remain in these with the Beloved: so that in the house of bread our infancy may be nourished; in the house of the flower of purity and holiness our adolescence may grow; and in the house of peace our patience may be strengthened by suffering for Christ. In the first there are three breads by which we must be refreshed. “Which of you will have a friend and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves’?” [Note: [Col. 0745] Luke 11.] The first [Col. 0745B] shows us heaven; through the second our heart ascends into heaven; the third is the living bread who descended from heaven. The first is the bread of doctrine; the second, tears arising from desire for heavenly things; the third, the Eucharist. The first gives us the foundation of faith; the second, consolation in our present exile; the third is provision for the journey here and delight in the kingdom. Of the first: “Bread strengthens the heart of man” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ps. 103.]; of the second: “My tears were my bread day and night” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ps. 41.], and: “Thou shalt feed us with the bread of tears” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ps. 79.]; of the third: “Man ate the bread of angels” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ps. 77.]. The first is eaten in the tabernacle of beauty; the second with the water of tears; the third with the drink of the Lord’s blood. As a figure of the first, there were twelve loaves of the bread of presentation in the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0745] Lev. 21.]; as a figure of the second, [Col. 0745C] an angel placed bread and a vessel of water at the head of Elijah sleeping under the juniper tree [Note: [Col. 0745] 3 Kgs. 19.]; as a figure of the third, Melchizedek offered bread and wine to Abraham returning from battle [Note: [Col. 0745] Gen. 14.]. Behold, with these the infancy born in Bethlehem is nourished with the Beloved. Let us proceed as far as Nazareth, so that there our adolescence may grow with the Beloved. Therefore, according to its threefold interpretation, we must first be holy, secondly clean, thirdly flowering: holy, that we may cleanse our sins; clean, that henceforth we may preserve ourselves from falling; flowering, that abounding in virtues we may delight in contemplating the flower, which is Christ. Of the first: “Keep my soul, for I am holy” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ps. 85.].—“When I have been sanctified [Col. 0745D] in you, I will pour clean water upon you” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ezek. 36.], namely, water by which you may be clean after sanctification. “Wash yourselves,” by sanctifying yourselves; “be clean” [Note: [Col. 0745] Isa. 1.], by guarding yourselves henceforth from sin. “Create in me a clean heart, O God” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ps. 50.].—“Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0745] Matt. 5.]. This is the twofold sanctification, concerning which Moses says: “Be sanctified today and tomorrow; on the third day ye shall see the majesty of God in yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0745] Exod. 19.], namely, because you will be flowering; hence: “The righteous man shall flourish as the palm tree” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ps. 91.]. The palm tree, which is Christ, flowers [Col. 0746A] through virtue and has at its summit the sweet fruit, namely the vision of the divine majesty: here in a mirror, there face to face. Behold, here adolescence has grown; in the vision of peace let patience be strengthened.

We see three peaces in this village while remaining with the Lord: the first at the last judgment; the second in the kingdom, free from every temptation; the third with the Creator formerly offended. Of the first: “Let rottenness enter into my bones, and let it swell beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0745] Hab. 3.]; of the second Job says: “The beasts of the earth shall be at peace with thee” [Note: [Col. 0745] Job 5.]. The beasts of the earth are the temptations of this world. Of the third he himself promises, as was said: “I think thoughts of peace” [Note: [Col. 0745] Jer. 29.] both here and in the future.

*Let us rise early for the vineyards.* The vineyard is religious conduct. [Col. 0746B] In the morning it is drenched with dew; at noon it thrives in the sun’s heat; in the evening it warms the neighbouring places. Thus holy conversion first has dew, that is, grace begun; secondly, the ardour of divine love; thirdly, the fragrance of a good odour. The first concerns oneself; the second, God; the third, one’s neighbour. Of the first Job says: “Dew shall remain in my harvest” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ch. 29.]; of the second: “Do not consider me dark, because the sun has discoloured me” [Note: [Col. 0745] Song 1.]; of the third: “I, as a vine, have brought forth the sweetness of fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0745] Sir. 24.]. Paul was in the first degree when he said: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0745] 1 Cor. 15.]; in the second when he said: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0745] Rom. 5.]; in the third when he said: “We are Christ’s good odour to God among [Col. 0746C] those who perish and among those who are saved” [Note: [Col. 0745] 2 Cor. 2.].

*Let us see whether the vineyard has flowered, whether the flowers bear fruit, whether the pomegranates have flowered.*

[THO.] The vineyard flowers when the Church first receives the devout rudiments of faith and confession. The flowers bear fruit when the faith and devotion of the saints are made prompt also for the exercise of righteous work, lest their faith be found idle or dead without works [Note: [Col. 0745] Jas. 2.]. The pomegranates flower when those who have advanced in faith and right action also acquire the desire to suffer for righteousness. For pomegranates, since they are blood-red in colour, signify the passion both of Christ and of the martyrs. Rightly does the Bride seek her Beloved’s presence in all these things, because without him she can neither act well nor think well nor do anything else. But if these words are read in the person of the ancient Fathers, by “morning” we understand Christ’s incarnation, which they ardently desired to see and, with him, to advance others. The vineyard is the Church; the vine is Christ: “I,” he says, “am the true vine; you are the branches” [Note: [Col. 0745] John 15.]. The vine of this vineyard is lowly in appearance; its flower is medicinal; its fruit is, “wine gladdens the heart of man” [Note: [Col. 0745] Ps. 103.]. Lowly on account of its twistedness; medicinal because it drives away the serpent; it gladdens [Col. 0747A] the human heart through the sweetness of its drink. In the first we observe Christ’s humility; in the second, the defeat of demons; in the third, the joyful resurrection. The Beloved was humble in the manger, humble in the world, humble on the cross. In the manger, laid in mean cloths, “because there was no room for him in the inn” [Note: [Col. 0747] Luke 2.]; in the world, while they cried to him, “Thou hast a devil” [Note: [Col. 0747] John 7.], exposed to the mockery of the Jews; on the cross, where he was seen as though leprous, struck, and humbled by God [Note: [Col. 0747] Isa. 53.]. “The branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine” [Note: [Col. 0747] John 15.], nor can it flower. This vine flowered with three flowers: with the flower of chastity, with miracles, and with the shedding of blood—first at the nativity, secondly in preaching, thirdly in the passion. Through this threefold flower [Col. 0747B] the vineyard—that is, the Church—flowered through him. This flower is medicinal. For when the vineyard flowers, all serpents flee from it through the power of the flower. There are three kinds of serpents which flee before this threefold flower: namely, the wantonness of the flesh, the malice of the world, and Satan’s cunning. By the flower of chastity the wantonness of the flesh is conquered; by the flower of miracles the malice of the world is driven away; by the flower of blood the devil’s cunning is stopped. The first serpents are those which Pharaoh’s magicians made in Egypt, where the children of Israel served in mud and brick—that is, in fleshly pleasure; the second persecuted those same people in the desert because of their malicious murmuring; the third was in paradise, seducing Eve by its cunning. It should be noted that in this [Col. 0747C] Song the flowering vineyard is treated three times: here, “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys and to observe whether the vineyards had flowered” [Note: [Col. 0747] Song 6.]. Likewise: “The fig tree has put forth its green figs; the flowering vineyards have given their fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0747] Song 2.].
