Likewise, in the present passage: “Let us see whether the vineyard has flowered, whether the flowers bear fruit.” First it is said simply: “Whether the vineyards had flowered”; secondly: “The flowering vineyards have given their fragrance”; thirdly: “Whether the flowers bear fruit.” First Christ was received by men simply as an infant of good disposition and pure life. Secondly, through miracles he was recognized as not merely man but also God. Thirdly, when he had shed his blood, the fruit of immortality was received from him. On account of these flowers he said: “I am the flower of the field [Col. 0747D] and the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0747] Ibid.]. He was the lily of the valleys because he was humble in chastity. He was the flower of the field, which is in open view—said to be a violet—because he was made manifest through working miracles. Of the flower it is said: “Hear me, ye divine fruits, and bear fruit like a rose planted beside streams” [Note: [Col. 0747] Sir. 39.]. For he was the rose reddened with blood in the passion. The streams of waters are the various goods of graces. He was above them, not beneath them, as Lord of all graces; and by dying he bore fruit, obtaining life both for himself and for us. Let us therefore see whether the flowers bear fruit. From these flowers we expect a threefold fruit: the fruit of virtue, [Col. 0748A] the fruit of work, and the fruit of immortality. Therefore through the flower of chastity the fruit of virtue is possessed. Hence it is said: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall arise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” [Note: [Col. 0747] Isa. 11.], etc. Jesse means “refreshment.” Therefore from him arose the flower of chastity, in whom the gifts of the Holy Spirit more gladly rest. Through the flower of miracles come works of virtue. For on account of those things seen to be done by Christ, people performed deeds. Hence Aaron’s rod flowered and was therefore chosen to minister in the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0747] Num. 17.]. Through the flower of blood we possess the fruit of immortality. Hence Solomon: “The almond tree shall flower, the locust shall grow fat, and the caper plant shall be scattered, because man shall return to the house of his eternity” [Note: [Col. 0747] Sir. 12.]. This almond tree [Col. 0748B] was the cross, which flowered with Christ’s blood; through him the caper plant—that is, our corruption—is destroyed, and thus man will return to the house of his eternity. Let us see also whether the pomegranates have flowered. The red pomegranates signify martyrs. They first have a desire to suffer; secondly, they offer themselves for martyrdom; thirdly, they willingly endure martyrdom. Thus they flower in the desire for martyrdom; grow when they offer themselves to martyrdom; ripen and become red when they suffer willingly. Hear the desires of the flowering Apostle: “Not only,” he says, “am I ready to be bound in Jerusalem, but also to die for the name of Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0747] Acts 21.]. Hear him offering himself to martyrdom: “Let us run,” he says, “to the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher [Col. 0748C] of faith” [Note: [Col. 0747] Heb. 12.]. Hear him enduring martyrdom: “Thrice was I beaten with rods, once I was stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck” [Note: [Col. 0747] 2 Cor. 11.].

*There I shall give thee my breasts.*

[THO.] The breasts are understood to be the teachers of the Church. She gives these breasts to the Lord when she offers in his service both the deeds and words of her preachers, so that they may beget new children for the Beloved. There are breasts of brute animals, such as mares, which nourish only their own young. And there are those which nourish their own young and also afford some usefulness to human beings, such as cows’ and sheep’s. And there are those suited only for nourishing human beings, such as women’s. The first signify persons dissolute both in speech and morals; the second, ornamented in speech but disordered in morals; the third, orderly in both [Col. 0748D] speech and morals.

The first make disciples only like themselves; the second, disciples like themselves in conduct but different in speech; the third, disciples acceptable to God in both speech and morals. Of the first it is said: “Even the dragons have uncovered the breast; they have suckled their young” [Note: [Col. 0747] Lam. 4.]. Of the second, Ezekiel’s words: “The breasts of thy maturity have been broken” [Note: [Col. 0747] Ezek. 23.]. A woman is called mature when she is capable of a man and fit to bear children; this a preacher possesses through preaching. But her breasts are broken if he has evil conduct. Of the third: “Thy two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle” [Note: [Col. 0747] Song 4.], on account of good conduct [Col. 0749A] and good speech. To the first the Lord says: “You traverse sea and land to make one proselyte; and when you have made him, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0749] Matt. 23.]. Nor is this surprising: “Night tells knowledge to night” [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 18.]. Hence that satirist rightly says [Note: [Col. 0749] Juv., *Sat.* VI.238]:

> Of course you expect a mother to hand down honourable ways,  
> or morals other than those which she herself possesses? Moreover, it is useful…

To bring forth a shameful little daughter for a shameful old woman. Of such persons David says: “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 13].” Behold what they are like in speech: “Their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways [Note: [Col. 0749] Ibid.].” Behold what they are like in conduct. Of the second sort it is said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me [Col. 0749B] [Note: [Col. 0749] Matt. 15].” Likewise: “Do what they say; but do not do what they do [Note: [Col. 0749] Matt. 23].” Of these also, in Leviticus: “You shall not sow your field with diverse seed [Note: [Col. 0749] Lev. 19],” as it is written: “To speak well and live badly is nothing other than to condemn oneself by one’s own voice.” But the Lord said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds, and take my covenant upon your lips? Yet you hate discipline and have cast my words behind you [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 49].” These are those “who speak peace with their neighbor, evil things [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 27],” etc.

Of the third sort: Hear the Apostle, how he nourished by the word. For he says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food [Note: [Col. 0749] I Cor. 3].”—“If I preach to you,” he says, “there is no glory for me in this. For necessity lies upon me. Woe is me if I do not preach [Note: [Col. 0749] I Cor. 9].” And how he instructed Timothy to nourish [Col. 0749C] by the word: “Preach the word,” he says; “persist, out of season and in season [Note: [Col. 0749] II Tim. 4].” And by conduct: “In all things show yourself an example of good works—in teaching, in seriousness, in integrity—so that he who is on the opposing side may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say of you [Note: [Col. 0749] Titus 2].”

Of these breasts, which are good, some keep them from the beloved, some place them at the beloved’s disposal, and some give them to the beloved. The first are those who expend in no useful work the grace bestowed on them by God; the second expend it for temporal fellowship; the third, for charity alone. The first hide the Lord’s talent wrapped in a napkin [Note: [Col. 0749] Matt. 25]. The second sell sheep, oxen, and doves in the Temple [Note: [Col. 0749] John 2]. The third return to their lord with profit the talent entrusted to them [Note: [Col. 0749] Matt. 25]. To the first it is said: “See that you do not [Col. 0749D] receive the grace of God in vain [Note: [Col. 0749] II Cor. 6].” And Paul says to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you [Note: [Col. 0749] I Tim. 4].” “Cursed is he who hides grain in a time of famine,” says Solomon [Note: [Col. 0749] Prov. 11]. “Hidden wisdom, hidden treasure: what use is there in either [Note: [Col. 0749] Ecclus. 41]?” To the second it is said: “Freely you have received; freely give [Note: [Col. 0749] Matt. 10].” Otherwise the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian will cling to Gehazi [Note: [Col. 0749] IV Kings 5]. Job says: “Fire shall devour the tents of those who gladly accept gifts [Note: [Col. 0749] Job 15].” And: “He who shakes [Col. 0750A] his hands free of every gift, he shall dwell on high [Note: [Col. 0749] Isa. 33].”

For there is a gift from the hand, a gift from the tongue, and a gift from service. To the third it is said: “Drink water from your own cistern and streams from your own well [Note: [Col. 0749] Prov. 5],” that is, let the grace bestowed on you by God benefit you, and nevertheless benefit others. Hence it is added: “Let your fountains be poured abroad, and divide your waters in the streets [Note: [Col. 0749] Ibid.].” Thus Paul: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty [Note: [Col. 0749] I Cor. 15].” The same man says elsewhere: “According to the grace given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation, but another builds upon it [Note: [Col. 0749] I Cor. 3].”—“Let him who thirsts come and drink, and I will give him freely the water of life,” as it is said in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0749] Apoc. 22].

The grace of the first is figured in that manna which, [Col. 0750B] because the children of Israel kept it contrary to the command, began to swarm with worms [Note: [Col. 0749] Exod. 16]. Likewise Onan, son of Judah—who is called “their sorrow”—when he ought to have raised up offspring for his deceased brother Er, spilled his seed upon the ground when he approached Tamar, his brother’s wife [Note: [Col. 0749] Gen. 46]. The grace of the second is signified by Esau’s birthright, which he gave to his brother Jacob for a meal of red lentils [Note: [Col. 0749] Gen. 25]. The grace of the third is figured in the oil of the woman whose son supplied vessels while she poured the oil in [Note: [Col. 0749] IV Kings 4], and in the oil and wine which the Samaritan poured upon the man who fell among thieves [Note: [Col. 0749] Luke 10].

The breasts of the Church are preachers, whom the Church, the bride, gives when she sends them to govern, imitating their teaching and conduct, as though sucking milk from breasts. Solomon prefigured these breasts when he made in the [Col. 0750C] Temple two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high, with wings of five cubits [Note: [Col. 0749] III Kings 6]. It was fitting that Christ, who had come to perform mercy, should appoint for us, in place of breasts, men of mercy; and that for those who had fallen through Adam’s folly he should appoint knowledgeable men—he who “teaches man knowledge [Note: [Col. 0749] Ps. 93]”—so that through them he might make man understand; he who “came not to destroy the Law but to fulfill it [Note: [Col. 0749] Matt. 5].”

These two cherubim are Peter and Paul. They were made of olive wood because they are men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not passed into oblivion. They are called cherubim—that is, “fullness of knowledge”—because they did not love the knowledge of fanciful disputations, but the knowledge of God more [Col. 0750D] than holocausts. They are said to be ten cubits high because, spiritually, by fulfilling and teaching the precepts of the Law, they shall receive with us, who labor in the Lord’s vineyard, individual denarii [Note: [Col. 0749] Matt. 20].

See the milk that proceeds from these two breasts. In the cherubim we have knowledge; in the olive wood, mercy. Behold a twofold milk. In the ten cubits is the perfection of the divine Law: knowledge, that there may be knowledge of God and of ourselves; mercy, that there may be compassion for one’s neighbor; [Col. 0751A] observance of the Law, that the execution of God’s commandments may be perfected in us. Of the first: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the Law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts [Note: [Col. 0751] Mal. 2].” And in the same place: “My people have perished because they had no knowledge [Note: [Col. 0751] Ibid.].” For this purpose the spirit of knowledge was given to the apostles.

Of mercy Job says: “The stranger did not remain outside, and my door stood open to the traveler [Note: [Col. 0751] Job 31].” And he adds: “For compassion grew up with me, and came forth with me from my mother’s womb [Note: [Col. 0751] Ibid.].” Therefore these are men of mercy. Behold the milk of the breasts. Of the Law it is said: “Great peace have those who love your Law, and there is no stumbling-block for them [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 118].”

There is knowledge followed by punishment; there is half-complete knowledge; and there is complete knowledge. The first knows God’s will, but does not [Col. 0751B] abandon wickedness. The second, though it deals with temporal affairs, nevertheless keeps purity. The third wholly follows God’s will. The first is pagan, because pagans do this. The second is political, because cities rightly order temporal matters. The third is apostolic, because apostolic men submit themselves to the divine will.

Of the first: “It would have been better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back [Note: [Col. 0751] II Pet. 2].” Of the second Paul says: “I know how to be hungry and how to be filled; how to abound and how to suffer need [Note: [Col. 0751] Phil. 4].” Likewise: “Let priests who know how to preside well be held worthy of double honor [Note: [Col. 0751] I Tim. 5].” Of the third the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew who it is that asks you for a drink, perhaps you would have asked him to give you living water [Note: [Col. 0751] John 4].”

The prophet complains of these: “There is no mercy, [Col. 0751C] no truth, no knowledge of God in the land [Note: [Col. 0751] Hos. 4].” Of this Paul says: “I judged that I should know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified [Note: [Col. 0751] I Cor. 2].” Likewise: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he, the just judge, is able to preserve my deposit until that day [Note: [Col. 0751] II Tim. 1].”

O Peter, where is that word by which you denied the Lord, saying to the maidservant: “I do not know what you are saying [Note: [Col. 0751] Matt. 26]”? Likewise, you began to swear and curse that you did not know the man [Note: [Col. 0751] Ibid.]. You too, Paul, when you kept the garments of those stoning Stephen [Note: [Col. 0751] Acts 7], when you did not cease to persecute Christ and his members [Note: [Col. 0751] Acts 9], when, that is, you received letters from the rulers [Note: [Col. 0751] Ibid.]—then you knew something other than Christ crucified. And he says: “But I acted ignorantly in unbelief [Note: [Col. 0751] I Tim. 1].” Therefore I who was formerly a teacher of cruelty now offer milk from the breast of mercy; [Col. 0751D] I who formerly sinned through ignorance now, as it were from a breast, offer knowledge abundantly to many. “God,” Peter says, “allowed me to fall, so that I might raise up those who had fallen.”

These were prefigured in Samuel when he said to Saul: “You will find two men leaping over great pits [Note: [Col. 0751] I Kings 10 according to the Septuagint].” For they leapt over the great pit when they passed from sin to righteousness, from the devil’s snare to Christ’s free way, from dread of eternal death to confidence. Hence the prophet says: “For you who are upon the earth there shall be terror and pit and snare [Note: [Col. 0751] Isa. 24].” The snare [Col. 0752A] is diabolical seduction; the pit, obstinacy; the terror, eternal punishment. The snare of diabolical seduction is so that one may fall into temptation; the pit of obstinacy, so that one may come into despair; the terror of eternal punishment, so that one may be ready for final condemnation.

Of the snare: “They prepared a snare for my feet and bowed down my soul [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 56].” Likewise: “Our soul has been delivered from the snare of the hunters [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 123].” Of the pit: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the pit which he made [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 7].” Likewise: “Foxes have dens, and birds of heaven nests [Note: [Col. 0751] Luke 9].” Of terror: “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away [Note: [Col. 0751] Ps. 111],” because “there is a terrible expectation of judgment and a fiery zeal which will consume the adversaries [Note: [Col. 0751] Heb. 10].”

They had knowledge in [Col. 0752B] the conversion of sinners, the guidance of converts, and the divine calling. In that conversion they had knowledge, strength by which they could endure labors, and courage by which they could resist tyrants. Behold, on the three bases we have lions, oxen, and cherubim. See Paul as a lion: “Neither death nor life, nor principalities nor powers, will be able to separate me from the love of Christ [Note: [Col. 0751] Rom. 8].” Behold: “The righteous is confident as a lion [Note: [Col. 0751] Prov. 28].” See the laboring ox: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck [Note: [Col. 0751] II Cor. 11].” Hear the cherubim: “Behold, my land cries out against me, and I have eaten its fruits without payment [Note: [Col. 0751] Job 31],” namely, with the knowledge by which it may be converted.

157 “These are the breasts which I shall give you,” says the bride. It should be noted that she gives breasts by which Christ [Col. 0752C] is nourished in his assumed humanity; there are breasts by which he is nourished in the steadfastness of faith; and there are breasts by which he is nourished in charity. The first are offered by the Virgin Mary; the second are supplied by preachers in the Church; the third are bestowed by the devout soul. By the first the Savior’s flesh is nourished; by the second, the Mediator’s faith; by the third, the fervor of love.

Of the first: “The Virgin alone, full of heaven, nursed at her breast the very King of angels [Note: [Col. 0751] Office of the Church].” Of the second, especially in reference to Peter and Paul and their imitators, it is said: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among lilies.” Of the third the prophet says: “Give them, O Lord—what will you give them? Withered breasts [Note: [Col. 0751] Hos. 9],” and a shield, hardness of heart. For those have withered breasts who neither offer living milk for Christ nor offer to God the milk of charitable devotion, to whom be honor [Col. 0752D] and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us lodge in the villages; let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the flowers bring forth fruit, whether the pomegranates have flowered. There I will give you my breasts.

[CARD] In these words the mother shows the concern which she bears for the Church: how she urges the Son to visit her and see her progress, so that by visiting he may supply what is lacking. Therefore she says: Come, my beloved, let us enter into the field; let us visit [Col. 0753A] those who are in the field and split the soil of human hearts with the ploughshare of preaching. Come, my beloved, let us lodge in the villages, making our dwelling among those who, living together in love, live under one rule. Let us rise early to plant vineyards in faith; let us see whether the vineyard has blossomed through the beginning of good work; whether the flowers bring forth fruit through the completion of a good beginning; let us see whether the pomegranates have flowered—whose red flower signifies, in faithful men designated by those trees, the desire to imitate the Lord’s Passion. And the lady adds: There I will give you my breasts, that you may taste my intercessions for the Church, which proceed from my breasts, through which, as we said above, her own piety and mercy are signified.

[Col. 0753B] The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates.

[THO.] The gates of Christ and the Church are the same teachers who were denoted by the name of breasts. They are breasts because by doctrine they nourish little ones; they are gates because they introduce those whom they have nourished into the kingdom of heaven. Hence in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0753] ch. 21], the city which John saw is said to have twelve gates, that is, the twelve apostles. At these gates the mandrakes gave forth fragrance, because both the apostles and their followers spread abroad the renown of spiritual virtues issuing from themselves.

The mandrake is an aromatic herb whose root has the shape of a human body; its fruits, however, have a sweet smell. It has this power: it induces sleep in sick persons suffering the discomfort of sleeplessness. Likewise, if bodies must be cut because of a medical concern, its [Col. 0753C] bark, mixed with wine, is given them to drink, so that, lulled to sleep, they do not feel the pain. Likewise, it heals those so afflicted by nausea that they can neither retain food nor take pleasure in it. The food of the soul is the word of doctrine, which some disdain to hear or, having heard it, neglect to commit to memory.

There are four gates: the first to the west, the second to the north, the third to the south, the fourth to the east. Ezekiel was shown a building [Note: [Col. 0753] Ezek. 8] in which the first is left unmentioned because it is useless, while the other three are shown to him because they are of great usefulness. Through the first there is departure; through the second, return; through the third, advance; through the fourth, entrance. Departure is into the darkness of worldly blindness; return to the grace of healing; advance [Col. 0753D] in the fervor of charity; entrance into the splendor of brightness. At the first, man falls into guilt; at the second, he rises again through repentance; through the third, he walks in righteousness; through the fourth, he penetrates the mysteries of heavenly blessedness. The first is the gate of error, the second of satisfaction, the third of fervor, the fourth of light.

The first is the Dung Gate, read of in Ezra [Note: [Col. 0753] II Ezra 3]; the second is that at which the Lord raises up the young man, the only son of his mother [Note: [Col. 0753] Luke 7]; the third is the Beautiful Gate, at which Peter raises up the lame man so that he may walk uprightly [Note: [Col. 0753] Acts 3], where the work of charity is performed; [Col. 0754A] the fourth is the gate of Bethlehem, where there was a spring whose water David desired [Note: [Col. 0753] II Kings 25].

Of the first: “They drew near even to the gates of death [Note: [Col. 0753] Ps. 106].” Of the second: “Enter by the narrow gate [Note: [Col. 0753] Matt. 7].” Of the third: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered through them, I shall confess to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0753] Ps. 117].” Of the fourth: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tents of Jacob [Note: [Col. 0753] Ps. 86].”

Through the first Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, went out and was violated [Note: [Col. 0753] Gen. 54]. The prophet invited the Synagogue to the second, saying: “Return, virgin Israel, to your cities [Note: [Col. 0753] Jer. 31].” Of the third Solomon cries out: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn [Note: [Col. 0753] Song 6]?” Paul hastened toward the fourth when he said: “We who have believed shall enter into that rest [Note: [Col. 0753] Heb. 4].”

The mandrake resembles man in every respect except [Col. 0754B] the hair. Christ is whole in divinity and humanity; but the righteous man who enters by these gates is a mandrake, made like the body of Christ—that is, his humanity—through a change into a religious life. “The head of Christ is God [Note: [Col. 0753] I Cor. 11],” to whom the righteous man cannot be made like in those things which Christ does by divinity, such as the working of miracles.

Therefore the life of the righteous gives fragrance at our gates, that is, at the final three. For at the first the life of the sinner dead four days gives a stench; at the second the life of one who has returned gives the fragrance of ointment; at the third the life of the righteous, the fragrance of incense; at the fourth the life of the devout contemplative, the fragrance of spices. The first gives a stench when he scandalizes others by the unclean example of his life; the second gives the fragrance of ointment when by his return he heals others, calling them toward [Col. 0754C] the remedy of divine mercy; the third gives the fragrance of incense when by prayers he obtains divine help for himself and others; the fourth gives the fragrance of spices through the sweetness of his devotion.

Of the first it is said: “Lord, by now he stinks, for he has been dead four days [Note: [Col. 0753] John 11].” As a figure of the second, “the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment [Note: [Col. 0753] John 12],” because Mary anointed the Lord’s feet. Of the third it is said in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0753] ch. 5]: “The elders had harps and golden bowls full of fragrances, which are the prayers of the saints.” Or the harp is the voice, and in the fragrances is the sweet richness of prayer. Of the fourth: “The smoke of the spices rose in the sight of the Lord from the hand of the angel [Note: [Col. 0753] Apoc. 8].”

Likewise, we find these four gates in [Col. 0754D] Christ’s sacraments, all understood in a favorable sense. The first is eastern, the second western, the third northern, the fourth southern. The first is the Virgin’s womb; the second is the Savior’s side; the third is the grip of infernal rapine; the fourth is entrance into the heavenly homeland. Of the first Ezekiel says [Note: [Col. 0753] ch. 44]: “This gate shall be shut; no man shall enter through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it.” Of the second: “Enter by the narrow gate [Note: [Col. 0753] Matt. 7].” Of the third: “I said in the midst of my days: I shall go to the gate of hell [Note: [Col. 0753] Isa. 38].” Of the fourth: “Be lifted up, [Col. 0755A] everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 23].”

These gates were closed in the prophets because they were obscurely foretold by them; but now, with the Gospel flashing forth, they stand open. The first was opened at Christ’s birth—opened, I say, not by the corruption of virginity, but by the manifestation of Christ’s birth. The second was opened in his Passion; the third at Christ’s descent into hell and resurrection; the fourth in his Ascension. By the opening of the first the world was enlightened; by the second man was redeemed and washed from sins; by the third captive man was freed from hell; by the fourth the Holy Spirit was sent.

Of the first it is said: “For you who fear my name the Sun of righteousness shall arise [Note: [Col. 0755] Mal. 4],” for “we have seen his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father [Note: [Col. 0755] John 1].” Of the second: “In [Col. 0755B] your blood you redeemed your captives from the pit in which there was no water [Note: [Col. 0755] Zech. 9],” and: “For he first loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood [Note: [Col. 0755] Apoc. 1].” Of the third: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell [Note: [Col. 0755] Hos. 13],” for bands of captives, now free, follow Jesus. Of the fourth: “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men [Note: [Col. 0755] Eph. 4],” that is, the sevenfold Spirit.

In these the mandrakes—that is, the conduct of the righteous—give fragrance: in the first when they imitate Christ’s humility; in the second when they conform themselves to him through suffering; in the third when they carefully flee the torments of hell by bravely repelling the devil’s devices; in the fourth when they raise their desires toward heaven. At the first David gave the good fragrance of humility, saying: [Col. 0755C] “I will dance before the ark of the Lord, and will become more lowly in my own sight [Note: [Col. 0755] II Kings 2].” At the second the Apostle gave the good fragrance of suffering, saying: “From now on, let no one trouble me; for I bear the marks of Jesus Christ in my body [Note: [Col. 0755] Gal. 6].” At the third David gave good fragrance by fleeing hell, saying: “Lord, you have drawn my soul out of hell; you saved me from those descending into the pit [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 29],” and: “My soul, like a sparrow, has escaped from the snare of the hunters [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 123].” At the fourth David gave good fragrance by raising his desire toward heaven, saying: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 41],” and: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 83].”

Likewise, the twelve apostles are called gates; hence in the Apocalypse [Col. 0755D] [Note: [Col. 0755] ch. 21] John saw twelve gates in that city, Jerusalem, which was shown to him. Likewise, Christ is called the gate: “I,” he says, “am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall enter and go out and find pasture [Note: [Col. 0755] John 10].” All enter by this gate.

Likewise, we find this division: there are gates of Zion, gates of righteousness, and everlasting gates. The gates of Zion are the Church’s sacraments, through which we enter the Church. The gates of righteousness are the intermediate virtues [Col. 0756A] which we exercise in time. The everlasting gates are the chief virtues, which we shall possess also in the future. At the first, prelates give fragrance by preaching; at the second, religious give fragrance by living justly; at the third, the perfect give fragrance by devoting themselves to God alone.

Of the first: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God,” says that outstanding preacher [Note: [Col. 0755] II Cor. 2]. Of the second: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field, which the Lord has blessed [Note: [Col. 0755] Gen. 37].” Of the third: “Your fragrance has stirred eternal desires within me [Note: [Col. 0755] Office of the Church].”

Likewise, there are gates of death, gates of the world, gates of hell, and gates of heaven. The gates by which we enter the world are corrupt sensuality and blind cupidity; hence: “They drew near even to the gates of death [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 106].” The gates of hell are blind despair and hard obstinacy; hence: [Col. 0756B] “The gates of hell shall not prevail against her [Note: [Col. 0755] Matt. 16].” The gates of heaven are humble patience, which is the iron gate leading to the city [Note: [Col. 0755] Acts 12], and concord in love, which is the eastern gate [Note: [Col. 0755] Ezek. 8]. The first gates belong to the children of this age, the second to the children of Gehenna, the third to the children of God. The first find error at their gates; the second prepare for themselves through theirs an everlasting stench; the third find at theirs, as mandrakes, the fragrance of life.

Of the first: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they did not find the way to an inhabited city [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 106].” Of the second: “Fire, sulfur, and a stormy blast are the portion of their cup [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 10],” for sulfur by its stench signifies an everlasting stench. Of the third: “I, like the vine, have brought forth sweetness of fragrance [Note: [Col. 0755] Ecclus. 24].” For the vine—which, as we have said, signifies the gates of heaven—by enduring pruning signifies patience; by its crookedness and lowliness, humility; and by wine, which is warm in nature and gladdens the heart of man [Note: [Col. 0755] Ps. 103], it signifies the fervor and delight of divine love.

Likewise, there are seven gates of Jerusalem: the Old Gate, the Fountain Gate, the Sheep Gate, the Horse Gate, the Dung Gate, the Fish Gate, and the Valley Gate [Note: [Col. 0755] II Ezra 2, 3]. Likewise there are seven beatitudes, enumerated there: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0755] Matt. 5],” etc. By one reckoning, the first are angels, the second patriarchs, the third prophets, the fourth apostles, the fifth martyrs, the sixth confessors, the seventh virgins. The first is heavenly, the second faithful, the third shadowy, the fourth judicial, the fifth terrible, the sixth [Col. 0756D] exemplary, the seventh marvelous.

It is called the Old Gate because it was founded at the beginning of Jerusalem’s birth: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth [Note: [Col. 0755] Gen. 1],” that is, angelic and human nature. Hence Jacob, waking, said: “This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven [Note: [Col. 0755] Gen. 28].”

The Fountain Gate was that through which there was an exit to the spring of Gihon, where Solomon was anointed king by Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet [Note: [Col. 0755] III Kings 1]. By it the patriarchs are signified: 158 for from them faith and the worship of the one God began and flowed to us [Col. 0757A] as streams from a fountain. Thus Prudentius says of Abraham: “The faithful old man is the first way of believing.”

The Sheep Gate was beside the Temple, and animals were led through it for sacrifice. These are the prophets, of whom Samuel first “made those of one disposition dwell in a house [Note: [Col. 0757] Ps. 67],” like a flock in a sheepfold. It is called shadowy because they prophesied under figures of deeds and coverings of shadows.

The Horse Gate was so called because they dismounted their horses there when they went up to the Temple; beyond it riding was not permitted. These are the apostles, so called because of their speed, since “suddenly their sound went forth into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world [Note: [Col. 0757] Rom. 10].” As their figure, the prophet Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0757] ch. 6] saw red, white, black, and variegated horses. This [Col. 0757B] gate is judicial, for it was said to the apostles: “You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel [Note: [Col. 0757] Matt. 19].” Hence the Church sings [Note: [Col. 0757] Hymn from the Common of Saints]:

> Princes of the churches,  
> Triumphant leaders in war,  
> Soldiers of the heavenly court,  
> And true lights of the world.

The Dung Gate was that through which the city’s filth was carried out. These are the martyrs, whose bodies were reckoned as dung. Thus David says: “They poured out their blood like water round about, and there was none to bury them [Note: [Col. 0757] Ps. 78].” Likewise David: “They gave the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of [Col. 0757C] the earth [Note: [Col. 0757] Ibid.],” because “they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, and died by the slaughter of the sword [Note: [Col. 0757] Heb. 11].”

The Fish Gate faced the Mediterranean Sea, and merchandise of fish was brought through it into the city. These are the confessors, who amid the whirlpool of vices are borne against the assaults of the waves of the world—that is, temptations—and are shaken by surrounding storms, yet are not cast down. These are the few little fishes with which the Lord satisfied four thousand men [Note: [Col. 0757] Matt. 15]. It is called exemplary because, together with the word of teaching, it supplies us with an example of life.

The Valley Gate led to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. These are the virgins, set in the valley of humility, because virginity and humility are associated virtues. Hence the blessed Virgin says: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid, behold, [Col. 0757D] from this time all generations shall call me blessed [Note: [Col. 0757] Luke 1].” It is called marvelous. For what is more marvelous than to lead an angelic life upon earth? To live in the flesh, yet not according to the flesh, is not merely above the flesh, but angelic.

We may also understand these gates morally. Let the first, then, be grace; the second, contrition; the third, outward penance; the fourth, holy meditation. And now let us discuss these four. The first, then, is grace, namely the Old Gate. For it is the beginning of the good things we have done; it is also heavenly. For through it [Col. 0758A] an angel came forth from heaven, Christ came forth, and the Holy Spirit came forth: the angel to visit, Christ to redeem, the Holy Spirit to console. The angel came to visit against the devil’s temptations; Christ, to redeem from infernal punishment; the Holy Spirit, to console in this misery. Hence Jacob saw angels ascending and descending, and he anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit the stone beneath his head—that is, Christ—and said: “This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven [Note: [Col. 0757] Gen. 28].”

The second, namely the Fountain Gate, is contrition. This fountain has three streams: by the first it washes one infected by the stain of sin; by the second it laments a neighbor’s failing; by the third it waters a devout affection. For it seeks to cleanse itself, to aid its neighbor, and to desire God. David desired this water when he desired water [Col. 0758B] from the spring which is at the gate of Bethlehem [Note: [Col. 0757] II Kings 3].

The third is the Sheep Gate, which is also called shadowy. There are three flocks: a flock of swine, a flock of goats, and a flock of sheep. Of the first it is written that the Lord sent evil spirits to enter the herd of swine [Note: [Col. 0757] Matt. 8]. Of the second: “Your hair is like a flock of goats that have climbed up from Mount Gilead [Note: [Col. 0757] Song 4].” Of the third: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing [Note: [Col. 0757] Ibid.].” We do not read that swine are offered in sacrifice; a goat is offered for sin, a sheep as a holocaust [Note: [Col. 0757] Lev. 22]. Therefore the first do not enter the gate, the second enter it, and the third are brought into the Temple. The first are swine, who are hurled into the sea—that is, sinners who shall be tormented in hell. The second are penitents who are afflicted for their sins; [Col. 0758C] the third are righteous persons who burn with charity, so that they may become more righteous.

Of the first: “To whom I swore in my wrath: They shall not enter into my rest [Note: [Col. 0757] Ps. 94].” Of the second: “Enter by the narrow gate [Note: [Col. 0757] Matt. 7].” Of the third: “The sons of Zadok shall enter into my sanctuary and minister to me [Note: [Col. 0757] Ezek. 44].” This gate is called shadowy because sacrifices are a shadow of things to come; or because these works must be done in secret; or because, although merit is visible, the reward is not yet disclosed.

The fourth is the Horse Gate. By the name of horses three classes of people are designated: the lustful, the proud, and those devoted to honours. The first remain outside the gate because of their uncleanness; the second because of their pride; the third in order that, having for a time laid aside their worldly concern, they may have a greater abundance of contemplation. Of the first: “Their discharge is like the discharge of horses” [Note: [Col. 0757] Ezek. 23]; of the second: “He will not delight in the strength of a horse, nor in its legs” [Note: [Col. 0757] Ps. 146]; of the third: “You mount upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” [Note: [Col. 0757] Hab. 3]. This gate is called judicial, because, when the soul returns, it knows more truly how to judge between truth and falsehood, good and evil, temporal and eternal things.

There follow three other gates. The first is that of confession, the second of imitation, the third of humility. The first is the Dung Gate; for when we confess our sins, we cast out, as it were, dung outside the gate [Col. 0759A]. There are three such dung-heaps: the first is sins; the second, temporal goods; the third, the misery of the world. Of the first: “Those who were brought up in scarlet have embraced dung” [Note: [Col. 0759] Lam. 4]; of the second: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen” [Note: [Col. 0759] Sirach 22]; of the third: “Raising up the needy from the dust, and lifting the poor from the dung-heap” [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 112]. This is called terrible; for while the hearer of confession preaches, he instils fear at the point of death, the trembling of horror at the judgment, and darkness in hell. Hence David: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me” [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 54].

There follows the Fish Gate, namely, that of imitation. There are three kinds of fish which we ought to imitate: those of the river, of the pond, and of the sea. The first are those who live in the world by their own labours [Col. 0759B], devoting themselves to almsgiving, and these have been tested by the witness of faith. The second are enclosed in a cloister: they are narrowed and afflicted. The third, in martyrdom, have experienced mockery and blows. This gate is called exemplary. We ought to imitate the first, that we may know how to live in society in the world; the second, that we may know how to keep solitude in the cloister; and the third, that we may be able to possess constancy in martyrdom. In all these, patience is necessary; hence in Leviticus: “You shall not eat fish, whether of river, pond, or sea, which have not fins and scales” [Note: [Col. 0759] Lev. 11].

There follows the Valley Gate, that is, humility. There is a fruitful valley, a grain-bearing valley, and a valley of lilies. The first is the humility of sinners, the second that of the righteous, the third that of virgins. [Col. 0759C] The humble sinner is watered with tears; the humble righteous person is heaped with the grain of virtues; the humble virgin rejoices in the pleasantness of purity. Of the first: “You send forth springs in the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 103]; of the second: “The valleys shall abound with grain” [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 64]; of the third: “Flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys surrounded her” [Note: [Col. 0759] Office of the Church]. This gate is marvellous. For it is marvellous that it destroys the pride which hurled down the whole human race. What pride hurled down from heaven, humility carries back to heaven.

“The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates.”

[CARD.] The mandrake is a herb which induces so deep a sleep that a person might be cut open and feel no pain. By mandrakes are signified the pursuits of contemplation [Col. 0759D], which make a person sleep so deeply amid his pleasures that he neither feels nor attends to separation from his carnal enemies and worldly affairs. He therefore says: “The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates,” that is, at the gates of the five senses—then truly *our* gates, if the fragrance of the mandrakes reaches them and excludes from them the worldly smell. For if the soul sleeps well inwardly, it shuts off its senses from outward things. There follows:

“All fruits, new and old, I have kept for you, my beloved.”

[THO.] The new and old fruits are the commandments or promises [Col. 0760A] of the New and Old Testaments, all of which the Church has kept for her Beloved. For she knows that he alone is the one who gave the commandments of both and who renders worthy rewards to those who keep them. He alone gave commandments and promised rewards: to the ancients through angels, to us through himself; lesser things to them, greater things to us.

Again, the old fruits are the Fathers of the Old Testament, none of whom, however holy, could enter the kingdom before the Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension. But the new fruits are the righteous of the New Testament. The Church foreknew that both were to be saved through the grace of Christ who was to come into the world.

There are four new fruits: first, the incarnation of the Saviour; second, the beginning of a new manner of life; third, the progress of humility; fourth, the fruit of perfect [Col. 0760B] virtue. Of the first, Job says: “My days have passed like ships carrying fruits” [Note: [Col. 0759] Job 7], which Gregory expounds concerning the Incarnation. Of the second, in Leviticus: “When you enter the land which the Lord will give you, and plant fruit-bearing trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins” [Note: [Col. 0759] Lev. 20], that is, vain glory from the new way of life. Of the third: “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valley” [Note: [Col. 0759] Song 6]. For humility is signified by the valley. Of the fourth: “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard” [Note: [Col. 0759] Song 4]. The pomegranates are martyrs, red through the shedding of blood; the fruit of the orchard which is in them is the perfection of virtues.

The first fruit brings health; the second tastes of austerity; [Col. 0760C] the third provokes vomiting; the fourth gives appetite: the health of true faith, the austerity of penitence, the vomiting out of pride, and the appetite for heavenly sweetness. Thus the first fruit brings health to the ancients by fragrance, to those present by taste, and to those to come in the resurrection by strength and beauty. Hence Wisdom herself says: “Like cinnamon and balsam giving forth fragrance, I gave forth an odour; like choice myrrh, I gave the sweetness of fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0759] Sirach 24]. Like cinnamon, pleasant in fragrance and taste, he gave fragrance at his birth; like myrrh, which is bitter, at his Passion; like balsam, which preserves the body incorrupt from decay, at his Resurrection. This threefold fragrance he gave to the ancients for faith.

He gave taste to those present, manifesting himself to them in the flesh; hence: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 33], [Col. 0760D] and: “Those who eat me shall still hunger” [Note: [Col. 0759] Sirach 24]. To those to come he will give the sweetness of strength through incorruption, and of beauty through the sight of himself; hence: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on splendour” [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 92].

The second fruit tastes of the austerity of penitence; hence: “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 144]. Such a person cries: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 6]—“For your sake we are put to death all the day long” [Note: [Col. 0759] Ps. 43]. The third fruit causes the vomiting out of pride, to which the Apostle exhorts us: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough” [Note: [Col. 0759] 1 Cor. 5]. And another apostle: “Putting away all malice, and all deceit and [Col. 0761A] hypocrisy, and envy, and all detractions” [Note: [Col. 0761] 1 Pet. 2], etc. The fourth fruit provokes an appetite for heavenly sweetness. The Apostle invites us to this, saying: “Set your minds on the things above, not on things upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0761] Col. 3]; and David: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” [Note: [Col. 0761] Ps. 41]. Hence the bride says in this Song: “Eat, friends, and be drunk, beloved ones” [Note: [Col. 0761] Song 5].

Of these four fruits the prophet says: “He has wounded us, and he will heal us” [Note: [Col. 0761] Hos. 6]. Through the first, penitence will strike; through the second, he will heal us, causing us to vomit out pride; through the third, he will revive us after two days, namely, those of the aforesaid beginning and the progress of humility, giving us heavenly taste; through the fourth—which is, namely, a certain quickening of spiritual life following in these two days—on the third day he will raise [Col. 0761B] us in body and soul, namely, after the two preceding days of the Law and the Gospel.

The first new fruit consists in the ineffable union of God and man; the second, in subjection to Adam’s oldness; the third is new by being reshaped away from the proud devil; the fourth is new by being conformed to Christ. Of the first: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” [Note: [Col. 0761] Jer. 31]; of the second: “Let us walk in newness of life” [Note: [Col. 0761] Rom. 6]; of the third: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, 159 and put on the new man, who was created according to God” [Note: [Col. 0761] Eph. 4]; of the fourth: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” [Note: [Col. 0761] Ps. 102].

This eagle is Christ, into whose likeness we are renewed when, leaving sins behind, we conform ourselves, insofar as our weakness permits, to his virtues and works, so that after death we may be re-formed by him. To hear that Christ is the eagle, listen to John the Apostle: “I heard,” he says, “the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0761] Rev. 8]; this we understand of Christ’s Ascension.

These things have been said concerning the new fruits. There are three old fruits: original sin, carnal pleasure, and temporal vanity. Adam gathered the first in paradise; the two elder presbyters gathered the second as they lay hidden in the orchard while plotting against Susanna’s chastity; the third occurs in the book of Ecclesiastes: “I,” he says, “acquired male and female servants for myself, and planted orchards and trees of various kinds; and I saw that this was vanity and affliction of spirit” [Note: [Col. 0761] Eccl. 2].

The Church keeps those first new fruits for her Beloved in order to be rewarded. But she keeps these old ones for him [Col. 0761D], either to remit them or to punish them eternally: original sin she remits through the washing of baptism; carnal pleasure through confession and mortification of the flesh; temporal vanity through confession and renunciation of the world. For of the first the Beloved says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0761] John 3]; of the second: “Whoever hates his life in this world keeps it unto eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0761] John 12], that is, his carnal life; of the third: “Unless one renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” [Note: [Col. 0761] Luke 14]. [Col. 0762A] Great possessions are indeed causes of vanity.

Otherwise, all these are kept for the Beloved to be punished eternally, unless we make satisfaction for them while time is granted to us. For we owe three things to God, three to our neighbour, and three to ourselves. We owe these three to God: reverence to majesty, obedience to truth, and patience to kindness. We ask that these three things, which we owe to God and do not pay, may be forgiven us. We owe our neighbour our ability, our knowledge, and our will: in assistance, in counsel, and in desire—to the beggar, the undiscerning person, and the perverse person. We likewise owe ourselves three things: the supports of life, living without the stain of crime, and walking in righteousness. Of the first: “Food, a staff, and a burden for an ass; bread, discipline, and work for a servant” [Note: [Col. 0761] Sirach 33]; of the second: “Blessed is the man found without stain” [Note: [Col. 0761] Sirach 31]; of the third: [Col. 0762B] “He who walks in righteousness and speaks truth, that man shall dwell in the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0761] Isa. 33]. Because we do not pay these, we say: “Forgive us our debts” [Note: [Col. 0761] Matt. 6].

We may understand this bride, whom we have heard keeping new and old fruits for the bridegroom, as the blessed Virgin assumed into heaven by her Son. While she presents to her Son the good deeds which she performed under the Law as old fruits, and those which she performed under grace as new, she says: “I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valleys, and to see whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had budded” [Note: [Col. 0761] Song 6]. The fruits of the valleys are the fruit of humility, which she had under the oldness of the Law; the pomegranates, whose seeds are red, are works of charity which she acquired [Col. 0762C] under the newness of grace. Therefore, lest she seem envious of so great goods, she invites all to receive the gifts of such great grace, saying: “Pass over to me, all who desire me, and be filled from my offspring” [Note: [Col. 0761] Sirach 24].

One who strives to reach the desired goal by running, forgetting what lies behind, stretches forward to what lies ahead [Note: [Col. 0761] Phil. 3]. For the person whose desire is inflamed is not burdened by running through the course until he reaches the prize. Therefore let us not be overcome with weariness, whom the imitation of so great a Virgin cheers. She says: “Pass over to me, all who desire me.” First, one must desire these fruits of the orchard; second, pass over; third, receive fullness: desire them with burning longing, pass over with fervent running, and receive fullness with a rejoicing mind. [Col. 0762D] In the first, the soul suffers languor; in the second, labour; in the third, it receives honour.

Of the first, the bride says: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my Beloved that I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0761] Song 2]. She was in the second when she said: “The watchmen of the city found me; they struck me and wounded me” [Note: [Col. 0761] Song 5]; likewise: “I will rise and go about the city; through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves” [Note: [Col. 0761] Song 3]. Paul was in burning desire when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0761] Phil. 1]. He was in fervent labour when he said: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for Christ [Col. 0763A] in Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0763] Acts 21]; likewise: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course” [Note: [Col. 0763] 2 Tim. 4]. He aspired to the third when he said: “Henceforth a crown of righteousness is laid up for me” [Note: [Col. 0763] Ibid.]; and Mary now rejoices that she is in it, saying: “I sat beneath the shadow of him whom I desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0763] Song 2].

The blessed Virgin ascended thither; hence: “Mary has been assumed into heaven; the angels rejoice, praising and blessing the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0763] Antiphon for the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary]. This assumption is threefold, and on this account we ought to rejoice. Christ was assumed; Mary was assumed; the predestined person will be assumed. Christ by the Father, Mary by the Son, the predestined person by the Judge. Of the first: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had dined with his disciples, was assumed into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0763] Mark 16]; of the second: “Mary was assumed into heaven; the angels rejoice, [Col. 0763B] praising and blessing the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0763] Antiphon for the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary]; of the third: “Two shall be in one bed: one shall be taken and the other left” [Note: [Col. 0763] Luke 17].

Christ’s assumption procured for us the mission of the Holy Spirit; Mary’s assumption makes remembrance of us before Christ; the assumption of the elect receives incorruption. O how the first is to be celebrated, by which the human spirit is renewed by the Holy Spirit! O how the second is to be venerated, by which the sinner is reconciled to God! How the third is to be desired, in which the whole human being is restored! But now let us treat of the second, that of our Virgin, who today offers to her Beloved new and old fruits and thus invites us to emulate her: “Pass over to me, all who desire me” [Note: [Col. 0763] Sirach 24]. But she herself shows why she is to be desired, so that we may follow her form.

[Col. 0763C] “I,” she says, “like a vine have brought forth the sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers are fruits of honour and uprightness” [Note: [Col. 0763] Ibid.]. Hear fragrance, uprightness, honour: the fragrance of good repute; the uprightness of holy conduct; the honour of the flower, namely, the Lord’s Incarnation. Note in the vine fragrance; in the flower, honour and uprightness. She herself was a vine emitting fragrance. Her Son was the flower, conferring honour and uprightness upon his mother. Of the fragrance: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” [Note: [Col. 0763] Song 4]; likewise: “Its inestimable fragrance was very great in her garments” [Note: [Col. 0763] Office of the Church]. Of the fruit of honour:

> You, a mother with virginal honour,  
> Chastely prepared, with sacred womb,  
> A chamber of the breast for the Lord of angels.

[Note: [Col. 0763] Hymn on the Virgin.]

[Col. 0763D] She received uprightness from her Son, namely from Wisdom incarnate, so that she could say: “Many good things came to me together with her, and innumerable riches through her hands” [Note: [Col. 0763] Wis. 7].

Likewise, when a vine is green it produces shoots; when it flowers it drives away serpents; when it bears grapes, and these are pressed in the winepress, it gladdens the human heart [Note: [Col. 0763] Ps. 103]. When it is green through grace, it produces shoots of virtues; when it flowers, it drives away serpents, namely the temptations of demons; when it produces clusters, that is, when it gathers in the unity of faith, it gladdens by hope the hearts of those who doubt, after being pressed out unto the shedding of blood through Passion [Col. 0764A]. Hear of the shoots: “Who is this who comes forth like the dawn rising, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” [Note: [Col. 0763] Song 6].

It flowered with a threefold flower: there was an outward flower, an inward flower, and an upper flower. The first was the holiness of conduct, the second virginity, the third Christ’s humanity. Of the first: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” [Note: [Col. 0763] Song 2]; of the second: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies” [Note: [Col. 0763] Song 7]. The grain of wheat, that is, Christ, was in her womb amid the lilies of holy conduct and virginity. Of the third: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0763] Song 2]. This flower drives away serpents, that is, demons.

Hear of the clusters: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” [Note: [Col. 0763] Acts 4]. Put them in the winepress: “The saints experienced mockeries [Col. 0764B] and blows, moreover also bonds and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted” [Note: [Col. 0763] Heb. 11], etc. Hear the wine of joy: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for him” [Note: [Col. 0763] Acts 5].

Hear further of the shoots, that you may desire great things: “I am the mother of fair love, and fear, and knowledge, and holy hope” [Note: [Col. 0763] Sirach 24]. These shoots put forth abundantly. Hear of the shoot of love: there is carnal love, natural love, and spiritual love. The first is loved by fornicators, the second by relatives, the third by the children of God. The first for the sake of desire or pleasure; the second for the sake of advantage; the third for the purity of the heart. The first has condemnation, the second some slight excuse, the third has reward. Of the [Col. 0764C] first: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” [Note: [Col. 0763] Ps. 4]. Of the second: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have?” [Note: [Col. 0763] Matt. 5]. Of the third: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your mind” [Note: [Col. 0763] Matt. 22], etc. The first is shameful, the second vapid, the third beautiful. Behold the “mother of fair love.”

There follows, “and of fear.” This fear is neither servile nor initial, but filial. The first belongs to sinners, the second to the dead, the third to the perfect. Of the first: “There is no fear in love, because this fear has punishment” [Note: [Col. 0763] 1 John 4]; of the second: “Perfect love casts out fear” [Note: [Col. 0763] Ibid.]; of the third: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever” [Col. 0764D] [Note: [Col. 0763] Ps. 18].

These are the new and old fruits which today the blessed Virgin Mother presents to her Son, fruits which she kept for him by living religiously, conceiving chastely, and giving birth devoutly. Today she presents them after ascending to heaven after him. May Jesus Christ bring us there, “to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen” [Note: [Col. 0763] Rom. 16].

“All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you.”

[CARD.] In this saying the Virgin’s perseverance in good works [Col. 0765A] is shown. Thus she says: O my Beloved, all fruits—all the works of good fragrance which I have done, both old, proceeding from the commandments of the old Law, and new, produced by evangelical precepts—I have kept for you without the stain of infection or the decay of corruption, as welcome gifts of hospitality to be presented. There follows:

## CHAPTER VIII.—“Who will grant me that you might be my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother?”

[THO.] This is the voice of the righteous of old, who believed that the Lord was equal and consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit. They also desired to see him in human form and consubstantial with human beings. Our mother, whose breasts he sucked, is the blessed Virgin—not by nature but by grace—through whom she bore such a brother for us. Or the mother is the Synagogue, in which and from which, through the Virgin, the Beloved assumed human flesh and was nourished in infancy.

Christ is our brother for three reasons: by reason of the flesh he assumed, by reason of religion, and by reason of the inheritance to be shared. Of the first there is no doubt: “For he is our flesh and our brother” [Note: [Col. 0765] Gen. 37]. Of the second: “Whoever,” he says, “does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother and sister and mother” [Note: [Col. 0765] Matt. 7]. Likewise, concerning the apostles: “Tell my brothers,” he says, “that I shall go before you into Galilee” [Note: [Col. 0765] Matt. 28]. Of the third: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined, he made conformable to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” [Note: [Col. 0765] Rom. 8].

He established the first brotherhood [Col. 0765C] in Mary, the second in the Church, the third from the Father in the homeland. For he received from Mary that of which it is said: “He himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” [Note: [Col. 0765] Isa. 53]; while living on the cross, and in the Church, by his grace, “he makes those of one manner dwell in a house” [Note: [Col. 0765] Ps. 67]. According to the third brotherhood, he prepares for us “an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, reserved in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0765] 1 Pet. 1].

Every Christian has three brothers: the first afflicts, the second neglects, the third loves and therefore corrects. The first afflicts through malice; the second neglects through sloth or carnal friendship; the third loves and corrects through abundance of charity. The first is dangerous because false; the second useless because mistaken; the third to be imitated because true. Of the first Paul says [Col. 0765D]: “Danger among false brothers” [Note: [Col. 0765] 2 Cor. 11]. Of the second the Lord says in Genesis: “From the hand of a man and of his brother I shall require your souls” [Note: [Col. 0765] Gen. 9]. Of the third, again the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone” [Note: [Col. 0765] Matt. 18].

Likewise, of the first: “Whoever says that he loves God and hates his brother is a liar” [Note: [Col. 0765] 1 John 2]—“For whoever hates his brother is a murderer” [Note: [Col. 0765] 1 John 3]. Of the second: “Whoever has the substance of the world and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him, how does the Father’s love abide in him?” [Note: [Col. 0765] Ibid.]. There is not only [Col. 0766A] the worldly substance of bodily possession, but also knowledge; for the need to lack spiritual things is greater than the need to lack temporal things. The third is called: “I was a brother of dragons and a companion of ostriches” [Note: [Col. 0765] Job 30].

Joseph had these three kinds of brothers. The first were the sons of the maidservants, who sold him; the second were the sons of Leah, who consented; the third was Benjamin, son of Rachel, his full brother, who mourned his absence with his father. This one was born among us, given to us, and condemned for us: born of a mother, given by the Father, condemned by a brother. Of the first and second: “A child is born to us and a son is given to us” [Note: [Col. 0765] Isa. 9]. Of the third: “Whom the Jews condemned to death” [Note: [Col. 0765] Mark 14]. He was given to us so that we might give ourselves for ourselves, to appease the Father’s wrath; born among us [Col. 0766B] that he might honour the lowliness of our weakness; condemned for us that he might cleanse us from sins, free us from hell, and open the kingdom of the heavenly homeland.

Thus he was born among us as a ransom, given to us as consolation, and condemned for us as a reward. The first, lest we remain hateful to God; the second, lest we be forever confounded by our misery; the third, lest we be captives forever in this exile. Hateful, because “all have sinned and need the grace of God” [Note: [Col. 0765] Rom. 3]; confounded, so that each might say in the distress of his mind: “I have been cast away from before the face of God’s eyes” [Note: [Col. 0765] Ps. 30]; captive, so that the despairing person might say: “I shall go to the gates of hell” [Note: [Col. 0765] Isa. 48].

This brother, thus given, born, and condemned, is said to suck the breasts of our mother. There are four kinds of breasts. The first breasts are Gentiles and Jews; the second, the Lord’s disciples, such as the apostles; the third, the breasts of Sacred Scripture; the fourth, arguments for falsehood. Of the first: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe deer” [Note: [Col. 0765] Song 4]; of the second: “Your breasts are better than wine” [Note: [Col. 0765] Song 1]; of the third Solomon says: “Whoever presses the breasts firmly to draw forth milk produces butter” [Note: [Col. 0765] Prov. 30]; of the fourth Job says: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why, when I came from the womb, did I not perish at once? Why was I received upon knees? Why was I nursed at breasts?” [Note: [Col. 0765] Job 3]?

Christ is therefore nourished from the first breasts, a little child from the second, one advanced in age from the third, and one led astray from the fourth. Christ, lest the instruction of childhood appear to be despised by him; the little child, that he may be instructed in faith and morals; the person advanced in age, that the secret sacraments of the Church may be understood; the deceived person, that he may flatter himself about impurity [Col. 0766D]. Therefore Christ’s mother is the Church of Gentiles and Jews, whose breasts he sucked when, sitting among the teachers, he listened to them and questioned them [Note: [Col. 0765] Luke 2], though he was not ignorant.

It should be noted that Christ sucked the breasts of his mother, pressed the breasts of Scripture, and poured into the breasts of the disciples. He sucked, that he might be nourished with the milk of bodily food; he pressed out the milk of wisdom; he poured in the milk of grace. Of the first: “The Virgin alone nursed at her breast, filled from heaven, the very King of angels” [Note: [Col. 0765] Office of the Church]. Of the second: “He opened the disciples’ understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” [Note: [Col. 0765] Luke 27].

[Col. 0767A] He interpreted to the disciples travelling to Emmaus, “beginning with Moses and all the prophets” [Note: [Col. 0767] Luke 27]. He poured out milk because, seated upon the mountain, he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0767] Matt. 5], etc. It will not be useless to pursue the milk of these breasts.

Now those poor in possessions are of many kinds. Some accuse God in their hearts because of the affliction of poverty; others are even-minded in the acquisition of possessions; others take poverty upon themselves by their own deliberate resolve. The first blame God for their want; the second give thanks for their need; the third cut back even what nature requires. Among the first was Job’s wife, when she said to her husband: “Bless God and die” [Note: [Col. 0767] Job 2], because, as the poet says [Note: [Col. 0767] Juvenal III, 152]:

> [Col. 0767B] Unhappy poverty has nothing harsher in it  
> Than that it makes people ridiculous.

To such persons it is said:

> Remember to bear the burden of poverty patiently.

Among the second was Job, when he said: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away” [Note: [Col. 0767] Job 1], etc. Among the third was Paul, when he said: “To this present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poor, we are beaten with fists” [Note: [Col. 0767] 1 Cor. 4]; likewise: “We are in want, but not reduced to destitution” [Note: [Col. 0767] 2 Cor. 4].

You have heard how the first is ruinous and wretched, the second burdensome and secure, the third fruitful and praiseworthy. Of the first, in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0767] ch. 3]: “You say, ‘I am rich and need nothing,’ though you are wretched and poor and blind and naked and miserable.” Of the second [Col. 0767C] Jerome says: “The poor man, rich in an exalted conscience, sleeps more securely on the ground than the wealthy man in purple amid gold.” Of the third: “Though Christ was rich, for our sake he became poor, that through his poverty we might become rich” [Note: [Col. 0767] 2 Cor. 8]. Such people say: “Lord, behold, we have left all things and followed you” [Note: [Col. 0767] Matt. 19]; this is praiseworthy. Hear the fruit: “You who have followed me, who have left all things, shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ibid.]. This is poverty of possessions.

But poverty of spirit is better. Those who possess it first strive to regard their sins as grave, to diminish their virtues in their own estimation, and to regard their own person as worthless. In the first presumption is avoided, in the second self-exaltation, in the third ambition. The first say: “I have sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea.” [Col. 0767D] The second say with Job: “Behold, there is no help for me in myself” [Note: [Col. 0767] Job 6]; likewise: “You do not go forth, O God, in our powers” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 43]. If the third are called to a share in a task of responsibility, they plead their own insufficiency, saying: “I am not a physician, and there is neither bread nor clothing in my house” [Note: [Col. 0767] Isa. 3]. I am not a physician to heal, bread to instruct, or clothing of upright conduct to give an outward example. Behold one drop of milk. Another follows:

[Col. 0768A] “Blessed are the meek” [Note: [Col. 0767] Matt. 5]. There is a meekness given by nature; there is one which follows peace; and there is one which grows amid the pressure of tribulation. The first is preparation for virtue, the second its beginning, the third its perfection. Of the first: “He will teach the meek his ways” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 24]; likewise: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 131]. Of the second: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0767] Matt. 11]; and: “He was the meekest of all men who are upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0767] Num. 12]. Of the third: “Like a lamb led to slaughter, he did not open his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0767] Acts 8]; hence: “He will guide the meek in judgment; he will teach the gentle his ways” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 24]. There follows the third drop:

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Note: [Col. 0767] Matt. 5]. There is mourning of compunction, mourning of desire, and [Col. 0768B] mourning of love. First we ought to weep for our own sins; second, for the misfortunes of others; third, for the eternal life which we desire. Of the first: “Every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 6]. Of the second: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep over the slain of the daughter of my people?” [Note: [Col. 0767] Jer. 9]. Of the third: “My tears were bread to me day and night” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 41]. There follows the fourth drop:

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” [Note: [Col. 0767] Matt. 5]. There is a threefold righteous person: one who “will spring up like a lily” [Note: [Col. 0767] Hos. 14]; one who “will flourish like a palm tree” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 91]; and one who, “if overtaken by death, shall be at rest” [Note: [Col. 0767] Wis. 4]. Let the first be the righteous person who “lives by faith” [Note: [Col. 0767] Gal. 3]; [Col. 0768C] the second, one who “will not be grieved, whatever may happen to him” [Note: [Col. 0767] Prov. 12]; the third, one who “is confident like a lion” [Note: [Col. 0767] Prov. 28].

The first “will spring up like a lily”: from the pallor of penitence, which is in the root, to the greenness of virtues; from greenness to the whiteness of innocence; from innocence to golden charity; from charity to the fear of God. The second “will flourish like a palm tree,” one who “will not be grieved, whatever may happen to him,” because, just as the palm does not lose its greenness either in winter or in summer, so this person does not lose virtue either in prosperity or adversity. The third, “if the righteous person is overtaken by death, he shall be at rest”: those who, while preaching righteousness, are killed for its sake will pass to the life where they shall be satisfied. Its fifth drop:

[Col. 0768D] “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” [Note: [Col. 0767] Matt. 5]. The merciful are those who perform the six works of mercy which we have frequently stated and therefore passed over briefly: namely, feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger in hospitality, consoling the sorrowful, visiting the sick and imprisoned, and burying the dead. For this mercy on earth they will obtain mercy in heaven. Hence: “Lord, your mercy is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0767] Ps. 35]. The sixth drop:

[Col. 0769A] “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God [Note: [Col. 0769] Matt. 5].” In the heart there are ugliness, weakness, and uncleanness: ugliness of thoughts, weakness of pleasures, and uncleanness of deeds. Of the first it may be said: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved [Note: [Col. 0769] Song 4]”; the second says: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed [Note: [Col. 0769] Jer. 27]”; of the third: “The soul that sins shall itself die [Note: [Col. 0769] Ezek. 18].” In the first case, “Dead flies spoil the sweetness of ointment [Note: [Col. 0769] Eccl. 10]”; in the second, “Little foxes destroy the vineyards [Note: [Col. 0769] Song 2]”; in the third, serpents poison the children of Israel [Note: [Col. 0769] Num. 21].” But if these things are removed, they will be pure in heart, and thus they shall see the Lord. It follows:

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God [Note: [Col. 0769] Matt. 5].” These are, first, those turning back from their own anger; secondly, [Col. 0769B] those enduring sufferings for Christ; thirdly, those making peace among the discordant. The first are sinners, the second patient persons, the third peacemakers; and thus they shall be called sons of God. It follows:

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake [Note: [Col. 0769] Ibid.].” This is righteousness: that you provide your body with necessities, your soul with spiritual things, your neighbor with counsel and assistance, and God with fear, love, and honor. Of the first: “Food, a staff, and a burden for an ass [Note: [Col. 0769] Ecclus. 33].” Of the second: “Have mercy on your own soul by pleasing God [Note: [Col. 0769] Ecclus. 30].” Of one’s neighbor: “If a person is overtaken in any offence, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of gentleness [Note: [Col. 0769] Gal. 6].” Of God: “Fear God and keep his commandments [Note: [Col. 0769] Eccl. 12].” Again: “You shall love [Col. 0769C] the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself [Note: [Col. 0769] Matt. 22].” Again: “Honor the Lord with your substance [Note: [Col. 0769] Prov. 3].” Because the blessed suffer persecution for this righteousness, the Lord, preaching these things, poured grace into the minds of the apostles so that they might preach the kingdom of heaven. May Jesus Christ deign to bring us to it, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

*Would that I might find you outside and kiss you, and that now no one might despise me.*

[THO.] For the Beloved was within, since “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God [Note: [Col. 0769] John 1].” But in order that he might be found outside, “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us [Note: [Col. 0769] Ibid.].” [Col. 0769D] The patriarchs and prophets saw him within by contemplation, not with the eye of flesh; the faithful were able to say: “We have found the Messiah, who is called Christ [Note: [Col. 0769] Ibid.].” For what he says aptly suits such persons: “Would that I might find you outside and kiss you.” Those who saw him face to face and spoke to him mouth to mouth kissed him when found, so that what was asked at the beginning of this Song might occur: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”; and now let no one despise me, as formerly when I was little, because God was known only in Judaea [Note: [Col. 0769] Ps. 75]. But now, [Col. 0770A] appearing outside, God is known everywhere, because “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth [Note: [Col. 0769] Ps. 18].”

Even to the angels human nature seems more precious than before. Prior to Christ’s coming they permitted themselves to be worshipped by human beings, but afterwards they did not, because he said to John: “See that you do not do this [Note: [Col. 0769] Rev. 19].” Three things are proposed: finding, kissing, and release from contempt. The first occurred in the Incarnation; the second, in the sending of the Holy Spirit; the third will occur at the final judgment. In the first is the gift of knowledge; in the second, the pledge of intimacy and honor; in the third, the magnificence of honor. Hence that father recognized his prodigal son when he found him; offering him a kiss, he showed a sign of love and intimacy; clothing him in the first robe and making a banquet for him, he honored him [Note: [Col. 0769] Luke 15]. Thus the disciples [Col. 0770B] recognized the Lord in the breaking of bread [Note: [Col. 0769] Luke 24]. “Have I been with you so long,” he says, “and have you not known me? [Note: [Col. 0769] John 14].” Hear of love and intimacy: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him [Note: [Col. 0769] Ibid.].” Of the third: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored [Note: [Col. 0769] Ps. 138],” and: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him [Note: [Col. 0769] John 12].”

This Beloved is sometimes found inwardly, sometimes outside, sometimes above. Inwardly, in the obscurity of the prophets; outside, in the flesh he assumed; above, with the Father in majesty.
