Of the first it is said: “We found him in the fields of the forest [Note: [Col. 0769] Ps. 131].” Of the second: “We have found the Messiah [Note: [Col. 0769] John 1],” and, as the prophets said, “We have found Jesus of Nazareth [Note: [Col. 0769] Ibid.].” [Col. 0770C] Of the third: “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord [Note: [Col. 0769] Ps. 131].”

John the Evangelist knew these discoveries. Of the first he says: “The light shines in the darkness [Note: [Col. 0769] John 1],” that is, Christ, light amid the obscure prophets; of the second: “The Word was made flesh [Note: [Col. 0769] Ibid.]”; of the third: “In the beginning 161 was the Word [Note: [Col. 0769] Ibid.].” The Bride received his kiss in the sending of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit was given for three purposes: the remission of sins, strength, and the working of miracles.

Hence the Lord breathed upon the apostles, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them [Note: [Col. 0769] John 20]”; this occurs for us in baptism. He was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands: [Col. 0770D] this occurs for us in confirmation, for strength. He was given to the apostles on the day of Pentecost for the performance of miracles. These are the three kisses which the Beloved gave the Bride as a pledge of love: the first, that she might be reconciled; the second, that she might be strong; the third, that she might be admirable and beautiful—reconciled from sins, strong against the assault of temptation, admirable and beautiful through miracles.

The father gave the first kiss to reconcile the prodigal son [Note: [Col. 0769] Luke 15]. Jacob gave the second to his father Isaac, when, because of his [Isaac’s] enfeebled strength, [Col. 0771A] he gave him food [Note: [Col. 0771] Gen. 27]. Rachel gave the third, and because she was beautiful she entered into his marriage [Note: [Col. 0771] Gen. 29]. Afterwards, lest she be despised, he will honor her. The Lord honors his friends in the world, honors them at judgment, and honors them in the kingdom: in the world, by gathering them among Christ’s soldiers; at judgment, by separating them from the servants of the devil; in the kingdom, by placing them at God’s right hand. Of the first: “Glory and honor and peace to every human soul that works what is good [Note: [Col. 0771] Rom. 2].” Of the second: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him [Note: [Col. 0771] John 12].” Of the third: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored [Note: [Col. 0771] Ps. 138].”

This threefold finding also occurs morally. The soul likewise finds him now inwardly, now outwardly, now above: inwardly through the sweetness of devotion; outwardly through the form of religious life; above through the joy of certain recompense. Hence in the third chapter [Col. 0771B] of this Song the finding of the Bridegroom is treated. Of the first it is said: “A little after I had passed by, I found him whom my soul loves [Note: [Col. 0771] Song 3].” But, in order to attain the third, she adds: “I shall not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me [Note: [Col. 0771] Ibid.]”; afterward I shall find him in his glory. Of the second it is said here: “Would that I might find you outside,” that is, that when I have outwardly learned the form of your religious life, I may be able to imitate you. Of the third: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love [Note: [Col. 0771] Song 5].” For the beloved asks holy souls that through their guidance she may be led to behold God’s face.

It follows: “That I might kiss you.” There is a kiss for the remission [Col. 0771C] of offence; a kiss for attaining a thing desired; and a kiss in thanksgiving. The first is so that sins may be forgiven; the second, so that spiritual gifts may be bestowed; the third shows how great the gifts received are. Mary Magdalene offered the first at the Lord’s feet [Note: [Col. 0771] Luke 8]. Jacob gave the second to his father Isaac, that he might give him a blessing of the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven [Note: [Col. 0771] Gen. 27]. Dying Jacob gave the third to his son Joseph, as though returning thanks to him because he had supported him in the time of famine [Note: [Col. 0771] Gen. 49]. And by the merit of the three kisses, “now let no one despise me.” For people are usually despised because of an offence in their own person, which the first kiss remits; or because of poverty, which the second kiss relieves; or because of ingratitude, which the third [Col. 0771D] kiss redeems. Therefore this is the reason why she ought not to be despised: namely, because she has obtained these kisses.

David desired this finding, kissing, and exaltation when he said: “Appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh [Note: [Col. 0771] Ps. 79].” Appear before Ephraim, whose name means “fruitfulness,” that I may produce worthy fruits of repentance. Appear before Benjamin [Note: [Col. 0771] Ps. 79], whose name means “son of the right hand,” that, believing you through miracles to be the Son of God, I may kiss you with the affection called forth by your presence. Appear before Manasseh, whose name means “forgetfulness,” that, having forgotten temporal misery, [Col. 0772A] I may be honored because of hope in future glory.

It should be noted that on the day of the Epiphany he appeared to us in three ways: in the manger, in baptism, and at the wedding feast. In the first, by the illumination of the star [Note: [Col. 0771] Matt. 2]; in the second, by the manifestation of the whole Trinity [Note: [Col. 0771] Matt. 3]; in the third, by the transformation of water into wine [Note: [Col. 0771] John 2]. In the first it was shown that he had come to enlighten us to know sin and to produce the fruit of repentance; in the second, that he might reconcile us to the whole Trinity; in the third, that “this mortal” might “put on immortality” [Note: [Col. 0771] 1 Cor. 15]. Of the first: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women [Note: [Col. 0771] Song 1],” etc.; again: “Do repentance [Note: [Col. 0771] Matt. 3].” Of the second: “I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction [Note: [Col. 0771] Jer. 29].” For the Lord restores peace, reconciling things below with things above in himself. Of the third: “This corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal [Col. 0772B] immortality [Note: [Col. 0771] 1 Cor. 15].” Thus “he will reform the body of our lowliness, made conformable to the body of his glory [Note: [Col. 0771] Phil. 3].”

We have obtained the first through Ephraim, whose name means “fruitfulness,” that is, through the fruit of repentance; the second through Benjamin, whose name means “son of the right hand,” namely through the performance of works; the third through Manasseh, whose name means “forgetfulness,” namely through forgetting temporal things. Let him therefore first appear before Ephraim, that we may bring forth worthy fruits of repentance. “Great,” says the Apostle, “is the mystery of godliness: which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, believed in the world, and received up into glory [Note: [Col. 0771] 1 Tim. 3].” Behold Christ in the manger, called the mystery [Col. 0772C] that was manifested in flesh—in the manger; justified in spirit, since by divinity he was without sin; appeared to angels, that is, manifesting himself to the apostles, as an example that we should bring forth worthy fruits of repentance. Let us be justified in spirit by contrition of flesh. Let us appear to angels—that is, to priests—by confession; let us be manifested in flesh by bodily satisfaction. For thus he will appear before Ephraim.

O truly great mystery of godliness, through which the unclean received purity, the slave freedom, and the miserable happiness: purity from the dregs of sin, freedom from the yoke of the devil, happiness from the calamity of this exile. Of the first: “For he shall save his people from their sins [Note: [Col. 0771] Matt. 1].” Of the second: “If the Son of God has set you free, you shall be truly free [Col. 0772D] [Note: [Col. 0771] John 8].” Of the third: “Those whom he foreknew, he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son [Note: [Col. 0771] Rom. 8].” Behold, he appeared before Ephraim.

Let him appear before Benjamin, whose name means “son of the right hand,” through spiritual works. In baptism, that is, when the heart has been purified, let the whole Trinity appear in order to help Benjamin to act. For in works it is necessary that the worker know, will, and be able. The first makes the work ordered; the second, voluntary; the third, perfect. For the first, the Son will assist with wisdom; for the second, the Spirit [Col. 0773A] with goodwill; for the third, the Father with foreknowledge. Otherwise, concerning the first, it will be said: “He was unwilling to understand so as to do good [Note: [Col. 0773] Ps. 35].” Concerning the second: “The sluggard would not plough because of the cold; therefore he shall beg in summer, and it shall not be given him [Note: [Col. 0773] Prov. 20].” Concerning the third: “This man began to build and was not able to finish [Note: [Col. 0773] Luke 14].”

Therefore the Son gives understanding, the Holy Spirit the affection of love, and the Father confirms the result. Ephraim, then, has the fruit of repentance and virtues; but Benjamin should carry their works through. Yet there are works of beasts, works of human beings, works of angels, and a divine work. The first is for the body’s need; the second, for the spirit’s benefit; the third, for delight; the fourth has perfect charity. The first is animal, the second spiritual, the third spiritual [*spiritale*, in a distinct sense], the fourth [Col. 0773B] wonderful. Of the first the Lord says: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you [Note: [Col. 0773] Ps. 127].” Of the second: “Work while it is day [Note: [Col. 0773] Ecclus. 51].” Of the third: “Admonishing yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs [Note: [Col. 0773] Col. 3].” Of the fourth: “He who believes in me shall also do the works that I do [Note: [Col. 0773] John 14].” These are the four works of virtues, whence the prophet: “Under their wings there were human hands in four parts [Note: [Col. 0773] Ezek. 1].”

Behold, “the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared [Note: [Col. 0773] Titus 3].” O how great is the kindness that gave the Son, gave the Spirit, gave himself, gave us temporal goods, gave spiritual goods, gave eternal goods. Temporal goods, because those who fear God lack nothing [Note: [Col. 0773] Ps. 33]; spiritual goods, [Col. 0773C] because “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights [Note: [Col. 0773] Jas. 1]”; eternal goods, because “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what he has prepared for those who love him [Note: [Col. 0773] 1 Cor. 2].”

Therefore the grace of God appeared to humanity, teaching us to be Manasseh. For, after the fruits of repentance and the works of virtues, a person ought to forget sin, forget the world, and forget himself: the desire of sin, the care of the world, and care for his own body. Of the first two: “Forget your people and your father’s house [Note: [Col. 0773] Gen. 12].” Of the third the Lord says: “Whoever has forgotten his garment, let him not return to take it up [Note: [Col. 0773] Matt. 24].”

The Beloved, therefore, is found outside with Ephraim through penitential satisfaction; with Benjamin he is kissed [Col. 0773D] through prayer, praise, and preaching; with Manasseh, through forgetting temporal things, so that no one may despise the Bride because of any defilement from earthly things. Thus with Ephraim let her say: “I am black but beautiful [Note: [Col. 0773] Song 1]”; again: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0773] Ps. 51]”; again: “I, like a vine, have borne the sweetness of fragrance [Note: [Col. 0773] Ecclus. 24].” With Benjamin she kisses him in praise, prayer, and preaching, so that he himself, having been kissed, may say: “Your lips, Bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue [Note: [Col. 0773] Song 4].” With Manasseh he has been found; therefore, “let no one despise me,” says the Bride, because there he presents the Bride glorious, [Col. 0774A] without spot or wrinkle [Note: [Col. 0773] Eph. 5]. Rather, let her say: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun? [Note: [Col. 0773] Song 6]” Who is this who ascends from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her Beloved? Our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

*Who will grant me, etc.*

[CARD.] In this chapter the mother shows her desire concerning her Son, her desire concerning the preservation of the remnant of the Jewish people. She says therefore: “Who will grant you to me as my brother”—a brother in human nature; likewise in legal teaching, whence she adds: “Sucking the breasts of my mother,” that is, of the Law or the Synagogue. Christ then sucked its breasts when he fulfilled in himself the Law’s ordinances [*incramenta*, probably “precepts/requirements”], [Col. 0774B] when he questioned the teachers who were the breasts of the Synagogue. “Who,” I say, “will grant me to find you alone outside and kiss you?” She desires to find him alone, namely in his divine nature, in which he is alone and has no human companionship. She desires to find him so that she may know him not merely in the prison-house of flesh, but may find the immensity of deity, which is enclosed by no boundary and contains and encompasses all things. She desires so to find him that she may kiss him: namely, that seeing him present, as it were face to face [Note: [Col. 0773] 1 Cor. 13], she may delight in his love.

Having said these things concerning what she desires in her Son, she shows her desire for the conversion of her people. Thus connect the wording: “And who will grant that now [Col. 0774C] no one may despise me?” For indeed the blessed Virgin is still despised by unbelieving Jews, since they do not believe her to be the mother of God, but blaspheme her as the mother of a sinful man. She herself shows how or when this will happen—that no one may then despise her. It is as if she said: “I shall seize you by the force of my prayers and lead you into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her who bore me [Note: [Col. 0773] Song 3],” as was explained above. And after I have brought you in, from then on the Jew, having become faithful from unbelieving, will not despise me; for whoever honors the Son honors the Mother also. It follows:

*I shall seize you and lead you into my mother’s house. There you will teach me, and I shall give you a cup of spiced wine and new wine from my pomegranates.*

[THO.] I shall receive one who comes with ready and faithful [Col. 0774D] devotion, and with every desire embrace your instructions. You also, returning to heaven after the dispensation of the flesh has been accomplished, I shall lead with joyful lights and proclaim with joyful voice before all. The house of Mother Church is the blessedness of the eternal homeland, where that portion called the mother is already present. The Church militant always strives to lead the Beloved there—not by its own strength, but by whatever devotion, prayers, and proclamations it is able, preaching that this is to be accomplished.

“There you will teach me” the precepts of the Gospel. Or, in that heavenly Church after judgment, you will show us all things that are now obscure to us. “And I shall give you a cup of spiced wine”: she gives him this cup [Col. 0775A] when, for benefits received, she returns to him the grace of love. Nor is it pure wine, but wine spiced by the testimony of good works. And because there are those who shed their blood for Christ, namely martyrs, she adds: “and new wine from my pomegranates,” which by their redness signify the blood of martyrs. *Malagranata* are the same as *punica* [pomegranates], but are called *granata* because of their multitude of seeds, and *punica* from their country, namely Africa.

But who are you, that you should seize the incomprehensible One? Yet because he took hold of the seed of Abraham, and not of angels, you trust that in the flesh in which he took hold of it, you can take hold of him. First, therefore, detect; secondly, rebuke; thirdly, take hold. After these things you will be able to seize him. First detect sin, secondly rebuke what has been detected, [Col. 0775B] thirdly take hold of what has been rebuked. Detect by knowing, rebuke by confessing, take hold by curbing. Thus Pharaoh, Sarah’s abductor, detected Sarah’s lie, because she had said that she was Abraham’s sister: “Remember,” he says, “that you have been found out [Note: [Col. 0775] Gen. 20].” Of the second Job says: “I rebuke myself, and do penance in ashes and dust [Note: [Col. 0775] Job 42].” Of the third: “Their foot was caught in this snare which they hid [Note: [Col. 0775] Ps. 9].” Now you can seize his humanity, so that afterwards you may seize his divinity.

Therefore, first seize the diligence of his work; secondly, seize his discipline; thirdly, his righteousness. The first is for driving away idleness, the second for strength against laxity, the third [Col. 0775C] as an adornment for receiving the Beloved worthily. The strong woman performed the first energetically, for “her fingers seized the spindle [Note: [Col. 0775] Prov. 31].” Of the second David says: “Lay hold of discipline [Note: [Col. 0775] Ps. 2],” etc. Of the third: “Whoever keeps righteousness shall lay hold of it [Note: [Col. 0775] Ecclus. 15].” He provided us an example of the first in his life, of the second in his Passion, and of the third in his Resurrection.

Again, we seize him in our heart, we seize him in the sacrament, and we seize him in the kingdom: in the heart, through desire; in the sacrament, in order that he may diminish sin and increase merit; in the kingdom, that he may be the reward of labor. Again, with respect to divinity we presume in some measure to seize him: first through reason, secondly [Col. 0775D] through devotion, thirdly through revelation divinely inspired. The first draws us to some small knowledge of him, the second to love, the third to wonder. The first comes by considering creatures; the second by resting in him; the third by contemplating his great works. Of the first: “The invisible things of God are understood and seen through the things that have been made, from the creation of God [Note: [Col. 0775] Rom. 1].” The second says: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and rest? [Note: [Col. 0775] Ps. 54]” For doves have wings, namely virtues joined with simplicity, by which one ascends to devotion, [Col. 0776A] in which one rests. But since in the third it is not so much one’s own virtue as the divine power that raises one to wonder—where one’s own wings do not suffice—God spreads out his wings, receives him, and bears him upon his shoulders [Note: [Col. 0775] Deut. 32]. In this apprehension, indeed, “The Lord alone was his guide, and set him upon the high land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields, suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone [Note: [Col. 0775] Ibid.],” that is, delighting in the richness and sweetness of heavenly things. Thus, having seized him, she leads him into her mother’s house.

I believe that this is that sevenfold woman of whom Isaiah says: “Seven women shall seize one man, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over [Col. 0776B] us; take away our reproach’ [Note: [Col. 0775] Isa. 4].” This man is Christ, whence: “A woman shall encompass a man [Note: [Col. 0775] Jer. 31].” He is called “one” antonomastically—that is, by eminence above all others.

These seven women signify the Church, which is virgin; and therefore it is denoted by the number seven, which is a virgin number, because beneath the first limit it alone neither begets nor is begotten. He was detected, grasped, and seized: detected by the patriarchs, grasped by the prophets, seized by the apostles; first through faith, secondly through revelation, thirdly through the Incarnation. As a figure of the first, one of the two women disputing before Solomon detected that her son was not dead but alive [Note: [Col. 0775] 3 Kings 3]: that is, the Church from the patriarchs, [believed] Christ would rise from the dead, [Col. 0776C] whereas the Church from the Jews [held him] perpetually dead. Of the second: “The ploughman shall overtake the reaper [Note: [Col. 0775] Amos 9].” The ploughmen are the prophets; the reaper is Christ. Of the third the Bride says: “I shall climb the palm tree and seize its fruits [Note: [Col. 0775] Song 7].” Thus this sevenfold woman seizes him: renewed by seven sacraments, strengthened by seven virtues, and governed by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Thus he too seized us. “For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham [Note: [Col. 0775] Heb. 2].” He seized us by taking an animate body. He [took hold of] us when he bestowed his divinity upon us. Here he suffered four harms, which, in order to repair them, he wishes to be apprehended: hunger’s lack of food, want of clothing, diminution [Col. 0776D] of the head, and the crime of injured majesty. By the first all were weak, by the second ashamed, by the third erring, by the fourth marked by public disgrace. Of the first two Isaiah says: “I am not a healer, and there is neither bread nor clothing in my house [Note: [Col. 0775] Isa. 3].” Again, of the first: “All my people groaning and seeking bread [Note: [Col. 0775] Lam. 1],” and: “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them [Note: [Col. 0775] Lam. 4].” Of the second: “You are wretched and poor, blind and naked and miserable [Note: [Col. 0775] Rev. 3].” Of the third: “Their enemies became the head [Note: [Col. 0775] Lam. 1].” Of the fourth: “All who glorified [Col. 0777A] her despised her, because they saw her shame [Note: [Col. 0777] Lam. 1].”

But Isaiah says that at Christ’s coming we recover these things. Of the first: “He who gives seed to the sower shall also give bread to eat [Note: [Col. 0777] Isa. 55].” Of the second: “Arise, arise, put on the garments of your glory [Note: [Col. 0777] Isa. 52].” Of the third: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar [Note: [Col. 0777] Isa. 30].” Of the fourth: “On that day you shall not be ashamed because of all your abominations by which you transgressed against me [Note: [Col. 0777] Ezek. 9].” And Virgil, prophesying Christ’s Nativity [Note: [Col. 0777] Eclogue IV]:

> Gradually the field shall grow yellow with soft ears of grain,  
> and the red grape shall hang from uncultivated brambles,  
> and hard oaks shall sweat dewy honey.

Of the second:

> The ram himself [lacuna] in the meadows [lacuna]  
>   
> [lacuna] shall change his fleeces from mud.  
>   
> [Col. 0777B] Of its own accord crimson dye shall clothe the feeding lambs.

Of the third:

> [lacuna] Assyrian amomum shall spring up everywhere.  
> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.

Of the fourth:

> Under your leadership, if any traces of our crime remain,  
> they shall become void, freeing the lands from perpetual fear.

According to the Gospel, there are three loaves; hence: “Friend, lend me three loaves [Note: [Col. 0777] Luke 11].” The first is that of tearful contrition, the second of teaching, the third of the Eucharist. The first feeds the weak, the second strengthens those fleeing the world, and the third confirms those serving in God’s army: so that the first may be refreshed, the second may advance, and the third may not fail. Of the first: “You shall feed us with the bread of tears [Note: [Col. 0777] Ps. 79].” Of the second: “You who inhabit the land [Col. 0777C] of the south, meet the fugitive with loaves [Note: [Col. 0777] Isa. 21].” Of the third: “Bread may strengthen the human heart [Note: [Col. 0777] Ps. 103].”

The angel brought Elijah the first under a juniper tree with water [Note: [Col. 0777] 3 Kings 19]. The table of proposition possesses the second, which belongs to priests alone [Note: [Col. 0777] Num. 4]. The third was the hearth-cake given to the prophet by the woman of Zarephath [Note: [Col. 0777] 3 Kings 17]. The bread which is Christ was the price on the cross, provisions on pilgrimage, and humanity’s reward in the kingdom. Of the first, when he gave it to his disciples, he said: “Eat: this is my body, which shall be given for you [Note: [Col. 0777] Matt. 26].” Of the second: “Give us this day our daily bread [Note: [Col. 0777] Matt. 6].” Of the third: “Man ate the bread of angels [Note: [Col. 0777] Ps. 77].”

The first was bran bread, because of the likeness of sinful flesh; the second, barley bread, [Col. 0777D] because of the misery of the world; the third, fine wheaten bread, because it was without the bran of vice and sin. Of this fine flour the Law commands a threefold sacrifice to be made: from an oven, from a griddle, and from a frying pan. The first, from the oven, was in the conception, because he was conceived in his mother’s womb by the fire of the Holy Spirit. The second, from the griddle, was because he was cooked by the fire of tribulation on the gibbet of the cross. The third, from the frying pan, was because, cooked by the fire of charity in the oil of gladness, he rose joyfully from the tomb. “Behold the bread that descends from [Col. 0778A] heaven and gives life to the world [Note: [Col. 0777] John 6].”—“Eat, friends, and be intoxicated, beloved ones [Note: [Col. 0777] Song 5].”—For blessed is the one who shall eat this bread in the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0777] Luke 14].

It follows: clothing. There is a threefold garment. The first is that of religious conduct; the second, of strong virtue; the third, of splendor. We use the first in the cloister, the second in battle, the third at a feast. The first is because of nakedness, the second against the attacks of enemies, the third for joy. Of the first John says in the Apocalypse: “I advise you to buy gold tried and pure, that you may become rich, and to put on white garments because of the shame of your nakedness [Note: [Col. 0777] Rev. 3].” Of the second the Apostle says: “Put on the armor of faith, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil [Note: [Col. 0777] Eph. 6].” Of the third [Col. 0778B] it is read that Judith the widow, about to go to the camp of Holofernes, “put on the garments of her joy [Note: [Col. 0777] Jud. 10].”

The first garment is of haircloth, the second of iron, the third of purple and linen. According to the first, the Ninevites clothed themselves in sacks at Jonah’s preaching [Note: [Col. 0777] Jon. 3]. The Lord clothed Adam and Eve, because they were naked, in tunics of skins [Note: [Col. 0777] Gen. 3]. According to the second, “Judas Maccabaeus put on a breastplate like a giant, and protected the camp with his sword [Note: [Col. 0777] 1 Macc. 3].” According to the third, of the strong woman: “Purple and linen are her clothing, and she shall laugh on the last day [Note: [Col. 0777] Prov. 31].”

According to the first, Christ at his birth was found in the manger in lowly swaddling-clothes [Note: [Col. 0777] Luke 2]. According to the second, in his Passion he was clothed in a scarlet cloak, which is the color of blood [Note: [Col. 0777] Matt. 27]. According to the third, in the Transfiguration he was shown in a white garment like [Col. 0778C] snow [Note: [Col. 0777] Matt. 27]; and also in his own flesh. For at the Nativity he was “made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man [Note: [Col. 0777] Phil. 2]”; in the Passion, in a sack cut apart by death; in the Resurrection, beautiful in a robe—namely, the robe in which he reigns in heaven.

Let us therefore be clothed, first in garments of repentance, secondly in garments of warfare; thirdly we shall be clothed in garments of glory. But lest we be *acephali*, that is, without a head, the name of the Lord must be invoked over us [Note: [Col. 0777] Isa. 4]. There are three such names: the first, Christ; the second, Jesus; the third, Son. He had the first in the world, he will have the second at judgment, and the third in the kingdom. Invoked through the first, he came to us; through the second, called as advocate, he will stand for us at judgment; through the third, called back, he will transfer us into the kingdom, [Col. 0778D] where he will receive us as fellow-heirs. Of the first: “The remnant of Israel shall call upon the name of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0777] Zeph. 3].” Of the second: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous [Note: [Col. 0777] 1 John 2].” Of the third the Bride says: “Return, my beloved [Note: [Col. 0777] Song 2].”

Through the first he endured with us the tribulation of the world; through the second he will plead our cause before the Father; through the third he will receive us as companions into the inheritance. Of the first: “When I called, you heard me, O God of my righteousness; in tribulation you enlarged me [Note: [Col. 0777] Ps. 4].” Of the second: “We have an advocate [Col. 0779A] with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins [Note: [Col. 0779] 1 John 2].” Of the third: “Return, my beloved; be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of Bether [Note: [Col. 0779] Song 2].” Therefore “seek the Lord while he may be found, while he is near [Note: [Col. 0779] Isa. 55].” Behold, the diminution of the head has been removed, because “your name has been invoked over us; yet do not abandon us, O Lord our God [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 37],” because reproach still remains. Therefore “take away reproach [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 118].”

There are three kinds of reproach: the first, of temporal punishment; the second, of iniquity; the third, of everlasting calamity. The righteous endure the first patiently, the wicked the second shamelessly, the condemned the third without cease. The first, because they await their reward; the second, because they do not fear [Col. 0779B] God’s judgment; the third, because they did not seek a remedy for sin. Of the first: “We have become a reproach to our neighbours, a mockery and derision to those around us” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 78]. Of the second David says: “Cut off my reproach, which I have feared” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 118]. Of the third it is said: “He struck his enemies on their hind parts; he gave them everlasting reproach” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 77]. But Christ removed all these things. For he lessened the first when he assumed it in the virginal womb. He erased the second in baptism, which was falsely laid upon him because of the likeness of sinful flesh. The third he shall not know at all, and he shall turn it away from the righteous by the reproach of the cross.

If you cast the first against him, he himself replies: “And for your sake I became greatly a reproach to my neighbours, and a terror to those known to me” [Col. 0779C] [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 88]. Against the second he says: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the rejection of the people” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 21]. And, in order to turn away the third, he says: “Father, zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 68]. Therefore he takes away the last through the shame of the cross, the second through mercy, and has changed the first into glory for the righteous.

It should be noted that one finds the house of the father, the house of the mother, and the house of the brother. Of the first: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” [Note: [Col. 0779] John 14]; of the second, here; of the third it is said: “He makes those of one manner dwell in a house” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 67], in which “it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 132]. The house of the father is the whole fabric of the world; the house of the mother, the heavenly homeland; the house of the brother is cloistered confinement. In the [Col. 0779D] first the Father works even now; in the second the mother rejoices; in the third the brother is tested. Into this house the soul of the righteous leads the Beloved by working in accordance with grace bestowed.

It follows: **There you will teach me.** The Beloved teaches us in this exile; he will teach us in the kingdom. There are four ways by which he teaches us here: by the setting forth of a commandment, by the harshness of the scourge, by the novelty of a miracle, and by subtle inspiration. The first, that we may know the way of truth; the second, that we may see the burden of our infirmity; the third, that we may know his [Col. 0780A] power; the fourth, that we may attend to his goodwill toward us. The way of truth, lest we wander. The burden of our infirmity, lest we put confidence in man. This is done for five reasons: that he may correct us from iniquity; lest anyone grow proud of virtue bestowed; that virtue may become known to men; that he may restrain others by its example; and that the crown may be amassed and increased. Thirdly, that we may know his power and flee to him in necessity. Fourthly, that we may attend to his goodwill toward us and thus love him.

163. Of the first David says: “I have chosen the way of truth” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 118]; of the second: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” [Note: [Col. 0779] Jer. 17]; of the third: “His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away” [Note: [Col. 0779] Dan. 7]; of the fourth we say: “The kindness and humanity of God our Saviour appeared” [Col. 0780B] [Note: [Col. 0779] Titus 3]. These four things are signified by the four diverse forms of Ezekiel’s living creatures [Note: [Col. 0779] Ezek. 1]. The human form, belonging to the rational creature, has the instruction of commandment; the form of the ox, which is sacrificed, has the harshness of the scourge, namely in the infirmity of the flesh; the form of the lion, which is a marvellous animal, has the novelty of miracle; the form of the eagle, which flies aloft, is subtle inspiration, which comes from above. Hence it follows concerning them: “They had faces and wings in four directions” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ibid.]. Faces—that is, consciences—by which we may consider these four things; wings, by which we may follow these four kinds of teaching.

Paul was instructed by these four things. For a commandment was set before him when he and Barnabas were set apart to preach the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0779] Acts 13]; [Col. 0780C] the harshness of the scourge, when he was struck by the Lord in the city [Note: [Col. 0779] Acts 21], and elsewhere stoned and beaten [Note: [Col. 0779] Acts 14]; the novelty of miracle, when light from heaven shone around him, he heard a voice, and saw no one [Note: [Col. 0779] Acts 9]; subtle inspiration, when he was caught up as far as the third heaven [Note: [Col. 0779] 2 Cor. 12].

It follows:

**And I will give you a cup of spiced wine.**

There is pure wine; there is wine infused with honey; there is wine seasoned with aromatic spices. The first is simply called wine, the second *mulsum* [honey-wine], the third *pigmentum* [spiced wine]. The first gladdens the human heart [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 103], the second sweetens it, the third strengthens diseased inward parts. The first was given us to drink by Christ, the Son of God; the second by the Holy Spirit; the third will be given by the Father in the kingdom. For the first is the birth of the Saviour; the second, [Col. 0780D] sevenfold grace; the third, the presence of eternal majesty.

It should be noted that wine gladdens, warms, and cleanses the decay of wounds. Christ’s coming gladdened us by his birth, cleansed sins by the shedding of his blood, kindled us to his love, and encouraged us to suffer by his Passion. Of the first: “The mountains shall rejoice before the Lord, because he comes to judge the earth” [Note: [Col. 0779] Ps. 97]; hence, when he himself was born, the angels sang for joy: “Glory to God in the highest!” [Note: [Col. 0779] Luke 2]. Of the second: “For he first loved us [Col. 0781A] and washed us from our sins in his blood” [Note: [Col. 0781] Rev. 1]. Of the third: “Be imitators of God, as most beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering to God” [Note: [Col. 0781] Eph. 5].

This wine gives great strength to Christ’s soldiers; hence *vinum* [wine] is so called as though nourishing the strength of the mind. But *mulsum*, which is the grace of the Holy Spirit, makes the soul become rich, sweet, and melted. It becomes rich by devotion, sweet by rejoicing in tribulation, and melted by compassion for its neighbour through works of mercy. Of these three it is said: “Eat rich foods” [Note: [Col. 0781] 2 Esdras 8]—behold the first; “and drink *mulsum*” [Note: [Col. 0781] Ibid.]—behold the second; “and send a portion to those who have prepared nothing for themselves” [Note: [Col. 0781] Ibid.]—behold the third. This *mulsum* soothes hearts; hence it is called *mulsum* as though soothing by the sweetness of honey.

Third follows *pigmentum*, that is, spiced wine, which we shall have in the Father’s presence and whose wondrous sweetness we shall enjoy. Hence *pigmentum* is so called as though “the pious taste of the mind”; it will also heal us from every corruption, when “this corruptible shall put on incorruption” [Note: [Col. 0781] 1 Cor. 15]. The soul offers the first wine by conforming itself to the humility of Christ’s birth; *mulsum* in the joy of spiritual grace; spiced wine in the homeland, when love gives thanks to the Beloved for all these benefits bestowed upon it.

**And the Church will give new wine of pomegranates.**

The pomegranate has a dark hue in its rind, redness in its seeds, and whiteness beneath the seed. In the first is the affliction of confessors, in the second the redness of martyrs, in the third the strength of virgins. The Church offers [Col. 0781C] the new wine of these: the purity of life of confessors, the shedding of blood of martyrs, and the chaste purity of virgins. The righteous soul likewise offers these three together. For from the dark hue of affliction, the redness of charity, and the whiteness of chastity it has here pressed the new wine which it will offer to the Beloved—namely, the desire to behold majesty. Nor only this: David also foresaw in the Spirit other gifts which the sons of the Bride would offer him in this exile, when he said: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring offerings” [Note: [Col. 0781] Ps. 71].

Four kings are here signified, who come to worship the Lord. The first is joyful, the second strong, the third hidden, the fourth vehement: joyful in gladness, strong in battle, hidden in cloudiness, vehement in fire. In the joy of heavenly felicity; in the battle both of bodily and spiritual adversity; in the cloudiness of humility; in the fire of charity. The first is the king of Tarshish, interpreted “investigation of joy”; the second, king of the island, which is shaken by the waves of the sea; the third, of Arabia, which is called “humble”; the fourth, king of Sheba, which is called “fire.” The first is Solomon, called “peaceful,” for in peace is joy; hence: “O Lord, the king shall rejoice in your strength” [Note: [Col. 0781] Ps. 20]. The second is David, called “strong of hand”; hence: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord mighty in battle” [Col. 0782A] [Note: [Col. 0781] Ps. 23]. The third is Hezekiah, called “the Lord strengthens”; for the Lord comes in humility to strengthen us. Thus Job says: “When I sat as a king with an army surrounding me, I was nevertheless a comforter of mourners” [Note: [Col. 0781] Job 29]. The fourth is King Josiah, called “where is the Lord’s incense?”

The first king investigates joy in three ways: the joy of the world, the joy of his own spirit, and the joy of heaven. The first is concerned with a passing thing, the second with one’s own righteousness, the third with heavenly glory. In the first he finds nothing but vanity, in the second worthlessness, in the third everlasting felicity. Therefore this king must so govern his steps through these joys that he does not plunge into the first; that he does not revel in the second, so as to consign penance to forgetfulness; and that he pours himself out in the third. For Solomon says of the first: “I judged laughter to be error, and I said to joy: Why are you vainly deceived?” [Col. 0782B] [Note: [Col. 0781] Eccl. 2]. Of the second David says: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise befits the upright” [Note: [Col. 0781] Ps. 32], and it follows: “Give thanks to the Lord with the harp” [Note: [Col. 0781] Ibid.]. Of the third: “Saints and righteous, rejoice in the Lord: God has chosen you as his inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0781] Office of the Church].

The first are the scouts of Jericho [Note: [Col. 0781] Josh. 2], which means “moon,” that is, the world because of its changeableness. The second are the scouts of Laish, which is called “unto salvation” or “for itself,” which the tribe of Dan, having no inheritance, acquired [Note: [Col. 0781] Judg. 18]. The third are the scouts of the promised land. “By Pharaoh’s life, you are all spies,” Joseph says [Note: [Col. 0781] Gen. 42]. These are Solomon’s ships, which brought from Tarshish gold, silver, elephant tusks, apes, and peacocks [Note: [Col. 0781] 2 Chron. 9]. The first bring gold, namely of heavenly [Col. 0782C] brightness; the second silver of innocence and purity; the third the remaining three things that signify worldly vanity. Of the first it is said that that city shall be golden [Note: [Col. 0781] Rev. 21]; the second is “silver tested by fire” [Note: [Col. 0781] Ps. 11]; the third is “vanity of vanities” [Note: [Col. 0781] Eccl. 1].

Therefore the scouts of Jericho found elephant tusks, that is, the world’s malice; apes, that is, buffoonery; and peacocks, the vanity of worldly favour. Of the first: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows” [Note: [Col. 0781] Ps. 56]. Of the second Paul says: “Let neither shamefulness, nor foolish talk, nor buffoonery—which is not fitting—be named among you” [Note: [Col. 0781] Eph. 5]. Of the third: “When he dies, he shall take nothing with him, nor shall his glory go down with him” [Note: [Col. 0781] Ps. 48].

The scouts sent into Laish—that is, to investigate [Col. 0782D] the soul’s salvation—in the house of Micah, whose name means “What is here?”, find an ephod, that is, the whiteness of innocence in the soul, and likewise *seraphim*, a graven image, and a molten image [Note: [Col. 0781] Judg. 18]. The *seraphim* signify foolish imaginings; the graven image, perverse deeds; the molten image, superfluous speech. They remove these from Micah’s house when they drive them from the heart. But there are also found there the things which are on the candlestick of the tabernacle, namely cups, little spheres, and lilies. The cup is continence full of the spiced drink of devotion; the little spheres are the cycle of life chastened by the lathe of correction; the lilies are the loveliness [Col. 0783A] and increase of virtues. But the scouts of the promised land—that is, of heaven—bring a cluster of grapes, pomegranates, and figs: grapes, the joy of the Lord’s resurrection; pomegranates, the future unity in heaven of angels and humankind; figs, the sweetness of the divine vision.

But it should be noted that the kings of Tarshish offer gold, the kings of the islands myrrh, the kings of Arabia frankincense, and the kings of Sheba a censer of incense [Note: [Col. 0783] Ps. 71; Matt. 2]. Gold signifies spiritual brightness; myrrh, the bitterness of tribulation; frankincense, humility; the censer, inflaming charity. Thus the three scouts offer gold: the scouts of the world, dark gold; the scouts of the spirit, gold tried by fire; the scouts of heaven, pure gold. The first is the brightness of a good life, but [Col. 0783B] mingled with temptation; the second is the brightness of teaching with the zeal of charity; the third is the brightness of the heavenly homeland with knowledge of truth. The first belongs to subjects, the second to prelates, the third to contemplatives. Concerning the first, the prophet saw “a man girded at the loins with *aurum obryzum* [fine gold]” [Note: [Col. 0783] Dan. 10], that is, unrefined [as the text explains]. Of the second it is said in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0783] ch. 3]: “I counsel you to buy gold tried and tested by fire.” Of the third, in the same book [Note: [Col. 0783] ch. 21]: “That city,” he says, “is pure gold, like clear glass.”

It follows: **“Kings of the islands.”** An island is so called as though *intus solum* [land within], for an island is land surrounded on every side by water. Therefore the kings of the islands are those who so govern islands that they are not submerged and destroyed by the force of flooding waters. [Col. 0783C] An island is subject to a threefold danger. It is diminished by the hidden erosion of waters, shaken by the onset of a storm, and submerged by flooding waters. But a wise king defends it against these harms. Against the first he sets wooden fences into the earth and water; against the second he builds walls of stones; against the third, so that people may escape, he raises a tower.

This island is the soul amid the waves of the world—that is, temptations; the king who governs it is reason. The first erosion, therefore, is the deceitfulness of the devil, or the world, or the flesh; the onset of the storm is the perversity of heretics; the flooding of waters is the wickedness of worldly tyrants. Of the first Job says: “A falling mountain crumbles away” [Note: [Col. 0783] Job 14]. Of the second he adds: “And a rock is removed from its place” [Note: [Col. 0783] Ibid.]. And to show whence this happens, he adds: “Waters hollow out the stone, [Col. 0783D] and by their overflow the earth is gradually consumed” [Note: [Col. 0783] Ibid.]. Of the third: “The deep surrounded me, and the sea covered my head” [Note: [Col. 0783] Jonah 2].

But against the first the king of the island should make a fence of watchfulness; against the second, a wall of Scriptures and prayers; against the third, a tower of virtues. Of the first: “Whoever breaks down a hedge shall be bitten by a serpent” [Note: [Col. 0783] Eccl. 10]. Of the second: “Surround us, O Lord, with your unconquerable wall” [Note: [Col. 0783] Office of the Church]. Of the third: “Be for us a tower of strength against the face of the enemy” [Note: [Col. 0783] Ps. 60]. In this tower there is safety from the waters, because it is high; but the prophet says who ought to [Col. 0784A] dwell in it: “He who walks in righteousness and speaks truth, who casts away avarice arising from oppression and shakes his hands free from every gift—he shall dwell on high; the strongholds of rocks shall be his lofty refuge” [Note: [Col. 0783] Isa. 33]. But, placed amid such bitterness, why do these men offer myrrh to the king?

But it should be noted that myrrh was offered to Christ three times: first in the manger, second on the cross, third in the tomb. The first was the offering of the Magi, the second of the Jews, the third of the devout. The first was for signification, the second for mockery, the third for anointing: to signify mortality; to mock holiness; to anoint against the decay of corruption. We offer the first when we grieve over our dwelling in this misery; the second when [Col. 0784B] we endure mockeries and reproaches, so that in hell we may be free from the devil’s mockery. We offer the third when we labour bravely, so that our body may be forever free from corruption. Of the first: The Magi offered the Lord “gold, frankincense, and myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0783] Matt. 2]. Of the second it is said: “They gave him wine mixed with myrrh to drink” [Note: [Col. 0783] Mark 15]. Of the third: Joseph, that noble councillor, bought “about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes” [Note: [Col. 0783] John 19].

This is the offering of the strong king; the king hidden beneath the cloudiness of humility brings his own offering. This king is a measured love of one’s own lowliness, just as, conversely, the king of pride is love of one’s own praise. But there is a humility which descends, one which exceeds, and one which proceeds.

164. It descends into sluggishness, exceeds moderation, [Col. 0784C] and proceeds to righteousness. This king rouses the first with a goad, restrains the second with a bridle, and subjects himself to the judgment of the third. Peter was in the first when he said: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0783] Luke 5]; of which David says: “My soul has been humbled into the dust” [Note: [Col. 0783] Ps. 43]. Eleazar was in the second when he indiscreetly placed himself beneath an elephant and was crushed by it [Note: [Col. 0783] 1 Macc. 6]; of this David says: “Had not your law been my meditation, I might perhaps then have perished in my humiliation” [Note: [Col. 0783] Ps. 118]. In the third, at Jonah’s preaching, the Ninevites were covered with sackcloth [Note: [Col. 0783] Jonah 3]; of which David says: “I was humbled exceedingly” [Note: [Col. 0783] Ps. 107].

This king offers frankincense, that is, the fragrance of a good life, both inward and outward, so that he may say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” [Note: [Col. 0783] 2 Cor. 2]. It should be noted that frankincense is first crushed, second [Col. 0784D] burned, and third produces smoke. It is crushed into powder, burned by fire, and smoke is produced by heat and moisture. In the first, tribulation causes a person to call himself dust and ashes; in the second, desire produces the melting of the soul; in the third, tears and prayer are sent forth. Of these three David says: “I am afflicted and exceedingly humbled; I roared from the groaning of my heart” [Note: [Col. 0783] Ps. 37]. Of the second: “Lord, before you is all my desire” [Note: [Col. 0783] Ibid.]. Of the third: “And my groaning is not hidden from you” [Note: [Col. 0783] Ibid.].

Job was in the first when, afflicted and sitting on the dung-heap, [Col. 0785A] he scraped his sores [Note: [Col. 0785] Job 2]. Of the second: “My soul melted away” [Note: [Col. 0785] Song 5]. Of the third: “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke?” [Note: [Col. 0785] Song 3]? Behold the king of Arabia, hidden beneath the cloudiness of humility, according to the poet [Note: [Col. 0785] Ovid]:

> If skill lies hidden, it profits; if discovered, it brings shame.

For the Bridegroom says to such a one: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves’ eyes, apart from that which lies hidden within” [Note: [Col. 0785] Song 4].

It follows: the king of Sheba, which is called “fire.” For he is the vehement king, through the fire of charity; he is righteousness set aflame, and he will offer a censer full of living coals [Note: [Col. 0785] Ps. 71]. This fire is threefold: the first he sends forth outside himself, the second he retains about himself, the third he raises above himself. The first is the correction of one’s neighbour; the second, [Col. 0785B] one’s own stirring to action; the third, divine love. In the first he corrects a sinner; in the second he rouses himself to labour; in the third he tastes the heavenly flavour. Of the first: “In the fire of my zeal the whole earth shall be devoured” [Note: [Col. 0785] Zeph. 1]. Of the second: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it burn?” [Note: [Col. 0785] Luke 12]. Of the third: “Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love” [Note: [Col. 0785] Office of the Church].

Thus this king—that is, righteousness—must so rule that he does not overthrow his neighbour, afflict himself excessively, or become so enticed by the love of God that he postpones care for himself and his neighbour. Concerning the first, Job said to his friends, who reproved him indiscreetly: “Consider the paths of Tema, the ways of Sheba” [Note: [Col. 0785] Job 6]. Concerning the second: “The queen [Col. 0785C] of Sheba came from the south to hear the wisdom of Solomon” [Note: [Col. 0785] 2 Chron. 9], in order to learn from him how she might kindle herself with fervour. Concerning the third it is said: “All shall come from Sheba, bearing gold and frankincense, and proclaiming praise to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0785] Isa. 60]: gold, namely the brightness of a good life, by which one’s neighbour is instructed through example; frankincense, devotion and prayer, through which one is enriched for the praise by which God is honoured—to whom belong honour and glory.

**There you will teach me.**

[CAR.] This adverb *there* refers to the preceding adverb *outside*. It is as though she said: “When I find you alone outside, there you will teach me what I did not know before, so that I may know you then as you are; and I in turn will offer you the dedicatory offerings of my merits, [Col. 0785D] which, bestowed by grace from you, I have received.” This is what follows: “And I will give you a cup of spiced wine.” By spiced wine she means charity seasoned with the honey of devotion and the spices of good works; “and I will give you new wine of my pomegranates.” By pomegranates she denotes companies of good works contained under the cells of individual virtues; the sweet pleasantness proceeding from them is called “new wine of pomegranates.” And “of mine” is significantly added, because no others can be compared with her pomegranates. Afterwards, because she shows herself concerned for the preservation of her people, she repeats, for the same sense and the same reason, the verse which [Col. 0786A] she had previously introduced above:

**His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.**

[THO.] His left hand—that is, the sacraments of his incarnation and the gifts of his presence; but his right hand is the rewards which the elect will receive at the end, in which will be the vision of majesty and the glory of glorified humility. This left hand is placed beneath the Bride’s head, that she may inwardly be sustained by these spiritual gifts; but the right hand is above her head, that in the homeland she may be rewarded with eternal goods.

It should be noted that the Bride first seeks a kiss, then comes secondly to Christ’s conversation, and thirdly here hastens to an embrace. For first she said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0785] Song 1]. Secondly follows: “Behold, you are beautiful, [Col. 0786B] my friend,” and she: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved” [Note: [Col. 0785] Ibid.]—behold, conversation. But here: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me”—behold, embrace. In the kiss is a sign of peace; in conversation, of familiarity; in the embrace, of spiritual union: peace, by which the Beloved’s anger and indignation are excluded; familiarity, by which the secret of his will is opened; spiritual union, by which vehement love is shown and the Bride becomes one spirit with the Bridegroom.

As a figure of this union, Jacob kisses Rachel when he finds her, speaks with her secondly, and thirdly is received into her embraces [Note: [Col. 0785] Gen. 29]. This Bridegroom, Christ, kissed the Church, his Bride, in the patriarchs; spoke to her in the Law and the prophets; and embraced her when he stretched out his hands [Col. 0786C] for her on the cross. He kissed her in the patriarchs when reconciliation began through them, as he says to Noah after the flood: “I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven, and it shall be a sign of the covenant” [Note: [Col. 0785] Gen. 9]. Thus God gave them the kiss of reconciliation, which was shown by abundance of possessions, favour in events, health of bodies, and the ordering of morals—as with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

This kiss foreshadowed that which Isaac gave to his son Jacob, when he gave him two kids to eat [Note: [Col. 0785] Gen. 27]. In Jacob is Christ; in Isaac, the ancient Fathers, from whom Christ was born according to the flesh. And for them he offered two kids: one, namely his flesh, like sinful flesh; the other, namely our sins, which he himself killed when he sacrificed his flesh for us on the cross.

The Beloved had [Col. 0786D] conversation with the Church in the Law and the prophets. For he gave them the Law, in which he showed them three things: he forbade what must be avoided, set forth what must be observed, and showed in figures what must be done. The first, as in: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” [Note: [Col. 0785] Exod. 20]. The second, as in: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” [Note: [Col. 0785] Ibid.]. There are ten commandments of the Law, of which the last three concern love of God, the first seven love of neighbour. In figures he showed what must be done, as he spoke to Moses concerning the making of the tabernacle: “See,” he says, “that you make all things according to [Col. 0787A] the pattern which was shown you on the mountain” [Note: [Col. 0787] Exod. 25]. For that mountain is Christ, in whom was shown the form of the spiritual tabernacle, which is built in us out of virtues—namely, when we conform our life to Christ’s manner of life. In the prophets, too, he foretold the things to come concerning Christ. Behold the conversation of the Bride and Beloved.

He also embraced her with a most loving embrace when he stretched out his hands upon the cross, to draw the Bride to himself; and, in a close embrace, united her spiritually to himself, according to: “He who clings to God becomes one spirit with him” [Note: [Col. 0787] 1 Cor. 6]. There his left hand was beneath our head—namely, his flesh, which was given as a price in order to sustain our soul, which is the head. His right hand embraced us from above, that it might be our reward.

[Col. 0787B] O vehement embrace, in which water came forth from the side, blood from the heart, and the soul from the body! Water for regeneration, blood for redemption, the soul for liberation: for regeneration, because he saved us; for redemption, because he delivered us from the devil’s power; the soul for liberation, when, descending to hell, he led forth the Fathers. Of the first: “I saw water flowing from the temple, from the right side; and all to whom this water came were made whole” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ezek. 47]. Of the second: “In the blood of your covenant you redeemed your prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” [Note: [Col. 0787] Zech. 9]. Of the third: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” [Note: [Col. 0787] Hos. 13].

And morally: the Beloved kisses the soul by reconciling it through forgiveness of sins; he converses with it by opening his will—that is, the way in which it ought to walk; [Col. 0787C] he embraces it by suspending it between the left arm of virtues and the right arm of heavenly promises. He kissed those toward whom he “abounded, so as to turn away his anger and not kindle all his wrath; and he remembered that they are flesh” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 77]. So was Paul when he said: “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost—I who was the foremost blasphemer, persecutor, and injurious man, and persecuted the Church of God, obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” [Note: [Col. 0787] 1 Tim. 1].

Those have conversation with the Beloved who inquire what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God. Paul sought it thus: “Lord,” he said, [Col. 0787D] “what do you wish me to do?” [Note: [Col. 0787] Acts 9]. And the Lord said: “I will show you how much you must suffer for my name” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ibid.]—behold, conversation. Afterwards one comes into the embraces of the Bridegroom. For he places beneath our head—that is, our soul—the left arm, namely the virtues by which we are sustained on the way; and he places the right arm beneath it by promising good things in the homeland. Hence: “Length of days is in his right hand, and in his left are riches and glory” [Note: [Col. 0787] Prov. 3].

Hear how Paul taught us to claim the left arm: “Let us live soberly, piously, and justly in this world” [Note: [Col. 0787] Titus 2]—behold, [Col. 0788A] the left arm. “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ibid.]—behold, the right arm. The Bridegroom’s right hand holds, leads, and receives: it holds the falling person, leads the walking person, receives the one who arrives. First, lest he fall in temptation; second, lest he stray from the way of righteousness; third, that he may hold the throne of glory. Of these three David says: “You have held my right hand; in your will you have led me; and with glory you have received me” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 72]. Likewise, of the first and second: “There your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 138]. Of the third: “My soul has clung after you; your right hand has received me” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 62].

The first says: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 93]. Here: “When he falls, he shall not be dashed down, because the Lord [Col. 0788B] places his hand beneath him” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 36]. For if he falls, he shall not fail to rise; indeed, he shall say: “The Lord is my light and my salvation: whom shall I fear?” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 26]. The second says: “Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 85], and: “Send forth your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 42]. The Lord leads such meek persons; hence: “You led your people, as you lead all, by the hand of Moses and Aaron” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 76]; likewise: “He who leads Joseph like a sheep” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 79]. The third says: “Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 118], so that afterward he may say: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ps. 29].

This is the hand of which Ezekiel says: “Behold, [Col. 0788C] a hand seized me by the lock of my head, lifted me up between heaven and earth, and set me in the temple at Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0787] Ezek. 8]. Behold these three things. First it held him when it seized him by the lock of his head; it led him when it lifted him up between heaven and earth, namely into the air, so that no impediment of earth might make his path crooked; it received him with glory when it set him in the temple at Jerusalem, which means “vision of peace.”

Elijah bore the figure of these three. Of the first, when fleeing from the face of Jezebel—that is, temptation—he fell asleep from weariness beneath a juniper tree; but the Lord held him, because there he found angelic consolation. Of the second, when he walked in the strength of food given by an angel for forty days and forty [Col. 0788D] nights. Of the third, on Horeb, the mountain of God [Note: [Col. 0787] 3 Kings 19]. Thus it is rightly said: “Length of days is in his right hand, and in his left are riches and glory” [Note: [Col. 0787] Prov. 3]: riches, namely of virtues; glory, indeed eternal already, though meanwhile there is delight in heavenly things; but length of days is in the right hand, because the blessed shall live forever beneath his shadow.

Thus it is rightly said: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.” The left hand is called divine correction; the right, delight in the love of God. But let us see how this comes about. The Lord’s left hand holds a scourge, his right a fan: [Col. 0789A] the scourge of affliction, the fan of delight. First the human being is scourged; second the spirit is stirred by the breeze. The left hand sometimes touches, sometimes rebukes, sometimes weighs down.

165. It touches the righteous, rebukes the sluggish, weighs down the wicked: the righteous, that they may be tested; the sluggish, that they may be stirred up; the wicked, that they may be called back.

From the first: “Have pity on me, at least you who are my friends, for the hand of the Lord has touched me” [Note: [Col. 0789] Job 19]; of the second: “By the strength of your hand I have failed under rebukes” [Note: [Col. 0789] Ps. 38]; of the third: “Day and night your hand lay heavy upon me” [Note: [Col. 0789] Ps. 51]. Likewise, of the first: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch” [Note: [Col. 0789] Song 5]. But “the righteous man shall not be saddened, whatever may happen to him” [Note: [Col. 0789] Prov. 12]. Yet he says with the prophet: “Let rottenness enter into my bones” [Note: [Col. 0789] Hab. 3], [Col. 0789B] because in this way he is tested; hence: “You visit him at dawn and test him suddenly” [Note: [Col. 0789] Job 7]; and David says: “Test me, Lord, and prove me” [Note: [Col. 0789] Ps. 25]. Again: “You have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire” [Note: [Col. 0789] Ps. 65].—“For fire tests gold, the furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation tests righteous men” [Note: [Col. 0789] Ecclus. 27].

The second says: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me” [Note: [Col. 0789] Ps. 140]; and the Apostle: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” [Note: [Col. 0789] II Tim. 4]. Therefore do not reject the Lord’s rebukes, “for he himself wounds and heals” [Note: [Col. 0789] Job 5]. On account of the third: “Moses’ hands were heavy” [Note: [Col. 0789] Exod. 17], namely, for punishing the wicked. But Hur and Aaron supported them, because the kindness of the Holy Spirit and the mercy of Christ ensure that those who endure are not broken. Thus God calls back the wicked; and unless they are converted, it is said to them: [Col. 0789C] “I called and you refused; I stretched out my hand and there was no one to heed it” [Note: [Col. 0789] Prov. 1].

Accordingly, the Lord’s left hand touched Job, rebuked Hezekiah, and lay heavy upon Paul. Job endured manfully; Hezekiah wept bitterly; Paul, when called, yielded to the Lord’s will. Hence he himself says: “I who was a blasphemer and persecutor have nevertheless obtained mercy” [Note: [Col. 0789] I Tim. 1]. Behold the Lord’s left hand. This is the hand of the Lord which appeared to Belshazzar, writing these three words upon the wall: “Mene, Tekel, Peres” [Note: [Col. 0789] Dan. 5]. *Mene* first says: that is, he has counted your goods; *Tekel* secondly says: that is, he has weighed your goods, which have been found few because of your sloth; *Peres* thirdly says: that is, you shall be divided from the kingdom unless, called by me, you return.

[Col. 0789D] I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes it.

[THO.] Here the “daughters of Jerusalem” are called the weak, who, although they are occupied with secular concerns—by which they sometimes impede contemplatives, designated here by the name “beloved”—nevertheless tend toward the kingdom. Yet they build with wood, hay, and stubble, and by these they importunately awaken the bride from the sleep of contemplation. But before she herself willingly returns for the common benefit of the brethren, they should not presume to awaken her.

Some awaken the devil; some awaken [Col. 0790A] the bridegroom, that is, the soul; some awaken God: the devil for temptation, the soul for labour, and God now for consolation, now for wrath. Of the first, Job says: “Those are ready, he says, to awaken Leviathan” [Note: [Col. 0789] Job 3]. For they awaken him when they voluntarily expose their senses to the world and nourish foolish thoughts in their heart. Thus the Lord says to Jerusalem, in the figure of a woman, through the prophet Ezekiel: “The opposite of the custom of women has happened in you: wages are given to all women, but you have given wages to your lovers” [Note: [Col. 0789] Ezek. 16].

They awaken God for consolation when they cry out to him in tribulation. Thus, when the little boat was endangered among the waves while he slept, the disciples awakened him, saying: “Save us, Lord; we are perishing” [Note: [Col. 0789] Matt. 8]. They awaken him to wrath when they test him; hence he himself says: “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” [Note: [Col. 0789] Matt. 22]. And Moses: “Why do you test the Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0789] Exod. 17].—“Neither test God as some tested him and perished by serpents” [Note: [Col. 0789] I Cor. 10].—“These provoked the Most High to anger in the waterless place. And the Lord awoke as one asleep, like a mighty man overcome with wine” [Note: [Col. 0789] Ps. 77].—“And the Lord was enraged in fury against his people” [Note: [Col. 0789] Num. 11].

At times some awaken the bride on account of disturbance; at times in order to obtain consolation; at times she awakens herself by her own will. The first are dead flies which spoil the sweetness of ointment [Note: [Col. 0789] Eccles. 10]. If the soul thus awakened does not consent to folly, it returns with greater profit. This is Sarah, [Col. 0790C] Abraham’s wife, who was turned away and torn from her husband’s side by Pharaoh’s attendants, but remained untouched and returned to her husband with gifts. When, for the sake of consolation, she herself cries out through the prophet: “He sent me to announce good news to the meek, that I might console all who languish” [Note: [Col. 0789] Isa. 61].

By her own will she is awakened from contemplation in four ways: through private curiosity; to forestall the devil’s plot; because of necessity; and for her own benefit. The first was Dinah, who went out from her father’s house to see the women of the region and was violated by Shechem son of Hamor [Note: [Col. 0789] Gen. 34]. The second was Judith [Note: [Col. 0789] Judith 13], who went out from her city to the camp of Holofernes, who was plotting evil against her people, and took away his head—that is, overthrew the beginning of the devil’s [Col. 0790D] temptation.

The third goes out from necessity, in order to heal the sinner already tossed about by sins. This is Mary, Moses’ sister, who went out from her father’s house and walked beside the channel of water, so that by some means she might help her brother Moses, who as a little child was struggling in a papyrus basket amid the waves [Note: [Col. 0789] Exod. 2].

The fourth goes out for her own benefit, so that, having seen another’s example and acted herself, she may return more eagerly to contemplation. This is Ruth, who went out [Col. 0791A] from her own land with her mother-in-law Naomi, whose name means “beautiful,” and gathered ears of grain in the field of Boaz, so that both she and Naomi might be fed; and thus she afterwards deserved to attain marriage with Boaz [Note: [Col. 0791] Ruth 4], that is, contemplation of the bridegroom.

Thus, first, when the soul is awakened by itself, it first goes out from contemplation of heavenly things to meditation upon the Scriptures; secondly, to remembrance of its sins; thirdly, to compassion for its neighbours. From there it proceeds to care actively for them. This is shown by a comparison: someone goes out from the bedchamber into the house, from the house into the portico, from the portico into the street, and from the street into the field. For the soul goes out from contemplation of heavenly things to the Scriptures, as though into a bedchamber; thence into the house, that is, into remembrance of sins; thence to compassion for neighbours, as though into the street; and thence to active care [Col. 0791B] for them, as though into a field.

In contemplation alone we rest. In the other things we labour: in meditation upon the Scriptures we labour, fearing that we may lose the rewards of the righteous; in remembering our sins we labour and groan, lest we be condemned; in compassion for our neighbours there is labour of the heart; in caring actively for them there is labour of deed. In the first we are admonished; in the second instructed; in the third moved; in the fourth we merit. Scripture warns us what we ought to do; remembrance of sin teaches us to repent; compassion moves us to love. Through good work, however, we merit that he may help us who help others.

That father comes to mind who went out to meet his prodigal son [Note: [Col. 0791] Luke 15]. He sees him coming from afar, runs to meet him, embraces him, kills the fatted calf, arranges a chorus, and strikes up the music. Thus the merciful Father returns from contemplation, on account of care for the sinner returning to repentance. He sees him coming from afar through compassion; meets him through forgiveness; embraces him by making him intimate with himself; kills the calf by preaching the mortification of the flesh; [Col. 0791C] plays instruments by teaching harmony and unity of conduct. Thus mercy invites the despairing; charity draws the invited person; mercy pacifies the one drawn; cheerfulness makes him secure; affability makes him familiar; familiarity opens the secret place; the opening of secrets preserves friendship; preaching instructs; harmony of conduct makes one a friend to one’s neighbour, and humility makes one a friend to God. This, then, is the necessary reason why the bride wishes herself to be awakened.

[Col. 0791D] Then one must labour greatly to discover that rest from which the bride is forbidden to be awakened. First, therefore, there must be the vigilance of circumspection; secondly, progress in righteousness; thirdly, that rest which is wisdom will be found. The first enables one to foresee the devil’s plots for oneself and for others; the second enables one to advance oneself and promote others; in the third one offers one’s whole self to God.

That wise man shows us this ascent, though in reverse order; for he says: “Blessed is the man who shall remain in wisdom, who shall meditate upon righteousness, and who shall consider the circumspection of God in his understanding” [Note: [Col. 0791] Ecclus. 14]. Three things have been set forth: circumspection, righteousness, [Col. 0792A] wisdom. The first instructs Christian warfare; the second examines conscience; the third makes us eager for patience. The first feeds us with the bread of life, lest one enter through the windows; the second with the bread of understanding, lest conscience be enveloped in the darkness of ignorance; the third gives us the water of wisdom to drink, so that we may be affected by the sweetness of wisdom.

Of the first: “Behold, sixty mighty men, of the mightiest of Israel, surround Solomon’s bed” [Note: [Col. 0791] Song 3]. Of the second: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks” [Note: [Col. 0791] Song 1]. Again: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” [Note: [Col. 0791] Song 2]. Of the third: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0791] Ibid.]. Christ is this tree. We are under his shadow, so that his fruit—that is, the certain recompense, sweet to us—may keep us unharmed from the heat of worldly tribulation; its savour, tasted by us, invites us to suffer willingly.

Now there is the circumspection of man, the circumspection of the spirit, and the circumspection of God. The first is against temporal harms; the second against the devices of vices; the third against impediments to divine love. The first prevents anyone from misusing temporal things; the second prevents virtue from being deceived by the resemblance of vices; the third prevents love within us from diminishing.

In the first, it must be observed that there are some who acquire both temporal and spiritual riches badly, spend them badly, and lose them with grief. Let Achan son of Carmi serve as an example: he took improperly the gold bar, [Col. 0792C] the silver shekels, and the very fine cloak from the accursed spoil of Jericho [Note: [Col. 0791] Josh. 7]. He used them badly by hiding them in the earth and lost them with grief, being stoned because of them. In the gold bar wisdom is signified, by which he might benefit others; in the silver, eloquence, by which he might instruct them; in the cloak, honourable conduct, by which he might invite others.

There follows the circumspection of the spirit. In the Song it is said: “Behold, sixty mighty men, of the mightiest of Israel, surround Solomon’s bed” [Note: [Col. 0791] Song 3]. This bed is the soul of the righteous man, around which strong men stand, “holding swords and highly trained for war” [Note: [Col. 0791] Ibid.]: first, so that no place may be left unguarded; secondly, so that the trouble of temptations may be repelled; thirdly, lest there be ignorance in fighting. These mighty men are the inner senses, which surround the wall of virtues [Col. 0792D] with unceasing vigilance, as in Ezra: “They set guards,” he says, “each around his own house, from among the inhabitants of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0791] II Ezra 4], so that it may be said: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set guards” [Note: [Col. 0791] Isa. 62].

These are they who hold the sword against the plots of vices: the sword upon the thigh, against pleasure of the flesh; the sword in the hand, against the vanity of the world; the sword in the mouth, that they may fight by prayer against the malignity of the devil. Of the first: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” [Note: [Col. 0791] Ps. 44]. Of the second: “Two-edged swords are in their hands” [Note: [Col. 0791] Ps. 149]. Of the third: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” [Note: [Col. 0791] Eph. 6]. Of these [Col. 0793A] Paul says: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God” [Note: [Col. 0793] II Cor. 10].

He had a sword upon his thigh who killed Agag, the very fat one. The sons of Israel had it in their hand, who held a sword with one hand and laid a stone with the other. In the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0793] ch. 1]: “He who sat in majesty had a sword in his mouth.” For circumspection, the living creatures were full of eyes before and behind. For the scruple of conscience, it is commanded that the breast and vital parts be brought near it; this pertains to righteousness. For the purity and sincerity of wisdom, there is fine flour fried in oil.

But now let us deal with conscience. There is good righteousness and bad righteousness. Good righteousness is threefold: it is good, secure, and glorious. The first is healthy; the second serene; the third pleasant. Healthy, because it is bounded off from wickedness; serene, because it is freed from the perversity of worldly care; [Col. 0793B] pleasant, because it already moves amid the joy of angels. In it the Bride rests, of whom it is said: “Do not awaken her until she herself wishes.”

Of the first: “The fullness of the law is charity” [Note: [Col. 0793] Rom. 13]. From a pure heart comes a good conscience. Of the second, Job says: “Behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who knows me is on high” [Note: [Col. 0793] Job 16].
