Of the third: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0793] II Cor. 1]. The first says: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” [Note: [Col. 0793] Song 5]. The second says: “Our bed is flowering” [Note: [Col. 0793] Song 1]. The third: “I sleep, but my heart watches” [Note: [Col. 0793] Song 5].

The first is the woman of whom it is said in the Law: “When you take a captive woman, if she pleases you, she shall shave all the hair of her body; afterwards you shall take her as wife” [Note: [Col. 0793] Lev. 14]. The second is the strong woman in Solomon, who provides for her household and, weaving a garment for her husband, conducts business [Col. 0794A] [Note: [Col. 0793] Prov. 31]. The third is the bride in the Song, who delights in the bridegroom’s kiss and embraces [Note: [Col. 0793] Song 1].

She wished to be given to drink of the water of wisdom when she said:

> Grant me to gaze upon the fountain of the good; grant that, having found the light,  
> I may fix the clear-seeing eyes of my soul upon you.  
> And shine with your splendour; for you are serenity itself:  
> you are eternal rest for the devout; to behold you is the end.

Therefore, “blessed is the man who shall remain in wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0793] Ecclus. 14], that he may rest there and that the Bridegroom may say: Do not awaken her, 166 until she herself wishes. Therefore one must keep watch in circumspection, reflect in wisdom, and watch diligently in righteousness. “Until she herself wishes”: in circumspection she wishes to be awakened when the severity of temptation threatens; in righteousness, when usefulness appears; in wisdom, she wishes to be at leisure when devout sweetness grows rich.

When, therefore, it is said: “Do not rouse her or awaken her,” the importunity of subordinates is restrained; the Bride is reserved the sweetness of contemplation; and to God, that his majesty may be praised by the Bride, is reserved the joy of the kingdom for all. May our Lord Jesus Christ lead us to it, to whom are honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.

[CARD.] The Son also, seeing her so fittingly solicitous, because she ought not to be made anxious, repeats, in the same sense and for the same reason, the aforesaid verse: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.” There follows:

## BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793C] Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?

[THO.] The Church of the Gentiles comes up from the wilderness, because, having for a very long time been forsaken by God, she now reaches his grace by advancing in the steps of faith and good work. Hence Isaiah foretold: “The deserted and trackless places shall rejoice; the wilderness shall exult and flower like a lily” [Note: [Col. 0793] Isa. 35], overflowing with those delights of which the beloved above said: “How beautiful and how lovely you are, most dear one, amid delights” [Note: [Col. 0793] Song 7]—that is, amid desires for heavenly life.

Rightly is she leaning upon her beloved, without whom she could not only ascend to the heights but not even rise again. This is what Judaea cries out, wondering at the conversion of the Gentiles. There are three kinds of delights: temporal, spiritual, and [Col. 0793D] heavenly. The first belong to secular or carnal persons, the second to religious persons, the third to the blessed. The first are goods which people acquire for use or misuse; the second are virtues, or things connected with contemplation; the third make one perfectly happy.

The first are misused by those “whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame” [Note: [Col. 0793] Phil. 3]; the second are used by those who seek the things above and set their minds on the things above [Note: [Col. 0793] Col. 3]. These kindle others. The Blessed Virgin kindles, ascends, surpasses: she kindles the lukewarm, ascends into heaven, surpasses the angels; she kindles the lukewarm through charity, ascends the heavens through holiness, and surpasses the angels in dignity.

Of the first it is said: “Holy Mary, help the wretched, aid the fainthearted, restore the tearful” [Note: [Col. 0793] Offic. Eccl.]. Hence it is said: “Chosen as the sun” [Note: [Col. 0793] Song 4], she who ascends; likewise: “The scent of your garments is like the scent of incense” [Note: [Col. 0793] Song 9]. Of the second: “Today the Virgin Mary ascends into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0793] Offic. Eccles.]. Of the third: “You have been exalted, holy Mother of God, above the choirs of angels” [Note: [Col. 0793] Ibid.].

Those will enjoy the third kind who “shall be intoxicated [Col. 0794D] by the abundance of God’s house” [Note: [Col. 0793] Ps. 35], where man shall eat the bread of angels [Note: [Col. 0793] Offic. Eccles.]. The first flow away; the second flow abundantly; the third flow together. Let us therefore consider the first, for they consist in care for the flesh, in abundance of [Col. 0795A] riches, in power, in knowledge, and in the glory of nobility.

Of these the Wise Man says: “He who delicately nourishes his servant from youth will afterwards find him rebellious” [Note: [Col. 0795] Prov. 29]; and Job: “There are those who count thorns as delights” [Note: [Col. 0795] Job 30]. Of care for the flesh the Apostle says: “Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies” [Note: [Col. 0795] Rom. 13]. These are enjoyed by those who “take up tambourine and lyre and rejoice at the sound of the instrument; they spend their days in prosperity and descend in a moment to hell” [Note: [Col. 0795] Job 21]. They say: “Come, let us fill ourselves with wine and costly perfumes; let not the flower of time pass us by; let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither” [Note: [Col. 0795] Wis. 2]. They do not remember that “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” [Note: [Col. 0795] Isa. 40]. To them Isaiah says: “The moth shall be spread beneath you, [Col. 0795B] and worms shall be your covering” [Note: [Col. 0795] Isa. 14].

Of riches the Apostle says: “Command the rich of this age not to think lofty thoughts or to hope in the uncertainty of riches” [Note: [Col. 0795] I Tim. 6].—The wise man says: “To be rich without riches is wealth; but set virtues before riches,” because “they have slept their sleep, and all men of riches have found nothing in their hands” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 75]. Therefore, “if riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 61]. For in life they afflict, at death they abandon, and after death they exclude a person from the kingdom.

Of the first two Boethius says [Note: [Col. 0795] *The Consolation of Philosophy*, III, met. 3]:

> Although the greedy man may compel inexhaustible wealth  
> to flow for him in a torrent of gold,  
> adorn his neck with pearls of the Red Sea,  
> and plough rich fields with a hundred oxen,  
> gnawing care does not leave him while he lives,  
> and fleeting wealth does not accompany him when he is dead.

Of the third the Saviour says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0795] Matt. 19].

> Riches have shattered the ages through shameful luxury;  
> luxurious love is nourished by riches.  
> —Ovid [Note: [Col. 0795] Ovid]

There is a power displeasing to God, and there is a power pleasing to God. The former displeases him when a person glories in it and oppresses others; hence: “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 51]. You glory, I say, but:

> … No power lasts long, says the poet [Note: [Col. 0795] Ovid].

For the Lord “has cast down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” [Note: [Col. 0795] Luke 1]. But you, proud and powerful, “therefore God shall destroy you forever; he shall pluck you up and [Col. 0795D] remove you from your tent” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 51]. Hear another wise man: “Terribly and swiftly shall he appear to you; most severe judgment shall be passed upon those who rule” [Note: [Col. 0795] Wis. 6]. Mercy is granted to the humble, “but the mighty shall suffer mighty torments” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ibid.].

There is another power that pleases God. “God,” he says, “does not cast away the mighty, since he himself is mighty.” But what kind? Hear the philosopher [Note: [Col. 0795] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, III, met. 5]:

> Let him who wishes to be powerful  
> tame his fierce passions,  
>
> [lacuna]  
>
> [lacuna]  
>
> For although distant India  
> tremble beneath your laws  
> and remotest Thule serve you,  
> yet if you cannot drive away dark cares  
> and banish wretched complaints,  
> that is not power.

“God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” [Note: [Col. 0795] I Cor. 1].

> Divine power plays among human affairs,  
> and the present hour scarcely possesses certain trust.

Likewise, there is a knowledge that displeases God. Some are wise in order to do evil. This is not wisdom descending from above, but earthly, animal, devilish. Through earthly wisdom temporal things are desired too greatly; through animal wisdom the flesh is dissolved into pleasure; through devilish wisdom God and the poor are oppressed by injuries.

The first is against spiritual poverty, the second [Col. 0796B] against sobriety, the third against charity. When the Lord asked Peter three times whether he loved him [Note: [Col. 0795] John 21], he showed us three degrees of charity. There is charity that cannot be put to sleep, charity that cannot be separated, and charity that cannot be overcome. Of the first: “I sleep, but my heart watches” [Note: [Col. 0795] Song 5]; and: “Watch, stand firm in faith, act manfully, be strengthened; let all that you do be done in charity” [Note: [Col. 0795] I Cor. 16]. Of the second: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ?” [Note: [Col. 0795] Rom. 8]. Of the third: “This is true brotherhood, which could not be violated by conflict.” Again: “They may be killed; they cannot be bent.”

The first is incapable of sleep because it is stirred by the goads of languor; the second is insuperable because it is bound by the bonds of sweetness; the third is insuperable because it is strengthened by the fire of fervour. Of the first: “Daughters of Jerusalem, [Col. 0796C] tell my beloved that I languish with love” [Note: [Col. 0795] Song 2]. Of the second: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” [Note: [Col. 0795] Song 1].—“For your spirit is sweeter than honey, and your inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ecclus. 24]. Of the third: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames.”

In the first, as has been said above, the soul has three anxieties, which draw it away from worldly anxieties. For it fears foulness, lowliness, and fickleness: the foulness of impurity, the lowliness of poverty, and the fickleness of instability. First, lest the beloved depart because of sin; second, lest he disdain to return because of poverty in virtues; third, lest, through delay of the reward, it fall into weariness. In the first it shall say: “I am stuck fast in deep mire, and there is no firm ground” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 68]. In the second: “The Lord came to the fig tree, from which he expected fruit; finding none, he cursed it, and it immediately withered” [Note: [Col. 0795] Matt. 21]. Of the third it was said: when they “go up to the heavens,” awaiting heavenly rewards, “and descend unto the depths,” wearied by their long expectation, “their soul languished in evils” [Note: [Col. 0795] Ps. 106] through weariness; for “hope deferred afflicts the soul” [Note: [Col. 0795] Prov. 13].

> [lacuna] The soul, while it conceives future kingdoms,  
> consumes its joys in long desire.

[Col. 0797A] Against these three things the bride sought a remedy when she said, against the first: “Strengthen me with flowers” [Note: [Col. 0797] Song 2], that is, with purity against sin; “Surround me with apples” [Note: [Col. 0797] Ibid.], that I may possess an abundance of virtues; “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand shall embrace me,” lest I fall into weariness. Again, she is shown to have been shaken by these things: by the first when the beloved says, “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish in you” [Note: [Col. 0797] Song 4]; by the second when she says, “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple trees” [Note: [Col. 0797] Ibid.]; by the third when she says, “I have found him whom my soul loves; I held him and shall not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me” [Note: [Col. 0797] Song 3]. Behold love incapable of sleep.

Inseparable love is bound by three cords, because “a threefold cord [Col. 0797B] is not quickly broken” [Note: [Col. 0797] Eccles. 4]. These are the goods of nature, the gifts of grace, and the promises of glory. In the first we were created; in the second recreated; in the third restored. Of the first: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0797] Gen. 1]; and: “The invisible things of God, understood through the things made from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, including his everlasting power and divinity” [Note: [Col. 0797] Rom. 1]. Of the second: “If anyone is a new creature in Christ, old things have passed away” [Note: [Col. 0797] II Cor. 5]. Of the third: “He shall reform the body of our lowliness, making it conformed to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0797] Phil. 3].

Of these bonds the Lord says through the prophet: “I shall draw them with cords, with the bonds of charity” [Note: [Col. 0797] Hos. 11]. Concerning love incapable of sleep it was said: “If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, [Col. 0797C] he would regard it as nothing.” Concerning inseparable love it is said: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.”

Charity is insuperable in those who are “rooted and founded in charity” [Note: [Col. 0797] Eph. 3], that is, made firm by a threefold fervour. The first fervour is that a person may rescue his conscience from sin; the second, that he may rescue his soul even from purgatory; the third, that he may rescue body and soul from this inseparable exile, and thus take his prey away from the devil.

On account of these three, when Achish said to David [Note: [Col. 0797] I Sam. 27], “Where have you made a raid today?” he answered: “Toward the south of Judah,” which means “confession”; “toward the south of Jerahmeel,” which means “the mercy of God”; “toward the south of the Kenites,” which means “my nest,” or “my treasury,” or “my possession.” For conscience is freed by the first fervour through confession; by the second through God’s mercy, which is in heaven; and body and soul are freed from this exile through fervour for attaining eternal blessedness. For it is said: “The sparrow finds herself a house, and the turtledove a nest where she may lay her young” [Note: [Col. 0797] Ps. 83]; of the second: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0797] Matt. 6]; of the third: “In their own land they shall possess double” [Note: [Col. 0797] Isa. 61].

There are those who wish to know in order to glory. Hence the poet says [Note: [Col. 0797] Persius, *Satires* I.27]:

> Your knowledge is nothing unless another knows that you know this.

> Yet it is pleasant to be pointed out with the finger and called: “There he is.”

Hence it is said: “Knowledge puffs up; charity builds up” [Note: [Col. 0797] I Cor. 8].—“Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent before yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0797] Isa. 54]. Of the knowledge that pleases God it is said: “He who adds knowledge adds labour” [Note: [Col. 0797] Eccles. 1]. Whoever therefore needs such knowledge should ask it from the Lord, who gives abundantly to all; for “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” [Note: [Col. 0797] I Cor. 1].

Of nobility it says in the same place: “God chose the ignoble things” [Note: [Col. 0797] Ibid.]. Hear the philosopher [Note: [Col. 0797] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, III, met. 6]:

> Every race of humankind on earth  
> rises from the same origin;  
> for there is one Father of all things,  
> one who supplies all things.  
> Why make noise about lineage and ancestors?  
>
> [Col. 0798B] If you look to our beginnings  
> and to God our Maker,  
> none is base-born,  
> unless, fostering worse things through vices,  
> he abandons his own origin.

Therefore, if you are wicked and boast of your parents’ nobility, hear what the poet says [Note: [Col. 0797] Juvenal, *Satires* VII.139]:

> The very nobility of your ancestors begins to stand against you  
> and to hold a bright torch before your shameful deeds.

For, as the same poet says [Note: [Col. 0797] Ibid. 141]:

> Every vice of the soul contains a crime more conspicuous in itself  
> in proportion as the sinner is thought greater.

The same poet tells you what nobility is [Note: [Col. 0797] Ibid. 20]:

> … Nobility is virtue alone and unique.

Therefore I would rather that you were low-born and virtuous than noble and [Col. 0798C] vicious. Hence the same poet says [Note: [Col. 0797] Ibid. 269]:

> I would rather Thersites were your father, provided that you were  
> the son of Aeacides and took up the arms of Vulcan,  
> than that Achilles should bring you forth resembling Thersites.

These are temporal delights. But there are three spiritual delights: a pure conscience, devotion, and joy in heavenly things. Of them David says: “The beautiful places of the wilderness shall grow rich, and the hills shall gird themselves with exultation” [Note: [Col. 0797] Ps. 64]. The wilderness is the human heart; its beautiful places are a clean conscience. These beautiful places grow rich through devotion; they become hills by contemplating heavenly things; they gird themselves with exultation by ascending thither with joy.

Job possessed the first when he said: “Behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who knows me is on high” [Note: [Col. 0797] Job 16]. Of the second and third, it is said in the same place concerning the hypocrite: [Col. 0798D] “He shall not see the streams, the rivers of honey and butter” [Note: [Col. 0797] Job 20]. Butter is the richness of devotion; hence: “Let my soul be filled as with fatness and richness” [Note: [Col. 0797] Ps. 62]. Honey, however, is joy in heavenly things; hence: “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 0797] Ecclus. 24].

To such a soul it is deservedly said: “You have become beautiful and lovely in your delights.” Hence in this Song: “How beautiful and how lovely, 167 most dear one, you are amid delights!” [Note: [Col. 0797] Song 7].

It is dear in conscience, dearer in devotion, [Col. 0799A] dearest in joy. Paul experienced the first when he said: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0799] II Cor. 1.]; the second when he said: “The love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Note: [Col. 0799] Rom. 5.]; the third when he said: “But our citizenship is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0799] Phil. 3.]. Thus also the prudent virgins had the pure lamps of conscience [Note: [Col. 0799] Matt. 25.], while within they had the oil of devotion, and the fire of love and brightness by which they see heavenly things and rejoice in them. The bride abounds in these delights: in these three senses according to the threefold interpretation of this word. In the first sense she *affluit*, that is, she “washes away the dregs”; in the second, she *affluit*, that is, “flows with affection”; in the third, she *affluit*, that is, “flows copiously,” namely, abundantly. Of these Job says: “Then [Col. 0799B] you shall abound in delights in the Almighty, and shall lift up your face to God” [Note: [Col. 0799] Job 22.]. Solomon says of them: “Delights do not become a fool, nor does it become a servant to rule over his master” [Note: [Col. 0799] Prov. 19.].

The third kind consists of heavenly delights, of which it is said: “Asher—his bread is rich, and he shall provide royal delicacies” [Note: [Col. 0799] Gen. 49.]. Asher is interpreted “blessedness”: he is Christ himself, who will give blessedness in the homeland. The devil departed from these; hence: “You were in the delights of the paradise of God” [Note: [Col. 0799] Ezek. 28.]. True delights are where the Father prepares a place, the Son gives food, the Holy Spirit gives seasoning, the angel gives song, and human beings give dancing. The Father gives the place of immortality; the Son gives food, by the sight of which we shall be satisfied—namely, his glorified body; the Holy Spirit gives the seasoning of love; the angel gives a song of praise; human beings give dancing in thanksgiving. Of the first: “To sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give to you, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” [Note: [Col. 0799] Matt. 20.]. Likewise, Christ ascended above the heavens and prepared for his most chaste mother a place of immortality. Of the second: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 16].—“You will fill me with joy by your countenance, delights at your right hand unto the end” [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 15]. Of the third: “The south wind will blow everywhere,” that is, the Holy Spirit, “and its perfumes shall flow” [Note: [Col. 0799] Song 4], namely, the seasoning of love, so that we may joyfully drink the sober intoxication of the Spirit. Of the fourth, Isaiah heard the seraphim singing: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of Hosts” [Note: [Col. 0799] Isa. 6]. Of the fifth: “For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall arise, and you shall go out and leap like calves from the herd” [Note: [Col. 0799] Mal. 4].

These are the [Col. 0799D] heavenly delights. But lest we suppose that the bride has these from herself, it is added: *Leaning upon her beloved.* First the bride goes; second, she strives; third, she leans. She goes when she withdraws from sin; she strives by ascending through the steps of the virtues; she leans when she trusts in her beloved’s aid, attributing none of her good things to herself but to God. Of the first it is said: “Take up your bed and walk” [Note: [Col. 0799] Mark 9.]; of the second: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0799] Isa. 2.]; of the third: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 113]. For without her beloved [Col. 0800A] she can do nothing; but he himself leads her in a cloud by day and in the illumination of fire throughout the night [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 77]. She could not endure the burden and heat of the day [Note: [Col. 0799] Matt. 20] unless she were in the shadow of him whom her soul loves [Note: [Col. 0799] Song 2]. For what place would be safe for her from the terror of the night [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 90], especially in a place of horror and vast solitude [Note: [Col. 0799] Deut. 32], unless he himself sent forth his light and his truth [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 42]? How could she temper the heat of concupiscence for herself unless the power of the Most High overshadowed her [Note: [Col. 0799] Luke 1]? From where would she illuminate the darkness of ignorance unless, in his light, she saw light [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 35]? Hence she says to him: “For you light my lamp, O God” [Note: [Col. 0799] Ps. 17], and so forth. Therefore she receives from the bridegroom two remedies against two principal evils: the cloud of refreshment against the concupiscence of the flesh, and the light of revelation against the [Col. 0800B] ignorance of the mind. Blessed are those for whom the beloved was a veil by day and a light of stars by night, spreading a cloud for their protection and fire to shine for them through the night [Note: [Col. 0799] Wis. 10]. The bride receives these things as she leans upon her beloved.

Because the Virgin Mary ascended to these delights, the Church invites us thus to rejoice with her [Note: [Col. 0799] Antiphon for the Assumption of Blessed Mary.]:

> “Today the Virgin Mary ascended to heaven; rejoice, because she reigns with Christ for ever.”

Here it should be noted that this Virgin departs from the world; Mary ascends to heaven; the Queen surpasses the angels; the Mother approaches the Son. The first is so because today she is snatched away from this wicked age, leaving the world. Of the second: “Mary has been assumed into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0799] Ibid.]; of the third: “The holy Mother of God has been exalted above [Col. 0800C] the choirs of angels” [Note: [Col. 0799] Ibid.]; of the fourth: “Because she reigns with Christ for ever” [Note: [Col. 0799] Ibid.]. Thus it is evident how remote virginity is from the world, how capable of grasping heavenly mysteries is the brightness of a pure understanding, how greatly human dignity was then exalted, and how near to God is humble virginity.

Jerome shows how remote virginity is from the world thus: “To live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not a human life but an angelic one”; hence: “Virgins follow the Lamb wherever he goes” [Note: [Col. 0799] Rev. 14]. For these are the violet skins in the tabernacle, above the goats’-hair coverings and the reddened ram-skins [Note: [Col. 0799] Exod. 26].

Now it must be known that the devil bound the human race to himself in three ways: by foulness, baseness, and misery. By foulness, from original sin; by baseness, from birth; by misery, [Col. 0800D] in life. Through the first a human being is defiled; through the second cast down; through the third he suffers countless deficiencies. Of the first: “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed?” [Note: [Col. 0799] Job 14]. Of the second: “I said to corruption, ‘You are my father’; and to worms, ‘My mother and my sister’” [Note: [Col. 0799] Job 17]. Of the third: “A human being born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” [Note: [Col. 0799] Job 14].

But so that these things might be alleviated through the blessed Virgin, against the first her virginity flowered in the flesh; against the second she gave birth without intercourse; against the third [Col. 0801A] she gave birth and did not suffer pain. Against the first, therefore, virginity gave fragrance; against the second, conception gave honor; against the third, childbirth gave rest. Of the first: “Like choice myrrh I gave forth sweetness of fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ecclus. 24]. There is infected myrrh, accepted myrrh, and choice myrrh. The first is bitter repentance, and yet one does not cease from sin; the second is repentance by which sin is washed away; the third is affliction by which the crown of the righteous is increased. The first was given on the cross, which, “when he had tasted it, he would not drink” [Note: [Col. 0801] Matt. 27]; the second at the tomb for anointing; the third was offered to the Lord by the Magi [Note: [Col. 0801] Matt. 2], together with the gold of wisdom. Hence: “You alone were chosen in the female sex in the world, and you remain Mother of God the Savior, eternally a virgin” [Note: [Col. 0801] Antiphon from the Office of Blessed Mary.].

Of the second: “My flowers are fruits of honor and uprightness” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ecclus. 24]. Hence she came to meet [Col. 0801B] us like an honored mother, so as to say: “I took root among an honored people” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ibid.]. Of the third: “In all things I sought rest” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ibid.], and so forth. But it should be noted that there is a threefold rest. For she sought rest within herself, rest above herself, and rest around herself. The first was that of the Son; the second, that of the Holy Spirit; the third, that of the human race. The first was in the womb of the Virgin, in which Christ willed to become incarnate; the second was the infusion of graces in Christ, so that it could not be separated from him; the third will be the salvation of the human race, which God willed to save through the blessed Virgin. Of the first: “He who created me rested in my tabernacle” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ibid.]; of the second: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding” [Note: [Col. 0801] Isa. 11]; of the [Col. 0801C] third: “In all things I sought rest,” and so forth. Likewise: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, unless upon the humble, the quiet, and the one trembling at my words?” [Note: [Col. 0801] Isa. 66]. Mary was humble; Christ was quiet; the Christian trembles at the words. Of the first: “The Lord looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0801] Luke 1]; hence: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ibid.]. Of the second: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to announce to the meek” [Note: [Col. 0801] Isa. 61]. He was quiet because “he was led as a lamb to the slaughter, and did not open his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0801] Isa. 53]. Of the third: “O Lord, by fear of you we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0801] Isa. 26]. Thus this Virgin, acting in this way, departed from the world, because she is snatched away from this wicked age. Therefore, following her example, let us die to the world [Col. 0801D] so that we may attain chastity.

It follows: “Mary ascended to heaven.” Mary is interpreted “star of the sea.” Morally, this is in us the brightness of pure understanding, by which we penetrate the secrets of heaven. Hence the Apostle says: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” [Note: [Col. 0801] I Cor. 2], and: “With unveiled face we behold the glory of God” [Note: [Col. 0801] II Cor. 3]. This Mary has a threefold ascent: she ascends spiritually, wonderfully, and bodily. First above herself; second above human nature; third to the heavenly homeland. First through her own [Col. 0802A] humility; second through Christ’s incarnation; third through her own glorification. Of the first: “She lifted herself above herself” [Note: [Col. 0801] Lam. 3]. Of the second she herself says: “He who is mighty has done great things for me” [Note: [Col. 0801] Luke 1], and so forth. Of the third: “All generations shall call me blessed” [Note: [Col. 0801] Ibid.].

Of the first: “Who is this who ascends through the wilderness like a wisp of smoke from perfumes?” [Note: [Col. 0801] Song 3]. Of the second: “Who is this who ascends from the wilderness, abounding in delights?” Of the third: “I saw the beautiful one ascending like a dove above streams of water.” Therefore, first she ascends through the wilderness; second, from the wilderness; third, above streams of water. First, she is polished in spirit and body by the thorns of discipline; second, having trodden the rare path of discipline, she is made delightful by the flowery sweetness of heavenly things; third, she is raised to heaven by the flowing streams of graces, as though by wings. The first is through the fervor of holy conduct; the second through the benefit of overshadowing and the Lord’s incarnation; the third through the glory of exultation.

Hence the Bridegroom calls the bride now to the refuge of the rock, now to the flowering garden, and now invites her to the throne. First, that she might experience the harshness of Christ’s Passion; second, the flowery delight of spiritual goods; third, that she might approach the majesty of her Son. Of the first: “Come, my dove, into the clefts of the rock, into the hollow of the wall” [Note: [Col. 0801] Song 2]. Of the second: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride” [Note: [Col. 0801] Song 5]. Of the third: “Come, my chosen one, and I shall place my throne in you.”

See whether perhaps she is the woman who was seen standing above Boethius’s head: of most venerable [Col. 0802C] countenance, with burning eyes; at one time she showed herself visible in a size proportionate to ordinary humanity, as regards the first ascent. But at another time she seemed to touch heaven with the summit of her head, as regards the second. When she raised her head still higher, she seemed even to pierce heaven itself, as regards the third. You may also apply some of the foregoing descriptions to the blessed Virgin, so that from her we may take the model by which we ought to ascend after her.

She was called of most venerable countenance, of vivid complexion, with eyes burning and keen beyond the power of any human being. A venerable countenance means gravity of character; the color of her face means the truth of religion; burning eyes, love; penetrating eyes, the brightness of understanding. Through the first frivolity is excluded; through the [Col. 0802D] second, the false religiosity of hypocrites; through the third, false compassion and fraternity; through the fourth, blindness to worldly things. He wished to appear of venerable countenance who said: “Show me your face” [Note: [Col. 0801] Song 2]; hence Job: “The light of my face did not fall to the ground” [Note: [Col. 0801] Job 29]. Of complexion: “Moses’ face became radiant when the Lord looked upon him” [Note: [Col. 0801] Exod. 20]. The face of hypocrites is radiant, but it is not radiant through the Lord’s regard. Of burning eyes, in the Apocalypse: “His eyes were like a flame of fire, as if in a burning furnace” [Note: [Col. 0801] Rev. 1]. Of penetrating eyes: “The bird has not known the path, nor has the eye of the vulture [Col. 0803A] seen it” [Note: [Col. 0803] Job 28]. For through the sharpness of its sight a vulture sees a corpse beyond the sea. The sea is the world; the vulture indeed sees within it the corpse, that is, our flesh glorified. Mary, star of the sea, while still living in the world saw this spiritually; today she begins to see it in presence: behold, Mary ascends to heaven.

It follows: “The Queen surpasses the angels.” Thus human nature is honored. For she who through Eve had been bent beneath Satan’s feet is through Mary exalted above the choirs of angels. She whom through Eve the devil drew into destruction precedes the merit of angels in Mary. She who through Eve was made shameful is through Mary made [Col. 0803B] glorious above the angels. Of the first, the demons said: “Bend down, that we may pass over,” as the prophet says [Note: [Col. 0803] Isa. 51]. But against this: “You have been exalted, holy Mother of God, above the choirs of angels” [Note: [Col. 0803] Antiphon for the Assumption of Blessed Mary.], and so forth. Of the second: “Through Eve, by the envy of the devil, death entered the world.” But against this: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you alone have surpassed them all” [Note: [Col. 0803] Prov. 31]. The daughters are said to be souls still serving in the world, souls already reigning with God, and angelic powers. Of the third: “All who glorified her despised her, because they saw her shame” [Note: [Col. 0803] Lam. 1]. But against this:

> O how you shine with glorious light,  
> Royal offspring of David’s line;  
> Lofty Virgin Mary, seated  
> Above all heaven-born beings of the ether.  
> [Note: [Col. 0803] Church Hymn.]

Behold how she surpasses the angels.

It follows how she approaches the Son: “Rejoice, because she reigns with Christ for ever.” The soul reigns first under Christ, second in Christ, [Col. 0803C] third with Christ. First through the mortification of vices; second through the practice of virtues; third through glorification. Now it should be observed that a ruler possesses purple, a sceptre, and a crown. Thus from purple comes beauty, from the sceptre firmness, and from the crown honor: the beauty of brightness, the firmness of peace, the honor of majesty. By the first, those who behold rejoice; by the second, rebels are subdued; by the third, those who marvel show reverence. In the first, you will rejoice as one reigning with Christ when “they shall shine like the sun [Col. 0803D] in the kingdom of their Father” [Note: [Col. 0803] Matt. 13]. You will rejoice in the sceptre when the spirit does not desire against the flesh, nor the flesh against the spirit [Note: [Col. 0803] Gal. 5]. You will rejoice in the crown when it is said: “You have crowned him with glory and honor, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0803] Ps. 8].

Thus the Son called her who was departing from the world, ascending to heaven, surpassing the angels, and approaching the Son, saying: “Return, return, Shulamite; return, return, that we may behold you” [Note: [Col. 0803] Song 6]. Behold, through these four things “return” is said four times. Likewise: “Come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned” [Note: [Col. 0803] Song 4]. Therefore rejoice if, with her, you depart from the world through the mortification of vices; ascend to heaven through knowledge of heavenly things; surpass the angels through contemplation of God; and approach the Son by sighing for his exaltation, so that, through the intercession of the blessed Virgin, we may reign with him while reverencing his majesty.

“Who is this who ascends from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved?”

[CARD.] These are the Son’s words, as though he were wondering about his Mother. The blessed Virgin indeed ascended through the progress of merits. She ascended through the degrees of dignities, she who rises like the dawn, is beautiful as the moon, and chosen as the sun [Note: [Col. 0803] Song 6]. She also ascended from the support of this present life, being assumed above the choirs of angels. Moreover, she ascended from the wilderness, namely from the world, which she thus abandoned [Col. 0804B] and regarded as a wilderness that she turned away from it all her affection. She is said to abound in the delights of graces and virtues, and to lean upon her beloved; for, lest she lose the delights in which she abounded, she relied not upon her own merits but upon his grace—he who bestows grace and merit and adds reward besides. It follows:

> “Under the apple tree I raised you up; there your mother was corrupted, there your mother who bore you was violated.”

[THO.] The apple tree most fittingly signifies the wood of the holy cross, upon which he himself hung, concerning whom it was said above: “As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons” [Note: [Col. 0803] Song 2]. Under this tree, therefore, the beloved raised up the Synagogue, whom through faith in his Passion he recalled from everlasting death. Under this tree her mother and progenitress was [Col. 0804C] corrupted and violated—namely, the greater and older part of that same people, which, deceived by the persuasion of its leaders, chose Barabbas, recklessly crying out: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” [Note: [Col. 0803] Matt. 27]. And indeed, she was beneath the cross not by believing, but by obstinately calling down this vengeance upon herself. The Lord, separating the faithful from her association, exhorts her to keep fixed in her heart the memory of the grace bestowed upon her.

The Church teaches us of three mothers: the first was Eve, the second the Synagogue, the third Mary. The first was mother of the human race, the second of the Church militant, the third of the Savior. For Eve was the beginning of the human race; the Synagogue gave birth in the shadow [Col. 0804D] to the sacrament of faith; the third gave birth to Christ, who is “the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” [Note: [Col. 0803] John 1]. Hence Eve is called the mother of all living; the Synagogue, “the separation of flocks”; Mary, “star of the sea.” In the first obedience was broken; in the second faith was corrupted; in the third virginity remained incorrupt. The first because she was deceived; the second because she was unbelieving; the third because she was overshadowed by the Holy Spirit. Of the first, the Apostle says: “I fear lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted” [Note: [Col. 0803] II Cor. 11]. Of the second, David says: “Because they did not [Col. 0805A] believe in God, nor did they hope in his salvation” [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 77]. Of the third: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Note: [Col. 0805] Luke 1].

The first was through the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; the second through the tree of the holy cross; the third through the tree which is the wisdom of God. Through the first the covenant between God and humanity was broken; in the second the Synagogue was corrupted by the scandal of the cross; through the third the Virgin remained incorrupt, and the human race will become incorruptible. Hear of the broken covenant: “God placed the human being in paradise to work it and keep it” [Note: [Col. 0805] Gen. 2]. These are the covenant terms; but they were broken when, expelled from paradise, he heard: “Cursed is the earth in your work” [Note: [Col. 0805] Gen. 3]. Hear of the scandal of the cross: “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power [Col. 0805B] of God” [Note: [Col. 0805] I Cor. 1]. Hear of the incorruption of the human race: “This corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing immortality” [Note: [Col. 0805] I Cor. 15].

It should be noted that under the tree of the cross some are summoned, some are raised up, and some are raised again from the dead: the healthy are summoned, the sick are raised up, and the dead are resurrected. For these have something of Eve’s former tree: the healthy have hardness, by which they are slower in devotion; the sick are wearied by temptation; the dead delight in lying in their iniquity. But the first are summoned through the power of the cross, that they may advance in good; the sick are raised up, that they may shake off temptations; the dead are raised again, lest they remain four days in the tomb. To the first it is said: “Work while it is day” [Note: [Col. 0805] Ecclus. 51], and: “Walk [Col. 0805C] while you have the light” [Note: [Col. 0805] John 12]. To the second: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human; God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear” [Note: [Col. 0805] I Cor. 10]. To the third it is said: “Awake, you who sleep, rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” [Note: [Col. 0805] Eph. 5].

The hardness of the first is figured in Abraham, who, while beneath the hard oak—that is, the oak of Mamre—was summoned by an angelic vision, namely when he saw three and worshiped one [Note: [Col. 0805] Gen. 24]. The raising from the disturbance of temptations found in the second is figured in Leah, lying under a juniper, that is, among the thorns of temptations, who is raised by an angelic visitation. The resurrection of one lying dead in the pleasure of sins is figured in Nathanael, lying under a fig tree; whence he was called by the Lord, though he had long lain beneath the sin of the law [Col. 0805D].

There is also a mortal tree, namely justice, beneath which the soul is refreshed. It is planted in the soil of good will; rooted in the depth of humility; grows through desire; spreads branches through example; bears the fruit of good work; and feeds the hungry with the sweetness of contemplation. Of this tree blessed Job says: “A tree has hope: if it is cut down, it grows green again, and its branches bud” [Note: [Col. 0805] Job 14]. As Gregory says in the *Moralia*: by the name “tree” are sometimes signified the cross, sometimes a righteous man, and sometimes the incarnate wisdom of God.

In the wood [Col. 0806A] of the cross we have the hope of salvation. But when this is said here of a tree, it is applied to the justice of any righteous person. The tree of justice has hope, because the righteous person awaits the recompense of future blessedness. If it is cut down, it grows green again: for when the righteous person is afflicted in the death of suffering for the truth, he is restored in the green vigor of eternal life; and he who flourished here through faith will flourish there through sight. There its branches bud, because from compassion for the righteous, the faithful are often multiplied in love for the heavenly homeland and receive the green vigor of spiritual life, while they rejoice that he acted bravely.

The soul, together with its virtues, is satisfied from the fruit of justice. The tree of life, according to the form of a human being, is Christ in the midst of the Church. This tree has hope because, if it is cut down, it will grow green again: although Christ could be killed, through the glory of the resurrection he returned again to the green vigor of life. Its branches bud so that, through his resurrection, the faithful may multiply and grow far and wide. The fruit of this tree is the flesh and blood of Christ. This tree, namely the wisdom of God, was from eternity the food of angels; incarnate, it was the redemption of sinners; in the resurrection, the salvation of the righteous; in the ascension, the consummation of joys. What went before in the head is fulfilled through him in the body. Through the apple tree—that is, the cross—he endured shame; through it he himself, and we through him, come to glory: “For the glory of Lebanon has been given to him, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon” [Note: [Col. 0805] Isa. 35].

But let us see when our mother was corrupted beneath the tree. O detestable bargain of [Col. 0806C] Adam, by which all his posterity was poisoned with guilt, weighed down by the burden of misery, deprived of the fervor of love, and disinherited from the promised glory! Truly it was poisoned with guilt, to which the Prophet says: “Woe to the sinful nation, the people full of iniquity, the wicked seed, the criminal children!” [Note: [Col. 0805] Isa. 1]. Truly weighed down by the burden of misery, to which it is said: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” [Note: [Col. 0805] Gen. 3]. Thus “a human being is born for toil, and a bird for flying” [Note: [Col. 0805] Job 5]. Truly deprived of the fervor of love, for the whirlwind wind came from the north [Note: [Col. 0805] Ezek. 1], by which iniquity was multiplied and not merely the love of many, but the love of all, grew cold [Note: [Col. 0805] Matt. 24]. Truly disinherited from glory, because humanity changed its glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 105]. And so: [Col. 0806D] “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” [Note: [Col. 0805] I Pet. 1].

But paternal mercy, pitying human labors, “sent forth his Word and healed them, because he rescued them from their destructions” [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 106].—“Surely he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” [Note: [Col. 0805] Isa. 53]. Against the third evil it is said: “He shall send forth your word and melt them, and waters shall flow” [Note: [Col. 0805] Ps. 147].—“I came,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it should burn and be kindled?” [Note: [Col. 0805] Luke 12]. Against the fourth Peter says: “Blessed be God, who has begotten us again to a living hope, unto an incorruptible, undefiled, [Col. 0807A] and unfading inheritance preserved in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0807] I Pet. 1].

Thus the Son of God came. But against these evils, “the beauty of Carmel was given to him” [Note: [Col. 0807] Isa. 35]: the knowledge of circumcision, so that misery might be diminished and guilt inflicted [reading uncertain]. Sharon, which means “succession,” was given so that love might be kindled in us. The glory of Lebanon, which means “whitening,” was given so that the delight of restored blessedness might be ours. Therefore, that we may flee guilt and punishment, let us first consider circumcision. First we must withdraw, second cut down, third circumcise: withdraw by fleeing impending sins; cut down sins already clinging to us; circumcise the occasions that generate sin.

Of the first the Apostle says: “Flee fornication” [Note: [Col. 0807] I Cor. 6].—“For whoever touches pitch shall be defiled by it” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ecclus. 13]. Of the second: “Rend your hearts and [Col. 0807B] not your garments” [Note: [Col. 0807] Joel 2]. As though he said: Cut down the sin that clings to your hearts. Of the third Abraham is told: “Circumcise every male of your household” [Note: [Col. 0807] Gen. 17], namely all occasions that surround the heart in order to draw it into sin.

In the first sense we properly withdraw in three ways: first by fleeing sin, second by fleeing imminent danger, third by fleeing present exile. The first is for purity; the second, for the benefit of the brethren; the third, for eternal blessedness. Joseph displayed the first when his mistress, a harlot, seized the hem of his cloak and said: “Sleep with me” [Note: [Col. 0807] Gen. 39]. The second appeared in Paul when he was lowered in a basket through the wall [Note: [Col. 0807] II Cor. 11]. Of the third the Bride says: “Flee, my beloved; be like a roe or a young stag [Col. 0807C] upon the mountains of spices.”

Therefore let us cut from the flesh gluttony, lust, idleness, and adornment. This is the Levite’s wife, whom, after she was violated, he cut into twelve pieces. From evil work let us cut down evil intention, envy, hatred, anger, and so forth. This is the ox which Saul cut up [Note: [Col. 0807] I Sam. 11], which is said to have been cut into twelve pieces. From good works let us cut down vain glory. This is the cloak which Ahijah the Shilonite cut into twelve pieces [Note: [Col. 0807] III Kings 11]. Hence: “The watchmen of the walls took away my cloak” [Note: [Col. 0807] Song 5].

It follows that we must circumcise the causes that generate sins. Moses taught this circumcision thus: “When you enter the land and plant fruit-bearing trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins” [Note: [Col. 0807] Lev. 19]. Hear the foreskins: “There are six things that the Lord hates, and a seventh that his soul detests: [Col. 0807D] haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands shedding innocent blood, a heart devising most wicked thoughts, one uttering lies, a false witness, feet swift to run toward evil, and one who sows discord among brothers” [Note: [Col. 0807] Prov. 6]. Behold, “the beauty of Carmel was given to him” [Note: [Col. 0807] Isa. 35]—to him “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0807] I Pet. 2]—now in the head, now in the members. In the head, whence the Bride says: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely” [Note: [Col. 0807] Song 1]. But [Col. 0808A] how? “His head is finest gold; his eyes are like doves” [Note: [Col. 0807] Song 5]. And in the body the Bridegroom says: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn?” [Note: [Col. 0807] Song 6], and so forth.

We have heard how our mother Eve or the Synagogue was corrupted beneath the apple tree, namely the tree of the knowledge of good and [evil; the OCR reads “good and good”] [Note: [Col. 0807] Gen. 2]; and how she was also raised up through Christ beneath the tree of the cross. To him was given the knowledge of circumcision, through which our corruption might be raised up. Sharon too was given to him, namely succession: that is, the fire of the Holy Spirit was sent by the Father through him. Hence: “I came to cast fire; what do I desire but that it should burn?” [Note: [Col. 0807] Luke 12]. Thus love may blaze through him, and ardor may kindle the neighbors. But because “the beauty of Carmel was given to him” [Note: [Col. 0807] Isa. 35], he was circumcised not from guilt but from misery. For we have heard: “He had neither form nor beauty” [Note: [Col. 0807] Isa. 53]. Now we have heard the angels singing: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe, advancing in the abundance of his strength” [Note: [Col. 0807] Isa. 63].—“For we saw him as leprous, struck by God, and humiliated” [Note: [Col. 0807] Isa. 53]. But Jesus is “white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands” [Note: [Col. 0807] Song 5]. Likewise: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” [Note: [Col. 0807] Isa. 53]. Behold, all the Lord’s beauty has been exalted above the stars.

Now Sharon was given to him, to dry up those who are fluid, kindle the cold, and enlighten the blind. He wished to be dried who said: “Burn my reins and my heart” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ps. 25]; likewise: “Burn our reins and heart, O Lord, with the fire of the Holy Spirit.” But some are fluid through superfluity in worldly things; some are fluid in doing the will of the flesh; some are fluid in ambition for dignities. This fire dries them up. In the first sense, the Red Sea was dried up before the children of Israel [Note: [Col. 0807] Exod. 13]. In the second, the bed of the Jordan [Note: [Col. 0807] Josh. 4]. In the third it is said: “You dried up the rivers of Ethan” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ps. 73], which means “flying.”

He wished to kindle the cold when he said: “Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love” [Note: [Col. 0807] From the Office of the Church]. Of light it is said: “The divine fire came, not burning but illuminating, not scorching but shining” [Note: [Col. 0807] Ibid.]. Behold, Sharon was given to him. But the glory of Lebanon was given to him: namely, the delight of the homeland both to him and to us through the wood of the cross. For beneath the tree he raised us up by that resurrection through which we shall rise with him in glory, he himself granting it, “to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen” [Note: [Col. 0807] Rom. 16].

> “Under the apple tree I raised you up; there your mother was corrupted, there your mother who bore you was violated.”

[CARD.] It signifies the tree of the cross, which it denotes by the apple tree, because in opposition to Adam’s fruit of condemnation this tree bore the fruit of salvation, Jesus Christ. Like an apple, he feeds and gives us drink through the sacrament of his flesh and blood. Beneath this apple tree Christ says to his mother, “I raised you up,” so that you might understand the answer [Col. 0809A] which I gave you at the wedding when you said to me: “They have no wine” [Note: [Col. 0809] John 2]. For then I answered: “What is that to me and to you, woman?” [Note: [Col. 0809] Ibid.]. I raised you up so that you might understand this answer when, as you stood beside the cross, I said to you: “Behold your son” [Note: [Col. 0809] John 19]. You were seeking wine from him through a miracle, but he tastes death from that which he has from you. And it is added: There, namely under that tree, your mother, the Synagogue, which does not believe Christ, was corrupted by the fault of unbelief. There your mother who bore you was violated by cruelty, she who killed her Creator. It follows:

> “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.”

[THO.] Set me upon your heart by thought, upon your arm by action, so that within there may be “charity [Col. 0809B] from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith [Note: [Col. 0809] I Tim. 1],” and that the devotion of the heart may outwardly appear through works for the glory of God. “A seal,” he says. We are accustomed to tie something upon a finger or hand, so that by it we may remember what we have resolved to do. By this comparison, therefore, the Lord warns us to remain mindful of his commandments. Hence of the law which he gave: “It shall therefore be as a sign upon your hand [Note: [Col. 0809] Exod. 13].” Thus the Beloved is placed as a seal upon the heart when we retain in memory in our heart those things which he did and taught. He is placed as a seal upon the arm when we carry into outward effect those things which we hold in memory concerning him. This seal, or signet, bears within itself an image of the Beloved, which is threefold, as we have already said; but we repeat it in order to add something.

For there is the image of divinity, the image of our weakness, and the image of glorified humanity. In the first we were made, that we might exist; in the second we were restored, that we might be good; in the third we shall be perfected, that we may be blessed. In the first we are initiated; in the second we advance; in the third we shall be brought to completion. In the first we were formed and are re-formed; we are conformed to the second; into the third we shall be transformed. Of the first it is said: “God created man in his own image and likeness [Note: [Col. 0809] Gen. 1],” and: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind; and, putting off the old man with his deeds, put on the new man, who was created according to God, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him [Note: [Col. 0809] Ephes. 4].” Of the second: “Those whom he foreknew, [Col. 0809D] he predestined to be made conformable to the image of his Son [Note: [Col. 0809] Rom. 8].” Of the third: “With unveiled face we behold the glory of God, so as to be transformed into the same image from glory to glory [Note: [Col. 0809] II Cor. 3].”

The first image, therefore, consisted of memory, understanding, and good will. This is the form of the Trinity. For the Father is called memory, lest he seem like a forgetful calf; the Son, understanding, lest he seem, like a little child, less capable of truth; the Holy Spirit, good will, lest anyone suppose that there was no love in them. Therefore we were created in these three faculties, that we might remember, understand, and love the Lord. But when the first man sinned, memory [Col. 0810A] was turned into forgetfulness; understanding into ignorance; good will into hardness of heart. Of the first: “They forgot God who saved them, who did great things in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0809] Ps. 105].”—“Let sinners be turned into hell, all the nations that forget God [Note: [Col. 0809] Ps. 9].” Of the second: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances [Note: [Col. 0809] Ps. 24].” Of the third: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit,” says Stephen [Note: [Col. 0809] Acts 7].

Again, there is a sealed signet, a signet partly opened, and a signet now revealed. The first is the humility and lowliness of the righteous; the second, the writing of the prophets; the third, the kingdom of heaven. For in the first is shut up the treasure of virtues; in the second the grace of the sacraments is opened; in the third [Col. 0810B] the glory of the blessed is revealed. Of the first Job says: “He shuts up the stars under a seal [Note: [Col. 0809] Job 9],” calling virtues stars. Of the second John says in the Apocalypse: “You are worthy, Lord, to open the book and to loose its seven seals [Note: [Col. 0809] Apoc. 5].” Of the third the same writer says: “From every tribe of the children of Israel there were twelve thousand sealed [Note: [Col. 0809] Apoc. 7],” as though already in glory.

The first, then, is sealed because the righteous conceal their virtues in order to exclude vain glory; the second is partly manifest, so that the faithful may progress through it; the third is revealed to the righteous on their journey, that they may run there ardently, and is manifest to the blessed, that they may now rejoice in their glory. Again, some bear Christ’s seal in the body, some in the heart, some upon the forehead. The first is the seal of our weakness; the second, the seal of divinity in the heart [Col. 0810C]; the third, the seal upon the forehead—at one time the preaching of the Passion, at another of Christ’s glorified humanity. They bear it in the body by afflicting themselves; in the heart by remembering, understanding, and loving God; on the forehead by glorifying Christ’s Passion and the victory of the cross. Of the first Paul says: “Henceforth let no one trouble me; for I bear the marks of Jesus Christ in my body [Note: [Col. 0809] Gal. 6].”

There is a threefold image in the heart: the image of creation, the image of re-creation, and the image of likeness. The first is that of reason, the second of grace, the third of the Trinity. In the first we were created; through the second we were re-created; for the third we were created. In the first man goes to and fro in the knowledge of natural things; in the second he passes to contemplation of the heavenly city; [Col. 0810D] in the third he passes beyond to perfect love of God. Of the second David says: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us”—that is, the brightness of your Son, who enlightens us by renewing in us the seal of divinity, so that we may possess his memory, understanding, and love; and therefore, “you have given joy to my heart [Note: [Col. 0809] Ps. 4].” Of the third the angel says to the four angels: “Do not harm the earth or the trees until we have sealed the servants of God upon their foreheads [Note: [Col. 0809] Apoc. 7].” This can be understood of the seal of the cross. Of the seal of glory it is said, concerning that same angel: “I saw an angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the sign [Col. 0811A] of the living God [Note: [Col. 0811] Apoc. 7].” Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I will take you, Zerubbabel, my servant, and will set you as a seal, because I have chosen you, says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0811] Hag. 2].”

It should be noted that some bear on their foreheads the seal of the earthly man; some, the seal of the devil; some, the seal of Christ crucified; some, the seal of Christ glorified. The first are those who reveal in themselves, by word and deed, the enticement of the flesh; the second reveal the devil’s sign, pride; the third openly both bear and preach the disgrace of the cross; the fourth, the glory of the resurrection. As a figure of the first, King Uzziah had leprosy on his forehead, by which he was cast out [Note: [Col. 0811] II Chron. 26]. Goliath, as a figure of the second, received a stone in the forehead, by which he was struck down [Note: [Col. 0811] I Sam. 17]. The Israelite people received the Tau [Col. 0811B] upon the forehead [Note: [Col. 0811] Ezek. 9], that is, the sign of the cross, by which it was delivered from the destroyer. Aaron had a golden plate hanging upon his forehead [Note: [Col. 0811] Exod. 28], by which he was raised to the priesthood. On it was written *he*, *ioth*, and *vau*, namely the Tetragrammaton, which means: “This one is the beginning of the Passion of life.”

But let us, as we have borne the image of the earthly man, bear the image of the heavenly. The first are enemies of the cross of Christ, “whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who savour earthly things [Note: [Col. 0811] Phil. 3].” Upon this first seal is written: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die [Note: [Col. 0811] I Cor. 15].”; upon the second is written: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High [Note: [Col. 0811] Isa. 14].”; upon the third is written: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord [Col. 0811C] Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0811] Gal. 6].”; upon the fourth is written: “He will transform the body of our lowliness, making it conformed to the body of his glory [Note: [Col. 0811] Phil. 3].”—“What is present is momentary and light and works in us, beyond measure in sublimity, an eternal weight of glory [Note: [Col. 0811] II Cor. 4],” that is, prepares glory.

The Apostle showed us the pattern of the seal, that we might imprint it upon ourselves, when he set forth the manner of Christ’s Passion thus: “He delivered his soul unto death, and was numbered with the wicked; and he himself bore the sin of many, and prayed for transgressors that they might not perish [Note: [Col. 0811] Isa. 53].” You have heard the distress of death, the disgrace of contempt, heavenly compassion, and the perfection of charity. In the first he brought to completion our [Col. 0811D] deficiency; in the second he disclosed the heart infected by Jewish malice; in the third he sought our advancement; in the fourth he showed the affection of charity. Behold: for us life dies, glory is put to shame, health is made weak, majesty makes supplication.

Of the first: “Let the life of all die; let the life of all rise again.” Again: “The life of the world is suspended, through whom the dead rise again.” He was that Elisha who raised the dead man cast into the tomb in which he lay [Note: [Col. 0811] IV Kings 4]. He is the serpent upon the wood which did not live, and [Col. 0812A] yet delivered from death those who looked upon it [Note: [Col. 0811] Num. 21]. Hear the second, namely glory put to shame: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory [Note: [Col. 0811] I Cor. 2].”—“For they changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay [Note: [Col. 0811] Ps. 105],” when they crucified him among thieves as among brute animals. The sun in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0811] ch. 12], which “became as a sackcloth of hair,” prefigured this shame.

Hear concerning the third, namely that health is made weak: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you [Note: [Col. 0811] Ps. 40],” and “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed [Note: [Col. 0811] Jer. 17],” and “Save me, and I shall be saved [Note: [Col. 0811] Ibid.],” and “I perform healings today and tomorrow [Note: [Col. 0811] Luke 13]”: behold health. Hear weakness: “We saw him as though a leper, struck by God and humbled. Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows [Col. 0812B] [Note: [Col. 0811] Isa. 53].” This is Samson [Note: [Col. 0811] Judg. 4], strong but weakened through the beloved woman, and thus stirred up—that is, Christ weakened because of love for the Church.

The fourth is that majesty makes supplication: he entreats the sinner, entreats the righteous person, and entreats the Father. The sinner, that he may come to his senses; the righteous person, that he may advance; the Father, that he may forgive the one and increase grace in the other. Hear him entreating the sinner: “Return to me, and I will return to you [Note: [Col. 0811] Hos. 14],” and: “Why will you die in your sins, house of Israel [Note: [Col. 0811] Ezek. 33]?” He is the angel who dealt with the healing of Tobit [Note: [Col. 0811] Tob. 11]. He entreats the righteous thus: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0811] Ps. 33].” He is the angel having a golden censer in his hand, [Col. 0812C] standing beside the altar of the temple [Note: [Col. 0811] Apoc. 8], that is, the heart of the righteous person. He also entreats the Father, as he himself says: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete [Note: [Col. 0811] John 14],” and: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do [Note: [Col. 0811] Luke 23].” Hence two cherubim, whose name means “fullness of knowledge,” stood over the mercy-seat [Note: [Col. 0811] Exod. 25]. That mercy-seat is Christ, who became “the propitiation for our sins [Note: [Col. 0811] I John 2],” as though making supplication to the Father for us.

“Soul” is called an invisible substance, temporal life, sensibility, or a thing beloved. By the first man subsists; by the second he lives; by the third he desires; the fourth is the thing which he desires. “My soul shall live for him, and my seed shall serve him [Note: [Col. 0811] Ps. 21].” Of the second Paul says: “I do not make my life dearer to me than myself [Note: [Col. 0811] Acts 20].” Of the third: “My soul has longed [Col. 0812D] to desire your justifications at all times [Note: [Col. 0811] Ps. 118].” Of the fourth Christ says through David: “My eye is troubled in anger, my soul and my belly [Note: [Col. 0811] Ps. 30].” For in the troubled soul of Christ was reason, which is the eye of the inner man; and in the Passion there were his soul and the affection, or unanimity, of the apostles, whom he loved as his own soul. Christ laid down the first in death; he delivered the second to death; the third was sorrowful unto death; the fourth was redeemed in death.

Hear concerning the first: “I have power,” Christ says, [Col. 0813A] “to lay down my soul, and power to take it again [Note: [Col. 0813] John 10].” For he laid it down in death when it was separated from the body. Of the second: “He delivered 170 his soul unto death and was numbered with the wicked [Note: [Col. 0813] Isa. 53].” [The printed “170” is evidently an OCR or textual intrusion.] Of the third he himself says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death [Note: [Col. 0813] Mark 24].” Of the fourth he says through the prophet David: “My lips shall rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed, O Lord [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 70].” The soul is also called the man himself. Hence: “The soul that has not been afflicted on this day shall perish from his people [Note: [Col. 0813] Lev. 23].” This holy soul was delivered by the Father, delivered by Christ, and delivered by Judas: by the Father in exposing it to death; by Christ in obeying the Father; by Judas in handing it over to the Jews for a price.

In the first is shown the Father’s generosity; in the second [Col. 0813B] the Son’s charity; in the third Judas’s wickedness. Of the first the Church sings: “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us men [Note: [Col. 0813] Office of the Church].” For Christ was “delivered for our offences [Note: [Col. 0813] Rom. 4].” Of the second we have here: “He delivered his soul unto death, and was numbered with the wicked [Note: [Col. 0813] Isa. 53].” Of the third Christ himself says to Judas: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss [Note: [Col. 0813] Luke 22]?” Therefore the Father delivered the Son, that through him he might call lost man back to the heavenly kingdoms; Christ delivered himself, that by his blood he might reconcile us to the Father; Judas delivered Christ, that he might satisfy his thirst for greed. Thus the Father delivered him as a price for redemption; the Son gave himself up as a victim for sacrifice; Judas delivered him like a wolf to devour him.

Of the first it is said: [Col. 0813C] “He sent redemption to his people [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 110].” For he is the ram substituted for sacrifice in place of Isaac [Note: [Col. 0813] Gen. 22], that is, humanity for divinity. Of the second: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he opened not his mouth [Note: [Col. 0813] Isa. 53].” Divine wisdom incarnate offered itself for us. It was the daughter of Jephthah who freely offered herself when she came to meet her father returning from battle [Note: [Col. 0813] Judg. 11]. Jephthah means “opening”; here he signifies the fathers from whom Christ’s faith was made manifest. Of the third Jacob says: “A most evil beast has devoured my son Joseph [Note: [Col. 0813] Gen. 37].” Joseph means “increase,” that is, Christ, who increased “in wisdom and age before God and men [Note: [Col. 0813] Luke 2].” And we increase in good things in him and through him. As a figure of his sale, Joseph’s brothers [Col. 0813D] sold Joseph himself to the Ishmaelites, and the Ishmaelites led him into Egypt [Note: [Col. 0813] Gen. 37], which is interpreted “darkness.” For Christ was sold by Judas; he came into the darkness of death, the darkness of the tomb, and the darkness of hell. Behold how life dies.

There follows how glory is put to shame. Let us therefore consider the cause for which he suffers, the person under whom he suffers, and the thief with whom he suffers. For he suffers for the wicked, he suffers under the wicked, and he suffers with the wicked. In the first is shown the work of divine condescension; in the second, the innocence of divine subjection; in [Col. 0814A] the third, the example of humiliation. The first is so that God may be loved more greatly; the second, lest man disdain to submit; the third, lest anyone exalt himself. Hear how he suffered for the wicked: “He was wounded for our sins, bruised for our crimes [Note: [Col. 0813] Isa. 53]”: behold the cause for which. Hear by whom: “The souls of the ungodly raged against me, and my heart was weighed down over them.” Again, they said: “Let us all unjustly beat the righteous man with words.” Hear among whom: “He was numbered with the wicked [Note: [Col. 0813] Ibid.].” Again: “They cast me among the lawless,” etc. Behold how he is put to shame.

There follows how health is made weak: “Though he was God, he became man, that he might bear our sins.” But note what he deferred, what he bore, what he took away, what he bestowed, and what he brought back: [Col. 0814B] he deferred vengeance; bore punishment; took away guilt; bestowed grace; brought us back to our homeland. He deferred vengeance, patiently awaiting repentance; bore punishment, supplying by mercy what was insufficient; took away guilt, cleansing us from every defilement of flesh and spirit [Note: [Col. 0813] II Cor. 7]; bestowed grace, by which we may advance in good; and brought us back to our homeland through repentance, carrying the sheep that had gone astray back to the flock [Note: [Col. 0813] Matt. 18].

Hear of the first: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” says Paul [Note: [Col. 0813] Rom. 2]. Of the second Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 0813] ch. 53]: “Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our offences, and we placed upon him the iniquities of us all.” Of the third: “You forgave the wickedness of your people; you covered all their sins [Col. 0814C] [Note: [Col. 0813] Ps. 84].” Of the fourth: “He led captivity captive and gave gifts to men [Note: [Col. 0813] Eph. 4].” Of the fifth: “He spread his wings and took him up, and carried him upon his shoulders [Note: [Col. 0813] Deut. 32].”

An example of the first was that he rebuked Peter because he cut off the servant’s ear [Note: [Col. 0813] John 18], so that the servant might be preserved for repentance. Of the second, the Samaritan, who carried the man wounded by robbers to the inn [Note: [Col. 0813] Luke 10]. Of the third, that he cleansed lepers and washed the disciples’ feet [Note: [Col. 0813] John 13]. Of the fourth, that he fed the crowd with five loaves [Note: [Col. 0813] Matt. 14]. Of the fifth, that he himself bore his cross [Note: [Col. 0813] John 19], through which, as by a ladder, he brought us back to heaven. Behold brotherly compassion.

There follows the perfection of charity: namely, that he prayed for transgressors that they might not perish [Note: [Col. 0813] Luke 23]. Of transgressors, some approach, some enter, [Col. 0814D] some depart, and some return. Some approach sin; some enter the depth of evils; some depart by setting an example through evil work; some return, compunct, to the fruit of repentance. For these transgressors he prayed: for the first, that they might not fall into temptation; for the second, that they might not remain in obstinacy; for the third, that they might not corrupt others by their perverse deed; for the fourth, that they might make satisfaction and advance in satisfaction.

He taught us the first prayer—that is, to pray thus for the first: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive [Col. 0815A] our debtors [Note: [Col. 0815] Matt. 6].” For the second: “And lead us not into temptation [Note: [Col. 0815] Ibid.],” that is, do not lead us inwardly, into the depth of evils. For the third he prayed at Lazarus’s tomb, saying: “I thank you, Father, because you always hear me [Note: [Col. 0815] John 11].” Lazarus is their figure. For the fourth, thus: “Sanctify in your name those whom you have given me [Note: [Col. 0815] John 17].” Perhaps it is for these four that the Apostle says: “I desire that in the Church there be prayers, entreaties, petitions, thanksgivings [Note: [Col. 0815] I Tim. 2].” Behold the perfection of charity.

But charity may be perfect, more perfect, or most perfect. It is perfect to forgive an offence; more perfect to pray for enemies; most perfect to do them good. Christ did the first in Mary Magdalene; the second in this prayer; the third by giving himself for sinners in his [Col. 0815B] Passion.

“Set me.”

[CARD.] The Beloved must be placed upon the heart and arm, so that heart and hand, will and action, may serve his love in due subjection. He must be set as a seal—that is, as a signet—by which those who are not friends are excluded from secrets; namely, so that the devil may be excluded from thought and action. The Beloved must also be set as a signet upon heart and arm, so that, as a seal bears the king’s image and name, so will and action may be formed in Christ; so that they may be designated by his name and called Christian from Christ, as Isaiah says: “This one shall say, ‘I am the Lord’s,’ etc.; and this one shall write with his hand [Col. 0815C] to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0815] Isa. 44].”

Therefore the Son says to the mother: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm”; and this is easy because you love me. For love is so strong that nothing resists its power. This is what follows:

“For love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell; its lamps are lamps of fire and flames. Many waters cannot quench charity, nor can rivers overwhelm it.”

[THO.] The strength of this love—that is, charity—is shown both in the Head and in the members. In the Head, love is strong as death, because he loved us so greatly that he endured death for us; hence he himself says: “No one has greater charity than this: that someone lay down his soul for his friends [Note: [Col. 0815] John 15].” The jealousy with which he was jealous for us is hard as hell, because no adversities could call him back from care for us, just as hell cannot be softened by the torments of the wretched. The lamps of fire and flames—that is, of love—are the hearts of the elect, who with all their powers subject themselves to love of their Creator and love their neighbours as themselves. These lamps are of fire, by which they burn inwardly, and of flames, by which they shine outwardly. A lamp of fire was he who said of Jesus: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way [Note: [Col. 0815] Luke 24]?” The Lord taught us to be a lamp, saying: “Let [Col. 0816A] your light shine before men [Note: [Col. 0815] Matt. 5].”

The many waters which cannot quench charity, and the rivers, are assaults of temptations that attack the souls of the faithful either visibly or invisibly. But hearts rooted and founded in charity are not moved [Note: [Col. 0815] Eph. 3], as it is written: “When you pass through the water, I will be with you, and rivers shall not overwhelm you [Note: [Col. 0815] Isa. 43].” And of the house founded upon a rock it is said: “The rivers came, the winds blew, and it was not moved, because it was founded upon a rock [Note: [Col. 0815] Matt. 7].”

In these five clauses five qualities are ascribed to charity: first it is called strong; second, hard; third, fiery; fourth, unquenchable; fifth, immovable. In the first it possesses patience; in the second, continence; in the third, ardour and brightness; in the fourth, prudence; in [Col. 0816B] the fifth, perseverance: patience against ignorance, prudence against the turbulence of worldly care, perseverance against instability of mind. Of the first: “Charity is patient [Note: [Col. 0815] I Cor. 13].” Of the second the Apostle says: “I pray that your charity may abound more and more in all sense and knowledge, so that you may approve better things and be sincere [Note: [Col. 0815] Phil. 1],” that is, continent from softness of life.
