Of ardour: “It bears all things [Note: [Col. 0815] I Cor. 13].” Of light: “It is kind [Note: [Col. 0815] Ibid.].” For kindness is liberality in material things that builds others up when they see a person distribute what is his own to the needy. Of prudence: “Charity is not ambitious, does not seek what is its own [Note: [Col. 0815] Ibid.].” For it is great prudence to act amid temporal care in such a way that one does not seek honours for [Col. 0816C] God’s sake, nor demand back all that is one’s own. Of perseverance: “Charity never fails [Note: [Col. 0815] Ibid.].”—“Who shall separate us from the charity of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword [Note: [Col. 0815] Rom. 8]?” Behold one who perseveres.

This is strong charity. But charity may be strong, stronger, and strongest. Let us, that is, raise it into a kind of tree and say how strong it is in the root, stronger in the trunk, and strongest in the summit. It has its root in purpose, its trunk in experience, and its summit in rejoicing amid scourges: “When you hear the sound of one marching in the tops of the pear-trees, then you shall go forth to battle [Note: [Col. 0815] II Kings 5].” This is expounded differently elsewhere. Of the first the Apostle says: “Rooted and founded in charity [Col. 0816D] [Note: [Col. 0815] Eph. 3].” Of the second, as was said above: “Who shall separate us from the charity of God?” Of the third the same Apostle says: “But I wish to know the charity of Christ that surpasses knowledge [Note: [Col. 0815] Eph. 3].” For the charity by which we rejoice in tribulation surpasses all knowledge.

Hear David, strong in the root—that is, in purpose: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength [Note: [Col. 0815] Ps. 17].” Hear Job, strong in the trunk—that is, in experience: “Even if he kills me, I will hope in him [Note: [Col. 0815] Job 13].” Hear those placed in the summit—that is, in joy amid tribulation: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name [Col. 0817A] of Jesus [Note: [Col. 0817] Acts 5].” This charity is strong as death because in it they spent their temporal life. It follows:

“Jealousy is hard as hell.” Again, charity is hard, harder, and hardest: hard in cutting away superfluity, harder in restricting necessity, hardest in abandoning one’s own will. Of these the Apostle said: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke [Note: [Col. 0817] II Tim. 4].” Reprove, for cutting away superfluity; entreat, for restricting necessity; rebuke, that one may abandon one’s will. Of the first it is said in the Law: “When you have taken a captive woman, if you wish to have her as your wife, she shall shave all the hair of her flesh [Note: [Col. 0817] Lev. 14],” that is, superfluities. Of the second the Apostle Paul says: “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery [Note: [Col. 0817] I Cor. 9],” namely by withdrawing things necessary [Col. 0817B] for the body. Of the third Peter says: “Lord, behold, we have left all things and followed you [Note: [Col. 0817] Matt. 19],” even one’s will, as the expositor says: “He leaves everything who has not retained even the will to possess.”

By these three hardnesses our persecutor, the devil, is slain. Perhaps these are the three spears by which Absalom, pursuing his father, was killed [Note: [Col. 0817] II Kings 18]. As a figure of these three, Christ endured three hard piercings on the cross. He was pierced by nails in hands and feet, by thorns in the head, and by a spear in the side [Note: [Col. 0817] Luke 23]. He was pierced in feet and hands as if to indicate that the superfluities of our works must be cut away; in the head, where the senses are active, to show that we must restrain our senses [Col. 0817C] even from what is necessary to them; in the heart, where the seat of the will is, to teach us that our own will must be plucked out from our heart. This charity is hard as hell, which torments the damned without utterly killing them. For in this hardness we torment ourselves, but we ought not utterly to kill ourselves.

It follows: charity is fiery. But note what is said: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames.” In a lamp four things are found: the lamp is a clear vessel; it contains oil within; the oil nourishes the fire, which gives heat and brightness. Thus the lamp signifies a pure heart; the oil, devotion; the heat of the fire, ardour of desire; the brightness, an example for neighbours and contemplation of heavenly things. Such a lamp was John, namely “burning and shining” [Col. 0817D] [Note: [Col. 0817] John 5]. The lamp was a clean heart; devotion was the oil; he had ardour in correcting, conversing, and loving; he shone in teaching, in showing Christ, and in contemplating heavenly things. John was a lamp burning with charity and shining by example and the gift of understanding; hence: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames.”

Again, there was a vision of living creatures “like burning coals of fire, and like the appearance of lamps [Note: [Col. 0817] Ezek. 1].” There was one burning in soul, burning 171 in hand, and burning in tongue. In the soul, by the heat of love; in the hand, by the fervour of action; in the tongue, [Col. 0818A] by the ardour of prayer and preaching. The first was figured in Ezekiel by the man who was like a flame of fire from the loins upward; hence: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall blaze forth [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 38].” The second was the man who entered among the wheels beneath the cherubim and filled his hands with coals of fire [Note: [Col. 0817] Ezek. 10]; hence: “Burning lamps in your hands [Note: [Col. 0817] Luke 12].” The third was in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0817] ch. 6]: the seraph who took a coal from the altar with tongs and touched the prophet’s mouth. Hence the Holy Spirit appeared in tongues of fire [Note: [Col. 0817] Acts 2].

Again, he shone inwardly, outwardly, and above. Inwardly, by knowledge of discernment between good and evil; outwardly, by the beauty of honourable religious observance; above, by understanding of the whole Trinity. Of the first: “See lest the light that is in you become darkness [Col. 0818B] [Note: [Col. 0817] Luke 11].” Of the second: “Let your light shine before men [Note: [Col. 0817] Matt. 5].” Of the third Job says: “Who will grant that I might be as in former months, when God guarded me, when his lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked in darkness [Note: [Col. 0817] Job 29]?” He understood at baptism the Father in the voice, the Holy Spirit in the dove, and the Son in the flesh.

That Magdalene, weeping at Christ’s feet [Note: [Col. 0817] Luke 7], purified the lamp—that is, her heart; by preparing the spices for burial, she procured devotion; by frequently running to the tomb, she showed the love of longing. Fourth, she was enlightened when Christ appeared to her in the form of a gardener [Note: [Col. 0817] John 20]. Thus in the first we prepare lodging for the Beloved; in the second we await him with joy; in the third we meet him as he comes; [Col. 0818C] in the fourth, when he knocks, we open with the brightness of lamps.

And in Ezekiel: “There was the likeness of living creatures like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps [Note: [Col. 0817] Ezek. 1].” If you wish to cleanse the lamp—that is, the heart—hear James: “Cleanse your hands, sinners; purify your hearts, you double-minded [Note: [Col. 0817] Jas. 4].” Consider the woman who, at Elisha’s command, poured in oil [Note: [Col. 0817] IV Kings 4], that you may possess the oil of devotion. For this woman is new love, which at the beginning has little oil—that is, devotion—in her house, that is, in her heart. The son is outward work, which prepares the vessels of hearts.

Fire is useful to you for three purposes: it consumes, kindles, and illuminates. It consumes guilt, kindles sloth, and illuminates ignorance. Of the first: “Our God is a consuming fire [Note: [Col. 0817] Deut. 4].” [Col. 0818D] Of the second: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will except that it burn [Note: [Col. 0817] Luke 12]?” Of the third: “He spread a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 104].” Of the first: “For in the fire of my zeal all the earth shall be devoured [Note: [Col. 0817] Zeph. 3],” that is, everything earthly. And: “Let fire devour your enemies [Note: [Col. 0817] Isa. 26],” that is, unlawful impulses. Of the second: “Was not our heart burning within us,” concerning Jesus, “while he spoke to us on the way [Note: [Col. 0817] Luke 24]?” Of the third: “In your light we shall see light [Note: [Col. 0817] Ps. 35].”

There follows concerning unquenchable and immovable charity. It is unquenchable when it administers the benefit of the brethren so prudently [Col. 0819A] that excessive care, creeping in secretly and gradually, does not invisibly overthrow it. For such temptations are simply called waters. But charity is immovable when the assault of violent and open temptation cannot move it from its constancy; that temptation is here called by the name “river.” Of these Job said: “A falling mountain crumbles away, and a rock is moved from its place. Waters hollow out stone, and by a flood the earth is gradually consumed [Note: [Col. 0819] Job 14].” For the mountain is a man exalted in charity. But if he lacks prudence, that charity crumbles away like the earth of a mountain gnawed by stealthy and incessant waters. This is what he says: “By a flood the earth is gradually consumed.” The rock, however, signifies a man strong and constant in charity; but the continual assault of temptations, by its violence, hollows him out like an unceasing river, until at last he falls in a single onset. Hence it is said: “Waters hollow out stone.” But if charity is prudent and steadfast, many waters will not quench it and rivers will not overwhelm it.

“If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as though it were nothing.”

[THO.] How true this saying is was made evident in the first apostles and in their countless followers. For love they gave all that they had in the world, and thought that they had lost nothing, provided that they received true goods in heaven. The Lord showed this by two parables in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field” [Col. 0819C; Note: [Col. 0819] Matt. 13]; and another: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls” [Note: [Col. 0819] Matt. 20]. In these it is shown that everything ought to be given for the love of God.

We know that there are three houses, in each of which there is a threefold substance which may be given for love: the first is the house of money, the second of discipline, the third of wisdom. Of the first the Apostle says: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver” [Note: [Col. 0819] 2 Tim. 2]; of the second: “Who makes those of one manner to dwell in a house” [Note: [Col. 0819] Ps. 67]; of the third: “Wisdom has built herself a house” [Note: [Col. 0819] Prov. 9].

The first is material; the second is the house of religious life; the third is the spiritual house in the secret place of the heart. The first is made from the rough and hard material of stones and timbers; the second from the concord of brethren; the third from the harmony of virtues. In the first [Col. 0819D] are the resources of temporal goods; in the second the luxury of bodies is restrained; in the third the treasure of virtues is guarded. The first has a foundation of perishable wood or stones; in the second the foundation is Christ; in the third, charity, which is called the Holy Spirit. Of the first: “All the foundations of the earth shall be moved” [Note: [Col. 0819] Ps. 81]. Whatever stones and whatever constructions there may be, “there shall not remain one stone upon another which shall not be destroyed” [Note: [Col. 0819] Matt. 24].

The second is well founded upon a firm rock [Note: [Col. 0819] Matt. 7]. Hence the Apostle says: [Col. 0820A] “As a wise architect, I laid the foundation” [Note: [Col. 0819] 1 Cor. 3]. And he shows what that foundation is: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0819] Ibid.]. Upon this the apostles built gold—that is, Christians fervent in charity; silver—that is, those resonant and gleaming with divine utterances; precious stones, conspicuous for works of virtue. They also built weaker persons: wood, namely those somewhat hard in works of mercy; hay, namely those tender in their flesh; stubble, namely those given to a certain frivolity. Yet they shall be saved because of the merit of the foundation.

The Most High himself founded the third [Note: [Col. 0819] Ps. 86]. Hence the Apostle: “Rooted and founded in charity, and built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” [Note: [Col. 0819] Eph. 3]. Hence Isaiah: “I will lay [Col. 0820B] your stones in order” [Note: [Col. 0819] Isa. 54], that is, I shall arrange virtues within you; and he adds: “I shall found you upon sapphires, and shall make jasper your battlements, and your gates of carved stones” [Note: [Col. 0819] Ibid.]. Sapphire has the colour of heaven and signifies charity, upon which the other virtues are founded and which is heavenly in origin. Jasper is green in colour and signifies the verdure of faith. It is placed in the battlements, because true faith overcomes demons; hence: “The saints conquered kingdoms through faith.” The carved stones are patience. The gates are made from these, because patience, like a gatekeeper, is the guardian of virtues.

In the first house material food is eaten; in the second, the paschal lamb; in the third, the stream of the river, the torrent of butter and honey. The first is consumed from necessity, the second with sobriety, the third in intoxication. Of the first it is said to the apostles: [Col. 0820C] “Into whatever house you enter, remain there until you depart, eating and drinking what they have” [Note: [Col. 0819] Luke 10], and this was for their necessity. Of the second: “In the same house you shall eat it.” But how? With sobriety. Hear: “You shall gird your loins,” against luxury; “you shall have shoes on your feet,” against an abundance of earthly things; “holding staffs in your hands” [Note: [Col. 0819] Exod. 12], so that you may have a defence against the violence of demons. Of the third: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” [Note: [Col. 0819] Ps. 25].

Thus in the first house is the substance of temporal goods; in the second, the substance of bodies; in the third, the substance of virtues. We can have these three substances either against charity, sometimes without charity, or we give them for charity. We expend temporal things against charity, as did that prodigal son when he lived luxuriously with prostitutes [Note: [Col. 0819] Luke 15]; we abuse our bodies for their pleasures; we vainly glory in the substance of virtues themselves. James says: [Col. 0820D] “You have feasted upon the earth and nourished your bodies in delights” [Note: [Col. 0819] ch. 5]. Again: “Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, and closes his bowels against him—how does the charity of the Father abide in him?” [Note: [Col. 0819] 1 John 3]. Behold temporal goods [Col. 0821A] used against charity.

Again, we use the substance of the body against charity when we pride ourselves on strength or beauty. But “grace is deceitful and beauty vain” [Note: [Col. 0821] Prov. 31], and “cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” [Note: [Col. 0821] Jer. 17]. To one who uses virtues against charity it is said: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” [Note: [Col. 0821] 1 Cor. 4].

They use these things without charity, as do those who give goods to their friends, not for God’s sake but for carnal affection; who render service to others with their own bodies for the sake of social courtesy; who possess the substance of virtues from mere habit. Hence the Apostle: “If I speak with the tongues of men and angels but do not have charity, I have become as sounding bronze [Col. 0821B] or a clanging cymbal. And if I have all knowledge, etc., I am nothing” [Note: [Col. 0821] 1 Cor. 13]. Behold virtues without charity. “And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor” [Note: [Col. 0821] Ibid.]: behold temporal goods without charity. “And if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” [Note: [Col. 0821] Ibid.]: behold the substance of the body without charity.

But we use these three substances by giving them for charity and despising them as though they were nothing: namely, when we leave temporal goods for God’s sake; when we expose the body to martyrdom; when we attribute our virtues to God and not to ourselves. Of the first the Apostle says: “The things which were gains to me have become losses for Christ, for whose sake I have counted all things losses [Col. 0821C] and reckon them as dung, that I may gain Christ” [Note: [Col. 0821] Phil. 3]. Of the second: “Let rottenness enter into my bones and seethe beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0821] Hab. 3]; and: “The saints experienced mockeries and beatings” [Note: [Col. 0821] Heb. 11], etc. Of the third Paul says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Note: [Col. 0821] 1 Cor. 15]; and: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” [Note: [Col. 0821] Ps. 113].

Therefore, when we use these things against charity, we are dragged down to lower things; without charity, we are reckoned as nothing; with charity, we are lifted up before God. Of the first David says: “My substance is in the lowest parts of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0821] Ps. 138]. Of the second the same man says: “My substance is as nothing before you” [Note: [Col. 0821] Ps. 38]. Of the third David says joyfully to God: “My substance is with you, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0821] Ibid.].

He gave the whole substance of his house [Col. 0821D] for love who said: “I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them; I did not turn my face away from those who reproached me and spat upon me” [Note: [Col. 0821] Isa. 50]. If that evangelical saying is true—indeed, because it is true—“No one has greater charity than that someone lay down his life for his friends” [Note: [Col. 0821] John 15], our Saviour seems not merely to rise to the worship of charity, but to exceed the bounds of charity. In order to give his servants a remedy for this misery, he sustained the loss of his temporal life. To relieve our poverty, he made an exceeding abundance [Col. 0822A] of himself. For love he gave his body, gave his soul, gave his spirit: his body for persecutors, his soul for sinners, his spirit into the Father’s hands. He gave his body to be scourged; his soul to die for sinners; his spirit to be kept for the coming resurrection.

In the first he gave us an example of patience; in the second he exceeded the limits of human misery; in the third he showed us from whom we must expect the reward of our warfare. Of the first he says: “I gave my body to those who struck me, my cheeks to those who plucked them” [Note: [Col. 0821] Isa. 50]. Of the second: “He delivered his soul unto death; he was reckoned among the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0821] Isa. 53]. Of the third: when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit, he said to the Father: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” [Note: [Col. 0821] Luke 23].

In the first, hear the example of patience: [Col. 0822B] “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps” [Note: [Col. 0821] 1 Pet. 2]. Of mercy: “His mercies are over all his works” [Note: [Col. 0821] Ps. 144]; again: “In the land of the Lord he is gracious to you.” This is not human misery but divine mercy. Hear from whom we ought to expect the reward of our warfare: “When you pray, enter your chamber; and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” [Note: [Col. 0821] Matt. 6]. God, he says, renders the reward for the labours of his saints [Note: [Col. 0821] Matt. 20].

“I gave my body,” he says, “to those who struck me” [Note: [Col. 0821] Isa. 50]. The mind is astonished, nature recoils, understanding shrinks from the striking of that body which walked upon the sea with dry feet [Note: [Col. 0821] Matt. 14]; by whose touch [Col. 0822C] the sick are healed; at whose fragrance the dead return to life; which was born of a virgin upon earth, which he glorified in heaven, which angels worship. Who can bear that those cheeks should be plucked, cheeks which, flowering in the bloom of youth, could move even their enemies by their appearance? Cheeks which, as the Bride says, are “like beds of spices planted by perfumers” [Note: [Col. 0821] Song 5]? Who can bear that face to be dishonoured with spittle, which shone like the sun in the Transfiguration [p. 172] [Note: [Col. 0821] Matt. 17]? Where is he who was “fairer in form than the children of men” [Note: [Col. 0821] Ps. 44], since “we saw him as though leprous, struck by God, and humbled” [Note: [Col. 0821] Isa. 53]?

How were those feet, beneath which the prophet saw the work of sapphire [Note: [Col. 0821] Ezek. 28], and those “rounded hands, golden” [Note: [Col. 0821] Song 5], fixed with nails? For what reason was that body pierced by a lance, in which all wisdom is hidden [Note: [Col. 0821] Ecclus. 20], which was girded [Col. 0822D] at the breasts with a golden belt [Note: [Col. 0821] Rev. 1]? Was dominion placed upon his shoulder when he was fastened to the gibbet of the cross? Did his head, “the finest gold” [Note: [Col. 0821] Song 5], deserve to be crowned with thorns? You marvel, he says, that I emptied myself to the measure of human weakness [Note: [Col. 0821] Phil. 2]; but how could the whole human being be healed unless the Hebrew had contracted himself to the measure of the daughter of the Shunammite? “We saw him,” he says, “as leprous, struck by God, and humbled” [Note: [Col. 0821] Isa. 53].

Leprous with wounds and bruising; struck with the lance; [Col. 0823A] pierced by nails and thorns; humbled by the shame of insults. Elisha sent his servant Gehazi, and the child was not raised; his staff—that is, the Law—was laid upon him, “and there was neither voice nor perception.” Elisha himself came, and the child was raised [Note: [Col. 0823] 4 Kings 4]. A priest and a Levite passed by the man wounded by robbers; behold, the Samaritan came, who poured in wine and oil [Note: [Col. 0823] Luke 10]. You marvel at the cross; but how could the Israelite people, wounded by serpents, recover unless they looked upon the serpent raised upon the wood [Note: [Col. 0823] Num. 21]? How could Jacob return to his father with two companies unless he crossed the Jordan with this staff [Note: [Col. 0823] Gen. 32]?

“Whoever wishes,” he says, “to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” [Note: [Col. 0823] Matt. 16]. Whoever wishes to come after me to the heavenly city, let him deny himself, doing not his own will [Col. 0823B] but the Father’s; let him take up his cross, imitating my Passion; and let him follow me through the virtue of obedience. Thus Isaac followed his father to be sacrificed, carrying the wood of the cross; but his father carried the fire and the sword [Note: [Col. 0823] Gen. 22]: the fire of love and the sword of suffering. Hear the fire: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” [Note: [Col. 0823] John 3]. “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” [Note: [Col. 0823] Matt. 16].

“Go now, and hesitate to bear what he himself bore,” says the poet [Note: [Col. 0823] Ovid]. But with what pains, do you suppose, was he afflicted? Hence the Virgin Mary, and likewise John the Evangelist:

> The rod mourns its flower; the beloved laments love.  
>   
> The virgin mourns her flower withering under the penalty of death.  
>   
> Now he drinks at supper; the beloved mourns in love.

[Col. 0823C; Note: [Col. 0823] Hymn of the Blessed Virgin.]

Therefore he underwent the difficulty of death in order to destroy the power of death. For Eleazar would not have killed the elephant unless he had placed himself beneath it [Note: [Col. 0823] 1 Macc. 6]. Thus “by dying he destroyed our death, and by rising he restored life” [Note: [Col. 0823] Preface of the Mass]. Gathering all these things together into one, “my beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall abide between my breasts” [Note: [Col. 0823] Song 1]. For who

> Of the Myrmidons, Dolopians, or soldier of stern Ulysses  
>   
> Could restrain himself from tears?

[Note: [Col. 0823] Vergil, *Aeneid* II, 7.]

There, repose is in labour, glory is put to shame, health is sick, life dies. O Jew: for whom do you spread garments [Note: [Col. 0823] Luke 19], extend triumphant palm branches [Note: [Col. 0823] John 12], offer the olive of peace, applaud with the pleasantness of flowers [Col. 0823D], and sing “Hosanna!” [Note: [Col. 0823] Ibid.] in a ringing voice—and surely spread garments—for him whom afterwards you stripped of his seamless tunic [Note: [Col. 0823] John 19]? You offer triumphal palm branches to him over whom, when you sought to triumph, he himself triumphed equally over you and over death. You bear the olive of peace, yet excluded from your peace him who “is our peace, who made both one” [Note: [Col. 0823] Eph. 2]. You brought forth pleasant flowers, yet through you “the flower of Lebanon withered” upon the cross [Note: [Col. 0823] Nah. 1], because he who is “the flower of the field and lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0823] Song 2] withered through you. And you cry, “Hosanna!”—that is, “Save, I beseech you”—to him upon whom afterwards [Col. 0824A] you cry: “Away, away, crucify him” [Note: [Col. 0823] John 19]. Whence came to you, wretch, so sudden a change, that you crucify against the Law him whom just now you called king?

In all these things he says: “I did not turn my face away from those who reproached me and spat upon me” [Note: [Col. 0823] Isa. 50]. Christ is said to have had a face of misery, a face of experience, and a face of glory. The first was that of one fighting; the second, of one journeying; the third, of one reigning. The first was that which David changed before King Achish [Note: [Col. 0823] Ps. 35]; the second, that of Joseph, who was “beautiful in appearance and fair of face” [Note: [Col. 0823] Gen. 29]; the third, that of Moses, because Moses’ face became radiant while the Lord looked upon him [Note: [Col. 0823] Exod. 34]. Of the first: “I set my face as the hardest rock” [Note: [Col. 0823] Isa. 50]. Of the second it is said: “His face was set toward going to Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0823] Luke 9]. Of the third, in the Transfiguration [Col. 0824B], “his face shone like the sun” [Note: [Col. 0823] Matt. 17]. In this face he reigns and is glorified for ages of ages. Amen.

**For love is strong as death.**

[CARD.] Charity is indeed strong as death in action—indeed, even stronger. Death separates a human being from worldly things by extinguishing affection; charity separates by subjecting affection to God. Death separates the soul from the body, a human being from father and mother, children and friends, possessions and riches, and all other things loved in the world; and it does this by extinguishing life. Charity, however, so separates that it does not extinguish life, but changes it for the better. In this, too, it is stronger than death: it does not fear death [Col. 0824C], but rather desires it, as was apparent in the Apostle, who longed “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0823] Phil. 1].

And while love is strong as death in acting, in suffering jealousy—that is, love—is said to be hard as hell, because its constancy is not broken by tribulation, distress, persecution, hunger, nakedness, peril, or the sword [Note: [Col. 0823] Rom. 8]. For just as those who are in hell cannot be broken by any torments or any cuttings, so charity is broken by no violence of torments. The lamps of charity are called lamps of fire and flame, because our fragile hearts, signified by lamps, if we hold the treasure of charity in these earthen vessels, burn with love and are illumined by knowledge of the truth in such a manner that they cannot be obscured by the darkness either of worldly wisdom or [Col. 0824D] of heretical perversity.

It is likewise said that many waters cannot extinguish charity. These waters are the rains of temptations descending from the powers of the air: namely, that overflowing shower of which Ezekiel speaks [Note: [Col. 0823] ch. 13], which rushes upon and overthrows the wall that has no writing, by which is signified the manner of life of the person who is not solidly and firmly bound together with the mortar of charity. Therefore the waters, or rains, of temptations do not extinguish charity, because they are absorbed by the heat of charity itself [Col. 0825A]; nor do rivers overwhelm it. By rivers are signified all transitory things; and they do not overwhelm charity because waters which have already flowed away and those which are yet to come do not touch it, while the contact of present things is measured by a single instant.

Charity itself, when it is possessed, is held so dear that, “if a man gives the whole substance of his house for love, he will despise it as though it were nothing.” For whatever is left or lost for its sake is wholly reckoned as nothing—indeed, as loss and dung [Note: [Col. 0825] Phil. 3]. It follows:

**Our little sister has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?**

[THO.] By a great dispensation of charity the Lord calls the Church a sister, and the sister of the Synagogue, so that [Col. 0825B] the Synagogue herself might remember that through grace she too had been made sister to her Creator, and might rejoice in the added grace and fellowship of her own sister. But because she still needs the consolation appropriate to a newborn, he adds, as though taking counsel for her salvation: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?”

The Lord addresses the Church when he instructs her concerning everlasting salvation, whether through the hidden illumination of his Spirit or through the open voice of preachers. “What,” he says, “shall we do for our sister when she is to be addressed?” Namely, at our coming in the flesh. She is to be addressed by me, by the apostles, and by the Fathers. Here four points must be noted. The Church is called a sister, little, without breasts, and to be addressed. She was made Christ’s sister through participation in grace; little through her recent conversion; without breasts because she shares milk and lacks the word of righteousness; she is to be addressed so that she may pass to the nuptials of her beloved and thus advance in the begetting of offspring.

She is a sister through grace, by which he assumed our humanity and made us children of God by adoption [Note: [Col. 0825] Rom. 8]. As a little one, she grew through baptism and Christ’s preaching; she began to have breasts through the calling of the apostles; she passed to the nuptials of her beloved through the Passion; she conceived through the sending of the Holy Spirit; she gave birth through the apostles’ preaching. Of the first the Apostle says: “The grace of God and of our Saviour Jesus Christ has appeared to all people, teaching us” [Note: [Col. 0825] Tit. 2]. Of the second Peter says: “Like newborn infants, desire rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow [Col. 0825D] unto salvation” [Note: [Col. 0825] 1 Pet. 2]. They were already growing when he said: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men” [Note: [Col. 0825] Mark 1]. She passed to the nuptials of her beloved when through his Passion “he betrothed her to one husband, to present her as a chaste virgin to Christ” [Note: [Col. 0825] 2 Cor. 11]. She was made fruitful by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit and gave birth; hence it was said to the apostles: “Preach the Gospel to every creature” [Note: [Col. 0825] Mark 16].

She was a sister through predestination; as a little one, she grew through calling; she took on breasts through justification; she was addressed and made a bride through glorification. “Those whom he predestined, those he also called,” says the Apostle; [Col. 0826A] “those whom he called, those he also justified; and those whom he justified, those he also glorified” [Note: [Col. 0825] Rom. 8].

Morally, the soul of a righteous person becomes the sister of the beloved, just as Christ became obedient to the Father even unto death [Note: [Col. 0825] Phil. 2]. Hence he himself says: “Whoever does the will of my Father, that one is my brother and sister and mother” [Note: [Col. 0825] Matt. 12]. She is little by humility, reckoning herself of no importance; but she is magnified when God exalts her by reward. Hence it is said: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0825] Matt. 23]. She has no breasts while she does not care to display outwardly her good conduct and manners for the edification of others, fearing lest she rise into pride. But the Lord, to show how secure she is in this, gives her a blessing. Thus Jacob says to his son Joseph: “The God of your father shall be your helper, and the Almighty shall bless [Col. 0826B] you with blessings of heaven above and blessings of the deep lying beneath, with blessings of breasts and womb” [Note: [Col. 0825] Gen. 49].

The blessing of heaven above is love of God, and it is in the right breast; the blessing of the deep lying below is fear of hell, and it is in the left breast. But just as in the womb a child is first conceived, then born and nursed, so fear and love are first considered in the secret heart and then are displayed outwardly to others in word and deed, as though flowing from breasts. Afterwards the beloved addresses her so that she may be brought to his nuptials. Behold: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in variety” [Note: [Col. 0825] Ps. 44].

In addressing her thus, the beloved instructs her to hear the commandments of God, understand what she hears, obey what she understands, leave carnal things by obeying, and reject the world. This is what he comprises in that verse. Behold the first: “Hear, daughter, and see”; the second: “Incline your ear”; the third: “Forget your people”; the fourth: “And your father’s house”; the fifth: “And so the king shall desire your beauty” [Note: [Col. 0825] Ibid.], and shall take you in marriage. For of this marriage it was said: “Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife” [Note: [Col. 0825] Gen. 2; Mark 10]. Christ left his Father when, though equal to the Father, he emptied himself by assuming flesh [Note: [Col. 0825] Phil. 2]. He left his mother when, as though despising the flesh assumed from her, he exposed himself to the Passion. Thus he cleaved to his wife because he did not afterwards leave her.

We read in the Gospel of three marriages prefiguring [Col. 0826D] the marriage of Christ and the Church. The first took place in the Incarnation; the second, in the Ascension; the third shall take place in the general resurrection. He made the first for mortals, the second for angels, the third for angels and human beings. In the first he refreshes the poor; in the second he gladdens the rich—that is, the angels; in the third all “shall feed and lie down, and none shall make them afraid” [Note: [Col. 0825] Zeph. 3]. Of the first it is said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who makes a marriage for his son” [Note: [Col. 0825] Matt. 22]. Of the second: “Be like people awaiting their lord when he returns from the marriage” [Note: [Col. 0825] Luke 12]. Of the third: “When the bridegroom came, those who were prepared entered with [Col. 0827A] him into the marriage” [Note: [Col. 0827] Matt. 25].

In the first the bride receives a dowry; in the second the bridal chamber is prepared by God and the angels; in the third she shall be brought in. A dowry is what is given to a wife so that she may have a means of living if she happens to be deprived of her husband; among jurists this is called a *donatio propter nuptias*, a gift on account of marriage. For properly speaking, a *dos* is what is given to the husband with the wife. She was as though deprived of her husband when Christ ascended to heaven; but she received a dowry when she received the Holy Spirit to console her. “We have received the pledge of the Spirit,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0827] 2 Cor. 5]. Of the second he says: “I go to prepare a place for you” [Note: [Col. 0827] John 14]. Of the third: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Note: [Col. 0827] Matt. 25].

There is also the marriage which took place at Cana of Galilee, where Christ changed water into wine [Note: [Col. 0827] John 2]. This marriage is moral [Col. 0827B]: affection, as bride, marries reason, as bridegroom. For reason rules the affections. At this marriage there are six jars holding water which is changed into wine [Note: [Col. 0827] Ibid.], provided that Jesus is present. There are six jars because there are six movements of affection. The first three are: desire of carnal pleasure, desire of temporal wealth, and desire of renowned praise. Of the first: “You have feasted upon earth and nourished your hearts in luxury” [Note: [Col. 0827] Jas. 5]. Of the second: [p. 173] “Woe to him who gathers evil greed to his house, that his nest may be on high” [Note: [Col. 0827] Hab. 2]. Of the third: “Whoever thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself” [Note: [Col. 0827] Gal. 6].

In the first is the water of luxury; in the second, of avarice; in the third, the water of vain glory. But when Jesus comes—that is, when the desire [Col. 0827C] for salvation comes—the water of luxury is changed into the wine of bodily affliction; the water of avarice into the wine of merciful liberality; the water of vain glory into the wine of self-contempt and humility. John the Baptist, clothed in camel hair, drank of the first [Note: [Col. 0827] Matt. 3]. And Paul says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” [Note: [Col. 0827] 1 Cor. 9]. Of the second Job says: “The stranger did not remain outside, and my door stood open to the traveller” [Note: [Col. 0827] Job 31]; and Tobias: “If you have much, give abundantly; and if little, take care to impart even that willingly” [Note: [Col. 0827] Job 4]. Of the third, Abraham says: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” [Note: [Col. 0827] Gen. 18]; and Job: “He who has lowered his eyes shall be saved, and he who has been humbled shall be in glory” [Note: [Col. 0827] Job 22].

The other three are these: contempt for God, hatred of one’s neighbour, and negligence [Col. 0827D] of oneself. The first has the water of ingratitude, the second of cruelty, the third of dissipation. Of the first: “They forgot God who saved them, who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, terrible things in the Red Sea” [Note: [Col. 0827] Ps. 105]. Of the second: “The daughter of my people is cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness” [Note: [Col. 0827] Lam. 4]. Of the third: “Ephraim is like a deceived dove, without heart; strangers have consumed his strength, and he did not know it” [Note: [Col. 0827] Hos. 7].

But the first is changed into wine, as Job says: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away” [Note: [Col. 0827] Job 1]; and John [Note: [Col. 0827] rather Peter, 1 Pet. 2]: “If, while doing good and [Col. 0828A] being struck, you endure, this is grace before the Lord.” Of the second: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0827] Matt. 11]. Of the third: “The children of Israel appointed guards from among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, each one opposite his own house” [Note: [Col. 0827] 2 Ezra 7]. The first water is changed into wine, namely thanksgiving; the second into gentleness; the third into watchfulness. Tobias drank of the first wine [Note: [Col. 0827] ch. 4], giving thanks to God for the goods restored to him. Of the second, Moses: “He was the meekest of all people who were upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0827] Num. 12]. Paul drank of the third, for he watched over himself when he said: “I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind” [Note: [Col. 0827] Rom. 7].

The jars are of stone when a person is obstinate in evil or confirmed in good. This woman—that is, affection—has only water in her jars when she does not marry reason. The jars are empty when she marries reason, but Jesus, who is called Saviour, is not invited to the marriage because affection is subjected to reason not for the salvation of souls but perhaps for vanity or profit, as the philosophers did. But when Jesus is invited, water is changed into wine.

**Our little sister has no breasts.**

[CARD.] These are the words of Christ’s companions, namely the prophets, who present the Blessed Virgin to the Lord as fit for him to assume flesh from her, and say: “Our sister, the Virgin Mary, is little through humility of mind, and is pure and clean like a tender young heifer, who [Col. 0828C] does not yet have breasts.” But Christ, as though accepting the virgin offered to him, adds: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?” Namely, on the day when the archangel Gabriel addresses her. And while the companions are silent, the whole Trinity replies, saying:

**If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her. If she is a door, let us fasten her with boards of cedar.**

[THO.] By the name of wall or door the Lord is customarily signified. He is rightly called a wall, because he protects his Church on every side lest it be plundered by enemies; a door, because we enter the Church, or the kingdom of heaven, only through Christ or through fellowship with him. Of the first: “A wall and a fore-wall shall be set in it” [Note: [Col. 0827] Isa. 26]. [Col. 0828D] Of the door, the Saviour says: “I am the door” [Note: [Col. 0827] John 10]. He was a wall appearing in flesh; the fore-wall was the revelation of prophecy. The Church defends that wall by proclaiming his Incarnation.

Or a wall and a door may mean any of his stronger members, who both defend others and introduce them into the kingdom. These are silver battlements when, by the brightness of their eloquence, they defend the virtues both of others and of themselves. Cedar boards are the incorruptible examples of the ancients, like cedar. The door is fastened with them when their abundance is supplied to other teachers for their completion. Or [Col. 0829A] cedar boards are the breadth of virtues, in which those who bring others with themselves into government ought to abound.

There are four cities which have walls and battlements: the first Babylon, the second Jericho, the third Jerusalem, the fourth Zion. A city is the dwelling together of many. In Babylon there dwells the confusion of sinners, for its very name is interpreted “confusion.” Its wall is obstinacy; its battlement, despair. Hear the city: “But you hate discipline and cast my words behind you; if you saw a thief, you ran with him” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 49], etc. Hear the wall of obstinacy: “When the sinner has come to the depths of evils, he despises” [Note: [Col. 0829] Prov. 18]. Hear the battlement of despair: “My iniquity is greater than I deserve to be forgiven,” says Cain [Note: [Col. 0829] Gen. 4].

In the city of Jericho, which is called “moon” because of mutability, according to the saying, “The fool changes like the moon” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ecclus. 27], the multitude of citizens is the variety of worldly things. Its wall is prosperity. Its battlement is faithless security. Hear the city: “Everything which is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life” [Note: [Col. 0829] 1 John 2]. Hear the wall of prosperity: “The turning away of little ones shall kill them, and the prosperity of fools shall destroy them” [Note: [Col. 0829] Prov. 1]. They raise the battlement of faithless security, “who trust in their own strength and glory in the multitude of their riches” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 48]. Hence Job says: [Col. 0829B] “I saw a fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty” [Note: [Col. 0829] Job 5].

Jerusalem is called “vision of peace,” for in it dwells the peace and harmony of virtues. [Col. 0829C] Its wall is patience; its battlement, wisdom in watchfulness; its inhabitants are harmonious virtues, which Paul sets forth: “Charity, peace, joy, patience, goodness, kindness” [Note: [Col. 0829] Gal. 5], etc. The wall of patience preserves possession; hence: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” [Note: [Col. 0829] Luke 21]. The battlement of wisdom extends sight far off in order to foresee; hence that wise man says:

Consider what follows, and foresee whatever threatens ahead. Thus a heavier blow strikes the enemy, and so wisdom conquers malice [Note: [Col. 0829] Wis. 7.]. Zion is called a watchtower. For within it the citizens are visions of heavenly blessedness; its wall is love of Christ, and its bulwark desire for him. Hence Isaiah: “Zion, the city of our strength; [Col. 0829D] the Savior shall be set in it as wall and outer wall” [Note: [Col. 0829] Isa. 27.]. God prevented the walls of Babylon from being completed by taking away understanding of languages, because stubborn counsels are the source of evils. Hence the Apostle: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” [Note: [Col. 0829] I Cor. 15.]. Joshua destroyed the walls of Jericho by a sevenfold circuit and the sound of trumpets [Note: [Col. 0829] Josh. 6.]. For by the preaching of the seven virtues, or the seven sacraments, or the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, our Savior—whose name Joshua signifies—destroys the world’s prosperity and faithless security. Hence he himself says: “Take courage: I [Col. 0830A] have conquered the world” [Note: [Col. 0829] John 16.]. “Surround us, Lord,” cry the inhabitants of Jerusalem, “with your unconquerable wall.” Yet great distress is required for the walls of Jerusalem—that is, patience—to be built: as the children of Israel returning from captivity set a stone with one hand and held a sword with the other for defense. But the walls and bulwarks of Zion are built by frequent contemplation of heavenly things. For the more we contemplate what is above, the more abundantly we love and desire Christ. Of Zion thus strengthened the prophet cries: “Strangers shall no longer pass through her” [Note: [Col. 0829] Joel 3.]. Yet under Judas Maccabaeus strangers held the citadel [Note: [Col. 0829] I Macc. 3.]. For many live well and cleanse themselves by confession, whom nevertheless worldly care and malicious spirits hinder as much as they can, lest through contemplation of heavenly things [Col. 0830B] they rise to the intensity of love and desire.

In the moral sense, the wall of the faithful soul is the structure of good works; its bulwarks are vigilant custody; or the wall is the order of virtues, and the enemies are carnal affections that interrupt that order. The Lord permits this wall to be destroyed when the soul does not resist vices. Hence Jeremiah: “The Lord resolved to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0829] Lam. 2.]. The Lord resolves to destroy these walls while he patiently awaits sinners; he resolves and destroys when he abandons the impenitent to be punished by enemies. Even the towers are handed over to enemies when vices dominate the more eminent virtues: “I have given,” says the Lord, “the walls of her towers into the hand of the enemy” [Note: [Col. 0829] Jer. 47.]. The first wall is indissoluble, because it is of fired bricks; the second [Col. 0830C] can be crossed, because it is of heaped-up earthworks; the third is strong because it is iron; the fourth is splendid because it is of precious stones. Of the first: “My belly shall sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for a wall of fired brick” [Note: [Col. 0829] Isa. 16.]. Of the second, to Ezekiel: “Take a brick for yourself, and draw Jerusalem upon it”; and among other things it is said, “You shall heap up an embankment” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ezek. 1.]. Of the third, in the same book: “Take for yourself an iron pan, and set it as a wall between yourself and the city” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ibid.]. Of the fourth: “And the structure of the wall was of jasper stone” [Note: [Col. 0829] Rev. 21.]. The bulwarks of these latter two are golden through charity, silver in preaching, and of precious stones in action.

A door is said to be Christ, a door a prelate, and a door [Col. 0830D] the human faculty of perception. Of the first: “I am the door” [Note: [Col. 0829] John 10]. Of the second, Job: “Who shut up the sea with doors, when it burst forth as though proceeding from a womb?” [Note: [Col. 0829] Job 38.] The sea is the world; the womb is the conception of carnal thought. Of the third: “Set a guard, Lord, upon my mouth, and a door of restraint about my lips” [Note: [Col. 0829] Ps. 140.]. The first—that is, Christ—is sometimes closed and sometimes opened. He is closed to the reprobate: “Those who were ready entered with him into the wedding, and the door was shut” [Note: [Col. 0829] Matt. 2.], namely, to the foolish virgins. He is opened to the predestined, as Job says: “My door was open to the traveler” [Note: [Col. 0829] Job 31.], namely, to one [Col. 0831A] making for the kingdom of heaven. The third is closed to the wicked: “Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0831] Acts 13.]. It is opened to the kindly: “My sheep hear my voice” [Note: [Col. 0831] John 10.]. Thus God shut the door of the ark against the waves of the flood and opened it when they had ceased [Note: [Col. 0831] Gen. 8].

In human beings there is a threefold door, namely a moral one: the first is that of sense-perception, the second of understanding, the third of affection. The first is the operation of the senses, the second discernment, the third deliberation. The door of the senses is closed against worldly enticements lest they enter into the interior. Thus Lot, when the Sodomites pressed him, shut the door behind himself [Note: [Col. 0831] Gen. 19.]. But if enticements enter, they are held at the door of discernment, so that there it may be determined whether a thing is good or evil. Thus it is said to the woman pouring [Col. 0831B] oil: “Shut the door upon yourself and upon your son” [Note: [Col. 0831] IV Kings 4.], namely, when you have detected evil. But if it escapes as far as the door of deliberation, so that the soul deliberates whether to act or not, the door must be shut. Hence: “When you pray, enter into your chamber; and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” [Note: [Col. 0831] Matt. 6.].

The first is opened so that, in praising the Creator, it may behold the beauty of creatures, or so that it may take an example from good people. Thus, when Moses went out to the tabernacle, the children of Israel stood at the doors of their tents [Note: [Col. 0831] Num. 16.]. The second is opened to what is good after it has been distinguished from evil. Thus Abraham, standing at the door of his tent, saw three men: he saw three and adored one [Note: [Col. 0831] Gen. 18.]. The third is opened when the good, distinguished from evil, knocks at [Col. 0831C] the door of deliberation and is judged to be done; it is then brought into effect, and so the soul directs itself toward God. Thus Elijah saw the Lord passing by at the door of the cave. Hence he himself says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” [Note: [Col. 0831] Rev. 3.].

These doors are joined with cedar planks because of cedar’s fragrance and incorruptibility. For the first door, which is Christ, was incorruptible: “We have heard that Christ remains forever” [Note: [Col. 0831] I John 2.]; and fragrant, as the Apostle says: “Blessed be God, who through us everywhere makes manifest the fragrance of his knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0831] II Cor. 2.]. The second door also—that is, prelates—is fragrant, as the Apostle teaches Timothy: “A bishop,” he says, “must be blameless, hospitable, prudent, [Col. 0831D] sober, chaste, a teacher” [Note: [Col. 0831] I Tim. 3.]: here is fragrance. Hear of incorruptibility: “Not given to wine, not violent, not quarrelsome, not covetous” [Note: [Col. 0831] Ibid.]. The third door likewise—that is, the inner and outer senses—is incorrupt, as the Apostle teaches: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your senses should be corrupted from the charity of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0831] II Cor. 11.]. Hear another apostle teaching good fragrance: “Who is wise,” he says, “and disciplined among you? Let him show his works from good conduct” [Note: [Col. 0831] Jas. 3.]. These doors are joined with cedar planks. But this [Col. 0832A] *compingere* is said from *compingo, compingis, compegi*, meaning “to form,” not from *compingo, compingis, compinxi*.

“If she is a wall, let us build silver bulwarks upon her; if she is a door, let us join her with cedar planks.”

[CARD.] By these words the Virgin is introduced as replying, as though she said: “Let it happen to me as you have said, and build silver bulwarks upon me, because

> I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower, since I became before him as one finding peace.

[THO.] I am rightly called a wall because I have been built together from divine stones; because I have been united by the cement of charity; because I have been placed upon an immovable foundation; because no blow of the heretical battering ram can [Col. 0832B] cast me down.

There are also in me certain persons endowed with exceptional virtue; and they are called towers because they do not fear the attacks of the perverse. They are breasts when they feed little ones with simple teaching. And by the generosity of that very one I have received this: from the time when I became before him as one finding peace—that is, from the time when he deigned to grant me the gift of his peace through the word of reconciliation. I acquired this strength not from myself but through him, from the time when he bestowed upon me the gift of my peace. Therefore I wish still to speak of that peace.

There is true peace, disordered peace, feigned peace, and rejected peace. Peace is true when it is simply maintained by both parties; disordered when God is offended for the sake of preserving peace with one’s neighbor; feigned when it is not held inwardly as it is outwardly displayed; rejected when it is offered by one person and refused by another.

Again, your peace sometimes perishes. But the righteous person first finds it, secondly reveals it, thirdly brings it forth. It perishes when God is offended; the righteous find it when God is reconciled; they reveal it when God is reconciled and this is shown in word and deed; they bring it forth when peace is restored by them among those in discord. Peace perishes, as it is written: “There is no peace for the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0831] Isa. 48.]. It is found in reconciliation, whence the Lord says: “I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction” [Note: [Col. 0831] Jer. 29.]. The Apostle teaches how to reveal it: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which [Col. 0832C] no one shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0831] Heb. 12.]. David urges bringing peace forth: “Keep innocence and behold equity, for there is a remnant for the peaceable person” [Note: [Col. 0831] Ps. 36.], that is, for one making peace. Behold: in such persons the bride is a wall—that is, in those who walk in peace. For because of peace she herself is called a wall: peace itself is a wall. This wall is founded when peace is found; it grows when peace is revealed; it is accumulated when peace is brought forth. This wall of peace surrounds all who are united in peace, as citizens of one city, and makes them rest secure in the Lord, so that they say: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” [Note: [Col. 0831] Ps. 4.]. The Lord too rests in them and with them, because, as David says: “In peace his place was made, and his dwelling in Zion” [Note: [Col. 0833] Ps. 75.].

In Zion there was a tower, to which the bride compares her breasts: allegorically, the prelates in whom is the dwelling of the Beloved. There is peace from hell, peace from the world, and peace from heaven. Peace from hell is agreement with vices and iniquity; peace from the world is tranquillity in riches and happiness; peace from heaven is the tranquil possession of graces in a good will. The first is most evil, the second dangerous, the third most secure. The first is savage peace, the second adulterous peace, the third true peace. Of the first: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, those things which he possesses are in peace” [Note: [Col. 0833] Luke 11.]. Of the second: “I do not give you peace as the world gives peace” [Note: [Col. 0833] John 4.]. Of the third: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” [Note: [Col. 0833] Ibid.]. Of the first two [Col. 0833B] it is said: “Peace, peace, and there was no peace” [Note: [Col. 0833] Jer. 6.]. Jesus did not come to send those peaces, but to cast them out, so that there might be room for this third peace.

“Therefore the strong man armed,” that is, the devil, “was guarding his courtyard.” First he knocks at the door, secondly withdraws into a corner, thirdly possesses the courtyard: the door, namely the bodily senses; the corner, secret thought; the courtyard, sinful wandering. The first, so that he may enter; the second, so that he may deceive; the third, so that he may possess. At the door he speaks “peaceful words deceitfully” [Note: [Col. 0833] I Macc. 7.]. In the corner he entices with the kiss of false security; in the courtyard he strikes with the sword. Joab followed this order when he killed Amasa [Note: [Col. 0833] II Kings 20.]. For first he said, “Greetings, brother”; secondly, “he took hold of his chin and kissed him”; thirdly, “he seized a dagger, struck him, and killed him.”

Therefore, because worldly peace, which consists in riches, is transitory: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” [Note: [Col. 0833] Ps. 61.]. For some place their heart beneath riches, some upon them, and some against them. Those place it beneath who cultivate frugality; those place it upon them who are devoted to prodigality; those place it against them who meet their own needs from their possessions. The first are ministers of avarice, the second servants of vain glory, the third children of temperance. Of the first:

> Avarice seethes, and with wretched desire the heart  
> seeks; and, wretched when it has found, withholds and fears to use.

To these the Lord says: “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy” [Note: [Col. 0833] Matt. 6.]. The second see:

> How money, a queen, confers both lineage and beauty.

[Col. 0833D] And therefore:

> He will be a perpetual slave who does not know how to use a little.

Of them it is said: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” [Note: [Col. 0833] I Tim. 6.]. To the third:

> Virtue is a mean drawn back from vices on either side.

To these it is said: “If you have much, give abundantly; if little, strive gladly to share even that” [Note: [Col. 0833] Tob. 4.]. The rich man to whom the Lord said, “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything you have and give to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0833] Matt. 19.], represented the first type. The richly clothed man [Col. 0834A] “who feasted splendidly every day” [Note: [Col. 0833] Luke 16.] represented the second. Those who said, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” [Note: [Col. 0833] Matt. 19.], represented the third. From these comes worldly peace. Hence Hezekiah said: “The word of the Lord is good; nevertheless, let there be peace in my days” [Note: [Col. 0833] IV Kings 20.]. But “pray for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0833] Ps. 121.]. This is true peace, which comes down from heaven.

There is true peace, truer peace, and truest peace. True peace is the grace of unanimity among brethren; truer peace is patience in tribulation; truest peace is the power of God and the wisdom of God. The first is true because among brethren there is “one soul and one heart” [Note: [Col. 0833] Acts 4.]; the second is truer because the assaults of temptations do not dissolve it; the third is truest because “he is our peace, who made both one” [Note: [Col. 0833] Eph. 2.]. Of the first: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which [Col. 0834B] no one shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0833] Heb. 12.]. Of the second: “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable” [Note: [Col. 0833] Ps. 119.]. The third is “the peace of God which surpasses all understanding.” Of the first two the prophet says: “Lord, you will give peace” [Note: [Col. 0833] Isa. 26.], peace because we have hoped in you. Of the third he says: “Behold, I shall turn toward them like a river of peace” [Note: [Col. 0833] Isa. 66.]. In this peace we esteem, or await, our rest. Hence: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” [Note: [Col. 0833] Ps. 4.].

Let us set up a tower: let Christ be in its foundations, the apostles in its walls, and the martyrs in its bulwarks. It possesses height and strength. Hear of its strength: “The floods came, the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it could not be moved, for it was founded upon a firm rock [Col. 0834C] [Note: [Col. 0833] Matt. 7.],” namely Christ. Hear also of its height: “Who are these that fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” [Note: [Col. 0833] Isa. 60.] For these build for us another tower. At its lower level are the works of human beings; at its middle level, the works of angels; at its highest, the works of God. Human works are penitence toward oneself, mercy toward one’s neighbor, and piety toward God. Angelic works are to praise God, to perform his embassy, and to visit us. There are three works of God: works of creation, works of restoration, and works of formation. Of the first it is said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0833] Gen. 1.]. Of the second: “Behold, a great prophet will come, and he himself will renew Jerusalem.” Of the third: “Who will reform the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0833] Phil. 3.].

Again, a tower is built [Col. 0834D] for us: in its foundation is shadow, in its wall body, and at its summit spirit. Or, in other words, the same thing: in its foundation is figure, in its wall reality, and at its summit truth. Figures were the things done under natural law and under written law. Realities are the visible sacraments of the new law, signified in those earlier things—for example, baptism. Spirit or truth is the spiritual and invisible grace bestowed upon us through those visible sacraments. Morally, however, a tower is raised: its foundation is right thought; its wall prudent meditation; its summit clear contemplation [Col. 0835A]. In it charity commands, reason orders, and sense-perception accomplishes. Those who are in this tower cry: “Be for us, Lord, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy” [Note: [Col. 0835] Ps. 60.]. And there the Lord broke powers, bow, shield, sword, and war. In the bow is deceitful opposition; in the sword open assault; in the shield concealed defense of one’s sins; in war open protection of one’s own error. We say that this last tower is the two moral breasts, namely reason and affection: “and my breasts are like a tower.”

> I am a wall.

[CARD.] She adds also: “And my breasts are like a tower, since I became before him as one finding peace.” The Blessed Virgin is indeed the wall of our defense, and upon her the whole Trinity built silver bulwarks. [Col. 0835B] For the whole Trinity built this in her for the defense of the Church: that by her prayers, sounding sweetly, she might drive back the enemy. This is signified by silver, which sounds more sweetly than other metals. Therefore, when she had said, “I am a wall,” she added, “And my breasts are like a tower.” As though she said: “My mercy and my piety, by which—as by breasts—I nourish the children of the Church with the sweetness of my intercessions, are a tower of defense, namely a refuge and security for sinners. And this has been so from the time when I was made so accepted, so pleasing, so beloved before him, that I was as one finding peace: that is, truly finding peace and making it between God and man, so that I might be peace-making, like the wall of the true peacemaker, the wall of the Mediator’s mediatrix.”

But understand in this way what is said: “If she [Col. 0835C] is a door, let us join her with cedar planks.” Christ calls himself a door, and this wall is here called a door, but in different senses. Christ is called a door—that is, an opening, or a way by which one enters into life. This belongs to him alone; thus he says of himself distinctively: “I am the door” [Note: [Col. 0835] John 20.], and no other. A door is also called a joining together of boards by which entrance into the house is shut against ill-wishers. Hence it is also said here: “If she is a door, let us join her with cedar planks.” The Blessed Virgin is a door in the Church, opposing malicious spirits lest they enter and approach her devotees as they wish. This door has been joined together by the Holy Trinity with as many planks as there are virtues and privileges of dignities in her. These planks are called cedar planks because they are incorruptible [Col. 0835D] and fragrant, and because, rooted deeply through humility, they grew to an immeasurable height. It follows:

> The Peaceful One had a vineyard in that which has peoples.  
> He handed it over to keepers; a man brings a thousand silver coins for its fruit.

[THO.] The Church speaks to her young companions. The Bridegroom is Solomon, that is, the maker of peace. In his peace was that vineyard—that is, the Church—of which the Gospel says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard” [Note: [Col. 0835] Matt. 20.]. This vineyard has peoples [Col. 0836A], since it has been gathered from Jews and Gentiles. The keepers of this vineyard are prophets, apostles, and their successors. The keepers are angels, who care for it on his behalf. “Each man brings a thousand silver coins for its fruit.” Here “man” means any perfect person who leaves behind all his temporal goods in order to possess its fruit. The fruit of labors undertaken temporarily for the Lord is the enjoyment with the Lord of everlasting rest and kingdom. Hence he says: “I have appointed you that you may go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit may remain” [Note: [Col. 0835] John 15.].

This vineyard is the soul, for which four advances appropriate to every vineyard are here shown: first, a temperate breeze; second, shoots; third, guardianship; fourth, abundance of fruit. They are the breeze of peace, the shoots of virtue, the guardianship of vigilance, and the fruit of eternal recompense. In the breeze of peace new growth is nourished; in the shoot of virtue, once nourished, it is strengthened; through the guardianship of vigilance it is protected from failure; in the fruit of eternal reward its labor is completed. The Apostle invites us to the breeze of peace when he says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation, giving no offense to anyone” [Note: [Col. 0835] II Cor. 6.]. He invited us to the strength of virtue, saying: “I beseech you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, with humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in charity” [Note: [Col. 0835] Eph. 4.]. Christ urged guardianship in the Gospel: “If the householder knew,” he says, “at what hour the thief would come, he would surely watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” [Note: [Col. 0835] Matt. 24.]. He encouraged us toward [Col. 0836C] fruit when he spoke the words already cited: “I chose you and appointed you that you may go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit may remain.”

Therefore, to nourish new growth, the breeze of peace is first necessary, lest the pestilential north wind extinguish it. This wind commonly harms in three ways: frost, hail, and rain—frost of sloth, hail of adversity, rain of prosperity. Sloth instills dread of future hardship and obstructs one’s manner of life. The hail of adversity strikes violently and breaks the already mature shoot of virtue. The flood of prosperity flatters and causes the flower of inward devotion and of outward integrity, displayed as an example, to wither. Of the first Solomon says: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he shall beg in summer, and nothing shall be given [Col. 0836D] him” [Note: [Col. 0835] Prov. 20.]. Again: “The sluggard hides his hand under his armpit and does not bring it even to his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0835] Prov. 19.]. Of the second it is said: “The boar out of the wood has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it” [Note: [Col. 0835] Ps. 79.]; and: “All her persecutors have overtaken her in the midst of straits” [Note: [Col. 0835] Lam. 1.]. And Hezekiah says: “My generation has been taken away and folded up from me like a shepherds’ tent” [Note: [Col. 0835] Ps. 38.]. Of the third the prophet says: “The flower of Lebanon has withered” [Note: [Col. 0835] Nah. 1.]. And Jeremiah: “How the gold has grown dark; the finest color has changed!” [Note: [Col. 0835] Lam. 4.]. Again: “All her beauty has departed from the daughter of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0835] Lam. 1.]; and: “All who glorified her have despised [Col. 0837A] her, because they saw her disgrace” [Note: [Col. 0837] Lam. 1.]. This is enough concerning the vineyard which belonged to Solomon in that place, that is, in the breeze of peace. It follows concerning the shoots of virtues. These are the peoples dwelling in the soul. Thus the passage says: “Which has peoples,” that is, the virtues dwelling in the soul.

Therefore, in order that the shoots of virtue may grow, the vineyard—that is, the soul—must be watered by divine grace. It is watered by devotion, of which there are three kinds: zeal, compassion, and benevolence. Thus it is watered in three ways: by zeal, compassion, and benevolence. Devotion is a good fervor of mind which the mind, unable to contain it, manifests by definite signs. It therefore includes zeal against those who oppose God’s will; compassion is toward those who suffer calamity; benevolence is that by which a person shows himself ready to one who asks. But, to speak truly, it must be watered from the fountains of Israel. The seven fountains of Israel are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, often mentioned: the Spirit of wisdom, the Spirit of understanding, the Spirit of counsel, the Spirit of fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge, the Spirit of piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord.

From the Spirit of wisdom flows the water of teaching; the Spirit of understanding sends out the stream of providence; from the fountain of counsel proceeds a vein of consolation; from the fountain of rectitude proceeds the strength of good work; the fountain of knowledge sends forth the groan of sorrow—for “he who adds knowledge adds sorrow”; the fountain of piety renders the due of compassion; and the rivulet of fear gives the fruit of confession. Thus the vineyard is watered as if by seven [Col. 0837C] fountains, so that the shoots of virtues may grow.

Among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, first is fear, which suits the humble, of whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0837] Matt. 5.]: not puffed up, not setting their minds on high things, but fearing [Note: [Col. 0837] Rom. 11.]. Second is piety, which suits the meek. For one who seeks piously honors holy things, does not criticize, does not resist: this is to become meek. Third is knowledge, which suits those who mourn for the evils they have done. Fourth is fortitude, which suits those who hunger and thirst, because, desiring joy, they labor for true goods and desire to turn away from earthly things. Fifth, counsel, suits the merciful, because the sole remedy for being freed from such great evils is to forgive others and lend to them, as we wish done to ourselves. Sixth, understanding, suits the pure in heart, who with a purified eye can see what eye has not seen. Seventh, wisdom, suits the peacemakers, in whom no rebellious movement exists, but all things obey the spirit. See how the breeze of peace nourishes new growth, and how the shoots of virtues likewise grow. But we have labored for nothing unless we guard them. Hence it follows:

“He handed it over to keepers.” But we have said that the keepers of virtues are vigilance. There are four things by which vigilance is exercised: fear, care, necessity, and affection. Fear is anxiety about danger; [Col. 0838A] care is concern to escape disadvantage or gain advantage; necessity is the obligation to give or the need to receive; affection is the desire to enjoy. Fear presses down, care draws down, necessity binds, affection wounds. Thus, when we extend the branches of a tree, either we put weights upon it to press them down, or hang weights beneath it to draw them down, or carefully fasten stakes beside it and tie its branches so that they may not rise upward but spread out broadly, or we graft shoots into its bare trunk so that, growing there, they may clothe the tree. Fear, then, is like a weight placed above; care like a weight suspended below; necessity is like the stake that binds; affection like a grafted shoot that wounds by being inserted.

These four arise from the four kinds of evils that a human being suffers in this world: the wrath of God, the vanity of the world, the weakness of human condition, and the devil’s envy. The wrath of God occurs when we are worn down by scourges; the vanity of the world occurs when, exceeding the measure of necessity, we turn to pleasure; the weakness of human condition is that we are easily injured by adversities and recover strength for doing good only with difficulty; the devil’s envy occurs when, at his instigation, we are inflamed toward vices. Thus God’s wrath presses us down by fear; worldly vanity, by inviting or introducing superfluous concerns, drags us downward; the weakness of human condition binds us with grievous necessities; and the devil’s envy wounds us by inflaming us with illicit desires. Therefore, by cautiously considering these things, we more easily avoid falling.

Therefore [Col. 0838C], with the shoots of virtues thus guarded, it remains for us, leaving all things, to strive to receive the fruits. For this is to leave all things: to bring a thousand silver coins. Thus: how are “the poor in spirit” blessed? Behold, the fear of pride is left behind, but the fruit is received: “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0837] Matt. 5.]. “Blessed are the meek”: behold, cruelty is left behind, and the fruit is received, “for they shall possess the earth”—here, namely, their own soul; hereafter, their body and soul, or the heavenly homeland. “Blessed are those who mourn”: behold, the joy of the world is left behind, but they receive the fruit, “for they shall be consoled by the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0837] Ibid.]. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness”: you have abandoned injury to neighbor and to God, but you receive the fruit, “for they shall be filled” [Col. 0838D] [Note: [Col. 0837] Ibid.]: “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom,” says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0837] Luke 22.]. “Blessed are the merciful”: you have left behind hardness of heart, but hear the fruit: “for they shall obtain mercy” [Note: [Col. 0837] Matt. 5.], in the judgment where forgiveness will be granted them. “Blessed are the pure in heart”: you have left behind the unclean enticements of the world, but the fruit follows—namely, the vision of God—“for,” he says, “they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0837] Ibid.]. “Blessed are the peacemakers”: you have left behind seditions, but the fruit is to be a child of God, “for,” he says, “they shall be called children of God” [Note: [Col. 0837] Ibid.]. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution”: you have left behind vengeance and murmuring, but you have the fruit, namely [Col. 0839A] “the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0839] Matt. 5.]. Thus a person brings these virtues, leaves their opposites, and receives the fruit.

> Solomon had a vineyard in that place.

[CARD.] Therefore the friends and companions of Christ, as though replying to the Virgin’s words, “I became before him as one finding peace,” add what happened in that peace which the Lady found. It is said that in that peace—which she found in the Lord’s good pleasure when, in her womb, the divine nature was united to human nature in the kiss of reconciliation and peace—a vineyard was made for the peace-making man, namely Solomon. And so that it may be understood as a spiritual vineyard, it adds: “Which has peoples; he handed it over to keepers.” As though it said: That vineyard which was made for Solomon so as to be his own has peoples, because it is the Church gathered together from many peoples; and he, the peace-maker, handed it over to keepers, namely the prelates of the churches. What fruit the Lord of the vineyard and the keepers receive from the vineyard the following statement shows, when it says: “A man brings a thousand silver coins for its fruits.” The man, namely Christ the Lord of the vineyard, who alone is truly a man through unfading vigor, brings for its fruit—that is, in place of fruit—a thousand silver coins: this is perfect praise. For a thousand signifies perfection, and silver the sound of praise; and this is assigned to the divine perfection, to which nothing is lacking and nothing else accrues from his vineyard except praise and matter for praise. How greatly the Lord loves this vineyard is shown by a brief interpolation [Col. 0839C], introduced as though in the person of the Lord, saying:

> My vineyard is before me. A thousand are yours, O Peaceful One, and two hundred for those who guard its fruit.

[THO.] “My vineyard is before me,” etc. Before I arrive at the customary explanation, let me first set forth certain perhaps not negligible preliminary observations. Let us see how great is the solicitude of our Lord for his Church; for all who treat Holy Scripture testify, both in the prophets and in the Gospel, that the Church is understood by the vineyard. Therefore, he says, “My vineyard is before me”; whence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age” [Note: [Col. 0839] Matt. 28.]. Thus the merciful Lord always has his vineyard before his eyes, nor does it lack what is necessary. Before departing he gave it means by which it might receive an increase of virtues; he gave it remedies against vices, namely the seven ecclesiastical sacraments.
