Therefore, dearest son in Christ, considering the reverence and devotion which we know you have shown the Roman Church from times long past, we have thought fit to establish by this present document that the Scottish Church, which is in a special sense a daughter of the Apostolic See, shall be subject to it directly, without any intermediary.

Within it the following episcopal sees are known to exist: namely, the churches of Saint Andrews, Glasgow, Dunkeld, Dublin, Brechin, Aberdeen, Moray, Ross, and Caithness. [Col. 0921D] No one except the Roman pontiff, or a legate sent from his side, may pronounce a sentence of interdict or excommunication within the kingdom of Scotland; and, if such a sentence is pronounced, we decree that it shall be invalid. We add that henceforth no person who is not from the kingdom of Scotland may exercise the office of legate there, unless the Apostolic See has specially sent him for this purpose [Col. 0922A] from its own body.

We prohibit controversies arising in that kingdom concerning its possessions from being brought for examination before judges situated outside the kingdom, unless an appeal has been made to the Roman Church. If any documents obtained contrary to this statute of liberty should come to light, or should hereafter happen to be obtained without mention of this concession, no prejudice shall thereby arise to you or to the kingdom itself concerning the grant of this prerogative. Moreover, we ratify the liberties and immunities granted to you, to that kingdom, or to the churches established within it by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and hitherto observed; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times. [Col. 0922B]

Therefore let no person at all infringe this page of our constitution and prohibition, or in any way oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third Ides of March, in the first year of our pontificate.

[Note: [Col. 0921D] In the year 1188 Clement III exempted the churches of the kingdom of Scotland from the jurisdiction of the English metropolitan see, as is clear from the rescript of that pontiff, quoted in the same place by Baronius. Yet, through a lapse of memory, he again presents it here under the name of Celestine III. Labbe did the same in volume X of the *Councils*, where he reports it both under the name of Clement III and under that of Celestine III. Brompton, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1191—the last year of Clement III—attributes that privilege to Clement III, omitting part of the subscription. Nor can there be any doubt that it was omitted by that pontiff; [Col. 0922D] for already under his predecessors a dispute had arisen between John, bishop of Dunkeld, and Hugh, bishop of Saint Andrews, as may be seen in Hoveden’s *Annals*, where he ascribes the privilege in question to Clement III, and in Baronius in various places. The error appears to have arisen because, when a certain copyist had written the opening words of the rescript as follows, “C., bishop, servant of the servants of God,” some later interpreted the letter C. as Celestine and wrote: “Celestine, bishop, servant of the servants of God,” etc. PAGIUS.]

LXV. He grants the abbot of the monastery of Saint Sixtus at Piacenza the use of a ring. (Lateran, March 18.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar. Casin.*, II, 222.]

[Col. 0922C] CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son . . . . abbot of Saint Sixtus of Piacenza, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that, through the diligent exercise of our office, it be brought to its proper effect. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, inclined by your just petitions, we have thought fit, through the kindness of the Apostolic See, to grant you the use of a ring on feast days, so that, for the honour of God and of your church, you may use it in the solemnities of Mass and may then wear it without any opposition. Therefore let no person at all infringe this page of our concession, [Col. 0922D] or rashly presume to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXVI. He takes the Florentine monastery of Saint Peter under protection and confirms its goods. (Lateran, March.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 103.]

[Col. 0923A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, MARIA, abbess, and the sisters of the monastery of Saint Peter Major, situated in the suburb of the city of Florence, both present and future, for ever.

The Apostolic See ought to grant protection to prudent virgins who, under the habit of religion, with lamps kindled by works of holiness, continually prepare themselves to go forth to meet the bridegroom; so that they may be able to persevere more steadfastly in their religious purpose, in proportion as they are more generously defended by an apostolic grant against the storm of worldly [Col. 0923B] waves. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Anastasius of happy memory, receive the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter Major, situated in the suburb of the city of Florence, under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. Whatever possessions and goods the said monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s aid, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and to those who succeed you.

[Col. 0923C] Among these we have thought fit to name expressly: the church of Saint Felix situated near the Ema, which Azo, formerly bishop of Florence, of good memory, canonically granted you, to be held, governed, and administered in perpetuity according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. We confirm by apostolic authority all the possessions which the noblewoman Gisla lawfully bestowed upon your monastery, and decree that they, confirmed to you and to those who succeed you, shall remain unshaken for ever; establishing that neither you nor those who succeed you may alienate that same church from your monastery under any title whatsoever.

[Col. 0923D] Therefore we decree, etc. If anyone therefore, etc.; but for all, etc. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Mel[ior], priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, John, bishop of Tusculum, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 0924A] I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Mersus, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, . . . days before the Kalends of April, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1192, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

LXVII. To [Aynard], archbishop of Vienne, and his suffragans: he commands them not to allow their parishioners to be prevented from bestowing goods upon the Carthusian Order. (Lateran, April 1.)

[*Privileges of the Carthusian Order*, fol. 3b.]

[Col. 0924B]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishop of Vienne and his suffragans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint of our beloved sons, the prior and brothers of the Carthusians, we have been informed that certain tyrants in your regions strictly forbid the people of their lands—though they are not serfs—to bestow upon them, when they enter their religious order or when they make a testament disposing of their final wishes, anything at all, even of the movable goods which they lawfully possess, or to leave such goods to them by testament. No person of sound understanding either judges or fails to recognize how contrary this is to all humanity and how opposed to the reason both of the canons and of the whole civil law. [Col. 0924C] Therefore, by apostolic letters we direct and firmly command your whole body that each of you shall carefully and strictly forbid all his parishioners to presume henceforth to impede such alms. If anyone proves contemptuous of this command, or attempts to harass those brothers over alms already received or yet to be received, his diocesan bishop shall not delay, all appeal and objection being set aside, to restrain him from such presumption by a sentence of excommunication and an interdict over all his land.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXVIII. He takes the monastery of Saint Justina under protection and confirms its possessions and rights, imposing upon the monks an annual payment of one Byzantine coin. (Lateran, April 7.)

[MORIONDI, *Monumenta Aquensia*, vol. I, p. 97.]

[Col. 0924D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the LORD abbot of Saint Justina and his brothers, both present and future, professing their religious life . . . . . . .

Whenever a request is made to us that is recognized as consistent with religion and honour, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and, in accordance with the petitioners’ truthful account, furnish assistance consonant with reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions [Col. 0925A] and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and establish by the privilege of this present document, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Justina, in which you are dedicated to divine service, which belongs directly to the Roman Church. First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order . . . which is known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict shall there be observed inviolate for ever.

Accordingly, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and free to you and your successors. [Col. 0925B] Among these we have thought fit to set forth expressly:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with its possessions, tithes, and first fruits; the church of Saint Michael built in the same city, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Saviour of Ritorto; the church of Saint Mary of Fontanigallo; the church of Saint Mary of Borio; the church of Saint Nicholas of Cannova, with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Michael of Puzol; the church of Saint Justina of Danaveta; the church of Saint Benedict of Coloniga; the church of Saint Justina of Pertice, with all their appurtenances; the possessions and all the rights [Col. 0925C] which you have in the village of Sezadii; the right which you have in the church of Saint Mary built in that village; the tithes, the fourth part, and the rent in that same place; the church of Saint James of Castronovo with its appurtenances; whatever you have in one Carpeneto and in the other, and in Borio, Castronovo, Fontanigollo, Ritorto, Danaveta, and Pertice.

Certainly, no one may presume to demand or extort from you tithes of your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, nor of the produce of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world who are free and unbound, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brothers, after making profession in the monastery, [Col. 0925D] from leaving it without his abbot’s permission, unless he has obtained admission to a stricter religious order; nor may anyone dare retain one who leaves without a letter of guarantee from the community. You shall receive chrism and holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks or clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to supply them to you freely and without any improper condition. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer . . . . . . who is in communion with the Apostolic See, and who, supported by his own authority, shall provide what you request.

When there is a general interdict [Col. 0926A] upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We also prohibit anyone from pronouncing against you or your church a sentence of excommunication or interdict without a mandate from the Roman pontiff, or from harassing you with new and undue molestations. Furthermore, we ratify the ancient immunities and reasonable customs granted to your monastery and hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain inviolate for ever. We further decree that burial in the monastery shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving [Col. 0926B] the rightful claims of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are brought.

When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it by any trickery of usurpation or by force, except one whom the brothers, by common consent or by the wiser counsel of the greater part of the brothers, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, have provided to be elected.

Therefore we decree that no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, remove them, or harass it with any vexations whatever; rather, all things shall remain intact for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, [Col. 0926C] saving the authority of the Apostolic See and, in the aforesaid churches, the customary right of the diocesan bishops. As a sign of this liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and our successors one Byzantine coin each year.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly attempting rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, after a second . . . . . . . . warning, does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve their rights to that same [Col. 0926D] place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the reward of good conduct and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Subscribed and sealed under the seal of the pontificate.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, . . . ., priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul. I, H., cardinal of Saint Clement, of Tusculum. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. [Col. 0927A] I, C., deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, L., deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, R., deacon-cardinal of Saint Martha.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and canon of the Lateran, on the seventh Ides of April, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1192, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

LXIX. He grants William, bishop of Lucca, authority to confer benefices, even those under lay patronage, if no one else has been presented by their patrons within a specified period. (Lateran, April 12.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, ed. Lucca, IV, 179.]

[Col. 0927B]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, bishop of Lucca, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the office of apostleship entrusted to us by God, we are bound to have care for all the Churches and, with the Lord as author, diligently to attend to their welfare. As you have stated, however, appointments to churches in your diocese are very often unduly delayed because patrons are drawn in differing directions by their wishes; and consequently their goods are greatly dissipated. Therefore, wishing by apostolic authority to remedy this evil, following the example of Pope Urban, our predecessor of happy memory, we have thought fit to grant you by this present document that, when patrons disagree concerning the presentation for churches whose appointment belongs to you, if, after your admonition, they do not return to agreement within the term established at the Lateran council, then, after that term has elapsed, you shall be free, notwithstanding any objection or appeal, canonically to appoint suitable persons to those churches. [Col. 0927C]

Given at the Lateran, on the second Ides of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXX. He takes the monastery of Saint Mary of Lucedio under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Lateran, April 14.)

[IRICUS OF TRENT, *Three Books of Affairs of the Fatherland*, in the dissertation, p. 15.]

[Col. 0927D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Lucedio, and his brothers, both present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetual remembrance.

It is fitting that those living the religious life should have apostolic protection, lest an assault of any rashness either draw them away from their purpose or—God forbid!—break the strength of their sacred religion. Therefore, [Col. 0928A] beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, after the example of Alexander, Lucius, Urban, and Clement, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and strengthen by the privilege of this present document, the aforesaid monastery of the Blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary of Lucedio, in which you are dedicated to divine service. First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in your monastery according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the observance of the Cistercian brethren, shall there be observed inviolate for ever.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically [Col. 0928B] possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s aid, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to name expressly:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery was built, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Alerii with all its appurtenances; the territory of Stodeganda with all its appurtenances; the land which belonged to the bishop of Vercelli, lying next to the monastery; the grange of Montarolio with all its appurtenances; the grange of Ripaemezana with all its appurtenances; the grange of Poblato with [Col. 0928C] all its appurtenances; the grange of Montiscalvo with all its appurtenances; the island of Ugerii and the island beside the Po. Likewise, the grange of Salmaria with all its appurtenances; the land situated on the island of Bremide; the chestnut grove of Zibrana. Moreover, we confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, by apostolic authority, the possessions at Pobleto which you bought from the abbot and brothers of Saint Michael of Clusa, and the chapel of that place, canonically granted in perpetuity to your monastery by the aforesaid abbot and brothers for an annual rent of ten solidi, as is contained in the authentic documents made concerning the matter and as you possess it peacefully.

Certainly, no one whatsoever may presume to demand tithes from you on the fruits of your labour which you cultivate with your own hands [Col. 0928D] or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, or from the produce of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen who are free and unbound, fleeing the world, and retain them in your monastery without any opposition. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brothers, after making profession in your house, from leaving it without your abbot’s permission; nor may anyone dare retain one who leaves without a letter of guarantee from your community. If anyone should nevertheless presume to retain them, you may by our authority pronounce the regular sentence against those monks or lay brothers of yours.

Further, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide for [Col. 0929A] your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from rashly committing violence, robbery, or theft within the enclosure of your monastery and the enclosed bounds of your places or granges; or from setting fire, seizing a person, or killing. Certainly, if bishops demand anything from you beyond the obedience due, or princes of the land demand anything contrary to the liberty granted by our predecessors and by ourselves, you may, by apostolic authority, refuse what is demanded, lest on that pretext your order, which has hitherto been free, be bound by the snare of human servitude. If bishops therefore pronounce any sentence on persons belonging to you or on your Church on this account, we decree that sentence to be void as pronounced contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See. We further prohibit by apostolic authority any new undertaking from being made within half a league of your abbey that might prejudice the liberty and peace hitherto preserved for you. In your own causes, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, you may bring forward competent brothers as witnesses and, by their testimony, as justice requires, repel violence and vindicate your right. [Col. 0929B]

Therefore we decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, or harass it with any vexations whatever; rather, all things shall remain intact for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly attempting rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning does not correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve their rights to that same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0929C] Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good conduct and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Landulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Michael, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of Saint Martin, title of Saint Equitius. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 0930A] I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Godfrey, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Sunfundi.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Giles, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1192, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

LXXI. To the dean and chapter of Rouen.—He permits them, during an interdict, to celebrate the divine offices without solemnity. (In the Lateran palace, April 16.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 616.]

[Col. 0930B]

CELESTINE, etc.

Since the whole Church of God, spread far and wide across the extent of the world, forms one Catholic—that is, universal—Church, redeemed by the price of the blood of her bridegroom; and since, as the uniformity of faith and doctrine joins diverse limbs into one body, if any one of them suffers injury, its harm cannot occur without injury to the others—although the head is offended more than the rest in proportion as it is more deeply affected by each one’s suffering and united to them by a firmer bond. For this reason, since the Roman Church is the head and mistress of all, we, though unworthy, preside over it; [Col. 0930C] and the oppression of any one Church more grievously shakes and afflicts us, and more forcefully moves us to compassion, in proportion as it more especially hopes for aid from us in adversity and as every Church has been accustomed to invoke more devoutly and confidently the protection of the Apostolic See against the violence of wicked men.

As we have been informed by letters from some of you and many others, and have already learned from the reports of many, the charity of all has grown cold through the increasing wickedness of the unrighteous, so that now scarcely any reverence is shown to the churches of God or to their ministers; the sanctuary of the Lord is trampled down by force, the teachings of faith are despised, and scarcely can any persons be found who, after very many enormities, add [anything] so as to rise again. Instead, in vengeance for preceding sins, they heap further and more grievous enormities upon offences hitherto committed; they rejoice when they have done evil (Prov. II), the wicked are proud while the poor man is set on fire (Ps. X), and they exult in carrying out works of iniquity. [Col. 0930D]

But since the wickedness of evil men has become so strong that remedy or assistance cannot be found in man, recourse must be had to the protection of the Creator; and prayer and every pious work must be pursued more earnestly, so that the condescension of heavenly mercy may graciously look upon us, may not permit man to prevail further over us, and may not allow him to delight longer in the oppression of the Churches. For only then can we securely hope for and await help from above, when we have diligently fulfilled those things [Col. 0931A] which belong to our office. Let us briefly set out what has been reported to us especially concerning the Church of Rouen and provide such remedies as we can. . . . (Something appears to be missing here.)

Moved, therefore, by this consideration, and likewise inclined by your prayers, we have thought fit to grant you by this present document that, when there is a general interdict upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. If, in the meantime, any of your canons or clerics, fortified by the ecclesiastical sacraments, should be called from this life, you may commit them to burial in the cemetery of your church without the solemnity of the office, with holy water and a cross, prayers [Col. 0931B] being offered in a low voice. Therefore let no person at all, etc.

Given in the Lateran palace, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the second year of our pontificate.

LXXII. At the request of Bishop William, he takes the Church of Lucca under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Lateran, April 21.)

[*Memorie edoc.*, IV, I, *Racc.*, p. 48.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, bishop of Lucca, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Both the order of reason requires, and consideration of ecclesiastical advantage invites us, to love our brethren and fellow bishops with more abundant charity and to strengthen the Churches entrusted to their governance more generously by the protection of the Apostolic See, so that, in carrying out the office they have assumed, they may always be more vigilant in proportion as they see themselves remaining more secure against the assaults of wicked men. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop William, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive the aforesaid Church of Lucca, over which, by God’s will, you are known to preside, under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, following the example of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Alexander II, Paschal II, Calixtus II, Urban II, Lucius III, and Urban III, of happy memory; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. [Col. 0931C] We establish that whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to name expressly:

The court or estate of Lucca with its suburbs and villages, holdings and lands belonging to it wherever situated; namely, the village called Suburbanum; the church and meadow called Saint Columban’s; the church of Saint Peter called Summaldi, with its appurtenances; the parish church of Lunata and the tithe of Carignano; the land belonging to the abbey of Saint [Col. 0932A] Donatus; and the rest which appears to belong to that estate. To these we add the parish church and estate of Marlia, with the church of Saint Terentius and with all its holdings, lands, and every appurtenance; also the two castles of Moriano with all their appurtenances and adjacent lands, as you are known hitherto to have held them; and the land called Cerbajola; likewise the castle called Fundannum with all its appurtenances; as well as the castle of Decimo and its parish church, with everything belonging to it; also the parish church of Gallicano; the land of Censpiano; and the castle and tithe of Verrucla in the Alps; likewise the tithing-right of Verrucla near Bojanum.

We also include the parish church and castle of Saint Mary called “At [Col. 0932B] the Mount,” with all its appurtenances, and land in the village called Surrexeri; the castle and estate of Saint Gervasius, with everything belonging to them; the parish church of Ficeclo with its chapels; the chapel of Saint Vitus of the Arno Valley; the parish church of Padule with its chapels, the estate of Capannore, and whatever right you have in that parish district; the parish church of Sibiliano with all its chapels and everything else you have in that parish district; the parish church of Aquis with all its chapels, the estate of Vivaio, and all else belonging to you in that parish district; the parish church of Triballo (Tripallo) with all its chapels; the parish church of Miliano with all its chapels, estate, and appurtenances; the parish church of Apiano with all its chapels and [Col. 0932C] everything you have in that parish district; the parish church of Saint Stephen with all its chapels.

Furthermore, adhering to the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Calixtus of pious memory, we grant to you and to your successors, out of the kindness of the apostolic see, the use of the pallium during the solemnities of Mass in your church; provided, however, that you use it only on those days on which this has been granted to you by our predecessors. Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid any monastery or church to be built within your bishopric without the consent of yourself or your successors, saving the privileges of the apostolic see. We likewise forbid monks to make catechumens among the people, to perform anointings of the sick, or to impose public penances, without the permission of yourself or your successors. But if the people of a parish should assemble at a monastery for participation in the divine office, these same sacraments shall be administered through a chaplain-priest to whom the bishop has entrusted governance of the people and care of souls, while the reasonable customs of the other churches are nevertheless preserved. [Col. 0932D]

With respect to parish churches held by monks within your bishopric, following the decree of Pope Urban II of blessed memory, we ordain that no priests shall be installed in them without the authority of yourself or your successors. Rather, when they become vacant, the abbots and priors to whom these churches belong shall present them to you, and you shall entrust the care of souls to those presented, if they are suitable; provided that they are answerable to you concerning the care of the people and their ecclesiastical order. [Col. 0933A] Moreover, if the monasteries or churches of the Lucchese diocese have causes against one another, and a complaint is brought to the bishop by one party, the dispute shall be settled by his judgment, without prejudice to the authority of the Roman Church. We also more strictly prohibit anyone from admitting persons excommunicated or placed under interdict by the bishop of Lucca into forbidden communion.

Moreover, by this present writing we enact that the bishop of Lucca shall be elected not through the violence of any laypersons, but by the canons of the Church according to canonical enactments. Furthermore, we confirm to you and to your successors the possessions which you hold by grant or confirmation of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Alexander II and Paschal II. We order that the judgment reasonably rendered, as the public instrument records, and hitherto observed, between your predecessor and the abbot of Ficeclo by Ildeprand, formerly bishop of Pistoia, Argentus, archpriest, and R., primicerius of Lucca, concerning tithes, churches, and other matters, shall be observed in future times. [Col. 0933B] We likewise decree that the renunciation made by Bulgarus, count of Ficecla, to John, your predecessor, concerning certain possessions and churches, as contained in the public instrument of Gerard the notary, shall remain in force henceforward. We hold valid, and confirm by apostolic authority, the canonical customs which from ancient times you have had, and are known still to have, in the monastic parish churches and elsewhere in your bishopric, both in receiving synodal dues and in other matters. [Col. 0933C]

Furthermore, out of reverence for the Church entrusted to you, the aforesaid Father and our predecessor Pope Lucius, moved by the prayers of you and your canons, as also of the clergy, consuls, and people of your city, granted you and your successors, with the counsel of his brethren, the use of the cross throughout your bishopric, and confirmed it by apostolic authority. Following in his footsteps, we decree that this shall remain firmly established.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for you and your successors, to be of use to you in every respect, without prejudice to the authority of the apostolic see. [Col. 0933D] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowingly attempting rashly to act against this charter of our enactment, after a second or third admonition, does not make amends for his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to stern vengeance.

But upon all who uphold the rights of that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 0934A]

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. (There follow the subscriptions of fourteen cardinals.)

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

Privilege for the abbey of Boschetto, or Vallis Lucida, by which the supreme pontiff receives the aforesaid monastery under the protection of Blessed Peter and himself, decreeing that the monastic order, known to have been established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian Order, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. (Fragment.)

[Col. 0934C]

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albanus, bishop of Albano. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the church of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal of the title of St Clement, bishop of Tusculum. I, Romanus, cardinal-priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 0934D] I, Gratianus, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bernard, cardinal-deacon of St Mary the New. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of the title of St Gregory at the Golden Veil. I, Nicholas, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Lothair, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the Ides of May [15 May], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### LXXVI. He receives the monastery of St Arnulf at Metz under protection and confirms its goods and possessions. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 15 May.)

*[History of Metz, III, Preface, p. 153.]*

[Col. 0935A]

**CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BURCHARD, abbot of the monastery of St Arnulf, and to his successors professing the regular life, for ever.**

A pious request ought to be brought to fulfilment by the effect of the will, so that faithful devotion may attain its notable result and the benefit sought may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore we graciously grant your just requests; and, following in the footsteps of our Fathers and predecessors of happy memory, Leo, Calixtus, Innocent, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, [Col. 0935B] we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of St Arnulf, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting it, by the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the churches, villages, possessions, and everything [Col. 0935C] which the most serene sons of the Roman Church—kings and emperors, namely Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, Arnulf, Charles the Bald, Zendibold, Otto, Conrad, and Henry—bestowed upon that monastery in pious devotion, or which, having been given by other faithful of Christ, they confirmed by the authority of their privileges. We ordain that these shall serve perpetually for the use of the abbot and brothers serving God there, and shall always remain whole and unshaken, without any contradiction, for their maintenance; namely: Mareolas (Marieulle), with its church and tithe; eighteen manses at Ars (Ars-sur-Moselle); Jussiacum (Jussy), with church and tithe; the church of Gravei (Gravelotte); the church of Arcis (Ary); Floriacum (Fleury); Flaviniacum (Flavigny), with church and [Col. 0935D] tithe; Nungardum (Nauroy-le-Sec), with church and tithe, of which one fourth belongs to the priest; Vigiacum (Vigy), with church and tithe and the ban of thirty manses; the church of Romeliacum (Remilly), with the entire tithe; furthermore Maurivilla (Morville), Baldrecurt (Baudrecourt), and eighteen salt-boiling sites at Vic and Winemunt; Devillare (Dévillers), with church; Tilium (Martille), with church; and Caminetum (Cheminot) and Buxerias (Bouxières), with their churches, which Queen Hildegard gave to St Arnulf together with tithe, fishing rights, woods, vineyards, waters and watercourses, mills already constructed, or to be transferred and built at any place above the river Seille within the ban of the aforesaid estate, wherever it shall please the brothers’ stewards. [Col. 0936A]

Pomeriolum (Pomérieux), moreover, together with and through which the oft-mentioned monastery was endowed in ecclesiastical fashion by St Pope Leo IX; Laium (Lay-Saint-Christophe), likewise, with church and tithe, one fifth of which belongs to the priest, and with the ban which a certain countess named Eva, together with the wood called Heis and every profit from it, and the water-meadow of the same village with bridge, fishing, and *vesnia* on the river Meurthe, had assigned for the maintenance of the brothers; Bivera (Bivère, near Trier), with church, given to that monastery by Countess Fredelinde and confirmed by authority of Emperor Conrad; and whatever St Arnulf possesses within the bishopric of Trier; [Col. 0936B] namely, the church of Vilers, Walen, Sira Melbranc (in the bull of Innocent and Alexander III, Mellanc), with church; Corlinges (Kerlange), with church; Dogaganen; Catinges, with church; and the remaining possessions which the aforesaid saint has in the bishopric of Metz, and in the bishoprics of Toul and Verdun; the cell of Aulegia (Oley), with church and tithe; the cell of Chiniano (Chiny), built in honour of St Walburga, with the churches belonging to it, namely Florenville, Orgeio, Tintiniacum, Casa Petra, and St Cecilia, which Count Arnulf gave to St Arnulf; furthermore, the cell situated in the forest called Fault (Fault in the forest of Remilly), bestowed upon and confirmed for the aforesaid saint by the venerable lord Stephen, bishop of Metz; [Col. 0936C] also the mill situated near the sandbank, to be transferred to whichever bank of the river Seille they wish, within the right of that monastery; the church of St Victor, situated in the suburb of St Stephen; the church of Wisse, with tithe and one quarter of a mansi; the hundred [district] of the borough with the ban under which the monastery of Blessed Arnulf was built, together with eleven manses of land; Campaneola (Champigneulles), with ban, church, and the entire tithe; a third part of the tithe in every respect from the church at Porchericourt; a third part of the allod of Cariseium (Cherisy), belonging to the alms of the poor; the allod of Sarlei (elsewhere also called Colmes), which the matron Judith gave to God and St Arnulf [Col. 0936D] for her soul; the church of St Benignus, with tithe; two houses situated within the city, one called the House of the Holy Cross, the other the Hall of the Romans; a certain garden and the house called Brinul, which Gerard gave.

All these things—namely the villages, churches, and possessions—we confirm to you, and through you to the same monastery, in perpetuity, as you reasonably possess them. We further establish that, apart from bishops and abbots, seven priests of the same monastery, and three canons of the house of St Stephen—the primicerius, dean, and first cantor—no one shall presume to celebrate Mass at that altar without the consent of the abbot and brothers of that place. We also order that, as has been established by our predecessors, no archbishop or bishop may presume to violate that altar or prohibit divine services there, unless he has first received permission from the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0937A]

Moreover, we decree that you and your successors shall have in the same place two annual markets: one on the feast of St Arnulf’s nativity, and the other on the anniversary feast of its dedication, as you have hitherto held them peacefully; and by the authority of this privilege we order that this dedication shall always be celebrated there solemnly by all. Likewise, in paternal affection, Abbot Burchard, we establish and grant to you and your successors in perpetuity that, on the feast-day of that dedication and on other principal feasts, you may wear sandals and a dalmatic in the celebration of Mass, as has been granted to you by our predecessors [Col. 0937B] and hitherto observed; we admonish your discretion that, as this honour is increased, so may love for the Most High increase within you. Further, no advocate may presume to demand anything from the affairs of the monastery beyond the customary judicial due of an advocate.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved whole, to be of use in every respect to those for whose governance and support they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Metz. [Col. 0937C] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future knowingly attempts rashly to act against this charter of our enactment, and, after a second or third admonition, fails to make amends for the offence by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0937D]

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Mel[ior], cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal of the title of St Clement, bishop of Tusculum. I, Romanus, cardinal-priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, Gratianus, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, cardinal-deacon of St Adrian. [Col. 0938A] I, Soffridus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Bernard, cardinal-deacon of St Mary the New. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the Ides of May [15 May], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### LXXVII. He receives the monastery of St Vincent at Metz under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 15 May.)

*[History of Metz, III, 156.]*

[Col. 0938B]

**CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FRANCO, abbot of St Vincent’s at Metz, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.**

Whenever something is requested of us which is known to accord with religion and uprightness, it becomes us gladly to grant it and to give appropriate support in accordance with the petitioners’ will when that will is consonant with reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, [Col. 0938C] we graciously grant your just requests, receive the aforesaid church of St Vincent, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order, known to be established in that place according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 0938D] Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of St German at Castello [Note: [Col. 0937D] Chaté-Saint-Germain], with all its appurtenances, in this manner: that you shall henceforth hold, as the right of the proper pastor, the altar together with its endowments and tithes, which in former times belonged to the priest, and the altars of the chapels; and that you shall appoint there a worthy vicar at your discretion, with no opposition hindering your will. After your election, he shall receive care of souls from the bishop, and, content with the portion assigned to him by your ordinance, shall not presume to lay hand upon any other things or possessions of the church. [Col. 0939A] It shall be his duty to observe synods and pay synodal dues; but it shall be yours to place the sacred vestments and altar vessels in diligent custody, to pay the rent at appointed times, and to install monks in that church according to your decision and will.

In that village of Castello, the hill of St German and the entire tithe belonging to the same church; also a dwelling in the same village, and whatever your monastery has hitherto possessed there; the tithe of the fields of Champenoys [Note: [Col. 0939D] Champenois, today dependent upon the commandery of Malta]; Amanvilers [Note: [Col. 0939D] Amanvillers], with chapel and whatever belongs to its ban; at Anceyum [Note: [Col. 0939D] Ancy], the church and five manses of land, with demesne vineyards and ban; on Mount St Quentin, the vineyard of John and Putayn, the tithes of those vineyards, [Col. 0939B] and the other vineyards which you possess there; one mansi at Longa-villa [Note: [Col. 0939D] Longeville-devant-Metz]; at Cheseles [Note: [Col. 0939D] Chazelles], rent-paying vineyards with ban; the church of St Marcellus [Note: [Col. 0939D] Parish of St Marcel] before your gate, and part of the tithe of St Martin [Note: [Col. 0939D] Tithes between the Pont des Morts and the Pont-Thieffroy], as you have hitherto possessed them; the village of St Julian [Note: [Col. 0939D] St Julien], with church, ban, and hundred [district], with all its appurtenances; a vineyard in Aculeus, bestowed for St Gorgonius before the greater church; at Alerias [Note: [Col. 0939D] Place unknown], six manses with ban, demesne vineyards, and tithe; the churches of St Lawrence [Note: [Col. 0939D] Vallières], with the appurtenances which you possess from it; the church of St Amand at Aneriacum [Note: [Col. 0939D] Ennery]; part of the tithe with the right which you hold in that church, and the lands which you possess there; at Littinges [Note: [Col. 0939D] Lutanges], five quarter-units [*quartarii*] [Col. 0939C] of land with the right which you hold in that church; the estate of Corzelles [Note: [Col. 0939D] Courcelles-sur-Niéd], with church, ban, and all its appurtenances; the estate of Challey [Note: [Col. 0939D] Chailly-sur-Niéd], with those things belonging to its ban; the allod of Sorbers [Note: [Col. 0939D] Sorbé], with church and the tithe of your fields; the church of Velers [Note: [Col. 0940D] Villers-l’Orme], with tithe; the village called Wbrisia [Note: [Col. 0940D] Varize], with church and a market held every Saturday in its precinct, and whatever belongs to its ban; at Jovilla [Note: [Col. 0940D] Juville], the church and whatever belongs to its ban; six manses at Trummacum [Note: [Col. 0940D] Tragny], and eight at Taysey [Note: [Col. 0940D] Taisey], with bans and demesne lands; one mansi in Lymucort [Note: [Col. 0940D] Lenoncourt]; the village called St Martin before Marsal [Note: [Col. 0940D] St Martin-devant-Marsal], with [Col. 0939D] ban and church; in the village of Marsal, twenty-nine and a half rent-paying [Col. 0940A] sites, and that land on which four sites are situated; in the village on the river Oran [Note: [Col. 0940D] This village has been destroyed. It was near Villeau-Pré], the rents and revenues which you possess there; before Verdun, the village of Duniacum [Note: [Col. 0940D] Dugny], with church and whatever belongs to its ban; the church of Sinoncort [Note: [Col. 0940D] Semoncourt near Dugny]; the church of St Clement at Arnavilla [Note: [Col. 0940D] Arnaville]; and the chapel of St Gengulf at Brocey [Note: [Col. 0940D] Brocq], and two shares of the offerings, both of the living and the dead, made in those churches; likewise the tithes of all the fields of Bukinella belonging to the ban of Brocey; the church of St John of Siryfontaine [Note: [Col. 0940D] Place unknown]; the church of Nonsart; eight and a half manses of land at Acerum; the cell of the monks of St Vincent on the Moselle, in the ban of Caliniacum [Note: [Col. 0940D] Chaligny]; in the village of [Col. 0940B] Caliniacum, the church with its appurtenances and whatever you possess in that ban, together with an annual rent of thirteen solidi in the currency of Châlons, which the brothers of that place owe you on the feast of St Vincent; and, in German territory, the cell of monks called Offainbac [Note: [Col. 0940D] Offembach, a priory in the duchy of Deux-Ponts].

We also decree that the monastery of St Vincent, which looks toward the episcopal see of Stephen, proto-martyr of Christ, and its abbot, when acting in the bishop’s stead, may celebrate Mass with dalmatic and sandals on the feast of the Invention and the Nativity of that proto-martyr, and likewise on the dedication of the church, as was granted to them by John, Benedict, Urban, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs of happy memory. Surely, no one may dare to demand or extort tithes from your newly cultivated lands [Col. 0940C] which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. It is also lawful for you to receive into conversion clerics or laymen who are free and absolved, fleeing from the world, and to retain them without opposition. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, to leave it except for the purpose of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare to retain a departing brother without letters of the community giving security. We order that chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred [Col. 0940D] orders shall be supplied to you by the diocesan [Col. 0941A] bishop. Furthermore, we decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remain intact.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved whole, to be of use in every respect to those for whose governance and support they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future, etc. [Col. 0941B]

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Mel[ior], cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal of the title of St Clement, bishop of Tusculum. I, Romanus, cardinal-priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 0941C] I, Gratianus, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, cardinal-deacon of St Adrian. I, Soffridus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Bernard, cardinal-deacon of St Mary the New. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of [Col. 0941D] Aegidius, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the Ides of May [15 May], in the tenth indiction, in the year one thousand one hundred and ninety-two of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### LXXVIII. He orders Seffrid, bishop of Chichester, and the abbots of Reading and Waltham to “absolve the clerics of Lambeth from the oath, sworn to Baldwin, former archbishop of Canterbury, to observe the new chapel.” (Rome, at St Peter’s, 16 May.)

*[TWYSDEN, Writers of English Affairs, II, I, 1593.]*

**CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Chichester, and to his beloved sons the abbots of Reading and Waltham, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

It is especially fitting for the governance of the supreme pontiff that, just as he desires that the provisions he reasonably makes be observed by his successors, so he ought inviolate to preserve the good institutions of his predecessors, established by the judgment of prudent deliberation preceded by reason. Since, therefore, our predecessors Urban and Clement of happy memory, acting with the counsel of their cardinal brethren, annulled the building of a new chapel and the installation of clerics, carried out to the prejudice of the community of the church and apparently likely to produce serious grounds for scandal, and expressly forbade the chapel thereafter to be observed or divine offices to be celebrated in it, [Col. 0942B] we, desiring what they are known to have established in this matter to enjoy perpetual stability, hold it ratified and firm and order it to be observed without opposition from anyone.

And because the canonical enactments judge void and useless whatever follows from this, or is done on account of that which has a cause of perpetual prohibition and has been forbidden by a canon established by supreme pontiffs; and because the civil laws likewise declare the same, we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, by authority of the apostolic see, you shall publicly declare the clerics of Lambeth absolved, on our behalf, from the oath of observing the new chapel which they swore to B[aldwin], former archbishop of Canterbury. Setting aside appeal, you shall strictly command them that they must no longer observe the new chapel [Col. 0942C] or the church of Lambeth, nor thereafter minister in it either personally or through their agents; and you shall restrain by ecclesiastical censure, without delay or appeal, those who presume to resist our command. No letters obtained from the apostolic see shall obstruct this, if the tenor of these letters has been concealed.

But if all of you cannot be present for carrying this out, nevertheless two of you shall carry it out.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June [16 May], in the second year of our pontificate.

### LXXIX. He grants the abbot of the monastery of St Denis “that, notwithstanding a frivolous appeal, he may freely perform the duty of his office in correcting monks and lay brothers.” (Lateran, 23 May.)

*[DOUBLET, History of Saint-Denis, 525.]*

[Col. 0942D]

**CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of the monastery of St Denis, etc.**

It was represented before us on your behalf that the monks and lay brothers of your monastery frequently interpose the obstacle of a groundless appeal so that you cannot proceed to correct them as pertains to your office; and so, because you cease such correction on that account, their offences remain unpunished. On this matter you asked that provision be made for you by the apostolic see. Therefore, not wishing that what is known to have been instituted as help for the oppressed should be turned into a means of escape for sins, by the authority of this document we grant you that, notwithstanding a frivolous appeal, you may freely perform the duty of your office in correcting those same monks and lay brothers, etc. [Col. 0943A]

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June [23 May], in the second year of our pontificate.

### LXXX. He receives the monastery of St Mary in Flumine under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 27 May.)

*[UGHELLI, Sacred Italy, II, 578.]*

**CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . , abbot of St Mary in Flumine, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular [Col. 0943B] life, for ever.**

A pious request of the will, etc.; following the example of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order, known to be established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Vallombrosan brethren, shall remain there inviolate for all time, etc. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the parish church of St Lawrence at Nocero, with its tithes, offerings, [Col. 0943C] testamentary bequests, and chapels—namely, the chapel at Casa Figaria; the chapel of Blessed Donatus, with all its possessions and appurtenances; the chapel of Paulo with its appurtenances; and the chapel of Petroniano and the chapel of Monsignano, with their tithes and testamentary bequests; one half of the parish church of St Peter at Ceneto, with half the tithes of that parish church; the chapel of St Peter Marsius with its appurtenances; the chapel of Baio with the possessions belonging to your monastery; the chapel of St Mary of Trexano; the chapel of Gagliano; the chapel of Pablexio, with its possessions and appurtenances; the chapel of St Quiricus with its possessions; the chapel of Vergniano with its appurtenances; the chapel of Bivano, the chapel of Alphiano, and the chapel of Ravaldino [Col. 0943D] with their possessions; the castle of Monte Vecchio, with estate and all its appurtenances; the estate of Nucero; the possessions of Ravaldino with all their appurtenances; the possessions of St Lawrence at Nucero; the possessions from Collina of Icoleis as far as the boundary; likewise the liberties and immunities bestowed upon your monastery by Frederick, Roman emperor ever august, of revered memory, and confirmed by the counts of the castle of Caro and of Castrum Novum through public documents and oaths duly sworn. Confirming these by apostolic authority, we decree that they shall be observed inviolate for all time.

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority the grant justly made to you by T. and O., bishops of Liviensis, as authentically contained in their writings. [Col. 0944A] Surely no one may presume to extort from you tithes from your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. It is also lawful for you to receive into conversion clerics or laymen who are free and absolved, fleeing from the world, and to retain them without any opposition. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the said monastery, to leave it except for the purpose of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare to retain a departing brother without letters of the community giving security. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they must answer to him [Col. 0944B] concerning spiritual matters. We further decree that no one within the bounds of your parishes may presume to establish a new church or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving the privileges of the apostolic see. Furthermore, burial in that place shall be free, etc.

We therefore decree, etc., without prejudice, etc. If anyone, etc. But upon all, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. [Col. 0944C] I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Goffredus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 0944D]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### LXXXI. He receives the church of Saints Andrew and Nicholas of Empoli under protection and confirms the possessions and privileges of its canons. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 27 May.)

[LAMI, *Monuments of the Florentine Church*, vol. IV, p. 109.]

CELESTINE III, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the plebanus and canons of the church of Saints Andrew and Nicholas of Empoli, and to the ecclesiastical persons canonically to be instituted there, present and future, for ever.

[Col. 0945A] Equity’s force and reason’s order require that we grant effect to just petitions, especially when piety assists the petitioners’ will and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid parish church of Saints Andrew and Nicholas of Empoli, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the liberality of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just causes, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 0945B] Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the churches of Saint Lord, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Lucy; the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Donatus; the church of Saint Mamas; the church of Saint Michael; the church of Saint Stephen; the churches of Saint Christopher and Saint James; the church of Saint Peter; the church of Saint Martin; the church of Saint Christina; the church of Saint Leonard; the church of Saints Simon and Jude; the church of Saints Hippolytus and Cassian; the church of Saint Justus; the church of Saint Rufinus; the church of Saint James; the church of Saint Fridianus; [Col. 0945C] the church of Saint Donatus; the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Angelus; the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Martin; the church of Saint Angelus; the church of Saint Pontianus; the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Bartholomew; and the church of Saint Mary, with all their appurtenances.

Moreover, no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on newly cultivated land which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. Since tithes are known to have been granted, under both Old and New Law, to the ministers of churches, we forbid under threat of anathema any layperson to presume to burden you by demanding tithes. By apostolic authority we further decree that no one may withdraw parish [Col. 0945D] churches subject to your parish church from their due obedience and subjection to you and your church, or presume in any manner to oppress you or that church with new and improper exactions or burdens. We hold valid the ancient rights and reasonable customs of your church hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times.

We direct that chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, the ordination of clerics to be promoted to holy orders, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments be provided to you by the diocesan bishop without any exaction. In the parish churches which you possess, your plebanus for the time being shall appoint clerics, as has hitherto [Col. 0946A] been observed; nor may anyone rashly presume to install any layperson or cleric in them. Furthermore, we forbid anyone within the bounds of your parish to presume to construct anew a church or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, while the privileges of the Roman pontiffs remain intact. We also prohibit anyone from pronouncing against you or your church a sentence of excommunication or interdict without just and reasonable cause.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we confirm to you, and through you to your church, the tithes which you have peacefully possessed for forty years. We decree further that the burial ground of your parish church shall be free to you, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who have [Col. 0946B] chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; provided always that the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remain intact. Upon the death of you, the present plebanus of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any cunning of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall, in the fear of God, determine to elect.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every respect of those [Col. 0946C] for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowingly opposing this document of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here [Col. 0946D] they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Demetrius, bishop of Tusculum. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 0947A] I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand [Col. 0947B] of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### LXXXII. He confirms to the canons of the church of Saints Peter and Andrew at Paderborn the estate of Helmgeldere and their privileges concerning the election of provosts and bishops. (Lateran, 30 May.)

[SCHATEN, *Annals of Paderborn*, I, 893.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons B., provost, and the canons of the lesser church at Paderborn, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0947C] It is fitting that we yield to the pious wishes of sons and readily give our assent, so that they may be the more devoted to us and to the Roman Church insofar as they know themselves to have been more fully heard. Therefore, beloved sons, canons of the lesser church at Paderborn, giving ready ear to your petitions, we confirm to you and your successors for ever the estate at Hemgeldere, which B., the pious provost of your church, released from lay hands and assigned to the common use of the brethren; and also the arrangement which the same provost established among us with the brethren’s consent: namely, that every brother among you who dies shall, from the day of his death until a year has elapsed, retain his stipend, to be spent for some work of piety [Col. 0947D] or to discharge his obligations if he happens to be burdened with debts.

Likewise, we confirm your free election of your provosts, which you have possessed until the present time, and also the election of your bishop, which you have customarily celebrated together with the canons of the greater church in your city. Furthermore, confirming firmly to you at the same time the annual meals which you have had with those same canons from earlier times, we command by apostolic authority that these be inviolably observed. Whoever rashly attempts to act against this document of our confirmation should know that he will without doubt incur the indignation of almighty God and of His apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May], in the second year of our pontificate.

### LXXXIII.

1. He ordains Albert, bishop-elect of Liège, deacon “on the Saturday of the solemn fast of the Ember Days celebrated at Pentecost.” (*Aegidius of Aulne, Life of Albert*, in Chapeaville, *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, II, 145.)

2. He commands Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, to “confer upon Albert, bishop-elect of Liège, the gift of consecration.” (Sigebert, continuation of *Aquicin[lacuna]t.*, 1192, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores*, VI, 429.)

3. He writes to William, archbishop of Reims, “that, if the archbishop of Cologne should decline to carry out the apostolic command concerning the consecration of Albert, bishop-elect of Liège, through fear of imperial power, the archbishop of Reims should nevertheless carry it out.” (Aegidius of Aulne, *Life of Albert*, p. 145.)

4. “To all the clergy and people, and to ecclesiastical and lay persons of every dignity and office throughout the whole bishopric of Liège, he commands and strictly enjoins, under peril to each person’s rank, that all obey Albert of Louvain; that all, released from the faith and oath which they had made to the provost of Bonn, whom the emperor had intruded, make a pledge and oath of subjection and obedience to Albert, whose election he approves.” (*Ibid.*) (Rome, at Saint Peter’s

[Col. 0948B]

### LXXXIV. He receives the convent of Saint Cosmas at Taliacozzo under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 1 June.)

[GATTULA, *History of the Abbey of Cassino*, vol. II, p. 804.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, Mabilia, abbess of the monastery [Col. 0948C] of Saint Cosmas of Talliacotio, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as consistent with religion and propriety, we ought gladly to grant it and to bestow suitable support upon the petitioners’ wishes. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of Alexander, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically [Col. 0948D] possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of popes, the liberality of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and to those who succeed you. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.
