The church of Saint Vitus with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Camerata with its appurtenances; the right which you have in the church of Saint Andrew at Clereto; one half of the offerings in the churches of the castle of Talliacozzo on the feasts of Easter and the Nativity of the Lord, and one half of the offerings for the dead; the burial of the leading men of the aforesaid castle; the burial of the hill of Bufara, with half the offerings for the dead; the tithes of the mills located in [Col. 0949A] the valley of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and thirty seed-measures of land in its channel; vineyards, lands, woods, houses, and cottages which you possess in the aforesaid castle; two mills; twenty-two feet of land, with which men of your monastery have been enfeoffed; the church of Saint Mary of Sorbo with all its appurtenances; one half of the mill of John Trotta; one half of the wood at the head of the water-source; and the wood of Colle de Coci within its boundaries.

Furthermore, we hold valid and firm the renunciation, promised before our aforesaid predecessors, which the nobleman Bartholomew of Talliacozzo made before many persons concerning the wrongful customs which he exacted from your monastery. By apostolic authority we forbid that the same Bartholomew or his [Col. 0949B] heirs at any time presume to impose those customs upon the monastery.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for your benefit and that of your successors in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the due right and reverence of the monastery of Cassino. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future knowingly attempts rashly to act against this document of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself answerable [Col. 0949C] before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. [Col. 0949D] I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Tusculum. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Goffredus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New. I, Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Aegidius, [Col. 0950A] deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the Kalends of July [1 July], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### LXXXV. He receives the monastery of Altorf in Alsace under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 8 June.)

[SCHOEPFLIN, *Alsatian Diplomas*, I, 297.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WALTER, abbot of the monastery of Saint Cyriacus in Alsace, called the High Monastery, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetual memory.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as consistent with religion and propriety, we ought gladly [Col. 0950B] to grant it and to bestow suitable support upon the petitioners’ wishes. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Cyriacus in Alsace, in which you are devoted to divine service, following the example of Leo, pope of happy memory, our predecessor; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order, known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, shall there be inviolably observed for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and peacefully [Col. 0950C] possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of popes, the liberality of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery was constructed, with all its appurtenances; the public court of Altorfh; a free advocate; its workshops, mint, and shops with all their rights; the court of Tutelheim, with the ban of that village and the jurisdiction commonly called *Masth*; the court of Jethol with its ban; the chapel of Blessed Michael; the church of Berbach [Col. 0950D] with its appurtenances; the church of Grindebroch with its appurtenances. We grant in perpetuity, freely to it and its successors to administer for the building of a new monastery, the aforesaid chapel of Blessed Michael and these two churches, Berbach and Grindebroch. Also: the chapel of Gierbaden; the court of Tamboch with its appurtenances; the court of Argent near Saint Aurelia with its appurtenances; the court of Tetvitre with its appurtenances; the courts of Ergerhenns and Mestershem with their appurtenances; the court of Sigoltesheim with its appurtenances; and the court of Wolfenganheim with its appurtenances.

You may also receive into conversion clerics and laypersons fleeing the world who are free and released from obligations, and retain them in your monastery without any contradiction. [Col. 0951A] Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, to leave it without the permission of his abbot; and no one may presume to retain one who has departed without a guarantee in your common letters. If anyone presumes to retain them, you may by our authority pronounce the regular sentence against your monks or converts. When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and ordinations of clerics or monks to be promoted to holy orders [Col. 0951B] from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things freely and without any improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

By this present document we also forbid anyone to dare demand or extort anything from you or your monastery beyond the ancient custom hitherto observed, except what your generosity voluntarily judges fit to bestow upon anyone. We also prohibit you, son abbot, or your successors from presumptuously enfeoffing, selling, alienating, or pledging any goods of the monastery through personal recklessness. [Col. 0951C] We hold valid and confirm by apostolic authority the liberties reasonably granted to you or the monastery by ecclesiastical or secular persons, together with the ancient and reasonable customs hitherto observed there.

Moreover, son abbot, you may use the mitre and ring, gloves and sandals, on the principal feasts; and we will that you be free from every jurisdiction and power of your diocesan bishop. We decree further that the burial ground of the place shall be free, so that none may oppose the devotion and final will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the rights of those churches from which [Col. 0951D] the bodies of the dead are taken remain intact. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, determine to elect.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the ecclesiastical or canonical [Col. 0952A] right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowingly opposing this document of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance.

But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

[Col. 0952B] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the sixth day before the Ides of June [8 June], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### LXXXVI. He confirms Sifrid, provost-elect of Saint Martin’s at Worms, and decrees that “this provostship shall never thereafter be assigned to the bishop of Worms, but its care and administration shall always be exercised through its own provost.” (Rome, at Saint Peter’s.)

[JAFFÉ, *Regesta*, p. 892.]

### LXXXVII. To all priors and brethren of the Carthusian Order he grants “that no prior or brother among them may be free to appeal without the consent and will of the chapter of his own house, or of its greater and sounder part.” (Lateran, 6 July.)

[*Privileges of the Carthusian Order*, fol. 4.]

[Col. 0952C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all priors and brethren of the Carthusian Order, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since you are separated from all agitations of worldly tumults not only in mind and profession but also by the situation and dwelling-places of your houses, you must take the utmost care lest, for the sake of some temporal advantage, you again be plunged into the whirlwinds of the world contrary to the purpose [Col. 0952D] of your order; and lest, deceiving yourselves under the appearance of what is right, you rashly involve yourselves in the disputes of lawsuits in order to acquire temporal advantage or avoid temporal disadvantage. Therefore, desiring also to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we firmly prohibit any of your priors or brethren from having liberty to appeal, by any rash presumption, without the consent and will of the chapter of his own house, or of its greater and sounder part.

Moreover, whenever you hold the general chapter, as you customarily do every year, if perhaps all cannot assemble, whatever shall have been reasonably and prudently established by the major prior of the order with the counsel of the greater and sounder part shall be held valid and firm [Col. 0953A] and shall be observed without objection by all brethren of your order.

Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this document of our prohibition or rashly act against it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of July [6 July], in the second year of our pontificate.

### LXXXVIII. He confirms the possessions and rights of the canons of the church of Saint Mary of Savona. (Rome, 7 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Sacred Italy*, IV, 735.]

[Col. 0953B] CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, provost, and the canons of Saint Mary of Savona, and to their successors canonically appointed, for ever.

“Whenever a request is made to us,” etc., as far as “to bestow suitable support.” Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, etc., as far as “we strengthen it.” Decreeing, etc., as far as “to specify the following by their proper names”:

The church of Saint Mary Magdalene with all its rights; the churches of Saint Stephen and Saint Pontius with all their rights; the church of Saint Saturninus and all the parochial rights of Savona, except that which was assigned to the churches of Saint George and Saint Peter; the hospital of Saint Maurus with all its rights; the right which you possess in offerings from Naulo; the tithe of both wine and grain; and the tithe of all that comes [Col. 0953C] into the bishop’s *Can.* [reading uncertain], as contained in the instrument of Amicus of blessed memory, formerly bishop of Savona; *Scarsolarum*, of brides, and of the blessing of ships [the construction is uncertain]; one half of the offerings which are given for those who choose burial at any church of the city; the right which you have in the *cellae* at Lavagnola, in Legino, and in Signo and its territory, and in Cugliani and its territory; all that you possess at Mallis; and whatever you possess in Lombardy, in Savona and its county; the church of Saint Thomas with all its rights; and the meals which the bishop of Savona owes you at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and the Assumption of Saint Mary.

Further, wishing with paternal kindness to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority your bishop to harass you or your church. We hold acceptable the liberties and immunities granted to your church, together with its ancient and reasonable customs, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. We decree further that the burial ground of your church shall be free, so that none may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remain intact. Upon the death of you, the present provost of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of intrusion or by force, except one whom the canons by common consent, or the sounder part [Col. 0954A] of the canons’ counsel, shall determine before God to elect.

Therefore we decree that no one, etc., as far as “saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.” If, therefore, etc., as far as “let him be subject to vengeance.” Upon all, etc., as far as “find the rewards of peace.” Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Benedict, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New. [Col. 0954B] I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at Rome, through the hands of [lacuna], on the Nones of July [7 July], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### LXXXIX. He receives the Carthusian house under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Lateran, 9 July.)

[*Privileges of the Carthusian Order*, fol. 4b.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0954C] sons, the prior and brethren of the Carthusian house, present and future, professing the eremitical life, for ever.

Since through God’s grace you excel in great glory of merits and, having chosen the solitary life, devote yourselves more strictly to divine contemplation, the good repute of your religious life induces us to attend with all diligence, by a common and particular obligation, to your tranquillity and to preserve your rights. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the footsteps of Alexander and Lucius, our predecessors of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves your Carthusian house in the wilderness, in which you are devoted to divine service, [Col. 0954D] and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the order of eremitical life, known to have been established in that place according to God, shall there be inviolably observed for all time. Furthermore, we confirm to you and your successors all possessions granted to your house by Christ’s faithful out of pious regard and possessed by you within your boundaries: namely, within the place called Clusa and the rock enclosing the valley and extending as far as the boundary-ridge enclosing and dividing Comba-Chalda, and reaching the middle rock above Bochgesos; then another boundary-ridge which stretches upward as far as the rock of Bovinant; thence another boundary-ridge which [Col. 0955A] runs downward along the ledge of Plataneti from Bovinant as far as the rock beside the furnace of la Follia.

Likewise, from that mountain which extends from the same rock as far as Mount Aillinart; and from Mount Aillinart it extends downward beside Morta westward as far as the rock above Carreria. From this rock it extends as far as the rock called Pertuso. Finally, it stretches downward to the river called the Dead Guier; and from the Dead Guier it rises along the rock enclosing Lesser Carreria as far as Terrassia; and from Terrassia, along the ledge of Plataneti and through la Follei Durtieres as far as Januarius; and from Januarius, as the Alps slope toward Proveysieu, as far as Calmeta Goncelim; and from Calmeta Goncelim [Col. 0955B] it extends along the ledge as far as the rock of Chalvienton; and thence descends by Bernard’s rock as far as Clusa.

Since the donors of these possessions forbade fishing, hunting, and the taking of birds, and prohibited within the aforesaid boundaries the pasturing and passage of sheep, goats, and all domestic animals, we likewise confirm that prohibition by apostolic authority.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we strictly interdict and, under threat of anathema, forbid anyone within your boundaries to seize persons belonging to your houses, commit theft or robbery, set fire, or commit homicide; or in any way molest persons coming to your houses [Col. 0955C] or returning from them. Thus, out of reverence for God and for your places, within these boundaries not only you and your brethren, but also others, may have full peace and tranquillity.

You may also receive into your conversion clerics or laypeople fleeing the world who are free and released from obligations, and retain them in your community without anyone’s opposition. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave your cloister without his prior’s permission; and no one may presume to retain one who has departed without a guarantee in the common letters.

No one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your labor which you cultivate with your own hands [Col. 0955D] or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals. We further enact that within half a league of the boundaries of the possessions which you hold, no religious person may build any structure whatsoever or acquire possessions. You shall receive the consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of your clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, is in grace and communion with the Apostolic See, and is willing to confer these upon you freely and without any improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you choose, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Moreover, by apostolic authority [Col. 0956A] we forbid any bishop or any other person whatsoever to compel you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit in a secular court concerning your own property or possessions; nor may anyone, unless invited, presume to come to your houses in order to celebrate ordinations, hear cases, or summon public assemblies; nor may anyone hinder the regular election of your prior or interfere in any way, contrary to the statutes of the Carthusian Order, in installing or removing the person who is prior for the time being. Furthermore, should bishops or other rulers of churches pronounce a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict against your monastery or the persons established there, or against your hired laborers because [Col. 0956B] you do not pay tithes or on any pretext concerning matters granted to you by apostolic favor; or should they pronounce such a sentence against your benefactors because they have charitably rendered you some benefit or service, or have assisted in labor on days on which you work and others observe a holiday, we decree that this sentence is to be annulled as having been issued contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See. Nor shall any letters have force which are found to have been obtained without naming the Carthusian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges. We also enact that, because of general interdicts laid upon territories, your monastery, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, shall not be compelled to abstain from divine offices.

Upon the death of you, who are now prior of the same place, [Col. 0956C] or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any trickery of surreption or by force, unless the brethren, by common consent or by the majority of the brethren of the sounder judgment, in the fear of God and according to the approved institutions of your Order, have decided that he should be elected.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and maintenance of those for whose benefit they were bestowed shall be preserved whole and unimpaired, to be of advantage to them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 0956D] person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this text of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. [Col. 0957A] I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, John, cardinal of the title of St. Clement, bishop of Tuscany. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of St. Mark, of the title of Equitius. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, John, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary the New. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Prison of Tullianus, on the seventh Ides of July [Col. 0957B], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

## XC. He confirms certain privileges of the prior and brethren of the Carthusians.  
*(Lateran, 12 July.)*

*[Privileges of the Carthusian Order, fol. 4.]*

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and brethren of the Carthusians: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Desiring to provide all the more willingly for your peace and tranquility because you are more closely devoted to divine service and, established upon the height of contemplation, are removed far from the tumult of earthly things, we more readily assent to your pious petition [Col. 0957C] and more gladly bestow apostolic favor. Therefore, in order that the institutions of your Order may possess lasting firmness, we decree that they shall henceforth remain ratified, as they have been approved and observed by those who use them rightly; and we confirm them by the authority entrusted to us. We enact that in the houses of your Order diocesan bishops may not review, or weaken contrary to the will of the prior and of the greater and sounder part of the chapter, the disciplinary penalties imposed upon offending brethren according to the institutions of the Order.

Nor may any bishop interfere or intrude uninvited in elections of priors, which your Order has hitherto held free by apostolic authority; nor may he extort from the priors [Col. 0957D] of the houses an unusual or unlawful obedience; nor may anyone attempt, contrary to the right owed to priors and to the institutions of the Order itself, to regulate the obediences and offices of the houses. Nor may anyone rashly presume to remove a brother from his cell without the prior’s permission, or to enter it and, by drawing him aside for conversation, break the silence—something which has never hitherto been permitted. Nor may anyone burden the houses of your Order with unlawful exactions or impositions. In houses assigned solely to the reception of brethren of the Order itself, no other person may presume to lodge, lest through him or those attending him the brethren’s quiet and silence be disturbed. Nor may anyone, usurping the office of prior in the chapter, interfere in any manner, against the institutions of the Order and apart from the will of the prior and brethren, either in disciplinary matters or in arranging [Col. 0958A] other business of the houses.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may violate this text of our prohibition and constitution or rashly act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth Ides of July, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XCI. He takes the monastery of St. Mary of Pomposa under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 13 July.)*

*[MORBIO, Histories of Italian Municipalities, I, II, p. 76.]*

[Col. 0958B]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANSELM, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary situated on the island of Pomposa, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as suited to religion and uprightness, it becomes us to grant it willingly and to give fitting support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just requests. Following the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Celestine, Eugenius, Anastasius, Adrian, Alexander, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, and under our own protection, the monastery of Pomposa, [Col. 0958C] in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We enact that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God willing, through the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the entire *massacella* called Materaria and the entire estate called Mausculi; one entire property called Casalae Publicum; [Col. 0958D] the estate called Nepotis and that called Caput Bovis; land and vineyard as you now hold and possess them by right of blessed Peter the Apostle; likewise, the bank of the River Alemonis on both sides adjacent to the estate called Prata, that bank extending from Agaziolo to the field of Bodullus; land and vineyard near the walls of the city of Ravenna, together with the entire shaded ground from the Little Gate of Augustus to the Taurensian Gate; one entire garden at the place called Ponte Calciato, in the district of St. Andrew, bounded on two sides by the right belonging to St. Andrew himself and on the other two by the public road; and the entire estate called Lacus Sanctus, with all its property and appurtenances, including its parish church, chapels, and ecclesiastical titles—namely, those of St. Mary, St. Martin, [Col. 0959A] St. Peter, and St. Venantius—with tithes, first-fruits, and all their rights; together with the fishery called Tidini, the archpriest’s ditch, and the fishery called Falce with the place called Montezello; Lacus Sichus, with the banks of the rivers Po and Gaurus on both sides as far as the sea; and, from the place called Conca Agata on one side as far as the sea, the whole place called Massenzatica, within the boundaries of the entire place and territory of the estate called Lacus Sanctus: on one side, the millrace of Volta Laterchli descending into Aquiliolo; from the River Rubba to Elia, and through the marsh to the middle of Curba, and beyond Curba to the Po above Policini; and beyond the Po above Policinum as far as the *gazum* of the bishopric of the Church of St. Comacchio [Col. 0959B] and as far as the river called Coesi; on the other side, the watercourse descending into Concha Agatuli and through it into the Gaurus; on the third side, the marsh extending between the stream of Agellus and Massenzatica as far as Montezella and Vedetoza, flowing into the Po; on the fourth side, Vacellinus, Ager Malus, and the channel of Vincareto running toward the arm of the river.

Moreover, we grant you the entire fishery called Volana, together with the stream of Sadalino and the greater Gavalena belonging to that fishery, with the parcels on both sides likewise belonging to it, as formerly they entered the sea. In the diocese of Concordia, the church of St. Martin at Fana; in the diocese of Ceneda, the church of St. Peter at Colice, those of St. Daniel and St. Andrew of Busco with their chapels; the church of St. Martin at Cambanardo; the church of St. Mary at Runco Marzolo; those of St. Helena and St. Mary at Vidore; and that of St. Bona with its chapels; the church of St. Mary at Castello, and others which you possess in those districts. In the diocese of Vicenza, the church of St. Mary at Turpise and the church of St. Blaise at Castro Vivarii; in the city of Verona, the church of St. Matthew; in the diocese of Brescia, the churches of St. Mary at the seat of Marculf, St. Mary of Cognomario, and St. Mary of Susilano; in the diocese of Cremona, the church of St. Stephen at Cavalaria with all its appurtenances; in the diocese of Asti, the churches [Col. 0959D] of St. Mary of Flexo and St. John of Cerro with all their appurtenances; in the diocese of Bologna, the churches of St. Mary of Arcellata with all its appurtenances, St. Venantius with all its appurtenances, St. Blaise of Luzaco with its whole court, St. Martin at Turrisella, St. John of Castagnolo, St. Blaise at Falcetto, and another church at Granarolo; in the same city, the church of St. Syrus. In the city of Modena, the church of St. Mary; at Castro Soleria, the church of St. John; in its village, the church of St. Michael; in the city of Ferrara, the church of St. Agnes; at Cattinaria, the church of St. Mary; at Bauria, the church of St. Mary; at Finale, the church of St. Michael and the church of St. Mary; at Votulato, the church of St. Peter; in the city of Faenza [Col. 0960A], the church of St. Clement; at Prate, the church of St. Lawrence; in the diocese of Livy, the church of St. Mary; at Manumizola, the churches of St. Michael and St. Mary of Rocca with their chapels; at Rimini, the church of St. Mary at Tribio; in the diocese of Urbino, the churches of St. Leo of Folia, St. Angel of the Island, St. Mary of Petia, St. Martin at Ulmeta, St. Heraclian, and St. Angel; at Provegio, the churches of St. Mary at Cateneto with its chapels, St. Mary of the Bond with its chapels, St. John of Prugneto with its chapels, and St. Mary of the Castle of San Marino with its chapels.

We grant all these things to you, your lawful successors, and brethren living religiously, to possess in perpetuity; provided that every year you pay to us and our successors, without difficulty, three silver solidi as rent. By public authority we also enact that the place itself and the things belonging to it shall be subject to no ecclesiastical person except the Roman pontiffs. No one shall presume to extort tithes from you on new lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals. You may receive into conversion clerics or laymen who are free and released from secular life and fleeing from it, and retain them without any opposition. You shall receive chrism and [Col. 0960C] holy oil from the bishop of Comacchio, if he is Catholic and is willing to give them to you freely, without an improper exaction; otherwise, for receiving these same sacraments, you may have recourse to whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. You may also receive the blessing of the abbot of your monks, the ordinations, and the consecrations of altars of your monastery and of those situated in the estate of Lacus Sanctus from whichever Catholic bishop you choose, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, who shall grant what is requested.

By a lasting decree we also enact that neither you, beloved son in the Lord, abbot, nor any of your successors may be compelled to attend the synod of any bishop, unless summoned by the Roman pontiff or his legate. Moreover [Col. 0960D], we decree that no archbishop or bishop may inflict a burden upon your monastery or exercise authority in it or over its property. No mortal may, against the will of the abbot and brethren of the monastery, exact *fodrum* or impose other exactions upon the tenants or villagers, male or female servants belonging to the monastery, or upon its cells, villages, castles, or parish churches; rather, may you always be cherished under the protection of the Apostolic See and, if necessary, preserved in its jurisdiction.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance [Col. 0961A] and maintenance of those for whose benefit they were bestowed shall be preserved whole and unimpaired, to be of advantage to them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this text of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that each may here receive the fruit of good action and [they] may find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 0961B] Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Lani., priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, John, cardinal of the title of St. Clement, bishop of Tuscany. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of St. Mark, of the title of Equitius. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, John, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary the New. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St. Gregory at the Golden Veil. I, John, bishop of Palestrina.

[Col. 0961C] Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and canon of the Lateran, on the third Ides of July, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

## XCII. He declares that the church of Schardeburg was given to the abbot and convent of Cîteaux by Richard, king of England.  
*(Lateran, 30 July.)*

*[HENRIQUEZ, Rule, Constitutions, and Privileges of the Cistercian Order, p. 232.]*

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Cîteaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily give assent to the just desires of petitioners and fulfill, by a result corresponding to them, vows which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring favorably in your just requests, we confirm for your community by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of this present writing, the church of Schardeburg with all its appurtenances and liberties, as the authentic documents issued concerning it by our dearest son in Christ Richard, illustrious king of England, attest. By a pious grant he gave that church to you for the maintenance of the abbots of the General Chapter, with the will and assent of our venerable brother Geoffrey, then-elect archbishop of York, as his authentic document testifies, and as is contained in the letters of our venerable brother John of Anagni, bishop of Palestrina, then legate in England. [Col. 0962A] We enact that no person whatsoever may violate this text of our confirmation or rashly act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of October, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XCIII. He confirms the goods of the Roman churches of St. Mary of Lady Rose and Blessed Lawrence, situated in Castel Aureo.  
*(Lateran, 4 October.)*

*[Collection of Bulls of the Most Holy Vatican Basilica, vol. I, p. 74.]*

[Col. 0962B]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, our primicerius and rector of the churches of St. Mary of Lady Rose and Blessed Lawrence, situated in Castel Aureo, and to all the clerics of those churches, present and future: in perpetuity.

The authority of the Apostolic See, over which, although unworthy, we preside by the Lord’s disposition, admonishes us to labor with prudent care for the well-being of all churches and to strengthen them with apostolic protection, lest they be harassed by the assaults of wicked persons. If we are bound to exercise pastoral care toward those far away, much more strongly ought we to discharge this duty toward churches built in the city of Rome, as toward special children. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just requests, after the example of our predecessors of happy memory Alexander, Lucius, and Clement, we fortify you, beyond the common protection, with a special privilege. Whatever possessions and goods the aforesaid churches now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, through the grants of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, we confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity by apostolic authority. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The same Castel Aureo with its appurtenances, [Col. 0962D] namely, the high and ancient walls surrounding it, together with houses and chambers joined externally on every side to those same walls; the garden beside that castle with its appurtenances and the upper parts of the crypts; the population outside the gate of the said castle, on the side of Campitelli and the district of St. Angel, as far as the borgo, on both sides of the road; and the fishpond with the tower of Salitula as far as the arch of the Sellaio-makers; and, on the side of the Pine, beside the aforesaid walls, on both sides of the road; the church of St. Lucy with its appurtenances; the church of St. Felix; and the estate called Ordeolus with its appurtenances; the estates called Porcaritia, Caput Caballum, Galeria, Rofanione, Servilianum, and Arcionem—or by whatever other names they are called—with vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, [Col. 0963A] cultivated and uncultivated lands, marshes, hills, valleys, and all else belonging to those estates.

Also, the holding concerning which you made an agreement with the church of St. Celsus, situated in the aforesaid place called Galeria; and the Saracen furnace with its boundaries and all its appurtenances, situated outside the gate of Blessed Peter, about eight miles distant from the city of Rome along the Via Cornelia, within these boundaries: on the first side, the small holdings belonging to the deaconry of St. Angel, as the ditches and watercourses divide them; on the second side, the small holdings belonging to the monastery of St. Andrew the Apostle, of the handmaids of God, as the ditches, watercourses, and boundaries divide them; on the third side, the estate of Vivarolus; on the fourth side, the land of the bishopric of St. Rufina and the estates of Memolus and Priscellus, as is contained in the authentic writings of Gratian, Gregory, Lady Rose, and Imilla, of blessed memory, founders of those churches.

Also, the strips of saltworks which you possess in the greater field, in the *pedica* called Serpentaria, in the old *pedica*, in the *pedica* called Fossatum Maius, and in the *pedica* of Caesarius. The boundaries of the strips which you possess in the *pedica* Serpentaria are: on the first side, the wood and Mount Calvarellus; on the second side, the heir of Benedict de Judice and the church of St. Sylvester; on the third side, your ditch and Carrara; on the fourth side, Greater Carrara. The boundaries of those which you possess in the old *pedica* are: [Col. 0963C] on the first side, a pool; on the second, a ditch; on the third, another ditch; on the fourth, Carrara. The boundaries of another strip which you possess in the same *pedica* are: on the first side, the church of St. Lawrence; on the second, your ditch; on the third, the strip of St. Sylvester; on the fourth, Carrara. The boundaries of those which you possess in the *pedica* of Caesarius are: on the first side, a pool; on the second, the heir of Lotterengus; on the third, Octavian; on the fourth, Carrara.

One meadow situated within the field of Merulus, as Pope John XIX, of blessed memory, gave it by pious devotion to your aforesaid churches; two houses situated at the bath of Miccinus, one held by the sons of Gerard of Conecclo and the other by the heir of John the Jew; three other houses in the same place, one held by the heir of John de Statio and Theodinus, another by the heir of Paul Guido of Rajano, and another by the sons of Paul Pipi; and the crypt, which Romanus, son of Paul Pipi, also holds. [Col. 0963D] In the district of Parione, two houses joined into one; one house situated at Scortecclari, not far from the church of St. Simeon; one half of the water of two mills situated on the River Tiber; the garden Casalino, situated in the district of the Marble Horse, nearly before the church of St. Agatha in the Deaconry; eight plots of vineyard, four on one side of the road and four on the other, situated inside the Pincian Gate beside the city wall; six plots of vineyard lying together in the completed gardens; four and a half plots of vineyard situated in Alban territory, two in the estate called Casa Intronata and two and a half in the estate called Torignanum; one enclosed vineyard in the territory of Ariccia, at the place called [Col. 0964A] Mandre beneath Mount St. Eleutherius; three houses which you possess inside the city of Ostia, joined to the wall of that city, on the right as one enters by the city gate; lands and vineyards situated in the same territory, not far from Stagno and Bucina; four small farmsteads and two crypts, with a court before them and gardens behind them, with their entrances and exits, situated outside the gate of the same city and not far from Ostia, in the place called Calcaria; all the lands which you possess in the estate called Calabriceto, and others in the estate of Ciciliani; and half of the two estates called Mauri and Casale. All these things the aforesaid Lord Gratian, most noble consul and duke of the Romans, as is found in ancient instruments, gave to your often-mentioned churches.

Likewise, two saltwork *pedicae*, one called Petrella and the other Cannuzetti, with ditches, pools, watercourses, and places for making *antippla*, with entrances, exits, and all appurtenances, situated in the field of the saltworks of Ostia, with the following boundaries: on the first side, the bridges and boundary-markers of Tibur; on the second, a wood; on the third, Maselum; and on the fourth, Carrara. These Paul, a most noble man, consul of the Romans and son of Count Viunisi, gave for his soul in the time of Lord Pope Adrian the Younger. As this was confirmed for you by our predecessors of happy memory Alexander, Lucius, and Clement, and is contained in their authentic writing, we confirm it to you in perpetuity by apostolic authority and fortify it by the protection of this present document. [Col. 0964C] We further enact that your aforesaid churches, namely St. Mary and St. Lawrence, shall be subject to no one but the Roman pontiff, and that both those churches and all else which you possess shall remain in the liberty in which they are known to have stood from ancient times until now.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid churches, take away their possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and maintenance of those for whose benefit they were bestowed shall be preserved whole and unimpaired, to be of advantage to them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this text of our [Col. 0964D] constitution, then, after a second and third warning, unless he corrects his offence by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. [Col. 0965A] I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal of the title of St. Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany. I, John Felix, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Susanna. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of St. Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 0965B] I, Goffredus, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, John, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary the New. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Prison of Tullianus, on the fourth Nones of October, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III. [Col. 0965C]

## XCIV. At the request of Bishop Mark, he confirms the liberty, privileges, and possessions of the Church of Venice. *(Fragment.)*  
*(Lateran, 11 November.)*

*[UGHELLI, Sacred Italy, V, 1249, where the reader is referred back to the privilege granted to the Church of Castello by Pope Lucius II; see Patrology, vol. CLXXIX, no. 7. Celestine’s bull was given: “At the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Prison of Tullianus, on the third Ides of November, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.”]*

## XCV. He grants Conrad, bishop of Regensburg, authority to absolve those who, fighting for the Church of Regensburg, committed acts of arson.  
*(Lateran, 12 November.)*

*[RIED, Diplomatic Codex of Regensburg, I, 274.]*

[Col. 0965D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother . . . bishop of Regensburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more numerous are the matters which the usefulness or necessity of subjects requires to be fulfilled by the episcopal office, the more mercifully ought apostolic favor to be present and, where its authority is necessary, to be applied more benignly. As you have represented to us, the Church subject to your governance and care is often attacked through the recklessness of perverse men; and consequently it is necessary that its faithful [Col. 0966A] resist their malice. At their instigation, these faithful frequently incur the guilt of arson. Therefore, for the correction of the wickedness of those whom neither fear nor reverence for the supreme Judge restrains from burdening churches, we have thought fit to grant your brotherhood that, should any of the faithful of your Church, or any of those who resist such men for its protection by your command or that of your ministerials, happen for any reason to incur guilt of arson, you shall freely have authority by this present document to absolve them and impose penance, without any objection or appeal. With regard to the matter on which you thought fit to consult the apostolic oracle—what you should do concerning those who, owing to the war among various princes dwelling in your bishopric, [Col. 0966B] happen for some reason to commit arson—we answer you by these present letters: namely, that you are to exercise ecclesiastical punishment against them until they have made suitable satisfaction and carried out what the canons prescribe.

Given at the Lateran, on the second Ides of November, in the second year of our pontificate.

Lead seal: Celestine, Pope III.

## XCVI. He approves the foundation of the Church of St. Peter at Marchtal.

*[HUGO, Premonstratensian Annals, vol. II, Documents, p. 83.]*

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons MANEGOLD, provost of the Church of St. [Col. 0966C] Peter at Marchtal, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: J. H. P. P. M. [uncertain abbreviation as printed].

Apostolic protection ought to be present for those choosing the religious life, lest an attack of any rash person perhaps recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and under our own protection the aforesaid Church of St. Peter, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we enact that the canonical order which is recognized as instituted in the same [Col. 0966D] place according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall there be observed inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, through the grant of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Mary, situated in the same village, with its parishioners, serfs, and right of patronage, which the noble duke of Swabia freely granted you over one of the prebends of that church; [Col. 0967A] and the estates, courts, houses, orchards, gardens, and woodland called the Church’s Endowment; and the fishing which you have in the River Danube flowing beside that same village; two parts of the tithes which you have in the church of Bilringen, and in Wacchingen, Willer, and Smalstertin; a mill at Zwisalten; the estate with court which you have at Ambra, with the chapel situated there, its vineyards, tithes, and other appurtenances.

Moreover, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you on the produce of lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the feed of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen who are free and discharged from secular life, and retain them without any objection. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave it without the provost’s permission; and let no one dare retain a departing brother without letters of authorization from the community. We likewise forbid that you be compelled to pay to any bishop or other person more for your tithes than their predecessors have reasonably been accustomed to receive during the fifty years preceding the present time.

When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, [Col. 0967C] consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things to you freely, without improper practice or exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever prelate you prefer who enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See; supported by our authority, he shall provide what is requested.

Furthermore, we forbid anyone, within the bounds of your parish, to dare build anew a chapel or oratory without the consent of both the diocesan bishop and yourselves, without prejudice to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We also altogether forbid archbishops, bishops, [Col. 0967D] archdeacons, deans, and all other ecclesiastical or secular persons to impose upon you new and unlawful exactions.

We further decree that the burial-place of that establishment shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Furthermore, by our authority you shall be free to redeem and lawfully release from the hands of laymen the tithes and possessions belonging by right to your churches which are held by laymen, and to restore them to the churches to which they belong.

Upon the death of you, the present provost of that place, or of any of your successors, [Col. 0968A] let no one be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. Moreover, desiring with paternal concern to provide henceforth for your peace and tranquillity, under threat of anathema and by apostolic authority we forbid anyone within the enclosures of your houses or granges to commit robbery or theft, set fire, rashly seize or kill a person, or dare exercise any violence.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away or diminish its possessions, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted by pious liberality for the government and support of those concerned shall be preserved whole and unimpaired, to be of use to them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to act against this text of our constitution, after a second or third warning, etc., etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### XCVII. To the prior and brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem: he confirms the church of Reichartsrode to them.  
*(Lateran, 17 December.)*

[USSERMANN, *Episcopatus Wirzeburgensis*, Documents, p. 54.]

[Col. 0968C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior and brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honorable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought, through the care of our office, to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your just prayers, we confirm to your devotion by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the church of Rictardrode, which you justly and peaceably possess through the donation of Albert of Hollo and the grant of the venerable bishop of Würzburg, your diocesan bishop, as is contained in that bishop’s authentic instrument. Let no person whatsoever therefore infringe this text of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the second year of our pontificate.

### XCVIII. He sends letters to all bishops, abbots, provosts, and the other clergy established throughout the kingdom of Denmark.  
*(Lateran, 23 December.)*

[PERTZ, *Archiv*, VII, 884.]

[Col. 0969A]

### XCIX. To the bishops of Lincoln and Rochester.—Concerning the annulment of the sentence invalidly pronounced by the Archbishop of York against the Bishop of Durham.  
*(Lateran.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 595.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the bishop of Lincoln and [GILBERT], bishop of Rochester, and to his beloved son the abbot of Burgh: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as we ought to preserve unimpaired those measures which are established by our venerable brother-bishops with prudent circumspection and prior deliberation, so it is incumbent upon us, by more complete foresight, to correct measures undertaken with insufficient consideration and restore them to their proper state. Therefore, since our venerable brother Geoffrey, Archbishop of York, had pronounced a sentence of excommunication against our venerable brother Hugh, Bishop of Durham, and certain others, and since, when their messengers came into our presence, the sentence and certain other articles had been fully debated on both sides in our consistory: recognizing that the sentence launched both against him and against the others [Col. 0969C] had been issued without due consideration and fortified by no support of reasonable cause, we publicly declared, on the counsel of our brethren, that it was invalid, annulling it and forbidding it to possess any authority.

Accordingly, so that what we have decreed may be publicly announced through your districts, we command you by apostolic letters to proclaim throughout your churches, by the authority of the Apostolic See, that the said sentence has been annulled, so that the people of the faithful may safely extend the fellowship of brotherly communion both to that bishop himself and to the others unjustly bound together with the bishop, and may by no means on this account withdraw from communion with them.

Given at the Lateran.

### C. To the abbot and convent of Lirum [Lérins?].—Concerning burials.

[Col. 0969D]

You wished to be informed by us how that clause customarily inserted in our privileges concerning “the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken” ought to be understood and explained. But since differing enactments of our predecessors have issued on this point—Leo judging that the said right was sometimes a third part and at other times a half, and Urban III judging it to be a fourth—we give the following answer amid this diversity: as blessed Jerome says, let each province abound in its own judgment, and according to the reasonable custom of the region that right shall, in the varying circumstances of places, be reckoned at approximately a half, a third, or a fourth part.

Given at the Lateran, in the second year.

## YEAR 1193

### CI. Bull for the canonization of St. Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim.  
*(Rome, at St. Peter’s, 8 January.)*

[MABILLON, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, VI, I, 251.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Hildesheim, to his beloved sons the clergy of that city, and to all the faithful established throughout his diocese: greeting and apostolic [Col. 0970B] blessing.

Since the wonderful and glorious Maker and Creator of all things frequently appears in His saints and deigns through them to reveal His works to His faithful, we have judged it fitting, and at the same time honorable to the Almighty, humbly to receive and hear the things which He willed by His grace to show in Bernward, bishop formerly of Hildesheim, of celebrated memory; and moreover to number him in the company of the saints.

Accordingly, having been informed concerning his merits, praiseworthy life, and many miracles through our beloved son Cencius, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina; through our venerable brother Conrad, Archbishop of Mainz; through other [Col. 0970C] bishops; through our beloved son Thideric, abbot of the church of St. Michael at Hildesheim; and through honorable and religious persons of that province; and having more fully learned his illustrious reputation, worthy of commemoration, after diligent deliberation with our brethren we have judged that the aforesaid most reverend man should be numbered in the catalogue of saints; that his venerable body should be raised from the bosom of the earth and placed among the relics of the saints, so that there it may receive from Christ’s faithful the service of due veneration in constant devotion, and that they, through his blessed and God-pleasing intercession, may obtain forgiveness for their sins.

Therefore we command your whole community by apostolic letters that, publicly proclaiming what we have so solemnly established concerning this saint, you shall henceforth take care to honor the same saint with due observances, so that through his propitious intercession the Creator of all may deign mercifully to hear your devout prayers which you offer Him.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CII. He writes to the archbishops and bishops established throughout England that the armies which went to the East did not fulfill expectation because of dissensions. He wishes the princes to be admonished, once discord has been stilled, to bring aid to the Holy Land.  
*(Rome, at St. Peter’s, 11 January.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 597.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0971A] brethren the archbishops and bishops established throughout England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, in order to repel the injury done to the Christian people and wipe out the stain upon the common faith which the filth of pagans perniciously and violently impressed upon it in the capture of the Holy Land, called the Lord’s inheritance; and also in order to restore the holy city and the Lord’s Sepulchre from the defilements of Saracens and other occupiers besides, and by the help of heavenly mercy to take it from their power, the Apostolic See, recognizing its duty, has often sent legates from its side and letters of admonition through diverse parts of the world, and, trusting in divine mercy, has bestowed great indulgences upon those going there: although, as your brotherhood can perceive, very many have resolutely and devoutly girded themselves for these undertakings through its exhortations, and so many of Christ’s faithful have frequently gathered in the lands beyond the sea for this purpose that their multitude seemed to outnumber their assailants by no small margin, and even to prevail in resources [perhaps *animi*, “spirit”] and strength; nevertheless they were unable to make much progress or harm those who contended against them. This was because, as may be understood from the outcome, the efforts and actions of those who had gone to those regions greatly displeased the Lord.

Thus, deservedly because of their other sins—since they trusted not in God but in their own strength, and the fear of God was not before their eyes—their hearts were permitted to be darkened by preconceived pride, so that they did other things entirely unbecoming, provoking against themselves by their perversities the divine judgment. Yet because the Lord is rich in mercies, and although, to curb the obstinacy of evildoers and bend the necks of stiff-necked men, He sometimes lays the hand of discipline upon them as a remedy—oppressing in order to raise up, striking or scourging in order to heal—if we return to Him with due humility, corrected for our sins, and adopt the firm resolve henceforth to observe with more ardent zeal the commandments of the Creator, we can hope without any hesitation that He will assist us more abundantly and favorably [Col. 0971D] and grant us from heaven a complete victory over the enemies of Christ’s name, so that all the hardships we have hitherto endured may be consigned to oblivion, with all who hate Zion driven back and falling in deserved confusion, they who have presumed to defile it with Gentile pollutions.

Those who attentively and diligently examine what threats divine power uttered against the people of Israel when it entered the land mentioned above by promise will have no hesitation in answering why our undertaking begun for God has not attained its hoped-for results. For they were told to abstain from the contagions and pollutions of the inhabitants of that land, and not to consider their vices worthy of imitation, lest these things befall them for their ruin; rather, with firm resolve and every effort of mind and intention, they were to keep the law of the Lord. If they obeyed these admonitions devoutly and humbly, one of them would defeat a thousand, and ten would defeat ten thousand. They later learned this by most certain experience, when a few of them slaughtered a great and almost infinite multitude of their enemies; and, while they devoted themselves to the divine commandments, there was no city or fortification able to avoid their assault or escape their power by any effort or counsel.

But when their children—who, as it is said there, did not know the Lord—rashly began to fall away from observance of what had been laid upon them by legal promulgation, their enemies, forming ranks against them, frequently subjected them to their power. The Israelites in turn subdued those enemies through divine help when, repentant of their offenses and acknowledging their guilt, they humbly turned to God in pious devotion. You may therefore recognize quite unmistakably that, when the fruit of hoped-for victory was taken from the Christian army by arising dissensions, the cause was the frequent [perhaps *frequentius*, “more frequent”] growth of quarrels and hatreds in the army, because “they made flesh their arm, and their hearts departed from the Lord” (Jeremiah 17).

If, therefore, we wish without great labor to obtain in every respect a glorious triumph unto the destruction of our adversaries, let us not lose heart because of the hardships hitherto endured. Rather, seeking the mercy of the Creator in humility and contrition of heart, we shall be able, for their perpetual confusion, to hope for an invincible victory through the accustomed benevolence of heavenly favor. Moved by this consideration, we have enjoined upon all the princes of the world, for the remission of sins, that, for love of God and regard for their own salvation, if anyone has conceived resentment against another for any cause, and has despised a human being, he must forgive for the Creator’s sake; so that no further occasion may be given for mutual discord, which, as you know, has hitherto both deprived us of the fruits of victory and brought the danger of death, with no benefit whatsoever, upon a very great part of the multitude.

With their whole hearts they should endeavor to find counsel among themselves by which, in the meantime, that small remaining portion of the Lord’s land held under Christian power may be kept secure from seizure by the hands of the wicked, defended without fear against the attacks of the impious, and a multitude of the faithful may once again be equipped to go there in due and devout humility and, having wholly conquered and trampled down the fury of its occupiers, liberate the entire land and the Lord’s Sepulchre.

Furthermore, because this gives us and the whole Christian people an overwhelming cause for tears, and because we ought in every way to grieve rather than rejoice while the land where the Lord’s feet stood and the sacraments of our salvation were accomplished is held under Gentile occupation, we utterly forbid tournaments, which were devised as occasions of rejoicing and for training young warriors in prowess. Whoever wishes to exercise himself should go to that land, where both the strength of his soul can be displayed manfully and profitably.

Let them likewise strive to devote themselves to unity and the harmony of peace among themselves, so that no one may wage war against another or dare repel an injury by arms; but rather they should labor together to restore, by diligent effort and work, the minds of those at variance.

But if anyone—though we do not believe it—setting aside the fear of God and despising reverence for us and the Christian faith, should presume in any rashness to act against this, let him know that we have strictly enjoined upon you and the other archbishops and bishops to place under ecclesiastical interdict the lands of those who stubbornly persist in such an undertaking, and, if necessary, to bind their persons with the bond of excommunication, and to ensure that both sentences are inviolably observed. Therefore, commanding you strictly through apostolic writings, we direct that, setting aside all delay and objection, you apply yourselves to promptly fulfilling what we have said and labor throughout your dioceses, without delay or appeal, to carry it into effect.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the third day before the Ides [Col. 0973C] of January, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CIII. He forbids Bishop Berno and the chapter of Hildesheim either themselves rashly to diminish the body of St. Bernward without the authorization of the abbot and brethren of St. Michael, or to permit others to diminish it; nor may they allow the offerings of the faithful to be disturbed.  
*(Lateran, 21 January.)*

[JAFFÉ, *Regesta*, p. 893.]

### CIV. He takes the monastery of St. Michael of Hildesheim under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 27 January.)*

[Ibid.]

### CV. At the request of Bishop O[mer], he confirms certain possessions of the church of Ribe.  
*(Lateran, 30 January.)*

[SHUM, *Hist. af Danmark*, VIII, 698.]

[Col. 0973D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother O., bishop of Ribe: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The equity of law and the established custom of the Church alike require that things reasonably possessed receive the authority of confirmation from this See, which was founded by Jesus Christ Himself upon the firm rock because of the merits of blessed Peter. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your just requests, we confirm to you and to the church itself by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the gifts and grants, made with prudent deliberation by our dearest son in Christ Canute, illustrious king of the Danes, and his predecessors, to the church of Ribe, concerning half of all things pertaining to royal right in the city [Col. 0974A] of Ribe, except Forban, Worck, and forty marks of Sagn; just as that church itself possesses them justly and without dispute, and as they are expressly contained in the authentic documents of the same king and of our venerable brother A., Archbishop of Lund and legate of the Apostolic See.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this text of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CVI. He forbids the successors of Peter, bishop of Roskilde, to alienate Castle Hafn, which is to fall to the church of Roskilde after the death of A[bsalon], Archbishop of Lund.  
*(Lateran, 12 February.)*

[THORKELIN, *Diplomata Arna-Magnæana*, I, 64.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, bishop of Roskilde: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0974C] When what is just and honorable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the care of our office. Therefore, concurring with grateful assent in the just petition of our venerable brother A., Archbishop of Lund and legate of the Apostolic See, by this present document, under threat of anathema, we forbid any bishop who may from time to time be in your church to alienate from your church the castle of Hafn, which will devolve upon your church after the death of that archbishop.

We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this text of our prohibition or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume [Col. 0974D] to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of February, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CVII. Privilege granted to the abbot and monks of Fécamp.  
*(Lateran, 24 February.)*

[*Neustria pia*, 244.]

CELESTINE … to his beloved sons the abbot and monks of Fécamp …

You requested of us that, if anyone should ask us to commit cases known to be in litigation between yourselves and others to persons of Rouen, whom you reasonably regard as suspect, you should by no means be required to consent, since your monastery could thereby suffer no small loss in its rights. Since everyone may in law refuse a judge whom he considers suspect, and wishing to provide for your indemnity in this respect, by the present letters we grant you that, if the aforesaid persons of Rouen are appointed by us judges in any case against you, without any mention having been made of this rescript, you shall not be bound to answer your adversaries before their tribunal.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CVIII. He confirms to Omer, bishop of Ribe, “all revenue of royal right which country-dwellers call *Querset*, while townspeople call it *Skot* and *Quersent*, and half of every royal right which is enrolled to the royal power in the city of Ribe, with these three exceptions: Forban, Strandwerc, and cases involving forty marks, which Sweyn Grathe, king of the Danes, remitted to all the Church’s tenants, both townsmen and country-dwellers.”  
*(Lateran, 25 February.)*

[TERPAGER, *Ripae Cimbriae*, 175.]

[Col. 0975B]

### CIX. He takes the monastery of St. Benedict of Ringsted under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 26 February.)*

[*Daenische Bibliothek*, III, 140.]

[Col. 0975C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANGSGAR, abbot, and the convent of Ringsted, and to all who profess the regular life there, present and future: in perpetual remembrance.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized as befitting religion and honor, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and provide suitable assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously granting your just requests, we receive your monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.
