First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted there according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Accordingly, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by God’s favor, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

The *Schot* of St. Mary from the two parts of Zealand called Susle; the indulgence of those coming to the tomb of St. Canute, together with offerings and alms; the *Schot* of St. Canute in Zealand and Halland; the offering of St. Margaret and of St. Canute the martyr; the freedom of bailiffs and tenant-farmers granted to you by royal authority; and the king’s right over bailiffs and tenant-farmers granted to you by that same king.

Moreover, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you on newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the feed of your animals. You may also receive into your conversion clerics or laymen, free or released from secular life, and retain them without any objection. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, to leave it without the permission of his abbot, unless for the sake of a stricter religious observance; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters of authorization from the community.

Furthermore, we hold valid the ancient liberties, immunities, and reasonable customs granted to your church and observed hitherto, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. We direct that chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks or clerics to be promoted to sacred orders be provided to you by the diocesan bishop without any improper practice. When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice.

Moreover, we decree that the burial-place of the establishment itself shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, [Col. 0976C] let no one be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, everything granted for the government and maintenance of those concerned shall be preserved whole, for their use and benefit, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to act against this text of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offense by due satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe punishment.

But may all who preserve their rights to that same place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that [Col. 0977A] they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church.

I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### CX. To the abbot and convent of Fécamp.—That they may remove from their benefice those who do not personally serve their churches.  
*(Lateran, 27 February.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 615.]

[Col. 0977D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son R., abbot of Fécamp: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more specially the monastery entrusted to your care belongs by right to the Apostolic See, the more kindly ought we to hear the things which you reasonably judge should be requested from us. Moved by this consideration, we have thought fit to grant you by this present document that you may, after canonical warning and without impediment of appeal, remove any vicar of your churches who refuses to serve them in his own person.

Furthermore, we grant to you and your brethren that, if anyone summons one of you before a secular judge concerning any debt, you shall not be obliged to answer, lest your monastery be burdened through such an occasion, as is frequently said to have happened. Let no person whatsoever, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of March, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CXI. He receives the monastery of St. Mary of Ferraria (diocese of Teano) under protection and confirms its goods and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 2 March.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 554.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons NICHOLAS, abbot of St. Mary of Ferraria, [Col. 0978B] and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Those choosing the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either turn them back from their purpose or, which God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously granting your just requests, we receive into the right and property of St. Peter and the holy Roman Church, after the example of our predecessors of blessed memory Lucius and Clement, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing: the aforesaid church of St. Mary of Ferraria, which you built for divine service upon an estate granted to you in pious donation by the noble Richard, formerly count of Sangro; likewise the exchange which you made with our venerable brother Matthew, Archbishop of Capua, and the Church of Capua, from whom you received two ruined churches—namely, the church of St. Martin, in which [Col. 0978C] you have determined to institute the Cistercian order, and St. Lucy’s—with all their estates, as you possess them in the public instrument; and the place where the church of St. Angelo stands, together with that church itself and its estate.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by God’s favor, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

The estates which W., illustrious in memory, king of Sicily, granted you: namely, the *startia* of Camillano, the *startia* of Palmento and the garden of Vallerari; the *startia* of Saint Stephen and of Pantanolli; and the Rivo of Janulo and of the Spring of Stella, and of Saint Peter of Lacusancto; the use of the pastures and of all the woods in the same holding; Vajani; the *startia* of Flasi and of Piedimonte, which Tancred, illustrious king of Sicily, gave you in the holding of Teano; the holding which you possess at Intromonte and in all its parts; and whatever you possess at Vairano; the estate which John the notary granted you beside the river Volturno; and whatever Hugh of Prata granted you; whatever you possess in the territory of Saint Angel, [Col. 0979A] and all the pastures in the land of the same Hugh; and what you possess at Catalasca; the estate of the level wood, which you possess by the gift of Gimundus; the land which the noblewoman Matthia and the aforesaid Hugh granted you on the river Lete, where you have a fulling-mill; the church of Holy Cross with its holding; the rights in churches which you possess at Naples; the benefice which the nobleman John, count of Alife, gave you in that city; and the houses and lands which you possess there; the holding of W. of Latina, which the nobleman Geoffrey of Montefuscolo gave you; the estate which Count W. of Caserta granted you in the holding of Tenescia, which had belonged to John Basso, knight; the mill which Count Roger of Molina granted you at Isernia; and the mill of Pintima, [Col. 0979B] which Malgerius Torellus gave you; and what you possess at Petra, Martiano, and Isernia; the houses, shop, and lands which John Richard gave you at Capua; the houses which Peter of Alife gave you in the same city; and what Sergius granted you at Aversa.

Furthermore, of the produce of your labours, which you cultivate at your own hands or expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, etc. It shall also be lawful for you to receive free clerics or laymen, etc. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, etc. But one departing, etc. And if anyone perhaps, etc.

Moreover, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide henceforth for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from daring rashly to commit theft or robbery, set fire, seize or kill a person, or exercise any violence within the enclosure of your places or [Col. 0979C] granges. Further, by apostolic authority we prohibit the establishment henceforth of any new habitation within half a league near your abbey from which any prejudice may arise to the liberty and peace hitherto preserved for you. But the ordinations of your monks by the diocesan [bishop], etc.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See, etc. If, therefore, anyone in future, etc. But for all preserving their rights to that place, etc., may there be peace, etc. Amen.

[Col. 0979D] **PERFECT MY STEPS IN THY PATHS.** [Saint Peter; Saint Paul.]

Celestine, pope the third.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul and Pam[?]. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cencius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. [Col. 0980A] I, Geoffrey, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, priest-cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, indiction II, in the year 1192 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

## CXII. He receives the monastery of Saint Mary of Esrom under protection and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Lateran, March 5.)*

[THORKELIN, *Diplom. Arna-Magn.*, I, 281.]

[Col. 0980B]

**CELESTINE**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WALBERT, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Esrom, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: for ever.

Those choosing the regular life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions [Col. 0980C] and receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary of Esrom, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of the present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order which is recognized to have been instituted in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through the grant of popes, the largesse of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favour, acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to set forth the following in their own terms:

[Col. 0980D] The place itself where the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its adjacent lands and appurtenances; the cloister itself of Esrom, with its woods, meadows, mills, fisheries, and all its appurtenances; Willingeruth, Hafraholem, Byrgisholm, Sande, Thumathorp, Toteholt, with all their appurtenances; Halese, with everything belonging to it; Stenholt; the houses of Saint Martin; Hiarnethorp; Cracadal; Mothorp in Halland; and Glumstenswigh, with their villages, meadows, woods, and remaining appurtenances; likewise the tithes of the parish called Esbernetorp, [Col. 0981A] which Absalon, archbishop of Lund, gave you and confirmed by an authentic document.

Furthermore, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you from the produce of your labours, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals. It shall also be lawful for you to receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and released from the world, and to retain them without any opposition.

Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from being permitted to leave it without the leave of his abbot; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves without a letter of authorization from the community. Further, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide henceforth for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by [Col. 0981B] apostolic authority anyone from daring to commit theft or robbery, set fire, seize or kill a person, or exercise any violence within the enclosures of your places or granges.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree that, as has been established by our predecessors, no bishop or other person shall compel you to attend synods or secular courts. Nor shall anyone, against your will, presume to come to your houses in order to celebrate ordinations, prepare chrism, hear cases, or summon public assemblies.

We also decree that if the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, after being asked three times at intervals and with fitting humility, should perhaps refuse to bless a substitute [Col. 0981C] abbot, that abbot may bless his own novices and perform the other acts belonging to his office, until the same bishop reconsiders his hardness and does not refuse to bless the abbot who is to be blessed.

Furthermore, if a bishop demands from you anything beyond the obedience due, or the princes of the land demand anything contrary to the liberty of the order granted by our predecessors and ourselves, you shall be free, by apostolic authority, to deny what is demanded, lest on this pretext the aforesaid order, hitherto free, be bound in the snare of human servitude. We add that no bishop may impede the regular election of your abbot or in any way interfere, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian order and the authority of our privileges, in appointing, removing, or deposing [Col. 0981D] the abbot who is in office at the time. If bishops issue any sentence on this account against your churches or persons, we decree that sentence void, as pronounced contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See.

When you cannot have access to your own bishops, if a bishop of whom you have full knowledge happens to pass through your district, you may receive from him, and from neighbouring bishops when the diocesan see is vacant, the blessings of vessels and vestments, the ordination of monks, and the consecration of altars; provided, however, that no prejudice thereby hereafter arises against your own bishops.

[Col. 0982A] We also forbid by apostolic authority anyone to place under interdict or bind with the bond of anathema your neighbours or hired labourers because they have helped you to work on days when you work and others keep holiday; or on any pretext relating to those things granted you by apostolic favour; or your benefactors because, from charity, they have bestowed on you any benefits from their own property or service.

If anyone pronounces a sentence of excommunication or interdict against any member of your household, so long as he remains in your service, on account of the withholding of tithes or of any other matter granted by the Apostolic See to your order, you may absolve them in danger of death. And if their priests, humbly asked, should perhaps refuse or maliciously delay to do this, you may administer to them the ecclesiastical sacraments. It shall also be lawful for you to pronounce, by our authority, the regular sentence against your monks or lay brethren who leave your cloister without their abbot’s permission, should anyone presume to retain them against your will.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose government and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 0982C] person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ our Redeemer, and be subject at the Last Judgment to strict vengeance.

But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve their rights to that place, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of the Church of Albano. [Col. 0982D] I, Octavian. I, John, bishop of the Church of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany. I, Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Guy, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callistus. [Col. 0983A] I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of Saint Mark, of the title of Equitius. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cinthius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Somfridus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, priest-cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia. I, Findantius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Gravous, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 0983B] I, Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Cencius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Lucy in Orthea.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the third day before the Nones of March, indiction XI, in the year 1192 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

## CXIII. To A[bsalon], archbishop of Lund, he declares that the castle of Hafn is to pass to the church of Roskilde after his death.  
*(Lateran, March 20.)*

[THORKELIN, *Dipl. Arna-Magn.*, I, 65.]

[Col. 0983C]

**CELESTINE**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother A., archbishop of Lund, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honourable is requested from us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the care of our office. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, moved by your just prayers, we confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion, and strengthen by the protection of the present writing, the castle of Hafn which W., illustrious in memory, king of Denmark, granted to your brotherhood; which you justly and peacefully possess under his gift, and which our beloved son Cencius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence [Col. 0983D] in Lucina, then legate of the Apostolic See, confirmed to you by the authority which he exercised.

For the greater clarity of the matter, we have thought fit to append below the authentic document of confirmation by that cardinal, whose text is as follows:

Cencius, by the grace of God priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, legate of the Apostolic See, to A., by the same grace archbishop of the Church of Lund, legate of the Apostolic See and primate of Sweden: greeting and the affection of deepest love.

While we exercised the office of legate in Denmark, we learned beyond doubt that W., illustrious in memory, king of Denmark, granted the castle of Hafn to your brotherhood, and that, under the condition imposed, you piously gave it to the church of Roskilde: namely, that you should hold it while you lived, but after your death it should freely devolve upon that church. Having therefore regard to the confirmations of Lord Popes Urban and Clement, and also of the canons of Roskilde under the terms of the aforesaid condition, we confirm to you by the authority which we exercise, and strengthen by the protection of the present writing, your just and undisputed possession of it with all its appurtenances.

[Col. 0984A] Namely, the village of Hafn; the estate of Ottherslef with all its appurtenances, namely Saereslef, Solbiarga, Walese, Wikislef, one *mansus* at Walbi, [Col. 0984B] Brunshoga, S . . brethorp, the estate of Grafnatofte, Mirthoga, Barsvertha, and Wigarum with all their appurtenances; the estates of Husfrekop and Averahi; and the estates of Burgabi and Martharum with all their appurtenances.

Moreover, we confirm by the present document to your beloved person the whole share of the goods which your castellan Nicholas, of good memory, acquired either in Falster or in Zealand, according to the terms of the agreement made between you, whether that share came to you in the partition effected before his death with his heirs. In addition, we entrust to your oversight and governance the churches of Hafn, Brunshoga, and Amabe, which you had previously assigned to the castle, so that, all claim ceasing, you may have free power to dispose of them; [Col. 0984C] and after your death both the churches and all the aforesaid possessions shall freely return to the church of Roskilde and its bishop without any habitation whatsoever.

Moreover, because, as we have learned, both the advantage of the people of Zealand and the affairs of the kingdom often require your presence in Zealand, we confirm to you by authority of the present writing that whoever is canonically appointed bishop in the bishopric of Zealand shall, whenever you wish to be present, share a common table with you under due honour and reverence as with the head of the household. He himself shall employ his own counsel and discretion in conducting his affairs; and, as a son obedient in all things to his father, he shall not presume to evade relieving your labours in Scania whenever you wish and necessity requires.

[Col. 0984D] Since we have granted these things to your person for just reasons, we intend that they shall not extend beyond your person. After your death, whoever is archbishop in Denmark at the time shall, by reason of this our confirmation, have no claim in the aforesaid matters over the bishop of Zealand or his bishopric.

Therefore let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly act contrary to it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0985A] Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CXIV. He orders the rights of the bishop of Lucca and of the Camaldolese prior concerning the church of Saint Jucunda to be preserved.  
*(Lateran, March 30.)*

[MITTARELLI, *Annal. Camaldul.*, IV, App., p. 184.]

**CELESTINE**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother . . bishop, and to his beloved sons, the chapter of Lucca and the Camaldolese prior: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The duty of the care entrusted to us urges us so to ensure that the rights of some persons are preserved whole that through them no unjust condition may be covertly imposed upon others. We therefore make known [Col. 0985B] to you that it was not our intention that, when the religious order was changed in the church of Saint Jucunda, the Church of Lucca should suffer any diminution or injury of its right or honour.

Accordingly, we prohibit and strictly forbid you, son prior, or brethren of your profession, or your successors, in any way to presume to take away, lessen, or disturb the honour and right which belong to the bishop and canons of Lucca in the aforesaid church. Rather, you should always preserve these for them peaceably, in their full integrity and with fraternal charity.

And lest, on such an occasion, any discord should hereafter arise among you, or—God forbid—the Church of Lucca should ever suffer any diminution of its right at the hands of you brethren of the Camaldolese order or your successors, we will and decree, establish by the present document, and firmly ordain to be observed for ever, that you—the bishop and canons of Lucca, or your successors—shall peaceably obtain, without any molestation from the aforesaid brethren or anyone else, and henceforth always hold undisturbed, the due right, honour, and custom which you have hitherto had in that monastery and its parish, in their proper integrity.

[Col. 0985C] But we decree that it shall be lawful to no one, etc., [to contravene] our constitution, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CXV. Bull for the monastery of Fécamp.—He forbids churches subject to the monastery of Fécamp to be placed under interdict.  
*(Lateran, April 1.)*

[MARTEN, *Anecdot.*, I, 652.]

[Col. 0985D]

**CELESTINE**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses the churches of the monastery of Fécamp are situated: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the monastery of Fécamp belongs especially to the jurisdiction of Saint Peter, it ought neither to be doubtful nor uncertain to you that injuries done to the brethren serving the Lord there are regarded as especially redounding upon the Roman Church. Therefore, by [Col. 0986A] apostolic authority, we strictly command all of you not to place under interdict, without a manifest and reasonable cause, the churches of the aforesaid brethren that are subject to you by diocesan law; nor, on account of one church from which some offence may perhaps at times arise, to burden by any sentence the others in the same diocese—as we have learned has hitherto been done by some of you.

Furthermore, if a parishioner of any of your churches must be struck by canonical discipline, the whole parish shall by no means be deprived of the celebration of divine worship because of the fault of one person, unless it is the lord of the place who has sinned or has the support of others in his fault. Nor shall anyone dare to pronounce against the monks of that church a sentence of excommunication [Col. 0986B] or interdict contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See. Know that if any one of you presumes to act contrary to the terms of this prohibition, by God’s authority we shall by no means leave his deed unpunished, and what has been perpetrated to the injury of the aforesaid brethren shall have no force.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CXVI. He confirms the substitution of Premonstratensians for the monks of Saint Vincent at Wrocław.  
*(Lateran, April 7.)*

[HUGO, *Annales Praemonst.*, vol. II, proofs, p. 292.]

[Col. 0986C]

**CELESTINE**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and canons of the monastery of Saint Vincent: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned from the letters of our venerable brethren the archbishop of Cologne and Syroslaus, bishop of Wrocław, your diocesan, and many others, that monks of the Black Order had been established in your monastery; but because those monks, by living badly, squandered the goods of the monastery and, though repeatedly asked, did not take care to correct their own transgression, it was feared that the same place, once renowned, would through their negligence suffer irreparable loss and almost fall into utter poverty. Therefore, with the assent of the noblemen Duke Boleslaus and Counts Peter, Wlodimir, [Col. 0986D] Dimili, and Leonard, patrons of this place, who are greatly grieved at its ruin, you have, by provident deliberation, established men of the Premonstratensian order in this monastery.

Believing, therefore, that this is a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, and moved by both your prayers and those of the aforesaid nobles, we confirm by apostolic authority your aforesaid arrangement, as reasonably made by you, and strengthen it by the protection of the present writing. Therefore let no person infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly, etc., act contrary to it.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CXVII. Bull confirming goods granted to the monastery of Saint Vincent at Wrocław.  
*(Lateran, April 8.)*

[Ibid., p. 691.]

[Col. 0987A]

**CELESTINE**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CYPRIAN, abbot of Saint Vincent at Wrocław, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in the Lord: in perpetual remembrance.

Those choosing the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions [Col. 0987B] and receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Vincent, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of the present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is recognized to have been instituted in that place according to God, the Rule of Saint Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through the grant of popes, the largesse of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favour, acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to set forth the following in their own terms:

[Col. 0987C] The place itself where the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Martin at Wrocław; the chapel at Legnica, with its villages and revenues; the market established for eight days on the feast of Saint Vincent; the tavern at the end of the bridge; the market at Kostenbluts; the tavern at Polonica, with the villages of Grabssin, Socolnice, Chenesce, and Sobasisce, which Duke Wladislaus gave you in exchange for half of Trebnica; Wirbrice, Odram, Crescenicam, and Olava, which Count Peter gave; Goreck, which Beronis gave; Pacostaus gave the village of Tasson; Countess Ultonissa gave [Col. 0987D] another village; Sandironius [gave] Sueccino; Jordan, another; Christon near Legnica, Audine, Battoma, Coleson, Divigor, Vejovo; Vitoslaus, Zaseph; Andrew, Laurentry; Sulislagus, Polsnicam; Praga, Saloriam; Pros gave the village of Nazarenove; Gustis gave Rattibor; Ragobina gave Plumascu; Dobeslaus gave [a gift not specified]; Albertus, Vidaon; Duke Wladislaus gave Sevarios with all his progeny, and their villages Mevinec, Golissa, Suanis, Suilgut, Susem, Uronice, and Ares. Robert, bishop of Wrocław, conveyed to the same monastery the chapel of Saint Michael, built beside the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary, with all its appurtenances. Duke Mezories gave the market at Chenese and freedom from tavern-dues to the market and its people.

Furthermore, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you from the produce of your labours.

[Col. 0988A] Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole, for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose government, support, and freedom they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the Last Judgment to divine vengeance.

[Col. 0988B] But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve their rights to that place, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, indiction XI, in the year 119[2?] from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine.

## CXVIII. He confirms the privileges of the citizens of Pisa established by Guy, former king of Jerusalem, and his wife Sibylla, King Richard of England, and Conrad, former marquis of Montferrat.  
*(Lateran, April 8.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 417.]

[Col. 0988C]

**CELESTINE**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the citizens of Pisa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The solicitude of the Apostolic See is exercised with more kindly care toward those whose faith and devotion it has learned through more certain experience, and whose zeal it knows to serve many benefits. Moved therefore by this consideration, and no less by your prayers, we have judged that the liberties, immunities, and other things which our beloved son, the nobleman G., formerly king of Jerusalem, together with his wife Sibylla, granted and confirmed by the protection of his writing to you in consideration of your manifold zeal and labour for that kingdom, [Col. 0988D] and which our dearest son in Christ Richard, illustrious king of England, and C., of good memory, formerly marquis of Montferrat, held ratified and valid—as these things were advisedly and prudently done by them and are fully contained in the documents made on this matter—should be strengthened by apostolic authority and secured by the protection of the present writing.

Therefore let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our protection or rashly act contrary to it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles [Col. 0989A] Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CXIX. He receives the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, April 16.)*

[PÉRARD, *Recueil*, 267.]

**CELESTINE**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benignus, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for ever.

Whenever what is recognized as befitting religion and uprightness is requested from us, it is fitting that we grant it with willing [Col. 0989B] heart and render suitable aid to the petitioners’ wishes. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Benignus, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of the present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order which is recognized to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through the grant of popes, [Col. 0989C] the largesse of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favour, acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to set forth the following in their own terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is built, with all its appurtenances. In the diocese of Langres, the cell of Saint Amator, with the church of Saint Ferreolus and its precincts, both the churches and the other things belonging to it; the cell of Montigny; the cell of Nogent with the chapel of the same castle; the cell of Saint Mary at Saxon’s Spring; the cell of Saint Stephen, with the chapel of the same castle at Wangion River, [Col. 0989D] with everything belonging to them; the cell of Grancey; the place of Clement’s Meadow, called Morey, in which the converts reside. And we command that those same converts be perpetually subject to the church of Dijon, and that they may not, through anyone’s contrivance, withdraw themselves from subjection to you or to the church of Dijon.

By apostolic authority we confirm the half-share of the mint, decreeing that without the abbot’s permission it shall neither be reduced nor increased, nor transferred elsewhere; and also your share of the toll, establishing that henceforth no person at all may harass the same monastery concerning these matters, or thereby inflict upon it any annoyance or diminution. The estate of Dianetum with its appurtenances; the estate of Casnedum, likewise Casnetum, Ispanniacum, Marcenniacum, Norgias, Veresas, Sariacum [Col. 0990A] and its tithe, Longovicum, Asiriacum, Plumberias, Prunedum, Escheriacum, Flaceiacum, Magnum Montem, Vinarias, and Sauriacum in the forest, with their tithes.

In the diocese of Toul, the cell of Bertiniaca Court; the cell of Solini Mount, with the churches, estates, lands, and everything belonging to them. In the diocese of Autun, the cell of Belna, with the churches of Viliacum and Caslegium, and of Pratum Ferreoli, with all their appurtenances; the cell of Sarmatia; the cell of Bertaud’s Court; the cell of Arnetum with everything belonging to the same. In the archdiocese of Besançon, the cell of Saint Marcellus; the cell in the estate of Anson; the cell of Sarcophagis; the cell of Logia Novella; the church of Torpa near Salins; the cells of Saint Peter and Saint Michael; [Col. 0990B] the chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene, and everything belonging to it. In the diocese of Chalon, the cell of Saint Mary, the cell of Paluel, with everything belonging to them. In the diocese of Valence, the cell of Saint Genesius of Mount Madrianus with its appurtenances, the church of Vuilpileriis, and those of Cornaz and Glum. In the diocese of Bayeux, the cell of Saint Vigorus, with its appurtenances. In the diocese of Sens, the cell of Saint Benignus at Vulnon, with all its appurtenances; the cell of Eschino, with all its appurtenances; the cell of Ruth, with those things which belong to it; the chapel of Iles, with the tithes and lands granted there. In the diocese of Geneva, the church of Villare with all its appurtenances. In the diocese of Lausanne, the cell of Saint [Col. 0990C] Mary Magdalene of Barlay, with the churches and lands granted there; the church of Saint Philibert and Saint John the Baptist; the church of Longovicum; the church of Sareium; the church of Asiriacum; the church of Fainaium; the church of Saint John at Laudon; the church of Vivariis; the church of Villare; the church of Plumbariae; the church of Prunedum; the church of Missiniacum; the church of Spaniacum; the church of Casnedum; the church of Marcenniacum; the church of Norgiis; the church of Varesiis; the church of Escheriacum; the church of Saint Apollinaris; the church of Orgeolum; the church of Saint Germanus of Lariacum; the church of Hulmetum; and the church of Ruz, in which religious women reside. And we forbid those religious women ever rashly to withdraw themselves [Col. 0990D] from your subjection.

We also confirm by apostolic authority, as is contained in his authentic charter, the hospital-house assigned for the reception of the poor, which Dominic surnamed the Rich, with the consent of his brother Ewrard, granted to your church for perpetual possession, and which M., bishop of Langres of good memory, confirmed; forbidding that, by the craft of any faction, that same house be withdrawn from your subjection. We likewise confirm to you twenty-five pounds of Dijon currency, which Hugh, duke of Burgundy of illustrious memory, and fifteen pounds which his son Odo, duke of Burgundy, granted you to receive annually from the toll of Dijon.

[Col. 0991A] Certainly, from your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals, let no one at all presume to demand or extort tithes from you. We also grant that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated or under interdict, while the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remain safeguarded. Moreover, in the parish churches which you hold, you may choose clerics and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they are answerable to the bishop concerning the care of the people, but to you concerning temporal matters.

Furthermore, you may receive into conversion clerics or laymen who are free and absolved, fleeing from the secular world, and retain them in your monastery without any objection. We further forbid any of your brethren, after having made profession in your house, to leave that house without the permission of his abbot, except for the sake of a stricter religious observance; and no one may dare retain one who departs without the security of your common letters. Moreover, by the present decree we decree that the liberties, immunities, and ancient reasonable customs of your monastery shall remain whole and unimpaired. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any trick of subreption or by violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, [Col. 0991C] in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, shall judge ought to be elected.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be kept whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly attempting rashly to act against this document of our constitution, after a second or third warning, does not correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. [Col. 0991D] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. [Col. 0992A] I, . . . . . ., cardinal priest of Saints Peter and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Tusculum. I, Romanus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saint Mark, of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Goffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia. I, Fidantius, of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. [Col. 0992B] I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter . . ., bishop of Saint Rufina. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

[Col. 0992C] Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1193 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

## CXX. Privilege for the Church of Genoa (Lateran, 23 April)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 619.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons OGERIUS, provost, OTHO, archdeacon, and the canons of Genoa, present and future, canonically appointed, forever.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that effect be granted to just petitioners, especially when the piety assists the petitioners’ wishes and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Genoa, in which you are devoted to divine service, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Alexander, Urban, and Gregory; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and undiminished for you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify these by their proper names:

Namely, the church of Saint Lawrence at Acre with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary Magdalene with its appurtenances; the church of Saint James of Galignano with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Quic. with its appurtenances; the church of Veguli and the church of Saint Bartholomew of Stallano with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Antoninus of Auripalatio with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Saviour of Sarzano with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Sesto, with the tithes and possessions of the same place; the grants of Gibellet and other places which Bertrand, count of Saint-Gilles, [Col. 0993B] reasonably made to your Church, as is recorded in his charter, and which you lawfully possess.

Furthermore, we decree to be valid and command to retain force the grant which Syrus, archbishop of Genoa of good memory, made to you concerning the tithes and tithe-lands of Genoese citizens, inasmuch as it was reasonably made and is contained in the authentic charter of that archbishop. We hold valid, and by apostolic authority confirm to you and your successors, the honourable and reasonable customs which until now you have had with respect to offerings of the living, candles, and other offerings for the dead whose funerals you are invited to attend; likewise the ancient and reasonable custom which you have in receiving the ancient offerings of the Church, or in other revenues or processions of that Church itself. Furthermore, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Lucius of blessed memory, we decree that you may celebrate a Mass for the dead on the day following their burial in the church in which they have been buried, provided that you yourselves did not celebrate during the funerals because you were detained by some impediment. We also decree that, when the archbishop is present but cannot celebrate Mass because of some impediment, you too may freely celebrate; and that the same archbishop may pronounce sentence against none of the canons without the counsel of the others, and, if he does pronounce it, it shall have no force. We decree that this statute, hitherto observed among you, shall remain firm and inviolate. [Col. 0993D]

We further grant and confirm by apostolic authority that the arrangement prudently made, with the assent and will of Hugh, archbishop of Genoa of good memory, concerning the number of clerics to be received in your Church shall remain unshaken and stable—unless, perhaps, the resources of the Church should increase to such an extent that the number of canons can and ought rightly also to be increased. We grant that the arrangement made among you, providing that your chapter shall have authority canonically to punish a brother who has wickedly separated himself from the community of the chapter in managing the Church’s interests, shall remain in force. Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority the sentence known to have been reasonably pronounced on your behalf concerning the church of Saint Bartholomew, [Col. 0994A] regarding the legacy of William Gata, by judges delegated from the Apostolic See, as it is contained in the authentic charter. We also deem valid and strengthen by this present privilege the composition made between your Church and the abbot of Saint Syrus concerning the place of benediction and the manner of obedience, insofar as it was made and accepted on both sides without impropriety and is contained in a public document.

We confirm by authority of the Apostolic See the sentence canonically pronounced by the abbot of Saint Andrew of Sesto, by apostolic delegation, between you and Brother Justus. We also grant that the provost of your Church, with the counsel of his archbishop, may bind with the bond of anathema those who withhold tithes from that Church or presume to take away its property. When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. By apostolic authority we also forbid anyone to presume to pronounce against you or your Church a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without an evident and reasonable cause.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be kept whole for the benefit of those for whose [Col. 0994C] governance and support they were granted, serving them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical right of the diocesan bishop, and the due reverence owed to the archbishop of Genoa. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to act against this document of our constitution, after a second or third warning, and does not correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. [Col. 0994D] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Mel[ior], cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. [Col. 0995A] I, Jordan, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Tusculum. I, John Fel[ix], of the title of Saint . . . . I, Romanus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cinthius, cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Fidantius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Grat[ian], cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 0995B] I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orfea.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1193 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

## CXXI. To Meinhard, bishop of the Livonian people, he congratulates him on the progress of the preaching he has begun, etc. (Lateran, 27 April)

[*Mittheilungen aus dem Gebiete der Geschichte Liv-, Esth- und Kurlands*, vol. III, p. 323.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MEINHARD, bishop of the Livonian people: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having heard the proclamations of praise reported concerning your deeds, and having learned from those coming from there of the progress of your preaching begun there, we render abundant acts of thanksgiving to the Creator, who deigned both to inspire in you such a will and, out of the multitude of His mercies, to grant it a fitting outcome. For since He Himself says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), whatever good has been begun or accomplished by a human being must without doubt be attributed to Him.

Although we have been taught by the apostolic trumpet that willing is within our reach, yet that we cannot accomplish or attain anything unless He both precedes it, insofar as the work requires, by His grace and brings it to completion by that same grace; without this, human striving is consumed in vain and useless labour and utterly comes to nothing. Yet because you recognize the fruits of your teaching begun, in that with much sweat and labour you have offered for tasting to those ignorant of the Lord’s law the heavenly bread: although the embrace of Rachel, in which you are refreshed in the cloister, may in some measure draw you back, nevertheless do not shrink at all from the undertaken labours of Leah, who by divine grace proves more fruitful in offspring; rather embrace them all the more and more confidently, because from them a more abundant fruit arises and they serve usefulness to the greatest degree.

For it is expedient both for the unbelievers, who need heavenly teaching, that you set before them the way of light and salvation; and for those newly converted, that you continually break for them the bread of sustenance and strengthening toward what is better, lest—God forbid—if your care in this matter should cease, they fail on the path they have begun because their daily provision does not abound, and thus the sweat of the labour begun be shown, through the ensuing failure, to have been shed uselessly. [Col. 0996A] Therefore persist, venerable brother, both in person and through others whom you judge should be joined to you for their life, merit, and teaching; and strive with every effort that, through your ministry, the people serving the Creator may increase both in number and in merit, by the words of teaching and examples of deeds.

For we, with the counsel of our brethren, grant you by the authority of this present letter full power to associate with yourself those whom you consider necessary and recognize as suited to the ministries. And so that you may carry this out with a more secure conscience, and may know that the office of preaching has been imposed upon you by us, as also upon those whom you judge should be associated with you, we bestow upon you our paternal blessing for the performance of this work. Moreover, because many from various orders have hitherto come, and perhaps will come in the future, to this pious office at your urging or through their own devotion, we grant you free authority, by apostolic authority, to dispense with them concerning food, drink, and even clothing, and to assign them the office of preaching. It will therefore be yours to conduct yourself in these matters in such a way that the hoped-for benefit of Christ’s teaching may through your care accrue more abundantly to those in need, and that through so pious a zeal, together with your brethren who continually undertake this kind of labour, you may be able more fully to obtain the reward of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0996C] Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, 1193.

## CXXII. He grants John, dean, and the chapter of Rouen that, “when a general interdict of the land is in force, they may celebrate the offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.” (Lateran, 11 May)

[CHERUEL, *History of Rouen*, vol. I, p. 256.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, dean, and the chapter of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since it is fitting that human affection should be continually occupied with the praises of the Creator, it does not seem inappropriate if, on occasion, something is relaxed from the severity of ecclesiastical discipline, so that the proclamations of divine praise need not be wholly silenced. For although, especially on account of the offences of certain persons, solemn celebrations have been prohibited and sentences pronounced against their unrestrained conduct, such sentences may nevertheless be mitigated in the case of those who are not participants in the guilt, who abhor the wicked persons against whom the Church takes action, and who, as far as they can, avoid communion with them.

Moved, therefore, by this consideration and likewise inclined by your prayers, we have thought fit to grant you by this present document that, when there is a general interdict of the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued [Col. 0997A] voice. You may also commit to burial in the cemetery of your church, without the solemnity of an office, but with holy water and a cross and prayers offered in a humble voice, your fellow canons and clerics who, fortified in the meantime with the ecclesiastical sacraments, are called from this life.

Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this document of our indulgence or, with rash audacity, act against it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the third year of our pontificate.

## CXXIII. He receives the Church of Blessed Peter of Guastalla under his protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Lateran, 15 May)

[AFFO, *History of Guastalla*, I, 351.]

[Col. 0997B]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GIBERT, archpriest of the church of blessed Peter situated in the district of Varistalla, and to its brethren, present and future, canonically appointed, forever.

Since without the worship of true religion neither the unity of charity can endure nor fitting service be maintained, it is appropriate to apostolic authority to love religious persons and to foster with the protection of the Apostolic See places which exist by the power of blessed Peter and are known especially to belong to the Roman Church. [Col. 0997C] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of that prince of the apostles and of ourselves the aforesaid church of blessed Peter, situated in the district of Varistalla. It is known to belong by right to the Roman Church; it was raised from a chapel to a parish church by our predecessor Pope Gregory V of happy memory; and it has been strengthened by the privileges of his successors, the Roman pontiffs Paschal, Innocent, Eugenius, Adrian, Alexander, and Gregory of holy memory. We strengthen it by the privilege of this present document, decreeing that whatever possessions, goods, or tithes that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant and liberality of kings, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by God’s favour, shall remain firm and undiminished for you and your successors.

We also confirm to you by apostolic authority the tithing rights of the lands of your entire estate, whether they are now cultivated or shall later be cultivated, and likewise the lands reasonably granted to your church by public charters by the abbots of Saint Sixtus of Piacenza, just as you are known now to hold them peacefully. Furthermore, we have likewise thought fit to confirm by apostolic authority to your church, just as you have hitherto held and now reasonably possess them, public penances, matrimonial cases, excommunications of offenders, the institution, removal, and building of churches, and every other spiritual matter throughout your whole parish, except those which belong exclusively to the episcopal office. [Col. 0998A] We grant you free permission to receive chrism, holy oil, church consecrations, and clerical ordinations from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. Furthermore, we decree that no one may presume to build a church within the bounds of your parish, unless it is to be subject to you, without your permission. We also decree that the chapels of Saint Bartholomew, Saint George, Saint Martin, and Saint James, belonging to the right of your church and secured to you by our aforesaid predecessors, shall remain perpetually subject to you.

[Col. 0998B] We therefore decree that no archbishop, bishop, abbot, duke, marquis, captain, judge, castaldus, or any other person whatsoever may disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, serving them in every way, while the authority of the Apostolic See remains reserved to all. As a token of this liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay three bezants each year to us and our successors. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to act against this document of our constitution, after a second or third warning, and does not correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power or honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. [Col. 0998C] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. [Col. 0998D] I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Roland, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint E . . . . I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Tusculum. I, John Felix, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Romanus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. [Col. 0999A] I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary, of the title of Callistus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Goffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Germanus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary Major. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. [Col. 0999B] I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary Major. I, Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Horibea.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the Ides of May, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1193 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Celestine III.

## CXXIV. He receives the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Rumon of Tavistock under his protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Lateran, 29 May)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 998.]

[Col. 0999C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HERBERT, abbot of Tavistock, and his successors regularly appointed forever.

The authority of the Apostolic See entrusted to us urges us to give the protection of guardianship to places and persons which duly seek its aid with devotion. For just as no effect ought to be granted to those who seek unjust things, so the petition of those desiring what is lawful and just should not be delayed. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Herbert, we graciously assent to your just petitions and decree that the monastery of Tavistock, dedicated in honour of blessed Mary and Saint Rumon the confessor, which belongs by right to the most holy Roman [Col. 0999D] Church, shall remain solely under its protection and ownership; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods, ecclesiastical as well as secular, that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by God’s favour, shall remain firm and undiminished for you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify these by their proper names:

The church of Blessed Mary and Saint Rumon the confessor at Tavistock, in which the abbey seat is located, with the same town, the market of that town, its chapels, and all other appurtenances; Middleton, and the church of Saint Constantine the confessor built in that town, with all its appurtenances; Hatherleigh, with the church of Saint John the Baptist founded in that town and all its appurtenances; Boryngton, with the church of the Holy Trinity situated in that town; Lega and Abbedysham, with the church of Saint Helen built there; Werdegete, Ordleg, Auri, Tornebury, Ruaburga, and one house in the city of Exeter; Devenebury and the church of Blessed Mary founded there; Wella, Daggecumba, Plymstok, Raddon, Hundetorre, Odatrew, Savyok, and the church of Blessed Mary founded there; Anton, with the churches founded there and their appurtenances; Rame, Tregrenon, Penhangar, Talcar, Wulrynton, with the mother church of Saint Paternus, the chapels of the same [Col. 1000B] town, and all things belonging to it; Oskereville; Pourton, with all liberties and free customs reasonably conferred upon you.

Moreover, within the Isles of Scilly: the island of Saint Nicholas, the island of Saint Sampson, the island of Saint Elidius, the island of Saint Theona the virgin, and the island called Hutho, with their appurtenances; and all churches and oratories built throughout the Isles of Scilly, with their tithes, offerings, and other appurtenances; two *bescatae* of land on the island of Aganas, and three *bescatae* of land on the island of Ennox. Also the church of Saint Michael of Rocta, with its lands and revenues; the church of Lamberton, with all its appurtenances, granted in free and perpetual alms to you and your monastery by W. Giffard, lord of the land; confirmed by B., bishop of Exeter of good memory; and assigned from you, with the assent of J., formerly bishop of Exeter, on condition that three poor persons be fed daily and other works of piety performed. The church of Saint Peter of Montocranihton, with the land of Nordecumba and its other appurtenances.

Upon the death of you, Herbert, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any trick of subreption or by violence, except the one whom the brethren, by common counsel or the sounder part of the counsel, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, shall decide, without anyone’s objection, ought to be elected abbot. We also decree that the custody of your house and the administration of your goods and possessions shall remain in your hands until provision has been made for your church. [Col. 1000D] We also decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated or under interdict, while the canonical right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remains safeguarded. We also grant that, when your churches are vacant, you may apply them to the use of hospitality, which is to be continually observed in your house, by choosing suitable chaplains for them. When presented to the diocesan bishop, these chaplains shall be answerable to him concerning spiritual matters and to you concerning temporal matters; provided that the bishop shall have no power whatsoever, without reasonable cause, to reject those presented to him.

[Col. 1001A] Certainly, from your newly cultivated lands and from those things which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from your animals, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you; rather, let them be reserved for you and applied to the uses of hospitality.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever, not even a bishop, rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to be of use in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. But if at any time any writing or privilege contrary to this liberty granted by us to you and your monastery, and confirmed by the authority of the present privilege, should come to light, it shall in no way prejudice that liberty. Moreover, as a token of this liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay annually to us and to our successors three gold pieces for the monastery of the Blessed Mary and of the aforesaid confessor Saint Rumon.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should attempt rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to stern vengeance at the last judgment.

But let all who preserve the just rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good conduct, and hereafter may find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June [29 May], in the year 1193 from the Incarnation of the Lord’s Nativity, in the third year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Celestine III.

## CXXV. He receives the convent of Sixena under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 3 June.)*

[BOSIO, *Dell’istoria della sacra milit. di Giov.*, I, 388.]

[Col. 1001D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, the prioress and sisters of Sixena, present and future, professing the regular life: perpetual greeting.

The Apostolic See ought to extend its protection to prudent virgins who, under the habit of religion, with their lamps lit, continually prepare themselves to go forth to meet the Bridegroom, lest an assault of any rash person either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their sacred religious life. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the monastery in which you are devoted to the service of God, and we fortify it by the privilege of the present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by God’s favour, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The estate, the new *praesinena*, *sena* [the reading is uncertain], [lacuna] of newly cleared land which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense; and from the increase of your animals, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you. It shall also be lawful for you to receive into your religious community free and unbound persons fleeing from the world, and to retain them without any objection. Furthermore, we prohibit any one of your sisters, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving it without the prioress’s permission, except for the purpose of embracing a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who departs without a guarantee in letters of the common community.

When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, it shall be lawful for you, with the doors closed, excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells not rung, and the voice subdued, to celebrate the divine offices. Furthermore, by Apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from pronouncing against you or the monastery a sentence of excommunication or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause. Moreover, we confirm by Apostolic authority the regulations reasonably made in that monastery, with the assent of our most dear daughter Sancia, illustrious queen of Aragon, by our venerable brother the bishop of Huesca and our beloved son the master of the Hospital of Amposta, together with other religious men.

Upon the death of you, who are now prioress of that place, or of any woman who succeeds you, no person shall be set over the house through any device of fraud or violence, except one whom the sisters by common consent, or the greater and sounder part of the sisters’ counsel, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, determine ought to be elected.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose support they were granted, to be of use in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to the master of the Hospital of Amposta.
