If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should attempt rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless such a person corrects his offence by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of power, honours, and dignity; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to stern vengeance at the last judgment. But let all who preserve that place’s rights have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good conduct and may find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia. [Col. 1003B] I, Peter, bishop of Porto. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana. I, John, bishop of Tuscania and Viterbo, cardinal priest of Saint Clement. I, Romanus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callistus. [Col. 1003C] I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saint Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Bran., cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. [Col. 1003D] I, Nicholas, deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, through the hands of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the third day before the Nones of June [3 June], in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1193 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Celestine III.

## CXXVI. He receives the monastery of Mount Saint Peter (Heisterbach) under protection and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(Lateran, 10 June.)*

[LACOMBLET, *Urk. fur die Gesch.*, vol. I, p. 374.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [Col. 1004A] to his beloved sons HERMANN, abbot of the monastery of Mount Saint Peter, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

It is fitting that apostolic protection should be present for those choosing the religious life, lest an assault of any rash person either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their sacred religious life. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God and Virgin, on Mount Saint Peter, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of the present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institutions of the Cistercian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grants of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s help, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself on which your monastery stands, with all its appurtenances; the grange called Burge, with all its appurtenances; the lands, woods, and whatever you possess in the territory of Megdenheim; the vineyards, houses, and fields which you possess at Bunne, Zudendorp, and Dudensdorp. We also ratify and confirm the annual payments from your tithes granted to you by your bishops with the common and voluntary assent of the archdeacons and parish priests of that time. We confirm to you as free the aforesaid possessions, with all their appurtenances, which you possess in woodland, open country, meadows and pastures, waters and watercourses, and with all other liberties belonging to them.

Indeed, from the produce of your labour which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, gardens, shrub-grounds, vineyards, enclosures, and fisheries, or from the increase of your animals, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you. It shall also be lawful for you to receive as converts clerics or laymen who are free and unbound and flee from the world, and to retain them without any objection. Furthermore, we prohibit any one of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving that place without his abbot’s permission; and no one shall dare retain one who departs without a guarantee in letters of the common community. Should anyone nevertheless presume to retain him, it shall be lawful for you to pronounce the regular sentence against such persons, whether monks or lay brothers.

We strictly forbid anyone to grant personally, or alienate in any other manner, lands or any benefice bestowed upon your church, without the consent of the entire chapter or of its greater and sounder part. If any donations or alienations are made otherwise than as stated, we decree them void. We further prohibit any monk or lay brother bound by profession to your house, without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, from standing surety for anyone or borrowing money from anyone beyond the amount established by the prudent determination of your chapter, unless for a manifest advantage to your house. If he presumes to do so, the convent shall not be bound in any way to answer for those matters.

Furthermore, it shall be lawful for you, in your own cases, whether involving a civil or criminal question, to employ the testimony of your brethren, lest through lack of witnesses your right should fail in any respect. Moreover, by Apostolic authority we prohibit any bishop or other person from compelling you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit to secular judgment concerning your own property or possessions; nor shall anyone presume to come into your houses in order to celebrate ordinations, hear cases, or summon public assemblies; nor to hinder the regular election of your abbot, or to interfere in any manner, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, with the installation or removal of whoever may at the time hold that office.

But if the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, when fittingly requested with humility and devotion, should refuse to bless the appointed abbot or to confer upon you the other things belonging to the episcopal office, it shall be lawful for that abbot, if he is a priest, to bless his own novices and exercise the other functions belonging to his office; and it shall be lawful for you to receive from another bishop all that has been improperly denied by your own bishop. We add that, in receiving professions submitted by abbots who have been blessed or are to be blessed, bishops shall be content with the form and wording known to have been established from the beginning of the Order: namely, that the abbots themselves ought to profess, with their Order preserved, and shall not be compelled to make any profession contrary to the statutes of their Order.

For consecrations of altars or churches, holy chrism, or any ecclesiastical sacrament, no one shall dare, under pretext of custom or otherwise, to extort anything from you; rather, the diocesan bishop shall furnish all these things freely. Otherwise, it shall be lawful for you to approach whatever Catholic bishop you prefer, being in the grace and communion of the most holy Roman See, who, relying upon our authority, shall furnish you what is requested. If, however, the see of the diocesan bishop should happen to be vacant, you may freely and without objection receive all ecclesiastical sacraments from neighbouring bishops, provided that no prejudice is thereby created in future against your own bishops.

And because you do not always have the opportunity of your own bishops, if a bishop in communion with the Roman See, as we have said, and fully known to you, happens to pass through your region, you may, by authority of the Apostolic See, receive from him blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks. Moreover, if bishops or other rulers of churches pronounce a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict against your monasteries or persons living in them, or even against hired labourers because you do not pay tithes, or on any pretext concerning matters granted to you by Apostolic generosity; or against your benefactors because in charity they have rendered you any benefits or services, or helped you work on days when you work and others rest, we decree that such a sentence shall be annulled as pronounced against the grants of the Apostolic See. Nor shall any letters have force which are obtained while concealing the name of the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of Apostolic privileges.

Moreover, desiring with paternal care to provide in future for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by Apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your establishments or granges from committing robbery or theft, setting fire, shedding blood, rashly seizing or killing a person, or daring to employ violence. Furthermore, we confirm by Apostolic authority, and fortify with the privilege of the present writing, all liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.

We decree, therefore, etc.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. [Col. 1006D] I, Jordan, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Romanus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callistus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Soffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 1007A] I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the fourth day before the Ides of June [10 June], in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1193 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Celestine III.

## CXXVII. He answers the questions of Walter, archbishop of Rouen, concerning appeals, etc.  
*(Lateran, 17 June.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 630.]

[Col. 1007B]

We commend your prudence with due praise, because, in questions of law about which you sometimes doubt, you judge that the Apostolic See should be consulted, to which indeed the ancient Fathers decreed that all difficult questions and cases ought fittingly to be referred. You have asked us whether, when a case is committed with appeal excluded, and the defendant brings a counterclaim against the plaintiff before the same judge—or before the same judges, which may lawfully be done under the provisions of both canon and civil law—and the plaintiff appeals in the matter of the counterclaim, such an appeal ought to be entertained.

Our judgment is that, since in this matter the plaintiff and defendant have one and the same case, both ought to employ the same law concerning the remedy of appeal. Therefore, we believe that an appeal thus brought is not to be entertained. For, Christ himself, who is Truth, bears witness that we have learned that whatever persons wish others to do to them, they must themselves do likewise; nor does the jurist differ from this conclusion. Hence the *Authentica* beginning “and follows,” in which this is expressly laid down concerning the making of a counterclaim, and elsewhere it is ordained that a person shall use against another the same law which he has thought fit to establish against him. Therefore, just as they desire that justice be done to them in accordance with the mandate, with appeal excluded, so, for the same reason, they must answer the counterclaimant in his just claim.

Second, you ask whether, when several articles are placed in one commission and appeal is expressly forbidden, with appeal excluded, in only one of them, an appeal is valid if it is lodged concerning the others. We answer as follows: since, according to blessed Gregory, words serve intention, and our intention is that appeal shall take effect in respect of all the articles included in our commission when justice has not been opposed, appeal is understood to be prohibited in all of them. For it makes no difference whether the prohibition of appeal occurs at the beginning, in the middle, or even at the end, since, as the express arguments of both laws teach us, provisions appearing at the beginning of rescripts often extend to the middle and end, and provisions at the end to the beginning and middle.

Third, you seek instruction whether, when someone refuses a judge as suspect, he must allege the ground of suspicion, and, unless the ground is manifest, is bound to prove it before that same judge; and whether the judge may proceed in the case if the person alleging suspicion is unwilling or unable lawfully to prove its ground. To your inquiry we have thought fit to give the following answer: when someone asserts that he regards a judge as suspect, he must allege the ground of suspicion before that same judge, lest otherwise he be able at will to evade, merely for purposes of delay, the judgment of anyone whatsoever. But the parties must be compelled by the same judge who is called suspect to agree upon another judge or judges who are not too remote. If before them the ground of suspicion is not proved within a suitable time, then the challenged judge shall exercise his authority; but if before them a manifest ground of suspicion is proved, the challenged judge must refrain from hearing the case. Reason itself dictates this, and it is proved by many examples, that suspect and hostile persons ought not to be judges; for, as an established decretal forbids, no one can give a more welcome or agreeable gift to an enemy than to commit to him the prosecution of matters in which he intends to injure and damage another.

[Col. 1008C]

Finally, you raise the further question whether a judge may determine whether an appeal has been made frivolously or on reasonable grounds, and, if the appellant does not allege a reasonable ground of appeal or does not prove what he alleges, whether the judge is bound, by reason of that appeal, to abstain from hearing the case. Here we see fit to determine nothing other than what has been determined by our predecessors and by the jurists of both laws. For the law has provided that, once an appeal has been lodged, whether received or not, nothing ought to be altered in the meantime. Likewise, canonical ordinances provide that those who wish, or who must do so, may have recourse to the Roman Church as to their head, and may appeal without any hindrance whatsoever; indeed, one who is permitted everywhere by the ordinances of the sacred canons to appeal is to be freely allowed to proceed to appeal without any custody, excommunication, condemnation, or spoliation. Therefore, when a judge sees that a case heard before him has been suspended by an appeal, he shall abstain from hearing it as soon as possible.

In the fifth place, you ask to be informed whether, when a case is entrusted to three or more judges, so that if all cannot be present two may nevertheless proceed, a defendant summoned only by two is necessarily bound to appear; and whether, if he has been summoned by only two, or, having been cited by several, has appeared before two while a third neither comes nor excuses himself by letter, as often happens, the two present may proceed with the case, determine it, and bring it to a canonical conclusion. Our answer in this case is as follows: unless one of the delegated judges has shown, by a trustworthy messenger or by a written excuse sent in due form, that he cannot be present, even though this could not otherwise be canonically established concerning him, the remaining judges ought not to proceed to hear the case; and those who proceed in this manner shall be deemed to have done nothing. For the ancient provision of the Apostolic See was to delegate such hearings and decisions more willingly to two rather than one, and to three rather than two, since, as the sacred canons attest, a judgment is complete when confirmed by the opinions of several persons. Indeed, a person would be proved to have exceeded the limits of his mandate if he presumed to judge otherwise than according to the form of the rescript received.

We add that where it is set down in the commission that, if all cannot be present, two shall proceed, and if any one of them, though able, refuses to be present, the two may nevertheless proceed in the case—although that third judge is to be very severely blamed because he has evaded or despised execution of the Apostolic mandate. We say the same in every respect when a case is committed to two, with the proviso that if both cannot be present, one may nevertheless proceed.

The sixth question put to us on your behalf was this: when a case is entrusted to certain judges, and it sometimes happens that the defendant objects against the plaintiff that he cannot stand in court because he is bound by a sentence of excommunication, if the defendant is unwilling or unable immediately to prove that the plaintiff is excommunicated, whether the plaintiff ought nevertheless to be heard until the truth of what is objected against him has been disclosed. We remove this doubt as follows: if the person making such an objection does not immediately, or within a suitable period, lawfully prove what he asserts, the plaintiff must be permitted to be heard without any impediment. But if it becomes evident from the plaintiff’s confession or by any other lawful means that the plaintiff is bound by excommunication, he may be absolved by the delegated judges according to the form of the Church—provided, however, that, if he has been excommunicated by the ordinary or delegated judge for another just and evident cause, he must be sent to the excommunicator to be absolved. If that person acts maliciously, the delegated judges may freely pursue the matter according to ecclesiastical rite, so long as it is not a class of excommunication whose absolution is reserved to the Apostolic See. It is a settled point of law that this is so concerning delegated judges to whom both the principal and the ancillary matter have been entrusted. But if he is absolved by those judges, he must first swear that he will obey the mandate of the Church.

You further ask whether, before those delegated judges or before the ordinary judge by whom he was excommunicated, he is bound to answer in the same case for which he was bound by excommunication, and whose mandate he ought to obey. In this case we answer that he must stand before the excommunicators themselves concerning the case for which he was excommunicated and obey their mandate, unless that matter has been specially delegated by the Apostolic See to another. If the excommunicators maliciously delay, the delegated judges shall exercise the same jurisdiction in that matter as in the principal and ancillary matters.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July [17 June], in the third year of our pontificate.

## CXXVIII. He confirms the rights of the hospital before the greater church of Siena.  
*(Lateran, 17 June.)*

[MURATORI, *Antiq. Ital.*, IV, 585.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [Col. 1010B] to his beloved sons INCONTRATO and the brethren of the hospital situated before the greater church of Siena: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

Although unworthy, we are placed in such a position that we ought, by admonitions and exhortations in the Lord, to strengthen the devotion of the faithful from good to better, and more graciously to extend the favour of our Apostolate to their just desires and petitions. Since, as is said, the canons of Siena have alienated for their own pleasure, and to no good effect, the greater part of the possessions of that hospital, and, moved by a zeal of avarice, are attempting both to harass the work of piety laudably and moderately carried on by you and others in the Lord through alms and other benefits conferred there by the Lord’s bounty, and to violate the instrument of agreement drawn up, accepted, and approved with the consent of both parties, and to subject you to their obedience: wishing to provide now and in the future for the security of you and of the hospital itself, we have thought fit by the present document to grant that neither you nor your successors shall in any respect be bound to answer to those canons or their successors, while preserving the tenor of the instrument drawn up by the hands of Raymond, judge and notary of Siena, and received and approved by both parties.

Holding that agreement to be valid and firm, as it was reasonably made, approved, and accepted by both parties, we grant you and your successors, upon the death of the rector of that hospital, full power, with every obstacle of appeal and contradiction removed, to elect and appoint there a suitable person who shall preside over the brethren according to God, understand how to devote himself to the reception and support of pilgrims and poor persons, and to the improvement of the house entrusted to him, and enlarge it by pious efforts and good works. Therefore let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our grant or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July [17 June], in the third year of our pontificate.

## CXXIX. He confirms the constitution of Boleslaus, bishop of Vác, made with the approval of Job, archbishop of Esztergom, concerning the annual celebration of a synod on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary (8 September).  
*(Rome, 20 June.)*

[FÉJER, *Codex diplomaticus Hungariae*, II, 290.]

[Col. 1011A]

## CXXX. At the request of Bishop William, he receives the Church of Melfi under protection and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(Lateran, 29 June.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 925.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, bishop of Melfi, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Placed by the Lord’s ordering upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love our brother bishops, whether near at hand or far away, with brotherly charity, and, with the Lord’s help, beneficially provide for their peace and tranquillity. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the Church of Melfi, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, and fortify it by the privilege of the present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grants of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s help, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors.

Following the example of our predecessors Paschal and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, we further enact by Apostolic authority that no episcopal see shall at any future time be established in the town of Lavello, near Melfi, as has hitherto been observed. Rather, we confirm that town itself, together with its appurtenances and boundaries, to you and to your episcopal successors, to be governed, held, and administered in perpetuity by episcopal right. Moreover, we decree that the estate of Salsula, Gaudiana, and the possessions of Saint John of Iliceto shall always remain the Church of Melfi’s own property, just as they were granted in his time and confirmed by his charter by Duke Roger of good memory. By the present page of privilege we establish the same concerning the tax paid by the Jews, the revenue from the baths, villein renders, tolls, mills, vineyards, fields, and all other things which that duke bestowed upon your Church within or outside the city of Melfi. Further, we enact as perpetual law that whoever hereafter succeeds, by God’s authority, as bishop in the Church of Melfi shall receive the grace of consecration from the pontiff of the Apostolic See.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 1012A] rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved inviolate and whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to be of use in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly should attempt rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to stern vengeance at the last judgment. But let all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good conduct and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1193 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Celestine III.

## CXXXI. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Bagnoregio.  
*(Lateran, 25 July.)*

[MITTARELLI, *Annales Camaldulenses*, IV, appendix, p. 187.]

[Col. 1012C] CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons AUGUSTINE, archpriest of the Church of Bagnoregio, and his brethren, present and future, professing the religious life: in perpetuity.

The authority of our office admonishes and invites us, etc. Celestine confirms for the Church of Bagnoregio the grants which his predecessors Innocent, in 1136, Adrian IV, in 1156, and Alexander III, around 1181, had made to that church, as contained in the bulls already mentioned.

### CXXXII. At the request of Bishop Theodinus, he confirms the boundaries of the diocese of Theano, the possessions and privileges of its bishops. (Lateran, September 29.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 557.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THEODINUS, bishop of Theano, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Although, by the Lord’s disposal, we have been placed, unworthy as we are, on the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love our brother bishops, whether near at hand or far away, with brotherly charity, and, with the Lord’s help, beneficially provide for their peace and tranquillity. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop Theodinus, acceding to your just requests and following the example of our predecessors of happy memory—Paschal, Adrian, Alexander, Lucius, and Clement, Roman pontiffs—we decree by the authority of this present writing that all the boundaries of the parish, as they are known to have been defined in the privilege of Pope John XVIII, of revered memory, granted to Bishop Sandrarius, shall remain wholly intact in perpetuity both to you and to your successors: namely, on the first side, where the water of Sextus enters the River Vulturnus, and as that river descends as far as Mount [Col. 1013D] Anezone, and as the land of that mountain rises and reaches the boundary of Melanico; on the second side, as the land runs from the mountain called Petra Molaria and from Mount Majone, descends into Decempondera, proceeds to the *stafilum* [uncertain local term], descends [lacuna] from the little bench or ridge (*scabellum*), and at that very watercourse (*rigazo*) enters the Sagone, as the same Sagone proceeds to the place called Balurum, where the stream called Porti seems to join it; on the third side, where one ascends along that stream as far as the bridge of Censano, and turns by the channel into Ponte Fracto, ascends into the valley and proceeds to Cartelera, reaches the ford called Area, ascends to Castellucum, and thence proceeds to the watercourse which runs beside the church of St. Mary situated in Baloneo Majore, [Col. 1014A] and that watercourse enters the river of Gavigliano; on the fourth side are that same river and the water called Branta, which goes to Silicum, then proceeds to the fork of St. Martin, and thence runs through those mountains and descends through the valley of Almagno into the aforesaid water of Sextus.

Within these boundaries lie the city of Theano and the following castles: Petra Molaria, Rocca Romana, Riardus, the castle of St. Felix, Sajanum, the castle called Petra Marzana, Bairanum, Pensinae, Praesentianum, Minianum, Caminum, Casale Caspuli, Rocca Banterani, Cucuruzium, Mertula, Gallucium, Rocca of the Holy Cross, [lacuna] the territory of Marzanellum, Cajanum, the settlement of St. John, and others included therein; likewise monasteries and churches of clerics or monks.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the Church of Theano now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Furthermore, we decree that the clerics of that bishopric, of whatever order they may be, shall remain under your jurisdiction and withdrawn from lay power. For, since a question had formerly arisen between Peter, your predecessor of good memory, and the clerics of Minianum concerning payment of the cathedraticum, Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory—then priest-cardinal of the title of St. Praxedis—and John, deacon-cardinal of Saints [Col. 1014C] Sergius and Bacchus, acting under delegation from the Roman pontiff, investigated the case. Having received suitable witnesses, they found that the predecessors of that bishop had received twelve denarii from each priest of Minianum for forty years under the name of cathedraticum; and, having learned from the assertion of many persons that such a custom was observed in the provinces of Capua and Benevento and in the other neighbouring provinces, they adjudged that the said cathedraticum was to be paid, in accordance with custom, to him and his successors by the priests of the aforesaid castle. We decree that this judgment, pronounced by the aforesaid Lucius when cardinal and known to have been confirmed by Adrian of holy memory, by the said Lucius, and by Clement, our predecessors as Roman pontiffs, shall remain unimpaired for all future times.

Moreover, we ratify and decree to remain unimpaired for future times the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to the Church of Theano by our beloved son, the nobleman Gimundus of Rocca Romana, as is more fully contained in an authentic instrument drawn up on the matter. For greater security, we have ordered that instrument to be inserted word for word in this present charter. It reads as follows:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. In the year 1189 of his Incarnation, in the twenty-third year of the reign of our lord William II, by God’s grace magnificent king, in the month of February, in the seventh indiction: every Christian ought to devote himself all the more earnestly to the honour of Holy Mother Church and to her right, inasmuch as he receives the beginning of his rebirth in her womb [Col. 1015A] and through her awaits the attainment of everlasting life. Therefore, we, Guimundus of Rocca Romana, wish it to be known to those present and absent that, whereas manifold and diverse disputes concerning specified articles had arisen between lord Peter, our venerable father in Christ, bishop of Theano, on behalf of his Church, and [lacuna], we finally endeavoured, through conferences of mutual friends, to arrive at unity of peace and concord.
>
> “For the same venerable bishop maintained that priests and clerics living in our territory were frequently burdened and oppressed by us and by our bailiffs through unlawful and unjust exactions and through tolls levied upon their animals. The said lord bishop also raised a question concerning the third part of the tithe from our demesne, which we did not permit him to possess wholly and peacefully, as our father lord Andrew, of good memory, formerly lord of Rocca Romana, had granted it to his Church. He further complained that we did not allow him to make use of the church of St. John at Clusas, in accordance with the tenor of his privilege, which had been granted to the Church of Theano by the aforesaid lord Andrew, our father.
>
> “Accordingly, desiring that the fullness of peace and concord should be restored, after taking counsel with friends and certain of our faithful men, and also for the salvation of the souls of our grandfather and father and for the redemption of our sins, in the presence of Nicholas, judge of Theano, Peter the notary, and the other witnesses subscribed below, we have endeavoured to arrive at the following concord and agreement concerning the aforesaid articles.
>
> “We grant and establish with perpetual force that priests and clerics dwelling in our territory, who hold no lay patrimony or tenement from us, shall suffer no molestation from us or from our bailiffs in their persons or property; rather, assistance shall be required from them. But should they perhaps freely choose to give us something as a favour, they shall be permitted freely and without disturbance of mind to serve God and the Church. If, however, there are any who hold a patrimony or tenement from us, assistance shall be required from them according to what we require from their brethren, or on account of the rights attaching to the patrimony or tenement.
>
> “If any cleric or priest is accused criminally or civilly, or is summoned concerning lost ecclesiastical property [the text is defective], whether by the bishop or by another person before the bishop, all examination, judgment, and correction shall belong to the bishop and chapter of Theano. But if any cleric or layman wishes to summon any priest or cleric of our territory before the archpriest whom the bishop shall appoint in our territory, or amicably before the syndic of the assembly of our territory, he shall be free to do so if the matter can there be decided. If it cannot be determined by them, and either party appeals to the greater church, or if a sentence is to be reconsidered, the matter shall be referred to the cognizance of the greater church. In all these matters neither we nor [Col. 1016A] our bailiffs shall in any way intervene in the judgments or coercive measures concerning clerics or priests.
>
> “We shall allow the clerics and priests of our territory not only to come to the greater church in solemn procession on the feast of St. John before the Latin Gate, but shall also compel by the fullest coercion those unwilling to come. Moreover, we shall not in any way harass, or cause to be harassed, with any oppression, burden, or exaction, laymen and faithful persons of the Church of Theano dwelling in the hamlet of Anguillari and Scarpato or in other adjacent places. As regards their lordship, I shall restrain and judge [them]; let the Church of Theano and its rectors be free [the wording is corrupt or uncertain]. Should they die intestate, their possessions and goods shall devolve freely and without condition upon the Church of Theano.
>
> “Neither we nor our bailiffs shall seize their animals and goods, or cause them to be seized, nor shall we intervene in any way against them or their property. This exception alone is made: at Easter and at the Nativity of the Lord they shall make a visitation at Vexeniis, according to the custom observed toward our predecessors, because they and their churches enjoy security in our territory and receive benefit therefrom in pasture, wood, and water, like the other inhabitants of our territory. But if in a last will, prompted by their ultimate intention, any of them wishes to favour us in respect of movable goods by leaving us something, they shall be free to leave to us, just as to any other outsider, according to their will, without coercion by us or our bailiffs.
>
> “We freely and absolutely grant to the Church of Theano the third part of the tithe of our demesne, to be held as lord Andrew, our father, granted it to that Church. Finally, we freely and absolutely relinquish the church of St. John at Clusas according to the tenor of the privilege granted by our father to the same Church, saving that Bonus Homo, the canon who has acquired that church by grant of the aforesaid bishop, shall hold it peacefully and quietly during his lifetime, and that the annual observances shall be performed by the canons of the aforesaid Church according to the tenor of our privilege. Upon the death of the said Bonus Homo, the bishop shall hold that church in demesne and shall possess it freely and without contradiction.
>
> “We confirm this our concession concerning the aforesaid articles, constitutions, ordinance, and agreement by delivery into your hands, lord venerable father, lord bishop of Theano, on behalf and in the name of your Church, in the presence of the aforesaid judge, notary, and subscribed witnesses; and we bind ourselves and our heirs never to act against this our concord, agreement, and grant toward you, the aforesaid venerable bishop, on behalf and in the name of the said Church.
>
> “For if we, the aforesaid Guimundus, or our heirs, or anyone acting in our name or on our behalf, should consent by any contrivance to break, remove, or alter this writing and its contents, or attempt to repudiate any part of it, we and our heirs are bound to pay as a penalty one hundred gold bezants to you, the aforesaid venerable bishop of Theano, to your successors, and to the party of the said Church, and to fulfil all the foregoing provisions. This charter and its contents shall always remain firm and stable; and for the fulfilment of all these things [lacuna] we have given you, the aforesaid venerable bishop of Theano, [a pledge or guaranty], and have provided sureties by agreement. If necessary, we have bound ourselves and our heirs to be distrained against by you, your successors, and the party of the said Church, in respect of our movable and immovable goods, lawfully and unlawfully [as the text reads], up to the law.
>
> “Thus we, the aforesaid Guimundus of Rocca Romana, have made known to the aforesaid venerable father Peter, bishop of Theano, on behalf and in the name of the aforesaid Church of Theano, what was done and fitting for us; and we requested you, Peter the notary, who were present, to write it. I, Peter the notary, wrote this and was present in the territory of Theano, in the place called Verclanicum.”

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved unimpaired and whole for the benefit in every respect of those uses for which they were granted, namely their governance and support, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this charter of our constitution, rashly attempts to violate it, and, after a second or third admonition, does not correct that presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power or honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be excluded from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 1017D] I Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I John, bishop of Tusculum, cardinal of the title of St. Clement. I John Felix, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Susanna. I Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Anastasia. I Guido, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mary across the Tiber. I Hugh, priest-cardinal of Saints Sylvester and Martin, of the title of Equitius. I Gregory, deacon of the title of St. Mary in Portico. I Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Aquiro. [Col. 1018A] I Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil. I Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1193 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of lord Pope Celestine III.

### CXXXIII. He informs the abbot and convent of Vallombrosa that John Gualbert, founder of the Vallombrosan congregation, has, at the request of the abbot and convent of Passignano, been enrolled among the saints. (Lateran, October 6.)

[*Acta Sanctorum*, July, vol. III, p. 338.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Vallombrosa, greeting and apostolic blessing.

God is glorious in his saints and wonderful in majesty. He not only rewards his ministers, who minister to him truly and sincerely, with an unfading prize and eternal reward, but also makes them worthy of commendation in this present life through the manifestation of many miracles and, according to the prophetic word, causes them to be held in everlasting remembrance and solemnly venerated by all. No Catholic indeed doubts this, since Holy Scripture also bears witness that the Lord is praised in his saints, and that whoever honours them wholly honours the Lord himself, as he testifies when he says: “He who honours you honours me, and he who receives you receives me” (Matt. 10:40). And likewise: [Col. 1018C] “What you have done for one of these least of mine, you have done for me” (Matt. 25:40).

And reason itself proves it fitting that, since the almighty Father has willed to distinguish the coheirs of his Son with that honour which he willed for the Son himself, the Son praying and saying: “Father, I will that where I am, there also may be my minister” (John 12:26); and again: “If anyone serves me, my Father who is in heaven will honour him” (John 12:26), human beings, fashioned from clay, should celebrate and venerate on earth the memory of one whose name is believed to be written in heaven.

Moved by this consideration, when we had received the petitions of our beloved sons George, abbot, and the convent of the monastery of Passignano, together with your testimony and letters, requesting that we should wish to enroll and associate in the catalogue of saints John of illustrious [Col. 1018D] memory, formerly abbot and founder of the congregation of Vallombrosa—who was a prudent and faithful servant of his Creator, gave the household committed to him its measure of wheat in due season, and, because he had been faithful over a few things, was after his death set by the Lord himself over many things; whom the Lord distinguished by many privileges of miracles and, as is said, still continually glorifies in these times—it seemed to us, and was resolved by the common counsel of the brethren and of neighbouring bishops and other prelates of the Church, that we should await testimonies concerning the manner of life and miracles of this good man.

[Col. 1019A] At length, after receiving the testimony and petitions of bishops, abbots, priors, archdeacons, parish priests, provosts, ecclesiastical and monastic communities, and others concerning the life, conduct, and miracles of that same minister of Jesus Christ, and having sought and held an assembly of our brethren concerning his canonization, we gave thanks to the Creator, who ever multiplies his Church with new offspring and adorns it with the flowers of roses and lilies. We canonized the aforesaid blessed John and decreed that he should be added to the number of Christ’s confessors. With humble prayer we beseech the King of all confessors that, through the prayers and merits of that same confessor—who pleased him by his bright and conspicuous deeds—we may be delivered from imminent dangers and experience his patronage in our necessities.

We therefore command and enjoin your devotion through apostolic letters that you rejoice spiritually in the aid of so great a patron, whom Italy herself bore and nourished, and that you commemorate his memory on a fixed day among the other confessors with solemn veneration, endeavouring to observe his feast and extolling in him divine omnipotence. For, if, according to the Lord’s attesting word, one is proved to love God who keeps his commandments, it is known from the fruits of the aforesaid holy man that he can and ought to be effectively heard by God. He was not a deaf hearer of evangelical preaching; reckoning the joys of the world as [Col. 1019C] dung, he abandoned them, and, following in Christ’s footsteps, not only established monastic observance in your monastery, but also built seven monasteries; finally, after restoring the monastery of Passignano, he ended his present life there by a praiseworthy death.

Yet among his miracles the first and principal one is found to be this: for a work of mercy prudently and mercifully shown to someone who had sinned against him, while that person lay prostrate before him in the form of a cross, the image of the Crucified is said to have inclined its head toward him while he was still engaged in secular service.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of October, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXXXIV. He takes the church of St. John of Calcinaia under protection and confirms its possessions and rights. (Lateran, November 13.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, III, 1179.]

[Col. 1019D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUIDO, parish priest of the church of St. John of Calcinaia, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as consistent with religion and honour, it becomes us to grant it willingly and to give assent appropriate to the petitioners’ wishes. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Guido, parish priest, we graciously accede to your just requests; and, following the example of Adrian and Alexander, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own protection the aforesaid church, which, by God’s grace, you are known to govern, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have thought it proper to specify among them the following in their own terms:

The churches of St. Mary and St. Michael of Monteclo; the church of St. Leonard of Cerbaria and the church of St. Prosper in Blentina; the church of St. Peter of Curte and St. Justus; the church [Col. 1020B] of St. Andrew of Sala and the parish of Bassiliano; the church of St. Fridianus in the place called Tredecim; in the village called Rapida, the churches of St. Lawrence and St. Christopher; the church of St. Martin of Pontedera; the churches of St. Michael of Travalda and St. Thomas; in the village called Calcinaria, the churches of St. Quiricus, St. George, St. Fridianus, St. Andrew, St. Lawrence, St. Stephen, and St. Michael.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority the judgment canonically rendered between you and the vice-lord of the Church of Pisa and the parish priest of Vico by Villanus, formerly archbishop of Pisa, of good memory, as contained in his authentic instrument. For greater firmness in this matter, we have decided that this judgment should be inserted word for word in this charter of ours.

Since it is fitting for everyone, and especially for those upon whom episcopal care is imposed, with watchful mind and diligent effort to restore to peace and tranquillity matters that are contentious and to impose an amicable end upon litigants—especially upon ecclesiastical persons and servants of God, who ought not to litigate and who are scarcely permitted on any ground to presume to contend before the tribunal of a secular magistrate—I, Villanus, by God’s grace archbishop of the Church of Pisa, having carefully heard the questions of litigation and controversy that had arisen between Homicius, venerable vice-lord of the Church of Pisa and parish priest of Vico, and Gerard, parish priest of Calcinaria, concerning a certain chapel and its [Col. 1020D] parish, built in honour of St. Fridianus in the place called Tredecim: the aforesaid vice-lord and parish priest of Vico contended that they belonged to his right, while the parish priest of the aforementioned parish church of Calcinaria asserted, on the contrary, that they likewise belonged to his right. The case having been long and extensively pursued on both sides in our presence, and finally submitted to your arbitration by the consent of both parties, with the counsel of our most learned assessors Master Benencasa, Judge Manfred, and Carpinus, we determined it by our arbitration or award as follows.

The baptismal church of Vico shall peacefully and quietly possess by parochial right the three principal houses which came from Tredecim to dwell there, and this shall in no way diminish the territory of the aforesaid church. These principal houses having thus been held in perpetual right, we further grant to the same parish of Vico one whole half of all the territory of the aforesaid chapel. But we grant and confirm to the parish of Calcinaria, freely, absolutely, and by perpetual right, the church itself and the other half of all the territory of that church of St. Fridianus, together with half of the farmsteads, apart from the three aforesaid houses.

Therefore, to settle the discord of both parties and so that peace and concord may henceforth exist between them, we have resolved to distinguish the matter of the parishes in the manner stated and have decreed that this decision be observed unimpaired, and that no secular or ecclesiastical person shall have leave to violate it. If either party, knowing this charter of our arbitration or award, rashly attempts to act against it and, after a second or third admonition, does not make satisfaction, let that party be excluded from the body and blood of the Lord. May salvation, peace, and Christ’s blessing be upon one who observes it. That this our arbitration or award may remain firm in perpetuity, we have impressed it with the attestation of our seal.

We also grant that the burial-place of that church shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving nevertheless the canonical right of those churches from which they have been taken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, [Col. 1021C] diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved unimpaired and whole, for the benefit in every respect of those uses for which they were granted, namely their governance and support, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the right and due reverence of the archbishop of Pisa. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this charter of our constitution, rashly attempts to violate it, and, after a second or third admonition, does not correct that offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I Albinus, bishop of Albano. I Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I John, bishop of Palestrina. I Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Cecilia. [Col. 1022A] I John, bishop of Tusculum, of the title of St. Clement. I John Felix, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Susanna. I Romanus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Anastasia. I Guido, priest-cardinal of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callistus. I John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I Centius, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I Soffredus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Praxedis. I Bernard, priest-cardinal of St. Peter in Chains, [Col. 1022B] of the title of St. Eudoxia. I Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Portico. I Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Aquiro. I Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil. I Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I Bobo, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore. [Col. 1022C] I Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Via Lata. I Cencius, deacon-cardinal of St. Lucy in Orchea.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Aegidius, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the Ides of November, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1193 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of lord Pope Celestine III.

### CXXXV. He grants William, archbishop of Ravenna, leave to convey certain goods to the people of Argenta by emphyteutic right. (Lateran, December 3.)

[RUBEI, *Historia Ravennatis*, p. 361.]

### CXXXVI. He instructs the provost of Mount St. Walburga, G., cantor of St. Gereon, and the scholasticus of St. Mary ad Gradus at Cologne, to order the inhabitants of the village of Winsae to pay a certain tithe to the monastery of Deutz. (Lateran, December 25.)

[LEDEBUR, *Allgemeines Archiv*, XV, 285.]

[Col. 1022D]

### CXXXVII. To [William], archbishop of Ravenna. (Lateran.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 634.]

[Note: From these letters was taken chapter *Ut super aliqua*, 8, *De rebus ecclesiasticis non alienandis* (“Concerning ecclesiastical property not to be alienated”).]

“Concerning certain matters,” etc.; and below: “You have also asked how the provision contained in the formula for conferring the pallium is to be understood, namely: ‘We confer upon you the pallium, that you may use it in your church and within every church of your province.’ If, however, it happens that you leave the church vested in sacred garments, whether in procession or otherwise, you must by no means use the pallium.”

Given at the Lateran, in the third year.

### CXXXVIII. To [Sicard], bishop of Cremona. (Lateran.)

[Ibid.]

“Although the remedy of appeal,” and below: “Therefore, wishing with pastoral solicitude to guard against so great an inconvenience to clerics and to remove from laymen material for disparaging clerics or coercing them under the same judgment, we have thought it right to answer you as follows: if a case concerning any cleric subject to you is brought before your fraternity, and the matter in dispute does not reach a value of forty solidi, we do not impose upon you an obligation to defer proceedings merely because the cleric, on that account, considers it necessary to appeal to the Apostolic See; rather, if you prefer, you may determine the case without impediment from the appeal, unless a manifest and reasonable ground of suspicion against you has been shown.”

Given at the Lateran, in the third year.

### CXXXIX. To the bishop of Viterbo, concerning tithes. (Lateran.)

[Ibid., col. 635.]

[Note: Chapter *Ex parte*, 21, *De decimis* (“Concerning tithes”).]

A complaint has been laid before us on behalf of our beloved sons, the canons [Col. 1023C] of your church: certain cultivators, although they have sown different seeds in the same field or garden, whether at the same time or at different periods of the year, nevertheless do not pay the canons tithes from the produce of those seeds. Some, moreover, do not take care to pay tithes from the yield of their fields until they have first deducted certain expenses incurred in transporting the produce to the threshing-floor or granaries. Since by this the canons themselves and the Church of God suffer no slight injury, whereas it is ordained that tithes be paid to the Levites without expenses, we command your brotherhood by apostolic writing that, after diligently investigating the truth, if you find that the matter stands thus, you shall compel those cultivators, by ecclesiastical censure and with every contradiction and appeal set aside, to pay tithes from all the fruits [Col. 1023D] of their estates, with no expenses deducted, but rather whole and undiminished tithes. By our authority you shall strictly prohibit them from henceforth attempting such things through any greed or presumption.

Given at the Lateran, in the third year.

### CXL. To the abbot of Vézelay, concerning divorces. (Lateran.)

[Ibid.]

As you state, it often happens in your parish that women leave their husbands on account of fornication, and are known to remain so until the husbands’ death. When the husbands have died, and the women claim from the kinsmen to whom their inheritances pass [Col. 1024A] their dowry together with their dower-right, those kinsmen deny them a hearing and refuse restitution, because the women are thought to have made themselves unworthy of it precisely by having chosen to leave their husbands on account of fornication. (Moreover, in your petition you added that, when cases are delegated to you by the Apostolic See, you insert the apostolic rescript in the letters of citation, so that, on seeing it, a person summoned by another may deliberate whether to appear—not at the first and second canonical citations, but only at the third, peremptory one—while the plaintiff appears at every citation and sets out his claim in law; and when the defendant, intent on delaying him, then first seeks time for deliberation, while the plaintiff offers him the authentic copy so that he may compare it with the rescript [Col. 1024B] received at the first citation, you assert that, over so long a period of citations, he could, if he wished, have had full time for deliberation. Since, therefore, you desire instruction concerning what is to be done in each matter, we answer as follows in the first case:) if a woman leaves her husband on account of her own fornication, whether by judgment of the Church or through her own fickleness, and is not afterwards reconciled with him, then upon his death she has no legal right to reclaim her dowry or dower-right. In the second case, we say that, when the defendant has been summoned to judgment in the manner stated above, if from the rescript sent to him he could be fully informed concerning the matter for which he was sued, further time for deliberation is not to be granted, but the examination of the case should instead proceed and its due conclusion be imposed.

[Col. 1024C] Given at the Lateran, in the third year.

### CXLI. To a Certain Person, on Excommunication.

[Ibid., col. 636.]

It was asked of us on your behalf whether, if someone has pronounced thus, “Whoever commits theft shall be excommunicated,” this general sentence is restricted to the subjects of the excommunicator himself, or extends generally to all who are not under his jurisdiction. To this we say that only subjects are bound by such a sentence, unless perhaps a higher and more ample authority has been conferred upon him by the delegating authority. (Furthermore, we were asked whether, if a judge has pronounced thus: “Unless you make satisfaction to Sempronius within ten days, know that you are excommunicated, [Col. 1024D] suspended, or interdicted,” and the person against whom such a sentence is pronounced appeals in the meantime but makes no satisfaction by the stated deadline, is he bound by such a sentence, or is he protected by the lodging of the appeal? It seems to us, however, that an appeal ought to prevent the effect of a sentence of this kind.

Given at the Lateran, in the third year.

### CXLII. To the Bishop of Ancona.—On a Sentence of Excommunication.

[Ibid., col. 637.]

He informed us, etc., and below: But we do not doubt that those clerics who knowingly and willingly participated with persons excommunicated by us, and admitted them to offices, [Col. 1025A] are involved in the same sentence together with them; and, in order to obtain the benefit of their absolution, we wish them to be sent to us with a statement in your letters.

### CXLIII. To the Prior and Chapter of Dehum.

[Ibid., col. 637.]

Of blessed memory, etc., and below: After this first confirmation had, as it were, been produced in our court, a second was presented, in these terms: “Likewise, let the following clause be inserted in those later letters: notwithstanding any letters of confirmation, let the case be heard and brought to its due conclusion.” The question was whether the first letters ought thus to be revoked. To this we say that the first would be wholly annulled by the later ones. But if it were said—as is more frequently customary in apostolic rescripts—“provided that no letters prejudicing truth and justice stand in the way,” or in another form of words, so long as it did not expressly refer to letters of confirmation, we expressly say that the first would retain its force until fuller knowledge were obtained of an unjust or false sentence.

### CXLIV–CXLV. He Grants to the Monastery of St Augustine at Canterbury That No One May Presume to Burden Its Abbot or Monks with Any Sentence Unless Sent from the Side of the Roman Pontiff. (Fragment.)

[TWYSden, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, II, 1840.]

CELESTINE, bishop, etc.

Since your monastery, and below: Wishing, with paternal solicitude, to provide for your peace and [Col. 1025C] tranquility, by apostolic authority we prohibit the Archbishop of Canterbury, his archdeacon or official, or any legate under pretext of his legation, from entering the monastery, burdening its abbot or monks with any sentence, troubling them with expenses, or attempting to place under interdict or excommunicate your churches, clerics, or men, unless he has been sent from the side of the Roman pontiff or has received from him a special mandate expressly directed to you by name.

### CXLVI. He Forbids Hubert, Archbishop of Canterbury and Legate of the Apostolic See, to Require “Obedience” from the Abbot and Monks of St Augustine.

[Ibid., 1841.]

[Col. 1025D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HUBERT, Archbishop of Canterbury, etc.

If you carefully consider how much favour and honour the most holy Roman Church, your mother, has bestowed upon you in these days, we firmly believe and hope that you will direct your actions toward those things which ought deservedly to please her. For we do not believe that your Fraternity is unaware that your predecessors were never shown the favour which we have taken care to show you in our own time; and therefore you must take the greatest care lest you do those things by which you may appear to offend us in any respect. You should know that it has come to our hearing that, after you undertook to exercise the office [Col. 1026A] of legation entrusted to you, you urgently demanded that our beloved sons, the abbot and convent of St Augustine’s, Canterbury—who belong directly to us, without any intermediary—should render you obedience. If this is true, it grieves and troubles us all the more because it appears to have been undertaken against us and the Roman Church. For we have never heard that legates whom we have sometimes sent from our side to various provinces demanded this from any churches.

Therefore, unwilling to pass over with closed eyes this burden laid upon the aforesaid church, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters wholly to desist from such a design and to cease from the burdens imposed upon that church by other churches, so that we may hear no complaint concerning you; [Col. 1026B] for, however sincerely in the Lord we may love your person, we could not endure this patiently.

### CXLVII. He Notifies R[oger], Abbot of St Augustine’s, Canterbury, Concerning the Preceding Letter. He Forbids Him to Render “Obedience” to Archbishop Hubert.

[Ibid.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son R., Abbot of St Augustine’s, etc.

Since the church committed to your care, and below: Concerning the matter in which, as we have learned, our brother Hubert, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, demanded obedience from you and your brothers, we have sent apostolic letters to him that he may cease from burdening you. We also will, and firmly prohibit by apostolic authority, that if he should ever consider demanding it from you, you are not to presume to render him any obedience.

## YEAR 1193.

### CXLVIII. To Canute, King of the Danes. (Fragment.)

[PERTZ, *Archiv*, VII, 884.]

… For our venerable brother Waldemar, Bishop of Schleswig, has informed us that W., your brother, the duke, violently took from him and his church castles, possessions, and many goods. …

### CXLIX. Bull in Favour of St James of Provins. (Lateran.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, *Instr.*, 61.]

[Col. 1026D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother the Bishop of Orléans and to the beloved sons the Abbot of St Evurtius and the Dean of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the grave complaint of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of St James of Provins: although the church of St Quiriacus at Provins had been granted to those canons, so that the order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine might be observed there in perpetuity; and although Pope Innocent, our predecessor of happy memory, receiving their persons [Col. 1027A] and goods under his protection, had perpetually strengthened the observance of the order in that church by the safeguard of his privilege … nevertheless, in the course of time they were compelled by secular violence to abandon that place and take refuge in a certain hospice. And although the sacred canons prohibit under pain of excommunication that places once known to have been assigned to religious observances should be returned to the worship of secular clerics and to more lax customs, regular canons were expelled, and a community of secular clerics was introduced there by lay power. When the aforesaid regulars had formerly set forth their complaint before Pope Alexander, our predecessor of pious memory, and obtained from him letters of restoration, both [Col. 1027B] the letters of restoration and all the documentary and privilege charters upon which they might at any time have relied were taken from them and burned so that they could never be recovered. And when so great an injury had been inflicted on them, thoroughly frightened by the threats of their persecutors, they groaned and grieved among themselves but had not until now dared to raise any action concerning such violence and injuries.

Accordingly, entrusting this entire matter to your discretion and steadfastness, in which we have great confidence, we command you by apostolic letters to go to the place, or to summon without delay before you the persons necessary for this purpose, and to inquire diligently into the whole course of the affair, having only truth and God before [Col. 1027C] your eyes. Setting aside every personal favour, do not delay to determine by our authority, with the impediment of appeal removed, whatever is canonical in these matters; bring this dispute to such an end that no complaint concerning it need henceforth be carried to us. If any persons rashly undertake to oppose you so as to prevent your proceeding in this affair according to God and the apostolic mandate, restrain them by our authority, without the impediment of appeal, through ecclesiastical severity from the audacity of such presumption. If all of you cannot be present for the execution of these matters, nevertheless let two of you carry them out.

Given at the Lateran … in the third year of our pontificate.

## YEAR 1194.

### CL. He Confers the Office of Apostolic Legate upon Adalbert, Archbishop of Salzburg. (Lateran, 21 January.)

[HANSIZIUS, *Germania sacra*, vol. II, p. 306.]

[Col. 1027D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother ADALBERT, Archbishop of Salzburg, legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by the office of service entrusted to us, we are bound to extend the gaze of our consideration to all, whether near or far away, and, in matters pertaining to God, to provide as far as divine grace may enable us—since all cannot, as would be expedient, approach our presence—we must entrust the burden of so great a care to certain of our brethren and fellow bishops, in whose fidelity and ability we have complete confidence. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, considering the dangers of travel and the many obstacles which may arise, especially amid the wickedness of this age, for those who must make their way from such distant regions to the Apostolic See, we confer upon you, throughout your entire province, the office of legation, by counsel of our brethren, placing great confidence in your prudence and in the sincerity of faith which you bear toward us and the Roman Church. By the authority of these presents we command that, acting in our stead, you correct and amend by apostolic authority whatever you see needs correction; foster and preserve what is well ordered; and strive to restore to a better condition whatever you recognize to be wicked or to have strayed from the path of rectitude. We also will that sentences which you reasonably pronounce against the contumacious or rebellious shall retain complete force until due amendment.

Given at the Lateran, 21 January, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CLI. He Confirms to the Monastery of Steingaden Goods Granted by Duke Welf. (Lateran, 28 January.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, VI, 503.]

[Col. 1028C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons the provost and brethren of the monastery of Steingaden, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant consent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect the requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of St Peter and ourselves your monastery and persons, together with all that you now rightfully possess or may hereafter, by God’s favour, acquire through just means. We especially confirm to you, and through you to the monastery itself, by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of the present writing, those goods which Welf, of blessed memory, formerly duke—who is known to have built that monastery and endowed it with many gifts—granted and delivered to it in pious devotion.

[Col. 1028D] Therefore let no one at all presume to infringe this page of our protection and confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 28 January, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CLII. He Takes the Monastery of St Lawrence of Aversa under Protection and Confirms Its Goods and Privileges. (Lateran, 8 March.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 220.]

[Col. 1029A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons MATTHEW, abbot of the monastery of St Lawrence of Aversa, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just petitioners be granted their requests, especially when piety supports their wishes and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your [Col. 1029B] just petitions and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Urban, Alexander, and Lucius, receive under the protection of St Peter and ourselves and strengthen by the privilege of the present writing the aforesaid monastery, which belongs in a special manner to the jurisdiction of St Peter and in which you are devoted to the service of the Lord. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the generosity [Col. 1029C] of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, acquire by God’s favour, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. We also confirm by apostolic authority to you and to the same monastery all churches, villages, and towns which it rightfully possesses. We prohibit in every way Masses without the consent of the abbot or brethren, lest any occasion be afforded to secular assemblies in the retreats of the servants of God. Certainly, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you from your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals. Nor may any bishop interdict or excommunicate the monastery itself or its cells.

You shall receive chrism, [Col. 1029D] holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks or clerics belonging to the monastery who are to be promoted to sacred orders, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, provided that, supported by our authority, he grants what is requested. We prohibit any bishop from excommunicating or suspending from office the chaplains or clerics who serve the monastery itself or its cells, or summoning them to synod. Further, because of the special liberty of the monastery itself, which is known to adhere directly to the Roman Church without intermediary, and for the honour and reverence of the most glorious martyr Lawrence, whose relics are deposited there, we grant to you and your [Col. 1030A] successors the use of the mitre everywhere in celebrations of divine worship and the daily use of the ring.

It shall also be lawful for you and your successors, without anyone’s objection, to receive clerics or laypersons who are free and released from obligations and who wish to come to your monastery for the purpose of conversion, whether in life or at death. We further decree that the burial-place of that site shall be free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and last will of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, without prejudice, however, to the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Upon your death, or that of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over the monastery by any cunning of subreption or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the choice of the greater and sounder part of the brethren, in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, have provided to be elected. The person elected, moreover, shall approach the Roman pontiff to receive blessing.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct the offence by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But let all who preserve the rights of that place enjoy the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.
