Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, Bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter Pozzillus, Bishop of the title of St Rufina. I, John, Bishop of Palestrina. I, Albinus, Bishop of Albano. I, Pandulph, cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve [Col. 1030D] Apostles. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of St Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, John, cardinal of the title of St Clement, Bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany. I, Romanus, cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of St Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen. I, Horatius, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, Soffredus, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca. [Col. 1031A] I, Gratian, cardinal of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of the title of St Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Aquiro. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of the title of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Robert, cardinal deacon of St Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on 8 March, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1193 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

[Col. 1031B] Sign of Pope Celestine III.

**DIRECT MY STEPS IN YOUR PATHS.**

### CLIII. To the Chapter of Modena. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 27 April.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Memorie storiche modenesi*, IV, p. 13.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons the provost and chapter of Modena, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The fervent and sincere devotion which you show toward us and the Roman Church moves and urges us more readily to grant you our favour in the things which you justly request, especially when you seek from us matters concerning the peace and welfare of your church. For we have learned from a rescript of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, that you formerly, after carefully considering the resources of the Church of Modena and with deliberate counsel, decreed that that church should have no more than fourteen canons, or fewer, unless the means of the church should increase by the Lord’s gift so that it could honourably maintain more. We therefore, assenting to your petitions, hold the aforesaid constitution ratified and confirmed; following the example of that predecessor of ours, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 27 April, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### CLIV. He Exempts the Priory of Bromholm from the Authority of the Monks of Acre. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 7 May.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 635.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman WILLIAM de Glanvill, advocate of the priory of Bromholm, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1032A] Although we are bound to consider the welfare of every person, we must give particular attention to the interests of those who have dedicated themselves to religion and, as far as we can with God’s help, bear their burdens. We have learned that, when your predecessors had, from regard for divine mercy, founded a certain house on their estate at Bromholm and endowed it with possessions so that brethren might serve the Lord there under the religious habit, the monks of Acre, because at request they sent two of their fellow monks to that house in order to teach the brethren more fully the observance of their order, do not hesitate to burden that house with their own monks who are blind, lame, infirm, and deprived of bodily strength, and to withdraw and remove from it brethren suited to the observance of the order and to the house itself.

Wishing, therefore, with paternal solicitude to provide for the preservation of the aforesaid priory and to cut away by the sickle of apostolic correction what is wrongly attempted against it, by the authority of these presents we grant to you, and through you to the said house, that the aforesaid house of Bromholm shall remain perpetually free, without the impediment of appeal or objection, from the unlawful jurisdiction and molestation of the aforesaid monks of Acre. We further add that, upon the death of the person who at present presides as prior over the aforesaid house, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of subreption or force, except one whom your discretion and the brethren, by common counsel or by the choice of the sounder part, in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, [Col. 1032C] provide to be elected prior.

Therefore let no person whatsoever presume to infringe this page of our grant or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 7 May, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### CLV. Bull for the Reform of the Monastery of St Caesarius at Arles. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 10 May.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, I, *Instrumenta*, p. 100.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother ***, Archbishop of Arles, greeting, etc.

It has been reported to us that a certain monastery of nuns was established and founded by Blessed Caesarius, formerly bishop of Arles, within the walls of your city, on a certain allodial estate, upon the condition that they should render reverence and obedience to his successors. Although their monastery was endowed from the goods of your church, as is contained in ancient and other privileges, the nuns, growing corrupt with the fatness of iniquity over time, presume to impair the ancient dignity and reverence of their mother Church and to turn away from its obedience. Thus they are granted free licence to roam about the city and borough and to presume many other things contrary to their honour. For, as we have heard, they elect abbesses and other persons in their church according to their own judgment; admit as many sisters as they wish; presume publicly to visit the sick throughout the town; and veil women by themselves. All these things disfigure the appearance of their religious profession and seem gravely to derogate from the dignity of your Church. Therefore, lest archiepiscopal authority and the dignity of your Church suffer a more harmful loss of their rights in this respect, and lest the nuns themselves be found notably disobedient, we have commanded the abbess and nuns of the aforesaid monastery by apostolic letters to render to you and your Church obedience both due and devoted, and no longer presume any of the foregoing acts. We therefore command your Fraternity by apostolic letters not to delay to recall them from their rashness to their former devotion and reverence for your Church, by our authority and with the impediment of appeal removed, and to restrain them entirely from attempting the foregoing acts.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 10 May, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### CLVI. He Commands the Bishops of Arezzo, Siena, and Pistoia, When Requested by the Abbot and Monks of Passignano, to Raise the Body of St John Gualbert “from the Place Where It Lies and Wholesomely Stir the Devotion of the Faithful to Venerate Him.” (Rome, at St Peter’s, 23 May.)

[*Acta Sanctorum*, July, vol. III, 339.]

[Col. 1033C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, the Bishops of Arezzo, Siena, and Pistoia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that it greatly advances our salvation if we keep celebrated remembrance on earth of those whose continual intercessions in heaven we hope will aid us, by recalling their merits in solemn praises. Therefore, when our beloved son Gregory, abbot of the monastery of Passignano, came to the Apostolic See and offered before us and our brethren many certain proofs of the holy conduct, life, and merits of the blessed confessor John, whose venerable body rests in his church, [Col. 1033D] we, having heard of the glory of his virtues and miracles and that among the fleshly he had had a spiritual life, and among humankind an angelic conduct, judged that he—now freed from the body and already worthy to be with Christ—should be enrolled, by counsel of our brethren, in the catalogue of saints, lest we should seem in some measure to detract from his due honour and glory if we allowed one sanctified by God to lack any longer the veneration of human devotion.

Since, therefore, his lamp has hitherto so burned in this world that, through God’s grace, it has deserved to be placed not under a bushel but upon a lampstand, burning in itself through works of charity and shining upon others by example, we admonish and exhort your Fraternity in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters that, when requested by the aforesaid abbot and his brethren, you are to go together to the said monastery and, with the honour and reverence proper to such matters, solemnly raise the body of the holy man from the place in which it had been laid, as is fitting for a saint; wholesomely stir the devotion of the faithful to venerate him; and proclaim that he is to be specially observed each year on an appointed day with a solemn feast.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 23 May, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### CLVII. To the Dean and Archdeacons of the Church of Lincoln.—Against Geoffrey, Archbishop of York. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 31 May.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 601.]

[Col. 1034B]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons HAIME [Note: [Col. 1033D] Perhaps HAIMON. HARD.] Dean of Lincoln, and ROGER of Leicester and WINEMER of Northampton, archdeacons established in the diocese of Lincoln, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our most beloved sons Simon, dean, and the chapter of the Church of St Peter at York have represented to us that, after an appeal had been lodged with us, the clerics of the chapel of our venerable brother, the archbishop of that church, and certain other persons of the same city, [Col. 1034C] were intruded into the cathedral church, to the grave prejudice of those canons. Having excluded the vicars and clerics of that church, they presumed to minister there and, contrary to approved and ancient custom, to overturn the order of the church by usurping the places and stalls of persons in choir and chapter. Wishing to oppose such presumptions as is fitting, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if what we have stated is true, you compel those presumptuous persons, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal set aside, to render due satisfaction in your presence to the Church of St Peter itself and to the canons concerning these matters. Cause also the losses which are established to have been inflicted upon the aforesaid chapter by those clerics to be repaired as justice requires. If all of you cannot be present to execute these matters, nevertheless let two of you carry them out.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 31 May, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### CLVIII. He Commands the Bishops Arpinus of Polignano and William of Conversano to Assemble at the Monastery of St Benedict of Conversano, Formerly Abundant but Now Most Destitute through the Fault of Its Superiors, and to Arrange for the Election of a Suitable Abbot. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 2 June.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VII, 703.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable [Col. 1035A] brethren A., Bishop of Polignano, and W., Bishop of Conversano, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we ought to exercise pastoral care for all churches, it is especially fitting to provide for those which belong directly to the Roman Church without intermediary. It has come to our hearing that the monastery of St Benedict of Conversano, which had been enriched with many possessions and resources and in which forty monks formerly dwelling under the Rule of Blessed Benedict rendered service to the Lord, is said to have been reduced through the negligence of its superiors to such poverty that scarcely three or four monks can in any degree be found there who can celebrate the divine offices as regularly and devoutly as they ought. Although we believed that the same monastery would be restored through the Bishop of Molfetta, to whom its administration had been entrusted by apostolic authority, the opposite occurred in every respect: after all the goods of the aforesaid monastery had been taken away, he sought flight and left the monastery entirely stripped of all its property.

Wishing, therefore, that the monastery itself, which belongs directly to the Roman Church without intermediary, should suffer no further loss through the absence of a shepherd, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters that you go together to the aforesaid monastery and grant the monks authority to elect an abbot from the body of the monastery, if a suitable person can be found in it; otherwise, let them arrange to elect from elsewhere such a superior as may enable the monastery to receive welcome growth both in spiritual and temporal matters. In order that provision may more swiftly be made for that monastery by our authority, which we likewise will, command, and enjoin, take care to carry this out without delay.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 4 July, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### CLIX. He Commands M[ichael], Archbishop, and M., Archdeacon of Sens, to Judge between the Chapter of Chartres and the Countess of Chartres. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 6 June.)

[*The Penitential of Theodore*, II, 567.]

[Col. 1035D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother M., archbishop, and to the beloved son M., Archdeacon of Sens, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As Henry the archdeacon, Reginald the provost of Masengeio, Simon of Berou, Ralph of Bellovidere, Germund of Levesvilla, and the chapter of Chartres represented to us in a communication sent to us: when, in accordance with the customary liberty of the Church of Chartres, they recalled Gilbert, Laurence, William, Robert, and Andrew—laymen of Chartres received under the care and likewise the protection of that church—to their domestic service, the countess of Chartres, without any failure of justice, together with her supporters who are of your province, violently seized one of the aforesaid servants, namely Gilbert, and despoiled both him and the others of all their goods and property without due process of law. And after many injuries had been inflicted upon the aforesaid clerics on this account, the matter was submitted by both sides to arbitrators, no security, however, having been provided on the clerics’ side. Yet the arbitrators, with the parties present before them, refused to render a full award, asserting that they ought not to arbitrate concerning their customs or liberties, and that they were not bound to do so by the terms of the submission.

They nevertheless declared, according to their own will, that the aforesaid servants should remain more freely in the service and under the ecclesiastical protection of those clerics until the approaching feast of the Nativity of Saint John, and no longer, without the arbitrators’ permission, enjoying full restitution of the things taken from them. Since, therefore, the aforesaid clerics acknowledged themselves bound by oath to uphold the customs and liberties of their church, and consequently could not in good conscience endure their infringement, they asked that provision be made for them in this case by letters of our commission.

Therefore, by apostolic writings, we command your prudence diligently to admonish and induce the aforementioned arbitrators to seek a way of perfect concord between the aforesaid parties. But if those arbitrators should perhaps refuse to do so, or to settle them concerning the question already mentioned according to what is consonant with reason, then, by our authority, summon the parties before you; and, after diligently hearing and examining what has been alleged on either side, settle the case by means of justice, all appeal set aside. Nor are you to allow the aforesaid clerics, so long as they are willing to submit to justice before the arbitrators or under your examination, to be deprived of possession of the aforesaid servants, or to suffer any rash act done unjustly or contrary to the approved liberties or customs of their church—without prejudice from any letters, should any appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See, that are contrary to truth and justice.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth Ides of June, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

CLX. To [Adelard], bishop of Verona: he commands him to receive an oath from the duke of Austria. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 6 June.)

[TWYSDEN, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, I, 675.]

[Col. 1036D]

Pope COELESTINE to the bishop of Verona.

We will, and by apostolic writings command and enjoin, that you receive from the duke of Austria an oath, together with such other security as you know to be expedient, that he will in every respect and without fraud obey our commands which we may convey to him through you, or by letter, messenger, or messengers. Once this has been received, command him by virtue of that oath to release all the hostages of the king of England; to remit every condition which he has imposed upon him; and, restoring in full to him and his people the offerings made to him by them and whatever he received from the unjust ransom of that king, to cause those hostages to return safely to their own homes, and henceforth not to attempt such acts. Moreover, let him make suitable satisfaction for the injury and damages inflicted.

When these matters have been duly fulfilled and carried out, grant him and his people the benefit of absolution, and lift the interdict to which his land was subject. Likewise, after absolution has been granted to the same duke and his people, command them, under obligation of the aforesaid oath, to proceed as quickly as they can to the regions of Jerusalem and to remain for as long in Christ’s service as the aforesaid king is known to have remained in captivity. Should they fail to observe this, reduce him and his people, all appeal set aside, to the same sentence of excommunication.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth Ides of June, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

CLXI. To the bishop of Lincoln.—He orders an inquiry into the misconduct of the archbishop of York. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 8 June.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 599.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Lincoln, and to his beloved sons the archdeacons of Northampton and the prior of Pontefract, greeting.

The Lord Jesus Christ, mediator of God and humankind, whose providence is not deceived in its ordering, willed that the headship and teaching authority of discipline for the whole Church should be reserved to the most holy Roman Church, and that all other churches should be subject to its governance and correction. Thus, a special fullness of power having been granted to it, it belongs also [or: is proper to it] to correct the transgressions of the rest and to approve by the authority of the apostolic majesty what is laudably done.

Therefore we, who by divine dispensation have been raised to its governance, wish to love our brothers and fellow bishops with such caution and discretion that we may not seem to prefer affection and familiarity for them to the duty of our calling; especially since the love by which one is bound to love a person, not that person’s error, has its limits.

Now it has come to our hearing through the representation of persons and of the chapter of the church of York; and the testimony of our beloved sons Robert of York, Roger of Selebi, and eleven other abbots of the Premonstratensian Order appears plainly to establish the same: namely, that our venerable brother Geoffrey, archbishop of York, despising the obligations of the office entrusted to him, and idly occupied with hunting, hawking, and other military pursuits, has since his promotion devoted neither hand nor effort to the ordination of clerics, the dedication of churches, or the holding of synods, nor has he blessed any abbot. Yet, against both clerics and abbots, he has been accustomed, according to his own impulse, indiscriminately to let loose his tongue for cursing and excommunication.

He empties and overturns the liberties and approved customs of his church; appeals, which are ordinarily a remedy for the oppressed, he has brought into contempt, to the injury of the Roman See. Many persons, because they had lodged appeals to us, he caused to be harshly confined in prison chains; after appeals had been made to us, he stripped members of his church of honours and benefices; disregarding appeals, he subjected certain canons to excommunication; the privileges of the Roman pontiffs are rendered wholly ineffective in his presence by his authority; and anyone who might otherwise be safe by producing our privilege loses before him the desired benefit of protection.

When anyone happens, by judges delegated through our authority, to be restored to a church or possession of which he had been deprived, he immediately finds as an enemy the very person through whom the judgment ought to have been executed. For he has deprived many thus restored, and, attacking churches through his servants, is alleged to have broken down church doors and violently expelled them. He has also perniciously caused very many to incur the guilt of perjury, withdrawing them by a kind of coercive necessity from the obedience which they had promised under oath to render canonically to their archdeacons.

Moreover, attacking the cathedral church with a multitude of armed men, he caused the chapter-house doors to be violently broken open and carried away; and he caused the goods of the canons and of many others, who had deposited their belongings both in the church and in the treasury, to be forcibly detained. On account of all these matters the chapter of York appealed to our hearing.

We have further learned from the testimony aforesaid that, when churches are at times vacant, he does not admit suitable persons presented to him by those to whom presentation belongs; rather, he assigns them either to boys or to persons of lesser respectability, himself exercising both the office of presenter and that of institutor. Or he causes them to remain vacant solely at his own will, so that their revenues may be applied to his own uses, and he does not hesitate to retain for himself what was due for the maintenance of some honourable cleric.

They added also that, although spiritual gifts ought to be distributed freely and without corruption, he frequently, when he grants a church, either divides it into portions contrary to the canonical statutes of the Church, or retains in it a new and unlawful pension; and he absolves very many excommunicated or suspended persons only when money intervenes. Religious and honourable men are despised and contemptible in his sight, whereas base and suspect persons readily obtain his familiarity and favour. Thus, if he lives in this manner and his conduct consists in such things, it is to be feared that he is for the flock entrusted to him a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal, rather than an example of instruction or a support and defence against spiritual wickedness.

Since, therefore, the matters set forth above demand the care of an inquiry, we have thought fit to commit the investigation of them to your prudence, in which we have full confidence. By apostolic writings we command you to go to the church of York and, having summoned the abbots, priors, and other ecclesiastical persons of the diocese of York, to inquire diligently whether he has governed the church and province of York so uselessly and perniciously. If lawful accusers appear concerning the foregoing matters, hear what they may choose to allege against the aforesaid archbishop; and, after diligently hearing and examining them, take care to transmit to us the depositions sealed with your seals, appointing the parties a suitable term within which, sufficiently prepared, they may come to the Apostolic See to receive there, God granting it, what is canonical.

But if accusers are lacking and public reputation is against him, require him, by our authority and with the impediment of appeal removed, to make canonical purgation with three bishops and an equal number of abbots. If he should fail in this, cause him, suspended from the archiepiscopal office and administration, to be presented before the apostolic presence, so that there, with the Lord’s assistance, he may be more fully instructed how he and those like him ought to minister in the house of God. If the same archbishop should wish to allege anything against them, hear it likewise and transmit it to us enclosed under your seals, so that what is canonical may be determined concerning these matters.

Moreover, if the said archbishop, in evasion of our command, should lodge an appeal or set out to come to the Apostolic See before your summons reaches him, set him a term of three months within which he must personally appear before us. If he does not do so, then, by our authority and with appeal removed, declare him from that time suspended from every pontifical office and from the administration of the archbishopric. If all of you cannot be present for carrying these matters out, nevertheless let two of you execute them.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth Ides of June, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

CLXII. He takes the Church of Nidaros under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 15 June.)

[THORKELIN, *Diplomata Arnamagnæana*, II, 13.]

[Col. 1039D]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HEIRIC, archbishop of Nidaros, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

We desire that the dignities and rights of our brothers and fellow bishops be preserved with such care and diligence that, in those matters in which they reasonably request apostolic favour, they may perceive it to assist them with greater kindness. Accordingly, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously grant your just requests and receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves your person and the Church of Nidaros, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same Church of Nidaros now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. We likewise confirm by apostolic authority, to you and to that church, the liberties and immunities which the church subject to your governance is known hitherto to have obtained by grants of kings, especially of King Magnus of Norway; and we decree that they shall possess perpetual validity.

It shall also be lawful for you and your successors, in chapels founded or endowed by royal liberty, just as in other churches or chapels of your province, to institute suitable persons without the kings’ consent or presentation, in accordance with the renunciation which those kings are shown to have made of their right of patronage by public instruments and their privileges.

Furthermore, we decree that in elections of bishops and abbots of your province no force, power, authority, or consent of king or prince shall intervene, nor shall anyone obtain an office of ecclesiastical prelacy through their favour, except one whom those to whom the election belongs judge, by unanimous election, to be more suitable for the vacant church in knowledge and character.

Desiring also that the clerics of the kingdom of Norway enjoy their due liberty, by this present document we strictly prohibit any bishop, abbot, or cleric—since they do not possess royal rights—from being compelled to take up arms, go on campaign, or expend anything of his own for that purpose. An exception is made if necessity of such gravity threatens that this is permitted by the diocesan bishop after consultation with the wiser and more discerning ecclesiastical men. If, however, any cleric who holds no ecclesiastical prelacy and is not specifically assigned to a ministry or office which he cannot leave without loss to the Church is permitted by his bishop to follow an expedition, let him serve there in such an office as is fitting for his profession or order.

In particular, we decree that priests or clerics and laymen assigned to the service of the martyr Saint Olaf, and all other priests dwelling in countryside or town, who are exempt by the privilege of royal piety, shall be wholly free from those compulsory public services which are called in the Norwegian language by the fixed and proper term *Laeidangir*.

Moreover, we grant you the right to send to Iceland thirty measures of flour, called by the proper name *Lest*, for purchasing garments for the use of the ministers of Saint Olaf, particularly at those times when the abundance of the country permits it. We also confirm by apostolic authority to the same church the customs dues owed annually to the church of Saint Olaf from one ship arriving from Iceland. We will and decree that all who come to its church for devotion and pilgrimage, whether strangers or natives, in time of war or peace, shall enjoy especial and secure protection in going and returning. We decree that those found guilty of molesting such persons shall be subject to the canonical penalty established against them by general determination.

We decree that ecclesiastical burial is to be denied to those whom pilgrims happen to kill in such a conflict in their own defence. We wholly prohibit clerics from appearing before secular judgment in cases forbidden by canon law; and we decree that those who attempt, contrary to the common prohibition and our special prohibition in this matter, to submit themselves to secular judgment shall be canonically punished at the discretion of the diocesan bishop.

No one whatsoever may destroy churches that have been consecrated, or for any reason transfer them from place to place, without permission of the diocesan bishop. Nor may any king or prince alter the approved and written laws of the country without the consent of the bishops and the counsel of the wise, nor alter, to the detriment of churches or clerics and contrary to ancient custom, monetary penalties imposed upon clerics or laymen; nor may he require an oath of fealty from any bishop or abbot who does not possess royal rights, either before consecration or blessing or afterwards. In giving tithes from their lands and dwellings, kings must in every respect follow the canonical sanctions.

Likewise, by the authority of this present document we grant you, according to what your predecessors are known to have held, that it may be lawful for you and your successors—not for pleasure but for your and the Church’s advantage—to buy birds, namely falcons, goshawks, and grey [birds; perhaps grey falcons], as has hitherto been observed by your predecessors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and maintenance of those concerned shall be preserved whole and shall be of benefit to their uses in every respect, the authority of the Apostolic See being preserved in all things.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting rashly to act contrary to this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning does not correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance.

But let all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Coelestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavianus, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tusculum. I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Saint Callistus. I, Huguccio, cardinal priest of Saint Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cynthius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Soffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Aegidius, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1194, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Coelestine III.

CLXIII. He takes the Church of Saint Peter of York under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 16 June.)

[WILKINS, *Concilia*, I, 503.]

[Col. 1042D]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SIMON, dean, and the chapter of the church of Saint Peter at York, and to their successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Since the Roman Church, over which by the Lord’s gift we preside, has always customarily attended with pious generosity to the just requests of petitioners, it is fitting and appropriate that those whose faith and devotion in its honour and reverence are proved by certain experience should trust in its special protection and defence, and should be able to be fortified against the attacks of evil men as with the shield of a desired defence.

Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests, receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves your church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it with the privilege of this present writing. Therefore, whatever possessions and whatever goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the vill of Dalton with its appurtenances; the vill of Cotom with its appurtenances; the vill of Brothton with its church, mill, and all other appurtenances; the vill of Helperby with its appurtenances; the land of Ulfrikby with its appurtenances; the land of Gisppesmare with its appurtenances; the land of Ledesham with its appurtenances; the land of Hoton with its appurtenances; the church of Burgo with its chapel and all other appurtenances; the church of Lanum with its chapel, the tithes of the archbishop’s mills, and all other appurtenances; the church of Burton with its appurtenances; the church of Lesyngton with its appurtenances; the church of Quetungkebur with its appurtenances; the church of Saint John at York Bridge; the church of Saint John in the Marsh; the church of Saint Lawrence in Walmgate, with its appurtenances within and outside the city; the church of Saint Andrew in Hecmangergat; the church of Saint Mark in Coney Street; the church of Saint Mary beyond the Ouse; sixty shillings from the manor of Patrington; two marks of silver from the fair of Saint Peter in Chains at York; eleven shillings from synodals for the chantry, and one hundred shillings for the chantry, and one hundred shillings belonging to the master of the schools.

We also confirm to you and your successors the ancient and reasonable customs of your church hitherto observed, and decree that they shall be firmly observed in your church in future times without anyone’s contradiction. Furthermore, by apostolic authority we prohibit your archbishop, whoever he may be at the time, from daring, without the consent of the dean and chapter, to pronounce any sentence of excommunication, interdict, or suspension against the dean, any person, the canons, or their servants—whether clerics or laymen—contrary to the immunity which your predecessors and you have hitherto enjoyed; or from excluding them from choir or from entry into churches. If he presumes to do so, we decree that the sentence shall have no force.

We further decree that the dean canonically appointed in your church according to God shall not be bound, under the pretext of an ecclesiastical benefice, to render homage to the archbishop contrary to the customary liberty and custom hitherto observed in your church.

Moreover, desiring with paternal concern to provide that you suffer no injury in matters known to belong to you, we confirm to you and your successors the free election of the master of the hospital of Saint Peter at York, as your church has hitherto possessed it by ancient and approved custom; so that whoever is to be appointed at the time may be appointed only through your customary election. And lest the condition of your church suffer alteration or disturbance through any rashness regarding reasonable observances, we declare valid, and decree to possess perpetual force, the dignities, liberties, and immunities reasonably granted to you and your church by kings, princes, or your archbishops, and approved by Roman pontiffs, or contained in authentic documents of kings, princes, archbishops, bishops, and Roman pontiffs.

We further prohibit the archbishop or any other person, contrary to the ancient and approved liberty of the church of York, from presuming to burden your persons, canons, clerics, or men with pecuniary penalties in the customary and due excommunications, or to remit without due satisfaction sentences which your chapter, according to the ancient and approved custom of your church, has reasonably judged should be pronounced against unlawful invaders or rash detainers of its goods or possessions, and against persons grievously offending against your men.

We also decree that the institution of canons or persons shall be free, as has been observed from the very foundation of the place: namely, that an honourable and suitable person to whom your archbishop judges a vacant prebend or dignity in your church should be granted shall, according to the ancient custom of your church, be presented to the dean and chapter. Once received by the chapter as a canon, that person must be invested with book and bread by the hand of the dean and chapter; then, having been received into the kiss of the brethren, he shall take the customary and due oath to preserve fidelity to your church, to defend to the best of his ability its liberties and customs consonant with right, and not to disclose the secrets of the chapter. Then, by order of the dean and chapter, he shall be installed by the hand of the precentor, as is customary. But if anyone has been introduced into your church by any person contrary to the ancient and approved custom, he shall be regarded neither as a person nor as a canon.

If your archbishop does not confer a vacant prebend or personate in your church upon a suitable person within the time prescribed by the form of the Lateran Council, after canonical admonition has been given, it shall be lawful for you, by apostolic authority and notwithstanding anyone’s opposition or appeal, to confer it contrary to the statutes of that council.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and maintenance of those concerned shall be preserved whole and shall be of benefit to their uses in every respect, the authority of the Apostolic See being preserved. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act contrary to this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless that person corrects the offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But may all who preserve the rights of that place receive the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our protection, confirmation, prohibition, and concession, or rashly act contrary to it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let that person know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

CLXIV. He commands the chapter of Tarragona to declare William Raimund, who cruelly killed Archbishop Berenguer in the city of Girona, anathematized and to place his land under interdict; further, under penalty of excommunication and interdict, to exhort the king and queen of Aragon to banish William and his accomplices from the whole kingdom, restore to the church of Tarragona the things taken away, and make satisfaction for the injuries. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 17 June.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 643.]

[Col. 1045C]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of Tarragona, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It would be more fitting to lament than to write concerning so heinous a crime as that which William Raimund, a son of iniquity, presumed to perpetrate with obstinate and persistent audacity: he did not fear to lay wicked hands upon his father and lord, [Col. 1045D] Archbishop Berengar of blessed and pious memory—whose niece he had taken as wife—and to butcher him mortally with a cruel sword. For William himself, as we have heard, was the archbishop’s man and had received many benefices from him; he had also married, as we have said, the archbishop’s niece. Yet, devising a ruinous deception, he sent a messenger—the interpreter of his conceived wickedness—to the bishop, saying that his wife, namely the bishop’s niece, wished to confer and deliberate with him about a certain matter. Therefore, when the archbishop came to Gerona because he was expected to do so on that account, William met him as though peacefully and, according to the prophetic oracle, like a deceitful man carrying evil vessels, wickedly wounded him [Col. 1046A] and threw him from the mule upon which he rode to the ground.

O monstrous crime, worthy of every detestation! By it the laws of peace and Christian religion are violated, and a son’s weapons are sharpened against his father. Rather, according to the prophet, that sword ought to have been turned into a ploughshare and the spear into a pruning-hook (Isa. 2). But, that the iniquity of this wicked man might issue forth from his fatness, he was not content to inflict a mortal wound upon him. After striking him a third time, when the archbishop began to make confession to the chaplain who was present, this man of blood—though clothed in the habit of the Cistercian order—feared neither God nor respected man. Having cast off human pity and clothed himself in diabolical ferocity, he strove with all his strength to prevent the confession.

Nevertheless, the Author of [Col. 1046B] supreme mercy, who wills that none should perish (2 Pet. 3), at last granted the archbishop the grace of confession. During that confession, while the persecutor raged against him with the sword, the archbishop, following the priest’s counsel, spared his murderer and unceasingly implored God for him, in imitation of the glorious first martyr. Finally, that insatiable murderer, having at first left him half alive upon the ground and gone as far away from him as, it was thought, two or three crossbow-shots might be discharged, returned, like a twisting serpent—or rather a crab—and inflicted so many wounds upon him that there was scarcely a place left for wounds. And, omitting nothing of his malice, indeed discharging all the venom which he had drunk in with savage mouth, he descended from the horse on which his pride had set him and, after so many and such atrocious wounds, spilled out the archbishop’s brain with the point of his sword. [Col. 1046C]

Alas! Why do you compel mortal hearts, detestable monster of wrath? Behold how shamefully you have caused the shepherd of the Church to be slaughtered; behold, the pillar of the Church falls! But what follows? By the hand of Him whose right hand performs mighty deeds, the son of Belial shall be trampled down; iniquity shall lie to itself, and the evil deed—not, we say, of a man, but of one who is no man—shall pay the penalty due. Rise up, therefore, zealous defenders and sons of God’s Church; courageously discharge the duty of your office. Let not Tarragona province alone mourn this accomplished crime, but all Spain, indeed the whole of Christendom; and in this [Col. 1046D] grief let it be struck with even greater astonishment, since not only this archbishop, but also the third after him, under the rule of one and the same prince, were both slain by the sword within this period. Nor is the cause for sorrow diminished but increased by the report that the illustrious king and queen of Aragon not only do not grieve over this evil, but even add affliction to the afflicted and crush your Church, already broken by repeated blows.

For when—if the report is true, as we greatly wonder—a complaint about these matters was immediately sent before them, they did not take care to administer justice. They were unmindful of that saying of Isaiah: “A king shall reign in justice, and princes shall rule in judgment” (Isa. 32); and of that precept of the Wise Man: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” [Col. 1047A] (Wis. 1). Thus it has come about that this utterly wicked man, fearing no rigor of justice, wanders about wherever he wishes with unrestrained steps, as if he had killed a sheep or calf; and the affair has become an evil and ruinous example. To such a degree is this so that no ecclesiastical person goes even a mile from his own seat without fear of danger, while the reverence owed to your Church and its ministers has almost withered away and vanished into the wind. For clerics—who are counted as the chosen and royal race, a people for God’s possession, and Christ’s own flock—have been reckoned as sheep for slaughter, made a reproach to their neighbors, an object of scorn and derision.

The aforesaid king and queen, both personally and through their agents, as well as through Hospitallers and religious persons, have afflicted your Church, both within the city [Col. 1047B] and outside it, with numerous losses and grave injuries. Since it has been reduced almost to nothing, and is thus torn apart in the slaughter of its shepherds through the wickedness of the children of men, no one is now found who dares submit his neck there to episcopal service. Therefore, because so heinous a crime ought not to be left uncorrected or unpunished, but such great crimes must be punished so that those who hear of them may not dare to commit similar acts, we command you by apostolic letters and, in virtue of obedience, strictly enjoin you under penalty of loss of offices and benefices and under threat of anathema: setting aside every excuse, delay, and appeal, you shall take care solemnly to declare the aforesaid William, son of perdition and treachery, and his accomplices, both clerics and laymen, to be anathematized, with bells rung and candles lighted; and you shall place all their land, and any other land in which they are present, under interdict. Do not relax the sentences which you pronounce until the anathematized William and his accomplices come before the Apostolic See.

We decree, moreover, that those clerics who gave counsel or consent that the aforesaid bishop should perish are to be deprived forever of ecclesiastical benefices. Without any exception, command all knights and other laymen in the territory subject to your Church by metropolitan right to pursue that wicked man and his followers as most desperate Saracens; [Col. 1047D] and let them in no way share with him in fire or water under the interdict. Nor may they presume to deal with him in any sale or purchase, in supplying provisions, or in receiving lodging, until he comes barefoot upon the ground, in great abstinence and harsh clothing, to the Apostolic See.

Furthermore, with all diligence admonish the king and queen and the other princes and barons, firmly enjoining them on our behalf to banish the oft-mentioned William and his accomplices from the whole kingdom; to restore to your Church everything taken from it; to confiscate the property of those who committed the aforesaid crime; to make satisfaction to the Church for the losses and injuries inflicted; and to permit it to remain peacefully in possession of its property and in freedom of election. [Col. 1048A] If, after your warning, they do not do these things, then, setting aside every favor and fear and removing every obstacle of contradiction or appeal, supported by the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and by our own, pronounce upon the persons of the king, queen, and others, and upon their lands, sentences both of excommunication and interdict, and cause them to be observed without challenge.

We therefore will, and by apostolic letters commanding you direct, that you take care to agree canonically and unanimously upon some suitable person and endeavor, by electing him, to nominate him archbishop, through whom the condition of the Church may be set in order and it may experience every benefit both spiritual and temporal. Show yourselves in every respect helpers and fellow-workers in pursuing the matters aforesaid, so that, as true sons, you may show by your inward grief over the trampling of your mother and the killing of your father.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July [17 June], in the fourth year of our pontificate.

## CLXV. He receives the Church of Halle, called “at the New Work,” under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 17 June.)

[LUDEWIG, *Rel.*, V, 63.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Dudo, provost of Halle, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, [Col. 1048C] in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by the Provider of all good things, so that we may cherish religious persons and endeavor by every means to advance those who please God well. For no apostolic service is pleasing to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the Church of Halle, called “at the New Work,” in which you have long been devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we establish that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted there according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God being favorable, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify these by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the parish in Halle; the churches of Saint Gertrude and Saint George; the chapels of Saint Paul, Saint Lambert, Saint Nicholas, and Saint Giles; the chapel in Gevekeosteyn; [Col. 1049A] the churches of Trote and Motzelitz; the churches of Dugaw and Cormbecke; the church of Stuvene, with all its appurtenances and all revenues belonging to the aforesaid churches or chapels; and the archdeaconry of Halle, extending to these boundaries: from the river Saale to Schrisize, and from the river Elster to the Vona. Moreover, the new village adjoining your church, with all its liberties and possessions; likewise the mills and fishing rights situated in the river Saale, with the gardens and meadows surrounding that river; nine holdings in the march of Halle; the tithe granted for the village of Honstede; nine holdings and four jugera belonging to a mill in Wizeke; one hundred holdings in Swinze, which Frederick, emperor of blessed memory, granted to your church; and thirty holdings [Col. 1049B] in Juterbock, which Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg of happy memory, bestowed on that church. We confirm to you, and through you to your church, by apostolic authority, all vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, and watercourses known to belong to your church and to lie within the boundaries noted above.

You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and released from secular bonds, who flee from the world, and retain them without any contradiction. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your church, from leaving that place without the permission of his provost, except for the purpose of entering a stricter religious order; and no one may dare retain one who departs without letters of the community guaranteeing him. We also forbid anyone, without a manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against you or your churches, or to burden you with new and unlawful exactions. We hold valid the ancient liberties and immunities and reasonable customs granted to your church and observed hitherto, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired forever. Furthermore, we forbid anyone within the bounds of your parish to dare construct a new chapel or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop and of yourselves, without prejudice, however, to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. When a general [Col. 1049D] interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

We will that chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordinations of your canons or clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders shall be supplied to you freely and without improper exaction by the diocesan bishop, if he is Catholic and enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See. We also decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. [Col. 1050A] On the death of you, the present provost of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any cunning of usurpation or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder counsel of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly attempt in future rashly to act against this document of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his fault by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. [Col. 1050B] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Giles, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July [17 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1194 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III. [Col. 1050C]

## CLXVI. He receives the convent of Saint Mary at Heinsberg under protection and confirms its possessions.

[HUGO, *Annales Praemonstratenses*, I, documents, p. 651.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved in Christ, the mistress holding office and the sisters of the church of Saint Mary at Heinsberg, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1050D] … Graciously assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolably for all time. …

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the possessions which you have in Heinsberg; the property which you possess in Humberse and Hoenge; and other property confirmed to your monastery by Philip, archbishop of Cologne, of blessed memory, and by Ralph, formerly bishop of Liège—we confirm these to you by apostolic authority. … [Col. 1051A]

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Giles, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the sixth day before the Nones of July [2 July], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1194 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

## CLXVII

1. To John, abbot of the monastery of Saints Facundus and Primitivus at Sahagún, and his successors, he grants “that, provided they are priests, they may give solemn and pontifical blessing in that monastery and in its other churches, and may, without appeal, bind or loose both clerics and laymen residing in the borough, in the preserve, and in other exempt churches.” He adds other privileges.

2. To John, abbot, and the convent of the monastery of Saints Facundus and Primitivus at Sahagún, he grants “that no person whatsoever, except the Roman pontiff or a cardinal legate of the Apostolic See, may pronounce upon their monks dwelling anywhere a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict.” He adds other privileges.

3. To the same persons, he declares that the monastery was founded by Berengar of Medina. (Lateran, 14 July.)

[ESCALONA, *Historia de Sahagún*, p. 563 ff.]

[Col. 1051B]

## CLXVIII. He grants Roger, abbot of the Neapolitan monastery of Saint Severinus, the use of a ring. (Lateran, 20 July.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullarium Cassinense*, II, 225.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1051C] son Roger, abbot of Saint Severinus of Naples, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of the Apostolic See has always been accustomed to cherish those whom it knows to be faithful and devoted to it, and to adorn them with some distinguished ecclesiastical honor as a token of special favor. Therefore, considering the devotion which you are known to have toward blessed Peter and ourselves, so that you may always be more devoted toward us and the Roman Church, and that others who see it may be more greatly encouraged to such devotion, we have thought fit to honor your person and church with a special favor. Since, therefore, the use of a ring has been granted to you personally at the request and earnest solicitation of our beloved son Albert, our subdeacon and chaplain, who is especially dear and acceptable to us, by apostolic kindness we have thought fit to grant forever the use of that same ring to you and, through you, to your successors canonically appointed.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [20 July], in the fourth year of our pontificate. [Col. 1051D]

## CLXIX. He receives the monastery of Bonne-Espérance under protection and confirms its property and privileges. (Lateran, 10 November.)

[HUGO, *Annales Praemonstratenses*, vol. I, documents, p. 304.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Robert, abbot of the church of Blessed Mary of Bonne-Espérance, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, [Col. 1052A] in perpetuity.

Those who choose the religious life ought to have the protection of the Apostolic See, lest an attack of any rashness either turn them aside from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, following the example of Alexander, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary of Bonne-Espérance, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution [Col. 1052B] of the brethren of Prémontré shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s help, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify these by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all lands, woods, meadows, waters, pastures, and all its appurtenances. The land of Bergesies and the adjoining possessions in the territory of Bruile, with the annual revenues which you have in those villages. The portion of the tithe at Lestines which you hold from the canons of Walcourt for an annual rent of eight Valenciennes pounds; and the mill which you possess in the same village from the church of Saint Mary of Cambrai, for an annual rent of six measures of grain, payable according to the lesser measure. The mill of Vallibus. The lands and revenues which you possess in the territory of Vellerella Sicca. The estate of Riverioles, which Henry the knight, together with his wife Matilda and his children, through the hand of Baldwin, count of Hainaut, for the sake of alms, made free from every land-rent belonging by right to himself; and whatever else he gave you by title of alms. The portion of land [Col. 1052D] formerly belonging to Saint Saviour. Another portion of land called Lemeis. The allod of Ramelgies. The land which you possess from the Templars in return for an annual rent of twenty-three measures of grain and the same quantity of oats, payable according to the lesser measure. Fifteen *binaria* of allod which two lay-sisters gave you as alms. The whole tithe of your lands and livestock at Ramelgies. Certain endowments at Merbioles, for which you pay the canons of Saint Ursinari fifteen Valenciennes solidi yearly. The wood called Roseria, and all that is known to belong to the estate of Riverioles. The estate of Daegnies, subject to an annual rent of ten measures of grain payable to Bado’s heirs. The portion of the tithe of the same village which you hold for rent. [Col. 1053A] The mill, and everything which you possess there by right in lands, meadows, and waters. The estate of Gays, with all its appurtenances, and the tithe of the livestock of that estate, which you possess from the church of Saint Humbert of Marigoles for a rent of five Valenciennes solidi. The estate of Marteri, with all its appurtenances. The portion of land which you have from the church of Saint John of Valenciennes, subject to a rent of five measures of oats, two and a half measures of good wheat, two and a half measures of good rye, thirteen denarii, and the same number of capons, which you owe them each year. The entire tithe of grain and livestock of the estate of Morteri, for which you pay yearly to the canons of Cambrai ten measures of grain and three Valenciennes solidi. Everything which you possess in the borough of Valenciennes and in the place called Cortanna. The estate of Regenies, with all its appurtenances, namely lands, meadows, waters, woods, and pastures. The land of Corriel. The estate of Saint Nicholas with its appurtenances. The estate of Courrières with its appurtenances, subject to a rent of five Nivelles solidi owed to the abbess of Nivelles and the same amount to Gillard’s heirs. The estate of Bostelen with its appurtenances, and the tithe of the livestock of that estate, for an annual rent of five Valenciennes solidi, which you pay upon the altar of Theozies. The tithe of livestock from the estate within the abbey, for an annual rent of six Valenciennes denarii payable to the canons [Col. 1053C] of Cambrai. The altar of Leugnies, and that village itself with all its appurtenances. The altar of Curcellis and the allod of Saint Foillan, subject to an annual rent of sixty Namur solidi, which you pay each year to the canons of Saint Foillan at Fosses. The greater tithe and everything which you possess in the same village. The altar of Gennetines, and the entire tithe and endowments of that village. The altar of Orbais with its appurtenances. The altar of Carneriis with its appurtenances. The altar of Morlangueis with its appurtenances. The altar of Haina Saint Paul. The altar of Fellny. The altar of the Cross. The altar of Ressais. The altar of Mont-Saint-Aldegonde with its appurtenances. The altar of Mont-Sainte-Geneviève with its appurtenances. The altar of Herchelina with its appurtenances. The altar [Col. 1053D] of Senessia, together with the endowments and the whole tithe of that village and all its appurtenances. The altar of Rues Famelico. The mill of Berkellies, the lands, and everything which you possess there. The tithes, mill, and revenues which you possess in the village of Merbiis.

No one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on lands newly brought under cultivation which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and released from secular bonds, who flee from the world, and retain them without any contradiction. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, from leaving that place without the permission of his abbot; and no one may dare retain one who departs without letters of the community guaranteeing him. When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

In the parish churches which you possess, you may appoint four, or at least three, of your canons, one of whom shall be presented to the diocesan bishop so that he may entrust him with the care of souls; provided that he shall answer to the bishop in spiritual matters, but to you in temporal matters and in observance of the order. Furthermore, in your own cases, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, you may use the testimony of your brethren, lest your right suffer loss in any respect through lack of witnesses. [Col. 1054B] For chrism, holy oil, consecrations of churches, ordinations of clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders, the installation of an abbot in his seat, or any other ecclesiastical sacraments, no one may dare demand anything from you, whether under pretext of custom or in any other manner. We also forbid anyone, without a manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce against you or your monastery a sentence of excommunication or interdict, or to burden you with new and unlawful exactions.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any cunning of usurpation or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder counsel of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the order of the brethren of Prémontré. Wishing also to provide hereafter with paternal concern for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your houses or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft; set fire; shed blood; seize [Col. 1054D] or kill a person.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this writing, all liberties and immunities granted to your order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably bestowed upon you by kings and princes in pious devotion.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly attempt in future rashly to act against this document of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his fault by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. [Col. 1055A] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
[Col. 1055B] I, Albinus, bishop of Albano.  
I, Octavianus, bishop of Ostia and Velletri.  
I, John, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Pan., cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles.  
I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia.  
I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, of Viterbo.  
I, Guy, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus.  
I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Martin at Equitius.  
[Col. 1055C] I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill.  
I, Cinthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, Soffredus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes.  
I, Bernard, cardinal-priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia.  
I, Fid., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus.  
I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Prisca.  
I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico.  
[Col. 1055D] I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Lothair, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.  
I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo.  
I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint … in Via Lata.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the fourth day before the Ides of November [10 November], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1194 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

## CLXX. He receives the monastery of Holy Cross at Donauwörth under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 16 November.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, XVI, 17.]

[Col. 1056A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Everard, abbot of the monastery of Holy Cross at Wörth, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetual remembrance.

By the administration of the office entrusted to us, we are obliged to labor for the welfare of churches and to strengthen them by the protection of the Apostolic See, so that they may not be harassed by the unlawful molestations of anyone. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, following the example of Innocent, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, receive under the protection of that prince of the apostles and our own the aforesaid monastery of Holy Cross, in which you are devoted to divine service and which is known to belong to the right and property of blessed Peter; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in your monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God being favorable, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, [Col. 1056C] offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify these by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with its gardens, meadows, woods, holdings, and all its other appurtenances. We confirm to you and, through you, to your church by apostolic authority the tithes of your court of Cenoviale and the tithes of the newly cleared land called Wicharfruth, as you possess them justly and without dispute. Moreover, let no one presume to demand or exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands and at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics and [Col. 1056D] laymen, free and released from secular life, and retain them without any contradiction. Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving that place without his abbot’s permission, unless for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters of the community granting leave and providing assurance. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Moreover, we forbid anyone within the boundaries of your monastery’s territory to dare build anew a chapel [Col. 1057A] or oratory without the consent of both the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We further prohibit altogether the imposition of new and unlawful exactions by archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, deans, or any other ecclesiastical or secular persons. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of your monks or clerics who are to be advanced to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to furnish these things freely, without abuse or any exaction; otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer who enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See [Col. 1057B], and who, supported by our authority, shall provide you with what is requested.

Furthermore, we recognize as valid the ancient liberties and immunities and the reasonable customs granted to your church and hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken shall be preserved.
