Accordingly, on land belonging to the monastery of Saint Alexander, we caused a cross to be set up by our venerable brother Bernard, bishop of Parma, and also a stone to be blessed for the construction, at the head of the bridge, of a church in honour of God and in memory of Blessed Cecilia, virgin and martyr, to be subject to that monastery of Saint Alexander.
>
> “But lest a dispute concerning the boundaries of the parish should hereafter arise between the old and new churches, we define the parish so that all who dwell on the land of that abbess, and the houses of those of Cistelle, and six others, and any new houses which may arise toward the hills, shall be parishioners of the new church. We decree that the priests and clerics who shall from time to time serve in that new church shall, outside those boundaries, receive none of the parishioners of the aforesaid old church for contributions of bags or staffs, nor for offerings on the principal feasts, nor women rising after childbirth, unless by permission of the priests of the church mentioned above; and that they shall observe the general and spiritual interdicts of the bishop, or of the chapter if the episcopal see is vacant; shall come to chapter like the other chaplains; and shall observe whatever is decreed there.”

Therefore let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly act contrary to it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 13 Kalends of May [April 19], in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCV. Privilege for the church of Saint Genesius. (Lateran, April 24.)

*[BALUZ., Miscell.*, ed. Mansi, III, 426.]

[Col. 1085B] CELESTINE, bishop . . . to his beloved sons GREGORY, provost of Saint Genesius, and his brethren, present and future, to be canonically established, for ever.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled with the resulting effect of its desire, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, most beloved sons in Christ, since, inspired by divine grace, you have resolved to conform your conduct and serve almighty God under the discipline of canonical life and in common according to the institution of the holy Fathers, we rejoice in your desires with paternal affection. Hence, following the enactments of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Alexander II, Paschal, Eugenius, Anastasius, Alexander, Lucius, and Clement, we strengthen by the authority of this privilege the order of canonical life which you have professed and receive your church under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which that parish is situated, with all its appurtenances; a fourth part of the tithes of your whole parish; and everything which Bishop John, of happy memory, granted to your canonical church: the house of the lepers, with the church of Saint Lazarus beside the same parish and its appurtenances; all things lawfully given to you by the Lombards of San Miniato and confirmed by charters; and a third part of the alms offered for the dead buried anywhere within the bounds of the parish, as was granted and confirmed in writing to you by our predecessor Paschal, of good memory.

Likewise, in the borough, the church of Saint Giles with its appurtenances; the church of Saints Christopher, Justus, and Angel above the borough, with all their appurtenances. Also in the same borough, the church of Saint Peter; and, in the castle of San Miniato, the church of Saint Mary with its appurtenances, in both of which divine offices shall always be celebrated by those appointed there through our provision; and whatever right you have in that same church of Saint Mary through the church of Saint Christina. Likewise, the church of Saint Bartholomew with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Blaise; the church of Saint Stephen; the church of Saint Lawrence of Nocida; the church of Saint Peter above the Fountain; the church of Saint Andrew beside Ciculum Castle; the church of Saint Michael within the walls; the church of Saints James and Lucy; the church of Saint Donatus of Faugnana; the church of Saint Martin of Castilione; the church of Saint Hippolytus of Marzana; the church of Saint Mary of Calenzano; the church of Saint Quintin; the church of Colle; the church of Capriano; the church of Canneto; the church of Saint Mary of Montarso; [Col. 1086B] the church of Monterotundo; the church of Planatole; the church of Brusciano; the church of Saint Stephen of the Tower; the church of Saint Peter of Marcignana; the church of Saint Donatus of the Island; the church of Saint Angel of Rophia; the church of Saint Philip of Pinu; and the church of Saint Prosper of Montalprandi, with all their appurtenances; and whatever may hereafter be built within the bounds of a single parish. Also, whatever right you have in the estate of San Miniato, at Empoli, Monterappoli, and in the estate of Marrignana.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Unde, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo [Col. 1086C] and Tusculum. I, Guy, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Callistus in Santa Maria in Trastevere. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Martin. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen. I, Cinthius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Soffredus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, priest-cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Fidus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Velletri. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 1086D] I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Santa Maria in Portico. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Santa Maria in Agro. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint George at Velabrum [printed *Vellaurentis*, sic]. I, Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Santa Maria in Cosmedin [printed *Carmeld.*, sic]. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelo. I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of Santa Maria in Via Lata.

Done at the Lateran, through the hand of Cirinus [Cinthius], deacon-cardinal of Saint Lucy in Hortea [sic], chamberlain of the lord pope, on the 8th day before the Kalends of May [April 24], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1194, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

CCVI. To the provost and canons of Saint George of Ganaceto in the diocese of Modena—He confirms all their goods and privileges. (Lateran, April 25.)

*[MURATORI, Antiq. Ital.*, V, 209.]

[Col. 1087A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, provost of the church of Saint George of Ganaceto, and his brethren canonically appointed, for ever.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled with the resulting effect of its desire, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefits requested may usefully and undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Lucius, Urban, Gregory, and Clement, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid church of Saint George of Ganaceto, in which you are devoted to divine service. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grant of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances, and the other things which you hold in the estate of Ganaceto and in your parish. Whatever you hold at Villanova, Saliceto, Soleria, in the estate of Lamina, Campo Galliani, Albareti, Citanova, Bajoaria, Pirradelle, Curli, Cugnenti, Rammi, Fredi, Malliagalli, Nirano, Monte Ursi, Casale, Cugnone, and Montegibio. The church of Saint Zeno of Lamma; the church of Saint Matthew, which is beside the River Situle, with all their appurtenances. In the bishopric of Bologna, the possessions which you hold in the estates of Saint Mark, Restalini, Manzolini, and Montebelli. In the bishopric of Reggio, the possessions which you hold in the place called Saint Fabian, Fontana, Substiliolo, Casale Montalto, and Querzole. In the bishopric of Ferrara, the possessions which you hold in the district of Ficarolo, at Sadriano, in the estates of Manegii and Trecente, and in the village of Saint Anastasius, together with the lake called Dampnarolo.

No one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes of your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or of the increase of your animals. You may also receive clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, into conversion, and retain them without any objection. Further, since tithes are known to have been granted to ministers of churches by both Old and New Law, we forbid, under sentence of anathema, that you be harassed by laymen in the exaction of tithes.

Moreover, we forbid anyone, within your parish which includes the estate of Ganaceto, to presume to build a new church or oratory without the assent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving nevertheless the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices with closed doors, excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells not rung, and voice suppressed.

We also hold valid the liberties and immunities, as well as the ancient and reasonable customs, justly granted to your church by the bishops of Modena and other persons and hitherto observed; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times. We grant you free power to hear matrimonial cases for your parishioners, impose private and public penances, and elect a prelate and brethren, as has been known to be reasonably and peacefully observed in your church for forty years.

Moreover, we have received from the instrument of our above-mentioned predecessors Lucius, Urban, Gregory, and Clement that, with the consent of Gerard, archbishop of Ravenna of good memory, you prudently decreed that your church should be content with only eight canons, since its resources do not suffice adequately to maintain more. We, who by the office entrusted to us ought and wish to approve the good acts of all persons, following the example of the aforesaid predecessors, decree that this constitution, as it was canonically made by you and is contained in the authentic instrument of the same archbishop, shall stand ratified and strengthen it by the page of this present writing—unless in the course of time the resources of that church should be increased, so that a fitting sufficiency of necessities could be supplied to more persons.

Further, by apostolic authority we decree that no one shall presume, without manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce an interdict upon your church, or a bond of excommunication or sentence of suspension upon you. The sentences canonically rendered by the bishop of Modena, of good memory [name lost in a lacuna], in the case between you and Priest Stephen concerning the church of Saint James of Aqualonga and parochial right; and by Theobald, bishop of Ferrara of good memory, by delegation of Pope Lucius, in the question litigated between you and Isaac, former abbot of Vangaditio—we hold these valid and confirm them by apostolic authority, insofar as they are reasonably contained in their authentic writings and have been put into execution.

Moreover, we decree that the burial-place of that establishment shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict.

We therefore decree, etc.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. [Col. 1089A] I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto. I, Pand[ulf], priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Jordan, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Pudentiana, called Pastor. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Martin. I, Soffredus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, priest-cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Gra . . . ., deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 1089B]

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Centius, deacon-cardinal of Saint . . . . . in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the 7th day before the Kalends of May [April 25], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1195, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

CCVII. He praises the purpose of Henry, king of the Romans, to procure peace, send aid to the land of Jerusalem, and promote more effectively the common good of the Christian people. He commends his legates. (Lateran, April 27.)

*[JAFFÉ, Regesta Rom. pont.*, p. 900, from the Reichersberg codex.]

[Col. 1089C] To his dearest son in Christ H[ENRY], illustrious emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although by the common obligation the Roman pontiff is bound to hold and love the Roman emperor in the bonds of charity, we nevertheless, out of special [affection], ought to embrace your Highness, upon whose head we have placed the imperial crown with our own hands. Indeed, we have continually embraced you in relation to God, for we have desired and desire with our inmost wishes the salvation of your soul.

But the excesses of your men were the reason why we for some time suspended our pen from writing to you. Since your power did not resist their rashness, we feared that favourable imperial assent had been added to their evil deeds and that they had acted by your command. Yet, because the heart of a prince is in the hand of God, who turns it wherever he wills, more abundant thanks must be rendered to the King of kings. For you have shown us more fully, both by your letters sent to our brethren and filled with much devotion, and through legates of great rank, the sincerity of devotion which you are bound constantly to show toward your mother, the Roman Church.

For they humbly brought word concerning the procurement of peace, the sending of aid to the land of Jerusalem, and the improved advancement of the common good of the whole Christian people. From many indications it has appeared to us that your settled purpose is, through a more earnest zeal for correction, to amend whatever has been outrageously done by your people, and wholly to direct your ways toward him in whose dominion lie all powers and the rights of kingdoms: through whom kings reign and princes rule; who gives salvation to kings and causes emperors to proceed by the royal way; whom he makes happily to rule.

If the Apostolic See has refrained until now from writing to imperial Highness, it did not do so from contempt or arrogant pride, but because it earnestly desired that you might, as it were, be awakened from sleep to make satisfaction to the Church, which seemed to have been most grievously offended, and, like a dutiful son, to placate your mother in these matters. For we ought not to have acted otherwise, since we could not effectively invite distant persons to devotion to the Church, nor avoid the scandals of others, unless, by temporarily withholding the address of apostolic greeting from you—who ought to be the special son and defender of the Roman Church, and than whom no secular prince is closer to it—we endeavoured to induce you to do precisely this.

Therefore, since according to the Apostle’s teaching we admonish those whom we hold dear, we exhort imperial Majesty as earnestly as we can: considering what the Redeemer of humankind affirms in his Gospel, “It profits a man nothing if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his soul,” strive to pass beyond temporal goods and exercise imperial power on earth in such a manner that you do not lose but rather gain eternal goods, and may receive in heaven the unfailing prize from him whose dominion endures for ever; who truly redeemed humankind not with perishable gold or silver, but with his own blood poured out.

You will assuredly obtain this from the Lord himself if you always set him before your eyes; if you preserve inviolate the rights of his Church; and if you amend and cause to be amended with all speed those things which have been presumptuously undertaken to the offence of the divine Majesty and the manifest injury of that Church. Having fully conceived good hope in this matter from imperial prudence, although we decided to send three men, yet our venerable brother, the bishop of Palestrina [John], being hindered by bodily infirmity, we have, by counsel of the brethren, thought fit to send to your presence our beloved sons P[eter], priest-cardinal of Saint Cecilia, and G[ratian], deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian—men prudent and discreet, eminent in the Roman Church, and always devoted to the welfare of Church and empire. We have carefully entrusted to their mouths what they will more diligently make known to your principal Highness on our behalf. We wish their words to receive the same faith as if they had been spoken in person from our own mouth.

You therefore, dearest son, since you see that our silence has been broken and that the instruments of our voice have been loosened to write to you, so receive the language of apostolic greeting and blessing that it may find in you the desired fruit; and that for the happy condition of your empire and the safety of your person the universal Church may unceasingly intercede with God, and the Emperor of heaven may, at the Church’s prayers, direct your steps into the way of eternal salvation.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of May [April 27], in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCVIII. Privilege for the monastery of Lucca, in the diocese of Olomouc. (Lateran, April 27.)

*[HUGO, Annal. Praemonst.*, II, Proofs, p. 47.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of the monastery of Lucca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman Church is accustomed, by the office of its habitual piety, to love more earnestly devout and humble sons and, like a loving mother, to cherish them with the protection of her defence lest they be troubled by the molestations of wicked men. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, considering the devotion which you are known to have toward blessed Peter and ourselves, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons and monastery, together with all goods which it now reasonably possesses or may hereafter acquire, God propitious, by just means.

In particular, we confirm to you, and through you to that monastery, by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the possessions and other goods which Otto, duke formerly of Bohemia, of good memory, and his mother Maria granted to your monastery out of pious devotion, insofar as you possess them justly and without dispute. Therefore let no person whatsoever rashly disturb your persons or monastery or its goods, infringe this page of our protection and confirmation, or rashly act contrary to it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of May [April 27], in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCIX. He confirms the agreement made between Henry, provost of Hadmersleben, “and the nobleman Gardulf concerning the site of the church of Saint Stephen, through the intervention of C[onrad], archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Sabina.” (Lateran, April 27.)

*[JAFFÉ, Regesta*, 901, who says that this privilege survives on the back of a bull of Eugenius III, given in 1145, on 26 October. (See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, no. 42), which is preserved in Berlin in the possession of D. G. B. Friedlander.]

[Col. 1091D]

CCX. He receives the monastery of Ranshofen under protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Lateran, April 29.)

*[Monumenta Boica*, II, 325.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ETICHO, provost of the church of Saint Pancras the Martyr at Ranshofen, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those who choose the religious life, lest perhaps the assault of any rashness [Col. 1092A] either turn them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of St Pancras the Martyr, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other [Col. 1092B] just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church itself of St Pancras the Martyr, with its tithe and parochial right; the chapel of St Michael situated in the same place; the chapels of Neuchirchen, Haetenperig, Geroltzberig, the chapel on Mount St Giles, and the chapel of St Stephen the Protomartyr at Praunawe, with their appurtenances; the chapel of Hochwerich with its appurtenances, in that liberty in which Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg of good memory, reasonably confirmed it to you by his own writing: namely, that no one, except that archbishop himself [Col. 1092C] and the diocesan bishop and the provost of your church, ought to exercise any authority there.

Whatever right has been granted in chapels throughout whatever regions by the ministerials of your church—namely, at Ror on the boundary of Chremsmünster, in the chapel of Nonspach, in the parish of Althaim and Heinchirchen, in the parish of Zeidlarn, and in other places near or far which are free from parochial jurisdiction—we confirm to you by this present document, as has hitherto been observed.

We also will, and by apostolic authority command, that the boundary of the same church of St Pancras be inviolably observed for you and that church: the boundary which Henry II, emperor of the Roman Empire, of revered memory, with his bishops—namely Dietmar, archbishop of the Church of Salzburg; Pernger, bishop of the Church of Passau; and Nicenus, bishop of the Church of Laodicea, together with thirteen other [Col. 1092D] bishops—prudently established, and which Conrad II, king of the Romans, confirmed to that church by his authentic charter. It begins, namely, from Eltnawe as far as Gruzensewen, Grewen, and Bibenpach; Rantwinsbrunen, thence to Iden; also Raperch, Wiwersengen, and Berchsteig; Rechingen likewise and Huolvowen; and Langen by the game trail; the chapel of St George the Martyr; then Swarzegreben and as far as Auwerbach; then through Adelbrechtzberch; then through Puchchirchen; then in the river Maeticha—as is contained in your ancient privileges and is known to have been observed down to these times.

[Col. 1093A] Moreover, no one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the food of your animals. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars, and the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the grace and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these to you freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may freely have recourse to whichever bishop you prefer who enjoys the grace and communion of the Apostolic See; supported by our authority, he shall supply what is requested.

Upon the death of yourself, the present provost of that place, or upon your transfer to the government of another place, [Col. 1093B] or upon the death of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the greater or sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine.

Further, because your house has been so constituted that the advocate of the duke of Bavaria’s goods in those parts is also advocate of that place, we forbid either him or any of his subordinates to harass that place with unjust burdens. Rather, in the duke’s stead, as he himself established and confirmed by his charter, that advocate must defend and protect it together with its serfs and possessions, on this condition: that he hear both your complaints and those of your serfs, and administer fitting [Col. 1093C] justice, provided that the cases are such as do not require an ecclesiastical court. For this, however, he shall demand no *parata* from you, but shall receive only from the granary of the duke then in office, according to the ancient institution, what is due in his time.

Furthermore, that advocate shall have no power of disposition over your cloister, serfs, or possessions. We utterly forbid anyone to impose unlawful exactions upon you or upon your serfs. We also decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches [Col. 1093D] from which the bodies are taken are preserved.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may presume, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of St Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1195, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

CCXI. He receives the convent of Vilich under his protection and confirms its possessions and rights. (Lateran, 29 April.)

[LACOMBLET, *Charters for the History*, vol. I, p. 380.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess of the monastery of Vilich and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

The Apostolic See ought to grant protection to prudent virgins who, under the habit of religion, continually prepare themselves with lamps kindled by works of holiness to go forth to meet the Bridegroom. [lacuna] We decree that the monastic order known to have been established in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

[Col. 1094B] [lacuna] You may also receive into conversion persons fleeing the world who are free and unencumbered, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid any of your sisters, after making profession in that monastery, to leave that place except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain a departing sister without letters of authorization from the community.

When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We will that the blessings of nuns and the ordinations of your chaplains who are to be promoted to sacred orders be provided to you without improper exaction by the diocesan [Col. 1094C] bishop.

Furthermore, we decree that burial in your monastery shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. Upon the death of yourself, the present abbess of that place, or of any of those who succeed you, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the sisters, by common consent, or the sounder part of the sisters’ counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb [Col. 1094D] the aforesaid monastery, etc.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Albinus, bishop of Albano.  
I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri.  
I, John, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia.  
I, Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of St Pastor at St Pudentiana.  
I, John, cardinal of the title of St Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany.  
I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of St Callistus at St Mary in Trastevere.  
[Col. 1095A] I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of St Martin at Equitius.  
I, Soffredo, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes.  
I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of St Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia.  
I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of St Adrian.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Aquiro.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of St Theodore.  
[Col. 1095B] I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of St Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1195, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

CCXII. He writes to [Michael], archbishop of Sens, that he is grieved that King [Philip], without consulting the Roman See, has divorced I[nggeborg], sister of Canute, king of the Danes, and has received Cent., his subdeacon and notary, and his letters with too little respect. He annuls that sentence of divorce. He commands that, if “the king, while she lives, should wish to bring in another wife, he is to take firm care to forbid him.” (Lateran, 13 May.)

[Ralph de Diceto, *Images of History*, in TWYSDEN, *Historians of England*, I, 681.]

[Col. 1095C]

POPE CELESTINE, to the archbishop of Sens, greetings.

Since, in the kingdom of France, Catholic princes—promoted by divine institution through the most holy Roman Church, whose faith and unity they have preserved—have always been cultivators of justice, they have obtained by a certain prerogative the privilege of blessing and grace. Even when we still held a lesser office, we willingly promoted their exaltation and glory, and more willingly gave counsel for their advancement. But now, called to the summit of the apostolate, we have embraced with the arms of paternal charity our dearest son in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of France, successor to his predecessors of revered memory in both goodness and prudence. We desire more earnestly to honour him with worthy titles and, insofar as we can with God, to exalt him. [Col. 1095D]

However, after the joyful and welcome report had first reached the Apostolic See that a marriage had been solemnly and lawfully contracted between our dearest sons in Christ—the aforesaid illustrious king of France and Queen I., illustrious sister of our dearest son in Christ, K. [Canute], illustrious king of the Danes—we afterwards heard that, concerning that marriage, at the perverse suggestion of certain persons, something had been presumed in a disorderly manner and not without injury to ecclesiastical honour. We are deeply grieved by this, both because of the injury done to God and because of the infamy inflicted upon those giving advice and consent. Indeed, had the royal majesty considered more attentively, and likewise those who were accomplices in this presumption reflected with themselves upon the greatness of the sacrament of marriage, we believe this course would not have been taken.

For it is plain to anyone who turns over the divine page that the Lord himself instituted marriage: in Paradise, before sin, for the duty of propagating offspring, saying, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. I); and outside Paradise, after sin, as a remedy for avoiding fornication. Hence the first man himself, inspired by the Holy Spirit, says: [Col. 1096B] “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II).

The Lord also indicated how great is the dignity of marriage and with what circumspection and seriousness proceedings concerning it ought to be conducted. When he was asked whether it was lawful to dismiss a wife, and when he was asked concerning an inheritance to be divided jointly between two brothers, he was silent in one case and answered thus in the other: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, commits adultery” (Matt. V). By this he plainly showed that the Church, in the adjudication of marriages, as a matter more difficult than other cases, ought to proceed with greater seriousness than in other matters. And since he says elsewhere, “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX), one may perceive how grievously that person sins, and how greatly he must fear the wrath to come, through whom the religious observance of so great a sacrament of Christ and the Church is disturbed. [Col. 1096C]

Moreover, it is not free from the fault of rashness that, in a matter so arduous and difficult, the judgment of the Apostolic See was not sought, so that it might either be canonically concluded by it or entrusted to persons who would decide the matter in accordance with canonical statutes and with the order of law preserved. Here there has plainly been a proceeding contrary to the venerable councils of the holy Fathers, which judged that greater and more difficult questions ought to be referred by all to the Apostolic See. This is observed most devoutly to the present day not only by the Gallican Church, except in the present case, but also [Col. 1096D] by churches much more remote.

To begin there briefly: is this not recognized as one of the chief and most arduous matters, since it concerns persons of such eminent royal standing, descended from the royal stock of their forebears, and turns upon a cause so difficult that, according to the statutes of the Fathers, it ought to have been reserved for the tribunal of the Roman Church? If even the most distant barbarians preserve unimpaired this and the other privileges of this See of blessed Peter, over which we, though unworthy, preside, how much more diligently are those bound to observe them who are nearer, are Latin, and are sustained more abundantly and frequently by the benefactions of the aforesaid See? He certainly does not err lightly who does not fear to oppose the privilege of blessed Peter and to act contrary to canonical sanctions.

But the prelates of the Church who offered support or counsel in this matter ought, if for no other reason, at least from fear of punishment, to have abstained from such conduct. They ought particularly to have recalled with anxious minds what is recorded in the sacred canons concerning Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier, and Gunther, archbishop of Cologne, who deserved to be struck with sentences of deposition because, in the matrimonial cause of King Lothair and his wife Theutberga, wickedly and rashly departing from the standard of equity, they transgressed the canonical sanctions. That the transgression here was equal or greater is shown by the very evidence of the matter.

For after the queen had been joined in marriage to the aforesaid king by words in the present tense, with mutual consent expressly declared, after oaths had first been sworn on both sides, with the priestly blessing added according to custom, after she had been anointed queen and honourably crowned, and after she had also been carnally known by him, as is reported, nothing ought so disorderly to have been attempted against her by anyone while she was undefended and ignorant of what was being done—as she did not know the language of the French. [Col. 1097B]

But we, who hold that king—Catholic and greatly devoted to the Roman Church—in the special inward affection of charity because of his forebears of illustrious memory, desire to provide more for the salvation of his soul and the integrity of his reputation than to satisfy the will of those who give him evil counsel. Accordingly, through our beloved son Cent., subdeacon, our notary, and legate of the Apostolic See, specially sent for this purpose, and through our letters, we asked, admonished, and earnestly exhorted his excellency; and for the remission of sins we enjoined upon him that, attentively considering the Gospel saying that it profits a person nothing to gain the whole world while suffering the loss of his soul (Matt. XVI), he should, while he had time, be concerned for the salvation of his soul, treat with marital affection the aforesaid wife whom he had removed from himself by evil counsel, and not seek to lend an ear in this matter to those who, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, imitate the hostile man who scattered tares in a well-sown field and count it gain if they can sow hatred and discord [Col. 1097D] among some persons.

But, as we have learned, that king did not receive the aforesaid legate and our letters with the devotion that was fitting. Yet we, as the Lord knows, although troubled on this account, are more deeply grieved for the salvation of his soul, concerning which we ought to take more earnest thought. We wish him always to do what ought to please his Creator and prevent him from incurring loss to his soul. Therefore, taking into consideration the public instrument concerning the genealogy sent to us by our venerable brethren, the archbishop of Lund and his suffragans, and the public report, we annul and wholly invalidate, with the counsel of our brethren, that sentence of divorce pronounced contrary to the order of law. By apostolic letters we command and order your brotherhood that, if the aforesaid king, forgetful of his condition, should perhaps wish to bring in another wife while she is alive, you are firmly to ensure, relying on apostolic authority, that this is forbidden him.

Given at the Lateran, the third Ides of March. [Note: At [Col. 1097D], “May” seems to be required. JAFFÉ.] In the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXIII. He gives William, archbishop of Reims, cardinal of St Sabina and legate of the Apostolic See, and his suffragans the same commands as in the preceding letter to the archbishop of Sens.

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 624.]

CCXIV. He informs Philip, king of the French, that “that sentence of divorce [made with Ingeborg] has been invalidated and annulled by him.” He exhorts him to “receive his wife and treat her with marital affection.”

(MARTÈNE, *Expanded Collection*, I, 1007.)

[Col. 1098B]

CELESTINE, etc.

“Since, in the kingdom of France,” etc., as above, Epistle 212, in almost the same manner as far as “sow discord.” But we, taking into consideration the public instrument concerning that genealogy sent to us by our venerable brethren, the archbishop of Lund and his suffragans, and the public report, wholly invalidate and annul, with the counsel of our brethren, that sentence of divorce pronounced contrary to the order of law. Therefore we ask, admonish, counsel, and enjoin upon your royal excellence, for the remission of sins, that for God’s sake and for the salvation of your soul you receive the aforesaid wife of yours and treat her with marital affection. For if, by dismissing her in such a manner, you perceive that you have incurred any stain of sin on this account, we mercifully pardon it to you by the authority of blessed Peter and Paul.

We wish, however, that your royal highness should not be unaware of the disposition we hold in the Lord toward your person: if we could in any way tolerate this deed while preserving our honour and the salvation of your soul, we should by no means have proceeded so far [Col. 1098D] in this matter; but, although you yourself, as we believe, do not fail to know it, we could not pass it by with closed eyes, without injury to conscience and danger to your soul.

CCXV. Confirmation of sentences of excommunication and interdict issued by the authority of Walter, archbishop, against the citizens of Rouen. (Lateran, 15 May.)

[Works of Peter of Blois, p. 796.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren Walter, archbishop of Rouen, and his suffragans.

Since all the Churches of God, spread far and wide throughout the whole extent [Col. 1099A] of the world, constitute one Catholic—that is, universal—Church redeemed by the price of the blood of her Bridegroom, and since, just as diverse limbs make one body, unity of faith and doctrine binds them together, if any one of them is injured, that offence cannot occur without injury to the others, and especially injury to that Church in which the head is more greatly offended than in the others, insofar as it is more affected by regard for each and adheres to them by a stronger bond.

For this reason, since the Roman Church is head and teacher of all, we who, though unworthy, preside over it are more gravely shaken and afflicted by the oppression of any Church; and we are moved more strongly to compassion insofar as assistance is more specially hoped for from us in adversity, and every Church has been accustomed, against the violence of wicked people, to invoke more devoutly and securely the protection of the Apostolic See.

As letters from some of you and many others have made known to us, and as we have already learned from the reports of many, the charity of all has so grown cold, as the wickedness of evildoers increases, that scarcely any reverence is now paid to the churches of God or their ministers. The sanctuary of the Lord is trampled by force, the teachings of faith are despised, and scarcely can any persons be found who, after very many enormities, add something by which they might rise again. Rather, in vengeance for former crimes, they heap still graver offences upon the enormities hitherto committed; they rejoice when they have done evil, the impious are proud while the poor person is burned, and they exult in the commission of wicked deeds. [Col. 1099C]

But because the wickedness of perverse persons has grown so strong that remedy or help cannot be found in human beings, recourse must be had to the protection of the Creator. We must apply ourselves more earnestly to prayers and every pious work, so that the heavenly mercy may graciously look upon us and no longer allow humankind to prevail over us or permit it to delight any longer in the oppression of Churches. For only then may we safely hope for and await help from above, when we have diligently performed those things which belong to our office. Let us briefly set forth what has been reported to us concerning the Church of Rouen and seek to apply such remedies as we can.

When it became necessary for you formerly, brother archbishop, while our dearest son in Christ Richard, illustrious king of the English, was on pilgrimage or in captivity, to occupy yourself with the affairs of the realm, the people of your city, stirred by diabolical prompting, broke out in hostile and cruel fury against your cathedral church, other churches subject to you, and their ministers. They plundered their goods and inflicted upon them exceedingly grievous injuries and insults. Hence, after taking counsel with prelates and other religious and learned men, you pronounced a sentence of anathema against those evildoers, since, though admonished, they scorned to repent.

But they, making that sentence—which had been pronounced for their correction and salutary shame—an incentive to wickedness, afterwards persecuted the churches and their ministers more fiercely and obstinately. They presumed to kill some of those ministers cruelly, mutilate others in their sexual organs, beat others severely, and subject them to very many insults. They demolished the houses of the canons, set fire to and burned some of them, and during the days of Easter uprooted their livestock enclosures and shrubs. [Col. 1100A]

Although after some interval of time those same evildoers offered an oath, confirmed by sacrament, that they would observe your command in these matters and make satisfaction, they afterwards stubbornly scorned to fulfil it. Therefore, sharing with paternal concern in the many burdens of that Church and of those subject to it, and wishing to apply the remedy of apostolic protection to such great oppressions, we have decreed that the aforesaid sentence, since it was issued reasonably and according to law, is to be held ratified and valid. By apostolic letters we strictly command your brotherhood that, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, every Sunday and feast day throughout all your dioceses you shall announce and cause to be announced that sentence publicly, with bells rung and candles extinguished, and cause it to be observed until they have restored what was taken, made satisfaction for the damages so cruelly inflicted and injuries done, and those bound by the same sentence have made suitable satisfaction. At the very least, they are to present themselves before us, on the testimony of the archbishop’s letters, for absolution and penance concerning such great offences. [Col. 1100B]

If, on account of such injuries, you or any of you judge that other sentences ought canonically to be pronounced, we command that they be publicly proclaimed until due satisfaction has been made. Furthermore, because, by the hidden judgment of God, other injuries followed upon the aforesaid injuries—injuries outrageously inflicted upon your canons, brother archbishop, and other clerics by the army of France—and because no satisfaction whatever was made despite frequent admonition by you and others concerning the goods taken and damages inflicted, you, after taking counsel with priests and other men, subjected to sentence of interdict that territory especially subject to your diocese. Certain clerics living in that territory, who scorned to observe your sentence, [lacuna: the source breaks off after “sentences of excommunication and …”]. [Col. 1100D] We command that sentences of interdict be observed inviolate until suitable satisfaction has been made to you, to the churches, and to the clergy against whom the injuries were committed.

Given at the Lateran, the Ides of May, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXVI. He grants and confirms to the abbots of St Chrysogonus the faculty, obtained from his predecessors, of using pontifical insignia. (Lateran, 18 May.)

[FARLATI, *Sacred Illyricum*, V, 65.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son VINCENT, abbot of St Chrysogonus of Zadar, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since we believe you to be a devoted and faithful son of the Church, we willingly attend to your honour and have thought fit to honour [Col. 1101A] your person by some special privilege, so that you may persist more fervently in devotion to us and to the Roman Church, knowing yourself to have been adorned by us with ecclesiastical honour and dignity. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, considering your devotion and prudence, we have thought fit to grant you the use of the mitre, ring, staff, and sandals—as your predecessors are known hitherto to have had them through the favour of the Apostolic See—so that by authority of the Apostolic See you may freely use these ecclesiastical insignia in solemn processions and principal feasts of your church, both within your monastery and in the churches belonging to it.

No person whatsoever, therefore, may infringe this document of our concession or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let that person know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1101B]

Given at the Lateran, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fifth year of the pontificate.

CCXVII. He forbids the privileges of the chapter of Chartres to be infringed. (Lateran, 2 June.)

[*The Penitential of Theodore*, II, 507.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . the dean and chapter of Chartres, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We ought to employ every careful concern and effort [Col. 1101C] so that the privileges and liberties reasonably granted by us and our predecessors to the churches of God may always remain in force; and, lest they be broken by the assault of anyone’s rashness, it is especially incumbent upon us to provide against this with the authority granted to us. Therefore, by authority of these present letters, we strictly forbid any archbishop, bishop, or other person whatever to presume to undertake anything contrary to the privileges granted to you by the Apostolic See which might produce prejudice in any respect to you or to your Church. If anyone should nevertheless presume to do so, we decree that the act shall be wholly void and without effect, etc.

No person whatsoever, therefore, may infringe this document of our prohibition and constitution, [Col. 1101D] or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let that person know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth Nones of June, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXVIII. He commands the canons of St Quentin not to injure the privilege granted by him to the canons of St Pecinna. (Lateran, 15 June.)

[COLLIETTE, *Memoirs of Vermandois*, vol. II, p. 525.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the dean and chapter of St Quentin, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since by our authority the beloved sons, the canons of St Pecinna, [Col. 1102A] have been forbidden to admit through you any person into their church as canon and brother until the prebends of that church have been restored, according to ancient and approved custom, to the number of eight prebends, you appear openly—something we regard as grievous and troubling—to be striving against that prohibition of ours. You presume to appoint certain persons in it, so that those prebends may not be reduced to the aforesaid number. Therefore, by authority of these present letters, we command and enjoin you not to presume in any way to derogate in any respect from that prohibition, but to preserve it wholly unimpaired in its force. Otherwise, know that we have firmly commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Arras, relying on our authority, to restrain you from your presumption by ecclesiastical censure, with the obstacle of appeal removed. [Col. 1102B]

Given at the Lateran, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXIX. He commands [Michael], archbishop and archdeacon of Sens, not to permit certain privileges of the chapter of Chartres to be infringed. (Lateran, 19 June.)

[*The Penitential of Theodore*, II, p. 564.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother the archbishop and beloved son . . . the archdeacon of Sens, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1102C] Since, on behalf of the beloved sons . . . the dean and chapter of the Church of Chartres, we have lawfully pronounced a judgment concerning the customs and liberties of that Church relating to the admission and delivery of the burgesses of Chartres to the service of those canons; since the ancient and reasonable customs of that Church—which our venerable brother . . . bishop of Chartres is bound by oath to observe, in the approved form of that oath—have been fully confirmed by us; and since the Apostolic See has graciously granted them that no one may rashly act contrary to the privileges of that Church unless he has a special mandate from the Apostolic See concerning this matter; since they have been granted free faculty to recall to their own service their male and female serfs who presume to act against them on the occasion of the commune [Col. 1102D] or of any rebellion; since the settlement amicably concluded and put into writing between the bishop and chapter of the Church of Chartres concerning the *precariae* of Normandy, Masengeio, Ungreio, and Alversio, and concerning the provostships of Nogent, Fontenay, Amilly, and Belsia, has been confirmed by the protection of apostolic authority and granted to them; and since it has been granted that neither they nor any of them may be compelled to answer before a secular judge, except in a case concerning possessions held secularly, or when a defendant wishes lawfully to prove before those before whom he is summoned the objections that he makes against them:

At the request of our beloved son R., canon of Chartres, who has not ceased to labour, opportunely and inopportunely, in advancing the affairs [Col. 1103A] of his Church, we have wished, through the care of your discretion, to provide with paternal concern for that Church, lest those things granted by us or strengthened by the safeguard of our letters might through anyone’s rashness be rendered void. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion to cause the foregoing provisions to be observed irrevocably by our authority. If any opponents should appear and, after your admonition, decline to desist from their wickedness, strike them with ecclesiastical censure, setting aside appeal; and cause them to be more strictly avoided by all until they return to their senses. No letters shall stand in the way, if any appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without mention of the tenor of these letters.

[Col. 1103B] Given at the Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXX. He decrees that no canon is to be drawn before a secular court except in a matter of fief. (Lateran, June?)

[Same work, p. 437.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Chartres, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant consent to the just desires of petitioners, and, with the outcome following, fulfil requests that do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, [Col. 1103C] beloved sons in the Lord, concurring favourably with your just petitions, by the authority of these presents we grant you that no one may hale you or any one of you before a secular court, unless a dispute arises, by reason of a fief or of any other secular possession, concerning some matter pertaining to it; or unless someone summoned by you before a secular judge wishes, in that judge’s presence, to prove objections which he has brought against you. We decree that, should anyone presume to contravene this indulgence of the Apostolic See, you may pronounce against him a sentence of ecclesiastical coercion, without appeal.

Let no person whatever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our grant or, by rash presumption, [Col. 1103D] to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, [lacuna] before the Kalends of July, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXXI. He confirms the award rendered between Taon, abbot of Fontana Taonis, and Massarius, pleban. (Lateran, 3 July.)

[ZACHARIA, *Anecdota medii aevi*, p. 347.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Taon, abbot, and the brethren of Fontana Taonis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1104A] When what is just and honourable is sought from us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought, through the care of our office, to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favourably assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this writing, the award which our beloved sons Sinibald, pleban of Villiano, and the priest Papa, rector of the church of St Saviour, reasonably promulgated between you and Massarius of Montecuccoli concerning the churches of Stagiano, St Simeon of Stagiano, and Podio Montiscuccoli, as was enjoined by both parties and is more fully contained in the instrument drawn up on that matter. For greater security, we have ordered that instrument to be inserted [Col. 1104B] word for word into this present page, and it reads as follows:

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, eternal God, in the year 1192 from his Nativity, in the reign of Lord Henry, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, in the tenth indiction. Whereas litigation and controversy had arisen between Taon, abbot of Fontana Taonis, litigating on his own behalf and in the place and name of his church, on the one side, and the pleban Massarius, litigating on his own behalf and in the place and name of the *plebs* of Montecuccoli, of which he appears to be custodian and rector, on the other, concerning namely the church of Stagiano, St Simon of Periano, and Podio Montis Cuccoli, where that *plebs* itself is built and established, it pleased both parties to commit this litigation and controversy to us, Sinibald, pleban of Vigliano, [Col. 1104C] and the priest Papa, rector of the church of St Saviour, in order that we might settle it by our free and independent arbitration in whatever manner pleased us.

We therefore, the aforesaid arbitrators, wishing to put an end to this controversy and wholly to quiet it, having taken the counsel of prudent men, and especially of Lord Bono, venerable bishop of Pistoia, and having also examined and read the privileges and charters produced on the matter by both sides, enact and decree, and declare by award and arbitration, that henceforth the aforesaid church of St Minias of Stagiano shall be under the authority of the pleban of Montecuccoli: namely, that he may and is bound to send there a priest to celebrate divine worship, the pleban receiving from it whatever accrues to that church on account of the people of Stagiano, whether from fief or [Col. 1104D] from offerings of both the living and the dead. If, however, the pleban wishes to place there his own priest, he may do so, provided that this is done with the abbot’s consent and that the abbot does not maliciously oppose him.

Concerning the chapel of St Simon of Periano, we order and enact as follows: from this hour forward the abbot may place in that church whatever priest he wishes, without consulting the pleban. The priest placed there shall, within the next eight days, go to the *plebs* and receive from the hand of the pleban the people belonging to that *plebs*, and the pleban shall invest him with them. The priest shall promise obedience to the pleban concerning that people, in this manner: whatever sentence the pleban may pronounce upon the people or any member of the people, that priest shall observe it and cause it to be observed. The priest shall be bound [Col. 1105A] to go to the *plebs* for litanies, feast-days, baptism, and the burial of the dead.

Concerning the feast of St Simon, we award and confirm by arbitration whatever the abbot of Furculis and Master Minias established: namely, that the pleban shall go every year to the feast of St Simon, accompanied only by two clerics, and shall be honoured, as the pleban Massarius, both in the divine offices and at the table, spiritual as well as bodily; but the people of that chapel shall hear the daily offices in the aforesaid chapel. For the litanies and feast-days of the *plebs*, and for baptism, they shall go to the *plebs*.

Concerning the *plebs* of Montecuccoli, we declare and decree that henceforth the abbot shall have or claim no right or action in the *plebs* or in the hill, except only this: the pleban or rector who at the time is in that *plebs* [Col. 1105B] shall annually, henceforth in the month of January, pay or cause to be paid to the abbot, or to his certain messenger, four pounds of good oil as a rent, by the proper market pound of the city of Pistoia, and nothing further. If he does not pay at the appointed time, he shall be bound to restore double.

We also enact that neither the abbot nor any of his monks may impose penance upon anyone of the people of the aforesaid *plebs* without the pleban’s permission. Nevertheless, whoever from the entire body or district of the *plebs* wishes to choose burial at the abbey shall not be forbidden by the pleban or his clerics, provided that he gives, or causes to be given, to the pleban a fourth part of whatever he adjudges from movable goods. Moreover, the pleban of the aforesaid *plebs* shall be bound once yearly to visit the often-mentioned abbey [Col. 1105C] with the whole people of the *plebs* in procession with litanies.

We add further, and firmly enact, that if at any time either party attempts by rash presumption to act against any one or more of the aforesaid provisions, and does not observe all that has been enacted above by us and pronounced by award and arbitration, the disobedient party shall pay twenty pounds of good Pisan denarii as a penalty to the other party which observes the award. Once this penalty has been given and paid, all the aforesaid provisions shall nevertheless always remain firm and enduring in their full force.

All this was done in the city of Pistoia, in the palace of the lord bishop, in the presence of the aforesaid Lord Bono, bishop of Pistoia; Nivaldus, provost; Boso, archpriest; the priests Melior Basilius and Accompagnatus, [Col. 1105D] fellow canons of St Zeno; also in the presence of Corso, ordinary judge; Daliottus, son of Pedrone of Montpellier, formerly [son] of Martin; Jacobus Daliottus; Marseppus, formerly [son] of Guidaloctus; Actis, formerly [son] of Niger; Jacobus of Pistoia; Averardus Melani; Ugolino and Cacciaquerra, formerly [sons] of Guerrier; and very many other summoned witnesses. Lord Gregory, monk and priest and chamberlain of the aforesaid abbey, consented to all the foregoing and gave his assent. Likewise Gerard, monk, gave his assent to all the foregoing. Rufus, called Raynerius, cleric of the same abbey, promised always to hold all the foregoing firm and ratified. Likewise Parisius, Bardus, Geoardus, Bellinus, Picciolius, and Maganutus, lay brethren of the same abbey, promising always to hold firm [Col. 1106A] and inviolate all that was enacted and awarded above, consented to it in every respect.

On behalf of the *plebs*, the priests Bonus and Armisius, Calincio the subdeacon, Bernard the canon, and Leonard, cleric of the *plebs*, assented to all the foregoing. I, Avianus, judge of Lord Frederick, of divine memory, emperor of the Romans, and notary of the Sacred Palace, was present at all the foregoing; hearing and seeing these things pronounced by the aforesaid arbitrators, I faithfully wrote them down at their command, adding or subtracting nothing, and reduced them to a public instrument.

Let no person whatever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or, by rash presumption, to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur [Col. 1106B] the wrath of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXXII. He grants privileges of indulgence to the church of St Mary and St Theobald at Metz. (Lateran, 4 July.)

[*Histoire de Metz*, III, 160.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of St Mary and St Theobald, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we are bound to direct pious solicitude towards all churches militant, we nevertheless ought especially to foster and embrace more closely those whose planting is new and which still rest upon tender roots; [Col. 1106C] and because they do not possess sufficient resources for those who serve God in them, they need to be nourished more abundantly from the breast of our consolation. Accordingly, beloved sons in Christ, considering your praiseworthy purpose and fervent devotion in divine worship—you who have planted a new community of canons from your estates and are raising a new church from its foundations, although you lack resources of your own—we ratify and confirm by apostolic authority that which our venerable brother Bertrannus, bishop of Metz, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, has conferred upon you.

Therefore, whoever twice yearly, namely on Easter Monday and on the day of the dedication of your church, celebrated on the feast of the blessed martyr [Col. 1106D] Lawrence, visits your church as a pilgrim, shall know that, by God’s authority and ours, he is absolved from the sins of his fathers and mothers which involved no injury; we remit penances and sins that have passed from their memory, and forty days from the penances imposed upon them. Furthermore, if any persons propose to visit the thresholds of the saints and wish, with the consent of their bishop or of the person whom the bishop appoints in his place, to contribute to your church from the resources necessary for their journey, for the remission of their sins, we grant them, by God’s authority and ours, that journey and pilgrimage.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXXIII. He grants the archdeacon, archpriest, and primicerius of the church of Siponto the use of mitre, *podium*, and ring. (Lateran, 11 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VII, 828.]

[Col. 1107A]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother HUGH, archbishop, and to the beloved son, the chapter of Siponto, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since you, brother bishop, have conducted yourself praiseworthily in our service from times long past, we have considered it fitting, at your request, to honour the church of Siponto granted to you. Therefore, by this present page we grant that the archdeacon, archpriest, and primicerii of the same church, [Col. 1107B] and their successors, shall henceforth be adorned with mitres, *podia*, and rings. We therefore decree that no person whatever may infringe this page of our concession or, by rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXXIV. To H[ubert], archbishop of Canterbury, legate of the Apostolic See, and his suffragans, he commands that they exhort people to bring aid to the land of Jerusalem. He wishes King Richard to be admonished to send there well-equipped knights and infantrymen. (Lateran, 25 July.)

[Radulf of Diceto, *Imagines Historiarum*, in TWYSDEN, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, I, 684.]

[Col. 1107C]

COELESTINE, bishop ... to the venerable brethren, the archbishop of Canterbury, legate of the Apostolic See, H[ubert], and the suffragans, and to the beloved sons, the prelates of churches established in the province of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The merciful and compassionate Lord, who, in order to restore by his mercy the fall of humankind, did not hesitate to take flesh from a virgin’s womb and to undergo the peril of death, does not wish us—whom he redeemed from darkness and the shadow of death by his death—to be delivered once more into the hands of the enemy because our merits demand it. In his mercy he chastens every son whom he receives, sometimes correcting us by warnings and at other times by scourges, so that, when we see that such things and greater are owed to our merits and sins, we may more readily and willingly incline to a better life.

But since in our days the wickedness of modern people has increased to such a degree that we are corrected neither by the warnings of Holy Scripture nor by the scourges of our infirmity, he has willed to lay his hand heavily upon us and to deliver the land of his birth—something which we cannot recount without bitterness of heart—into the hands of the pagans. Thus, justly lamenting with the prophet, “O God, the nations have entered into thy inheritance” (Ps. 78), etc., we have heard with our ears what some have been granted to behold for greater compunction: the corpses of the saints [Col. 1108A] given as food to the birds of heaven and their blood as drink to the beasts of the earth.

We have likewise heard of the abomination of desolation made in the holy place: there, it is said, the Hagarenes have made a brothel of prostitutes where formerly stood the table of breads and the holy offering; and there, to this day, stands a stable for beasts where the body of Christ both lay buried and was customarily received by the faithful. Even the saving sign—the most sacred wood of the Cross, in which the Apostle spoke figuratively when he said, “But we must glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6), in which are our salvation, life, and resurrection, through whom we are saved and made free—has, when that land was overrun, through the sins of the Christian people, passed into the power [Col. 1108B] of those who detest alike the Crucified One and the cross, and pursue the children of the Church with every effort.

Moreover, Jerusalem, once the vision of peace and the land promised to the ancient fathers, where our Lord chose to suffer for us and to show sure proofs of his divinity, and which used formerly to be visited with the deepest and most frequent devotion by professors of the Christian faith, is trodden under the feet of the wicked and polluted by the filth of those to whom it had once been an object of fear and horror. Stripped of its former glory and riches, bereft and deserted by religious worshippers, it turns to lament over itself: “How solitary sits the city once full of people; the mistress of nations has become like a widow” (Lam. 1:1).

[Col. 1108C] What worshipper of Christ, then, mindful of so great a desolation, can hold back tears? Who, hearing the misery of this calamity, does not grieve with the mourning dove? Who can receive consolation for this boundless grief, when there is no one among all her beloved to console the weeping Church? Gird yourselves therefore, brothers, to proclaim the word and glory of God to the peoples. Let those who may wield the material sword against the persecutors of the faith gird themselves, that they may swiftly avenge by retribution the injury done to the cross. Let those who are permitted to devote themselves solely to prayers and contemplation gird themselves, that they may appease the Lord by unceasing prayer. For behold, Satan has demanded us, that he might sift us like wheat in this tribulation (Luke 22:31). Behold, whoever is not now with Christ shall, according to the teaching of evangelical [Col. 1108D] authority, be turned away. And whoever is not moved at present by the wrong done to the Crucified One must not place confidence in another saving sign.

Nor do we wish to admire the prudence of certain persons if the various rulers of the world, who hitherto have gone forth against the Saracen people with spear and sword, have achieved, as it were, nothing at all. For the Lord does not save those who trust in his mercy by spear and sword, but will save them in the multitude of his mercies. Nor have our merits yet advanced so far that we have moved the wrathful Lord to mercy and healing. Although the sons of Israel once went up, armed at the Lord’s command, against the tribe of Benjamin to avenge the death of the Levite’s wife from Mount Ephraim, [Col. 1109A] they nevertheless could not overcome them at all until, having been put to flight by them once and a second time, they had purged their own excesses and iniquity.

Ascend, therefore, beloved, in hope to the high heart, so that the Lord may be exalted in his wondrous works. Pour out your hearts before him, that God may add mercy, preserve his mercy in wrath, and after storm and weeping bring joy. Let those who have hitherto taken up military arms among Christian peoples take the sign of the cross; let them neither despair because of their small number nor glory in their multitude. For if they wish, in due humility, to hasten to the defence of the land of Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension, the Lord who destroys wars, who cast Pharaoh’s chariots and army into the sea, [Col. 1109B] will teach their hands for battle and their fingers for war, immediately blow away the multitude of pagans like chaff before the wind, and wipe them out like mud from the streets.

But you, brothers, archbishops and bishops, to whom, after the pontiff of the supreme see, the care of all and solicitude for souls has been entrusted, must labour by unceasing prayers to the Lord and continual preaching to the peoples subject to you, so that, taking the sign of the cross, they may gird themselves to confound and refute the persecutors of the Christian faith. For we hope—and you yourselves ought to hope—that the Lord will cast out the net in the word of your preaching and prayer, and in his favour raise up for the defence of the [Col. 1109C] eastern province such persons that God will arise more through the compelling force of their merits than through confidence in arms; his enemies shall be scattered, and those who hate him shall flee from his face.

For those who, for love of the Godhead, undertake the labour of this expedition and strive to carry it out insofar as lies in them, we grant, by the office of authority bestowed upon us by God, that remission of the penance imposed through priestly ministry which our predecessors are known to have established in their times: namely, that those who undertake the labour of this journey with contrite hearts and humble spirits, and die in penitence for their sins and in the right faith, shall obtain full indulgence for their offences and thereby eternal life. Whether they survive [Col. 1109D] or die, they shall know that, by the mercy of almighty God and the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul and our own, they will receive remission of the satisfaction imposed for all sins of which they have made rightful confession.

From the moment that they take the cross, their goods, together with their households, shall remain under the protection of the holy Roman Church and likewise of archbishops and other prelates of God’s Church. They shall suffer no legal claim concerning those possessions which they held peacefully when they took the cross, until their return or death is most certainly known; meanwhile, their goods shall remain whole and undisturbed. Those, moreover, who send from their goods aid to that land shall obtain pardon for their sins, according to the [Col. 1110A] direction of their prelates.

But upon you, brother archbishop, to whom the care of the legation of the kingdom of England has been entrusted by the Apostolic See, we have thought fit to impose the labour of this honour, commanding you to exert yourself by unceasing exhortations with our dearest son in Christ, Richard, the illustrious king of the English, that he send well-equipped knights and foot-soldiers for the defence of the land of Jerusalem. As you travel throughout the province of England, press them with preaching in season and out of season, so that, taking the sign of the cross for the defence of Christendom, they may visit the land beyond the sea. But upon you, brother bishops and beloved sons, prelates of churches, we command by the authority of these presents that you receive and treat with honour your said archbishop, as legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 1110B] and obey his wholesome admonitions and commands.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXXV. At the request of Bishop Oddo, he confirms two castles to the church of Penne. (Lateran, 31 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1125.]

COELESTINE ... to the venerable brother ODDO, bishop of Penne, greeting ...

When what is just is sought from us ... Therefore, venerable brother in Christ ... the two castles, namely Puliano [Col. 1110C] and Colle Alto, with all their appurtenances, which by your care and diligence you acquired for the church of Penne, ... we confirm and strengthen by the protection of this writing. Let no person whatever ...

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of August, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXXVI. He commands archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established throughout all Alamannia and Germany to induce the people “to assist the region of Jerusalem in persons and goods, in accordance with the just direction of P[eter], cardinal priest of St Cecilia, and J[ohn], cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill.” (Lateran, 1 August.)

[SUDENDORF, *Registrum*, I, 82.]

CCXXVII. By letters to the chapter of Blessed Martin of Tours, he forbids a rent or lease of church property exceeding ten pounds to be granted without security; then he decrees that canons absent from the offices shall be deprived of the six denarii which they received daily from the common fund. (Lateran, 30 August.)

[*Défense de Saint-Martin de Tours*, 27.]

[Col. 1110D]
