COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of Blessed Martin of Tours, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of the Apostolic See, over which, by the ordering of divine mercy, we preside though unworthy, moves us to provide with paternal solicitude, insofar as divine bounty permits, [Col. 1111A] for the welfare of churches; and if practices which seem likely to bring them loss are observed in them under the pretext of a corrupt custom, it becomes us diligently to remove them as a duty of our office.

Indeed, it has come to the hearing of our apostolate that you often grant the rent or lease of your church’s revenues, without receiving guarantors or pledges for them, to the person offering the higher fixed price, having received from him only an oath as security; and on this account it frequently happens that, when he has not paid the price, he incurs perjury and the Church incurs harm and loss. Therefore, wishing that these matters be prevented henceforth, by the authority of these presents and under anathema we forbid you henceforth to presume to grant a rent or lease of church property exceeding [Col. 1111B] the sum of ten pounds to anyone without adequate security by guarantors or pledge; nor may you rashly attempt to confer upon one person more than three leases having a value greater than ten pounds.

Furthermore, we have been told that it frequently happens in your church that, when the divine offices are celebrated, certain canons either remain in the cloister or, constrained by no reasonable cause, roam about everywhere at their own will like vagabonds; although others attend the celebration of the divine worship, they themselves are absent from those offices. Consequently, that church is often deprived of the solemnity of divine worship, and the other canons are furnished with an occasion for wrongdoing. [Col. 1111C] By the authority of these presents we decree that, whenever the divine offices are celebrated, if any canon is absent—unless perhaps he judges that he must be absent for a reasonable cause and with permission received from the chapter—the six denarii which every canon is accustomed and entitled to receive daily from the common fund shall be entirely withheld from him, all contradiction and appeal ceasing; so that those whom divine love does not induce to the service of the Saviour may at least be compelled by the withholding of their due stipend.

Let no person whatever be permitted to infringe this page of our prohibition and constitution or, by rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 1111D].

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of September, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CCXXVIII. He takes the church of Auch under protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Lateran, 12 September.)

[Cl. de BRUGELES, *Chronicle of the Church of Auch*, 40.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother BERNARD, archbishop of the church of Auch, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetual remembrance.

Placed, by the Lord’s disposition, on the exalted watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love our brother bishops, both those nearby and those far away, with fraternal [Col. 1112A] charity, and to provide with paternal solicitude for the churches entrusted to them by God. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ Bernard, archbishop, we graciously grant your just requests; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of Auch, over which, by God’s favour, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future obtain, by the grant of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

We further add that the [Col. 1112B] church of Auch, which is known to have been subject to the most holy Roman Church alone, ought to be subject to absolutely no other power, but shall remain in that liberty which Clovis, once king of the Franks, of revered memory, granted it in pious devotion after freeing it from Saracen hands, and which he increased with many and various gifts and possessions. He added that whatever right he possessed in that church or city should, from that time and forever, accrue wholly to the use of the archbishop of that place and his successors, as the aforesaid king is known to have granted to the archbishop who then presided over the said church and as [Col. 1112C] your predecessors have possessed hitherto.

Furthermore, whatever the aforesaid church of Auch has hitherto possessed within the city or outside it, on this side of the river Ercius or beyond it, by parochial right or by right of landed property, in lands and mills, within those boundaries, namely, which have been marked out and fixed by a truthful delimitation from ancient times:

The church of Saint Lawrence outside the walls; the church of Saint Martin with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter; likewise, the quarter-shares of all the churches which your predecessors were accustomed to hold and receive under their custodian, as they themselves are known to have possessed them from the time of Austind, formerly archbishop of Auch, of blessed memory, who is said to have acquired those same [Col. 1112D] quarter-shares, and as your predecessors are known to have held them: all these we confirm to you and your successors by the text of the present privilege.

In Armagnac: the church of Nugarol with its entire parish, just as Count Bernard, with his wife Naupasia and his sons Gerald and Otto, formerly sold it to the Church of Auch itself, reserving no right in it or in its appurtenances for themselves or their descendants, and confirming that sale, with additions from their property, upon the holy Gospels; the church of the castle of Cornelian, with houses, possessors, tithes, offerings, and the cemetery of its parishioners; the church of Saint Saturninus of Sotiens, with the castle itself and its appurtenances; the church of Saint [Col. 1113A] Peter of Vic, with the castle itself and its appurtenances, with its tithes and cemeteries; the church of Lugajan.

In Pardiac: the church of Saint Christopher and Saint Mary of Marcelian, with its tithes and offerings.

In Astarac: the church of Idrac, with the castle itself and its appurtenances; likewise the castle of Lamaguère, with the church itself, tithes, lands, and people; the church of Saint Venancia, with the whole village, and what it possesses in the church of Durofort; the church of Arbeissan; the church of Vignau; the church of Gaubissan; the church of Artigue; the church of Castelnau; the church of Sajan; and the rent which it possesses in the grange of Artigues, namely thirty measures of wheat from J. Pala; the church of Barrads; the church of [Col. 1113B] Pipios; the church of Orbessan.

In Magnoac: the church of Saint Mammet.

In the city of Elne: the church of Saint Mary, with its tithes, offerings, and the cemetery of its parishioners. In the borough itself, the possessions and houses which you own there.

In Ausan: the church of Agraulet, with vineyards and its other appurtenances; the church of Fremosens and Saint Peter of Genens, and the church of Saint John of the Spaniards, with their possessions and other appurtenances; the church of Lafite; the church of Castillon, with tithes, offerings, and its other appurtenances; the church of Principanian; the church of Bretos; the church of Saint Giles of Peyrusse.

In the archdeaconry of Juliac: one half of the revenues of the church of Lavignac. In Corrensac: the church of Saint John, Saint Bibian, and Saint Martin of Berdale, with their appurtenances, tithes, and cemeteries; the church of Cabesolas; the entire village of Saint Christina, with lands, vineyards, and hamlets.

In Angles: the church of Insula and the right which you possess in that same village; the church of Saint Michael of Crotera; one third of the church of Saint John of Ordesan; the tithes of Barser; the church of Villeneuve; the church itself of Despeiroli; the church of Basian; the church of Despesos; what you possess in the church of Rutissan and in the church of Saint John; the church of Arcaiag.

In Spain: the churches of Pedrola and Azoer, with their lands, tithes, and offerings; [Col. 1113D] the houses and possessions which you own at Tudela. In Sarreria: the church of Saint Ferreolus and Saint Frajolf.

We likewise confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors the bishoprics listed below, subject to the metropolitan jurisdiction of the Church of Auch: namely Bigorre, Lescar, Oloron, Dax, Bayonne, Aire, Bazas, Comminges, Couserans, and Lectoure.

Moreover, by the liberality of the Apostolic See, we grant your brotherhood the use of the pallium, that is, the fullness of the pontifical office. You are to use it on those days on which you know your predecessors used it: namely, on the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Stephen the Protomartyr; the Circumcision of the Lord; Epiphany; Hypapante [the Presentation]; [Col. 1114A] Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; Easter; Easter Monday; the Ascension; Pentecost; the three feasts of blessed Mary; the nativity of blessed John the Baptist; the commemoration of All Saints; the solemnities of all the apostles; dedications of churches; consecrations of bishops; ordinations of clergy; the principal feasts of your church; and the anniversary day of your consecration.

It is therefore especially fitting that you provide diligently and prudently for preserving the honour of this vestment through modesty and vigour of conduct; that the adornments of your moral character should accord with it; and that, with the Lord as author, you may be conspicuous in both respects; that you, whom the office of pastoral care binds, may show love . . . . . [Col. 1114B] to the brethren, and that you may also follow . . . . . with all; that you may devote yourself to pious works, abound in virtues, and that in your breast the breastplate of judgment may shine, joined with active conduct signified by the shoulder-piece. Thus proceed before God and in the sight of men, so that you may furnish the flock entrusted to you an example of virtue, and that even your adversaries, seeing your good works, may glorify your Father who is in heaven. Let there be in your speech words of edification and in your mind the fervour of zeal. Beyond all these things which befit your office, act with such moderation that you may appear frequently to embrace what the dignity of the pallium demands, and may be able to gain eternal glory for yourself in heaven.

Following the example of our predecessors of happy [Col. 1114C] memory, the Roman pontiffs Calixtus, Innocent, Lucius, Eugenius, Anastasius, Adrian, and Alexander, we decree that bodies of the dead shall henceforth be buried at the same mother Church of Auch. Thus no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated or under interdict; without prejudice to the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Further, no one in the province of Auch shall henceforth dare to possess church cemeteries or ecclesiastical benefices by hereditary right. Should anyone attempt this, let him be struck by canonical censure.

By apostolic authority we also forbid clergy, [Col. 1114D] monks, or any religious persons knowingly to receive in churches those whom you or your officials have placed under interdict or excommunicated, or to celebrate the divine offices in their presence; to admit those same excommunicated persons to the religious habit; or, if they have died, to bury them. Nor may anyone presume to act against a sentence canonically promulgated by you, unless danger of death is imminent, so that, if the person cannot have your presence, one bound by the sentence may, after prior satisfaction, have to be absolved by another according to ecclesiastical form.

[Col. 1115A] We likewise confirm to you the ancient and reasonable customs and regular observances concerning canonical order and the appointment or removal of persons which your predecessors have hitherto maintained. We also add that you, brother archbishop, may by our authority, after taking counsel with the regular canons, establish regulars in the Church of Auch; and that in the chapter of regular canons you shall have free power to dispose of and freely confer the honours and benefices, dignities and offices of that church, solely upon regular persons and not upon others. Neither you nor any other person may introduce secular canons into that church. Moreover, we decree that the Church’s benefices and dignities which that church or your canons at present possess justly and canonically shall be conferred from among those regular canons, and not from other persons, except with the consent of the greater [Col. 1115B] and sounder part of the chapter.

We also decree, and command you, brother archbishop, to observe inviolably, that whoever wishes to become a canon in the aforesaid churches of Saint Martin outside the city, Saint Nicholas of Nugarol, Saint Saturninus of Sotio, Saint Peter of Vic, Saint Candida of Jeguno, and Saint James of Idrac, shall first present himself to the chapter of the Church of Auch. In its presence, and with its consent and authority, he shall receive canonical status, being devoted to divine service in the named churches; and he shall always humbly render to that mother church, as to his spiritual mother, the obedience and reverence due to it, as has hitherto been customary and observed.

We likewise decree, according to the decree of Pope Urban of blessed [Col. 1115C] memory, that in parish churches within your bishopric which monks hold, they shall appoint priests with your counsel. Those priests shall receive from you, with the abbots’ consent, the care of the parish; they shall render account to you for the care of the people, but shall render to the abbot due subjection concerning temporal matters belonging to the monastery.

Upon the death of you, the archbishop of that church, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of intrigue or by force, except the person whom the regular canons of that church, by common consent or by the counsel of the sounder part, shall, in the fear of God and according to the institution of the holy Fathers, have provided to be elected. [Col. 1115D] No secular person or power may thereafter, on any pretext, presume to intrude or interfere in that election, or in any way impede or disturb it.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all things shall be preserved unimpaired and entire for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, without prejudice, of course, to the authority of the Apostolic See.

If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. [Col. 1116A] I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Santa Rufina. I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, title of Calixtus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saint Martin, title of Equitius. I, Lentinuus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Fid., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. [Col. 1116B] I, Gerald, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on 12 September, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1195 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Celestine III.

## CCXXIX. To the bishops of Bayeux, Avranches, Sées, and Coutances.—Concerning a sedition raised by the citizens of Rouen against the canons, and the satisfaction to be made to them. (Lateran, 11 October.)

[MARTÈNE, *Anecdota*, I, 659.]

[Col. 1116C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops of Bayeux, Avranches, Sées, and Coutances: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint of our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Rouen, it has come to the hearing of our apostolic office that the people of Rouen, in rash audacity, destroyed the wall of the atrium of the church of Rouen, together with certain buildings [Col. 1116D] attached to it. When you came to the city, you carefully admonished the said people and commune in a spirit of gentleness to take care to render fitting satisfaction to God and Holy Church for so enormous an offence. But although they had been admonished again and again both by us and by the beloved son, the aforesaid dean of Rouen, they utterly scorned to make amends.

You, as we learned from your letters, pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon them with the authority and consent of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Rouen. But they, at the prompting of the spirit of wickedness, breaking forth into greater insolence, laid profane hands upon the priests of the Lord during Holy Week before the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection; [Col. 1117A] they killed some of them, and shamefully and wickedly mutilated the genitals of others after subjecting them to abuse. On the very day of the Lord’s Resurrection, they partly demolished and partly burned the houses of the canons of the Church of Rouen, and moreover cut down their shrubs at the roots. At last, after many admonitions and the repeatedly renewed commands of our dearest son in Christ, Richard, illustrious king of England, all alike swore, touching the holy Gospels, that they would obey the judgment of the Church without any evasion in all the matters written above.

Thereafter, when you had been summoned and came to the aforesaid [Col. 1117B] city, and your discretion imposed upon them the observance of the judgment in accordance with their sworn oath, you called prudent and discerning men to your assistance and, with the consent and authority of the aforesaid archbishop, firmly decreed that the commune of that city should be bound to make full restitution for the damages; that it should without any difficulty restore the wall of the atrium of that church which the commune itself had destroyed, together with its attachments and appurtenances; and that it should not delay restoring the houses of the canons and clergy of Rouen which it had demolished and burned. Those members of the commune, however, who had rashly laid violent hands upon canons or clergy were, after making fitting satisfaction to those injured, to hasten to the Apostolic See to obtain the benefit of absolution.

[Col. 1117C] Since no one may rashly act contrary to an oath given, by our letters we command and strictly order those same citizens to take care, as they promised and are bound by oath to do, to make satisfaction in such a manner that full satisfaction may be rendered to God and the Church whom they have offended, and their devotion may thereby deservedly be commended. If, however, they delay to carry out your command, by the tenor and authority of these presents we command your brotherhood, under strict injunction, to cause the sentence pronounced by you against that same people—which we ratify—to be put into execution, any appeal set aside.

[Col. 1117D] Given at the Lateran, 11 October, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXX. To the citizens of Rouen.—On the same matter. (Lateran, 11 October.)

[Ibid.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the people of Rouen.

Know that we do not extend to you a word of greeting, not because of our harshness, but rather because of your contumacy. Indeed, from the complaint of our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Rouen, it has come to the hearing of our apostolic office that you rashly destroyed the wall of the atrium of the church of Rouen, together with certain church buildings [Col. 1118A] attached to that wall. When our venerable brothers, the bishops of Bayeux, Avranches, Sées, and Coutances, came to the city of Rouen, they carefully admonished you and the commune in a spirit of gentleness to take care to render fitting satisfaction to God and Holy Church for so enormous an offence. But although you had been carefully admonished again and again both by those bishops and by the aforesaid son, the dean of Rouen, you utterly scorned to make amends.

As we learned from their letters, they pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon you with the authority and consent of our venerable brother Walter, archbishop of Rouen. But you, at the prompting of the spirit of wickedness, breaking forth into greater insolence, laid profane hands upon the priests of the Lord during Holy Week before the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection; you killed some of them and, after subjecting others to abuse, shamefully and wickedly mutilated their genitals. On the very day of the Lord’s Resurrection, you demolished for the greater part, and for the remaining part consumed by fire, the houses of the canons of the church of Rouen; and you moreover cut down their shrubs at the roots. At last, after many admonitions and the repeatedly renewed commands of our dearest son in Christ, Richard, illustrious king of the English, you all alike swore, touching the most holy Gospels, that you would obey the judgment of the Church without any evasion in all the matters written above.

Thereafter, when the aforesaid [Col. 1118C] bishops, having been summoned, came to that city to impose upon you observance of the judgment in accordance with the oath you had sworn, they called prudent and discerning men to their assistance and, with the consent and authority of the aforesaid archbishop, firmly decreed that the commune of your city should be bound to make full restitution of the damages and things taken away; that it should without any difficulty restore the wall of the atrium of that church which the commune itself had destroyed, with its attachments and appurtenances; and that it should not delay restoring the houses of the canons and clergy of Rouen which it had demolished and burned. Those members of the commune who had rashly laid violent hands upon canons or clergy were, after making fitting satisfaction to the injured parties, to hasten to the Apostolic See to obtain the benefit of absolution.

Since no one may rashly act contrary to an oath given, we command and strictly order your whole community by apostolic letters to take care, as you promised and are bound by oath to do, to make satisfaction in such a way that full satisfaction may be rendered to God and the Church whom you have offended, and your devotion may thereby deservedly be commended. Otherwise, know that we ratify the sentence which those bishops pronounced and shall cause it to be put into execution through them.

Given at the Lateran, 11 October, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXX bis. He receives the church of Saint Mary of Neuchâtel under protection and confirms its donations, goods, and possessions. (Lateran, 20 October.)

[MATILE, *Monuments de l’Histoire de Neuchâtel*, I, 35.]

[Col. 1119A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, provost, and the canons of the church of Saint Mary of Neuchâtel, present and future, canonically . . . . . . . . . . . . . in perpetuity.

. . . . . . To grant the petitions of those who ask for what is recognized to accord with justice and religion is required both by the force of equity and by the order of reason, especially when the will of the petitioners . . . . . . . . . . . and truth do not leave [lacuna]. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, [Col. 1119B] we graciously assent to your just petitions, and . . . . . . . . . . . . . receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of the present writing, the church of Saint Mary of Neuchâtel, in which you are devoted to divine service. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, the Lord granting it, acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself where the aforesaid church is situated, with [Col. 1119C] all its appurtenances; the vineyards and other things which you possess there; the church of Haris with all its appurtenances; the church of Furnis with all its dependencies and appurtenances; the vineyards and other things which you possess at Sarrières; the land and other things which you possess at Pusoz; the land which you possess at Marens; the land and other things which you possess at Finis; the land and other things which you possess at Boudeviler; and those things which you possess elsewhere.

[Col. 1119D] We will that chrism, holy oil, consecrations of your altars or churches, the ordinations of your canons and clergy who are to be promoted to orders, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments be supplied to you freely and without any exaction by the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See. Moreover, by apostolic authority we strictly forbid anyone to presume to pronounce upon you or your churches a sentence of excommunication or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause, or to harass you with novel and unlawful exactions.

In the parish churches which you possess, you shall be free to elect priests and present them to the diocesan bishop, who, if they are suitable, shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they must answer to him concerning spiritual matters and to you concerning temporal matters. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated or interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Furthermore, we ratify the liberties and immunities, as well as the ancient [Col. 1120A] and reasonable customs, granted to you and your church and observed hitherto; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscania. [Col. 1120B] I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, title of Calixtus. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Martin . . . . . I, Cencius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Geoffrey, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Fidus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praeneste. [Col. 1120C] I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. [Col. 1120D] I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on 20 October, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1195 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Celestine III.

## CCXXXI. Privilege for the monastery of Le Bec. (Lateran, 17 November.)

[Works of Lanfranc, p. 333.]

CELESTINE, bishop . . . , to his beloved sons WALTER, [Col. 1121A] abbot, and the convent of Le Bec: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman Church has customarily, in fulfilment of its habitual duty of compassion, to love its devoted and humble sons more earnestly and, lest they be troubled by the annoyances of wicked persons, to cherish them, like a loving mother, with the protection of her safeguard. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify with the patronage of the present writing, your persons and your monastery with all its appurtenances, and all that you presently possess or may in the future, by just means and with the Lord’s aid, acquire. We decree that no [Col. 1121B] archbishop, bishop, archdeacon, dean, or any ecclesiastical person, superior or inferior, not even a legate of the Apostolic See unless he has a special mandate, may presume to subject you, your monastery, your individual churches or other possessions, or their guardians or administrators, to a sentence of suspension, interdict, or excommunication; or by any audacity demand or extort from you or your tenants anything that may bring you vexation or burden, or derogate from the ancient customs of your monastery. Should this be attempted, it shall have no force and shall wholly fail.

We also forbid any ecclesiastical person to presume, through favour or any personal connection, to confer any of your churches [Col. 1121C] upon another, retain it for himself, inflict upon you vexation or burden in this matter, or accept a person presented to him by a layperson. Rather, he shall receive only the person whom, from regard for charity, you judge should be presented to him. If he should delay receiving or instituting that person, then by our indulgence you may retain your vacant churches in your administration until they are provided, upon your presentation, by the diocesan bishops.

Wishing likewise to uproot the greed of certain persons, we forbid anyone to compel you to establish monks in your houses which you are able to retain, without loss, under your own control.

Moreover, by apostolic authority [Col. 1121D] we grant you permission, by common consent, freely and suitably to assign your churches, with their appurtenances, in whatever province or diocese they are known to be situated, to the refreshment of the poor and the reception of guests. No one may, by force, power, or any rash act, withdraw those churches from the use and benefit of the poor and guests. You may also receive clerics and laymen fleeing the secular world for conversion, and retain them without any opposition. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, provided that you exclude those whom you know to be excommunicated or under interdict. We also decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish [Col. 1122A] of those who decide to be buried there.

Further, if any patron or parishioner of one of your churches should be placed under interdict for a particular offence of his own, we grant by apostolic authority that, even while excluding them, you may admit to divine service your other parishioners who were not their accomplices, and assist them both in death and life according to the custom of the Church. We have also thought fit to add that you, son abbot, and your successors shall have, by indulgence of the Apostolic See, free authority, without anyone compelling you, to remove priors from your priories [Col. 1122B] for definite and established reasons, according to the Rule of blessed Benedict and the ancient custom of your monastery hitherto observed, and to substitute others whom you judge suitable.

Upon the death of you or of any successor, or if he is called by God to the higher rank of dignity, no secular, ecclesiastical, or lay person may presume to take part in your election, unless perhaps he has been invited to do so at the request of all the brethren, or of the greater or sounder part of them.

When, according to God and the rule of your order, you have elected someone as abbot, present him to your diocesan bishop. If that diocesan delays confirming his election or, without delay and without a known fault, conferring the hand of blessing upon the person elected, you may approach any other bishop who, provided he is Catholic and enjoys the favour of the Roman [Col. 1122C] pontiff, shall endeavour to grant what is requested.

We also forbid anyone to presume within the bounds of your parish churches to establish an oratory or church without your consent, or to demand or extort tithes from you from newly cultivated lands which you cultivate by your own labour or at your own expense, from the produce of gardens, or from the offspring of your animals.

Moreover, by this present document we have thought fit to forbid any archbishop, bishop, archdeacon, dean, or even legate of the Apostolic See to seek to demand or extort from you, or from your house beyond the circuit of its walls, any procuration or anything under the name of procuration. [Col. 1122D] We command that this be observed with the moderation appropriate to better-endowed houses; but in smaller houses, whose means do not suffice for this, we wholly forbid it to be done. Wishing also to provide for your peace and tranquillity in future, we strictly forbid any archbishop, bishop, archdeacon, dean, or their officials to summon you to court concerning any complaints, except by special mandate of the Apostolic See. But if anyone wishes to pursue a claim at law against you, he shall proceed judicially: in the regions on this side of the sea, before our beloved sons the abbots of Saint Victor and Saint Geneviève and the cantor of Paris; but in the regions beyond the sea, before the abbots of Westminster, Saint Alban, and Saint Edmund, to whom we write concerning this matter.

[Col. 1123A] Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may lawfully infringe this document of our protection, permission, or prohibition, or rashly act contrary to it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on 17 November, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXXII. He receives the monastery of Saint Mary of Germerode under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Lateran, 20 December.)

[KUCHENBECKER, *Analecta Hassica*, IX, 148.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1123B] sons LOUIS, provost of Saint Mary at Germerode, and his brothers and sisters, present and future, professing the regular life.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized to accord with right and religion, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford appropriate support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, after the example of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Mary of Germerode, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of the present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order [Col. 1123C] which is recognized to have been established according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of Prémontré shall be observed inviolate in your house for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s aid, acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, which Count Ruckerus of Bilsteynn granted to God and Blessed Mary for the remedy of his soul, together with the adjoining court [Col. 1123D] and all its appurtenances—villages, courts, homesteads, lands cultivated and uncultivated, roads and trackless places, woods, groves, meadows, pastures, streams, waters, and watercourses—with all things belonging to it, whether justly and lawfully acquired from the offerings of the faithful or by its own labours.

Likewise, the courts of Wolffartrodt, Arnolffrodt, Luprestadt, Reymetshussenn, Sigersshusen, Voothmanrodt, Fridericdorpp, Rudolffshusen, Honedhe, Welssbech, Ruchellinge; and the salt which is paid annually to the church at Sothe; and the entire village of Berharssdorp. Moreover, possessions situated in these villages: Grucinge, Herboltsshusenn, Francquartsshussenn, Vorwerch, Bolestedde Cvera, Hosnolre, Luderbech, Rudansshusen, Iletre, Berthen, Heppenrodt, Hasla, Rodenkirchen, [Col. 1124A] Gozenwinden, Wolsten, Holsten, Holtzhusen, Hasla, Tense Trintberch, Huntzenrodt, Hassbach, Mutherodt, Hempenrodt, Tunnefelt, Bassendrot, Hermensassen, Johendorpp, Rinerichdorpp, Wissener, Theffer, Elkenhagen.

Certainly, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the produce of your newly cleared lands. You may also receive clerics, laymen, and sisters who flee the world, being free and discharged from it, for conversion, and retain them without any opposition. Whenever a general interdict shall be in force . . . , you may, with doors closed, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, in a subdued voice and without ringing bells, celebrate the divine offices. Upon the death of . . . , the present provost of the same place, [Col. 1124B] or of any of his successors, no one shall be set over it through any stealth, cunning, or force, except one whom the brothers and sisters, by common consent—or the sounder part of the counsel of the brothers or sisters—shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, decide ought to be elected.

Nor shall anyone usurp the advocacy, except the eldest of the founder’s lineage, who shall exercise that office without all violence and wrong, and shall be bound to defend it against the assaults of evil men, so long as he wishes to preserve the right of advocacy for himself. We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated or under interdict; yet the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken shall remain unimpaired [Col. 1124C].

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be kept whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical jurisdiction of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, attempts rashly to contravene this charter of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed [Col. 1124D]; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the discerning Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Cencius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1114 [read: 1195], and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine.

## CCXXXIII. To Simon, Dean of York—Concerning the administration of that diocese.  
*(Lateran, 23 December.)*

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXII, 604.]

[Col. 1125A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SIMON, dean of York: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the government of the universal Church has, by the favouring grace of God, been committed to us, though unequal to it, and since we are bound to guard against the misfortunes of each of its churches and provide for their welfare, we must take the greatest care lest churches suffer temporal or spiritual loss from the very source from which we believe their honour and advantage are being secured. [Col. 1125B] For when, after weighing and diligently examining a person’s merits, we suspend someone from the exercise of his rank in proportion to his deserts, and remove him temporarily from the governance of churches, we must provide for those deprived of a pastor’s care such a person as knows how both to settle the disputes of litigants and correct the offences of subjects, and, insofar as the duty of his office permits, loves and cherishes them.

Therefore, since the archbishop of York, as his deeds and contumacy required—having abused our patience and neither desisted from his iniquities nor presented himself before us within the term mercifully granted to him—has by our authority been suspended from the use of the pallium, the exercise of episcopal office, the administration both of spiritual and temporal matters, and the receipt of benefices, we have considered it proper, by the authority of these present letters, to grant to your discretion that, with the counsel of the canons resident in the Church of York, you may correct the offences of clerics in the diocese of York and canonically determine the disputes of complaining clerics and laypeople of the diocese of York that require settlement by ecclesiastical judgment; and, setting aside appeal, punish with canonical severity anyone who contumaciously chooses to resist in this matter, until our care shall otherwise provide for that church. Let no person therefore [Col. 1125D] infringe this page of our grant or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXXIV. To the clergy of York—On the same matter.  
*(Lateran, 23 December.)*

[Ibid., 605.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons all abbots, priors, archdeacons, and other clerics, counts and barons, [Col. 1126A] and all others established in the province of York: greeting and apostolic blessing.

You may see how mercifully the Roman Church has proceeded in the matter of the archbishop of York if you carefully consider the tenor of our letters, which each party has obtained from the Apostolic See at different times. For when it reached the hearing of our apostolic office, as the beloved sons the dean and chapter of York and no few abbots, priors, and other prelates of the Church established in the kingdom of England had reported, that the said archbishop, neglecting the duty of his pastoral office, involved himself in secular affairs and devoted the whole zeal of his mind, not to divine worship, the ordination of clerics, the dedication of churches, the holding of synods, or the blessing of abbots, but to hunting and hawking, and practised other things that seriously detract from the office and honour of the pontificate entrusted to him: we did not immediately pronounce judgment against him. Rather, we committed an inquiry into his reputation to our venerable brother, the bishop of Lincoln, and our beloved sons the archdeacon of Northampton and the prior of Pontefract [otherwise: Saint—], wishing to deter the archbishop himself from his offences either by threat of suspension, if the matters reported to us were established, or, if they could not lawfully be proved, by requiring him to undergo canonical purgation with three bishops and an equal number of abbots. [Col. 1126C]

But because that archbishop appealed to the Apostolic See before the citation of the said judges reached him, the said judges, in accordance with the tenor of our letters, granted him three months and arranged to assign him the Kalends of June as the date by which he was not to delay prosecuting the appeal he had lodged. Thereafter, when the archbishop himself had set out to come to the Apostolic See, fearing that, because of the harshness of the weather, some danger might befall him personally, he requested from us by letters and messengers that we mercifully extend the date appointed for him. We granted his request, believing that he would repent all the sooner of his offences if he found us more gracious and ready to hear his petitions; and we set the Octave of Blessed Martin, then next to pass, as the date for him to prosecute his appeal and clear himself. Nevertheless, we instructed the aforementioned judges that if the archbishop then neglected to present himself before us, they were thereafter to proceed in accordance with the tenor of the earlier letters and carry out what had been entrusted to them by those letters. [Col. 1126D]

But when that stated time had now passed, and he neither came to the Roman Church nor sent any representative to excuse his absence in any way, considering his disobedience and contumacy, we suspended him from the use of the pallium, the exercise of pontifical office, the administration of temporal as well as spiritual matters, and the receipt of benefices. By apostolic letters we instructed the aforementioned judges publicly to announce throughout the diocese and province of York that he had been suspended by us. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command all of you that you shall in no way presume to obey the said archbishop or his officials, whether in spiritual or temporal matters. If disputes arise among any of you established in the diocese of York which ought to be settled by ecclesiastical judgment, bring those controversies before our beloved son Simon, dean of York; humbly accept and steadfastly observe his judgment. Know that, by the customary mercy of the Apostolic See, we have granted to that dean that, with the counsel of his canons resident in the Church of York, he may correct clerical offences and determine disputes in the diocese of York, whether of clerics or laypersons requiring an ecclesiastical hearing. [Col. 1127B]

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXXV. To the bishop of Lincoln—On the same matter.  
*(Lateran, 23 December.)*

[Ibid., 606.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Lincoln and his beloved sons [Col. 1127C] the archdeacon of Northampton and the prior of Pontefract [otherwise: Saint—]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the most holy Roman Church, founded in perpetual stability upon the immovable foundation—that is, the true cornerstone—and since Truth itself said of itself, “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16), received through the merits of blessed Peter mastery and primacy over all churches; since the Lord declared to the prince of the apostles, “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 13); and since the same prince of the apostles heard from the Lord, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matthew 16), and thus received judicial power not only over bodies but also over souls: we, whom not our own merits but divine mercy alone has called to the summit of the supreme pontificate, if we wish to frame our judgments rightly and with prudent deliberation and not abuse the power entrusted to us, ought, insofar as human frailty permits, to follow the example of him upon whom the Apostolic See is founded, from whom it received the care of the other churches and the fullness of the power of binding and loosing. [Col. 1127D]

For God is wonderful above all things, and the depth of divine counsel unfathomable. Although His judgments are incomprehensible and His ways unsearchable, if we rightly observe some of the things He does below, He indicates to us and to other prelates of churches a pattern for judgment to imitate. For when, according to the Gospel, He ordered the barren tree in His vineyard to be cut down lest it occupy fertile ground, He first said: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and find none; therefore cut it down” (Luke 13). [Col. 1128A]

Reflecting continually within ourselves upon this, though we are least among men and subject to the defects of human frailty, when we heard of the offences of the archbishop of York and reports of his dishonourable life and unprofitable conduct were recounted before us and our brethren, we did not immediately pronounce judgment against him. Rather, following the example of Him whose mercies are above all His works, we did not cease, over no small period, to labour for his correction by repeated letters and commands, so that the barren tree might put forth fruit and recover its lost vigour: at one time recalling him by our admonitions to the way of salvation, at another deterring him by threat of suspension from office and benefice from the paths of his wickedness and error. We believe this is manifest to you, who have come to know the entire sequence of events and the course of the affair in due order. [Col. 1128B]

Indeed, from the representations of persons of the chapter of the Church of York, this has come to our hearing; and the testimony of our beloved Robert of York, Roger of Selby, and eleven other abbots of the Premonstratensian Order appears plainly to establish it: that Geoffrey, archbishop of York, despising the sacraments of the office imposed upon him, was uselessly occupied with hunting, hawking, and other military concerns; that after his promotion he applied neither hand nor effort to the ordination of clerics, the dedication of churches, or the celebration of synods; and that he blessed no abbot. Yet against clerics and abbots alike he was accustomed, according to his own impulse, indiscreetly to let loose his tongue in cursing and excommunicating.

He nullifies and overturns the liberties of his church and its approved customs. Appeals, which ought to be remedies for the oppressed, he has brought into contempt, to the injury of the Roman See; and he caused several persons, because they had made an appeal to us, to be tightly bound in prison chains. After an appeal to us had been made, he stripped persons of his church of honours and benefices; disregarding an appeal, he subjected certain canons to excommunication. Privileges of the Roman pontiffs are wholly deprived of force in his presence and by his authority; and one who might otherwise be safe forfeits, by displaying our privilege before him, the benefit of the protection he sought. [Col. 1128D]

Whenever anyone is restored, by delegated judges acting under our authority, to a church or possession taken from him, he immediately finds as an enemy the man through whom the judgment should have been executed. For he deprived several persons so restored, and, violently attacking their churches through his agents, is accused of having broken down their doors and driven them out by force. He caused very many to incur the guilt of perjury to their ruin, drawing them away by a kind of coercive necessity from the obedience which they had sworn to observe canonically toward their archdeacons. [Col. 1129A]

Moreover, attacking the cathedral church with a multitude of armed men, he caused the chapter-house doors to be violently broken and carried away, and caused the goods of the canons and many clerics—who had deposited their property both in the church and in its treasury—to be held by force. For all these matters the chapter of York appealed to us. We have also learned from the testimony aforesaid that, when churches are at times vacant, he does not admit suitable persons presented to him by those to whom the presentation belongs. Instead, he assigns them either to boys or to less respectable persons, exercising at once the office of presenter and institutor; or he causes them to remain vacant at his own mere pleasure, in order that their revenues may be applied to his own uses and that he may not fear to retain for himself what was due for the support of some respectable cleric. [Col. 1129B]

They further added that, although spiritual gifts ought to be distributed freely and without corruption, when he grants a church or divides it into portions contrary to canonical statutes, he frequently retains in it for himself a new and improper possession [perhaps: pension]; and he absolves very many excommunicated or suspended persons only when money intervenes. Religious and respectable men become despised and contemptible in his sight; base and suspect persons easily obtain his familiarity and favour.

Since we heard such profane reports not once but often, and since the letters of the aforesaid and of other prelates established in the kingdom of England and the province of York had repeatedly impressed them upon our ears, desiring to deter him from his offences and recall him to fulfil the obligation of his pastoral office, we committed an inquiry into his reputation to you. You were to summon abbots, priors, and other ecclesiastical persons of the diocese of York and investigate the truth of the foregoing matters more diligently. If lawful accusers proceeded against him, then, after hearing the allegations on both sides and reducing the depositions of witnesses to writing, you were to send them, secured by your seals, to the Apostolic See; and to appoint the parties a suitable date on which they should present themselves before us to hear judgment. [Col. 1129C]

We recall that the same letters also contained this: if accusers failed, yet public reputation stood against him, you were to require his purgation with three bishops and an equal number of abbots, setting aside the impediment of appeal. If he should fail in this, you were to cause him, suspended from archiepiscopal office and administration, to be presented before us. But if the said archbishop appealed to the Apostolic See before your citation reached him, you were to grant him a delay of three months; and if within that period he neglected or delayed to prosecute the appeal he had lodged, you were to announce him as suspended by our authority from every pontifical office and the administration of the archbishopric. [Col. 1129D]

Now, because that archbishop, before he was cited by you to answer the case, as he informed us by his letters and messengers, took care to appeal to the Apostolic See, and you assigned him the Kalends of January as the date for prosecuting the appeal: wishing to spare him labour and expense, and fearing that, if he came to Rome in the summer season, some danger to his person might arise from the harshness of the weather [perhaps: “fearing lest, if…”], when, as had been reported to us, he had set out to come to the Apostolic See and was ready to answer the crimes objected against him, by the customary kindness of the Apostolic See we considered it proper to extend for him the date for prosecuting his appeal until the Octave of Blessed Martin then next to pass. We suspended everything obtained against him until that same date and restored to its previous state whatever had been altered by us or others after the appeal to us had been lodged, under colour of the earlier letters. [Col. 1130B]

By apostolic writings we also explicitly commanded you that, unless he presented himself before us on the Octave of Saint Martin, you should not delay in any respect to proceed according to the form of the first commission, with every impediment of contradiction and appeal removed. But because the said archbishop, abusing our patience, neither came to the Roman Church nor sent any representative who might excuse even his absence—and although we mercifully took care to await him for no small time beyond the term fixed for him—he appears by that very fact to have confessed the charge, in that he neglected to present himself before us. We therefore suspended him from use of the pallium, exercise of every episcopal office, administration both of spiritual and temporal affairs, and receipt of the benefices of the Church and province of York, so that, at least thus returning to his senses from obstinacy in his wickedness, he might not compel the censure of canonical severity to be exercised more forcefully against him. [Col. 1130C]

Therefore, by apostolic writings, we command and enjoin your discretion publicly to announce in every church of the diocese and province of York that he has been suspended by us. On our behalf, strictly command all clerics and laypeople of that province not to presume to obey the archbishop himself or his officials in temporal or spiritual matters until we determine otherwise concerning that archbishop. We also command, and wish it announced through you in the diocese of York, that if disputes happen to arise among any persons which should be settled by ecclesiastical judgment, they are to refer them to the hearing of our beloved son Simon, dean of York. We entrust to him, with the counsel of the canons resident in the same church, the correction of clerical offences and the decision of controversies among litigants, both clerics and laypeople; they are humbly to accept and firmly observe his judgment. [Col. 1130D]

Furthermore, we decree to remain ratified everything which, under the authority of our letters and before notice of the second letters reached you, you wisely and reasonably determined in matters concerning that archbishop, whether respecting restoration of things taken away or other matters. We command that, fortified by our authority and proceeding to the Church of York, you continue according to the tenor of the earlier letters both in the inquiry into reputation and in making restorations to the canons of what was taken from them, notwithstanding the appeal or absence of the said archbishop and notwithstanding letters hitherto obtained to the prejudice of the first letters. [Col. 1131A]

Moreover, by the authority of these present letters, we enjoin you to judge wholly void and without effect the sentence of excommunication pronounced by that archbishop, after the appeal to us had been lodged, against certain canons, vicars, clerics, and servants of the canons of the Church of York. Nevertheless, as a greater precaution, you shall absolve by authority of the Apostolic See the said canons and the others named in that sentence. But all those who laid violent hands upon Benedict, clerk of the aforesaid dean, Walter the priest, Richard of Semare, and five clerics of Cavel, and other clerics of the Church of York, or who ordered violence to be inflicted upon them, you shall announce to be held, appeal set aside, under the bond of excommunication until they have made fitting satisfaction to those injured and come to the Apostolic See to be absolved, with testimony in your letters. If all of you cannot be present for carrying these matters out, let two of you nevertheless execute them. [Col. 1131C]

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXXVI. He confirms the judgment delivered by Archbishop Michael and M., archdeacon of Sens, between the chapter of Chartres and Countess Adela of Blois.  
*(Lateran.)*

[*The Penitential of Theodore*, II, p. 565.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons G., dean, and the chapter of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

If litigants were afforded license to revoke what has been established by judgment or agreement, an end would be imposed upon lawsuits in vain, and judicial authority would be reckoned as nothing. But the approved institution of the Fathers of old, desiring to restrain the malice of litigants, adopted the practice of reducing to writing, for greater caution and perpetual validity, the decisions of judges confirmed by authority; and the Roman Church customarily confirms by apostolic letters what has rightly been determined by its command. [Col. 1131D]

Now, when a dispute concerning the liberties and customs of the Church of Chartres was pending between you and our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman Adela, countess of Blois, after arbitration had been carried out by our venerable brother William, archbishop of Rheims, cardinal of Saint Sabina and legate of the Apostolic See, and by Adela, illustrious queen of the Franks, the matter was committed by the Apostolic See to our venerable brother M., archbishop, and our beloved son M., archdeacon of Sens. After they had lawfully cited the parties and fully understood their arguments, they pronounced a definitive judgment in your favour. [Col. 1132A]

Thereafter, when the same case was brought before us by appeal, both parties having sent representatives with open letters of ratification, we entrusted it, together with a question arising concerning a certain indulgence, to our beloved sons Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Martin, and P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, for hearing. In their presence, with representatives of both parties appearing, the representative of your church humbly requested confirmation, on the grounds stated, of the judgment of the aforesaid judges. But the opposing party made many arguments that the said judgment ought not to be confirmed by apostolic authority, instead requesting for the countess a certain indulgence contrary to your customs, which your envoy contended should be rejected on the grounds he presented. The aforementioned hearers laid the matter and the arguments of both parties concerning each question before certain of our brethren by written communications at our command; and, by their counsel, they received additional witnesses from your side concerning certain articles. [Col. 1132B]

When all these matters had been referred to the common deliberation of ourselves and our brethren, and the merits of the parties had been examined, by the common counsel of our brethren we judged that the indulgence sought contrary to your customs, to the detriment of the Church of Chartres, must be wholly annulled. Considering also the justice of the judgment issued in your favour by the aforementioned judges under our authority, we confirm that judgment by the authority of these present letters, precisely as it was contained in the authentic instrument of the judges themselves, and strengthen it with the protection of this present document. For greater caution, we have caused that authentic instrument, read in our presence, to be inserted in this letter word for word. It is as follows:

“To the most excellent Father and lord, Celestine, supreme pontiff by divine election: M., most humble minister of the Church of Sens, and M., archdeacon of the same church, greeting and obedience, both due and devoted in all things. [Col. 1132D]

“Let your holiness know, most reverend Father, that, when a controversy arose between the beloved sons, the chapter of Chartres, and Adela, noble countess of Blois, concerning the liberties and customs of the Church of Chartres regarding the receiving and protection of servants, and concerning certain servants of those same canons received, for their domestic service, under the Church’s protection according to the same customs; and also concerning a submission to arbitration made by the parties to our most excellent lady Adela, queen of the Franks, and the venerable Father William, archbishop of Rheims: a mandate of yours was issued to us in the following form:

“‘Celestine, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother M., archbishop, and his beloved son M., archdeacon [Col. 1133A] of Sens: greeting and apostolic blessing. Just as Henry the archdeacon,’ etc. See letter 159 above.

“Accordingly, most holy Father, in accordance with the tenor of your rescript, we summoned the parties before us. Having heard their allegations and diligently examined the attestations produced on both sides, we finally, relying upon the counsel of prudent men and jurists, brought the matter to definitive judgment in the following form. We judged the submission made to the lady queen and the lord of Rheims, and the arbitration pronounced by them, wholly void and without effect: both because no penalty had been established in the arbitration, and because it had plainly become known to us that the arbitration was pronounced contrary to the terms of the submission. [Col. 1133B]

“We adjudged to the Church of Chartres the liberties and customs proved by the testimony of lawful men and set down below. We decree that the canons of the same church may freely receive and protect the burgesses of Chartres who have entered their domestic service—except the servants of the prince of Chartres—enjoying the same liberty and immunity as the canons themselves, together with their goods and households. They must, however, abandon every kind of trade and usury, except that at harvest-time they may buy and sell grain, and at vintage-time wine, as they please, just as the canons do. They may make cloth from the fleeces of their own sheep and sell it without payment of the lay customary due; and, if anything needed for its completion is purchased elsewhere, they may do this without payment of toll. [Col. 1133C] They may deal with all their livestock and its produce under the same liberty.

“Therefore, falling devoutly at the knees of Your Majesty, we humbly beseech you to add to our definition, pronounced by your authority, the strength of apostolic confirmation and cause it to be observed inviolably.”

Let no person therefore infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of . . . , in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXXVII. He receives the monastery of Saint Mary of Dauleio under protection and confirms its property and privileges.

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, II, Documents, p. 408.]

[Col. 1133D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WARNER, prior of the monastery of Saint Mary of Dauleio, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as consistent with religion and honour, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and extend apostolic protection to the just desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully grant your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary [Col. 1134A] of Dauleio, in which you are devoted to divine service. We strengthen it by the privilege of this present document, first decreeing that the monastic order which is known to have been established in that monastery according to the Rule of the Lord and of Blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, with the Lord’s assistance, acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have considered it proper to specify the following in their own terms:

[Col. 1134B] The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances, etc. . . .

You may also receive clerics or laymen who flee the world, being free and released from it, for conversion, and retain them without any opposition. Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving that place without the permission of his prior, unless for the sake of a stricter religious observance; and no one shall dare retain those who depart without a common letter of authorization. Whenever a general interdict of the land shall be in force, you may, with doors closed, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice, celebrate the divine offices. In the parish churches [Col. 1134C] which you possess, you may elect priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are found suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they owe accountability to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters.

Moreover, we hold ratified the liberties and immunities granted to you and your monastery, as well as the ancient and reasonable customs hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times. We also decree that the burial-place of the same house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated or under interdict; yet the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken shall remain unimpaired [Col. 1134D].

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical right of the diocesan bishop, and the due reverence owed to the monastery of Saint Aper. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make fitting satisfaction for the offence, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him or her know that he or she stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given in the year 1195.

## YEAR 1196

### CCXXXVIII. To Hubert, Archbishop of Canterbury—Concerning the affairs of the Holy Land. (Lateran, January 12.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 610.]

[Col. 1135B]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUBERT, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It was represented before us on your behalf that many persons in England have taken up the Lord’s cross in order to visit the Lord’s Sepulchre and to bring suitable assistance to that Holy Land upon which the Lord’s feet stood. Although they are able to fulfil their vow, they nevertheless withdraw themselves from carrying it out, at the peril of their souls. There are also some who, although they have received the cross, cannot duly fulfil the vow they have made because of poverty, bodily weakness, or another just cause. But since your brotherhood has thought fit to consult us as to what should be done concerning these persons, by the authority of this letter we answer you, commanding by apostolic writing that you compel, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, all those who have made such a vow, as stated above, and who possess resources sufficient to fulfil it, to perform that which they are said to have vowed freely, unless there is a just reason for omitting it.

As for those who, because of poverty, bodily weakness, or another just impediment, cannot duly fulfil the vow which they are known to have made, we wish that, once the truth of the matter has been established before you, you impose a suitable penance upon them and grant them permission to remain. You must firmly enjoin them that, as soon as they are given the free ability to carry out their vow, they are not to defer its fulfilment by any delay. But those whom you know, because of bodily infirmity, to be wholly unable to pursue their vow in person are to send across the sea, at their own expense, one suitable person or more, according to the means available to them, to remain there in the service of Jesus Christ for a year or longer, at your discretion.

Given at the Lateran, 12 January, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CCXXXIX. To Walter, Archbishop of Rouen—That he restrain those who despised the censures of the Church. (Lateran, January 13.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 617.]

[Col. 1136A]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the Archbishop of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that those who arrogate to themselves a proud bearing against their prelates and, persisting in contumacy, neither observe their sentence nor heed their admonitions or commands, ought to be punished no less than the obedience of the devout and humble deserves reward and commendation from all. For unless the pride of the contumacious is subdued and cast down by the authority of the Apostolic See, ecclesiastical order will perish, and encouragement and opportunity for wrongdoing will increase for everyone.

For, as you have reported, it has come to the hearing of our apostolic office that, when you bound certain persons with the bond of excommunication because of their offences and decreed that they be avoided by all, certain religious and other persons established in your diocese rashly presumed to receive them into their communion and admit them to the celebration of divine offices. Although such persons are by the law itself bound by a lesser excommunication and thereby excluded from participation in the Body and Blood of Christ, nevertheless, that they may repent more quickly and turn back from their wickedness, if upon your warning they refuse to desist from their presumption and to render fitting satisfaction for what they have hitherto attempted, we grant you by the authority of this letter full power to bind them with the bond of excommunication and forbid them ecclesiastical communion. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of January [13 January], in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CCXL. He commands Albert, Bishop of Vercelli, and the Abbot of Lucedio, under penalty of anathema, to forbid the monks of Saint Just from administering ecclesiastical sacraments to the burgesses of Susa contrary to the privilege of the canons of Oulx. (Lateran, January 20.)

[*Cartulary of the Church of Oulx*, p. 106.]

### CCXLI. He grants Gerard, Bishop of Bologna, authority, if priests of churches both in the city and in the diocese of Bologna die, to appoint others to their offices. (Lateran, January 27.)

[SAVIOLI, *Annals of Bologna*, II, II, 183.]

[Col. 1136D]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GERARD, Bishop of Bologna: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since suitable persons ought to be appointed in the churches of God, and others ought to be instituted in the place of those who die within a fixed period according to the statutes of the Lateran Council, we are deeply troubled whenever this is done otherwise; and, that it may be corrected more quickly, we more readily employ apostolic authority. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, favourably assenting to your petitions, we grant you by this letter authority to appoint, in accordance with the Lateran Council, other persons in place of those who die in those churches of the city and diocese of Bologna which are subject to you by diocesan law and in which two or more priests customarily minister, according to their means, notwithstanding any opposition or appeal in this matter.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, infringe this charter of our concession or rashly act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let that person know that he or she will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, in the year of the Lord 1195, 27 January, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CCXLII. He takes the monastery of Saint Mary of Baumgarten under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Lateran, February 9.)

[WURDTWEIN, *Nova Subsidia Diplomatica*, vol. X, p. 170.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons MAXIMIAN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Bongarth, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those who choose the religious life, lest the assault of any rash act either turn them aside from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Holy Mary, Mother of God and Virgin, at Bongarth, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it with the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the monastic order, which is known to have been established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the said monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their proper names:
