The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; and, at the adjoining grange of Bongarth, the cultivated and uncultivated land of Cilkenberth; the mill of Heisco with the adjoining vineyards and meadows; likewise, whatever you possess in vineyards, arable lands, meadows, woods, and other things near the village of Ephekeb and its dependencies; the vineyards of Borsperch and Birkereth; and also the mill which our venerable brother Conrad, Bishop of Strasbourg, caused to be built; the land of Salemberch; the grange of Howarth; the land of Tecelin and Humbert, and whatever you possess in that grange; the grange of Anesseim with all its appurtenances; the alms-gift of Walfrid of Bissoffheim, in vineyards, lands, meadows, courts, houses, and a mill at Ergesseym; the grange of Baldenem with all its dependencies; the grange of Hanso with the tithe and all its appurtenances; the grange of Fossa with all its dependencies.

Likewise, rights of use in the woods and pasture for your animals for all your needs throughout the whole territory of the castle called Spicemberg; the arable lands and vineyards of Tambach; and the vineyards of Blineswilre, Nothehalt, and Cella. No one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes from the produce of your labour, which you cultivate by your own hands and at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, from your fields and brushwood, or from the increase of your animals.

You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and absolved, fleeing from the world, and retain them without any opposition. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, to depart from that place without the permission of his abbot. No one shall dare retain a person departing without the common security of letters; should anyone nevertheless presume to retain such a person, you may pronounce the regular sentence against those monks or conversi. We more strictly forbid that lands or any benefice granted to your church be given personally to anyone or alienated in another manner without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater and sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than as stated, we decree them void.

Moreover, we forbid that any monk or conversus bound by the profession of your house, without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, stand surety for anyone or borrow money from anyone beyond the amount established by the provision of your chapter, except for the manifest benefit of your house. If he should presume to do this, the convent shall in no way be bound to answer for it. Further, in your own causes, whether involving a civil or criminal question, you may use the testimony of your brethren, lest your right be lost in any respect through lack of witnesses.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we forbid any bishop or other person to compel you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit to secular judgment concerning your own property or possessions; or to presume to come to your houses for the purpose of celebrating ordinations, hearing causes, or convoking any public assemblies. Nor may anyone impede the regular election of your abbot, or in any manner intervene, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, in installing or removing the one who may at the time hold that office.

If the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, when duly requested with fitting humility and devotion, refuses to bless the abbot who has been appointed and to confer upon you the other things belonging to the episcopal office, the said abbot, provided that he is a priest, may bless his own novices and perform the other functions belonging to his office. You may receive from another bishop all things improperly denied you by your own bishop. We add, however, that, in receiving professions offered by abbots who have been blessed or are to be blessed, bishops shall be content with the form and wording known to have been established from the origin of the Order: namely, that the abbots themselves must make profession with their Order reserved to them and are not to be compelled to make any profession contrary to the statutes of their Order.

For the consecration of altars and churches, for holy oil, or for any sacrament of churches, no one shall dare, under pretext of custom or otherwise, to extort anything from you; rather, the diocesan bishop shall provide all these things freely. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the most holy Roman See; relying on our authority, he shall provide what is requested. If the see of the diocesan bishop should happen to be vacant, you may meanwhile freely and without opposition receive all ecclesiastical sacraments from neighbouring bishops, provided that no prejudice is thereby created in future against your own bishops.

Since you sometimes lack access to your own bishops, if a bishop who is in communion with the Roman See, as stated above, and of whom you have full knowledge, should happen to pass through your area, you may receive from him, by authority of the Apostolic See, blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks. But if bishops or other rulers of churches pronounce a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict against your monasteries or persons established there; or against your hired labourers because you do not pay tithes, or for any matter among those granted to you by apostolic favour; or against your benefactors because out of charity they have bestowed upon you benefits or services, or have helped you work on those days upon which you work while others observe a holiday, we decree that such a sentence, as pronounced against the grants of the Apostolic See, is to be invalidated. Nor shall letters have force which are shown to have been obtained without naming the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges.

Moreover, wishing by paternal care to provide henceforth for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosures of your places or granges, to commit robbery or theft, set fire, shed blood, rashly seize or kill a person, or dare to commit violence. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen with the privilege of this present writing, all liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to correct that presumption by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him or her know that he or she stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. [Col. 1140C] I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, [bishop] of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, John, by God’s grace cardinal priest of the church of Saint Clement. I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saint Mark, of the title of Equitius. I, Cencius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Soffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Fidantius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. [Col. 1141A] I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angel. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, 9 February, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1195 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### CCXLIII. He grants the Abbot of Longpont that “no one may demand procurations in the granges belonging to the monastery or exact homage from its servants.” (Lateran, February 6.)

[*Chronicle of the Abbey of Longpont*, 105.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son the Abbot of Longpont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although the general care of all churches rests upon us, and we ought, so far as we can with the Lord, to provide for their needs, nevertheless we both wish and ought to assist with more devoted care religious persons who have resolved to serve the Lord in the silence of the cloister and wholly remove their wills from the contests of litigation, and to defend them from the molestations of wicked persons. For it has come to our hearing, as you report, that certain powerful persons demand that costly procurations be supplied to them in the granges belonging to your monastery; and, when they wish to obtain them, they violently take your goods to pay such expenses. Others seize and despoil certain hired labourers dwelling in the service of your monastery, and strangers who are subject to them on no ground whatsoever, and by wrongful presumption compel them to render homage.

Therefore, unwilling that your monastery should henceforth be harassed by such vexations, by this present charter, under threat of anathema, we forbid anyone to presume in the granges of your monastery to extort such undue procurations, to compel by any pretext persons dwelling in the service of your monastery to render homage, or unjustly to take their property from them. Let no person, therefore, infringe this charter of our prohibition or rashly act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let that person know that he or she will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1142A] Given at the Lateran, 6 February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CCXLIV. To [Aegidius], Bishop of Modena: he affirms the right to institute canons in the churches of his bishopric. (Lateran, February 12.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Memories of Modena*, IV, 18.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother [AEGIDIUS], Bishop of Modena: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we have been called to the governance of the universal Church, not by our merits but by the Lord’s ordering, we ought to extend the attention of our consideration to such matters that we may correct and improve those things which are undertaken in them contrary to canon law and approved custom, to the prejudice of our brethren and fellow bishops. For it has come to us from the tenor of the letters which you sent to the Apostolic See that, although the institution of clerics in the churches of your diocese belongs to you by right and approved custom, the beloved sons, the archpriests of Saint Vitus and of Baisoria, after your election, without your knowledge or any consultation with you, received Master Martin, provost of your church, and certain others, as is said, as canons; rejecting and entirely disregarding those on whose behalf your brotherhood had taken care to intervene and make request.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, assenting to your petitions, we entirely annul and decree to be invalid such appointments, undertaken without your knowledge, in the aforesaid churches and in the others in which you are known to possess the right of institution. We decree that, as has hitherto been observed in your diocese, no one may be admitted as a cleric in churches subject to you by diocesan law without your authority; and, if admitted, such an appointment shall have no validity. Moreover, by the authority of this letter, we grant your brotherhood authority to subject to excommunication those who presume rashly to disturb or take away the possessions of the churches of your diocese, unless, after your threefold warning, they decide to desist from the audacity of their presumption; and, without appeal, to command that they be avoided by all.

[Col. 1142D] Given at the Lateran, 12 February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CCXLV. Privilege for the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem. (Lateran, February 13.)

[Eug. de ROSIÈRE, *Cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre*, 233.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GAUFRID, prior of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and his brethren, present and future, professing the religious life: in perpetuity.

Whenever that which is known to accord with religion and uprightness is requested of us, it becomes us gladly to grant it and to give suitable support to the desires of the petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, following the example of our predecessors of pious memory—Honorius, Innocent, Celestine, Lucius, Eugene, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs—receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it with the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established in that church according to God and the Rule of Saint Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their proper names:

One half of all offerings which belong or are brought to the Lord’s Sepulchre; but of wax, the church shall always have two thirds—one for the church’s lights and the other for the service of the canons—while only the remaining third shall accrue to the use of our venerable brother the monk, your patriarch, and his successors. You shall also have all offerings of the life-giving Cross, which is assigned to your custody, except on Good Friday alone or when necessity compels the same patriarch or his successors to carry it on campaign; likewise the high altar in your choir, with all offerings accruing to it; the prison also, and its altar, with everything offered there; the altar of Saint Peter and Saint Stephen, and the Finding [of the Cross], with all altars and all offerings; the altar at the head of the Holy Sepulchre, which is parochial, with its offerings; the chair behind the high altar, and everything offered there, or at any of the aforesaid altars, when the patriarch celebrates Mass, whether offered to his hand or at his foot; likewise all offerings of the *compassus* [term uncertain], which is in the middle of your choir; the square between the church gate and the columns, and the other square between those columns and the Hospital of Saint John, extending in its length and breadth; also the houses, shops, lands, and whatever you possess in the quarter of the church and patriarch, and may hereafter justly acquire; and all houses, shops, and lands which you possess inside or outside Jerusalem.

Likewise, all the ovens of Jerusalem except two—one belonging to the Hospital and one to the Latina—and especially that which the patriarch restored to you on the testimony of Peter, Archbishop of Tyre, and which he had held on loan from you. Furthermore, the church and cemetery outside David’s Gate, beside the road to Bethlehem; likewise one half of the possession which King Baldwin I gave to the aforesaid church of the Lord’s Sepulchre in exchange for the bishopric of Bethlehem; all tithes of the city of Jerusalem and of the entire bishopric, except the tithes of the *funde* [uncertain term], reasonably granted to you by Arnulf, Patriarch of Jerusalem of good memory, as you now possess them peacefully; and also such other tithes as you may lawfully acquire in that city and bishopric in the future. We confirm these to you and your church by apostolic authority.

At Nablus, the land which Amalric, illustrious King of Jerusalem, gave you in the new borough; the church which you began to build there, with its cemetery, by concession of Amalric, Patriarch of Jerusalem of blessed memory; and whatever right you have at Nablus and in its district. The twenty-one *casalia* [rural settlements] which Duke Godfrey gave, with their appurtenances, to your church; likewise the villages which you have built, namely Greater and Lesser Machomaria and Bethtsurit, and all others which you are to build wherever Latins shall dwell, with churches and the full integrity of parochial jurisdiction and right. Likewise, Thecue with all its appurtenances, and the church of Quarantine with its appurtenances; Geladia and the land which you bought from John Gomagno; and all the *casalia* with their appurtenances which you bought from Hugh of Ibelin.

The church of Saint Peter at Joppa, with the full integrity of its honour and dignity, as you now peacefully possess it; and the tithe which you have received throughout that entire county from the king, religious persons, and all Christians. Whatever right you have at Ascalon and in its district; whatever right you have under the power and lordship of the lord of Arsuf, at Caesarea and throughout its bishopric; the castle of Fe[n]iculus, the house near Cayfas, Gebul, and Lo Cara; and all that you reasonably possess or shall possess in the whole archbishopric of Nazareth, the bishopric of Acre, and the entire archbishopric of Tyre.

Likewise, everything which you possess or may, by God’s gift, lawfully acquire in the whole patriarchate and kingdom of Jerusalem; whatever right you have at Mount Pilgrim and throughout the bishopric of Tripoli, and at Antioch and throughout its patriarchate and principality, or may lawfully acquire in future, God granting. Furthermore, all possessions which you have on this side of the sea in the kingdom of Sicily—namely, in Sicily itself, Calabria, and all Apulia—first, the church of the Holy Sepulchre and Saint Lawrence at Brindisi with all its appurtenances; at Barletta, the church of the Holy Sepulchre with all its appurtenances; the church at Troia with all its appurtenances; at Benevento, the church of Saint Theodore with all its appurtenances. Whatever right you have or shall have at Rome and in all its territories, in Tuscany, and throughout Italy; moreover, everything which the aforesaid Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre is known lawfully to possess, or may in future acquire by the Lord’s bounty, throughout the kingdom of France and all provinces lawfully subject to it, as well as in all the kingdoms and counties of Spain, or anywhere in transalpine regions. We likewise confirm to you and your successors forever all ancient and reasonable customs of the church. You shall have free power, nevertheless by common counsel, to dispose of these and your other possessions and goods for the honour of God and the advantage of your church.

When the Patriarch of Jerusalem crosses the sea, the prior and canons then serving in the same church shall, as is just, guard and govern the house and household of the patriarch, and all things belonging to his right, inside and outside, until he returns. Upon the death of the patriarch of that place, no one shall be set over it through any deceitful contrivance or violence, except the person whom the canons of that place, by common consent, or the sounder part of the canons, shall canonically determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the institutions of the holy Fathers.

We likewise confirm to you by apostolic authority the stations of the Temple of the Lord, Mount Sion, the Mount of Olives, and the Valley of Jehoshaphat on their feast days, as the Church of the Lord’s Resurrection has always customarily held them; so that, in the patriarch’s absence, the prior then in office may solemnly celebrate Mass there and hold a procession with the canons. We further add that you may condemn by a sentence of interdict and excommunication, during the absence of your patriarch, your malefactors—especially those who take tithes from you—who belong to your parish, within or outside Jerusalem, unless, after lawful warning, they make satisfaction.

We also decree that neither patriarch nor prior may sell, alienate in any manner, or mortgage the church’s goods except by the common counsel of the canons, or of their sounder part. Goods already known to have been alienated from your church to its harm and detriment you may lawfully reclaim. We further enact that neither patriarch nor prior may, without the counsel and consent of the chapter or its sounder part, send any of you to an obedience on this side of the sea, suspend him from his office, or remove him from the fellowship of the canons, except on account of his manifest public fault, or one to which he has confessed or of which he has been convicted. Moreover, the Body of the Lord and ecclesiastical burial shall not be denied to your confreres unless they are excommunicated or personally named in an interdict.

To the foregoing we add that the patriarch shall not dare to demand by obedience from the canons or confreres anything from the goods of your church to which he has no legal right. No one shall presume to demand tithes from you from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. Further, we confirm to you one half of the possessions which are common between you, as in England, Denmark, Germany, Poland, Ruthenia, Avagia, Hungary, Constantinople, and all its territories, in which you ought to contribute one half of the expenses.

[Col. 1146A] We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, carry off its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved unimpaired and entire for the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right and reverence due to the Patriarch of Jerusalem. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly possessing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office, and let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; [Col. 1146B] let him be cut off from the most holy Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. [Col. 1146C] I, Melior, priest-cardinal of the title of Pammachius, of Saints John and Paul. I, Jordan, priest-cardinal of the title of Pastor, of Saint Pudentiana. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscania. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Martin in Equitius. I, Cintius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Sofredus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Fidantius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus. [Col. 1146D] I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Girard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angel. I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the Ides of February, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1195 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

## CCXLVI. He confirms the exchange of the “estate of Bocharn,” made by the provost and chapter of the Church of Augia with C[onrad], bishop, and the canons of Regensburg.

*(Lateran, 15 February.)*

[**Monumenta Boica**, I, 223.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost and chapter of the Church of Augia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant our assent to the just wishes of petitioners, and bring to effect the vows which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously concurring in your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, for you and through you for your church, the exchange of the estate of Bocharn which you concluded with our venerable brother C., bishop, and with our beloved sons, the canons of Regensburg. Since it was reasonably and without any impropriety made and accepted by both parties, and is contained in the bishop’s own authenticated instrument, we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. [Col. 1147B]

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1147C]

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCXLVI bis. To the clergy, nobles, and people of Cyprus.

He announces that, at the request of King Amalric, he has delegated the archdeacon of Laodicea and Alan, chancellor of Cyprus, so that on this island, hitherto schismatic, they may determine, notwithstanding an obstacle of appeal, whatever concerned the provision of endowments for the Church.

*(Lateran, 20 February.)*

[DE MAS-LATRIE, *History of the Island of Cyprus*. Paris, 1854, octavo, Part I: Documents, p. 599, from the cartulary of Venetian Saint Sophia, charter no. 2.]

[Col. 1147D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy, nobles, and people of Cyprus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

God founded the firm foundation of the Church upon the rock in the unity of faith. From the beginning of its birth, having conferred power upon blessed Peter and his vicars, He granted primacy to the Roman See and bestowed upon it the pre-eminence of all teaching. From it, indeed, throughout the many and diverse regions of the world, churches are brought forth as daughters from a mother and are nourished at her breasts with the milk of one doctrine for the edification of the faithful. It belongs to that See to furnish necessary instruction, so that all may receive the rules of teaching from the place where Christ established the primacy of the whole Church; so that she who is recognized as mother of every priestly dignity may also be the teacher of ecclesiastical reason to her children at the breast. For it is possessed by divine privilege, and the enactments of the holy Fathers more clearly declare, that those who at any time think otherwise and endeavor to oppose divine institutions—claiming teaching for themselves not from God, drawing knowledge not from the fountain, and following the tracks of their own will—are proved utterly to stray from the unity of faith and dangerously to strive to wander upon devious paths. [Col. 1148A]

Now, since, as we plainly perceive from the tenor of the letters of our beloved son, the nobleman A., lord of Cyprus, he possesses, solely by God’s inspiration, knowledge in the singleness of faith; and, recognizing the Roman Church as the head and teacher of all churches, he endeavors zealously to lead back the island of Cyprus—whose lordship, we believe, was conferred on him by divine rather than human power—having at last been recalled from its errors through his diligent effort, from the brutish leaven of the schismatics to the unity of the orthodox mother Church. This has been more plainly reported to us through his messenger, our beloved son Master B., archdeacon of Laodicea, a prudent and discerning man. We therefore render abundant thanks to almighty God and commend very highly in the Lord the fervor of his devotion. [Col. 1148B]

Indeed, we have certain confidence in his integrity, since, among other things, we reckon as a powerful inward proof that his brother, the former king of Jerusalem, of revered memory, placed himself as a wall of defense for the Church and displayed his steadfast integrity in many ways. [Col. 1148C]

[Note: [Col. 1147D] King Guy of Lusignan.]

Moreover, having heard the petitions of his devotion and sincere faith, earnestly presented to our apostolic office, and wishing with favorable assent to advance his purpose and desire, we have thought fit to entrust our authority in this matter to the said Master B. and to our beloved son A[lan], chancellor of Cyprus, so that whatever they shall judge ought worthily to be determined with God concerning both tithes and the endowments to be bestowed upon the Church, they shall not delay to establish by our authority, without hindrance from an appeal; and we shall hold it ratified and cause it to be inviolably observed.

[Note: [Col. 1148D] Alan, who became archbishop of Nicosia.]

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your whole community, under obedience, to take care to furnish and provide them, appeals set aside, with diligent effort, favor, counsel, and assistance, so that in these matters they may have a free and desirable course in the Lord. [Col. 1148D]

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCXLVII. He takes the Church of Saint Alban at Basel under protection and confirms its property and rights.

*(Lateran, 21 February.)*

[SCHOEPFLIN, *Alsatian Diplomatic Records*, I, 302.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THEODERIC, provost of the Church of Saint Alban, founded in the territory of Basel, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever. [Col. 1149A]

Whenever a request is made of us which is known to accord with religion and uprightness, it is fitting for us willingly to grant it and to impart apostolic protection to the just desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Saint Alban, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time. [Col. 1149B]

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself where the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances. In the city of Basel itself, the churches of Saint Alban and Saint Martin, as bounded by the River Birs; the church of Bussissenheim, with its dependencies and all its rights; the right which you have in the church of the village called Kemps, and half of the village with its appurtenances; [Col. 1149C] the church of Haegendorf in the village called Lower Basel; the church and village of Appenwilre, with their appurtenances; Loerrach, with its church and all its appurtenances, in vineyards, fields, meadows, and woods alike; the church of Howingen with its appurtenances; the church of Candro with its appurtenances; the church of Aenschossingen with its appurtenances; the wood situated beside Saint Alban; mills on the bank of the Birs, with adjoining meadows; three parts of the tithes in the village called Huningen—on the condition, however, that the priest of that village and of Saint Martin is to receive the fourth part; Rinwilr, Leidinchoven, Habenchesheim, Guzwilre, [Col. 1149D] Sierentze; in the village called Westhalda, one estate with vineyards; Ufheim, Marswilre, Ramspach, Michelenbach, Oberwilr, Bratello, Gelterchingen, Durmin, Hollnstein, Metten, Bladolsheim, Biningen, Magstat, and Utingen, with all their appurtenances.

We likewise confirm for you by the page of this present privilege those possessions and goods which Burkard, bishop of Basel of good memory, granted to your church and confirmed by the protection of his writing. You may also receive clerics or laymen, free and released from secular life, who flee the world for conversion, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving that place without the permission of his provost, except in pursuit of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain one who has left without letters of authorization from the community. [Col. 1150A]

Furthermore, by apostolic authority, we strictly prohibit anyone from presuming to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against you or your churches without manifest and reasonable cause, or to burden you with new and unlawful exactions. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We further decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or expressly interdicted—without prejudice, however, to the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. [Col. 1150B] Moreover, by apostolic authority we confirm for you and your church the liberties and immunities, as well as the ancient and reasonable customs, granted to you and hitherto approved.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your aforesaid church, carry off its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical right of the diocesan bishop, and the due reverence of the monastery of Cluny. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc. [Col. 1150C]

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1195 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

## CCXLVIII. He takes the monastery of Saint Peter at Aldenburg under protection and confirms its goods and privileges.

*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 25 February.)*

[*Chronicle of the Monastery of Aldenburg*, ed. Van de Putte, p. 106.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HERMANN, abbot of Saint Peter of Aldenburg, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever. [Col. 1150D]

To grant effect to just petitioners is required alike by the force of equity and the order of reason, especially when piety supports the wishes of petitioners and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time. [Col. 1151A]

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s help, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The site itself upon which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; one third of the tithe of the entire parish of Aldenborgh; moreover, one third of the tithe, all offerings, and everything which proceeds from the altar of Saint Mary, except the benefices belonging to the priesthood. All these things, subject to an annual payment of eight pounds and eleven shillings, which you must pay every year, as is contained in the privileges of the Church of Tournai, we confirm for you by apostolic authority; the tithe of Eer[.....]ghem; and the land which you possess at Aldenborgh. [Col. 1151B]

Let no one presume to demand or extort from you tithes on your newly cleared lands (*novalia*) which you cultivate by your own labor or expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive clerics or laymen, free or released from secular life, who flee the world for conversion, and retain them without any opposition. We further prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving that place without his abbot’s permission, except in pursuit of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain one who has left without authorization from the community of brethren. [Col. 1151C]

We also strictly forbid any bishop, archdeacon, their officials, canons, or other clerics, under pretext of any custom, to claim the right or permission to demand from us a silk cope or anything else for the confirmation, enthronement, or blessing of the abbot. If they demand anything from you for these things, since this is detestable and contrary to reason, you may freely refuse what they ask. If the land is under interdict, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice. We further decree that burial in that place shall be free, and that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted—without prejudice, however, to the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. [Col. 1151D]

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any stratagem of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the counsel of the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, carry off its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the use and benefit of those for whose governance or support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offense by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his office and honor; let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; [Col. 1152A] let him be cut off from the most holy Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 1152B]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Cencius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1195 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

## CCXLIX. He takes the convent of Saint Mary of Kluaynard under protection and confirms its goods and privileges.

*(Lateran, 26 February.)*

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, II, 1043.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, AGNES, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Kluaynard, and the sisters of that house, present and future, professing the religious life, forever. [Col. 1152C]

The Apostolic See ought to afford protection to prudent virgins who, under the habit of religion, with lamps lit by works of holiness, continually prepare themselves to go forth to meet the Bridegroom, lest an assault of any rashness either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their sacred religious life. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Kluaynard, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that monastery according to the Rule of the Lord and of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Froensian brethren (*Froenses*), shall be immutably observed there for all time. [Col. 1152D]

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s help, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and those who succeed you. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The site itself where the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; Lesnabenny, [Col. 1153A] Grhlem, Balinchuleman, and Rosinbardan, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Luscha, with ten ridges of land in the adjoining field, granted as alms by John, archbishop of Dublin; Cuodmua, Arrd, Grenog, Lesamulin, and Kellathlechty, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Dublin, with the villages of Balinsgellan, Kelmactalmanais, Kelbrigi, and Glenduah, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Damliay, with the village of Balimleochid and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Thermunkechin, with the village of Achadersamid and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Scrin, with the adjoining field of Dumdonnuill and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Odra, with the village itself and all its appurtenances; [Col. 1153B] the church of Saint Brigid of Athrim, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Kenenus, with its dwelling in that city and the village of Disnerthicechan; the church of Saint Mary of Favor, with the village of Kellarthalgach and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Durmaig, with its possessions; the church of Saint Mary of Kluaynmacnois to the east, with the village of Kellogainechan and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary to the west, with the village of Drumalgach and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Evachdun, with the village of Kelgel and its appurtenances.

Let no one presume to demand or extort from you tithes on your newly cleared lands (*novalia*) which you cultivate by your own labor or expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive free and released persons who flee the world for conversion, and retain them without any opposition. We further prohibit any of your sisters, after making profession in your house, from leaving that place without her abbess’s permission, except in pursuit of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain one who has left without letters of authorization from the community. [Col. 1153C]

When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We also prohibit any archbishop, bishop, or any other person, unless requested by you, from presuming to summon public assemblies in your monastery or to conduct lawsuits or other business there, unless he has received a mandate on this matter from the Roman pontiff or his legate. We absolutely forbid new and unlawful exactions to be imposed upon you by archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, deans, or any other ecclesiastical or secular persons. [Col. 1153D]

Furthermore, we have thought fit to prohibit any archbishop, bishop, or other person from being permitted to demand or receive unjustly from you, for your tithes, anything other than what has been demanded by their predecessors up to the present time. You have, by our authority, full liberty to redeem and lawfully free from the hands of laymen the tithes and possessions belonging by right to your churches which are held by laymen, and to restore them to the churches to which they belong. We also confirm for you, and through you for that monastery, the tithes which your monastery has possessed without challenge for forty years and now reasonably possesses. [Col. 1154A]

Moreover, we decree that your ancient liberties and protections, and the reasonable customs granted to your monastery and hitherto observed, shall remain inviolate in future times. We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted—without prejudice, however, to the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. [Col. 1154B]

Upon the death of you, the present abbess of that place, or of any woman who succeeds you there, no one shall be placed over it through any stratagem of intrusion or by force, except one whom the sisters, by common consent or by the counsel of the sounder part of the sisters, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. Furthermore, desiring henceforth to provide with paternal concern for your peace and tranquility, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from committing robbery or theft within the enclosures of your places, shedding blood, rashly seizing or killing a person, or daring to use violence.

We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, etc., on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1195 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III. [Col. 1154C]

## CCL. To the master and brethren of the Order of the Temple.—Concerning tithes.

*(Lateran, 26 February.)*

[ROSIÈRE, *Cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre*, 273.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the master and brethren of the Order of the Temple, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our apostolic office has been informed by the complaint of our beloved sons, the prior and canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre, that you presume, contrary to the order of law, to revoke and render void an agreement concluded and put into writing between yourselves and them concerning the tithes which you possess, or will hereafter possess, in places belonging to them or to their church. For, although it had been agreed between you that each year you would faithfully pay to them and to their successors, without any opposition, one half of all the tithes from the aforesaid places, you do not keep your promise and do not at all fear to reduce the portion due from the said tithes. [Col. 1154D]

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your whole body and, by virtue of obedience, enjoin you that, just as you wish your own privileges to be kept whole and inviolate for you by us, so you must yourselves inviolably observe these obligations towards them, lest repeated complaints coming to us on this matter should deservedly provoke us to act against you. [Col. 1155A]

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCLI. He urges the Count of Toulouse to repair the losses inflicted upon the monastery of Saint-Gilles; otherwise, he declares that he will be excommunicated by the archbishops of Bourges, Narbonne, Arles, and Aix.

*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 1 March.)*

[*History of Languedoc*, III, Proofs, p. 181.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman the Count of Toulouse, greeting, etc.

While we held a lesser office, we loved your father, of revered memory, with a sincere affection of charity. After it pleased the divine will to place us, though unworthy, in the Apostolic See, we resolved not to forget that ancient affection, but to transfer the marks of that same charity to your person—unless your conduct should hinder our intended purpose. Yet such reports of your actions are brought to us that our mind, though unwillingly, is compelled to withdraw from the ardor of that affection. Nor can that true and wholehearted love retain its strength toward you unless appropriate satisfaction follows for the rash offenses by which, as we have heard, you have already prepared a precipice for yourself. [Col. 1155B]

For we have heard—and have conceived no little grief in hearing—that, having no regard for the justice of churches and religious places out of any consideration of divine mercy, you have violently destroyed the church of Asperano and the buildings there, together with everything belonging to that church. Our beloved son, the abbot of Saint-Gilles, asserts that he spent more than sixty thousand solidi on those buildings. You have also hostilely destroyed the church of Scieura, plundering at your own pleasure their harvests at Cassanici and Stagello; you have violently stripped the church of Saint Genesius of all its goods; you have likewise deprived the house of Saint Amantius of all its goods; and you have violently seized a certain mill and the harvests of that same house, and have presumed unlawfully to retain them to the ruin of your soul. Nor was your fury turned aside by these acts. Rather, so that the perversity of your malice might be more clearly displayed, to the detriment of the monastery of Saint-Gilles—which belongs directly to us without any intermediary—you have rashly presumed to build a certain castle on its allodial land. [Col. 1155C]

In this offense, indeed, apart from the other injuries which, as is plainly evident in the instrument authenticated by your seal, are said to have been inflicted by you upon that monastery in violation of your oath, the abbot and convent of that place are required to endure a most grave and damaging prejudice. Therefore, since we so embrace that house that we ourselves suffer grievously any loss inflicted upon it as though it were inflicted upon us, we command your nobility by apostolic letters and strictly enjoin you under threat of anathema to cause the aforesaid castle to be demolished without delay; and, concerning the other injuries and losses inflicted upon the aforesaid monastery, to make full satisfaction, so that no ground for complaint against you may remain to the abbot and convent, and to preserve that monastery unharmed in all its rights. [Col. 1155D]

Otherwise, know that we have strictly commanded our venerable brethren, the archbishops of Bourges, Narbonne, Arles, and Aix, and their suffragans, that, by our authority and with every contradiction, delay, and appeal set aside, they bind you and all your bailiffs and supporters with the bond of excommunication and subject your whole land to interdict. They are not to delay renewing these sentences publicly every Sunday, with lighted candles and ringing bells, and are to cause them to be solemnly renewed throughout all the churches of their dioceses. In all other lands to which you may come, while you are present there, they are to forbid the celebration of divine offices, until you have rendered suitable satisfaction in all the matters set forth above. Know for certain that, if you choose to persist in your begun malice, we release all your men from the oath of fealty by which they are bound to you. [Col. 1156A]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of March, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

## CCLII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Wedinghusen.

*(Lateran, 7 March.)*

[HUGO, *Premonstratensian Annals*, vol. I, Proofs, p. 117.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CHRISTIAN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Wedinghusen, and his brethren, present and future, professing an excellent life, forever. [Col. 1156C]

Those who choose the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest an assault of any rashness either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their religious life. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Lawrence at Wedinghusen, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren shall be inviolably observed there for all time. [Col. 1156D]

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s help, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The site itself on which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the estate at Marselde, which Count Henry of Arnsberg—who, moved by pious consideration, founded your monastery [Col. 1157A]—granted, with the consent of his sons Henry and Godfrey, to the same monastery to possess in perpetuity, with all its appurtenances; the estate called Evenho; the hill called Echols; the hill called Cetus; one holding at Weltere; one holding at Eenole; one holding at Buren; one holding at Hagenen; one holding at Holthausen; Grinele; Hagenbole; Mollensclea; Wige; the tithe of Wanden, which you possess by the gift of Everhard of Arthei and his brother Jonathan; Eoolbem in Wirte, which the aforesaid brothers Henry and Godfrey, by prudent deliberation, granted to your monastery with all its appurtenances; and the right held in the convent of nuns at Rumbecke.

Furthermore, no one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes from your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense [Col. 1157B], from your gardens and shrubs, your fisheries, or the increase of your animals. You may also have clerics or laymen, receive into the monastery those released from the world and fleeing to it, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your monasteries, to leave that place without the permission of their abbot; and no one shall dare retain one who departs without the common authorization contained in your letters. We further prohibit any bishop or other person from asking or receiving from you for your tithes more than has been granted by predecessors and required up to the present time.

When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land [Col. 1157C], you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, is in communion with the holy Roman See, and is willing to provide these to you without any improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you wish who possesses the grace and communion of the Apostolic See, and who, relying upon our authority, shall supply what you request.

Moreover, we forbid anyone, within the bounds of your parish [Col. 1157D], to dare build a new chapel or oratory without the assent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We also entirely prohibit new and undue exactions by archbishops, archdeacons, deans, and all other ecclesiastical or secular persons. We decree also that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved.

Furthermore, by our authority you have free power to redeem and lawfully free from the hands of laymen the tithes, possessions, and rights belonging to your churches which are held by laymen, and to restore them to the churches to which they belong [Col. 1158A]. Desiring also, with paternal concern, to provide henceforth for your peace and tranquility, we confirm by apostolic authority that within the enclosures of your houses or granges no one may dare commit robbery or theft, set fire, shed blood, rashly seize or kill a person, or perpetrate violence. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the privilege of this writing all liberties and immunities granted to your order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted by kings, princes, and the faithful.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, seize its possessions, retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop [Col. 1158B]. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our confirmation, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance [Col. 1158C]. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ottomanus, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor [Col. 1158D]. I, John, cardinal of the church of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tusculum. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cintius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Loffricius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of Saint Peter, of the title of Eudoxia. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. [Col. 1159A] I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Centius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the Nones of March, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1196 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Celestine III.

### CCLIII. To the Chapter of Nidaros.—He forbids any layman in the diocese of Nidaros to exercise ecclesiastical jurisdiction.  
*(Lateran, 17 March.)*

[THORKELIN, *Diplom. Arna-Magn.*, II, 17.]

[Col. 1159B]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of Nidaros: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since ecclesiastical dignities and spiritual jurisdiction ought to be foreign to lay persons, we cannot sufficiently wonder that, after the canonical ordinances of Pope Adrian, our predecessor of happy memory—who established three archdeaconries in your Church and directed that a single dean be ordained—you complain that ecclesiastical jurisdictions are exercised by laymen and that undue authority in spiritual matters is granted to them. Therefore, desiring to remove so detestable an abuse from the Church of Nidaros, we expressly forbid by the authority of the present letter that any layman in your diocese exercise ecclesiastical jurisdiction or hear or determine causes which require settlement by ecclesiastical judgment [Col. 1159C].

Therefore let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our prohibition and constitution or rashly act against it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CCLIV. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Maurice of Agaunum.  
*(Lateran, 2 April.)*

[See GUICHENON, *Bibl. Sebus.*, p. 262.]

[Col. 1159D]

### CCLV. He grants William, abbot of Saint Maurice of Agaunum, the use of the mitre and ring.  
*(Lateran, 6 April.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, 431, Documents.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, abbot of Saint Maurice of Agaunum: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the monastery of Saint Maurice is subject to the Holy Roman Church and exists under the protection of Saint Peter, we believe it fitting and reasonable that it should rejoice in the prerogative of a special privilege bestowed through the Apostolic See [Col. 1160A], so that its liberty may be recognized in the gift and its dignity displayed in its adornment. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, considering the devotion which your Church has always shown toward the Roman Church, and also considering the constancy in religious life which, on the testimony of many, we have learned that you possess, we have judged that the use of the mitre and ring should be granted to you and your successors through the kindness of the Apostolic See, for use within your church at the solemnities of Mass on feast days. Let no person, therefore, infringe this page of our grant or rashly act against it. If anyone should presume to do so, let him know that he will incur the wrath of Almighty God and the indignation of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1160B]

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CCLVI. To Berard, archbishop-elect of Messina, he confirms “the whole tithe of the river Dionysius.”  
*(Lateran, 10 April.)*

[PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, vol. I, p. 400.]

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, in the fifth year of the pontificate.

### CCLVII. He decrees that Greek and Latin abbots shall provide the necessary procurations for Berard, archbishop-elect of Messina, when visiting his diocese.  
*(Lateran, 13 April.)*

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1160C]

Bernard—whom Lellus calls Bernardus and Bonfiglius calls Bertius—was a monk of Saint Benedict and bishop of Messina. Pope Celestine III gave him authority, by a diploma issued at the Lateran on the Ides of April, in the fifth year of his pontificate, the year of salvation 1196, that when he visited his diocese he might compel Greek and Latin abbots to provide the procuration owed and customary to him.

### CCLVIII. To [William], bishop of Maguelone.  
*(Lateran, 22 April.)*

[GARIEL, *Series praesulum*, etc., vol. II, p. 245.]

[Col. 1160D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Maguelone: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although unworthy, we have been raised to the height of the supreme pontificate; it is fitting that we admit the just petitions of all and especially foster in the Lord the rights of our brothers and fellow bishops. For when due honor is kept unimpaired for the governance of churches, ecclesiastical vigor gains strength and ecclesiastical discipline can never perish. It has indeed come to the knowledge of our apostolate that, whenever the archdeaconry and sacristy in your church happen to become vacant, those whose assent you are bound to seek for the conferral of those dignities, while raising no reasonable or canonical objection to the persons named by you, maliciously endeavor to impede your appointment [Col. 1161A] and, led by their own will, oppose the appointment itself.

Therefore, unwilling that the appointment to customary dignities in churches should be delayed through anyone’s malevolent evasions, we grant this privilege to your brotherhood by the present letter. If those whose assent you are bound to request in appointing the aforesaid dignities raise no reasonable or canonical objection against the persons named by you, and, having been lawfully required, do not prove such an objection, you may, notwithstanding entirely their opposition or appeal, appoint by apostolic authority a suitable person of that church to the aforesaid vacant dignities within the period established by the Lateran Council.

We decree, therefore, that no person may infringe [Col. 1161B] this page of our grant or rashly act against it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

### CCLIX. To [William], bishop, and the chapter of the Church of Maguelone.  
*(Lateran, 22 April.)*

[Ibid., p. 247.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Maguelone and to his beloved sons, the chapter of Maguelone [Col. 1161C]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although unworthy, we have been raised to the summit of the supreme pontificate in order that we may bestow in the Lord worthy rewards upon the good for their merits and, as far as we can, oppose the malicious acts of individuals.

For, as we have received by a truthful report, both you, brother bishop, and your predecessor of good memory, when you came to the Roman Church, were taken captive and stripped of all your possessions, and your companions were forced to pay ransom. Even now, because the malice of very many persons abounds in your regions, many canons and men of the Church of Maguelone are frequently seized by your parishioners and neighbors. Desiring, as far as we can, to provide against injury to you and your church, we grant you by the present authority [Col. 1161D] that whoever in your diocese seizes a bishop, canons, or men of the Church of Maguelone, or violently takes away their goods, and after canonical warning does not take care to correct his offense by worthy amendment and make appropriate satisfaction to you and your church, shall thereafter, as an excommunicated person, be strictly avoided by all. His land and the place in which that wrongdoer lives, and in which the captive person or stolen goods are held, shall be subjected to ecclesiastical interdict until due satisfaction is made.

Therefore no person may infringe this page of our grant or rashly act against it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation [Col. 1162A] of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

### CCLX. He forbids the prior and monks of Saint Pancras of Lewes to pay certain pensions or “to promise churches to anyone before they fall vacant.”  
*(Lateran, 27 April.)*

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 93.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, . . . . prior and monks of Saint Pancras of Lewes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Things wrongly undertaken contrary to the order of law, to the prejudice of churches, must be corrected by apostolic authority [Col. 1162B]. Since, by the duty of the service laid upon us, it is incumbent upon us to consider with paternal concern each church scattered throughout the whole world, we must consult their welfare and are bound to relieve their burdens.

We have learned that, at the insistence of certain nobles whose favor you could not easily refuse, you promised the first, second, and third churches that should become vacant to certain clerics, to whom meanwhile you paid fixed pensions; and your church is seriously burdened by paying them. Therefore, granting apostolic favor to your petitions, by authority of the Apostolic See we absolve you and your church from promises of this kind and decree that you are not bound to pay such pensions [Col. 1162C]. We strictly forbid you to presume to promise churches to anyone before they become vacant, or to invest anyone with them.

Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our absolution and prohibition or rashly act against it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

### CCLXI. He confirms to the chapter of Parma Ponte Litia, with its chapel.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 29 April.)*

[AFFO, *Storia di Parma*, III, 309.]

[Col. 1162D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GIRARD, archdeacon, and the chapter of the Church of Parma: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honorable is requested of us, both the rigor of equity and the order of reason require that, through the care of our office, it be brought to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gladly consenting to your just petitions, we confirm to your devotion by apostolic authority Ponte Litia with its chapel, as you justly and without dispute possess them [Col. 1163A], and strengthen them by the protection of this writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly act against it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

### CCLXII. Bull for the nunnery of Crisenon.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 1 May.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, Documents, 140.]

[Col. 1163B]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, SARAH, abbess of Crisenon, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

The Apostolic See ought to extend its protection to prudent virgins who, under the habit of religion, with lamps kept alight by works of holiness, continually prepare themselves to go forth to meet the Bridegroom, lest an assault of any rash person recall them from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of Eugene, our predecessor of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid place of Crisenon, where you are devoted to divine service [Col. 1163C], and strengthen it by the privilege of this writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have judged the following to be expressly named:

The place itself on which your convent is situated, with all its appurtenances; the oven in the market of Auxerre; the oven of Saint Gervais, with the right of use in the wood of Bar; the mills in the meadows; the enclosed vineyard; the pond at Santolives; eighty *brunelli* of salt; [Col. 1163D] the right of use in the wood of Fretai. At Baserne, two *modii* of grain; in the mills of the son of the nobleman Narioudus, one [measure], and another in the rents of Galfrid; and a third part of the allod, in wood and plain, waters, and all customs and usages; and two *modii* of wine in the enclosure of Narioudus, lord of Baserne; and at Baserne one *sextarius* of wheat. At Chistri, ten shillings of annual rent; at Valan, rent and grain; at Monasterellum, the church with the presentation of the priest, twenty shillings and ten pounds of wax, fifty shillings from the toll of the village of Liniac, and half the lesser tithes; in Campis, the tithe of wine and grain; at Apoignis, ten shillings of annual rent; at Saint-Cyr, the tithe of grain and other produce; at Malliac-villa, half the lesser [Col. 1164A] tithes, and from Malliac castle the tithe of Roan.

Again, at Auxerre, two ovens by the Feschel gate, the oven of Saint Eusebius, and several vineyards; the mills of Cren. At Rippa, three *sextarii* of grain and five shillings of annual rent; at Noers, one *modius* of grain from the mill of Montet; at Ultenatum, an oven; in the fields of Mondefeis, part of the tithe; at Malliac, ten pounds from sales; the right to use deadwood in the wood of Arsiac; at Marriac, sufficient use of land, stone, and woodland for the operation of the mills of Cren; at Pré-Gilbert, a grange with its territory, rent, customs, and usages; the church of Luchiac, with the presentation of the priest; the village of Lissi with its appurtenances [Col. 1164B], and the church of that village with the presentation of the priest; the grange of Charmei with its territory; the mills of Arsiac, the tithe of grain and wine, two shillings of annual rent, and a fourth part of the offerings at three feasts; the grange of Vertennac with its territory; the vineyards and houses of Varziac with their appurtenances; the grange of Chalmes with its territory; at Truciac, rent and customs; at Sementeron, a third of the tithe and the whole lesser tithe; half the tithe of Chassi; rent and usages at Crevent; rent at Jussi; rent and customs at Colunias; at Château-Censoir, the annual allowances of the canons’ prebends; at Nuiliac in Champagne, half the tithes; at Lisigni, ten shillings of annual rent; [Col. 1164C] at Fonroone, half an oven; likewise confirming to you the right which you hold in the monastery of La Ferté.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. Upon the death of you, the present abbess of that place, or of any who succeed you, no one shall be set over it through any craft of intrigue or violence, except one whom the sisters by common consent, or the sounder part of the sisters’ counsel, shall in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict provide to be elected.

[Col. 1164D]

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your aforesaid convent, seize its possessions, retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, all things are to be preserved whole for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to their benefit in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orchea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the Kalends of May, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1196 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Celestine III.

### CCLXIII. He commands Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, to allow the monks of Thorney to appoint a successor in place of their deposed abbot.  
*(Lateran, 6 May.)*

[TWYSDEN, *Hist. Angl. Scr.*, I, 696.]

[Col. 1165A]
