CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HUBERT, archbishop of Canterbury.

Since the tares which threaten to choke the wheat harvest must be cut from the Lord’s field by the apostolic sickle, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters: once the abbot of Thorney has been removed both from administration and from the office of abbot, you are to grant the monks, by our authority and setting aside the obstacle of appeal, permission to elect a suitable person as abbot. Furthermore, lest the aforesaid abbot’s offense remain unpunished [Col. 1165B], we will and command you by the authority of this letter to have him arrested and committed to prison custody until you receive our decision in this matter.

Given at the Lateran, on the day before the Nones of May, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CCLXIV. He takes under protection the Church of Saint Mary in Port at Ravenna and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(Lateran, 11 May.)*

[FANTUZZI, *Mon. Ravenn.*, II, 167.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons VARDO, prior of the church of Saint Mary in Port at Ravenna, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

The authority of the Apostolic See entrusted to us urges us to grant the protection of guardianship to places and persons which duly seek its aid with devotion. For just as no assent should be granted to those seeking unjust things, so the lawful and just petition of those who ask ought not be delayed—especially of those who, through integrity of life and praiseworthy ordering of conduct, rejoice in serving Almighty God. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, with all that belongs to it, after the example of Innocent and Adrian, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors [Col. 1165D], and strengthen it by the privilege of this writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God favoring it, through the grant of pontiffs, the gift of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have judged the following to be expressly named:

The place itself on which the aforesaid church is situated, together with the whole island; the place called Corrizolo with its marsh beside the Bidente, and Badarenum, extending to the harbor of Gaius Caesar and to the road that runs [Col. 1166A] beside the hills of Saint Severus as far as the sea; whatever rights you possess in the region of Ravenna, both in the city and outside it; the water-mill with its redemption-payment and appurtenances outside the gate of Saint Lawrence at Ravenna, where you constructed a mill beside the bridge, on the upper and outer side of that bridge, which you hold by right of blessed Peter under an annual rent of one denarius of Luccan coin payable to the Roman Church; whatever rights you possess in the bishopric of Cervia—saltworks, fisheries, and houses, with lands and vineyards situated in the place called Bovaredo; the place of Saint Pellegrinus with lands, vineyards, fields, and meadows; and whatever rights you possess in the bishopric of Cesena, together with the church of the Holy Cross, which belongs by right to blessed Peter, and with all you possess in that vicariate.

[Col. 1166B] Whatever you possess in the county of Osimo; whatever you possess in the county of Senigallia; the place called Monte della Croce, with the chapel built there; whatever rights you possess in the bishopric of Fano, with the chapel called Saint Mary of the Sea; whatever rights you possess in the bishoprics of Pesaro and Rimini; whatever you possess in the bishopric of Forlimpopoli and the bishopric of Forlì, with the chapel of Saint Augustine; whatever rights you possess in the bishopric of Faenza, with the chapel of Saint Mary called *in Stratella*; whatever you possess in the bishoprics of Imola and Bologna, or in the district of Medicina and the parish of Veterana; whatever rights you possess in the county of Mantua, with the church of Saint Bartholomew and the church of Saint Mary of Venice, with all their appurtenances [Col. 1166C]; whatever you possess in the bishoprics of Padua and Treviso and in the bishopric of Chioggia; whatever you possess in the bishopric of Comacchio and in the places called Gatula, Vincareta, and Fossa-Bovaria, with all the valleys and marshes belonging to those appurtenances; whatever you possess in the woodland district of Ferrara, with the chapel of Saint Margaret; and whatever Walter, Moses, Anselm, and Gerard, archbishops of Ravenna of good memory, granted you out of pious regard in the estate of Costanciago, at Sandolo, at Argenta, or in other places and estates.

Also, whatever has been granted to the same church by the bishops of Fermo, Rimini, Cesena, Cervia, Forlì, Comacchio, and Mantua; whatever your predecessors acquired from Alipontus, abbot of Saint Andrew of Cereto in the region of Istria, by *emphyteusis* [Col. 1166D, a hereditary lease], or was granted by other abbots of other monasteries. Furthermore, whatever the abbots of Saint Apollinaris in Classe and Saint John the Evangelist, and the cantors of the Church of Ravenna, have granted you, as is contained in their authentic documents.

You may also receive into conversion in your congregation clerics fleeing the world, without objection or harassment from any bishop or provost; and you may yourselves associate laymen from any parishes with your community for conversion to regular discipline, unless they are bound by some lawful obligation. No bishop or provost may forbid you this. Nor may any brother of the same church, after making profession with you, be permitted on any pretext to leave your cloister or house without permission of the prior of your church or of the common congregation [Col. 1167A]. If any professed cleric or layman leaves your cloister or house and, after warning, refuses to return, the prior then in office of that church shall have authority from the Apostolic See to suspend and excommunicate such a person from his offices; and no bishop or abbot may presume to receive or retain one suspended or excommunicated. We grant all these things by apostolic authority so long as the practice of canonical order, God granting, remains vigorous among you.

Furthermore, by our authority you may give the clerical tonsure in your place to those who wish through profession to live according to the rule [Col. 1167B]. You shall have permission to receive the ordination of your clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, if at any time the Church of Ravenna has no bishop, or if its bishop is known not to be Catholic, or if he is unwilling to grant this to you freely. Certainly, no bishop or episcopal official may dare demand from you tithes of the fruits which you gather anywhere by your own labor and expense. We decree also that the burial-ground of your sacred places shall be wholly free: no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict.

In addition, by the authority of the present privilege we decree that your aforesaid church, together with all its possessions everywhere, shall be exempt from every extraordinary service. Thus, if it should happen at any time that the archbishop of Ravenna, or any other bishop in whose parish you have a church or possessions, or, upon the death of an archbishop, clerics or laymen of that church, must travel to the Roman pontiff or to the emperor on any business, they may dare impose upon you no exaction in silver, mounts, or any other expenses from the goods of that church, nor ever impose a burden on you by lodging there [Col. 1167C]. Furthermore, if war breaks out and the citizens of Ravenna or of other cities, or the inhabitants of other places, levy a contribution for soldiers or for defending city or castle, we likewise command that your aforesaid church shall be exempt from every exaction [Col. 1167D].

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, seize or diminish its possessions, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved whole for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to their benefit in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future, etc. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, etc.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. [Col. 1168A] I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tusculum. I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Callixtus. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saint Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 1168B] I, Cinthius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Soffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1196 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Celestine III.

### CCLXV. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Paris.  
*(Lateran, 14 May.)*

[*Cartulaire de Notre-Dame de Paris*, I, 26.]

[Col. 1168C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MAURICE, bishop of Paris, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The more renowned the noble and glorious Church of Paris is because it is the seat of the king of the Franks, and in its love and reverence for blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, venerable brother Bishop Maurice, etc., as in the privilege of Innocent II, as far as: “are known to pertain.”

The episcopal jurisdiction likewise in the following abbeys and all their parishes or parishioners: namely, in the abbey of Latiniacum, the abbey of Fossatum, the abbey of Saint Magloire, the abbey of Saint Victor, the abbey of the Valley of Saint Mary, the abbey of Sarneia, the abbey of Herivallis, the abbey of Hermeniarum, the abbey of Mont-Estif, the abbey of the nuns of Montmartre, the abbey of Hedera, the abbey of Kala, the abbey of Gif, the abbey of Saint Cyriacus, and the abbey of the Deep Valley; and in the church above Argenteuil.

Desiring also to provide for the peace and tranquillity of the Church of Paris, etc., as in the privileges of Innocent II and Lucius II.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucia in Orthea, chamberlain of our lord pope, on the second Ides of May, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1196, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Celestine III.

CCLXVI. He confirms the customs of the chapter of Mâcon. (Lateran, 15 May.)

[SEVERTIUS, *Chronological History*, II, 146.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of Mâcon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those things which are wisely established and confirmed by our brethren exercising the office of legation ought to be strengthened by protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we approve the reasonable customs of your church hitherto approved, which our beloved son Melchior, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, then legate of the Apostolic See in those regions, approved and confirmed, as they are contained in his authentic document. For greater firmness in the future, we have caused it to be inserted and copied word for word in this present letter. Its tenor is as follows:

Melchior, by the grace of God cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Mâcon: greeting in the Lord.

The pious desires of worthy wills ought to be assisted with the greatest care, so that, if they lack any firmness, they may attain their effect through the favour of their superiors.

[Col. 1169C] Certainly, when you, beloved dean, came into our presence to promote the affairs of your church, you humbly requested that we confirm the approved customs of that church. You also showed that they had been strengthened by an authentic document of Stephen, formerly bishop of Mâcon, of good memory. We therefore, assenting to your just petitions, have thought fit to establish by this present authority that, whenever the bishop of Mâcon has been duly consecrated, he shall first promise to observe, with every vigilance and care, the customs and rights of the church, and of the chapter or clergy over whom he presides.

These, moreover, are the things which the church has hitherto possessed by custom and right. The bishop must not, when he wishes to answer in the common chapter concerning a canon or any other person of the choir of the church or clergy, commit an injustice or compel others [to do so]. Whenever he is called upon concerning an injury or loss inflicted upon the canons or clergy of the same church, especially concerning possessions and goods belonging to the church, he must immediately administer fitting justice against the wrongdoers.

The bishop must not take part in the election of canons or the granting of prebends, except that canons elected in chapter receive the book from his hand as investiture. Likewise, when the deanery or the office of cantor is vacant, the chapter has free authority to elect without the bishop. Thereafter, when a person has been elected by common consent, the bishop, summoned for this purpose, confirms the dignity by ascending to the place of honour in the choir. The bishop shall choose, from the church, such archdeacons as he wishes and wherever he wishes; but he shall present those elected in chapter, [Col. 1170A] and thereafter shall give them investiture in the choir into their respective seats.

If a bishop is chosen from the body of the church, whatever possessions he holds from it immediately revert to that body. They nevertheless remain in common possession until he is consecrated; or, if he is perhaps rejected, he shall recover his possessions.

Each year the bishop owes three general procurations (meals) in the refectory: the first at the Nativity of the Lord, the second on the feast of the Passion of Blessed Vincent, and the third at Easter; and three spiced provisions: the first in Advent for the abbey, the second for the sacristy, and the third for the bishopric.

The bishop has no exactions from the chaplains belonging to the chapter, except that, according to his means and at a suitable time, he must not refuse lodging if it should be necessary. Because the bishop is sacristan, he must repair the ruined roofs of the church, recast broken bells, and [the chapter: all remaining buildings of the church, towers, pavement, etc.]; he must also provide what is necessary for divine offices, both lights and other things, and likewise a candle in the refectory for guests of the church.

All these things which have hitherto been observed without contradiction in your church we hold valid and firm, and, by the authority of the legation which we exercise, confirm them, forbidding under threat of anathema anyone rashly to presume to oppose them.

In order that these things may indeed be observed inviolably—here and henceforth Pope Celestine resumes the discourse—we have caused this present page to be strengthened by the impression of our seal; we confirm it by this present page and support its legal force by the protection of this written instrument. We further decree that the constitution which the same cardinal, with the counsel of our and your venerable brother the bishop, established concerning those clerics who were negligent in the divine offices of the Church of Mâcon, shall remain wholly firm and unimpaired, and that none of you or your successors shall presume by any rashness to violate it.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of His apostles Saints Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of May, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CCLXVII. He decrees upon whom, among the clergy of Modena, the burden of expenses should fall at the arrival or passage of legates of the Apostolic See and of the metropolitan. (Lateran, 21 May.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 1055.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Modena: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By letters recently sent to our apostolic office, your brotherhood has taken care to inform us that there has from ancient times been such a custom in your city: on the first day the bishop, on the second the canons, on the third the abbot of Saint Peter, and on the fourth the clerics of that city ought to provide for legates of the Apostolic See. In this you alone are greatly burdened, because, when at times a legate of the Roman Church or your metropolitan remains in that city for only one day, you alone furnish him with provision, and the others who are obliged [to do so] provide you with no aid of assistance.

Therefore, not wishing that you should be burdened, as is unfitting, in receiving them, we have thought fit to establish by this present page that, if at any time a legate of the Roman Church or the metropolitan does not remain in the city of Modena for as many days as would enable him to receive the individual aforementioned procurations in their order, those who are bound to furnish procurations shall take care to reimburse you proportionately from that procuration, so that you may not be unduly burdened in furnishing procurations and the due honour and service may be rendered to the Roman Church by those who are bound to render it.

Given at the Lateran, 12 days before the Kalends of June, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CCLXVIII. He commands S[icard], bishop of Cremona, not to allow the church of the Holy Cross at Cremona to suffer injury, to the detriment of the administration of the monastery of Nonantola, at the hands of its patrons and neighbours. (Lateran, 4 June.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of Nonantola*, II, 324.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother S., bishop of Cremona: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1171C] Upon the complaint of our beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Nonantola, it has been brought to our hearing that the church of the Holy Cross of Cremona belongs specially and by right to them; and that until these times they have been accustomed to appoint and remove there its prior, monks, and chaplain. Yet the patrons and neighbours of that church, setting aside ecclesiastical reverence, are attempting to hold that church at their own will, to the prejudice of the abbot and convent, and to install a prior and chaplain there contrary to the order of law. It has further been added that they have pledged a certain vineyard of that church against the will of those residing there.

Since these things, if true, ought not to be passed over with closed eyes, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters effectively to warn and induce the said presumptuous persons to leave the said church to the aforementioned abbot and convent of Nonantola to administer in the liberty in which they have been accustomed to administer it, without anyone’s opposition, and to redeem from their own goods the aforesaid vineyard. If necessary, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal being set aside.

Given at the Lateran, on the second Nones of June, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CCLXIX. Confirmation of the agreement between the archbishop and the clergy of Split. (Lateran, 15 June.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum Sacrum*, III, 226.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the archbishop and to his beloved sons the canons of Split: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since a dispute concerning various articles was pending between you, brother archbishop, and the clergy of your city, you brought it before our sight so that, examined under our judgment, it might be brought to a due conclusion. You, brother archbishop, were asking those clerics to pay you the fourth part of the tithing and offerings from the body of the city which was due to you. You also requested that, whenever you or your successors should go to the Roman Church, those same clerics should give you suitable assistance.

They replied to you as follows: your predecessors were obliged to provide for five weekly ministers—the priest, namely, deacon, subdeacon, acolyte, and sacristan—for the entire week, and this seemed unbearable to them. Thus they agreed with the canons that, in compensation for the aforesaid procurations, they themselves should have the fourth part of the tithing and offerings from the body of the city, as is expressly contained in the writings of your predecessors Gaudius, Gerard, and Peter, of good memory. They further requested twelve meals, to be received on fixed and specified feasts of the year, Saturday drink-allowances, and the procurations to be furnished to three weekly ministers on each Sunday.

Since we, occupied with many and various affairs, could not attend to these matters, we granted you as auditors our venerable brother J[ohn], bishop of Viterbo, cardinal of Saint Clement, and our beloved son C. de Sancto Apostolo, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. In their presence, after many disputes and allegations on either side, you adopted sounder counsel and agreed as follows: you clerics shall assign the fourth part of the tithing and offerings of the city to the archbishop; and you, brother archbishop, through your procurator shall annually give the aforesaid clerics twenty perperi from that fourth part of the tithing and offerings in compensation for the aforesaid procurations, while whatever remains of that fourth part shall be applied to your own uses and benefit.

Moreover, you shall give them only six meals on the stated feasts of the year, namely on the feast of Saint Domnius, Pentecost, the translation of Saint Domnius, Saint Anastasius, Saints Cosmas and Damian, and Saint Vincent; Saturday drink-allowances; and procurations for three weekly ministers on every Sunday. You shall render the aforesaid clerics perpetually exempt from all other assistance which you had demanded as due from the clergy of the whole city, both for yourself and for your successors.

Holding this amicable agreement, made with the assent and will of both parties, valid and firm, notwithstanding the aforesaid writings or any others appearing to prejudice the archbishop himself, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present instrument.

[Col. 1173A] Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of His apostles Saints Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 17 days before the Kalends of July, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CCLXX. To the bishops of Skradin and Knin. (Lateran, 15 June.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum Sacrum*, III, p. 227.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops of Skradin and Knin: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When our venerable brother your archbishop and his canons were present before us, those canons began to raise against the same archbishop a claim concerning the tenth part of the tithing which arises throughout the whole archbishopric outside the city, and they urgently requested it from him. But because they had not come sufficiently prepared for this matter, we have thought fit to commit it to your examination and to have it brought to a due conclusion. Therefore we command your brotherhoods by apostolic letters to summon the parties, hear what they may see fit to put forward on either side, and terminate the cause between them by justice or agreement.

[Col. 1173C] Given at the Lateran, 17 days before the Kalends of July, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CCLXXI. He enlarges the privileges and possessions of the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Fécamp, subject only to the Roman pontiff. (Lateran, 25 June.)

[*Neustria Pia*, 242.]

Although, by reason of the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by God, we ought generally to honour and love religious men and preserve their rights to the churches committed to them, we ought nevertheless to provide with more devoted care for those known to adhere particularly to Blessed Peter by a more special prerogative. The monastery of the Holy Trinity of Fécamp, founded in religion, has indeed long been noble and renowned, and subject to no one but the Roman pontiff. For all these reasons, we judge that the place deserves ampler favour and benevolence, and we wish affectionately to cherish it beneath the pious bosom of the Apostolic See.

But since, as you have explained to us, you sent one of your monks to England, with the privileges of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, to defend the liberty of the monastery of Fécamp, and while crossing the sea between your land and England that monk was struck by a violent storm and lost the privileges along with the other things he possessed: therefore, wishing to provide lest, because you do not have those privileges, your right might in any respect be diminished or disturbed, we confirm by the page of this authentic instrument all dignities, liberties, and benefices granted to your monastery by the Roman pontiffs, our predecessors. We receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all the churches named below, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

We establish that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God favouring, acquire by the grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit expressly to name the following:

[Col. 1174B] Namely, the churches of the entire parish of Fécamp: the church of Eslcetot, the church of Limpivilla, the church of Turmovilla, the church of Witeflou, the church of Palluel, the church of Saint Riquier, the church of Ingovilla, the church of Saint Valery, the church of Magnaville, the church of Wellis, and the two churches which are at Dunum. At Rouen: the church of Saint Gervais, the church of Saint Mary of Wasto, the church of Saint Albin above Sedan, and the church of Torvilla. In the diocese of Lisieux: the church of Dudecheravilla. In the diocese of Bayeux: all the churches of Argentiis with their appurtenances, all those of Dimondevilla, and the church of Saint Gabriel.

[Col. 1174C] In England: the church of Staninges with its chapels. (In *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. II, the priory of Cogges is recorded in the district of Oxford.) In France: the church of Aviscomont; also the abbey of Bernay, the abbey of Saint Taurin of Évreux, and the abbey of Saint Bertha of Torne. We confirm their administration to you and, through you, to the Church of Fécamp.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected from their own community or, if necessary, from another, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The person elected shall proceed to the Apostolic See, or to whatever Catholic bishop he prefers, to receive blessing by the permission and mandate of the Roman pontiff.

No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you of your new lands which you cultivate with your own hands or resources, or from the produce of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and unencumbered, fleeing from the world, and retain them without any opposition. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, to depart from it unless he has obtained permission to enter a stricter religious life; nor shall anyone dare retain one who departs without letters of authorization from your community.

[Col. 1175A] You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the ordination of your monks or clerics, and the consecration of the aforesaid altars or churches from whatever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall supply what is requested. Moreover, we establish that the abbot of that place shall not be compelled to attend any council unless summoned by the Roman pontiff or his legate. Nor shall your church, or its abbot, monks, clerics, or servants in churches wholly exempt from episcopal jurisdiction, be interdicted from divine offices or subjected to excommunication by anyone other than the Roman pontiff or his legate.

When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice. We further decree that the burial-ground of that place is free; no one shall oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving, however, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

In the parochial churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust to them the care of souls, so that they shall be accountable to him for spiritual matters and to you for temporal matters.

Whatever dignity, liberty, or benefice the monastery of Fécamp is known to have obtained from the Apostolic See, we likewise grant and confirm to you and your church. No bishops, officers of bishops, or any persons whatsoever may impose any exactions or molestations upon the abbey of Fécamp, the aforesaid churches, or the clerics serving them; rather, they shall remain free and undisturbed, so that they may more freely fulfil their vows to almighty God.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1175D] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour, and know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and at the final judgment be subject to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1176A] Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucia in Orchea, chamberlain of our lord pope, seven days before the Kalends of July, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1196 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Celestine III.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavianus, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter Fornerius, bishop of Santa Rufina. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscania. I, Guido, cardinal priest of Saint Mary and Saint Callixtus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 1176B] I, Cencius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Joffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Frederick, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Gratianus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerardus, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 1176C] I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.

CCLXXII. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Mary of Vangadizza. (Lateran, 26 June.)

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, IV, Appendix, p. 202.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ALICHO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Vangadizza, etc.

The authority of the Apostolic See, over which by the Lord’s authorship we preside, exhorts us to labour for the condition of churches and to establish with more earnest diligence those things arranged for their peace. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and strengthen by the privilege of the Apostolic See the aforesaid monastery of Vangadizza, in which you are dedicated to divine service. As is known, it was founded by Hugh, formerly marquis, of revered memory, was endowed with liberty by our predecessors in holy memory—Sylvester, Callixtus, Innocent, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs—and belongs by a special prerogative to the right of Blessed Peter and the Holy Roman Church.

We establish that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly [Col. 1176D] possesses, etc., shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit expressly to name the following:

The estate of the abbey in which the monastery stands, with the parish church of Saint John; Vangadizza with the church of Saint Michael; the estate called Salvaterra with the church of Saint Antoninus; Cavazzana with the church of Saint Lawrence; the church of Saint Andrew of Ramipalo with its appurtenances. Within the city of Verona, the church of Saint Saviour with all its appurtenances. Whatever possessions you have in Illasi and in Bardolino and in any places within the diocese of Verona. Within the diocese of Vicenza, the land of Albareto. In the diocese of Padua, the church of Saint Peter situated at Monselice with all its appurtenances; part of the valley of Almerico with the church of Saint Andrew; at Este, the church of Saint Firmus and the church of Saint Peter with their appurtenances; at Palso, the church of Saint Michael; possessions in the court of Ville and elsewhere in that diocese.

[Col. 1177B] In the diocese of Adria: Venezze with the church of Saint Martin; Prosetta with the church of Saint Leo; at Contina, the church of Saint Sixtus; at Goviano, the church of Saint Bartholomew; in the village of Comeda, the church of Saint Peter; and whatever other possessions you have in the same diocese or county. Possessions in the diocese of Ferrara; and in the diocese of Bologna, the church of Saints Simon and Jude of Urbisano with its appurtenances.

Finally, wishing to preserve without any opposition the enactments of our aforesaid predecessors, we decree that the monastery itself, placed under the protection of the Roman pontiffs alone, shall remain altogether free from the lordship of other bishops, together with all the churches which it is known now to possess or may hereafter justly acquire, and exempt from every synodal exaction.

Therefore, son abbot, you and all your successors may peacefully possess all your churches with their cemeteries, baptisteries, chapters, and synods, and administer them through your own priests, notwithstanding the opposition of any bishop. We establish with perpetual validity that the promotions of your other clergy, the consecrations of churches, and the confirmations of children dwelling in your villages shall be performed, in reverence for the Apostolic See, by such Catholic bishops as you choose to invite, without any taint of simoniacal sale intervening.

[Col. 1177D] By authority of this present privilege, priests at any time appointed in parish churches and churches of the monastery are granted the right to impose penances upon the peoples committed to them for public as well as secret sins. The resolution of questions arising from marriages and also more difficult cases shall belong to those same priests, so that they may refer them to you, son abbot, and your successors to be decided according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers.

Moreover, it shall be your concern each year to receive the most holy chrism, through your delegates, from whatever Catholic bishop you prefer, and to distribute it when received, according to custom, to the baptismal churches, as you are known in every respect to have done hitherto.

Certainly, in consideration of piety, we grant you to possess in their entirety all the tithes of the abbey, together with those of Vangadizza, Salvaterra, Cavazzana, and Ramipalo, and from the territory of Prosetta, Saguedo, and Venezze. In other places, however, you shall claim by our authority the tithes of estates cultivated at your own expense and of your revenues, just as you have held them without challenge for the past forty years and have been accustomed to do.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of deceit, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict from their own community or that of other religious, if—God forbid—no suitable person is found there. The person elected shall proceed to the Roman pontiff for confirmation.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucia in Orthea, chamberlain of our lord pope, six days before the Kalends of July, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1196 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of our lord Celestine.

CCLXXIII. He commands Albert, bishop of Vercelli, and Peter, abbot of Lucedio, to make peace between Archbishop Boniface and the canons of Genoa. (Lateran, 11 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, IV, 881.]

[Col. 1178C] CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ALBERT, bishop of Vercelli, and to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Lucedio: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Considering with prudent reflection the praiseworthy purpose of goodness and the purity of steadfast faith which you exercise in good works, we frequently urge you to the service of many people and entrust to you the execution of numerous affairs with greater confidence.

We wish you to know that, although in whatever office we have been established we have always loved the Church and city of Genoa with a certain prerogative of sincere affection, and have embraced its persons with an even closer bond of charity, we have rejoiced with great joy and exultation over the unanimous concord and true tranquillity of peace which, God cooperating, has hitherto flourished in that city. From it, as may be understood from the manifest evidence of events, many benefits have come first to Genoa itself and afterwards to all Christendom. With most ready will, we desire that they should never at any time cease from so praiseworthy a purpose and commendable work.

But the enemy of the human race, who does not love united wills, but dwells in the hearts of those at variance and wickedly labours to cause divisions, has sown tares between our venerable brother Boniface, archbishop of Genoa, [Col. 1179A] and his canons. Those who had been sons through concord have become estranged from paternal favour, and paternal love no longer caresses them in its customary manner.

We command your discretion by apostolic letters personally to go to the aforesaid city and labour most earnestly to restore peace and concord between them. You are to induce the archbishop more diligently to remove from his heart the resentment conceived there, to love his canons with paternal kindness, and, if they appear to have incurred any fault by offending him, not to recall it to mind but utterly to forgive it from heartfelt affection, and to learn, as a good father, to feel sympathy and show mercy toward his sons.

Thereafter, turning your admonition to the canons themselves, you shall endeavour to induce them to love their archbishop more earnestly as a father and ruler of their souls; to honour him; to adhere to his corrections; to endeavour to obey his salutary admonitions; and not to dissent from his will.

Finally, if—God forbid—the parties perhaps refuse to comply with your admonitions and decide to persist in their hardness, hear what may be put forward on either side and, according as God inspires your hearts and you know to be expedient, bring the disputes arising between them to an end by means of justice, without impediment of appeal.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth Ides of July, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CCLXXIV. He permits Hugh, abbot of Cluny, “to correct in the abbeys belonging to the monastery of Cluny whatever he judges should be corrected according to God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the statutes of the order.” (Lateran, 5 August.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, 95.]

[Col. 1179C] CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HUGH, abbot of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honourable is sought from us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought, through the diligence of our office, to its due effect. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, yielding to your just requests, we grant you by the authority of this present document free authority, all contradiction and appeal being set aside, to correct in the abbeys belonging to the monastery of Cluny whatever you see should be corrected according to God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the statutes of the order, and to establish there whatever ought to be established.

We also hold valid and firm any sentence which you judge ought canonically to be pronounced against the contumacious and rebellious; with God as author, we shall cause it to be observed inviolably.

No person, therefore, shall be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of His apostles Saints Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of August, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

CCLXXV. He commands [Michael], archbishop of Sens, and the abbot of Saint Columba to compel the count of Nevers to restore the house of Colenges to the priory of La Charité. (Lateran, 6 August.)

[*Ibid.*]

[Col. 1180A] CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the archbishop of Sens and to his beloved son the abbot of Saint Columba, established in the diocese of Sens: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the representation of our beloved sons the abbot and convent of Cluny, you are to know that we have learned the following. At the time when our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the Franks, set out for Jerusalem, their priory of La Charité, through the penance [Col. 1180B] and sins of its inhabitants demanding it, had been burdened by an excessive load of debts; and Peter of Croyon, servant of the noble count of Nevers, afflicted and harassed them severely. The prior and brethren of that place were therefore compelled to offer for sale, in order to raise thirteen thousand solidi for the prior, the house at Colenges belonging to that prior. As a result, the priory of La Charité was greatly damaged and burdened.

Although, at the urging of the aforesaid abbot of Cluny, the count subsequently swore upon the holy [Col. 1180C] Gospels, in the presence of our venerable brother W., archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest of Santa Sabina and legate of the Apostolic See—who was then administering the care and government of the kingdom of France together with our dearest daughter in Christ, the illustrious queen of the Franks, mother of the king—that he would restore in actual payment, to the prior and brethren of La Charité, the aforesaid house with all its appurtenances, for their peaceful possession; nevertheless, afterward he was unwilling to perform what he had sworn, although, as is said, the brethren were willing to repay him that money.

Since, therefore, the care and concern of all churches has been entrusted to us, and since we desire, as we ought, with solicitous paternal affection to provide for the indemnity of the said priory of La Charité, we firmly command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters to labor effectively, by our authority, to admonish and induce the aforesaid count of Nevers—who, as is said, occupied the same house of Cobenges in his servant’s name and converted it to his own uses—and the servant himself, if the aforesaid house was restored to him, so that he shall not fail to return that house to the aforesaid priory without any difficulty, upon receiving back from them the money repaid; provided that, anything built upon it by the count or the aforesaid servant shall not be charged to the brethren, but shall be made good from the revenues received from the house.

But if the same count or the servant refuses to make restitution, relying on our authority compel both the count himself and any others holding the house, by sentences of excommunication and interdict, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed, to restore that house with its aforesaid appurtenances to the brethren. Cause both sentences to be inviolably observed until fitting satisfaction has been made, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See. If both of you cannot be present to carry this out, you, brother archbishop, shall nevertheless execute it.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXVI. He declares to the canons of the Venetian church of St. Saviour that the church of St. Bartholomew was granted by Bishop Mark. (Lateran, August 8.)

[CORNELIUS, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, XIV, 124.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . . the prior and canons of St. Saviour of [Col. 1181B] Rialto: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honorable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought through the solicitude of our office to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority—and fortify with the protection of this present writing—the church of St. Bartholomew, granted in pious deliberation by our venerable brother Mark, bishop of Castello, to you and your successors, with its treasury, books, ornaments, houses, other possessions, and appurtenances, in order to avoid the scandal which frequently arose between you and . . . . the plebanus [parish priest] thereof. We confirm it to you and, through you, to your church, just as you lawfully and peacefully possess it and as it is fully set out in the writing of that bishop.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or, with rash boldness, to act contrary to it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of August, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXVII. He commands archbishops, bishops, abbots, deans, and other prelates of churches to excommunicate lay plunderers and harassers of the Cluniac brethren, and to remove clerics from their benefices. (Lateran, August 8.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, 96.]

[Col. 1181D]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren archbishops and bishops, and beloved sons abbots, deans, and other prelates of churches to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Not without grief of heart and great disturbance have we learned that ecclesiastical censure is so relaxed in many regions, and the severity of canonical sentences so weakened, that religious men—especially those endowed with greater liberty through privileges of the Apostolic See—everywhere suffer injury and robbery from wrongdoers, while scarcely anyone is found to aid them with appropriate protection and to set up a wall of defense in support of the innocence of the poor.

[Col. 1182A] In particular, our beloved sons, the brethren of Cluny, complaining both of their frequent injuries and of the daily failure of justice itself, have asked that all of you be stirred by apostolic letters, so that you ought to rise with ready magnanimity for them in their tribulations against their wrongdoers, and that through our assistance they may be able to recover breath from the straits and oppressions they endure.

Therefore we strictly command all of you by apostolic letters that, if any persons, at the instigation of the devil, lay violent hands on any of those brethren or their converts; irreverently seize their property, houses, or the possessions of their people; extort tithes of their labor or produce in contempt of the privileges [Col. 1182B] of the Apostolic See; or unjustly withhold things left to the said brethren by the wills of the deceased—you shall strike them, if they are laymen, with a sentence of excommunication, candles being lighted and appeal removed. Clerics, however, appeal being removed, you shall suspend from office and benefice. You are not to relax either sentence until they have rendered full satisfaction to the aforesaid brethren; and especially those bound by the bond of anathema for violent laying on of hands are to deserve absolution from that bond only by coming to the Apostolic See with letters from the diocesan bishop. Moreover, you shall subject to a sentence of interdict those villages in which the goods of the aforesaid brethren or of their people are violently withheld, for as long as they are held there.

[Col. 1182C] Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of August, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXVIII. He commands Master Leo, procurator at Constantinople, to compel the heirs to pay the bishop of Castello (Venice) tithes from the goods of John Canalo-Lupi. (Lateran, August 12.)

[CORNELIUS, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, vol. XIII, p. 223.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Master LEO, procurator at Constantinople: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother, the bishop of Castello, has submitted to us a complaint alleging that the tithes lawfully due to himself and his church from goods [Col. 1182D] formerly belonging to John Canalo-Lupi are unjustly withheld from him and unlawfully denied to them. Therefore, unwilling that the said bishop should suffer injury to his right, we command you by apostolic letters that, whenever requested by the messenger of the aforesaid bishop, you compel the heirs and executors of the same deceased person, by ecclesiastical censure and as justice requires, appeal being set aside, to make the due payment of those tithes.

We also will and command that you preserve the said bishop unharmed, by our authority, in all his rights, and especially in the tithes which his predecessors have hitherto held and which are known reasonably to belong to himself and his church, [Col. 1183A] notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See prejudicial to truth and justice.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of August, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXIX. He confirms for Joachim, abbot of Flore, “constitutions concerning the life of the monks and of the monasteries subject to his cenobium, and concerning goods possessed by the brethren and their number.” (Rome, August 25.)

[*Acta Sanctorum*, May, vol. VII, p. 125.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOACHIM, abbot, and the convent of Flore: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When you, son abbot, were present before us, [Col. 1183B] you explained to us in your reports that you had made certain constitutions concerning the life of your monks and the monasteries subject to your cenobium, concerning the goods to be possessed by the brethren, and concerning their number. You earnestly requested that we confirm them so that they might be observed in those monasteries and by those brethren. Inclining therefore to your prayers, we confirm by apostolic authority the aforesaid constitutions, as prudently made by you, firmly forbidding that the form of those constitutions be weakened in the aforesaid monasteries by anyone’s rashness.

Let no person whatsoever, etc.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXX. He permits [Aegidius], bishop of Modena, to punish the disobedience of certain clerics. (Lateran, November 8.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Memorie Modenesi*, IV, 18.]

[Col. 1183C]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Modena: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, beyond the common obligation of charity, we embrace you as our dearest brother with a special bond of affection, it is altogether pleasing and welcome to us that the honor due to you and the customary obedience should be rendered by your subjects without any diminution; and, so far as we can do so consistently with our honor, [Col. 1183D] we direct our care and diligent effort to this end. We have heard—and could not fail to wonder on hearing—that the clerics of the parish of Baioaria and certain others subject to you by diocesan law, taking advantage of archiepiscopal protection and stubbornly raising the horns of pride against you, attempt with such presumption to withdraw the obedience due to you that you are unable to correct their offenses or oppose their wrongful acts as is fitting.

Therefore, lest the aforesaid clerics continue longer to rejoice in their rashness and serve the vice of disobedience according to their own will, by the authority of these presents we grant you free faculty to make arrangements concerning both the clerics of the aforesaid people and the other clerics of your diocese, according to ancient and reasonable [Col. 1184A] custom, all obstacle of appeal being removed, and to order matters as justice requires.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or rashly act contrary to it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXXI. He commands the archbishop of Ravenna and his suffragans, under penalty of excommunication, to admonish the citizens of Modena to restore what they have taken from the monastery of Nonantola. (Lateran, November 14.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Storia di Nonantola*, II, 324.]

[Col. 1184B]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishop of Ravenna and his suffragans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

At the hearing of our apostolate, upon the complaint of our beloved sons B., abbot, and the convent of the monastery of Nonantola, it has been reported that the citizens of Modena, having no regard for the worship of churches, violently despoiled their churches of books, vestments, and other furnishings, and their people of oxen and all household goods, on the pretext of a certain levy. Desiring therefore, by reason of the charge of administration [Col. 1184C] entrusted to us, more vigorously to repel lay violence from harassment of churches and their ministers, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you admonish and effectively induce the aforesaid citizens of Modena to restore without difficulty to the aforesaid abbot and convent what they wickedly took from the said churches.

But if they should persist in contumacy, strike the principal authors of that wrongdoing with a sentence of anathema, all appeal being set aside; subject that land to ecclesiastical interdict; and, every Sunday and feast day, with candles lighted and bells rung, cause those sentences to be publicly renewed throughout all the churches of your dioceses and observed by all until they have rendered suitable satisfaction [Col. 1184D] for all the aforesaid matters.

Given at the Lateran, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXXII. He commands the bishop of Arras, the abbot of St. Victor, and the prior of St. Martin-des-Champs in Paris to subject the Church of Chelles to the Church of Paris. (Lateran, November 23.)

[Collection des Cartulaires, IV, 65.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Arras, and beloved sons the abbot of St. Victor and the prior of St. Martin-des-Champs in Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1185A] Since we are human and bound by the law of human nature, it should not seem remarkable to us if some scruple sometimes arises in our acts, in accordance with what is human. Long ago, when our beloved son Martin, priest of the Church of Chelles, came as messenger into our presence and presented to us, on behalf of the same church, a certain instrument authenticated by the seals and testimony of prudent men, by which the Church of Chelles asserted itself to be exempt from the jurisdiction of the Church of Paris, we gave complete credence to the writing and granted to that messenger letters of our protection concerning the said exemption.

Later, when the aforementioned messenger tried to obtain from us a privilege concerning the same matter, the Church of Paris, recognizing that this was being attempted to its prejudice, sent its beloved son Master Thomas to the Apostolic See to act on its behalf. When the messengers of each church were therefore present before us, we appointed as auditors our beloved sons B., cardinal-priest of the title of St. Mary in Trastevere, and G., cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico. After the parties had disputed before them for some time, the aforesaid Master Thomas maintained before us that the Church of Chelles ought to be subject to the Church of Paris, on the authority of privileges of the Roman pontiffs of blessed memory Innocent, Eugenius, Alexander, and many others; also by reason of the blessing of the abbess and the consecrations of virgins performed by the bishop of Paris; and because for thirty or forty continuous years it had rendered obedience and procurations at the time of visitation, as well as other temporal dues, to that bishop, the archdeacons, and their predecessors.

[Col. 1185C] He also produced for us an instrument fortified by the seals and testimony of our beloved sons H[ugh V], abbot of St. Denis, and R[obert IV], abbot of St. Germain-des-Prés, Paris. From its tenor we learned that, when our venerable brethren the bishops of Amiens and Tournai, together with the same abbots, were arbitrators appointed by agreement in the aforesaid dispute between the Churches of Paris and Chelles, they received the letters of both churches and imposed on each side a penalty of five hundred pounds for observance of the award. The abbess, moreover, had given security by oath in this matter, while she and her convent claimed exemption and liberty on the basis of certain privileges allegedly granted to them by certain bishops of Paris.

After hearing the allegations, carefully examining the authentic documents, and also hearing the abbess’s judicial confession—namely, that she had received the rite of blessing from the bishop of Paris and had promised subjection and obedience to the Church of Paris by a profession written in her own hand and placed upon the altar—the said bishops and abbots discussed peace. Since no means of settlement could be found, they consulted prudent men concerning the question and condemned the Church of Chelles.

[Col. 1186A] When the abbess appealed this decision to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Franks, he did not admit the appeal, since the laws do not permit appeals from arbitrators; he declared that the Church of Chelles differed in no prerogative of liberty from the other abbeys which, by authority of privileges of the Apostolic See, are subject to the Church of Paris. Since the oft-mentioned abbess, unafraid to disregard the binding force of her oath, refuses to obey that sentence, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the foregoing is true, you cause the said Church of Chelles to be subject to the Church of Paris as to its mother church, by ecclesiastical censure, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed. Letters of exemption, executory letters, or indulgences obtained from us by the aforesaid abbess and convent, and the appeal made to the aforesaid king, shall not hinder you.

[Col. 1186B] If, however, the matter stands otherwise, summon the parties before you, hear what they choose to submit on either side, and bring the case to a canonical conclusion, appeal being removed; and cause whatever you decree to be inviolably observed by the parties through ecclesiastical censure.

If all of you cannot be present to carry this out, nevertheless two of you shall execute it.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXXIII. By letters to [Odo], bishop of Penne, he confirms “the sentence of deposition pronounced against the clerics of Arsita.” (Lateran, November 30.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1125.]

[Col. 1186C]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Penne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is equitable and consonant with reason that measures established by those delegated by us, after due consideration, should remain firm and unimpaired and be strengthened by the protection of our confirmation, so that they may in no way be violated thereafter through anyone’s presumption. Long ago, as you assert, the clerics of Arsita, bound to your church by an oath of fidelity, failed to observe an interdict [Col. 1186D] imposed on them by you; subsequently, by you and by our venerable brother the bishop of Valva, acting by our authority, they were involved in a sentence of excommunication. Because they observed neither sentence, a sentence of deposition was pronounced against them at our command by you and the aforementioned bishop, as your report has made known to us.

Desiring, therefore, that what has been done concerning them may possess in future times the strength of due firmness, so that they may in no way glory in their wrongdoing, since they do not hesitate to raise the heel against their prelates, we confirm by apostolic authority the sentence of deposition pronounced by you and the aforesaid bishop against the clerics of Arsita, as reasonably pronounced and not set aside by the remedy of a lawful appeal, [Col. 1187A] and fortify it with the protection of this present writing.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may, etc. If anyone, however, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXXIV. Bull for the nuns of St. Julian of Auxerre. (Lateran, December 3.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, *Instrumenta*, 142.]

COELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishop of Sens and the bishop of Nevers: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint sent to us by our beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess and nuns of St. Julian of Auxerre, [Col. 1187B] we have learned that, although our venerable brother the bishop of Auxerre ought, as a good father, to foster them with blessings and not disturb with the tumult of disputes the tranquillity of religious life which they appear to have embraced, he—something we can scarcely believe—harasses and attacks them in many ways on the pretext of an indulgence obtained from the Apostolic See.

Although that indulgence was granted by us to the bishop through the benevolence of the Apostolic See for the improvement of the monastery, he, as is said, uses the power allowed him not for the benefit of that monastery but, giving attention to temporal gain rather than considering the salvation of souls, wearies them by assailing them with continual lawsuits [Col. 1187C] and gravely injures and disturbs their rights. Although they ought to have him as defender of their rights, they experience and recognize him as their adversary. When they seek through his officials to obtain justice against wrongdoers against the monastery, so many and such great burdens are inflicted upon the monastery by him and his agents that, unless they are soon assisted by the clemency of the Apostolic See, they must, as they say, abandon the habit of the religious life they have embraced and go into exile from the monastery.

[lacuna] the abbess . . . the church of Colanges, in which there is a right of presentation . . . presented W. of Saint-Pris, a cleric. . . . refusing his institution, while raising no canonical objection against the person, he also refused to admit the presentation made by the abbess. . . . [lacuna] we neither will nor ought that, just as it is unfitting for him, he should harass the aforesaid monastery on the pretext of our indulgence, especially since we have received from many prelates of those regions testimony concerning their [Col. 1187D] praiseworthy religious life and honorable administration. By our writing we . . . to the same bishop . . . firmly command that he shall not harass that monastery with undue molestation and shall allow the abbess and nuns peacefully to serve the Lord in their holy habit; and, if he is known to have offended them unreasonably in any matter up to this time, he shall correct this himself without delay.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid bishop is unwilling swiftly to correct the matters we have stated, you restrain him, as you see fit, from undue harassment of the aforesaid monastery, abbess, and nuns, all obstacle of appeal being removed; and that you take care, by apostolic authority, to protect and defend both that monastery and the nuns in all disputes. . . . [lacuna] if both of you cannot be present to carry this out, you, brother archbishop, shall nevertheless . . . [lacuna]

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of December, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

[LANG, *Regesta*, I, 366.]

[Col. 1188B]

## CCLXXXVI. He commands the abbot of Heimerod and the scholastic of the cathedral church of Trier to judge between the brethren of St. Peter’s, Mainz, and their provost Siegfried of Eppenstein. (Lateran, December 12.)
