You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of monks [Col. 1215C] or clerics to be advanced to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things freely and without any improper condition. Otherwise you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Furthermore, by this present decree we establish that, upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any stratagem of fraud or by force, save the man whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall deem to be elected in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. We prohibit, under threat of anathema, the exaction of tithes from laypersons. We also forbid anyone to presume to build a church or oratory within the boundaries of your parishes without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, while the privileges of the Roman Church remain intact. [lacuna] Moreover, holding valid the liberties and immunities granted, in consideration of piety and religion, to your monastery and its people by our predecessor Pope Alexander of blessed memory, [Col. 1216A] or by the archbishops and dukes of Aquitaine and also by the other barons of that land, we confirm them by apostolic authority. We establish that, as is known to have been enacted by our said predecessor, no ecclesiastical or secular person shall presume to compel your inhabitants to bear arms or to extort unlawful exactions from them. [lacuna] Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved.

[Col. 1216B] Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, or to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those concerned shall be preserved whole, to be of benefit to them in every way, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this page of our constitution, rashly presumes to contravene it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his fault by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; [Col. 1216C] let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, John, cardinal of the title of St. Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tusculum. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of St. Mary in Trastevere, [Col. 1216D] of the title of Calixtus. I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of St. Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Sosfredus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Praxedes. [Col. 1217A] I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Prisca. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Gran . . ., bishop of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, cardinal-deacon of St. Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Aigro. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 1217B] I, Lothair, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Bobo, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Censius, cardinal-deacon of St. Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the sixth Ides of May, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1197 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

### CCCIX. He receives the canonry of St. Mary of Pesaro under protection and confirms its goods. (Lateran, 12 May.)

[COLLUCI, *Antichità Picene*, vol. IV, Appendix, p. XXXII.]

[Col. 1217C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RAMBALD, provost of Blessed Mary of Pesaro, and his brethren, the canons now established and those to be established in the future, for ever.

Placed, by the Lord’s disposal, in the governance of the Apostolic See, we are bound, with the Lord’s assistance, beneficially to provide for all churches and mercifully to assent to the just requests of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously granting assent to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid canonry of St. Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, following the example of our predecessors—the Roman pontiffs Alexander II, Nicholas II, and Eugenius III, of holy memory—and strengthen it by the privilege of this writing. We establish that whatsoever possessions and goods that canonry now reasonably possesses, or may hereafter, God favouring it, acquire by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The demesne house which you inhabit, situated beside the church of Pesaro; the other houses and gardens situated around it, with the chapel of St. John; [Col. 1218A] the church of St. Clement with all that you possess in its parish; the church of St. Nicholas beside the Sea Gate, with its parish and all its appurtenances; the church of St. Angel of Gattullo, with all that you possess in its parish; the church of St. Columba, with its parish and the possessions which you have in it; the church of St. Martin of Ruibale, with its parish and appurtenances; the church of St. Bartholomew of the Mount, with its parish and other appurtenances; the church of St. Marina and the oratory beside Mount Conspejan, with its parish and all its appurtenances; the church of St. Zeno, with its parish and appurtenances; the parish which was formerly St. Andrew of Bernard, with all that you possess there; the parish church of St. [Col. 1218B] Christopher and St. Quiricus, with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Apollinaris and the church of St. Hermas, with their parishes and all their appurtenances; the field and vineyard outside the Colline Gate; the vineyard beside the bridge of the Foglia; whatever you possess in the suburb of Gattullo; the vineyard of Scopetuli; whatever you possess in the estate of Gallione and in the estate of Granarole, or in its church; in the estate of Bonci, in lands, vineyards, and olive-groves; whatever you possess in the church, parish, and possessions of St. Cassian; those things which you justly hold in the church of St. Heraclian; and whatever you possess throughout the diocese of Pesaro, with tithes, first-fruits, income from the living, lands, vineyards, gardens, [Col. 1218C] olive-groves, woods, meadows, pastures, and fishing-rights—we confirm all these by apostolic authority.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid canonry, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, all things granted for the governance and support of those concerned shall be preserved whole, to be of benefit to them in every way, without prejudice to the power of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this page of our constitution, rashly presumes to contravene it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; [Col. 1218D] let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the reward of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. [Col. 1219A] I, John, bishop of Viterbo and cardinal-priest of the title of St. Clement. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of St. Mary in Trastevere. I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of St. Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cinthius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Prisca. I, Fra . . ., cardinal-deacon of Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Aquiro. [Col. 1219B] I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Peter at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Bobo, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of . . . . . . . . . . . . . Cencius, cardinal-deacon of St. Lucy in Orthaea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the fourth Ides of May, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1197 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

### CCCX. He confirms the agreements made between the abbess of St. Alexander and Hugh, canon of the Church of Parma and archpriest of the parish church of St. Pancras. (Lateran, 28 May.)

[AFFO, *Storia di Parma*, III, 311.]

[Col. 1219C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ GUILLA, abbess, and the sisters of St. Alexander of Parma, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those matters which are established harmoniously or reasonably by judicial decision must remain firm and unimpaired; and lest, with the passage of time, they relapse into the anxiety of renewed contention, they must be fortified by apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, favourably assenting to your petition, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this writing, the agreement [Col. 1219D] reasonably made between you and Master Hugh, canon of Parma and archpriest of the parish church of St. Pancras, concerning the church of St. Andrew of Fabrore: as it was made without impropriety, received by both parties, observed hitherto, and is known to be contained in the instrument drawn up for that purpose.

Therefore, let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to act against it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1220A] Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXI. He affirms for the monastery of St. Denis the patronage of the church of Blessed Mary of Medonta, granted by Philip, king of the French. (Lateran, 28 May.)

[DOUBLET, *Hist. de Saint-Denys*, p. 527.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of St. Denis, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever we are asked for something known to accord with religion and honour, it is fitting that we grant it willingly [Col. 1220B] and afford appropriate support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, mercifully assenting to your just requests, we hold valid and firm the grant to you of the patronage of the church of Blessed Mary of Medonta, made by our dearest son in Christ Philip, illustrious king of the French; we confirm that grant by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the privilege of this writing. We establish that, when the canons of the aforesaid church of St. Mary die, monks of your house shall be appointed in their place, so that through them service to God may be rendered more acceptably and continually in that church. Furthermore, whatsoever possessions or goods that church now reasonably possesses [Col. 1220C] or may hereafter, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, acquire through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, all things granted for the governance and support of those concerned shall be preserved whole, to be of benefit to them in every way, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 1220D] person, knowingly acting against this page of our constitution, rashly presumes to contravene it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to divine vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1221A] I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia. I, John, cardinal of the title of St. Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tusculum. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of St. Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus. I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of St. Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cinthius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, Sosfredus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Praxedes. [Col. 1221B] I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Prisca. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, cardinal-deacon of St. Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Nicholas, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal-deacon of St. Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year [Col. 1221C] 1197 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

### CCCXII. He confirms the sentence rendered by Burchard, abbot of Ebersberg, and Conrad, provost of St. Andrew’s at Freising, between the brethren of Garz and the provost of Au. (Lateran, 2 June.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, I, 64.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . ., provost and brethren of the church of Garz: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those things which are established on the authority of the Apostolic See, with reason guiding the decision, ought to be strengthened by apostolic protection lest they relapse into the anxiety of renewed contention. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favourably assenting to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this writing the judgment canonically issued by our beloved sons Burchard, abbot of Ebersberg, and Conrad, provost of the church of St. Andrew at Freising, delegated judges of the Apostolic See, concerning the controversy over the church of Purtin, which was being litigated between you and our beloved sons . . . ., provost and chapter of Au. This judgment awarded the aforesaid church to you and your church; it was reasonably rendered by them and has not been suspended by a lawful appeal. For fuller evidence of this act, we have thought fit to insert in this [Col. 1222A] page of ours the judgment itself, word for word; its tenor is as follows:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.
>
> I, Burchard, abbot of Ebersberg, and I, Conrad, provost of the church of St. Andrew at Freising, having received a mandate from the apostolic lord concerning the dispute which was being litigated between the brethren of Garz and Au over the church of Purtim, that we should settle it by his authority, summoned both parties by apostolic authority to meet in the metropolitan place of Salzburg, granting them a postponement so that they might come prepared on both sides. We therefore sat in the baptistery church there to hear the case of both parties.
>
> The . . . provost of Garz and [Col. 1222B] his brethren accordingly asserted that they would prove that they had possessed the church of Purtim by just title for forty years and more, and that they had been violently dispossessed of that possession during the schism, when Egelolf, the emperor’s chaplain, was intruded by the emperor himself into that provostship, because of the hatred borne toward Albert, archbishop of Salzburg, who then presided over that church. The same Albert, wishing because of his hatred of that intruder to remove the church of Purten from the aforesaid usurper, permitted it for a time to the provost of Au. Conrad, now archbishop of Mainz, who then presided over the church of Salzburg, restored the repeatedly mentioned church, at his first chapter, to the church of Garz, in whose peaceful possession they remained until the brethren of Au, on the pretext of apostolic letters, again violently expelled them, though they had neither been summoned nor convicted.
>
> We therefore, having heard the proof set forth above, by which their rightful possession and their violent ejection by the brethren of Au were proved, restore the aforesaid church of Purten to the church of Garz by the authority delegated to us from the Apostolic See, and restore the provost of Garz and his brethren to possession of that chapel with its appurtenances. Henry, a priest and sworn parish incumbent of the church of Salzburg, declared that the church of Garz possessed the church of Purtem with its appurtenances in good faith and by just title in the time of Hugh and Henry, provosts of the church of Garz, for more than forty years, until [Col. 1222D] the time of the schism, when they were violently expelled. Ulscaleus, sworn custos of the church of Salzburg, declared that the church of Garz had justly possessed the aforesaid church of Purten for forty years, until the brethren of Au violently entered it. Conrad, dean of Plidelveschirchen, declared on oath that the lawful possession of the Garz brethren in the church of Purtin had been known to him for sixty years. Berthold, priest of Sewen, declared on oath that the lawful possession of the Garz brethren in the aforesaid church had been known to him down to the time of Egelolf, who, during the schism, was violently intruded by the emperor into that provostship; because of his hatred for him, Lord Archbishop Albert allowed it to the provost of Au, and later Lord Conrad, now archbishop of Mainz, [Col. 1223A] restored it in its entirety to Provost John.”

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly act against it. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth Nones of June, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXIII. He forbids the abbot and monks of Fécamp to provide the archdeacon of Caux with an annual procuration. (Lateran, 3 June.)

[*Neustria pia*, 245.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of the monastery of Fécamp: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although, by the duty of the apostolic office entrusted to us, we are bound to care for all churches, we ought nevertheless to devote special attention to the preservation from loss and burden of those which are directly subject to us. For it has reached our hearing, through your complaint, that the archdeacon of Caux, on the pretext of the hospitality which Henry, your abbot of good memory, charitably and generously afforded from time to time to that archdeacon and his predecessors, does not hesitate to demand from your monastery an annual procuration contrary to the privileges of the Roman Church. We therefore, unwilling that the aforesaid monastery should endure so great a burden, prohibit your whole community by the authority of this letter from being answerable to that archdeacon in any respect concerning the said procuration. We establish that no person whatsoever may infringe [Col. 1223C] this page of our prohibition or rashly act against it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third Nones of June, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXIV. He admonishes the monks of Nonantola not to retain an improper custom in assigning the monastery’s possessions. (Lateran, 4 June.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Storia di Nonantola*, II, 325.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [Col. 1223D] to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Nonantola: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as things established through prudent deliberation for the benefit and advancement of churches ought to remain firm and unimpaired, so things tending toward their diminution or loss, undertaken through the insolence of certain persons, must be abolished and wholly extirpated. It has reached our hearing that you, adhering most outrageously to a certain improper custom, do not hesitate, while a tenant is alive, to grant by another lease the possessions of the monastery which had previously been leased to that tenant. Thus, if the first lessee dies without an heir, the possessions which after his death ought by right to revert [Col. 1224A] to the monastery itself pass by succession to others, even though the said monastery suffers very great loss thereby; although both by the authorities of the holy Fathers and by a special command of our predecessor Pope Urban of blessed memory, you have been deprived of the power to do this. Therefore, wishing to provide for your honour and protect your monastery from loss, we command and enjoin your whole community by apostolic letters that, wholly abstaining from such leases and alienations, you shall by no means henceforth burden the frequently mentioned monastery with the load of debts. We also strictly forbid you and the priors of your obediences to presume in any manner to sell or alienate rents or possessions belonging to the monastery itself or to its obediences. If anything has been undertaken contrary to the prohibitions of both our said predecessor and ourselves, we wholly annul both the aforesaid leases and the alienations of possessions, and decree that they have no force.

Given at the Lateran, on the second Nones of June, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXV. He grants to Hugh, abbot, and the brethren of St. Denis that no one may dare pronounce a sentence of excommunication against them. (Lateran, 13 June.)

[*Cartulaire de N.-D. de Paris*, I, 137.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [Col. 1224C] to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot, and the convent of St. Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Recalling that in your monastery, which is known to surpass all those around it, purity of order and regular observance have always flourished so greatly that the authority of your reputation and honour, diffusing the fragrance of good conduct into diverse parts of the world, has made your house and the reverence of its name celebrated, and even rich in temporal resources, we have judged that this safeguard of favour should be granted to you and to your church: that it may exclude from you the injuries and excesses of assailants, and that your flock, living in innocence of life, may rejoice that it is exempt from [Col. 1224D] secular disturbance. You have humbly reported to our apostolic office that it frequently occurs in your regions that, although it has been granted to you by authority of the Apostolic See that prelates of churches may not pronounce a sentence of excommunication against you except by mandate of the supreme pontiff or of a legate of the Roman Church, church prelates, out of hostility to this freedom—which, as we have learned, they ought not to envy but rather to congratulate—arbitrarily suspend your churches from the celebration of divine worship because of monks’ offences, and pronounce sentences of excommunication against your people and those in communion with you.

Therefore, wishing to provide for you and your church in this matter with paternal concern, we strictly prohibit by the authority of this letter anyone, because of monks’ offences, so long as they are willing to submit to the command of their abbot as their ordinary judge, [Col. 1225A] from daring to pronounce a sentence of suspension or excommunication against your churches or people, or against those bound to pay you tithes or other revenues, or from undertaking anything on that pretext to your prejudice. Should anyone in his own rashness proceed to do so, we decree by apostolic authority that the sentence itself is wholly void and of no effect.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our prohibition and constitution or rashly act against it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, [Col. 1225B] let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of June, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXVI. To the archbishop of Rouen—What action is to be taken against plunderers, invaders, or burners of churches. (Lateran, 2 July.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 620.]

CELESTINE, bishop, to the archbishop of Rouen, etc.

When we are asked for what is just and honourable, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the diligence of our office. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, assenting to your petitions, we grant you by the authority of this letter that, whenever anyone presumes to invade the churches of your province, or their rights or possessions, by plunder, arson, or any other means, if those invaders are of your province, you may, without impediment of appeal, pronounce sentences both of excommunication against their persons—excepting our dearest sons in Christ, the illustrious kings of France and England and their households—and of interdict upon their lands. If, however, such wrongdoers are from another province, and, when you have requested their bishops concerning this matter, satisfaction has not been made to those injured, your brotherhood may, appeal being set aside, pronounce against them a sentence of excommunication and a sentence of interdict upon those lands which they possess within the boundaries of your province. No one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth Nones of July, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXVII. He receives the monastery of Amelungsborn under protection and confirms its goods, rights, and privileges. (Lateran, 27 July.)

[FALKE, *Codex traditionum Corbeiensium*, 854.]

[Col. 1226A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HOIKON, abbot of the monastery at Amelungsborn, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetual remembrance.

For those choosing the religious life, it is fitting that apostolic protection should be at hand, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions [Col. 1226B], and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present document, the aforesaid monastery at Amelungesborn, in which you are devoted to the divine service. We first decree that the monastic order which is known to have been established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, God being gracious, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. [Col. 1226C] Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the estate or endowment of your monastery at Elersen [Note: [Col. 1225D] Allerseni, by the Holzminne and the Weser.]; at Adololdesse [Note: [Col. 1225D] Arolzen, a village in the district of Altersen.]; at Oderkese [Note: [Col. 1225D] Oelkassen, in the district of Wickensem, within the principality of Wolfenbüttel.]; at Erdeshuse [Note: [Col. 1226D] Erzhusen, a village on the Leine, in the district of Grenc.]; at Grene; at the long enclosure in Suthe; at Gese; at Luderdesse; at Aldentheib; at Waltenstide; at Oudenhusen; at Swalenhuse; at Salinis; at Hachem; at Volenberge; at Nienhachem; at Osterse; at Reinlevessen; at Reinwardesse; and at Guddingen; together with meadows, vineyards, lands, woods and brushwood, rights of use and pastures, in woodland and plain, waters and mills, roads and paths, and all their other liberties and immunities. [Col. 1226D]

No one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes from the produce of your labours which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, gardens and brushwood, your fisheries, or the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and released from secular obligations, who flee from the world, and retain them without any objection.

Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving that place without the permission of his abbot; [Col. 1227A] and no one shall dare retain one who has left without the guarantee of letters issued jointly by you. If anyone should presume to retain him, you may pronounce the regular sentence against such monks or lay brothers. We strictly forbid, further, that lands or any benefice granted to your church may be personally bestowed upon anyone or alienated in any other way without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater and sounder part. If any donations or alienations are made otherwise than has been stated, we decree them void.

We also prohibit any monk or lay brother bound by profession in your house, without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, from standing surety for anyone or borrowing money from anyone beyond the amount established by the prudence of your chapter, [Col. 1227B] unless this is for a manifest benefit to your house. Should anyone presume to do so, the convent shall not be bound in any way to answer for these matters.

Furthermore, in your own cases, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, you may use the testimony of your brethren, lest your right should fail in any respect through lack of witnesses. Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid any bishop or any other person to compel you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit your own property or possessions to secular judgment; nor shall anyone presume to come to your houses for the purpose of celebrating ordinations, hearing cases, or convening public assemblies. Nor may anyone obstruct the regular election [Col. 1227C] of your abbot or meddle in any way, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, in installing or removing the person who is abbot at the time.

But if the bishop in whose parish your house was founded, when duly requested with fitting humility and devotion, refuses to bless the abbot who has been chosen and to confer upon you the other things belonging to his office, that abbot—provided he is a priest—may bless his own novices and exercise the other functions belonging to his office; and you may receive from another bishop all that has been improperly refused by your own. We add that, in receiving professions presented by abbots who have been blessed or are to be blessed, bishops shall be content with the form and wording established from the beginning of the Order: namely, that the abbots themselves must profess while preserving their Order, and shall not be compelled to make any profession contrary to the statutes of their Order. [Col. 1227D]

For the consecration of altars or churches, for holy oil, or for any other ecclesiastical sacrament, no one whatsoever shall dare to extort anything from you on the pretext of custom or by any other means; rather, the diocesan bishop shall provide all these things to you freely. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer, provided he enjoys the favour and communion of the holy Roman See, and he, relying on our authority, shall grant you what is requested. If the see of the diocesan bishop should happen to be vacant, you may meanwhile receive all ecclesiastical sacraments from neighbouring bishops without objection, [Col. 1228A] provided that no prejudice thereby arises in future to your own bishops.

Since you do not always have access to bishops, if it should happen that a bishop in communion with the Roman See, as stated above, and one of whom you have full knowledge, passes through your district, you may receive from him, by authority of the Apostolic See, blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks. But if bishops or other rulers of churches pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against your monasteries or persons established therein, or even against your hired labourers because you do not pay tithes, or on any ground connected with the concessions granted you by apostolic kindness; or if they pronounce the same sentence against your benefactors [Col. 1228B] because, out of charity, they have given you some benefactions or services, or helped with work on those days on which you labour while others keep holiday—we decree that such a sentence, as pronounced against the grants of the Apostolic See, is to be annulled. Nor shall letters obtained with the name of the Cistercian Order concealed, and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges, have validity.

Wishing also to provide in future, with paternal solicitude, for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your establishments or granges to commit robbery or theft, set fire, shed blood, seize or kill a person rashly, or dare to use violence. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority and fortify by the privilege of this present document all liberties [Col. 1228C] and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in future, etc.

[Col. 1228D] I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto. I, John, cardinal of the title of St Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany. I, . . . (here a space was left for one of the cardinals). I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. (Here again a space was left for an absent cardinal.) I, Soffredus, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of St Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of St Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. (Here a space was left for one absent.) [Col. 1229A] I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Lothair, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. (Here a place was assigned to an absent deacon.) I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Angel. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of St Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of St Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1197, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### CCCXVIII. He confirms to the monastery of Steingaden the church of Widergeltingen. (Lateran, 7 August.)

[Monumenta Boica, VI, 503.]

[Col. 1229B]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son the provost of the church of Steingaden: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant consent to the just wishes of petitioners, and bring to effect, by the result that follows, vows which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, concurring favourably with your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your monastery, the parish church of Wildrikeltingen, just as the monastery itself possesses it lawfully and without dispute; and we fortify it by the protection of this present document. [Col. 1229C]

No person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or, with rash boldness, oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of August, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXIX. Privilege for the monastery of Tepl. (Lateran, 7 August.)

[Hugo, *Annales Praemonstratenses*, vol. II, Proofs, p. 372.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1229D] sons the abbot and canons of Tepl: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman Church customarily loves more earnestly, by the duty of its accustomed piety, its devoted and humble children; and, lest they be troubled by the vexations of wicked people, cherishes them like a loving mother beneath the safeguard of its protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, considering the devotion which you are known to have toward Blessed Peter and ourselves, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves your persons and the church in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all goods which it reasonably possesses at present or may hereafter, by lawful means and with the Lord’s help, acquire.

In particular, we confirm the village called Tepl, with its toll and all [Col. 1230A] its appurtenances, which the nobleman Ibroznata, count of Bohemia and founder of your monastery, granted you by provident deliberation. We likewise confirm, by apostolic authority, to you and through you to your church, and fortify by the protection of this present document, the liberty of your people in respect of levies, and the land lying between Sandow and the border of Bohemia, which Henry, bishop of Prague, of good memory, is said to have granted to your church while administering the duchy of Bohemia; all as you justly and peaceably possess them and as is contained in the authentic documents drawn up concerning them. We decree that, should you find yourselves burdened in any matter, you may freely appeal to the Apostolic See.

No person whatsoever may infringe this page of our [Col. 1230B] protection, confirmation, and grant, or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of August, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXX. He receives under protection the church of St Mary of Arzilla of Fano, and confirms its goods and privileges. (Lateran, 10 September.)

[Mittarelli, *Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. IV, p. 208.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Berard, prior of the church of St Mary [Col. 1230C] of Arzilla, and his brethren, present and future, professing the religious life: in perpetuity.

For those choosing the religious life, it is fitting that apostolic protection should be at hand, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present document, the aforesaid church of St Mary, which is of the special right and property of Blessed Peter, and in which you are devoted to the divine service. We first decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to God and the Rule of Blessed [Col. 1230D] Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s help, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, which the nobleman Valerus, count of Fano, built by provident deliberation and to which he granted the possessions written below, with all its appurtenances; the hospital near the aforementioned church; and the chapel [Col. 1231A] of St James with its hospital, which the aforesaid count built at his own expense, with all its appurtenances; one house in the city of Fano; nine gardens near the aforementioned church; one vineyard on the plain of the borough with its appurtenances; all vineyards that formed the dower of Adjuta; at Malliano, the vineyards which the same count acquired from Duke Hugh; one field in the place called Paludis; one field beside the seashore; one field at the stream of Arcu; one field beside the pool of Volte; one field which formerly belonged to Honesti Albert; one field beside St Maurus; and the whole olive grove which belonged to Buccebatalle.

No one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from your gardens and fisheries, [Col. 1231B] or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion and retain without objection clerics or laymen, free and released from secular obligations, who flee from the world. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your church, from leaving that place without permission from his prior, except in pursuit of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who has left without the guarantee of letters jointly issued by you.

When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, [Col. 1231C] consecrations of altars and churches, and the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to holy orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys communion with the most holy Roman See, and is willing to furnish these things to you without any improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic prelate you wish, provided he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See; relying on our authority, he shall provide what you request.

Further, we absolutely forbid the imposition of new and undue exactions by archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, deans, or other ecclesiastical or secular persons. We likewise decree that the burial ground of the place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of those churches from which bodies of the dead are taken being nevertheless preserved. [Col. 1231D]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. As a token of this liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and our successors one bezant each year. [Col. 1232A] If, therefore, in future, etc.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Guy, cardinal priest of St Mary in Trastevere, of the title of St Callistus. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of St Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of St Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of St Adrian. [Col. 1232B] I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Angel.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of St Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the fourth day before the Ides of September, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1197.

### CCCXXI. He confirms to the canons of St Mary of Runc the tithes of the newly cleared lands of Runc and Stamphen. (Lateran, 27 September.)

[See Biancolini, *Serie cronologica dei vescovi e governatori di Verona*, Verona, 1749, quarto, p. 83.]

[Col. 1232C]

### CCCXXII. He confirms the donations, foundations, and endowments made by Guy, lord of Salion, for the establishment of canons in the church of Blessed Mary of Salion. (Lateran, 22 October.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, IV, Documents, 25.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and canons of Blessed Mary of Saux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When that which is just and honourable is sought from you, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought, through the diligence of our office, to its due [Col. 1232D] effect. Now, as we have plainly learned from the tenor of the letters of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Lyon, our beloved son the nobleman Guy, lord of Saux, for the remedy of his soul newly established you as canons in the church of Blessed Mary in that castle; and he freely gave to you and to that church many possessions and revenues, granted other concessions and liberties, and that same archbishop confirmed this work of piety of the nobleman by the document he issued.

Therefore, considering the praiseworthy act of that nobleman, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to that church, your foundation and the grants and benefactions made to you and to the same church, as they were reasonably made and as are contained in the authentic document of the aforesaid nobleman; and we fortify them by the protection of this present document. [Col. 1233A] No person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXXIII. He writes to the brethren of Marmoutier concerning the repair of a certain chapel. (Lateran, 8 November.)

[Morice, *Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire de Bretagne*, I, 728.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the abbot and convent of Marmoutier, etc.

[Col. 1233B] A petition presented to us on your behalf stated that John Gruel and R., knights, had formerly built a certain chapel and assigned it revenues sufficient for the maintenance of two monks, etc. And since, in the course of time, many evils and inconveniences had arisen in those regions because of wars and the dreadful storms of warfare, and the aforesaid chapel had for some years remained destitute of ministers, the clerics of the Church of Delle oppose the repair of that church, etc. We, etc., grant that you may undertake the repair of this chapel, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXXIV. He directs [Rainald], bishop of Mâcon, [Robert], bishop of Chalon, and the dean of Lons, to compel Rainald, lord of Château-Rainald (diocese of Chalon), and Gilo of Belfort (diocese of Besançon), to restore property taken from the priory of Louinco, belonging to the monastery of Tournus. (Lateran, 25 November.)

[Juenin, *Nouvelle histoire de Tournus*, Documents, p. 180.]

[Col. 1233C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the bishops of Mâcon and Chalon, and to his beloved son the dean of Lons, established in the diocese of Besançon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint brought before us by our beloved sons, the monks of Tournus, that [Col. 1233D] Rainald, lord of Château-Rainald in the diocese of Chalon, and Gilot of Belfort in the diocese of Besançon, violently take away and retain, to the prejudice and injury of their priory of Louinco, alms which their predecessors had bestowed upon it by last will for the good of their souls, together with certain other goods. Since, therefore, we ought not to tolerate injury to the rights of the aforesaid monastery, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if you find the foregoing to be true, you compel the said R. and G., by sentence of excommunication and interdict upon their lands, without appeal, [Col. 1234A] to restore everything taken away and make fitting satisfaction to the prior of that house for damages and injuries. If all of you cannot take part in carrying this out, nevertheless let two of you carry it out.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

On the lead seal: CELESTINE POPE III.

### CCCXXV. He appoints the bishop of Lodi judge between the bishop of Pavia and the canons of Piacenza. (Lateran, 11 December.)

[Campi, *History of Piacenza*, II, 376.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Lodi: greeting and apostolic blessing.

You are to know that, as our venerable brother the bishop of Pavia has represented to us, it has come to our hearing [Col. 1234B] that, although we had committed to our venerable brother the bishop of Bobbio the hearing of the case pending between that bishop and the canons of Piacenza concerning certain tithes, the bishop of Pavia cannot approach the presence of the said bishop of Bobbio without grave danger and fear to his lands and person because of a war which has arisen between one of his castles and the marquis Malaspina.

Therefore, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide for both parties and, through your prudent diligence, to impose a due end upon the case, we command you by apostolic letters that, notwithstanding the aforesaid letters, if proceedings have not yet lawfully begun under them, [Col. 1234C] summon the parties before you; decide between them, without appeal, what justice requires; and cause your decision to be inviolably observed.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of December, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### CCCXXVI. He confirms to Leontius of the monastery of St Saviour at Messina and to his monks tithes donated by William, archbishop of Reggio. (Fragment.) (Lateran, 29 December.)

[Pirri, *Sicilia sacra*, vol. II, p. 981.]

. . . We confirm by apostolic authority the tithes of your possessions in the territory of Messa, which our brother William, archbishop of Reggio, with the consent of his chapter, remitted to your church and concerning which a dispute had arisen, as you possess them peaceably. [Col. 1234D]

No person, therefore, may, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

### CCCXXVII. To the archbishop of Canterbury—concerning the restoration of monks in the church of Coventry. (Lateran?)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXII, 612.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the archbishop of Canterbury, the bishop [Col. 1235A] of Lincoln, and the abbot of St Edmund: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as we in no way wish the measures wisely established by our predecessors to be annulled or infringed, so we wish measures obtained from them by deception, to the detriment of ecclesiastical propriety, to be corrected and restored to a better condition. For, as we have heard—indeed, as we know well—a monastic order has existed in the Church of Coventry almost from the first establishment of the Christian faith in England, and its members served with such regular observance that they deserved to be privileged by the Apostolic See and endowed and enriched by kings of England of illustrious memory.

We grieve deeply that our venerable brother the bishop of Chester, on the strength [Col. 1235B] of certain letters which, it is said—and which we can scarcely believe—he procured from Pope Clement, our predecessor of good memory, by a false representation, without the knowledge of ourselves and our brethren, violently expelled the beloved sons, the prior and convent, from that monastery and established secular canons there. Since this brings disgrace upon monastic religion and upon the whole discipline of the Church, and since it is not our intention that the aforesaid predecessor, unless deceived, should have lent authority or favour to so great an irregularity, we command you by apostolic letters and strictly enjoin you, by virtue of obedience, that, notwithstanding the aforesaid letters or any other privileges of confirmation or [Col. 1235C] indulgence, you remove from that monastery the secular clerics instituted there by the aforesaid bishop. Without hindrance from any litigation, restore the monastic order there, bringing back the monks expelled from it and establishing [perhaps: restoring] therein persons who ought and desire to observe the Rule of Blessed Benedict.

Compel the said bishop and all holders of the goods of that church, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to restore them. We further will and command that, relying on our authority, you annul the donations, grants in fee, leases, and alienations of the possessions of that church made by the same bishop from that time onward; striking with canonical censure, without the obstacle of appeal, those who presume to act contrary to this. Declare excommunicated those who laid violent hands upon the aforesaid monks, and let them come to the Apostolic See with testimonial letters from you to receive absolution. [Col. 1235D]

Given, etc.

### CCCXXVIII. He receives the monastery of Cysoing under protection and confirms its rule and possessions.

[Buzelini, *Gallo-Flandria*, 364.]

[Col. 1236A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of the church of Cysoing and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Since, by the Lord’s inspiration, you have professed the regular life, we provide with paternal concern for your peace and offer you apostolic protection, lest you be harassed by the vexations of evil men. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present document, the aforesaid church of St Callistus, in which you are devoted to the divine [Col. 1236B] service. We first decree that the canonical order known to have been established in your church by Raynald, formerly archbishop of Reims of good memory, according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the institution of the brethren of the church of St Denis of Reims, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, [Col. 1236C] or other lawful means, God being gracious, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place in which your church is situated, with its tithes and free tenants, so that no one shall have the right of advocacy over them; the church, grange, and land of Lovilio, with the full tithe and the lodging due from the whole village; the wood of the prebends; Malum-Alnetum; the wood called Salengretum; and the property of that same village and of Cysoing, in arable land, meadows, woods, marshland, and waters, as it had been possessed from ancient times; also the course of the spring of Burgela, which the church may conduct through its necessary works without anyone’s prohibition; the church of [Col. 1236D] Asli, with the full tithe, arable land, and the priest’s *mansus* [Note: [Col. 1235D] Here and in the following places, *mansus* seems to denote a house.]; the church of Bosni, with the full tithe, grange, and tenants; the church of Camphain, with the full tithe and tenants; the church of Bouvines, with the full tithe and *mansus*, grange, both in the land and *curtis* [Note: [Col. 1235D] This word, here and often elsewhere, denotes a village. [Col. 1236D] In Flodoard: “A certain priest of the *curia* of Bovonis”—for that is what the village is called.] of St Amand and in other lands; the church of Gruson, with the full tithe; the church of Genech, with the full tithe, *mansus*, and grange; the church of Cobrin; the church of Summinio, with the full tithe, the land-rent of the whole village, tenants, and a free *mansus*; the chapel of Hornen, with [Col. 1237A] the full tithe and land-rent; the manor of Beaurepaire, with woods, waters, marshland, fishpond, and arable land; the manor of Vitri, with land, tenants, and the right which you have in the revenues and tithes of that village; the church of Cheren; the church of Fys (Lys); the church of Toufles; the chapel of Hestberga; the manor of Crespelan, with land-rent, tenants, and the whole village, so that no one but the abbot alone may exercise justice or advocacy there; a stone house on the hill of Tournai, so that its revenues may be assigned in perpetuity to the use of the sick of the church; the houses of Messines; five solidi which the count of Flanders pays for the orchard.

Certainly, no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We also decree that the burial-place of that site shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict—while preserving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave the cloister without his abbot’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without the guarantee of letters from the community. You may receive for conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and released from secular obligations, and retain them without any opposition. We also prohibit any bishop or archdeacon from pronouncing against you or your churches a sentence of excommunication or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause, or from burdening you with novel and unlawful exactions. Upon the death of yourself, abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the greater part of the brethren of sounder counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

Furthermore, we strictly forbid any bishop, archdeacon, their official canons, or other clerics from having power or permission to demand from you, under the pretext of any custom, a palfrey, silk cope, or anything else for the confirmation, enthronement, or blessing of your abbot.

> **Note [Col. 1237D].** Consult what we have said above concerning the privileges of the Church of St. Martin. Moreover, these words appear also to have been directed against the advocates of this abbey, who formerly sought to claim a palfrey for themselves.

If they demand such things from you, since this is detestable and contrary to reason, you may freely refuse them what they ask. Moreover, desiring with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquillity, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone within the enclosure of your establishments to dare commit violence, robbery, or theft, or to detain, seize, or kill persons.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit, in every way, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If therefore in future, etc.

Thus signed:

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church, etc.

**A.D. 1191–1198**

[Col. 1238B]

### CCCXXIX. He takes the Church of St Thomas of Paraclete (Æbelholt) under protection and confirms its possessions and rights.

(LANGEBEK, *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, vol. VI, p. 142.)

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot of the Church of St Thomas of Paraclete, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1238C] The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, in order that we may love religious persons pleasing to God and strive by every means to advance religion. For no service is ever rendered pleasingly to God unless it proceeds from the root of charity and is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore all lovers of the Christian faith ought to love religion and to foster more attentively venerable places together with the persons devoted therein to divine service, so that they may be troubled by no molestations of wicked people or wearied by vexatious burdens.

Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests and receive the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, strengthening it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we establish that the canonical order which is recognized to have been instituted in your church according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of St Victor of Paris, shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favor, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by name:

[Col. 1239A] The site itself on which the aforesaid church is built, with all its appurtenances; the church of Therby with its tithes; one third of the tithes of the church at Alsentorp; one third of the tithes of the church of Annesse; one third of the tithes of Haelsinghe; one third of the tithes of the church of Craekom and Eskilso; the holding at Synderby with woodland, fields, and meadows; land at Saerflouae; the holding at Jolighe with the village belonging to it, meadows and fields, and a mill situated beside Vaerebro; the holding at Hathelosae with woods, meadows, and fields; the entire village of Naetveth, with woods, meadows, fields, and fisheries; the village of Tiaeraeby with its church, woods, meadows, and fields; land at Halt with a parcel of woodland; land at Tolletorp with woodland; land at Frithtoph; the holding at Haelsingae with woodland, fields, and meadows.

[Col. 1239B] Certainly, no one whatsoever may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on those of your granges which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. You may also receive for conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and released from secular obligations, and retain them in your church without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your place, to leave that place without his abbot’s permission except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without the guarantee of letters from your community.

[Col. 1239C] In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose clerics and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the cure of souls to them, so that they shall be answerable to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. We also grant that the burial-place of that site shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who have decided to be buried there, unless perhaps they are excommunicated or under interdict—while preserving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing little bells, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, and in a subdued voice. Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the part of the brethren of sounder counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact and unimpaired for the benefit, in every way, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 1240A] If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt rashly to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

### CCCXXX. He takes the monastery of Locus Dei under protection and confirms its possessions.

(LANGEBEK, *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, V, p. 189.)

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Locus Dei: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the diligence of our office. Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously granting assent to your just prayers, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves your persons together with all the goods which you now reasonably possess or may hereafter acquire by just means, with God’s favor.

[Col. 1240C] In particular, we apostolically confirm to you and, through you, to your monastery, and strengthen by the protection of this document, those goods which our venerable brother Omer, bishop of Ribe, is known to have granted you by pious resolution after the example of his predecessors, just as you possess them lawfully and without dispute and as is contained in authentic documents of that bishop, of our venerable brother Absalon, archbishop of Lund and legate of the Apostolic See, and of Eschel, his predecessor of good memory.

Therefore no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your persons or goods, or infringe this page of our protection and confirmation, or presumptuously oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His apostles, Blessed Peter and Paul.

### CCCXXXI. He takes under protection the leper-house of the valley of Bugnes and declares that “a portion of the forest of Cantastra is exempt from every exaction.”

(*Histoire ecclés. d'Abbeville*, p. 387, on the testimony of BRÉQUIGNY, *Table chron.*, IV, 47.)

## SPURIOUS

[Col. 1241]

### I. Privilege for the monastery of Murbach. (Lateran, 22 May, A.D. 1190.)

[MARTEN., *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 633.]

[Col. 1241A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SINTBERT, abbot of the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul and of the martyr Leodegar at Murbach, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

It accords with apostolic governance to assist with kindly compassion those distinguished by pious religion, and to grant cheerful assent, with eager devotion, to those asking for what is just and religious. From this, beyond doubt, we especially deserve the reward of gain from God, Creator of all, if venerable places, suitably ordered, are without doubt brought into a better state. Therefore, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery, situated beside the bank called Murbach, now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favor, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

[Col. 1241B] Certainly, no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. You may receive for conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and released from secular obligations, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave that place without his abbot’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without the guarantee of letters from the community. When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of that site shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who have decided to be buried there, unless perhaps they are excommunicated or under interdict—while preserving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

[Col. 1241D] Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by the common consent of all, or the part of the brethren of sounder counsel, shall judge fit to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. Furthermore, after deliberation we decree this: at suitable times the matter shall be reported to our ecclesiastical solicitude, so that monastic religion may be directed according to regular observance and ecclesiastical concord may be maintained in fitting fashion, lest perhaps—God forbid!—under the pretext of this privilege the purpose and manner of your uprightness should somehow be turned aside from the norm of justice.

[Col. 1242A] We grant the bishop of Basel no power at all in that place to conduct or order even the smallest matter, except in accordance with the common will of the brethren and the abbot. Nor do we permit a sentence of excommunication to be imposed upon the abbot himself or his monastery, for any cause whatever, by any bishop or archbishop other than the bishop of the Apostolic See alone. We further specifically ordain that the same monastery, with its precinct and all its appurtenances, shall be free from every incursion by any persons, and likewise exempt from all services and burdens whatsoever imposed by the bishop of Basel, all bishops, episcopal officers, kings, emperors, dukes, counts, and all persons.

[Col. 1242B] Concerning the appointment of an advocate, we decree that no one may obtain this office as though it were due to him by hereditary right, except one appointed by the common election, or the sounder election, of the brethren. That advocate, however, must never unjustly or violently lay hands upon that place or upon the possessions of those serving God there. Without the abbot’s consent, he may not burden the monastery itself, the peasants of the monastery, or its household with frequent attendance or lodging; nor may he extort any exactions from them. Nor may he conduct among them any judicial pleas unless invited by the abbot. From the many judicial pleas called *justitiae*, he may receive no more than the one-third which is owed him by custom—and that only from those pleas to which he has been invited by the abbot. If he violates these provisions and is found useless to the monastery, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his fault, he shall be removed and another, if they so wish, or none, if they so wish, shall be substituted.

[Col. 1242C] We decree that that place, endowed with complete liberty, shall always be secure and free, both from the jurisdiction of all mortals and from every rash disturbance of vexations; that there shall be a perpetual abbey there; that it shall always be protected under the guardianship of the Apostolic See; and that a gold Byzantine coin shall be paid yearly to the apostolic palace as a sign of perpetual liberty. Beyond the due payment of that census, nothing further may in any way be demanded from it for the services of the Roman Church. We also grant, by licence of our apostolic authority, to you and to your successors the use of the dalmatic and sandals in the solemnities of Mass, in accordance with the privileges of our predecessors.

[Col. 1242D] The abbot shall be blessed only by the Apostolic See, from which he ought to receive blessing; and if he is accused of any crime, he shall await judgment only from that same Apostolic See. We have also thought fit to add generally that whatever is known to have been granted to the monastery of Murbach by the authority of any of our predecessors, kings, or emperors shall also be confirmed and strengthened by our apostolic authority through this our privilege. We establish under apostolic censure and under the solemn adjuration of divine judgment that none of our successors—Roman pontiffs, kings, dukes, marquises, counts, archbishops, or persons of any rank or condition—may ever dare to attempt anything contrary to this privilege.

[Col. 1243A] If anyone should presume to do so, let him know that he is indissolubly bound by the bond of our anathema until he makes worthy satisfaction. But whoever, out of regard for this privilege, preserves it and ensures that it is not infringed in any respect, may deserve to obtain from God, the rewarder of all good things, the grace of blessing and forgiveness of his sins, so that he may rejoice in the heavenly dwelling. Amen, amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Guala, cardinal-priest of the title of St Martin at the Equitius. I, Stephen, cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, Thomas, cardinal-priest of the title of St Sabina. I, Pelagius, bishop of Albano. I, Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum. I, Otto, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St Angelo. I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of St Theodore. I, Stephen, cardinal-deacon of St Adrian. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.
