[Col. 1243D] Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Master Gunther, notary of the lord pope, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1190 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### II. Privilege for the monastery of St Modestus at Benevento. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 3 April, A.D. 1195.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VIII, 127.]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RICHARD, abbot of the monastery of St Modestus, built in the city of Benevento, and to his successors canonically elected: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1244A] Placed, by the Lord’s ordering, upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we are bound by the office of our apostolate diligently to consider the condition of all Churches. Yet we wish, and ought, to devote still more careful attention to those places in which the fervour of religion and observance of order are maintained and which are subject directly, without any intermediary, to the Roman Church. Accordingly, beloved son Richard in Christ, we graciously grant your just requests and receive under the special protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of St Modestus, which is known to belong to the right and property of the Roman Church, and strengthen it by the written instrument of this present privilege. First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity. We establish that whatever possessions or goods that monastery justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favor, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to note:

[Col. 1244B] The place in which the monastery itself is situated, with all that pertains to it both within and outside the city of Benevento: namely, the church of St Nazarius situated beside the aforesaid monastery; the church of St Angelo at the Rufina Gate; the church of St Nicholas situated in the suburb of the same gate; and also the other churches which they possess outside the named city, together with houses, storehouses, a bathhouse, olive groves, vineyards, mills, lands, gardens, meadows, woods, and *ischiae* [uncertain: possibly water-meadows or islands].

[Col. 1244C] We further will that both you, dearest son, and your successors may, by your own authority and without the opposition of any bishop, summon whichever bishop you wish for the consecration of your churches or the ordination of your clerics. No one may presume to celebrate solemn Masses unless invited by the abbot of that monastery. By apostolic censure we entirely establish and prohibit every ecclesiastical and secular dignity from introducing into the aforesaid venerable monastery any condition whatever or any new custom. You may also receive clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and released from secular obligations, and retain them without any opposition. Archbishops and bishops may not place under interdict the churches subject to your monastery, or their priests or clerics, nor excommunicate parishioners. If any person holding the patronage of a church wishes to give it to your monastery, he may do so by permission of our grant.

[Col. 1244D] We ratify the ancient and reasonable customs, immunities, and liberties granted to you and your monastery and observed hitherto, and decree that they shall remain whole and unimpaired in future times. We grant that you, beloved son Richard, and your successors serving the Lord perpetually in the same monastery may possess the mitre and ring. Upon your death, now abbot of the same place, or that of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the greater part of sounder counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The man elected shall come to the Roman pontiff to be blessed. Moreover, we decree that the burial-place of that site shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict—while preserving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 1245B] rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, all things shall remain whole and unimpaired, to benefit in every way those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this our constitution, should attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to divine vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of the Lord, so that they may receive from Him the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Celestine, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, John, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Cecilia. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of St Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia. [Col. 1245D] I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of St Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Joffrey, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St Theodore.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hands of Giles, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, on the third day before the Nones of April, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1195 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III.

### III. He replies to Philip, bishop of Beauvais, that he deservedly suffers adversity because “he put off the peaceful prelate and put on the warlike soldier”; and because, with his aid, “the king of France, who was bound by a bodily oath sworn to the king of England to preserve unharmed both towns and lands, had shamelessly acted against faith and oath, violently occupied the king’s towns, and cruelly ravaged his land with a hostile hand.” He adds that “the king of England, at last returning from captivity, had manfully confronted the king of France; and that humility had fought against pride, right and equity against wrong, moderation and restraint against arrogance and intemperance.” He adds that “he had sent supplicatory letters to the king of England on Philip’s behalf.”

(MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 611.)

[Col. 1246A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother PHILIP, bishop of Beauvais: greeting, and may you hasten to return from your deviation.

[Col. 1246B] Though things have gone badly for you, this is no wonder: for he deserves the hatred of all who proves himself the common enemy of all. For you put off the peaceful prelate and put on the warlike soldier; inverting the order and sequence of things, you have rashly borne a shield in place of a mitre, a sword in place of a stole, a coat of mail in place of an alb, a helmet in place of a mitre, and a lance in place of a pastoral staff—claiming that you wished to repel force by force, as you allege, but in truth fighting not for your country but against it.

For we may now publicly proclaim concerning your France: “Woe to the land whose king is a child” (Eccles. 10). For your king was bound to the king of England by a bodily oath, solemnly sworn, faithfully to preserve unharmed both his towns and lands, at least until his return from his pilgrimage. Yet, shamelessly violating faith and oath, he violently occupied the aforesaid king’s towns and cruelly ravaged his land with a hostile hand. At last returning from captivity, that king manfully confronted your king, placing his hope not in multitude but in the Lord God. For wars are won not by an abundance of men or forces, but of virtues.

[Col. 1246C] On behalf of the king of England, humility has thus far fought against pride, right and equity against wrong, moderation and restraint against arrogance and intemperance. For men richly endowed with virtues, not military strength, achieve victory. Laws and rights permit an injury inflicted by arms to be driven back by the remedy of arms. Now at last, though late, the king of England has shown his own courage and spirit; for it is difficult for enclosed virtue to remain hidden, for the heat of courage to be extinguished, or for the spark of worth to be crushed and contained. Virtue does not know how to be shut in, and fire when pressed down bursts into flame.

[Col. 1246D] You have shown yourself, in your folly and insolence, not merely counsellor but accomplice of your lord’s unbridled madness. You sought and found; you knocked and were knocked down; you deservedly fell into the pit you made; where you were found, there you were judged. Thus, as we gather from the tenor of your letters sent to us, while charging us with your country’s excesses, you strive to turn your own fault against us, calling us lukewarm and dissembling. What then, if a sheep rises against the shepherd, or a son against his father? He will not be a shepherd who did not feed it, nor a father who does not regret having raised it. It is therefore harmful in a man to cloak malicious cunning under the appearance of simplicity.

[Col. 1247A] Nevertheless, we have sent supplicatory letters to the king of England on your behalf. Having considered thoroughly the character of your capture, in such a case we cannot and ought not command, but only plead. A victor must be overcome wisely, for it is written: “Wisdom overcomes malice” (Eccles. 7). We plead for you not inopportunely but suitably; for the importunate urgency of prayers is evidence of distrust. Patient waiting more readily obtains what is owed than an importunate request extorts it.

Meanwhile, bound in chains and given over to lamentations, bear your chains and lamentations gently and patiently, according to the poet’s words (OVID, *Heroides*, V, 7):

> Whatever you suffer deservedly must be borne gently.
>
> A punishment that comes undeservedly comes to be lamented.

And that which the belly gains at the expense of shame must deservedly be expiated by lamentations.

Given, etc.

### IV. To those who visit the altar of St Mary in the church of St Stephen at Bologna and “extend helping hands for the condition and preservation of that church,” he grants remission of sins. (Lateran, 8 May.)

[*Acta Sanctorum*, February, vol. II, p. 48.]

[Col. 1247C]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Christ’s faithful: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The glory of eternal life, with which the wondrous goodness of the Creator of all crowns the blessed host of heavenly citizens, ought to be gained by the power of merits from those redeemed at the price of blood poured out from the precious body of the Redeemer. Among these merits, one is recognized as especially great: that the majesty of the Most High be praised everywhere, but especially in the churches of the saints.

Therefore, in the temple of the glorious protomartyr Stephen, called the Jerusalem of Bologna, which Petronius, servant of God and bishop of that city, raised and constructed after the likeness of the sepulchre of our Lord Jesus Christ at Jerusalem, there rest the relics of very many saints, especially the bodies of the martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, Florian with forty companions, five bodies of the Innocents, and St Juliana the widow. There, moreover, almost all the mysteries of our Saviour Jesus Christ are represented and displayed with the utmost devotion; and there God, most good and great, works many miracles through the interceding merits of those saints.

[Col. 1248A] We ask and exhort all of you in the Lord, imposing upon you remission of sins, that you come in humility of spirit to the aforesaid temple to implore from the Lord pardon for your offences. For, wishing beneficially to invite Christ’s faithful to merits, as it were through rewards, and trusting in the mercy of almighty God and the authority of His apostles Blessed Peter and Paul, we mercifully remit and grant:

[Col. 1248B] To all who are truly penitent and confessed, whenever they visit in devotion the altar of the Virgin St Mary in the said temple and extend helping hands for the condition and preservation of that church: two hundred years; the altars of St Peter and of the Innocents: six hundred years; of St James: one hundred years; of St Catherine: one hundred and fifty years; of St Mary Magdalene: one hundred and fifty years; of St John the Baptist: one hundred and sixty years; of St Stephen: three hundred years; of St Agnes: two hundred years; of the Holy Trinity: three hundred years; the column resembling that on which our Redeemer was scourged: two hundred years; likewise of St Juliana: one hundred years; and of the holy martyrs Vitalis and Agricola: two hundred and fifty years; and to those who visit the tombs of Blessed Florian and his companions situated in the said church: four hundred years; and the place called Calvary: three hundred and sixty years.

[Col. 1248C] Likewise, to those who annually visit the said temple on the feasts of the Nativity of the Lord, Circumcision, Epiphany, Ascension, Pentecost, St Stephen, and the celebration of All Saints: seven hundred years. To those who enter the sepulchre fashioned in the likeness of the Lord’s sepulchre on the Friday of Holy Week, on Easter, the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and on the two following days each year for devotion’s sake, and extend helping hands, we mercifully grant them full remission from the penances imposed upon them for all their sins, and decree that it shall remain perpetually valid.

> **Note [Col. 1247D].** “It was to be valid.”

[Col. 1248D] Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

[Col. 1247]

## DECREES OF CELESTINE III

[Col. 1247D] I. He replies to the bishop of Ambule[n] [otherwise, Abule[n]] that “the Templars, Hospitallers, and others having oratories in their houses are not permitted to place bells in them and ring them publicly.” (AUGUSTINE of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 417.)

II. He orders the bishop of Abie[n] [otherwise, Amiens] to restore what had been taken from a priest. (AUGUSTINE of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 382.)

[Col. 1249A] III. To Ralph, bishop of Angers, he grants that those “who cannot attain the honour of the priesthood because of the impediment of age, if he recognizes that this alone stands in the way, may be tolerated until the time when he finds them fit to undertake the burden of priesthood.” (MANSI, XXII, 634, 550.)

IV. He exhorts the patriarch of Aquileia to see that “provosts and others to whom, according to the custom of the land, authority is known to have been assigned to bestow prebends upon certain persons in the place of those dying, do not substitute for the deceased their own sons whom, while established in holy orders, they have begotten.” (MANSI, XXII, 642, 627.)

V. He forbids all judges of Benevento that “any of them should presume to act as advocate except in his own case, or perhaps when he is bound to provide patronage to some church or by reason of an obligation of generosity.” (MANSI, XXII, 626.)

[Col. 1249B] VI. He replies to the chapter of Bisiuco that, if a layman “at the command of the abbot in whose service he resides, has presumed to lay violent hands upon a cleric, monk, or lay brother,” both abbot and layman are to be regarded as excommunicated until they come before the Apostolic See. (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 421.)

VII. He replies to the bishop of Brugna [Brugnatensis]: first, that “one who asserts that he has incurred an automatic sentence of excommunication can obtain the benefit of absolution only through the Apostolic See”; secondly, that “bigamous priests and husbands of widows are not to be admitted to the celebration of divine offices, whether their wives are living or dead.” (MANSI XXII, 637.)

VIII. He replies to the [arch]bishop of Brindisi concerning those who “have taken an oath unwillingly in order to preserve life and property.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, II, title 24, ch. 15.)

But in the question set forth fifth—whether those who have taken such an oath unwillingly in order to preserve life and property are released from the bond of the oath—we judge nothing other than what our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, are known to have judged: they released such persons from the bonds of the oath.

Yet, in order that the matter may be handled more prudently and an occasion for swearing falsely removed, they should not be told so expressly that they need not keep their oaths. But if they do not observe them, they are not on that account to be punished as for a mortal crime.

IX. He replies to the bishop of Saragossa that, “when a prebend is vacant and several of those enrolled there break out in an appeal, if they have not pursued the appeal within forty days, canonical election is to proceed.” (MANSI XXII, 571.)

[Col. 1249D] X. He replies to the archbishop of Canterbury that “an appeal is not to be deferred to when the adversary is prepared immediately to prove that the appellant despoiled him after the appeal had been lawfully lodged.” (MANSI XXII, 641.)

XI. He replies to the archbishop of Canterbury that, “if a criminal question is being litigated in a matrimonial cause, the matter ought to be determined not through an intermediary person, but through the principal matrimonial cause itself.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 365.)

XII. He replies to someone consulting through W., dean of Cathalaven, that “a woman who, believing her husband dead, has assumed the religious habit and, after his return, has been removed from the monastery, is not to be compelled against her will, after her husband’s death, to observe the rule.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 394.)

XIII. He informs the bishop of Le Mans that he has confirmed the abbot-elect of Pelicea. (*Decretals of Gregory*, I, title 6, ch. 13.)

[Col. 1250A] XIV. He commands certain persons to compel the archbishop to restore what he has taken from the monastery of Dol. (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Appendix*, IV, 370.)

XV. He commands certain persons to compel a certain knight to pay B., archdeacon of Leun. [Dol], “tithes from the proceeds of a mill.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 391.)

XVI. He commands certain persons to order that tithes of hay from certain lands be paid to B., archdeacon of Dol. (Ibid.)

XVII. He replies to the archbishop of York concerning a marriage. (*Decretals of Gregory*, IV, title 17, ch. 10.)

“Having reported to us …” And below: “We reply to your Fraternity as follows: since justice based on public decency prohibited a marriage from being contracted between them, the marriage contracted ought to have been separated. Consequently, since the children are excused neither by the Church’s permission nor by their father’s ignorance, they do not appear to be admissible in any way to succession to their father’s estates.”

[Col. 1250B] XVIII. He commands the bishop of Exeter to rescind leases of ecclesiastical estates made by canons. (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 387.)

XIX. He grants the abbot of St. Facundus that, “whenever he is required to produce his privilege or any indulgence whatever, the document is to be read aloud only by the judge, in the hearing of the opposing party, so that the privilege is in no manner handed over for copying.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 374.)

XX. He replies to the bishop of Vamo [perhaps Fano] that “judicial duels are to be tolerated neither concerning the presentation of churches nor in other cases.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, V, title 35, ch. 1.)

XXI. He grants the bishop of Faenza leave to restore to its former condition the monastery of Granden., which its prior had, without his authorization, subjected to the monastery of Cerat. (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 417.)

[Col. 1250C] XXII. He commands all the oblates of the monastery of St. Peter of Fertum to obey the abbot. (MANSI XXII, 627.)

XXIII. He writes to the archbishop of Otranto concerning Jo., who was ordained priest by a Greek bishop not “at the four seasons” [Ember seasons]: “For the future,” he says, “we do not wish mixtures and customary combinations of rites to be observed in ordinations.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 358.)

XXIV. He commands the bishop of Lincoln and the abbots of Thaniae and Labrire to compel G. Bochis to restore a church to a certain priest. (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 376.)

XXV. He commands the bishop of Lincoln and Abbot T. to declare [or judge] Lucy, widow, daughter of G. and A., “legitimate.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, IV, title 17, ch. 11.)

XXVI. He commands the bishop of Lincoln, the prior of Fractoponte, and the archdeacon of Marin. to compel G[alfrid], [Col. 1250D] archbishop of York, to restore money received from R., the provost. (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 412.)

XXVII. He replies to the chapter of Lucca [perhaps Lucera] that the clerics of Bari who, after suspension by Bishop Vigilius [perhaps of Vigili], obtained ecclesiastical benefices are to be deprived of those benefices. (MANSI XXII, 570.)

XXVIII. He replies to the chapter of Magdeburg that, since N., archdeacon of Le Mans, “although he is their church’s dean, has nevertheless chosen his residence rather in the regions of France, and for a period now of ten years their church has been unable to have his presence,” they are to elect a new dean unless he returns when summoned. (*Decretals of Gregory*, III, title 4, ch. 8.)

XXIX. He replies to certain persons that the son of the knight C., whom his father “caused to assume the monastic habit while he was in no way of the age of discretion, in a monastery of the province of Mainz,” is not to be compelled to retain the habit if he does not wish to do so. (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 393.)

[Col. 1251A] XXX. He commands the archbishop of Vidros [Nidaros] to “abstain from communion with one who has incurred a sentence of excommunication by the sacrilegious laying-on of hands, although he has not been formally denounced.” (MANSI XXII, 633.)

XXXI. He commands the [canons of Poitiers] to admit Hug., subdeacon of Le Mans, whom Jordan, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Pudentiana, had made a canon of their church, “fully as a brother and canon, and to assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 363.)

XXXII. He writes to the prior and canons of St. Ranerius that they should not doubt that an oath sworn concerning a fixed number of canons may be altered by the authority of the Apostolic See. (MANSI XXII, 633.)

XXXIII. He commands certain persons to excommunicate I. de Malafrena and I., son of Cavalca, and their associates, who violently broke into the church of Miliaton. and other churches of the diocese of Reggio. (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 421.)

XXXIV. He replies to [Walter], archbishop of Rouen, that “those are to be regarded as absolved who have incurred excommunication for laying hands on clerics or other religious persons and have at the time been absolved by cardinal-legates sent from the side of the Roman pontiff, although the legates do not show that they possess an express mandate concerning these matters.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 420.)

XXXV. He writes to [Walter], archbishop of Rouen, concerning the right of religious communities to present prelates. (BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, III, 369.)

The dignity of the Apostolic See is acknowledged, granted to it by the Lord himself in blessed Peter, so that where any point of doubt arises, recourse is had to its pronouncement, and what it decrees in reply must be received and observed by all without any hesitation. For it has been represented to us on your behalf that in your province it often happens that, for churches in which communities are known to have the right of presentation, their abbots, either in person or by letters, present suitable persons to the diocesan bishops. After such persons have been presented and received, the monks or communities of another order sometimes object—sometimes before institution, sometimes after it—and protest. You seek a clear reply from us as to whether an institution already made, or one still to be made, ought to be impeded on this account.

[Col. 1251D] To this we have thought fit to reply as follows: namely, that presentations made by such prelates must be understood to be made with the consent of their communities, without which they cannot acquire any validity. Therefore, when it is established that the consent of the convent, or of its greater and sounder part, was absent, such institutions ought to be annulled—unless, by an ancient and approved custom or a granted liberty, some of them can prove that the consent of the community entrusted to them ought not to be required in the bestowal of churches or benefices.

Given at the Lateran.

XXXVI. He writes to [Walter, archbishop of Rouen?] concerning James, a priest, who is not to be regarded as excommunicated. (Ibid.)

James, the bearer of the present letters, having come to the Apostolic See, showed us in his statement that, while he was celebrating the morning offices, a certain nun entered the church and, playing with another cleric, created an impediment preventing him from rendering due service to God. The said priest, therefore, moved so that he might more freely devote himself to the celebration of divine offices, laid hands upon her in order to put her outside the church. Since she would not leave, he forced her, while dragging her, to remain within the church; but you avoided him for this as excommunicated and cause him to be avoided by others.

[Col. 1252A] Therefore, by apostolic authority we command you that, if the matter stands thus, you are henceforth not to avoid him, since on this account we see that he is not in any way bound as excommunicated.

XXXVII. He replies to the dean of Rouen, consulting him on various matters. (*Decretals of Gregory*, II, title 4, ch. 2.)

[Col. 1252B]

“Prudence …” And below: “You have indeed consulted us whether, when a cause is committed with appeal excluded, and the defendant counter-sues the plaintiff before the same judge, while the plaintiff raises the obstacle of an appeal against the counterclaim, such an appeal ought to be deferred to. We judge that, since plaintiff and defendant have the same condition, and each ought to be assessed under one and the same law regarding the remedy of appeal, just as the plaintiff desires that justice be done to him according to the rescript of the mandating authority, with appeal excluded, so in the same way justice ought to be rendered to the counterclaimant in his own case.”

XXXVIII. He writes the following to the suffragan bishops and dean of Rouen: “Certain letters have been sent by forgers recently discovered in the City [Rome], which we fear may be accepted by some as genuine. Therefore we command that, if you can discover any such persons—whom you will be able to recognize by comparison of the seal and by the character of the style—you cause them to be seized and kept in close custody until this has been reported to us.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 415.)

XXXIX. He commands certain persons that, “since Jews have occupied a large part of the parish of St. Laud, unless the Jews dwelling in the city of Rouen arrange annually to compensate the church of St. Laud and the other churches whose parishes they hold occupied for the tithes and all other revenues which they would receive from faithful parishioners if those parishioners lived there: they are to bind with the bond of anathema all those marked with Christ’s character who attempt to render service to Jews, borrow anything from them or repay what has already been borrowed, enter into sales or leases with them, or make any other contract, greet them, or hold conversation with them.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 391.)

[Col. 1252D] XL. He grants the bishop of Senigallia that, “when an appeal to the Apostolic See has been made by one of his subjects, he may compel the appellant to set out for the Apostolic See within twenty days after the appeal has been lodged.” (MANSI XXII, 627.)

XLI. He replies to the bishop of Teramo [perhaps Chieti] that the marriage of C. is not to be dissolved, although “after he had sworn that he would take V.’s daughter as wife, he changed his mind” and married another. (MANSI XXII, 633.)

XLII. He grants the abbot and convent of Vercelli that, if archbishops, archdeacons, archpriests, and deans “should presume, when visiting their churches, to exceed the number of mounts and persons established at the Lateran council, and demand procuration for them,” they may refuse it. (MANSI XXII, 630.)

[Col. 1253A] XLIII. He commands the faithful established in the province of Vianensis [perhaps Vienne] that “before deducting expenses from all goods collected, they are to pay tithes fully and duly to the churches, saving the privileges of the Roman Church.” (MANSI XXII, 571.)

XLIV. He rescinds this custom [of certain churches]: “when the election of some prelate is to be confirmed, the convent is to name two persons, to be secretly communicated to the patriarch or prince, so that they may have the power either to elect one of these or another person, or wholly to invalidate the election.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, I, title 6, ch. 14.)

XLV. He replies to a certain archbishop that “it does not seem fitting that he lend his pallium to another, since the pallium does not pass from one person to another.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, I, title 8, ch. 2.)

XLVI. He replies to a certain archbishop concerning presentations. (*Decretals of Gregory*, III, title 10, ch. 6.)

“It is known …” And below: “Since it often happens in your province that, for churches in which communities are known to possess the right of presentation, their abbots, either in person or by letters, present suitable persons to diocesan bishops, and, after those persons have been presented and received, monks sometimes object, sometimes before and sometimes after [institution]. We reply that presentations by prelates must be understood to be made with the consent of their communities, without which they have no validity. Therefore, if it is established that the consent of the convent, or of its greater and sounder part, was absent, such institutions ought to be annulled—unless, by ancient and approved custom or a granted liberty, some can prove that the consent of the community entrusted to them need not be required in the bestowal of churches or benefices.”

[Col. 1253C] XLVII. He replies to a certain bishop concerning those who, having been absolved from excommunication by judges more remote from Rome, “remain in an illicit union of consanguinity.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, I, title 31, ch. 6.)

Your Fraternity has informed us that certain of your parishioners, when they are marked by excommunication for an illicit union of consanguinity or affinity, procure letters from judges more remote from the Apostolic See. By these letters, after they have been absolved from excommunication, they remain in the aforesaid wicked union, because the delegates do not come to the place where witnesses can be produced, nor send anyone to receive them, and thus the case does not obtain its due effect.

And below: Since no one ought, through the malice or negligence of a delegated judge, to find support for remaining in the union of an iniquitous conjunction, we give your Fraternity this reply: whenever the matters we have described occur in your diocese, you may lawfully recall those so absolved into the former sentence of excommunication and keep them bound by that same sentence until the case begins to make lawful progress in the reception of witnesses and in other respects.

XLVIII. He writes to a certain bishop that, “on the occasion of an oath sworn not to alienate the property of the Church, he should not neglect to make salutary provision for a needy people concerning the furnishing of basilicas.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, III, title 48, ch. 6.)

XLIX. He replies to a certain bishop concerning the marriage of G. (*Decretals of Gregory*, IV, title 12, ch. 4.)

The letters sent to us by you showed [Col. 1254A] that, after G.’s wife had died, he carnally knew her daughter—his own stepdaughter. Afterwards, having taken another woman as wife, he did not fear publicly to commit an illicit act with his stepdaughter, returning like a dog to its vomit. Since you have sought advice on these matters, we answer in this present letter that, while living with his lawful wife and supplying her necessities, he is not to know her so long as he lives, unless she requests it of him; and then he is not to approach her without great sorrow of heart. Moreover, while he remains with her, he is to do penance for incest and adultery according to the moderation of your judgment; and if he survives her, he is thereafter to remain perpetually without hope of marriage.

L. He replies to a certain bishop that Henry, a priest, “although he himself did not fight in the duel, but someone fought for him, ought not to minister in holy orders.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, V, title 14, ch. 2.)

[Col. 1254B] LI. He commands a certain bishop to allow V., a deacon, to enjoy a certain benefice. (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 361.)

LII. He replies to a certain bishop concerning B., a cleric who, after “betrothing a certain girl, was promoted to be a canon.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 383.)

LIII. He grants a certain bishop that the illegitimate son of a certain knight may “be promoted to holy orders.” (Ibid., p. 360.)

LIV. He commands a certain bishop to have W., a subdeacon, “avoided by all as excommunicated until he dismisses the woman from his companionship.” (AUGUSTINUS of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 403.)

LV. He replies to Master Columba concerning delegated cases. (*Decretals of Gregory*, I, title 30, ch. 2.)

You have undertaken to ask us whether a general legate in the province may, before or after cognizance, take cognizance of a case which we have delegated to another, or in this way impede the progress of our commission which we send to the delegated judge.

[Col. 1254C] We reply that, because a special mandate derogates from a general one, a legate cannot impede a commission specially made to another. And if a judgment has already been pronounced according to the form of our mandate, the legate cannot in any way invalidate it unless he receives a special mandate concerning this matter; nevertheless, if it was reasonably rendered, he may confirm it and order its execution.

LVI. He replies to someone concerning “what incapacity is meant by the clause frequently inserted in letters: namely, that if two, three, or even more persons to whom letters are directed cannot all be present together to execute them, one or more of them may nevertheless execute them.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, I, title 3, ch. 13.)

LVII. He replies to someone that, “even if nothing had been proved against R. before the bishop of Dulmen. and his co-judges, the judgment nevertheless had to stand unless R. showed that it should be invalidated.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, I, title 9, ch. 6.)

LVIII. He commands someone to order a certain church restored to D., a priest. (*Decretals of Gregory*, V, title 1, ch. 12.)

LIX. He replies to someone concerning “the indulgence of Pope Adrian of happy memory, then bishop of Albano and legate to Norway, by which all the people of that land were permitted to contract marriage in the sixth degree.” (*Decretals of Gregory*, IV, title 14, ch. 3.)

LX. He replies to the questions of a certain person concerning spiritual kinship.

(MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 638.)

[Col. 1255A]

You pursue the praiseworthy care of the episcopal office, because in matters concerning which you are uncertain you consult your mother, the Roman Church, and ask to be instructed by her. You state first that a certain man married a woman whose father had lifted him from the sacred font while he was a boy. The two spouses lived together for twenty years and had children, although from their fifteenth year their consciences had been troubled. Subsequently, however, after an action had been brought against them—by a process whose wording is corrupt—

> [Note: Col. 1255D. The passage is corrupt, as are many others below.]

it was established for the Church by witnesses above every exception that the man had been received from the water of baptism by the father of the woman whom he had married.

Since Zacharias and Deusdedit, Roman pontiffs, decreed that such a union must be separated, because there can be no doubt that spiritual kinship exists where the relationship of co-parenthood is contracted, especially between those through whom that co-parenthood itself is contracted, who are called brethren in divine law; and since the spouses had nevertheless lived together for so long, the length of time does not diminish sins but increases them. Moreover, since the Church, in the proper course of this case, recognized that contract as unlawful, it declared that the marriage must be dissolved according to the canons. Each, however, is to be admonished to provide for the other’s necessities according to his means. But the offspring born before such separation are, if nothing else stands in the way, to be considered legitimate.

[Col. 1255C] You ask further: when a marriage happens to be challenged, is sexual intercourse to be suspended, or for how long may it be tolerated or rather endured? The answer is that Alexander II expressly forbade spouses to separate from one another until a just examination of the case has taken place. And the decree of Pope Symmachus provides that subjects ought not abandon an accused prelate before the matters alleged have been clearly brought to light and the charge lawfully proved; all the more, therefore, when a question of marriage is at issue, one spouse accused need not be deprived of the right he has in the other.

You further added that someone contracted marriage with a girl not yet marriageable. When she eventually reached the age threshold and had been known by him several times, [Col. 1255D] after four or five years, when she had attained full age, she withdrew and alleged against the marriage, asserting that she had always dissented from him from the beginning. What she says is supported by witnesses, reputation, and excellent conduct. In this case, therefore, we judge that she ought not to be heard against the marriage, since before consummation, or before she reached lawful age, she did not protest when she could have done so. For, just as she could have dissented before consent—which is expected in the twelfth year according to canon law—so, once lawful age had arrived and she had consented even once to marital intercourse, she is without doubt deemed by ratification to have waived silence on this matter.

[Col. 1256A] Again, as you say, a certain man, having made a vow of chastity, swore that he would afterwards take a certain woman as wife. Asked by your Fraternity about this, and having consulted prudent men, we judge that, since a simple vow binds before God no less than a solemn one, he should do penance because he swore rashly, and should strive to observe the vow he made to God. But if, after making such an oath, he should of his own motion proceed to marriage, your question contains no ambiguity: a simple vow impedes the contracting of marriage but does not dissolve a marriage already contracted.

But you asked concerning Saracens who, while in captivity, killed the husbands of certain Christian women by plots and machinations: since they afterwards converted to the Christian faith, may they lawfully marry those women, or, if they do marry them, is that marriage valid? Here we agree with the ruling of the Council of Tribur: if they maliciously plotted the death of the husbands, then, although through the women’s influence they have joined the ecclesiastical faith, they ought neither to adhere to those women nor, if they have adhered to them, be tolerated. Such a dispensation could not be admitted without danger, since the Church does not wish so great an injury to be compensated by such gain.

[Col. 1256B] Certain Saracens, moreover, are known to have killed Christians in war, and Christians likewise Saracens. Afterwards Saracens converted to the Christian faith and joined in marriage the wives of those whom they had delivered to death in battle; Christians are likewise known to have done the same with Saracen women converted to the faith. Yet, after discovering the truth about the death of their former husbands, these women urgently seek divorce. We answer that, since neither Christians nor Saracens are known to have procured one another’s deaths, marriages of this kind may lawfully be contracted between the aforesaid persons; and persons thus united, of either sex, cannot lawfully obtain or seek divorce on account of their spouses’ deaths.

Likewise, you wished to propose the following case: a Christian man, through hatred, denied Christ, joined himself to a pagan woman, and had children by her; the Christian woman, abandoned to the reproach of Christ, proceeded to a second marriage with the consent of her archdeacon and bore children by it. It does not seem to us that, even if the first husband returns to the communion of the Church, she ought to leave the second husband and be surrendered to the first, especially since she is seen to have departed from him by judgment of the Church; and, as Gregory testifies, contempt of the Creator dissolves the right of marriage against one who abandons his spouse through hatred of the Christian faith.

[Col. 1257A] As to whether, when the first husband returns to the faith and does not wish to enter monastic life, he may, after the death of the first wife, take as wife the woman whom he had joined to himself in the pagan rite and who, because of him, has returned to our faith with her children; and whether children born before conversion are to be held legitimate by virtue of a marriage celebrated after conversion according to ecclesiastical rite; and likewise whether the children of the woman who, with the permission of her archdeacon, left her first husband and married a second husband, an unbeliever who became a Catholic man, are legitimate: the glorious teaching of the Apostle, which says, “If the unbelieving spouse departs, let him depart; a brother or sister is not subject to such servitude,” together with the decree of the aforesaid Gregory—namely, that it is not a sin, if one dismissed for God’s sake joins himself or herself to another, for the unbeliever who departs sins both against God and against marriage—and also the statement of our predecessor Alexander III of happy memory, “Such is the force of marriage that those born before it are held legitimate after the marriage has been contracted,” do not permit us to doubt in these matters. Thus, in these cases, free access is open to one wishing to enter religious life; the man who returns to the faith may lawfully marry, after the first wife’s death, the woman who has converted; and the children in the aforesaid case are to be held legitimate.

[Col. 1257C] You also decided to ask us whether, when someone is accused of having carnally known a woman, witnesses must be questioned on the basis of sight, or whether reputation in the neighborhood alone is sufficient; and whether sworn witnesses are to be believed when they confess that they know of the union, but affirm nothing from sight. We reply that, if suitable testimony is given from sight or hearing, reputation furnishes a strong presumption in agreement with it, and lawful supporting evidence is supplied, the testimony of the sworn witnesses must be accepted. For a careful and discerning judge, according to what is provided in civil law, will confirm his conviction in such cases from arguments and testimonies which he finds better suited to the matter.

Finally, you carefully asked how much time ought to be granted to persons naturally frigid for testing marital intercourse, so that, if they fail in it, they may be separated. We judge that, although different periods are allowed for this in ancient canons as well as laws, [Col. 1257D] in the present consultation the following is to be observed: if a naturally frigid man cannot use as a wife the woman whom he married from the time of the celebration of the contract, and if the frigidity cannot be proved earlier, he is to cohabit with her for up to three years according to the authentic legal text. When that period has elapsed, if he still cannot have intercourse, then, according to Gregory’s decree, if the woman can prove by just judgment that the man cannot have intercourse with her, she may marry another. But if he has married another, they are to be separated.

If both consent to remain together, however, the man is to have her, if not as a wife, at least as a sister. Or, if both confess that they have never joined one another, each is to swear, [Col. 1258A] touching the holy Gospels, with seven relatives—or, if relatives are unavailable, seven neighbors of good repute—that they have never become one flesh through carnal intercourse; and then the woman appears able to proceed to a second marriage. But if he takes another wife, those who swore are to be held guilty of perjury and, after their penalty has been completed, compelled to return to their former marriage.

Finally, you ask what may be objected after the publication of depositions to a witness who, before the oath or depositions, had nowhere been challenged, and to the witness’s person. Know that it has prevailed in the Roman Church by long custom that, before the oath or depositions, both prejudicial objections and the witnesses’ own lawful exception may be raised in law. If crimes are alleged against witnesses of which they have not previously been accused, but which are advanced by anyone merely by way of exception, proof of those crimes must certainly be produced before the case is concluded by judgment. For, since canonical enactments require that witnesses be without any infamy, suspicion, or manifest stain in giving testimony, [Col. 1258B] if only those crimes of which they were at another time convicted or to which they confessed are alleged against witnesses, they may be repelled from testifying; because, as Stephen and many other Roman pontiffs testify, their confession against others is not to be believed unless they have first proved themselves innocent.

[Col. 1258C] But if witnesses have been convicted of or confessed to crimes alleged merely by way of exception, they cannot be punished by the ordinary penalty, since the action against them does not proceed according to law and order. It is sufficient, therefore, that they be excluded from giving testimony, especially where the crime alleged against them does not appear to concern the case at issue.

Since we know you to be a prudent and discerning man, and since, when you are uncertain on certain matters, you seek advice from us with pastoral concern, we willingly answer you, to the extent that we can, from canon law and commend your prudence with fitting praise in God. In your communication you have taken care to set before us whether a woman who, while under the age of discretion, was handed over to a monastery by her parents, put on the religious habit, and received the blessing, but later left and joined herself to a certain knight, by whom she even had offspring, ought to be compelled to return to the monastery. She asserts that she left after she had acquired the power to consent, and declares that she received the blessing against her will.

[Col. 1258D] To your consultation we have thought fit to reply as follows. Since, as the collection of the council appears to lay down, either paternal devotion or one’s own profession makes a monk, and one to whom either of these is applicable is barred altogether from returning to the world, she does not appear able to cast off the yoke of the monastic profession undertaken by her. For it is not clearly established that she objected when she received the blessing, which those forbidden to do so receive only when of the age of discretion—especially if ratification followed. And even if it is established that she objected at some time, what was done before [Col. 1259A] has been confirmed. Nor is this contradicted by the apparently contrary sense admitted in the personal constitution of our predecessor, the holy man Leo: namely, that girls compelled by their parents’ command to receive the habit of virginity may abandon it without violation. That ruling is understood to concern a girl who is known to be of marriageable age, both because she has free choice in the matter and because, when placed under parental choice, she is not compelled to follow her parents’ will.

LXI. He writes to someone that “a merchant who has entered the religious habit can neither cast off the habit nor join any woman to himself in marriage.”

(*Decretals of Gregory*, III, title 32, ch. 10.)

LXII. He commands certain persons that, “if clerics residing at Paris have any secular cases, they are to decide them by canon law and not permit custom to prevail over written law.”

(*Decretals of Gregory*, II, title 2, ch. 9.)

[Col. 1259B]

LXIII. He replies to someone that he is not to allow B., a woman abandoned by A., to be harassed by Peter, a knight, concerning a certain house.

(*Decretals of Gregory*, III, title 17, ch. 4.)

LXIV. He replies to someone concerning clerics caught in theft, homicide, or perjury.

(*Decretals of Gregory*, II, title 1, ch. 10.)

“Since not by man …” And below: You have asked us on your behalf whether it is lawful for a king or any secular person to judge clerics of whatever order, whether caught in theft, homicide, perjury, or any crimes whatever. We reply to your consultation as follows: if a cleric of whatever order is lawfully caught and convicted of theft, homicide, perjury, or another crime, he is to be deposed by the ecclesiastical judge.

[Col. 1259C] If, after deposition, he is incorrigible, he must be excommunicated; then, as his contumacy increases, he must be struck by the sword of anathema. Afterwards, if, descending into the depths of evils, he remains contemptuous, since the Church has nothing further that it can do, he is to be restrained by secular power, lest there be further ruin of very many persons; thus exile is to be assigned to him or another lawful punishment inflicted.

LXV. He replies to someone concerning a certain dependent cell which wished to be exempted from the subjection owed to the mother church.

(*Decretals of Gregory*, I, title 8, ch. 10.)

Moreover, in the fourth place the following question arose: [Col. 1259D] a certain dependent house wished to be exempted from the subjection by which it was bound to its mother-house. And below: The brethren of that house, while acknowledging in law that they had formerly been subject to that house, reported that a dispute concerning this subjection had once been raised and settled by agreement, on the condition that, by paying a certain annual rent to the mother church, they should be exempt from subjection to the principal house. And below: The prior, on behalf of the greater church, accordingly maintained that it was not lawful to make a settlement concerning spiritual subjection. We therefore reply that, from the aforesaid confession of the brethren, judgment ought to be rendered against them, especially since that agreement—even though we could not ascertain what the dependent house was definitely bound to pay—appears to have contained simoniacal injustice.

### LXVI. He replies to someone concerning appointed judges.

*(Decretals of Gregory, book II, title 12, chapter 2.)*

[Col. 1260A]

Finally, we were asked whether judges appointed to take cognizance of possession and ownership, wishing to spare the parties heavy expenses, may hear the allegations of both sides together and likewise admit the witnesses together; then first hear the depositions concerning possession and pronounce according to their tenor. We reply that this may lawfully be done, since it is expressly provided in civil law.

### LXVII. He replies to someone concerning appeals.

*(Decretals of Gregory, book II, title 28, chapter 40.)*

Moreover, we were asked whether, if a judge has pronounced sentence in this form: “Unless you satisfy Sempronius within twenty [Col. 1260B] days, know that you are excommunicated, suspended, or under interdict,” and the person against whom the sentence is given appeals in the meantime but does not make satisfaction by the appointed day, he is bound by such a sentence, or is protected by lodging the appeal. It appears to us, however, that the obstacle of an appeal ought to prevent a sentence of this kind.

### LXVIII. He replies to someone concerning testimony.

*(Decretals of Gregory, book II, title 20, chapter 27.)*

Moreover, when someone is accused of having carnally known another: should witnesses be questioned concerning what they saw, or is the report of the neighborhood alone sufficient? Or should sworn witnesses be believed when they profess themselves aware of sexual intercourse [Col. 1260C] but affirm nothing from sight? We reply that, if suitable testimony from sight is given, or even testimony from hearing, and corroborating public report supplies a strong presumption, and other lawful supports assist, the testimony of sworn witnesses is to be accepted. For a prudent and discerning judge will confirm his own judgment from those arguments and testimonies which he finds more suited to the matter.

### LXIX. He replies to someone concerning public witnesses.

*(Decretals of Gregory, book II, title 21, chapter 7.)*

Moreover, if public witnesses, whom your city calls synodal witnesses, have once given testimony before you or your chapter in a matrimonial case, they ought not to be compelled to take an oath again concerning the same cause in the presence of a delegated judge, provided that the delegated judge is otherwise given assurance—unless perhaps an issue of a new question arises.

Such witnesses may lawfully be excluded from giving testimony on account of infamy, if, after having been received in the community, they happen to have incurred it. If at any time their testimony has erred not deliberately but in its utterance, and they correct themselves immediately, they ought not to be rejected; it is otherwise if they allow an interval before making their correction.

### LXX. He replies to certain persons concerning P., an acolyte, who took up arms with some men in order to resist robbers.

*(Decretals of Gregory, book V, title 25, chapter 4.)*

[Col. 1261A]

The contents of the letter [lacuna]. And below: Since the acolyte P., together with certain men, took up arms in order to resist robbers, and in that conflict three persons were mortally wounded by others, yet those homicides were committed neither by his act nor by his counsel. And below: We reply to your inquiry as follows: since you say that the aforesaid acolyte has adopted a better way of life, he may be promoted to the order of subdeacon and exercise ministry at the altar.

[Col. 1261]

## VARIANT READINGS FOR THE LETTERS TO CELESTINE III

### I. Guarinus, Abbot of Saint Victor, to Celestine.—He congratulates him on his promotion and commends to him the church of Saint Victor.

*(MARTÈNE, Amplissima Collectio, I, 266.)*

[Col. 1261B]

To the most holy lord and father CELESTINE, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: brother GUARINUS, humble servant of the poor of the Church of Saint Victor at Paris, together with the other brethren of the same place, offers the obedience due to so great a father and the fullness of reverence.

Holy Father, we give thanks to almighty God, who has entrusted to the sincerity of your faith the Church which He redeemed by the precious blood of His only Son, appointing you its supreme and sure shepherd. He had long known [Col. 1261C] you to be concerned for the salvation of the sheep, that you might bestow fatherly affection upon all, you who had previously watched on behalf of all. Indeed, He trusted that you were His friend, since He wished to say to you: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14), bowing beneath your feet the hills of the world and every height, when He chose to transfer you from a share in responsibility to the fullness of power. We believe that this might often formerly have happened to you, if the Almighty had so ordained and it had agreed with your own good pleasure.

But now, after the long experience of many days and the manifold knowledge granted you from heaven concerning those matters necessary to the honor and benefit of the holy Church, the Almighty has wished to place your eminence in a more exalted position within Christian religion, so that, through the ever-watchful prudence of your diligence, things harmful might long since be uprooted from the fruitful field which the Lord has blessed, while wholesome things might be planted more carefully.

Would that a living and enduring remembrance may cling to your heart of how swiftly those whose chair you have now succeeded to departed from this light: [Note: [Col. 1261D] Namely Lucius III, who sat only 4 years, 2 months, and 18 days; Urban III, who held the pontificate for 1 year, 2 months, and 25 days; Gregory VIII, who held it only 2 [Col. 1262D] months; and Clement III, who held the pontificate for 3 years, 2 months, and 10 days.] so that, by imitating while you may the examples of the holy apostles whose place you occupy, you may attain their rewards; and, through Him who brings near the end that hangs over us, by the favor of divine mercy, may receive a reward that will not end.

For all others who fear God, your elevation to the fatherhood is a common occasion for joy. But in this joy the church of Blessed Victor glories in a special privilege: by the gracious condescension of heavenly mercy it has hitherto found you a most benign father in its necessities and an invincible protector. Therefore, prostrate at the feet of your eminence, we earnestly beg that, for the remedy of your soul, you may deign to restore to your servants the holy interpretation of the Apostolic See concerning that word, obtained in its entirety by your authority, and to restore our cause in its entirety according to the former commission.

### II. Eleanor, Queen of England, to Celestine.—She implores the pope’s aid for the release of Richard, King of England, her son. (A.D. 1192.)

*[Works of Peter of Blois, ed. GILES, vol. II, p. 58, epistle 144.]*

[Col. 1262C]

To the reverend father and lord CELESTINE, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: A., by the wrath of God Queen of England, Duchess of Normandy, and Countess of Anjou, offers herself—a miserable mother—to him as a father.

I had resolved to be silent, lest I be accused of insolence and presumption, should the abundance of my heart and the violence of grief perhaps draw from me some insufficiently guarded word against the prince of priests. Indeed, grief, while it is in the heat of its burning, differs little from madness: it recognizes no masters, fears no companion, defers to and spares no one—not even itself. Let no one, therefore, wonder if the force of grief sharpens the moderation of my words. For I lament a public loss; but private grief has also struck roots beyond consolation in the depths of my spirit. For the arrows of the Lord are within me, and their indignation drinks up my spirit. Nations are broken apart, peoples torn in pieces, provinces laid waste; and the whole Western Church, exhausted by lamentations, [Col. 1263A] in a contrite and humbled spirit implores you, whom God has established over nations and kingdoms in all fullness of power. I pray you, let the cry of the afflicted enter your ears: for our calamities have multiplied beyond number (Psalm 39). Nor can you conceal these matters without the mark of guilt and disgrace, since you are the vicar of the Crucified One, Peter’s successor, Christ’s priest, the Lord’s anointed, even Pharaoh’s god. “Let judgment come forth from your countenance, O Father; let your eyes behold equity” (Psalm 16).

The hopes of the people depend upon your decision and upon the mercy of your see; and unless your hand grasps judgment more promptly, the whole tragedy of this evil will recoil upon you. For you are father of orphans, judge of widows, comforter of mourners and sufferers, and [Col. 1263B] a city of refuge for all. Amid so great a mass of miseries, one sole consolation common to all is awaited from the authority of your power. In hard circumstances the children of Israel consulted Moses, whose office you perform, and in their distresses fled to the tabernacle of the covenant.

Our king is in straits, and pressures hem him in on every side. Consider the condition—or rather the ruin—of the kingdom; the wickedness of the time; the cruelty of the tyrant, who unceasingly forges weapons of iniquity in the furnace of greed against the king. He holds him captive and confined in prison chains—him whom he captured on the holy pilgrimage, under the protection of the God of heaven and the guardianship of the Roman Church—and by holding him, kills him. For he despises God and His terrible judgments; he broods over his prey, and there is none who can snatch it from his hand. If the Roman Church, with hands clasped, is silent amid such injuries to Christ, let God arise (Psalm 67) and judge our cause; let Him look upon the face of His anointed Christ (Psalm 83). Where is Elijah’s zeal against Ahab? John’s zeal against Herod? Ambrose’s zeal against Valens? The zeal of Alexander III, who, as we have heard and seen, solemnly and terribly cut Frederick, the father of this prince, off from the communion of the faithful by the full authority of the Apostolic See?

Yet the tyrant treats the apostolic keys as a mockery and regards nothing but words as the law of God. All the more steadfastly, therefore, ought you to take up the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6). For it is written: “He who despises you despises me” (Luke 10). Therefore, if you do not wish to pursue the wrong done to yourselves or to the Roman Church, you may nevertheless not disregard the insult to Peter and the injury to Christ.

Let not the word of the Lord, then, be bound in your mouth; nor let human fear bury in you the spirit of freedom. It is more tolerable to fall into human hands than to abandon God’s law. “They trust in their strength and glory in the abundance of their riches” (Psalm 48), these enemies of Christ’s cross, “whose end is destruction and whose glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3). Whatever is taken from the need of churches and the poor, the gullet of insatiable greed devours. But the time is near when the Lord’s hand will inflict timely vengeance upon them, and what blessed Job declares concerning the wicked robber will come to pass: “He will vomit up the riches which he swallowed, and God will draw them out of his belly” (Job 20); [Col. 1264A] “he will pay for all that he has done, yet will not be consumed” (Job 18). And if for a time they escape human judgment, the divine judgment hanging over them is more terrible: their present joy is like a point, but the punishment of fire and worm is without end.

For what persecutor of innocence has ever been recorded as escaping the avenging hand of Him who “takes away the spirit of princes” (Psalm 75) and punishes the mighty mightily? Not to speak of the punishment of Gehenna, we often read how the finger of God, at His pleasure, transfers kingdoms and empires; how He raises powers as He wills and casts them down as He wills. I pray you, let secular exaltation not frighten you. Moab is proud, and his pride is greater than his strength; but, on the contrary, the name of the Lord is strength in abundance.

But what publicly grieves [Col. 1264B] the Church, provokes the people’s murmur, and does no small damage to your reputation, is this: in so great a crisis, amid so many tears and petitions from so many provinces, you have sent not even one messenger from your side to those princes. For relatively minor causes your cardinals, with great authority, often discharge embassies even to barbarian regions; but in so arduous, lamentable, and universal a cause, you have not yet sent even one subdeacon or acolyte. Today profit makes legates, not regard for Christ, not the honor of the Church, not the peace of kingdoms, or the people’s safety. What profit or gain could be more glorious for you than, through this king’s liberation, to exalt the summit of the supreme pontificate—that is, the priesthood of Aaron and Phinehas?

Indeed, you would not have much humbled the dignity of the Apostolic See had you gone in person to Germany for the release of so great a prince. For you ought not so negligently to desert in adversity one who had so dutifully honored you in prosperity.

Why do you not weigh in the balance of justice the benefits which Henry, the father of this king, of good memory, rendered to you, as we saw, in a moment of utmost need, against the tyranny which Frederick, on the other hand, exercised against you, the possessions of the Roman Church, and all who faithfully adhered to you? For when the aforesaid Frederick, supporter and author of the schismatic division against Alexander III, canonically elected, as you know, had conspired with the party of the apostate Octavian, and the Church everywhere throughout the world suffered under that shock of schism, the kings of France and England were assailed by embassies from both sides. And when the mind of the King of France, wavering uncertainly amid diverse counsels as to which side he should favor, fluctuated in doubt, King Henry, grieving that Christ’s tunic should be torn apart any longer, was the first to assent to Pope Alexander. By much prudent effort he drew the King of France also into agreement with the Apostolic See, fortified him with his counsels, confirmed him with his aid, and so placed Peter’s ship, already in imminent danger of shipwreck, in the safe haven of the shore.

We saw these things at the castle of Radulf, where he also satisfied the Roman demands, as they themselves publicly proclaimed as a miracle, by the more ample gifts of gold and silver supplied through royal generosity. [Col. 1265A] It therefore notably dishonors the glory of the Apostolic See if any ingratitude could ever erase the memory of so great a benefit. At some time, God avert it, the ferment of schism may spring up from a similar cause, and the memory of your present negligence and failure may then be a cause of groaning to some.

Although that crafty serpent, that twisting dragon, obstructs the king’s liberation by deceitful schemes, nevertheless we trust in the Lord that He will promptly look upon the face of His anointed Christ (Psalm 83) and “give dominion to His king” (1 Samuel 2). For our expectation has grown strong in certain hope and firm faith. The Church continually makes prayer to God for him. But God, who hears in the accepted time and helps in the day of salvation, will regard the prayers of the humble and will not despise their petitions (Psalm 101). For “the continual prayer of the righteous is very powerful” (James 5). At Joshua’s prayers the sun stood still, and the moon did not move over against the valley of Aijalon (Joshua 10). For by the prayers of the righteous it is obtained that the sun of righteousness does not depart from the sinner’s heart, and that the human mind, although inclined toward failure, is nevertheless established by the steadiness of virtues. By prayer not only is sin forgiven; by the benefit of prayers, the punishment of sin is also averted.

Therefore it is good for the king to await in silence the salvation of the Lord (Lamentations 3). For if he is now being purified by God in the furnace of tribulation—God who orders adversity and prosperity around him with the most health-giving moderation—his affliction will pass into glory, and, in place of double [Col. 1265C] shame and reproach, he will possess double blessings in his land. Blessed, therefore, is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence (Jeremiah 17). And indeed, just as public groans and universal tears are now offered for him, so, desired by the nations, he will in due time be welcomed amid common vows and the rejoicing of the whole earth. “O Lord, the king shall rejoice in thy strength” (Psalm 20); and the Roman Church, which now delays far too culpably in securing his release, will blush, not without tears, that in such great distress it did not help so great a son.

### III. Another letter by the same.—Of similar argument. (A.D. 1192.)

*[Works of Peter of Blois, ed. GILES, vol. II, p. 63, epistle 145.]*

[Col. 1265D]

To the most holy father and lord C., by God’s grace supreme pontiff: A., by the same grace Queen of England, Duchess of Normandy, and Countess of Anjou, wishes you health and abundance in the bowels of mercy.

“My soul is weary of my life.” For all that I feared has come to pass, and the expectation of a harsher outcome still cuts off every grace of consolation.

When did I not fear graver dangers as real? Therefore, considering my labor and grief, I am overthrown by faintness of spirit and tempest (Psalm 54). But I am already being poured out, and old age hastened by sorrow foretells to me the fewness of my days. I have often written to you and frequently offered the sacrifice [Col. 1266A] of my heart in a contrite and humble spirit (Psalm 50). Yet since I have once begun, I shall still speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes (Genesis 18). “Let me alone, Lord, that I may lament my grief a little” (Judges 11). For I do not know how it is that the surge of anguish is eased by weeping itself and the pouring forth of tears.

Long have I, lost woman that I am, awaited someone to soothe a mother’s grief, to say: “Joseph your son lives” (Genesis 45), “and has been brought out of the cistern, nor has an evil beast devoured him” (Genesis 37). O evil beast, more cruel than tigers, lamiae, and every beast: you who sold and delivered my son—the soldier of Christ, the Lord’s anointed, the pilgrim of the Crucified One—bound in chains to the emperor! Thus an adversary harder than himself was appointed over him, and he was transferred from prison to a labyrinth, from Scylla to Charybdis. Since the days of Judas Iscariot none has been found like him who so violated the law of the Most High, who so maliciously betrayed the righteous man. And these things were done secretly and in darkness; for they were works of darkness.

Father of mercies, I beseech you by the memory of the abundance of your sweetness (Psalm 144): deliver the innocent one from the lion’s mouth and from the beast’s hand. And what profit is there to you in his blood (Psalm 29), which will be required most strictly from your hand? Because we once believed that the Lord had resolved through you to show mercy to my son, we became joyful (Psalm 125). But now matters have been turned the other way: the devil triumphs far and wide; “wisdom overcomes malice” (Wisdom 7); and the report of my son’s capture, heard among the nations, rings through the streets of Gath and the crossroads of uncircumcised Ascalon amid solemn applause.

Alas, alas: the Lord has struck us with a grievous blow and a cruel chastisement. The tyrant has torn my entrails from me; while plundering churches he has acted wickedly in the land of the saints (Isaiah 26), and has worn down countless peoples with bitterness and mourning (Lamentations 1). In all these things His anger has not turned away, but His hand is still stretched out. He spares neither monks, recluses, hermits, nuns, nor lepers. For law and right, the fear of God, faith, religion, and honorableness have perished.

“Arise, why dost thou sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not reject us forever” (Psalm 43). Let the grief of this most unhappy sinner move you, supreme pontiff—or, if not that, at least the cry of the poor, the groans of prisoners in chains, the blood of the slain, the plundering of churches, and finally the general oppression of the saints. See how greatly the enemy has behaved maliciously in the sanctuary (Psalm 73). The Church’s enemies have gained strength; they have prolonged their iniquity (Psalm 128); strengthened as they are, they add transgression; “they add iniquity to iniquity” (Psalm 68), so that blood touches blood, their pride continually rises (Psalm 73), and the impiety of the moderns not only fills but exceeds the measure of their fathers. Certainly they ought to have been struck with a dreadful anathema, or rather thunderstruck.

Therefore let the bishop of the world arise, [Col. 1267A] and let your hand seize judgment like lightning. As Peter with one blow could destroy Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), and with one blow Simon Magus from the midst (Acts 13), so may you slay the wicked with the spirit of your lips (Isaiah 11). Otherwise you will appear, through consent, to enter into a bond with wickedness. But “those who turn aside into binding entanglements, the Lord will lead away with those who work iniquity” (Psalm 124). “Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O most mighty one” (Psalm 44)—that is, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6). Let your hand take judgment; by the power divinely conferred upon you, remove the rod of sinners from above the lot of the righteous; with the shield of your good will (Psalm 5) protect my son; and let not the son of iniquity further add to harm [Col. 1267B] the innocent one (Psalm 88).

Since the innocence of my royal son has testimony from those nearby and from those far away, you have no excuse concerning sin. What excuse could cloak your negligence and lack of care, when it is plain to everyone that you have the power to free my son yet withhold the will? Was not every kingdom and all governing power entrusted by God to the apostle Peter—and in him to you? (Matthew 16.) “Blessed be the Lord, who has given such power to men” (Matthew 9). No king, emperor, or duke is exempted from the yoke of your jurisdiction. Where, then, is the zeal of Phinehas? Where is Peter’s authority? Where is one who says: “The zeal of thy house hath consumed me”? (Psalm 68.) Let it appear that the two-edged swords in your hands and in the hands of your fellow bishops were not given to you in vain (Psalm 149). Say to the wicked: “Do not act wickedly”; and to transgressors: “Do not raise the horn” (Psalm 74).

May the revered succession of apostolic dignity not degenerate in Peter’s heir. Recognize your primacy, prove your zeal, gird yourselves for the work of strength, and honor your ministry (2 Timothy 4); let your glory pass down to posterity, and let another generation know (Psalm 77) how vainly that tyrant presumed and how powerfully the Roman See punished his presumption. It will assuredly turn to your peril and guilt if you keep your hands slack and impunity adds horns to the sinner. “For if these things are done in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23.)

I beg your fatherhood to recall what a great friend my husband the king, the father of this king, was, and how faithful he was to you; consider how kindly this successor to his father’s devotion has acted. Nor let it fall from your heart how zealously I promoted through him the affairs of your legates—indeed, your own affairs. If my affection toward you has ever grown slack in your necessities, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies (Psalm 7). Yet now I find the promises of your cardinals to be words and leaves; but trees are known not from leaves or flowers but from fruits (Matthew 7). And indeed we have known them from these fruits. It shames me to say what I wish it shamed them to have done: the tyrant had them as supporters of his wickedness, when they ought to have presented themselves as its avengers.

I loved you not in tongue and word but in deed and truth (1 John 3). “Is evil returned for good, and hatred for my love?” (Psalm 108.) To say one thing, with my lord’s peace, I tell him what Joab is sometime recorded to have reproached King David with: “You love those who hate you, and hate those who love you” (2 Samuel 19). Alas, how crime is disarmed of justice! How miserably the keys of the Church have lost their office! And where the glorious primacy of Peter ought to have shone forth, there pontifical authority is more shamefully crushed and made cheap. The wolf rushes into the sheepfold, the lion into the Church of God, and the solitary wild beast devours it (Psalm 79); nor is there one who goes up in opposition for the house of the Lord. And what I grieve more intimately and intolerably: the tyrant tortures my son, the supreme pontiff ignores it, and there is none to redeem or save him (Psalm 7).

If, then, there is any consolation in you, any strength of charity in Christ, any pity, any bowels of compassion—finally, anything savoring of a father’s affection and pontifical anointing—let all the people hear that wisdom is in you to execute judgment. But why dwell on such things? I run uncertainly and beat the air (1 Corinthians 9), and our groans vanish into the winds. The tyrant’s obstinacy is harder than adamant; and I know that no one can correct the man whom God neglects. My word has fallen to the ground and returns [Col. 1268C] to me empty (Wisdom 1); it does not prosper in those things for which it was sent.

Therefore the dreadful storm of tribulations overwhelms me; the deep of a terrible abyss swallows me; and the pit of despair presses its mouth upon me (Psalm 68). All our people give their hands to death and, wasting and withering from fear and expectation of the things coming upon the whole Western world, make a covenant with hell (Luke 21). But You, Lord God of hosts, who judge righteously, see that I suffer violence (Isaiah 38); judge my cause. And because I find no judge on earth, I, miserable and pitied by none, appeal the earthly judge to Your terrible tribunal. Unhappy woman that I am, why do I follow the impetuous force of my violent grief and set my mouth in heaven? Yet, Father, I beseech you, let your kindness patiently endure what proceeded from grief, not deliberation.
