I have sinned; and, to use the words of blessed Job, “What I have said, I wish I had not said; therefore I will add no more” (Job 39), and “I will put my finger upon my mouth” (Job 21). Farewell.

### IV. The same author’s third letter.—Of similar argument. (A.D. 1192.)

*(Ibid., p. 68.)*

To the reverend father and lord CELESTINE, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: A., miserable—and would that she were an object of pity—Queen of England, Duchess of Normandy, Countess [Col. 1269A] of Anjou, offers herself, a miserable mother, to him as a father of mercy.

The jealous distance of places prevents me, most blessed pope, from speaking with you in person; yet I must lament my grief a little. And who will grant that my words may be written down? I am distressed both inwardly and outwardly; hence my words are full of grief. “Fears are without, conflicts within” (2 Corinthians 7); nor am I free for a moment to breathe from the tribulation of evils and grief (Psalm 106), from tribulations which have found us exceedingly (Psalm 45). I have wholly wasted away in grief, and, when my flesh was consumed, my bone clung to my skin (Psalm 101). My years have failed in groanings (Psalm 30), and would that they failed altogether. Would that all the blood of my now-dead body, the brain of my head, and the marrow of my bones might be dissolved into tears, so that I might flow away wholly in weeping.

My entrails have been torn from me: I have lost the staff of my old age and the light of my eyes (Psalm 37). It would accord with my prayers if God condemned my unhappy eyes to perpetual blindness, so that they might no longer see the evils of my people. “Who will grant me that I might die for you, my son?” (2 Samuel 18.) Mother of mercy, look upon a mother in such misery; or, if your Son, the inexhaustible fountain of mercy, exacts a mother’s sins from her son, let Him exact the whole penalty from her who alone sinned; let Him punish the ungodly woman, and not take delight in the sufferings of the innocent one. Let Him who began it himself crush me, withdraw His hand, and cut me down; and let this be my consolation: that, while afflicting me with grief, He does not spare me (Job 6).

[Col. 1269C]

I, miserable and pitied by none, why have I come to the disgrace of this detestable old age? I had been mistress of two kingdoms and mother of two kings; my entrails have been torn from me; “my generation has been taken away and rolled up from me” (Isaiah 38). The younger king and the Count of Brittany sleep in the dust, and their most unhappy mother is compelled to live, so that she may be tortured without remedy by the memory of the dead. Two sons remained to console me; today they remain to me, miserable and condemned as I am, for my torment. King Richard is held in chains. His brother John ravages the captive’s kingdom with the sword and lays it waste with fire. In everything the Lord has turned cruel toward me and opposes me in the hardness of His hand (Job [Col. 1269D] 30). Truly His wrath fights against me; and therefore my sons fight one another—if it can be called a fight when one is oppressed in close bonds, while the other, adding sorrow upon his sorrow, endeavors by cruel tyranny to usurp for himself the kingdom of his exiled brother.

Good Jesus, who will grant me that You protect and hide me in hell until Your wrath has passed over (Isaiah 26), until the arrows which are within me cease, by whose indignation my whole spirit is drunk up? Death is my desire and life my weariness; and although I thus die unceasingly, I nevertheless desire to die more completely. I am compelled unwillingly to live, so that life may be food for death and material for torment. O happy those who, untouched by the mockeries of this life and the unforeseen events of an uncertain condition, have anticipated them by a blessed death!

[Col. 1270A]

What am I doing? Why do I stand still? Why do I delay, miserable woman that I am, and not go to see him whom my soul loves (Song of Songs 3), “bound in poverty and iron” (Psalm 106)? For how could a mother for so long forget the son of her womb? Affection softens even tigers toward their young, and even lamiae more cruel than they are. Yet I waver in doubt. For if I go, leaving my son’s kingdom, which is everywhere ravaged by grievous hostility, it will, in my absence, be deprived of all counsel and consolation. But if I remain, I shall not see my son’s face, which is most dear to me. There will be no one to work zealously for my son’s release; and, what I fear more, that most delicate young man will be pressed by torments for an impossible sum of money, and, unable to endure such affliction, will easily be driven to death by tortures.

O impious, cruel, and dreadful tyrant, who did not fear to lay sacrilegious hands upon the Lord’s anointed! Neither royal anointing, reverence for the holy journey, nor fear of God restrained you from such inhumanity. Yet the prince of the apostles still reigns and rules in the Apostolic See, judicial rigor stands in its midst, and it remains for you, Father, to wield against evildoers Peter’s sword, for which purpose He established you over nations and kingdoms. Christ’s cross preceded Caesar’s eagles; Peter’s sword precedes Constantine’s sword; and the Apostolic See takes precedence over imperial power. Is your power from God or from men? Did not the God of gods speak to you in the apostle Peter, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and [Col. 1270C] whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven”? (Matthew 16.) Why, then, do you so long delay—indeed, so negligently, so cruelly delay—or rather, not dare, to loose my son? But you will say that this power was committed to you over souls, not bodies. Granted: it is certainly enough for us if you bind the souls of those who keep my son bound in prison. It is easy for you to free my son, provided the fear of God drives out human fear.

Give me back my son, therefore, man of God—if indeed you are a man of God and not rather a man of blood—if you grow sluggish in securing my son’s release, so that the Most High may demand his blood from your hand (Gen. 9). Alas, alas, if the supreme shepherd is turned into a hired hand; if he flees from the face of the wolf; if he leaves the little sheep committed to him—or rather, the chosen ram, the leader of the Lord’s flock—in the jaws of the bloodthirsty beast! The good shepherd instructs and trains other shepherds, not that they should flee if they see the wolf coming, but that they should lay down their lives for their sheep (John 10).

May your own soul, I beg, be safe to you, provided that you strive to procure the liberation—not, I will say, of your sheep, but of your son—by repeated embassies, salutary admonitions, thunderclaps of threats, general interdicts, and terrible sentences. Indeed, you would lay down your soul for him, though for that same man you have hitherto been unwilling to speak or write even one word. The Son of God, according to the prophet’s testimony, descended from heaven in order to bring forth the prisoners from the pit in which there was no water. Would what befitted God be unbecoming to God’s servant? My son is tormented in chains; you neither descend to him, nor send to him, nor are you moved at Joseph’s affliction. Christ sees this and is silent; but he will abundantly repay, in the utmost severity, those who perform God’s work negligently (Jer. 48).

Envoys have now been promised us for the third time, yet they have not been sent: and, to tell the truth, they are bound rather than sent. If my son were prospering, they would have hastened to him at his mere summons, because they would expect rich harvests from their embassy, from his magnificent generosity and from the public advantage of the kingdom. And what gain could be more glorious to them than to free a captive king, restore peace to peoples, tranquility to religious persons, and joy to all? But now, [Col. 1271B] “the sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle” (Ps. 77); and in a time of distress, while the wolf crouches over its prey, dumb dogs either cannot or will not bark.

Is this that promise which you made us at Ralph’s castle with such protestations of affection and faith? What profit was it to give words to us simple folk, and to mock the vows of innocent persons with empty confidence? Thus King Ahab is said of old to have entered into a covenant of friendship with Ben-hadad, and we have heard that the outcome of their mutual affection was disastrous. Heavenly providence furthered with favorable auspices the battles of the brothers Judas, John, and Simon Maccabaeus; but when they sent an embassy to establish the friendship of the Romans, they lost God’s help, and the venal familiarity of those Romans was turned into weeping for them not once but often.

You alone compel me to despair—you who alone, after God, had been my hope and the confidence of our people. “Cursed is he who trusts in man” (Jer. 17). Where, then, is my hope now? You are, Lord, my God. To you, Lord, who behold suffering, are the eyes of your handmaid. You, King of kings and Lord of lords (1 Tim. 6), look upon the face of your Christ (Ps. 83); grant dominion to your servant, and save the son of your handmaid (Ps. 85); do not punish in him the offenses of his father or the wickedness of his mother.

From certain and public report we have learned that, after the death of the bishop of Liège—whom the emperor is said to have killed, though by a far-reaching hand, with a deadly sword—the emperor confines in the misery of prison the bishop of Ostia and four bishops of his province, as well as the archbishops of Salerno and Trani. Furthermore, what apostolic authority ought by no means to have concealed: Sicily, which it is established has been the patrimony of St. Peter since Constantine’s time, he has occupied by tyrannical usurpation, after embassies, supplications, and threats from the Apostolic See, to the perpetual prejudice of the Roman Church.

“In all these things his anger is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.” He has indeed inflicted grave injuries, but you can most certainly expect still graver ones shortly. For those who ought to have been pillars of the Church are shaken by reed-like instability in every wind. Would that they recalled [Col. 1272A] that, because of the negligence of Eli the priest ministering at Shiloh, the glory of the Lord was transferred from Israel (1 Sam. 1). This is no longer a parable of a past time, but of the present; for “the Lord rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle where he dwelt among men, and delivered their strength into captivity and their beauty into the enemy’s hands” (Ps. 77).

It is charged against their faintheartedness that the Church is trampled down, faith is endangered, liberty is oppressed, and deceit, patience, and wickedness are nourished by impunity. Where is what the Lord once promised his Church: “You shall suck the milk of the nations, and you shall nurse at the breast of kings; I will make you an everlasting exaltation, a joy from generation to generation” (Isa. 60)? Once the Church, by her own strength, trod upon the necks of the proud and lofty, and the laws of emperors followed the sacred canons. But now, with the order overturned, I shall not say merely the canons, but the framers of the canons, are constrained by perverse laws and execrable customs.

The detestable crimes of the powerful are tolerated; no one dares utter a word, while canonical rigor is exercised only upon the sins of the poor. Therefore Anacharsis the philosopher not without reason compared laws and canons to spiders’ webs, which hold fast weaker animals but let the strong pass through. “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together against the Christ of the Lord” (Ps. 2), against my son. One tortures him in chains; another lays waste his lands with cruel hostility. And, to use a common saying, one shears while the other flays; one holds the foot while the other strips off the skin.

The supreme pontiff sees these things and keeps Peter’s sword sheathed. Thus he adds horns to the sinner, and his very silence is taken as consent. For he appears to consent who, though able and bound to correct, does not rebuke; and patience that dissembles will not be free from the suspicion of secret partnership. The time of dissension foretold by the Apostle is at hand, so that the son of perdition may be revealed; perilous times press upon us (2 Tim. 3), so that Christ’s seamless tunic may be torn, Peter’s net broken, and the solidity of Catholic unity dissolved. These are the beginnings of evils (Matt. 8): we feel grave things and fear graver ones.

I am neither a prophetess nor the daughter of a prophet; yet grief suggested that I should say more concerning future disturbances—but it takes away the very words that it suggests. For it interrupts the spirit of sobbing, and sorrow, swallowing up the powers of the soul, shuts up the vocal passages in anxiety. Farewell.

## V. Instrument of renunciation made by Peter Latro and his nephew to Pope Celestine III. (A.D. 1193.)

[Muratori, *Antiquities of Italy*, V, 844.]

In the name of the Lord, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1193, the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III, the eleventh indiction, in the month of July.

We, Peter Latro, son of the late Peter Latro, for one half of the property hereafter specified; and I, John [Col. 1273A] son of Nicholas Maria John, appointed as additional guardian for Odo, son of the late Odo Peter Latro, whose grandmother and guardian is Lady Lucina, being appointed by the hands of Judge John Donadei to conduct litigation, discharge debts, and receive credits, as appears from the instrument of inventory written in the hand of Leo, notary—for that minor and for the other half of the aforesaid property—we both jointly and equally, in the presence of the lords judges John the Saxon Archarius and Henry Dativus, and, so far as the said minor is concerned, by their authority and decree, of our own free will renounce and, by right of settlement, generally relinquish to you, Lord Cencius, by God’s grace cardinal-deacon of St. Lucy in Silice, [Col. 1273B] and chamberlain of the lord pope, likewise agent and attorney specially appointed in this case for the aforesaid lord Celestine, by God’s grace supreme and universal Pope III, for the use and benefit of him and his successors forever, namely all those two hundred pounds of Pavia denarii which the late Lord Pope Innocent is acknowledged to have owed to Peter Latro, grandfather of me, Peter Latro, and great-grandfather of the said minor.

For those sums he granted in pledge and gave in benefice the castle of Saxum, the Old City, Gobita, and the hamlet called Vulgare, as appears by the privilege of the aforesaid Lord Pope Innocent. This also appears equally by the privilege which Lord Pope Alexander III made, with intent to renew it in like form and manner, to me Peter and to my brother Odo, father formerly of the said minor. In that privilege, for the same two hundred pounds of Pavia denarii, he mortgaged and granted to us in benefice the said castles, except the Old City, which we then relinquished.

Henceforth we invalidate and annul those privileges in all respects, so that they shall be held to have absolutely no force. We also relinquish to you, as stated, all those fifty pounds of revenues which, in a separate transaction, the aforementioned Lord Pope Alexander owed us, as has appeared hitherto in his privilege. We likewise invalidate and annul that privilege and entirely relinquish the aforesaid benefice of the castles.

Whatever right and whatever personal, real, or hypothecary action we have or could in any manner have against the aforesaid Lord Pope Celestine, and in his possessions and goods—especially in the said castles and hamlet mortgaged to us and granted in benefice—whether by right or occasion of the benefice, or by reason of the mortgage, the entire specified sum of money, its fruits, or its additions; and whatever we could hitherto seek or litigate against Lord Pope Celestine, in the said castles or his other goods, on any ground or occasion whatsoever: all this we relinquish to you, acting as attorney for him and his successors, as stated, generally and in every respect by right of settlement.

This is because you, on behalf of the said lord pope, whose attorney you are, and from his money, pay to me Peter Latro one hundred ounces of good gold in settlement for all my rights; and to me John son of Nicholas, on behalf of the said minor, in settlement by the aforesaid right and decree of the said judges, you give and pay another one hundred ounces of gold. I pay all of these, on behalf of the minor and by decree of the same judges, toward the paternal debt of that minor, to the sons of the late Lord Stephen the Norman, who have hitherto held in pledge at interest the minor’s share of the castle of Ceres, inside and outside Toris, as appeared hitherto from an instrument written in the hand of John Kalo, notary, which they returned to me cancelled.

Therefore I, John son of Nicholas, on behalf of the said minor, and I, Peter Latro, acknowledge you fully discharged from those two hundred ounces of gold and from every right of ours and of the said minor; and we waive the exception of unpaid money.

Because for a long time litigation or controversy, entangled in several questions, existed between us and the said Lord Pope Celestine and his predecessors—not only concerning the aforesaid benefice of the castles but also concerning all the aforementioned money granted as expenses—the said lord pope set forth this objection to us, saying that a benefice ends upon the death of either giver or recipient, and asserting with many allegations that all or part of the said money had been paid to us. We, however, strove to establish our claim not by other proofs but by the aforesaid privileges. At last, with the intervention of the lord cardinals and other prudent men on both sides, we came by amicable agreement to this settlement, since the laws permit a settlement between both an adult and a minor concerning a doubtful matter and uncertain litigation. Therefore henceforth the aforesaid lord pope and his successors shall always remain free and at peace concerning this matter.

Moreover, we promise that this right of ours, namely mine, Peter’s, and that of the said minor, in whole or part, has not been granted to anyone or otherwise alienated. And I, Peter, particularly promise that, if the aforesaid minor or anyone else on his behalf should at any time presume to act against this renunciation, I will make him desist. If I am unwilling or unable to do so, and if the said lord pope and his successors suffer any loss on that account—whether from this matter or from a grant or alienation of our aforesaid right, should one be shown to have been made, which God forbid—then, to the amount of the loss in either case, they may, by their own authority and without injury to law or proclamation before any court, seize by right of pledge such of my rural and urban properties and possessions as they choose, and be fully satisfied from them.

If I should wish to oppose this, I shall forfeit the right which I have in those goods and shall be bound to pay the same amount as a penalty. Knowing that the laws assist me because I act as surety for a minor, I wholly renounce that aid of right or law and every other aid introduced in this case on my behalf.

[Col. 1275A] Furthermore, I, the said Peter Latro, and the aforesaid John son of Nicholas, on behalf of the said minor, in all the aforesaid articles renounce every right and every exception by which we could in any manner invalidate all that has been said. Finally, I, Peter Latro, for myself and my heirs and successors, and I, John son of Nicholas, on behalf of the said minor and his heirs and successors, in the office which I perform, promise to you, acting as attorney for the said lord pope and his successors, as stated, to observe, defend, and fulfil this renunciation and all the matters set forth above, under penalty of double the aforesaid two hundred ounces of gold; and even if the penalty is paid, this instrument shall nevertheless remain in force.

I requested John son of Leo, notary, to write this in the aforesaid month and indiction.

Lord John son of Guido de Papa, witness. Lord Tostus son of Peter Deusvossalvet, witness. Peter son of Cencius, usher of the lord pope, witness. Paul Malagromus, usher of the lord pope, witness. Peter son of Robert, likewise usher, witness. Clement, usher, witness. I, John son of Leo, notary of the Holy Roman Church, having authority to appoint tutors and guardians, to emancipate persons, to issue decrees, and to determine maintenance, completed and executed this instrument.

## VI. Charter of renunciation made to Pope Celestine III concerning the city of Castellana by the sisters Constance and Sibyl, Hyacinth son of Peter Deusvossalvet, and the brothers Nicholas and Octavian. (A.D. 1195.)

[Muratori, *Antiquities of Italy*, II, 141.]

[Col. 1275C]

In the name of the Lord, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1195, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Celestine III, the thirteenth indiction, on the first day of February: we, Constance, wife of the late Andreotta, and Sibyl, wife of Hyacinth son of Peter Deusvossalvet, full sisters, daughters of the late Andrew de Baldoino; and also we, principally, Hyacinth son of Peter Deusvossalvet, and Nicholas and Octavian, brothers, sons of the late aforesaid Andreotta—all together, each for the share belonging to us—before the lords judges Saisson the primicerius, John Saisson the arcarius, and Peter Paul Rubeus, appointed judges, and in the presence of Lord Peter de Judice, advocate, and the undersigned witnesses, voluntarily renounce and generally relinquish to you, Lord Peter Saracenus, seneschal of the lord pope, agent and attorney of Lord Pope Celestine specially appointed for this purpose before the aforesaid learned men, for the perpetual use and benefit of the said lord pope and his successors and of the whole Roman Church, namely every suit and claim which we have made, sought, or could seek or make against the said lord pope and the Roman Church.

That is, we renounce all claim concerning the whole share formerly belonging to Peter de Attegia, namely in those thousand marks of silver which Lord Pope Adrian IV formerly owed to him and his associates. For these sums Adrian mortgaged and delivered to him by right of pledge the city of Castellana, its entire county, and Monte Alto, as appears from the privilege of the said Lord Pope Adrian. So far as the share of the said late Peter de Attegia is concerned, that privilege shall cease to have effect and be void and of absolutely no force.

This share belongs, or appears to belong, to us both by succession from the aforesaid Andrew de Baldoino and by a grant and mandate made specially to me, Hyacinth, for one half, and to me, Constance, for the other half, by Kiera, wife of Peter Latro and daughter of the late Farulf of Monastery, as appears from the public instrument which we deliver to you. It also belonged to the said Lord Andrew de Baldoino by succession from his late daughter Mary, whom he had begotten by Lady Albascia, his wife and daughter of the aforesaid Lord Peter de Attegia, as appears from the will of Lady Albascia herself, which we likewise give you on behalf of the said lord pope.

Whatever right and whatever personal, real, or hypothecary action, whether to bring an action or raise an exception, which we could have against the said lord pope and the whole Roman Church, especially in all the aforesaid property and pledges—namely the city of Castellana within and without, the whole county, and Monte Alto—and generally in all the patrimony of the Roman Church; and against any other person, by right, occasion, or reason of the entire share in the aforesaid thousand marks of silver that formerly belonged to Lord Peter de Attegia, together with their fruits, interest, additions, penalties, and every cause: we generally relinquish, cede, and assign all this to you, as stated, acting as attorney for the said lord pope and his successors.

Thus whatever we could hitherto, as regards possession and ownership, bring or defend in our own right and name concerning all the aforesaid things against any person, the said lord pope and his successors shall henceforth bring and defend in their own right and name; and so that they may proceed by a useful and direct action, we appoint you attorney of the said lord pope in the aforesaid matter.

We make this renunciation, concession, and assignment to you, as stated, on behalf of the said lord pope, for sixty-two and a half marks of silver, which you give and pay to us all, each according to the share belonging to us, on behalf of the said lord pope and from his money, acting as attorney, as stated. In respect of all these sums and of all our claim relating to the said share of Peter de Attegia in the aforesaid thousand marks of silver, we acknowledge full discharge; and we generally renounce, in every respect, the exception of unpaid money or silver and every other exception, if any, by which we could oppose the aforesaid lord pope and the Roman Church so as to invalidate what has been said and what will appear below.

Moreover, under a penalty of double the aforesaid sum of silver, we promise that we have granted, mortgaged, or otherwise alienated to no one this right of ours, in whole or in part. If anything of the property and possessions of the said city of Castellana, inside or outside it, and of its whole county, has been mortgaged by obligation of debt through us, or through the said late Lord Peter de Attegia, or through his heirs and successors, we promise to recover and release it from pledge out of the aforesaid sum of silver, under the penalty set out below.

If at any time, through an alienation or mortgage made by us or by the aforesaid Lord Peter de Attegia and his heirs and successors, the said lord pope and his successors, or the Roman Church, suffer any loss, then, to the amount of that loss, they may, by their own authority, without injury to law or proclamation before any court, seize by right of pledge such of our goods as they choose, so far as pertains to the said sum of silver. If we should attempt in any way to oppose this, we shall forfeit the right which we had in those goods, and shall be bound to pay double that loss to the Roman Church.

For such loss, should it occur—which God forbid—we, Hyacinth and Nicholas Andreotta, in particular bind our goods jointly and severally insofar as it concerns this matter, and hold them from the Roman Church for ourselves and our heirs by sufferance, renouncing every aid of right or law introduced for us in this case because we intervene in part for others. Henceforth the said lord pope and his successors, and the entire Roman Church, shall always remain undisturbed and at peace.

For ourselves and our heirs and successors, all of us aforesaid, men and women, promise you, acting on behalf of the said lord pope, his successors, and the whole Roman Church, to observe, defend, and fulfil all that has been said, under penalty of double the whole aforesaid sum of silver. Even if the penalty is paid, this charter shall remain valid. We requested John son of Leo, notary, to write it in the above-mentioned thirteenth indiction.

Peter Saracenus son of John Kinard, witness. Paul Malagromus, usher of the lord pope, witness. [Col. 1277D] Gregory son of John Bibentisaquam, witness. John son of Odo, witness. Lawrence Barbuccia, witness. I, John son of Leo, notary of the Holy Roman Church, having authority to appoint tutors and guardians, to emancipate persons, to issue decrees, and to determine maintenance, completed and executed this instrument.

## VII. Queen Ingeborg of the Franks to Celestine—That, neglecting her, the king has attached himself to the daughter of the Duke of Merania. (A.D. 1196.)

[Baluz., *Miscellanies*, ed. Mansi, vol. III, p. 21.]

The distress of unexpected sorrow compels me to lay before you a sorrowful beginning and, amid the groaning of my heart, to recount my grievances tearfully to your Apostolic office. It is now three years since the King of France betrothed me when I was of marriageable age and rendered to me, as natural order requires, the marital due. But afterwards, seduced by the instigation of the devil and the persuasion of certain malicious princes, he brought in and keeps as his wife the daughter of Duke S. He ordered me to be imprisoned in a certain castle, where I live in such proscription that I neither dare nor can lift my eyes to heaven.

He alleges no relationship of kinship, nor any cause of wrongdoing for which I ought to be separated from him; rather, he makes a decree out of his will, a law out of obstinacy, and madness out of pleasure. I grieve, indeed, and cannot avoid sorrow, since I eat bread in pain and am continually compelled to mingle my drink with tears [Col. 1278B] (Ps. 101); and I grieve not only for myself but also for the king, who [lacuna] gives Christians and all in his realm an example of malignity toward the orthodox faith.

Alas for grief! He does not fear to disregard the letters of your Holiness, refuses to hear the commands of the cardinals, despises the words of archbishops and bishops, and rejects the admonitions of all religious persons. But what I should say or do, I wholly do not know, since I am surrounded by countless distresses. Therefore, unless your mercy deigns to have mercy upon me, I shall shortly succumb to temporal death.

## VIII. Philip, Bishop of Beauvais, to Celestine—Concerning his capture.

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXII, 611.]

[Col. 1278C]

To the venerable lord and father, CELESTINE, supreme pontiff, PHILIP, bishop of Beauvais, greeting and the devotion of canonical obedience.

The favor of supreme dignity has raised your blessedness and manifold successes on high, recalling to mind that legal maxim: “He invites the innocent to crime who leaves the guilty unpunished.” It is now held almost as common knowledge among all the Churches how irreverently and inhumanely the King of England long ago rose up against his lord, the King of the Franks, like a man attempting to pull down a great mountain by encircling it with a rope.

Bringing with him fire [Col. 1278D] and sword, and supported also by apostate bands of Brabançons, he had invaded our country, laying it waste on every side. When I saw this, not forgetful of that legal maxim, “It is lawful to repel force by force,” and of the other, “Fight for your country,” I went out to meet the advancing enemies, mingled among the ranks of soldiers and citizens and the battle-line of nobles. But Fortune, stepmother to human designs, consigned the undertaking to an adverse outcome. I was captured there and subjected to heavy fetters and chains; neither the dignity of my order nor reverence for God brought me any remedy or mitigation.

Thus the King of England did not fear to rage like a wolf against the Christ of the Lord; and we do not suppose this unknown to your ears. Why, then, do you dissemble? What father would see his son go astray and remain silent? What father would not strike his son with the rod so that he might not run upon the sword? A father despairs of his son when he does not correct him with threats or the scourge. It is clearer than daylight that the King of England and his other accomplices, who violently laid hands upon us, have incurred the sanction of the said sentence.

We tearfully lay before your fatherhood the wrongs and enormous injuries inflicted upon us, with our tears; kindly grant our petition. For it is unworthy that the petition of subjects sent to you should return empty and vain, since it breathes humility and is supported by the protection of reason. Nor is he free from blame who, though able to correct, neglects amendment; nor is he free from the suspicion of secret complicity who ceases to oppose an open crime.

Therefore, holy Father, do not wonder that I have multiplied words of sorrow so often. Constant grief does not know—indeed, cannot—be buried within the enclosure of the breast. May your fatherhood prosper.

# ORDER OF MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

## THOMAS THE CISTERCIAN AND CARDINAL JOHN ALGRIN

Notices, 9. Dedicatory epistle, 15. Thomas’s preface to Pons, bishop of Clermont, 17. Prologue of John Algrin, 19.
